en: Dharma is the foundation of the entire world;
this is the Prajnapathshala Mandal Granthamala Mimamsa Kosha.
First Part. Editor: Kevalānandasarasvatī. Mārgaśīrṣa, bright fortnight, 4th day, Friday, Śaka year 1874.
The Publisher’s Note: The venerable feet of our teacher, the illustrious Kevalānandasarasvatī, have composed the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā-kośa* complete with its auxiliary sections and supplements.
The nature of this work has been explained in detail by him himself in the Introduction.
This treasury is to be published divided into six parts.

Its compilation has been entirely accomplished by the venerable Śrī Kevalānanda Svāmī over a very long period of time, following a thorough investigation of the Jaiminīya Tantra, along with its related commentaries (*bhāṣya*), sub-commentaries (*vārtika*), and other Mīmāṃsā treatises, as well as the *Kalpasūtras* and the four Vedas.
However, there is this distinction here: the method of exposition is presented by following a historical approach.

At the end of this volume, three appendices are included: an alphabetical index of Vedic citations found in the Bhāṣya, Vārttika, and other works, accompanied by references to their original locations and notes on difficult passages; a lexicon defining the technical terms used by ritualists (*yājñika*); and a compendium of the performance manuals (*prayoga*) for archetypal sacrifices such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Agniṣṭoma.
This work of publication was accomplished at great expense.

We respectfully submit that those of noble intellect who are devoted to Vedic learning shall attain an incomparable mass of merit by expending their own wealth upon this work. We offer our hundreds of thanks to the Education Department of the Bombay State for lightening the burden of its publication expenses by granting ten thousand rupees.

Furthermore, the sons of Mahādeva known as Keśava, through their example of the Vartaka brothers, have manifested supreme generosity by donating five thousand silver coins for the expenses of publication; thus, they are most worthy of praise. We also offer our heartiest congratulations to the two educational institutions: the Puṇyapattana Vidya Peetha, which provided one thousand silver coins for the printing of the first part, and the Mumbai Vidya Peetha, which contributed five hundred silver coins, thereby assisting in this work of publication.
The 4th day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, Śaka year 1874.
Lakṣmaṇaśāstrī Jośī, Tarkatīrtha, Director of the Prājña Pāṭhaśālā Maṇḍala and Chief Editor of the Dharmakośa: Index.

Salutations again to the sage Jaimini, who extracts the nectar of the Dharma.
The introduction to Mīmāṃsā is indeed ancient— it is heard that Mīmāṃsā has indeed been in operation among the ritual performances of the sacrificial priests for a very long time.
In the *Aitareya-brāhmaṇa*, regarding the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice belonging to the *agniṣoma*, a cake (*puroḍāśa*) on eleven potsherds dedicated to the deities Agni and Viṣṇu is mentioned.
Its two deities are Agni and Viṣṇu.

In this regard, a certain doubt was raised by some theologians (*brahmavādins*): "They say: since the cake is on eleven potsherds and there are two deities, Agni and Viṣṇu, what is their arrangement (*klṛpti*) therein, and what is their division (*vibhakti*)?"

In that regard, other proponents of Brahman replied: "The cake for Agni is on eight potsherds; that for Viṣṇu is on three potsherds. When the question arises as to how there is a rule regarding the eight potsherds for the offering to Agni, the following reasoning is cited: "The Gāyatrī indeed has eight syllables; the Gāyatrī is the meter of Agni. The meaning is this: because Agni and the Gāyatrī meter were produced simultaneously from the mouth of Prajāpati, they are inherently connected; and since the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables per foot, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni likewise consists of eight potsherds.

Now, if it is asked how the sacrificial cake for Viṣṇu has three potsherds (*trikapālatva*), he says in that regard: "For thrice did Viṣṇu stride this [world]. Since the entire universe was pervaded by Viṣṇu through three strides of his feet, it is appropriate that the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) of Viṣṇu has three potsherds, due to its connection with the triad of strides of the feet that pervade the universe (AitBr. 1.1.6–7).

Likewise, regarding the leading forward of Agni and Soma (*agniṣomapraṇayana*), when the Adhvaryu has given the instruction for the recitation (*anuvacanapreṣa*), it is stated by the rule, "He recites the *sāvitrī* verse beginning with 'O God, to the first father,'" that the Hotṛ priest must recite the Ṛgvedic verse addressed to the deity Savitṛ, beginning with "O God, [to] the *sāvitrī*. In this regard, the following doubt is raised: "They say: since he recites what is to be recited after Agni and Soma while they are being led forward, then why does he recite the *sāvitrī*?"
For the purpose of bringing forth Agni and Soma, a verse addressed to the deities Agni and Soma ought to be recited; how then is a verse addressed to the deity Savitṛ prescribed?
To this, the following answer is given: "Savitṛ indeed is the lord of all impellings (prasava); therefore, he recites a verse to Savitṛ.
For all actions proceed only through the impulse of Savitṛ; indeed, without the light of Savitṛ, no one is able to move even a single step from its place.
Therefore, Savitṛ rules over all the agreements regarding ritual actions;
consequently, for the sake of obtaining that agreement, at the commencement of the *praṇayana* rite, a verse dedicated to the deity Savitṛ alone must be recited.
Other numerous examples, indicative of the Mīmāṃsā method consisting of doubt and resolution, are to be found in the Brāhmaṇa texts.

Now, in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (3.1.2), it says: "For the Bahvṛcas investigate this very one in the Great Hymn; the Adhvaryus [investigate] him in the [Agni]laying; the Chandogas [investigate] him in the Mahāvrata.

The Bahvṛcas—those who have recited the Ṛks, i.e., the followers of the Ṛgveda—investigate, that is, deliberate upon, this very Supreme Self in the Great Hymn, which consists of the *śastra* recitations.

The Adhvaryus—the followers of the Yajurveda—investigate the Supreme Self in the mantras pertaining to the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), such as "They harness the mind and they harness the thoughts" (*yuñjate mana uta yuñjate dhiyaḥ*), and so forth.

The Chandogas are those who sing the *chandas* (Vedic hymns), namely the followers of the Sāmaveda; however, it is they who, during the Mahāvrata rite, investigate the Supreme Self within the mantras contained in that rite.
Here, the word "investigate" (*mīmāṃsante*) is employed as the very term directly denoting *mīmāṃsā*.
*Mīmāṃsā* is defined as the definitive conclusion arising from inquiry preceded by doubt.

This is the meaning: it is stated in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (2.1.2) that once, in order to restrain an elephant that was fleeing, Prajāpati ran after it—both in front and from behind. However, Prajāpati was unable to restrain the exceedingly swift animal, and exhausted, Prajāpati became perspiring.
Then he sat down and wiped the sweat from his forehead;
that water manifested in the form of clarified butter (ghṛta). In the meantime, the morning time for the fire-oblation arrived.
And a fire-oblation (homa) must be performed with clarified butter (ājya), since at that time no other substance was available. Therefore, Prajāpati took it in his hand to offer as the oblation.
Furthermore, because that clarified butter was produced from impure sweat-born water, Prajāpati fell into doubt.
Thus it has been said:
"He had doubts: 'Shall I offer? Shall I not offer? From that doubt arose birth."
"He who, knowing thus, hesitates, intends for what is better"— the meaning of this is: he fell into *vicikitsā*, that is, doubt, regarding that ghee produced from sweat.

What is this doubt? He states it: "Should I offer with this ghee—that is, should the oblation be performed by me with this ghee—or should I not offer—that is, the oblation should not be performed by me with this ghee? The doubt is whether or not this ghee is fit for the oblation. This is the origin of that very uncertainty (*vicikitsā*).
The meaning is that such a doubt as this arose regarding Prajāpati.

Any learned person who, being thus uncertain about the nature of Prajāpati, falls into doubt and investigates, he indeed perceives—that is, knows—the most excellent truth; he attains a definitive conclusion.
Thus, it is clearly stated here that the very nature of Mīmāṃsā consists in a definitive conclusion produced by investigation preceded by doubt.

It was deliberated whether some day belonging to the *Utsargiṇām ayana*—which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *Gavāmayana*—should be omitted or not (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.5.7): "The exponents of Brahman deliberate, 'Should it be omitted or should it not be omitted? They say, 'It must indeed be omitted,' and they say, 'It should be omitted on the new moon day and on the full moon day.
Here too, the word "they deliberate" (*mīmāṃsante*) is explicit.

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad as well (1.5.21), beginning with "Now follows the investigation of vows" (*athāto vratamīmāṃsā*), the unique functions of the sense organs with respect to the self (*adhyātma*) and of the deities with respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*) are investigated.

In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad too (5.11.1), among the great Vedic scholars (*mahāśrotriyāḥ*) such as Aupamanyava and others, it is clearly stated: "Having come together, they performed an investigation (*mīmāṃsā*): 'Who is our Self? What is Brahman?
Even if one accepts only the verbal form *mīmāṃsāñcakruḥ* ("they performed an investigation") as the action, there is no deficiency.
"Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the *hotṛ*-priests" (*Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra* 18.14.34).

Regarding this, the Ānartīya Bhāṣya provides the explanation that after the discussion on the performance of the *hotṛ* duties, the investigation of the *hotṛkā*s (the assistants of the *hotṛ*) remains to be addressed.

In the passage, "The exponents of Brahman deliberate: 'Should one take water after the sun has set, or should one not?'* (Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra 1.6.11), the meaning of the term *mīmāṃsā* as an investigation consisting of the adoption of the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions is clearly evident."
"O gods, you have ordained that food be equal for both the pure man who lacks faith and the impure man who possesses faith."
In the commentary on *Baudhāyana* 1.10.5, Govindasvāmin explains [the term] as "having deliberated" (*mīmāṃsitvā vicārya*).
Therefore, the word *mīmāṃsā* has the sense of investigation.

In the *Gautama-dharmasūtra*, after introducing a doubt with the words, "In that regard, they deliberate (*mīmāṃsante*) whether one should perform an expiation or not" (19.14), and after stating the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the proposition, "They say one should not perform it" (5), the reasoning for the prima facie position is presented by the statement, "For an action is not destroyed" (6).

Having stated the thesis of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words, "He should perform [it]; this is another [view]" (Sūtra 7), the author has cited the scriptural passages that prove it through the subsequent Sūtras beginning with, "Furthermore, in the *stoma* sacrifices... (Sūtra 8). Thus, by means of this adoption of the prima facie and final positions (*pūrvottarapakṣa*), the meaning of the term *mīmāṃsā* as "investigation" becomes clear.
Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should one perform the expiation? Should one perform it? (MīmSū 6.5.49).
(2|12) "One should not perform [it]," so they say; (3) for "action is never exhausted. (4) Therefore, one should indeed perform it, according to the evidence of the Śruti. (5)
Thus, here too, it is clear that the word *mīmāṃsā* refers specifically to specialized inquiry.
In every respect, the commencement of *mīmāṃsā* begins precisely with the birth of human beings.

Furthermore, it is not only humans who engage in *mīmāṃsā*; even animals such as cattle and birds, having first deliberated (*mīmāṃsitvā*) whether "this is edible" or "this is inedible," then consume their food.

Even birds such as forest sparrows, when the time for procreation arrives, deliberate upon their location and construct a nest with a favorable structure in a truly suitable place. Thus, deliberation (*mīmāṃsā*) exists even among animals; this very deliberation, increasing according to their intelligence, has over time reached a far greater degree of development.

In this regard, the Jaiminīya Mīmāṃsā system—which serves to enhance the excellence of the intellect of the wise, determines the meaning of Vedic sentences, and consists of an extraction from the flow of the investigation of sentence-meaning—begins with "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" and ends with "As the *yājyā-saṃpreṣa*, as the *yājyā-saṃpreṣa*," comprising sixteen chapters.

The Necessity of a Mimamsa Lexicon: A child, standing on his mother's lap or crawling on his feet, hears words uttered by his parents and others and observes the actions performed by them; after some period of time, he understands that "this is the meaning of this sentence.

In this very manner, hearing various kinds of words and observing the corresponding activities, he discerns the individual components of sentences in the form of *pada*s (words) and their respective meanings.
Likewise, he also comes to grasp, at first sight, the constituent parts of words themselves in the form of *prakṛti*s (bases) and *pratyaya*s (suffixes).
Thus, knowing the relationship of signifier and signified between words and their meanings, one engages in linguistic usage accordingly.
Even uneducated, illiterate people such as plowmen, cowherds, and shepherds are seen engaging in such usage.
This acquisition of the expressive power [of words] is called "grasping the capacity through usage."

The meaning is that through the very process of linguistic usage consisting of hearing and seeing— without even the knowledge of scripts and the like— the relationship between word and meaning, as well as between sentence and sentence-meaning, which exists in the form of signifier and signified, is understood as lasting for the duration of one's life solely by means of such usage.
However, one who desires knowledge exceeding that, by relying on means other than linguistic usage, acquires further knowledge.

The means for grasping the power of word-meanings have been stated by the ancients: "The elders declare that the apprehension of word-power comes from grammar, analogy, lexicons, sentences, usage, the remainder of a sentence, explicit explanation, and the proximity of a known word."
The elders state that the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*) arises from these means.
Among them, for one who is untrained, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is the primary means; some of the others are applicable as the case may be, while some do not apply at all.
For those who are learning and for the proficient, however, the lexicon (*kośa*) and grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) are preeminent.
For those well-trained in it, the lexicon (*kośa*) alone is such a valuable means for understanding diverse languages and so forth.
Lexicons such as the *Viśvaprakāśa* and the *Medinī* were composed by scholars of that time solely for the purpose of knowing the relationship between words and their meanings.
However, the *Amarakośa*, consisting of three sections (*trikāṇḍī*), is the most excellent among all these works for those endowed with proficiency in the divine language (Sanskrit).
For this very reason, there is a well-known saying: "The triad consisting of *Raghu*, *Laghu* (the *Laghukāumudī*), and *Amara* is as useful for the acquisition of grammatical knowledge as a mother.
Furthermore, various and diverse lexicons (*kośas*) of high and low quality have been composed by lexicographers to assist in the mastery of their respective languages;
and for the sake of worldly knowledge, great treasuries of knowledge (*jñānakośas*) have also been revealed by great men.
For there is great utility in lexicons;
just as there are lexicons of words and meanings, so too are lexicons of the subjects of various sciences extremely helpful.
Just as lexicons concerning the subjects of other sciences serve as aids to the study of a single science, so too does a lexicon of the subject matter of one's own science provide immense benefit.

For within a single scripture there are many texts, and it is not possible for one person to study all those texts; yet, if mastery of the subject matter contained in the scripture to be studied is attained, then knowledge of the desired portions of the subject can arise suddenly, without either labor or expense.

While we ourselves were studying the Dharmaśāstra and Vedānta, we repeatedly experienced stumbling and difficulty due to the lack of a treasury of Mīmāṃsā topics. For that very reason, the intention to compose this Treasury of Mīmāṃsā arose.
For this very reason, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa in the Śaka year 1858, I made a formal resolve and began the composition of the Mīmāṃsākośa.
At times, a certain portion of the writing already completed proved to be of great utility at other times.
The Vedas have four auxiliary sciences (vedopāṅgas): the Purāṇas, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā.
In that regard, there are the eighteen Purāṇas, beginning with the Brāhma, as well as the Upapurāṇas together with the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata;
Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika (the system of Gautama), Sāṃkhya (the system of Kapila), and Lokāyata;
and the Dharmaśāstra, which consists of the Smṛtis composed by Manu and others.
Furthermore, Mīmāṃsā consists of twenty chapters and is divided into two parts, the Pūrva and the Uttara, namely the *Ṣoḍaśalakṣaṇī* and the *Caturlakṣaṇī*.

In this regard, because Mīmāṃsā is a science of sentences (*vākyaśāstra*), it is beneficial to all—just like the science of words (*padaśāstra*) and the science of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaśāstra*).
Indeed, every linguistic usage, whether in the form of oral utterance or written expression, consists essentially of sentences.
The meaning of a sentence cannot be understood without an investigation into the relationship between the subject and the predicate, and so forth;
furthermore, the determination of the meaning of a sentence is not accomplished without Mīmāṃsā.
Therefore, for those who follow the Veda, Mīmāṃsā alone is useful for the purpose of ascertaining the meaning of sentences through such determination.

It is not only according to the Vedas that the determination of the meaning of a sentence occurs; rather, there is no dispute that for others as well, the determination of the meaning of a sentence arises precisely through the investigation of sentences (*vākya-mīmāṃsā*), whether by means of other words or in another manner. Although Jaimini’s Mīmāṃsā is the *Dharma-mīmāṃsā* and *dharma* is the Veda, in various sections (*adhikaraṇa*) he cites only Vedic sentences and, having refined them through *śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, and so forth, [establishes] the subject and the predicate by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not.
Mīmāṃsā determines the meaning of a passage by ascertaining its intended sense in a manner that does not contradict other statements.

It is no cause for wonder that, through the logical principles (*nyāya*) that establish the determination of the meaning of Vedic passages, the entire body of literature in the divine language—including the *stuti*, *purāṇa*, *itihāsa*, *kāvya*, *nāṭaka*, *ākhyāna*, *kathā*, *ākhyāyikā*, and *kāthāsaritsāgara*—as well as works in various vernacular languages, can be subjected to inquiry, understood, and determined.
Furthermore, the term "mīmāṃsā" signifies revered inquiry.

From the root *mān*, which signifies "to honor" (*pūjā*), the suffix *san* is applied according to the rule *mānavadhadān* etc. Furthermore, this suffix *san* has the sense of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) based on the Vārttika *mānejijñāsāyām*.
Although the word *jijñāsā* denotes the desire for knowledge (*jñānecchā*), it refers by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the inquiry (*vicāra*) that is to be accomplished by that desire.
And thus, the word *mīmāṃsā* has the sense of "venerated inquiry. The veneration of this inquiry here consists in its being supported by reasoning (*tarka*).
And reasoning consists of deliberation (*ūha*) and elimination (*apoha*), as well as the form of logic (*nyāya*).

*Nyāya* is the method established by worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*), and it generally consists of the reasoning that establishes the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttarapakṣa*).

Indeed, it is this very [method] that is referred to by the term *nyāya* in such expressions as "by the principle of the section on *tad*" (*tadadhikaraṇanyāyena*) or "by the principle of the section on *aḍ*" (*aḍo'dhikaraṇanyāyena*). And worldly convention exists in some cases.

For this very reason, they cite the maxim from the section concerning the invalidity of that which contradicts the Śruti—namely, "Who indeed deserves to obtain what has been carried off by horses through donkeys?"—as its foundational principle.

While the study and teaching of this Mīmāṃsā are becoming increasingly diminished day by day, its utility remains immense for both ancient scholars who practiced the traditional sciences and for modern ones.

Furthermore, when those in the courts of justice deliberate upon the meaning of sentences from the ancient Dharmaśāstras and other texts, a state of great difficulty arises without recourse to Mīmāṃsā.
Without Mīmāṃsā, the study of the Vedānta scriptures—and especially of the treatises on Dharma—stumbles at every step.
For most [legal and philosophical] works are commenced by relying upon the established principles of Mīmāṃsā;

indeed, they cite Mīmāṃsā maxims here and there, such as "by the principle of distinctness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktvanyāya*), "by the principle of the singularity of the cup" (*grahaikatvanyāya*), and "by the section concerning relative strength" (*balābalādhikaraṇanyāya*).
For this very reason, this effort in composing the Mīmāṃsākośa is fruitful. Enough of this. Now, the subject matter of the Kośa:

In this *Mīmāṃsākoṣa*, there is a compendium of three categories: all the *adhikaraṇas* (topic-sections), scriptural and worldly *nyāyas* (principles of reasoning), and *laghusiddhāntas* (concise conclusions).

Among these, the *adhikaraṇas* are of four types: those found in the *bhāṣya*s on the twelve chapters (*dvādaśalakṣaṇī*), those in the *saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* *bhāṣya*, those in the *Bhāvacandrikā*, those in the *Tautātikamatatilaka*, and the *adhikaraṇas* from Kevalānanda’s commentary.

In the sections concerning the commentaries (*bhāṣya*), first, a heading indicating the subject matter of the section (*adhikaraṇa*)—prepared either by ancient editors or composed by us—is presented. Following that is the *sūtra*, accompanied by the chapter (*adhyāya*), section (*caraṇa*), section number (*adhikaraṇa*), and *sūtra* number. Next comes the *bhāṣya*, then the *vārtika*. Then follow the verses from the *Śāstradīpikā* and, in some places, its prose portions. After that is Somanātha’s *Saṅgati* (also known as the *Mayūkhamālikā*), which provides the connection between the topics, the meaning of the *sūtra*, and in some instances, the meaning of the entire treatise. Next is the verse, or verses, from the *Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara*. Then follows the *Śāstradīpikā*. After that is a quarter-verse from Maṇḍanācārya’s *Mīmāṃsā-anukramaṇikā* that sets forth the subject matter of the section. Finally, there is the corresponding portion from Śrī Śaṅkara Bhaṭṭa’s *Mīmāṃsāsārasaṃgraha*.
This concludes the section consisting of the verses of the *Śloka*.

Furthermore, in the initial portion of this manuscript, the *Nyāyabindusaṃgraha* composed by Vaidyanātha, known as Tatsat, was included; however, later, due to fear of the bulk of the work, the *Nyāyabindusaṃgraha* was omitted.

Regarding these topics (*adhikaraṇas*) discussed in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Tantravārtika*, the *Ṭupṭīkā-vārtika*, and the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*—these three have been collected here letter by letter. This is because the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārtika* are the original source texts (*ākaragrantha*), while the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* represents a refined stage according to the *Nayapaddhati* method. Furthermore, for the topics belonging to the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, after first presenting the ancient available headings or reconstructed titles in alphabetical order, the *Bhāṭṭacandrikā*—which is synonymous with the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*—is then presented.

The *Tautātitamatātilaka*—also known by the alternative title *Bhavaprasāda*—is a work composed by Bhavadeva that elucidates the subject matter of the *adhikaraṇas*. It generally follows the Prābhākara position in each *adhikaraṇa* before refuting it; thus, it is a treatise older than the *Śāstradīpikā*.
Its extent corresponds exactly to that portion of the *Bhāṣya* for which the *Tantravārtika* is complete;
that is to say, it begins from the first *pāda* of the first *adhyāya* and extends only as far as the end of the third *adhyāya*.
Even therein, we have obtained and printed only up to the very end of the second chapter; therefore, only that much has been compiled.
This constitutes the second type of section (*adhikaraṇa*).
Having presented the first sūtra of each section according to the order of the letters, that text has been inserted in its respective place.
Now, for the purpose of understanding the meaning of all the sūtras word by word, a new commentary has been composed by us. This has been arranged according to the topical sections (adhikaraṇas).
Therein, having first presented the initial sūtra according to the order of its syllables, the section of the commentary is summarized.

Thus, it should be understood that in this compendium (*kośa*), the *bhāṣya-adhikaraṇas* and *saṃkarṣaṇa-adhikaraṇas* are to be found according to the headings arranged by the order of the letters (*varṇakrama*), whereas the *tautā-adhikaraṇa* and *vṛtti-adhikaraṇa* are to be found according to the order of their respective sūtras arranged by the sequence of letters.
In these four types of *adhikaraṇas*, the *ḍamaru* symbol (the damaru-sign) has been placed at the beginning. Now, the *nyāyas*.

The *akṣāmbhyañjananyāya*, the *agnisaṃmārganyāya*, the *aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*, and others such as these belong to the Mīmāṃsā system; some belong to the Uttaramīmāṃsā (Vedānta) system, and some belong to the Vyākaraṇa (Grammar) system. Even those formulated as *paribhāṣās* (technical rules) are designated by the term *nyāya* in works such as the *Śelara*. Furthermore, there are others in the form of verses found in various source texts such as the *Vārtikas* by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* and others; all of these have been collected here as far as they could be obtained.

For these [principles] are cited as authoritative means for determining meaning in the treatises on Dharmaśāstra, in various other types of technical (śāstrīya) treatises, and in the treatises on Mīmāṃsā itself. Consequently, their compilation is indeed necessary. Several names for these Mīmāṃsā principles are found here and there, such as the *parṇatā-nyāya*, the *parṇamayī-nyāya*, the *parṇamaya-adhikaraṇa*, and so forth.

In that regard, one particular name is presented as a heading (*śīrṣaka*) at the beginning of a topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth, while the remainder are presented according to the order of their syllables.
Furthermore, just like scriptural principles (*nyāya*), there are also worldly principles;
indeed, many such worldly principles are presented in Mīmāṃsā treatises themselves for the purpose of determining the meaning of a topical section.

And these too must certainly be included. If maxims that have been identified as such are indeed to be inserted here in this treasury, then what offense has been committed by the learned? Thus, all worldly maxims found in works such as the *Laukikanyāyasahasra* and others have been collected by us.
All these maxims have been arranged in alphabetical order and placed in their respective locations.
In the *Nyāya* and other systems, the ḍamaru symbol is placed at the beginning of each topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), just as it is placed at the beginning of each syllogism (*nyāya*).
Thus, our rule is that only the ḍamaru symbol should be inserted at the start of a topical section and likewise at the start of a syllogism.
However, because this was not determined from the very beginning, it did not reach the printing process until page 184.
After that, this very *daṇḍaka* was accepted everywhere.
In that context, what is called "reasoning" (*nyāya*) is a collection of sentences consisting of an inference for the sake of another (*parārthānumāna*).
And that [collection] may have two members like the Buddhists, three members like the Mīmāṃsakas, or five members like the logicians (*tārkika*).
The judgment document of the judge is also a *nyāya*.

However, there is this distinction: whereas a *nyāya* possesses brevity of body and consists of aphorisms (*sūtra*), a judgment document possesses elaborateness of body and consists of commentaries (*bhāṣya*).
Nevertheless, *nyāya*, *nirṇaya*, and the pentad beginning with the *pratijñā* (the five-membered syllogism) are synonyms.

*Rītiḥ*, *prakāraḥ*, and *paddhatiḥ*—these also constitute the meaning of the term *nyāya*. For instance, the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* (30.6.9) states: “He recites those [Nārāśaṃsī verses] by way of *pragrāha*, just as in the case of the *Vṛṣākapi*; for the *Vārṣākapa* follows this rule (*tan-nyāya*) of the *Vṛṣākapi*. The meaning of this is: he recites those mantras known as the Nārāśaṃsīs by way of *pragrāha* (i.e., in a specific sequential manner).

The Brāhmaṇacchaṃsin recites with both *pragṛhya* (protracted) and non-*pragṛhya* vowels. Just as he recites the hymn named *Vṛṣākapi* by dividing it into quarters (*pādaśas*), so too must this recitation— the *Vārṣākapaṃha*, which is the service (*sevada*) dedicated to Vṛṣākapi— be performed.
Therefore, one attains—that is, reaches—the *nyāya*, meaning the method or mode consisting of the analytical recitation (*vigṛhyaśaṃsana*), of that hymn named after Vṛṣākapi.
Here, Sāyaṇācārya has taken the word *nyāya* to mean "method" (*prakāra*).
Furthermore: "Śunaḥśepa said to his father Ajīgarta: 'He who would commit a sin once, he might commit it again after that.'"

"You have not departed from the Śūdra way; undoubtedly this has been done by you" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 33.5.4). Regarding this, Sāyaṇa comments: "You have not departed (*apāgāḥ*) from the Śūdra way (*nyāyāt*), that is, you have not become removed (*apagataḥ*) from the cruel conduct associated with the low caste.
Thus, *nyāya* means conduct, manner, or method."

"Whatever is of fewer number, that one should perform first; thus they complete each respective number that is to be completed. This very principle has been illustrated with examples, such as in the twenty-three-night sacrifice: "the five-day period, the six-day period, and the twelve-day period," according to the *Śāṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra* (13.15.11), which states: "By this, he completes each respective number. Regarding the phrase "he should protect the castes from the stages of life according to the rule" (*Gautama Dharma Sūtra* 11.9), the commentary of Maskari explains that "according to the rule" (*nyāyataḥ*) means by a path that does not contradict worldly custom or the scriptures.

Regarding the statement, “Reasoning (*tarka*) is the means for the attainment of *nyāya*” (29), Maskari’s commentary states: “In the context of attainment (*adhigama*), *avadhāraṇe*, *tarka* is inference (*anumāna*).
By this, it is made clear that the meaning of the term *nyāya* is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) consisting of the five members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase “one should practice spiritual disciplines (*yoga*) accompanied by *nyāya*” found in Āpastamba’s *Dharmasūtra* (1.22.19), the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda explained the word “accompanied by *nyāya*” as “endowed with logical justification (*upapatti*)”.
And thus, *nyāya* means logical justification, reasoning, or argument.
The consensus of those who know the *nyāya* is that "instruction for the ignorant should be by means of primary [terms]" (*ĀpDhS* 2.8.13).
This sūtra states that it is not proper to designate the *kalpasūtras*—which are for the ignorant—by words denoting primary [Vedic categories], such as "Chandas," "Veda," or "Brāhmaṇa."

Having thus explained that "the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the consensus of those who know logic (*nyāyavid*)," the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpūjyapāda stated: "These two—the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion—are to be clearly seen in the section on the *Kalpasūtras* (Brahmasūtra 1.3.6).

By this, it is understood that in the sections of the *Adhvara-mīmāṃsā*, the logical arguments (*yukti*) that establish the *pūrvapakṣa* and *siddhānta*, as well as those that serve as their seeds, are denoted by the term *nyāya*.
For example, the statement "a cognition of a qualified object does not arise without its qualifier having been apprehended" is the seed of the section on the generic form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*).

Or, for example, "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained from any other source" is the seed of the *Kartradhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the agent), and so forth. Furthermore: "And its [the Vedic injunction's] universal applicability is understood because of that same principle."
For it belongs only to some, while for others it does not exist at all.
Thus says the Vārttika (1.3.188, p. 216).
Its meaning is "by means of the words for sound.

Regarding this, the Sudhā (p. 207) states: "That power which possesses the logic (*nyāya*)—that is, the reasoning (*yukti*)—for that omnipresence is *tanmāyā*; the state of being that is *tannyāyatvam*."

In response to the inquiry, "What kind of reasoning (nyāya) is this?", [the author] says: "Not of many. Here, the meaning of the word *nyāya* as "logical argument" (*yukti*) has been explicitly stated by the author of the *Sudhā*. Furthermore, the word *nyāya* is employed numerous times within the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtras*.

And in all such instances, the word *yukti* is generally understood to mean "logical," "proper," or "fitting," as in the sūtra: "By the term *anyāya*, [it is meant] the absence of scriptural authority" (1.3.126).

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "And this is not the rule (*nyāya*), that all words which are similar and which apply to a single meaning must necessarily have an uninterrupted traditional lineage."

The author of the *Laukikanyāyasaṃgraha* states: "All worldly examples and all worldly discourses (such as those found in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha* and others, including the stories of Dāmbhyāla and Kaṭāca) can be cited as *nyāyas*.
The conclusion is that, by taking the meanings of 'manner', 'method', 'way', and 'reasoning' as the basis, all scriptural and worldly *nyāyas* have been compiled in the *Mīmāṃsākoṣa*.
Now, the third part of the *Koṣa* is titled *Laghusiddhānta*.
And here, "lightness" does not mean having few words;
for some [works] may be large even in terms of their verbal expression.

Therefore, whether small or large, any portion of a Mīmāṃsā treatise that is distinct from its primary subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) and distinct from its formal reasoning (*nyāya*) is technically termed a "light conclusion" (*laghusiddhānta*).
At the beginning of these [entries], the symbol for *tārā* has been placed.

This is the method employed in the arrangement of the statements of the *Laghusiddhāntakaumudī*: when certain words from the sūtra-texts are to be inserted, the word found therein is first entered according to the sequence of case-endings, such as the nominative (*prathamā*) and so forth; even within that, it is entered according to the sequence of numbers, such as the singular (*ekavacana*) and so forth.
Following that, the compound words (*sāmāsika-pada*) formed by those [elements] are inserted in accordance with the sequence of the letters (*varṇakrama*), as appropriate.

In this work, the statements of the established conclusions (*siddhānta*) have been divided according to their respective subject matters and arranged in accordance with their meaning; even so, the sequence of the letters has not been neglected as appropriate.
Furthermore, these established conclusions have been extracted from various Mīmāṃsā treatises, for the most part exactly as they were seen, letter by letter.
However, regarding those situated in the majority [of the tradition], even when some have performed alterations such as changing the syllables (*akṣara*) and so forth,

some are in the form of sugar-candy (*śarkararūpa*), while others consist of the extraction of the intended meaning (*tātparyoddhāra*). Therefore, because they are inclined toward demonstrating the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), even when viewing through the phrases (*phakkikā*) of ancient texts consisting of syllables exactly as they were seen, the editor is not at fault.
Our system of phonemes and the rules of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) are as follows:
the vowels are thirteen— *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, lṛ, e, ai, o, au*—
along with the *anusvāra* (-) and the *visarga* (:).
The *ka*-group, the *ca*-group, the *ṭa*-group, the *ta*-group, the *pa*-group, the *ya*-group, and the *śa*-group—these are the thirty-five consonants.
Thus, there are forty-eight phonemes (*varṇas*).
They are to be understood according to the sequence already stated.
Consequently, at the time of examining the consonants following the vowels, we have adopted this sequence: first the *anusvāra*, then the *visarga*, and then the *ka*-group and so forth.
This very sequence is established by the Tantras and is indeed well-known in the world;
furthermore, the inclusion of the *anusvāra* and *visarga* among the consonants is not a new innovation.

For it is stated in the *Ṛk-prātiśākhya*: "The anusvāra is either a consonant or a vowel" (1.15), and "Everything else is exclusively consonants" (1.16). By this rule, it is determined that the visarga is indeed a consonant.

In that context, since the status of the anusvāra as a consonant is accepted through a fixed option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*), there is no risk of contradicting one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

In this regard, those who accept the rule that the *anusvāra* must always be replaced by the following homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) in editions such as the Kāśī and Kālīghāṭa prints, print [the words] simply as *saṃnayataḥ* and *asaṃnayataḥ*.

In that case, there arises a doubt as to whether there is an internal word-division (*avāntarapadabheda*) as *sam + nayataḥ* or *sav + nayataḥ*. Demonstrating the consistency [of his view], he says: "One who performs the act of bringing together (*sānādhya*) is called *saṃnayan*; however, those who do not perform it in that manner are *asaṃnayantaḥ*."
Furthermore, no one here accepts the word "sat" as being included within the compound; rather, it is simply the prefix "sam.
If that were the case, the printed forms "sannayataḥ" and "sānādhyaṃ" would indicate a highly ambiguous reading.
In such instances, we have adopted a method throughout so that no ambiguity may arise.

Where there is the unification of words (*akhaṇḍapadaikya*), there the *parasavarṇa* (the substitution of the following sound) is indeed applied to the letter *na* or the letter *ma* (which, from the perspective of common usage, is the *anusvāra*). However, where an option (*vikalpa*) such as "or [the substitution applies] at the end of a word" (*vā padāntasya*) is prescribed, there the *parasavarṇa* is not applied at all; for example: *saṃgatiḥ*, *saṃtardanam*, *saṃpādanam*, *sānādhyam*. But in cases such as *prasaṅgaḥ* and *prasañjanam*, the *parasavarṇa* is indeed accepted.

In all cases, the *visarga* has been inserted as a *visarga* itself; it has not been changed to a *śar* when followed by a *śar*, nor has there been elision of the *visarga* before a *kharpara* *śar*.
However, in instances such as "yastu" and "visargastu," a *śar* has sometimes been applied and sometimes not.
In cases such as "tha eva," where the word division is either "thaḥ eva" or "tha eva," the form—whether "thaḥ" or "ye"—has been inserted according to the sense, without applying sandhi.

Thus, it should be understood whether the application of rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, *ādguṇaḥ*, *vṛddhireci*, *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*, *eṅaḥ padāntādati*, and *eco'yavāyāvaḥ* has been accepted according to the necessity of making [the phonetic forms] manifest. If the operation of the rules of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) were not required, how could there be the consequence of a deficiency in the expressive power [of words]? To illustrate this somewhat, one should also observe the placement of the introductory markers (*avataraṇacihna*) right there.

In the printed edition of the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara* with the commentary of Bhūtiśa, on page 14, it is printed as: "ata eva 'aṇo 'pragṛhyasya' ity etadekavākyatāpannād 'adaso māt' ity etat—" (therefore, because of this being in syntactic agreement with "aṇo 'pragṛhyasya," [the rule] "adaso māt" [is applied]).
Upon reading this, the speaker indeed suffers distress.
How can even learned scholars consider such a printing to be correct? Thus, the mind of Māhātmyapaṇḍita is grieved.
If indeed that very statement of Śekharācārya had been printed as "ata eva 'aṇo'pragṛhyasya' ityetadekavākyatāpanna-'adaso māt' iti," then what a great loss would have occurred!
On page 133 of that very book, [the reading] "bhinne 'pyatra" etc. was printed.
In this regard—[as in the phrase] "even when [the word] is split" and so forth—what effort is required from the printer in the act of printing?

Generally, in the application of the rules of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) and in the insertion of punctuation marks (*avataraṇacchidāna*), no consideration for the ease of comprehension by the reader, nor any discrimination between what is essential and what is not, is made at all during the printing process; thus, there is a great lack of discernment.
Nevertheless, in the printing of our own work, we have deliberately adopted a relaxation of the rules of euphonic combination for the sake of the reader's convenience.
Regarding matters such as "mo'nusvāraḥ," a certain degree of boldness has been adopted in the form of a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*).
Where one should have printed either "prayojanamiti" or "prayojanam iti," it was printed as "prayojanaṃ iti.
Where one should have entered either "jñānamitiḥ" or "jñānam anumitiḥ," it was entered as "jñānaṃ anumitiḥ."
This convention of ours is intended solely for the convenience of the speaker; therefore, we should not be criticized by those learned in the scriptures.

It should be understood that in every respect, we have adopted a relaxation of the rules of euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) for the sake of allowing speakers easy entry into this profound and deep subject.
It is also true that in some instances, it was not possible to act in such a manner due to other reasons.

The authors—their works which have been included in this treasury, as well as those which could not be included—are all pointed out for the sake of knowledge according to the context; and their accepted works, as well as how they were accepted, are likewise indicated. Their dates, having already been established by scholars, are cited here as available, rather than through an independent investigation. For example:

The ancient Mīmāṃsā teachers: Ātreya appears three times—as in *phalamātrayo nirdeśāt* (4.1.8), *mūlayānantaryamātreyaḥ* (5.1.8), and *nirdeśādvā trayāṇāṃ syādaganyāgheye hyasaṃbandhaḥ kratuṣu brāhmaṇaśruterityātreyaḥ* (6.1.26).
Ālekhana appears once—as in *vyuddha bhāgamyastvalekhanaḥ* (6.1.17).
Āśmarathya appears once—as in *anirute'bhyudite prākṛtībhyo nirvapedityāśmarathyaḥ* (6.5.16).

Aitiśāyana: thrice—“According to Aitiśāyana, there is a single mantra for all” (3.1.44); “Or rather, according to Aitiśāyana, this [rite] should be like a conjunction, because it is connected with the fruit; therefore, it is a ritual act” (3.1.44); “Because of the mention of a specific gender, it is connected with the male, according to Aitiśāyana” (6.1.6).

Kāmukāyana: twice—“And likewise, Kāmukāyana cites the observation of another purpose” (1.1.98); “Kāmukāyana says [the offering] should be once, because of the contradiction regarding the measure” (1.1.162).

Kārṣṇājini: twice—“In the case of a sacrifice, Kārṣṇājini held that the mention of results is merely commendatory” (4.1.17), and “It would be a family tradition, says Kārṣṇājini, because it is possible for only one [to follow it]” (6.7.35).

Jaimini: five times—“Actions also [are to be repeated], says Jaimini, because they are for the sake of a result” (3.1.4); “But Jaimini [holds] there is no difference in the action” (6.3.4); “But Jaimini [holds] its repetition” (8.3.7); “And [it is] more and different, says Jaimini” (9.1.28); “Because of falling under another’s authority, according to Jaimini” (12.1.17).

Bādarāyaṇa: “That is authoritative, because Bādarāyaṇa [holds it] to be independent,” 1.1.5; “But at the end, Bādarāyaṇa [says],” 5.1.19; “But as for the class, Bādarāyaṇa [says],” 6.1.8; “But as for the injunction, Bādarāyaṇa [says],” 10.8.44; and “In the division of the context according to the rule, Bādarāyaṇa [prescribes] the performance,” 1.1.165—thus five times.
Bādari is mentioned four times: in *dravyaguṇasaṃskāreṣu bādariḥ* (3.1.3), *nimittārthena bādariḥ* (6.1.27), *kālābhyāse 'pi bādariḥ karmabhedāt* (8.3.6), and *varṇe tu bādariḥ* (9.1.32).
Lāvukāyana is mentioned once: in *vipratiṣedhāttu guṇavantyataḥ syāditi lāvukāyanaḥ* (6.7.37).
Similarly, the word *eka*, used in the sense of "others," appears ten or eleven times in the forms *eke* and *ekeṣām*.
Thus, specific references to the ancient Mīmāṃsā teachers are found in the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī*.
Since the *Saṃkarṣa-sūtras* are no longer extant, nothing can be said regarding the subjects mentioned therein; nevertheless, something will be discussed later.
Among these, Ālekhana is mentioned by Āśvalāyana in his own *Śrautasūtra* (6.1.29), as is Āśmarathya (6.1.20).
Kārṣṇājini is mentioned in the Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra at 1.14, and Bādari at 4.96.
Furthermore, it is impossible to determine whether these teachers were contemporaneous or belonged to different periods, nor whether they hailed from the same region or different regions.

Furthermore, it is impossible to speculate whether Mīmāṃsā-sūtra texts belonging to each or some of these [ancient teachers] actually existed, and that Jaimini compiled their views here after finding them therein; or whether they were found in dialogues, supplements, or specific discussions; or whether, having been obtained through the lineage of gurus, they were incorporated into his own sūtras, and so forth.

Nevertheless, having examined the names of the ancient Nirukta teachers mentioned by the master Yāska in the *Nirukta*, or having obtained them from other sources, the commentator on the *Nirukta*, Durgācārya, has established that "there were thirteen *Niruktas*. Likewise, observing these names of ancient Mīmāṃsā teachers, one must consider whether their works on Mīmāṃsā themselves existed, taking into account the differences or non-differences in place and time.

The tradition holds that the venerable great sage Jaimini is the author of the *Śrutilakṣaṇa* known as the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra*, which consists of twelve chapters (*dvādaśalakṣaṇī*) and provides an extensive exposition of categories beginning with the distinctions between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-bheda*) and ending with incidental discussions (*prasaṅga*), as well as the *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa*, which expounds upon miscellaneous topics concerning *dharma*.
The venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpūjyapāda maintains that the venerable Bādarāyaṇa is the author of the *Tulakṣaṇa* known as the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā*.

The traditional consensus is that the use of the term "Jaimini" in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* and the use of the term "Bādarāyaṇa" in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* are not contradictory, as they are intended to reveal specific nuances of his own intention.
Furthermore, the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi* maintains that Jaimini alone is the author of all twenty chapters [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras].
Modern scholars maintain that Jaimini was some disciple or successor of [Bādarāyaṇa] who composed the Sūtras for both Mīmāṃsās;
only on this basis is the mention of the names Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa in both systems consistent.
(Siddhāntacandrikā, commentary on the Śāstradīpikā, Tarkapāda, p. 4).
Furthermore, the relationship consisting of the lineage of teachers (*gurugarbhakrama*) has been stated here by some as follows:

Brahmā proclaimed the Mīmāṃsā to Prajāpati; he [Prajāpati] to Indra; he [Indra] to Agni; he [Agni] to Vasiṣṭha; he [Vasiṣṭha] to Parāśara; Parāśara to Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana; and he [Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana] to Jaimini, who, immediately after receiving this instruction, composed this treatise on logic (*nyāya*).

It has been stated: "Who indeed—whether Brahmā, Maheśvara, or Prajāpati—proclaimed this Mīmāṃsā? Prajāpati [proclaimed it] to Indra, Indra to Āditya, and Āditya to Vasiṣṭha"; such is the alternative reading.

Therefore, the statement of Jaimini—that "the generic form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of a word"—is established. This is the Jaimini, author of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtras*, as pointed out by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) at *Bhāṣya* 1.1.5 (p.
52). All the *sūtras* of the twelve chapters (*dvādaśalakṣaṇī*) composed by him are collected here in this treasury.
Regarding Upavarṣācārya:
the *Kathāsaritsāgara* states that he was the teacher of Pāṇini, the author of the *Vyākaraṇa*.
As for the time of Pāṇini, according to the view of Rājwade, it is the 8th century BCE.
Citrāvāśāstri, however, states that "according to the opinion of Rājavāḍe, the time of Pāṇini is 1200–900 [BCE], and according to the opinion of Kāle, it is 700 [BCE] from the present.
The venerable Upavarṣa had a commentary (*vṛtti*) on the twenty-chapter *Mīmāṃsā*.
Śabara Svāmī mentions him by the titles *Vṛttikāra* and *Upavarṣa*, as will be cited further below.

In the *Śārīrakabhāṣya*, the venerable Pūjyapāda [Śaṅkarācārya] makes the following mention: in the commentary on the *sphoṭa* theory at *Brahmasūtra* 1.3.28, he states, "The venerable Upavarṣa maintains that the phoneme (*varṇa*) alone is the word (*śabda*)," and in the sūtra 1.3.53, "One [is the soul], because of its existence when there is a body," he notes, "The venerable Upavarṣa, in the context of discussing the existence of the self in the first system (*tantra*), made the declaration: 'We shall explain this in the *Śārīraka*.

There are six worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

Furthermore, there are six means of valid cognition regarding *dharma*: injunction (*vidhi*), explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), mantra, name (*nāmadheya*), traditional law (*smṛti*), and the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).

There are six means of establishing the distinction between ritual acts (*dharma*): difference of word (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), name (*saṃjñā*), accessory quality (*guṇa*), and difference of context (*prakaraṇāntara*).

There are six means of knowledge for the application (*viniyoga*) of ritual acts: direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*, i.e., order), and name (*samākhyā*).

There are six means of determining the order (*krama*): direct assertion (*śruti*), purpose (*artha*), textual sequence (*pāṭha*), position (*sthāna*), primacy (*mukhyatva*), and commencement (*pravṛtti*).
The word, the name, and the characteristic— these three are the means of extended application (atideśa).
The principle of "occupying the place" (sthānāpatti) is the means of modification (ūha).
There are three grounds for sublation (bādha): substitution (pratyāmnāna), prohibition (pratiṣedha), and loss of purpose (arthalopa).

Regarding the categories of objects (padārtha): they are sevenfold, consisting of substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), action (karma), generality (sāmānya), inherence (samavāya), power (śakti), and absence (abhāva).
Among these, substances are eleven: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, mind, darkness, and sound.
"For time is beginningless for us" (Dharmottarapradīpa 6.1.15, p. 1356).
The sense organs are six: the nose, tongue, eye, skin, ear, and mind.
Among these, the olfactory, gustatory, visual, and tactile organs are, respectively, of the nature of earth, water, fire, and air.
The auditory organ has space as its essence.

The mind is atomic in dimension; it is an internal organ that, by its own independence, has as its objects the self, its conjunction [with the self], the qualities [of the self], and the universals residing therein.
He has no independence regarding external objects.

Contact (*saṃnikarṣa*)—the conjunction between the object and the sense organ—is threefold: conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), and inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*).

There are twenty qualities (*guṇa*): color, taste, smell, touch, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, momentum, unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort.
The conjunction of conjunctions is not admitted.
Number is a distinct category of reality. Action, consisting of motion, is one and the same.
Generality is twofold, consisting of the higher and the lower. There is both difference and non-difference between generality and that which possesses generality.
Generality is of the nature of a universal (jāti).
It is eternal, one, and follows many.
By accepting the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), their non-difference is established.

There is both difference and non-difference between the universal and its possessor, between the part and the whole, between the quality (*guṇa*) and the qualified (*guṇin*), and between the action (*kriyā*) and the agent of the action (*kriyāvat*).

Inherence (*samavāya*): That relation by which a single substratum, through its own connection, generates a cognition colored by itself in the substrate; it is not, however, a relation of inseparable existence (*ayutasiddha*). Potency (*śakti*): It is threefold—innate (*sahajā*), adventitious (*āgantukī*), and word-potency (*padaśakti*).

In the ninth [chapter], in the sūtra: "Or rather, because it is preceded by the word, the ritual act of sacrifice should be primary; the mention of the deity is subordinate" (9.1.9), the deity's subordination to the sacrifice is stated according to the principle of the co-utterance of the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished (*bhūtabhavyasamuccāraṇanyāya*). Having raised the objection: "But is it not understood from the context that the deity is also intended as the desired object of the ritual act?", [the author] replies: "We do not deny its status as the intended object."

By the Bhāṣya statement, "The intended nature of the deity associated with a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix or in the dative case is understood from the sentence" (Bhāṣya, p. 1652), the status of mere sound as the deity is refuted; for if a collection of meaningless phonemes lacks the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it cannot be joined with a *taddhita* suffix or a dative case-ending, and thus by the mention of such a connection—and by the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*)—the status of mere sound as the deity is rejected.

And in the tenth [book], under the sūtra *vidhiśabdasya mantratve bhāvaḥ syāt tena codanā* (10.4.23), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is raised that since the deity can be denoted by any synonym whatsoever in acts such as *āvāhana* (invocation), there is no regard for the specific word used in the injunction, such as "Āgneya" and so on. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached by arguing that because the connection of the oblation with the deity is enjoined by the word "Agni" within the injunction—namely, "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni"—the very same word found in the injunction must be uttered when performing the mantra-function of designating the deity. Then, having asked, "What indeed is this thing called a 'deity' (*devatā*)?", two alternative views are presented: first, that Indra and others residing in heaven are the deities; and second, that whatever is referred to by the word "deity" in the Veda—such as in "Agni is the deity," "Vāyu is the deity"—is the deity. Both of these are rejected because they fail to include things like days and tigers. According to his own view, he states in the Bhāṣya: "Deities are those who partake of the hymns (*sūkta*) and those who partake of the oblations (*havirbhāj*).
