From this, it is understood that the "object" (*artha*) is characterized by being the object of praise and the object of intent. Furthermore, the Bhāṣya states: "There will be the status of deity for things—whether embodied or unembodied, conscious or unconscious—that are conceived by scripture as being for the sake of some particular object. This declares that even embodied and conscious entities can have the status of deity. Finally, the Bhāṣya says: "Or rather, she (the deity) is that for whose expressive word one forms the resolve: 'Having remembered the word, I shall offer the oblation,' or 'I shall offer the oblation' while uttering the word. Because the root *diś* means "to utter," it is declared that the status of deity belongs to the expressed meaning (*vācya*) through the word being uttered, or through the word being remembered in an injunction such as "One should sacrifice to Prajāpati mentally. Anticipating the objection, "If this is so, then one might as well designate Agni by any word whatsoever," he begins by saying: "This would indeed be so, if the word 'Agni' were uttered merely for the purpose of conveying the meaning, and if the meaning itself were conveyed merely for the purpose of connecting it with the oblation. He concludes: "In the capacity of being an instrument of sacrifice, the deity does not exist by way of its form (*rūpa*)."
"By what means, then? By the word through its connection," and so forth—in this passage from the Bhāṣya (Bhā. p.
1928), the status of the word as the deity is refuted by the mention of that which is distinct from the word yet connected to it.
Thus it is said.
Now, something from the *Kutūhala* is cited by way of illustration:

"As for that which is refuted in the ninth [chapter], in the section beginning with *'Or rather, the deity should be the motivator'* (9.1.4.6), regarding the view that deities possess physical forms (*vigraha*) and so forth—that is merely a statement made for the sake of argument (*prauḍhivāda*)."

"The deity is the word alone, not the meaning; likewise, the claim that the meaning devoid of the positions regarding bodily form (*vigraha*) and so forth is the deity is merely the prattle of disguised Buddhists. The followers of Karma-Mīmāṃsā are proponents of atheism (*nirīśvaravādin*); the common report that they hold no position regarding the bodily form of the deity and such refers specifically to those who are one-sided followers of that [Mīmāṃsā] school who are disguised Buddhists. "Salutation to Him whose body is pure knowledge, whose divine eye is the three Vedas, who is the cause for attaining the highest good, and who bears the meaning of the *Sauma* [mantra]."
This is because the venerable teacher Bhaṭṭa Kumārila, at the beginning of his *Ślokavārttika*, describes the nature of Īśvara;

and because in the *Śāstradīpikā*, in the third chapter, second quarter, under the section on "Indicative Mark and Order" (*liṅgakrama*, 3.2.7–9), he states: "Since [the deities] are established in the Mantras, Arthavādas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth as having the form of creating, protecting, and so on, and since they are understood to exist even outside of ritual action—such as being the presiding deities of heaven and the like—there is no lack of the status of being an agent.
Therefore, for Vedic believers (*āstika*), there exists the position that the deities possess bodies and other such attributes. This much, at least, is certain.
Thus [it is said].

In the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, however, in the section concerning the deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*), the view that the grace of the deity is the motivating factor was refuted precisely by accepting the existence of the *apūrva*. Here, however, the objection—that the grace of the deity itself should be the motivating factor without accepting that *apūrva*—is refuted as a relevant point of discussion. Regarding this, [the author] states: "In no way is there acceptance of a physical form (*vigraha*) and so forth; rather, the deity is the word alone. As for its referent (*artha*), on account of the support provided by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), some conscious or unconscious entity may be accepted, but not one possessing a physical form and so forth."
The summary of Jaimini’s position is that in the context of worship and the like, only a superimposed (āhārya) meditation on the Supreme is required; however, [the author] concludes:
"Even for me who speaks thus, my speech is defiled; therefore, Lord Hari alone is my refuge.
But this must be considered: Jaimini did not exclude the existence of deities.

"Ritual action (*yajñakarma*) should be primary, while the mention of the deity is subordinate"—this much alone Jaimini has stated (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 9.1.4.9). It is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra that in the granting of the fruit, ritual action alone is primary, whereas the deity is merely subordinate; such indeed is the intended purport (*tātparya*) of Jaimini.
This is the reading of the collection of the Sūtras (*sūtrāṇāṃ saṃhitā*).
It is determined that the recitation of the Sūtras composed by Jaimini originally existed as a *saṃhitā* prior to [the division into individual rules], just like the Sūtras of Pāṇini.

For this very reason, the statement of the Vārttika—“Or rather, the conclusion is ‘teṣvadarśanādavirodhasya’; or the Sūtra begins with ‘teṣvadarśanādavirodhasya’” (1.3.7)—is consistent. Furthermore, the *Sudhā* (p. 999) states: “‘Śiṣyate samāptivat’ [is the reading] in the *saṃhitā* of the Sūtras (2.4.19–20); even by means of the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *a*, a separation is possible.”

In many of the Sūtras, it is also observed that they take the form of verses or even parts of verses, such as: "From the one joined with the last of the principal [elements], everything ceases" (*nivartate*—though this word would later appear in reverse order at 10.1.15); "But in that case, it should be like the *prayāja*s" (10.1.16); "But in the case of the sacrificial post, because it is merely a location, the cessation [of the rule] is perceived" (*pratīyate*—though this word would later appear at 10.1.10); "Or rather, because it is a subordinate element, its consecration is perceived" (11); and "The same applies to the *ājyabhāga* offerings" (16).
And so forth.

Furthermore, we entertain the conjecture that all these sūtras may have existed in the very remote past either exclusively in verse form, or as a mixture of prose and verse (campū) like the *Campūrāmāyaṇa*.
This is suggested by the mention of the teacher Upavarṣa, the author of the *Vṛtti*.
The examples provided by Śabarācārya are cited [as follows]:

On page 25 of the commentary on 1.1.5, the Bhāṣya states: "But the author of the Vṛtti explained this passage differently, beginning with 'tasya nimittaparicchedaḥ' and so forth," continuing until the end: "that alone is the incorrect cognition, and no other."
It must be considered how extensive this *Vṛttimantha* is.

In the *Mīmāṃsādarśana* published by the Ānandāśrama, at the end of the commentary on the fifth sūtra and before the commentary on the sixth sūtra, it is printed: "The restatement of the Vṛttikāra’s opinion is completed.
By this, it becomes clear that everything from the words "the Vṛttikāra, however" onwards constitutes the entire commentary on the fifth sūtra as the Vṛttikāra’s opinion.

In the *Ślokavārttika* printed by Caukhambā, however, immediately before the *Nirālambanavāda*, at the end of the twenty-sixth verse, it is printed that "the work of the Vṛttikāra is completed," and in the portion of the commentary (*Ṭīkā*), it is printed as "thus ends the opinion of the Vṛttikāra in the *Nyāyaratnākara*. Consequently, the version from Ānandāśrama appears to be established differently. Furthermore, even in the *Bṛhat* [commentary], prior to the *Nirālambanavāda*, it concludes with: "Therefore, it is established that for whomsoever the instrument (*karaṇa*) is defective and for whomsoever there is the cognition that 'this is false,' only that cognition is incorrect, and no other."
Furthermore, in the *Ṛjuvimalā*, the passage from the *Bṛhatī* is introduced with the words: "He concludes for the sake of the topic: 'Therefore, it is established.

And at the end of the *Nirālambanavāda*, because it is a Śūnyavāda, [the commentary] states: "'And weakness is the incapacity for action; it is not the capacity arising from the production of another effect,' as stated in the text of the Vṛttikāra. From this, it becomes clear that the text of the Vṛttikāra was already completed prior to the commencement of the *Nirālambanavāda*.

And at the commencement of the Vṛttikāra’s exposition, it ought to have been stated that "the examination of the cause [of cognition] is for the purpose of refuting the absence of an objective basis (nirālambanatā).
Yet this was not stated by the Vṛttikāra.

Is there then some other point that ought to have been stated? It is replied: he has stated another point in order to demonstrate a further argument that serves as a means of proving the meaning of the Sūtra's principle as previously explained.
And likewise, the *Bṛhatī* states: "Thus, the statement of the definition of all means of valid cognition [is established] for that which is other than that.

And in the *Ṛjuvimalā*: "In the previously mentioned explanation [of the Sūtra on Perception], there is no intent to provide a definition; rather, the intent is to show that [perception] is not a cause [for knowing Dharma].

But in this explanation [by the Vṛttikāra], since it aims to demonstrate the application of that sūtra by way of its being a definition, the statement of the definitions of all means of valid cognition is established."

It has been stated that "the application of all the definitions of the means of valid cognition [is for the purpose] of demonstrating non-deviation, which results in the rejection of the theory of baselessness (*nirālambana*). By this also, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that the Vṛttikāra’s text was completed even before the discussion on the baseless theory.

If the entire Vṛtti-text were part of the sixth section (*adhikaraṇa*), then the mention in the *Śabdapariccheda* (p. 45)—"The venerable Upavarṣa says: 'The letters *ga*, *a*, and *visarjanīya*'"—would not be consistent.
Therefore, it is established that the completion of the *Vṛtti* occurred prior to the *Nirālambanavāda* [section]. (1.1.5, p.
45, Bhāṣya): "Now, what is the word in the expression ‘gauḥ’? It is the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the visarga," says the venerable Upavarṣa.
One should understand that by the term *vṛttikāra* (the author of the Vṛtti), Śabara Svāmī refers exclusively to the teacher Upavarṣa throughout.

Regarding the Vārttika on Sūtra 2.1.7.32: "In their application (*vṛtti*), the characteristic of these [mantras] is that they possess the nature of being intended for a purpose; benediction, praise, and enumeration are taught as secondary characteristics."

The general rule regarding the extensive application of mantras is considered to consist of: direction (praiṣa), seeking (anveṣaṇa), recitation following what has been asked (pṛṣṭhākhyāna), connection (anuṣaṅga), and functional capacity (sāmarthya).
Thus [it is said].
And the Bhāṣya states: "And this very point has been explained by the Vṛttikāra by way of providing examples;
even this is merely general."
And regarding Sūtra 2.1.8.33, the Bhāṣya states: "By the very statement of the definition of Mantra, the [definition of] Brāhmaṇa is established.

That which does not possess this definition is the Brāhmaṇa; thus, the Brāhmaṇa is established by elimination (*pariśeṣa*). However, the author of the Vṛtti, for the benefit of his students, has elaborated upon it: [a Brāhmaṇa is] that which abounds in the particle *iti*, is composed as a narrative (*upanibaddha*), and takes the form of a story (*ākhyāyikā*); [and it contains] 'reasoning (*hetu*), etymological explanation (*nirvacana*), censure (*nindā*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and injunction (*vidhi*)'."
The performance of services for others, traditional lore,
legal procedure, and analogy— these are the prescribed rules for a Brāhmaṇa.
This shall be the constant characteristic of the injunctions regarding all [castes].
"This too is generally so.
Thus says the Bhāṣya on Sūtra 2.1.12.16: "The capacity of the word *juhuyāt* (he should sacrifice) is this: that it expresses an effort qualified by the act of offering (*homa*)."

However, the oblation (*homa*) is not enjoined here as a means; rather, it is understood from the sentence that a specific effort, characterized by being the end to be accomplished, is based upon the curd.

For this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* stated: "The quality based upon the oblation will accomplish the fruit, just as a king's servant, relying upon the king, performs the king's work. Thus [it is said].
2|1|6|16: "Because [the rule] is seen mostly in the case of a specific [instance].
Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "This very sūtra is non-informative; it is indeed purposeless. Now, it must be stated: what is the proposition here, and how does the doubt arise?"

From the words of the author of the *Vṛtti*, we understand both the proposition and the doubt. Here, the venerable Teacher, having cited this example—"One should sacrifice a calf; for cattle are exceedingly fond of calves" (*vatsani-kāntāḥ*)—presents this doubt: "Does this verb *ālabhati* denote an act of sacrifice (*yajimat*), or does it signify the object to be sacrificed (*ālabhya-vacana*)?"
And therein he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "It is a designation for that which possesses a sacrifice" (*yajimat-abhidhāna*).

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "In this context, it is said that the venerable Upavarṣa cited this scriptural sentence—'One should touch the calf' (*vatsam ālabheta*)—in the section concerning the milking of the cow.
(3.1.3.6). Here, the *Bhāṣya* says: "This [statement] by Bādarāyaṇa—that subsidiariness (*śeṣatva*) resides in substances, qualities, and purificatory acts—is not definitive."
Now, in this regard, the venerable commentator, having reached a firm conclusion regarding the body [of the treatise], states:
"The status of being a subordinate (śeṣabhāva) with respect to the sacrifice is restricted solely to substances, qualities, and preparatory acts; in other cases, it is relative.
For the sacrifice, there is a state of primacy (pradhānabhāva) with respect to the substance, and a state of subordination (guṇabhāva) with respect to the fruit."

The fruit is primary in relation to the sacrifice, but subordinate in relation to the person; the person is primary in relation to the fruit, but subordinate in relation to such acts as the measuring of the *audumbarī* post. Therefore, there is an equality of status [between the two].
"Substances, qualities, and purificatory acts are invariably subordinate to the sacrifice.
Regarding this, the Vārttika says: "Intending to explain the four sūtras otherwise according to the opinion of the Vṛttikāra, he says: 'Now, here the Blessed One...

[Sūtra 7.1.16] "And thus the scripture would be purposeless. This sūtra means: "And this being so, the scripture of extended application (atideśa-śāstra) would be purposeless, because its subject matter would be impossible to carry out."

"Therefore, it is not logical for even the word [to have] a location," having thus explained according to his own view, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "The author of the Vṛtti, however, thought that the science of chanting (*gānaśāstra*) would otherwise become meaningless in common usage. His intention was: 'When a way out exists, it is not right to accept such a great effort on the part of the learned as being fruitless. (8.1.12) Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "But in order to avoid the prolixity [involved] in the substitution of every individual word, the author of the Vṛtti adopted the general term 'as in the original' (*prakṛtivat*) for the purpose of extended application (*atideśa*)."

Regarding 10.1.12.14, the Bhāṣya states: "This has been said by the Vṛttikāra: 'Or rather [the word is eternal], for the comprehension of meaning is preceded by the word; therefore, the accomplishment of the meaning [occurs]. " Regarding 10.5.1.53–54, this section (adhikaraṇa) is explained in two ways in the Bhāṣya:
therein, the first explanation follows the Vṛttikāra, while the second is according to his own view.

For this very reason, in the *Bhāṭṭa* [school], it is stated: "In this regard, the Vṛttikāra, having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the statement ‘the Ṣoḍaśin [cup] is in the latter [part]’ is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), concludes with the final position (*siddhānta*) that because the phrase ‘the Ṣoḍaśin is in the latter’ restricts [the rule] to ‘on the following day of the two-night sacrifice (*dvirātra*)’, the optional performance of the Ṣoḍaśin cup in the two-night rite is set aside. Furthermore, it is said: "But the Bhāṣyakāra has explained it differently."
The intention regarding that has been set forth in the passage beginning with "tasyām āśayaḥ" (Sūtra 12.2.7–8;
2.22–23). The ancient commentators on the Vṛtti accepted a single topical section (*ekādhikaraṇya*) for these two Sūtras.
Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "But some maintain that there is a single topical section."
The *Vārttika* states: "These two topics (*adhikaraṇa*) are indeed distinct.

And the *Tantraratna* says: "Because of the difference in the scope of the two principles (*nyāya*), these two topics are indeed distinct; one should not consider the unification of the topics under a single heading (*aikādhikaraṇya*) made by other commentators to be correct merely on the basis of hearing the word 'or' (*vā*).
[This concludes] the textual variations found in the *Bhāṣya*.

The textual variations found in the Ānandāśrama edition of the Bhāṣya, in the Prābhākara *Bṛhatī*, and in the *Anudita-bhāṣya* are here collected. In that regard, not the entire Bhāṣya has been cited in the *Bṛhatī*; however, regarding those portions which have been cited, some textual variations are observed therein, and this is the investigation of them alone. Here, "Bhā. signifies the reading of the Ānandāśrama edition of the Bhāṣya, while "Bṛ. signifies the reading of the Bhāṣya as situated in the *Bṛhatī*.
Above each of those, the two marks on the bronze seal should be understood as signifying, respectively, "page" and "line.
Regarding the characters of the costume, there is a distinction: those letters are arranged such that one letter after each [pair] is set in a larger size.

It should be noted that the two subject matters, although not connected by differences in the textual reading (*pāṭhabheda*), have been included solely for the purpose of making known the different systems (*prasthāna*) of the *Bṛhatī* commentary on the *Bhāṭṭa* school. The first [subject matter] concerns the "sixfold discussion" (*ṣaṭpakṣī*), while the second occurs in the context of the sequence [of the sūtras], namely: "Both are indicated here by the injunction" (*ubhayamiha codanayā lakṣyate*).

Regarding the passage from the Bhāṣya beginning with "In the world, regarding those objects... (*loke yeṣvartheṣu...*), the author of the Vārttika has stated the six meanings mentioned by the first commentator [Kumārila] in the verse: "They explain six meanings of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with 'In the world'... (*Ślokavārttika* 1.1.1–26).
However, the author of the *Bṛhatī* explains the same meaning exactly as it was heard [in the *Śābarabhāṣya*]:

“An investigation of the various kinds of Vedic sentences is to be conducted here,” according to the *Bhāṣya* (4.2); and “An investigation of the meaning of Vedic sentences is to be conducted here,” according to the *Vṛtti* (7.8).
Furthermore, “Moreover, we certainly do not [hold this] here,” according to the *Bhāṣya* (4.3); and “Moreover, this being so, we certainly do not [hold this] here,” according to the *Vṛtti* (7.11).
“He will prohibit the inquiry into Dharma and will subsequently establish immediate succession;

for in that case, the sentence would be split,” so says the Bhāṣya (512). “He prohibits the inquiry into Dharma and teaches immediate succession later on; for then the sentence would be split,” so says the Vṛtti (513). “In one [interpretation], ‘having studied the Vedas’ is enjoined while immediate succession is restated; in the other, the opposite,” so says the Bhāṣya (515). “In one [interpretation], ‘having studied the Vedas’ [is enjoined]; in the other, the opposite,” so says the Vṛtti (715).

"But when the Veda has been studied, two things follow: one must return from the teacher's house and one must investigate the Vedic statements. In this regard, [the injunction] 'one should not return from the teacher's house' is an instruction for the purpose of how one might investigate the Vedic statements"—thus says Bhāṣya (516). "Furthermore, when the Veda has been studied, two things follow: one must return from the teacher's house and the Vedic statements must be investigated; therefore, the instruction 'one should not return' is for the purpose of how one might investigate the Vedic statements"—thus says Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya-vārttika (815).
‘And the sacred tradition (āmnāya) must not be transgressed,’ so says the Bhāṣya (511); ‘and the sacred tradition must not be transgressed,’ so says the Vṛtti (813).
‘For here there is no [intentionality] regarding immediate sequence (ānantarya),’ so says the Bhāṣya (615); ‘for there is no [intentionality] regarding immediate sequence,’ so says the Vṛtti (915).
‘The suffix -ktvā is used to denote priority of time,’ so says the Bhāṣya (615); ‘for the suffix -ktvā is used to denote priority of time,’ so says the Vṛtti (1016).
‘Or [it is] because study has a visible purpose,’ Bhāṣya (616); ‘And study has a visible purpose,’ Vṛtti (1016).
‘Nor is this bathing for an invisible purpose,’ Bhāṣya (71); ‘And this is not for an invisible purpose,’ Vṛtti (1112).
‘Of another action,’ Bhāṣya (81); ‘Even of another action,’ Vṛtti (1110).
‘It must be done; however, having studied the Veda, one should not perform the ritual bath in haste,’ so says the Bhāṣya (812). ‘It must be done;
having studied the Veda, one should not perform the ritual bath in haste,’ so says the Vṛtti (1111).

“This country is secure and well-supplied with food; therefore, I dwell in this country,” so says the Bhāṣya (814); “This country is secure and well-supplied with food; therefore, I live in this country,” so says the Vṛtti (1214).

“For one who has not studied the Vedas would not be able to investigate the Vedic sentences for the sake of dharma,” so says the Bhāṣya (817); “For one who has not studied the Vedas would not be able to investigate the Vedic sentences for the sake of dharma,” so says the Vṛtti.
“The desire to know [dharma] is for the sake of dharma,” so says the Bhāṣya (912); “For the desire to know is for the sake of dharma,” so says the Vṛtti (1314).

“‘Of these propositions’” (*etāsāṃ pratijñānām*)—thus [it is read] in the *Bhāṣya* (916); “‘of these propositions’” (*āsāṃ pratijñānām*)—thus in the *Vṛtti* (1416). “‘This is stated as contradictory: that it speaks and yet is false’” (*vipratiṣiddhamidamucyate, bravīti vitathaṃ ceti*)—thus in the *Bhāṣya* (1411); “‘This is declared to be contradictory: that it speaks and yet is false’” (*vipratiṣiddhamidamidhīyate, bravīti ca vitathaṃ ceti*)—thus in the *Vṛtti* (2116). “‘For instructions arise even from delusion; when there is no delusion, they arise even from the Veda’” (*upadeśā hi vyāmohādapi bhavanti, asati vyāmohe vedādapi bhavanti*)—thus in the *Bhāṣya* (1619); “‘For instruction arises even from delusion; when there is no delusion, it arises even from the Veda’” (*upadeśo hi vyāmohādapi bhavati, asati vyāmohe vedādapi bhavati*)—thus in the *Vṛtti* (2413).
‘For indeed, it may even be erroneous,’ so says the Bhāṣya (1712); ‘For indeed, it may even be erroneous,’ so says the Vṛtti.

‘But the cognition [of dharma] is directly perceived through the words of the Veda,’ so says the Bhāṣya (1718); ‘But the cognition [of dharma] is directly perceived from the words of the Veda,’ so says the Vṛtti (2612).

‘Therefore, the object characterized by the Vedic injunction is that which brings about the highest good (*śreyaskara*),’ so says the Bhāṣya (1719); ‘Therefore, dharma is that which brings about the highest good,’ so says the Vṛtti (2713).
Regarding the phrases “*yo hi yāgam anutiṣṭhati*” in the *Bhāṣya* (1710) and “*yo yāgam anutiṣṭhati*” in the *Vṛtti* (2719), as well as the *Bhāṣya* statement (1819):

“*ubhayam iha codanayā lakṣyate artho ’narthaś ca*,” [the author] deliberated further through objections and their resolutions, stating: “*ubhayādikas granthaḥ sādhyasādhanasaṃśritaḥ*” (*Ślokavārttika* 220).

Regarding this, Ratnākara (verse 224) states: "The Bhāṣya should be construed as follows: 'Both are indicated by the injunction—the goal to be accomplished and the means thereto; and the goal to be accomplished is also twofold: beneficial and harmful.
However, in the Bṛhatī, this effort [to provide such an interpretation] was not adopted.

For it has been stated there as follows: "In order to demonstrate the purpose of the word 'artha' (meaning/purpose) through its positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the author of the Bhāṣya said, 'Both the beneficial (*artha*) and the harmful (*anartha*) are indicated here by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*). Furthermore, following a question, he stated: 'What is the beneficial? That which leads to the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. What is the harmful? That which leads to transgression (*pratyavāya*), such as the Śyena sacrifice. Thus, the nature of dharma and adharma is described as being characterized by the attainment of the highest good and the occurrence of transgression respectively. By demonstrating this, it is effectively stated that both are indicated by the Vedic injunction."

And the *Ṛjuvimalā* states: "The author of the *Bhāṣya* has said that both [types of action] are characterized by *codanā* as being either beneficial (*artha*) or harmful (*anartha*). And: "The construction of the *Bhāṣya*-author is as follows: 'In this context, both are indicated by *codanā*, namely the beneficial and the harmful.
The beneficial is that which has an unprohibited result, and the harmful is that which has a prohibited result.
Among these, the term 'beneficial' is included so that the harmful might not be designated as *dharma*.'"

‘The Śyena and other [sacrifices] are not understood as things to be performed,’ Bhāṣya (1913); ‘The Śyena and others are not understood as having the nature of being performed,’ Vṛtti (2815). ‘How is this understood? Bhāṣya (2717); ‘How is this understood? Vṛtti (p. 4910).
‘For when the mind is afflicted by the eyes and other [senses],’ Bhāṣya (279); ‘If the mind is afflicted by the eyes and other [senses],’ Vṛtti (52|7).

‘It cannot be said that [the dream-cognition] is not different from the waking cognition because it is a cognition,’ so says the Bhāṣya (30.2); ‘It cannot be asserted that it is other than a cognition,’ so says the Vṛtti (56.7).

‘But the falsity of the dream-cognition arises from something else,’ so says the Bhāṣya (30.3); ‘For the falsity of the knowledge of the void [in a dream] results from another cause,’ so says the Vṛtti (57.1).

‘Perceptual cognition has an external object as its domain, not another cognition as its domain,’ so says the Bhāṣya (32.1); ‘For perceptual cognition has an external object as its domain, not a [subsequent] cognition as its domain,’ so says the Vṛtti (63.1).
‘yaducyate’ is from the Bhāṣya (32.3); ‘yadyucyeta’ is from the Vṛtti (66.5).
‘jñāte tvanumānāt’ is from the Bhāṣya (32.4); ‘jñāte cānumānāt’ is from the Vṛtti. ‘api ca niyatanimittaḥ’ is from the Bhāṣya (35.4); ‘dṛṣṭaśca niyatanimittaḥ’ is from the Vṛtti (69.4).
‘Otherwise, even in the case of taking up threads,’ Bhāṣya (35|5); ‘for otherwise, even in the case of taking up threads,’ Vṛtti (69|5).
‘By seeing the absence from the house while Devadatta is alive,’ Bhāṣya (38|2); ‘by seeing the absence from the house of the living Devadatta,’ Vṛtti (84|7).
‘Now, let perception and the other [means] indeed be other means of valid cognition,’ Bhāṣya (32|3); ‘let perception and the other be other means of valid cognition,’ Vṛtti (95|8).

‘upalabhbhakāni’ in the Bhāṣya (99|6), ‘upalabhbhanāni’ in the Vṛtti (95|8). ‘There is also some scriptural statement that contradicts what is perceived’ in the Bhāṣya (41|1), ‘and there is some Vedic statement that contradicts what is perceived’ in the Vṛtti (100|4). ‘It designates the body’ in the Bhāṣya (41|2), ‘it designates the body’ in the Vṛtti (100|6).

‘And that does not go to the heavenly world,’ so says the Bhāṣya (41.4); ‘and that does not go to heaven,’ so says the Vṛtti (100.6). ‘A statement of this kind, which contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is not authoritative (*apramāṇa*),’ so says the Bhāṣya (41.5); ‘and such a statement, contradicting the means of valid cognition, is not authoritative,’ so says the Vṛtti (100.8). ‘There is no connection at all between a word and its object,’ so says the Bhāṣya (43.1); ‘there is indeed no connection between a word and its object,’ so says the Vṛtti (103.7).
"Or [the question] 'Is it authorlessness?'—how so?
(Bhāṣya 43.9); "Or [the question] 'Is it authorlessness?'"
"How so?"—thus [in] the *Vṛtti* (103.8).
"'Of the primary [agent] in the utterance of sound'"—thus [in] the *Bhāṣya* (43.2). "'From the utterance of sound, of the primary [agent]'"—thus [in] the *Vṛtti* (103.9).
In the *Vṛhatī* (105, 107) and in the two *Pṛṣṭha* [commentaries], however, the reading *mā-pāṭhaḥ*, namely “in the utterance of sound” (*śabdoccāraṇe*), is cited.

Bhartṛhari’s commentary (*bhā.*) states (43|3): “the relation characterized by conjunction” (*saṃślepalakṣaṇaṃ saṃbandhaṃ*), while the *Vṛtti* says: “intending the relation of conjunction” (*saṃśleṣasaṃbandhaṃ abhipretyocyate*).
“‘It would be stated by you with the intention that it is an effect,’” so says the Bhāṣya (43.3); “‘It would be stated by you that it is an effect,’” so says the Vṛtti (103.10).

“‘But as for the relationship consisting of the state of being supported and so forth, it is simply untenable in the case of a word,’” so says the Bhāṣya (43.4); “‘Relationships such as being supported and so forth [or ‘relationships of being supported’] are simply untenable for a word with respect to its meaning,’” so says the Vṛtti (103.11).
On page 107 of the *Vṛtti*, however, the reading “*yaunādayastu saṃbandhāḥ*” is cited [from the *Bhāṣya*].
Thus, “*yo hyatra*” is from the *Bhāṣya* (43.5), while “*yo'tra*” is from the *Vṛtti* (107.5).
Furthermore, “*saṃjñāsaṃjñilakṣaṇaḥ*” is from the *Bhāṣya* (43.6), whereas “*saṃjñāsaṃjñilakṣaṇaḥ saṃbandhaḥ*” is from the *Vṛtti* (107.7).

“Another phoneme, accompanied by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, is the conveyor [of meaning],” says the Bhāṣya (46|1); “Another phoneme, accompanied by a specific latent impression produced by the preceding phonemes, is the expressive [word],” says the Vṛtti (114|6).
“Even in the absence of another object, such a cognition arises,” says the Bhāṣya (50|4); “Even in the absence of another object of that kind, such a cognition arises,” says the Vṛtti (127|6).
“Even trees do not exist,” says the Bhāṣya (51|2); “Trees indeed do not exist at all,” says the Vṛtti.

‘“It would be faulty; even in the absence of a forest, the cognition of a forest would follow,” so says the Bhāṣya (51.5); “It would be faulty; even in the absence of a forest for you, the cognition of a forest would follow,” so says the Vṛtti (130.2). “Forgetfulness would be possible,” so says the Bhāṣya (55.2); “Forgetfulness is possible,” so says the Vṛtti.
“The perception of even that which exists occurs,” so says the Bhāṣya (55.3); “The perception of even that which exists occurs,” so says the Vṛtti (137.2).’
‘It is said’ (*ucyate*)—thus in the *Bhāṣya* (66.3); ‘To this it is said’ (*atrocyate*)—thus in the *Vṛtti* (166.4).

‘On one day seen, on another day I saw him’ (*anyedyur dṛṣṭe aparedyur aham imam adarśam*)—thus in the *Bhāṣya* (66.3); ‘On one day seen, on the following day I saw him’ (*anyedyur dṛṣṭaḥ paredyur aham imam adarśam*)—thus in the *Vṛtti* (166.4).

‘The other, indeed, is he who was on another day’ (*aparo hy asāv anyedyuḥ*)—thus in the *Bhāṣya* (66.4); ‘For the other is he who was on another day’ (*aparo hy asau yo hi anyedyuḥ*)—thus in the *Vṛtti* (166.6).
“Therefore, there exists another distinct from that,” so says the Bhāṣya (66.5); “therefore, there is no other distinct from that,” so says the Vṛtti (166.6).
“Surely he perceives the impermanent as impermanent,” so says the Bhāṣya (69.2); “surely he sees the impermanent as impermanent,” so says the Vṛtti (166.9).
“Granted that consciousness may be discarded, but not the objects,” so says the Bhāṣya (71.5); “granted that consciousness may be discarded, but not the object,” so says the Vṛtti (186.5).

‘This is not so; for if conjunctions and disjunctions were to assist the auditory organ without reaching it, then those situated in near and distant places would perceive the sound simultaneously,’ thus says the Bhāṣya (79.1). ‘This is not so; for if they assist without reaching [the organ], then those situated in near and distant places would perceive the sound simultaneously,’ thus says the Vṛtti (218.1). ‘[The sounds] produce [the perception] as far as the region extends,’ thus says the Bhāṣya (79.6). ‘Producing [it] as far as the region extends,’ thus says the Vṛtti (222.6).

“‘But that which belongs to one part of what exists,’” so says the Bhāṣya (80.9); “‘Just as this [is said] of one thing that exists,’” so says the Vṛtti (225.2). “‘Granted, the locations themselves may be distinct,’” so says the Bhāṣya (82.5); “‘Granted, the locations themselves might be distinct,’” so says the Vṛtti (233.3). “‘Being distinct, they are deluded by similarity,’” so says the Bhāṣya (88.2); “‘Even though they are distinct, they are deluded by similarity,’” so says the Vṛtti (244.4).
“‘The intellect and action are also those two,’ so says the Bhāṣya (88.5); ‘For the intellect and action are also those two,’ so says the Vṛtti (245.5).
‘Sound arises from conjunctions and disjunctions when the wind is stirred up,’ so says the Bhāṣya (90.14); ‘Wind... sound arises,’ so says the Vṛtti (252.9).
‘Even though it is innate,’ so says the Bhāṣya (91.10); ‘If it is innate,’ so says the Vṛtti (254.8).”

In the passage beginning with *bṛhatyeva* (277.4), the restatement is made as ‘yadyapi autpattikaḥ’. Bhāṣya (92.5) says, ‘these words have been employed’, while Vṛtti (278.1) says, ‘for these words have been employed’.
Bhāṣya (93.3) says, ‘when a certain word-meaning is understood’, while Vṛtti (279.4) says, ‘when a certain object is understood’.
“From some word heard for the first time,” so says the Bhāṣya (93.7); “from some word heard for the first time,” so says the Vṛtti (280.3).

“For it is observed that meanings are understood even from a sentence heard for the first time,” so says the Bhāṣya (93.9); “for it is observed that meanings are understood even from a sentence heard for the first time,” so says the Vṛtti (280.6).

Here, in the Bhāṣya as well, in the immediately following line, the word *śruta* itself is repeated in the phrase “if they were to understand from what is heard for the first time” (*yadi prathamaśrutādavagaccheyuḥ*), and not the word *avagata*.
Therefore, it appears that even previously, the word *śruta* itself must have been used in the Bhāṣya.

Thus [it is said]: “But surely, even by those who know the meanings of words, the relationship with the sentence-meaning will be understood as uncreated” (Bhāṣya 94.2); and “But surely, even by those who know the meanings of words, the relationship with the sentence-meaning is understood as being indeed uncreated” (Vṛtti 281.6).

"For those who have been refined by the knowledge of the meaning of the words will understand that very same meaning through hearing it a second time and so forth," thus says the Bhāṣya (94.3); "Those who have been refined by the knowledge of the meaning of the words will understand that very same object through hearing it a second time and so forth," thus says the Vṛtti (281.7).

“Or if it is the final phoneme in the sentence that conveys the meaning, then the assistance [derived] from the knowledge of the word-meanings would not be possible,” so says the Bhāṣya (94.4). “Or if it is the final phoneme in the sentence that conveys the meaning, what assistance then could possibly be derived from the knowledge of the word-meanings? so says the Vṛtti (281.11). “But surely this will be the case,” so says the Bhāṣya (94.8). “But surely this will be possible,” so says the Vṛtti. “That is not so.”
"How indeed?"—thus Bhāṣya (94.10); "Not at all;
how indeed?"—thus Vṛtti (282.9). "Even from a mental injury—that is, when the meanings of words are not ascertained from these uttered words."

"Then they would not necessarily comprehend the meaning of the sentence, if it were separate from [the meanings of] its parts," so says Bhartṛhari (97.8). "Due to a mental lapse, even when words have been uttered, their word-meanings are not grasped; at that time, they do not necessarily comprehend the meaning of the sentence.
And they would not necessarily fail to comprehend the meaning of the sentence, if it were separate from [the meanings of] its parts," so says the Vṛtti (291.9).
"He indeed understands it as possessing the quality of whiteness," so says the Bhāṣya (98.2); "He indeed understands the substance as possessing the quality of whiteness," so says the Vṛtti (294.8).
"There is no connection of this [word] with the collection of words," so says the Bhāṣya (98.3); "There is no connection of this with the collection of words," so says the Vṛtti (295.5).
"But that which is based on direct audition (*śrauta*)," so says the Bhāṣya (98.3); "But that which is based on direct audition," so says the Vṛtti (295.7).
"‘This is indeed so’" (*satyameva evametat*)—thus in the *Bhāṣya* (98.4); "‘This is indeed so’" (*satyamevemetat*)—thus in the *Vṛtti*.

In this manner, within the *Tarkapāda*, at eighty locations where the lines of the *Bhāṣya* have not been cited, variations in the readings from the Ānandāśrama edition of the *Bhāṣya* have been observed.
As for the other *Bhāṣya*, however, one can only speculate as to how many or what kind of reading variations might exist.

The Critique of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya by the Vārttikakāra: Whatever criticisms have been offered by the Vārttikakāra here and there regarding certain sūtras and the Bhāṣya, and whatever has been explained otherwise, all of that is presented here for investigation as it has been found. This presentation will follow the order of the text;
moreover, it will be done only in brief, for a detailed presentation would result in excessive prolixity.
Even the refutation of certain [alleged] grammatical operations by the author of the Vārttika might occur right here.

Although defects such as improper composition are observed in some sūtras that differ from those presented in the Vārttika, and although such matters ought indeed to be demonstrated in this context for fear of digression, we shall nonetheless set aside that burden upon those who investigate the sūtras and establish our point by adducing a single example.

And an example is as follows: in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *ṛtvikphalaṃ karaṇeṣvarthavattvāt* (3.1.16), after presenting the doubt whether the fruit belongs to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented that "therefore, the fruit of the officiating priest is to be wished for. Then, in the sūtra *svāmino vā tadarthatvāt* (3.8.27), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: "therefore, the fruit of the sacrificer is to be wished for.
In this case, the contradiction is not established by the two phrases "the fruit of the officiating priest" and "of the sacrificer" alone.

Whether one reads "The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) should desire the fruit; the master (*svāmī*) should desire the fruit," or "In both cases the nominative [is used]," or "The fruit belongs to the officiating priest; the fruit belongs to the master"—the latter way of reading is more appropriate.
This is the general direction.

In this regard, it should be understood that those words which are well-established in common usage for certain meanings should, whenever possible, be understood as having those very same meanings in the Sūtras.

"The meaning of these [sūtras] is not to be mentally supplied (*adhyāhāra*) or otherwise interpreted through technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*)," so it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* at the beginning of the treatise.
Nevertheless, in many sūtras, the commentator himself has provided explanations by employing mental supply and other such methods.
This very point was explained in the *Ślokavārttika* for the purpose of indicating the general direction.

For example: "In the case of those [words] that partake of the remainder, there would be elision; this is the assumption of an ellipsis" (*Ślokavārttika* 1.1.54); or, "Alternatively, it would belong to those that partake of the remainder, because of a specific cause" (*Ślokavārttika* 6.1.3). In these *sūtras*, without the supply of the word "elision" (*lopaḥ*), the expectancy of the question "What would happen? would not be pacified; thus, the ellipsis is accepted. Now, as for transposition (*vipariṇāma*):
"Because of the distance from the animal, the case-ending is transposed."

(55) Regarding the sūtra *paśośca viprakarṣastanmadhye vidhānāt* (12.1.32), for the sake of semantic consistency, the word *viprakarṣa*, being in the nominative case, is changed to the ablative, and the word *vidhāna*, being in the ablative, is changed to the nominative. Alternatively, there is a connection through mediation (*vyavadhāna*). In the sūtra *loke sanniyamāt prayogasaṃnikarṣaḥ syāt* (11.1.16), the word *loke* is connected with the word *saṃnikarṣaḥ*. This is based on the principle stated in *padena vyavadhāne tu loke sanniyamāt* (55).
And that [rule] is separated by the two words "asanniyamāt" and "prayoga.
As for the separation by a sūtra, it is established in the case of the "pānavyāpad" [section]:
"Doṣāt liṅgālloke syāt" (3.1.28) and "pānavyāpacca."

Although the two sūtras beginning with "tadvat" (3.1.32) are separated by three intervening sūtras, nevertheless, by the word "tadvat," the worldly term is referred back. Now, as for the modification: "In the case of the general injunction regarding the animal sacrifice, the sūtra itself was modified."

(56) The sūtra, "The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice is common to all, because there is no distinction in the context" (3.1.18), establishes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the procedure is the same for all animals. However, since this would lead to a lack of connection with the subsequent sūtras beginning with "And because of its position, [it belongs] to the preceding one" (3.1.19), the author first formulates the prima facie sūtra and then, having set it aside, applies it differently to the position that it belongs to the *savanīya* animal sacrifice, as stated in the Bhāṣya: "The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice would be common to all if there were no distinction in the context; however, there is indeed a distinction in the context."
Alternatively, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*):
"And because the fires have their own specific times,
the application of the properties of the gift is logical through a syntactical split."

In the sūtra, "Because all those [materials] have been employed, and because the fires have their own specific times" (3.1.39), two distinct topics (*adhikaraṇa*) are explained by resorting to a division of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, after stating in the two sūtras, "In the *Abhyudayeṣṭi*, there should be the removal of defects; it should possess its own properties because it has already commenced" (9.4.1) and "And because of the instruction regarding the boiled [milk]" (42), that the properties of the offering-materials (*deyadharma*)—namely curd and ghee—must be performed in the *Abhyuditeṣṭi*, the subsequent two sūtras, "Or rather, there is a removal because of the injunction for another time, as in the case of the *caru* and the *payas*" (43) and "The mention of the boiled [milk] is for the purpose of a secondary characteristic" (44), state that the properties of the offering-materials are to be omitted.

Since these two [present] sūtras and the two preceding ones constitute a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) due to their syntactic unity, it might appear that the duties regarding what is to be given (*deyadharma*) for one who has risen [after dawn] are being discussed; however, having separated them from that, the Commentator has explained this as a distinct topical section concerning one who desires cattle. Now follows the acceptance of the secondary sense (*gauṇasvīkāra*): "This assumption of a quality (*guṇakalpa*) has been made."
"(Ślokavārttika 57): 'But [the word] is innate; [it applies] to what comes from a cow, and likewise to the uṣṇih and kakubh meters.
And because of the observation of a specific distinction, there is likewise prosperity.'"

(58) In the phrase "autpattikastu," the word *autpattika* is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) to mean "inherent" (*svābhāvika*). The word *gavyasya* is used figuratively to refer to the *Gavām ayana* sacrifice by virtue of its mere connection with the cow, even though the term literally denotes a product or a part of a cow. In the rule "uṣṇikakubhorante darśanāt" (5.1.36), the word *kakup* is used figuratively to denote the *triṣṭubh* meter. In the rule "darśanād viśeṣasya tathā'bhyudaye" (10.3.55), this word *abhyudaya* is accepted as being used figuratively for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which serves as the means for prosperity (*abhyudaya*).

In this regard, a certain figurative meaning of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the nature of Prajāpati has been described in the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding that, the *Vārtika* begins by stating: "In this context, while it is true that [the statement] has a basis, its status as a mere praise (*stuti*) would be lost;
therefore, without abandoning its status as praise, we describe it as being true in its own literal sense. This is what is explained there.

Regarding the Bhāṣya on Sūtra 1.1.17, which states, "Words of praise, while praising, will be helpful to the performers by making the ritual acts attractive," [the author] explains this differently than it is heard [in the literal text]. By the Vārttika beginning with, "But they do not accept this interpretation;
for if there were an extraction of the suffix," etc., the position mentioned in the Bhāṣya—that there is an extraction of the injunctive suffix—is refuted.
Here, in the Bhāṣya on 1.2.1.12, it is stated: "In the case of the two mantras of mixed gender, 'Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā' and 'Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā'."
"It is stated in the Vārttika that this example was written erroneously,
because the gender and the deity of the two [mantras] are mutually mixed.
For instance, the mantra beginning with 'Agnir jyotir jyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā' is a mantra of mixed gender."

Regarding the passage at 1.2.1.13, p. 302: As for what the author of the Bhāṣya stated—that by using the word *dravya* (substance) in its contrary sense [to denote quality], through a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the quality residing in that substance, and because the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected in an *asamartha-samāsa* (compound with incompatible members), the word would not be expressive of a substance for one who maintains the theory of *ākṛti* (form)—this should be understood as being both unstrained and suitable for the employment of a quality mentioned in a different grammatical case (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the passage at 1.2.1.33, p. 319: The author of the Bhāṣya has stated the cause of doubt to be "because there is a cognition of the universal (*sāmānya*) and because action is possible in the individual (*vyakti*)."
This is incorrect, because the individual (vyakti) is also perceived; how then can it be maintained that only the genus (jāti) is perceived?
Moreover, if the individual were indeed being perceived, there would be no doubt at all as to what is being denoted by this [word].
Nor is the possibility of action a ground for being denoted, for that would entail the same consequence for other individuals as well.
Therefore, one should consider the cause of doubt to be exactly what was stated previously (Sūtra 2.1.19–22).

The purpose (*prayojana*) of this section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya in three examples: the ladle made of *śamī* wood at the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice, the *abhrathṛtha* offering, and the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) made of *tarasa* flesh.
This has been refuted in the Vārttika with the words, "But they do not properly accept the purpose of this section," and so forth.

Regarding this, there is a *vārttika*: "In another commentary (*vṛtti*), however, only four causes of differentiation are cited—namely, difference of word, technical name, quality, and fruit.... That appears to be incorrect.... Therefore, since there is identity of the word, the postulation of a different word is the work of another author of a commentary.
Thus, that other commentary is refuted.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "It is heard here in the Bahvṛca-brāhmaṇa. The Vārttika states: "One need not be overly insistent on whether it is heard in the Bahvṛca-brāhmaṇa or the Adhvaryu-brāhmaṇa" (the meaning being that the author of the Bhāṣya has made an error).
Regarding the Vedic statement, "One performs the *agnihotra* for as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam agnihotraṃ juhoti*),

it is stated in the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) commentary on the *arthādhikaraṇa* at 3.1.17 that "here, however, the ritual elements such as the giving [of the oblation] are enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Having refuted that with the words "And this appears improper," etc., the *Vārttika* establishes the *pūrvapakṣa* in a different manner, beginning with "Therefore, it should be explained thus," etc.
An extensive exposition, however, is the subject matter of another treatise (see *Nibandha* 3.1.14, p. 310).

As for that which was shown by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), while demonstrating the scope of the faultless restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*), namely the two possible verbal expressions regarding the desired and the undesired: "it is for the purpose of naming this [cord]" and "he does not take it [otherwise]";
and as for the reason stated: "because the taking [of the cord] is already established by the very form of the mantra."
That is incorrect.
Sūtra 3.2.19 states: "There is no conflict between direct statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and context (prakaraṇa).
Regarding this, the Vārttika says: "Now the author of the Bhāṣya is seen."
At the beginning, the Commentator stated: "This is not a single sentence, namely the entire *sūktavāka*; rather, there are many sentences here.

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* shows its untenability with the words: "But even this which has been stated is not correct, because—as in the case of the *vaiśvānara* sentence—the unity of the sentence is directly perceived through the common [tantra] words," and so forth.

Having stated the purport of the *Bhāṣya*: "And it should be understood that even in the *Bhāṣya*, because the *sūktavāka* is possible [therein], the plurality of even a single [entity] has been mentioned," he says: "Likewise, the *Sūtra* also must be understood in this very way—that the term *kṛtsna-sūktavāka* (the whole *sūktavāka*) is applied merely by virtue of the association with its own deity-words for both [sections], since there is no division of the context; thus, everything is without contradiction."

Regarding the statement in the *Vārttika* that refutes the *Bhāṣya*: "As for the syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) shown by the author of the *Bhāṣya*—[namely], 'if a mantra from the *Daśataya* were enjoined while disregarding the context, the sentence would be split']—that is common to all injunctions involving multiple qualifications," [the following applies]:
In Sūtra 3.3.10, the word "by the majority" (*bhūyastvena*) is used; however, this explanation of "majority" provided by the author of the *Bhāṣya* is not tenable.
This is the Vārttika.

Regarding the section on the *ahīna* (3.8.15), after stating, "That which was said by the author of the Bhāṣya—that [the Jyotiṣṭoma] is not abandoned (*ahīna*) because of the sacrificial fee or the officiating priests, and therefore the Jyotiṣṭoma is an *ahīna*—is incoherent," the Vārttika demonstrates its incoherence.
(3.9.131) "The undertaking is repeated, however, for the purpose of removing the notion of difference produced by another Bhāṣya."

For the other [view] holds that these two sūtras—*“And the unenjoined rite [is established] because of the difference [of the recipient]; that [rite] would apply to the first [recipient] on account of the indicative mark”* (3.4.130–31)—could have been explained even in the preceding section.
Thus says the Vārtika.

In another Bhāṣya, however, based on the word *ārthija* in the sūtra, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is an offering on four potsherds to Varuṇa for the one who receives the horse.

This sūtra (3.5.8) was explained by the author of the Bhāṣya as constituting a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*). However, the Vārttika, having refuted that view, explained it as a supplement to the preceding section. [The Vārttika argues: "There are indeed other sections where a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established through reasoning and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached through a scriptural statement (as the author of the Bhāṣya explained the section on sūtra 3.5.8).
