likewise, the procedure (itikartavyatā) also assists the instrument at that very same moment.

If the agent were to attain the status of an agent in one moment while the heaven were to exist in another, and the instrument were likewise to bring about the result in a different moment, then in that case there would be no relationship at all between the object to be produced (*bhāvya*) and the producer (*bhāvaka*).
Therefore, there must be simultaneity between the heaven and the sacrifice; and in the same way, there must be simultaneity between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Thus, these possess the same time—so says the *Vārttika*.

In the *Bhāṣya* on 1.1.3.19–22, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated that the two acts of joining and releasing the fire (*agniyoga-vimokau*) are for the sake of the primary rite alone (*pradhānamātrārthau*), and not for the sake of both the primary and its subsidiaries (*sāṅgapradhānārthau*).

However, in the *Vārttika*, having refuted the reasons given in the *Bhāṣya* with the words "This is not tenable" (*naitadyuktam*), etc., the established conclusion is stated as "for the sake of both the primary and its subsidiaries. Furthermore, at 1.1.4.5, having asserted that "this interpretation (made by the authors of the *Bhāṣya*) is incorrect," the reasons for its incorrectness are demonstrated.
Regarding what is stated in the *Bhāṣya*, "It is performed with reference to the aggregate (*samudāya*)," that is incorrect;

for the aggregate is not enjoined with respect to the fruit (*phala*), as has been established in the *Vārttika* on 1.1.4.8 (31). Having restated the explanation of the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vārttika* refutes it by stating, "This is correct," and so forth, concluding that "this being the case, whether through modification (*vikāra*) or non-modification (*avikāra*), the very subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) does not arise. Then, beginning with "Therefore, it is explained otherwise," it provides an alternative explanation.
In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on [Jaimini] 12.1.12–14, it is stated that the establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) also serves the purpose of securing the deities (*devatāparigraha*).

However, in the *Vārtika*, it is argued: "In reality, the establishment of the fires is not understood to be for the purpose of securing the deities, neither from the perspective of fact nor from the perspective of the scriptural word.

Furthermore, having stated, "As for what was said—that the securing of the deities is accomplished by the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering—that too has been refuted," the [opponent's] position is shown to be untenable.

In this [sūtra] 12.1.12.22, the *pañcadaśarātra* sacrifice is mentioned as an example in the Bhāṣya. There, the Vārttika refutes this by stating, "In this sūtra, the *pañcadaśarātra* sacrifices are not examples," and so forth. Having asked, "What then is the example here?", it provides another example characterized by the absence of specific names and other such particulars, beginning with, "Where five sacrifices are enjoined together toward a single result," and so on.

In the *Tantravārttika*, however, the example has been clarified by the passage beginning: "One desiring cattle should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dātṛ; a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Pradātṛ; and curds, honey, ghee, water, and parched grains (mixed together) as an offering to Prajāpati"—thus [constituting] seven sacrifices. That very same point is stated in the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā*.

12|1|12|20: "And because there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the object [of cognition]—since a particular [such as Kauṇḍinya], which is delimited by others [i.e., other Brāhmaṇas] and is determined by a single [cognition], cannot [otherwise] be established—the sublation [of the general rule by the particular] is described [in the Bhāṣya] in this way, so that this may not occur; that too has been stated. For there is no injunction that the scripture must be favored.
If it were merely a matter of favoring the scripture, then once the offering of curd had been performed, the scripture would be favored; thus, the offering of curd would apply to both cases."
And this [position] is not accepted.

Therefore, the *Vārttika* states: "That very sublation which we have described regarding the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites—beginning with the words 'because they culminate in human purpose' in Sūtras 1.4.11–12—is precisely what applies here.
Now, the criticisms and other arguments presented by the author of the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā* against the Sūtra, the Vṛtti, the Bhāṣya, and the Vārttika are set forth.
And that [criticism] follows strictly the order of the text.
Among these, some are merely restatements by the author of the Vārttika intended as refutations of the Bhāṣya.

(In this *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*, something has been said eighty-four times in total: five times regarding the Sūtras, three times regarding the Vṛttikāra, twenty-seven times regarding the Bhāṣya, twenty-three times regarding the Vārttika, eleven times regarding differences between the views of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika, twice regarding the Prabhākara view, once regarding the view of Bhavadeva, seven times in general, and thus eighty-four times altogether.)

The commentators (the Bhāṣyakāras) established the conclusion that when there is a contradiction with a directly revealed Vedic text (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), or even in its absence where greed and the like are observed, the Smṛti lacks authority because there is no basis for inferring an underlying Vedic text (*mūla-śruti*).
The author of the Vārttika, however, stated that the Sūtra intends to mean that as long as a Vedic text is not observed, there is non-authority characterized by the failure of ritual performance.

Regarding the word *sṛṣṭi*, the Bhāṣyakāra says it is a figurative restatement (*gauṇyā anuvāda*) of only those *sṛṣṭi* mantras obtained through indicative mark (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*). (Bhāṭṭa 1.3.2).
The author of the Vārttika, however, states that here the placing [of the bricks] qualified by the mantra is what is enjoined (1.4.17).

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), on the other hand, established the conclusion that in the case of "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*), because the existence of that which is understood through the verb—even though not explicitly mentioned—is present, the connection with the root *juhoti* (to offer) is possible precisely through that [verb]; thus, it is indeed a subsidiary element of the *prayāja* offerings.

However, because this [word *muṇan*] lacks expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) when construed with *juhoti* through a relationship such as anteriority (*pūrvakālatā*), and because there is no evidence that *juhoti* refers exclusively to the *prayāja* offerings, and because the matter has already been largely settled by the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the author of the *Vārttika* explained it otherwise.

The author of the *Bhāṣya*, on the other hand, stated that since the *pavamāna-havis* offerings are neither subsidiaries of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice in their specific form nor present [in the context], the acts such as the choosing (*varaṇa*) must be subsidiaries of all archetypal sacrifices (*sarvaprakṛti-yajña*), or else subsidiaries of all sacrifices (*sarva-yajña*).

The author of the Vārttika, however, states that the Pavamāna oblations do not have the nature of being subsidiary to the fire-installation (agnyādhāna), and that the acts such as the formal appointment of priests (varaṇa) and so forth are indeed subsidiaries to all sacrifices.

(3.1.12). The author of the Bhāṣya maintains that because the fire-installation belongs to the Yajurveda, the subsidiary elements of the installation must also possess the quality of low-voiced recitation (upāṃśutva) characteristic of that Veda; the author of the Vārttika, however, introduced a different point by stating that the accent to be adopted is that of the Veda in which the application (viniyoga) occurs, not the accent of the Veda in which the rite is originally produced.

(3.1.32). The author of the Bhāṣya accepted the placement of the *saṃtardana* (the thickening of the sacrificial post) within the very context (prakaraṇa) itself, treating this as a desired conclusion.
The author of the Vārttika, however, has stated that [the rule] applies to all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), including the *vicchidya-stoma* which is distinct from the *agnihotra* (Sūtra 3.1.11).

As for the alternative view presented in the Mūla—that the injunction “*nivītam manuṣyāṇām*” is a prescription as a subordinate element of rites such as the *ātithya*, which have humans as their primary focus—that has been disregarded.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is precisely that it is a subordinate element of those ritual acts within the context (*prakaraṇa*) that have humans as their primary focus.
In reality, however, this is not an injunction (vidhi).

Since the offering of the substance itself is the means for accomplishing the sacrifice, the remaining portion is the disposal of the remnant; these are the "rites for the remnant" (śeṣakāryāṇi), according to the Commentator (bhāṣyakāra).

The Author of the Vārttika, however, maintains that the entire cake on eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla) is the oblation (havis), while the act of throwing it [into the fire] is the disposal of the substance.
He states that by the term *juhoti*, only the act of throwing [the offering] into the fire is conveyed.

(Sūtra 3.4.18): "In this case (regarding the *surā* in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice), there is no remaining residue (*śeṣa*) at all, because the injunction for the oblation (*homa*) is prescribed specifically for that which is faultless; furthermore, since the residue of what has been offered—which is mentioned in the scriptural statement—is subject to another disposal (*pratipatti*), it belongs to the category of disposal prescribed by extended application (*atideśika*).
And this has been stated according to the view of the author of the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya.

Even if, according to the method stated in the *Vārttika*, another sacrifice with *surā* as its substance is enjoined for the purpose of consecrating the deity, even then there is an absence of a remnant (*śeṣa*), just as before.
(3.5.3) The Prābhākara view—that the status of being an *adhvaryu* and so forth consists in possessing an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the formal selection (*varaṇa*)—is refuted;

because in the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the word *hotṛ* is used prior to the selection in the injunction, "The *hotṛ* recites the *sāmidhenī* verses," and because the same [usage] would apply to the *satra* sacrifices as well.

Furthermore, as for what was stated in the *Vārtika*—namely, that since the *hotṛ* and *adhvaryu* cannot perform the *praiṣa* (directions) and *vacana* (utterances) belonging to the *āgnīṣomīya* sacrifice and others as a single unitary act (*ekapadārtha*), there must be an injunction for the *maitrāvaruṇa* priest—that too has been disregarded. This is because the word "yajati" (sacrifice) is explicitly recited in the *hautra* (the *hotṛ*'s portion) regarding the *āgnīṣomīya* and other rites; thus, by means of the name (*samākhyā*), the *hotṛ* is obtained through the extension (*atideśa*) of the *adhvaryu* and other roles. Even though that [application to the *hotṛ*] is set aside by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "hotaryaja" (O Hotṛ, sacrifice), the *maitrāvaruṇa*, who is his subordinate (*tatpuruṣa*), is indeed obtained for the word "yajati" as well as for the other words that form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with it. Therefore, that [objection] is ignored.

3|7|22: Regarding the passage, "The *taras* [omentum] cakes are the *savanīya* cakes," when the reading is—as taught by Bhavadeva and others—"The *puroḍāśa* cakes are the *savanīya* cakes," then, because of its primacy, it is clear that the function (*kārya*) of the *puroḍāśa* itself is the objective (*uddeśyatva*).

3|8|23: As for the fact that the author of the *Bhāṣya* and others, having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that even all property acquired through specific means is solely for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that acquisition (*arjana*) is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and that even the restrictive rule (*niyama*)—though subservient to the sacrifice—is indeed for the sake of the person; that... [is as follows].

The assumption of a fruit for the restriction regarding acceptance (pratigrahaniyama) is disregarded because, if it were for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha), then even the wearing of gold and similar acts would result in being for the sake of the sacrifice; furthermore, [this view] has already been refuted by that [previous argument].

Regarding the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stated by the author of the Bhāṣya and others—that because the fire has a clearly visible form, it lacks the quality of being a substance to be offered, and thus, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), burning with sacrificial vessels (*yajñapātra*) as the instrument would be impossible in a rite involving forfeiture—it was overlooked because, in the *pūrvapakṣa*, there exist separate vessels for purposes such as pouring out (*uddavana*), and even though those do not serve as means for the sacrifice (*yajñasādhana*), their status as "sacrificial vessels" is established through the application of the term "weapon" (*āyudha*) due to their functional utility, thereby making the burning possible.

Regarding the point stated by the author of the Bhāṣya and others—that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), if the whey (*vājina*) is destroyed, it would be produced again by bringing in fresh curd, just as in the case of the destruction of the clotted curd (*āmikṣā*), whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the rite is completed with clarified butter (*ājya*)—that purpose has been set aside because it is equally applicable even in the prima facie view, since the completion with *ājya* on the occasion of the destruction of the sacrificial oblation (*havirvināśa*) and so forth will be explained by the force of the injunction in the sixth book.

In the beginning of Sūtra 4.1.9 (*samānayanaṃ tu*), the term *samānayana* refers to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth belonging to that specific time; for otherwise, the established doctrine—that the act of pouring together (*samānayana*) which refines the clarified butter (*ājya*) does not serve as the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the clarified butter itself—would be untenable.

Furthermore, the Sūtras should be interpreted by the wise in this very sense (namely, that the accent is not the motivator for acts such as sprinkling), and not in the sense stated by the author of the Bhāṣya (that the accent is not the motivator for its own production).

4|2|1: Nor is it correct, as stated in the root-text, that because this [Agnimāruta-śastra] does not have its sentences following [the principal action] like the Vaimṛdha sacrifice, and because the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*)—due to the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the expectation of a fruit—presumes its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*).

For even if there is an expectation of that [fruit] in the originative injunction, since the application (*viniyoga*) is possible through another sentence by accepting a general "desired object" (*iṣṭa-sāmānya*) as the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*), it is improper to presume subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) on the basis of a weaker means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that when the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) is performed on the full moon day, there is no performance of the New Moon sacrifice (darśa) on the following new moon day because the time has passed—this should be understood to apply even in the view that the establishment takes twelve nights, provided the full moon time does not occur on the day following the establishment.

The position stated in the root-text—that *krama* (sequence) is simply the nature of a collection of antecedence and succession residing in multiple ritual items, such that "after this specific item, that specific item [occurs]"—is disregarded because it is not explicitly stated in the Vedic word (*aśābdatvāt*). Furthermore, in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), when some ritual items are omitted, such a collection of antecedence and succession residing in that many items becomes impossible; thus, even if one were to perform the rite in a different order, no deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) would result. Therefore, that view is set aside.

Regarding the point that, having accepted the view of "extension" (*vitati*) as the introductory principle in the root text, it was stated that all of this constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*): that [view] has been set aside because extension, being non-verbal, is unfit to be an object of injunction; because if it were enjoined with reference to multiple initiations (*dīkṣā*), a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would result; and because an injunction regarding the agent is necessary for the initiation of the leader (*unnetṛ*).
(5|1|9) The citation of the scriptural passage mentioned in the root text is not to be respected.

5|1|9. Since the sages (*ṛṣi*) and others are beginningless, and since other sages can also arise at the beginning of a cycle of creation (*saṃsāra*), there certainly exists eligibility (*adhikāra*). Thus, the demonstration of non-eligibility stated in the *Bhāṣya* is to be disregarded.

As for the division mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* regarding the twelve hundred—namely, "fifty-six by one, and likewise fifty-six by the other"—that is set aside because the twelve hundred are prescribed [as a total], and thus the combination of both is possible even therein. Alternatively, the intention of the *Bhāṣya* is the cessation of two sets of twelve hundred.

Regarding the hearing of the singular number in such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (svargakāmo yajeta), at the root level, singularity is not intended to be significant, because the word *svargakāma* refers merely to the desire for heaven.

Alternatively, even if [the word] refers to the qualified person (*adhikārin*), since that person is the objective (*uddeśya*) [of the injunction], their qualification is not intended to be significant; thus the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was formulated as "one, two, or many agents. This was set aside because, since a distinct human effort directed toward the fruit has not been previously established, it must be enjoined, and therefore it is logical to intend the qualification of the agenthood (*kartṛtva*) in each instance; furthermore, even if that [agenthood] were not intended in the term *svargakāma* (desirer of heaven), there is no obstacle to its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, and so it was disregarded.

In the discussion concerning the substitute (pratinidhi), the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra* (6.2.2) establishes the following as the final position (*siddhānta*): since there is no absolute difference between a substance and the action [performed with it], the difference in the substance would lead to a difference in the ritual act (*karmabheda*), and so forth; thus, there is only one individual instance of the ritual act existing on the surface of the world, though its mere manifestation (*abhivyakti*) differs. However, this has been set aside because—even if the action is dependent upon the substance—it is impossible to suspect a difference in the essential nature (*vaijātya*) of the action due to the differences in those substances; furthermore, if the final position were that the action resides in the individual instance, it would result in the destruction of the unseen potency (*apūrva*). Moreover, if that [action] were produced by the manifestation, it would entail the necessity of resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *yajati*.
In the root text (Mīmāṃsāsūtra) at 6.3.2, two distinct sections are established regarding the substitution for both types [of sacrificial materials]. I have omitted them here due to their clarity.

Regarding the destruction of a portion and so forth: if, after the portions have been taken out, there is the destruction of what remains in the *pātrī* or the *kumbhī*, then according to the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, since the gift of the substance constitutes the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the sacrifice is performed with that very same material even in the absence of the subsequent rites for the remnants (*śeṣakārya*).

However, according to the view of the Vārtikakāra, because the sacrificial oblation consists of the entire *puroḍāśa* measured by the amount of rice poured out, and the *sāṃnāyya* consisting of the entire quantity of milk, the sacrifice must be performed with another material, as the oblation itself has been destroyed even when only what was in the *pātrī* is lost.

Regarding what was stated in the *Mūla* under the view of a separate action—that because curd and milk are enjoined as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), there would be the consequence of taking only worldly, unrefined curd, and thus there would be no possibility for the application of the curd prepared for the *darśa* sacrifice—that has been set aside; for since that [consequence] applies equally to the view of "cooking together" (*saha śrapayati*), it is necessary that they be enjoined precisely as sacrificial oblations (*havis*).

6|5|1. As for the alternative view stated here by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*)—that the word "he should divide" (*vibhajet*) does not enjoin a removal (*apanaya*), but rather enjoins a gift in the form of a general division, whereby one should give the sacrificial oblation belonging to the previous sacrifice to the deities of the modified rite (*vaikṛta*)—this gift being common to both the *upāṃśuyāja* and the *āgneya* offerings;
whereas the removal of the previous deities follows by implication (*arthāt*).

In that regard, although there is an establishment of other substances due to specific statements, the giving of clarified butter (*ājya*) from all three [cups] occurs solely on the basis of the general statement. However, since there is no authority for taking the original oblation (*prakṛtahavis*) in the absence of a rule for its removal, and because this would result in the general statement being reduced to a mere general injunction regarding a different ritual action, that view is utterly disregarded.

(6.5.2) Having separately stated the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra and the intention of the Vārttikakāra concerning the number of initiations (*dīkṣā*) in the Soma sacrifice, he has indicated that both are indeed logical.

As for the other discussion conducted in the *Mūla* regarding the establishment of extended application (*atideśa*), namely whether ritual properties (*dharma*) are prompted by the sacrifice (*yajati*) or prompted by the *apūrva*, that was disregarded because even if they were prompted by the sacrifice, it would still be possible for them to be prompted by the specific sacrifice under discussion; otherwise, even if they were prompted by the *apūrva*, that [extended application] would not follow, and thus there would be no risk of redundancy with the *Āvāhika* section.

Just as the word *itara* (the other) is established in common usage as denoting what is proximate, it is likewise established in common usage as denoting what is similar to that which was previously mentioned; for instance, in the expression, “A blanket and a silk garment are to be given to Caitra and Maitra; the other [item] to Viṣṇumitra,” there is a cognition precisely of that which is similar to the aforementioned, just as there is of the proximate.
Therefore, the statement by the author of the Vārttika that similarity to what was previously mentioned is not denotable should be disregarded.

Having stated the views of the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Bhāṣya regarding the rule *pañcasaptareṣu* (Pāṇini 7.1.17–21) under the heading of the locative case (*adhikaraṇe*), and having then stated something contrary to that beginning with the words "but in reality" (*vastutastu*), [the author] begins by saying, "Therefore, disregarding the Bhāṣya, this [section] is explained as follows," and concludes: "Because the sentences concerning the fire-altars (*agni*) and the fuel (*dhana*), etc., are equal in their status as rules of extended application (*atideśavidhi*) by virtue of their propriety, the Sūtra 'not so, because they serve another purpose' (*netarārthatvāt*) is intended to state the purpose consisting of the form of the breast-sucking (*stanapāna*) which is enjoined.

And that very thing is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the status of the extended-application sentence as a rule for subsidiary elements (*aṅgavidhi*); such is the meaning of the Sūtra on the observation of indicative marks (*liṅgadarśana*).
This is what was stated.
In the *Rathantara-adhikaraṇa*, it was stated: “However, other positions found in the *Bhāṣya* have not been recorded here because they are untenable.

Having begun by stating, “The author of the *Bhāṣya*, having explained only two *adhikaraṇas* through seven *sūtras* (7.1.19–22 [20–23 Ke., 23–25 Ke.], and 23–25 [24–26 Ke.]),” he concluded at the end: “Therefore, even for the author of the *Bhāṣya*, there is no room for the criticisms raised in the *Vārttika*.
Furthermore, beginning with, “As for the justification of the *Vārttikakāra*’s view,” he provided that justification.

In reality, however, because the *khalvālī* is prescribed for the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the word *yūpa* does not possess the power [to denote] the consecrations and so forth; thus, the extension of those consecrations by way of "substitution" (*sthānāpatti*)—as stated in the Sūtra—is also inconsistent with the aforementioned view of the sacrificial post. Furthermore, the Bhāṣyakāra’s citation of this [text, "One should offer a *saurya* oblation"—namely, "At each *prayāja*, one offers a *kṛṣṇala* weight of gold"] as an example of a scriptural injunction is improper, as it falls under the fifth category [of analogical extension].
We do not understand the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra, who considers the production of the fruit to occur in such cases [concerning the desires for specific qualities].

As for the conclusion reached by Pārthasārathi—having accepted the *Āgneya* nature of the *vārtika*-accent and, on the grounds that the two *abhimarśana* mantras serve two purposes, establishing a fixed application (*vyavasthā*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*) through an option (*vikalpa*) based on the requirement of association with another principal rite in one *Āgneya* sacrifice, yet concluding that in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) there is an unfixed option because of the absence of such a cause for fixation due to the lack of that association—that has been disregarded; for the deliberation on the option of mantras belongs properly to the twelfth book (*adhyāya*), and since there is no discussion of extension (*atideśa*) here, it would result in a lack of connection to the current chapter; furthermore, since the distinction between the various *Āgneya* sacrifices has already been established, their identity is untenable.

(In fact, here the refutation of the Vārtika is also intended. In Janaka’s sacrifice, after restating the four days as "four days consisting of the *trivṛt*," the injunction of the *trivṛt* nature is made; since this *trivṛt* nature is a subsequent instruction (*utpannaśiṣṭa*), it is weak. Therefore, the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra is that even these six days possess the character of being modifications of the six-day period within the twelve-day sacrifice.
However, in reality, this very [sentence] is the injunction of a ritual act qualified by the *trivṛt* nature.)
Furthermore, the numerous descriptions provided here at the beginning have been omitted because they are redundant and of no practical use;
however, it should be understood that they were included by the original author for the purpose of explaining the entire treatise.

As for the point raised by the author of the *Bhāṣya* regarding the Aśvamedha sacrifice—wherein, based on the injunction "The Traidhātavīyā is the *dīkṣaṇīyā*," the Traidhātavīyā is prescribed for the purpose of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, namely the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer—it was stated that the purpose [of this discussion] is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the properties (*dharma*) of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* are extended [to it], whereas according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is the properties of the well-known Traidhātavīyā itself that apply. This is not correct; for even in the final conclusion, there is no obstacle to its taking the place [of the original] just as in the prima facie view. In reality, however, this Traidhātavīyā is not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Therefore, in the absence of a desire for the [original] dharma, how could there be an application of the principle of extension by analogy (*sthānāpatti*)?

As for the point stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* regarding the *Māsāgnihotra*—that the modification (*ūha*) of low-voicedness (*upāṃśutva*) applies to its institutor—that has been disregarded; for when there exists a tone obtained through extension by name (*nāmātideśa*), whether it be contradictory or non-contradictory, it is impossible for the low-voicedness obtained through extension by means of the indicative mark of the injunction (*codanāliṅga*) to take effect.

Furthermore, as for what was stated in the Vārttika and other works—that there is an extension (*ūha*) of the *upāṃśu* (whispered) quality in passages such as "Before the *upasads*, they proceed with the *saumya*"—that too has been set aside because an extended rule (*atideśa*) postulated on the basis of the *saumya* alone is stronger than the extended application of the *upāṃśu* quality prescribed by a general rule.

As for the fact that in the root text (*mūla*), during the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) was not accepted as a qualifier of "extension" (*vistāra*)—in the passage "While extending the sacrifice, they restrain their speech"—and instead its status as a property of the ritual portion (*bhāga-dharma*) was asserted, that was disregarded because it is difficult to establish the connection of the word "sacrifice" elsewhere without "extension," and because no word denoting a "portion" is heard there.

The Commentator (*vṛttikāra*), however, established the following conclusion (*siddhānta*): the installation of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) is not the meaning of the term "commencement" (*ārambha*); rather, it is a specific form of determination (*adhyavasāya*), synonymous with "resolution" (*saṃkalpa*), in the sense of "this must be performed by me."

The *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice, being for that purpose, must indeed be performed even in a modified (*vikṛti*) rite, even when it is devoid of the *anvādhāna*. Furthermore, in the archetypal (*prakṛti*) rite, because the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is made only once for all lifelong performances subsequent to the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), the *anvārambhaṇīyā* is performed only once. That is not correct. Because the various lifelong performances are occasioned by the specific life-situations occurring at their respective times, they present themselves only at those specific times; thus, there is no basis for a single, universal resolve (*adhyavasāya*) encompassing them all. Since the determination [of performance] occurs only through the influence of the specific causes of each particular life-period, there is no evidence for a resolve common to all of them.
Therefore, the commentators and others have established this conclusion: the word *ārambha* denotes "determination" (*adhyavasāya*).
*Ārambha* is precisely the instigation of one who has not yet begun.

The *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice has that as its purpose; it renders the performer fit for undertaking [the rite]. Thus, the *ārambhaṇīyā* is the first constituent element (*padārtha*) belonging to the initial performance, consisting of an injunction to instigate one who has not yet begun with respect to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
And that [introductory rite] must be performed once for the sake of the primary purpose.

As for what was stated in the root text—that the *ārambhaṇīyā*, being performed at the commencement of the first performance, benefits all performances, and therefore, having been performed at the start of the first performance, it alone serves as the benefit for all—that has been disregarded; for if the benefit produced by the *anvārambhaṇīyā* were to persist as long as one lives, it would follow that it would also serve as a benefit in the modified (*vikṛti*) rites by way of "extended application" (*prasaṅga*). Conversely, if it did not persist, it could not serve as a benefit even in the second and subsequent performances.

9|1|11: As for the fact that the Commentator, in the case of the *nirvāpa* mantra (*devasya tvā*, etc.), established its specific application to the *nirvāpa* by explaining that the word "horse" (*aśva*) is used figuratively (*gauṇī*)—referring to the husband and wife because of their role in the giving of the horse during the *ādhāna*—this was intended with the understanding that there is an absence of superimposition (*āhāryāropa*) in the Veda due to the absence of a person capable of performing such a superimposition.

9|1|12: As for the fact that the Commentator stated that the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—"the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) is upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)"—is also appropriate only in the context of the *pragrayana*, for here a literal grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not possible due to contradiction.

Therefore, it was stated that by accepting figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) only for the term "midday pressing" (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*), one understands the meaning to be "those which are recited in the Sāmaveda as constituting the collection of the midday pressing, those are sixty. However, since figurative indication is necessary, this [interpretation] has been set aside because of parsimony (*lāghava*); for it is possible to establish that very same nature [of being sixty] even for those [verses] brought from the *Daśatayīs* by figuratively indicating only the verses used in the Stotras of the midday pressing.

9|1|6, Section 2: As for the consideration by the author of the *Bhāṣya* regarding whether there should be a bringing together (*samānayana*) or a transposition (*pragrayana*) of the other two *anuṣṭubh*s, that has been disregarded because it would result in redundancy. 9|1|6, Section 2: The mention of the *naudhasa* by the author of the *Bhāṣya* is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin who recites the *naudhasa*; for since the [Brahman priest] has the *bṛhat-sāman* as his *pṛṣṭha*, only that [the *bṛhat*] is applicable, and thus there is no possibility of the *naudhasa* applying. This is because in the *Gavāmayana*, the *abhīvarta* alone is specifically prescribed as the *brahmasāman*.
9|1|6, Section 4: In the *Mūla*, having accepted *sthānāpatti* (substitution) as consisting in the capacity to perform that function, its fivefold nature is stated.
Although in all cases the cause of substitution is indeed a similarity (*sādṛśya*), nevertheless, because there are five factors that act as its auxiliaries, it is said to be fivefold.

9|1|11: Having refuted the notion of *sthānāpannatva* (the state of being a substitute) as stated in the *Mūla*, and having demonstrated that even the examples cited in the *Mūla* are inappropriate, [the author] says, "Therefore, since the methods stated in the *Mūla* are untenable, it should be stated thus," and then states another method and explains the examples in the *Bhāṣya*.

In [Jaimini Sūtra] 9.1.11, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) resolved the matter by accepting the very point at issue: that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of non-conflicting properties such as *saṃmīlana* for the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* chants, whereas there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding conflicting properties such as those pertaining to Viṣṇu.
The Vārttikakāra, however, states that even for *saṃmīlana* and the like, there is only an optional choice (*aicchika-vikalpa*) and not a combination.

As for what was stated in the root-text—that the threshing is not enjoined as an end in itself within the archetype (*prakṛti*), but rather as a means to a specific instrument of the *apūrva*—that is not correct; for if that were the case, there would result a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in the archetype itself should one perform threshing or other operations as substitutes for rice (*vrīhi*).

As for the argument presented in the *Mūla* to establish this position—that in the case of the phrase "twenty-six are its ribs" (*ṣaḍviṃśatir asya vaṅkrayaḥ*), the repetition of the word heard in the text is justified because this sentence primarily expresses a connection between the number twenty-six and the animal, and must therefore be repeated for each individual animal in order to manifest that connection—this is untenable, because the genitive case, which signifies the relationship, functions as a subordinate element (*guṇa*), making any suspicion of its being the primary element (*prādhānya*) impossible.

Furthermore, since the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is not itself verbal (*aśābdatva*), it cannot constitute the subject matter (*sūtratā*) of the aphorism; and even if it were primary, its manifestation would still be possible even when [the word] is supplemented. Since there is no evidence for repetition, [this view] has been disregarded. Regarding this point (in the sūtras 9.1.7.21), the author of the Bhāṣya, following his interpretation of the sūtras, maintained a single topical section (*aikādhikaraṇya*) with slight differences, while the author of the Vārttika adopted two topical sections (*adhikaraṇadvaya*). This I have disregarded, as my endeavor here is merely to record the essential subject matter (*prameyamātra*).

In [the discussion on] *praśasā bāhū* (9|1|12), the Commentator and others have already resolved this: since the sacrificial knife (*svadhiti*) is directly enjoined, it would be cumbersome to assume an injunction based on the wording of a mantra (*māntravarṇika*); therefore, the word *praśasā* refers merely to its excellence. Furthermore, that point was disregarded because the sentence "Having performed the ten *prayāja* offerings, he says, 'Bring the *śāsa*'" was written down, thereby establishing that the *śāsa* is also enjoined for the animal sacrifice.

Regarding the statement in the *Mūla* under a different interpretation (9|1|14), where the example "One desiring long life should offer a *caru* of gold pieces (*kṛṣṇala*) in clarified butter to Prajāpati" is cited, and it is said that threshing is set aside because there is no purpose for it in the form of producing satisfaction in the gold pieces—that was a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintya*) assuming that the gold pieces serve as the material source (*prakṛti*) for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) to be offered.

Under 10|1|1, the intention of both the author of the Sūtra and the author of the Bhāṣya is that in the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, the function of the offerings dedicated to deities such as the Aśvins is indeed archetypal (*prākṛta*), whereas the function of those dedicated to deities such as Indra-Agni is non-archetypal (*aprākṛta*).

The author of the Vārtika, however, maintains that due to the specific quality (*guṇa*), a distinct ritual action is indeed enjoined—one which takes the form of the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*) animal sacrifice and is based on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). (Jaiminisūtra 10.1.19). As for what was stated in the root-text (*mūla*)—namely, that where the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) functions as a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*), there the bones alone perform the actions such as the touching (*anvārambha*) and so forth; and that even though they are insentient, their status as agent (*kartṛtva*) is established because they serve as the substratum for the activity residing in the state conducive to the touching—it should be said in response to this: in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), the one denoted by the word "sacrificer" is the living self (*jīvātman*) alone who is designated as the agent of the sacrifice.
The body, however, does not possess agency;
and the agency of the self exists solely by virtue of being the substratum for action. Nor is such agency impossible for one who is dead.
Therefore, it is better to establish the agency of the deceased self in the primary material itself through the medium of consent, and thus the ritual should be performed by you without fail.

Regarding the statement in the *Mūla* that the original qualities (*prākṛtaguṇaka*) do not apply under the view that the deceased has the right [to the offering], that was disregarded because it was already stated in the eighth [book] that they do not apply in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), and because there is no purpose in discussing a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintya*).

As for the seventeen-earthenware-pot (*saptadaśaśarāva*) sacrifice of Bṛhaspati, the meaning—namely, that one should prepare a vessel measuring four and a quarter earthenware pots in accordance with the number [of portions] and perform the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) four times with it—has been determined by all, including the author of the *Bhāṣya* and the commentators such as Karka.

It occurs to me, however, that rather than subverting the *agnihotra-havaṇī* (the sacrificial ladle) which is the direct means of accomplishment, and the handfuls [of grain], it is more appropriate to subvert the number, which serves as the means for the pouring (*nirvāpa*) by way of delimiting each individual handful.
In reality, however, even that [number] is not subverted;
for there is no fault even if the delimitation of the handfuls—which functions within the pouring of as much material as exists for the sacrifice—is subverted.
But the Lord knows the truth.

(10.1.27) The intention of the Bhāṣya is that in common worldly practice, since parched barley (*dhānā*)—which were originally unhusked—is well-known to be re-husked after roasting, one should perform the subsequent step (re-husking) even if it overrides the natural sequence, for the sake of the purpose at hand, provided it possesses the same characteristics as the original.
However, the author of the Vārttika [states] that the state of being parched barley (*dhānātva*) occurs twice, [once] when they are unhusked and [again] after roasting.

Since parched grains (*dhānā*) are obtained only after roasting barley that has already been properly softened by soaking, it follows that threshing must be performed according to its original nature—that is, prior to roasting. Therefore, parched grains are not the illustrative example here; rather, it is the *mantha* (gruel).

Regarding the point here where the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), having raised the objection that the *upavīta*—which is obtained through extension (*atideśa*) and prescribed for the sake of all rites—is set aside by the *nīvīta* (wearing the sacred thread around the neck) enjoined in the *Śyena* sacrifice by the text "the priests proceed with the *nīvīta*," which serves as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agents engaged in the performance, he concludes the established position (*siddhānta*) that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) because the former is for the sake of the beginning [of the rite]. However, if that were for the sake of the beginning, it would follow that even in the case of *śrāddha* and other such rites, the *upavīta* would have to be combined with the *prācīnāvīta* (wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder).

Since it is impossible to combine specific modes—such as wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavīta*) or around the neck (*nivīta*)—which are enjoined by the knowledge of their respective rites and depend upon the lifelong *sattra* sacrifice or the one-night *sattra*, this [position] has been disregarded.

As for the statement that, having raised the doubt regarding the cessation on that day of the original milk-vow (*payovrata*) by means of the horse-flesh meal (*aśvaśana*) prescribed in the rule "when the six-day period has concluded, one should eat horse-meat under the Maghā asterism," it was asserted that there is a combination because of its being for the sake of nourishment—that has been disregarded; for since horse-meat is unfit for sustaining the body, it cannot perform the function of the milk-vow, and thus there is no basis for the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), and furthermore, there is an absence of the milk-vow during the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*).

Regarding the passage *agnisāṃ dvirātre 'vaikhānasaṃ pūrve 'han sāma bhavati, ṣoḍaśyuttare* (At the Agniṣṭoma-like Dvirātra, the Vaikhānasa Sāman occurs on the first day; the Ṣoḍaśin [cup] is on the latter), the Vṛttikāra established the following: having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the phrase *ṣoḍaśyuttare* constitutes an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), he concluded as the final position (*siddhānta*) that because the phrase *ṣoḍaśyuttare* serves as a restrictive specification (*upasaṃhāra*) of the rule *uttare 'han dvimātrasya*, it sets aside the optionality of taking the Ṣoḍaśin cup on other occasions involving two measures.

The Bhāṣyakāra, however, established the following: having raised the prima facie view that it is a restrictive specification (*upasaṃhāra*), he concluded as the final position that it is merely a commendatory statement (*stāvakatva*).

Regarding the point where the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), having not mentioned the *tryanīkā* as taught in the original injunction (*aupadeśikī*), but instead citing the *tryanīkā* belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāhika*) associated with the nine-day period—which applies to the first half of the *gavāmayana*—and having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of repetition like a "beaten stick" (*daṇḍakalita*), then explained the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the extension [of the ritual] to its own place (*svasthānavivṛddhi*) and the supporting indicative mark (*liṅgadarśana*):
that is incorrect.

For, since it has been established that the application of the ten-day period contained within the twelve-day sacrifice occurs in all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), the *tryanīkā* associated with the nine-day period cannot possibly apply; thus, [the Commentator's position] is untenable.
Therefore, the discussion (*adhikaraṇa*) should be applied by taking the directly taught (*aupadeśikī*) three-day period (*tryanīkā*) exactly as stated in the Vārtika.

However, even according to the Vārtikakāra, this much must be considered: where in the archetype (*prakṛti*) a ritual duty (*dharma*) pertains to a deficient portion, but in the ectype (*vikṛti*) that same portion consists of more days, and those additional days are not of the nature of the original constituent parts of that portion—as in this very case, when the directly taught three-day period is absent and one considers it through hypothetical reasoning (*kṛtvācintā*)—how is there the attainment of the duties pertaining to that portion?

Regarding the statement by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) that the *maśvasya* [offering] is called "twelve-day" (*dvādaśāha*) because of its context (*prakaraṇa*), that is disregarded because such a designation would also apply to the *vaimṛdha* offering.

Furthermore, as for his claim that the *maśvasya* is called "twelve-day" because it is perceived to assist the subsequent duties by producing satisfaction to whatever extent and in whatever measure, that too is disregarded because, if that were the case, it would result in the knowledge of only two or three such items.
The sūtras should also be applied to this point in 10.6.19.

Regarding this point, the application of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya—namely, that there is an established option (*vasthitavikalpa*) between the utterances *svāhākāra* and *ṣaṭkāra*—should be inferred here by the wise.

As for the point explained by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) regarding this indicative mark (*liṅga*), "The omentum (*vapā*) is indeed now on the left side," which he interprets as follows: if there were no separate ritual action, it is logical that the remnant of the *prayāja* is not overwhelmed because it remains in its original state through the sprinkling over the animal of the sacrifice; however, if it were a separate ritual action, a new *prayāja* would have to be performed for that purpose, and since the sprinkling over the omentum would be accomplished by that very [new] *prayāja*, the observation of its being "not overwhelmed" would be illogical—this interpretation has been set aside. For even under the view that it is a separate ritual action, just like the *paśupuroḍāśa* and the *savanīya* oblations belonging to the midday pressing, it falls within the framework of the *savanīya* sacrifice (*savanīyatantra*), and thus a repetition of the *prayāja* does not occur due to the principle of incidental application (*prasāṅga*).

Regarding 11.2.11, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) first presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that since the fire (*agni*) serves all purposes, the yoking of the fire (*agniyoga*) is for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite; therefore, the unyoking (*vimoka*) of the fire should be performed only at the very end of everything. He then establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the unyoking should indeed take place at the end of the principal rite alone. However, the Author of the Vārttika (*Vārttikakāra*), using the very same reasoning stated by the Commentator, treats the view that the yoking is for the sake of the principal rite alone as the prima facie position, and explains the Sūtras according to the final conclusion that it is for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite.

Regarding the Prābhākara position that, even though both the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) and the *prayogavidhi* (performance injunction) are present, there is no performance [of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, etc.,] in the animal-cake sacrifice (*paśupuroḍāśa*) due to a lack of purpose—that view is disregarded because it follows that when one performs the *prayāja* and other rites as enjoined by the injunction with their specific qualifying attributes, no purpose would be served by the absence of those enjoined attributes.

As for the fact that in this section the root text accepts the *prayogavidhi* (injunction of performance) and establishes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the sublation of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), while establishing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by accepting the *codaka* and sublating only the *prayogavidhi*, that has been disregarded because it is devoid of logical justification and lacks purpose.

Regarding the point here that the author of the Sūtras and others, while conceding that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice serves the primary rite alone, have resolved the issue by stating that since the word "Viśva" (all) in the term for the deity of the primary rite—*vaiśvadeva*—denotes everything, and since all the gods are understood to be the deities, the deities of the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) are also included within that [comprehensive] acceptance, thereby establishing the principle of *prasaṅga* (incidental benefit); this has been set aside because the word "Viśvadeva" is understood to refer to a specific group [of deities] based on the traditional authority (*smaraṇa*) of the *Trikāṇḍī*, which states "the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas," and because there is no evidence for the view that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* serves the purpose of accepting the deities of the primary rite alone.

Regarding what was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that in the Pañcadaśarātra sacrifice, on the first day of the Agniṣṭut, the Aindrī [verse] should be employed for the sake of greater conformity—that has been set aside; because the Subrahmaṇyā invocation serves the purpose of manifesting the deity, and since the manifestation of Indra achieves the very same function as the manifestation of Agni, it is understood that two distinct Subrahmaṇyās belonging to both deities must be performed.

Regarding 12.1.17, other commentators have stated that "numerical majority" (*bhūyastva*) does not set aside "primacy" (*mukhyatva*); rather, having formulated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on numerical majority specifically in the case of the *Paśukāmeṣṭi* sacrifice, and having established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) based on primacy, the two sūtras should be explained as belonging to a single topical section (*aikādhikaraṇya*). This [position] has been disregarded because, in the world, even a fortress previously occupied by those with few resources can later be seized by many who arrive subsequently.

Regarding the point stated by the author of the Bhāṣya—that because the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *svara* (the wooden sword) is seen at the end of the Soma sacrifice in the text, "When the sacrifice has not yet concluded, he throws the *prastara* along with the cloth," the framework (*tantra*) of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice must be extensive—it was disregarded because that disposal at the end is justified simply by the fact that the *svara* is common to all three animals; thus, it is not a unique indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the extensiveness of the *savanīya* framework.

Regarding what was stated by the author of the Sūtras— that when Agni alone is obtained [as the deity] for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering according to the procedure (*tantra*) of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), the sentence "he cuts off [the portion] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" is meaningful as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to that— the alternative view expressed there,
namely that the meaning of the verbal root alone is enjoined here and the word *sviṣṭakṛt* has its literal sense disregarded, is merely a display of boldness (*prauḍhimātra*).

Regarding the fact that the author of the Bhāṣya did not cite a specific substance for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) here in the event that the *agnihotra* offering is not performed before sunrise—that was overlooked because it is logical that [the rule] serves to remove the fault caused by the transgression of time for those who offer after sunrise; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that those who offer before sunrise would have to perform expiation at all times.

12|3|6. As for this instance where the author of the *Vṛtti*, Śabara-svāmī, has been criticized by the author of the *Vārttika*, and the author of the *Vārttika* has likewise been criticized by the author of the *Bhāṣya* (Śabara-svāmī), and even the author of the *Vārttika* by the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*—there is nothing in that which brings reproach to our established tradition (*samaya*).
For this is simply the inherent nature of creation:
from the very origin of human beings until the end of time, there has been, is, and will continue to be, a constant conflict between the ancients and the moderns.
For the moderns, having delved into the ancient [traditions], perceive certain existing or non-existing defects therein through their own favored subtle scrutiny;
and while setting aside those defects, they either establish some new doctrine or some new statement for the moderns, or they modify the reasoning that supports the previously established doctrine.
By this very method, atheists refute theists, and theists refute atheists.

Even atheists quarrel with one another, and likewise do theists. The doctrine of Kapila is not pleasing to the followers of Kaṇāda; the doctrine of Kaṇāda, in its entirety, is not pleasing to those such as Akṣapāda; and all three of these are not pleasing to the Mīmāṃsakas.

Even among the Mīmāṃsakas, the author of the Bhāṣya does not tolerate the ancient authors of the Vṛttis; the author of the Vārttika does not tolerate the author of the Bhāṣya; and Khaṇḍadeva, the modern Mīmāṃsaka, does not tolerate the author of the Vārttika.
Furthermore, Bhavadeva refutes Pārthasārathi, Khaṇḍadeva refutes Pārthasārathi, and in certain respects, Murārimiśra—who is intent on destroying Advaita—refutes Khaṇḍadeva.

Indeed, in all the treatises, there is a perpetual conflict between the "New" (Navya) and the "Ancient" (Prācīna). Moreover, this status of being "new" or "ancient" is not determined by a royal seal stamped at any particular point in time.
Those who are new today become old tomorrow. Those who are new after a full year were old last year, and those who were new last year are old this current year.
For as the wheel of time revolves, so too do perceptions change accordingly.
Therefore, there is nothing at all surprising here.
The wonder, however, is this alone: that we consider all this to be stable even as it is expanding.
Let this suffice for now.
By citing the shifting of views among ancient and ancienter Mīmāṃsakas, our intention is this: that even Mīmāṃsā follows the method of other treatises and is not a nihilistic doctrine.

As for the ritualists (*yājñikas*), however, certain elements regarding the performance of sacrifices and so forth are explained by the Mīmāṃsakas in one way, while they are explained in another way by the ritualists.

It is said that the ritualists (*yājñika*) compose certain independent treatises of their own decision according to their respective *kalpasūtras*, yet the established conclusions of Mīmāṃsā do not regard them as such. Several instances of this have been pointed out in the *Bhāṣya* and other works. In this regard, the author of the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* has refuted the ritualist doctrines in many places, while in some instances he has even adorned them.
A collection of these is presented here:
first, a single passage from the *Bhāṣya*, then several from the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā*,
and some from the *Bhāṭṭacandrikā* on the section concerning *saṃkalpa* (the formal resolve) are also indicated in their respective locations.

The ritualists (yājñikāḥ) do not approve of this; they perform a modification (*ūha*), [saying]: "O food, come! O giver of much, red-hued one, smoke-bannered, far-seeing one! (Bhāṣya 9.1.15.42–44).
