Furthermore, the injunctions for ritual action authorize the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and his spiritual power (*medha*), not the wife; such as "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires" and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," and so on.

And it is stated in the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa*: "Therefore, even one who is without a wife should perform the *agnihotra*. Furthermore, this has been made explicit by the authors of other ritual manuals (*kalpa*) who state that the fires exist even in the absence of a wife.
To this effect, Bharadvāja says: "Now, if he should be without a wife, his consecration is performed with both—the *aupāsana* fire and the *agnihotra* fire."

Likewise, Jaimini states in the *Talavakārakalpa*: "If the wife of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) dies after [the husband] has produced a son, he should cremate her with fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*) or with the *saṃtapana* fire.
Similarly, Āśvalāyana says: "[One should cremate] the wife of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) with ordinary fire.

Furthermore, the practice of ancient cultured persons (*śiṣṭas*) is also observed in this matter, as in the cases of Kaṇva, Vibhāṇḍaka, Bhīṣma, and others, as well as that of the blessed Lord Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.

Furthermore, even regarding the wife’s joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*), there is no equality with the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). As the Mīmāṃsaka has stated: "For her, only that which is prescribed [is required], such as the benediction (*āśis*) and celibacy (*brahmacarya*), because of the inequality" (MīmSū 6.1.24). Therefore, it is established that even in the absence of the wife, there is no cessation of the rituals.
— Rudradatta 1.6.

(By this, the discussion conducted by the authors of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārtika*—Bhaṭṭa Umbeka, Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, and others—in the section on the authority of traditional conduct (*sadācāra-prāmāṇya*) within the first chapter, third section (*adhikaraṇa*), concerning the performance of sacrifice, is explained.)
In the Mīmāṃsā (10.3.7), it is established that in the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, the garment (*vāsaḥ*) prescribed as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) supersedes the standard *āhārya* fee.

However, Baudhāyana, having stated regarding the *śyāmāka-āgrayaṇa* that "he gives a garment after the full moon," and regarding the *vrīhi-āgrayaṇa* that "he gives the first-born calf after the full moon," has made an extension (*atideśa*) for the *yava-āgrayaṇa*, stating: "The ritual procedure is the same as that of the *vrīhi-āgrayaṇa*."

Thus, although both the cloth (*vāsas*) and the calf (*vatsa*) are indeed [prescribed] as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to their respective contexts, it is stated that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) with the subsequent sacrificial fee (*anvāryadakṣiṇā*).
This constitutes the point of divergence from the Mīmāṃsā. (BaudhŚrSū 3.2)
"From the indicative mark [in the text], 'the garment is combined with the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) in the case of śyāmāka,' it follows that this is so.
Rudradatta [states] at 6.8: 'In the case of the Āghāra libation and the continuous stream, the connection with the beginning must not be forgotten.'"
Rudradatta [on *Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.4].

In the Mīmāṃsā, however, in the section on the *ādhāra* (the base-offering) at 1.2.1.2, and in the section on the *dhārā* (the stream-offering) at 1.2.1.1, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the ritual action and so forth, as well as the mantra and so forth, are to be performed together; the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the ritual action and so forth, ending with the mantra, are to be performed together.

Regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) preceded by the Soma sacrifice, the Mīmāṃsaka has established in the section *svakāle syādavipratiṣedhāt* (5.1.5.19–20) that there is a sublation of the time for the Soma sacrifice based on the scriptural statement: "He who, having performed the Soma sacrifice, establishes the fires, need not inquire [about the lunar day] nor [the lunar mansion].

Rudradatta says: "They consider this to be a sublation of the time for the Soma sacrifice; however, that is incorrect, because from the context it is understood that the time for the *ādhāna* is being sublated by this, and because of the mention of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
Indeed, no specific lunar mansion has been prescribed for the Soma sacrifice such that it could be prohibited here."
Therefore, the sublation of the time for the Soma sacrifice is improper.
Regarding the time for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), it is stated: "And the castes of the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*)," and "This work should be performed by those who belong to the three castes.
This time for the *ādhāna* belongs to those who, being included within the three castes, are devoted to their own sacred fires and construct the chariot.
Rudradatta [on *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 5.1].

However, in the *Mīmāṃsā*, in the section concerning the chariot-maker (*rathakārādhikaraṇa*, 6.1.12, sūtras 44–50), it is established that the chariot-maker is not one of the three higher castes, but rather a specific mixed caste. Yājñavalkya states: "From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇa mother, a chariot-maker is born."
The Māhiṣya is born from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother; the Karaṇī is born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother.
The chariot-maker (rathakāra), who is synonymous with the Saudhanvana and denoted by the term Ṛbhu, has been established as one for whom the laying of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is prescribed.

In the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, Baudhāyana (1.14) has stated that the mantra beginning with "I prepare your seat" (*svonaṃ te sadanaṃ karomi*), which consists of half-verses, serves as the instruction for spreading clarified butter (*ājyopastaraṇa*) upon the vessel.

However, Āpastamba and Satyāṣāḍha (Satyāṣāḍha Śrautasūtra 1.27.1) maintain that the preparation of the seat for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—which is synonymous with spreading the butter—is performed with only the first half-verse, while the placement of the cake upon it is performed with the second half-verse.

Furthermore, in the *Mīmāṃsā*, within the section concerning relative strength (*balāvalādhikaraṇa*) and specifically the section on indicative mark (*liṅga*) versus syntactical connection (*vākya*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established—just as by Āpastamba and not as by Baudhāyana—that the indicative mark is stronger than syntactical connection.
[This concerns] the *upāṃśuyāja*:
"The *upāṃśuyāja* has clarified butter as its oblation; it occurs only at the full moon sacrifice, and belongs to Viṣṇu, or Agni-Soma, or Prajāpati."

Since Baudhāyana and others prescribe the *upāṃśuyāja* even on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), the word "only" (*eva*) is used in the phrase "only on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsyām eva*) for the purpose of excluding that [view]. Rudradatta [comments on this at] 2.6.
This entire matter has been established in the Mīmāṃsā under the section beginning with "Or Prajāpati [is the deity], because of the dharma" (10.8.17.51–61).
In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, however, the upāṃśuyāja is prescribed even for the new moon sacrifice;
that it should not be performed according to the Āpastamba Kalpa is another matter.
In the Ātithyā ceremony, there are two separating blades made of ikṣu grass.
Regarding the two *aikṣavya* [separators]: Rudradatta states that some say they are "leaves of the sugarcane" (*ikṣuparṇe*) or "roots of the *kāśa* grass.
Satyāṣāḍha says, "The two *ikṣuśalākā* are the *vidhṛtī* [separators]. Jyotsnā comments: "The two *ikṣuśalākā* consist of the bark of sugarcane; some say they consist of the leaves of sugarcane."

In the *Mīmāṃsāvārtika*, however, it is concluded that the two separating blades (*vidhṛtī*) are made of sugar-cane parts, as these are established in common worldly usage; likewise, it is established that they are made from the roots of *kāśa* grass. Regarding this point, since there is no supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) by Gautama (Satyāṣāḍha) here to serve as authority for using the roots of *kāśa*, Satyāṣāḍha’s intention is that the meaning established in common worldly usage alone should be accepted.

The intention of the Mīmāṃsaka school is that while the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) for the word *āśvalāyana* in the sense of "made of *kāśa*" is as clear as it is, there is no such supplementary statement for the word *aikṣavya* in the sense of "having *kāśa*-roots"; nevertheless, [the meaning] must still be sought out.
Thus [ends the discussion of] the *caturhotṛ* mantras.
"Among those [Caturhotṛ formulas], those that are connected with the sacrificial session (*vihāra*) belong to one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*); the others belong to both.

Among those Caturhotṛs, those which are connected with the sacrificial session—such as "One undertaking the New and Full Moon sacrifices [should employ] the Caturhotṛ," and so forth—belong only to one who has established the sacred fires.

However, those which are not connected with the sacrificial session—such as the Daśahotṛ and others in passages like "He who should desire, 'May I beget offspring,'" and so forth—belong to both the one who has established the sacred fires and the one who has not.
In that regard, for one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni), the oblation is offered either in the Āhavanīya fire or the Aupāsana fire;
for one who has not established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), it is in the Aupāsana fire.
— Rudradatta 1.15.

In the Mīmāṃsā (6.8.1.9–10), however, it is established as the final conclusion that in the case of the *caturhotṛ* offerings, only one who has not yet consecrated the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) is entitled to perform them.

Regarding the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice performed when the moon rises while the offering is still in progress: this is not a rule for one who prepares the *sāṃnāyya* milk-offering, because of its connection with the *sāṃnāyya*.

And Āśvalāyana says: "In the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice, when the moon has risen before [the time for the offering]. Bharadvāja says: "This [rule] applies to one who does not perform the *sāṃnāyya*, according to one view; it applies to one who does perform it, according to another. (Rudradatta 9.1)

In the Mīmāṃsā (6.5.1.21–24), however, having raised the prima facie view that "it should belong to one who prepares the Sāṃnāyya because of the connection with the Sāṃnāyya," the established conclusion was reached that "because of the connection with the vegetable offering (auṣadha), it belongs to both"—that is, to both those who prepare the Sāṃnāyya and those who do not.

Regarding the *Candramyudita-iṣṭi* (the sacrifice performed when the moon has risen after the new moon), once it has been performed, there is an option for performing the *Iṣṭi* again; as it is said: "One should sacrifice with one [offering], or one should sacrifice with two."

Having said this, Rudradatta spoke again: "When the object [of the sacrifice] has been set aside, these three alternatives from other treatises are stated: one may perform the sacrifice again exactly as the original (prakṛti), having left it unmodified; or, having performed the Abhyuditeṣṭi, one may sacrifice again according to the original rite; or, having extended [the ritual] only up to the Aupavasathya day, one may sacrifice afterwards. This is clearly stated in the Vaidhāyanīya (Dvaidha-sūtra)," and so forth. Regarding the heating of the Tryambaka offerings, Āpastamba states as an option: "Having heated them, or having offered them [without heating]," and so on.
In the *Mīmāṃsābhāṣya*, however, it is stated that the passage concerning the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*)—the very statement of the *mīmāṃsā* regarding the sprinkling—is an *arthavāda*.
Furthermore, in the *Śāstradīpikā*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached: "Therefore, there is no option; the sprinkling is indeed mandatory.
[This concludes the discussion on] the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*.
"These belong to Dakṣa, thus they are Dākṣas; their course is the Dākṣāyaṇa.
Who, then, is Dakṣa? "He who is energetic," says the author of the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya.
Rudradatta, however, says that the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* is so called because the sacrifice was seen by Dākṣāyaṇa;

this is based on the statement of Manu, "The sacrifice of Dākṣāyaṇa," and because of its association with other [proper names] such as the *Sārvaseniyajña*, the *Vāsiṣṭhayajña*, and the *Śaunakayajña*.
[He also mentions] the *Niṣādasthapati*.
"By this very [rite] one should cause the Niṣādasthapati to sacrifice. (The Niṣāda is a hunter; the Sthapati is a chief; he is both a Niṣāda and a Sthapati).
For that is his sacrifice (it is prescribed with reference to him).
And that same [fire] is also implied here by the term "as far as necessary" (*yāvadartham*), even in its inclusive sense (*abhividhi*).
According to some, the *iṣṭi* sacrifice is performed in a common (worldly) fire;
in that case, the formula "O preparer of the oblation, come! (*haviṣkṛdādhāva*) and so forth should not be recited for a Śūdra.
Rudradatta: 9|4.
The knowers of logic maintain that for a wife, the ritual action is exactly as prescribed in every case (based on the *mīmāṃsā* principle at 6|1|6|24:
"Because her [the wife's] performance of the rites is equal to what is stated for him [the husband]").
But Bharadvāja has stated: "The wife's purificatory rites are the same as [the sacrificer's], with the exception of shaving.
(Rudradatta 4.1).
Regarding the eleven sacrificial animals, the (Āpastamba) Sūtra states: "For each animal, there are two spits for the omentum, two pots, and heart-spits."

Regarding this, Rudradatta says: "But surely, it has been stated in the *Paribhāṣāpāda* that in a group of animals of the same species there is a single performance (*tantra*) of the cauldron and other implements, whereas in a group of different species there is a distinction (*bheda*). Furthermore, the experts in logic have stated: 'In a group of animals, because the cauldron, the spit, and the omentum-cooking vessel serve a common purpose (*prabhutvāt*), there should be a single performance' (Jaimini Sūtra 11.4.8.33). Likewise: 'But in the case of the *jālma* offerings, there should be a distinction because of the inequality of the cooking' (Jaimini Sūtra 10.4.10.40). Therefore, it must be stated what the scope of this injunction is."
It is said:
this rule applies where animals of a single species are dedicated to various deities, such as seventeen animals for Prajāpati;

however, where animals of a single species are dedicated to the same deity, as in the case of seventeen animals for Prajāpati, there is *tantratva* (commonality of performance)—this is the distinction.
Thus, (11.42) by this, the contradiction between Āpastamba and Mīmāṃsā due to a difference in subject matter is resolved.

Furthermore, regarding the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*), the rule that the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) of the original establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*) are superseded by the feeless fees of the re-establishment is established in the Mīmāṃsā under the section (10.3.5.20–23): "In the case of an occasional modification of the qualities of the *agnyādheya*."
This has been explained.

However, in the Āpastamba [Śrautasūtra], it is prescribed: "He gives the sacrificial fee for both: that pertaining to the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya) and that pertaining to the re-establishment of the fires (paunarādheya)," as stated by Rudradatta on 5.8.
The throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastarapraharaṇa*):
"While the *sūktavāka* is being recited, he throws the grass-bundle together with the branch into the *āhavanīya* fire, [reciting] 'O Maruts, you are the spotted ones (*pṛṣatayaḥ stha*)'.
The *sūktavāka* is the section beginning with 'idaṃ dyāvāpṛthivī', intended for the proclamation of the deities of the sacrifice; at the time of its recitation, he throws the grass-bundle."
"He does not utter *svāhā*" means that he does not utter the *svāhākāra* in the mantra "You are the speckled ones of the Maruts. [Objection:

But since the *svāhākāra* is already unobtained simply because there is no act of offering (*ajuhoti*), what is the purpose of this prohibition? [Response: True, it is not obtained; nevertheless, it is prohibited as an objection raised according to the view of others.
For this is the view of the followers of Jaimini: there exists an injunction for sacrifice, namely, "He throws the grass-bundle (*prastara*) with the *sūktavāka*."

In this context, the *sūktavāka* occupies the place of the *yājyā* (offering verse), the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is the substance (*dravya*), the deities are those indicated by the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*), and the act of throwing (*praharati*) constitutes the meaning of the sacrifice (*yajati*).
However, the intention of the author of the Sūtras (Āpastamba) is that this is rather an injunction regarding the time for the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prastara*.
For this very reason it is said: "while the *sūktavāka* is being recited."
Rudradatta: 3|2.

This view was stated in the Mīmāṃsā, under the *sūktavāka* principle (2|1|5|11–15), in the section [beginning with] "And in the *sūktavāka*, there is an injunction regarding time. Furthermore, according to the system of Āpastamba, the example "He throws the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the *āhavanīya* fire while the *śaṃyuvāka* is being recited" is likewise identical.
Therefore, it has been stated by Rudradatta: "In the case of the *anūyamāna* [formula], it is as before.
"As before" means: "in the case of the *sūktavāka* being recited as *anūyamāna*," and so forth. Regarding the choosing of the *pravara*: "He chooses three seers who are authors of mantras."

Alternatively, one chooses one, two, three, or five mantra-authors according to what is possible—namely, one for one who has a single *ṛṣi* ancestry, three for one with three *ṛṣis*, and five for one with five *ṛṣis*.
Thus says Āśvalāyana: "He chooses as many ancestral *ṛṣis* of the sacrificer as there may be" (1.3.1).

Others, however, maintain that even for those with five *ṛṣis*, only three are to be chosen; they hold that those with only one or two *ṛṣis* have no entitlement to the rite at all, and that the injunctions "he chooses one" and "he chooses two" are merely partial restatements (*avayutyānuvāda*) of the rule regarding the number three.
And likewise, the Mīmāṃsakas [state]: "There would be the loss of one who lacks a lineage of ṛṣis" (MīmSū 6.1.1.143).
(The intention is that this is not tenable.
— Rudradatta, 2.5.
Regarding the throwing of the *prastara* bundle:
Baudhāyana has stated (1.19), "Having uttered the direction, 'Recite the *sūkta-vāka*,' one throws that (*prastara*) as if upwards.

By this, it is established that the throwing of the *prastara* occurs at the time of the recitation of the *sūkta-vāka*; however, there is no evidence whatsoever for its occurrence when those two [the *sūkta-vāka* and the *śaṃyuvāka*] are absent.

In the commentary and sub-commentary on the *Āpastamba* [Kalpasūtra] composed by Rāma and Kauśika, however, the *śruti* is cited as stating: "The *prastara* is the oblation; the *sūktavāka* is the *yājyā*.
Furthermore, it is established that the *sūktavāka* is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the bringing of the branch (*śākhāharaṇa*).
Moreover, the throwing away (*praharaṇa*) of both the *prastara* and the branch is declared to occur simultaneously.

In Rudradatta’s commentary (*vṛtti*), however, this is the view of the followers of Jaimini: "There is indeed an injunction for sacrifice in the statement, 'He casts the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*.

In that case, the *sūktavāka* occupies the place of the *yājyā* (offering verse), the *prastara* is the substance (*dravya*), the deities are those indicated by the words of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*), and the verb 'he casts' (*praharati*) has the meaning of 'he sacrifices' (*yajati*).
The intention of the author of the Sūtra, however, is that this is rather an injunction regarding the time for the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prastara*.

Therefore it has been said: "when the *sūktavāka* is being recited. (The intention of Āpastamba is that the statement, "He throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*," is an injunction regarding time. This has been stated. Regarding this, Satyāṣāḍha says: "'Recite the *sūkta*,' he gives the command; the Hotṛ begins the *sūktavāka*" (2.10.20).
"The Adhvaryu throws the *prastara* and the branch into the fire" (21).

Regarding this, the *Vaijayantī* states: "Although the author of the *Bhāṣya*, relying on the view of Jaimini, has stated that 'the mantra ends with the word *svāhā*', even that is to be reconsidered."

Therefore, it is established that the *sūktavāka*—which reminds one of the deities intended for sacrifice and produces a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the intended deities such as those of the *ājyabhāga* offerings whose names end in *-sviṣṭakṛt*—has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), while [its role] as part of the sacrifice has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Thus, the *sūktavāka* is not a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the throwing of the grass-bundle (*prastara-praharaṇa*); rather, the connection "he throws the grass-bundle with the *sūktavāka*" is a conjunction of time (*kālārtha-saṃyoga*). This is the opinion of the ritualists Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, and Satyāṣāḍha.
Jaimini, however, states: "And in the case of the *sūktavāka*, there is an injunction of time, because it serves another purpose" (3.2.51).

Having presented the prima facie view that "He throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*" is an injunction regarding the time [of the action], the author states: "Or rather, it is an instruction (*upadeśa*), for the word 'offering-verse' (*yājyā*) does not [apply] to this.
Or rather, there should be an instruction of the mantra with respect to the throwing of the *prastara*.
And by doing so, the term "offering-verse" becomes justified [in the statement]: "The *sūktavāka* itself is the offering-verse; the *prastara* is the oblation."
And the sacrifice is that which strikes;
"if it is argued that it is a disposal," [the reply is: "it has been firmly established."

For some, the following elements belonging to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* archetype do not exist: the non-kindling of the fires (*ananvādhāna*), the taking up of the vow (*vratopāyana*), eating forest food (*āraṇyāśana*), keeping watch (*jāgaraṇa*), the giving of the *anvāhārya* rice-offering, and the binding and unbinding of the wife’s hair. This is because these are already established by the sacrifice called *soma*. Furthermore, whatever other subsidiary elements depend upon the context (*prasaṅga*) for their application also cease; for example, the touching of water with the formula "thou art the light of the three" (*tridhud asi*), the choosing of the Brahman priest (*brahmavaraṇa*), and so forth. However, the non-kindling of the fires is performed at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* initiation, and the binding of the wife’s hair is likewise performed there, as they are otherwise established.
Satyāṣāḍha and Bharadvāja, however, prescribe the undertaking of the vow (*vratopāyana*) for the rites following the *avabhṛtha*, such as the *udavasānīyā* and others.

This is not the intention of the Teacher (meaning Āpastamba); for the *patnīsaṃyāja* is established by implication in those rites following the *avabhṛtha*, since the *yoktra* has been discarded at the *avabhṛtha*.
— Rudradatta.

"O preparer of the oblation, come! for a Brāhmaṇa; "O preparer of the oblation, come hither! for a Rājanya; "O preparer of the oblation, run hither! for a Vaiśya; "O preparer of the oblation, hasten hither! for a Śūdra.
The mention of the Śūdra is intended for the Niṣāda-sthapati (the chief of the Niṣādas).
— Rudradatta.

Now, the explanation of the chapters and so forth of the Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa: In the Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa there are four chapters, and since there are four quarters (caraṇas) in each chapter, the total number of sections (akṣaras) is sixteen. Furthermore, all the topical sections (adhikaraṇas) combined amount to 342. [This concludes] the Yūpapāda.
Kālapāda;
Agnipāda; Grahapāda.
The section on the Ṛṣis, the section on the choosing [of priests], or the section on the bricks;
the section on the portions [of the sacrificial victim].
The quarter of the *preṣa*,
the quarter of the *homa*, and the quarter of the *sāmidhenī*.
The *nigadapāda* and the *vaṣaṭkārapāda*.

Regarding the mention of the *saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa* by the author of the Śābara-bhāṣya and others: he will state (at 2.4.20), "In the *Saṃkarṣa*, it will be said that Vanaspati is a modification of Sviṣṭakṛt."

In the *Saṃkarṣa* [Pūrva Mīmāṃsā], under the sūtra "May our breath come from afar, from the intermediate space, from the sky, from the earth; you are immortality; for breath, thee," the application of the mantra is stated by means of its concluding portion: "he breathes over the gold" (Su.
p. 686). Furthermore, according to the principle to be stated in the *Saṃkarṣa*—"Or rather, every day, because it is enjoined"—the oblation of the Kauṇḍapāyins is to be performed once every day.
In the Siddhānta, however, because the ritual action is one and the same, it should be performed in the evening and in the morning according to the archetypal form, just as in the original model.
Sūtra-pṛ. 788.

In the second chapter of the *Saṃkarṣa*, in the section (sūtra 2.1.26) beginning with "In the middle [form], the fire is piled after the *citi* has been performed, because it is assisted by the archetypal [rite]," the doubt arises as to whether the duties pertaining to the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) should be performed or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the *auttaravedika* duties. This is because the two fires—the one on the *uttaravedi* and the one being piled—have different purposes, and since the fire on the *uttaravedi* is understood to be absent [in this case], the duties of the *uttaravedi* do not apply. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached by considering the scriptural statement: "Having performed the *citi*, the fire is piled on the *uttaravedi*. Although this indicates a combination (*samuccaya*), the ground prepared by the act of piling (*cayana*) serves as a substratum for the fire mentioned in the accusative case in the injunction "he piles the fire" (*agniṃ cinute*). Since this ground is fit to be a substrate for the fire, and since the purpose of the *uttaravedi* is the placement of the fire—as seen in the statement "he places the fire on the *uttaravedi*" (*uttaravedyām agniṃ nidadhāti*)—there is a functional identity despite the difference in purpose. Furthermore, just as in the cases "he places the oblations on the *vedi*" and "he places the oblations on the *barhis*," where the *vedi* and *barhis* are used alternatively, here too, because the ground and the *uttaravedi* are obtained optionally, there is no restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) governing them. Consequently, since their mutual independence is not perceived, there is no contradiction in their combination. Thus, even when the piling is combined with the *uttaravedi*, the duties of the *uttaravedi* should apply to the fire placed upon it. By stating this, the author of the *Tantravārttika* will establish the extension of those duties based on the fact that the *uttaravedi* is a subordinate element (*adhikāra*) of the fire-piling, having first refuted the prima facie view that it is not such a subordinate element. This will be demonstrated through the characteristic of obtaining the duties of the *uttaravedi*.

And by the statement of a collective [inclusion] as if they were established, there—by way of excluding the status of being subordinate (*adhikāra*) to that which is sublated (*bādha*)—it will be stated therein that the sublated form lacks such subordination.

Su. P. 949: Even regarding the prohibition of the *anūbandhyā* cow in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, since it is recorded in the Taittirīya Śākhā—beginning with "He who mounts their sacrifice mounts the gods," and then referring to the skin of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* with "This is its vow"—one might suspect that this is a *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation) due to a different connection (*saṃyogāntara*). However, having raised this doubt, it will be stated in the *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa* (1.3.8) that this refers specifically to the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*. Therefore, there is no reason here for it to be considered a *paryudāsa*.

*Sūtra-pṛṣṭha* 1393. In the *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa* (1.1.15), regarding the *śāmitra* [the slaughterer], it will be stated that in the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he is to be chosen from among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the cup-bearers (*camasin*), and the assistant priests (*adhvaryu*); in the second, from among the officiating priests; and in the third, from among the cup-bearers alone. In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, his function will be assigned to the *adhvaryus*. *Sūtra* 3.7, page 28. Furthermore, the *Saṃkarṣaṇa-sūtra*, "Or rather, he is not fit for the status of an officiating priest," should be explained as intending that he is not eligible for the role of an officiating priest insofar as it pertains to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the sacrifice.

Bhaṭṭa [says this]. Somanātha, however, states: "After the performance of the *cayana* (piling) has brought about the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the fire, since that consecration—which consists in the placing of the fire upon the mound (*sthaṇḍila*) produced by the *cayana*—lacks an inherent fruit of its own, it must be understood as culminating in the completion of the ritual (*kratu*). Therefore, in the *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa*, it is established that the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice possesses both [the fires] as its substrate; it does not have the *cayana* as its substrate, nor is it a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the fire. Thus he says.
4|3|18. In the *Saṃkarṣa* (2|1|26), because of the statement, "It is mixed on the *uttaravedi*," the combination (*samuccaya*) of the fire-altar (*agni*) and the *uttaravedi* will be explained.

*Bhāṭṭa* 10|8|11. In the *Saṃkarṣa*, regarding the section on various offerings (2|3|16), under the subsidiary aphorism (*guṇasūtra*) "And because of the observation of another purpose" (*anyārthadarśanācca*), the commentator Bhavasvāmin has explained it as follows: "The statement concerning the application (*viniyoga*) of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses reveals a distinction in the offerings (*pradānabheda*). [One should sacrifice] following the first [verse], then [one should sacrifice] following the middle one; having followed the middle one, [one should sacrifice] following the last one; the last one..."

"A human being should sacrifice with the first [verse]; thus, all [verses] become *anuvākyās* and all become *yājyās*. (Parimala on Brahma Sūtra Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa 3.1.28.43). Furthermore, in the Brahma Sūtra Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa, the statement "Inanimate things are unfit for worship because of the absence of the fruit [of liberation] and the opposite [result]" is intended to strictly prohibit their worship altogether.

Advaita 2.4.327. In the fourth [chapter], third [section] (the second exposition in the sixth topic) of the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, the following is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Having cited the scriptural passage, "One should meditate upon that deity for whom the oblation has been taken up when about to utter the *vaṣaṭ*," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is raised that what is intended is merely meditation on the nature of the deity as known from the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, mantras, and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*). The final conclusion is reached as follows: because one hears words such as "belonging to Agni" (*āgneya*) or "belonging to Indra" (*aindra*) which designate the deity, and because there is no reason to abandon that [word] which is the first to present itself; and because when an action is impossible with respect to the word, the cognition of the action is understood to apply to the object; and since meditation is possible here with respect to the word, meditation must be performed upon the word "deity" itself.
Ku. 4.3.16, Section 2.

In the second book of the Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa, in the fourth section of the second chapter (Adhikaraṇa 26), under the heading "Ṛtāṣāḍ ṛtāmeti yathārthaviniṣkarṣo'rthapṛthaktvāt" (The extraction [of mantras] should be according to their meaning because the objects are distinct), there arises the following deliberation: In the mantra "Ṛtāṣāḍ ṛtāmeti gandharvaḥ sa idaṃ brahma kṣatraṃ pātu tasmai svāhā; tasyauṣadhyo'psarasa ūrjaṃ nāma tā idaṃ brahma kṣatraṃ pāntu svāhā," should the masculine-denoting and feminine-denoting words be extracted and employed separately for each oblation (*pratihoma*), or should they be used exactly as they appear in the text? This is the inquiry.

Ku. 2|1|14|42, p. 150: The formulas beginning with "ṛtāṣāṭ ṛtadhāmā" and so forth, which are recited prior to "tasmai svāhā tābhyaḥ svāhā," constitute the various turns (paryāyas); and these occur before the formula "bhuvanasya pate.

This very point will be elaborated upon in that same section concerning the deities (the Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa, 2|4|27), under the discussion of the statement "he offers with six [turns]," as in the case of "he offers the Sāvitra oblations.
Ku. 2|1|1|42: In the Rāṣṭrabhṛt mantras, even if a portion is understood differently according to its knowledge, it is employed in the preceding mantra because there is no contradiction.

This is clear from Devasthāmin’s commentary on the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* (2.4.26): "Because when the preceding mantra is being employed, the subsequent portion that has already been employed can be connected [to it] by virtue of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), since in worldly poetry we observe the connection of masculine words even when they are separated by feminine words. Furthermore, in *Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa* 2.1.1.42, it will be stated in the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* (2.1.2) that both possess the status of deity (*devatātva*): Agni possesses the status of deity characterized by being the object of the mantra, whereas Samidh and the others possess the status of deity characterized by being the recipients of the oblation (*havirbhāj*). Thus, both are deities.

Ku. 2|1|2|2. In the second section of the second chapter of the Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa (2|1|2), the following scriptural passage is cited in the Bhāṣya: "When the Adhvaryu says, 'Recite the offering prayer for the kindling-sticks (samidhaḥ),' this is a cryptic form pertaining to Agni; he is actually saying, 'Recite the offering prayer for him.'"

Ku. 2.1.2.2. In the second section of the second chapter of the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, regarding the preliminary argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) stated in the sūtra: "In that case, there is no instruction of the name of the deity, because it is nameless," the opponent argues that in the *yājyā-praiṣa* (the call for the offering verse) "yajā," the name of the deity should not be instructed. This is countered by the sūtra: "Or rather, it exists, on account of observations [of Vedic texts] to the contrary," which states: "If one were to say, 'Sacrifice to Tanūnapāt,' or 'Sacrifice to the Iḍās,' there would be a repetition (*jāmi*)."

Having established the final position (*siddhānta*) that the censure of the designation of deities (*devatā-ādeśa*) in the *prayāja* offerings implies a rule for designating deities elsewhere, [the author] raises an objection: "The designation of deities is recited in the *prayājas*; its prohibition is stated regarding the others" (ŚB 11.7.4.2). This refers to the censure in another recension (*śākhā*)—such as "If one should say, 'Sacrifice to Tanūnapāt,' or 'Sacrifice to Iḍ,'" etc.—of the designation of deities which is directly enjoined there by the words "Sacrifice to Tanūnapāt. Therefore, there is no designation of deities other than in the *prayājas*, since there is an absence of such specific injunctions as "Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, one should say, 'Sacrifice to Indra,'" or "Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, one should say, 'Sacrifice to the Maruts,'" and so on. This objection is resolved by the sūtra: "In some recensions, it is recited for that purpose: 'Recite for such-and-such; sacrifice! (ŚB 11.7.4.3). This means that in every instance, such as the *yājyā-praiṣa* (the call to recite the offering verse), the designation of the deity must be performed, as it is directly enjoined in another recension. The occasional mention of "Sacrifice to Indra," and so forth, is merely a reiteration (*anuvāda*).
Nor should it be argued that because the number is not obtained in such cases as "one should recite twenty-one," there is no possibility of another recitation qualified by that number;

for, according to the principle of the fourth chapter, second section of the *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa*— namely, "the archetype is to be followed"— there exists the status of being the archetype for the obligatory recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses, due to the similarity with the recitation.
Ku.

In the second [section] of the fourth [chapter] of the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, under the heading: "When [an action] is enjoined without connection to a deity, the deity is understood through implication, just as there is a connection with humans in the case of rice for a meal," the following is established: Regarding injunctions such as "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between" (*upāṃśuyājam antarā yajati*), which are enjoined without a connection to a deity, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since no deity is apprehended through the words themselves, the substance should be offered even without a deity. However, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached by stating that because the deity is understood from the *yajati* (sacrifice) itself through the general and specific forms found in the *mantra*-text, the relinquishment of the substance for the sake of the deity is indeed possible. In the subsequent section (3), under the sūtra: "'The *sūktavāka* is the *yājyā*; the *prastara* is the oblation; the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) are the first of the oblations to be offered,'" the prima facie view is presented: the throwing of the *prastara* and the placing of the fuel-sticks are of the nature of an oblation (*homa*), because the supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*)—"The *sūktavāka* is the *yājyā*, the *prastara* is the oblation"—and "The fuel-sticks are the first of the oblations to be offered"—make them known as *homas*, and because the specific deity is obtained from the *mantra*-text. The final conclusion is established by the sūtra: "'Or rather, it is praise; it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *prastara*, because of proximity; the fuel-sticks are for the purpose of kindling. This means: [The *prastara* is not an oblation, but] it is praised as being one by way of its being an oblation. The throwing of the *prastara* is a disposal (*pratipatti*) because the *prastara*, having already been mentioned with the accusative case ending (*prastaram*), is present [as the object]; and the placing of the fuel-sticks has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) because it serves the purpose of the two fires. Thus, the conclusion is reached.

Regarding the statement, "Or rather, it is an instruction, for the word *yājyā* [is used] up to the *nāka-saṃmāna*" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.12), Deva Svāmin has stated in his commentary that this is a *kṛtvā-cintā* (a hypothetical discussion).

In the first section (1.1.1) of the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, under the sūtra *Ku.* 3.1.5.13, it will be explained that in the sentence "He performs the *anuyāja* with the words *vīhi*," the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is enjoined; and because this is prescribed by another scriptural passage, a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) is enjoined as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *Somayāga*.

In the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, under *Ku. 3|1|16|35*, having raised the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) argument that "because of the extraction according to the actual meaning—'not having performed [the rite], one should not go to the next world,' and because of their distinctness" (2|4|26), it will be established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by the sūtra "or rather, according to the traditional recitation" (*yathāsamāmnātam vā*). This is because the application of each preceding mantra occurs in an intermingled manner exactly as they are recited; and since the pronoun "to them" (*tābhyaḥ svāhā*) is intermingled with each preceding mantra, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is satisfied by taking the presentation of the immediately preceding word.

In the second [section] of the fourth [chapter] of the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, under the sūtra "(1) When an offering is enjoined through connection with a deity, the act of giving is the oblation, just as in common worldly usage" (*devatāsaṃyogena codyamāne pradāna āhutiryathā loke*), this will be explained in detail: "The oblation consisting of the sacrificial material must be cast into the fire; the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice) is not merely the act of relinquishment.
In the *Bhaṭṭacandrikā* on the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*, a mention of the ancient teachers Ālekhana, Āimarathya, and Kāṣrṇājini—those who were ritualists—is found.
There, in the section concerning the *sāmidhenī* verses, it is revealed in scripture: "One should recite three triplets for a Kṣatriya.
And those triplets are to be taken as Gāyatrī, Jāgata, and Anuṣṭubh meters.
For a Vaiśya, the *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*, and *anuṣṭubh* meters are used.
Regarding the statement, "They are indeed *gāyatrīs*," Ālekhana maintains that the original rule (*prākṛta-vidhi*) is set aside by this occasional modification (*naimittika-vikāra*).

Āmarathi, however, maintains that because a restriction based on a specific meter through a mere explanatory passage (arthavāda)—such as "there are these eight oblations, for the Gāyatrī has eight syllables"—is improper both as a restrictive rule and as a sublation of the archetypal (prakṛta) norm, the re-enactment of the injunction serves a purpose by way of excluding other triplets (tṛca). Thus, he says that only the Gāyatra triplets of the archetype are to be taken.
Saṃkarṣa. 4.2.1.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the release of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati has been mentioned.
In this regard, the view of Kāṣrṇājini is that the very act of untying the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) constitutes the meaning of the term "release" (*utsarga*).
(Saṃkarṣa 1.1.4). After having laid down the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick, one must perform the touching with the *sūdadohas* verse.

The ritualists (*yājñikas*), however, maintain that both [the *samidh* and *tanūnapāt* offerings] share a single mantra. Whatever refutation and other arguments have been made regarding the Sūtra and Bhāṣya in the *Bhaṭṭacandrikā* on the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* (2.1.41), those are now summarized.
The commentary on this [section] is that composed by Devasvāmin, and not the Śāvara-bhāṣya. In the Bhāṣya, however, these four topics (adhikaraṇas) have been explained by treating them as one.

As for the final sūtra, "And because of the observation of an indicative mark" (*liṅgadarśanācca*), it has been explained for the sake of universal application: when the injunction (*praiṣa*) "The oblation is cooked; the slaughterer is ready," occurs, the indicative mark—"He responds three times, 'It is cooked'"—makes known the identity of the agent for both the act of slaughtering (*śamana*) and the act of cooking (*śrapaṇa*).

The intention [of the author] is that, since it is determined in the archetype (*prakṛti*) that the act of cooking (*śrapaṇa*) is to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest, etc., [the same applies here].
Regarding *Saṃkarṣa* 1.1.15:

"The sacrificial animals end toward the south"—since the binding of the animals has been established by the injunction of the offering through the sequence beginning from the northeast (*īśāna*) and ending with the southeast (*ādhānya*), and since the same [rule] would apply to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as well because no closer proximity to the primary act is obtained in its remaining part, the injunction that they "end toward the north" (*udagapavarga*), which is being applied, must be interpreted in a way that does not contradict the proximity of the connection.

And thus, having measured nine sacrificial posts (yūpas) in the order of the animals and passing over the position for the tenth, one should fix the tenth at the south-east corner of the altar (vedi) and the eleventh in the north-eastern part of it.
The author of the Bhāṣya maintains that if this were so, there would be a violation of the sequence for only the two—the last and the penultimate.

However, the Teacher (Ācārya), because there is no difference in their being based on direct scriptural statement (vācanikatva), accepts that in the archetype (prakṛti) there is indeed an option (vikalpa).

In the sūtra, "The second [portion] belongs to the *pañcāvattin* at the *āghāra* and the *sviṣṭakṛt*," since there is no absence of the word "or" (*vā*) and so forth to refute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), even in the absence of the phrase "of some" (*ekeṣām*), both [positions] are indeed established conclusions (*siddhānta*) according to different recensions (*śākhā*). Having prescribed, "He cuts from the middle," and having censured the cutting from both halves in the passage beginning with "When he cuts from both sides," the text clearly prescribes, "He cuts from the upper half. Thus, because the cutting occurs at the very place of the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offering, the three-fold cutting (*trivada*) of the oblation is accomplished through the two-fold cutting; such is the intention of the Bhāṣya.

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that even for the throwing of the *prastara*, having established that it is purely a directly-contributing (*saṃnipāti*) act, its status as a remotely-contributing (*ārādupakāraka*) act is discussed as a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtācintā*) because of the previous introduction.

As for the fact that the *Bhāṣya* cites the mention of "days" (*ahan*) alone in such scriptural passages as "rites for the gods on an inauspicious day," "these two days are indeed pure and fit for sacrifice," and "on the following day he sacrifices to the deities"—and treats this as the reason [for the term "day"] being used here—that contradicts the intention of the Sūtra-author, who, by stating "the word 'night' is established otherwise," intends [by "otherwise"] both the context of the ritual procedure (*tantra-prakrama*) and the sense of the full twenty-four-hour period (day and night). For both of those [conditions] are equally possible in the case of the word "day" (*ahaḥ*) as well.

The Commentator, however, having reached the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that both [the days] are indeed times for sacrifice—based on the sūtra "The two times" (*Saṃkarṣa* 3.1.2) and such scriptural statements as "On the day when [the moon] is seen both before and after, one should worship; when it has become full, one should sacrifice," and "That which is the earlier full moon is Anumati, that which is the later is Rākā"—established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of this sūtra (located in *Saṃkarṣa* 3.1.16): because there is no direct statement of a duality of time in those [passages], and because of indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "There are twelve full moons in a year," he concluded that each [term] refers to a single time.

As for the alternative interpretation (*varṇaka*) presented in the *Bhāṣya*, that is merely another description of this very same section (*adhikaraṇa*) by means of different sentences, with the sole purpose of demonstrating a variation in the reading of the *siddhānta-sūtra*.

As for what was stated in the Bhāṣya—that because the *atigrāhya* cups also possess the status of being "cups" (*graha*), they necessarily share the same characteristics as other cups, and thus their offering must be accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call alone, rather than having the nature of a double oblation (*dvirhoma*)—that point is to be reconsidered, because it is contradicted by the fact that this rule is inconsistent in the case of the *dadhi-graha* and others, and because at the end of the subsequent section, the author of the Sūtra himself explicitly prescribes the use of the mantra beginning with "For breath, thee! (*prāṇāya tvā*) during the oblation.

Thus, the mind is like a thief in being concealed, and speech is habitually prone to falsehood; however, gold is free from these two defects.

Regarding the two cups, the Aśvābhyagraha and the Ādābhyagraha, which are prescribed in the *Aupāṃśuvākya* section, the commentary—relying on the investigation of principles—concludes that these two cups are indeed optional (kāmya). This is because, compared to the assistance rendered to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the fruit of "overpowering enemies" (*abhrātṛvyatā*) is more immediately presented by the statement, "The Ādābhya cup is for one desiring to overpower; the Aśu cup is for one desiring vigor. This being the position reached, [the conclusion is] that both purposes are served by the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyoga-pṛthaktva*), because otherwise the two statements—“He indeed sacrifices with an oblation who, having taken the *adābhya*, sacrifices to Soma,” and “The life and breath of him depart who takes the *aṃśu*”—would result in meaninglessness.

Just as in the case of the *agnihotra*, although it accomplishes both [purposes] by virtue of being directed toward both an originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) and a fruit-injunction (*phala-vidhi*), its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) is established by the two injunctions within this specific context.

Regarding the *Aṃśu* and *Dābhya*: because even for the *Aṃśu* and *Dābhya*, one must depend upon an investigation into their placement that is consistent with avoiding defects such as *tyādi*, the injunction for the production (*utpatti-vidhi*) of the *Aṃśu* and *Dābhya* occurs precisely there, due to the superior force of the contextual statement (*prākaraṇika-vākya*).
On this basis, they are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇa-vidhi*) within the section on the *Upāṃśu-yājyā-kāṇḍa*.

Since it is possible for those two [the *upāṃśu* and *yajus* mantras] to follow their respective original forms (*prakṛti*) precisely through the dependence on the substance of the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*), it follows that their application occurs at a different stage according to the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: by the principle of "the scriptural mention of both due to abundance" (*bhūyastvena ubhayaśruti*, Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.10), because the injunction of the subordinate qualities (*guṇavidhi*) is contained within the *upāṃśuyāja* sentence itself, the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*) is also located there. And since there is no order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) with respect to other constituent parts (*jāti*) therein, the application of those two occurs precisely at the time of the intermediate performance (*āntarālya-kāla*).

In reality, even if the injunction is accepted as residing in the *aupānuvākya* section itself, since it must be inserted only after [the *sāmidhenīs*] whose sequence is already established by the principle of "But at the end, according to Bādarāyaṇa" (5.1.9.169), it is proper to accept its own sequence in order to avoid the redundancy of its repeated recitation within the context; thus, there is no difference in the result between the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions.

If it is argued that, by the force of the Brāhmaṇa text and the mantra-text, the performance [of the rites] for the Upāṃśu, Antaryāma, and other vessels is already established as complete, then for that very reason, the performance therein is established even in the case of the full-moon sacrifice (pūrṇamāsa).

In fact, the establishment occurs precisely through the Vedic sequence: "Having performed with the Dadhigharma, he performs with the two Ājya offerings"; this is indeed a rule of acquisition (prāptisūtra).
The same applies to the placing of the animal heads.
Saṃkarṣa 313.14.
The duties of the day (*ahardharma*), such as the *sādana* (placing), apply to both the *Aṃśu* and *Dābhya* cups as well.
That which is taught at a distance is not connected with others due to the lack of proximity.

Commentary: That which is taught from afar belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma, such as the *aupasada-anuvākyā-kāṇḍa* [section on the invitatory verses for the Upasad rites], in which the *Aṃśu* and *Dābhya* cups [are mentioned].

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the ritual properties of the cups (graha-dharma) prescribed in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma be performed, or not? What is the prima facie view? They should not be performed, because they are not present [in that context].
Just as, by the statement "he mixes the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa with milk," the mixing applies only to the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa and not to all of them.
In this way, this class of dharmas also belongs only to those [acts] situated within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), not to all [acts].
Or rather: by way of digression, the contradiction between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*) is examined.

In that regard, since the context is set aside, it is understood that the properties of the cups (*graha-dharma*) apply to the cups mentioned in the context; thus, the status of being for the sake of what is taught outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta-arthatva*) is refuted as impossible.
Therefore, he says it is "unconnected" (the Sūtra: *ārāc ciṣṭam*).
Or rather, it is "connected," because that [activity] is for the sake of the ritual act, since the activity is caused by it.
Bhāṣya: Or it is connected with the dharmas.
Such a case would constitute a non-contextual application.
Why? Because syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*).
For if they were performed otherwise, they would not benefit the Jyotiṣṭoma.
It is said:
they are auxiliaries because they serve that purpose— that is, because they serve the purpose of the Jyotiṣṭoma— since they exist for the sake of the two parts.
This duty of the cup belongs to that [cup];
it is for the purpose of the cup and serves as an auxiliary to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
It ought to apply to every cup that assists the Jyotiṣṭoma in whatever way.
Therefore, the ritual properties (*dharmas*) of the *graha* vessels must be performed for the *aṃśu* and *adābhya* vessels as well.

Alternatively—since the context (*prakaraṇa*) is a restrictive factor, these [properties] belong only to that which is the means for the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma; thus, while being excluded from the *surā-graha* and other such vessels, they remain established within the context.

However, for those [vessels] for which even the status of being a non-performance [of the main rite] exists, they ought to possess the ritual properties by virtue of the connection with the direct statement (*vākya-saṃyoga*), according to the same principle as before.
The possession of *dharma* (ritual properties) also applies to the *aṃśu*, *graha*, and others. It is established by specific instruction (*nirdeśāt*).
Commentary: As for what was said—that "one mixes the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup with milk"—that is correct.
In the case of the *śravaṇa* (direct statement), because it is explicitly stated, it sets aside the context (*prakaraṇa*) for the sake of establishing a specific rule;
here, however, the opposite is the case.
There, the context applies to all [days], whereas the direct statement applies to specific ones.

But here, with respect to all the cups (*graha*), there is a direct statement (*vākya*); with respect to specific ones, there is the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, these ritual properties (*dharma*) belong even to those not within the context.
This concludes the section on the Aṃśu and the Ābhya cups (Section 3).

That which is taught as "unconnected" (*anārabhya*) refers to those two cups, the *Aṃśu* and the *Dābhya*; they are not connected with the [cup-related] properties (*dharma*), because the connection belongs only to that which is taught in the immediate context (*saṃnidhāna*). [The reading in the Sūtra here is *itaraiḥ saṃnidhānāt*. As for the verse: "The properties of the cups are not applied to the pair of *Aṃśu* and *Dābhya* when stated outside of a specific context;
either they are performed [there], or—by virtue of the context—the first [option applies], while by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*), the latter [option applies] here."
Therefore, those properties belong to them [the cups].

Bhaṭṭa: When the properties of the cups would result in being purposeless with respect to the essential nature of the cup itself, the term "cup" indicates its status as a means for the *apūrva* (unprecedented spiritual merit) resulting from the practice of the cup, according to the principle of the regulation of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.2, second section), and not its status as a means for the *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

And for this reason, since the means [of the sacrifice] is present [in the mind], and because it is defined as being a means to the previously established [apūrva], one might initially conclude—on the grounds that these rules were taught outside of any specific context—that the ritual duties (dharma) pertain only to those means to the apūrva that are present here. However, this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because other [sacrifices] are permitted here through the context (*prakaraṇa*), even those taught outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*) are brought to mind; and since there is no evidence for restricting the scope of the statement (*vākya-saṃkoca*), they apply to all [sacrifices].

Therefore, by whatever means of knowledge—whether strong or weak—a substance is understood to be a means [to the apūrva], the Vaiyyadhika [rite] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to all such sacrificial oblations (*havis*).

In reality, however, both the *aṃśu* and *adābhya* cups, even though they are mentioned outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), are established by the very same sentence within the context; thus, they are exactly equal [in status].

*Nyāyabindu*: When it is argued that the properties of the cups apply only to those cups mentioned within the specific context (*prākaraṇika*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because there is no difference in their being means for the sacrifice (*yāgasādhanatva*), these properties apply even to those mentioned outside of a specific context.
*Māṇḍana*: "The *aṃśu*, *graha*, and so forth, are first in the archetype (*prakṛti*)."
Śaṅkara says: "The properties of the *grahas* serve all purposes.
This is the section concerning the *aṃśu* and *ādābhya*.
The injunction for the *aṃśu* and *ādābhya* *grahas* applies specifically to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which is taught as independent (*anārabhyādhīta*)."
Because it lacks a material substance, it would be a mere subsidiary of the ritual action.

Bhāṣya: It is not heard in the context of any [specific] ritual that "He indeed sacrifices with an oblation who, having drawn the Adābhya cup, sacrifices to Soma," nor likewise that "The life-span and breath of him depart who draws the Adābhya."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this a separate sacrifice involving the cup (graha), or is it an injunction regarding the cups within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice? What is the prima facie view? That it is a separate sacrifice. Why? Because of its connection with a previously unknown name.
In the original archetype (prakṛti), there is no sacrifice bearing this name,
nor is there any cup (graha) that corresponds to these;
therefore, it is a distinct sacrifice.
But surely neither the substance nor the deity is mentioned.
Let it be that there is no substance or deity; nevertheless, the word "yajati" (he sacrifices) is explicitly present.
Therefore, the conclusion reached is that one performs a distinct ritual act—a sacrifice known by the names *adābhya* and *aṃśu*.
This being the case, we reply: when the name *adābhya* is heard as a mere name, we say that it is the injunction of a specific repetition of the drawing (*graha*) within the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.
Why? Because this secret name belongs first and foremost to the drawing (*graha*), not to the sacrifice, since its connection is direct with the drawing and not mediated by anything else.
Furthermore, the term *aṃśu* is undoubtedly the name of a drawing (*graha*).
Nor does a difference in the cups (graha) entail a difference in the sacrifice (yāga).
Furthermore, neither the material nor the deity is explicitly mentioned, such that the act of taking up the cup (grahati) would constitute a statement containing a sacrifice (yajimat).
As for what was said—that the word "sacrifices" (yajati) is itself directly injunctive—it is simply not possible for it to enjoin a separate ritual action.
For that [term] denotes the sacrifice as enjoined, since there is no distinction;
therefore, by the word "yajati," the Jyotiṣṭoma is understood.
It is thus established that another *graha* (cup) practice, namely the *Aṃśu* and *Dābhya*, is enjoined.
Alternatively, regarding the *Aṃśu* and *Dābhya* cups studied as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*), there is a threefold doubt, similar to the case of the *Ālabhya* and others (2.3.16).
Having refuted those two positions, it is asserted that this is an injunction pertaining to the sacrifice (*yajimatī codanā*).
Furthermore: "The capacity to differentiate is established even in the case of a name that pertains to the subject matter;
how much more so, then, in the case of one not pertaining to the subject matter, where there is no cognition of non-difference at all?"
For this name is not established for anything in the archetypal ritual (*prakṛti*), such that its repetition would necessitate the performance of a distinct action.
Therefore, we consider that within the general injunction of the *graha* offerings, the *jyotiṣṭoma*—which serves as the archetype—is enjoined for the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) and others.
Nor is there any similarity to the case of the calf-offering (*vatsālambha*).

Since the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is directly perceived in one case, and since in the other case a distinctness is postulated through an unerring name (*saṃjñā*), the performance of all the *Jyotiṣṭoma* rites is obtained by means of the verb *gṛhṇāti* (he takes), resulting in the establishment of a connection between the substance and the deity. Therefore, [one might conclude] that this is a different sacrifice. To this, it is replied: [The established conclusion is as follows: Since the root *yajati* is directly perceived in both instances, and since the name is not invariably indicative of a difference in the ritual action, the verb *gṛhṇāti* does not bring about the application of the entire set of *Jyotiṣṭoma* characteristics; rather, it merely indicates the extraction of the Soma juice. Consequently, the connection between the substance and the deity is already established by the original injunction of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. Thus, there is no separate sacrifice. This is the final position.
"That in which only a name is apprehended upon its mention,
being even less substantial than the mere touching of a calf— that is designated as adravyatva (insubstantiality)."

First of all, the deity is indeed remote (*dūraprathā*). [This is so] because, in the case of the statement "he sacrifices for Soma" (*somāya yajate*), a specific sacrifice is already obtained as the subject of the restatement (*anuvāda*); furthermore, since it is heard later, it is logical that this is a restatement of a deity already established by the wording of the mantra—"having taken [the portion] for Soma, *soma svāhā* to Soma"—and thus there is no possibility of it being an injunction of a deity. Therefore, it is said to be remote.
As for the substance (*dravya*) which follows the path of the cup (*graha*), that too is not established by anything;
for a substance cannot be characterized without a genus (*jāti*) and a quality (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, when another [action] is determined by the connection [with the word], there is no substance belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma by which it could be understood that "one takes the Soma.
Nor does the root *gṛh* (to take) deviate from the Jyotiṣṭoma,
because it denotes mere taking in general.
Nor are these two the names of sacrifices, such that they would divide it;

rather, they stand in grammatical apposition with the act of drawing [the cup], as is the case with both of them. Indeed, we ourselves accept that there is a distinction between the acts of drawing in this instance.
And by that much alone, it does not become a different sacrifice.

Furthermore, even when the substance and deity are present, the status of such [acts] as being "possessing a sacrifice" has been refuted in the rule: "And preparatory acts are not injunctions [of a sacrifice]" (2.2.18).
In this case, however, even that [substance and deity] is not found.

Even the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) that occurs in the *adābhya* passage is enjoined by means of an affix whose injunctive force has been transferred [from another injunction], according to the logic of the *revatī-vāravantīya* section (2.2.27).
Therefore, this is simply an injunction for the act of drawing [the cup] (*grahaṇa*) with reference to the sacrifice.
If it is asked, "How is there a connection of the *aṃśu* with the sacrifice?"—if it is replied, "By means of the Jyotiṣṭoma, which is presented through the general term 'draws' (*gṛhṇāti*)."
However, there is a further recitation of these very two [mantras] for the Taittirīyas within the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.9–10).
Since they serve a different purpose elsewhere, they will effect an application to the ritual action (*karmaviniyoga*).
Just as in the case of the two *sādana* mantras...
There is no action of one who is without desire; no such action is seen anywhere here.
Whatever a living being does, all that is the activity of desire.
This is the principle [stated in] Manu 2.4.
By this it is taught that for a person, desire alone is the seed of all objects and the source of all actions and instruments.
Desire is that which causes a man to long for an object—whether seen or heard—even without an investigation into its connection with the means of yoga or the attainment of yoga.
The desire for worldly objects is here denoted by the word *kāma*.
For this very reason, it was said by the Blessed One: "This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of *rajas*;
all-devouring and greatly sinful—know this to be the enemy here."
(Bhagavadgītā 3.37).
Sāhasrī 522.
[§] Furthermore, because it is not something to be produced, there would consequently be a distinction.
The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that, just like the gift of land in the Viśvajit sacrifice, lack of faith (*aśraddhāna*) must also not be practiced.

Consequently, because the gift of cows is prescribed, and since lack of faith is again something that ought not to be done—due to the statement that it is improper to give "maned [animals]" (*na kesariṇo dadāti*)—there would be a distinction.
This distinction consists in the fact that while the giving of cows and other such items is enjoined, the giving of wealth consisting of horses and the like is prohibited.
This is not a case of figurative application (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*).
And in that regard: "Because praises are dependent upon injunctions, figurative application is not [accepted] here;
rather, because the injunction is primary and there is no contradiction, it is postulated."

For that which is being enjoined must be something to be performed (*sautavya*), not something to be praised (*stutya*) as an injunction; furthermore, an injunction pertains to an object not already established by other means. Thus, it does not deviate from its literal meaning. Even if this were to begin as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), then the injunction might perhaps be subordinated to the first cognition; however, this [passage], "The pebbles are smeared," begins as an injunction.

Therefore, if an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not serve the purpose of that which has been specified as a general rule (*sāmānya*), it becomes meaningless and is thus unable to function independently. Furthermore, since the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) is capable of being effective even without an explanatory passage, it is not proper for the latter to perform its function. However, because there is no other recourse, the explanatory passage may speak by the force of the injunction; and while a particular (*viśeṣa*) can indicate a general rule because it is never found apart from it, a general rule cannot indicate a particular because it deviates from it. Therefore, the phrase "vṛttacchadaḥ" is intended to indicate the mere quality of oiliness (*sneha*).

Whether it be a desire or a statement, the rule regarding clarified butter (ghṛta) applies when it resides in a general context; however, in determining the purpose of an oily substance, there is an injunction even without a commendatory passage (stuti).
5|1|9: "If one does not find gold, one should place pebbles smeared with ghee, for ghee is splendor.
This statement occurs in the context of the *Sāvitracayana*; some say it applies to the *Caturhotṛcayana*.

However, even though the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) brings to mind a specific sacrifice, there is no occasion to assume that this remainder restricts the injunction, because the injunction is understood to apply to all cases, and thus—due to the absence of doubt—the logic of the *aktādhikaraṇa* (the section on "smeared [pebbles]") does not apply here.

Bhāṭṭa: [Objection] Since in the *vākyaśeṣa* (concluding explanatory passage) only those sacrifices consisting of a single *stoma* are mentioned, and since it is they alone that are grasped by the word "others," it is appropriate that the injunction regarding the subsequent time applies to them alone, according to the principle of the *aktādhikaraṇa*. [Response] This is not so, because the *vākyaśeṣa* can be explained in another way. 5|1|15:

Regarding the rule "In cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the *vākyaśeṣa*," just as in the case of "One should place the smeared pebbles (*aktāḥ śarkarāḥ*) [on the fire]," the doubtful word *akta* occurring in the opening statement is determined by the word *ghṛta* (clarified butter) found in the *vākyaśeṣa*, and is not sublated—[if you say this, we reply: no.

Here, the conclusion of the injunction as dependent upon corroboration has been shown. For it is established therein that what is doubtful in the injunction is determined by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), but not that what is doubtful at the beginning is [determined] by the conclusion.

Bhaṭṭa: Having prescribed the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) for the purpose of purchasing Soma, it is stated that when she is being led to the place of purchase: "He follows her for six steps; he draws a line with a stick at the seventh step; he offers an oblation of gold in her footprint; then he takes the seventh step with his joined palms so that it does not slip; he should direct the axle toward the east in the *havirdhāna* shed. In this context, the lubrication of the axle (*akṣabhyañjana*) is also a motivator (*prayojaka*) for leading the one-year-old cow, just like the purchase itself, because the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgatva*) is equal in both cases, as in the case of the produced [result].
For, since the dust of the footprints is indicated by that very word in the context of the eye-anointing (*akṣabhyañjana*), they are an auxiliary part of that [anointing].

Furthermore, the fact that the "foot" (*pada*) is defined by the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is understood from the subsequent mention in another scriptural passage, "her seventh step," and thus she too is an auxiliary part of that [foot].
Consequently, because the act of leading—which serves the purpose of the purificatory rite of restriction—is for the sake of both, it must be performed by both.

Nor does the word [for the cow] become a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*) simply because the one-year-old cow is obtained through the act of purchase; for, since the purchase is already established, the injunction of the subsidiary acts—which have the result of making her the "impeller" (*prayojaka*)—is logically consistent with the acceptance of her as such prior to that point. Furthermore, even so, there is no occurrence of the *puroḍāśakapāla* logic (where the term refers back to something already known), because the word [for the cow] itself would necessarily imply the result by its very nature if it were to refer only to the one-year-old cow as qualified by being impelled by the purchase.
Because it is accepted that [the passage] has as its sole purport the nature of the one-year-old cow itself.

This being the position reached, because of the excessive complexity of the injunction (*vidhigaurava*) and the resulting assumption of an unnecessary potency (*śaktikalpanāgaurava*), it is understood that the word "her" (*sā*)—by its very nature of referring back to what precedes—functions as a restatement (*anuvādaka*) of the words in the context (*prakaraṇa*) which it depends upon. Consequently, since it is determined that the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) is subsidiary only to the act of purchase (*kraya*), it follows that even her leading forward (*nayana*), which is a subsidiary of that [purchase], is intended solely for that purpose. Therefore, the anointing of the axle (*akṣabhyañjana*) or the oblation at the footstep (*padahoma*) and so forth are performed for the sake of the action by means of the leading forward of the one-year-old cow prompted by the purchase; they are not themselves the motivators (*prayojaka*) of either the cow or her leading forward.

Therefore, when a one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) being led for the purpose of purchase happens by chance to fall into a pit at the seventh step, she is not led again for the purpose of anointing the axle. Just as the one-year-old cow is not employed again even if the purchase of the axle is omitted, so too for the purpose of anointing the axle, any dust whatsoever must be taken; for when a subordinate element (*guṇa*) is omitted, there is no occasion for the omission of the primary element (*mukhya*).
The *homa*, however, is indeed a *śrāvaṇī* because it is an auxiliary that assists from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*).
As for its performance according to one's capacity, whether it is performed in the *āhavanīya* fire or without any specific substratum—this is another matter.

Nyāyabindu: Having begun with the statement, "He buys [the cow] with a one-year-old heifer" (*ekahāyanyā krīṇāti*), it is further heard: "He steps forward with her footstep after footstep; he takes up the seventh footprint with his joined palms; with that [dust], he should anoint the axle. Since both the purchase and the anointing of the axle are accomplished by the leading of the one-year-old heifer, it might be argued that both are the motivators for that leading. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: because the one-year-old heifer is mentioned specifically for the purpose of the purchase, the leading of her is also for the sake of the purchase as a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for her. As for the anointing of the axle, it subsists upon the dust from the footstep of the one-year-old heifer who is being led for the sake of the purchase; therefore, in the absence of such dust, the task may be performed with any other dust. Thus is the conclusion.
Maṇḍana: "Even the *padakrama* [recitation] is forceful (*ojas*).
12. Śaṅkara: Like Maṇḍana.
Om. Binding with the eyes is the dharma of cattle.
Bhāṣya 3.6.1.8: *Akṣṇayāvaḥ* (diagonally) refers to something ending in *-āv*. Here, *vakrala* denotes a curve; and in this context, it refers to the rivalry between the two opposite corners.
For example, the rope that is joined outside at the *darśa* [sacrifice] is stretched diagonally across the altar (*vedi*), starting from the southwest corner and facing toward the northeast corner.
Therefore, there is even a partial connection to animal sacrifice.
And thus Satyāṣāḍha says: "With the mantra, 'I bind you, O divine oblation, with the noose of Truth,' he fastens [the cord] upon the right foreleg and over the head" (4.1.8).
The meaning of this is that he fastens it with the mantra beginning with "of Truth."
Where? On the right foot, that is, on the front foot.
There are two feet in the front part of the body and two feet in the rear part of the body;
these are both the right and the left.
There, on the right front foot and on the head, there is the binding of the fetters (*pāśapratimoka*).
When the binding of the fetters has been performed upon the body of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) in this manner, the bond becomes imperishable (*akṣaya*).
Who?

"Oṃ, for the sake of imperishability, [he prepares] food consisting of rice-gruel and thread, and for the sake of going to the windless state, he transforms the blue bedding, seat, and food. Bhāṣya 10.3.1.32, 10.4.1.48. Ke. (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad).

Oṃ. Because they are unbroken and so forth, the properties of being unblemished (*amīlāsa*), being whole (*abhūta*), and being desirable (*iṣṭaka*) belong [to the bricks], but they do not belong to the properties of the first layer (*prathamaciti*).
Therefore, those properties exist even in the *citriṇī* and other bricks belonging to the unblemished layers.

Oṃ. The Theory of Non-apprehension (Akhyātivāda). Now, the fact that all cognitions are in accordance with reality (yathārtha) is being established. If it is argued that if all [cognitions] were in accordance with reality, the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous would not be established, we say no.

Just as for you [the Yogācāras], even though there is a specific nature to cognition, some [cognitions] are in accordance with reality while others are not, so too, even while all are in accordance with reality, the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous is logically possible.

If it is argued that the establishment of the distinction [between valid and invalid] follows from the fact that defects in the cause are not sublated, then let the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous be established by that very same principle.

If you argue that for you [the Mīmāṃsakas], there is no sublation because cognition is always in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*), then how is sublation possible even in the case of a particular cognition for you? If you say that it is postulated because we observe a cognition such as "this is not silver" even regarding a particular cognition, then let it be postulated on the grounds of observation alone, even while maintaining that all cognition is in accordance with reality.

However, this is the distinction: for you, [the cognition] is erroneous due to its nature as a cognition; for us, however, it is erroneous due to the sublation of practical activity (*vyavahāra*).
