Therefore, by that very same reason, there is a distinction between what is true and what is false, and by that same reason, there is a distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous; thus, the two positions are equal. Now, if the cognition of silver does not arise with respect to the mother-of-pearl, then how is the inclination toward silver on the mother-of-pearl explained? It is not necessary to maintain that the cognition of silver arises with respect to the mother-of-pearl itself, because the inclination toward silver on the mother-of-pearl occurs simply through the cognition of silver with respect to [what is actually] silver.

If it is argued that there is no activity toward one object based on a cognition of another, that is true; however, it is likewise never observed that a cognition appearing as one thing is produced from something else.
Furthermore, it is not observed here that activity arises even from a cognition that does not correspond to its object.

If it is argued that [the correspondence] is postulated because the occurrence of activity toward silver would otherwise be inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*), then, by that same inexplicability, one should merely postulate that a cognition whose object is one thing serves as the cause for activity toward another; what is the use of the doctrine of "cognition conforming to reality" (*yathārthajñāna*)? If it is maintained that even in the case of a cognition conforming to reality, its status as the cause of activity toward another remains established, then for you [the opponent], the status of a cognition appearing as one thing being produced toward another is exactly the same.

If it is argued that the establishment of this status is achieved through the presence of a defect in the cause and the absence of a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), then let the establishment of status be exactly the same for us as well.
Therefore, all [cognitions] are identical because they otherwise involve a misconception.
The occurrence of activity is established precisely through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the object;
for coreferentiality is not the name of a relation between a property and its locus that is devoid of mutual distinction.

Even in the case of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), the activity "this is silver" arises from the grasping of the universal *rajatatva* (silverness) as residing in a particular object, not from the grasping of a relation.

Therefore, even in other cases where no such relation exists, activity occurs because the grasping of the relation—which consists in the non-apprehension of difference—is accompanied by the recollection of the universal *rajatatva*.

For this very reason, there is no room for the objection that "due to the non-grasping of the distinction [between the remembered and the perceived], simultaneous activity and non-activity would result," because activity proceeds from an uninterrupted manifestation.
Therefore, because it prevents the ongoing worldly practice of treating silver as real, the subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya) is also logically established.

If it is argued that the cognition has the mother-of-pearl as its object because it arises from the application of the sense organ to the mother-of-pearl, [we reply] that even if it is a memory of silver, it is logically consistent with having the form of silver in relation to the intended object.

If it is argued that there would be the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) regarding the dissolution (*lopa*) and so forth [of the object], then why does the cognition of silver not arise for you even in the case of the dissolution and so forth? If it is argued that it is because of the absence of similarity (*sādṛśya*), and if it is further argued that [if there were similarity] there would be the cognition "this is silver," then why is it not recognized as "having mother-of-pearl as its object" when it actually has mother-of-pearl as its object? If it is argued that such recognition does not arise simply due to a defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*), then for us as well, the non-recognition of "that" [as silver] occurs precisely due to a defect in the cause; thus, all these points of inconsistency are exactly the same.

It must be expressed as appearing through the determination of its object (*viṣaya-vyavasthā*), and not as the attainment of fitness for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*), because that would entail the consequence that non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpa*) is without an object.
Nor can it be the previous [state of] unfitness, since that very [state] does not exist.
If it is "appearing," then this very cognition is the determination of the object as it truly is (*yathārtha-nirūpaṇa*).
If that cognition which determines an object as "this" is the object's domain,
then it is established that even in non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka) cognition, the object itself is the specific content of the cognition.
In this case, however, there arises a cognition of silver characterized by its relation to silver as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*).
Otherwise, the cognition of silver would not have the mother-of-pearl as its object.

Therefore, since [your argument] that "it is non-correspondent because it is erroneous and because it is a cause of purposeful activity" is refuted by the contradiction with the very means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*), and since the very designation "cognition of silver" entails the admission that its object is silver, your thesis that its object is mother-of-pearl is sublated by that very [designation].

Furthermore, if it were correspondent, the inference—based on the reasons such as "because it is a cognition" and "because it is a cause of worldly transaction"—would be flawless, as it would establish its non-manifestness [as non-correspondent].

Thus, even when an argument from presumption (*arthāpatti*) is presented, everything remains consistent with reality; therefore, by the very logic previously stated, there is no other way to account for it.
Furthermore, erroneous cognition does not arise merely from the absence of a cause.
If you argue that it arises solely from a defect in the cause, we reply that defects are only causes for the subversion of an effect, not for the production of a different effect.

If it is argued that a sprout of a plantain tree arises from a burnt seed of a mango tree, [we reply] that in that case, there is a complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*). If a defect were also part of the causal complex, then the defect itself would not exist; consequently, the effect would not be as it truly is.

Furthermore, if all cognition were non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārtha*), one would never be attached to anything; moreover, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of unreality, since silver does not exist in the form of mother-of-pearl. Even doubtful cognition (*saṃśaya-jñāna*) possesses correspondence with reality because it takes the form of memory (*smṛti-rūpatva*).
Therefore, it is established that all this cognition is indeed correspondent with reality. (Prābhākara-vivaraṇa, pp. 16–23).

Refutation of the Theory of Non-apprehension (Akhyativada): In cases such as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there is no apprehension of a relation, because there is a lack of evidence for it.

Rather, there is merely a non-apprehension of the non-relation between the two objects of memory and perception—the universal "silver-ness" and the individual substrate; it is not "apprehension otherwise" (anyathākhyāti).
Indeed, this non-apprehension consists precisely in the non-apprehension of the non-relation.
And thus, they say that because knowledge whose object is non-connection (*asaṃsarga*) is the cause of both activity and worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), it is extremely parsimonious (*atilaghvī*).

To this we reply: since there is no decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) between the two qualifiers of a specific cognition—namely, "having non-connection as its object" and "having silver as its qualifier"—there results the cumbersome assumption (*kalpanā-gaurava*) of two separate causal relations (*kāryakāraṇa-bhāva*).

Thus, while the cognition of taskhood (*kāryatā*) is generally the cause of activity, in cases where activity occurs due to an error regarding taskhood, there arises the necessity of postulating two distinct causal relations—due to the lack of a determining factor (*viniigamanāviraha*) regarding the qualifier-qualified relationship between the absence of non-relation as an object and having taskhood as a qualifier.
The same applies to invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).

In a case where there is an apprehension of invalidity (*apramā*)—which is of the nature of an error—consisting in the cognition that "this has the property of being an effect qualified by the absence of knowledge," since that [apprehension] is itself invalid, it lacks the relation of qualifier and qualified between "not having the relation [of the object] as its content" (*saṃsargāviṣayakatva*) and "having the property of being an effect" (*kāryatvaprakārakatva*). Consequently, due to the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), one would have to postulate a causal relationship (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) between these two, which results in excessive complexity (*atigaurava*). Therefore, such a case is not included here; for it is untenable for it to be the cause of the non-occurrence of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
Thus, it is logical that only the apprehension of a cognition qualified by silverness—which is of the nature of a misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*)—is the cause of activity and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that such a view leads to the confusion between error and non-error, because Maitra’s activity would result from the cognition "Caitra possesses the cognition of silver, since he possesses the cognition of [its] being an effect.
This is not a fault, because his error is sublated precisely by the subsequent absence of that conviction;

or because we accept that activity arises either from a cognition of silverness as a qualifier with a momentary delay following the cognition of another's cognition of silverness as a qualifier, or by accepting that activity arises from a cognition that does not have [the other's] cognition as its object.

Alternatively, since the cause for an activity directed toward silver—characterized by the property of being an activity whose object is silver—is the cognition of silver as having the qualifier "silverness" (i.e., a cognition where the objective content of silver is not determined by silverness), there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
Furthermore, "non-inclusion" (*asaṃgrāhyatva*) is not the cause of every activity, for otherwise activity would result at all times.

Rather, in the case of activity produced by valid knowledge (*pramā*), the cause is the certainty regarding that effect and its cause; whereas in the case of activity other than error, it is "non-inclusion. Thus, there is the complexity of postulating such a causal relationship.

For me, however (the Mīmāṃsaka), in every instance of activity, the cause is the certainty regarding that causal factor; thus there is parsimony (*lāghava*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. *Maṇi*, pp. 26–27.
The maxim of the resort to the last resort (*agatikagatinyāya*): *Sāhasī*, 683.

Where no other course exists, even that which is not continuous is accepted; for the acceptance of what is disagreeable is the resort of a person who has no other way. If one traveling by the great road should somehow become stuck, he would then desire to go even by a footpath.
The *padapāṭha* itself is its path.

For, since there is no fault when there is an equal optionality (*tulyavikalpatva*), one [of two options] is resorted to in certain cases according to the maxim of "going where there is no other way" (*agatikagatinyāya*).
How much more so, then, in the case of an unequal optionality regarding the status of authority (*prāmāṇya*) separated by different levels (*kakṣāntarita*)?

174. Immoral conduct (*anācāra*) consists in approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*). (An *agamyā* is a woman who should not be enjoyed, namely the wife of another; approaching her means enjoying her.)
Or.
In the *kayāśubhīya* hymn and others belonging to Agastya, there are exactly eleven *sāmidhenī* verses.
There are fifteen verses seen by Vāmadeva;
there are likewise as many [verses] in Agastya’s *Kayāśubhīya*.
With reference to each of these individually, it is recorded in the scripture: "They should be the *sāmidhenī* verses, as well as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*."

In this regard, because the word "and" (*ca*) makes it clear that all [verses] are to be employed in both cases, the status of being *sāmidhenī* verses belongs to the fifteen [verses] by way of their combination.
Although only four are required for the purpose of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, the application of the fifteen occurs through optionality.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [we reply]: since it is improper for there to be a discrepancy in the injunctions—such as an instruction regarding the whole in one case and an instruction regarding a single part in another—the first and the last [must be used].
Agni: 16. Agni; "Agni cittvā" (Agni, having been perceived), 17. Agni; the Āhavanīya and others:
this [fire] is exhausted; henceforth it is the Gārhapatya—so says the Śruti.

vi. 12 | 16. *Sabhya*: that which exists in an assembly (*sabhā*). The assembly hall (*sabhā*) is the chief house; it is a place where gambling with dice and the adjudication of legal cases take place.
According to the view that [the fire] is established upon a lotus, it is separate.
But according to the view that the *tretā* fire-altar is established, the *āhavanīya* fire alone is to be worshipped.

Some who study the *agnicayana* bring a water-pot for their teacher, while others do not. (Bhāṣya 2.4.2.8, p. 632). [If it is argued: "There may be a difference in ritual action due to a difference in scripture," [we reply: Now, that specific duty (*dharma-viśeṣa*) which has been mentioned for the purpose of acquiring knowledge and so forth, does not assist the ritual action, because of the absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other such means of proof.
Bhāṣya 2.4.2.4:
"Having piled the fire-altar, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī.
(The meaning is that after performing the piling of the fire-altar along with its accompanying rites, the Sautrāmaṇī must be performed.)
Having churned the fire near the sacrificial post (yūpa), he takes [the fire] and offers an oblation.
This occurs in the Jyotiṣṭoma at the set of eleven sacrificial posts (yūpaikādaśinī).
In this context, churning is intended, not proximity.
And the felling of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is a common ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Bhāṣya 1.1.2.3, 26–29. It is heard in scripture regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*): "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn; (a Rathakāra should establish them in the rainy season)."
"That action is for the sake of a purpose" (tat karmārtham) is the accepted position.
Bhāṣya 1.1.3.2: Having established the sacred fires, everyone forms a resolution: "I shall perform the Full-moon and New-moon sacrifices with leaves and leaf-cups."
Bhāṣya 1.1.1.35: From Agni the Ṛgveda was born.
Bhāṣya 3.1.3.2: The designations of Agni are *agni*, *śuci*, *pāvaka*, *dhūmaketu*, *kṛtānu*, *vaiśvānara*, *śāṇḍilya*, and so forth.

Bhāṣya 10.4.2.1–23: Just as the *ādhāna* (consecration) is a subordinate element (*guṇa*) of Agni for the purpose of its refinement (*saṃskāra*), so too the *pavamāna-havis* offerings are subordinate elements of Agni alone.

Bhāṣya 3.1.3.22: The bodies of Agni are forty-three in the Soma sacrifice: the *parṇā*, the *śamitrāḥ*, and those belonging to the *aupayaja* animal sacrifices of the *paśumedha* constitute six; the four *nirmanthyas*; and together with the *āgnīyīya*, there are five *mahāmaya*s. Thus, [the total is] 28 + 6 + 4 + 5 = 43.
This is according to the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
3|2|16. Regarding the fire: [the fire] for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is not [the same as] that for the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other rites;
for that [latter] is prescribed according to the distinctions of the *agnihotra* and so forth (p.
413). The functions of the fire are burning, cooking, and illuminating.
Bhāṣya 8.4.1: "The first oblation belongs to Agni; the second belongs to Prajāpati; [they are] the Sāmidhenī verses.
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 875: Even among the fires, the ritual action is not fixed for all of them by everyone; they are intended for both the archetype (prakṛti) and the modification (vikṛti).

Bhāṣya 3.1.9.39–40: A fault is heard of regarding the removal of the fires outside their proper receptacle, and an expiation is also prescribed. For the Āhavanīya and other fires are consecrated by a specific location; they must not be led elsewhere without their place of sacrifice.
"Verily, he whose consecrated fire goes out is deprived of his senses and his vigor," and so forth.
Śābarabhāṣya 2.2.8, p. 221: The prefix *vi-* in *somaviṛṣyate* is connected with the verb *ṛṣyate*;
the meaning is that it occurs as an alternative (*vikalpe*).
"Apakṣāyati" means that it goes out from its place;
by the word "ādi," there is an inclusion of the expiatory formulas such as "He should collect that [embers]," "This is one for you," and so forth.
(In reality, however, "apakṣāyati" means it cools down, becomes extinguished, or is destroyed.)
And thus, the statement regarding the extinguishing [of the fires] is not relevant to the present topic, because its purpose is to describe the defects arising from the destruction of the fire.
(Ke.
At the concluding rite (*paridhānīya-karma*), the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the fires and the sacrificial vessels consists of depositing them upon the body of the sacrificer.

Bhāṣya 1.1.3.13–44.42, 44: When the fire has gone out during the course of a ritual, the oblations intended for the *laukika* (worldly) fire are not interrupted; rather, they are performed in the *laukika* fire, and not in the *śrauta* (Vedic) fire.
Su. p. 782: The initiation rite (*upanayana-homa*) is performed in the *laukika* fire, but not in the *śrauta* fire. Vi. [Viṣṇu-smṛti].

6|8|2. The sacrifice of the Niṣāda chief is performed in the common (laukika) fire. 6|8|3. For a religious student (brahmacārin) who has broken his vow of chastity (avakīrṇin), there is an expiatory animal sacrifice in the common fire.
VI.8.4. This shows the absence of meat-cooking in the Vaihārika fires;
except for the animal sacrifice (paśubandha), one avoids touching meat near the Vaihārika fires.
Bhāṣya 1.2.1: 15. Without the connection to a deity, the offering of the oblation into the fire is not established.

Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1521: The Pavamāna fires are for the purpose of consecrating the fire; for the Pavamāna fires are indeed for the sake of the fire. Bhāṣya 3.6.4.12: It has been stated that those Pavamāna fires are for the purpose of consecrating the fire.
Bhāṣya 3.6.6.13: The *sāmidhenī* mantras are those which kindle and illuminate the fire.
For the purpose of kindling the fire, there are eighteen large and long fuel-sticks (*samidh*) beginning with ten. Ke. (Kaiyaṭa).

Regarding the sūtra *agnisvakālatvāt* (3.1.9.139): by this [sūtra], it is stated that the fires will serve all purposes (*sarvārtha*), and thus they possess the quality of being for all purposes (*sarvārthatva*) because of their own time (*svakālatvāt*).
Furthermore, "because of their own time" means because of their independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to the knowledge [of the ritual] and so forth. Or.
On page 1039, under the sūtra *agnayaśca svakālatvāt*, it is stated that the fires (*agni*) serve the purpose of both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*).

On page 1528 of the *Sūtra* commentary: for whatever has a transferred (*ātideśika*) means of operation (*dvāra*) in the modification, only that which is studied outside the context of the commencement (*anārambhādhīta*) goes to the archetype, as in the case of the *parṇatā* (being made of *parṇa*-wood) and so forth. For in that case, the means of operation, namely the *juhū* ladle, is [established] in the modification by way of transfer (*atideśataḥ*).

Since the state of being made of *parṇa* wood is already established by the excellence of the ten [sacrificial ladles], the re-enjoining of *parṇatā*—though stated twice—is not redundant because the door [of application] is one of extension (*atideśika*); however, since there is no such redundancy here, the attainment of the *āhavanīya* fire occurs precisely through direct injunction (*upadeśataḥ*). This is the principle of the locus [known as] "the fires" (*agnayaḥ*).

*Soma*, 3.4.18, p. 239. In the section *agnayaśca svakālatvāt* (3.1.9.39)—concerning the form of the *antarāgārbhīya*—it was not accepted that the root *juhoti* found in the sentence regarding the *āhavanīya* fire applies universally to all injunctions for oblations (*sarvahomavidhi*). Rather, it was accepted as applying only to those *āman-homa*s and others that are taught specifically in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) and are not merely extended by analogy (*atideśa*).
*Rasāyana*, p. 187.
The mantra "agnim citvā" is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, not an auxiliary of the *citi*.

Regarding the injunction "Having built the fire-altar (agni-cit), one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī," because there is no temporal connection [between the two acts], the Pavamāna oblations—which are auxiliary (ārādupakāraka) rites—are also seen to have the nature of substances (dravya), as they possess the character of being materials for the Agnihotra.

Regarding the statement, "Having built the Śyenaciti, one desiring heaven [should perform the sacrifice]," when it is argued that—due to the requirement of a ritual action based on a specific result—the Sautrāmaṇī must be a subsidiary part of that very [action], it is established by the principle (Nyāya 2.3.1.23) that because the two proximate acts of preparing the altar and piling the fire have no requirement for direct-contributing subsidiaries (*ārādupakāraka*), they are connected to the sacrifice itself; thus, like the *Sāgnicitya* sacrifice, since it has the act of piling (*cinoti*) as its purpose, the Sautrāmaṇī is a subsidiary of the sacrifice and must be performed immediately after the sacrifice.
Saṃkarṣa 1.1.15:
The giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-dāna*) in the Agnicayana is a subsidiary of the sacrifice.

Regarding the scriptural injunction, "Because of the nature of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, one should accomplish [the goal] by means of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this accomplishment through fees—just like the granting of boons—is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the piling of the fire-altar (*cayana*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Since sacrificial fees serve the purpose of hiring (as wages) and thus lack intrinsic spiritual purpose (*anarthatva*), and since they are employed for the performance of the ritual procedure (*prayoga-prayuktatva*) and possess a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), they are an auxiliary part of the sacrifice itself.
(Saṃkarṣa 1.1.17).
Furthermore, when it is said, "Bring Agni for the *agnihotra*," the "Agni" referred to is other than the *āhavanīya* fire.

Having heard the scriptural statement, "When he brings [Agni] for the office of the Hotṛ, he brings Sviṣṭakṛt," one understands that the fire being kindled for the purpose of the Hotṛ is indeed Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, who possesses the quality of being Sviṣṭakṛt and whose nature is that of the deity of the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. Furthermore, from another scriptural passage, "By what he offers in the Āhavanīya, by that this fire of his becomes pleased," it follows that through connection with the oblation, [Agni] becomes pleased; thus, the identity of Sviṣṭakṛt with the Āhavanīya fire itself is established. Consequently, both conditions—the single performance of the act and its purposefulness—are fulfilled.

And since the distinction among the fires based on their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is easily established, [the author] says: "The *āhavanīya* fire itself is the *sviṣṭakṛt* fire," according to the scriptural text (*śruti*).
Consequently, in the *nigada* formula "Bring the gods for the *agnihotra*," there is a modification (*ūha*) of the word "gods" (*apaḥ*).

As for the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "Because the two deities are designated as the carriers of the oblation (*havyavāhana*), they are designated by the term *sviṣṭakṛt*; therefore, when the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is made with the entire oblation, there is an omission of the invocation of the deities."

That is not so; for the invocation of the respective deities is prompted solely by the names of the respective sacrifices. Thus, even when the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is omitted, since there is no omission of the respective sacrifice, the invocation of the deity cannot be omitted. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because of the connection with the prefix *abhi*, the root *iṣ* (from which *iṣitaḥ* is derived) signifies "desire. Although the status of the agent who performs the action of "entering" (*praveśana*)—as determined in the *triṣṭup* verse—is restricted to the *āhavanīya* fire alone, nevertheless, due to the identity of the *sviṣṭakṛt* derived from the root *yaj* (with the prefix *su-*), one must accept a distinction based on limiting conditions (*aupādhika-bheda*) for that which is essentially one. Since no limiting condition is heard of that would sustain both [the *āhavanīya* and the *sviṣṭakṛt*] simultaneously, the *āhavanīya* fire itself is the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
Saṃkarṣa 4.1.9:
The fire—namely the Āhavanīya and others—is for the purpose of all sacrifices and rituals;
and the fires [are established] because they have their own specific times.
This is a portion of the sūtra: "(They [the fires] are for all purposes: because the fire employed [for one purpose] belongs to its own time)" (3.1.9.39).

Alternatively—those fires such as the Āhavanīya and others, their being for all purposes is indeed irrelevant; nor is it mentioned by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*), because even the reason of "belonging to its own time" is incapable [of proving it].
Furthermore, there is no consideration of a counter-argument regarding either the thesis or the reason.

And if "being for all purposes" is asserted with reference to worldly activities, then, since it has already been determined in the discussion of the statement, "The sacrificial hall should accomplish the purpose of worldly people because of its capacity" (1.2.1.1), followed by, "Or rather, it should be for Vedic purposes because of the specific mention" (1.2.1.3), this matter need not be further deliberated upon.

As for the claim that the fire-rituals (*agnikārya*) prescribed by the Vedas serve all purposes for both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*), this too need not be further deliberated upon, as it has already been settled by the statements: "In a case of doubt, it should be the worldly one, for all this [is worldly]" (7.3.1.30), "Not the Vedic one, because of the lack of specific direction" (31), and "Likewise, there is an accumulation of these because of their equality" (32).
This is refuted by the very words of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) found in the Bhāṣya.
Therefore, it is explained thus: "The opponent's position that the fires have a universal purpose (*sarvārthatva*) was never even established."

What then? It is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) itself that is stated here through a division of the sūtra’s wording, following the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) inferred by means of the logic set forth in the *adhikaraṇāntara* sūtra (3.6.1.2).
Nor is this universal applicability dependent upon the requirement for fire.
What then? [It is] with reference to the conceptualization of the original nature (*prakṛti*).

In that regard, by means of the scriptural tradition concerning what is not specifically commenced (*anārabhya-adhīta*), [the author] constructs the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttara-pakṣa*) regarding the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) itself:
"The fire" refers to the *āhavanīya* and other such fires. 18.
[The two views are] true; [the question is: do the Āhavanīya and other fires serve the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*), or rather, do they serve all purposes?

In this regard, since it has been argued that "that serves the purpose of the archetype, just as in the case of others who maintain the theory of commencement" (3.6.154) and "or [they belong] to the archetype because of being mentioned twice" (3.6.152), the following is stated:
these [fires] serve all purposes; they should serve the purposes of both the archetype and the ectype (*vikṛti*).

Why? Because [the fire] flows [continuously], just as at its own time; this has been explained under the sūtra: "Or rather, it is for all purposes, because the installation has its own specific time" (3.6.15).
However, this status of being for all purposes cannot be understood as applying to every single case.
"In those cases where the door is turned away, there too a dependence exists;
entities reach such a state and are not independent in any way whatsoever."
For those *davihoma* offerings whose specific forms are enjoined by the scripture,
the *āhavanīya* fire must be used in those sacrifices alone, because no other injunction applies to them.
It is heard in the scripture: "That which is an oblation is for the Āhavanīya fire. It does not say, "They should sacrifice.

Therefore, one must necessarily wait for the injunction regarding the Āhavanīya until the door [of its application] is reached through extension (*atideśa*), as in the cases: "He offers in a square vessel," "In that he offers the *graha* cups," and "In that he offers the *camasa* vessels."

"Therefore, there would be a certainty here [regarding the *āhavanīya*] either through extension (*atideśa*) from the archetype (*prakṛti*) along with that [archetype], or because of the fault of double-statement (*dviruktatva*)."
And likewise, in the rule "tāsāmadhiḥ prayātavat" (3.6.166), the fact that [the term] functions as the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyarthatva*) is shown as if it were already established.

Similarly, because the modified *puroḍāśa* cakes have the oblation (*havis*) heard directly in the text, there is no need for the *gārhapatya* fire; thus, the hearing of the word *gārhapatya* must be understood as obtained through extension from the archetype (*prakṛti*). Having concluded the discussion regarding the fires (*agni*), the subsequent sūtra is commenced concerning the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
"The meaning of the base [word] should be external for all purposes, just as in the case of the *parṇa* [leaf].
The principle of the *parṇa* applies to what is extended by analogy (*atidiṣṭa*), but when it is directly enjoined (*upadiṣṭa*), it is all-pervading."

If it is argued that— just as the injunction regarding the *parṇa* (the palāśa tree), namely "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* hears no evil report," has the ladle as its primary purpose (*prakṛtyartha*), so too, since the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not for the sake of a specific ritual result, the consecrated *āhavanīya* fire is the primary purpose—
this is not so, because of the disparity between the two cases. In the sentence concerning the *parṇa*, the entry of the *parṇa*-quality into the ritual depends upon the *juhū* as its medium.
And that *juhū* ladle, being prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) to all modifications (*vikṛti*).
In the entry into the seasons for the sake of the *āhavanīya* fire, the oblation (*homa*) is the gateway;
and since that too is prescribed in the archetype, it is extended to the modification, such as the *ariṣṭha*-oblations and others for progeny.

In such a case, by the sentence "He offers in the Āhavanīya," the fire is prescribed only for the archetype (*prakṛti*); however, in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is extended (*atidiśyate*) along with the oblation. Therefore, the *parṇa*-rule applies there.

But as for the oblation that is specifically enjoined in the modified sacrifice—such as the *āman-homas* in the *Sāṃgrahaṇī* and others—since the oblation, which serves as the means (*dvāra*), is being enjoined in the modified sacrifice, the end (*dvārin*) cannot be determined by the sentence even in the modified sacrifice, just as in the archetype.
Therefore, the *barhis* grass is for all purposes.

Bhaṭṭa: The fires such as the Āhavanīya and others are enjoined by statements taught in connection with the *anārambha* [section] as restatements (*anuvāda*) of the *homa* and other rites, according to the logic of the *parṇatā* [wooden ladle]; thus, they serve only the purpose of the *prakṛti* (archetypal) *homas*.

In the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice), however, those very *homas* and other rites are obtained through extension (*atideśa*). Since there is a discrepancy regarding the time of their occurrence, the fault of *dviruktatva* (redundancy) is quite evident.

Even those [fires] such as the *āmanahomādi* which are unprecedented (*apūrva*), they too cannot be established as constituent parts (*aṅga*) without a connection to a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*); and since the modified sacrifice first requires the assumption of an extended application (*atideśa*) in order to adopt constituent parts whose auxiliary functions (*upakāra*) are already established, this applies to all cases. Furthermore, that [extended application] is impossible without the attainment of the *āhavanīya* fire in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*). Therefore, in their case as well, there is "double-stated-ness" (*dviruktatva*). Consequently, the *āhavanīya* fire is not obtained in them through direct injunction (*upadeśa*), nor is it obtained through extended application for the purpose of spreading grass in the sacrificial post-hole (*yūpāvaṭa*).

Therefore, since it follows that [the fires] exist even without a specific locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it is true that for those [rites] obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), there is an instruction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth.

However, in the case of new rites (*apūrva*), because this [instruction] is not taught in connection with the commencement [of the rite], its attainment is established only through direct instruction.

For the *āmanahoma* and other such elements do not constitute subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) without a connection to a modified rite (*vikṛti*); for in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the verbal comprehension reaches its conclusion even by taking the general "desired result" (*iṣṭasāmānya*) as the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*).
The fire-altar (agni) is that of the Uttaravedi (19), because the construction of the fire-altar is logically established as an injunction for the Āhavanīya fire by way of reference to it;
therefore, those [fires] also serve all purposes.

(From here on, "to the north of the sacrificial post," etc. Śaṅkara: [This refers to] those for whom the fires have been established in the same manner. The fire on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*) is only a single part of the *śālāmukhīya* fire, not the whole of it.

It is traditionally taught (*samāmnātam*) that "they lead forward the fire first" (*prāg agniṃ praṇayanti*). Because this refers to a specific leading forward (*praṇayana*), it applies to every *āhavanīya* fire, including that on the northern altar (*auttaravedika*); for from this point onward, that very fire serves as the locus for all oblations by virtue of being the *āhavanīya*. This is because the Śruti mentions the *āhavanīya* as the destination (*apādāna*). And since there is no other [destination] when it is absent, there is no distinction here. For this very reason, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "that which was in front becomes behind," and the statement, "he follows the former fire," etc., using the terms "former" and "latter," is consistent with the many instances involving the *Śālāmukhīya* and the *Āhavanīya*.
Saṃkarṣa 3.2.19:
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the fire [is consecrated] at its conclusion; thus it would be worldly [in nature], not at the conclusion of the Dīkṣaṇīyā.

Although the Āhavanīya fire exists after the conclusion of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, it follows from the aforementioned reasoning that it is merely worldly (*laukika*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because of the scriptural statement, "The deities, having taken possession of these [fires], support the sacrificer," the consecration (*saṃskāra*) consisting in the appropriation of all the deities of the Soma sacrifice has not yet ceased; therefore, upon its cessation, since that [appropriation] also ceases, the fire must be maintained until the very end by re-establishing it (*agnimādhiyaiva*). In reality, however, since the *dīkṣā* belongs to the Soma sacrifice, its cessation is also for the sake of that [Soma sacrifice]; thus, the fires become worldly only at the conclusion of the Soma sacrifice, not at the completion of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.

For this very reason, the Śruti text—"In the Veda, the wife does not speak; the sacrifice does not pass him by, for the Soma-sacrifice is as if it has not yet concluded"—indicates through the prohibition of the *abhyavandana* at the conclusion of the Soma that the fire possesses a truly transcendental (*alaukika*) nature. Furthermore, even during times when no ritual act is being performed, the observation of the *Āhavanīya* fire is justified by the rule: "Having brought the sacrificial food (*vrata*) across behind the *Āhavanīya*, he hands it over. In the case of the *Prāyaṇīya* and other such rites, there is no need for a fresh kindling (*punar-praṇayana*), as the purpose is already accomplished through the principle of *prasaṅga* (extended application).
Saṃkarṣa 3.2.20:
Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is indeed a specific deity who presides over the Gārhapatya fire.

It might be argued that, being mixed with the nature of the *āhavanīya*, it would be a certain fire whose very form is that of a deity, since the capacity for the *sviṣṭakṛt* function belongs to the deity itself. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhānta is as follows]: because of the scriptural statement, "The *gārhapatya* is the *sviṣṭakṛt*," and because the status of *sviṣṭakṛt* is possible for it through its connection with several oblations, the *sviṣṭakṛt* is indeed a specific deity who resides within the *gārhapatya* fire.
(Saṃkarṣa 4.2.10).

Regarding the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*): the general nature of the non-piling is illustrated here. In the *agniṣṭoma* and other rites, they perform the piling of bricks upon the northern altar (*uttaravedi*).
And that, having been spread out like a hawk swooping down upon its prey, they generally fashion into the shape of a hawk (*śyena*).
Furthermore, many other [fire-altars] shaped like tortoises are mentioned in the Veda.
In that regard, in the first application of the piling (cayana), there are one thousand bricks of various shapes, and the sacrificial altar (vedi) is knee-deep.

Therein, there are five bundles of grass (prastaras) and, for each subsequent layer, a layer of earth (purīṣa); thus, with five layers of earth, the piling is performed as a five-layered structure (pañcacitika).
Two hundred bricks are laid down for each layer (*prastara*).
In the practice of the second piling (*cayana*), there are two thousand bricks.
With two layers and one filling of earth (*purīṣa*), this constitutes one layer; in this manner, there are exactly five layers.
Thus, there are ten *prastara* layers and five *purīṣa* layers; the altar (*vedi*) is knee-high.
But in the third performance, there are three thousand bricks, fifteen *prastara* layers, five *purīṣa* layers, and the altar is face-high.
In that case, three *prastara* layers and one *purīṣa* constitute one layer (*citi*); thus, there are five layers in total.
"The layer ends with the loose soil"—this is the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*).
There are also performances [of this rite] even on the fourth day; in that case, the measurement of the bricks would indeed be greater and greater.

Then, having chosen the eight officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and having offered the *sāvitra* oblation as well as certain other offerings, they take up the fire, seize the horse and the donkey, and go to the place where the nails are to be cut.

Having dug up other earth, they wrap it in a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), place it upon the back of a donkey, and bring it; the horse, however, [does so] by treading upon the ground and so forth.

Having mixed powdered bricks, potsherds, bamboo, and the like with the earth, moistened it with water, and formed it into a lump, they bake a square hearth (*ukhā*) for the purpose of establishing the fire.
Then, they prepare the five animal heads—of a man, a horse, a bull, a ram, and a goat.

Having recited the *sāmidhenī* verses, having performed the pouring of the clarified butter (*ājyāghāra*), and having performed the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, he offers twelve *dīkṣā* oblations—six pertaining to the *adhvara* and six pertaining to the fire (*agni*)—in accordance with the Śruti.
Then, by means of heating the aforementioned *ukhā*, he produces the fire named *ukhya*.
Having placed fuel sticks (*samidh*) therein, he places the *ukhā* containing the fire upon the disciple.
Having fastened that distinguished golden ornament (*rukma*) on his chest, he fastens the *śikhya* [ornament] upon his shoulder.
Having performed the *viṣṇukrama* steps and so forth, he removes the *śikhya* from his neck and places it upon the throne (*āsandi*).
Then follow the six initiations (*dīkṣā*).
They prepare the bricks;
they bake them by means of a cover.
Then, having designated [the spot] as the *gārhapatya*, he pours the fire that has been raised over it down upon it.
Then, at a distance in the southwestern direction, he lays down three Nairṛta bricks;
upon them, the empty space and so forth. This is the second Agnicayana. This is the Agnicayana.
The piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana) 21. [He] piles the fire-altar. He places [the brick] with [the verse]:
"The one who dwells within, the gatherer... [and so on] regarding the Gārhapatya fire.

An investigation into whether the construction of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) possesses fruit or is fruitless follows the *parṇamayī-adhikaraṇa*. Having performed the preceding and subsequent *pravargya* and *upasad* rites, one approaches [the altar].

The discussion regarding whether [the ritual] is original (*prākṛta*) or modified (*vaikṛta*) is established in the section concerning the *agni-atigrāhya* offerings. First, the primary piling (*cayana*) must be performed;
therein, at the beginning, on the site of the piling.
The investigation into permanence and impermanence is established by the *godohana* example in the [Pūrva Mīmāṃsā] section;
[it is said]: "With a plough drawn by six oxen, he tills the earth;
there are seven furrows in the fields."
The discussion concerning the modification of the altar (*vedi*) occurs in the second chapter on transference (*saṃkrama*).
It is established [in the following manner]: "In the fourth [chapter], regarding the phrase 'wild plants for one who does not plow,' he offers the herbs" (2.1.26).
This is settled.
Su. Pṛ. 149. In the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana):
having sprinkled [the materials], he piles together the unbroken blades of grass (apūri-leṣṭhāni) of the plants;
then the āti—
The Sāvitra oblations are to be performed prior to the Dīkṣaṇīyā; [the sacrificer] performs the rites beginning with the Bhāṣika. (Bhāṣya 5.2.1)

Then, at the time of the piling (*cayana*), in the section concerning the *dvaitika* [sacrifice] under the rule *svartha-śabdena* (Pāṇini 2.3.188), the initial statement is rendered self-sufficient; thus, having set aside the view that the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) serves to provide the deity, and by accepting that the word *bṛhaspati* refers to the Brāhmaṇas, it is determined—on the grounds of its being a eulogy—that the purpose is the praise of wild rice (*nīvāra*).
As for the "Parākrama" [section], it is heard in scripture: "The oblation consists of wild rice (*naivāraścaruḥ*)" and "Because he piles this brick."

In this matter, when considering whether the purpose of the *caru* is for sacrifice—such that what remains after performing the sacrifice must be used for piling—or whether it is for the purpose of piling itself, the conclusion is that this is solely for the purpose of piling, not for sacrifice.
(Bhāṣya 2.3.18). Many mantras recited for the purpose of shaving have been mentioned.

In the ritual application (*prayoga*), however, the number fourteen is prescribed by the statement "it occurs with fourteen. That number is not to be understood as starting from the first mantra; rather, having set aside the sequence according to the context, one may begin either at the end or at the beginning of the first mantra according to one's own will, until it is complete.
Whether the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) has been performed or not, the covering (*āvaraṇa*) of the various seed-syllables (*bīja*) is carried out.
In this regard, these are the mantras:

Vi. 10.5.6. Regarding the mantras recited in the *agnicayana* for the purpose of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) and for the purpose of shaving (*vapana*), when their number is prescribed in the scripture, they are to be employed without restriction; it is not only the first ones that are used.
This is the section concerning the exception to the omission of others.
Bhāṣya 10.1.14: "There are five layers (*citayaḥ*). Here, by the word *citi*, the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is denoted from one perspective, not the entire altar (*vedi*).

Saṃkarṣa 2.1.17: "'He places [the bricks] as the vital breath (*prāṇa-bhūta*). Here, the laying down of the bricks is enjoined by way of restating the mantra obtained through indicative power (*liṅga*) and grammatical derivation (*karaṇa*). And although the term 'vital breath' occurs only in the first mantra, nevertheless all the mantras associated with it are indicated by the expression 'vital breath'."
VI. 14|1|18: The bricks are to be laid down with all the mantras as recited, and not with the mantra "Fill the world, fill the gap" alone.
Those mantras which are additional are employed in other ritual applications.

Saṃkarṣa 2.1.15: Filling the deficiency. When the mantras commenced for a particular altar (citi) have been completed, the laying down of bricks must be performed by repeating the two mantras, "Fill the world, fill the gap" (*lokaṃ pṛṇa chidraṃ pṛṇa*), and not merely by repeating those [original] mantras that were first commenced. 2.1.16: When there is a repetition of the *lokam-pṛṇā* [verse], there is also a repetition of its mantra.
Where there is a plurality of meanings in the mantra, there its repetition occurs.

Just as in the case of the *lokampūṇā* brick (*agni*), the bricks are taught independently (*anārabhyādhīta*). This is a defect of the fire-altar construction (*agnicayana*), not a defect of the piling itself (*citidoṣa*). *Bhāṣya* 11.4.12.
Therefore, they should be placed all at once, and not for each individual layer (citi).
5.3.16–16. The characteristics of bricks—the measures—must be performed for all bricks except those that serve as the *citriṇī*.
3.6.12.35. Since the *citriṇī* is not an integral part (*anaṅga*) of the piling (*cayana*), there is no repetition [of its placement].
VI. 5|1|6: Satyāṣāḍha has stated that the *bhūteṣṭakās* are to be laid down in the third layer (*citau*).
"To the Earth, Svāhā!"—thus [are] the twelve *bhūteṣṭakās* (12|1|17). [Question: Among the bricks prescribed in the Brāhmaṇa, where is their placement? [Answer: In the middle layer (*madhyamacitau*).

VI.5.1.7: "He lays down [bricks] connected with creation. Mantras associated with the act of creating are expressed by the term "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*), such as "Brahman was created," "the beings were created," and so forth.
And thus, this word "sṛṣṭi" is a mantra-recitation, not an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi);
rather, it is an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
Here, by way of restating the mantras obtained through their indicative power (liṅga) and their instrumental function, the placing of the iṣṭakās is enjoined.

1|4|17: The properties of bricks (*iṣṭakā*) should not be performed in the *raudra* *gāvīdhuka* oblation nor in the *sarvopadha* [oblation], because the placing of all the bricks (*sarvopadhāpana*) is prescribed for the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) independently (*anārabhya*), and because the depositing of the oblation (*carunidhāna*) is performed only at its completion; thus, there is an absence of that specific requirement. Saṃkarṣa. 2|1|10: The oblations of the *devasū* sacrifice are heard of in relation to the fire: "He offers the *puroḍāśa* of the *agnīṣomīya* [sacrifice] and then offers the oblations of the *devasū*. In that case, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the animal *puroḍāśa* must be performed [and therefore, by extension, the procedure applies to the subsequent offerings].

Bhāṣya 12.1.2 (1–8): Regarding the performance of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) in the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicaya*), it is said: "This Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed piled for the sake of the heavenly world; the set of eleven [stakes] (*ekādaśinī*) belongs to the fire. If one were to fix the set of eleven stakes in the fire, he would thereby exclude himself from the heavenly world by means of the thunderbolt (*vajra*). If he were not to fix them, he would ruin the animals with the *svaru* stakes. He fixes a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*); thus he does not exclude himself from the heavenly world by the thunderbolt, nor does he ruin the animals with the *svaru* stakes. Therefore, eleven animals are to be bound to a single post.
In that case, if the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is accepted, the arrangement must be performed for each individual animal.
In the Siddhānta, there is indeed a difference of opinion. [The Bhāṣya on Jaimini Sūtra 4.4.24 states: "The duties of one who has built the fire-altar (*agnicit*):

Having built the fire-altar, he should not descend toward anyone for a year (he should not rise from his position); the fire-altar does not rain upon him as long as he lives, nor should he run; he should not approach women (but he may approach his lawful wife); having built it a second time, he should not approach the wife of another; having built it a third time, he should not approach any woman at all, or he may approach his own wife.
Satyāṣāḍha (Śrautasūtra 12.1.15–17) states that if the fire-altar is for the sake of specific desired qualities (*guṇakāma*), then there is the undertaking of these observances.

*Duṣa*. 10|8|11|127. The *citi* (altar-pile) is fivefold and occasional (*naimittikī*). Following the construction of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), when the occasion of instability (*apratiṣṭhā*) arises, there is only one [additional pile] for the sake of stability (*aṣṭārthā*). Depending on the specific application, the *citi* is prescribed either as part of the *agnicayana* or for the purpose of the fruit of stability. Bhāṣya 4|4|3: "The sixth *citi*—the year indeed establishes him who, having piled the fire-altar, does not find stability. There are five previous *citis*; then he piles the sixth *citi*. This refers to the fire-altar construction (*agnicayana*) performed specifically during the *upasad* days. 23. Regarding that which pertains to the fire-altar construction...

Thus, what is stated in the Śruti is not obligatory (nitya), but rather occasional (naimittika) due to the absence of a firm foundation. And so, while the five altars (citayaḥ) are obligatory and the fifth altar is also obligatory, the fire-altar consisting of five altars must be constructed. (Vi. 4.4.7)

[The mixing of the fires] occurs only during the Upasad days, and not prior to them. Since the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa texts read the section on the piling (cayana) later [than the Upasads], one might conclude that the mixing of the fires should take place before the Upasads. However, this being the prima facie view, the established conclusion is as follows: "On the day one intends to pile the fire, on that very day one should mix the fires. Because this injunction ordains the mixing (*samāsa*) of the fires on the same day as the Upasads—which are performed in a single day—the mixing must indeed take place during the Upasad days. (Saṃkarṣa 2.1.27)
There is no fixed rule that the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana) must be performed exactly three times, since it is possible to perform it on the fourth day as well.

It should be piled up exactly three times and not more than that, because the verses beginning with "He should pile it knee-high" prescribe the measurements for the piling only within the limits of the *svandila* (the sacrificial mound), and thus do not provide for more. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: it may be piled many times at will. For if those [verses] were intended as a restrictive rule (*parisaṃkhyā*) limiting the food [to three meals], it would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, those injunctions can be understood as merely prescribing a quality (*guṇa*) contingent upon the first meal. Moreover, there are indeed four types of meals, so that the following texts may remain meaningful: "Each subsequent one is greater," "Having piled the immediate [fire], one should not pile a smaller one," and "One desiring heaven should pile the largest [fire]. Thus, there are four meals.
Saṃkarṣa 2.1.30:

There is no permanent maintenance of the fire in the ukhā (cauldron) that has entered into the construction of the fire-altar. If there were permanent maintenance, there would be an option; for a prohibition cannot occur without a reason.
The Commentary states: Regarding that very *ukhya* fire, there is this consideration: whether it should be maintained perpetually or not, or whether it should not be maintained at all.
To this, it is replied:
regarding perpetual maintenance, there is an option; it may either be maintained or not.
Why? Because a prohibition cannot occur without cause.

There is indeed a prohibition regarding the maintaining [of the fire]: "One should not rekindle; if one rekindles, he produces a rival for himself"—so says the Śruti. (Note: Regarding the forms *pratisamidhyet* and *samidhyet*, there is another reading, *saminvīta*.)
And a prohibition becomes meaningful only when there is a possibility [of the action occurring].
For example, the prohibitions "one must not go" and "one must not eat" are applicable only when there is a possibility of going or eating.

Since such a possibility cannot arise without another scriptural injunction, an injunction enjoining the constant wearing [of the sacred thread] is inferred; thus there is an attainment [of the practice], and through the prohibition, its cessation [is established].
Therefore, it is not an option.
Because of its constant maintenance, there is a prohibition for one whose prosperity has departed.
The Commentary states: if at some time there were no possibility [of application] through direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), then another [text] might be inferred there.

However, there is an incidental Vedic injunction regarding the perpetual maintenance [of the fire] for one whose prosperity has departed: "The *āhnīya* fire belongs to one whose prosperity has departed.
Since the *āhnīya* fire is established as a permanent fixture, the perpetual maintenance of the *ukhya* fire also follows by implication;
therefore, the scripture prescribes it in that very manner.
Therefore, there is an inference from another scriptural passage.
Consequently, since there is no injunction for perpetual maintenance and because there would be an absence of purpose, there should be non-maintenance.

Having concluded the discussion concerning the fire intended for optional rites (*kāmyāgni*), he begins again with the perpetual fire (*nityāgni*) and considers whether it belongs to the primary [fire] as a matter of course.

Regarding the phrase "by one who has gone to the Abhricayana," the fact that it is a partial prohibition (paryudāsa) must be established by somehow bringing to mind a general statement concerning the locus of the Āhavanīya fire— based on the force of the scriptural injunction that "one should re-establish [the fire]" as being supported by the Āhavanīya— and then supporting that through the principle of exclusion.
It should be understood that, with respect to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), even by means of this [negation], the description as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is superior.
(Vi)—"Is his resolve (*dhṛti*) optional, or is there no maintaining at all?
Because of the negation and because it is a rule for what was to be imagined, not because of the warding off of what has already been attained."

Bhaṭṭa: However, in the case of the *nitya* [fire], since the condition of having lost the sacred fires (*gataśrītvam*) is equal, even though the perpetual maintenance (*ajasradhāraṇam*) is already established by the very fact of being an *āhavanīya* fire, it is not to be performed at all because it is excluded by the rule "one should not rekindle [the fire]" (*na pratisaṃdedhyāt*). This is merely incidental.

*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the *ukhya* fire, there is the view that its constant maintenance is established by the rule "one should not extinguish it," since a prohibition of maintenance presupposes the prior existence of a rule for such maintenance. To this, [the author] replies: because the *ukhya* fire occupies the position of the *āhavanīya*, its maintenance is already established even for one who has attained prosperity (*gataśrī*); therefore, what is prohibited here is the maintenance of the *ukhya* fire in that specific context, and not a rule for maintaining it [in general]. Consequently, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *ukhya* fire is indeed not to be maintained.
Maṇḍana: "There should be no constant maintenance of this [fire]. Śaṅkara: "And there is no maintenance for one who has attained prosperity."

By means of the fire intended for the optional rite (*kāmya*), which has reached the *abhri-cayana* (the piling with spades) and has struck the burning tree-cluster, [the fire] is placed beneath the *ukhya* fire-altar.
There is a mandatory combination (*samuccaya*) of both the optional and the constant [fires] in the injunction, because the desire is observed [in the text].
The Commentary states: "There is fire in the *ukhya* fire; he generates the fire by continuous heating."

Regarding that [fire], it is heard in scripture: "For one desiring Brahman-splendor, one should place [the fire] having taken it from the top of a tree; for one desiring fragrance, one should place it having taken it from the smoke; for one desiring rain, one should take it from the sky. In this regard, a deliberation arises: is there a combination of both the optional and the obligatory fires, or is the obligatory fire modified by the optional one?
To this, it is said:
In the case of the fire-pit (ukhā), there is a combination of both the optional and the obligatory fires.
Why? Because in this way, the injunction regarding the performance of the ritual, which encompasses all fires, is upheld.

[Objection: But surely, by the principle "But the occasional [rite] is a modification of the archetypal [rite], because of a specific connection" (3.6.13.10), the fire intended for a desired result will be a modification of the obligatory fire. [Reply:
It will not be so.
What is the reason? Because the desire is observed in relation to the injunction.

Regarding the non-consumption of the fire, this desire is heard: "One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should place [the fire] down without having carried it. This does not mean that for one desiring spiritual luster, this [act] serves the purpose of the fire-oblation (*agnihoma*).
If this is so, the result will arise from placing it down without having carried it;
as for the oblation, however, it remains as it was established, namely, in the *ukhya* fire alone.
And from their conjunction, there is a combination of the two fires.

Regarding the passage: "For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), having taken [the fire] from the top of a tree, he should place it on the *vārdhāgni*," it is deliberated whether there is a combination of the *ukhya* fire and the *vārdhāgni*, or whether the *vārdhāgni* is placed within the *ukhya*.
The conclusion is that there is a combination of both.
Why? Because desire is observed in connection with the injunction.
In the statement, "One desiring Brahman-splendor should install the fire," desire is heard as being restricted [to that specific act], not from any other fire.
If this is so, then the word, having fulfilled its purpose by effecting that restriction, is unable to exclude other fires; therefore, the result arises solely from the restriction itself.
And if the unconditioned fires were absent, ritual action would take place [inappropriately].
The Commentary states: "If the obligatory fire-altar (agni) were modified by the optional one, it would not exist at all.
In its absence, ritual action would occur even in the case of unconditioned [fires], such as those used for smelling incense (āghrādi)."
Likewise, the universal applicability of the *ādhāna* would be contradicted;
therefore, there is also a combination [of rites],
because that [fire] is for the sake of the deity.
The Commentary states: Furthermore, by the meditation upon the fire (agnyadhyāna), the deities are encompassed.
If that fire were to go out in the fire-pan (ukhya), then the deities would remain unencompassed.
Therefore, one should cause the fire to prosper through the meditation upon the fire.
From the removal [of the fire] performed for that purpose, there is the taking up of the fires from the deities;
or rather, it is a modification (vikāra) of that which was previously stated.
The Commentary says: "Or rather, it is a modification of the permanent (nitya) fire by means of the optional (kāmya) one."
Regarding this, it has been stated [in the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]: "But that which is without a specific cause is for the sake of the archetype; its modification [is for the sake of the ectype]" (3.6.13.10).
This was stated in general terms: "One offers in the Āhavanīya fire. Then, by the specific rule: "One desiring rain should sacrifice with the Vaiyāghrta [offering]," the general rule is set aside.
What is the reason? Because a universal (*sāmānya*), whose object is excluded from others within its own substrata, can also have an occurrence elsewhere;

and because a particular (*viśeṣa*), which is delimited by others and results in a definitive determination, would—were such [occurrence] impossible—lead to the consequence that its object does not exist. Thus, lest the instruction be rendered futile, [the universal must be admitted].
Now, as for what was said—that a desire is observed in the case of an injunction (*niyoga*)—to that we reply:

The statement "he should place it after having smelled it" is a specific scriptural injunction regarding the very same constant placing intended for the purpose of the oblation; [this applies] even here to one who has no desire [for the result], as in the case of the *āghrāda* oblation.
Furthermore, the repetition of the word "he should place" (*avadadhyāt*) is a direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*).

If there were a scriptural mention of desire (*kāmaśruti*) regarding the placing, then the placing itself would be enjoined; however, that which is not being enjoined cannot logically function as a means to a desired end.
And while that [rite] is being prescribed, because the word "and" (*ca*) has multiple meanings, the sentence is connected with that which pertains to the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*).
[It is] by means of that which pertains to the piling of the fire-altar.
It would be split;
therefore, the scriptural mention of desire pertains to the injunction.
What then? This permanent injunction is for the sake of the oblation itself; it is restated for the purpose of prescribing it without distinction.
As much as can be said—that one should prepare the *vaiyṛta* fire for the purpose of the oblation—is exactly this.
If this is so, then it is logical that in each of those occasional rites (*naimittika*), the eternal fire (*nitya*) is modified. [Durgasiṃha says:
"Because a universal, whose object is not excluded from its own substrata, can also have an occurrence elsewhere than that" (Bhāṣya).

"Let curd be given to the Brahmins; let buttermilk be given to Kauṇḍinya. In this case, the universal [property]—which has as its object that which is not excluded (avyāvṛtta-viṣaya) and whose object is undifferentiated (aparicchinna-viṣaya)—can still function with respect to other individual instances of the Brahmin group, even while depending on the particular [exception]. Therefore, since it is possible for the universal to function in other Brahmin groups besides the particular, namely Kauṇḍinya, the general rule remains fulfilled with respect to other objects.

"And because there would be the consequence of the non-existence of the object—since a particular [rule] is delimited by something else and determines that [object], and if that [delimitation] were impossible—the instruction would be rendered useless; lest this occur" (this is the Bhāṣya). Furthermore, as for the "particular": it is that which is delimited from other Brahmin-portions, such as those belonging to Kauṇḍinya, and which determines that [portion]. If that were impossible—that is, if such delimitation were not possible—there would be the consequence of the non-existence of the object, and the instruction would be useless. Therefore, even that particular rule must be accommodated.
However, the explanation given for the *vāyu* [sūtra] is incorrect.
The reason is that the favoring of the scripture occurs when the gift of curd is made; thus, the gift of curd applies in both cases.
However, this [latter case] is not carried out.
Therefore, that very sublation which we have described—whether it be obligatory or occasional—is precisely what takes place here.

Now, as for what was said—that the fruit [arises] from the kindling of the fire—this is replied: "Those [acts] are of two kinds" (2.1.13.6); thus, in the case of the kindling, a substance is intended to be prepared, and the refinement of the fire is indeed visible.
Therefore, it is established that [the term] refers to the purpose of protection.

Regarding the statement that "there would be ritual action even in the case of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) because of the scriptural declaration," we reply to that: the Bhāṣya says—"And as for what was said, that there would be ritual action even when the unconditioned does not exist, to that we say..."
Because of this statement, action would exist even with respect to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What could this statement not accomplish?
There is no burden too heavy for a statement.
As in the case of "he offers on the foot.
Furthermore, there would be a fault even in the case of conjunction.
The Bhāṣya says: Moreover, if there were a conjunction, there would be a connection of the Vedic [rite] with the worldly [one].

But in that regard, a defect is heard [in scripture]: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Śuci; for he whose fire is mixed with that which is used for cooking is most impure, as is the fire used for cooking. If it is argued that this is because of a scriptural injunction, [we reply: no.
The Commentary says: This is not a fault.
There is conjunction because of the scriptural statement.
No fault arises when that which is based on the scriptural statement is performed.
Regarding the other [case],
the Bhāṣya says: It is stated that,
according to the other view, the oblation in the unconsecrated vessels is based on a direct scriptural injunction (vācanika).
Thus, since it is explicitly stated in both cases, and since there is no fault, a modification (vikāra) is adopted on account of its being contingent (naimittika), not a combination (samuccaya);
for even in the case of the original rite (utsarga), the ritual act has already been performed.
The Commentary states: Now, as for what was said—that "because that [offering] is for the sake of the deity"—to that we reply.
Even upon the abandonment of the perpetual fire (*nitya-agni*), there is no contradiction in the acceptance of the deities, because the ritual act has already been performed.
The deities are accepted through the meditation (*adhyāna*) upon the fire, not by the fire itself.
Thus it is heard in scripture: "He who accepts the fire before [the new moon], he indeed shall sacrifice to the deities on the following day."
And that [offering] has been made to Agni;
by him the deities are encompassed.
Because of the scriptural statement regarding another fire, the sacrifice is performed [in that other fire].
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Śā—The cessation of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite by means of the optional (*kāmya*) one.
Having concluded the investigation into option (*vikalpa*) and combination (*samuccaya*), it is now considered whether combination indeed exists or not; this is the connection (*saṃgati*).

Since *soma* and *jāvanī* have the same purpose, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between them; however, because the fire in the *ukhya* and the fire in the *āhavanīya* have different functions, they are to be combined (*samuccaya*). This is the connection (*saṃgati*) arising from this point. In the Sūtra, the word *niyoga* means "attention" (*avadhāna*). Vi— "The optional fire is to be applied to the fire [already present]."
"Or else, [the fire] would be obstructed;
for this [fire] is distinct from the other due to the difference in its function, as there is no contingency of it being produced by desire.

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the fire in the *ukhya* [pot], it is said that "one generates the fire by continuous heating. By this, the *ukhya* fire is held by the sacrificer at the neck with a sling (*śikya*) in a vessel used for pouring libations (*āhavanīya*).
In that vessel, the Āhavanīya fire is contained within the *ukhya* [fire-pot].
Since this occurs subsequent to the initiation (*dīkṣā*), even though the Agnihotra has not yet been formally established, the oblations are performed as if they have been completed.

With reference to that, it is revealed in the Śruti: "For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), one should take [the fire] from the top of a tree while it is blazing and deposit it; for one desiring [scent], one should deposit it after having smelled [it]."

Thus, here we must consider whether, in the performance of optional rites (*kāmyaprayoga*), there is an incidental establishment (*prasaṅgasiddhi*) of the obligatory *āhavanīya* fire by way of sublation (*bādha*), or not. In this case, the act of placing (*avadhāna*) in the fire-pot (*ukhya*) is not enjoined for the sake of a result by means of the *āghāra* offerings and so forth—such that one might suspect an incidental establishment of the *camasa* cup by means of the *godohana* vessel—because the act of placing lacks the status of a substrate (*āśrayatva*), as it is not enjoined by any other injunction.
Therefore, it is simply the act of placing, qualified by the fire and having the fire-pot as its substrate, that is enjoined for the sake of a result.
Furthermore, because it depends on the omission of what is prescribed for the pouring of libations onto the Āhavanīya fire, the ritual application does not involve that [other] fire;
and even the contact of this Āhavanīya fire with another fire is not considered a fault, as it is based on a scriptural injunction.

And therefore, since there is no sublation of this constant *āhavanīya* fire even when one merely performs the placing [of the fuel] for the sake of another fire intended for a specific result, it follows that the *homa* and other rites should be performed right here. However, since the act of maintaining and placing [the fire] is already established by implication as being for the very purpose of the *homa*, even in the absence of being enjoined by another injunction, the loss of its substratum (*āśraya*) is untenable; thus, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), this is simply a connection between a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and a result. Consequently, through the cessation of this constant [fire], the requirement is fulfilled by incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

*Nyāyacindu*: Regarding the fire to be established on the *uvāya* altar in the *agnicayana* sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), [the fire] should be taken from the top of a tree while blazing; for one desiring sovereignty (*ādhipatya*), [it should be taken] from a frying pan.

On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*), because the obligatory act serves the purpose of the oblation (*homa*), whereas the optional act, being merely a form of taking [the fire], does not serve the purpose of the oblation. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that both the taking [of the fire] for the sake of the oblation and the mere taking [of the fire] are injunctions regarding the result for the other fire (*agnyantara*). Therefore, the obligatory is set aside by the optional.
Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Maṇḍana [states]: "The Veda is threefold.
Śaṅkara [states]: "The *āmnāya* is that which expresses desired objects."

In the section concerning the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), the optional fire (*kāmyāgni*) that is struck by a burning tree or similar object, as heard in the scripture, does not possess the status of the *āhavanīya*.
[Objection: "That [fire] should be the *āhavanīya*, because of its connection with the oblation (*āhuti*).
[Bhāṣya: That fire which belongs to the sacrificial ground (*vaihārika*) should indeed be the *āhavanīya*.
Why? Because of its connection with the oblation (*āhuti*). That into which one comes and offers is the *āhavanīya* fire; and into this [fire] the oblation is offered perpetually.
Therefore, this too is the Āhavanīya fire. Or rather, it is another [fire] that is brought forth and called "Āhavanīya.

The Commentary states: "Or it may be other than the Āhavanīya; for this one is not brought forth by being drawn out and then called [Āhavanīya], as in the injunctions: 'One should bring it from the Āghāra,' or 'One should bring it from the forest-fire.'"
Furthermore, the term *āhavanīya* is based on consecration (*saṃskāra*), because it exists during the consecrations and is absent prior to them.

As for the argument that [the name] arises from connection with the oblation (*āhuti*), once the status of being *āhavanīya* is established, the oblations are prescribed by the rule, "That which they offer in the *āhavanīya*.
Since these oblations are prescribed by means of that already established [status], their status does not derive from those oblations.
Therefore, it is the Āhavanīya.
The purpose [of this discussion] is the absence of the characteristics of the Āhavanīya.
Śā—This fire, which is for optional rites (kāmya), should be denoted by the term "Āhavanīya," because [the etymology] is "that into which oblations are offered" (āhūyate asmin).

Therefore, the properties of the *āhavanīya* fire—such as carrying away prosperity (*gata-śrī*) and so forth—should be performed here. This is not so; for this word "āhavanīya" denotes a specific consecration (*saṃskāra*) arising from the act of installation (*ādhāna*), and it cannot apply in the absence of that consecration.
Therefore, the properties of the *āhavanīya* do not apply here.
Soma: This is a contextual connection (*prāsaṅgikī saṃgatiḥ*).

Regarding its status as the *āhavanīya* fire, [the opponent might argue] that the injunction "one offers into the *āhavanīya*" prescribes the *āhavanīya* only when it already exists for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*); however, since the *āhavanīya* would then be defined by its being the locus of the oblation, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*). Furthermore, because the term is not used for the footprint (*pada*) and other such things even though they serve as loci for oblations, this term is purely conventional (*rūḍha*). Viśvarūpa: That fire is our *āhavanīya*, or rather, it is that which is designated by the application of the term "oblation" (*āhuti-yoga*).
Because of mutual dependence, it is thus [the case that] it arises from the *saṃskāra* (consecration) alone here.
Bhā—This very *kāmyāgni* (fire for optional rites) would be denoted by the term *āhavanīya*, because it is the means for performing the *homa* (oblation).

Therefore, there is a doubt based on mere possibility that the duties pertaining to the *āhavanīya*—such as maintaining the fire after it has attained its glory (*gataśrī*) and so forth—should be performed therein.

The words *āhavanīya* and the like denote specific consecrations (*saṃskāra*) produced by the rite of *ādhāna*; they cannot apply in the absence of that consecration. Therefore, in this context, the benefit to the fire provided by the maintenance of one who has attained prosperity (*gataśrī*) is not merely its physical preservation.
Therefore, it is understood that even in that case, one must first bring the sacrifice to completion.

Regarding the scriptural injunction, "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," there arises a doubt: since the Bṛhaspatisava is enjoined as a subsidiary (aṅga) of the Vājapeya, should it be performed together with it in a single performance during the autumn—the time of the principal rite—or rather at its own time, namely spring, as established by extension (atideśa)?
In this regard, [the principle is: "For the prescription of the place and time pertains to the principal rite along with its subsidiaries."
Because this [time] is also a subsidiary (aṅga) of that [principal rite], like other subsidiaries, there is a performance together with it.

The sense is that in the eleventh [book], under the sūtra *aṅgāni tu vidhānatvāt* (11.2.17), the connection of place, time, and agent with the principal rite along with its subsidiaries will be stated. For the Vājapeya is not enjoined as something to be performed in autumn; rather, this is an injunction of time for the performance—the activity directed toward the fruit—which is the means for the Vājapeya. This is because of the mention of the instrumental case in the expression *śāradi vājapeyena*.
