Since that very [rite], which constitutes the collection of factors for the fruit and is intended to be performed, requires a time, [the time is prescribed].

And since that activity is governed by the principle of the relationship between the subsidiary and the principal, the application is equal for both the principal and its own subsidiaries; thus, in the case of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), the same logic applies to the *agnicit* and to the *avyānī* oblations, because the productive operations (*bhāvanā*) terminate with their respective results.
However, for the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), the result to be achieved (*bhāvya*) is an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the fire;
and since that [unseen merit] arises immediately [after the act], this is the distinction.

Regarding the Soma sacrifice: the connection [of this section] is established because of the counter-argument based on the example of the "fire-obtainer" (*āhitāgni*), which was stated in the previous section’s *guṇasūtra*—"The vow follows immediately, because it has become that"—concerning the necessity of performing the *agnihotra* and other rites immediately after the *ādhāna*.

Regarding the rule *karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.2.1) and *bhūte* (Pāṇini 3.1.84): since the suffix *kvip* is prescribed for the root *ci* (*cinoti*) when "fire" (*agni*) is the object (*karman*) as an attendant word (*upapada*), it is the state (*bhāva*) that has fire as its object and piling (*cayana*) as its object which, having become past (*bhūtā*), serves as the cause; however, it is not the act of piling itself [that is the cause]. Furthermore, the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) becomes past through the accomplishment of the result (*phala*), because an action culminates in its result.
And here, the result consists in the maintenance of the fire, which is the primary purpose.

Therefore, because the causal condition (*nimitta*) exists in the form of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) centered on the consecration of the fire (*agni-saṃskāra*) performed during the piling (*cayana*), extending up to its completion along with its ancillaries (*sāṅgatya*), it is not logical to claim that "the undertaking of the vow (*vrata*) occurs immediately after the piling. However, since the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)—unlike the piling—lacks the status of being a subordinate act (*kratvartha*) and thus lacks the status of being a consecration for the sake of the means of the ritual procedure (*kalpa-pūrva-sādhana*), it possesses an independent, unseen result (*adṛṣṭa-phala*) residing in the fire. Consequently, there is no requirement for the consecrated fires (*āhitāgni*) to undergo the heating of the sacrificial vessels (*kalpa-taptīkṣā*).

However, regarding the *agnicit-vratas* (vows of the fire-piler): these vows, which are prescribed for one who has consecrated the fire through the act of piling (*cayana*), do not apply at all until after the piling is complete; this is because the status of being an *agnicit* does not exist merely by the placement of the sacrificial mound (*āṇḍila*) and other such preliminary acts. Thus, there is a disparity [between the two cases]. The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "The vow connected with the fire-piler should occur immediately upon the mere piling (*citamātre*), because the occasion (*nimitta*) has been reached. As stated in the Vivaraṇa: "'He should not run while it rains,' and so forth—[is this] when the piling is already completed, or even while it is being performed?"
Because the first scriptural statement serves as the occasion (*nimitta*), here the vows belong to the one who has piled the fire-altar (*agni-cit*).
Therefore, those vows are performed [only] when that [occasion] occurs.

According to the Bhaṭṭa school: the vows of the fire-piler, such as "one should not run while it rains," are prescribed for the sake of the person (as a human duty) either until death or for the duration of the rain, with the piling of the altar as the occasion; they are just like the vows of the one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni-vrata*), which are prescribed with the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) as the occasion.
In this case, the indication of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) occurs through the mere hearing of the words of the vow in both instances;
and its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is to be understood from the hearing of the scriptural mention of its fruit.

Regarding this *agnicid-vrata* (the vow of the fire-piler), since it is a cause (*nimitta*) for the mere act of piling (*cayana*)—just as the *bhūta-agni* (the completed fire-altar) is—it follows that the vow should be performed once the piling alone has been accomplished, similar to the vows of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: Since the words "in the action" (*karmaṇi*) and "when [the action] has occurred" (*bhūte*) are understood to carry over from previous rules, the rule *Pāṇini 3.2.91*, *agnau ceḥ*, prescribes the *kvip* suffix after the root *ci* (to pile) when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. Because the status of being an object (*karman*) would otherwise be inexplicable, there is an implication (*ākṣepa*) of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). Thus, it is understood that the cause is the completion (*bhūtatva*) of the very efficient force whose instrument is the piling and whose object is the fire (*agni*). Furthermore, since the fire denoted by the term *agnicit* (fire-piler)—namely, the fire called *jvalana*—cannot be the object of piling in its own essential form, it is understood to be the object only by way of being the receptacle (*ādhāra*) for the bricks produced by the piling. Since the state of being a receptacle persists until the conclusion of the *Sāṅgatyāga* sacrifice, it is only upon the completion of that sacrifice that the efficient force whose instrument is the piling and whose object is the fire is understood to have reached its state of completion (*bhūtatva*). Therefore, the status of being an *agnicit* occurs precisely at the end of that [sacrifice].

Regarding the term *āhitāgni*, although the past passive participle suffix (*kta*) indicates the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and it is understood that this very force, having come into being, serves as the occasioning cause (*nimitta*);

nevertheless, since the fire—designated by the act of kindling—is denoted only as the substratum for a previous kindling performed by another (the sacrificer's father), and such a fire is accomplished only at the conclusion of the kindling rite, the vows of the *āhitāgni* must likewise be observed only at its conclusion.

For the status of being the object of the action is not here heard in reference to the *āhavanīya* fire and the others, such that their accomplishment could be assumed to occur at the end of the cooking.

*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the injunctions such as "one should not run while it rains," which are the vows (*vrata*) of the *agnicit* (the one who has piled the fire-altar), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they must be performed immediately after the act of piling (*cayana*), just like the vows of the *āhitāgni* (one who has established the sacred fires). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Since the act of piling culminates in its fruit, the [vows] occasioned by it should be performed immediately after that [act]. The fruit of the act of piling is the benefit to the fire-altar (*agni-upakāra*), namely, the maintenance of the fire used as the means for the *homa* sacrifice; therefore, the occasional duty (*naimittika*) follows immediately after that. However, the distinction is that the fruit of the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), which consists of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the fire, occurs immediately [after the act itself]. This is the final position.

Maṇḍana: "When the sacrifice is completed, this is the vow. Śaṅkara: "But they perform it with the *im* mantra. In the fire-piling (*agnicayana*) and the *avyānī* oblations, Indra and other deities are indicated by the wording of the mantras (*māntravarṇika*).
In the Śrauta-sūtra it is heard: "He lays down these *ajyāni* bricks" and "Having offered the *Āgrayaṇa*, he offers these oblations.
Five mantras beginning with "To the one armed with a hundred weapons" (*śatāyudhāya*) are obtained according to the order of their recitation.

Even though the status of being the instrument of laying down is understood through the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "That which is for them" (*tad-anāsām*, Pāṇini 4.4.125), the deities are established by the words of the mantras themselves, because the word "these" (*etāḥ*) does not indicate that they are the instruments of the oblation.
It is established that [the term "these"] is appropriate as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is being performed, since the mantras are employed for the purpose of consecrating the bricks.

As for the deity, it may be postulated in accordance with general rules of interpretation. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: by the word "these" (*etāḥ*), there is a reference to the bricks; otherwise, the pronoun "these" (*enāḥ*) would result in a lack of coordination. Therefore, through a necessary reference to the *ṛc* verses, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "oblations" (*āhuti*) becomes untenable unless they are understood as such. Thus, in the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), these are the bricks; [and] in the piling of the fire-altar, this is the baking of the bricks.

The word "bhiriti" refers to the inevitability of transformation; in the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), it is to be understood through implication as referring to the laying down of specific bricks (*iṣṭakopadhāna*).
But the word *varṇa* itself is not intended to refer to that [the phoneme], because of the natural sense of the sūtra "due to the conjunction with sound" (*śabdasaṃyogāt*);
for there is no evidence to establish the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *varṇa* in the general sense of a line.

When it is argued that the word *varṇa* must be neuter because the lexicon states "but *varṇa* [is neuter] when referring to a syllable," [we reply: since the passage ending with "straight lines behind and in front, drawn in the middle" prescribes specific locations for bricks possessing various lines, and since the reading "all *varṇas*" (sarvān varṇān) indicates that the word *sarvavarṇa* refers to those very bricks introduced by the preceding injunctions; and since, once the intended meaning is grasped, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is justified due to the otherwise inexplicability of the text, there is an application-rule (*viniyoga-vidhi*) for as many specific parts as there are.

Regarding the Kūrma-citi (tortoise-altar) in the Agnicayana: in the Agnicayana, concerning the Kūrma-citi, the statement "facing east" is a description of the agent's face, whereas "facing west" is a description of the tortoise. Since the tortoise is the primary subject, there are scriptural injunctions stating, "He places it facing east," and "He places it facing west from the front. Because it is possible for both the agent and the object to face east, one might initially conclude that there is no fixed rule—that either the tortoise or the agent may face east. However, since an option (*vikalpa*) is improper, the statement regarding the agent's face is that he faces east.
The statement "the husband is prior" is merely a figurative expression (kūrmasukhavādaḥ) [regarding the wife].
(Saṃkarṣa. 2.1.20).
In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), the injunction "he places the ghee-bricks" refers to the placing of jars filled with ghee.

Regarding the passage "He places the *ghṛteṣṭakā*s," and so forth, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the placement is enjoined as being performed with the recitation of mantras such as "They have mixed the clarified butter" (*ghṛtaṃ mimikṣire*), according to the principle of the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks (Jaimini Sūtra 1.4.12–13). However, this is refuted: the placement refers to the substance *ghṛta* (clarified butter), because its presence is possible by filling a jar; for the *puṣkaraparṇa* brick alone possesses those indicative marks (*liṅga*), and there is an absence of both sequential order (*krama*) and specific ritual action (*karaṇa*) [for the mantras]. Furthermore, there is no contradiction, just as in the case of the *dhūpabha* and other such bricks.
*Saṃkarṣa* 2.1.24:

In the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), regarding the square bricks, there is an alternative name: "He lays down the circular bricks" (*maṇḍaleṣṭakā upadadhāti*). When it is argued that the "circular bricks" mentioned in the scripture beginning with "He lays down the circular bricks" should be circular in shape because their names are otherwise [than square], [the reply is: since these names do not conflict with the purpose of the ritual action consisting of the piling, they refer to the square bricks themselves.
Saṃkarṣa 2.1.25:

In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), during the fourth layer of bricks, the number [of bricks] should exceed three thousand. Furthermore, in those fourth layers of bricks, according to the rule beginning with "the first," there should be exactly one, two, and three thousand bricks respectively.

Since there is a prohibition against the smallest [measurement], and because no other number is prescribed for the three-thousand-fold [altar], it might be argued that the practice should remain as it was. However, since the numbers mentioned in the context are contingent (*naimittika*), they do not apply in the absence of their respective conditions; therefore, a different number must indeed be adopted.

In the *Saṃkarṣa*, regarding the measurements of the layers (*citi*) in the fire-altar construction (*agnicayana*), the measurement should be taken either from the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or from the officiating priest (*adhvaryu*).
It is heard in scripture: "The wings and the tail are each one fathom (vyāma) in measure.
In this regard, since the Adhvaryu is engaged in the ritual action and because there is no restrictive rule regarding his measurement, it follows that his measurement alone should be accepted;

for in the case of the injunction "He offers with a winnowing basket," we observe that the status of being an auxiliary to the ritual is what is grasped. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the correct conclusion is: because his measuring as equal to the Sacrificer has been enjoined, there is no restrictive rule [limiting the measurement to the Adhvaryu alone].
However, in the case of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), there is a disparity because it is set down for that very purpose;
*Saṃkarṣa* 1.4.10.
In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), the word "layer" (*citi*) does not refer to the grass-bundle (*prastara*), but rather to its constituent parts.

In the passage, "There are five layers (citis); he piles them up with five fillings (purīṣas)," each layer of grass-bundle (prastara) is denoted by the word *citi*, which ends in the suffix *ktin* used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
This is because we observe common usage such as, "One layer has been completed by the masons on the palace," etc.;
for this very reason, it does not refer to the act of piling itself.

And because that [act of piling] is a single unit, there is no room for repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the injunction "he piles the fire" (*agniṃ cinute*); thus, since it follows that the placing of the *puṣkaraparṇa*, the man (*puruṣa*), and the earth (*purīṣa*) occurs solely through the injunction of five layers (*prastara*), the scriptural prescription (*vācanika*) of their arrangement—each subsequent one being placed above the preceding—is consistent. This being the position reached—that the layers (*prastara*) are together with those [other materials]—we reply: although the act of piling (*cayanakriyā*) is one, it is divided into five parts due to the distinctions created by the intervening layers of earth (*purīṣa*); therefore, the word "piling" (*citi*) refers to each individual portion.

For this very reason, after stating, "One places the *svayamātṛṇṇā* and the *vikarṇī* on the two uppermost [bricks]," there follows a prohibition against placing any other bricks above them, such as: "One should not place another brick above," and so forth; thus, since the rule would otherwise result in uncertainty regarding the placement of all other bricks at the very top, the injunction is not contradicted even though the placement of the four [bricks] beginning with the *puṣkaraṇā* might have been subject to no fixed order. (Saṃkarṣa. 2.1.27). In the *agnicayana*, the characteristics of the altar (*vedi*) apply to the aggregate of the layers (*citi*) themselves, and not to the ground that serves as their support.

When it is argued that the characteristics of the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) should be performed for the ground of the piling (*cayanadhārabhūmi*), [the reply is: since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the *uttaravedi* is prescribed by the middle term [of the injunction], and in the ectype (*vikṛti*) Agni is prescribed in its very place, the characteristics of the *uttaravedi* apply to that which has taken over its function—just as in the case of the *dara*s or in the absence [of the altar] itself—but they do not belong to the ground beneath it.
Saṃkarṣa. 2.1.26.
In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), bricks such as the *citriṇī*s, which are not mentioned in the immediate context but are mentioned in the *lokampṛṇā* section, [are to be used].
Because that [Vedic recitation] was previously the guide for the world, its purpose is fully accomplished.
The Commentary states: In the *Aupānuvākya* section, bricks are enumerated:
"He lays down the *vajriṇī* bricks," "He lays down the *citriṇī* bricks," and "He lays down the *bhṛteṣṭakā* bricks."
In this regard, the following has been established: [the fire-altar] is to be placed upon the middle layer, or rather, upon the middle [altar].
Is it before the leading forth of the world [of the fire], or after? What is the prima facie view? "But at the end, according to Bādarāyaṇa" (5.1.19).
This being the position reached, it is replied:

prior to the *lokapraṇā* brick, because that [brick] serves a complete purpose, its completeness is heard in the scripture: "Whatever is deficient in this [altar], whatever is a gap, that he fills with this [brick]: 'Fill the world, fill the gap.
In the *agnicayana*, the *citriṇī* and other bricks [are used]... in the *agnicayana*, the *citriṇī* and other bricks are used.
And because the matter is unprecedented (*apūrva*), it is understood that the injunction would otherwise be purposeless;
therefore, the *lokapraṇā* should take place before the construction of the world-altar (*lokampṛṇā*).
Śā—Even in the case of the middle altar, the *lokapraṇā* should occur at the end.
The term "for the sake of completion" (pūraṇāya) indicates that [the insertion] occurs before the *citriṇī* and subsequent verses.
Soma: The connection [of this section] is established through the consideration of specific details by relying on what was previously stated.

Indeed, in the *Tatsiddhipeṭikā* (on Sūtras 1.4.23–28), beginning with the statement, "Some, however, support the view that this is a mantra-injunction (*mantra-vidhi*) regarding the passage 'He lays down the bricks' (*iṣṭīrupadadhāti*)," it is said: "Since the mantras beginning with 'With one [verse] they called' (*ekayā''hvata*) lack an unambiguous indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the act of laying down (*upadhāna*), there would be a futility of the injunction if they were intended for that purpose. Then it continues: "But since the laying down is already established [by other means], the direct injunction is purposeful even for the sake of the meaning of the mantra 'the middle one' (*madhyama*). (This is stated in the *Śāstradīpikā* on Sūtra 27, "Dhumā").

If it is argued: "Since the mantra is directly enjoined by a Brāhmaṇa passage, and because we accept that those things to be deposited by that mantra are connected with the middle layer (madhyamaciti), how can it be determined here that the brick does not belong to the middle layer?"—this is true.

Nevertheless, the mantra does not [apply] merely because of a direct injunction in the Brāhmaṇa, as is the case with the bricks themselves; rather, even if there were a direct injunction in the Brāhmaṇa, there must also be an indication that those bricks are to be laid down with that specific mantra, since the bricks are designated by terms such as "the variegated ones" (*citriṇī*) in passages like "he lays down the variegated ones."

And thus, in the case of the statement "He lays down the *sṛṣṭi* [bricks]," although there is an injunction of the mantra—which serves as a qualifier—by means of the word *sṛṣṭi*, which denotes the bricks to be laid down with the *sṛṣṭi*-mantras, the connection with the middle layer (*madhyamaciti*) is established because the bricks, which serve as the qualificands, are explicitly mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa.

In the present case, however, only the mantra itself—"Fill the world, fill the gap"—is heard in the explicit Brāhmaṇa; there is no mention of bricks to be laid down with that mantra. Therefore, no justification [for its placement] is possible.

Vi—‘Fill the world; erect it upwards, O Svāhā! Before that, [place] the Citriṇī bricks; before that, Bādarāyaṇa says, [place] the Pūraṇī bricks. Bhāṭṭa—Even in the middle layer, the placing of the Citriṇī and other bricks occurs immediately after the placing of the bricks belonging to the context (the Prākaraṇika bricks), and not before the Lokampṛṇā brick; because they are adventitious (āgantuka).

Nor can it be argued that because of the statement, "Whatever is deficient in this [altar], whatever is a gap, that he fills with this [brick]; fill the world, fill the gap," the *lokapraṇā* brick is placed at the end for the purpose of filling, and therefore the *citriṇī* and other bricks must be placed before it—this is what must be said. For, since the mantra’s purpose of filling the gaps is established by its very indicative power (*liṅga*), this scriptural statement lacks the character of an injunction for that specific purpose. Even if, by some means, the mantra were an injunction for that purpose, there is no evidence that the brick itself has that purpose.

Or, let it be granted that the mantra serves to fill a gap; yet, since the brick cannot be established without being preceded by that [mantra], the brick must also possess that [function]. Nevertheless, because that mantra has scope even in other layers (*citi*), there can be no sublation of the *citriṇī* bricks and others—which have no other scope—by the rule regarding their placement at the end [of the layer] (5.1.9). Nor does the worldly injunction, like the direct Brāhmaṇa text, have as its object only the middle layer; for this mantra, ending with the particle *iti*, is not employed as a word designating the bricks.

Nor should it be argued that [the injunction] lacks scope, because even if it were read as belonging to each specific layer (*cit*), it would result in its placement in that very layer; and if it were read within the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) of the piling (*cayana*), it would result in its placement in the final layer alone. How, then, can it be said to have scope?

Since the purpose is filling, and because the distinction [of the bricks] is established through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) itself due to its universal scope, this being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), it follows that if the *citriṇī* and other bricks were placed at the end, there would result the sublation of the very fruit of the *lokapraṇayā*, which consists in filling the gaps. Therefore, it is better to place the *citriṇī* and others before the *lokapraṇayā*, even by subverting the sequence following the laying of the previously mentioned bricks.

*Nyāyabindu*: Although the *citriṇī* and other [bricks] are placed at the end, they must be placed even before the *lokapraṇā*; for there is the scriptural statement, "Whatever is its unburned part, whatever is its fissure—that he fills with this [brick]," and because the *lokapraṇā* serves the purpose of making [the altar] complete. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). *Maṇḍana*: Those [bricks] are prior to the *lokapraṇā*.
"Those" refers to the *citriṇī* bricks.
Śaṅkara: "Either at the end of the world [of the altar] or at its conclusion.
In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), the placement of the *citriṇī* and other bricks occurs in the middle layer; otherwise, they would be at the end.
The Bhāṣya states: In the Aupānuvākya section, it is heard: "He lays down the citriṇī bricks," and "He lays down the vajriṇī bricks.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: are these to be laid down in the [upper] citi, or in the middle one?
What is the prima facie view? [They should be laid down] in the fifth [citi] alone.
The bricks have their sequence already established;
no others are desired by these [rules],
as is also seen from the indicative mark (liṅga).
The Bhāṣya states: "Or rather, the final layer is obtained; one lays down other bricks.
However, in the middle [layer], according to the scriptural statement, there are those possessing Brāhmaṇa-texts.
[This concerns] the bricks such as the Citrīyā and others in the Agnicayana sacrifice. 36
The Commentary states: These [bricks] do not belong to another layer.
To which one, then? To the middle layer.
Why? Because these bricks possess Brāhmaṇa-texts, and it is the middle layer that is prescribed for them in the sacred tradition.
"Whichever brick one may recognize as being accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa passage, that one should place in the middle of the layer.
But are not all bricks indeed accompanied by Brāhmaṇa passages?
No, he says.
Others [are determined] by the sequence of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) according to the traditional enumeration (*samāmnāya*).
Therefore, these [mantras] do not stand at the end. [The rule is:
when the performance has been established as occurring once, then the sequences are considered.
Is the *upapradhāna* (subordinate principal) for the *citrīyādīn* [rites] in the *samā* [sacrifice], or in the *madhyamā* [sacrifice]?
Since their sequence is already established when they are being explained, they are not studied as independent (*anārabhyādhītāḥ*).
Furthermore, the statement "whichever [cow]" is not something to be enjoined.
It is said:
"In the absence of a direct scriptural statement, there would be the status of being a *pratyakṣa-brāhmaṇa* (one who knows the Brāhmaṇas directly) and so forth;
for this verb *jñā*, preceded by the prefix *abhi*, functions in the sense of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
The statement would thus be merely the doctrine of *syādvāda* regarding the meaning;
however, the inclusion of *citriyādi* (the desire for variety and so forth) would therefore occur in the middle altar (*madhyamā citi*).

Since the prefix *abhi-* has the sense of "directing toward," and since being directed toward an object is impossible for anything other than cognition, the verb *jñā-* preceded by *abhi-* signifies direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*).
They also say that the word *jānāti* preceded by *abhi-* is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of direct perception.

And regarding the statement "vākyaṃ ca" (Śābarabhāṣya): the sense is that since the meaning of the sentence is not contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*), it must be stated that [the rule] is intended precisely for the purpose of sublation (*bādha*). Vi— "The [suffixes] *citrīyā* and so forth should be prescribed either before the highest person (*uttama-puruṣa*) or as secondary to it; they should be stated [to occur] immediately before the highest person or before the middle person (*madhyama-puruṣa*)."

The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains that for the *citrīyā* and other such bricks, the placement is in the middle layer (*madhyamaciti*) by virtue of the scriptural statement: "Whichever brick one recognizes as being accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa passage, that one should place in the middle layer.

For here, since the verb *jānāti* preceded by the prefix *abhi-* denotes perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*), and because the sentence must have a meaningful purpose, there is an injunction prescribing the middle layer with reference to those bricks enjoined in the Brāhmaṇa that are perceived [by the sacrificer].
As for the act of placing (*upadhāna*), however, it is the substratum (*āśraya*) [of the injunction] due to the context (*prakaraṇa*).

It has already been stated in the *Bhūmādhikaraṇa* (Bhāṭṭa 1.4.17) that the state of possessing an explicit Brāhmaṇa text entails being placed in the middle position as prescribed by a specific scriptural injunction.

Furthermore, the possession of an explicit Brāhmaṇa text cannot be a qualification of the subject (*uddeśyaviśeṣaṇa*), because the word "that" (*tat*) refers back to the qualified entity as a whole, thereby making a qualified reference possible.
Therefore, the placement occurs specifically in the middle layer (*madhyamaciti*).
And this is not a reversal of the context, because there is no distinction.

Regarding the *Nyāyabindu*, when it is argued that "the *citriyā* and others should be placed at the end," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they belong to the middle layer, based on the scriptural statement: "Whatever brick one recognizes as being accompanied by a *brāhmaṇa* passage, that one should place in the middle layer.
Maṇḍana states: "The *citriyā* and others are in the middle layer."
Śaṅkara says: "The Citrīyā and other [rites] end with this.
In the Agnicayana, there is no gift to a Brāhmaṇa in these three [cases]."

"Rudra, indeed, is this Agni; he has three arrows: directed backward, across, and forward. Whosoever piles the fire-altar, he comes under the power of these [arrows]. Having piled the fire-altar, by giving another [cow] among the three to a Brāhmaṇa, he pays homage to himself; moreover, he ransoms himself from them. Since it is thus heard in scripture, and since the gift of the "other" among the three [cows] also pertains to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) according to the previous principle, [it may be argued that] because the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) itself is Rudra, and because one is struck by his arrows, this gift is a taking refuge; and the statement regarding the ransom of oneself from them is appropriate only when performed in this manner.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the case of a subsidiary element belonging to a combined rite reaching its conclusion; for we observe the granting of a boon as a subsidiary element of the *rathantara* chant (Saṃkarṣa.
Likewise, in the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), when the maintained fire is destroyed, the *jyotiṣmatī* sacrifice is not to be performed.
"And because it is for the sake of another in the case of maintaining [the fire].
The Bhāṣya states: "This is handed down in scripture: 'The *gataśrī* fire is to be maintained; the *āhavanīya* fire is to be produced by friction.'"

As for the expiation for the *agnihotra* fire, [the scripture] says: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Jyotiṣmat; for him whose *agnihotra* fire, though not yet offered, goes out while being maintained.

In this regard, the following point is subject to doubt: when the fire that is to be maintained goes out, should this expiation be performed or not? What is the prima facie view? It should be performed.
For the occasion has indeed arrived;
this is the occasion here: the fire has been drawn out for the purpose of the Agnihotra.
Therefore, an expiation must be performed.
Is it not the case that this [rite] is for the sake of all ritual actions, and not for the Agnihotra alone? It is replied:
if it is said that because it is for the sake of the entire collection of ritual actions, it does not exist for the sake of the [Agnihotra] alone.

But as for the statement "for each one," which refers to all [the fires], that which is employed for one becomes employed for the *agnihotra* of all; yet this is not for the sake of the entire collection of rites, because the collection itself has not been enjoined, and there is no requirement toward the means [of the collection]. In that context, each individual rite requires its own act of drawing out [the fire].
Therefore, even though it serves all purposes, it exists for the sake of the *agnihotra*.

And thus, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for following [the fire] becomes applicable. Just as the acts such as sprinkling water around the fire (*paryukṣaṇa*), sweeping around it (*parisamūhana*), and removing grass (*tṛṇāpacaya*) are performed day after day in the case of the fire that is maintained, so too would the expiation be performed. This being the position reached, we reply:
And in the case of maintaining the fire after the *agni-cayana* has been performed, or upon the destruction of the maintained fire (37),
this expiation is not to be performed when the *Śrī* follows [the fire].
Why? Because it is for the sake of another.
For at that time when he has attained prosperity (*gataśrī*), the taking out of the fire is not for the purpose of the *agnihotra*;
rather, the fire taken out for that other purpose is maintained for all purposes.
The lifting up, however, serves that single purpose alone;
the carrying, on the other hand, is for the sake of all ritual acts.
Furthermore, no expiation is prescribed for following [the fire] when it is being carried for the purpose of the Agnihotra.
What then? It refers to the act of extraction (*uddharaṇa*). And here, the extraction is that performed by another; it is an extraction for the sake of another.
Even when the extraction is performed for the sake of that [other] for whose sake the extraction was intended, that same expiation applies.
Therefore, there is no need for an expiation (prāyaścitta) in this case.

[Duh: Having previously established that "being for the sake of another" (tādarthya) is characterized by the assistance provided even when it is partial, the intention here is to bind both the individual and the collective together, like the feeding of Devadatta and Yajñadatta; for whatever is accomplished by them collectively may be accomplished by even one of them alone.
That [act], however, is for the sake of the collective whole, like the fetching of leaves and water; it cannot be said to be "for one or the other.
Nor is that [act] itself enjoined.
Therefore, that lifting of the fire is for the sake of the Agnihotra as a collective whole for each individual.

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is that the purposefulness [of the ritual] is characterized by the Vedic texts and so forth; moreover, one whose prosperity has departed does not necessitate the extraction [of the fire].
For its maintenance is contingent upon a specific occasion;
it awaits that [occasion] as long as the ritual action persists.
The extraction was performed by way of a general indication;
let it serve that very purpose.
By way of incidental discussion, it also assists another matter.
Therefore, when [fire] has been drawn out for another purpose, there is no expiation for the sake of the *agnihotra*.

However, if the fire that was drawn out for the evening *agnihotra* is maintained by one whose prosperity has departed, and it is then drawn out again at the time of the morning *agnihotra*, does an expiation apply or not? We say:
it does apply, because the entire set of causal conditions is present.
Or rather, it does not exist;
for that [fire] was not drawn out merely for the sake of the Agnihotra. What then? It is with respect to the ritual procedure (*vyatya*).
The specific individual in reliance upon whom this [vow] was undertaken has indeed come to an end.
This is because of the context of morning and evening;
furthermore, this wearing [of the garment] is not for the sake of pleasure.
[This applies] to one who possesses human attributes, because of the departure of [divine] glory.
"Because they are for the sake of action, there would be ritual action regarding the others.
Commentary: Now, as for what was said—that items such as sweeping around and sprinkling water are performed with the fire being maintained—so too is the expiation; to this, it is replied:

It is appropriate that the acts of smoothing and so forth are performed, for they have been enjoined as purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), they are possible to perform, and their purpose has not yet been fulfilled.
However, the act of lifting [the vessel] has ceased because its purpose has already been accomplished.
Furthermore, the recitation [of the *adhyāya*] is restricted by specific place and time.
Therefore, this is the expiation for that.

The Śāstra states: "This expiation is heard [in the scriptures] when the fire has been drawn out for the sake of the Agnihotra. Since that which is maintained is intended for that purpose, it is maintained for the sake of all [sacrificial rites]."
It is not so;
for this [grain] is extracted for another purpose and is retained because it has reached its full measure.
That alone is the cause for its retention, since no specific reason for its retention is heard in the scripture.

For it is not heard in scripture that the fetching of the fire for a man who has already fetched it (*gataśrī*) is for the sake of all purposes, such that the act of fetching or the fire thus fetched would be universal; rather, it is merely for the purpose of maintaining it (*dhāraṇa*).

Therefore, when one fetches the fire with reference to some specific ritual action, he performs its mere maintenance by virtue of having already fetched it. When the fire is fetched upon the arrival of a particular rite, the fetching is for that rite alone, and the fire thus fetched is likewise for that rite alone.
Being maintained on account of a specific occasion (*nimitta*), it incidentally (*prasaṅgāt*) benefits the *agnihotra*; therefore, there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for its removal.

As for the *soma* sacrifice—previously, because there was no such purpose (*tādarthya*), there was no expiation for removing the fires used for the *darśa* and other rites; however, since that purpose exists here, expiation is appropriate. This is the connection (*saṃgati*) arising from the discussion of rising [from the seat]. One by whom prosperity (*śrī*) has been attained is "one who has attained prosperity" (*gataśrī*); his *āhavanīya* fire must be maintained.

In the Śruti passage, "There are indeed three who have attained prosperity: the learned man, the village headman, and the Kṣatriya," the term *gataśrī* (one who has attained prosperity) is well-known.

It is true that fire exists for the sake of the Agnihotra; nevertheless, the condition for the rekindling (*uddhāna*) is not merely that, but rather, as stated in the Śruti, "He whose fire has been taken out" (*yasyāgnir uddhṛtaḥ*). Thus, it refers to the taking out of the fire intended for that specific purpose.
And when the sacrificial fires have been extinguished, or when there is a destruction of the *dhārya* fire during the piling of the altar (*agnicayana*),
one worships with the *pṛṣṭha* verses at the piling of the altar.
It has been explained [in the *Tantraratna*] that it is heard in the scripture: "Three indeed have attained glory—the learned Brāhmaṇa, the Āmanin, and the Rājanya" (Vi.

9.4.8), and that the author of the Kalpasūtra states, "Aurva, Gautama, Bhāradvāja. Thus, it is explained as "one who has attained glory. Therefore, here, when the installation of the Āhavanīya fire has been performed on account of that [qualification], and at the time of the Agnihotra he should chant the *udgītha*, there arises the consideration: should the *jyotiṣmatī* recitation be performed for its presence or not? In this deliberation, since both the occasion (*nimitta*) and the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) exist, it must be performed.

Nor is there non-performance [of the extraction] even when the maintenance [of the fires] has been performed, because the extraction suitable for the performance of the *yoga* (conjunction) has not occurred; for since it is impossible to maintain what has not been extracted, the extraction—accompanied by mantras—is implied by the *tantra* (common procedure) for the sake of the *agnihotra-yoga* that is to be performed prior to that [maintenance].

This maintenance is not for the purpose of purifying the person on the occasion of having completed one's Vedic study (*gataśrī*), as that would entail the assumption of a separate result; furthermore, from the word "is to be maintained" (*dhāryaḥ*), the Āhavanīya fire is understood through its direct denotation to be the object of the action.

In the case of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) heard in the texts, although it does not explicitly state agency because its purpose is to indicate a causal basis (*nimitta*), it is not untenable; for example, as in "seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses for a Vaiśya" (*vaidyasya*, *saptadaśa vaiśyasya sāmidhenyaḥ*, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.6.3, Bhāṣya).
However, [the maintenance of the fire] is solely for the sake of consecrating the Āhavanīya fire.

Since the Āhavanīya fire does not exist apart from its maintenance, there arises the contingency of its being purposeless in its own form; consequently, there is the establishment of a consecration of the Āhavanīya that serves as a means for the *apūrva* of the sacrifice, by way of bringing about the presence of the specific sacrificial session (*kratusaṃsthā*) which is invariably associated with it.
Thus, the statement that wearing [the sacred thread] serves a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) is refuted by the *Tantraratna*.

For this very reason, since the rites to be performed exist for as long as one lives (*yāvajjīvam*), even if one wears it again after having lost its splendor (*gataśrī*), the accomplishment of wearing it for the duration of one's life is established.
However, under the view that it serves a human purpose, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would have to be sought for its lifelong duration.

Furthermore, by the very fact that it is for the purpose of all rites, its retention implies its extraction according to the maxim of the bronze vessel (*kāsyabhojinī-nyāya*) (JS 1.2.14.134). Because it assists the *agnihotra*, it implies the extraction as a necessary concomitant. Nor should it be argued that since the retention is possible even when the extracted butter has already reached the fire for some other ritual purpose, it cannot independently imply the extraction.

When no ritual action whatsoever is being performed at midday or other such times, it is precisely then that the condition of having "passed the time" (*gataśrī*) arises; since the maintenance [of the fire] is mandatory upon the occurrence of this occasion, the extraction [of the fire] must necessarily follow in accordance with it.
Therefore, because the occasion exists, the *jyotiṣmatī* oblation must indeed be performed.

This being the position reached: when the state of having finished the study (*gataśrītvam*) occurs in the midst of a ritual action, then [the rule for holding] applies because it necessitates the act of lifting; otherwise, if it were not necessitating, there would be the fault of inconsistency (*vairūpya*). By the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), the injunction for holding—which serves the purpose of lifting prompted by another—is enjoined with respect to the state of having finished the study as the occasion (*nimitta*) for that which has been lifted for the sake of some ritual action.

For this very reason, even though the occasion is restricted in accordance with that [injunction], just as in the case of the phrase "not harming" (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth, there is no contradiction in restricting the [occurrence of] living.

Therefore, because the fire is either maintained according to the *dhāraṇa* rite or the *agnihotra* rite, and because of the implication of its extraction (*uddharaṇa*), there is no non-performance of the occasional rite (*naimittika*) when the fire—which is a subsidiary of the fire to be employed in the *agnihotra* about to be performed—is destroyed; for the requisite occasion (*nimitta*), namely destruction characterized by having as its counter-positive (*pratiyogitā*) that which is delimited by being extracted, is absent.

Furthermore, since there is no reason for maintaining [the fire] when it has been drawn out for the sake of another rite, whereas there is a reason for maintaining it when it has been drawn out specifically for the *agnihotra*, how could there be an absence of the *āśrita* (dependent) [expiation] in another performance such as the *tantra*? If it is argued that—just like the destruction of the potsherds—the specific act of drawing out (*uddharaṇa*) which serves the purpose of the *yoga-vākya* (the ritual injunction) brings about the utility of the *yoga-vākya* precisely through the destruction of what was cut off, because the state of being consecrated (*jyotiṣmatī*) is the occasion (*nimitta*), otherwise an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result;
therefore, this expiation does not apply here.
Rather, it is established that what is prescribed in general applies only to the *manasthī-homa* and similar rites.
The *Nyāyabindu* states: "The *āhavanīya* fire is to be maintained by one who has attained *gataśrī*-status.
One who has attained *gataśrī*-status is one whose prosperity has departed.

In this regard, although the *uddhāna* (removal of the fire) must be performed at the time of the *agnihotra*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) should still be performed. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since the fire removed for another purpose is maintained [by the sacrificer] on account of the occasion of having completed the *Gataśrī* sacrifice, it assists the *agnihotra* by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Consequently, because there is no removal of the fire specifically for the sake of the *agnihotra*, the sacrifice is not required.
Maṇḍana states: "The sacrifice is not required when the fires are merely maintained. Śaṃkara states: "The sacrifice is not required when the fire is maintained for the sake of the *Gataśrī*."

In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), the injunction that "some bricks are placed facing west in the east, and others facing east in the west" is for the purpose of regulating the completion of the ritual action.
"In front, one lays down others facing west; behind, others facing east"—here too, one should perform the laying down [in that manner].

This is because the meaning of the word *paścāccis* has been determined in the section concerning the application of words (*prayuktādhikaraṇa*), and because of proximity (*saṃnidhāna*). Such being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since the injunction is for the purpose of regulating the attainment of desires by the Brahmavādins, and because we see a praise of the single arrangement of the circle of stars in the statement, "Therefore, the constellations turn both eastward and westward" (Saṃkarṣa 2.1.21).
In the context of the Agnicayana, in the injunction "He worships with the pṛṣṭhas," the word *pṛṣṭha* denotes the *ṛc* verses as its substance.

The term *pṛṣṭha* should refer to the ritual action (*karman*), because it is taught as being such. In the Bhāṣya it is stated: regarding the scriptural injunction in the context of the fire-altar, "He stands worshipping with the *pṛṣṭhas*," it is considered there whether the duties (*dharma*) of the *pṛṣṭhas* are to be performed or not.
And what are they?
At the piling of the fire-altar, he worships with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. At the piling of the fire-altar, he worships with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras].

The general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) are the syllables *hi* and so forth; the specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) are such as "while the *rathantara* is being chanted, one should meditate on the earth with the mind," and "in the *bṛhat*, [one should meditate on] the ocean," and so on.
What, then, is the prima facie view? To that he says: this must first be examined—does this word *pṛṣṭha* denote an action (*karman*), or does it denote a substance (*dravya*)?

Is it not already established that the word *pṛṣṭha* is a name for a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*) in the section [of the Jaimini-sūtra] beginning with "In which there is an instruction regarding a quality, there is a connection with the primary" (1.4.12–13)?
For it was stated in reference to those very injunctions: "seventeen *pṛṣṭhas*", "the *vairūpa* *pṛṣṭha*", and "the *vairāja* *pṛṣṭha*".
Now, however, this is being considered here in the context of the statement: "He worships with the *pṛṣṭhas*."
What, then, is appropriate here? To that he says:
"The word *pṛṣṭha* should refer to the action, because it is taught as being such.
That is, the word *pṛṣṭha* should be expressive of the ritual action.
Why? Because the instruction is of that nature.
Just as that instruction is of such a nature wherein this word "pṛṣṭha" is a name for the ritual action (*karman*), so too is this [present case] of that nature.
What is its being of that nature? It is the commonality of the word "pṛṣṭha."
In that context, the word *pṛṣṭha* is understood to denote the ritual action (*karman*), and that very [action] is the *āgrayaṇa*.
Therefore, here too, it must be understood as denoting that same [action], because there is no distinction [in the usage].
If it were otherwise conceived here, one single word would have multiple meanings.

What is the fault in that? When a *dvandva* compound is uttered, there would be doubt, and no comprehension of the meaning would occur. In that case, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would not be established;
yet, the employment of words is for the sake of linguistic usage.
Or else, another cause, such as the context and so forth, must be relied upon.
However, when there is a single meaning, the comprehension of the meaning is independent [of such factors].
Therefore, it is improper for a word to have multiple meanings.

Therefore, the word "pṛṣṭha" is a name for the ritual action (*karman*). When it is a name for the ritual action, if those actions themselves are being taught here, then their mention [in this context] is indeed purposeless.
On the other hand, if this [mention] is understood there as being for the sake of establishing that [the *pṛṣṭha* chant], so that this fault may not occur, then this present section is contradicted.
Therefore, on account of this similarity, it is not to be prescribed [as a separate act]. One "stands by" with the *pṛṣṭha* forms; that is, one stands by with the seven *pṛṣṭha*-type rites.
And that similarity arises through their common characteristics (*dharma*).
Therefore, the duties must be performed.
[Objection: Because of the instruction regarding the designation and because of the contradiction, the word *pṛṣṭha* should apply to the substances.
[Reply: The Commentary states—this is not so; the word *pṛṣṭha* refers to the ritual action (*karman*).
What then? The word *pṛṣṭha* should refer to substances;
that is, to the substances consisting of *ṛks*.
It is the designator of *ṛks* such as "abhi tvā śūra nonumaḥ" and so forth.
Why? Because of the instruction regarding the designation.
This is an instruction regarding the designation: "He worships with the *pṛṣṭha* [hymns]. The meaning is that he designates [the sun] by means of the *pṛṣṭhas*.
But how, again, can this verbal form *upasthāna* be understood as having the meaning of "denotation" (*abhidhāna*)? It is said:
because of the specific nature of the grammatical suffix (*upagraha-viśeṣa*). When used with a mantra, the verb *upatiṣṭhati* takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).

The mantra, however, is the instrument of the act of naming, not of the act of approaching. Approaching is performed either with the body or with the mind; therefore, the mantra serves the purpose of naming.
This is indeed a contradiction:
if the word *pṛṣṭha* is assumed to refer to ritual acts, then the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is contradicted;
for in that case, the mantra would not function as an instrument (*karaṇa*).

Now, if the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is followed, there would be a contradiction regarding the *upasthāna* [offerings]. In that case, the purpose of denotation would be undermined; therefore, following the middle voice is the logical course.
For the word *pṛṣṭha*, by denoting the mantra that accomplishes the *pṛṣṭha* stotra through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), possesses meaning;
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), moreover, is justified precisely by the mantra being the instrument.
Therefore, the status of being the means for accomplishing the *pṛṣṭha* is established by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) for the act of *upatiṣṭhati*.
From the indicative mark (liṅga) of the middle voice (ātmanepada), it follows that the purpose is denotation;
nor is the direct statement (śruti) sublated by the indicative mark.
It is said in reply:
In this case, the Vedic revelation (śruti) is not sublated; rather,
the verb *upatiṣṭhati* expresses its own primary meaning, namely "standing near," which serves the purpose of denotation.
The verb "tiṣṭhati" (he stands) indicates that one should stand near the fire in order to accomplish the naming [of the deity], because it is in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
[The opponent] says: even so, the mantra is the instrument for the naming, not for the standing; thus, there is indeed no connection between the standing and the mantra.
Likewise, the recitation "he stands near with the *pṛṣṭha*" would be meaningless. It is replied:
by bringing about the expression [of the deity], the mantra becomes the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the standing-near (*upasthāna*), because it accomplishes its purpose.
For that which is purposeless is not performed;
therefore, the word *pṛṣṭha* [is applied] only by means of the mantra.
And if it is within the mantras, there is no application of the ritual properties (*dharmas*).
For the properties of mantras are not themselves unrighteous.
[The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: The word "pṛṣṭha" denotes a substance.
Why? Because the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is prescribed when a mantra is employed as an instrument.
In this regard, since the act of making a mantra cannot occur without the intervention of the navel, a root (*dhātu*) [meaning "to stand"] is inferred as something beyond that.
Thus, there are two roots here: one heard and one inferred.
Of these, the root *tiṣṭhati* ("to stand"), which is obtained through semantic necessity, is restated (*anūdyate*).
The meaning of the prefix is a restatement (anuvāda), because its capacity [to convey that meaning] is already established.
That which is performed as an *upasthāna* (waiting upon) is done only by standing near it, not otherwise.
Therefore, through the force of the prefix (*upagraha*), the word *pṛṣṭha* indicates its own specific mantras.
If the word *pṛṣṭha* were understood as being like the word *śruti*, there would be an absolute requirement for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Therefore, the word *pṛṣṭha* denotes the mantra.

[The opponent] asks: "How can it, which expresses 'standing near' (*upasthāna*), function in the sense of 'denoting'? [The reply is: The meaning of the two [roots] connected with the verbal root is not contradicted, because it is obtained through the capacity of denotation.

But the other says: "The mantra is for the purpose of denotation, not for the purpose of standing near (upatiṣṭhati). If this is so, how can that which has denotation as its purpose come to have the purpose of standing near? It is replied:

Just as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other such purificatory rites (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), by making the person fit for receiving the fruit, operate within the context of the sacrifice and are for its sake; so too here, the function of the verb "to stand near" (*upatiṣṭhati*) is denotation. And thus, by performing that operation, they attain the status of being for its sake. The Śābarabhāṣya states: "First of all, no new ritual act (*apūrva karma*) is enjoined by the word 'upatiṣṭhati'."
The word "pṛṣṭha" also prescribes for that very [sāman] the status of being a pṛṣṭha-stotra.
It is said:
"Because it functions as a secondary term (*jaghanyavṛtti*), the word *pṛṣṭha* is equal to these [other words];
furthermore, the verbal root *upatiṣṭhati* denotes standing near."

The meaning of that [is as follows]: regarding the statement "the *pṛṣṭha* stands behind," one should approach and address the fire while standing near the means of accomplishing the *pṛṣṭha*, namely the *rathantara* and other [sāmans].
Therefore, it is established that this is an injunction for addressing (*abhidhāna-codanā*).

As for Soma’s point: although the word *pūpa* occurring in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not effect extension (*atideśa*), let the word *pṛṣṭha* occurring in the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*) possess the power of extension; thus, the connection [of the discussion] is stated.

In this regard, since the *ātmanepada* ending in "upatiṣṭhate" is prescribed by the rule "upānmantrakaraṇe" (Pāṇini 1.3.25)—which ordains the *ātmanepada* for the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *upa* when used in the sense of employing a mantra—it would not be tenable in the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) argument that this is an injunction regarding the *pṛṣṭha* as the object [of the action].
Consequently, one would have to accept a "transposition" (*vyatyaya*) according to Pāṇini 3.1.85, "vyatyayo bahulam," and such a transposition is improper.
Nor can it be argued that the *ātmanepada* occurs here by virtue of the rule "akarmakācca" (Pāṇini 1.3.16), which prescribes the *ātmanepada* for roots that are intransitive.

In passages such as "The two wings [are] by means of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans], the tail by means of the Yajñāyajñiya," the word *upatiṣṭhate* cannot be supplied [to the sentence]; thus, because it is not intransitive, the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) would be entirely untenable. Therefore, based on that very [use of the middle voice], the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is an injunction for the designation [of the mantras] as having the Pṛṣṭha-sāmans as their instrument.

However, that is incorrect; for even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), one must accept that the actions denoted by the word *pṛṣṭha* are indeed directly stated in the scripture (*śruti*), since other [mantras] cannot serve as the means for the Pṛṣṭha and Sadyaska sacrifices.

And thus, since the Śrutis consist in the denotation of qualities residing in a qualified substratum, and because there is a rule that they function as mantras (*mantrakaraṇatva*), it is possible for them to have a function in the sense of being a mantra—even as in the final Siddhānta view—by means of a word standing in proximity to their object; consequently, there is no lack of justification for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Therefore, the occurrence of the middle voice is not a defect in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Thinking thus, the author of the treatise (*Śāstradīpikā*) employed the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), even though it was somewhat unclear, with the intention that "there would arise a secondary sense (*gauṇī*) of inferior status. One should understand that the *ātmanepada* was used to demonstrate that, while rejecting the definition of denotation (*abhidhāna-lakṣaṇā*) for the root *upatiṣṭhati*, denotation is inferred by means of *upatiṣṭhati*; it was not intended as a formal logical justification (*siddhānta-yukti*) for the occurrence of the *ātmanepada* itself.

The meaning of the first sūtra is as follows: the word *pṛṣṭha* should denote the ritual action (*karman*), signifying the core of the stotra; the word *pṛṣṭha* should [denote the action] because, as seen in such injunctions as "the *rathaṃtara* is the *pṛṣṭha*," it is taught as denoting the stotra itself.
Vi—Regarding the question, "Do the properties of the stotra apply to the *pṛṣṭha* or not?
[the answer is: No, according to the principle of the Agnihotra, because of the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*) ending in the mantra.
Therefore, the word *pṛṣṭha* does not extend the ritual properties (*dharmas*) of the *stotra*.
[Bhāṭṭa: It is heard in scripture: "He stands upon the *agni-pṛṣṭha*.

In considering what is enjoined there by the word *pṛṣṭha*, since the word *pṛṣṭha* denotes a specific *stotra* and since it is impossible to enjoin that [specific *stotra*] in the rite of piling the altar (*cayana*) because it lacks plurality, it is concluded that the properties of the *pṛṣṭha*—which are distinct from the act of standing proximate to the root-meaning—are enjoined here as well, within the very productive energy (*bhāvanā*) expressed by the suffix.
Furthermore, because they possess the quality of being "back-parts" (*pṛṣṭha*), their status as *stotra*s (hymns) is established.

Moreover, even though the term is derived from a verbal root, its proximity [to the action] is due to its being the effect of the *akṣata* (unhusked grain), and thus it refers specifically to another ritual act.

Alternatively, according to the principle of the section on recitation (*pāṭhādhikaraṇa*, 9.1.7), since it is improper to accept a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense for the word expressing the "back-part" merely to conform to the plural number, one must indicate singularity and so forth by means of the plural; therefore, this is simply an injunction regarding the *jyotiṣṭoma* back-part within the context of the fire-piling (*cayana*).
Regarding their proximity, as before, they are subordinate to the *pṛṣṭha* stotras.
In reality, however, since the plurality of *pṛṣṭha* stotras has already been established for the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, all *pṛṣṭha* stotras indeed come to be enjoined by the *cayana*.

It is not, however, an injunction of the *pṛṣṭha* mantras or of the *rathantara* and other *sāmans*, because that would entail the fault of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the word "pṛṣṭha" occurring in the opening statement.
And thus, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) alone should be explained as being correct by virtue of its frequent occurrence (*bāhulakatā*), according to Pāṇini 3.1.85.

This being the case, although the word *pṛṣṭha* denotes the body, it is possible for it to refer to that which stands near [the body] by means of it; therefore, since it remains doubtful whether it serves as a restrictive factor specifically for the injunction of the *stotra*, it is more appropriate to interpret the word *pṛṣṭha* differently in accordance with the unambiguous middle voice.

For instance, by the traditional rule (smṛti) "after the prefix *upa*, [the Ātmanepada is used] when a mantra is the instrument" (Pāṇini 1.3.16), the Ātmanepada affix indicates that the mantra functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of standing nearby (*samīpāvasthāna*). Since this is possible through direct denotation (*abhidhāna*), even though a mantra cannot function as an instrument in an operation other than its own denotation, it is accepted as an instrument with respect to standing nearby by way of the denotation which serves as the purpose for that standing nearby. Consequently, in accordance with that, it is understood that the word *pṛṣṭha* refers to the mantra.

Therefore, by means of the relation of being the producer of the expression [of the deity] arising from standing nearby, the mantras possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to standing nearby; however, there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "expression" [as the primary meaning].

In reality, however, according to the principle of the *aindrādhikaraṇaka-stobha* (3.2.2), it is "expression" itself—qualified by the present action—that is enjoined by the verbal root through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In that case, the status of instrument belongs to the ritual act of the *pṛṣṭha*; as for standing nearby, it is merely restated here as already established by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra beginning with "abhi tvā."
However, by the term *pṛṣṭha-pada*, following the requirement of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the mantras that constitute the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* are indicated.

In reality, however, since it has been established in the *Kaustubha* on the *Citrādhikaraṇa* (1.4.3) that the word *pṛṣṭha* refers specifically to the *Sāmans* such as the *Rathantara* and others used in the *pṛṣṭha-stotras* through a conventional secondary sense (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā*) based on the purpose of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it is those very *Sāmans* that are enjoined as the instruments for the act of denotation.
And here, the status of the *Sāman* as the instrument for the act of denotation within the *stotra* is possible by way of manifesting the syllables of the *ṛk*.

For this very reason, since there is also the mention of the *yoni*-verses which serve as the basis for those [Sāmans], and because—as stated later in the text—"one Sāman is made into the *stotrīya*," they are applied specifically to the *stotra*; thus, there is no possibility of their being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the *abhivāna*.

Consequently, it is established that here the mention of the *rathantara* and other *ṣāḍahika* Sāmans, characterized by their basis in the *yoni*-verses, is enjoined as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*).

Furthermore, this discussion regarding the instructional aspect (*upadeśa*) concerning the Sāman portion is considered here merely on the basis of its prior understanding as a subordinate element of another [rite].

*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the passage "He stands behind the *agni*," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this is an injunction for a new ritual act (*apūrvakarman*), meaning that one standing near the *agni* should perform actions associated with the *pṛṣṭha* chants. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is a mere descriptive reference (*anuvāda*), meaning that having stood near the *agni*, one should offer it by means of the *rathantara* and other *pṛṣṭha* chants, because of the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating "the prefix *upa-* [is used] when a mantra is the instrument.
*Māṇḍana*: "There is no transfer of properties (*dharmātideśa*), nor does the word *pṛṣṭha* [denote the act itself].
*Śaṅkara*: "[The word *pṛṣṭhaiḥ*] indicates the means (*sādhanalakṣaṇā*)."
In the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana), there is application at the beginning of the principal rite, and the release of the fire at the conclusion of the principal rite.

The *agniyoga* (yoking of the fire) occurs at the time of the *soma*, because the consecrated ritual is for that purpose; since the goal is to be accomplished by means of the subsequent [rites], there should therefore be a release (*vimoka*) at the end of all the *parvan* sections. Commentary: Regarding the fire, it is heard in scripture: "With power and with ghee, I yoke the fire"—he offers this oblation; he thereby indeed yokes the fire. Again: "This sweet, swelling [oblation] of the waters"—with these words, he offers the *anuvimoka* (subsequent release).

In this regard, it is deliberated: does the yoking (yoga) serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, such that the unyoking (vimoka) must be performed upon the completion of everything; or rather, is the yoking at the beginning of the principal rite and the unyoking upon the completion of the principal rite?
What is the prima facie view? "The yoking of the fire... should be [performed]" (the entire sūtra).
The yoking should be at the beginning of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, and the unyoking should be upon the completion of everything.
What is the reason? It is heard without distinction: "With power and ghee I yoke Agni; he offers [the oblation]; he thereby yokes Agni.
And it is not heard that it is for this or that specific rite.
Because there is no distinction, it is understood to be for all purposes.
Moreover, when that [fire] is established, both the subsidiaries and the primary rites are performed within it;
therefore, for this reason as well, it is for the sake of all.
As it has been stated: "Or rather, it belongs to all, because of its being a subsidiary, since it is not connected with those [specific rites]" (3.1.12).
If liberation were for the sake of all objects, then liberation would have to be performed upon the cessation of every single one; for only then would the task of yoga be completed,
and liberation is for the purpose of yoga and liberation.
dup—(The written reading is compared with the *Tantraratna*); at the conclusion of everything, the release (*vimoka*) must be performed.
Why? Because by the statement "He yokes [him] to Agni alone," no specific distinction is understood as to whether the yoking occurs at the beginning of the principal rite (*pradhāna*) or not.
And since both the principal rites and the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) are performed within the fire—which is the locus for the consecration known as yoking—[the release must follow all].
Just as in the case of the injunction "he places the oblations on the altar," the placing of the oblations—
both the subsidiary oblations and the principal oblations— is not qualified by the principal oblations alone;
just as the sweeping (*saṃmārga*) performed at the Āhavanīya fire does not belong only to the subsidiaries, but rather [belongs to the fire itself].

Likewise here too, since there is no distinction regarding the fire, the application (*yoga*) pertains to all purposes; for it has been stated that the context (*prakaraṇa*) does not serve as a differentiator. And thus, when the application pertains to all purposes, its release (*vimoka*) must also pertain to all purposes.
Or rather, [the release occurs] upon the completion of the principal act, because it is for the sake of that.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, the release would not occur upon the completion of everything."
What then? Only upon the completion of the principal [sacrifice].
For it is heard in connection with the principal sacrifice: "He yokes with five; the sacrifice is fivefold; as great as the sacrifice is, so much he attains.
It is understood that he yokes for the purpose of reaching the sacrifice.
Therefore, there is a connection with the *pradhāna* and so forth.
If it is for the sake of the *pradhāna*, then once that *pradhāna* has been accomplished, the purpose of the yoga is completed; therefore, there is liberation (*vimoka*) therein.
A general injunction, when specifically connected with the sacrifice, serves the purpose of liberation.
Upon the completion of the principal [rites], there is release.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "He unites with five; the sacrifice is fivefold," which connects it with the sacrifice.
And the word "sacrifice" (yajña) denotes the principal [rites].
This is not correct; for the statement "he joins with five" is a sentence prescribing a quality (*guṇavākya*).
Therefore, because it forms a single syntactical unit with that [injunction], this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of the number itself, not of the joining.
By the force of the context as well, this is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) for that very [act], namely "the sacrifice is cooked," and not for the joining of the fire.

[To the question] "By what, then, is the injunction for the sacrifice stated?"—it is said that the ritual act is expressed by: "He offers the oblation with the words, 'I yoke the fire with power and with ghee.'"

And that which is being produced becomes desirous of an action. (It is not [desirous] of the destruction of qualities, nor of its own production. In that case, it becomes free from expectancy through whatever connection with a purpose is provided by context or by sentence—here, however, its purpose is provided by the sentence itself: the joining of fire (*agniyoga*; for it joins fire alone).
Furthermore, in that sentence there is no connection with sacrifice (by which it could be for the sake of the primary rite).

Even if there were a connection with sacrifice (in the very originative injunction), nevertheless, the word "sacrifice" denotes both the subsidiary sacrifices and the primary sacrifices as merely sacrifice in general. Therefore, because there is no distinction, the connection (relationship) is with sacrifice in its entirety.
And in the case of the *avabhṛtha* bath, there is a prohibition of that which is for the sake of the primary rite, because it is not part of the path.

The Commentary (Bhāṣya): And this being the case, the non-release of the selection of the ancestral lineage (ārṣeya-varaṇa), which is prescribed for the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), must be performed at the very end of all [rites].

Here, since it follows that the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) produced by the connection [of the rite] has its own final effect, this state of being the conclusion is understood through the force of the explanatory passage (arthavāda).

Therefore, regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the release of the fires (*agnivimoka*) occurs only at the conclusion of their own specific duties, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it occurs only at the end of the primary rites (*pradhāna*). This is because the supplementary statement, "The fifth oblation is the foot of the sacrifice," indicates its true purpose; and just as in the case of the rule "The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belongs to the Soma [rite]," it is understood to apply to all [rites] rather than being restricted solely to the primary ones. Consequently, even the selection of the priests (*varaṇa*) pertaining to the Soma rite—based on the scriptural passage, "If one were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call while already chosen, the blessing of the sacrifice would go to the enemy"—is for the sake of the primary rites alone, by virtue of the same logical principle (*nyāya*) as the engagement of the fires (*agniyoga*).

Consequently, in the *avabhṛtha* bath, which is an ancillary (*aṅga*) of the Soma sacrifice, the selection of the *hotṛ* priest—which would otherwise be obtained through extension (*atideśa*)—is excluded by the statement, "He does not choose a *hotṛ*. However, if the selection belonging to the Soma sacrifice were intended for both the ancillaries and the primary rite (*pradhāna*), then because the extension-based [selection] would be sublated by the direct (textual) [injunction], it would not even arise; thus, an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) would be untenable.
And although...
In the Agnicayana, there is the releasing of the sacrificial post and so forth (46). In the Agnicayana, the *lokaṃpṛṇā* mantras are not those belonging to the *Daśatayī*;
because they are not recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*), they lack the status of being constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the rite.

Since it is explained by the supplementary statement, "This indeed is the *chandas* of the seers (ṛṣis) which belongs to Agni, namely the *Yājñasenī*," [one might argue that the verses are those of Yajñasena]. This being the position reached, we reply: they are *āgneyī* (belonging to Agni), because the supplementary statement explains them as being for the purpose of recollecting the seers of the *Daśataya* collection, starting with "I praise Agni, Madhucchandas," and so forth. Furthermore, since it is enjoined that "one places [the bricks] with a *sūkta* for the sake of delimiting the *ṛc*s and *sāmans*," and since the term *sūkta* is well-known to apply only to the *Daśataya* collection and not elsewhere, the *Yājñasenī* verses are the instruments (*karaṇa*).
(Saṃkarṣa. 2.1.32)

In the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana), the rites such as the releasing of the sacrificial stakes (ruk-pratimocana) and others are to be performed after the purificatory consecrations (dīkṣā-saṃskāra).
If there is a conjunction (saṃnipāta), it should occur at the end as previously stated.
The Commentary states: After the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering], the *ruk-pratimocana* and subsequent rites are prescribed by the sacred text (*āmnāya*).
In that very sequence, the purificatory rites for the initiated (*dīkṣita-saṃskāra*) are obtained through the principle of extension (*codaka*).
In this regard, there is a doubt: is there no fixed rule, or should the releasing of the *ruk* and so forth come first, or should the consecratory rites (*dīkṣita-saṃskāra*) come first?

What is the prima facie view? There is no fixed rule; or else, just as the *ullāsa-bharaṇa* and other rites precede the *dīkṣaṇīyā* according to the order of the direct textual recitation (*pratyakṣa-pāṭha-krama*), so too should the releasing of the *ruk* and so forth [precede].
This being the case, we reply:
the consecratory rites (dīkṣita-saṃskāra) must be performed first.
Why? Because both the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama) with respect to the Dīkṣaṇīyā and the extended injunction (codaka) indicate that they are to be performed after the Dīkṣaṇīyā.
Regarding their mutual sequence, no manifest textual order (*pāṭhakrama*) of the *ullāsabharas* establishes priority there.
However, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is a prior recitation of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), whereas in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), the *rukṣapratimocana* comes later.
Therefore, the sequence should be exactly as stated: the modified rite at the end.
Now, for what reason is a "conjunction" (saṃnipāta) suspected? Is this conjunction not indeed manifest?
This statement regarding something that is not doubtful is itself doubtful.
For example: "Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and have sacrificed with many sacrifices..."
"If the scriptures were authoritative, they would have attained the supreme goal.
Therefore, there is no fault.

Dup—After the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, the consecration rites (*dīkṣita-saṃskāra*) have been performed; by the force of the general rule (*codaka*), they are obtained in the same manner [in the subsequent rites].

Now, it may be argued that rites such as the untying of the *ruk* and others are heard of as occurring after the *dīkṣaṇīyā*; even though these are to be performed according to the sequence obtained through the general rule, their posteriority is certainly not set aside.
Śā—In that case, by virtue of the direct textual recitation (*pratyakṣa-pāṭha*), [the rites] follow immediately after the *dīkṣaṇīyā*.
The wearing of gold ornaments and so forth should be performed first, followed by the consecration of the initiate (*dīkṣita-saṃskṛti*).
It is said:
"Consecration (*dīkṣā*) brings about the purificatory rites of the initiate in their proper sequence."
And for those [reasons] that have been presented, there is no reason for us not to act;
for, as before, there is a counter-position [based on perception]. (Perception...)

In the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana), one places a bull-brick. Regarding the rule for the constant flow of what has been heard in the agnicayana, there is no lack of confidence because it is not explicitly mentioned [elsewhere]; therefore, let that be merely optional (kāmya).
