As for the general statement found in the Taittirīya branch, "He offers the Vasordhārā," it is intended to enjoin the twelve [Vasordhārās] in a general sense.

In this regard, through the accomplishment of the intermediate performance (*avāntarakaraṇa*), the continuous sequence (*sāṃtatyam*) of all twelve oblations is established by the scriptural injunction. Since the word "continuous" (*saṃtata*) here denotes simultaneity (*sāhitya*), and since simultaneity between the mantra and the ritual act is thus perceived, one might argue that there is no conjunction of the beginning of the act with the end of the mantra. To this, we reply: although the word "continuous" is used in common parlance even for things that are not simultaneous, it would result in enjoining simultaneity only among the acts themselves. Therefore, because it does not subvert the temporal sequence—namely that the act follows the end of the mantra—as understood through reasoning, it cannot be taken as enjoining the simultaneity of the mantra, which is not otherwise established.

Nor should it be argued that such a rule for constant performance (*nityaprayoga*) is redundant because the concomitance of those [subsidiaries] is already established by the very fact that the performance must be expeditious according to the injunction of performance;

for that injunction is prescribed in order to obtain the penance occasioned by the sequence of Yajurvedic subsidiaries, which is not otherwise known through the application of the penance rules triggered by the faults prescribed by the hypothetical injunctions.

*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the statement, "He offers a continuous stream of clarified butter" (*saṃtatāṃ vasordhārāṃ juhoti*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the quality of continuity (*saṃtatatva*)—which consists of simultaneity (*sāhitya*)—relates to both the mantra and the ritual action, these two must be performed simultaneously. In response to this, [the established view (*siddhānta*) is as follows]: Since continuity consists of non-interruption (*aviccheda*), there is no requirement for simultaneity. Even if such simultaneity were required, because of the scriptural injunction, "He performs these twelve offerings," there is a plurality of actions; thus, the meaning of the word "continuous" (*saṃtata*) refers to the non-interruption of those very [individual acts]. This is because [continuity] is conveyed by the word "offers" (*juhoti*), whereas the mantra is not so conveyed.
Therefore, in this case as well, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is just as before.
Maṇḍana says: "In the *dhārā-yajña* as well, the sequence should be exactly the same. Śaṅkara says: "And [it applies to] the continuous stream of *vasu* (*vasordhārā*)."
"One should begin at the end of the mantra.

Regarding the statement, 'In the piling of the fire-altar, one lays down a bull,' there is another word 'bull' (*vṛṣabha*) which is to be laid down by means of the mantra, 'Thee, O Agni, the bull. Since the word 'bull' heard in the injunction 'one lays down a bull' can possibly refer to something to be laid down—just as in the cases of animals, bricks, and so forth—this is the prima facie view. However, since it is heard that such a bull is to be laid down in each layer (*citi*), and because laying it down in all five layers would contradict the rule regarding its knee-height, this word 'bull' refers to the single brick to be laid down by the mantra, 'Thee, O Agni, the bull.'"
*Saṃkarṣa* 2.1.22. In the *agnicayana* (fire-piling), the hawk-shaped altar (*śyenākṛti*) is purely optional (*kāmya*).

This is because the mantra "The divine eagle" (*divyaṃ suparṇa*) functions as an injunction, and since the optative suffix (*leṭ*) is heard in the sentence "Of birds indeed... (*vayasāṃ vai...*), it can be concluded that this is a restatement of the injunction "One desiring heaven should pile the hawk-altar" (*śyenacitiṃ cinvīta svargakāmaḥ*). Thus, due to its connection with the desire for heaven, the hawk-shape is both obligatory and optional, like the *aindravāyava* cup. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the Siddhāntin replies]: Since the specific shapes such as the hawk, the falcon, and so forth can be accounted for by a mere general reference (*anuvāda*), there is no evidence for assuming the presence of the optative suffix (*leṭ*). Therefore, the hawk-piling (*śyenaciti*) is purely optional (*kevalakāmya*).
The statement "it is eternal" is merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) of the ritualists (*yājñika*). (Saṃkarṣa.

2.1.40) In the case of the fire-piling (*agnicayana*), there is an omission of the consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as the formal installation (*ādhāna*), for the optional fire (*kāmyāgni*) that is prescribed in the scripture as being brought from a tree that is swaying.

In that [fire], the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are to be performed because they have been prescribed. Commentary: In that fire used for the maintenance of the sacred fires (*vaihārika*), the purificatory rites pertaining to the establishment of the fires (*ādhānika*) must be performed; because they have been prescribed.
For those [rites] belong to all ritual acts, since the establishment of the fires is a prerequisite for everything.

If they were not performed, that rite would be deficient in that constituent part and thus fruitless. However, they would fall away from their place. Commentary: They would fall away from their place; that is, the purificatory rites pertaining to the installation [of the fires].
Why? Because of its position.
This unconditioned [element] is heard in the same position as that conditioned [element];
because it is specific, it is the sublater of that.

If he has already ceased [from transmigration], for what purpose would the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) be performed? They would be performed so that he might become purified; there is no purpose here for one who is not purified. Therefore, they are omitted in his case.

Śabara: The purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) and so forth, should be performed there [in the forest], because purificatory rites are for the sake of the *homa* sacrifice, and this fire is the means for performing the *homa*. Bhāṣyakāra: It is true that this fire is the means for the *homa*, yet it is unrefined; since it has already attained a state of being refined [by its very nature], no purificatory rites need be performed here.
For it is not possible to impose a refinement produced by the churning sticks (*araṇi*) and mantras upon wood already brought from a tree.
Therefore, there are no purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) here.

Soma—[the connection is as follows]: since the *āhavanīya* fire also belongs to the optional fire (*kāmyāgni*), and because the purificatory rites for one who has attained prosperity (*gataśrī*) must be performed even there, this constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Thus is the connection.

Although the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is for the sake of the *āhavanīya* fire, nevertheless—because of the word "āhavanīya" in the injunction "one offers into the āhavanīya"—the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) produced by the *ādhāna* and the *pavamāna* [sacrifices] are applied to the *homa* (offering). Since it is impossible for those consecrations to be the direct substratum of the *homa*, it is understood that they belong to the fire which serves as the substratum for the *homa*. Consequently, since even the optional (*kāmya*) [fire] serves as the substratum for the *homa*, the consecrations must be performed for that as well; such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Alternatively, if one were to refer to the substratum of the *homa* already established by another sentence...

If the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) were to be performed [there], they would then be common to both optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory rites; however, this is not the case. Rather, it is the sentence "He offers into the Āhavanīya fire" itself which, while enjoining the rite of preparation, brings about the status of being an object for the oblation for that fire once it has been prepared.
Consequently, when the optional fire is employed in the piling of the consecrated fire-altar (*agnicayana*), how could it receive those preparatory rites?
Therefore, there are no preparatory rites there; such is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The meaning of the first sūtra is as follows: in that optional fire (kāmya-agni), the performance of the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) should take place, because they have been taught and prescribed as being for the sake of all oblations (sarva-homa). [Objection: "Is there not the rule here that [the rites] beginning with the installation (ādhāna) do not apply? [Response: That is so, because it is a subordinate element (śeṣa) to everything. [Rebuttal: No, because the state of being consecrated (saṃskṛtatva) does not fall away, and because the logic of the mantras is not possible [in this case]."

Commentary: For this very reason, the purificatory rites such as *ādhāna* (the formal installation of the sacred fires) do not apply to the fire used for optional (*kāmya*) rites; for that fire is denoted by terms such as *āṣṭra* precisely because it is unrefined, and because [purificatory rites] like *mayana* (cleansing) are impossible therein. Furthermore, since *ādhāna* is not something to be accomplished (*kṛtya*), there is no possibility of its application to that fire.
However, rites such as the sweeping and cleansing of the enclosing sticks (*parisara*), which serve as means for accomplishing the preceding ritual procedure (*kalpa*), certainly do take place.

*Nyāyabindu*: In that regard, it is argued that the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as *ādhāna* (the laying of the fires) should be performed, even though [the wood] is intended for the purpose of the *homa* (oblation). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that although it serves as the means for the *homa*, since the purificatory rites such as the recitation of mantras do not apply to the tree [itself], no such rites are to be performed here.
Maṇḍana: "The purificatory rite of *ādhāna* does not apply to this.
Śaṅkara: "Rites such as *ādhāna* do not belong to this."

In the Agnicayana sacrifice, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the initiation-offering mantras (*dīkṣāhuti-mantra*) prescribed [in the context of the fire-altar] with the Soma-related initiation-offering mantras.
This is because of the scriptural statement, "He initiates with six," which indicates a modification of those mantras due to their connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
Commentary: "His fire-altar is this," as in the passage, "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar."
In that context, there are initiation-oblations (*dīkṣā-hutayaḥ*), both archetypal (*prākṛtī*) and modified (*vaikṛtī*).

The archetypal ones are: "To Ākṛti, to Prayuj, to Agni, Svāhā! To Manas, to Medhā, to Agni Prayuj, Svāhā! To Citta, to Vijñāta, to Agni Prayuj, Svāhā! To Vāc, to Vibhūti, to Agni Prayuj, Svāhā! Likewise, the modified ones are: "To Ākṛti, to Prayuj, to Agni, Svāhā! To Medhā, to Manas, to Agni, Svāhā! To Dīkṣā, to Tapas, to Agni, Svāhā! To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni, Svāhā! O divine waters, vast and all-pervading; O firm Heaven and Earth, and the wide mid-region!"
May Bṛhaspati ordain [this] with the oblation, Svāhā!
May the Viśve Devas choose the mortal who leads him toward truth.
O All-Gods, you strive for wealth; may he choose glory for his purification, Svāhā! (Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā 1.4.7)
Thus [it is said].
With reference to these [verses], they recite: "He initiates with six.
In this regard, there is a doubt.

Is there the application of the modified (vaikṛta) offerings and the cessation of the original (prākṛta) ones, or rather, is there a combination of both the original and the modified? What is the prima facie view? Since it says "he initiates with six," there should be a modification of the mantras for those original oblations;
the original ones should be superseded by the modified mantras, because of their connection with the scriptural injunction.
The connection with the direct Vedic revelation belongs to the modified (vaikṛta) [mantras].
There are six modified mantras;
by the word "six," the modified ones are understood.
Therefore, there is sublation of the archetypal elements, not their combination.
Regarding the phrase "But because of the repetition of the principal," the *Bhāṣya* states: the word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position that there is sublation of the archetypal elements.
There is no contradiction; rather, there is a combination. Why? Because it is possible.

For where there is the possibility of the simultaneous occurrence of both the original (prakṛta) and the modified (vaikṛta), there the original is set aside by the modified; for if they were to be combined, there would be a repetition of the principal act. However, where repetition is explicitly enjoined as something that must be performed, in that case this fault does not arise—that is, the contingency of repetition does not apply.
Furthermore, here the scriptural injunction for the principal oblation is heard: "He offers twelve oblations.
Therefore, because this is possible, there is a combination [of the two];
the ritual action involving the mantra should be performed by repetition.
Commentary: This is not so; it is a case of combination (*samuccaya*).
Those archetypal elements obtained through the *codaka* (transfer rule) would be sublated by those [elements] directly heard in the modified (*vaikṛta*) rite.
Now, as for what was said—that when there is possibility, one does not sublate—[that is incorrect].
To this it is replied: there is no possibility.
How so? The six modified mantras are enjoined for the archetypal oblations in the fire by means of direct scriptural audition (*śruti*).
If these are subordinate acts, they must be performed with modified mantras;
therefore, the mantra-ritual should be repeated.
Consequently, the original (prakṛta) elements would indeed be set aside.
Alternatively, because each mantra is distinct, there should be no omission of the original [mantras]; rather, there should be repetition when another is recited.
Commentary: The word "alternatively" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position.
The oblations are performed with each individual mantra.
And due to repetition, there is a total of twelve.

Both the archetypal (*prākṛta*) mantras, which are obtained by virtue of being the meaning of the mantras, and the modified (*vaikṛta*) ones, which are obtained through direct scriptural statement (*śravaṇa*), are included. Furthermore, the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavacana*), which grasps all constituent parts, encompasses both sets.
Furthermore, sublation and optionality occur when combination is impossible; combination is not possible here.
For if there were sublation, the application of the injunction would be annulled.
Moreover, the modified (vaikṛta) elements are not heard of as being extracted once the oblation has been accomplished.
Therefore, because they are established from the word *homa*, those modified (*vaikṛta*) subsidiaries would lack a fixed rule;
for those modified ones are heard [as being performed] at the initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*),
whereas [the others] are heard [in the context] of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*).

Regarding the statement, “He initiates with six,” the injunction for the performance of the oblation takes up those [mantras] that are proximate, which are intended for offering and end in the word *svāhā*.
And both the archetypal (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*) mantras are proximate.
Therefore, there is a reason for the determination that "one takes these," and not others;
and it has already been stated that no fault arises from the performance of the primary [rites].
Consequently, [the rule] applies to the original (prakṛta) mantras.
Moreover, practice performed improperly is not effective;
the mantras are recited only once by the gods,
and it is by means of them that the consecrated person accomplishes his purpose.
Once the consecration has been performed by them and the purpose accomplished, a further repetition is not logical;
therefore, for this reason as well, there is no omission of the archetypal elements.
Furthermore, repetition is not possible when there is a sequence [of prior and posterior], because it is contingent upon a specific occasion.
Commentary: Furthermore, the words "prior" (*pūrva*) and "subsequent" (*apara*) occur [in scripture]:

"He offers six prior [oblations]," and "He offers six subsequent [oblations]. This is not possible for the modified (*vaikṛta*) oblations alone, as they are merely recited by name; for they are occasional (*naimittika*).
The subsequent sound has the preceding as its cause, and the preceding sound has the subsequent as its cause;
therefore, there is no abandonment of the original [sounds].
Furthermore, it demonstrates their identity.
The Commentary states: For this reason as well, we understand that there is no exclusion, but rather a combination.
Why? Because it shows the distinctness of those oblations:
"He offers both—the Āgnikī and the Āśvarkī."

Just as there is a collection of these mantras, so too, because they are offered into the fire and performed by the sacrificer himself, no such specific designation occurs. Otherwise, all of them would simply be "pertaining to the fire" (āgnikya),
in which case their distinctness would not be established.
And there is distinctness;
therefore, there is neither exclusion nor conjunction,
nor would there be an indistinct designation.
Commentary: For this reason also, there is no cessation [of the fire-altar construction]; rather, there is a combination.
Why? Because of the designation. There is a designation: "First the sacrifice (adhvara), then the fire-altar (agni); that which is the fire is the rite near the fire."
The designation "first of the sacrifice" and then "of the fire" is appropriate only if there is a conjunction, not in the absence of a distinction;
therefore, there is a conjunction.
[Śabara: In that case, it is by direct observation and by direct scriptural statement.
"Modified mantras set aside the original mantras because they serve a different purpose.
This being the prima facie view, we reply: "The modified mantras are not heard in scripture as being for the purpose of the oblation by means of a direct statement;
rather, their status as being for the purpose of the oblation is merely inferred from their being for the purpose of initiation (dīkṣā)."

And because the purpose [of the original] is established even by a mere approach accompanied by effort, there is no sublation of the archetypal [mantras] by the modified ones through replacement; rather, there is a combination. Therefore, there is a combination of both the archetypal and the modified mantras.

Soma: Although the Agni-jyotiṣoma sacrifice is not a relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), nevertheless, they establish—beginning with the relevant section—that the Saumika Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi is a modification of the Āgnika Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi, and that for one initiated by fire, both Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭis are indeed auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
The connection [of this section] arises from the objection that, as in the previous case, there is here too a sublation of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rule.

(Regarding the claim of the prima facie position—that since the modified [Vaikṛta] offerings, which are prescribed by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*), sublate the archetypal (*prākṛta*) mantras obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*) and thus constitute parts of the oblation, the twelve [oblations] should be offered with those very [mantras] repeated—[the author] says: This would indeed be so if there were a prescription of other mantras by direct scriptural statement specifically for the function of the archetypal mantras; however, this is not the case, because the scriptural statement makes known that those [mantras] are intended solely for the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Nor should it be argued that because mantras ending in *svāhā* cannot directly serve the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the word "initiates" (*dīkṣayati*) is stated to indicate the function of the original mantras;

for since the scripturally established fact that they serve the purpose of initiation is possible even by way of the oblations (*āhuti*), it is improper to assume that "initiates" indicates a different function.

And thus, in the absence of an explicit statement regarding the repetition of the oblation (*āhuti*), it must be stated that the purpose of the oblation is indeed implied; and since that [purpose] is established merely by the connection of the mantras with the oblations, there is no evidence for the repetition of the mantras. Therefore, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that their combination (*samuccaya*) alone is logical, by virtue of the repetition of the oblations. As for the meaning of the first Sūtra: "In the injunction 'he initiates with six,' there should be a modification of the mantras for those original (*prākṛta*) oblations, because other mantras are prescribed by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
The commentary (*vi.*) states: "'He initiates with six'—this understood [injunction] sets aside the original [mantras]."

"Or [if there were] a combination, there would be sublation because of the unity of the effect, and that [unity] is established by the sentence! [This is] equal to the case of the *dīkṣā* oblations in the fire, as known from the injunction 'one offers the *dīkṣā* oblations with the *sruva* ladle from the *ājya* vessel. For the sake of establishing twelve [oblations], there must be a combination without repetition! In the *Bhāṭṭa-some*, it is heard in scripture: "One offers the *dīkṣā* oblations, taking portions from the *ājya* vessel with the *sruva* ladle. And here, due to the plural number, there is a distinction of acts based on the number.

Due to the recitation of the mantras in the sequence of the ritual manual (*karmapaṭhaka*), as established by the subsequent reasoning (1.1.1.9.147–52), the principle of the *kapinjala* section (1.1.1.8–46) does not apply here. Furthermore, their status as subsidiaries to the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is established by the designation (*samākhyā*) "initiation oblations" (*dīkṣā-huti*).

Moreover, in the context of the fire-altar construction (*cayana-prakaraṇa*), after reciting another set of six mantras, the text declares through the statement "he initiates with six [mantras]" that they serve the purpose of initiation.
And regarding those [mantras] ending with *svāhā* which are prescribed in the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*),
since they are directly connected to the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*), it is undisputed that they serve that purpose by means of the oblations (*homa*) which constitute their subsidiary parts.

And immediately thereafter, by the statement "he offers twelve," there is an injunction of the number twelve with reference to the previously established *dīkṣā* oblations; thus, in the performance of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* involving fire, there is a repetition of those [oblations], just as there is a repetition of the eleven *prayāja* offerings.

In this regard, it must be considered whether, in all twelve repetitions, the mantras specifically prescribed in the section on fire (agniprakaraṇa) should occur twice by way of excluding the eight mantras generally prescribed, or whether they should occur without repetition through conjunction. Since it is understood that the general rule is set aside by the specific one, there would be no fault even if the repetition of the mantras were accepted according to the principle that "the subordinate follows each primary. This being the prima facie view, [we reply]: only the fact that they serve the purpose of initiation (dīkṣā) is heard in scripture for them, not that they serve the purpose of the oblation (homa).
That [purpose of the oblation] must be inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the exclamation *svāhā*.

And even if that [sublation] were understood through non-return (*anāvṛtti*), it would still be sublated in practice because there is no evidence for its acceptance as something to be performed. Therefore, there is indeed a combination with the six mantras prescribed by general rule.

For if these mantras had not been prescribed in the restatement of the *dīkṣā*-sacrifices, then—in the case of the statement "they proceed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (*apasavyena caranti*)—there might have been a sublation of the mantras prescribed by general rule in all archetypal (*prākṛta*) oblations, as in the case of the *agnipraṇayana*; but this is not the case, because it is heard in scripture that [the rule] applies specifically to the purpose of the *dīkṣā*.

In the performance (*cayana*) of the fire-altar, by virtue of the archetype (*prakṛti*), the fourth day of initiation (*dīkṣāha*) and its mantras—beginning with "To Ākṛti, to Prayuj, to Agni, Svāhā! and so forth—are obtained.
And here, six mantras beginning with "Ākṛtim" are enjoined for the initiation, according to the statement, "He initiates with six.
Furthermore, the number of those days of initiation is twelve, based on the scriptural injunction, "He offers twelve oblations."

In this regard, since there is both a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), the modified mantras (*vaikṛta-mantra*) should supersede the original ones (*prākṛta*).

Therefore, the conclusion reached is that all twelve oblations should be offered using those very [modified] mantras repeated [twelve times]. However, the final established position (*siddhānta*) is that since the purpose of the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is accomplished through the act of offering by means of a single performance, there is neither repetition nor supersession of the original.
Maṇḍana states: "But there should be a combination (*samuccaya*) of the initiation-oblations."
Śaṅkara says: "Even in the case of initiation mantras, there is no [such rule].
In the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana), there is a combination of the mantras prescribed by number, because in the case of those prescribed by number, combination is not [merely] contingent."

Commentary: Regarding those mantras for which a specific number is prescribed—such as in the case of the fire-altar ritual, where it is said, "He takes [the earth] with four [mantras], he digs with two, and he brings [it] with six"—there should be a combination (samuccaya) of them.
What is the reason? Because a number is expressed by the word; that number must be accepted.
And that number cannot be accepted except through combination.

He says: Even in the case of a collective [performance], that action is performed by those who are brought together [in conjunction] with the ritual act, not by those who are separated, because of the lack of conjunction.
If that were so, the number would not be accepted as a factor in the ritual act.
This is not a fault.
Through the expression of its meaning, the mantra becomes subordinate (aṅga).
And all these [mantras] express that very meaning.
Even so, it is by means of the immediately preceding form [of the mantra] that [the action] is performed; the others become merely for recitation (japa), like ordinary speech.
It is said:
they will not have an unseen purpose;
rather, they will repeatedly state that very same action.
For there is indeed the repeated use of a mantra for the purpose of performance, such as "do, do, let me do.

In that case, just as a mantra whose purpose is expression becomes a performer of what has not yet been expressed by virtue of its traditional recitation (*āmnāna*), so too, because of the statement "he takes [the vessel] with four," that which is performed with four becomes a performer of what has already been stated.
Therefore, even in the case of combination (*samuccaya*), there is no lack of a transcendental purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).
The combination is established.

As for those mantras associated with a number, such as "He takes [the earth] with four," and so forth—of these too, as before, there is an option; however, due to the force of the number, there is a combination.
For the number four, being an auxiliary to the ritual act, would not be integrated if there were no combination.

In this regard, it is determined by the force of the statement regarding the number that the previously employed mantras function as instruments by way of their residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), whereas the final one functions directly; therefore, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) [of all].

If there were a conjunction (*samuccaya*) [of all four mantras], then only that mantra by which the ritual act is accomplished would function as the instrument (*karaṇa*), while for the others, their purpose would be merely transcendental (*adṛṣṭārtha*); thus, since the status of all as instruments is understood through implication, the number four is not an injunction. Rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the number already established by cognition, namely: "He takes [the fuel] with these four mantras. This is because the application (*viniyoga*) of the mantras beginning with "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the Gāyatrī meter" is established by the indicative power (*liṅga*) itself through repetition.
The statement "by four" is intended solely for the purpose of prescribing a number;
for even in the absence of an indicative mark (liṅga), a mere restatement of what is already established is untenable, and thus it must be understood as a prescription of number—
this is the final conclusion (siddhānta).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: regarding those mantras for which a specific number is prescribed, there should be a combination (samuccaya) of them; because they are prescribed by way of number, their combination is logically established even in the absence of a simultaneous application (saṃnipāta) of all of them to the ritual action and so forth. [As stated in the Vṛtti: “In the case of ‘He takes [the earth] with four [mantras],’ is there an option (vikalpa) or a combination of the mantras? Option was [the view] previously; but it is not so here, because of their being the instrument (karaṇatva) in the aggregate.”

There is no separate instrumentality for each individual mantra, because instrumentality is perceived in the collection as a whole, characterized by the number four. In the *Agnicayana* sacrifice, however, those [mantras] enjoined by statements associated with the number—such as "He takes it up with four" and so forth—are to be used in conjunction (*samuccaya*). This has been stated in the *Mantrādhikaraṇakaustubha* (1.2.4.31–45). Nor is there any impossibility of further manifestation once something has already been remembered; for even that which is already remembered can be recalled again for the sake of producing a refinement (*saṃskāra*) or for the sake of clarity.

Therefore, even if one posits a disparity—namely, that by the force of the scriptural statement (*vacana-bala*), the aforementioned mantras serve as auxiliaries to the ritual action (*anuṣṭhāna*) through the medium of a sanctification (*saṃskāra*), whereas another serves directly—there is no fault.

The *Nyāyabindu* states: "In such cases as 'He takes [the fuel] with four,' there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) due to the number; for without that, the status of being a constituent of the ritual (*karmāṅgatva*) would be impossible for the number.

In that regard, it is determined by the power of the scriptural statement that the mantra functions as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) through the medium of a sanctification, while the last one functions directly. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Maṇḍana: "The number mentioned by you should be stated as a collective aggregate.
Śaṅkara: "It is a collective aggregate joined with the number. Oṃ: In the Agnicayana sacrifice, when there is no holding of the mouth for a year, there is the Vaiśvānareṣṭi.

The Vaiśvānara [offering] should be permanent, because it has the same number as the permanent [offerings]. The Commentary states: Regarding the fire-altar, it is heard in scripture: "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar. "If one who has not maintained the fire for a year piles the fire-altar, he will meet with calamity just as if the fire-wood were piled out of order; therefore, one should first offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. Vaiśvānara is indeed the fire-altar of the year. Just as one is born when the time arrives after having reached a full year, even so, having reached a full year, when the time arrives, he piles the fire-altar and shall not meet with calamity."

"This Vaiśvānara is indeed the dear body of Agni; he thus secures for himself the very dear body of him. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the Vaiśvānara offering obligatory (*nitya*), or is it occasional (*naimittika*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? Here too, it is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of what is already obligatory, namely: "The fault incurred by keeping the mortar for a full year is destroyed by the Vaiśvānara offering."

And its number becomes equal to that of the permanent [offerings]. It is said: "The oblations are so called because they are offered; there are these three worlds, for the purpose of ascending to these worlds.
However, the worlds lack the capacity to serve as oblations.
If, as the worlds are eternal, so too these oblations are eternal, then their connection with the worlds is established;
therefore, Vaiśvānara is indeed eternal.
Alternatively, it is because of the connection with what has arisen.
The Commentary states: When a [defect] has arisen, its removal through the utterance of the *nimitta* (the remedial cause) constitutes a conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
It is not the case that a defect which has arisen without such a conjunction serves the purpose of determining the fault.
Therefore, there is no contradiction here, as there is in the case of the *dadhi-graha* (the curd-cup).
For them, it is neither a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) nor something contingent (*naimittika*).
As for what was said—that the correspondence with the number of the worlds is only possible if [the sacrifice] is eternal, and not otherwise—that is an error.
Since there is a commonality between the three worlds and the three oblations (*havis*), it will be an explanatory praise.

The intention of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that in the passage "He who [performs] the Soma[-sacrifice], verily, [is] the year," the word *yat* does not serve to present the subject (*uddeśya*), because it is impossible for the word *yat*, which is construed as "he who piles the fire-altar for a year, he incurs ruin," to function as a presenter of the subject.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since it is impossible to refer (*anuvāda*) to an ornament that has not been obtained, and since there is a reference by the word "not having [worn]" to an ornament already obtained through laziness or other causes, the word *yat* (which) can function as the indicator of the subject (*uddeśya*), with the sentence ultimately meaning: "He who would not wear [it] should offer [it]. Thus, the referent is established.

The meaning of the first sūtra is as follows: "They are called *havīṃṣi* (oblations) because they are offered; these are the three worlds; for the ascent to these worlds. Thus, because the number of worlds corresponding to the oblations of the New Moon sacrifice, the Āditya sacrifice, and the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is the same as that of the eternal worlds, and because the worlds and the deities are eternal, it follows that the Vaiśvānara sacrifice must be eternal. [The commentary states: "Should the Vaiśvānara sacrifice at the piling of the fire-altar be considered obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)?
It is obligatory, just like the previous one, because of the word *yat* [in the text] and because there is no contradiction; otherwise, the latter view would hold."

In the *Bhāṭṭa* school’s interpretation of the fire-sacrifice (*agni*), regarding the scriptural injunction "He who [desires] a year... should offer," the sacrifice is indeed a contingent rite (*naimittika*) serving as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the event that, due to laziness or other reasons, one is unable to carry the fire-brand for a full year. This is because the word "who" (*yaḥ*), being in grammatical apposition with the agent, indicates that the agency in the action is the intended object (*uddeśya*), thereby conveying its status as a condition (*nimitta*). Therefore, like the *medana-homa* and similar rites, this is prompted by both the combined season and the contingency.
*Nyāyabindu*: It is heard in the context of the fire-sacrifice: "He who... should offer."
In that case as well, as before, the "supporting for a year" is considered to be merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), and thus its obligatory nature is maintained.

However, because the word *yat* (if) is used in conjunction with the agent, it establishes that the supporting for a year is a condition (*nimitta*); therefore, its status as a contingent rite (*naimittika*) remains settled.
Maṇḍana [states]: "For one who does not maintain the primary [means of subsistence] for a year, there is the sacrifice."
Śaṅkara says: "Vaiśvānara would be [the fire] on the occasion [of the rite].

Having been consigned into it at the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana), this [fire] is [used] in the annual piling of the fire-altar; [it is] Gāyatra. Having been consigned into it at the piling of the fire-altar, this [fire] is used elsewhere for the performance."

Since the act of depositing [the fires] serves as an auxiliary through another means, it is capable of performing the function of ownership; therefore, in the context of the *adhikaraṇa*, just as with the *ulba* (the fetal membrane), there would have to be a direct carrying away (*pratyakṣanayana*) of the *gārhapatya* fire and others as well. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because that which has gone outside without being covered by its seat necessarily becomes worldly (*laukika*), whereas the act of depositing is based on a scriptural injunction (*vācanikatva*) and lacks any specific designation (*samākhyāviśeṣa*), the carrying away must be done only after the fire has been deposited. (Sūtra 3.2.34).
Oṃ, in the piling of the fire-altar, there is no repetition of the offering of all-herbs.

If [the word] were to denote the mere property (*dharmamātra*), liberation would result from the meaning of the word through non-perception [of its purpose]. The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "But where the visible purpose does not exist—for example, in the case of those who maintain the sacred fire (*agnicit*), regarding the injunction: 'Having filled a mortar made from the root of an *udumbara* tree with all kinds of herbs, he threshes them;

he places that [mortar] there'—in that case, there is no purpose for the production of rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), because the purpose of the rice-grains, such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), has already been fulfilled."

Therefore, since the meaning of the word is established by a single performance, there would be no repetition. However, for those who maintain the position that "the word *avahanti* applies to the acts of raising and lowering the pestle only when the rice grains [are being threshed]," repetition would follow until the rice is fully prepared. But that is a very weak position.
For this reason, even in the absence of rice grains, the usage is observed in such expressions as "he threshes the *kaṇva*" and "he threshes the *kiṇva*.
Nor is this a figurative usage, because there is no contradiction [with the primary meaning].
Furthermore, by virtue of the established meaning of its constituent parts (*avayava-prasiddhi*), it is understood to denote merely the act of threshing itself.
Furthermore, the aggregate [of the word "pacati"] is not established as having a distinct meaning [other than the action];
rather, because the activity of cooking rice occurs most frequently, its usage there is predominant.
Therefore, this is a delusion.

In the case of the threshing of all herbs (*sarvoṣadha*), since a visible purpose is possible, the verbal meaning should be performed merely for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). Regarding this, the Sūtra—"But in the case of a mere duty (*dharma*), because no [visible] result is seen, there would be completion through the verbal meaning"—has been explained as a topical heading (*adhikaraṇa*) for the purpose of establishing that the threshing of all herbs has an unseen purpose; however, it is not [to be taken] as such [a formal section], because it belongs to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Rather, it is merely a counter-example.
Regarding the threshing of all the grains: is it to be performed repeatedly or only once?
It should be repeated, as in the previous case; for it is not so when the purpose is already visible [in the first instance].

In the Bhaṭṭa view, however, since the visible purpose is possible, the threshing has an invisible purpose; in that case, it is not at all [the case that] it is not for the sake of removing the husks.
For example, in the context of the fire-piling (*cayana*): "Having filled a mortar made of *udumbara* wood with all kinds of herbs, one threshes them; here he places that [mortar]."

In this context, since there is no application of the threshing (*vaituṣya*) of all the herbs (*sarvoṣadha*) at the outset, and on the contrary, it is understood that the filling with all the herbs—prepared by the rite of threshing—is for the purpose of preparing the mortar (*ulūkhala*) suitable for the placing (*upadhāna*), there is no possibility of an oblation (*āhuti*) even if the threshing were a refinement of the all-herbs in an invisible manner (*adṛṣṭavidhayā*), because it lacks the purpose of producing dehusking (*vaituṣya*).
This is even more so if the threshing is merely an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
The *Nyāyabindu* states: the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is no repetition of the threshing of all the herbs, because it serves an invisible purpose.

Maṇḍana: "In the case of *sarvoṣadhi*, there should be threshing only once. Śaṅkara: "But in the case of *sarvoṣadhi*, that (threshing) is [performed] once. [Regarding the statement] "In the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), one should pile it a thousand times," the word "thousand" does not refer to the ritual session (*ṛtu*).

Regarding the statements such as "One building [the altar] for the first time should pile it with a thousand," the words "thousand" and so forth refer to a sacrifice (ṛtu) where the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is a thousand. This is because we observe the use of the word "thousand" in reference to sacrifices in passages such as "having sacrificed with a thousand. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: Since it is understood that the word "thousand" is a qualifier of the verbal root *cinoti* (to pile), the interpretation that "one should perform the initial piling at a sacrifice where the fee is a thousand" would result in the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, as in the case of "one should pile it knee-deep," the "thousandfold nature" belongs to the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) itself.
(Saṃkalpa 2.1.12)
"Oṃ, in the piling of the fire-altar, you are the measure of a thousand"—this mantra applies to every layer of the altar.

Regarding the mantra "Thou art the measure of a thousand," its application—though established by the context (*prakaraṇa*) as applicable even to the layers (*citis*) consisting of two or three thousand bricks—is restricted by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra itself to those layers consisting of exactly a thousand bricks. Thus, it follows that the mantra is not to be used elsewhere. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: since the word "thousand" can refer to multiple numbers through figurative praise (*guṇavāda*) for the sake of eulogy, there is no contradiction between the indicative mark and the context; therefore, the mantra applies to all layers. (Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 2.1.14)

"Oṃ, in the construction of the fire-altar lasting a year, one desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should pile it with *gāyatrī* verses," and so forth; these apply only to those who desire specific fruits, whereas for those without such desires, the *ṛc*s must be in other meters.

When there arises the possibility of employing all the verses being brought forward without distinction, the rule is established as follows: because of the connection with specific desires in such injunctions as "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should pile the fire-altar with *gāyatrī* verses" and "One desiring vigor (*vīrya*) should pile it with *triṣṭubh* verses," those who desire those respective fruits should use verses in those respective meters; for those who do not have such desires, they should use verses in other meters.

In the *agnicayana* lasting a year (*sāṃvatsarika*), regarding the placement of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks: the *Āgneya-sūktas* brought in from the *Dāśataya* collection have no application in rites such as the *upasthāna*, which are distinct from the actual piling (*cayana*).

If it is argued that these sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are distinct from those prescribed by the archetype (*prakṛti*), and thus the archetypal fees are set aside, [we reply: this is not so, for there is no sublation of the archetypal elements. The duty of the fire-altar applies to each brick because of its collective nature, like the Full Moon sacrifice.

In the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), it is heard in the scripture: "He sprinkles the fire-altar with a thousand pieces of gold," and "He sprinkles the fire-altar with curds mixed with honey.
Likewise, it is also heard: "He drags [the altar] over with a cane branch and *avakā* plants," and "He drags [it] over with a frog.
Are these acts of sprinkling and dragging to be performed for each individual brick (*pratīṣṭakam*) upon every single brick, or are they to be performed only once for the entire collection of bricks?

Likewise, in the inquiry as to whether the word "fire" (agni) applies to the collection of bricks or to a distinct substance (dravyāntara) beyond that collection, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): The properties of the fire—the ritual duties of piling (cayana), such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and drawing lines (vikarṣaṇa)—should apply to each individual brick. This is because the word "fire" refers to the aggregate (saṃghāta), that is, the collection of bricks.

Therefore, since there is no distinction made regarding the fires characterized by the collection of the *cayana* (piling), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the drawing out (*vikarṣaṇa*) must be performed for all of them,

just as in the case of the *Paurṇamāsī*. Just as it is said, "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the full moon" and "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the new moon," and by the words *Paurṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā*, only the *Āgneya* and other offerings are intended, so it is here.

Or, just as in the case of the injunction "One should mix this [mixture] with the *Caturhotṛ* at the full moon sacrifice," the ritual duties (*dharma*) prescribed for the fire (*agni*) apply to the oblations such as the *Āgneya* and others indicated by that term—since those duties cannot possibly apply to the collective whole as a single entity—in the same way, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the word "fire" refers to the entire collection, and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and drawing out (*vikarṣaṇa*) are performed for each individual brick. [The Siddhāntin replies: This cannot be so; because the substance is a single unit, it is the bricks that are for the sake of that [fire].
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with a thousand pieces of gold and so forth, as well as the dragging (*vikarṣaṇa*) with a branch of *vetasa* and so forth, would apply to the fire (*agni*) as a single material caused by the bricks, and not to each individual brick. This is because of the unity of the substance; for the substance of the fire—which consists of five layers (*citipañcaka*) and is a composite whole (*avayavin*) commenced by the parts that are the bricks—is one.

And because the other bricks are for that purpose—that is, because they are constituent parts of the substance [of the altar]—and because of the understanding of the relationship between means and end established by the text "He piles the fire-altar with bricks," there is sprinkling and drawing only once; this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). However, due to the collection of injunctions, such would be the case at the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*).

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the analogy "like the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsīvat*) was cited. The proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) states its dissimilarity; the word "but" (*tu*) indicates this dissimilarity.
[The word "paurṇamāsī" is derived] from the collection of injunctions (*codanā*). The fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of elision (*vyalopa*).

Taking the collection of those injunctions—namely, the *Āgneya*, *Upāṃśuyāja*, and *Agnīṣomīya* sacrifices performed on the full moon day—as indicated by the word "paurṇamāsī," it is logical that the performance of the oblations (*havis*) characterized by them, or the properties of the fire-altar (*agnidharma*), [is intended]. Therefore, in the case of the term "paurṇamāsī" used for the full moon day itself, its status as such would consist in its being a denotation of the collection (*samudāyavācakatvena*), thereby possessing the nature of a collective.
However, in the case of *amā*, there is a different substance; thus, it does not possess that same nature, and this constitutes the disparity.

Therefore, the word *agni* denotes a distinct composite substance (*avayavidravyāntara*); because that [substance] is one, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and drawing out (*vikarṣaṇa*) are performed only once—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). A distinction between the two fire-drills (*araṇi*) is necessary due to the distinction between the fires, because if they were placed on a single [drill], a conjunction [of the fires] would result; for in the injunction regarding crossing a river—"they cross together with the fire-drills"—the plurality of fire-drills is heard. As for the statement "they cross with the two fire-drills," there is an option between duality and plurality according to other recensions (*śākhā*). This being the position reached, [we reply]: just as in the case of "they cross with a part of the chariot" and so forth, the mere accompaniment by fire-drills is enjoined for the purpose of crossing the river; thus, the mention of duality and plurality is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to refer to the distinction between the upper and lower fire-drills.
Alternatively, this is also possible under the view that the fires are perpetual (*ajasra*).
In the *Saṃkarṣa*,
it is stated that the fire addressed by the invocation "Bring Agni hither for me" is the Āhavanīya fire.

In the mantra "agnimagna āvaha," both the state of being external (*bāhyatva*) and the state of being internal (*vāhyatva*) are perceived in one and the same entity, because the designation is made with reference to both aspects.

This is logical, for in the mantra "svaṃ mahimānamāvaha," there is the perception of the one designated as "self" (*sva*) carrying his own greatness by himself. And that Agni, who consists of both these aspects, is precisely the deity of the *ājyabhāga* offering dedicated to Agni.

Based on the Vedic scripture, "He says, 'Bring Agni hither for me'; thereby he causes Agni to be brought for his share of the clarified butter," this being the position reached, [we reply]: because there is a contradiction between the agent of the act of bringing and the object of that action in a single entity, and because the term *svamahiman* is also explained as referring to Vāyu in the Kauṣītaki [Brāhmaṇa], and because of the scriptural hearing, "Having approached with the Sāmidhenī verses, [he says] 'Bring Agni hither for me,'" it is the manifest fire itself—the Āhavanīya—that is the bringer.

Therefore, even though there is a distinction between the *āhavanīya* fires, because they are stable and one, the duality is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) and thus not a determining factor; consequently, although there is no modification (*ūha*) of the vocative address, in the *avabhṛtha* rite there is a modification such as "O Agni, bring the waters" (*agnim āpa āvaha*). Because it is for that purpose—that is, because it is for the purpose of the primary rite along with its subsidiaries. Therefore, at the conclusion of the entire sacrifice (*sarvapavarga*), when the principal rite together with its preceding and succeeding subsidiaries is completed, there should be the release of the fire (*abhrevimoka*).
The meaning is that the application of the fire (*abhiyoga*) must be performed at the very beginning of all rites, and the release of the fire (*abhivimoka*) must be performed at the end of all.

This is a *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra according to the view of the Bhāṣya, whereas according to the view of the Vārttika it is a *siddhānta* (conclusive) sūtra; however, the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) remains the same—this should be noted.

Liberation does not occur at the conclusion of every subsidiary rite (*apavarga*), but rather it occurs at the conclusion of the principal rite (*pradhāna*); and the performance of *yoga* occurs at the beginning of the principal rite. This is because both *yoga* and liberation have that as their purpose—that is, they have the principal rite as their purpose. For it is heard [in scripture] that "he joins with five; being fivefold, he attains the sacrifice in its entirety," thus showing that *yoga* is connected to the principal rite.
The word "vādāt" (from the discussion) is for the purpose of excluding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
