A prohibition of both the selection of the Ārṣeya and the selection of the Hotṛ is appropriate because they are primary acts.

Since the selection of the Hotṛ is for the sake of the primary rite, and because its purpose is fulfilled upon the completion of that primary rite—meaning that the purpose or objective of the Hotṛ’s selection is such that it reaches its conclusion at the *avabhṛtha*—it is thus completed.

At the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), a prohibition must be made regarding the selection of the *hotṛ*, which is otherwise obtained by extension of the rule; for it has been stated: "He does not choose a *hotṛ*, nor one from a lineage (*ārṣeya*).
Therefore, these two acts—yoking and unyoking—are for the sake of the primary sacrifice.
Yoking is to be performed at the beginning of the primary sacrifice, and unyoking is to be performed at the end of the primary sacrifice.

And in the case of a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*), the binding and releasing should occur every day, because it is for that purpose; that is, because it is for the sake of the primary rites.
In the twelve-day session (*dvādaśāha*), the joining and the releasing should take place every day, since it serves that purpose and because it is for the sake of the principal acts.

Because it is stated in the Śruti: "He indeed releases [the yoke] day by day during the multi-day sacrifice (ahargaṇa)," therefore, even in the Abhri-cayana, the yoking (yoga) and the releasing (vimoka) are for the sake of the principal rite (pradhāna). Consequently, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the yoking occurs at the beginning of the principal rite and the releasing occurs at the end of the principal rite.
Some.

Regarding the statement *oṃ abhiyogaḥ somakāle*, since the fire (*agni*) is for the purpose of the primary rite together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅgatya-pradhānārthatva*), it is determined that the *abhiyoga* (the fastening of the yoke-pole) is also for the purpose of the primary rite together with its subsidiaries by way of that [fire]. Having thus proposed as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the unyoking of the fire (*abhivimoka*) should occur at the conclusion of the parvan together with its subsidiaries, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) will state the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the unyoking occurs at the conclusion of the primary rite alone. This is because of the scriptural text, “He yokes with five; the sacrifice is fivefold,” and because it is determined that the sacrifice is the primary offering; thus, it is understood that the *abhiyoga* is for the sake of the primary sacrifice alone. Therefore, the conclusion is that the unyoking of the fire occurs upon the completion of the primary rite.
Oṃ. Regarding the clarified butter for Abhirudra: in the Apabhṛta rite, it becomes worldly.

Even after the completion of the ritual (*karmāpavarga*), because the fire is still visible and because it has been drawn forth from the *gārhapatya* fire, its status as Vedic fire does not lapse according to the principle that "the continuity of the fire remains the same. Since there is no departure of the qualities characterized by consecration (*saṃskāra*) without the fire being extinguished, and since the scripture states, "Then it has departed," which is appropriate given the scriptural injunction for drawing it forth, one might argue that even when the *yāvaka* offering is made, the fire present at the conclusion of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is indeed Vedic. In response to this, we hold: even though the fire is being carried away after the placement in the kindling woods (*araṇī*), its nature remains consistent even upon the completion of the rite. This is because the consecrations exist only for the sake of the ritual purpose; the scriptures understand their persistence only as long as that purpose exists. Furthermore, the scripture stating "Then it has departed" indicates departure immediately after the oblation (*homa*). Therefore, although the fire is being carried away and remains in its original locus, once the consecrations have ceased, it becomes a worldly (*laukika*) fire during the *apāmārjana* rite.

For this very reason, by the passage beginning with "If the fire of one whose fire has been taken out goes out during the Agnihotra" and ending with "having brought those same embers together, he should think," the re-kindling by friction is prescribed specifically for the taking up of the fires prior to the completion of the Agnihotra.
By this, it is implied that upon the completion of that [Agnihotra], because those [embers] no longer exist, the fires become worldly (laukika).
Saṃkarṣa. 3.2.9.

Regarding the rule for mantras containing mixed indicative marks (*miśraliṅga*), there is also [the following]: "One offers the evening oblation with the mantra, *oṃ abhiyogyatijyotiḥ sūryaḥ svāhā*, and the morning oblation with *sūryo jyotirjyotiragniḥ svāhā*. (Su.
pṛ. 436). Furthermore, when it is said, "Agni is the deity," the cognition of the blazing fire arises.
Bhāṣya 3.2.12, p. 746: "Oṃ, 'May the god Agni, the Hotṛ, sacrifice to the gods'—this is the statement regarding the Āhavanīya fire.

In the *adhyupravara-nigada*, where the rule of common applicability to both [the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires] might have been expected in the phrase "May the god Agni, the Hotṛ, sacrifice to the gods," it is established that this refers specifically to the Āhavanīya fire because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the characteristic feature of the one who has been chosen, as seen later in the phrase "and may he speak through the word of the Brahman.
Saṃkarṣa 4.2.18.
Regarding the statement "Oṃ, the boy is a firebrand," the boy is not [designated] by way of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the firebrand.

What then? "That which is perceived in the boy—such as his tawny color and so forth—which is understood from the firebrand that characterizes its object, gives rise to the cognition of 'firebrand' in the boy due to similarity."
Or rather: [The theory of] "guṇādeśavāda" [is as follows]: by means of denoting its own primary meaning. Bhāṣya 1.4.12.23 (1), p. 354:
"When the word *abhri-māṇavaka* is uttered, there arises a cognition (*saṃpratyaya*) of the boy (*māṇavaka*); thus, the word *abhri* itself is the designator (*abhidhātṛ*) of the boy.
To this, it is replied:
A young brahmin is not understood from the word "fire.

People are seen to understand fire from the word "thunderbolt," disregarding the cognition of the young brahmin; but they are never seen to understand a young brahmin from the word "thunderbolt," disregarding the cognition of fire.

Whence is this [known]? Because wherever fire is intended to be expressed, the word *abhri* is invariably used there. For this very reason, although this [fire] is devoid of heat, it is not perceived as such;
therefore, the absence of heat is the cause for the application of this word *abhri*.
And since this [word "fire"] is not understood from that [word "boy"] when fire itself is not already known, therefore it is primary with respect to fire, not with respect to the boy. 3.2.11.
In the case of *abhir māṇavakaḥ*, [the dual form] is *abhir māṇavakau*.

It is understood everywhere that a word, though applied through similarity due to absolute difference [from its primary object], is not a denoter [of that object] because it lacks the characteristic of a cognition [directed toward it]. Vākyapadīya 3.1.6.12, p.
683. "The boy is like a spade" (*abhri-māṇavaka*).
For indeed, there is denotation even by way of a quality (*guṇa*).
Bhāṣya 3.2.14: *abhrimāṇavakaḥ* (the boy who is like a spade).

Even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the boy, [the word "spade"] denotes [the boy] because of similarity; it does not denote him when such similarity is absent. Furthermore, since its application is observed elsewhere where there is no similarity, and its meaning is not observed where there is no similarity, and because it functions as a qualifier, similarity itself must be conveyed first when the boy is being cognized. And since that [similarity] is not perceived unless the [spade] is known, the denotation of the "spade" occurs first.
And from that very connection, the understanding of the remainder [is obtained].
Vārttika 3.2.12, p. 748.
"May Agni Hotṛ know [the offering]"—in this *sugādāpana-nigada*, there is a mention of the Āhavanīya fire.

In the formula for the selection of the Hotṛ priest, *sugādāpananigada*, where the rule *abhrihotā vettu* might otherwise lead to uncertainty, the text states: *abhrihotyāhāgnirdevānāṃ hotā taṃ vṛṇīte* ("He says 'Agni is the Hotṛ'; Agni is the Hotṛ of the gods; him he chooses"). Following this, it is heard: *yo'gniṃ hotāramṛtāyurityāhavanīyaṃ punarvṛṇīte* ("He who says 'Agni as the Hotṛ for the sake of Truth' chooses again the Āhavanīya fire"). By the word "again" (*punar*), it is understood that the previously chosen Hotṛ is none other than the Āhavanīya fire. This is because the Brāhmaṇas are observed to employ the two—the blazing fire and the deity—interchangeably due to their mutual non-difference. (Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 4.2.19).
"Oṃ, Agnihotra, this oblation has been enjoyed"—this is the formula for the Gārhapatya fire.

In the *sūktavāka* mantra, "O Agni, you are the *sūktavāk*," because of the connection with the statement in the *sūtra*—"you are the *sūktavāk*"—and because of the determination of [Agni] as the *hotṛ* priest by virtue of the *āhavanīya* fire being directed toward him, and because in the phrase "the *agnihotrī* has enjoyed this oblation" (*agnihotriṇedaṃ haviḥ*) the instrumental case indicates merely the accompaniment of the *hotṛ*'s ritual action, and because that much alone is figuratively stated in such passages as "because he quickly traverses the space" (*tūrṇi haṅgyatvāt*), it follows that even the *āhavanīya* fire can be referred to as "the *agnihotrī*"; thus, this is a reference to that very same fire. To this, we reply: the instrumental case here denotes a characteristic mark (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*), and the reference is to the *gārhapatya* fire by virtue of its position.

Even though the connection with the recitation of the *sūktavāka* pertains to the *āhavanīya* fire, there is no reason why that which is read in proximity to the offering of the oblation (*havirjuhoti*) should not pertain to the *gārhapatya* fire; as stated in Saṃkarṣa 4.2.16: "It is like the cloud."

Just as, once the fires have been consecrated by the *ādhāna* ceremony, no further consecration is performed during their subsequent use, so it is here. (Ke. 9.2.12) It is like the case of the *agni*.

Just as in the passage: "Now, therefore, one performs sacrifices following the *agnihotra*: that [fire] with the *uktha*, that with the *atirātra*, that with the *caturrātra*, that with the *pañcarātra*, that with the *saptarātra*, that with the *ahar-rātra*, that with the *navarātra*, that with the *daśarātra*, and that with the *ekādaśarātra*," in these cases the piling (*cayana*) of the fire-altar can be performed, so it is here.
In this context, the word *abhri* means "piling" (*cayana*).

Bhāṣya 10.5.23.78: "Like the *abhri*. Just as for the fire that has been consecrated by a single installation (*ādhāna*), no further consecration is performed for it in subsequent rites, so it is here.

The Release of the Fire (agnivimoka): 60. The Release of the Fire is a specific type of oblation (*homaviśeṣa*) performed with the mantra "imaṃ stanaṃ madhumantaṃ dhayāpām" at the conclusion of the principal rite (*pradhānānta*)—or at the conclusion of the principal rite involving the fire-altar (*sāgnipradhānānta*)—in a sacrifice characterized by the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicityā*).
Bhāṣya 11.1.9.17. Oṃ. The Distribution of the Fires (*agniviharaṇa*) takes place in the Jyotiṣṭoma.

The various *harana* (carrying away) consists of the placement of the fires—having been taken from the *āgnīdhra* hearth—into the fires located at the *dhiṣṇya* altars for the disciples. There are eight *dhiṣṇyas*, which are fire-places in the form of small altars (*laghuvedi*), belonging to six officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who have performed the *praṇava*: the Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the Potṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Acchāvāka; the seventh belongs to the Āgnīdhra, and the eighth is the Mārjālīya. This is the ritual distribution (*viharaṇa*) therein.

In the injunction for the spreading of the fires (*agniviharaṇapreṣa*), the mantra "O Agnīdh, spread the fires" (*agnīd agnīn vihara*) is connected [to that act], but not to the rising. Thus, in the rule "Rising, he recites," the time is indicated by metonymy (*kālalakṣaṇā*); it is the time of rising at which the injunction for the spreading of the fires is to be performed. Therefore, the time is what is enjoined. (Vi. 3.2.4) *The Section on the Application of Mantras such as the Spreading of the Fires*.
The phrase "the section concerning rising and the utterance of speech" is to be seen in the *Vindī*.

Oṃ. The word "Agni," as heard in the injunction "he piles the fire" (*agniṃ cinute*), refers to the two internal forms consisting of the five layers (*citayaḥ*), and not to the mere collection of bricks.

Bhāṣya 9.1.26–27: The word "Agni," while presenting the mere genus (*jāti*), fulfills its purpose through the ordinary fire alone; it does not become a presenter of the Vedic [fire] without a qualifying term that denotes the consecrated states such as the *āhavanīya* and so forth.
VI. 7|3|2: The word *agni* [is used] by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for fire in general.

3|3|10: Although the word *agni* is a term denoting a universal, in the passage "he piles the fire" (*agniṃ cinute*), it functions and applies specifically to that which has been consecrated by the act of piling (*cayana*), due to the force of the context.
Vārttika 2|3|10|22: From the Vedic passage "May Agni strike down the Vṛtras," it is understood that the word *agni* denotes an entity capable of slaying Vṛtra.

Furthermore, because the fire denoted by the word *laukikadhrtyagni* (the fire for worldly maintenance) lacks that capacity [to perform Vedic functions], and because it would entail the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate a different power (*śaktyantara*) for a word that is not etymologically derived (*avyutpanna*) in another sense; and since the word *agni* is derived from the root *ag* (meaning "to go") with the suffix *ni* according to the Uṇādi-sūtra *ahnerlepaśca* (Uṇādi 4.99), which results in the formation of the word *agni*, there is no intended difference in form between the Vedic *agni*—which is etymologically derived—and the worldly *agni*—which is not so derived—due to the distinction in the analysis of their bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*).
(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 334).

Oṃ. The logic of the flame of fire (*agniśikhānyāya*): Just as by its very nature the flame of fire moves upward, so too the self moves upward; thus say the Ārhata followers. As it has been stated by Mādhava: "The upward flaming of the consumer of oblations is well-known" (1.2). In that same way, the self also moves upward.
For it has been stated thus in the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha-artha-darśana*: "Like a potter’s wheel, like lac that has lost its stickiness, like castor-oil seeds, and like a flame of fire.
Therefore they recite: "The planets, such as the moon and the sun, return after having gone and come;
but those who have reached the space beyond the world (*alokākāśa*) do not return even today."
Thus [it is] "sādṛśī. 706. *Oṃ* Agni and Soma are the deities (*devatā*).

However, in the case of *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction), there is another [compound] formed by the mutual association of the referents of the case endings that have been distributed [to each member], as in "Agni and Soma are the deities" (*agnīṣomau*), and so forth.
Bhāṣya 6.1.5: *Oṃ Agniṣṭut*.
This is a certain one-day (*ekāha*) sacrifice which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the Agniṣṭoma.
It is called "Trivṛt" because it is characterized by the Trivṛt-stoma in the Pṛṣṭha-stotra.
It is called the *Agniṣṭoma* because it has the *Agniṣṭoma* as its final form (*saṃsthā*).
[Vi. 2.1.12] Regarding the *Agniṣṭut*:

"The *Agniṣṭoma* consists of the *Trivṛt* stoma; having performed the *Agniṣṭoma-sāman* as the twenty-one-fold chant upon the *Vāyavyā* verses, one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with it. Having performed the *Vāravantīya* as the *Agniṣṭoma-sāman* upon the *Revatī* verses for this very same sacrifice, one desiring cattle should sacrifice with it. This is an injunction for a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*), and not a result arising from a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) such as the *Vāravantīya*.

Bhāṣya 2.1.127: In the Pañcadaśarātra sacrifice, the Agniṣṭut—by name—the initiator of the Āgneyī Subrahmaṇyā formula, is set aside by the Jyotiḥ and other sacrifices, which are initiators of the Aindrī Subrahmaṇyā formula. Bālakrīḍā, p. 132: In the Pañcadaśarātra, the Agniṣṭut is the first day; it is a modification (vikṛti) of the one-day (ekāha) Agniṣṭut.

VI. 1.2.13. In the case of the *agniṣṭut*, the *vidhvant* (the concluding ritual sequence) of the former [sacrifice] proceeds into the subsequent ones beginning with the *revatī* verses; for it will be stated (at 8.1.2.19) that because of the great magnitude of the intermediate commonality (*avāntarasāmānya*) of being a *nikāya* (a group of sacrifices), all the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) such as the *agniṣṭut*—which are designated simultaneously by the single term "Sādyaskas"—are included.
In the *agniṣṭut*, "the cups (*graha*) belong to Agni.

In that context, no modification (*ūha*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) hymns (*stotra*) and recitations (*śastra*) according to the deity is to be performed; rather, there is only the application (*adhikāra*).
Bhāṣya 10.4.24.9: In the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, regarding the cups (grahas), there is an injunction concerning the deity: "The cups belong to Agni.
10.4.2.3: In the Agniṣṭut, it is heard that "the Agniṣṭoma is threefold" (trivṛt).

Although in common worldly usage the word *trivṛt* denotes a threefold nature through its etymological derivation (*avayava-prasiddhi*), nevertheless, in the Veda, by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it signifies a *stoma*.
Therefore, among the nine *stotrīyās*, the state of being *trivṛt* (threefold) pertains specifically to the sequence of the *stoma*. (Vi.

10.6.7) In the *agniṣṭut*, during the first day of the fifteen-night sacrifice (*pañcadaśarātra*), although the *subrahmaṇyā* formula pertaining to Upastuta is obtained by the rule of extension (*codaka*), it should not be performed as one addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*); rather, for the sake of favoring the majority, it must be performed as one addressed to Indra (*aindrī*).

On the days from the second to the fourteenth, these [subrahmaṇyā formulas] belong to Indra alone. (In reality, however, both subrahmaṇyās should be recited on the first day; the intention of both the Bhāṭṭa school and the Bhāṣya-ṭīkā is that the manifestation of both must be performed. 1|2|17.
In the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, during the Pṛṣṭha-stotra, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman accompanied by the twenty-one-fold stoma (ekaviṃśastoma) is to be chanted upon the Revatī verses.
Bhā. 2|1|127. In the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, one desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should chant the Agniṣṭoma-sāman accompanied by the twenty-one-fold stoma upon the Revatī verses.
In the Agniṣṭoma, however, that [Sāman] is sung upon verses dedicated to Agni (Bhāṣya 2.1.127).

In the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, the Subrahmaṇyā formula is addressed to Agni; therefore, in place of the word "Indra," the modification (ūha) of the word "Agni" must be made as "Ama āgaccha" ("Come, O Agni").
However, phrases such as "Hariva āgaccha" are not subject to modification; rather, the Subrahmaṇyā invocation mantra should be accepted exactly as it is heard in the text.
Praise may also be performed even with qualities that are not actually present.

Regarding this, the ritualists (*yājñika*) perform a modification (*ūha*) [of the mantra], saying: "O Agni, come hither, O thou whose horse is red, O great giver, O smoke-bannered one, O Jātavedas, O all-seeing one!
(9.1.142–44). In the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice, the hymns (*stotra*) are extended by analogy (*atideśika*).

Vārttika 2.1.127, p. 553: Oṃ. In the Agniṣṭoma, the *trivṛt* (ninefold) nature—which is heard in scripture and consists of the form of the *stotrīya* verses—serves as a sublater of the *stoma* of other *stotras*. Since *trivṛt* is a numerical designation, it would constitute a modification of all numbers.
The Bhāṣya states: Thus it is heard in scripture, "The Agniṣṭoma is *trivṛt*."

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the number three apply merely as a means for the Agniṣṭoma, or is it restricted to the subject of the *stoma*? What is the prima facie view? The word *trivṛt* is used in common worldly usage to denote that which consists of three, as in "the threefold plough" (*trivṛt-sīra*) or "the threefold amulet" (*trivṛn-maṇi*).
Here too, in the expression "the *trivṛt* Agniṣṭoma," the Agniṣṭoma should be performed as connected with the number three.
Thus it is said.
In that context, it is stated that [the number] is connected to that [sacrifice] by way of delimiting the means for the Agniṣṭoma, and not directly, because number is a subordinate quality (guṇa).
Furthermore, no specific number whatsoever is being enjoined here as a qualification.
Because there is no distinction [between them], whatever is connected with the Agniṣṭoma and is delimited by number would be delimited by all [of those numbers].
By way of the commonality of being a number, one would alter that number.

For example, when it is said, "Devadatta is to be fed with curds, rice, and śāli-grain; Yajñadatta is to be fed with oil, just like Devadatta," because of the commonality of being a lubricant (*sneha*), the oil is employed for the function of lubrication alone, not for the function of boiled rice (*odana*).
In this way, even a number is employed only for the purpose of a numerical function, because the *stoma* possesses that characteristic.
The Bhāṣya states: "And it is not the case that there is a modification of all numbers."
What then? It would modify only the number that constitutes the *stoma*.
How so? Because the word *trivṛt* is seen elsewhere in the context of the *stoma*;

just as in the passage "The *trivṛt* is being chanted," its application to the *stoma* is determined, so too here in "The *trivṛt* is the *agniṣṭoma*," that same word being uttered should bring that very thing of all kinds to mind through inference.
Therefore, on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the *stoma*, one should modify only the number pertaining to that [stoma].
To this, it is replied: this is not correct.
For numerical words have unrestricted application;
for whatever number they are connected with, they denote that very number.
Thus it has been taught: "The Agniṣṭut is threefold; Agni is twofold."

Therefore, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the measure of the *viṣvajit*, it enumerates the *stotra*; and wherever else there will be something to be enumerated, it will enumerate that as well.
Consequently, the fact that it possesses the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the *stoma* is also not a reason for the opposite [conclusion].
To this, it is replied:

This word *trivṛt* is employed here in its well-known worldly sense of a specific number, as in the expression "the *trivṛt* being recited," which refers to the number nine in the context of a *stoma*.

Having stated "the *trivṛt* being recited," nine *stotrīyā* verses are mentioned; therefore, it is understood that the word applies to them. Likewise, a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) is also seen: "They are encompassed by the *tryambikā* [cakes] and equal to the *stoma*. By stating the equality of the nine potsherds with the *trivṛt-stoma*, this demonstrates the established usage of the word *trivṛt* in that sense.
Therefore, on account of established usage and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), this meaning is determined.
Even in common worldly usage, a specific meaning arises from coreferential application and established practice, as in the expression "This is Devadatta.

Consequently, this word *trivṛt* is observed elsewhere to have a specific number as its object; thus, when employed here as well, it brings to mind that very same [number] by virtue of its indicative mark (*liṅga*). For this reason, it is restricted to having the *stoma* as its object.

As for what was stated— that number indeed has an unrestricted scope and thus establishes a connection everywhere— this has already been refuted in the case of the *subrahmaṇyā* litany at the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice by rejecting the meaning of the individual components and accepting the collective sense.
And thus, since the enumeration belonging to others is not set aside, there will be favor toward the injunction.

Śā—In cases such as "The *agniṣṭut* sacrifice is threefold" (*trivṛd agniṣṭut*), where a specific meaning is not understood from the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), that is what is investigated here. (Although, in the case of "the anointed" [*akta*] and so forth, there is no determination of a specific meaning from the supplementary statement; rather, by virtue of conformity with the supplementary statement, a power (*śakti*) itself is postulated toward another meaning characterized as a group of nine hymns (*stotrīyā-navaka*). And once that power has been postulated, its non-departure remains even in the absence of a supplementary statement, so the absence of a supplementary statement is irrelevant. Nevertheless, since the power toward both the state of being threefold and the group of nine hymns is indistinguishable, it is necessary to employ a different principle (*nyāyāntara*) to establish the intent toward the meaning consisting of the group of nine hymns in instances where a supplementary statement is absent. Therefore, this is not covered by the section on "the anointed" [*aktādhikaraṇa*, Jaiminisūtra 1.4.23–29].)

Does the expression "possessing the three qualities" (*traiguṇya*) signify a modification of the number of all the ritual implements (*ṛtusādhana*), or does it signify a modification of the *stoma* itself by denoting a group of nine verses (*stotrīyānavaka*)? In this regard, out of a desire for the scripture to have a broad scope of application, [the view is held that] it refers to all substances (those substances which are associated with numbers in the archetype [*prakṛti*], all of them). This applies to the *abhiṣṭuti* and the *subrahmaṇyā-nigada*. 64. In the *abhiṣṭuti* and the *subrahmaṇyā-nigada*...

[The opponent says: "Or rather, [the mantras] refer to the prior and opposing positions, such as 'Indra’s two bay horses,' because the statement is purposeful by virtue of being accepted as having that [Indra] as its fruit.

If they do exist, then—in accordance with the indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of those statements—the recitation of these [mantras] even in the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*) serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), namely to manifest Indra himself through his own qualities, and not for the sake of the sacrificial oblation (*havirarthatva*); rather, it serves the purpose of avoiding the transgression of the opening of the pressing (*savanamukha*) and reaching the final performance."
Therefore, since fire is also manifested by means of its own qualities, it should be understood that Hari alone is the intended meaning in the phrase of the *subrahmaṇyā* liturgy.
Having set aside words such as "red" (*rohitavat*), words such as "red" and so forth are to be substituted; this being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), we reply:
While these qualities exist thus in those [passages], there is no authority for their presence in that [context].

As for the supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*) mentioned by you, they serve merely as praise; Indra is the deity there, not Agni, for in the *Indrastuti* there is no status as having Agni as the deity, since those [qualities] apply only to the cups (*graha*).

Thus, for this reason, those two [names] do not exist in that sense at all, because they are based upon that [substratum]. And therefore, by logical principle, the *subrahmaṇya* call is indeed not obtained [in that context].

Indra is celebrated by means of the qualities associated with his name; thus, Agni as well should be connected with those very same qualities. However, because [the *subrahmaṇyā*] is an auxiliary to the *graha* and *āghāra* offerings dedicated to the deity Agni, there must be an adaptation (*ūha*) such that the *subrahmaṇyā* formula becomes addressed to Agni.
They say that this is enjoined for the *savanamukhīya* offerings and others.

In that regard, just as in the case of the words "Soma" and "Sacrificer," an adaptation is prescribed here as well; even in the *savanamukhīya* oblation, since it consists of the *śukrāmantra*, there is complete consistency.

In this *Tantraratna*, although there is no modification (*ūha*) according to the logical principle, because it is well-established among ritualists (*yājñika*) in the case of the *abhiṣṭuti* [chant], and because of the scriptural injunction (*vacana*) regarding the repetition of the cups dedicated to Agni (*agnidevatya-graha*), which involves the recitation of a different prose formula (*nigada*) containing words such as "harit" and so forth, that very [formula] is to be performed. Even though the *subrahmaṇyā* is prescribed by direct instruction (*aupadeśika*), in the case of the *savanamukhīya* [rite], there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the original, unmodified form; thus, this section is established as being logical. This is because there is no evidence for the absence of the Indra-*subrahmaṇyā* in the modified rite, and it has been stated that the *subrahmaṇyā* belongs to those two [specific rites].

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: since words such as *harit* (green) and others are directly denotative (*padeśika*) with respect to their own meanings, it would follow that the investigation into *ūha* and *anūha* (adaptation and non-adaptation) would be irrelevant;
therefore, the view that [these words] do not apply to *harit* and so forth because they are not inherent (*asamaveta*) to them is indeed the better position.
Up to this point.
That [deity] would be perceived as qualified by Hari and others precisely as it is, and not as something to be modified (*ūhya*).
However, this is now considered: just as in the case of the word *indra*, does modification (*ūha*) occur in the words *hari* and so forth when they are applied to the deity, or not?
In that regard, modification would indeed occur only if the deity possesses a physical form and the like.
It should be inferred; do not say so, for praise is possible through the excellence of the object being praised.
On the basis of the authority of mantras, arthavādas, itihāsas, and purāṇas, even deities such as Hari and others [are included]. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the Subrahmaṇyā litany.

Because Indra is the one to be praised, the mantra beginning with "O Indra, come! O Hari, come! serves to manifest Indra for the purpose of praising Agni through the mention of his red color and other attributes.

When it is argued that there is a collection of names for Indra, [we reply] that, according to the principle of the section on deities (9.1.4), this is a sacrifice dedicated to a deity; and since there is no evidence that the mantras and other elements are directed toward him alone, the term *harit* and so forth is employed as a name. Because it is designated as the *savanamukhīya*, it is merely a recitation (*āhārya*) and not a praise (*stuti*). Furthermore, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), the *subrahmaṇyā-nigada* is also [of this nature]; thus, it is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) belonging to another deity, and therefore there is no modification (*ūha*) [of the mantra].
This is merely stated as the purpose of the section concerning the deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*), just as in the case of the formula "the essence of rice" (*vrīhīṇāṃ medha*).
And it serves no purpose in the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice. Furthermore, this purpose is stated only as a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvācintā*), assuming the absence of any other purpose.

Because of the statement, "The cups belong to Agni," when the *chandoga-sūtra* prescribes Agni as the deity for the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice—specifically in the opening libation (*savanamukhīya*) with the mantra, "O Agni, come first, O Rohita, O Dhūmaketu, O Jātavedas, [come]..."—then the *subrahmaṇyā* formula, having become that [Agni], is modified by the removal of the word "Indra" and the insertion of the word "Agni. Thus, the recitation of that very [formula] is completed; at that point, this traditional rule (*smṛti*), preceded by the presentation of logic (*nyāya*), is indeed established.

Nor does this lead to the futility of the statement "the Subrahmaṇyā belongs to Agni," because its establishment is not merely through logic (*nyāya*), but rather because it possesses the character of *śruti*—just like the recollection of the *Āgneya* and other offerings—and thus lacks the nature of mere inference (*tarka*).

Furthermore, in the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the reading [of the mantra] is indeed set aside by the principle of this very section (*adhikaraṇa*), since even the *savanīya* oblations at the commencement of the pressing (*savanamukhīya*) have Indra as their deity.

In that case, just as with the *barhiṣmatī* [mantra], one should understand that this specific mantra is the instrument for the particular deity of the *Subrahmaṇyā* invocation, just as in the case of [the rule] 3.7.1.

For this very reason, wherever there is a recollection of the *subrahmaṇyā* mantra—whether modified or unmodified—for the sake of the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the ectype (*vikṛti*), preceded by the presentation of a logical argument (*nyāya*), it follows that such a recollection must be based on direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*). Otherwise, if it were merely a tradition (*smṛti*), the presentation of the logical argument would be rendered useless, as it would result in the possibility of the *subrahmaṇyā* being recited from a Mīmāṃsā commentary or a non-Vedic manual (*anigada-pāṭha*). Thus, it was stated in the section on the *Kalpasūtras* (1.3.16) that when there is a contradiction with this principle, the *smṛti* is merely a fallacious appearance (*ābhāsatva*). [This applies] to the mantras of the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns in the *abhiṣṭuti*. 65. [This applies] to the mantras of the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns in the *abhiṣṭuti*.
*Nyāyabindu*: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, the *subrahmaṇyā-nigada* is intended to reveal the deity, beginning with "O Indra, come! O Hari-vant, come! and so forth.
In the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice, because of the injunction "the *subrahmaṇyā* belongs to Agni," one modifies [the mantra] to "O Agni, come!

Furthermore, words such as "Hari-vant" are also modified into forms such as "Rohita-vant" to denote attributes of the deity. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is no modification (*noha*), because there is no evidence for these being attributes of the deity, and they are modified merely for the sake of praise.
Maṇḍana [says]: "In cases such as *harivat-pada*, the *nohastu* (the non-substitution of *o*) should not be applied.

Śaṅkara [says]: "It should not be like *arivat*, etc., for the life-span (*āyus*). In the case of hymns (*stotra*), recitations (*śastra*), and mantras that are *prākṛta* (original), there should be no modification (*avikāra*).
Commentary: There is the one-day sacrifice (ekāha) called Agniṣṭut.

Regarding it, it is heard in scripture: "The cups (grahas) are dedicated to Agni. In this regard, there is a doubt: is there modification (ūha) according to the deity for the original stotras and śastras, or is there no change?
This is stated in order to set aside the notion of modification.

"If the deities of the planets were different [from those of the sacrifice], there would be a modification of the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns because they constitute the ritual action. Regarding this [sūtra], on whose grounds could such a notion arise that it should be set aside? It is for one of dull intellect who thinks that the denotation [of the deity] will be established.
Furthermore, even instruction given to those of dull intellect becomes fruitful.
Moreover, all those of dull intellect rely on something [external].
But if there is still no complete satisfaction with this, then it is described otherwise:

that which is the eighth topic in the second chapter (2.1.13–29) has this as its *prayojana-sūtra*: "If there is a difference in the deities of the cups (*graha*), there would be a modification [of the ritual] because the *stotra* and *śastra* are constituent parts of the action."

If the *stotra* and *śastra* are subsidiary acts (*saṃskārakarman*), what is the purpose? [The answer is: in the *agniṣṭud-ekāha*, there would be modification (*ūha*) according to the deity, as in the case of "the day has divinity. Alternatively, if they are principal acts (*pradhānakarman*), then because the *stotra* and *śastra* are acts, there would be modification when the deities of the cups (*graha*) are different. [Objection: "In the cups dedicated to Agni (*āgneya-graha*), there is no modification for the *stotra* and *śastra*, because they are acts of consecration (*saṃskāratvāt*).
[Reply: It is not so, because it is certain that they are principal acts (*arthakarmatva*).

In the *Bhāṭṭa-Agniṣṭut* sacrifice, by the statement "The cups (*graha*) belong to Agni," there is an injunction for other deities through a reference to the original (*prākṛta*) cups. Since the second book has established that the *stotra* and *śastra* are purposeful acts (*arthakarma*), the verses (*ṛc*) belonging to various deities from the archetype must be recited in the *stotra* and *śastra*; however, there is no introduction of a separate verse dedicated to Agni as the deity.
This [discussion] is merely a statement of the purpose of what was established in the second book.
And this should be considered as being based merely on the statement, "They praise with the Āgneyī verses," or as referring to another context.

*Nyāyabindu*: In the Agniṣṭut sacrifice, it is heard that "the cups (grahas) are dedicated to Agni. In that case, since the original hymns and recitations (*stotra* and *śastra*) serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there is no modification (*anūha*); this is clear.
The application [of the verses] is mixed; however, by the injunctions "they praise with the Āgneyīs" and "he recites the Āgneyīs," the application belongs to the Āgneyīs alone.
Thus, the mention of the "Agniṣṭut" is merely illustrative.
The scope [of this rule] is that case where, in a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), there is another deity, and due to a specific injunction, the verses dedicated to that other deity do not apply.
Therefore, it should be understood that in the Sūtra it is stated in general terms: "because the presiding deities of the planets are different."

In this context, the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that although *śruti* (Vedic texts) and *śastra* (recited hymns) are purificatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*), there is nevertheless modification (*ūha*) when the deity changes in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)—is untenable. This is because, by the prohibition of the *ṛc*s found in the statement, "This syllable indeed putrefies if one recites it [inappropriately]; therefore, one does not modify" (*pūyati vā etad akṣaraṃ yad enadanūhati, tasmād anūhaḥ*), it is understood that even if they serve to designate a deity, there is no modification. Rather, since the original *ṛc*s are incapable of designating the deity in the modified sacrifice, and because there is an absence of modification, the prima facie view should be described as follows: in the modified sacrifice, since the original *ṛc*s are unable to manifest the deity, one must bring in *ṛc*s from the *Daśataya* collection to perform the praise.

For this very reason, in the section concerning the *stotra* and *śastra* (2.1.13–29), regarding the view that [the verses] serve as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the deity, the injunction "he recites the *āgneyī* verses" would be redundant in the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice, because the *āgneyī* verses are already obtained by their own nature. Since it is established in the *guṇasūtra* (2.1.26) that "that statement is redundant" constitutes a sublation (*bādhaka*), and since the teachers (the authors of the *Vārttika*) have demonstrated that the very nature of the *ṛc*s is such that they are not subject to modification (*anuha*), and since the statement of the aforementioned prohibition has been cited as the authoritative source in the *Nyāyasudhā* (p. 664) regarding the absence of modification (*anūhatva*).

Therefore, having established the matter according to what was heard, it is indeed logical that the point for deliberation (*ūhapada*)—by means of *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical reasoning)—is intended to signify the cessation of the original form (*prakṛti*).

In the Sūtra, because of the term "action" (*karman*), the meaning is "because it is an action for the sake of the purpose" (*arthakarman*). [The question is: Is there modification (*ūha*) in the Āgneya cups, or not? [Regarding] the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns.
As for the argument "because it is a conditioned phenomenon," it is not so, because its status as an object of purposeful action is certain.

In the *Bhāṭṭa-Agniṣṭut* sacrifice, by the statement "The cups (*graha*) belong to Agni," there is an injunction of different deities through a reference to the archetypal cups (*prākṛta-graha*). Since the second book of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra* establishes that the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns are *arthakarma* (acts for a purpose), the verses belonging to various deities from the archetype must be recited in the *stotra* and *śastra*; however, there is no introduction of a separate verse dedicated to the deity Agni.
This [discussion] is merely a statement of the purpose established in the second book.
And this [point] is to be considered either as a reflection based solely on the statement "They praise with the Āgneyī verses," or as pertaining to another context.

VI. 11|5|9. In the Agniṣṭoma, the Ṣoḍaśī cup is to be drawn from the Āgrayaṇa vessel after the Ukthya cups have been drawn.
10|5|10. If the Ṣoḍaśī cup is drawn in the Agniṣṭoma, the sacrifice is indeed completed; by that, there is a reduction of the preceding days.

And the state of being established elsewhere must be accepted. 10.5.12. In the Agniṣṭoma, the Ṣoḍaśin cup is to be drawn for a Kṣatriya only at the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana), and not during the morning or midday pressings.
10.5.11. In the Agniṣṭoma, there is only one Savanīya seasonal animal sacrifice (ṛtupaśu); for it is stated: "In the Agniṣṭoma, the animal dedicated to Agni is to be immolated."
Bhāṣya 3.6.1.8: At the Agniṣṭoma, the performance of the slaughter of the Savanīya animal takes place at the time of the Ārbhava-pavamāna.
"In the archetype (prakṛti), the performance occurs at the time of the Ārbhava.
11.3.15.46: At the Agniṣṭoma, there is the commencement of the Stotra.
"One should turn back," with these words he introduces the *stotra* for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
The *stotra* is dedicated to Mahendra.
"One should turn back" is the mantra.

*Upākaraṇa* means the commencement or indication. (Vi. 10|4|2, Section 2). Regarding the selection of the Hotṛ in the Agniṣṭoma, it is stated: "He chooses the Hotṛ with the words, 'Agni is the Hotṛ; he is my Hotṛ; O Hotṛ, you are my Hotṛ. (Bhā. 12|1|2|8|137).

For in those [other] *saṃsthās*, the Soma is exactly as much as in the Agniṣṭoma, because of the scriptural statement, "Come with the ten fingers," and that same amount of Soma which is in the Agniṣṭoma is also present in the *ukthya* and other *saṃsthās*.
In the Ukthya and other sacrifices as well, only ten handfuls of Soma are to be taken;
because of the rule regarding the number of joints—namely, "it has three joints"—it is not possible to take one with many joints. O Sage!
And a combination [of these] is not possible here, because for that which has already been established, another form of establishment is incompatible. In this regard,

there is an optional choice according to one's desire between the forms of the Agniṣṭoma— which serves the purpose of the sacrifice— and the forms such as the Ukthya and others— which serve the purpose of the person.
*Bāla.*, p. 163: "The *agniṣṭoma* termination is the inherent nature (*nijambha*) of this [*jyotiṣṭoma*].
*Vārttika* 3.6.16.4, p.
1061: "The *agniṣṭoma* termination is inseparable (*avinābhūta*) from the *jyotiṣṭoma*."

When there is a repetition of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Agniṣṭoma terminus (saṃsthā) must necessarily be undertaken, as it involves the prescription of all the ritual duties. (Bhāṭṭa 5.3.13). Even after the first day of the Atirātra, the Udbhid and other sacrifices should be performed only after having completed the Agniṣṭoma terminus.
5|3|13: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice when it has the Agniṣṭoma as its concluding form (saṃsthā), there are one hundred and ninety stotriya verses;
this is not the case when it is joined with other concluding forms.

5|3|12: Regarding the rule that "the Ṣoḍaśin cup is to be drawn in both the Agniṣṭoma and the Ukthya forms," this is stated by the scriptural injunction: "One should draw [the Ṣoḍaśin] for a Kṣatriya in the Agniṣṭoma, and also in the Ukthya."

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice when it is concluded with the Agniṣṭoma form, three animals are prescribed: the Agnīṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anubandhya (Vārttika 3.6.178). By establishing the Agniṣṭoma as the concluding form, the accomplishment of the fourth enclosure (vihāra) follows from the injunction: "The Jyotiṣṭoma should be performed."

Saṃkarṣa 3.2.16: Prior to the performance of the Agniṣṭoma, sacrificial rites (kratavaḥ) that are modifications of the Soma sacrifice—whether consisting of a single stoma or multiple stomas—cannot be performed.
Vi. 5.3.15: The performance of the modifications of the Agniṣṭoma occurs after the time of the Agniṣṭoma.
Now, regarding the phrase "or by another," there is a discussion concerning the *saṃsthās* (terminuses), because of their proximity.

The Commentary states: "'Or by another'—is this a discussion concerning the *saṃsthās*, or rather concerning the modifications (*vikāras*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, such as the *ekāhas* and so forth? (This is the doubt).
What, then, is the prima facie position? It is that it concerns the *saṃsthās*."
Why? Because of proximity. The *saṃsthās* (termini) are proximate in that context;
their mention serves to support the context.
Duṣ: Now, regarding the phrase "by another," this refers to the sacrificial forms (*saṃsthās*).
Whatever is proximate to that which was previously mentioned is denoted by the pronoun.
And for the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya and other forms are proximate.

Therefore, having performed the Jyotiṣṭoma with the Agniṣṭoma as its concluding form, the Ukthya and other forms should be performed; there is no fixed rule regarding the Gavya and other sacrifices. (Now begins another section, a commentary not based on the Sūtra: Regarding the phrase "he who, without having sacrificed with this [Jyotiṣṭoma], [sacrifices] with another," both of these matters have been examined.
Now the meaning of the sentence is being examined:
Is the property of being first enjoined for the Agniṣṭoma, or is there a prohibition of being first for the subsequent sacrifices, or is there some other mode?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That the property of being first is enjoined for the Jyotiṣṭoma because of the context, and not a prohibition of being first for the others.
In that case, if it were so, then in the second and subsequent performances of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the result would necessarily fail to arise because of the absence of "primacy" (prāthamya).
Nor could there be a prohibition of primacy for other [performances],
since there exists no word expressive of such a thing.

Therefore, there is another mode. What, then, is it? Because the phrase "one who, having not performed these" (*ya ete nāniṣṭvā*) expresses a time prior to the *svādhyāya* (study/recitation), it first declares that the *agniṣṭoma* must be performed, and only afterwards [the performance of] the *gavāmayana* and so forth.

Consequently, by this sentence, the attainment of those [results] such as cattle is enjoined; by another sentence, heaven [is enjoined]. Therefore, there will be a result in the second and subsequent performances; thus, there is no fault.
Or rather, it is a mere praise, because of the absence of any indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: "If this is so, then there is no discussion regarding those who have authority over that [matter]. In that case, there is neither a transference (*vihāra*) nor a lapse (*āpatti*)."
By virtue of context and other such factors, those properties belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
If they were prescribed for the [gifts of] cows and so forth, then context and the other factors would be set aside;
in that case, there would be an assumption (āpatti) that contradicts direct perception.
This praise, however, is due to the absence of falling into [faults] and the absence of dwelling [in them];
or it is due to the cognition of the method, for praise would not occur without cause.
The Commentary says: "To this, it is replied:"
Although the occurrence (*āpatti*) and the departure (*vihāra*) are not explicitly prescribed, they are nevertheless prescribed by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
Those [elements] which are to be performed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) are understood to be performed in the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well, due to the statement of the *codaka*.
Thus, it is understood that when the occurrence and departure take place, it is by means of another [element].
For praise cannot occur without cause.

How could that other [element] be indicated by this praise? It is for this purpose that there is praise. Śā— "The *saṃsthās* themselves are expressed by the word 'other,' for they are the subject under discussion."

(Although, since there is no injunction for the *saṃsthās* within the scripture that enjoins the *jyotiṣṭoma-saṃsthās*, the context belongs to the sacrifice itself and not to the *saṃsthās*, nevertheless, it is precisely proximity (*saṃnidhi*)—characterized here as "context"—that is intended by the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*); for it is that alone which is referred to by the pronoun "by this" (*anena*), as it is the operative factor.)

And thus, in the phrase "by this," only the Ukthya and other forms of the previously mentioned Agniṣṭoma are proximate, not other sacrifices; therefore, since it is something other than the previously mentioned [Agniṣṭoma] that is proximate, the reference by the word "other" (anya) must be to the sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthās) themselves—this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). He states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "But there is no context (prakaraṇa) for the terminuses, because this is the section concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma, as indicated by its mention in the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa)."

"For by the word 'of sacrifices,' all of them are indeed included. [Objection: But if there is a connection with other words through the term *jyotiṣṭoma*, then by the phrase "by a *jyotiṣṭoma* other than the *agniṣṭoma*," it would be only the *jyotiṣṭoma* with the *ukthya* and other terminuses (*saṃsthā*) that is indicated, and not the other sacrificial rites (*ṛtu*). To this, he says: "*jyotiṣṭoma*... [etc.]

The meaning is as follows: because the word *jyotiṣṭoma* has no expectancy for anything else—since it is already complete by itself—it cannot be connected with another word such that there would be a relationship of qualifier and qualified in the manner described. Rather, when the question arises, "From what other [sacrifice]? the *jyotiṣṭoma*, being present at hand, is connected as the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) in the sense of "from something other than the *agniṣṭoma* which is under discussion.
Consequently, since all [other sacrifices] are distinct from the *jyotiṣṭoma* characterized by the *agniṣṭoma* form, this is indeed a reference to all of them.

This being the case, since the *saṃsthās* lack the nature of a sacrifice (*yāga*), and because the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are not authorized [with respect to them], it is logical that the section concerning the sacrificers applies.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tantraratna*: "Among the sacrifices—the *agniṣṭoma*, *atirātra*, *agniṣṭoma*, *ahīna*, and *satra*—this is the first performance."

Furthermore, the use of the term *yajña* (sacrifice) as common to all sacrificial forms (*saṃsthā*) is observed in both the Śruti and the Kalpasūtras, such as in the passages: "Prajāpati created the sacrifice" and "We shall explain the sacrifice.
Regarding this, the Teacher (the author of the Vārttika) [states that] there is one [commonality] among the modifications of the Agniṣṭoma... [of the modifications of the Agniṣṭoma].

The word "vāda" (discourse) indicates that by this sentence, the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) subsequent to the Jyotiṣṭoma is enjoined for all of them. Soma: [This] connection is established by depending on what precedes. Vi: Is the mention of its terminuses (*saṃsthā*) by another [text] for all of them, or for the first? The former.
"By means of the sentence, there is the statement of the entire qualification of that proximity.
Bhaṭṭa: Having determined the meaning of this word, the meaning of the other word is now determined.

Since the word "other" (anya) denotes that which is proximate to what has been previously mentioned, and since the *saṃsthās* (concluding rites) are proximate, it follows that the injunction of being subsequent to the Agniṣṭoma applies to them alone—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, this is not so; for first of all, there is no proximity of the *saṃsthās* within the context (*prakaraṇa*), because they are modified forms (*vikṛti*). Furthermore, the governing topic (*adhikāra*) belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma, as evidenced by the mention of that very sacrifice in the supplementary passage beginning with "This indeed... Moreover, when it is stated that among the sacrifices performed on the day of the Jyotiṣṭoma, the one named Agniṣṭoma is the first, other sacrifices such as the Udbhid are also included under the term "sacrifices" (*yajña*). Thus, the *saṃsthās* are not the intended referents.
Nor is there non-apprehension [of the forms] on the grounds that the configurations (saṃsthā) are not sacrifices;
for even in those cases, the substratum (āśraya) is a sacrifice.
And therefore, [it applies] to the Agniṣṭoma.
Regarding the Agniṣṭoma among the sacrifices [72]: it is established that in the Agniṣṭoma, there is no fixed rule for the sequence of the three animal sacrifices dedicated to Śakra and the others.
It is stated that in some cases, a priority based on the order of the sūtras occurs.
In this regard, [the opponent argues that] by means of this pronoun (*etena*), which is a general term (*sarvanāman*), all the *saṃsthās* are considered without distinction.
(This is the prima facie view. "Because two *saṃsthās* are optional (*vaikalpika*) in relation to the obligatory nature (*nityatā*) of the Agniṣṭoma."

For the *agniṣṭoma* termination (*saṃsthā*) is the inherent form of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and thus it is perceived as such, not as being joined with other terminations, because those others are adventitious (*āgantuka*).

Furthermore, due to the instrumental indication in the word "by this" (*etena*), the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) having the *jyotiṣṭoma* as its instrument is expressed by the word "having sacrificed" (*iṣṭvā*).

[Objection: Even when the *jyotiṣṭoma* is being employed in the various terminations, its status as the instrument for the efficient force of its own result is not lost; for in all cases, a ritual action prompted by another serves as the substrate (*āśraya*) for a desired quality (*guṇa*).

And thus, even when there is a connection with the *saṃsthās* (termini of the sacrifice), there is no inconsistency in the designation of the instrument (*karaṇa*); therefore, he says: "Nor is there an inclusion of the *saṃsthās* within the ritual productive operation (*ṛtubhāvanā*), because they exist for the sake of the fruit.

However, the *agniṣṭoma-saṃsthā* is included within the ritual productive operation; therefore, there is a reference only to that which possesses this *saṃsthā* [i.e., the *agniṣṭoma*] (the sense being that since the status of being an instrument belongs to that which is endowed with the procedure [*itikartavyatā*], it is logical to accept the designation of the instrument only for that which possesses the *saṃsthā* which is included within the procedure).
— *Soma*: The connection [of this section] consists in the fact that the investigation into the meaning of this word results in the establishment of the system set forth in the preceding section.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: by the word "by this," the Agniṣṭoma termination is indicated, because it is only that which has that termination which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*). [Objection: This [view] he refutes: "Is it the Agniṣṭoma with all its terminations, or the Agniṣṭoma alone? Since there is no distinction, let the Jyotiṣṭoma with all its terminations be described here."

The procedure for the Agniṣṭoma is primary here because it is his first sacrifice; by that [procedure], or by another, he obtains the other subsequent optional terminuses (saṃsthās). Bhaṭṭa: While there is no fixed order for those rites undertaken in separate performances, in some cases priority is established by a scriptural statement, such as: "This indeed... that possesses the Gārhapatya fire."

In this context, although the word *etad* (this) refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma in general, it nevertheless does not include all its forms (*saṃsthās*), but rather only the Agniṣṭoma form. This is because, as will be explained in the section concerning the Agniṣṭoma (*agniṣṭomādhikaraṇa*), the other forms are designated by different names, and thus their performance must necessarily follow the Jyotiṣṭoma; consequently, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is established that the Agniṣṭoma form must be performed first.
For this very reason, the Atirātra form is performed first only on account of the specific scriptural injunction: "Some perform the Atirātra first."

Or rather, let this word have as its primary fruit the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice characterized by the Agniṣṭoma termination; for it is precisely with reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma having the Agniṣṭoma termination that all the ritual properties are enjoined.
For this very reason, the statement "it has one hundred and ninety stotriya verses" is logically consistent.
Indeed, there are only that many *stotrīyā* verses in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* when it has the *agniṣṭoma* as its final form (*saṃsthā*), and not when it is joined with another final form.

And thus, it should be understood that even after the first day of the *Atirātra*, the *Udbhid* and other sacrifices must be performed only after having completed the *agniṣṭoma* form. *Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the passage "This very [sacrifice]... one should sacrifice by means of another," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the word "this" (*etad*) refers to a specific instance within the *Jyotiṣṭoma* comprising all its final forms, it refers to any of them. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the *agniṣṭoma* form is obligatory (*nitya*), the reference is specifically to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* in its *agniṣṭoma* form.
Maṇḍana: "But the Agniṣṭoma is for this purpose.
The meaning of "for this purpose" is the referent of the word "by this" (*etena*).
Śaṅkara: "The other [sacrifice] is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the Agniṣṭoma."
The subsequent *sattras* are to be performed after the *agniṣṭoma*.
In the *agniṣṭoma*, the *khara* (mound) serves for the purpose of the three animals;
it should be completed with the *khara* as the central ritual framework (*tantra*), because its time is determined by the axle.

Commentary: There is a sacrificial post-hole (khara) mentioned in the scripture: "He makes the hole for the sacrificial post. Does it serve as a common feature (tantra) for all that is heard [in the ritual], or is it distinct?
What is the prima facie view? Indeed, the hole serves as a common feature, because other things are also mentioned [in relation to it], owing to its being a single time.
Its own time for production does not exist;
it is employed at the time of the ritual action, as in the rule: "He anoints the animal while it stands in its natural form.
The distinction is understood that this [anointing] is for the sake of whichever animal is taken up at the time of the anointing.
Therefore: [Objection] But surely, in the case of "he makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," its production is for the sake of its own time;
indeed, this too is not merely internal to the performance.
Moreover, here the word *svaru* denotes an effect.
"He makes it harsh; he performs the function of the harsh.
For what reason? Because the harshness is known, whereas the function of the harsh is known to be the coloring of the animal.

But is it not seen that at the conclusion of the sacrifice there is the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *svaru*, as in: "When the *soma* sacrifice is completed, he throws the *prastara* [grass-bundle] and the *svaru* into the fire"?
That [conclusion] is only logical if it is common to both. Therefore, the *apavarga* (concluding rite) should occur at the end of the *dīkṣā* and *upasad*, not only at the end of the *dīkṣā-paśu*.
For this reason as well, it is common to both.
"Or it may be at that time, like the *prastara* [grass-bundle].
Commentary: That which was stated must be refuted.
Or rather, because it is an original injunction (*utpatti-vākya*), it is not like the *prastara* in its application (*pradeśa*).
Commentary: There is no offering of the *svara* at the time of the *anubandhya*.
What is the reason? This very [text], "At the end of the *soma*, he offers the *prastara* and the *svara* for the *ayaśas*," is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) for the offering.
By this, it is understood that the time of the *agnīṣomīya* is taken by virtue of the sequence.
If it were common [to all], then its appearance at the end of the *utsarga*—as a specific exception to the rule that the ritual act is completed upon hearing the entire text—would be logical.
But if it were separate, then it would be seen only at the conclusion of the *agnīṣomīya*.
Now, why is this not simply a statement? Because it is a statement made at the end of the Soma sacrifice regarding what was already applicable at the end of the *agnīṣomīya*.
This is not so;
by means of this single statement, two specific details regarding the *drāgulasa* would have to be enjoined— namely, the throwing into the fire and [the disposal] at the end of the Soma sacrifice—
and thus there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, that statement [of yours] is not correct.
As for the argument "like the *prastara*," it is because of the specific instruction regarding the *prastara*.
In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the throwing away (*praharaṇa*) of the *prastara* is prescribed: "He throws away the *prastara* with benedictions."
It is attained through practice by means of the prompter (*codaka*).
In that regard, it is appropriate [to consider] this in view of the duration of the subsequent connection, but this does not apply to one's own performance (*svapraharaṇa*).
Therefore, there is the introduction of Agni and Soma.

...thus, since there is only one first splinter (*śakala*) on a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is *tantratva* (commonality of performance). Furthermore, its collection must be performed at the very time of cutting the post for the purpose of removing confusion and for the purpose of avoiding loss or theft; thus, because it is a specific requirement of that which is being raised, there is *tantratva*.

The objection (*utthiti*) is that, because it does not serve the purpose of the Soma or the post, it cannot have *tantratva* like the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*). This constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "In the Agnīṣomīya [animal sacrifice], there would be a separate disposal (apavarga) for each part because they have their own specific times. However: "There should be one [disposal] with the splinters (svaru), because they share the same time; there is a distinction based on the time of the [main] animal. The first [part], consisting of a single chip, should be the common ritual core (tantra) because of its remaining status."
Commentary: Like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the wooden splinter (*svaru*) also serves as a common element (*tantra*) for all the *śrutas*.
Nor is there any need for its separate procurement at the time of initiation or at the time of performance;
in the *agniṣṭoma*, there is only one sacrificial post for the three animals. In the *agniṣṭoma*, there is only one sacrificial post for the three animals.
Furthermore, since that which has been appropriated possesses a discernible distinction, its destruction must be said to result precisely from its destruction [as a whole].

This is because, even at the end of the time of the material cause (*upādāna*), the first chip is designated as the *svaru* by the injunction, "The first chip that falls shall be the *svaru*"; and since that [chip] is a single entity, a division [into multiple parts] is logically untenable.

Nor should it be argued that, despite there being only a single throwing (*praharaṇa*), the plurality of the first chips is established by the injunction "the first [that falls]"; for [this would contradict the aforementioned principle].
Because its disposal (*praharaṇa*) is not logically possible, the perception of its "primacy" (*prāthamya*) depends entirely upon another fragment, since it is established as one with that [wood].

Furthermore, at the very time of cutting the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the *svaru* must be taken up for the purpose of removing delusion and for the purpose of preventing the theft of the Lord; thus, because no specific distinction is perceived there, it is the *svaru*.
For this very reason, the injunction for its final disposal at the end—stated as "When the Soma sacrifice is completed, he throws away the *prastara* and the *svaru*"—is also consistent.

Nor is this a rule regarding time for that which has become a subsidiary part of the Anubandhyā sacrifice; for when the general application [of the rule] is established by logic (*nyāya*), there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) to justify a restriction.
Therefore, in cases where the distinction is understood through logic alone—as in the case of the *prastara* bundle—a restriction is indeed accepted.

*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the group of five sacrificial chips (*śakala*), since it might be argued that another chip should be taken up after the first because of the group of five, [the conclusion is reached]: "That which is the first chip is the *svaru*. Because of this statement, only the final chip is to be taken; its taking up occurs at the very time of cutting the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) for the purpose of removing confusion. Thus, there is no specific selection [of a particular one], and therefore the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is indeed a single performance (*tantra*).
Maṇḍana: "The *svaru* should be one for the three animals. Śaṅkara: "When the sacrificial post is one, the *svaru* is a single performance (*tantra*)."
Oṃ: The common procedure for the consecrations of the sacrificial posts intended for the three animals in the Agniṣṭoma.
The *saṃskāras* (consecratory rites) are considered first because they pertain to the time [of the sacrifice].

The Commentary states: Regarding those consecratory rites of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) which are performed within the procedure of the animal sacrifice (*paśutantra*)—such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), anointing (*añjana*), the principal rite, and the two encircling ropes (*parivyāṇa*)—it is deliberated whether these should be performed separately for each individual animal, or whether they constitute a single performance (*tantra*).
What is established? First, the preparatory rites (saṃskāras) would apply to the sacrificial post (yūpa); they would not be as if the sacrificial post were the central framework (tantra).
What is the reason? Because it pertains to the time of the purpose (arthakālatvāt).
The purpose is the tethering of the animal.
These preparatory acts (saṃskāras) pertain to that specific time;
therein a distinction is apprehended:
they belong to that animal for whose sake they were performed at the time of its binding.
Since the other animal sacrifice has not reached its proper time, there is no performance for its sake; therefore, the practice is as follows,
such as the wiping of the fire.

However, these [times] belong to that specific period because they constitute the ritual act of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), since its properties are prescribed for that time, and because there is a scriptural statement regarding all [the times].
Commentary: It is true that they would be performed at those times if they were occasions for tethering [the animal];
however, these times belong to the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
How is this known? Because they constitute the action of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
These [acts] are not for the purpose of tethering;
rather, the sacrificial post is made by means of these, and the sacrificial post is for the purpose of tethering. Furthermore, that [post] is to be prepared during the initiatory rites (*dīkṣā*).
Because of the statement, "He cuts the sacrificial post during the initiations," and because it is prepared by means of purificatory rites (saṃskāras),
these purificatory rites belong specifically to the time of initiation.
Objection: In that case, only the cutting of the sacrificial post (yūpa) is heard in the scripture, not the making of the post itself.
Reply: It is said that there is no substance whatsoever designated as "the post" for which the cutting could be prescribed.
Thus, it is understood in this way: "During the initiations, one prepares the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by means of cutting and other such acts.
And the mention of "cutting" is for the purpose of illustration, because it is the primary act;
for the reason that the post does not become a *yūpa* through cutting alone.
Thus, these purificatory rites (saṃskāras) belong to the time of initiation itself;
yet, because of the statement regarding all matters that exist, some are assigned to other times, as for example: "After the Āgnimāruta [offering], they proceed with the after-offerings (anuyājas)."
Therefore, the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are also the underlying principle (*tantra*).
There is another interpretation of the phrase "the rite of the sacrificial post" (*yūpakarma*):
that which constitutes the rite of the sacrificial post consists of those preparatory rites intended for cutting [the wood].
This very post is being made by means of the operations of carving and so forth.
Just as when a sovereign is heard of once in connection with the Vājapeya sacrifice, a further performance of it would be useless;
therefore, there must be repetition.
If this were the case, then even in the instance of an animal already slaughtered, that very same sacrificial post (*yūpa*) ought indeed to be constructed.
True, it would be so, provided there were no prohibition against sacrificing with a postless [animal].
However, such a prohibition does exist.
Therefore it comes to pass:
just as that sacrificial post (yūpa) was prepared, so from that point it is relinquished. Its relinquishment is such that the sacrificial post is relinquished.
And it shows that the measurement is performed only once.

The Bhāṣya states: "Having encircled the sacrificial post (yūpa) with a triple-stranded cord, he dedicates the Savanīya animal. This indicates that the ritual properties of the post follow the act of encircling; thus, it shows the post to be measured and cut only once.
Otherwise, one would begin with sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) because of its primary status.
If it is argued that this is for the sake of immediate succession,
we say no.
Because it is established by its very nature (*prakṛti*).
For this reason as well, the *saṃskāras* (consecratory rites) constitute a *tantra* (common procedure).

Soma: Since the *tantra*-status of the consecratory rites does not arise without the *tantra*-status of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is a logical connection (*saṅgati*) because the present discussion proceeds to examine the *tantra*-status of those *saṃskāras* by relying upon the *tantra*-status of the *yūpa* mentioned in the preceding section.
For the acts of cutting and the other procedures, being independent of one another, each brings about the cognition of a refinement (*saṃskāra*) such as making a hole and so forth.

And those refinements, only when combined, are denotable by the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post), not individually; for it is only after the accomplishment of all those refinements that [the term applies], as in:
"In the Agniṣṭoma, the sacrificial post for the three animals. In the Agniṣṭoma, the sacrificial post for the three animals...

In the injunction "one should bind the animal," which is a sentence prescribing a ritual refinement (saṃskāra), the word *yūpa* cannot be applied to each individual [piece of wood] used for the specific cutting of the sacrificial post, as this would result in a plurality of meanings for the word; rather, that meaning must be conceived as belonging to those pieces only when they are combined.

Thus, first of all, regarding the production of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as a collection of preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*), since the acts that produce those preparations—such as hewing and so forth—are desired as a single unit, and because the sacrificial post cannot be produced by mere cutting alone, when it is stated, "One should make the sacrificial post by cutting during the initiations" (*dīkṣāsu chedena yūpaṃ kuryāt*), the cutting is taken as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all those constituent elements that have come down as being for the purpose of producing the sacrificial post. Consequently, the sentence-final meaning is established as: "During the initiations, one should produce the sacrificial post by means of all the constituent elements, beginning with cutting. Thus, the postponement (*apakarṣa*) of all these constituent elements is understood.
Is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) consisting of hewing and so forth distinct [from the sacrificial post] in the ritual system, or not?
It is not so; for it is subordinate to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which serves as its material cause.

Therefore, even in the case of three animals, the acts beginning with hewing and ending with anointing should be performed once for all (*tantra*)—just as in the case of the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

According to the Bhaṭṭa school, if the sacrificial post is common to all (*tantra*), then its purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as hewing, sprinkling with water (*joṣaṇa*), and sprinkling with clarified butter (*prokṣaṇa*), must also be performed once for all.

Nor should it be argued that because the injunction "he cuts the sacrificial post during the initiations" (*dīkṣāsu yūpaṃ chinatti*)—which prescribes only the act of cutting—is not present, and because acts such as carving (*takṣaṇa*) are performed only at the time of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, it is understood that they serve only that purpose; consequently, since a specific distinction is being grasped, there should be a repetition of the procedure upon the completion of that [Agniṣomīya] alone. For if the cutting were intended for the qualified [post], it would lead to an impossibility; if it were intended for the mere act of cutting, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the injunction regarding the time is made precisely with reference to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

The term *chinna* (cut) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the mere formative forces (*saṃskāra*) that produce it; and those formative forces which produce it are, according to the examination of the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of Bodhāyana and others, as well as the consensus of the sacrificial experts (*yājñika*), precisely the cutting and splitting required for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), just as the laying of the fire (*ādhāna*) and so forth are for the fire itself, but not the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), sharpening (*ajjana*), and so on.
Those [latter], however, like the wiping (*saṃmārga*) and other such acts, are merely producers of refinement (*saṃskāra*) once the post has already been produced.

Thus, even within this established rule, those which are indeed producers possess the quality of being performed once (*tantratva*), because no distinction can be perceived due to their occurring at different times, just like the sacrificial post.

As for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites which are purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*) performed upon the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) once it has been produced—since there is no scriptural statement regarding their displacement (*apakarṣa*), they must be understood as restricted to their specific place and time; nevertheless, because the sacrificial posts are one and the same across the *Ātithyā* and subsequent sacrifices according to the logic of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇanyāya*, 12.1.16), the sprinkling and other rites performed there [in the first instance] can benefit the others through *prasaṅga* (incidental application). Therefore, there is no repetition (*āvṛtti*) of those rites either. However, for Pārthasārathi Miśra, who asserts that all these purificatory acts are denoted by the word "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*), this would entail that they also belong to the time of initiation (*dīkṣākāla*), which contradicts the practice of ritualists (*yājñika*). Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the [textual] tradition (*śruti*).

Now, if one accepts another position—that there is a removal of the mere measure [of the wood] by resorting to the definition of this very lack of primary sense—then the resulting contingency of a specific location and so forth is indeed difficult to avoid.

Nor can two words, "in order to make a sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ kartum*) and "he cuts the *khadira* tree" (*khadiraṃ chinatti*), be supplied to avoid that [contingency], because indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is simpler than that.
