*Nyāyabindu*: Since only the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is brought forward [to the time of the animal sacrifice], while the other consecrations (*saṃskāra*) belong to the time of the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*), it follows that because of the specific mention [of the cutting], there should be a renewed performance for another animal. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): The meaning of "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*) is that one should produce the sacrificial post by means of cutting, since the post is not yet established [prior to the ritual]. Nor is it possible to have a post by mere cutting alone; therefore, the word "cuts" (*chinatti*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for cutting, hewing (*takṣaṇa*), and so forth. Alternatively, even if it conveys mere cutting, since the sacrificial post—which is the medium—is common to all [animals], the [consecrations] for those too constitute a single performance (*tantra*). This is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Maṇḍana: "And those consecrations (*saṃskāra*) are also a single procedure (*tantra*); they are not distinct.
By "those consecrations," he means the consecrations of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Śaṅkara: "In that case, there is a unity of procedure regarding the consecrations."
"In that regard, concerning the sacrificial post intended for the three animals:
'Oṃ! The *ṣoḍaśī* cup is to be drawn for both the *agniṣṭoma* and the *ukthya*, and the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is indeed the same.
Because of the connection with both the *ukthya* and the *agniṣṭoma*, there should be an *astṛta-śastra*; for when there is a difference in designation (*saṃjñā*), [the ritual details differ]."

Commentary: Regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, which is the archetype, this is recorded in scripture: "One should take [the cup] for a Kṣatriya at the *agniṣṭoma*; it should also be taken at the *ukthya*.
In this regard, there is a traditional doubt as to whether the *ṣoḍaśin* is without *stotra* and *śastra*, or with *stotra* and *śastra*.
What is the prima facie view? It should be without *stotra* and *śastra*.
Why? Because of its connection with the Ukthya and Agniṣṭoma.
There is a connection with the Ukthya and Agniṣṭoma, as it is said: "One should take [the Ṣoḍaśin] at the Agniṣṭoma for a Kṣatriya; it may also be taken at the Ukthya.
Thus it is stated that the Ṣoḍaśin is to be taken at both the Agniṣṭoma and the Ukthya sacrificial forms (saṃsthās).

Thus, this sacrifice becomes one that concludes with the *agniṣṭoma* form, provided that the cup (*graha*) is drawn there, even if neither the chant (*stotra*) nor the recitation (*śastra*) is performed.

For if there were a chant or a recitation, it would conclude with the *ṣoḍaśin* chant; in that case, it would not be one concluding with the *agniṣṭoma*, nor one concluding with the *ukthya*. Therefore, this statement is appropriate: "One should draw [the cup] for a Kṣatriya at the *agniṣṭoma*; it may also be drawn at the *ukthya*.
This is said in reference to the *jyotiṣṭoma* characterized by the *agniṣṭoma*, and not as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *agniṣṭoma* alone.
The sacrifice is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *stotra* and *śastra*, because the sacrifice possesses a fruit while the other two are fruitless.
Furthermore, it is by means of this [sacrifice] that the *agniṣṭoma* comes to be designated as the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and not otherwise.
Therefore, it should be without *stotra* and *śastra*.

Regarding the statement, "One should take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup for a Kṣatriya at the *agniṣṭoma*": since the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is taken at the *agniṣṭoma*, if it were performed with the *sastoma* and *śastra* [of the *ukthya*], the *agniṣṭoma* form (*saṃsthā*) would not exist.
And if the *agniṣṭoma* form does not exist, then—due to the absence of its cause—the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup itself would not even be applicable.
Therefore, that [case] is accepted where there is no obstruction of the cause (nimitta) regarding the basis of the stotra;
however, in this case, there would be an obstruction of the cause.
And how could it be "possessing the stoma and the śastra" if the Ṣoḍaśī were enjoined as a subsidiary (aṅga) of the Agniṣṭoma stotra?
That being the case, because the principal [rite] itself would be prescribed as a subordinate member (*aṅga*), the *stotra* and *śastra* would have to be performed;
however, this [sixteenth cup] is not prescribed as a subordinate member of the *agniṣṭoma-stotra*, because the performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice possesses its own fruit.
Furthermore, that which is fruitless cannot stand as the principal with respect to the *stotra* and *śastra*.
Or rather, it possesses both the stoma and the śastra, because they are its constituent parts.
Commentary: Or rather, the *ṣoḍaśī* [cup] is accompanied by the *stotra* and *śastra*.
Why? Because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that.
For the *stotra* and *śastra* are indeed auxiliaries of the sacrifice, being the causes for its performance (*grahaṇanimitta*).

How so? When the occasion has arrived—namely, "having taken up either a cup (graha) or having drawn out a ladle (camasa), he introduces the chant (stotra)"—the contingent rite (naimittika) occurs because of that future occasion.

Therefore, the Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice should be accompanied by both the chant and the recitation (stotra-śastra). For when the chant and recitation are to be performed, they constitute its constituent parts (aṅga).
The Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice possesses a fruit;
because it possesses a fruit, it requires auxiliary rites (*aṅga*).
If those [auxiliaries] were not performed, then the Ṣoḍaśī would not accomplish its own purpose.
Therefore, the stotra and śastra should be performed.
However, if they were performed, the Agniṣṭoma form [of the sacrifice] would not exist;
and if the Agniṣṭoma form does not exist, [the rite] must indeed be performed.
Therefore, it possesses both the Stomas and the Śastras;
this is the reading found in the manuscript (the portion in brackets being from the Kaṃsa, i.e., the Tantraratna).
And because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).

Commentary: This indicates the meaning of the term "liṅga" (indicative mark), namely that [the sacrifice] possesses the *ṣoḍaśī* stoma and śastra. How so? "Some sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) are vertical, while others are horizontal. Those in which the Hotṛ satisfies himself are vertical; those in which the Acchāvāka does so are horizontal. How is this an indicative mark? This is what is being stated.

There are only two types of sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*): those which conclude with the office of the Hotṛ and those which conclude with the office of the Acchāvāka. If the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice has its *stotra* and *śastra*, then it is thus;
otherwise, this *ṣoḍaśin* should conclude on the ground of the Adhvaryu.
Therefore, the Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice also possesses six stotras and six śastras; its status as a distinct sacrificial conclusion (saṃsthā) is due to a specific scriptural injunction.

Commentary: Now, as for what was said—that there would indeed be a difference in the concluding rites—it shall be so precisely because of the scriptural statement. Regarding that which was stated to end with the Agniṣṭoma, another conclusion is prescribed for it by virtue of that specific statement.
What statement indeed would one not accept?
For this reason also, it is said that [the sacrifice] is accompanied by both Stomas and Śastras.

Regarding the Śāstra: from such statements as, "One should take the Ṣoḍaśin [cup] at the Agniṣṭoma for a Kṣatriya," or "It should be taken even at the Ukthya," the Agniṣṭoma is established as the primary model (prakṛti).

In this regard, when there arises a doubt—whether at that time it should be without the *stomas* and *śastras*, or whether even then it should possess the *stomas* and *śastras*—the following is stated: "Upon the conjunction with the *ukthya* and *agniṣṭoma*, its [the Ṣoḍaśin's] *stotra* and other elements would not exist;
in the completion (*saṃsthā*) of the Ṣoḍaśin, there would be no status of being an *ukthya* or *agniṣṭoma*.
For the words *agniṣṭoma* and so forth denote the presence of specific *stotra* completions."

In the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* being established as a part of the *agniṣṭoma*, the sacrifice would not be an *agniṣṭoma*; thus, the injunction that "it should be taken up in the *agniṣṭoma*" would be contradicted. Therefore, it should be a *ṣoḍaśin* characterized by its own specific hymns (*stoma*).
(Now the established conclusion: "It is true that there is no fault because of the statement regarding the attainment of another *saṃsthā*;
rather, by the sublation of the previous *saṃsthā*, another *saṃsthā* itself is enjoined.
For that which was originally established as having the *ukthya* *saṃsthā* is [here] established as having the *agniṣṭoma* *saṃsthā* due to its excellence."

"Is this not likewise [prohibited] for a Kṣatriya? What then of one who has completed the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice?"—such is the meaning of that statement; therefore, it includes both the Stomas and the Śastras.
For the Stotra and the Śastra are directly enjoined as its constituent parts (aṅga).

"The hymn consists of twenty-one verses; the *hari* [verses] are the two *śastras* for the foundation"—thus is the *stotra* and *śastra* prescribed. For, in the absence of contradiction, would they not be performed for the *ukthya* and *agniṣṭoma* forms? Therefore, it possesses both *stoma* and *śastra*. Regarding the *ṣoḍaśin*: according to the *Tantraratna*, because of the context of the *ṣoḍaśin* and because of the context of sublation (*bādha*), the question is considered regarding the mere measure of that which lacks a *stotra* and *śastra*.

In this case, the *ṣoḍaśin* recitation is not prescribed by taking the *agniṣṭoma* and other terminuses (*saṃsthā*) as the occasion (*nimitta*); rather, regarding that sacrifice which has been enjoined as having the *agniṣṭoma* terminus or the *ukthya* terminus, for a Kṣatriya (*rājanya*), that sacrifice—though possessing those terminuses—is not to be performed with them, but must instead be performed with the *ṣoḍaśin* recitation. Thus, taking the Kṣatriya alone as the occasion, another terminus is enjoined by setting aside the previous terminus.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that when the *stotra* and *śastra* exist, there should be a difference in the terminus. [Vi]: The *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed related to the *agniṣṭoma*, characterized by the *stoma* and the *śastra*.
Or, when it is joined with that [term], the Agniṣṭoma is obtained, just as the *saṃsthā* (concluding rite) is obtained [by the name of its constituent].
Thus, the stotra indeed comes to be; for in this way, it is praised as "possessing the word *hari*" (*harivat*, i.e., joined with the word *hari*).
For it is accepted that when there is another ritual arrangement (*saṃsthā*), the *stotra* and *śastra* are then joined [with it].

Regarding this, the Bhaṭṭa [school] has stated in the section on "The Modificatory Nature of the Ṣoḍaśin" (10.1.13–4): "The *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice is a member of the archetype (*prakṛti*)," as established by the two statements: "One may take [the cup] even at the *agniṣṭoma* for a Kṣatriya," and "Even at the *ukthya*."
This is now raised as an objection:
here, the injunction for the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice (*ṣoḍaśi-saṃsthā*) as a subsidiary of the *agniṣṭoma* does not apply when the Kṣatriya is the occasion (*nimitta*).

For would it be the *saṃsthā* itself denoted by the words "agniṣṭoma" and so forth, or the Jyotiṣṭoma qualified by that [agniṣṭoma] *saṃsthā*? It is not possible in either case, because one *saṃsthā* cannot coexist with another *saṃsthā*.
For a *saṃsthā* (concluding rite) is that which follows another; thus, within a particular performance of a sacrifice (*kratu-prayoga*), there can be no other concluding rite once one has occurred.

Furthermore, it is impossible for the *ṣoḍaśin-stotra* to be the final element if the *agniṣṭoma-stotra* and others have already preceded it. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that there is an injunction for a different concluding rite by way of superseding each preceding one—is also untenable.

This is because it is impossible to determine the meaning of the sentence either by treating the *upamarda* as having the sense of "lack of faith" (*aśraddhā*) or by treating it as the relationship between the *ukthya* and the thing to be enjoined. Furthermore, even if there were an *upamarda* of the previous *saṃsthā*, since the sequence following the *ukthya* is not enjoined for the *ṣoḍaśin*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that [the *ṣoḍaśin*] occurs after the repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the *agniṣṭoma* would fail to be established. Nor can it be argued that the terms *agniṣṭoma* and so forth indicate the pure *jyotiṣṭoma* and that the injunction of the *ṣoḍaśin-saṃsthā* is made with respect to that [pure form], because this would result in the redundancy of the two sentences.

Therefore, in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin*, which is subordinate to the [Agniṣṭoma], there is merely the taking up of the cup (*grahaṇa*); having indicated that very act as constituting the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, it is enjoined either with reference to the terminuses (*saṃsthā*) such as the Agniṣṭoma, or with reference to the sacrifice qualified by those [terminuses].
And in that context, because of the connection with a deity, the repetition of the offering (*yājyābhyāsa*) is also implied by the sense.
However, this does not entail the performance of the hymn (*stotra*) which is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of that [offering].

Since there would be a contradiction resulting from the sublation of the *agniṣṭoma* and other *saṃsthās*, which constitute the primary elements of that [Jyotiṣṭoma], this being the position reached: first of all, the injunction for the taking of the cups (*grahaṇa*) is not intended with reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma as qualified by the *saṃsthās*, because that would entail the fault of secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even in the words *agniṣṭoma* and so forth.

Nor is it intended with reference to the *saṃsthās* alone, because since their status as subsidiaries of the *saṃsthās* is already established by the context (*prakaraṇa*), the use of the particle *api* for the purpose of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) would be illogical.

Nor is there an injunction [of the *agniṣṭoma*] as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* when the *saṃsthā* (the completion of the sacrifice) is the occasion (*nimitta*), because that would result in a lack of unity in the object to be enjoined (*uddeśya*), since the *rājanya* would also be an occasion.
Therefore, even though it is the first to be presented, the word *agniṣṭoma* itself must have *lakṣaṇā* (indication) either toward the *stotra* (laudatory hymn) or toward the repetition thereof;
and the locative case is a *satisaptamī* (locative of condition).

And thus, when the repetition of the Agniṣṭoma has been performed—this being the sense derived from the wording—the Ṣoḍaśin-saṃsthā itself, characterized by occurring after that repetition, is enjoined as an auxiliary of the Jyotiṣṭoma on the occasion of a Kṣatriya (rājanya).
Consequently, its permanent form is the Agniṣṭoma-saṃsthā, while its optional Ukthya-saṃsthā is set aside.
However, the optional Ṣoḍaśin-saṃsthā belongs to all [classes]; this is the distinction.

For this very reason, it should also be understood that the sequence following the *ukthya* belongs to the *ṣoḍaśin*, both in the optional performance (*kāmyaprayoga*) and in the *atirātra* sacrificial form.
This is indeed the authoritative position here: in the *agniṣṭoma* form, there is nothing such as the *ukthya* and so forth after the *agniṣṭoma* stotra;
however, in the *ukthya* form, the *ukthya* stotras follow it, but even after those, there is no *ṣoḍaśin* and so forth.
In the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrificial form (*saṃsthā*), however, the *ṣoḍaśin-stotra* follows it, but not the *atirātra* and so forth which follow that as well.
In the *atirātra* sacrificial form, however, the conclusion is reached by that [stotra] alone.

Therefore, here, in the optional (*kāmyā*) *ṣoḍaśin* sacrificial form and in the repetition of the *ṣoḍaśin* included within the *atirātra*, the sequence following the *ukthya* remains exactly as it was established.

However, when the *agniṣṭoma* arrangement (*saṃsthā*) is suppressed, since the status of being subsequent to the repetition of the *agniṣṭoma* is expressly prescribed by scripture, there is indeed the omission of the *ukthya* stotras.
And this very [sacrifice] receives the name "Atyagniṣṭoma," based on the scriptural statement from another school: "In the Atyagniṣṭoma, one should draw [the cups] for a Kṣatriya.

But when the *ukthya* arrangement is suppressed, because there is a specific reinstatement (*pratiprasava*) of the *ukthya* stotra alone in that case, there is no omission of the *ukthya* [cups] therein.
And since only the optional *ukthya* sacrifice is obtained [as a model], its displacement results in the non-performance of that [optional sacrifice] for the *rājanya*.
Otherwise, the word "even in the *ukthya*" (*apyukthye*) would become redundant. Alternatively, let there be no exclusion of the optional *ukthya* sacrifice.
This has been explained in detail in the *Kaustubha* on the *Rathantara-carana* (712).

Therefore, it is established that for a Kṣatriya, the *ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice, which consists of the *ukthya* and *agniṣṭoma* terminuses along with the *stomas* and *śastras*, should take place by superseding those terminuses.

As for the scriptural injunctions such as "One should take [the draughts] at the *atirātra* for a Brāhmaṇa," these do not enjoin a different terminus by superseding the previous one; for they are perceived as being distinct from the sentences regarding the *agniṣṭoma* and others, because they are restorations (*pratiprasava*) and lack the characteristic of "covering over" (*kapidhātu*).
If one were to accept a subsequent application (*anuprajñā*), it would result in the redundancy of the recitation of the *ukthya* and *vyakta* [mantras].
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the term *atirātra*, which presents itself first, to indicate the *stotra*.
Therefore, the term *ṣoḍaśin*, being the last mentioned and connected [to the context], alone indicates the repetition of the sacrifice (*tyāgābhyāsa*).

And its injunction is made either with reference to the *atirātra* as a specific form (*saṃsthā*) or with reference to the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice characterized by that form; for the sacrifice is already satisfied (*nirākāṅkṣa*) by the preceding [injunctions] alone.
Furthermore, due to its textual recitation (*pāṭha*), it is qualified by the time-period ending with the *atirātra* stotra.

For this very reason, since it is established as a permanent requirement (*nityavat*) for a Brāhmaṇa in that context, there is a prohibition—"one does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra"—intended to establish its optional nature (*pākṣikatva*).

Therefore, it should be understood that for a Brāhmaṇa there is an option (*vikalpa*), whereas for others there is none at all, precisely because of the absence of any authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishing it.
As for the statement written in some places, "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*," that [is to be understood] as "for a Brāhmaṇa at the *atirātra*," by means of these two [texts] alone.

"But the fire [is mentioned] because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga), as it is said: 'It is established. Now, this is not a consecration of the fire; rather, the fire is determined to be for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha). Nevertheless, in the subsequent sentence, "He sacrifices after the fire" (*agnimanuyajati*), there is the accusative case of the karmapravacanīya.
Because it requires another action, the act of sacrifice itself is connected with the arrangement.
Therefore, this is the meaning: the sacrifice by means of the Agnihotra and other rites is performed subsequent to the fire consecrated by the piling (cayana).

This being the case, since the piling is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), even in the statement "he piles the fire," the fact that the piling has the Āhavanīya fire as its object is determined precisely because it serves the purpose of the ritual.

In sentences such as "the praise of Agni" (*agneḥ stotram*) and "the recitation of Agni" (*agneḥ śāstram*), since it is untenable for the word *agni* to refer to the [physical] substance, they must refer to the sacrifice itself through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor can it be argued that there is no inconsistency even if the word *agni* retains its primary meaning in both these sentences— such that this would not be an injunction of a sacrifice, but rather an injunction of other preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*) similar to those in the archetype (*prakṛti*) and ectype (*vikṛti*)— and thus the injunction in the ectype would be redundant, since the rite could be obtained in the ectype by extension (*atideśa*) from the archetype alone.

Just as in the case of the injunction "He twice scoops from the middle and from the front part of the Agnihotra," where the purpose is not the literal quality [of the action] but rather the intended meaning based on the requirements of the ritual task, so too here the word functions by indicating the intended sense through the force of the action.
Consequently, the primacy of fire (*agni*) and the subordinate status of singularity (*ekatva*), and so forth, are to be applied in the same manner as previously explained.
It should be understood that even the word "tṛṇāni" (grasses) here is not intended to denote plurality.
Vārttika 3.1.14, pp. 722–23.

In the Agnihotra sacrifice, there is an *anugrahamantra*: "With speech as the Hotṛ, with breath as the Udgātṛ, with the eye as the Adhvaryu, with the mind as the Brahman, and with the ear as the Agnīdh—by these five divine officiating priests, I offer you."
This mantra should not be recited when lifting the fire for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

(Vi. 1.4.9) In the *agnihotra*, at the time of sunrise or sunset, the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) must be performed only upon the destruction of both the *āhavanīya* and the *gārhapatya* fires, and not even upon the destruction of one alone.
(6.4.8) In the *agnihotra*, cooking is prescribed on the *gārhapatya* fire, whereas in the *māsāgnihotra*, cooking is performed on the *prājahita* fire.
1.2.1.6: One should have the *jāti* performed at the *agnihotra*.
This should be seen under the section titled “The Topic of the Fruit of the Scripture” (*śāstraphalādhikaraṇa*).

The limit for the performance of obligatory rites such as the *agnihotra* is until one's death. Even for an aged person, performance is possible by employing assistants; thus, the limit of time is until life. For one without assistants, old age is the limit. For one who has lost his senses or whose offspring have perished, the limit is thirty years. Just as there are fixed alternatives (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*) regarding these periods of life and so forth, it is also possible to prescribe even a month for one who is extremely detached and has lost his senses or whose offspring have perished, as this too is a matter of fixed application (Su. p. 190). Furthermore, in the case of the obligatory *agnihotra* and other rites, if two of the prescribed materials are lost, the rite must be completed using a substitute (*pratinidhi*).
Bhāṣya 6.3.13–17: Words such as *agnihotra* denote meanings that are connected with substances and gender.
Vārttika 2.6.1244, p. 616: There is no requirement for the lifelong performance of rites such as the *agnihotra* at every single instance of their respective times;
this is the *agnihotra-nyāya*.

*Bhāmatī* 6.3.24–27: Since learned persons belonging to the three higher castes are already available for the performance of the *agnihotra* and other rites, these injunctions do not necessitate the acquisition of knowledge by those of the fourth caste (*caturvarṇa*). *Śāstradīpikā*, Tarkapāda, p. 6: When it becomes necessary for an initiated person to travel elsewhere, even in the absence of the *agnihotra* fire, the *agnihotra* must be performed after having [the fires] formally deposited (*samāropya*) within himself. *Saṃkalpa* 3.131: For the purpose of the *agnihotra*, when the fire that has been drawn out is extinguished, the *jyotiṣmatī* sacrifice is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and not the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
VI. 1|417. The sole duty of the Agnihotra consists precisely in the carrying forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana) and so forth.
Vārttika 2|1|126, p. 650. Since the Agnihotra, the Iṣṭi, and the Soma sacrifices do not have distinct purposes, an investigation into modification (ūha) must be undertaken.
Ci. 9|1|1, Section 1.
The Principle of the Name "Agnihotra" (7.3.11–14). In the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, the first day is named *prāyaṇīya*, and likewise in the *gavāmayana*.
If it is argued that there is an extension (*atideśa*) [of ritual details] from that [first day] to the other based on the principle of the name "Agnihotra," it is not so.
This is precisely the principle of the *māsāgnihotra*:
that rituals such as the *agnihotra* must be performed at their prescribed times.
"Because it is not a subsidiary to ritual action, the practice [of repetition] is enjoined as being for the sake of the person.
The Commentary states: They recite this: "One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as long as one lives.
This sacrifice is enjoined as being for the sake of the person.
It has already been stated that this practice is not a mere subsidiary of ritual action (2.4.11–17).
Now, a doubt arises here: should the offering be made continuously, or rather intermittently? What is the prima facie view? It should be continuous, because it is taught with reference to the person.
"This person [should act]"—thus it must be performed continuously.

For it is heard in scripture: "The Agnihotra is to be offered at dusk" and "at dawn in the morning," as well as "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day" and "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day.
This performance is not one in which all the constituent parts (aṅgas) are assembled simultaneously.
Therefore, there is no fault in being slightly deficient in time, as that [deficiency] is impossible in this context by implication.
The Bhāṣya states: "This is not so; that one must offer only when [the command] 'juhudhi, juhudi' has been uttered."
It is said that one should offer oblations in such a manner as one is able;
however, it is not possible to do so continuously.
By this, it is meant that food and recreation must be taken.
Therefore, one should always offer at times that are not incompatible [with other duties].

It is not taught that [the offering] depends on specific times. The Commentary states: "And this is not the case—that one should always offer whenever there is no conflict with the purpose of the *juhū* ladle."
This specific time is prescribed: "The Agnihotra is to be offered at dusk," and "at dawn in the morning.
Likewise: "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day," and "one should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day.
Therefore, it is not a matter of continuity.
He says: "But surely, even for one who lacks the [required] qualities, the performance and the time must be observed.
To this it is replied: Time is not a quality.
This has been stated to be the indicative mark (*nimitta*).

Therefore, at other times, because it would have been prescribed [only for that specific occasion], even what was performed would be as if unperformed. Consequently, the performance of that which depends on time must continue for as long as one lives.
The prescription of time is established from the observation of temporal indicators (*kāla-liṅga*).

The Commentary states: "Indeed, there is an indicator: 'He who, being a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should neglect either the full moon or the new moon day, falls away indeed from the heavenly world.
If the oblation were to be performed at all times, then what would there be to neglect? Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no continuous practice."
Śabara: It is heard in scripture, "as long as one lives.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the performance be continuous, or only at specific times—namely, the Agnihotra in the evening and morning, and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices on the full and new moon days?

In this regard, since the ritual is enjoined with "living" as the occasion (*nimitta*), and because in the case of an occasional rite (*naimittika*) there is no deficiency even when its performance is impossible due to the absence of the occasion, and since time is not a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), it is logical that the performance be continuous despite the omission of those specific times.
This being the position, we reply: even though time is a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), its abandonment is not reasonable. Why?
Because it is of a non-prescribable nature (*anupādeya-rūpatva*) with respect to that [action].

The principle of the Agnihotra (85); the principle of the Agnihotra-spoon: [these apply] to the injunctions regarding ritual acts. If something is to be adopted according to the injunction of performance, then it is appropriate that it be "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*).
Furthermore, because time is not something to be undertaken as an objective, this is the mode of expression there: "When this time has arrived, the rite must be performed.
Consequently, by implication, living at that very time becomes the occasion [for the performance], and thus there is no performance at another time.

By this, the two knowledges of Agni (agnividye) are also explained. For even those two, though established by the injunctions for study and installation, are accepted [as requirements] because they are not to be performed by the injunction of application (prayogavidhi).
The formulation of the statement is as follows: "One who possesses the fire and is learned is not qualified [for the ritual]."

Furthermore, there is the direct hearing of the qualification for one who performs [the rite] in the injunction itself, because such a statement is heard everywhere, as in: "He who, knowing thus, [performs] the Agnihotra.
Therefore, when that time arrives, the knower, having combined the other auxiliary factors (aṅgas) as far as possible, carries out the performance while maintaining the nature of the fire.

[Objection: Soma—[one might object] that based on the authority of Smṛti, just like the qualification of one who has been initiated, there must be continuous performance due to the scriptural text stating "as long as life lasts"; this is the connection [of the objection].

This injunction regarding the performance does not concern time alone, but rather concerns only those subsidiaries that are intended for the purpose of the application-injunction (*prayogavidhi*). One is not required to perform [subsidiaries] according to one's capacity merely by virtue of being enjoined by the application-injunction; rather, it applies only to that which is understood as something to be performed (*kartavya*) by the application-injunction.
For it can be said that "one should do what is to be done according to one's capacity," but not that "one should do what is not to be done."

Furthermore, since the person's duty is enjoined by the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*), at that very time it must be performed according to one's capacity; however, because time is not subject to such [personal] capacity, there is no requirement to perform it according to capacity in that regard.
As for the meaning of the Sūtra: the word "or" (*vā*) indicates a negation.
This repetition is not a subsidiary part of the ritual action (*akarma-śeṣa*), but rather a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
And therefore, [the practice] is to be performed continuously (this is the prima facie view).
Vi—“As long as one lives, it is continuous; or at its own time, or due to a specific occasion.
Since time is a subordinate factor, the last [alternative] follows from the principle of non-duality.”

Bhaṭṭa: In the case of the Agnihotra and other rites occasioned by life and so forth, since the occasion varies at every moment, there is the perception of a continuous performance of the occasional rite (naimittika) for each occasion; and in accordance with that, it will be stated later that it is impossible to abandon [the rite]. Furthermore, since time itself is an auxiliary (aṅga), its abandonment is logically consistent, and its purposefulness is established by its being restricted to optional (kāmya) contexts. Therefore, there is continuous performance. For this very reason, in the Soma sacrifice, because spring is the occasion, there is the perception of the entire procedure in each instance; thus, even when the time of the new moon and so forth is favored, there is no defect.

This being the position, [the author] replies: Since the scriptural injunction regarding the *nimitta* (occasion) must necessarily be restricted so as not to conflict with food, movement, and other such activities, that [injunction] is restricted by time as well—just as it is by the knowledge of the fire-altar (*agnividya*).

For even though time is an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*), it does not follow that the scope [of the rule] extends to all cases where one is capable; rather, only for that which is subject to the performance-injunction (*prayogavidhi*) is there a possibility of performance when one is capable, and only for that, in case of incapacity, is there a renunciation in accordance with the scriptural injunction regarding the *nimitta*.

And thus, just as in the case of the two *agnihotra* offerings, because they depend on being prompted by another injunction (*vidhi*) and are therefore objects of performance within the scope of that injunction, [the rule of continuity does not apply], so too for time (*kāla*), which—being something to be performed in its own right—is subject to the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) and is governed by the principle of "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*).
Even by means of an injunction regarding time, there is no continuous performance due to the restriction imposed by the hearing of the specific occasion (*nimitta*).

For this very reason, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed in the text, “He who, being a performer of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, should let the new moon or the full moon day pass,” applies only when there is an omission of the occasional rite (*naimittika*) at the prescribed time.

*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the rule “One should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives,” since this is occasioned by life, the rite must be performed even without the specific times of evening and morning or the month-long periods; for in the case of an occasional (*naimittika*) duty, there is no deficiency (*avaiguṇya*) when what is impossible to avoid is omitted. Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there should be continuous performance. In response, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: because the time for the auxiliary (*aṅga*) rites cannot be accomplished by human effort, they fall under the principle of acting according to one’s capacity (*yathāśaktyanyāya*). Therefore, life itself is the occasion for the rite only at those specific times [evening and morning], and thus there is no requirement for continuous performance. Maṇḍana: “The new-moon sacrifice (*darśa*) and other such rites should not be performed continuously. Śaṅkara: “There is no omission of the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) by failing to study [the texts].”

This is the principle of the *agnihotra*. Nor does there arise the fault of mutual dependence—whereby, if there were an injunction regarding time, there would be a name, and if there were a name, there would be an injunction of time by way of restating that [act]—because, in cases such as "on the full moon day with the full moon [offering]," the status of the term as a name is first determined through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) according to the principle of the *agnihotra*; subsequently, based on that, its status as the ground for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*) is determined through its connection with the time prescribed in accordance with it.
Bhāṭṭa 2.1.2:
The Principle of the Agnihotra-havaṇī.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that when the word *vaṣaṭkāra* is heard in the context of the *vaiśvadeva* [offering] within the *rājasūya*, it extends the properties of the nine potsherds (*navakapāla*), just as the word *agnihotra* [extends properties] in its own context.
VI. 3.16, The Principle of the Agnihotra. (This is indeed the principle of the Agnihotra: the principle of the name "Agnihotra.

The word *pṛṣṭha* in the phrase “*pṛṣṭhe upatiṣṭhate*” is employed in reference to the ritual performance of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*); by the principle of the term "Agnihotra," it extends the properties of the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* to the act of worship (*upasthāna*).)
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
It follows the logic of the *agnihotrahavaṇī* (the oblation-ladle used for the *agnihotra*).
Even in the absence of the vessels for the year-long rite, because of the logic of the *agnihotrahavaṇī*, the performance of the principal *kapāla-yāga* (pot-sherd sacrifice) is not precluded.

This is precisely the principle of the transfer of qualities (guṇalopa). Regarding the Agnihotra sacrifice (agnihotrahoma): the ritual duties (dharma) of the Agnihotra and other rites include specific sacrificial implements (yajñāyudha), such as "the Agnihotra-ladle and the winnowing basket," which is a wooden vessel used as the means for the pouring out of the oblation (nirvāpasādhana).
And this [offering] is included within the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*):
“He pours out the oblations with the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle”; “He collects the sacrificial implements.
Which [implements]?—The *agnihotra-havaṇī* is present because it is mentioned in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
PMS 10.2.163: A subordinate element (*aṅga*) is set aside by the principal (*pradhāna*).
For example, among the *pavamāna* offerings, the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle is set aside by the act of pouring out the oblation (*nirvāpa*).
Bāla. p. 132: Just as that [ladle] is called *agnihotrahavaṇī* when the *agnihotra* has been offered.
Śābarabhāṣya 10.2.17: "He offers the oblations with the Agnihotra-ladle" (10.2.16). [This applies] to the Darśa and other sacrifices.
Bhaṭṭadīpikā 10.2.16:

The evening Agnihotra is not performed on the Uttaravedi even when it occurs on the day of a Paśuyāga; however, if the Paśu ritual is postponed due to some accident, then it is indeed performed on the Uttaravedi.

In the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the carrying forward of the fires (*praṇayana*) has already been performed; this is considered as established by the very statement regarding the *taddhīnīya* [rite], according to the principle of the *diś* [section] (4.3.15–16).
By process of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it serves the purpose of bringing about the proximity of the ritual procedure.
Just as in the case of "the householder is not consecrated," the consecration is not enjoined;
for he is neither the sacrificer nor the Adhvaryu priest who is being enjoined as the agent, since all [roles] are already obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction).
What then? The sequence of consecrations, having been obtained without a fixed order, is here being regulated.
Thus, here too, a property is enjoined with respect to the sacrifice;
and a qualification of that which is being pointed out as the object is not intended to be significant.
Therefore, the intention is that there is the acquisition of the property upon the mere mention of the sacrifice.
"But if [the details] are prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), then those details being prescribed for one specific instance will apply even to another instance of that same kind;
therefore, in that case, modification (*ūha*) is established.
What is the intention? The means (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) are required by that which is being brought into existence.

Therefore, both [the sacrifice and the apūrva] are connected with that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), because of their mutual requirement; and that which is to be brought about is the *apūrva*.
Furthermore, the sacrifice is not accomplished without the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), because in common worldly experience, a sacrifice is a means that is incomplete in itself.
Thus, [the connection occurs] in that which is qualified.
Regarding the dharma of the Agnihotra and other rites, it is said that one should perform them.
When the sacrifice exists, these acts are auxiliaries to the *apūrva*; when it does not exist, they are non-auxiliaries, being merely ignorance.
Therefore, the sacrifice is the cause, whereas the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is the motivator.
This being the position reached, we reply:
the sacrificial act is primary; it is the effect of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
For that [result] is indeed heard as being the fruit.
The refinement (*saṃskāra*) which occurs when one sacrifices with materials belonging to that [deity] is prompted by the *apūrva*.
These [materials] are prepared on the grounds that they are for the sake of that [deity]; their connection is not with the act of sacrificing itself.
These are connected with the meaning of the root by means of the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*),
for that [statement] possesses expectancy, whereas the meaning of the verbal root does not.
Therefore, they are employed for the sake of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) and are caused by the *apūrva*.
As for what was said— that the status of the *apūrva* as an instigator (*prayojaka*) and its status as a causal occasion (*nimitta*) are untenable because of the difference in the mode of expression—
therein it is replied:
the status as an instigator is based on the scriptural injunction (*vācanika*), whereas the status as a causal occasion does not exist independently of the scriptural injunction.
If that by which one is engaged becomes its cause (nimitta), then it is as follows: for example, a garden is both the motivator and the cause for a gardener in the payment of wages;
when the garden exists, wages are given to him.
It maintains equality with wages; for there is no evidence that a garden arises from anything other than watering and so forth when they are absent.

Indeed, no causal complex (*sāmagrī*) distinct from watering and the like has been established for that which is delimited by being an *āgneya* (dedicated to Agni); if such were the case, then the exclusion of the property of being an *āgneya* would follow upon its being produced by that [complex].

However, by virtue of the force of the injunction itself, sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and so forth constitute the constituent parts of that [sacrifice]; since there is no evidence for their occurrence apart from that [sacrifice], there is no pointlessness in sprinkling and the rest being for the sake of the essential nature of the sacrifice.

For this very reason, even those factors that provide indirect assistance (ārādupakāraka) would be purposeless, since their purpose would merely be the essential form of the sacrifice itself. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: although the delimiting factor for the objecthood (*uddeśyatā-avacchedaka*) of acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) remains the same even when they serve as means for a sacrifice of a different class, nevertheless—just as in the case of being a means to the *apūrva*—the property of "rice-ness" (*vrīhitva*) does not enter into that [objecthood] according to the method to be explained hereafter. Consequently, the accomplishment of the result to be achieved by that act is unavoidable even in the case of *śyāmāka* grain.

In reality, however, being the means for a sacrifice of a specific class (*vijātīya-yāga*) is not the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*). This is because such a sacrifice is included within that which is delimited by the more pervasive property of "sacrifice-ness" (*yāgatva*); and since it is understood from common worldly experience that whatever is delimited by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is a cause for that [sacrifice], there is no obstacle to the occurrence of a sacrifice of that specific class even through rice and other materials—despite the absence of other substances—due to the force of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Consequently, the charge of pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) remains as it was.

Nor is there a rule that a universal, by being inherent in a particular cause, must necessarily produce an effect; for while this may be the case elsewhere, there is no evidence for such a postulation in the present context, and because the scriptural indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "that very [grain] should be offered as it is"—would otherwise be untenable.

For this very reason, having established the application of the rule through a different method, the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding grains and the like is justified as being for the sake of the result, even in the case of substitutes.
Therefore, all injunctions concerning substances and their preparations have as their object only that which serves as a means to the *apūrva*.

Since it is not possible for substance (*dravyatva*) and the like to be a cause with respect to that which is delimited by the unprecedented (*apūrva*) as a pervading factor—this being unestablished according to common worldly experience—the aforementioned counter-inference would follow.

Even in the case of remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), it is in this same manner that they possess the capacity to produce a suitability conducive to the generation of the *apūrva*; thus, the substance serves [the sacrifice] in this way, but its purpose is not the sacrifice itself, as that would result in futility (*ānarthakya*).
Because it produces the suitability for the sacrifice and other such acts, there is no contingency of it becoming the primary element.
The point that "there would be a destruction of its status as a subsidiary" (*aṅgatva-vighāta*) and so forth has been explained in detail in the *Kaustubha*.

As for the argument that the injunction for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth applies only to that which is delimited by the universal of rice-ness (*vrīhitva*), because figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not admitted in verbal cognition, and that subsequently—by the principle of the "Nishada-chief" (*naiṣādasthapati*, Pāṇini 6.1.13)—one assumes another sacrifice consisting of rice-grains qualified by sprinkling and so forth, thereby assuming they serve the purpose of the *apūrva* (transcendental result); that [argument] is refuted because, if the sprinkling and so forth, or the [rice] produced from them, were the objective (*bhāvya*) delimited by rice-ness, there would be a contradiction due to unfitness (*ayogyatā*), which acts as an obstacle to the verbal cognition itself, and thus figurative indication must be admitted.

Therefore, since the terms *vrīhi* and so forth indicate by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) that which is delimited by being a means (*sādhanatva*), the injunction for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites is indeed with respect to that [means] alone; thus it is established that these [rites] are prompted solely by the *apūrva*. Consequently, the modification (*ūha*) in the case of *śyāmāka* and other grains is proven. Nor does it follow—even under this view—that there would be an omission of ritual properties (*dharma*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) due to the absence of *vrīhi* and so forth, simply because those terms function as conditions (*nimitta*) through their non-occurrence; for there is no evidence that *vrīhi* and so forth serve as conditions, given the absence of any passage containing the relative pronoun (*yat*).

Because, according to the method to be explained, since the [result] does not enter into the status of being the delimitor of the objective (*uddeśyatāvacchedakatva*), it also lacks the quality of being an instigator (*anu-jñāpakatva*). For this very reason, only that which is temporally prior [to the action] possesses the state of being delimited by that [objective].

In reality, however, although the desire for a result may be an instigator, there is no evidence that an unestablished result can be an instigator; therefore, even a preceding factor that has become the result is not the occasioning condition (*nimitta*).
And by this very same direction, the status of being a cause (*nimittatva*) for the nature of a sacrifice (*yāgatva*) in cases of remote auxiliary acts (*ārādupakāraka*) has been refuted.
Therefore, since there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*), [the conclusion] is indeed established.
As for the numerous alternative interpretations (*varṇaka*) presented here in the root-text, they have been disregarded because they are redundant and so forth.

It should be understood that these [works] were composed by the original authors out of a fondness for the elaboration of their treatises. In the *Nyāyabindu*: Since threshing and other such rites serve the purpose of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) through the medium of rice (*vrīhi*) and other grains, it follows—given the absence of such a medium—that there is no modification (*ūha*) in the case of wild rice (*nīvāra*) and the like. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since rice and other grains serve as the medium by virtue of being the means to the *apūrva*, and since the status of being a means to the *apūrva* exists even in wild rice and the like in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is established that [the rites apply] because they are obtained through that medium; for the fact that they contribute to the *apūrva* is understood through the rule of extension (*atideśa*).

Thus, in the case of the rule "one threshes with the mortar and pestle that have been sprinkled," there is an adaptation (*ūha*) of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) to the new [implements] such as the winnowing basket and the nails.

Similarly, because mantras that indicate heaven—such as "Agni, the light"—are syntactically connected [to the ritual], there is an adaptation (*ūha*) in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*); this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Maṇḍana says: "The extension [of rules] (*atideśa*) was concluded in this [eighth] chapter, and again in the ninth."
The investigation of the extended (atidiṣṭa) ritual elements is as follows:

"Modification (ūha), however, is the alteration [of a mantra] in its practical application when it has fallen into a new position, due to the function of another element belonging to the original (prakṛti) rite;
it is declared to be that which is modified during performance."
Śaṅkara says: "The purpose is for the sake of crushing;
it is delimited by the state of being rice (*vrīhitva*);
or rather, it is the exclusion of its being for the sake of the sacrifice."
And in this context, regarding those [factors] that bring about a conjunction (*saṃnipātinaḥ*),
it is stated that the unprecedented (*apūrva*) serves as the cause;
or rather, it is the same for those that bring about a conjunction.
The Section on the Agnihotra (1.4.13.8).

When such a quality is heard [in the text], the power of the injunction is transferred even in the absence of the Agnihotra itself; [this concerns] the mantra for the drawing out [of the fire] for the purpose of the Agnihotra.

The term *mati* refers to what was stated in the *Agnihotra-adhikaraṇa*: "When another way [of interpretation] is possible, it is logical that the injunctive power (*vidhi-śakti*) should apply to only one [element]; thus, the injunctive power transfers to the subordinate element (*guṇa*). (Bāla-manoramā 2.1.6.17, p. 5.10). This means that in the *Agnihotra-adhikaraṇa*, it was stated that the injunctive power shifts to the quality. (Su. p. 790). This very section is the *Ādhāra-Agnihotra-adhikaraṇa*.

Even in the absence of the *agnihotra*, when the possibility arises for the initiated (*dīkṣita*) to travel elsewhere, the fires must be taken after having been formally deposited (*samāropya*). Prior to the release from initiation (*dīkṣā-nirmoka*), if the possibility of departure occurs, the formal deposit (*samāropa*) consists of taking the fires along with their placement in other vessels.

This is because, according to the injunction "Having offered the morning *agnihotra*, one should perform the formal deposit," the formal deposit is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *agnihotra*, following the principle established in the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice (Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 4.1.12).

Since for one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), there is an absence of the *agnihotra*, [one might argue] there is no connection with it; this being the prima facie view, we reply: because the ritual of consigning the fires (*samāropa*) serves as the means for the removal of the fires, or simply due to its immediate sequence, there is no evidence that the *vāstospatīya* oblation is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the *agnihotra*. Therefore, even in the absence of the *agnihotra*, the fires must be removed after having been consigned. (Saṃkarṣa 1.2.13). Furthermore, the mantra for the lifting of the fire intended for the *agnihotra* is not to be performed at the time of the lifting intended for the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, because the injunction for it does not apply when the time has not yet arrived. (Saṃkarṣa 1.2.14).

The Commentary: Regarding this Agnihotra, there is the mantra for the taking out [of the fire], beginning with "By speech, thee, as the Hotṛ; by breath, thee, as the Udgātṛ," and so forth. In that regard, this matter is subject to doubt: when the taking out of the fire is performed for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, should the mantra be employed therein or not? What is the prima facie view? Even when the fire has been taken out for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Agnihotra is indeed offered in it.
In that case, if no mantra is employed, the Agnihotra proceeds from a fire that has been lifted without a mantra.
Therefore, that lifting must be performed with a mantra.
Now, it might be argued that because the time [for the rite] would be lost, the lifting itself would be defective, and thus the Agnihotra [would not be valid].
And as for that: only the time has indeed passed;
however, the performance of the Agnihotra will still take place, even if it is deficient in its details.
If it is argued that the mantra must be recited in this way, we reply as follows:
when the Agnihotra is performed in a fire taken from another source, we declare—on the basis of the injunction—that it is a ritual action; therefore, no mantra should be recited therein.
That is not the extraction of the mantra;

therefore, one should not perform the extraction according to another's method. It is replied: But was it not already stated that the extraction of the Agnihotra will be deficient in its qualities? It is not the case that because of the absence of qualities, there is also an absence of the primary rite itself.

To this it is replied: Time is not a constituent quality (*guṇa*); rather, it is said that it exists as a causal condition (*nimitta*) for the production [of an action]. Therefore, if an action is performed in the absence of that causal condition, it becomes something unscripturally performed (*aśruta*).
Therefore, that extraction does not belong to the Agnihotra.
If the extraction does not belong to the Agnihotra, then the mantra should not be performed;
for in some respect it would be meaningless.

Śā—In the sequence of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, when the carrying forth of the fire (*agnyuddharaṇa*) is being performed, there arises a doubt: should the mantra for carrying forth the fire, which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Agnihotra, such as "By speech, [I carry] thee, O Hotṛ," and so forth, be employed, or not?
In this regard: "Even when the fire is carried forth for the sake of the Darśa, the Agnihotra proceeds;
the status of being a means (*sādhanatva*), though possessing the aforementioned properties, does not depend on a negative particle (*nañ*)."

Therefore, even though the lifting (*uddharaṇa*) is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *agnihotra*, the mantra must indeed be employed for the sake of measuring the time, simply by virtue of its being helpful to that [sacrifice], just as the properties of the *praṇītā* waters apply to the two vessels used for the sacrifice.
Even if the time cannot be a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), it is illogical to exclude the mantra.
(Thus it has been stated that even if one does not know the specific place for the lifting, the mantra is obtained merely through its helpfulness.)
Now, it must be accepted that the extraction itself is a subsidiary (aṅga) of the Agnihotra;

and thus, the mantra should be employed all the more readily. To this alternative view, he says: "Or rather, even this extraction is a subsidiary of the Agnihotra, and it may be performed even at an improper time; otherwise, due to the omission of the bringing forward (praṇayana) of the fire for the Agnihotra, there would be a deficiency (vaiguṇya). This being the position reached, it is replied: "But when the [proper] time—which is not a subordinate factor—is attained, the ritual act is enjoined."
It is with its ancillaries; therefore, prior to that time, there is no entitlement to perform the ritual.
And what is performed by one who lacks entitlement would be fruitless.
Consequently, before the [proper] time has arrived, neither the lifting of the fire—which is an ancillary of the *agnihotra*—nor its mantra should be performed.

Regarding *soma*: although there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when the fire is drawn out for another purpose in rites such as the *agnihotra*, it is stated that the mantra should still be recited when the drawing out is for another purpose; this constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*) by way of a counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*).
Even though the time [of the rite] may be brief, it is nevertheless not something to be adopted merely by the force of an injunction like other subsidiary elements (*aṅga*).
Consequently, once the time has arrived, the action is enjoined with reference to the person connected to that time.

Since the implements (*ājñāni*) are employed through the impulsion of ritual action (*karmanodanā*), and because there is no entitlement (*adhikāra*) prior to that time, an act performed by one who lacks such entitlement is purposeless. Thus, since there is no entitlement when the time has not yet arrived, the mantra cannot serve as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the extraction (*uddharaṇa*); therefore, the second alternative—which holds that the mantra is not to be employed—is untenable. Likewise, even if it were merely a means of assistance through the presence of a constituent part, the mantra would still be obtained as something that enters into the performance; thus, the first alternative is also untenable. Even though the extraction lacks the status of a constituent part, the mantra must nevertheless be employed precisely as a constituent part of the extraction.

And because, even in the case of the *uddharaṇa* (removal) which is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to that [rite], there is an absence of qualification (*adhikāra*), the mantra associated with the removal for the sake of the *agnihotra* is not to be performed by one who lacks qualification regarding its subsidiary. [This is illustrated by] the rule for the removal of cooked food when both fires in the *agnihotra* are extinguished; since there is no state of qualification at that time, the mantra does not enjoin its performance.

Since there is no possibility of performing [the rite] at an improper time because it would be unacceptable, and since that which is performed at an improper time is impossible to be fruitful, the application of the mantra at an improper time is not even a possibility. Thus,
the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that neither the maintaining of the fire nor its mantra is an auxiliary part of the Agnihotra, because [the time for it] has already passed.

It should be understood that because the *agnihotra* is established by the very act of lifting [the fire], there is no fault even in the omission of the *praṇayana* (carrying forward). As for the meaning of the Sūtra: "In the case of one whose *agnihotra* is spoken of as being for another..."
Maṇḍana: "The mantra is not enjoined for the act of looking;
there is an injunction for that [act], and in that case, the mantra would not apply because its time has not yet arrived.
Śaṅkara: "It is not so, because it begins with the mantra for taking up the fuel."
Or, for the extraction of the ten meanings of "vāk" and so forth, it is accompanied by mantras:

"Oṃ, in the case of the Agnihotra, when both fires are destroyed, there should be a re-establishment (punarādhāna) as an expiation (prāyaścitta), because there is no exclusion of the time [of the rite] here due to the specific cause."
The mind.

Bhaṭṭa: When the carrying forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) is performed for the sake of the ten [offerings], then, in that very same fire, the evening and morning *agnihotra* offerings are to be made; there is no taking away [of the fire] from that [original fire], nor is there its mantra.

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: Regarding the question whether or not the formula "O Agni, you have come with glory" (*yaśobhāvamī anugatau*) and so forth should be recited at the *agnihotra* sacrifice, [it is considered] in the context of the ten [cases]. [It is said]:

"If one should set [the fire] down while the sun is setting, or if the sun should rise while it is [still] unkindled, for him there is a re-establishment (*punarādheya*)"; this refers to the ritual lifting (*uddharaṇa*) of even that fire which has already been consecrated (*praṇīta*), which serves as the means for establishing its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *agnihotra*, and constitutes the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

In this regard, there is a doubt: when only one of the two [fires] has arrived, does the mantra—which is a constituent part of that [act]—still apply because it is the motivator for the act of leading forward (*praṇayana*), even though the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is not required; or rather, [does it apply] only when both have arrived?

What is established? The re-establishment (*punarādheya*) [of the fires] would apply because it occurs in the morning; in the case of the removal (*uddharaṇa*), there is an absence of occurrence in the afternoon.
It would be like the case of the rice-offering (*odana*).

Just as in the case of the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*, 6.4.12–23), because the principal fire and the act of removal are one, the time for its subsidiary [the *samayādhyuṣita*]— [The text ends here.]

When one or the other [fire] has arrived, there is the re-establishment (*punarādheya*); for when either one has come, because it is already established and because there is no need for a new undertaking,
the extraction (*uddharaṇa*) ought not to occur, lest it result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Just as in the case of the statement "I shall sacrifice here," even though the act of drawing [the fire] (*praṇayana*) does not possess the status of being a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the Agnihotra, the purposeful removal [of the fire] is intended;
likewise, there is this very connection: "I shall perform a good deed here.
This is because the status of being the agent (*kāraka*) of the Agnihotra exists precisely through that [connection].

Regarding the phrase "dup—yasyobhāvagnī tau," the meaning is that the following of the fire (*anugamana*) should extend only as far as the fire itself reaches. This is because the purpose [of the action] is the attainment of the mantra, which possesses the status of a governing factor (*adhipatya*) over the object. In this regard, whatever qualification is clearly expressed or found in another word constitutes the conclusion. Thus, having reached this position, [it is stated]: "The morning [rite] is for the sake of the *darśa* sacrifice intended by the seeker."

It has been stated that this [number] is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*) (in the section on the singularity of the cup, 3.1.7, because at the time of the act, the *agnihotra* is not present due to the absence of its occasioning factor;
and in the section on the oblation, etc., 6.4.16).

Here too, for the same reason—that being a subordinate part of it, the drawing of the water (*ādhāraṇa*) is all the more not present due to the absence of its time—it is not [the number] of the mantra that is intended.
The reasoning is as follows: regarding the statements "I shall sacrifice here" and "I shall perform good deeds here," there was at that time an expectation [of the ritual].

Nor is the sentence "I shall do this with the Agnihotra itself for the sake of avoiding faults through its own qualities" concerned with the Āhavanīya fire; for even though it is not the proper time, there is an implication of that [fire], since its accomplishment is established by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). That...

The statement "I shall perform the good deed" does not refer to the *gārhapatya* fire; for, since the ritual function of refinement such as the lifting [of the fire] is already obtained, it does not imply the necessity of that specific lifting alone. Thus, in these two sentences, two fires are observed.
Therefore, because that mantra and so forth involve even a slight contradiction; hence,

since the *prayāja* offerings and the *paśupuroḍāśa* are not auxiliary parts (*anaṅga*), even though they belong to the subsequent mantra, when the two fires are destroyed, the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) occurs— this is the illustration from the two cited statements regarding the fire.
This is not the ultimate meaning.

And thus, as in the case of "I shall sacrifice here" (*yathā iha yakṣye*) during the performance of the *hotṛ* function, because there is an absolute absence of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*), there is no possibility of a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) even in its absence.

Such final passages of the *Bhāṣya* constitute the text of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), not the text of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*); therefore, the mantra does not possess a figurative sense consisting in the absence of [denoting] another time.
Thus the author of the Vārttika says:
"The word 'pramādyāt' [is used] here with the intention of excluding [the application of the rule]; rather, it is established that there is indeed a sublation (bādha).
And this is concluded in the Tantraratna by the words 'on account of the indicative mark' (liṅgataḥ)."
[Question: What? [Answer: Even for the extraction of the ten meanings, there would be the production of the substance that assists the *agnihotra* sacrifice. This is the point of the *Nyāyabindu*.

Because [the rite] has been performed, the mantra for the extraction of the *ūrddhara* (the upward-moving breath), which is a constituent part of that [rite], is recited: "The Hotṛ [priest] [invokes] you with speech. Commentary:

When the substance [of the sacrifice] is destroyed, the production of that very same substance occurs here; such is the application [of the rule]. Because the means (*sādhana*) are specific [to the purpose], there is no lapse of time;
this is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
For its purpose is this: "How might it become a substance? and yet there is no omission of the mantra.
Alternatively, this is also an extraction;
the re-establishment of the fire is performed.
In this regard, this is the rule: it is performed together with two [fires], whether at the time of the subsidiary acts of the Agnihotra or otherwise;
not separately.

In that case, if only one arrives, it is not possible [to perform it], because the deficiency would arise from the omission of the carrying forward (praṇayana) of the single [fire] for the Agnihotra. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):
If both [fires] are destroyed during the Agnihotra, one should indeed re-establish the Agnihotra cooking fire; for otherwise, it would be defective.
Then he spoke a second time as well: "Even a single following of the fire is subject to re-establishment.
Daughter, if that [fire] is indeed the Āhavanīya, then it is the Āhavanīya."
Or rather, there are only two [options], because of the removal of two [syllables] while remaining in the same state, as in the case of the five-plate offering.
Since one of the two [fires] already exists for the purpose of the *homa*, it would not serve as the *homa* itself;
rather, the injunction for re-establishment (*punarādheya*) is based on its being the *tyāga-dakṣiṇā* (the sacrificial fee given upon relinquishment).
Therefore, the persistence of only one fire is not the reason [for re-establishment]; for that which is produced for the sake of the *homa* is the *āhavanīya*.
For this reason,
whether it be a Sūtra or a mantra...
It is a refinement (*saṃskāra*). And the word "refinement" does not apply even in the absence of a single refinement.
Bhāṭṭa: "The two [terms] *yaśas* and *bhāma*, following [the sun], arise as the sun rises."
And this consecration (*saṃskāra*) is for the purpose of the *homa* sacrifice;
for it is heard in the scripture: "If [the fire] should go out or set, the re-establishment (*punarādheya*) is indeed its expiation," and "he offers the oblation after having brought [the fire]."

When one [fire] has gone out, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been heard; does it apply even when each one goes out individually, or is there a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) when one is being re-established, or indeed a deficiency in both?

When considering whether this applies only when all the fires have gone out, because the cause for both is present, therefore, when one has gone out, there must be a re-establishment (*punarādheya*), since [otherwise] it would be impossible.

Even in that view, because [the individual] is not intended as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatvena*), this expiation applies even when each one is missing; for the Āhavanīya fire is non-worldly (*alaukika*), just like a Brāhmaṇa. Nor is its acquisition of self through the presence of spring and so forth dependent on the others, in the same way as it is with the Gārhapatya.

In the case of the *gyanu* (the *anvāhāryapacana*), since there is no other expiation such as the *prāyaścitta* for the *prātapatya*, its acquisition of self occurs through the arising of both [fires], not merely one alone.
The same applies to the *gārhapatya*.
It possesses the quality of being the object of a specific condition (*viṣayala*), because it has the non-existence of the rising of the sun and so forth as its specific condition.
Nor is origination for the sake of a specific purpose possible when that [purpose] already exists elsewhere.

Even so, because of the context, the hearing of the word "only" (eva), and the repeated performance, it arises together with the other [fire] when that is not yet present; for otherwise, it would be impossible for it to be a separate ritual act. Furthermore, in the origination-injunction (*utpattivākya*) regarding the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), all the fires are produced, and that [fire] indeed already exists.
For that which has arisen, it lasts as long as life.
Since the status of being a generator is already established, the determination of the object to be enjoined (uddeśya) must conform to the capacity of the injunction;
for a fault is heard [in scripture] regarding its abandonment.
Furthermore, it must be stated that there is no lack of determination;

for even in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the production of the *āhavanīya* fire is understood from scripture through its simultaneous production with the fires that are the objects of dedication, and not otherwise.
Because the specific qualification is not intended to be expressed [in that context].

For this very reason, according to the principle of the *Yogasiddhi* section (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 4.1.11–28), the re-establishment (*punarādheya*) of the fire-altar is occasional (*naimittika*), since both [conditions] are present upon the rekindling. Thus it is said: "It is true that at the time of the occasion, both are distinguished."
The yoga is indeed distinct.
This being the case, [it is said]: "In the bases, the requisites are occasional; however, this alone is not capable of producing [the result] for one."

Regarding the rule for the *punarādheya* (re-establishment of the fires), since the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice has already been established, and because the primary *āhavanīya* fire is available on its own *gārhapatya* hearth, there is no evidence for taking the *gārhapatya* from the middle [of the sacrificial ground] as one would in the case of a minor loss (*aṇunāśīvat*). Furthermore, when one’s own *gārhapatya* hearth is available, it is improper to take the *gārhapatya* from another; therefore, the cooking must take place in the *prājahita* fire itself.
Saṃkarṣaṇa 3.2.25: Thus the person (puruṣa) of Brahman.
This belongs to the third class;
he shares a third part in the third [class], and he receives four cows at the Soma sacrifice.

VI.3|7|17: The mantra "O Āgnīdhra, distribute the fires" is connected with the *praisha* for the carrying of the fire, but not with the rising [of the sacrificer] in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. 3|2|4: "The Neṣṭṛ consecrates the Āgnīdhra" in the Sattra.
3|3|17: In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is the exclusion of the original, complete *iḍā*-consumption by the Āgnīdhra through the *vanip* suffix.
The section on the wood-seller (*vanipū*).
Mānava Śrautasūtra 10.7.1.17: The etymological derivation of the word *agnīdh* is "one who has kindled the fire" (*agni ity edha*).
Keśava: In every Śrauta sacrifice, one of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is named *agnīdh*.
This very person is called the *agnīdh*.
"At the conclusion of each day, having entered the *āgnīdhra* shed, the *agnīdh* gives the command: 'O Subrahmaṇyā, summon the Subrahmaṇyā!
The use of the repetitive expression "at the conclusion of each" (*saṃsthite-saṃsthite*) indicates that there is no difference between the various Subrahmaṇyā invocations.
The *bhāṣya* states:
"And the *agnīdhra* is the *vaniṣṭhu*, as in the case of the *vyūhana*.
This is a rule of extension (*atideśa-sūtra*).
Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, it is heard in the scripture: "They carry away the *vaniṣṭhu* after it has been separated.
This *vaniṣṭhu* is a modification of the *iḍā*-portion;
for the *āgnīdhra*, it is the *vaniṣṭhu* alone and nothing else.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is like the *agnīdh* and the *hotṛ*; just as there is a modification regarding the consumption of the *ṛtviṅ-ṛca*, so it is here. This is the principle for the exclusion of all fires—both worldly and Vedic—which will be stated in the twelfth book [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*]: "On account of the specific designation, it should apply to the Vedic ones" (*nirdeśād vaidikānāṃ syāt*, 12.1.13). [See] Sūtra 3.7, page 40. For Agni and Varuṇa, one must necessarily perform the invocation using the term *sviṣṭakṛt*, such as: "O Agni and Varuṇa, bring the *sviṣṭakṛt*s," and so forth.
Bhāṣya 10.4.1.34–35: "Agni and Soma are the deities"—thus it is said.

Just as the status of being a deity belongs to Agni and Soma even when they are separate, yet their deity-status is one and the same, for that very reason the word "deity" (*devatā*) is used in the singular; likewise, the joint performance of the sacrifice by the husband and wife is explained, and therefore the verb "he should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is used in the singular.
Bindu 6.1.14: Agni-Soma, Viṣṇu, and Prajāpati are the deities of the Upāṃśuyāja, [to be chosen] optionally.

VI. 10.8.13. The preeminence of Agni and Soma in the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice is established by their mention in the passage, "Those two, Agni and Soma, said... (Su. p. 75). Because the deityhood of Agni and Soma is shared (*vyāsaṅga*), the oblation for Agni and Soma (*āgnīṣomīya-havis*) is not designated by the term *āgneya* (belonging to Agni) alone (Ratnākara 11.1.8; Ślokavārttika 8). The deityhood of Agni and Soma exists only when they are mutually dependent upon one another.

Because it has been stated, "The deities are Agni and Soma" (Śābarabhāṣya 6.1.4), the status of being a deity for Agni and Soma is not established by their own respective functions; rather, it is established by the mention of the sacrificer using the dative case. And since that mention is singular for those two, there is a unity of the deity-status therein.

Soma. The carrying forward of the Agni and Soma (agnīṣomapraṇayana) takes place on the day of preparation (aupavasathya) in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. [Vi. 5.1.14] Like the carrying forward of the Agni and Soma;

VI. 5.1.14. The acts such as the cutting of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which are recited after the carrying forward of the fires and Soma (*agnīṣomapraṇayana*), are displaced by the scriptural injunction and precede the *saumika* rites.

For sequence is expected only when [acts] are encompassed by a single injunctive statement.
And by virtue of sequence, a preceding word-meaning brings about the subsequent one;
therefore, when a preceding word-meaning is displaced, it displaces the others as well,

The principle of the *hṛdayādi* (heart, etc.):

The animal for Agni-Soma; milk [100]; the animal for Agni-Soma; the *sāṃnāyya* (curdled milk offering);
the animal produced for the sake of the sacrifice to Agni-Soma. When that has been offered, its remnants are to be disposed of.
Therefore, this rule regarding the performance of service toward the teacher has a visible purpose.

For those [animals], the sacrificial post (yūpa) is common to the whole ritual (tantra).
Oṃ. The animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (*āgnīṣomīya-paśu*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma;
however, the primary rite (*pradhāna*) is indeed the Soma sacrifice itself.

Vi. 3.7.2. Oṃ. Furthermore, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the *āgnīṣomīya* sacrifice must be performed by way of a single performance (*tantra*), because there is no distinction in the primary attributes among the twelve sacrifices of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*).
The concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) and other such rites are also performed by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Vārttika 9.1.8.32 states: "Because it is for the sake of the *āgnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice], the sequence of place and performance for the characteristics of the animal sacrifice will also apply;
the *āgnīṣomīya* animal is a modification of milk."
[The curd] should [be the substitute] for the *dadhi*, because of the similarity of form.
