Commentary: Even though it is a modification of the *sāṃnāyya*, it would be a modification of the *dadhi*, not of the milk.
Why? Because of the similarity of form.
The state of being wealth belongs to the embodied [sacrificial animal];
or rather, milk [is used] because of the commonality of time.
Commentary: Or rather, one should modify the milk for the animal sacrifice, not the curd.
The time for the *sadyaskrī* sacrifice is that of the animal sacrifice; milk also belongs to that same immediate time.
Curd, however, has a two-day interval because it is mediated by milk; thus, it is an external factor.
Therefore, it is offered later.
Commentary: In the case of the animal sacrifice, the milk comes first, followed by its sitting; curd does not.
And liquidity is indistinguishable. Commentary: Liquidity is common to both the animal and the milk; the animal flows, and the milk also flows.
Therefore, the animal is a modification of milk.
Śabara: Even in that case (regarding the *sāṃnāyya*), it would be a modification of curd, because of the commonality of being solid; or else, [it would be] a modification of milk.
For that [milk] is directly derived from the animal, whereas curd is derived from it;
for in the case of the animal, the derivation from the animal is direct.
Furthermore, the quality of being mobile is common to both the animal and the milk, and this quality is greater in the milk than in the curd.
Regarding the *soma* sacrifice: the connection [of this topic] arises from the specific consideration of its being a modification (*vikāra*) of the previously mentioned *sāṃnāyya*.

Since it shares the quality of originating from an animal (*paśuprabhavatva*) with curd, yet possesses the superiority of being more substantial (*ghanatva*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of curd should apply.

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since curd possesses only the quality of being substantial, whereas milk possesses both qualities—originating directly from an animal and being mobile (*gatimattva*)—the ritual procedure of milk should apply.

Vi—In this case, [the question arises] whether it is from curd or from milk; because of the similarity in the quality of thickness (*ghanatva*), it must be a modification of curd, as the property [of thickness] exists in milk only after the time of being processed into a substance for the sake of the animal sacrifice.
Bhaṭṭa—Even there, in the deliberation as to whether it is a modification of curd or a modification of milk, it is indeed a modification of curd due to the similarity in the quality of thickness.
Nor can there be a suspicion that it is a modification of milk based on the similarity of its direct origin from a cow;
for since causality consists in pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is supersensible and thus inferential, and as such is weaker than wealth which is accessible through perception.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: because we observe that the heart and other organs are modifications of milk that have remained for one day, the similarity of having remained for one day and the similarity of possessing their own inherent movement are indeed accessible through perception. Thus, by being assisted by these, the very notion of "wealth" (as the primary meaning) is sublated by the fact of its direct origin from the cow, and therefore it is certainly a modification of milk.

In the *Nyāyabindu*, [the objection is raised]: "Because it is [the product] of wealth and so forth... This being the position reached, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it belongs to the milk alone, because it originates directly from the animal.
Maṇḍana [states]: "But he would possess the nature of milk";
"he" refers to the animal.

Śaṅkara: "In that case as well, although there is no *prasaṅga* (extended application) because the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the *puroḍāśa* cake, and the *viṣṭakṛt* offering are not understood [to be included], nevertheless, since there is no difference in the function between the original (*prākṛta*) cooking of the animal and the cooking of the *puroḍāśa*, and since the *śāmitra* fire possesses the visible capacity for the cooking required by the original function, there is indeed *prasaṅga*. This section is appropriately connected for the purpose of refuting such a specific doubt."
The meaning is that, according to the Sūtra, the other [fire], the Gārhapatya, is employed by means of the Pauroḍāśika procedure.
Vi— "Another [offering] is the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) at the Śāmitra;
it belongs to the Śālyamukhīya fire because it is included within the ritual system of the animal sacrifice."

The cooking (*śrapaṇa*) prescribed for the *gārhapatya* fire is employed here; and in the eastern part of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, it is used to avoid any deficiency in the *homa*. As for the *śāmitra* fire, which is prescribed by the rule "he cooks in the *śāmitra* during the initiation (*daikṣa*)" for the roasting of the animal, that *śāmitra* fire does not apply to the cooking of the preceding animal-cake (*puroḍāśa*). Rather, the function of the *gārhapatya* is extended [to it] by the statement: "the *śālāmukhīya* itself becomes the *gārhapatya* thereafter"; thus, the *śālāmukhīya* alone is used.

Nor can it be argued that, because the term [śāmitra] is a general designation, the application of the *śāmitra* fire—prescribed by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) common to both the subsidiary and the principal rites—is established for the *śālāmukhīya* fire; for the word *śāmitra* denotes a connection with the act of quieting (*śamana*), whereas cooking possesses a connection with the act of heating (*pacana*). Furthermore, since that [connection with quieting] exists only in relation to the animal (*paśu*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the injunction for the *śāmitra* fire is understood as being restricted specifically to the cooking of the animal.
*Nyāyabindu*: "The *śāmitra* fire is for the purpose of cooking the animal."

Therefore, there arises the doubt: "The *puroḍāśa* cake should also be cooked in that very same place, because it depends upon the procedure for the animal sacrifice (*paśutantra*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since the *puroḍāśa* receives no benefit from the cooking of the animal, it must be cooked separately; that cooking must take place on the *gārhapatya* fire, for otherwise there would be a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in the ritual. Maṇḍana: "The cooking of the animal is not performed on the *śāmitra* fire. Śaṅkara: "The *śāmitra* fire is not used for the *puroḍāśa*. In the case of the *iṣṭikṛt* offering belonging to the *agnīṣomīya* animal *puroḍāśa*, there is no omission of the *sviṣṭakṛt* in the sacrificial formulas (*nigama*).
When there is an omission of a quality for that which possesses qualities, it should be as much as is stated in the Vedic injunctions.
The Commentary states: There is an animal sacrifice dedicated to Indra and Agni (Āgneya) in the Soma ritual.
Regarding this, it is heard in scripture: "At the performance of the animal sacrifice to Indra and Agni, one subsequently offers the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) dedicated to Indra and Agni."
In that context, a modification of the qualities of the Sviṣṭakṛt is heard in the injunction: "He sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the modification of the qualities of the Sviṣṭakṛt apply only to the sacrifice itself, while the original form remains in the remaining invocations (nigamas), or do the modifications apply everywhere? What is the prima facie view? When the modification of the qualities of Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is heard as being accompanied by those qualities [in the injunction], we reply as follows:
It is not said that there is an omission of a quality (guṇa) in that very [context]; rather, it would have to be so. And in the sacrifice, it is stated: "One should sacrifice to Agni.

If an omission of a quality were being asserted in the sacrifice, and if such an omission were determined to apply to all liturgical formulas (nigama), then something not heard in the scripture would have to be assumed.
And as great as the fault is in abandoning what has been heard, so great is it in the postulation of what has not been heard.
Therefore, the omission should occur only in the sacrifice, not in all the recitations (nigamas).
Or rather, [the rule applies] to everything, because of the unity of purpose.
The commentary states: Or rather, in every Vedic text, the word "Agni" in the term *sviṣṭakṛt* would lose its secondary meaning (*guṇa*). Why? Because of the unity of purpose (*aikakarmyāt*).
It is not only in the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering that the secondary meaning would be lost.
What then? It is in the performance of the sacrifice.
How so? The word "he sacrifices to Agni" is the injunction regarding the performance;
this is the statement.
It would be omitted in every application of the Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice;
for other Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifices are indeed contained within the Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice itself.
Therefore, there is omission everywhere.
In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa).
Regarding that, a loss of an accessory (guṇalopa) for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering—which is obtained through extension (codaka)—is heard in the text: "He sacrifices to Agni" (*agne yajati*).
Is this loss of the accessory restricted to the primary [offering] alone, or does it apply to all the ritual formulas (nigama)?

Since the word "yajati" (he sacrifices) is heard [in the text] with respect to the *pradhāna* alone, while in the remaining *nigamas* (concluding formulas) there is a designation associated with the quality of *sviṣṭakṛt* according to the archetype (*prakṛti-vat*), [this being the position reached, we reply: the injunction regarding the absence of qualities applies only to the performance; thus, there is an omission of the quality in all cases. Soma: [Objection: Even though the term *sviṣṭakṛt* was present in the preceding case, here it is stated that the designation in the *nigamas* lacks the word *sviṣṭakṛt*; how is this consistent?

Nor should it be argued: "Since, in the passage *'tathottarasyāṃ tatau'* (10.4.9.125), the word *ādi* (etcetera) is used as a means to express what must be stated in all *nigama* verses by way of a different application, and since here too the meaning of that [word] is established precisely through its application, how can there be a doubt based on its referring only to the primary [meaning]? For the difference in application arises from a slight difference in the *bhāvanā* (efficient force); and here, if there were a difference in *bhāvanā*, there would be a prescription for a distinct *bhāvanā*, which would result in the verbal root having an absolute lack of purport (*atyantatātparya*). Consequently, the suffixes [denoting the *bhāvanā*] would have no connection to the meaning of the verbal root. This is the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since there would be meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) if the word were merely connected with the form of the root-meaning, one must accept that even though it serves another purpose (*pārārthya*), it prescribes the performance of the *bhāvanā*.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: [The opponent argues] that in the archetype (*prakṛti*), when a quality is lost in the ectype (*vikṛti*), among the ritual formulas (*nigama*), the omission of the quality should occur only in those cases where it is explicitly stated and only in respect to that specific principal element (*pradhāna*) where the quality is lost, and not in all cases. This constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Vi— "The quality of *sviṣṭakṛt* is to be elided either in the sacrifice itself in all cases, or in the sacrifice according to the logic of the sacrifice, but not in the performance;
because the word *yajati* denotes the performance, it is to be elided in all applications (*nigama*) of the usage.
Because the word *yajati* expresses the performance (*prayoga*), it is to be elided in all applications (*nigama-prayoga*) of the usage.

Bhaṭṭa: In the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) belonging to the initiation rite (*daikṣa*), it is heard in scripture: "He sacrifices to Agni" (*agniṃ yajati*).

Since there is no evidence for a distinct ritual act (*bheda*), it is necessary that this be an injunction of the deity alone by way of reference to the sacrifice. It cannot, however, be an injunction intended merely to specify its subsidiary status within the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rite, because that [deity] is not already established in the *ājyabhāga* offering to Agni; and if it were enjoined in the offering to Soma (*saumya*), it would result in an unprecedented injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

Therefore, it is concluded with greater parsimony (*lāghava*) that this is indeed an injunction of a restrictive rule (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*) regarding the accessory alone, as in the case of the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice.

Furthermore, although that [deity] is produced from the substance only in the sacrifice—and not even in the *nigama* mantras, because in those [mantras] it would be subordinate as something to be consecrated, making its injunction impossible—nevertheless, since that deity enjoined in the sacrifice is established as performing the function of the archetype (*prakṛti*), it applies to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) as well; therefore, the name is applied to the deity alone, even when it is devoid of qualities.

Although in the archetype (*prakṛti*), in the invocations (*āvāhana*) and other formulas (*nigama*), there is indeed a mention of the deity as devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), nevertheless, in the *ādhvaryava* and *hautra* sections, the deity is mentioned as possessing qualities (*saguṇa*) in the first two *yājyā* verses; however, here even in those cases, the deity is mentioned as being devoid of qualities.
It should be understood that this point, though already established, has been stated for the benefit of the students.
*Nyāyabindu*: In the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*), the omission of the quality of the *sviṣṭakṛt* is heard [in the scripture]: "He sacrifices to Agni" (*agniṃ yajati*).

In that regard, the conclusion reached was that the omission of those [qualities] occurs only in the sacrifice itself, but not in the *nigama* (recited mantras); however, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the injunction regarding the absence of qualities applies only to the performance (*prayoga*), and thus there is an omission of qualities everywhere.
Maṇḍana: "In cases of the omission of qualities, it applies everywhere. Śaṅkara: "But that omission occurs in the performance."

The property of *upāṃśutva* (whispering/low voice) residing in those ritual acts occurring prior to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice is prompted by the intermediate *apūrva* (transcendental result) produced by those specific acts.
The *upāṃśutva* connected with the location [of the sacrifice] should belong to them because of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), and because that [property] exists there.

The *Bhāṣya* states: "In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is recited: 'This is indeed a secret (*tsarā*) part of the sacrifice; therefore, whatever is prior to the *agnīṣomīya* [sacrifice], they perform that in a whisper (*upāṃśu*). "

In this matter, the point at issue is as follows: Is this quality of being performed in a low voice (*upāṃśutva*) enjoined for those rites that occur prior to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, or is it enjoined by the *paramāpūrva* (the final transcendental result)? What is the prima facie view? This property is enjoined for those subsidiary *apūrvas* occurring prior to the *agnīṣomīya* which provide remote assistance (*ārādupakāraka*), as well as that which effects the purification of the primary substance; for this is connected with a specific place. Why is this so? Because of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Those things which are characterized by a specific region through conventional usage (*maryādā*) are connected to this ritual duty by direct statement (*śruti*):
"Whatever things are in this region, one performs them in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
[Objection: But surely the duty is enjoined by the syntactical connection (*vākya*) alone, not by direct statement.
We do not say that it is not by means of a sentence.

What then? It is by means of what is heard (*śruta*) that there is syntactic unity with a single [sentence], and not by means of that which is indicated (*lakṣita*), imagined (*kalpita*), or enjoined merely for the sake of being a subordinate part (*aṅgatā*) of that [context]; nor by means of that which is indicated or imagined in the context (*prakṛta*).
This is what is stated.

If it is argued that this property belongs only to those *apūrvas* (transcendental results) which are subordinate (*aṅga*), and not also to that *apūrva* which is the purificatory rite (*saṃskāraka*) for the substance of the primary (*pradhāna*) sacrifice—asking "Which one is that?"—the answer is: it is that which exists in the preceding stage and serves as a purificatory rite for the substance of the primary sacrifice.
It is said:
And because that exists there;
because such a thing as this exists in the preceding section.
For there is indeed a hymn named *Somapravahaṇīya* (beginning with "bhadraṃ naḥ," AitBr. 3.21–26).

Therefore, it will be a property of the location (*deśadharma*). Just as it is said, "One restrains speech when about to lead [the cows], and releases it together with the *haviṣkṛt* call," this duty pertains to those ritual items that exist in this particular location; it does not pertain to the primary apūrva.
In this same way, this [quality of] being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is also [to be considered].
In the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*), it was stated that the touching (*abhimarśana*) is prompted by the whole [sacrifice].

In connection with that discussion of the whole, there is another group which appears as if it were a whole—the group consisting of the repetitions of the cup-offerings (*graha-yajña*). Regarding that, it is now deliberated: is the quality of being whispered prompted by that [whole] (i.e., prompted by the *apūrva* of the Jyotiṣṭoma), or is it prompted by those constituent elements (i.e., prompted by the *apūrva* produced by the specific purpose of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice)?

Alternatively, the sublation of the *saṃskāra* is being considered for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*). (This is the connection.
By direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) applies to those ritual items that occur prior to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
[Objection: But surely this duty is already enjoined by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*) alone.
And yet, there is no third case-ending [expressing the agent]. It is replied:
True; however, the word "prāk" (before) must necessarily be rendered syntactically complete.
In that case, if a connection were made with the Soma sacrifice, the connection would be one inferred through the context (*prakaraṇa*).

If, however, it is connected with the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice], being connected with what is explicitly stated (*śruta*), it is connected with all those constituent elements (*padārtha*) that precede the Agniṣomīya, because they possess the quality of being grasped [by the injunction]. By the portion of the sūtra, "And because of its existence there," he states that these are the constituent elements which possess the *apūrva*.
Among those [rites], the rule that is prescribed is not purposeless;
just as it was stated [in the commentary on Sūtra 9.1.2, Varṇaka 2] regarding the restriction of speech at the Dīkṣaṇīyā [initiation] being a constituent element of the rite, so it is here as well.
"Because of the scriptural injunction" (*śrutinirdeśāt*). He uses the term "scripture" (*śruti*) with reference to the connection with the directly stated sentence (*śruta-vākya*).

Alternatively, it is connected by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with that which is preceded by the meaning of the words (*padārtha*), but it is connected by secondary indication of the secondary indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) with the supreme transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*).

First, the individual ritual acts (*padārtha*) are to be indicated by their respective *apūrvas*; by those [acts] thus indicated, the *apūrvas* [are indicated]; and by those, the supreme *apūrva* (*paramāpūrva*).

Thus, with reference to this "indication of what has been indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*), he cites the scriptural statement. Alternatively, the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, when uttered, brings to mind the ritual acts that precede it, but not the sacrificial portion (*yajñabhāga*).
Intending that, he cites the Śruti:
"Or [it belongs] to the sacrifice, because of its connection with it.
The Commentary states: By the word "or" (vā), the position is reversed.
This is not the case; it is not the property of those regions. Of what, then? It is the property of the supreme apūrva.
Why? Because of its connection with that.
There is a connection with that, namely a connection with the sacrifice, according to the text:
"That which is prior to the animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma is indeed a stealthy approach to the sacrifice."
Since there is no relationship of sublation between the two specific terms regarding that which is prior to the sacrifice,
it follows that there is an option (vikalpa) with respect to the primary rites such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā and others.
It is said: the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are the primary means for the production of phonemes;
however, in the word *yatkiñcit*, there is no production of any phoneme whatsoever.
And regarding speech (*vāc*): by means of what is expressed with praise (*varṇa*), that which is expressed without praise (*avarṇa*) is indicated.

Because of the use of the instrumental case in the expression "with the *pravarya* loudly" (*uccaiḥ pravaryeṇa*), there is consistency in both cases. The statement "in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) for the *prasava*" is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) based on propriety.

Regarding this purpose that has been described— that if this *upāṃśutva* (whispering) were applied by way of the location (*deśa*), it would result in its extension to the *māsāgnihotra* and other such rites—
it is replied: in those cases, another accent is obtained by virtue of their names, whereas *upāṃśutva* is obtained by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
The name is more powerful than the injunction;
therefore, another purpose has been stated for that which is not a name:
"Before the Upasads they proceed with the Saumya [offering], in the middle with the Tvaṣṭra, and after with the Vaiṣṇava."

Śabara: What is this "low-voicedness" (*upāṃśutva*)? Is it a property of the *prāgbhāga* (fore-part) of the Soma sacrifice, which, being a property of that [fore-part], is prompted by the remote *apūrva* (transcendental result), and therefore must be extended (*ūhya*) even to non-original (*aprākṛta*) items that initiate that [fore-part] in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*)? Or is it a property of those items preceding the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice—such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and so forth—which is prompted by their own intermediate *apūrva*, and therefore the property of being "not placed upon the fire" (*anadhihitatva*) should not be extended to non-original items such as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the calf (*vatsa*)? This is the doubt. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the low-voicedness belongs to the rites preceding the *agnīṣomīya*.

Since it has been established that those [rites] which bring about a direct contact (*saṃnipātin*) are prompted by the *apūrva*, there arises a logical connection (*saṃgati*) because of that context: it is established that for specific rites involving such contact, they are prompted by a specific *apūrva* characterized as an intermediate *apūrva*.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: "The state of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*), which is connected to the spatial direction of the eastern part, should be a property (*dharma*) of those ritual elements (*padārtha*) occurring therein, because of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
This is the sense: the word "eastern" (*prācīna*), being expectancy-laden (*sākāṅkṣa*), must have its expectancy satisfied by the meaning of its constituent parts.
In that case, the fulfillment of the expectancy [of the word "sacrifice"] by means of the word "yajña" is not possible, because of the proximity of the word "tsarā.
Therefore, another unmentioned word "yajña" would have to be supplied.
Consequently, the expectancy is satisfied by the mentioned word "agnīṣomīya."

And therefore, because the word *prācīna* (eastern) in the context of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice functions as a part-indicating term (*avayava-lakṣaṇa*) denoting a portion, it does not denote the ritual items (*padārtha*) residing in that portion; consequently, the property of *upāṃśutva* (whispering) belongs to that apūrva, since that apūrva exists in those ritual items which are proximate to the portion. Vi— "Is the *upāṃśutva* of the eastern part [connected] to the supreme apūrva or to the intermediate one? Since another [property], such as the place of the *yajñopagāna*, is heard as being spatially defined."

Bhaṭṭa: It is heard in scripture: "This [portion] is indeed the *tsarā* (the secret part) of the sacrifice; therefore, whatever is prior to the Agniṣomīya [offering], they perform that in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). In this regard, there arises a deliberation: is the quality of being performed in a low voice a property of the portion prior to the Agniṣomīya belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, and thus prompted by the *paramāpūrva* (ultimate transcendental result) of that [Jyotiṣṭoma]; or is it a property of those individual constituent acts (*padārtha*) situated in the portion prior to the Agniṣomīya, and thus prompted by the respective intermediate *apūrvas* produced by them? In this inquiry, it is undisputed that the words "that" (*tat*) and "this" (*tad*) do not serve as qualifiers for the object of reference (*uddeśya*), because the quality of being performed in a low voice is what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

And that [demonstrative pronoun] refers only to the eastern portion of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice previously introduced, and not to the individual ritual items (*padārtha*), because the word *prācīna*—according to the principle of the section on generic form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, 1.3.9)—denotes only the eastern portion; and since it is used in the singular number, the pronoun refers back specifically to that portion which was expressed by that [word].

For this very reason, since the object to be enjoined (*uddeśya*) is presented by that single pronoun alone, there is no "qualified location" (*viśiṣṭadeśa*), whether in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) or the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), even though the Agniṣomīya and other elements serve as qualifiers.

And in that context, the *agnīṣomīya* [animal] is a qualifier by way of being the object of the limit (*avadhi*) with respect to the portion (*bhāga*), and the sacrifice (*yajña*) is connected as the means through its performance (*prayoga*).

For this very reason, the word "sacrifice" is not a qualifier of the word "stealthily" (*tsarā*), because that would result in the qualification of something that is not even applicable (*aprasakti*).

Or, let it be that the word "sacrifice" is indeed a qualifier of the word "stealthily," by accepting the meaning that the sacrifice is concealed due to its separation from that [portion] by the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Nevertheless, because it is the subject under discussion, the "portion" (*bhāga*) is indeed that which is designated as the sacrifice (*yajña*).

This is also necessary even according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because in that view, the delimiting factor for the objective (*uddeśyatā'vacchedaka*) is precisely the ritual act (*padārtha*) occurring prior to the portion of the sacrifice subsequent to the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice].

And since there is no mention of individual ritual acts therein, and for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the delimiting factor for the objective is simply the portion of the sacrifice prior to the *agnīṣomīya*; the injunction of low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutva*) applies to that space delimited by it.

And since there is no direct connection with the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) in the [specific] portion, the mantras that constitute its constituent elements possess the status of being the means (*dvāratva*), by virtue of their inherent suitability.

Since the specific portion of the object intended (*uddeśya*) would result in being purposeless in its own form—because there is no evidence for the existence of a "prior transcendental result" (*pūrva*) produced by that portion, and because the restriction of subsidiaries such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* would otherwise be impossible (as discussed in the second interpretation of 1.1.2)—the very fact of being a means to the supreme *apūrva* produced by the connection with the portion is what is indicated by the mention of the portion. Thus, in cases such as the term *āgniṣomīya*, it is determined that the application [of the rule] is prompted by the *apūrva* of that portion, and not by the portion itself. In cases such as the term *āgniṣomīya*.

Since even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), novelty (*apūrvatva*)—defined as the absence of a prototype—is necessarily admitted through the postulation of extension (*atideśakalpanā*), this is not an illustration of the present topic (*prakṛtādhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, for the remaining [sacrifices] such as the *āgniṣomīya*, the ritual properties (*dharma*) are obtained through the archetypal injunction (*vidhyanta*) [as imagined to be the syntactic supplement].
How is this heard? It is said:
Whatever archetypal (prakṛta) constituent is heard mentioned in a modification (vikṛti), that very constituent the modification adopts, because it is thereby rendered free from expectancy.
For example, there is the hearing of the mention of the *ājyabhāga* offerings in the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice.
And here, too, an archetypal constituent is heard: "nine *prayāja*s."
Therefore, its requirement for completion is satisfied by that alone, as in the case of the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice.
The final position is that there is the origination of additional [elements]—as stated in the Sūtra—and the cessation of the archetypal ones;
thus, there is no contradiction with its being an archetype.

The Commentary states: "And in this way, there will be no conflict. What is the conflict? It is the assumption that [the rule] applies because of the nature of the archetype (*prakṛti*). That word of the injunction (*codaka*) does not refer to an archetype that is remote, separated by many sentences."

Regarding the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice (110): for those [offerings] that are modifications of the Agniṣomīya sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), the burden of a specific injunction (viśiṣṭavidhi) is logical;
moreover, the fault of enjoining the meaning of an entire sentence (vākyārthavidhi) is equal in both positions.
Regarding *Soma*: in the preceding two sections (*pādas*), sublation (*bādha*) was primarily established;

here, however, it is primarily established in relation to what is heard in a modified rite (*vikṛti*) because of its archetypal nature (*prākṛtatva*). Thus, they say there is a difference between the sections and an immediate succession.

That which is heard as an archetypal element endowed with non-archetypal qualities is the very example [of sublation], and not merely that which is modified (*vaikṛta*) according to the Prābhākara system, on account of its being directly taught (*aupadeśika*).

The meaning of the first *sūtra* is as follows: In a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because only the primary act (*pradhāna*) is explicitly mentioned by the word (*śabdavatvāt*), there is an "addition" (*adhikotpatti*) of the subsidiary elements (*guṇa*), such as the *prajāpati-vrata* and others, which arise as being qualified by other constituent parts (*saṃsthāntara*); it is not merely an injunction of the subsidiaries alone. Because of their proximity (*saṃnidhānāt*), the requirement of the modified sacrifice is satisfied by those very [subsidiaries] already present; therefore, there is no extension (*atideśa*). This is stated in the *Vṛtti*: "In cases such as the eleven *prayājas*, the injunction of the rule is set aside;
in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) and others, the injunction of the *sāmidhenī* verses and so forth does not apply."
This is not an injunction for special [details] and so forth, because they are obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).

Due to parsimony (*lāghava*), in the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma, [the details] are those of the *ātithyā* [offering]. In the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma, [there are] those pertaining to the *darśa*.

The Bhaṭṭa [view] is as follows: the same sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which was spread on the altar in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall for the sake of the *ātithya* and *upasad* rites by means of the mantra "O wool-soft one, do not harm me," is spread again to the west of the *uttaravedi* for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya* rite. This is because, due to the difference in location, the purification (*saṃskāra*) of that [grass] is not co-extensive there; thus, the repetition of the spreading—which effects the purification of the grass serving as the substrate—is necessary in accordance with the requirements of the purpose.

Therefore, since that act of spreading [the sacrificial grass] is repeated, the mantra belonging to it is also repeated; thus, there is no question of *prasaṅga* (extended application) or *tantra* (simultaneous performance) in this case, because the memory produced by the mantra recited at the time of the *ātithyā* sacrifice is not present at the time of the spreading for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.
This point is already established, but it has been stated here for the benefit of the student.

The *Nyāyabindu* states: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) which was spread in the *prāgvaṃśa* hall for the sake of the *ātithyā* is brought from there and spread again behind the *uttaravedi* for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya*."

In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the mantra for spreading, "I spread you, the woolly earth," applies only to what was previously performed, because it is common to the *barhis* grass. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since the act of spreading is expressed by the injunction "he spreads the altar with *barhis* grass," and since that [altar] is distinct [in each case], there must be a repetition of the mantra. Even though the *barhis* and the altar are the same, because the act of spreading is repeated, there is a repetition of the mantra associated with it; otherwise, it would result in the defect of being a mere subordinate quality (*tadguṇa*).
Maṇḍana says: "But they should recite the mantra again at the time of spreading."
Śaṅkara says: "The difference in the mind arises from the difference in place;
[this refers to] the mantra for the spreading of the mind. In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is the destruction of the Darśika [rite]."

"And because of the observation of indicative marks in the case of the animal sacrifice. Commentary: Regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is considered whether the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), or that of the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*). What is the prima facie view? It is exactly as in the previous case.
To this, the following reply is stated: "And in the animal sacrifice, because of the observation of indicative marks;
for in the animal sacrifice, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) is indeed that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

Why? Because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*): "He performs eleven *prayāja* offerings," and "eleven *anuyāja* offerings. Likewise: "Having poured the *āghāra* libation, he anoints the animal with the *juhū* ladle. But is this not merely an indicative mark? From what [source] is its application derived? From the commonality of the injunction (*codanā-sāmānyāt*).
What is the commonality? It is the nature of being a specific injunction (*vyaktoḍanātva*).
What is the particular instance (*vyakti*)? "The animal for Agni-Soma" is one;
"the milk for Indra" is another.

But Soma is [known] from another injunction. Regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni-Soma, the deity is established by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and the act of immolation (*ālambha*) is common to both the New and Full Moon sacrifices; thus, the immolation also occurs in the *iṣṭi*.

In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there exists a rule pertaining to the Darśa [sacrifice]: "One should seize the victim for Indra. Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing the visible subsidiary elements such as the seizing of the feet, there is a requirement for extension (atideśa).

Therefore, in that case, the *aiṣṭika* (sacrificial) procedure applies. Soma: But surely it is logical that the *darśapūrṇamāsa* [procedure] applies to the *iṣṭis* because of the presence of indicative marks (*liṅga*); however, in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), since there is no such indicative mark, the *aiṣṭika* procedure does not apply.

Nor is the introduction of the deity by means of a *taddhita* suffix an indicative mark of an *iṣṭi*, because that fact is not applicable as an indicative mark of an *iṣṭi* in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Nor is it taken as a subject [of injunction], because that is not observed in the context of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; thus, the connection [of this section] arises from the emergence of such a doubt. In this case, where this animal-person is in proximity to the purchase, the ritual duties are not prescribed there, but rather on the day of the Upavasatha.

Furthermore, when there is an expectancy regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for that [animal sacrifice], the application of the archetypal ritual details (*iṣṭikavidhyanta*) from another section—accompanied by supporting reasons—is unimpeded.

This is because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) found in the Sūtra, such as "He anoints the animal standing upon the grass," and because of the forceful injunctive mark (*codanāliṅga*). [Objection:
"In this case, the archetypal ritual details would not apply, due to the absence of the *kapāla* vessels and other such elements."
There may also be the status of having both a material (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*), because of the commonality with the *ājya* [libation].

"The animal for Agni-Soma" indicates the material and the deity; "He performs eleven *prayāja*s" indicates the possession of *prayāja*s; and "Having poured the *āghāra* oblation, he anoints the animal with the *juhū* ladle" indicates the *āghāra* and the touching (*ālambha*). Thus are the indicative marks (*liṅga*s). Bhāṭṭa: (From the eleventh to the nineteenth sūtra, the third section (*adhikaraṇa*) consists of nine sūtras here.)

In this context, however, the principle of *prakṛtārthādhikaraṇa* is understood by way of extension (*atideśa*). Similarly, in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) dedicated to Agni-Soma, its status as a modification (*vikāra*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) follows precisely from the fact that its deity is prescribed by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*).

Nor can it be argued that there is no such extension because the requirement for further rules is satisfied merely by the prescription of other specific duties, such as those concerning the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth;

for even so, the requirement remains because of the scriptural mention of other specific duties, such as the invocation (*āvāhana*), the placing of the offering (*āsādana*), and the water-pot (*kumbha*).
Furthermore, the *daikṣa* [initiatory rite], which is recited in proximity to the purchase (*kraya*) and is devoid of specific ritual details (*nirdharmaka*), first establishes this very requirement.

Consequently, once the performance on the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*) is understood through the statement "This [rite] is on the day of fasting," for that which has no further expectancy regarding archetypal details (*prākṛta-dharma*), there is no obstruction to the assumption of extended application (*atideśa-kalpanā*) even for the characteristics of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth—on the basis of the principle of the *upahoma* (5.2.9)—due to the necessity of performing the rite.

This same reasoning also applies to the indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "He performs eleven *prayāja* offerings" and "Having poured the *āghāra* libation into the *juhū* ladle, he anoints the animal."
Maṇḍana: "The sacrificial animal of the *iṣṭi* should be the *vihāra*.
Śaṅkara: "That [animal] should belong to the *agnīṣomīya* [sacrifice], not to the *iṣṭi*. That [position] is refuted.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, there is no portion for the Pratiprasthātṛ to consume.
And [the entitlement of] the Pratiprasthātṛ [arises] from the offering of the omentum (vapā).
Commentary: In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, a priest named the Pratiprasthātṛ is mentioned in the scriptures.
Regarding him, there is a doubt: should he have a share of the sacrificial remains (śeṣabhakṣa) or not?
What is established? That he should partake. Why? Because while cooking the omentum (vapā), the Adhvaryu performs his ritual duty, as it is said: "The Pratiprasthātṛ cooks the omentum.
Therefore, he should have a share of the consumption.
Or rather, it should be the *akṣa* (axle) because of the distinction in the ritual action, since that [offering] consists of the giving of everything.
Commentary: It should be the *akṣa*, namely the *pratiprasthātṛ*.
Why? Because in the sacrifice for which he has authority, there is no remnant of the substance belonging to the *adhvaryu*.
That person cooks the omentum, and its entirety is to be offered.
Since there is no remnant in that case, what would he eat? As for those parts where a remnant exists, such as the heart and so forth, the Adhvaryu has no authority over them.

In the case of the *vapā* (omentum) and other [offerings] that are *apūrva* (unprecedented), there is the attainment of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). And by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), the consumption (*bhakṣa*) belongs to the performer of that rite for which the remnant (*śeṣa*) is to be disposed of;
for in this way, it becomes a benefit to that [rite].

In the case of another ritual assistant (*anyakarmakara*) at the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, [the question arises regarding] the Pratiprasthātṛ. Regarding the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, does this Pratiprasthātṛ obtain a portion for consumption (*bhakṣa*) while making the portions (*avadāna*) from the heart and other organs? For there is the scriptural injunction: "Having placed [the vessel] to the south, the Pratiprasthātṛ makes the portions."
Regarding this doubt, the resolution is stated in the Bhāṣya.

In that regard, [the following is said]: "This section concerns that recensional branch (*śākhā*) in which the cutting out (*avadāna*) is performed by the Adhvaryu alone; this section concerns that recensional branch in which there is no statement regarding the cutting out of the heart and other organs being performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ. However, that [interpretation] is inconsistent with the literal text, because it contradicts the principle of the unity of all recensions (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*).

Consequently, the Bhāṣya intends to show that this is the governing topic (adhikaraṇa) for that branch of the ritual in which the Adhvaryu’s instruction regarding the cutting of portions (avadāna) is found;
and this alone is the appropriate resolution. However, in the case where the Pratiprasthātṛ performs the cutting of portions, he himself indeed has the right to consume [the remnant].

(The second resolution will be seen elsewhere—) As for the statement that this *avadāna* (cutting-off) is non-ordinary (*aprākṛta*), and that its non-ordinariness is due to its being the commencement of the offering (*pradāna*), as stated in the Bhāṣya—that is not correct. Even though this is not the commencement of the offering because another ritual act is enjoined in the middle—namely, "Having cut off portions for the deities, one should not yet offer them; one cuts off the portions for Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt"—nevertheless, this *avadāna* is solely for the purpose of the offering, not for the sake of some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

(Granted that the Pratiprasthātṛ may be the one who performs the cutting [avadāna], nevertheless, the original [prākṛta] act is not performed by the Adhvaryu. This is because the cutting performed in the middle—intervening between the offering to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt and the final portion—is not the commencement of the offering; since the commencement of the offering belongs to the original rite, there is otherwise a contradiction. Consequently, the cutting which is the original function for the consecration of the oblation must be performed by the Adhvaryu alone, and not by the Pratiprasthātṛ; thus, the meaning is that there is no possibility of his consuming [the remnant].)

The third rebuttal, however, has been refuted in the *Tantraratna* itself by providing a scriptural justification for that [position] through arguments such as those concerning meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The *Tantraratna* states as follows: "Indeed, it is not merely an implied matter that the act of taking the portion belongs to the Adhvaryu alone in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Since the act of taking the portion—which is established by implication through the injunction for the offering of what has already been taken—is performed by a single agent at the time of the actual offering, and because of the principle of uniformity (*sāmānyāt*), its performance by the Adhvaryu is indeed scripturally mandated. And while performing that [act], the Pratiprasthātṛ would certainly be entitled to the consumption [of the remnant]."
Therefore, it is truly the case that this is merely a *kṛtvācintā* (a hypothetical discussion for the sake of argument), or else [it refers to] "another portion.

However, in the view that the Adhvaryu takes the portion, there is no consumption (*bhakṣa*) by this [Pratiprasthātṛ], because the omentum (*vapā*) has been entirely exhausted; such is the meaning of the section.
Soma: There is a connection [of this topic] because it was stated that the consumption [of Soma] is performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ, who is engaged in the duties of the Maitrāvaruṇa.
Viśeṣa: Is there a consumption for the Pratiprasthātṛ or not? He [the opponent] says:
"There is, because he cooks the omentum (vapā); since the entire omentum is offered once it has been cooked."

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding that very case (the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice), there arises a doubt as to whether or not there is a consumption (*bhakṣa*) for the Pratiprasthātṛ as well. Since he too is an agent (*kartṛ*), the consumption should serve as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the agent.

For there is no evidence to suggest that a consumption which refines the sacrificial offering (*havir*) must necessarily refine the agent who performs the subsidiary act connected to that specific sacrifice; rather, following the logic of the "sprinkling of Prajāpati" (4.1.14), one merely postulates that what refines the offering also serves to refine the agent.

Therefore, since there is no obstacle to the Pratiprasthātṛ—who is the performer of the cooking of the omentum (*vapā*)—partaking in the remnants of the sacrificial offerings such as the heart and so forth, this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). However, since it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if the act were merely a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for any performer whatsoever, a necessary qualification must be applied. Since that qualification is present within its own sentence, we must conclude that the "eating" which serves as a purificatory rite for the sacrificial offering produces either a purificatory effect for the performer of the subsequent ritual acts connected to that specific sacrifice, or it generates a purificatory effect in the form of providing strength regarding those subsequent acts to be performed in connection with that sacrifice. In the case of the Pratiprasthātṛ, who is the performer of the cooking of the omentum, there is no possibility of eating remnants because the entire omentum is offered in the fire. Furthermore, since he is not the performer of the original (*prākṛta*) ritual acts connected to the heart and other organs, there is no possibility of him eating the remnants of those offerings. Thus, he does not partake in the eating.
For this very reason, even though the heart and other organs are prepared by him, because they lack the quality of being "ordinary" (*prākṛta*), he does not consume them.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the scriptural injunction states, "The Pratiprasthātṛ, having placed [the organs] to the south, cuts off the portions," it is understood that the cutting of the portions from the heart and other organs is performed by the Pratiprasthātṛ; therefore, there arises the contingency of his consuming the remnants thereof.

For this is not an extraordinary *avadāna* (portioning) distinct from the others; rather, it is an injunction for the *Pratiprasthātṛ* alone to perform the ordinary offering (*prākṛtahavirvyāghra*) by way of restating the ordinary *avadānas* or the *avadānas* intended for the ordinary purpose, because the placement to the south is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the fact that the southern buttock (*dakṣiṇaśroṇi*) is already established by the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Although, according to the writing of Pārthasārathi, there might be an option in other treatises for the cutting out of the heart and other organs to be performed by the Adhvaryu priest, nevertheless, even in the case where the Adhvaryu performs it, the consumption of the *lepa* (residue) and so forth by the Pratiprasthātṛ—who is the performer of the mere roasting of the omentum (*vapā*)—is not contradicted. This is because his role as the one who wipes away the scattered residue (*ākīrṇakara*) from the heart and other organs is not in conflict [with his eating], just like the blood and other such remnants.

If it is argued that, therefore, even though the cutting out (*avadāna*) of the heart and other portions is performed by both [the *adhvaryu* and the *pratiprasthātṛ*], the eating (*bhakṣaṇa*) by the *pratiprasthātṛ* is logically established—this is true; nevertheless, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the refinement of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*) does not consist in hiring (*ānati*). This is because such a refinement is already accomplished through the rule regarding sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Rather, it consists in providing strength for the performance of the archetypal acts yet to be done. And this [strength] does not exist for the *pratiprasthātṛ* at all after the eating, even though the cutting out of the heart and other portions was performed by him.

Therefore, there is no eating of that [heart, etc.]. Pārthasārathi, however, [holds that] regarding the portions of the heart and other organs offered by the Pratiprasthātṛ in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, for each individual victim in the Agniṣomīya sacrifice...
On the other hand, the designation of that [cup] as being for consumption is entirely baseless.
If, however, such is the practice of the ritualists (*yājñika*), then some archetypal (*prākṛta*) element occurring subsequent to the consumption must be followed.
And the utility of this section lies in its sublation of the [notion of] the sacrificer being the fifth [member of the group].

*Nyāyabindu*: Since the Pratiprasthātṛ performs the work of the Adhvaryu in the cooking of the omentum (*vapā*), it might be argued that he should partake of the *iḍā* portion. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: one should consume the remnants of that for which one is the primary agent. In this case, because the omentum has been consumed entirely by the Pratiprasthātṛ, there is no possibility of his consuming a remnant. Nor should it be argued that he must consume it because of the injunction, "Having placed [the meat] to the south, the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts [the portions]," since this refers to his role as the performer of the cutting of the heart and other organs.
This is accepted.
However, it should be understood that this section concerns the case where, in a particular recensional school (śākhā), the cutting of the portions (avadāna) belongs to the Adhvaryu alone.
Therefore, according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), when the Adhvaryu alone is the performer of the cutting, there is no consumption of the Ādābhya cup by the Pratiprasthātṛ.
Maṇḍana: "They do not prescribe the consumption [of the portions] by the Prasthātṛ in the animal sacrifice. Śaṅkara: "There is no consumption by the Pratiprasthātṛ [in the animal sacrifice].
In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is a distinct offering for each respective part.
1017. The animal sacrifice is performed with all [its parts], because it is enjoined as a whole.
The Commentary states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the Agnīṣomīya animal, as it is said, "When one who is initiated sacrifices the Agnīṣomīya animal.

Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the entire animal a single oblation (*havis*), or is there a distinct oblation for each limb? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That the entire animal is a single oblation.
Why? Because the whole is enjoined.
For the entire animal is enjoined with respect to Agni and Soma; the status of belonging to Agni and Soma does not apply to individual parts.
Therefore, having cut off the heart and other parts from the animal form, they are to be offered to Agni and Soma.
In the case of the animal-offering (*paśu-haviṣya*), there would have to be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the word "animal.

Therefore, the entire animal constitutes a single oblation. This is shown by the texts: "Now, indeed, the Kāpeyas say that one should take [the portion] from the front of the right foot; thus it becomes a portion taken from the whole animal," and "Now, indeed, the Āṭyaṇas say that one should take [the portion] from the front of the right foot; thus it becomes a portion taken from the whole animal. These passages demonstrate the taking of portions from the entire animal.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the entire animal constitutes a single oblation.
[Dvādaśalakṣaṇī, Adhyāya 2, Pāda 1, Sūtra 6–17] It has been established that such passages as "He cuts off from the heart and so forth" do not enjoin a sacrifice;
rather, this injunction of the sacrifice is "The Agnīṣomīya animal."
Are the heart and other organs the sacrificial offerings (*havis*), or is the individual animal, by virtue of its form as a "beast" (*paśu*), the offering?

Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: the connection with Agni and Soma is heard in the scripture in relation to the animal (*paśu*), not in relation to the heart and other organs.
If those [organs] were connected with Agni and Soma, there would be an indirect indication (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*).
From that *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice, because it is known [to be prescribed],

when the portions from the middle and the front part would otherwise be obtained, the specific locations such as the heart and so forth are enjoined; and there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding them.
Or rather, it is because each individual [cognition] is conceived separately, like the planets.
The Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that the entire animal constitutes a single oblation;
rather, there is a distinction of oblations for each limb.

Why? Because they are prescribed separately. For those who possess separate cognitions, it is prescribed: "He cuts a portion from the front of the heart; then he cuts a portion from the tongue; then he cuts a portion from the chest; he cuts a portion from the two forelegs; he cuts a portion from the two sides; he cuts a portion from the rectum.
Thus, the cutting of portions is heard in the scripture as being performed from the heart and the other specified parts.
This is not possible when the animal has already been dissected;
therefore, the animal must be dissected by means of the heart and other organs.
And while it is being dissected, the form of the animal no longer remains.
Thus, this follows:
the after-shape (paścākṛti) would assist the sacrifice being performed;
and by interposing that after-shape, it is not possible to directly delimit the substance of the sacrifice.

Therefore, since that form is great as the agent through the indirect sequence, the substance possessing that form is enjoined as the constituent element for each limb in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice— such as "He cuts from the tongue" and so forth— and in that case, the word *aya* would be a restatement (*anuvāda*).

How so? This word *ayam* (the term *ānantarya*) occurs in the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*). When the preceding and succeeding objects are both understood, then there is immediate succession. But when those two do not exist, of what could one speak as being "in between"?
If it is understood [from context], then the sequence is already understood from the recitation itself; in that case, the word *atha* would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, you do not accept the injunction of the constituent parts (*padārtha*), whereby both the words *atha* and *agra* would be restatements.
Therefore, the application (*avacāti*) is enjoined with respect to specific items such as the heart and so forth.
The same applies to the tongue and the other [senses].

And thus, that substance from which [the offering] is derived is the *havis*. Just as in the sentences "He takes the *āgrayaṇa* for Indra" and so forth, the substance is conceived separately, and that alone is the primary *havis*, so it is here as well.
Nor are these eleven immovable things unpleasing;
for [the opponent holds that] sacrifice consists merely in the giving of substances from the animal itself.
In this view, the very fact that it serves no purpose is the defect.
In these sacrificial verses, nothing unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*) is involved.
Even the injunction regarding the animal (*paśu*), by means of indication (*lakṣita-lakṣaṇā*), indicates the heart and other organs, which are then connected with Agni and Soma.
Thus, only those parts whose extraction is explicitly heard in the scripture are the means of accomplishing the sacrifice, not other parts.

Why? This word "animal" (paśu) was conceived as a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) after observing the sentences concerning the heart and so forth; it indicates only those things which were observed when it was first conceived. What occasion is there for other items not being heard in the text, such that it would indicate them as being the sacrificial oblation (havis)?
The deity is indeed the animal itself when no secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is present, because there is no other injunction;
it is the offering of the entire animal, just as in the case of the milk for Indra.

The status of being an oblation (*haviṣṭva*)—characterized by that which is renounced with reference to a deity—is properly predicated only of that which has a connection with a deity, because the rule "this is its deity" (*sā'sya devatā*) prescribes such a deity specifically for a *sūkta* and an oblation.

For this very reason, although the creeper is mentioned in the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*) "one should sacrifice with soma," it does not possess the status of an oblation; rather, as in the sentences "he takes the āgrayaṇa cup for Indra-Agni" and so forth, because the word *soma* is heard there in connection with a deity, it is that [extracted juice] alone which possesses the status of an oblation.
Thus, due to the connection with a deity, the renunciation of the animal itself is performed with reference to the deity.

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: "Just as in the case of the injunction, 'The milk for Indra [is offered] on the new moon day,' because of the connection with the deity, there is the relinquishment of the entire milk and not merely of the portion cut out (*avadāna*); so it is here.
This being the position, we reply:
"For the cutting (*yaṇḍana*) is seen in the case of the heart and other parts for the sake of the original purpose."
Therefore, the animal is connected to the deity by virtue of being its material cause.

Since the terms "heart" (*hṛdaya*) and so forth denote specific types of meat, it is not appropriate that they be taken as indicators for parts of the animal; for it is only the heart and other such organs that can logically constitute the *avadāna* (cutting-off). Furthermore, in the archetype sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the *avadāna* is for the purpose of preparing the oblation (*havis*); thus, here too, it is logical that the *avadāna* belongs to the oblation itself. And since this [act of cutting] is observed in relation to the heart and other organs, it is determined that the heart and the rest alone possess the status of the oblation. Nor is there a conflict between the statement of origin (*utpattivākya*) and the supplementary statement (*śeṣavākya*) regarding the animal being the oblation; for since the animal is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the heart and other organs, its connection with the deity is established even through its role as the means of accomplishing the sacrifice.
(Soma: And thus it is stated in the grammatical tradition [Vyākaraṇasmṛti], "In the case of a hymn and an oblation...").
For if there were a means of proof for an indirect method, then the animal itself would be offered directly.
However, there is indeed a means of proof in the form of the injunctions regarding the cutting out [avadāna] and the dismemberment [viśāsana] of the heart and other parts.

Therefore, the heart and other organs are the sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) to be offered to the deity, and from them alone the portion for the offering (havirdāna) is taken; that [animal] is the archetype (prakṛti) of the animal sacrifice.

Regarding Soma—after the discussion concerning the production of the Soma sacrifice, the discussion now concerns the animals and other components which are its subsidiaries, specifically the portions such as the middle and fore-quarters; thus they say there is both a change of subject (pādāntaratva) and immediate sequence (ānantarya).
Because the animal itself is not the sacrificial oblation, the ritualists' method of modification (ūha) is based on the formula: "I make the animal my own."

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that because the entire animal is enjoined as being connected to the deity, that whole animal alone constitutes a single oblation (havis).

[The refutation: "Is the entire animal the oblation, or is there a different oblation for each limb? It is the former, due to the injunction; it is not so, because of the distinctness of the portions cut off (avadāna)."
Therefore, there is a distinct sacrificial offering for each limb.

According to the Bhaṭṭa school: although in the originative injunction "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," the animal itself is understood to be the sacrificial offering (havis) in its connection with the deity—just as the cake (puroḍāśa) is—[it is nevertheless the limbs that constitute the offerings].

Therefore, although it appears that this [status of being a means] is established by that very [text] through the predominance of the deity, nevertheless—by considering the ritual injunctions such as "he dissects the animal," "he discards the blood," "he sprinkles the marrow," "he extracts the omentum," "he cooks the entrails in a pot," and "he cooks the heart with the heart-spit"—it is determined that, like Soma, its status as a means is mediated by the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
And it is logical that wood and other materials serve as means through the medium of flame, provided there is a succession of authoritative means for grasping the intended meaning.
Because there is no establishment of another [agent] through a dual operation.
Indeed, the animal is not perceived in acts such as slaughter, whereby its existence might lead one to postulate that it alone is the instrument (*sādhana*).
Even in the perception of the act of abandonment (*tyāga*) and so forth, there is merely an inference of a connection with the animal.
Otherwise, in the case of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, there would be no possibility of understanding the statement "the animal has perished" for the Maitrāvaruṇa priest.

Therefore, here, in accordance with the statements regarding slaughter (*viśasana*) and so forth, the animal itself is merely the material source (*prakṛti*) for what is to be offered, and not something to be offered directly; rather, it is its own constituent parts that are the offerers. Thus, those [parts] alone are the subordinates of the milk (*payas*). It is precisely in them that the properties of the milk apply.

*Nyāyabindu*: In the case of "the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," since the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) indicates that the animal itself is connected to the deity, there is a renunciation (*tyāga*) of the entire animal, just as in the case of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "He cuts first from the heart," there are eleven places of cutting, namely the middle, the front, and the lower parts.

Consequently, it might be argued that the animal itself is the sacrificial offering (*havis*). However, since it is the heart and other organs that are being cut, they alone possess the status of the *havis*. For cutting (*avadāna*) is indeed a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*) applied specifically to the *havis*.
The animal, however, is connected to the deity by virtue of being the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the heart and other parts.

Therefore, it is the heart and other such parts alone that should be offered to the deity; from those very parts the portion for the oblation (*havirdāna*) is taken and offered, since the animal is their material cause.
Maṇḍana [says]: "In the case of the animal sacrifice, the oblation should consist of the individual limbs."
Śaṅkara [states]: "The heart and other organs constitute the sacrificial offering (havis) in the animal sacrifice.
In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the injunction regarding the fruit [of the rite] finds its application."

In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) increases; he cuts the grass for the animal as it is. This *barhis* belongs to the *praśrān* (the preliminary offerings).

When the Savanīya animal sacrifice is present, [the *barhis*] applies to the Savanīya animal because of the qualification of the subsequent term (*uttarapada-viśeṣaṇa*), since the Savanīya animal is brought to mind. This is because the statement, "That which is the *barhis* of the Āditya [offering], that is for the Agniṣomīya," is weaker than the intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*).

Since, in the *Jāmadagnya* performance where there is a cutting of five portions (*pañcāvatta*), we observe the displacement (*utkṛṣṭa*) of the four-fold portion (*caturavatta*)—even though it belongs to the context—because its inclusion would otherwise be impossible; this being the position reached: [we reply that] because the word "uttara" (the latter) would entail a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) if it were a subsequent member of a compound, and because its application as the substratum for the cutting is prescribed specifically in the subsequent sentence, there is no displacement. This is because there is no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhaka*) between two things that have distinct functions. [End of section on] Resolution (*saṃkalpa*). 1.3.4.
In the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-paśu*), there is a consumption (*bhakṣa*) by the Maitrāvaruṇa priest.
Because of his non-ordinary status (*aprākṛtatva*), the Maitrāvaruṇa is not entitled to consume [the sacrificial portion].
Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the Agnīṣomīya animal sacrifice, according to the text: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the Agnīṣomīya animal."
In that case, there is the Maitrāvaruṇa priest as an officiant.

Regarding him, there is a doubt: does he have the consumption of the remnant obtained through the rule of extension (codaka), or not? What is the prima facie view? He is non-archetypal (aprākṛta); when the consumption is performed for him, the archetypal nature is not thereby established.
Therefore, because he is not a *prākṛta* (archetypal) priest, the Maitrāvaruṇa would have no right to consume [the soma].

Or rather, there may be consumption by the Maitrāvaruṇa, because he is a modification (*vikāra*) of both the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu, and because his duties are connected with those of both. This is the view of the Bhāṣya.

For he is indeed a modification of the Adhvaryu in the *praipas*, and a modification of the Hotṛ in the recitations (*anuvacanāni*); thus it is said: "Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the directions (*praṣyati*) and also recites (*anu āha*).

Consequently, because of his connection with those two functions, he obtains the portion [of the Soma] by implication (*arthāpatti*). Therefore, he should be one who partakes of the drink (*sabhakṣaḥ*).

Furthermore, because the Maitrāvaruṇa performs the duties of the Adhvaryu—since he issues the *praiṣas* (directions) for the sake of the consecration of the Adhvaryu and Hotṛ—and because he performs the duties of the Hotṛ—since he performs the recitations (*anuvacana*)—there is an entitlement to the *bhakṣa* (consumption).

As for Soma: just as the *vaniṣṭhu* (rectum) serves to set aside the *iḍā-bhakṣa* of the Āgnīdhra, so too it is said that the *vaniṣṭhu* sets aside the *iḍā-bhakṣa* of the Maitrāvaruṇa; this is the connection (*saṃgati*).

Although, because of the connection with the accusative case in the injunction "With the *vaniṣṭhu* [omentum] at the *āgnīdhra* [altar]," the consumption is for the purpose of the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the sacrificial offering (*havis*), nevertheless, since there is no restriction regarding the officiants such as the *adhvaryu* in that context, it does not serve even as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the offering in its aspect of being a restrictive rule. This is unlike the case of the injunction "He sprinkles the oblation with the remnant of the *prayāja*," where the sprinkling—which is for the purpose of the disposal of the *prayāja* remnant—also serves the purpose of consecrating the oblation, due to the restrictive rule that the oblation must have that remnant as its substratum.

And just as, so that the consecration of the oblation (*havis*) may not be lost, there is a sprinkling over all the oblations present and not just one, so too here, so that the consecration of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*) may not be lost, there is the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) by the Maitrāvaruṇa as well.
[Objection: "Is there no consumption for the Maitrāvaruṇa here, or is there? No; because it is not archetypal (*aprākṛta*). [Response: It exists, because it is included within the *dvayṛc-homa*."
That is the *bhakṣa* (consumption).
In the *Bhāṭṭa* school, the consumption of the *iḍā* portion taken from the archetype (*prakṛti*) is the consumption of the remnant (*śeṣabhakṣa*).

It has been stated in the sixth book (6.4.13) that, according to the principle of the sprinkling of the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings (4.1.14.33–39), the second [consumption] serves both for the disposal of the remnant (*pratipatti*) and for the purification of the agent (*kartṛsaṃskāra*).
Furthermore, the agent is intended as such by virtue of being the means for accomplishing that specific task, and not by way of his own individual identity as the *adhvaryu* and so forth.
Consequently, even the *maitrāvaruṇa* priest should consume [the remnant] in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), because he serves the purpose of the original (archetypal) functions.

For he has assumed the duties of the *adhvaryu*, since the original calls for commands (*praipa*) issued by the *adhvaryu*—such as "Let the Hotṛ sacrifice" (*hotā yakṣat*) and so on—are intended for the same purpose as the archetypal calls for commands issued by the *adhvaryu*, such as "Sacrifice" (*yajeti*).
Furthermore, since the *anuvākyās* for the *ājyabhāga* offerings and others—which are normally recited by the Hotṛ—are recited by the Maitrāvaruṇa, he performs the duties of the Hotṛ.
Therefore, because he has taken over that function (*kāryāpanna*), he too should consume the portion.

*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it was argued that the Maitrāvaruṇa does not consume the *iḍā* portion because his role is unprecedented (*apūrva*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since he performs the duties of both the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ through his commands (*praipa*) and recitations (*anuvacana*), his consumption serves as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the performer of the action. Thus, he must consume it.
In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is one portion for the Maitrāvaruṇa.
Following the completion of the sacrifice in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, Maṇḍana states: "The consumption of this very [portion] belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa."

Śaṅkara says: "The consumption by the *iḍā* [portion] would be commendable; however, for the Maitrāvaruṇa, it is prescribed otherwise. In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni-Soma, there is only one portion for the Maitrāvaruṇa."
He should have two shares because he has two functions.
Bhāṣya: Now, a doubt arises concerning the Maitrāvaruṇa priest himself: does the Maitrāvaruṇa receive two shares, or one share? What is the prima facie view? He should have two shares.
Because it is a modification of the Adhvaryu, it obtains the share of the Adhvaryu; because it is a modification of the Hotṛ, it obtains the share of the Hotṛ.
Therefore, it should have two shares.
However, because of its oneness, it should have only one share, since the division into shares is not explicitly stated in the scripture.
Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
[The cake] should not be divided into two parts; rather, it should consist of a single part. Why? Because a division is not mentioned in the scriptural text (aśrutibhūtatvāt).
In this context, neither a portion for the Maitrāvaruṇa nor a portion for the Hotṛ is heard [in the scripture].

For if both were indeed heard, then once one portion had been performed, following the completion of the sacrifice of the Agniṣomīya animal— at the point of the omentum (vapā) of the Agniṣomīya animal— [the procedure would follow].

One should not fear this, because even the prohibition [of touching] would have as its object the touching of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) occasioned by going seven times during the middle of the ritual season, and so forth—just like [the prohibitions] "one should not utter the end" or "one should not approach a woman. Since such touching would result in a deficiency of the ritual (*kratuviguṇya*), this injunction of the mantra is indeed for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) as a means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for that [deficiency].

And thus, since there is only one sacrificial post, the formula "these two are yours" (*etau te*) and so forth—which is recited again for the purpose of establishing the modification (*ūha*) of the mantra—is stated solely on the basis of logical necessity (*nyāya*).

Even though no purpose is obtained for the mere recitation of the inferred mantra in this way, there is no lack of a purpose for the application [of the mantra] in the passage beginning with "if two," because these three mantras, which are recited in proximity to the *daikṣa* [sacrifice], serve the purpose of establishing their displacement (*utkarṣa*) when an option (*vikalpa*) would otherwise arise according to the principle of the section on recitation (*pāṭhādhikaraṇanyāya*) at 9.3.5.15–20.

This being the prima facie view, [the following is established]: although, in reality, the sacrifice (*yajña*) does produce *duriṣṭa*—which is synonymous with sin—the deprecatory explanatory passage (*nindārthavāda*) proclaims the transfer of the *duriṣṭa* residing in the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), produced by the performance of the sacrifice, onto the one who touches the post. From this scriptural statement (*āgama*), it follows that this prohibition pertains to the period subsequent to the completion of the sacrificial performance. Furthermore, because this expiation (*prāyaścitta*), which serves to remove that defect, is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), its status as a human objective prevails, overriding the context (*prakaraṇa*) by means of its indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Therefore, based on the natural interpretation (*svārasya*) of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya, it should be understood that this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies only after the completion of the sacrificial post’s function (*yūpakāryāpavarga*), and not—even according to the natural interpretation of the Vārtika and other texts—upon a mundane touch occurring even in the midst of the sacrifice.

For this very reason, since the sacrifice is the cause of the sacrificial post's production, there is no fault even when a mundane touch occurs during the course of the sacrifice; for prior to the sacrifice, the cause [of the post] is absent, and thus there is no talk of an immediate or mediated sequence [of causality].

For this very reason, even the Smṛti-based expiation prescribed for touching [the sacrificial post] and so forth—namely, "it would be a sin" (*syāt*)—applies only to cases outside the ritual context, since no other basis (root text) for that prohibition need be postulated.

Alternatively, since that [Smṛti rule] has a general scope, it may apply even to worldly acts occurring within the ritual. In that case, however, it is logical to enjoin the *ālambhana* (touching) upon one who has proceeded by transgressing that [prohibition], with the priests as the agents.
In every respect, the recitation of the mantra has its purpose fulfilled only upon the completion of the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

For this very reason, it is established that these three mantras—which would otherwise be applied by virtue of a prohibitory statement—are prescribed as entirely independent in reality for the purpose of determining the defects arising therefrom; it is not the case that one [mantra] is a modification (*ūha*) of another.

*Nyāyabindu*: "If one should touch a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), one should say, 'This is for thee, O Vāyu'.
