Since this scriptural injunction regarding the touching of the post applies without distinction to both worldly and Vedic contexts, and because it is simpler to assume a result [of the rite] only in the Vedic context by means of the *prakaraṇa* (context), such is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since the prohibition of touching pertains to the worldly context, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) intended to remove that defect must also apply specifically there.
*Māṇḍana*: "The mantras would apply only to the touching in the worldly context. *Śaṅkara*: "In the world, there is a fault in touching the sacrificial post."
Oṃ: In the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, there is the fivefold cutting for the omentum and for all the limbs.
If it is according to what is heard [in the scripture]:
the Commentary states—In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, as it is said: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
Regarding that, this is enjoined: "Even if the sacrificer is one for whom four portions are prescribed, the omentum (vapā) must be prepared as five portions."

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: there is a doubt as to whether the *pañcāvatta* (five-fold portioning) prescribed for the omentum (*vapā*) sets aside the *caturavatta* (four-fold portioning) prescribed for the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), or not. What is the prima facie view? If you ask what the doubt is, it is: "No. Why? Because the *pañcāvatta* is set aside from the *caturavatta* only where it is itself prescribed, and not elsewhere.

Just as one does not set aside [the rule] during another season, so too the scriptural injunction regarding the fivefold cutting (*pañcāvatta*) ought not to be set aside even when it has not yet been reached.
[Duh]: "The omentum (*vapā*) must be made fivefold.

What is being enjoined here in your view, such that you think it applies even to the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*)? For in this case, the number is not enjoined by means of the location of the cutting; rather, it is the fivefold cutting itself that is enjoined by way of its designation.
And it has been stated that there is no intention to express a qualification of the subject (*uddeśya*), nor even of the subject itself.
Otherwise, since the cup (*graha*) would also not be intended [as the subject], the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) would apply to the *camasa* vessels as well.
Therefore, this is clearly distinguished by the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) and the cake (*puroḍāśa*).
"Not so, because of the unity of the injunction.
The Bhāṣya says: "This is not so; for this is a single injunction: 'When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.'"
In that context, it is heard [in scripture].
Therefore, by virtue of the context, it will apply to the apūrva (unseen potency) of the subsidiary parts.
He says: "But surely, by virtue of the syntactical connection (vākya), it ought to apply to the omentum (vapā)."
It is said: "No," for the omentum is the substance;
there is no purpose in its connection [with the mantra].
It is said:
the injunction regarding the performance of the omentum-offering (*vapā-prayoga*) will incorporate the fivefold cutting;
thus, there will be no fault.
Therefore, it is stated otherwise:
even this being so, the fivefold cutting (pañcāvatta) would be established in the subsidiary apūrva.
How? Because that injunction is indeed one.
The offering of the limbs (*aṅga-yāga*) is the offering of the omentum (*vapā-yāga*).
If the fivefold cutting (*pañcāvatta*) is connected with that [offering], then it ought to apply to the limbs as well.
But is it not the case that the fivefold cutting applies only to the omentum and not to the limbs?
It is said: this statement is not so; the word itself [indicates] fivefold cutting.
How then? "He cuts fivefold."
Since making it one-fold implies the exclusion of its being otherwise,
that state of being five-fold portions which exists without distinction cannot be set aside by a connection with the omentum (vapā).
Because there is no word that would set aside [the fourfold cutting], therefore the fourfold cutting does not apply to the subsidiary offerings.
Moreover, when it is known that such subsidiary offerings consist of five cuttings, there follows another injunction: "He shall cut those twice for the sacrificial oblation."
In that context, the mention of the "taking of the omentum" (*vapāgrahaṇa*) is heard as being established by its primacy for the purpose of characterizing the sacrificial offering (*havis*).
For if that were already established by an injunction, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, even in the case of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), there must be exactly five cuttings (*pañcāvatta*).
It is said: by this word *avatta*, a substance connected with the act of cutting (*avadāna*), expressed in the neuter gender and associated with the number one, is denoted;
and furthermore, the number five is prescribed for that [substance].

And if, while this [portion] is being restated, its gender and number were intended to be significant, and it were further qualified by the omentum (*vapā*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) according to the principle of the injunction regarding the cups (*graha-vidhi-karaṇa-nyāya*, 2.1.3).
Therefore, the number five is enjoined for that which effects the offering (*avadāna*). And that number, being enjoined, is connected with the sacrifice through the context (*prakaraṇa*).
And because there is no distinction in the context, that [rule] applies to all offerings.
Now, it may be argued that since the word "only" (*eva*) is heard, the exclusion of other numbers is understood, not the injunction of the number five.

Just as in the case of the statement, "One should recite twenty-five only," which is for the purpose of excluding twenty-four or two, and not for the purpose of enjoining twenty-five, so too here this [statement] serves to exclude the four-fold cutting, rather than being an injunction of the five-fold cutting.

Therefore, even the "five-fold cutting" (*pañcāvadāna*) is not obtained, because the sentence is intended for another purpose. It is said in reply: the five-fold cutting itself is what is enjoined (for, since there is no prior attainment of the five-fold cutting, a mere restatement [*anuvāda*] would be impossible; thus, its mention [in the text] must have fallen out by error, otherwise). And when that [five-fold cutting] is being enjoined, that which was previously obtained through the general rule (*codaka*) ceases to exist; thus, the primary and subsequent rites are secured, and that [mention of the five-fold cutting] is a restatement.
But where two [possibilities] are obtained in number, there the particle *eva* excludes one of them;
in that case, the meaning of *eva* is accepted.
Here, it exists according to the *tantra* system.
Śā—(The Siddhānta verse: "If the state of being five-fold were enjoined with reference to the omentum (*vapā*), it would be so;
however, here the number five is enjoined with reference to the act of cutting (*avadāna*).

Therefore, the state of being five-fold applies to all [the parts], and that is accomplished in the case of the limbs (*aṅga*) either by increasing the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and so forth, or by increasing the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) because of the injunction regarding two cuttings."

Therefore, even regarding the limbs, there is a restriction to five portions. [Objection: Even when there is a sublation of barley in the case of *soma*, there is no sublation of the four-fold portioning in the heart and other organs.
This is stated as the connection (*saṃgati*).

Regarding the statement that "here, at the cutting of the limbs, there shall be fivefoldness [of the portions] by means of a gold chip for the omentum," that is your alternative view; and its mantra is as follows.

Nor does the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) arise from enjoining the number of the cuttings with reference to the omentum, because the qualification of the number and the cutting is established through the compound itself even without the operation of an injunction; thus, there is no room for a syntactical split occurring after the injunction has already functioned. (Mīmāṃsākośa 16)

In reality, however, there is no injunction here for an extraction (*avadāna*) qualified by the number five; rather, there is an injunction for an extraction qualified by the number five with respect to the *vapā* (omentum) as expressed by the words. Through the distinction between what is already established and what is not yet established (*prāptāprāpta-viveka*), the injunction culminates in the number five alone, as in the case of "red-turbaned [priests]" (*lohitoṣṇīṣāḥ*). Otherwise, since the same logic would apply there as well, there would be no injunction for redness alone. And thus, although the number is the object of the injunction regarding the extraction when understood through the intended meaning (*tātparya*), because it is not so [directly] expressed by the words, there is no resulting split in the injunctive force (*prasara-bheda*).

And likewise, because of the consequence that the statement "those two [offerings] shall be double the oblation" would otherwise be rendered meaningless, and because the mention of the *vapā* (omentum) is intended to indicate all the oblations mentioned in the *pāśuka* section, the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvadāna*) is established for the heart and other parts as well.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that since the five-fold cutting is heard in the scripture specifically regarding the *vapā*, it sets aside the original four-fold cutting (*caturavatta*) only there and not elsewhere.
The refutation (*vi*) is: "Is the five-fold cutting only in the *vapā*, or even in the others?"
"From the direction of the *vapā* (omentum) it is without wings; from the direction of the *vadāna* (fore-offerings) it is the last.

For all sacrificers (*yajamāna*), both the fourfold and fivefold portions (*caturavatta* and *pañcāvatta*) are prescribed by the authors of the *Smṛtis* according to the distinction of *gotras*: "The Jāmadagnyas, the Vatsas, and the Vārṣṭiṣeṇas—these three [take] five portions;
all others take four portions."
Thus:
"The Jāmadagnyas, the Vatsavadās, and the Vārṣṭipeṇas,
as well as the Bhārgavas and the Aurvas, are declared to be those who offer five cuttings."

Thus it is found in the *Gobhilagṛhyasūtrabhāṣya*. **Bhaṭṭa:** Regarding the animal sacrifice (*daikṣapaśu*), there is a scriptural injunction: "Even if the sacrificer is one who offers four portions (*caturavattin*), the omentum (*vapā*) must be offered as five portions (*pañcāvattā*). Upon reflection as to whether this fivefold cutting applies only to the omentum or also to the other limbs, it is concluded that here there is no injunction of the number five by way of restating the act of cutting (*avadāna*). For if that were the case, since the heart and other organs would—by virtue of their connection with the act of cutting through the specific texts concerning them—be the sacrificial oblations (*havis*), the omentum would not be an oblation because it is subordinate to those other limbs; consequently, the act of cutting would not apply to it, as it would not be established by way of restatement (*anuvāda*). Therefore, the omentum is indeed the primary oblation.

Furthermore, because accepting the relationship of subject and predicate within a single word would result in the fallacy of breaking the "single flow" (ekaprasaratābhanga), it follows that here the act of cutting off (*avadāna*) itself is enjoined with reference to the body (*vapuḥ*), just as in the passages concerning the heart and other organs, for the purpose of establishing its status as the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). As for the number five (*pañcatva*), since it is already established by extension (*atideśa*) for those such as the Jāmadagnya sacrifice, it is merely a partial restatement (*pākṣikānuvāda*).

In reality, although the hearing of the word *ekāra* (the singular form) and the restatement (*anuvāda*) "one who offers four cuttings" suggest that this is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*)— even for the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvatta*)— in order to establish it as a constant rule common to both the Jāmadagnyas and non-Jāmadagnyas, nevertheless, according to the principle of the *camasa-adhikaraṇa* (3.1.8.16–17), since the term refers specifically to the fat (*vapā*) as the means of accomplishment, there is no possibility of five cuttings applying to the limbs (*aṅga*). Nor is there a release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, [only] in the case of the fat.

Since that [quality of being "connected"] exists in the limbs (*aṅga*), the sentence—"one cuts these twice each"—must enjoin the act of cutting qualified by that number; otherwise, the mention of the *vapā* (omentum) would result in its own redundancy. To avoid this, the mention of the *vapā* alone must be meaningful as a means of excluding the heart and other organs. Nevertheless, even if this were the case, it must be stated that [the term] serves as an indirect indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all the sacrificial materials under discussion.
Regarding the taking of the omentum (*vapā*):

even though [the rule] "There are indeed eleven portions of the animal; he cuts them off twice each" lacks the character of a general characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), the statement concerning the animal portions (*pārśvadāna*) in the limbs for the Jāmadagnya option would be redundant. This is because [those portions] are already obtained through the archetype (*prakṛti*), and since the five-fold cutting (*pañcāvatta*) applies to the omentum, the two-fold cutting is already established by its very nature as that which effects [the five-fold cutting].
Because it has the measure as its object;
for if it had all [the parts] as its object, there would be no pointlessness since the five-fold cutting would be established.
This being the position reached regarding the statement on the cutting of the animal victim:
Even though the cutting (avadāna) of the sacrificial oblation (havis) is already established by general rule, the explicit mention of "cutting" would otherwise be redundant.

Therefore, in order to avoid violating the principle of a single syntactic thrust (ekaprasaratā), the subsequent act must be understood as the cutting characterized by the five-fold portioning (pañcāvatta).
Since the entire purpose of the statement is thus fulfilled, it is logical that the mention of the omentum (vapā) is merely illustrative (upalakṣaṇa) of all such portions.
The prescription of the instruction regarding the ordinary act by means of the instruction regarding the body [of the animal] follows from the operation of extended application (atideśa).

Therefore, since the term "cutting" (avadāna) applies to the subsidiaries, the five-fold cutting (pañcāvattī) of the ordinary cutting itself is accomplished either through the spreading under (upastaraṇa), the cutting, and the pouring over (abhivāraṇa) performed in sequence, or through the spreading under, the cutting, and the pouring over performed in sequence for the animal-cutting.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
[The injunction] is prescribed by means of the teaching of the *vapā*.
For this very reason, in the second position, there are five—
Maṇḍana: "The *avadāna* (cutting) applies even to the heart and other parts.
[He argues that] the injunction is for the sake of establishing the necessity (*nityatva*) of the act, and regarding the portion of the *avadāna*, it pertains to the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
Śaṅkara: "The five-fold cutting (*pañcāvatta*) is the entirety."

It should be understood that this is for the sake of establishing its own validity and for the sake of avoiding the violation of the principle of single-directionality (*ekaprasaratā*). In either case, because the extended application (*atideśa*) is obstructed regarding the portions to be cut off (*avadāna*),
the invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) must be performed for the sake of the ritual action already present.
And because of this, in the sentences concerning the heart and other parts, the cutting (*avadāna*) is indeed for the purpose of preparing the omentum (*vapā*).
Furthermore, in the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) together with the cake (*puroḍāśa*), there would be a common ritual procedure (*samānatantra*);
the injunction is by way of subsequent reference (*anudeśena*).
Nor should it be argued: "Why could the reverse not be the case?
For, when the portioning of the animal (*paśvāvatta*) is enjoined by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to the portions (*avadāna*), there is the principle of a single flow of expression (*ekaprasaratā*).
Because destruction itself is the restrictive factor.
Nor is there an absence of the consecration at the time of production—the commentary states: "In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is the animal and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)."
In the case of those two [offerings], it is improper to insert another *saṃskāra* (consecratory act), because it is intended solely for the purpose of consecrating the *soma*.
Furthermore, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) pertaining to the *puroḍāśa* belongs to the *pāṅkta* [rite].

Here too, that same [principle applies]: [the consumption of the *abhiṣava* and so forth, as established in the previous section, is not common to all, because it is subordinate to the primary [act]—namely, the attainment of the fruit of the *pūrtīka* sacrifice.]

[The doubt] arises: should the release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) be performed at the time of summoning the *haviṣkṛt* for the sake of the *pāṅkta* ritual, since there is no obstacle to its subsequent performance due to the non-interference with other consecrations (*saṃskāra*), or is it for the sake of the *puroḍāśika* ritual? [The answer is:
because the consecration itself does not establish a difference in rituals apart from its own application.
In the same manner, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the final (siddhānta) positions are to be understood.

This is also a section of the topical discussion (adhikaraṇa); therefore, because the cutting out for the preparation of the omentum (vapā-saṃskāra-avadāna) itself is enjoined by means of the mention of the heart and other organs, it is so.
But surely there is no *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) in the case of the animal sacrifice, because it consists of [the offering of] herbs;
and since that [animal sacrifice] is characterized by the fivefold cutting (*pañcāvatta*), there must always be five cuttings even in the case of the heart and other organs.
Having established this—that they serve all purposes—it is thus considered.
This is inconceivable.
It is the attainment of speech;
namely, those actions which are established as being entirely dependent upon another.

Śā— In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, there is the *paśupuroḍāśa* (animal-cake). In that regard, since the call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*) exists in the sentences describing the aforementioned procedure by way of specifying those very materials such as the omentum (*vapā*), and because it is prescribed [there], and because the taking of portions (*avadāna*), which is already established by the context, is merely restated, [the call to the preparer] exists also in the case of the animal sacrifice.

It is considered: is the release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) at the first time for the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), or at the time of the cake-offering (*puroḍāśa*)? Because the animal-cake offering is incidental, [it follows] by the logic of the *pāṅkta*—as it is heard in the *Agniṣomīya* animal sacrifice: "Even though... [the *kaustubha* provides the detailed exposition].
Since the accomplishment of the purpose is achieved through the verbal expression, the purpose is not [fulfilled] by the verbal expression itself.
Therefore, the sacrificer is one who offers four portions of the animal; the omentum (vapā) must be made into five portions. Regarding that:
"The release of speech at the proper time"—this is the answer for one who thinks thus.
This suppression of speech pertains only to the omentum (*vapā*); it does not apply to the portions from the heart and other parts of the animal, because these have different substrates.
It is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*).
This [act] is a refinement of the agent;
therefore, according to the principle that "when the word has been released" (3.1.8), because the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is intended to be expressed,
the *pauroḍāśika* rites being performed would become deficient in merit.

Therefore, since there is a difference in the *apūrva* (transcendental result) regarding the omentum (*vapā*), this being the position reached, [we reply]: because the act of cutting off (*avadāna*) is already established, its relinquishment occurs at the time of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

The injunction for the five-fold portion (*pañcāvatta*) is made with reference to that [act], and because it is a qualification of the object of reference, the omentum is not [the subject of the injunction].

Since the accomplishment of the ritual purpose is achieved by the *pāṅkta* [fivefold] nature alone, the items belonging to the *pauroḍāśika* section are intended [to be included]; therefore, the mention of the *vapā* (omentum) is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Even though, in the case of the compound *pañcāvattā*, the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) is improper due to the entire word being a single unit, there is no loss of dharma; thus, as in the previous case, the release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) occurs exactly as before. This is the conclusion.
There is no connection [between the two].

Since the summoning of the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) is for the purpose of perceiving the time when speech has become manifest, even when the secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) has ceased, it is according to the principle of the cessation of the secondary characteristic.
In the *agniṣomīya* animal sacrifice, there is the release of speech; in the *agniṣomīya* animal sacrifice, of all seven...

Since there is the possibility of releasing speech (*vāgvisarga*) during the invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* for this [animal sacrifice] as well, there is no need for concern regarding the non-arising of the *vaṣaṭ* [in the case of the rule]: "In the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma, one chooses seven.
The meaning of the sūtra, however, is that there is a common ritual procedure (*samānatantratā*) for both the animal sacrifice and the cake offering (*puroḍāśa*).
The selection belongs to the agents alone.
It may be that the fivefold formula for choosing the priests (*vāgvyama*) should be followed until the end of the *pauroḍāśika* section.

Regarding the *daikṣa* [consecration], it is heard in the scripture: "Having chosen both the divine and the human *hotṛ*s, up until the point of the *śrāvaṇa* and *pratyāśravaṇa*, he chooses the Soma-offering priests."
Regarding this [act of] releasing speech (*vāgvisarga*) at the time of the *utkīrtana* or at the time of the *puroḍāśa*:

that which is prescribed in the middle [of the rite] is for the sake of all [the constituent acts], because it effects a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). As for the first [instance], due to its being the principal (*tantra*), it would be [for the sake of the whole]; or rather, the latter [instance] would be [for the sake of the whole] because it is a refinement of the agent (*kartṛsaṃskṛti*) through the utterance of speech.

Regarding the statement "he chooses seven," it is a figurative expression (avayutya-vāda), similar to the statement "they take ten. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhānta is as follows]: In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is prescribed. Furthermore, in the case of the animal sacrifice, even though the carrying forward of the *praṇītā* waters and the invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* are absent, there is the possibility that the time-limit indicated by them [could still apply]. Even if such a possibility were somehow non-existent, [the rule would still hold]. [The opponent objects: If the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call without having been chosen, they would cut off the head of the sacrifice; whereas if these [priests] utter the *vaṣaṭ* call after having been chosen, it is the sacrificer who cuts off the head of the sacrifice. Therefore, since the time-limit is defined by the act of choosing, how can this [rule] apply? [The author replies: It is possible because the time-limit is characterized by the act of choosing. And even if it were somehow impossible, [the rule remains valid]. *Bhaṭṭa:* In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the animal-cake is heard [in the scripture]. [The opponent argues: "If the officiating priests were to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call without having been chosen, they would cut off the head of the sacrifice; but if these [priests] utter the *vaṣaṭ* call after having been chosen, it is the sacrificer who cuts off the head of the sacrifice. Therefore, since the time-limit is defined by the act of choosing, how can this [rule] apply even if it were somehow impossible? *Note:* The text provided contains some repetition and minor orthographic variations typical of manuscript traditions. The translation above attempts to synthesize the core argument regarding the *paśupuroḍāśa*, the role of the *ṛtvij*s, and the nature of the time-limit (*kālavādha*) defined by the act of choosing (*dhṛtā*). The term *avayutya-vāda* refers to a secondary or figurative statement made by extracting a portion from a primary context. The discussion centers on whether the ritual requirements apply even when certain elements (like the *praṇītā* water) are absent in the animal sacrifice. The final sentence reflects the resolution that the rule holds despite apparent impossibilities.

By the statement "syāśīr gacchati" (the blessing goes away), there is a censure of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance when it is not performed; since the silence of speech (*vāg-vyama*) is specifically prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as a duty pertaining to each respective ritual act, the selection of only a few *vaṣaṭ*-utterers is thereby restricted.
For this very reason, because the priests (*ṛtvij*) and their duties exist in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it is established that these duties belong to them.

Having stated, "He chooses," [the text continues]: "He chooses the *ṛk*-metres; he chooses the Hotṛ; and there is that which belongs to the *pṛṣṭhya* and other such sacrificial elements, beginning with the leading forward [of the fires] and the *havir-kṛt* call, as well as the *āgnīdhra*, the *apratīc-chandas*, and so forth. By this passage ending with "he chooses speech," even items such as the *praṇayana*, the *haviḥ-kṛt*, the *brahmā*, the intermediate duties, and the *sānnāyya* are included in the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, because of the extension (*atideśa*) of those specific details to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) as well, it is indeed appropriate that their properties apply there too.
It is consistent; for although the office of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer would apply [to him] by extension, there is this restrictive injunction: "One does not choose the *acchāvāka*.
Nor is there a prohibition stating that in the archetype he stands between the *haviṣkṛt* and the *āhvāna*.

Saṃkarṣa, 3.4.9: Because [the animal sacrifice] is the subject of the injunction, the extension (*atideśa*) [of the ritual details] would not apply to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), since there is no invocation of the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation) in that case. Regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is said: "He chooses seven. [Thus, the specific rule applies only there.]
However, because it is intended as a reference to that very same reality, there is an extension of its properties;
it is a restatement of the agent, not a separate act of choosing.
It is to be carried out.
Therefore, regarding the animal sacrifice, the time for summoning the *haviṣkṛt* has been stated in the root text;
just as in passages such as "he chooses three," so too in the passage "he chooses seven," [the number] is indeed primary.

And therefore, since the accomplishment of the purpose—such as the production of offspring—is achieved solely through the employment of the fivefold speech (*pāṅkta-vāk*), the syntactic connection (*saṃkhyānvaya*) pertains to the meaning of the verbal root itself; because there is a plurality of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), there is no separate performance of the fivefold speech in the case of the seven steps during the animal sacrifice (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
However, if it is a case of incidental application (*prasaṅga*)—

Because it is subordinate even to that which is numerable; for, by the statement "having Agni as its deity," if one were to establish a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) regarding the injunction for the sacrificer, there would be a lack of consistency with the chapter.
Such [objections] are raised.
This is because the act of choosing (varaṇa) is also mentioned therein.

And since the selection (*varaṇa*) pertains specifically to the status of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterer, let this discussion proceed from that point regarding the consideration of the principle of common application (*tantratva*) in the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*).

Even if the previously mentioned selection is invariably for the purpose of purifying the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*), it follows that there is no separate performance of this [selection] enjoined by this specific statement; such being the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), we reply: since the other selections prescribed by this statement serve as remote auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), the priests distinct from them must be appointed through the mental concentration (*manaḥ-praṇidhāna*) which serves as a visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāraka*) for the verbal expression. Thus, there is a distinction regarding the progeny and so forth.

By process of elimination, it might be argued that they should be understood as being instrumental to the ritual action (*karmakāraka*); however, this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because, as stated previously, it is illogical for them to be merely indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), and because the selection (*varaṇa*) of the mind has already occurred, among the eight [priests] other than the sacrificer—specifically regarding the Adhvaryu, Pratiprasthātṛ, and Udgātṛ—the subsequent performance of the *puroḍāśika* rites after the release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) is governed by a mantra in the dual number intended for the selection. Consequently, since the selection applies to the seven [priests] among the Ṛtviks, there is neither a case of *tantra* (common application) nor *prasaṅga* (incidental application).
The statement "he chooses" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
*Saṃkarṣa*, 3.4.12.
*Nyāyabindu*: The invocation of the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt-āhvāna*) exists even in the case of animal sacrifice (*paśu*).
Oṃ. Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, it is considered whether the selection (*varaṇa*) of all seven priests should be performed according to worldly custom;
however, because the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), it is by means of the *pāṅkta* [formula] alone.
Or rather, how?
Since the accomplishment of the ritual task is achieved through the restraint of speech, the release of speech occurs only at the time of the animal sacrifice.

Regarding the doubt concerning the mantra "Agni is the divine Hotṛ" in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: because the restraint of speech is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the agent, the actions performed by one who has released his speech would be defective; furthermore, since the selection of the Hotṛ (*hotṛvaraṇa*), which is recited in the *Puroḍāśika* section, is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), [the release of speech] must therefore occur at the time of the *puroḍāśa*.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that for the two [the *ruṇa* and the *taditka*], the release of speech (*vāgvisarga*) is to be enjoined because they are Vedic; for others, however, it is the worldly [practice] that applies, thus it is "the release of speech.

When it is argued that the two [types of] animals follow the rule of the sacrificial animal (*paśudharma*), while the other follows the rule of the Soma sacrifice, [Maṇḍana] replies: "If the release of speech belongs to the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśa*) and also to the animal sacrifice, then they should be performed only as worldly [acts]."

In this rite prescribed by a single injunction, "He chooses seven," there is no option for a single [verse] because of the lack of suitability for diversity (*vairūpya*) in this ritual action. That release of speech occurs at that time; it is not [to be performed] here.
It is indeed that release of speech.
In this ritual, due to the impossibility of diversity, [the rule applies].

Regarding the black antelope horn used for scratching during the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, although the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is prescribed as a single injunction, its variation according to the different *savana*s (pressings) is accepted because it would otherwise conflict with the injunction for the disposal (*prāsana*) of that horn after the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
(Saṃkarṣa.)
Oṃ. In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering should be performed with three parts [of the victim] from what remains after the primary offerings (*anijyāśeṣa*).
It is desired that the *sviṣṭakṛt* be made from the remnants of the offerings, according to the model of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is an animal for the initiation rite (*dīkṣaṇīya-paśu*), as it is said: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma."
In that [original sacrifice], the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is obtained by extension (*codaka*).
Here, it is heard in the scripture: "He performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* with three portions.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the *sviṣṭakṛt* be offered from those three portions which are remnants of the sacrificial offerings (*ijyā*), or rather from those that are not remnants of the sacrificial offerings?
What is established? That [the number] is from the defects of the sacrifice.
Why? Because in this way, there will be conformity with the original meter (*prakṛticchandas*).
There are three limbs which are constituent parts of the sacrifice; when the sacrifice is being performed, the word "three" (*tri*) is also thereby accommodated.

Regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) dedicated to Agni and Soma (126): even when the fire has been formally consigned (*samāropa*), there is an injunction in the passage beginning with "yad vai" which prescribes [the offering] with reference to the *sviṣṭakṛt*.

Although these [elements] are enjoined as subordinate factors (*guṇa*) with respect to the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice, since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the latter half of the principal oblation (*pradhānahavis*) is also subordinate with respect to the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*), it is quite easy to establish sublation (*bādhakatva*) here, because they share the same objective domain (*samānaviṣayatva*).

Furthermore, with respect to the offering (*prakṣepa*), it is indeed a consecration (*saṃskāra*) within the archetype (*prakṛti*); for, since it serves as the means of accomplishing that [offering], it possesses the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the offering, and thus its having the same object (*samānaviṣayatva*) is established, thereby subverting what is extended by analogy (*atidiṣṭa*) through direct instruction (*upadeśa*).

In reality, however, even here, although the offering is a consecration of what has been used, because the aforementioned sacrifices are produced from the animal (*paśu*) and are therefore "scattered" (*ākīrṇakara*), it is logical that it is a consecration of them—just like the discarding of blood (*lohitanirāsana*) and so forth.
Even in that respect, the subversion occurs precisely because of the identity of the object.

Even here, although the substance is enjoined as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) with respect to the act of throwing (*prakṣepa*) by means of the injunction heard in the context itself, it is nonetheless possible for it to be the primary element (*pradhāna*) with respect to the act of throwing by virtue of the purpose-driven injunction; therefore, there is not even a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the instrumental case.

[Objection: Even so, since the portion consisting of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering was employed in the archetype for the purpose of consecrating two other substances, even if it is here employed for the purpose of consecrating a different substance, the consecration remains possible because it occurs with respect to each individual object to be consecrated; thus, there is no contingency of the prescribed [element] subverting the extended [element].

For in this case, it cannot be said that the Aindra mantra—which has its requirement for a purpose satisfied by being enjoined through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) as an auxiliary to the Gārhapatya fire—is here intended to bring about the mental representation of Indra and others; nor can it be said that the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, which has no further requirement since its purpose is fulfilled by being for the sake of consecrating the remnants of the Agni-oblation, is intended to serve as a means for the act of sacrifice.

Since the status of being a means for the purpose of sacrifice is already established in the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, it need not be postulated here; and since there is no reason why the benefit consisting of the disposal of the upper half of the offering material (*pradeya*) should not be extended here, there is no obstacle to the extension of the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation—which is the generator of that benefit—by virtue of its dependence upon it.

Nor is there any evidence for the claim that there is a sublation of the archetypal disposal when that which was obtained as the generator of the benefit is applied here as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a different substance; for it is possible, by way of a single performance (*tantra*), that it serves as a refinement for both.
Because there is no contradiction.

For here, there is no requirement for the expectation of a substitute (*pratipatti*) regarding the original material (*prākṛta-saṃskāra*), such that its inclusion would not be removed on the grounds of being a producer of that [substitute].

Nor does it follow from this that, in the case of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, even though a different deity is prescribed for the animal-cake (*paśu-puroḍāśa*)—and thus a non-original function is postulated—the original function is still extended (*atideśa*), leading to the undesirable consequence of performing the animal-cake offering again; for the original function, having been prescribed as being produced by another ritual act involving substances such as *surā* liquor, has no further need for a producer.

If it is argued that, in the present case, since the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is established as being performed by way of a single performance (*tantra*) due to its being a non-established residue of the primary act, it is appropriate to perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation by casting [the portions] together—this is true.
However, here too that same principle applies, because the requirement is fulfilled by the eating of the remnants of the oblation (*havir-śeṣa*).

For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), although the eating of the remnants of the oblation is prescribed without distinction in the text "They eat the remnants of the oblation," it is restricted because other disposal rites (*pratipatti*), such as the *sviṣṭakṛt*, are enjoined for the northern and southern halves of the rear portion.

In the present case, however, because the *sviṣṭakṛt* requires a purpose due to its connection with another function (*kāryāntara*), there is no restriction [of the scope of the rule]; thus, it is logical that the consumption of the remnants serves as a disposal (*pratipatti*) and as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the subsequent portion of the offering material. Therefore, it is established that the *sviṣṭakṛt* belongs only to those portions that are not remnants of the sacrifice (*anijyāśeṣa*). Even though the rectum (*guda*) is indeed a remnant of the sacrifice, nevertheless, the *sviṣṭakṛt* for the middle part of it is not obtained through extension (*atideśa*); rather, it applies only to the third part of the rectum intended for the subsequent portion. Thus, even so, it constitutes a different type of consecration.

*Nyāyabindu*: It is argued that the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent offerings should be made from the heart and the other [specified organs] alone; for the scriptural statement, "In that he offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* with the *vai*s," is intended merely to prescribe the number three for those very organs. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: because it would result in breaking the unity of the syntactical stream (*ekaprasaratā*) to prescribe the number three by way of a reference to the subsidiary parts (*aṅga-anuvāda*), and because other organs are mentioned in the supplementary passage—"From the two fore-legs, from the middle of the rectum, and from the three entrails he cuts off"—the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent offerings are made from those three alone. Since they serve as the scattered remains (*ākīrṇakara*), the scriptural injunction applies them to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, thereby setting aside the heart and the other organs. This is the final position.
Maṇḍana: "The phrase 'one should sacrifice with what [is left]' is not a subordinate element of the sacrifice.
Or rather, the reading is "because of its connection with the sacrifice.
Śaṅkara: "By others than those, [it is performed] with the three Sviṣṭakṛt [offerings]."
Regarding the invocation of Agni Sviṣṭakṛt for the purpose of carrying the oblation, the *nigada* (liturgical formula) beginning with "abhi hotrādyeti" occurs at that very point.

And that recitation of the *hotṛ* (the *hotrāmnāna*) is indeed for the purpose of the oblation (*homārtha*), because the word *hotrā* refers to the oblation; because even in that [recitation], there exists the quality of being the locus for certain oblations; and because its purpose as an oblation is declared by such texts as, "In which these [oblations] are offered" (*yasmin vaitad asāv āhutayo hūyante*). This being the prima facie view, [we reply]: the *hotra* is the action of the *hotṛ*, and that consists in the conveying of the sacrificial offering (*havyaprāpaṇa*). For this is determined by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of mantras such as, "O youngest one, carry the offerings (*havyā vahā*) today," and "By which path I may carry the offering to you. Furthermore, from the meaningfulness of the term *hotrā* and so forth, it is understood that it serves as the cause for the name "carrier of the offering" (*havyavāhana*).
Therefore, even in the absence of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings in the *śyena* sacrifices, the *nigada* "Agnim hotrāya" and so forth must certainly be recited.
(Saṃkarṣa 4.2.11).

Furthermore, even when the fire has been consigned into its source (*ātmasamāropa*), the re-descending of the fire (*pratyavaroha*) must be performed by churning it from the two kindling woods (*araṇi*).

If it were argued that, because both the fire and the self consist merely of a refinement (*saṃskāra*), the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the fire and the self could be combined like the fire and the araṇi wood—this being the position reached—it is replied:

no, because there is no possibility of combination since the fire and the means [of kindling] serve a single purpose; furthermore, there is no evidence for the view that the superimposition of the self is a mere refinement.
(Saṃkarṣa.)
It is likewise in the context of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
There is one section concerning the nature of the Self;
however, this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

In a non-contextual passage—that is, a place distinct from the context of the *cayana* (the piling of the altar)—the bricks such as the *sāma-trātā* and others would belong to the fire-altar (*agni*) itself, which consists of the aggregate of the five layers (*pañca-citi*). This is because of the principle of the "greatness of the context" (*tatra-mahat*) stated in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*). Just as the cups (*graha*) such as the *upāṃśu* and *āditya*, though mentioned outside the context of the fire-altar, are auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, so too are these bricks auxiliary parts of the fire-altar.
In the context of the Agniṣṭoma, it should be like that—in the context of the Agniṣṭoma, it would be so.
"Agni" refers to the fire-altar (agnicayana) and the Atigrāhya cups; the collection of these is "Agniṣṭomādya."

Since it is taught [as a model] for only certain modifications (vikṛti), such as the two-night sacrifice (dvirātra) and others, its application would, according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), occur only from the Agniṣṭoma in those specific modifications where it is explicitly taught, and not elsewhere. And the mention of the month (māsi) is likewise [to be understood in that same way].

Similarly, just as there is an instruction regarding the modification of another *atigrāhya*, so too in the case of the statement, "The monthly *grāhyas* are taken," the inclusion of the word "monthly" (*māsi*) is also a proof for the absence of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
Thus says the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).
And the particle *ca* is intended to conjoin another reason.

"Māsi-grahaṇam" (the grasping in the month) is a *karmadhāraya* compound expressing a possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) or a penetration (*apavedha*). Alternatively, "grasping" (*grahaṇa*) [is used] because of its equivalence.
He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), there would be an extension by implication (*codaka*) of both the fire-altar construction (*agnicayana*) and the *atigrāhya* cups, because the implication is equal for the *agniṣṭoma* day and for the other constituent parts.
The word "negation" (*bādha*) is intended to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
This is because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

"One should pile the *kaṅkacita*," "One should pile the *śīrṣacita*," and "In the Vājapeya, one takes five *atigrāhya* cups with five teeth"—from the observation of these indicative marks (*liṅga*), it is known that the [piling] of the Agniṣṭoma day is extended by the rule of transfer (*codaka*) to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).
This is another reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). And the word "and" (*ca*) is used precisely for the sake of this additional reason.
The taking up [of the vessels] would be subject to the same rule.

Since the fire-altar construction (agnicayana) and the *atigrāhya* cups are taught in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), their taking up in that modified sacrifice and in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) would be subject to the same rule;
that is, the prescription for both cases would be by means of a single rule alone.
Furthermore, the remaining [elements] are obtained in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) through the extended application (*codaka*), as in the case of the *agniṣṭoma* days.
By this, the objection raised in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, that "because of the direct instruction (*upadeśa*) in the unmodified sacrifice" (Sūtra 23)—is refuted.
The mention of "monthly" (*māsi*) is for the purpose of prohibiting repetition (*abhyāsa*).

Regarding what was stated by the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "the *atigrahya* cups are not to be taken" (Sūtra 24), he replies: "The *atigrahya*s are to be taken month after month. Thus, the mention of "month by month" (*māsi-māsi*) in the *Gavām ayana* sacrifice is for the purpose of prohibiting their repetition day after day, and it does not establish the absence of the rule of extension (*codaka*).

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the fire-altar construction (*agnicayana*) and the *atigrahya* cups proceed into the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) by means of the rule of extension.
In the case of the Agniṣṭoma, there would be no extension [of certain elements] to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) because of their specific designation for that sacrifice.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the *agni* prescribed by the sentence "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar" (*ya evaṃ vidvān agniṃ cinute*) and the *atigrāhya* cups prescribed by the sentence "These *atigrāhya*s are indeed the support of the sacrifice" (*upaṣṭambhanaṃ vā etad yajñasya yad atigrāhyāḥ*) are extended from the Agniṣṭoma to the modified sacrifice or not— the view is that they are not, because the *agni* is connected to the *ukthya* sacrifice by the rule "That [one] with the *ukthya*" (*tam ukthyena*).
Thus [it is said].
Likewise: "Verily, these Atigrāhyas belong to him who is oppressed.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the Agni-atigrāhya apply to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), or not?
What is established? That the *agnyatigrāhya* does not apply in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
*Agnyatigrāhya* refers to the fire and the *atigrāhya* cup;
that [combination] does not apply in the modified sacrifice.
Why? Because it is taught in the context of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

For that is taught in the modified sacrifice thus: "Now, therefore, he sacrifices to Agni with the *agniṣṭoma*; him [he sacrifices] with the *ukthya*, him with the *atirātra*, him with the *ṣoḍaśin*, him with the *vājapeya*, him with the *ṣaḍaha*, him with the *saptarātra*, him with the *daśarātra*, him with the *dvādaśarātra*, him with the *navarātra*, him with the *daśarātra*.

Likewise: "If they were to take up the *pṛṣṭhas* from what is taken up at the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*, they would take up the *pṛṣṭhas* from a wise sacrifice; if he were to take them up at the *ukthya*... and so forth.

Surely the injunction does not extend the *agnyatigrāhya* cup to [the sacrifice], since it is enjoined directly in a specific modification (*vikṛti*). And the mention of "every month" is likewise [not an extension]. The Commentary states: "And this is also handed down in the tradition: 'The *atigrāhya* cups are drawn every month.'"
If the extended application (codaka) were to apply here, there would be no such instruction as "they are not taken month by month.
And their taking [as cups] is equal [to the others]. The Commentary states: "Or rather, the *agnyatigrāhya* is indeed taken by means of the extended application (*codaka*)."
For there is no distinction between this [part] and the other parts;
it is not tenable to say that it takes up some parts and does not take up others.
And because of the observation of indicative marks.

The Commentary states: An indicative mark (*liṅga*) is seen even in a small measure, such as "one should pile [the fire-altar]" and "one should pile it as a head-pile (*śīrṣacita*), if one should desire, 'May I be born with a beautiful head in this world.
Likewise, "he takes five *atigrāhya* cups for Indra.
By mentioning the form of the *kañca* cup and the specific quality of being dedicated to Indra, this shows the application of the *atigrāhya* cup for Agni in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
The inclusion [of the details] would be governed by the same rule.
The Bhāṣya says: Now, that which was stated—that [the details] are taught in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti)—must be refuted. To this, it is replied:
That rule which is taught in a particular modification (*vikṛti*) applies equally to that modification and to the archetype (*prakṛti*);
as for the remaining modifications, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) brings it forth.
[Śabara] says: "The application of desires for subsidiary qualities (*guṇakāmanā*) occurs where there is an equal rule (*samānavidhāna*); in that case, it is logically consistent."

How so? In the archetype (prakṛti), there is an option: [the fire] is to be established either on the high altar (uttaravedī) or on the bare ground. That same option is obtained here by extension (codaka). Therefore, the restatement in this context will serve the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha).
Just as the repeated mention of the *khadira* wood serves a restrictive purpose:

if fire were mentioned in the context of the *dvirātra* and other sacrifices with the injunction "fire is to be performed here," then it would be a restrictive rule, just as in the case of "the sacrificial post is made of *khadira*."

This fire, however, has been prescribed without reference [to other rites] along with its specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Having prescribed it, its connection with the seasons is established through the intended purposes (*abhiprāyaiḥ*).
And these sentences belong to this very context.

Furthermore, the context (prakaraṇa) for the two-night sacrifice and others does not recur [in the subsequent sections], such that it could serve as a restrictor for what is obtained through the general rule (codaka) regarding the two-night sacrifice and others.
Therefore, by the general rule, the fire-altar for the two-night sacrifice and others is indeed optional.
The restatement, however, serves to indicate that when the fire-altar is present, there is the application of the rites intended for specific results (guṇakāmān).
The inclusion of the term "month" (māsi) is for the purpose of prohibiting repetition.
The Bhāṣya asks: "Now, how is it that the term 'month' is included? It is for the purpose of prohibiting repetition;
[the meaning is] that they are not drawn day after day, but rather they are drawn month after month.

Śabara: This is the fire which is not explicitly enjoined by a direct statement in certain modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), such as in the *ṣoḍaśin* and the *vājapeya*. In that regard, there arises a doubt: should it be performed there because it is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), or not?

Similarly, there are cups called *atigrāhya* which are mentioned in the archetype (*prakṛti*); they are also enjoined in some modified sacrifices, such as "one should take them in the *ukthya*, one should take them in the *pṛṣṭhya*, and they are to be taken in the *viśvajit*.
Regarding these as well, there is a doubt: should they be taken in other modified sacrifices or not?
In this regard, the *Codaka* [sūtra] states: "The *agni-atigrāhya* is not seen in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
Its mention in certain [texts] would otherwise be purposeless.
Therefore, for the sake of its meaningfulness, it is inferred that there is no [general] injunction (*pradeśa*)."
Therefore, wherever there is an instruction for this [rite], there alone is the performance;
it is said that, like the *advāntara* [sacrifices], its attainment from the primary scriptural injunction (*śrauta-katu*) is certain.
Because the purpose of the extended application (*codaka*) is complete, however, there is a further mention [of details] in some cases.
If it is indicated as having the same injunction (*sāmānavidhi*), one should not exclude extension (*atideśa*).
What is the meaning? When there is the same injunction, the application of the desire for qualities (*guṇakāma*) is certain.
In those modifications (*vikṛti*) where [the rite] is enjoined, the injunction is the same as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

In other modifications (*vikṛti*), however, there is acquisition [of elements] through the force of the extended injunction (*codaka*); thus, the prescription is not identical to that of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
And if they were subject to the same prescription (*samānavidhāna*), the purpose would be the application of the qualities desired for the *agni* and *atigrāhya* cups in those modifications.

In those [modifications] where the injunction does not exist, the qualities desired do not apply, according to the principle: "Or rather, there is non-application because of the difference in the ritual acts" (*nivṛttir vā karmabhedāt*, 8.1.14.24).

Thus, since there is a scriptural mention [of the fire-altar] in certain modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) for the sake of engaging in the desire for its specific qualities, it cannot be assumed on that basis alone that there is an absence of extended application (*atideśa*); therefore, extended application does exist. On this point, some say: "The fire-altar (*agni*), being taught outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), finds no place in the archetype (*prakṛti*) because it is intended to enjoin the *uttaravedi* altar which belongs to the context. And that which is not part of the archetype is not extended to the modified sacrifices. Therefore, its presence in the modified sacrifices occurs only through direct instruction (*upadeśa*); thus, it is not obtained in the *ṣoḍaśin* and *vājapeya* sacrifices due to the lack of such instruction."
"It is not by the *agniśrutī* alone" [meaning:

since the connection with the season is expressed by the *agni* sentence itself, its placement in the archetype is appropriate—this he says]. That is incorrect, because it is prescribed in the archetype as well by the *agniṣṭoma* sentence.
However, that [mention] will not have the modified fires (vikṛtyagni) as its intended meaning, because it would contradict the rule that the context (prakaraṇa) governs what is stated within it.
Indeed, it is not proper to restrict a sentence by means of the context.

Furthermore, since the primary rites (prakṛti) are self-sufficient and require nothing else, whereas the modified rites (vikṛti) depend upon extended application (atideśa), it is the primary rite itself that is denoted by this [term].
Since the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice denotes the *ṛtu* itself, its connection [with that] is established by syntactical statement (*vākya*); therefore, it cannot be set aside by the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Consequently, the fire-altar exists in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and thus it is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the ectype (*vikṛti*) sacrifices as well.

In that regard, because it is impossible to perform it in the Sārasvata sacrificial sessions (*satra*)—since they are accomplished in a single day (*ekadinasādhyatva*), whereas in those sessions the principal offerings must be performed on different days throughout the year—it may be built at will; however, it must be built in the Ṣoḍaśin and Vājapeya sacrifices.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: although there is no sublation (*bādha*) in the *dāvihoma* offerings because the mention of the word "Svāhā" occurs again in the form of a concluding repetition (*upasaṃhāra*), it is appropriate that there is sublation of the fire-oblation (*agni*) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) where it is mentioned again. This constitutes the logical consistency.

As stated in the *Vidhirasāyana*: "If, prior to the operation of an injunction regarding a result based on a quality (*guṇa*) residing in something else, the fire (*agni*)—already established as being connected to the sacrifice through direct instruction (*upadeśa*) or extended application (*atideśa*) within the context of the *Agni* section or the contexts of various specific sacrifices—were to be merely restated (*anuvādya*) as the substratum (*āśraya*) in injunctions concerning results based on qualities such as the *śyena*-shaped altar, then the subsequent connection of the fire obtained through extended application, which is perceived later, could not occur as the substratum while the directly instructed fire, already present in the intellect, is already connected as the substratum. Thus, for the sake of connecting that [extended fire] as well with that [result], a further direct instruction would be fruitful. However, this is not the case; because the connection with the sacrifice is already effected by sentences such as those concerning the *agniṣṭoma* and so forth, there is no possibility of restating the pure fire—as in the phrase 'one who knows thus' (*ya evaṃ vidvān*)—as the substratum before that point. Consequently, there is no evidence for the fire connected to the sacrifice itself to be the substratum. And since the pure fire cannot be the substratum, when one of the fires is connected to the sacrifice, it follows by implication that the fire connected to that sacrifice is the substratum."
And there is the status of being the locus for an unprecedented fire-altar (apūrvāgni-stheya).

Whether in those cases where the fire’s status as serving an unprecedented rite is based on direct injunction (aupadeśika), or in those where it depends on extension (atideśa), this is established without distinction in all such instances.
Therefore, the uniformity of rule (sāmānavidhya) exists for the purpose of attaining the results of the subordinate elements (guṇakāma).
That is to be considered.

This would indeed be so if pure fire possessed the fitness to be a substratum; but it is not so, because that which is pure, being of an established nature, lacks the fitness to be a substratum without the entry of an action.
And it has been stated in the fourth [chapter] of the *Tantraratna* (4.3.1.9): "The cognition of neutrality is dependent on two [factors], and action is likewise [dependent], but substance is not."

Furthermore, the established nature (*siddharūpatva*) of the fire-altar (*agni*) was accepted by Vidhirasāyana itself during its exposition of the statement: "The sentences such as 'Now, therefore, [one should worship] the fire-altar with the Agniṣṭoma' serve as the substratum for the fire-altar, which is understood from passages like 'One desiring cattle should pile the altar' to have the purpose of [attaining] a fruit."

And thus, just as an established entity requires a substratum for the sake of its own capacity to produce a result, so too, since an established entity can serve as a substratum, it requires entry into a ritual (*kratu*) for that purpose. Consequently, the fire (*agni*) that is connected to a ritual by means of sentences such as those concerning the *Agniṣṭoma* is precisely the substratum; it is the fire as qualified by its own function, and not the fire in its pure form. Therefore, the purpose of the repeated mention [of the fire] is established as being the attainment of the desire for a specific quality (*guṇakāma*).

For it is not the case that the fire, which is optionally associated with the *uttaravedī*, cannot have its re-enunciation in certain *vikṛti* sacrifices for the purpose of restriction; thus, there is no attainment of the accessory (*guṇa*) for the sake of a desired result (*kāma*).
The statement "that is its purpose" [refers to this].

Because the fire situated in the context of the primary sacrifice is more proximate to the attainment of the accessory-desired-results dependent upon it—being obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal extension) of the *dvirātra* and other such *kratu-vikṛtis*—it is appropriate that its very attainment constitutes the purpose.

However, where a proximate purpose is obtained—as in the case of the injunction regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, such as "On the following day, the cup of the two-night sacrifice is taken"—there the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is accepted as having its own fruit, even though it depends on the attainment [of the rite] through its respective original injunction (*codaka*).

But here, because a proximate purpose is obtained, restriction is not the purpose. [Tri: "There is neither extension nor non-extension; there is no such thing. The *atigrāhya* cups are many. It is not so.
Furthermore, in the case of a modification (vikṛti), this [repetition] would be like another injunction;
however, because of the equality between the archetype (prakṛti) and the modifications, there would be a restatement.
And when there is such equality, there is the application of those [rites] intended for specific qualities (guṇakāma).
As in the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*). And therefore, since there is no pointlessness in the subsequent injunction, there is indeed an extension (*atideśa*).

The Bhaṭṭas [hold] that by the statement, "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar," the fire-altar consisting of the piling (*cayana*) is enjoined for the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—known as the *Agniṣṭoma*—by means of the injunction studied outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), namely, "Then, therefore, he sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma after the fire-altar"; this is established in the second book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*, sūtras 2.3.10.12–23].
This is because the *Kaustubha* has established that the word *agniṣṭoma* occurring here refers to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
Likewise, regarding the cups known as *atigrāhya* which are taught as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*),
there is the section on the *atigrāhya* of Agni (Section 130), the section on Agni.

By the relevant statement, "The *atigrāhya* cups are indeed supports for this [sacrifice]," there is an injunction [of these cups] as being auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Jyotiṣṭoma. This being established, regarding certain modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), there is a re-statement of the fire-altar (*agni*) and the *atigrāhya* cups through such texts as, "That [is performed] with the *ukthya*," "That with the *atirātra*," and "They are to be drawn at the *ukthya*," and so forth. This re-statement is not intended to establish something previously unknown (*apūrva*), like the re-statement of the *ājyabhāga* offerings; for since this injunction—which occurs at the same time as the archetype (*prakṛti*)—lacks any established auxiliary benefit (*klṛptopakāraka*), it is impossible for it to sublate the extended application (*codaka*). Furthermore, the extended application (*atideśa*) is necessarily required for the sake of the *agniṣṭoma* and other such forms.

Therefore, if one were to mistakenly think that this [text] is intended solely for the purpose of excluding other *atigrāhya* cups in other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), then—since the injunction of those [other cups] exists in this specific modification—it would be impossible to find a basis for the extension (*atideśa*) of this matter to other modified sacrifices; thus, a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) would have to be asserted. And that [exclusion] is necessarily fraught with three defects (*tridoṣa*).

Nor should it be argued that, out of fear of redundancy (*vaiyarthyabhīti*), one accepts this [text] as a determinant of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) and thereby postulates that it prescribes the extension (*atideśa*) from another modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*);

for when a much simpler purpose is possible, it is improper to postulate an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) based on the assumption of the absence of a conflict with this [text], especially since the extension from a distant source is far removed.

For instance, there are instructions regarding equality even in certain modifications (*vikṛti*) with respect to the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as "one desiring heaven should pile the fire-altar by means of that which has been piled," concerning the qualities characterized by the forms of the hawk and so forth which depend on the fire-altar; these are for the purpose of their application in those modifications.

Otherwise, since the piling itself—which serves as the means in the archetype—would logically become the substrate (*āśraya*) in those cases, those qualities would not apply there according to the principle of self-nature (*ātmika-nyāya*).

However, since this rule exists, because there is no distinction in the status of being the substratum (*āśrayatva*) for both the piling (*cayana*) that serves as the means for the archetypal *apūrva* and the piling that serves as the means for the various modified (*vikṛti*) *apūrvas*, the attainment of the results of the subsidiary desires (*guṇakāma*) is established.
And thus, since the piling is optional in the archetype, its mandatory application (*niyama*) is also a purpose [of the rule].

For although it will be stated in the *Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa* (2.1.26) that, according to the statement "the fire is on the high altar" (*uttaravedyām agniḥ śrūyate*), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the [ordinary] fire and the high altar;

Nevertheless, by examining the Śruti and Kalpasūtras—namely, “If they are about to sacrifice” (*yajñi cepyamānā bhavanti*) and “Agni [is for] those desiring the first [portion] of Soma” (*agniḥ somādyaṃ cecchatām*)—an option (*vikalpa*) regarding Agni, whose counter-positive is his own absence, is indeed accepted.

For this very reason, even a performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma without Agni is accepted on the basis of the mere *uttaravedi*, due to the injunction: “He places the fire on the *uttaravedi*” (*uttaravedyāmagniṃ nidadhāti*). Consequently, since the same applies to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), the repeated mention in certain cases results in a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

For this restriction is not a verbal injunction (*śabda-niyama*) that occurs subsequent to the application of the extended rule (*atideśa*); if it were so, then because it would have already taken effect prior to the extended rule by virtue of being co-temporal with the archetype (*prakṛti*), it might be sublated by that extension. Rather, since this [restriction] has already taken effect previously, having been enjoined for the sake of the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the extended rule—which applies even subsequently—cannot be conceived as having the status of an enjoiner of that [sacrifice], nor can it be conceived as having a scope where that [restriction] is absent.

Therefore, the following argument is refuted: that since the purpose of engaging in the desire for qualities (guṇakāma) already present is available, it is illogical to assume a remote purpose dependent on the power of obtaining those respective extended applications (atideśa), which would require being led by such dependence.

This is because, in the absence of the aforementioned assumption of a purpose, this very [assumption] depends on the establishment of the meaning obtained through the extended application itself, and thus is dependent on the exhaustion of the extended application.
Consequently, when two lighter purposes are possible, one should not accept the acceptance of a result consisting of a heavy exclusion (parisaṃkhyā).

For this very reason, just as in other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), even in a *sattra* characterized by movement, lack of movement, and so forth, where the *atigrāhya* cups would not otherwise be obtained on a daily basis, the specific injunction—"The *atigrāhya*s are drawn month after month"—is appropriate.

Furthermore, in certain specific modified sacrifices, the prescription of the rule in a particular manner—such as "One should draw the *atigrāhya*s from the fifteen-night sacrifice" (*pañcadaśarātra*)—and other such specific prescriptions are also appropriate.
Therefore, the *atigrāhya*s must be performed in every modified sacrifice.
In the Sādhyas and the Sārasvata-sattra, [the fire] is used; however, in the Agniṣṭoma, it is not, because it is impossible.

The *Nyāyabindu* states: The fire in the form of a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), which is prescribed as a general rule (*anārabhya-vihita*) by such passages as "Then, therefore, they sacrifice with this fire, with that fire; him with the Ukthya, him with the Dvirātra," etc., is employed in certain instances both in the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*).
Likewise, there are the *atigrāhya* libations, which are remnants of the drawing of soma.
Furthermore, even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), they are established by specific injunctions: "They are to be drawn at the *ukthya*," and "They are to be drawn at the *vibhajati*.
Thus, this *agni-atigrāhya* is not extended (*atidiśyate*) to those cases where there is no such instruction.
Otherwise, if there were a modification of the altar (*cit*), it would result in the logical fallacy of the absence of an original injunction (*upadeśābhāva*).

This being the prima facie view, [we reply]: because the repetition of the text in certain cases constitutes an identical injunction (*samānavidhāna*), there is no cessation of extended application (*atideśa*); and this identical injunction exists for the purpose of engaging those desiring specific results (*guṇakāma*).

Since [the altar] is based on the fire-altar (*agni*) by such texts as "One desiring heaven should pile it with whatever [altar] he piles," when that [altar] is common to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), the engagement for the sake of the desired result occurs therein.

Otherwise, because there would be a lack of determination regarding the presence of the substratum in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the respective ritual procedure (*vṛtti*) would not apply. Therefore, there is an extension (*atideśa*) [of the procedure];
this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In that regard, in the Sādhyaka and Sārasvata sacrificial sessions (*sattra*), there is no *cayana* (piling of the fire-altar) because it is impossible; however, in the Vājapeya and other such rites, it does occur—this is the remainder [of the discussion].
Maṇḍana: “The *atigrāhya* cups belong to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
(Amiśra). Śaṅkara: “The extension (*atideśana*) of the fire-altar and the *atigrāhya* cups.”
The section on the fire-altar:
the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the fire.
Regarding the *agniṣṭut*, the word "season" (*ṛtu*) is understood from the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
The Commentary: Regarding this, there is the statement, “He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar” (*ya evaṃ vidvān agniṃ cinute*).

Having prescribed this, it is heard: “Now, therefore, he sacrifices to this very fire-altar with this [altar]; him with the Ukthya, him with the Atirātra,” and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the word *agni* denote a sacrifice, such that a distinct ritual action from the Jyotiṣṭoma and others is enjoined by the verb *cinute* (he piles), or does it denote a substance, such that it is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇa*) within the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites?
What is established? That it is a word denoting a sacrifice.
Why? Because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).
For an indicative mark is seen: "the stotra of Agni," "the śastra of Agni."
Likewise, [in the statement] "There are six *upasads* for the *Āgneya*," it is understood that the word "Agni" denotes that [sacrifice] which possesses the *stotra*, the *śastra*, and the *upasads*;
all of this belongs to the sacrifice.
Therefore, it is a word denoting sacrifice.
[Objection: But since there is an indicative mark (liṅga), let it be stated that it is a name (prātipadika).
To this it is replied:
Regarding the statement, “Now, therefore, they sacrifice to this very fire with these [offerings],” it is said that he brings about the sacrifice.
He specifies that fire as "this" (imam);
therefore, it is understood that it bears the name "Agni."
The prefix *anu* is also an *upasarga* that qualifies the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
This is appropriate only if Agni is the sacrifice;
therefore, the word *ṛtu* (season) is understood [in this sense].
Or rather—there is no doubt even in the case of "he piles the fire" (*agniṃ cinute*).

Is it an injunction for a previously unknown sacrifice (*apūrvayāga*), or an injunction for the mere act of piling (*cayana*), or an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhāna*) in the archetypal and ectype sacrifices?

In that regard, because it is mentioned again within the context (*prakaraṇa*) as possessing two parts, and because a mere purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) by itself cannot have a purpose, another ritual action (*ṛtvantara*) is inferred by means of the very name.

And likewise, there is the hearing of a fruit in the passage, "As if with Ṛc verses. Nor can it be said that the fruit arises from a mere subordinate quality (guṇa), because that would result in an inconsistency with the subject matter under discussion.
Furthermore, the exclusive marks of the Soma sacrifice, such as the *upasads* and so forth, are heard mentioned in both [passages] concerning Brahman.

Likewise, regarding these statements such as, "Now, therefore, they sacrifice to this very Agni with these [offerings]," therein the injunction is understood to be one that prescribes a sacrifice qualified by a name already established— just as in the cases of "he sacrifices to Agni" or "he sacrifices to the *samidhs*"— according to the rule, "And there is another scriptural passage which makes known that [name]" (*tatprakhyaṃ cānyaśāstram*). And the qualification for that very [sacrifice] is its designation as the *agniṣṭoma* and so forth.
The specific details of the first [altar], such as the two *āvratas* and so forth, are thus differentiated.
Alternatively, in the sentence concerning the rule for the sacrificial forms (*saṃsthā*), there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the root *yaji*.
This is possible only if, in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), the root *cinoti* (to pile) possesses the sense of sacrifice (*yajimat*).

Therefore, because of its grammatical coordination with the general term *yajati* (he sacrifices) at the very outset, it is determined that "Agniṣṭut" is the name of a ritual (*ṛtu*) from the start. Furthermore, the word "anu" is [explained] by the passage: "He who, having performed this [sacrifice], [offers] to Agni... and so forth.
It restates the sequence after the Jyotiṣṭoma:

"Or rather, he sacrifices after Agni with the sacrifices consisting of the Agniṣṭoma and other forms. This implies that if there is a sacrifice to Agni, then it can be performed as a subsequent sacrifice (*anuyajati*). For in all cases, priority and posteriority exist only in the division of things that possess a similar form and similar characteristics.
For example, as in the expression "he follows Devadatta.
If Devadatta also goes, then such following is logically possible;
likewise, so too is subsequent sacrifice (*anuyajana*).
Therefore, this is an injunction for the performance (*itikartavyatā*) as something heard [directly] or inferred.

In the latter interpretation, however, since this rite is performed after the *agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, it would be merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to them, and thus the mention of a fruit would be a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

In the former view, however, because it is independent, it serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of being an injunction for a fruit, according to the rule: "The fruit belongs to Ātreya, because of the specific mention" (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.18). This is the distinction.
Or it may be the substance, because the purpose is for that [substance].
