The Bhāṣya says: "Or it may be the substance; if it is argued that the word 'fire' denotes the substance.
Which substance? That which is the flame.
For here this [meaning] is well-established:
the injunction "he piles up" (cinute) means that the piling (cayana) prepares him and establishes him upon the altar.
Furthermore, the prefix *anu* will have the sense of "subsequently," meaning that after the piling has been completed, he sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

Or rather: "From the word 'atyantam ruddha' (completely obstructed), without resorting to a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) and so forth, the sacrifice is understood as not abandoning the fire."
The word "Agni" is not intended here as a derivative term (yaugika),

nor is it joined with syntactical split (vākyabheda), exclusion of that (tadvyatireka), or non-application of that (tadapradeśa), by which it might be understood as a name for a ritual action (karmānāmadheya).
As for what was said— that such [features] exist— it would be so only if the word "Agni" were heard as a subordinate part of the sacrifice (ṛtvaṅga).
And since it has not been obtained from anything as having that very nature, there is an absence of any other explanation for it.
Therefore, "these are indeed substances.

Regarding the question in the Bhāṣya, "Which substance?", this is a question intended to point out the contradiction with its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the act of piling (*cayana*).

The proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntavādī), however, considering that there is no contradiction because the relationship between the refinement and the object to be refined is possible through grammatical coordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya)—just as in the case of "one threshes rice"—states: "As for this [statement], 'he piles the fire'.

Therefore, since the word *agni* retains its well-known meaning and since the root *ci* (to pile) pertains to the injunction of a sacrifice, and because of the absence of a material substance (*dravya*) and a deity (*devatā*), the meaning of the injunction is determined to be simply this: "one refines the fire by means of piling.
In this way, the use of the accusative case is justified.
If, however, it were the name of a ritual action, there would be difficulty, as in the case of the *agniṣṭoma*.
If it is asked how the word "he performs the after-offerings" (*anuyajati*) [is to be understood], it is said in reply:
"He will perform the sacrifices consisting of the *ekāha*, *ahīna*, and *satra* types;
by the hearing of the word 'anu' (after), he will declare their performance.
For if this word "agni" were in grammatical apposition [with the others].
In that case, it would be difficult to understand [the meaning], if this were a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) in the sense of an object (*karman*).
However, this is a case of different grammatical coreference (*vyadhikaraṇa*); the second case ending occurs when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*.
Here, the meaning is as follows: "after the enkindling of the fire, [the sacrifice] is desired by means of the Agniṣṭoma and other rites."
And although the word *agni* denotes a general class, it functions here—by virtue of the context—to refer to the fire consecrated by the rite of piling (*cayana*).
The meaning is that one should sacrifice after the time of the consecration of the piling.
Therefore, these statements are intended for the purpose of bringing forward the portions of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

If it is asked: "What is the purpose of the restatement (*punarśruti*) in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), given that [the rule] has already been obtained by the injunction (*codaka*) itself?"—it will be stated in the tenth book: "'The mention [of the accessory] would be a common injunction' (10.8.11.27).

Furthermore, precedence (*paurvāparya*) does not necessarily occur only between two things of the same class; precedence also occurs between things of different classes, as in the case of "he eats after cooking," which is established without contradiction. As for the claim that in the expression "Devadatta follows Yajñadatta," an identity of action is understood, that is correct only when the agent alone is mentioned and no other action is specified.
In this case, however, there exists only the piling (cayana) intended for the consecration by fire; thus, it is not the same [as the previous case].
Because of its connection with that [piling], the sacrifice should be named after it, and by means of that, the injunctions of ritual duties [apply].
As for the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) mentioned—that the word "Agni" denotes a sacrifice—[that is addressed as follows].

Therefore, that [term] applies only to those words associated with the *liṅga* (the fire-altar), not everywhere; because among them there is a connection with the piled fire-altar (*cityāgni*), the word is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇaśabda*) for the sacrifice.
Thus, there is no fault in the fact that they are expressions for the ritual (*ṛtu*) and injunctions of its properties.
Or rather—in cases such as "the hymn of Agni" (*agneḥ stotram*) and so forth—the fire-altar serves as the substratum (*āśrayatva*).
A location connected with fire is indicated, but the sacrifice is not located therein;
nor is it the case that because a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is resorted to in one instance, it must be resorted to everywhere.
Therefore, since a direct application is possible, the piling up of the material itself is what is appropriate.

As for the discussion conducted by another commentator on this very same topic—concerning whether fire possesses a fruit or not, whether it is produced or eternal, and whether it is a modification of the *uttaravedi* or not—that was established under a different illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*) and a different topical heading (*adhikaraṇa*).
Since its occurrence here is impossible, it should be disregarded as merely a reflection appearing in the mirror of memory.
Therefore, it is established that a quality of this kind is not a differentiator [of rituals].
The investigation into whether [the act] bears fruit or is fruitless, as in the case of *sudhā*, is established in the *parṇamaya-adhikaraṇa* (4.3.1).

The investigation into whether something is archetypal (*prākṛta*) or modified (*vikṛta*), as in the examples of the fire-altar (*agni*) and the Veda, is established in the *agnyatirādhyā-adhikaraṇa* (10.8.11). The investigation into whether something is permanent (*nitya*) or non-permanent (*anitya*), as in the example of the *godohana* vessel, is established in the third *adhikaraṇa* (3.6.3).
The discussion regarding whether the *uttaravedi* is a modification (*vikāra*) or not a modification (*avikāra*) was established in the second chapter (2.1.26).

[Page 419] Śābarabhāṣya: Is the injunction "one should meditate upon Agni" a prescription for a sacrifice; or is it an independent injunction for a mere refinement (*saṃskāra*) of Agni; or is it a prescription of an accessory (*guṇa*) for sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*?
To that end, there is the doubt: does the word "Agni" function as the name of a sacrifice, or does it denote a substance (*dravya*)?
In this regard, it might be argued that there should be an injunction for a sacrifice; however, the following is stated in reply:

"Only the consecration consisting of the piling (cayana) of the fire-altar is enjoined. Its connection with a specific ritual (kratu) would be established by such sentences as 'Now, therefore, [the piling] of the fire-altar'."
This word *agniṣṭoma* is derived from fire (*vahni*), yet it is not a denoter of the sacrifice;
therefore, even in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, it is an injunction regarding a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
As for *soma*—the connection [of this discussion] is due to the opposition based on fire (*agni*) in the preceding section.
In the Siddhānta, sentences such as "Now, therefore, they sacrifice for Agni with this [offering]" (*athāto 'gnimagnimemānu yajanti*) are the ones that enjoin the *agni* offerings.

Since the *agniṣṭoma* terminus (*saṃsthā*) is to be inferred there, and since the *agni* offerings can have that as their substratum, the term "sacrifice" (*yāga*) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) in that very context to mean "by means of the *agniṣṭoma* terminus sacrifice.

However, it should be noted that in the sentences concerning the *uktha* and other terminuses, the words *uktha* and so forth refer exclusively to those terminuses themselves; they do not refer to sacrifices by virtue of being their denotable meaning (*śakyatā*), because it is precisely those terminuses—which possess results—that can function as the primary objectives (*śeṣin*) in relation to the *agni* offerings.
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the word *agni* is understood as the name of a sacrifice (*yāga*).

This is because we observe an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the form of a reference associated with the word "stotra" in the passage, "The stotra of Agni is this covering. Since the two words "stotra" and "agni" are connected to a single ritual (*kratu*), just as there is an inconsistency in the sentence containing the word "stotra," one should not accept that the word *agni* refers by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) merely to the ritual associated with it—in the injunctional sentence "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar" (*ya evaṃ vidvān agniṃ cinute*)—in the same way that [the word *agni*] is accepted as the name of a sacrifice. This is the intention of the final position (*siddhānta*).

Vi: "In the case of the injunction *agnim cinute* ('one piles the fire'), the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) refers either to the sacrifice itself or to a consecration (*saṃskṛti*). Because [the term *agni*] indicates the name of a sacrifice through its indicative power (*liṅga*) and because it is restated by means of the root *yaj*, this word *citi* is, by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the name of a substance—the fire—just like the act of installation (*ādhāna*).
The *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice is prescribed for the consecrated fire (*saṃskṛta-vahni*). Therefore, it is an injunction for a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra-vidhi*).
Bhāṭṭa: It is heard as an independent statement (*anārabhya-śruta*) that "one who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar (*agniṃ cinute*)."
In that context, the injunction is not for the purpose of preparing the fire by means of the root *ci* (to pile), but rather for the injunction of a sacrifice designated as "Agni. [As it is said:
"Now, therefore, they sacrifice to Agni with the Agnimāruta hymns; him [they sacrifice] with the Ukthya."
Section on the Fire-altar (Agnnyadhikaraṇa) 133: The establishment of the fire-altar (*agnyādhāna*) occurs in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

Regarding the subsequent statements such as "that [is performed] with the *Atirātra*, that with the thirty-two-fold [Stoma]," these refer to the *agniṣṭoma* and other terminuses (*saṃsthās*) which possess the quality of being a subsequent sacrifice to Agni (*agnyanuyajana*).

Indeed, the status of being an "after-sacrifice" (*anuyajana*) is not possible if Agni were itself the sacrifice, because the word *anu* is observed only in connection with a subordinate action, as in "Yajñadatta follows Devadatta."

And for this reason, because there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in enjoining both the word "fire" (*agni*) and the sacrifice within that very injunction, it is in the *vidvadvākya* alone that the sacrifice is enjoined through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the root *cinoti*.
And since it is unmanifest (*avyakta*), it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma. Furthermore, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the ritual is established by the subsequent sentences.

Since the piling (*cayana*) is already established by the statement "He piles the fire-altar with bricks" (*iṣṭakābhir agniṃ cinoti*), the verb *cinoti* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that piling, just like the verb *nirvapati*.

This being the prima facie view, we reply: because the word *anu* is seen in expressions such as "he eats after cooking" (*pākamanu bhuṅkte*) even in the absence of a connection with an identical action, it is not appropriate—on account of that [usage]—to assume that the words *agni* and *cayana* refer to the sacrifice.
Therefore, in the sentence concerning the knower (*vidvadvākya*), the piling itself is enjoined for this specific purpose.

Although by the word *agni* the burning fire itself could be understood, nevertheless, because that meaning would result in redundancy, it is determined—through conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍha-lakṣaṇā*)—to refer to the *āhavanīya* and other such fires. Consequently, piling (*cayana*) is enjoined as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) with reference to those fires. By virtue of its capacity as a purificatory rite, its purposeful intent consists in the establishment of the fires through the performance of the piling and other such rites.

When there is a requirement for the application of the consecrated fire (*agni*), its injunction as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is made by the sentence "Now, therefore" (*athātaḥ*).
For in that context, by the word *agni*, either the fire characterized by the refinements (*saṃskāra*) such as the completion of the piling (*cayana*) is intended,
or else the piling itself is denoted by the term *agni* through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

And although the word *agniṣṭoma* denotes a sacrificial conclusion (*saṃsthā*) according to the principle of the genus (*jāti*), it denotes the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself according to the principle of the individual (*vyakti*) due to its frequent usage, just as the word *pārtha* denotes Arjuna.

Therefore, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), being a *Jyotiṣṭoma* alone is the delimiting factor of the objective (*uddeśyatā’vacchedaka*), and not even the state of being an *agniṣṭoma* conclusion.

Although the piling (cayana) exists solely by virtue of its performance because it serves the purpose of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, nevertheless, there is no contradiction with the *tantra* (the general ritual framework) regarding the restoration of Agni’s status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the optional sacrifices (*kāmyayāga*), based on such statements as "one desiring cattle should pile [it]" (*paśukāmo ’gnim cinvīta*).

Furthermore, this Agni is optional (*vaikalpika*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*) according to the scriptural injunction, "Agni [is used] for those who desire [results] from Soma," and so forth. And in the modification (*vikṛti*), there is a combination (*samuccaya*) with the high altar (*uttaravedi*), due to the statement, "For one piles the fire upon the high altar."
And in the absence of that [altar], there is only the *uttaravedi* (northern altar), because of the scriptural injunction: "He places the fire on the *uttaravedi*.

Consequently, sentences such as "That [fire] with the *ukthya*" and so forth—being optional—are intended to provide a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) for specific modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), and to ensure the attainment of qualities whose fruits are the forms of the eagle (*syena*) and so on, which depend upon the piling (*cayana*). This will be explained in the tenth book (10.8.11–23–28). *Nyāyabindu*:

In the passage "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire," there is an injunction for a sacrifice designated as "Agni" (*agni-saṃjñaka-yāga*); however, the term "piles" (*cinoti*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the acquisition from the sentence "He piles the fire with bricks" (*iṣṭakābhir agniṃ cinute*), just like the verb "offers" (*nirvapati*).

Furthermore, the fact that the word *agni* is the name of a sacrifice is understood from the sentence "Then, therefore, they perform the sacrifice following the Agni [rite] by means of the Agniṣṭoma," because this is an injunction of the *agniṣṭoma* terminal form (*saṃsthā*) by way of referring back (*anuvāda*) to the sacrifice named *agni*, as in "that which one sacrifices with the *agni*, that is by the *agniṣṭoma*.

Likewise, the expression "they perform the sacrifice following" (*anuyajanti*) is also an indicator; for if the *agni* were not itself a sacrifice, it would be impossible for other sacrifices to follow it, since such a designation—as in "Yajñadatta follows Devadatta"—is used only between two things of the same class.
This being the position reached, we reply: here only the ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the piling (*cayana*) of the fire-altar is enjoined.

The connection with the seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu*) for that [rite] is established by sentences such as "Now, therefore, [he offers] to Agni" (*athāto 'gnim*), and the word *agni* is not an unmentioned name (*aśrutanāmadheya*).

Furthermore, the expression "he performs the after-offerings" (*anuyajati*) is appropriate even without the piling of the fire-altar (*cayana*), because the usage occurs even with heterogeneous things, as in "he eats after the cooking" (*pākamanu bhuṅkte*).
This is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Maṇḍana: "One should state the sacrifice by its name.
Śaṅkara: "The quality of fire (agni) is not part of the sacrifice.
Therefore, even for the purpose of securing the deities, the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) should not be performed in the Jyotiṣṭoma at the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites.
And because its purpose was already grasped previously.

The Commentary states: "It was said that the previously mentioned establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*), being of the *saumika* type, accomplishes the purpose in the *aiṣṭika* rites by way of incidental application" (12.1.10.19). That [point] is now being challenged.
The objection was raised because that [mantra] has the purpose of retention (*dhāraṇī*).
But it is not for the purpose of retention alone;
what then? It is both for the purpose of retention and for the purpose of securing the deity (*devatā-parigraha*).

For it is thus heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "With the words, 'May splendor be mine in the invocations,' he first takes hold of Agni; thereby he sacrifices on the following day to the deities who have already been taken hold of.

In that case, although the purpose of maintaining [the fire] is accomplished through the incidental application (*prasaṅga*) of the Saumika [rite], nevertheless, for the purpose of the formal acceptance (*parigraha*) of the deities, that Dāśīpaurṇamāsika rite belonging to the iṣṭi must be performed.
[The opponent] says: This is not correct.
The purpose of securing the favor of the deities (*devatāparigraha*) is also established as a matter of course.

Why? Because the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) has that as its purpose. Even in the *Soma* sacrifice, the offering of the wood-shavings (*śakalapādi*) for the purpose of securing the favor of the deities is heard in scripture: "One should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Agni-Viṣṇu at the consecration (*dīkṣaṇīyā*); Agni is the first of the deities, Viṣṇu is the last; in that he offers an eleven-potherd cake to Agni-Viṣṇu... [and so forth].
"Having grasped both the deity and the sacrifice from both sides, one undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*).

This very [act of *anvādhāna*] serves the purpose of grasping the deity; by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), it will accomplish the function of the rites belonging to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices. [Objection: Even if one accepts that the *anvādhāna* has the purpose of grasping the deity, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering] is nonetheless set aside [as redundant].

In reality, there is no evidence whatsoever for the view that the *anvādhāna* (the preliminary placing of fuel) is intended for the formal acquisition of the deities; thus, he states the ultimate truth: "In fact, it is not understood from the [text] that the *anvādhāna* is for the purpose of acquiring the deities.

If this were so, the statement—'By [reciting] "O Agni, may splendor be mine among all," he first acquires [them]; having thus acquired the deities through the previous [verses], he shines and sacrifices"—would make known its purpose as the acquisition of the deities.
However, such a statement cannot establish that it is for the purpose of acquiring the deities, because the sentence is merely an *arthavāda* (a commendatory or explanatory passage)."
The *anvādhāna* itself is praised by this [statement].
And in this way, there will be no assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*).
The mantra also accomplishes the subsequent [rite] by its own inherent power, and nothing else.
As for what was stated—that the initiation (*dīkṣaṇīyā*) constitutes the appropriation of the deity—that too is incorrect.
How so? By the term "being initiated" (*dīkṣyamāṇaḥ*), the agent is designated as one possessing knowledge; the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) indicates future time.
Furthermore, by the word "initiation" (*dīkṣā*), the purificatory rites such as shaving and cleansing are indicated.
Therefore, there is such an intention;
consequently, by the scriptural statement regarding the offering to Agni and Viṣṇu (āgnāvaiṣṇava),
such a refinement (saṃskāra) is enjoined in order to accomplish that initiation (dīkṣā).
Regarding that which is being enjoined, the explanatory passage (arthavāda), "He encompasses all the deities," serves as a praise for the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* offering;
such a passage cannot enjoin the encompassing of the deities.

Furthermore, if it were intended for the purpose of encompassing the deities, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), as it would simultaneously function as a refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) and as having the purpose of encompassing the deities.
And there would be the assumption of what has not been seen twice.
If it is argued that it is "like the remainder" (śeṣavat), the Bhāṣya says: It is replied, it is not established.
The *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice is for the sake of the principal [rite];
it functions in the appropriation of the deity of the principal [rite].
However, the remaining deities of the subordinate members (*aṅga*) have not been appropriated.
For the sake of its inclusion, the ritual pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapaurṇamāsika) should be performed among the iṣṭi-type rites;
however, the Vaiśvadeva is not [to be included].
The Commentary states: it need not be performed.
The *dīkṣaṇīyā* itself will accomplish the purpose of securing the deities by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).
But was it not said that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is for the purpose of securing the deities of the primary sacrifice?
Being for the purpose of securing the deities of the primary sacrifice, it secures the deities of the subsidiary rites as well.
How so? Because it is the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Indeed, there exists in the Soma ritual the Vaiśvadeva cup-offering (*grahayajña*).
Therein, all the deities are worshipped.
And within that [maṇḍala], there are also the limb-deities;
therefore, they are included.
There is no need for this Vedic fire-laying (*agnyādhāna*) performed for the purpose of appropriating that [fire].
Or rather, there may be [a need], because of the designation.
The Bhāṣya says: "Or rather, there may be a need for the Vedic fire-laying."
There is no inclusion of all deities. But surely they are included because "the Viśvedevas are sacrificed to"?
No, for not all deities are sacrificed to therein.
What then? It is a class of specific deities, such as the Sādhyas, Vasus, and Rudras. How is this known? From their specific designation.

There is a designation such as "Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Indra with the Maruts, Varuṇa with the Ādityas, Bṛhaspati with the Viśvedevas," which shows that the Viśvedevas are distinct from the Vasus and the others. For if all the gods were mentioned [by the term "Viśvedevas"], they would not be distinct from those [other groups] by means of the word "Viśvedeva."
Therefore, the term *viśvedeva* refers exclusively to a group [of deities].
If this is so, then the auxiliary deities (*aṅgadevatā*) remain unaddressed;
for their sake, the *anvādhāna* ritual pertaining to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices must be performed.
"Not so, because it is for the sake of a quality.
The Commentary says: "This is not so.
Why? Because it is for the sake of a quality."
By means of its name and designation, the Vaiśvadeva group can indeed be conceived.

The designation by means of qualities is seen in cases such as Bṛhaspati and others: Agni and the rest are associated with the Vasus and so forth alone, while Bṛhaspati is associated with all the gods, as well as with those others. It is just as a general comes accompanied by his own troops, a collector-general by his own force, and a king by all the forces, as well as by those others.
Furthermore, the Vaiśvadeva group must be postulated; however, all the deities are understood from the word itself.

Thus, the acceptance of the subsidiary deities (*aṅgadevatā*) for the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice is also accomplished by implication (*prasaṅgāt*), and therefore the establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices need not be performed for the sacrifices belonging to the Soma ritual (*aiṣṭika*).
Śā—Even though the establishment of the fires is for the purpose of accepting the deities, nevertheless it need not be performed in the *prāyaṇīyā* and subsequent rites.
For even in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiation offering], its purpose of securing the deities (*devatā-parigraha*) is heard from the scriptural statement itself.

Although, by the declaration "the initiation belongs to Soma," the *dīkṣaṇīyā*—being for the sake of the primary sacrifice—secures only the deities of the primary sacrifice, nevertheless, because all deities are present in the *vaiśvadeva-graha*, the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, while performing that securing, also secures the deities of the subsidiary rites (*aṅga-devatā*) by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).

Indeed, the word *viśvedeva* does not denote a specific group of deities, as there is no evidence for assuming a different meaning for the constituent parts of the word when its conventional sense is already available.

Therefore, because [the fire] is the speech of all deities, and because by its acceptance there is also the incidental acceptance of the limb-deities included within all [deities], the anvādhāna (the placing of fuel) need not be performed.
Alternatively, according to that accepted position, the anvādhāna must indeed be performed at the dīkṣaṇīyā [offering], but after that, it need not be performed.
[The opponent says: There is a connection [between the *anvādhāna* and the *dīkṣaṇīyā*] because of the distinction between the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and the commencement of a vow (*vratopāyana*).

Even though the *dīkṣaṇīyā* has the visible form of the acceptance of the deity (*devatāparigraha*), it serves as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the deity; thus, since that [deity] is employed in the ritual only when consecrated, it is possible for it to be the basis of what is to be accomplished (*bhāvyupajīvyatā*), just as life is the basis for the future unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa*) of the *anūyāja* offerings in the case of the animal sacrifice and others. Therefore, in the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, the *anvādhāna* must be performed for the purpose of accepting the deity. The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is: the previous *anvādhāna* would be dispensed with even for the purpose of acceptance, because the *dīkṣaṇīyā* itself serves that same purpose.

Vi— "The *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel) may or may not be for the sake of maintaining [the fires] for the gods; because it is unestablished [otherwise], it is not so, since it is established by the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. Bhāṣya—That which was stated—that because the *anvādhāna* is for the purpose of maintenance, there is no *anvādhāna* in the *soma*, *iṣṭi*, and other sacrifices—is now challenged and resolved.

The *anvādhāna* is not for the purpose of maintaining the fire; rather, by virtue of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "It is auspicious that one worships after first having taken possession of the deities," it is for the purpose of the formal acceptance of the deities.

Therefore, by the mantra-text of the verse "Enkindling [thee], O Agni... and the injunction "He first takes possession of the fire with the mantra 'Mine, O Agni, be vigor,'" all the archetypal deities are consecrated through this *anvādhāna*, which is characterized as an act of formal acceptance (*parigraha*), and are thus first indicated by the deity Agni. This is the meaning.

And therefore, even though the incidental maintenance of the fires (*agnidhāraṇa*) occurs [as a byproduct], since that is not its purpose, the *anvādhāna* must indeed be performed at the *Soma*, *Agniṣṭoma*, and other sacrifices for the sake of securing the deities (*devatāparigraha*).

This being the position reached: although that [offering] is for the purpose of securing the deities, nevertheless, because it is a means of merit, the remainder of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* passage states: "One being consecrated should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu; Agni is the first of the deities, Viṣṇu is the highest; thus, having secured the deities from both sides, he undergoes consecration. Since it is thus understood that its purpose is to secure the deities, the principle of *prasaṅga* (extended application) is rightly applicable in that very manner.

Furthermore, in the phrase "one being initiated" (*dīkṣyamāṇaḥ*), what is intended is merely the state of occurring at a subsequent time, not the state of being produced; thus, an explanation can be provided there as well.

Nor should it be argued that because of the statement "the initiations belong to the Soma [sacrifice]," the initiation is understood to pertain solely to the primary rite (*pradhāna*), and therefore, by the mere acceptance of its deities, the acceptance of the deities of the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) does not follow.

Even though initiation (*dīkṣā*) consists solely of the primary rite, there is no evidence that the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*—which brings about that initiation—has as its deity the deities of the *Āgneya* and other such constituent parts; rather, it is for the purpose of securing the deities common to both the subsidiaries and the primary rite.
As for the claim that the authors of the Sūtras and others, while accepting that the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* serves only the primary rite, [assign it] to the deity of the primary rite...

Regarding the argument that when the *vaiśvadeva* cup is drawn, because the word "viśva" (all) denotes everything, all deities are understood to be the recipients, and thus even the deities of the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*) are included by that inclusion—thereby establishing the principle of incidental performance (*prasaṅga*)—this has been refuted. For it is understood from the *Trikāṇḍī* lexicon’s traditional teaching—"āditya-viśvavasavaḥ"—that the term *viśvadeva* is a conventional designation (*rūḍhi*) for a specific group [of deities]; furthermore, since the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice has the purpose of securing the deities, there is no evidence to suggest it serves the purpose of the primary rite alone. Therefore, that argument is disregarded.
Therefore, even on the view that the purpose is the "appropriation of the deities" (*devatāparigraha*), the principle of extension (*prasaṅga*) applies correctly to the *prāyaṇīya* and other rites.

However, in the case of the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, since the appropriation of the deities is not yet known at that stage, the original (*prākṛta*) *anvādhāna* must indeed be performed for the sake of that appropriation of the deities.

In reality, however, since there is no evidence that the mention of Agni in the sentence concerning the *anvādhāna* of the *dīkṣā* day is intended as a designation of the deity, and since the *agnyādhāna* is understood—on the basis of its indicative mark (*liṅga*) and logical consistency—to have the mere purpose of maintaining the fire, and since the *dīkṣaṇīyā* is known through established scriptural statement (*śruti*) to produce consecration (*dīkṣā*), neither of these two rites has the purpose of "appropriating" the deity.

As for the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because it contains the restrictive particle *eva* in both instances and because there is no connection with the principal deity through the act of marking (*aṅkana*), it is merely a praise based on the absence of appropriation in that very context.

And for this reason, since the requirement is already fulfilled by extension (*prasaṅga*) through the taking up of the *soma* and the *āgnīdhra* fire even in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, there is no *anvādhāna* (the kindling of the fires) in that sacrifice either.

*Nyāyabindu*: The kindling of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) is also for the purpose of securing the deities, because of the scriptural text: "With the verse ‘O Agni, may splendor be mine,’ he first takes hold of the deities; having first taken hold of them, he shines and sacrifices. Thus, he secures the deities beforehand.

Thus, when the objection is raised that the *anvādhāna* (the ritual piling of fuel) must be performed for the sake of the *prāyaṇīya* and other sacrifices because it is intended for their purpose, [we reply]: since the maintenance of the fires can achieve its desired result, it is impossible to assume that its purpose is the "taking possession" (*parigraha*) of invisible deities, as that would be merely an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*). Even if such a purpose were possible, its accomplishment is achieved by the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice itself, because we hear an explanatory passage to that effect: "Agni is the first of the gods, Viṣṇu is the last; thus, having taken possession of them on both sides, he undergoes consecration (*dīkṣate*)."

Although, according to the statement "The initiation (dīkṣā) is for Soma," the Dīkṣaṇīyā [offering] is intended solely for Soma and thus the primary deity alone receives [the oblation], nevertheless, because the Viśvedevas are the deities there, the subsidiary deities also receive it.

And on this view, the *anvādhāna* must indeed be performed in the Dīkṣaṇīyā for the purpose of securing one's own deities; however, after that, it need not be performed—this is the distinction, which is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Maṇḍana says: "There is no *anvādhāna* here, nor is there a focus on other deities."
Śaṅkara says: "And [the rites] for one who has been initiated and one who has taken up the sacrificial fuel.
The establishment of the fires (agnyādhāna) in the Jyotiṣṭoma—[that] establishment of the fires need not be performed in the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other [preliminary] rites."
Because [the fires] have already been maintained, the establishment of the fires (*agnyādhāna*) does not exist in the *Soma* sacrifice.

The Commentary: Regarding the *Soma* sacrifice, in the ritual acts pertaining to the *iṣṭi* (such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*), there arises the question of whether the establishment of the fires, which is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), should be performed or not. It should be performed; in this way, the extended application will be upheld.
This being the case, it is said:
it should not be performed.
Why? Because of its being held [as a permanent rule].
That was done by Vidvatsna for the sake of Soma;
by him, Agni was sustained.
Furthermore, there is no need for the act of holding that which has already been held.
But is it not true that it was performed without mantras?
True, it was without mantras; however, it was nonetheless performed.
Furthermore, once something has been performed as a mantra, there is no repetition; therefore, it should not be done again. [Objection:
As before, since it has not been previously established, its separate performance must be undertaken—this is the connection.

That which is called *anvādhāna* is the initial act of placing fuel for the purpose of maintaining the fire immediately after the ritual distribution (*viharaṇa*), consisting of the activity of kindling by means of wood; it is an activity consisting of the placing of wood, and not merely the placing for the purpose of kindling.

Since the initial operation [of the fire] follows immediately after the *viharaṇa* (carrying forth of the fires), there is no possibility of performing the *anvādhāna* (replenishing of the fuel) repeatedly;
for, in the absence of a repetition of the *viharaṇa*, it is impossible to perform the *anvādhāna* again and again.
Regarding this, [the view is]: "The *anvādhāna* should take place at the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites, or it does not exist [there]; it does exist."

The objectors say: There is no [need for] the first kindling of the fires with mantras for one who has already performed the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) according to the procedure of the Soma sacrifice. Bhaṭṭa: In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the first kindling of the fires with mantras is prescribed either after the *praṇayana* or after the making manifest (*prāduṣkaraṇa*).

Although that [kindling] is obtained by extension (*atideśa*) in the Agniṣṭut and other Soma rites, such as the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*, it is not to be performed; for the kindling has already been accomplished prior to that, as part of the overall Soma ritual following the *praṇayana*.

Although that [act of kindling] is implied by the context and its purpose is already attained, nevertheless, because the ritual action has already been accomplished for that very purpose, there is no separate performance of it in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites. Nor can it be argued that since the kindling was performed once, it must be repeated with the mantra; for by the injunction, "With the mantra *mamāgne varcaḥ*, he first encircles the fire," the application of the mantra is prescribed only for the initial establishment of the fire (*agnyādhāna*) subsequent to the bringing forward of the water (*praṇayana*).

Nor does the repetition of the mantra apply to each act of holding [the fire] on the grounds that the first word, by virtue of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "fire," refers specifically to the *āhavanīya* fire—according to the principle that a subordinate element (*guṇa*) repeats for each primary element (*pradhāna*)—because Bodhāyana, having accepted that the first word functions as an adverbial qualifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) due to its application to the kindling of the *gārhapatya* fire, maintains that it pertains to the injunction for the initial kindling.

For this very reason, the view held by some—that the word *pūrva* (in the compound *pūrvair-yudh*) refers to "previous time" in order to conform to the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "Having performed the *samidhenī* offerings on the previous [day], one should sacrifice on the following day"—is refuted. This is because it would entail a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*), and because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to repeat the mantras for each of the numerous *samidhenī* fuel-sticks offered on the previous day. Furthermore, it would result in the impossibility of performing the *samidhenī* offerings and the *anvādhāna* (placing of the fire) at the same time as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), which is characterized by being performed on the same day (*sadyaḥ-kāla*). Moreover, the argument that the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are accomplished through "extended application" (*prasaṅga*) due to their being performed on the same day cannot withstand scrutiny.

Therefore, since the injunction of the mantra for the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel) is performed in exactly the same manner [as in the model sacrifice], its application (*prasaṅga*) to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites is indeed appropriate.

*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the question of whether the *anvādhāna* should be performed in the Soma-related sacrifices belonging to the *iṣṭi* class—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) being that it should be done—the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it need not be performed. This is because the *anvādhāna* serves the purpose of maintaining the fires, and since those fires are already maintained for the sake of the Soma sacrifice, the required purpose is accomplished through that very maintenance (*prasaṅgasiddhi*).
Maṇḍana: "But there is no initial application of the fires within the middle of the sacrifice."
The term *ādadhati* refers to the *anvādhāna*.
Śaṅkara states: "In the *Soma* sacrifice, that which was established at the *agnyādhāna* is the *anvādhāna*. *Anvādhāna*.
This is called *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel) and also *anvāhita*.

What is it? The *anvādhāna* pertaining to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices need not be performed separately in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, because it is accomplished by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*) through the ritual arrangement (*viharaṇa*) belonging to the Soma sacrifice.

The *anvādhāna* (the ritual piling of fuel) in the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, even for the purpose of securing the deities in the *iṣṭi*-type rites, need not be performed; for, just as with the principal deities, the subordinate deities (*ājñadevatā*) are already secured [by that act]. Bhāṣya 12.1.12.24–28. If the *anvādhāna* is for the purpose of securing the deities, it must nevertheless be performed separately in the *nirāhuti*. By the original *agnyanvādhāna*, the deities of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) are secured, but they are not secured by the [deities] such as Rakṣohā and the rest.

Regarding the *anvādhāna* (the preliminary rite of placing fuel), those ritualists who maintain that it is performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) alone do so based on this very mantra-text (*mamāgne varcaḥ*). However, even if they cite some other scriptural statement, there remains the deliberation as to whether the result varies according to the option between the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer, as in the case of optional rites, or whether it is invariably the duty of the sacrificer alone.
The conclusion is that it belongs to the sacrificer.
Or [it may be so]. Pāṇini 3.8.124:
The *anvādhāna* (the ritual of adding fuel) belongs to the office of the Adhvaryu priest when it is undertaken as part of a sacrificial session (*samāravyā*).
And thus, a mantra possessing such qualities performs the function of the Adhvaryu.
It is said that [the mantra] is recited by this [person];
therefore, the mantra belongs to the Adhvaryu.
Furthermore, even in the mantra "O Agni, may splendor be mine," one designates the sacrificer’s splendor as "mine" through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

Bhā. 3|8|13126: By means of the *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel), the fire is established; through that act of maintaining the fire (*agnyādheya*), there is the formal acceptance of the deities (*devatāparigraha*).
12.4.119: By means of the *anvādhāna* (the adding of fuel), the deities are encompassed, not by name.

Thus it is heard in scripture: "He who takes up the fire on the previous day shall indeed sacrifice to the deities on the following morning. 12.4.125: That the purpose of the *anvādhāna* is the encompassing of the deities is heard in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) [of the mantra]: "O Agni, may my luster be among the gods"—thus he first encompasses the fire; thereby the deities themselves are encompassed on the previous day, and he sacrifices on the following morning.
Even for the purpose of taking possession (*parigraha*), it indeed serves the purpose of pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*).

Among ritualists, it is well known that the first constituent act (*padārtha*) consisting of the placing of fuel (*anvādhāna*) and so forth constitutes the commencement of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
(Bhāṭṭa 9.1.11)

The primary purpose for the *anvādhāna* (adding fuel to the fire) and other such acts is that which is about to be performed; however, for the *sviṣṭakṛt* and others, it is that which has already been performed.
From the *anvādhāna* up until the *upākaraṇa* (the formal dedication of the animal), these acts are common to all [the offerings] and are performed once. (Durmūla 5.1.58)
Fire and other such things which are well known as the illuminators of jars and the like are not themselves of the nature of illumination, for illumination does not depend upon them.
Even when words denoting deities such as Agni are employed, there is no violation of Prajāpati’s status as the seventeenfold [sacrifice].

In cases such as "O Agni, recite" (*agne 'nubrūhi*), there is no reason to assume an addition of the word "Agni" in the formulas "Sacrifice to Agni" (*agniṃ yaja*) and "We sacrifice to Agni" (*ye yajāmahe agnim*) for the sake of joining with the respective deities; for this would result in the breaking of the seventeen-fold nature of the *śastra* (recitation). Furthermore, since there is no evidence for an improper assumption based on a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from a restrictive rule, it is appropriate to supply the required verbal form of the action by implication (*arthādhyāhāra*), just as in the case of "I cut" (*chinadmi*). Even if the word "Agni" were supplied, there is no evidence for a restriction that it must occur only at the beginning of the *praisha* (direction) and at the end of the response; rather, those two [formulas] should be employed with exactly two syllables and five syllables respectively. This being the prima facie view, we reply: even if the word common to all deities is supplied, the seventeen-fold nature of the *śastra* remains intact.

Furthermore, since the supplying of an implied meaning (*arthādhyāhāra*) has been rejected, and because there would otherwise result a violation of the established principle of having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) in the immediately preceding section—due to the absence of the specific deity-word and the specific act of renunciation (*tyāga*) required for the particular sacrifice—the name of the deity must be enjoined.

For this very reason, in other scriptures, in such injunctions as "Recite for that one" (*amuṣmā anubrūhi*) and "Sacrifice to that one" (*amuṃ yaja*), the word *adaḥ* (that) is heard as indicating the specific name of the deity. Likewise, the restriction of the referent of the deity-word is also derived from this very source, as seen in such formulas as "Come, O so-and-so" (*asāvehi*), "Having cut off that one" (*avadhiyāmuṃ*), and "This [I offer] to so-and-so" (*idamahamamuṣya*).

As for the argument that an indicative mark (*liṅga*) was stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*—namely, "In the case of the *tanūnapāt* [offering], one should say 'Sacrifice to Tanūnapāt! Recite for the *iḍā*s! [but] one should simply say 'Sacrifice, sacrifice!'"; and based on such indicative marks as "Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa* regarding the *adhvan* [offering] to the Maruts, one should say 'Recite for the Maruts! Sacrifice to the Maruts!'"—it follows that the deity-word is obtained elsewhere as well; this is not so. For in another scripture (*śāstra*), the reading is simply "Sacrifice to Tanūnapāt," and since the former [text] serves to prohibit that [reading], while the latter can be understood as a positive injunction, it actually proves the opposite. This has been stated in that very same work.
Saṃkarṣa 2.3.2:
*Agnyādheya*. It is simply the placing or establishing of the fires.

For a householder who has a wife and sons, three or five sacred fires must first be established according to the prescribed rite for the purpose of performing all the Śrauta rituals, such as the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, and the Jyotiṣṭoma. It is through this ritual that, once purified, the Śrauta rites are performed in the Āhavanīya and other fires.

This very act is designated by the terms *ādhāna*, *anvādhāna*, and *agnyādheya*. What is this *agnyādheya*? It is not performed for the sake of specific ritual fires (*agni*), but rather for the sake of all ritual acts (*karman*).

Thus it is said that [the fire-laying] is for all purposes (sarvārtha). Bhāṣya 3.6.15–16: The establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) is not for the sake of the Pavamāna offerings; rather, the Pavamāna offerings themselves are for the sake of the fires.

In the case of a conditional modification of the *guṇa* (accessory) in the *Agnyādheya*, there should be an additional gift of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), because of its connection with the scriptural statement.

Regarding the *Ādhāna*, the following sacrificial fees are heard in scripture: "One should be given; six should be given; twelve should be given; twenty-four should be given; a hundred should be given; a thousand should be given; an unlimited amount should be given.

Now, the conditional re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) is also heard in scripture: "He who, having established the fires, suffers loss of fortune, loss of cattle, or loss of sons, should establish them again" (*jyāniḥ* means loss or destruction).

In that regard, concerning the *punarādheya* (re-consecration) which is contingent upon a specific cause, since the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is already established [from the original *agnyādheya*], there arises the possibility of sublation (*bādha*) due to the modification [of the fee] by the following scriptural statements:

"A chariot repaired again is the fee," "A garment woven again is the fee," and "An ox that has calved again is the fee. Nevertheless, the giving of the fee should be additional because of its connection with the scriptural statement: "He gives both: those belonging to the *agnyādheya* and those belonging to the *punarādheya*."

Therefore, in the case of re-establishment (*punarādheya*), there is a combination of both sets of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*): those pertaining to the first establishment (*āgnyādheyika*) and those pertaining to the re-establishment (*puna-rādheyika*). It is not the case that either only the *āgnyādheyika* or only the *puna-rādheyika* fees apply; this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Regarding the other [fees], they are like those prescribed by the learned authorities (*śiṣṭa*) according to their respective places. He states another argument for the prima facie view:

In accordance with their respective places, without overstepping the sequence, and following the order, there remains the principle of the subsequent bringing forward (*abhyānayananyāya*) for the others— the modified rites distinct from the archetypal ones—
because these archetypal sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), such as one cow, six cows, and so forth, have been prescribed and remain [to be applied].
Therefore, there is a combination.
For the optional rites belong to their own specific context;
thus, setting aside the prima facie view reached by the two preceding sūtras with the word "but" (tu), he states the established conclusion.

If, however, the statements "the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is not-greedy again," "the garment is not-greedy again," and "the ox is not-greedy again" were to occur within the context of the original establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), then they would not set aside the sacrificial fee of that original establishment.

But since they occur outside of the context—meaning in the absence of the context of the original *ādhāna*—the qualities such as "not-greediness" prescribed for the re-establishment (*punarādheya*) apply specifically to the original *ādhāna* performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*) or as a regular obligatory rite (*nitya*).
Therefore, the sacrificial fees of the optional and occasional re-establishments are modifications of the sacrificial fee of the original *ādhāna*.
Furthermore, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for re-establishing the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) sublates the sacrificial fee of the original establishment; there is no combination (*samuccaya*).
It is a modification (*vikāra*), because the words of the Sūtra state: "For the optional rites are recited in the context of the removal [of the fires]."
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for re-establishing the sacred fires is a modification that supersedes the sacrificial fee for the original establishment;
for this reason, the optional materials for the sacrificial fee of re-establishment take precedence over those of the original establishment when they are set aside,
as in the case of the optional "Amṛtā" rite which lacks the "Apriya" verses.

By that same reasoning (*durvailena*), the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*ṛtvarthatva*) is obtained for [the suffixes] *śnā* and *rat* through their context (*prakaraṇa*). However, in this case, because the nature of the act of drawing [the Soma] as qualified by a deity—such as in the case of the *aindravāyava* and others—is composed of a non-worldly deity, it lacks worldly renown (*lokaprasiddhi*) like *śnā* and *rat*. Therefore, since the recitation of the *vyūha* in the twelfth chapter serves the purpose of establishing the status within the context by way of making known that very nature [of the act], and because there would otherwise be meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), one cannot conclude that the status of being for the sake of the sacrifice is obtained merely on that basis.
Thus it must be said.

Even so, because of the connection with the accusative case in expressions such as "aindravāyavam," there is an understanding that [the mention of the cups] is for the purpose of consecrating the substance used in the sacrifice; and since its status as being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) follows from that very fact, it is more appropriate to assume that the intention of that specific sentence is precisely that.

If, however, its purpose were merely to make known the mere form [of the cup], then, like the recitation of the *vyūha*, the mention of the cup would have been recorded as being primary in itself, rather than as something serving to consecrate a substance used in the ritual.

Therefore, because they are recorded here as being preparatory (*saṃskāraka*), the injunctions that prescribe the attainment of the *aindravāyava* and other cups—though they function with the intent of serving the sacrifice (*kratvartha*)—possess, even in the sentence connected to a specific desire (*kāma*), only the quality of being helpful by way of making their own nature known directly; however, this does not mean that they serve desire alone.

Furthermore, even the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in "speech is [the cup]" and so forth does not constitute a direct connection to the sacrifice; rather, such a connection must be inferred because these are restatements (*punarāmnāna*) of things already established by their respective individual injunctions.

Therefore, it is better to assume that [the mention] serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*ṛtvartha*) by virtue of its power as a preparatory act (*saṃskāraka*). Furthermore, the repeated recitation is indeed meaningful, because—as explained above—it excludes the status of being a substratum for the optional qualities such as the precedence of the *śukra* cup, which are intended for the sake of the *upaśantvartha* [sacrifices]. Thus, how could there be any pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) in that? Consequently, the very purpose is as stated in the text. The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: there should be a displacement (*apakarṣa*) of the *śukra* and other cups from after the *aindravāyava* cup to before the *upaśantvartha* cups; for, under the heading of the "holder of the stream" (*dhārāgrāhaka*), that very [displacement] has been established as the injunction for the optional precedence and so forth.
"He [the previously mentioned *pratikarṣa*] may be either at the beginning of the *sarva* section, or at the beginning of the *aindrāyava* section, or here without distinction;

or it may be at the beginning of the *āśraya*, or even at the beginning of the *dhṛti* in the *aindrāyava* section. Thus there is a doubt as to whether that aforementioned *pratikarṣa* should be placed at the beginning of the *sarva* section, or before the *aindrāyava* section.

In this matter, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, without distinction, [the rule applies] to all [soma-vessels] at the beginning. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that there is a displacement (*pratikarṣa*) [of the rule] to the Aindravāyava and subsequent vessels, because of the scriptural mention of the "holding of the stream" (*dhārāgrahaṇa*) and because it is stated in the *Śruti*: "They should hold it. The Bhaṭṭa school maintains that even this displacement is not possible, because there is no evidence for the term "vessel" (*graha*) to indicate such a restriction; rather, by virtue of the great context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), it is logical that the support [of the rite] belongs to all vessels. Furthermore, since the statement "this is indeed speech" (*vāg eṣā*) serves another purpose, it cannot be assumed to override the great context. Thus, the displacement is untenable.
[Objection: "Because it has the purpose of pacifying everything, [the drawing] must occur even before that.

This being the position reached, [we reply: since the purpose stated by the author of the *Tantra* has been refuted, and because another purpose also serves as a purpose only by way of harmonizing with the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), and because when that [context] is applied, the drawing of the stream (*dhārāgrahaṇa*) itself can logically be established as the substratum, the drawing of the *śukra* and others must occur earlier within those very [streams].

*Nyāyabindu*: Since there is no distinction, it follows that the *śukra* cup should be drawn at the beginning of all [the cups]. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: because the drawing of the *aindravāyava* and other cups is the context (*prakṛta*), the priority of the *śukra* cup is enjoined only with respect to that [specific sequence] as its substratum; therefore, there is no retroactive displacement of the priority from the very beginning of all [the cups]. This is precisely the purpose of the mention in the upcoming text, "The *aindravāyava* cups are drawn," namely, that they obtain the status of being the substratum. Maṇḍana: "Even in the case of an optional rite (*kāmya*), [the priority] would not apply to all the cups."
"Drawing back.
Śaṅkara says: "But that [drawing back] is based on the receptacle for the stream;
that is the state of being foremost."

*Amṛtā*:—(Sūtra 10.15.62) "In the beginning" (*agre*) means at the start. Regarding the *dhārā-grahas* (stream-cups) that are drawn at the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, the distinction as to which cup is to be drawn first is stated according to the difference in *sāman* chants: "If the Soma sacrifice has the *Rathantara-sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with the *Aindravāyava*; if it has the *Bṛhat-sāman*, those beginning with the *Śukra*; if it has the *Jagat-sāman*, those beginning with the *Āgrayaṇa*," and so forth.
In the case of the *bṛhat-sāman*, the *śukra* cup is drawn first, followed by the *aindravāyava* and the others; this is the rule everywhere.
This is indicated by the term "precedence" (*agratā*).
What is known is the specific position of the *amṛta* cup itself: that it should be placed before and in front of the two cups used for the *upaśanta* rite.
[The word] *bhā.* [stands for] *bhāṣyam*.
And its being for the sake of assisting that [means] its being the cause of that assistance.
Therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) even in cases such as the performance of a subsidiary part of a primary rite (*pradhāna-aṅga*) which produces a benefit for the primary rite itself.
Here, this should be understood:

even in the definition of that which serves the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the age of five years and so forth—which is dependent on the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and other rites performed at the time of a desired result (*kāmya*)—nor to the curd-offering and the like, which constitute a desired genus (*jāti*); for these two are not themselves things to be performed (*ananuṣṭheya*).

The definition of "being for the sake of the sacrifice" (*kratvarthatva*) suffers from over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the previously cited examples such as the cow and so forth. Furthermore, since both *ādhāna* (the fire-consecration) and *adhyayana* (Vedic study) are distinct from [the category of] sacrifices, and since they are not mentioned therein, there is an over-extension of the definition of "being for the sake of the sacrifice" to those cases as well. By this, the statement in the *Śāstradīpikā*—that "being for the sake of the sacrifice" consists in being connected as a procedure (*itikartavyatā*), while "being for the sake of the person" (*puruṣārthatva*) consists in being desired for that [sacrifice]—is also refuted.

There is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of "aiming at the human goal" (*puruṣārtha-lakṣaṇa*) with respect to *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) and *adhyayana* (Vedic study). Furthermore, because established entities such as *soma* and the like lack the status of being integrated as the "procedure" (*itikartavyatātvena*), both definitions would respectively suffer from over-extension and under-extension (*avyāpti*). If it is considered that even those [established entities] possess the status of being a procedure in relation to their own operations (*vyāpāra*) and so forth, then [the definition] is "burnt" (*dagdha*); for, since they serve both purposes, there is an absence of the desire for them [as mere ends] therein, and thus the definition of aiming at the human goal suffers from under-extension (*avyāpti*). This is how it should be understood.

(He quotes and refutes [the position] found in the *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* on the fourth chapter: Some maintain that "being for the sake of the person" (*puruṣārthatva*) consists in having a prescribability (*vidheyatā*) not determined by being an object desired by oneself or by being an object residing in a location other than oneself; whereas "being for the sake of the ritual" (*kratvarthatva*) consists in having a prescribability not determined by being an object residing in something distinct from what is desired by oneself. Here, "being desired by oneself" is as previously defined. Furthermore, "objecthood" (*uddeśyatā*) and "prescribability" (*vidheyatā*) are here understood as relations of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), and not as consisting of the states of being an end-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*) or being an action-to-be-performed (*anuṣṭheyatva*).
By this, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) even in cases where [an action] is not to be performed at a specific time;

nor is there over-pervasion (ativyāpti) in the case of permissive injunctions (*abhyanujñāvidhi*) regarding human goals (*puruṣārtha*), even when those various actions are enjoined with the aim of the absence of defects. Furthermore, since the enkindling of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and Vedic study (*adhyayana*) are enjoined with the aim of acquiring knowledge of objects other than what is sought by oneself, there is no fault even if their being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*) is accepted.

Regarding the sūtra "And the fruit [is not a subordinate element], because it is for the sake of the person" (3.1.3), some say that the designation of the fruit as being "for the sake of the person" is merely figurative, just like the designation of something as a "subordinate element" (*aṅga*). However, even that is not correct according to the literal sense.

For the mantra "agnim," by virtue of a scriptural injunction (*śruti*) inferred through its indicative power (*liṅga*), is enjoined with heaven—sought by the person—as its objective; thus, the definition of "being for the sake of the person" would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to that case.

For this very reason, because there is an absence of a non-determined status as the predicate (*vidheya*) due to the fact that the subject (*uddeśa*) is not distinct from what is desired by the agent himself, the definition of "being for the sake of the ritual" (*kratvarthatva*) also suffers from the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*).

Furthermore, in cases such as "one desiring rain should employ *hīṣ* as the *nidhana*," where *hīṣ* and so forth are enjoined with respect to rain through the relationship of being the substratum of the *nidhana* of the *saubhara* chant—which is not itself a means to that [rain]—the definition [of "being for the sake of the person"] suffers from over-extension (*ativyāpti*), while the definition of "being for the sake of the ritual" suffers from under-extension (*avyāpti*). (The meaning is: the definition of "being for the sake of the person" is over-extensive, and the definition of "being for the sake of the ritual" is under-extensive.)

For their status as human goals (puruṣārtha) is not accepted. Since there is no scriptural injunction [for them as independent goals], and since *hīṣ* and the others—prescribed as bases for the *saubhari*-finale (*nidhana*)—would otherwise apply indifferently as bases for the *saubhari*-finale intended for rain, the sentences "One desiring rain should make *hīṣ* the finale," "One desiring vigor (*ūrj*) should make [it] so," and "One desiring heaven should make *ū* [the finale]," merely establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding *hīṣ* and the others in relation to the *saubhari*-finale for those respective fruits.

Therefore, by the aforementioned relationship, although *hīṣ* and so forth are actually based upon the respective *nidhanas* of the *saubhara* for the sake of specific results such as rain, it is precisely through their connection to those *nidhanas* that *hīṣ* and so forth serve as the means to those respective results.

Nor should it be argued: "Even so, let there be an injunction of *hīṣ* and so forth based on their connection to the *nidhana* of the *saubhara*, while the terms 'desirous of rain' (*vṛṣṭikāma*) and so on indicate the *saubhara* as the means to rain;
thus, since the *saubhara* itself is not desired by the person enjoining it, there would be no other [result] at all. This cannot be maintained.

Because it is improper to resort to a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for that which is delimited by a heavy property (*gurudharma*) in order to conform to the parsimony of a subsequent restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), and because, in comparison to that, it is more appropriate to accept the injunction of *hīṣ* and so forth with reference to another fruit—as established in the fifth stage of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *Saubharādhikaraṇa* (2.1.3)—the conclusion (*siddhānta*) of that section would otherwise be untenable.

Therefore, by virtue of the parsimony of the restrictive injunction, the intended meaning of the conclusion in that very context lies precisely in the manner described; thus, that alone has been set forth in that section.

Therefore, how can it be appropriate to state that there is a single injunction regarding both the mention (*uddeśa*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*)? For this very reason, one should maintain the conviction that it is precisely according to the method stated therein.

In reality, in such passages as "One desiring rain should employ *hīṣ* as the *nidhana*," there is no injunction of *hīṣ* and so forth with respect to rain and the like through the aforementioned relationship; for if that were the case, it would be impossible for rain—which is heard as a qualification of the person desiring *hīṣ*—to be construed as the object of the injunction (*uddeśya*), and it would result in the word "desiring rain" (*vṛṣṭikāma*) involving a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of rain, and the verbal suffix (*śruti*) involving a figurative indication of being the object of an action (*karmatva*).

Therefore, rather than resorting to two distinct figurative indications (*lakṣaṇā*), it is more appropriate—given the single term *nidhana*—to assume a figurative indication of the *nidhana* as that which brings about rain within that very term, and to enjoin the *hīṣ* and other syllables for that specific purpose alone. This is because, if a second accusative case followed the word *nidhana*, it would result in a further figurative indication, since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) would then imply a status of being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvarthatva*). Nor should it be argued that our position necessitates accepting another figurative indication, on the grounds that we accept a possessive compound (*karmadhāraya*) in words such as *vṛṣṭikāma*.

Nevertheless, it is more appropriate [to interpret] the word *nidhana* through a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—wherein the objecthood (*karmatva*) is not delimited by its own delimitor of capacity (*svaśakyatāvacchedaka*)—with respect to the fourth [syllable], because it is possible for a word situated in proximity to the injunction to provide the objective (*uddeśya*), whereas a remote word is unfit for such a role. Furthermore, in your view, the restatement (*anuvāda*) of the word *nidhana* would be purposeless.

Nor is its utility [as a definition] due to its grasping the relationship (*saṃbandha*) or the intended meaning (*tātparya*); for since "being for the sake of the sacrifice" (*kratvarthatva*) is simply "being a distinct auxiliary (*aṅga*) supported by the parsimony of restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*)," there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the previously stated definition of *kratvarthatva*. If this is argued, we say no. Because the definition would over-pervade (*ativyāpti*) the eating of food and so forth performed at a marriage ceremony, which is enjoined with the intention of removing defects (*doṣābhāva*) and is thus for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). This is because the absence of a defect is not something produced; and since "causality" (*janakatva*) is a pervasive property, it is impossible to construct a definition based upon it.

Furthermore, [the definition] characterized as "having the purpose of a ritual action" (*karmārthatva*) suffers from the fault of being under-extensive (*avyāpti*) with respect to things that serve both purposes, pairs of things, and so forth.
Therefore, it should be stated as follows:

"The state of being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*) consists in possessing a status as a thing to be enjoined (*vidheyatā*) that is qualified by being an objective (*uddeśyatā*) directed toward a visible result (*dṛṣṭa*) desired by oneself, which is not delimited by being for the sake of the *apūrva*."

And this [definition] exists in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices enjoined with heaven as their objective (*uddeśya*), because there is no lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) when heaven and the like are of an unspecified manner; thus, the status of being the objective residing therein is delimited by "heavenness" (*svargatva*) and so forth.

Here, according to the method previously stated, the qualification of the objective as "not being delimited by the state of being for the sake of the *apūrva*" (*apūrvīyatvānavacchinnatva*) is added to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Agnihotra and similar rites.

In that regard, since it has been established in the commentary on (1.1.3) that the objective residing in heaven and the like is indeed delimited by the state of being for the sake of the *apūrva*, there is no fault.

Since there is no lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) in the form of [the injunction] "one should bring near" (*āivanīyādi*), the property of being an *āhavanīya* fire and so forth serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the objective (*uddeśyatā*). Consequently, the qualifier is the state of being a "predicability" (*vidheyatā*) that is defined by an objectivity not delimited by "being for the sake of the transcendental result" (*apūrvīyatva*). For this very reason, in the case of the passage beginning with "hīṣ etc.," although the objectivity residing in the *nidhana* (finale) is delimited by "being a *nidhana* that produces rain," there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because it lacks the property of "subsisting in what is desired by itself" (*svaprārthitatvavṛttitva*), even though it is not delimited by "being for the sake of the transcendental result."

Thus, *kratvarthatva* (being for the sake of the sacrifice) consists in possessing a predicatedness (*vidheyatā*) that is qualified by a subjecthood (*uddeśyatā*) distinct from the subjecthood characterized by the aforementioned status of being for the sake of a human goal (*puruṣārthatva*). And this "distinctness" from the aforementioned subjecthood consists in the absence of being delimited by the property of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*) of the aforementioned subjecthood. For the subjecthood residing in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices—which is qualified by the predicatedness of the injunctions regarding the *prājāpatya* and other offerings—possesses both absences mentioned above.

Since the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves are not the intended objects (*uddeśya*)—because they would otherwise be purposeless and because they lack the quality of being desired for their own sake—they are instead intended as the means to the *apūrva*. Therefore, the offspring and other such results serve the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*). If one were to state merely that there is no absence of being delimited by the *apūrva*, then in cases such as "he cuts the sacrificial post" (*yūpaṃ chinatti*) or "he sprinkles [it] with a thousand golden jars," there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the cutting and so forth. This is because, in the form of the post itself, there is no purposelessness, and thus the definition of being for the sake of the *apūrva* (*apūrvīyatva*) would be absent; consequently, the post and the like would become the intended objects of the injunction.
Thus, if one were to state merely the absence of the occurrence of being desired by oneself (*svaprārthita*), there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in the case of fire and the like;
therefore, the pursuit extends to the absence of both.
And so, [the definition applies] to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the like, by virtue of their being intended as objects of desire by oneself.

There is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), because [the example] possesses the absence of both [properties] due to being endowed with intrinsic nature (*svābhāvya*), and because it possesses the absence of the absence of being delimited by *apūrva*-ness due to its status as an objective (*uddeśyatā*) residing in heaven (*svarga*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the fact that the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) and other such acts serve the purpose of the ritual (*kratvartha*) is indeed accepted.
Now, an objection is raised: in the case of "He pours curds into the heated milk," it is accepted (as stated in 8.2.4) that the pouring of curds is enjoined with the milk as the objective.
Siddhānta:
In that case, milk (*payas*) is not the objective (*uddeśya*) by virtue of being a means to the *apūrva*.
This is because, prior to the operation of this sentence, there is no cognition of milk as a means to the *apūrva*, and therefore figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by the word "milk" is impossible.

For, unlike the case of rice where its status as a means to the *apūrva* is understood through a sentence such as "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*)—which functions independently of sentences like "they thresh the rice" (*vrīhīn avahanti*)—no sentence whatsoever, independent of the present context, has established that milk is a means to the *apūrva*. Consequently, since the delimiting property (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) would not have been previously presented, there could be no secondary denotation (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "milk" (*payas*) in the sense of the rice found in the sentence regarding threshing, based on that delimiting property. However, the sentence "That [offering] is the Vaiśvadevī sacrifice" (*sā vaiśvadevy āmikṣā*) refers back to the milk specifically indicated by the present context.

Because it is understood from scripture that [the *bṛhaspatisava*] is a constituent part of the preparatory application (*prayoga*), there is no purposelessness (*ānarthakya*) regarding either the essential nature of the *vājapeya* sacrifice or the nature of the supreme *apūrva* produced by it. Consequently, according to the principle of the *prakaraṇa-kalpita-vākya* (a sentence inferred from the context) or the *vaibhrathanyāya* (4.3.11), the *bṛhaspatisava* is not enjoined with reference to the *vājapeya* as a means to the *apūrva*; rather, it is enjoined with reference to the *vājapeya* as a means to the fruit consisting of sovereignty (*svārājya*). Furthermore, since an injunction made with reference to a qualification is necessarily required even when an injunction is made with reference to a subject, the *bṛhaspatisava* is enjoined with reference to sovereignty as well. Thus, in all cases where the definition consists of the inclusion of the deity desired by oneself, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the *bṛhaspatisava* to instances such as the *hīp* mantra mentioned by the Navyas.

Furthermore, if one examines closely, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the definition of being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*), which consists in being delimited by something not previously established (*apūrva*). Therefore, in the definition of being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārthatva*), the qualification "not being a delimiter of its own objecthood" (*svoddeśyatānavacchedakatva*) is added as a modifier to "being desired by itself" (*svaprārthitatva*). The word "itself" (*sva*) refers to that which is intended as being desired by itself.

Since universal sovereignty (*svārājya*) is a delimiter of the *Bṛhaspatisava* sacrifice—which resides in the *Vājapeya* and other rites—there is no over-extension [in the definition of *puruṣārthatva*].
That which is desired by oneself—that is, that which possesses the status of being the predicate (vidheyatā) as determined by a deity—is not "for the sake of the ritual" (kratvartha).
Therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti).

Furthermore, regarding the term "unprecedented" (apūrva), if there is an injunction for the sake of heaven as the unprecedented result, then because the injunction for the sake of the unprecedented is necessarily implied, all of this must be understood by taking the deity within the application of the unprecedented (apūrvaniyoga).
Each of these two kinds of auxiliary (aṅga) is further twofold:
established in form (siddharūpa) and consisting of action (kriyārūpa).
Among these, that which begins with the *mī* [roots] is established in form and serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*).
That which is of the nature of action and subserves the ritual purpose includes the *prayāja* offerings, the *avaghāta* (threshing), and so forth.
Likewise, that which is of the nature of an accomplished entity and subserves the human purpose includes curd, the *godohana* vessel, and so forth.
That which is of the nature of action and subserves the human purpose includes the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and so forth.
