And for the purpose of establishing the nature of ritual action (*kriyārūpaka*), it is twofold: *saṃnipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing) and *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly contributing).

Among these, a ritual act (*karman*) is *saṃnipatyopakāraka* when it possesses a prescriptive status (*vidheyatā*) determined by a state of being intended (*uddeśyatā*) residing in either the substance (*dravya*) or the deity (*devatā*).
Examples include sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), threshing (*avaghāta*), the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the cake offering (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth.

Regarding the injunction, "Having performed the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, one should offer the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) on eleven potsherds for Agni and Soma," it has been stated in the *Tantravārttika* (10.1.9) that this animal-cake is indeed for the purpose of consecrating the deity of the animal sacrifice, with the female gender [of the victim] serving as the objective reference. In this context, if the definition were merely "that which possesses a prescriptiveness (*vidheyatā*) determined by an objectivity (*uddeśyatā*) residing in a substance (*dravya*)," there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood," where properties like being made of *parṇa*-wood are established facts (*siddharūpa*) and are subservient to the purpose (*kratvartha*), yet do not reside in a substance. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "action" (*karman*) is necessary.
As for the claim that an action which effects the refinement of either the substance or the deity is a *saṃnipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing) action—
that is not correct.

This is because there is no single property of "being a refinement" (*saṃskāratva*) that resides solely in the purely visible refinement produced by the *prayāja* and other such rites as they pertain to the sacrificer, and thus a definition based on that [single property] is impossible.

Some, however, say that "directly contributing" (saṃnipatyopakāraka) consists in possessing a status as something to be enjoined (vidheyatā), which is defined by a purpose (uddeśyatā) delimited by being a means to the apūrva residing in either the substance or the deity.

Otherwise, even the Jyotiṣṭoma—though enjoined with reference to a person desiring heaven—would incur the status of being directly contributing, just like the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites enjoined with reference to the person [seeking initiation].
This is not correct.
Because the cutting and so forth are enjoined with reference to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they are not intended for the sacrifice itself.

Therefore, since there is no lack of purpose (*ānarthakya*) in their own form as possessing eight characteristics and the like, they are not intended for the sake of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency). However, it is established that the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites are indeed enjoined with reference to the person.

Since there is no possibility of that which already exists in a perfected form being the object of cultivation (*bhāvya*) when there is a requirement for such an object in the context of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), words such as "one desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) must, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), refer to heaven and the like [as the result].

Alternatively, if it is considered that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because [the definition] applies to things like the *uddiṣṭa* (the designated) since they are enjoined with reference to substances such as the *padārtha*, then let the inclusion of "being for the sake of the ritual" (*kratvarthatva*) be inserted into the present definition.
Or else, let the inclusion of "being delimited by the *apūrva*" be inserted according to the method of non-inclusion (*asamudghakarī*).
However, it should be understood that [the sacrifice] does not function as a qualifier by having heaven delimited by its connection to an *apūrva* (unseen potency) as its objective.
An *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly contributing factor) is precisely that action which is distinct from the aforementioned *saṃnipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing factor).
The term "distinct" (*bhinnatva*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *saṃnipatyopakāraka*.
It must be postulated that [the definition] overextends to actions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which serve human goals (puruṣārtha).
The inclusion of the term "action" (kriyā) is for the purpose of excluding those things that have the nature of an accomplished entity (siddharūpa) or serve the purpose of another (kratvartha).
Regarding these definitions, the wise should consider whether they follow or do not follow the definition stated in the original source (ākarokta); enough with this prolixity.
This Murāri is not the Murāri who was the author of the *Tarkasaṃgraha*;
rather, he is a more recent Khaṇḍadeva or similar figure, a poet among Mīmāṃsaka logicians.
Pārthasārathi himself [is the author], as his *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* has also been refuted elsewhere.
However, this composition of his, which does not exceed [the scope of] the *Sāmagrī*, is captivating to the minds of the learned.
Ke.
The fourteen-seven auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are employed for the first time [in the archetype].
Such [elements], when there is a different purpose in the modified rite (*vikṛti*), must be adapted (*ūhya*) for the sake of that specific function.
Furthermore, when the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is the cause for its connection with a property (*dharma*), that intrinsic nature is what constitutes the subsidiary.

In that case, although the *apūrva* is to be accomplished by means of that [subsidiary] which possesses the property, the *apūrva* does not become the cause for the application of the property; thus, it is not the motivator (*prayojaka*).
Since its own nature exists [independently], the property is not applied [to it].
In that case, modification (*ūha*) is not possible in a modified rite (*vikṛti*) because it would lack its original meaning;
[this is stated at] 9.1.2.12, pp. 1642–43.
For that which is not prescribed is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*), and what is not a constituent part is not included by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*).
For it will be stated [at 3.4.14.13]: "And that which is not prescribed does not become an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
Vārttika 3.4.14.15: Even if something is obtained through implication (*upacita*), if it is not subsumed under an injunction (*vidhi*), it does not become an auxiliary at all.
[Śabarabhāṣya] 3.6.1.10, p. 1036.
For no limb whatsoever can belong to anyone without providing some assistance.
For the principal does not enter into a connection with a principal through a subordinate limb.
Bhāṣya 10.8.17–19. In the Rājasūya sacrifice, the subordinate elements—the Aveṣṭi and the animal sacrifices—are not part of the common ritual framework (tantra).
Bhāṣya 11.1.18.10: It was understood in the preceding section (11.1.15–10) that the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), when joined with one another, perform a subordinate assistance (*anupakāra*).
The auxiliary parts bring about the perfection of the instrument (*karaṇa-pauṣkalya*).
Some auxiliary elements (aṅga) are indirectly beneficial (ārādupakāraka), while others are directly beneficial (saṃnipatyopakāraka).

"But the subsidiaries, because they are prescribed by rule, should be taught along with the primary acts" (11.1.12); thus it will be stated that even the subsidiaries are enjoined by the injunction of the primary act. (Ku.

Regarding the sūtra “But the subsidiaries [follow] because of their being prescribed,” the principle of the *antarāgarbhita* (intermediate inclusion) states that the knowledge of the subsidiaries is governed by the time of the primary rite (*pradhānakāla*). In the conclusion of the eleventh section (*ekādaśādhikaraṇa*), under the sūtra “But the subsidiaries,” it is established that those very same place, time, and agent that apply to the primary rite also apply to the subsidiaries. This declaration of the identity of the agent for both the subsidiary and the primary rites is only possible if the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is for the sake of all [the rites], and not otherwise.
(This refers to the prima facie view, *pūrvapakṣa*, at 3.7.10).

Regarding the maxim *‘aṅgāni tu vidhānatvāt’* (JS 11.1.12), its nature is as follows: there is indeed an expectation regarding time, namely, "At what time should that which is intended to be performed (*cikīrṣita*) be done? For one who desires a result, it is the very operation called *phalabhāvanā*—which has as its object both the primary rite and its subsidiaries (*sāṅgapradhāna*) as a collective causal complex for the result—that is intended to be performed, and not the primary rite alone; because if the performance of the subsidiaries were absent, the result would not be accomplished. Therefore, by virtue of this expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the connection with time belongs only to the primary rite together with its subsidiaries, and not to the primary rite alone, since the latter lacks such expectancy. (Somadeva, *Tantravārttika*, 4.3.18, p. 393).

[Objection: Is it not understood that *upāṃśutva* (the state of being whispered) applies only to that much which is enjoined by the Yajurveda? Thus, it would not apply to the chanting of Sāmans; for only the principal acts (*pradhāna*) and their subsidiaries (*aṅga*) are Yājurvedika, and therefore they alone would possess *upāṃśutva*.
[Reply: This is not so. For he will state later: "But the subsidiaries... (*aṅgāni tu*).
Or rather, as stated on page 890 [of the *Tantravārttika*], section 3.3.21:

"The connection with the agent exists only in the performance consisting of the operation directed toward all the constituent parts (*aṅga*)," this is the conclusion established in the section beginning with the words "But the auxiliary parts" (*aṅgāni tu*).
The thirty auxiliary elements (aṅga) mentioned are not the primary ritual procedure (tantra) in the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Bhāṣya 11.4.11–3: The auxiliaries are of two kinds: those that provide remote assistance (ārādupakāraka) and those that provide immediate assistance (sāmavāyika). Among these, the immediate auxiliaries are more significant than the remote ones.
For in that case, the first [direct application] is immediate;
however, in the case of indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*), there would be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the primary rite through an indirect connection.

(10.4.19.38) The auxiliary rites (*aṅgāni*) do not constitute a single integrated whole (*tantra*) for the *rājasūya* sacrifice, because the *tānūnaptra*, *vaiṣṇava*, and other rites possess their own distinct sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

11|4|11-3: The auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) are enjoined both concisely and in detail in the archetype (*prakṛti*). They are enjoined concisely as "he performs five *prayāja* offerings," and in detail as "he offers to the *samidhs*," and so forth.

It has been explained in the section on the "transgression of the subordinate and the principal" (*guṇamukhyavyatikrama*, 3|1|2|9) that the auxiliaries receive their designation from the primary [sacrifice].
These subsidiaries are observed to be on the same side as the principal; wherever the principal is, there they are understood to be.
If [the principal] is tomorrow, its subsidiaries are of that time; if [it is] today, their times are today.
Bhāṣya 11.4.16.23: The subsidiaries and the primary acts are equal to the agent, as in "In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the priests are fewer.
They are equal to the place, as in "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa on level ground.
They are equal to the time, as in "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day" and "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day."
11|1|10|16: When the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) are taught along with the principal act (*pradhāna*) for the sake of accomplishing the fruit, they are taught together.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the subsidiaries, such as the *prayāja* sacrifices and so forth, effect distinct types of assistance (*upakāra*) within the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that even though there is a difference in the gateways (*dvāra*), the assistance is one and the same.
Even though there is a difference in the doors [of entry] for rice, wood, a cooking pot, and so forth, their primary effect is indeed the production of cooked rice (odana).
For the auxiliary parts perform their functions only with regard to the visible purpose, because they are connected to the primary act.
Bhāṣya 11.1.17.35: The substratum does not assist the primary act (*pradhāna*) alone.
This is because at that time, the primary acts do not yet exist.
However, when all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) have been performed, then the prior potencies (*apūrva*) produced by them combine and assist the primary acts.

On the full moon day (paurṇamāsī), because of the connection of time with three [principal rites], the auxiliary elements (aṅga) are performed by way of a single performance (tantra). (The same applies to the new moon day as well.
[Dvaidhasūtra 11.1.4.11]: For the auxiliaries are taught for the sake of the principal rites;
how might the principal rites possess their auxiliaries?

Bhāṣya 11.1.10.54: Regarding the application (viniyoga) prescribed by means of the six criteria beginning with direct statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga), those things which are applied in the form "One should sacrifice at the Darśapūrṇamāsa" with reference to the *samid* and other such items are the auxiliaries (*aṅga*).

These are of two kinds: those of an accomplished nature (*siddharūpa*) and those of an active nature (*kriyārūpa*). Among these, the accomplished ones consist of genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), existence (*sattva*), and so forth.
And these have perceptible results.
Furthermore, actions are of two kinds: subordinate actions (*guṇakarman*) and principal actions (*pradhānakarman*).
These alone are [further divided into] those that assist by direct contact (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) and those that assist from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*).

The second position is that some cognitions (*jñāna*) are to be performed through combination (*samuccaya*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that all cognitions are to be performed through combination because they fulfill the requirement for an instrument (*karaṇākāṅkṣā*) by producing a single beneficial result. Vi. 11.1.3: The application of the cognitions in time follows the eleventh principle (11.2.13–10).

Soma. 5|1|17: Due to the statement of certain ignorant persons, there is a shift to another time even for those [rites] intended for all purposes, as in: "After the Āgnimāruta [offering], they proceed with the after-offerings (anuyāja). Bhāṣya 11|1|4|6.
But for the *ajña* rites, there would be a difference in the results due to the difference in the words [of the injunction], just as in the case of the *ṛtu* sacrifices.
The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Just as the result of the principal acts of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* which are inherent [to the sacrifice] is one, it is not so for the *ajña* rites.
But for those who are ignorant [of this], there would be a difference in the results;
that is, there would be a separate result for each ignorant person.
This is because of the difference in words—due to the difference in injunctions such as "He offers the *samidh* oblation" and "He offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation."
For perception belongs only to those who are ignorant and only to those who are gathered together.
It belongs only to those who are ignorant and only to those who are gathered together.

The Commentary: This is now considered: Is there an application of rites such as the Agnihotra even when they are joined with only a portion of their constituent parts, or must they be performed only by including all the constituent parts?

Now, what occurred there [in the previous section] was the statement, "There should be engagement when one has the capacity for everything" (6.1.1); therein, an inquiry was made regarding the obligatory path.

By this injunction, "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as long as one lives," this lifelong rule of performance is stated: does that require the inclusion of all constituent parts, or not?
Now, here is the consideration regarding the performance for the sake of the fruit:

with respect to this undertaking for the sake of heaven, enjoined by the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," is the performance necessarily regular (obligatory), or must there be a combination of all the auxiliary parts? What, then, is the prima facie view? It should be completed even with a single part, because the purpose is accomplished, just as in the case of other [optional] rites; and when [the others] are obtained, the subsequent [parts] would follow.
"Even by a single part, the ritual act would be completed for those who are ignorant; that is to say, it would be performed. Why? Because its purpose has been fulfilled.
That which was intended to be pervaded for the sake of heaven by means of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices—"
Regarding the two [sections] on the ignorant ones (*ajñāna*) taken together as one, the Vārttikakāras have refuted here the claim that they constitute separate topics (*adhikāra*).
Since even the *Śāstrīyadīpikā* and the *Bhāṣṭīpikā* do not accept a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), they have not been cited here;
the same applies to the *Nyāyabindu*.
Some say: "Is that assistance [rendered] by one, by some, or by all?
The first [case] is due to the fulfillment of expectations; the middle is due to the excellence of the result.
And in the case of simultaneity, like [the story of] the pigeon, it is because of the absence of a cause for renunciation."
They fulfill the desire for collective action through their mutual assistance.
Maṇḍana states: "The task is primary when joined with all its constituent parts. Śaṃkara states: "And there should be a conjunction of those [parts]."
Only when cognitions are combined do they possess a single cooperative efficacy.
However, because there is a difference in the words [denoting the cognitions], there would be a difference in their results, just as in the case of sacrificial acts (*kratuvat*).
Bhāṣya: Now the consideration regarding the Āgneyas is as follows: do the cognitions perform their function collectively, or by way of distinction?
In this regard, it is said:
just as there is a single result for primary elements that have come together, it is not so for those who lack knowledge.
For those who lack knowledge—

Only when the auxiliary elements (aṅgas) are combined is a single [result], such as the attainment of heaven, heard in the scripture. Because of the mutual requirement and proximity, this occurs: "This is the operation in this [context]," by which the sacrifice effects heaven.
When that [injunction] is being formulated, there is no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Alternatively, the injunction regarding the primary acts with respect to the fruit, and the injunction regarding the subsidiary acts with respect to the primary acts, is not contradictory.
How so? By means of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, an *apūrva* (unseen potency) which is the means to heaven is expressed.
The statement regarding that specific [action] is employed as follows:
"Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman for this very [sacrifice] upon the Revatī verses, one desiring cattle should indeed sacrifice with it.
Therefore, the performance of the subsidiaries is enjoined by the very injunction of the performance of the principal.
[Objection: Here, the procedure (itikartavyatā) is not enjoined by restating the sacrifice.
What then? The connection with the procedure is through the productive urge (bhāvanā) itself.
How so? When the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), which expresses the productive urge, is uttered, these expectations arise.
In that regard, for what purpose is it to be cultivated? That which is the human goal (puruṣārtha) occurs [as the result]. In the second [case], it is the instrument;
in the third, it is the agent.
Since it is precisely the limbs taken collectively that constitute "one" [in the sense of "among the limbs"], their collective application is indeed appropriate.

As for the fact that each individual limb is established as an independent means in both the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) and the applicatory injunction (*viniyogavākya*), this is like the case of the primary acts (*pradhāna*) in the originative injunction; it is defined in relation to intermediate functions (*antarakārya*), and thus there is no fault whatsoever.

For this very reason, in that case, there is the postulation of distinctness (*vaijātya*) regarding the intermediate effects (*avāntarakārya*), in accordance with the conjunction (*samuccaya*) understood from the injunction of performance (*prayoga*).

If the *apūrva*—which takes the place of the supreme *apūrva* and consists of an indivisible instrument (*akhaṇḍakaraṇa*)—were the primary [effect], then it would necessarily apply to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) as well; otherwise, it would not apply even there. What need is there for further elaboration? However, regarding the intermediate effect where it has not been previously determined by any other means of knowledge prior to the injunction of performance, since conjunction is understood through that injunction of performance, there is indeed the postulation of distinction (*bhedakalpanā*).

However, where unity alone is determined by necessity and the like—as in the case of *vrīhi* rice and so forth—even though this [alternative] is optional, there is no combination (*samuccaya*) when the performance-rule (*prayoga-vidhi*) prescribes the performance.

Or, where even for things with visible purposes (*dṛṣṭārtha*), such as the *citriṇī* brick and others used for a single animal and so forth, they do not fall within the scope of a single performance-rule, there—due to the absence of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that would grasp a combination—it should be understood that there is only an option (*vikalpa*) when the results are equal; but when there is a difference, there is an abundance of fruit. In the present case, however, by the performance-rule, there is a combination...

The Principle of Conflict Between the Quality of a Subsidiary and the Primary (Aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya) 160. Regarding the conflict between the quality of a subsidiary and the primary, the Bhāṣya states: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu at the Dīkṣaṇīyā [initiation rite]. In that very context, there is also the Sautrāmaṇī day.

The time for the *parvan* (the junction day) for those two [the Darśapūrṇamāsa and Cāturmāsya sacrifices] is established by the scriptural statement: "He who would sacrifice with the *iṣṭi*, with an animal, or with Soma, he should sacrifice on the new moon day or the full moon day.
However, when there are ritual options (*kalpa*) such as "one initiation (*dīkṣā*), three *upasads*," and so forth, then a contradiction arises.
In that case, the inquiry is: should the initiation be performed on the *parvan* day and the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) on a non-*parvan* day, or is it the reverse?
Since it is primary, the initiation (dīkṣā) must be performed.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
when there is a conflict between a quality of a subordinate member (aṅga-guṇa) and a quality of the principal (pradhāna-guṇa), in this case, the quality of the subordinate member shall be set aside.
Why? Because it is for that purpose.

An auxiliary is performed with its qualities so that the principal may be endowed with its qualities. If, while the auxiliary is being performed with its qualities, the principal becomes defective, what has been accomplished by that qualified auxiliary?
Therefore, the Soma-pressing (sutyā) should be performed on a festival day (parvan), while the initiation (dīkṣā) may take place on a non-festival day.

Regarding the rule, "He who desires [a specific result] should sacrifice with an animal or with Soma on either the new moon or the full moon day," a doubt arises because there is a multi-day interval between the preparatory rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* and the principal rite, the Soma sacrifice; consequently, it is uncertain whether the Soma sacrifice should take place on the lunar festival (*parvan*) day while the initiation (*dīkṣā*) occurs on a non-festival day, or vice versa. Since the initiation would naturally fall on the festival day due to its priority, the established conclusion is: "Because the performance of auxiliary rites is for the sake of ensuring the excellence of the principal rite, the principal rite itself must conform to the time of the festival.
(Page 167)

Regarding the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [initiatory rite] and the *soma* sacrifice, since their simultaneity is established by the scriptural injunction, "He who [desires] with the animal and the soma," and so forth, a deliberation arises as to which time should be favored when there is a possibility of two times under the alternative of one or more initiations (*ekādidīkṣā*). If there were no restriction, the preference would initially fall upon the properties of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* due to its being the primary [introductory] element. However, because the time of the *sutyā* (the day of pressing) pertains to the principal rite itself, it is that time which must be favored. All subsidiaries and their own ancillaries are performed for the sake of ensuring the excellence of the principal rite;
and when a direct connection to excellence is possible, one does not resort to a mere indirect succession.
Therefore, this is a favor granted to the time of the primary sacrifice.
This consideration regarding sublation has also been undertaken here because of the contingency of the coexistence of conflicting properties;
its connection [to the previous topic] is due to the fact that it favors the primary properties previously mentioned in relation to the Soma sacrifice.
However, it is not according to the view stated by others that when the time of the auxiliary (aṅga) is accommodated,

that very same time applies to the primary (pradhāna) by way of the auxiliary; such a connection [of the primary with the auxiliary's time] would result in the impossibility of the primary's time being established as heard in the scripture, because of the occurrence of *prasaṅga* (incidental application).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: when there is a conflict between the quality of a subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the quality of the principal (*pradhāna*), it is logical to favor the quality of the principal alone; for the subsidiaries are subordinate to the principal. As it is said: "Whether it be the time for the *iṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice, the initiation (*dīkṣā*), or the Soma sacrifice..."
"The first" means by virtue of being primary; do not say so, for the Pradhāna is [merely] a child's fancy.

Commentary: However, where the primary limb (*mukhyamaṅga*)—such as the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice which must be performed on the first day—or where there are many limbs—as in the case of the *Upasad*, *Gopīthya*, and animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*) on the *Upavasatha* day—the principal rite (*pradhāna*), though occurring later and being singular, such as the *Soma* sacrifice to be performed on the fifth day, takes precedence over the conflict with the time-period (*parvakāla*) prescribed by the injunction "He who desires [this]," etc. This is because the limbs exist for the sake of the excellence of the principal; thus, in the event of a conflict, the excellence of the limbs is rendered ineffective. In common worldly experience, it is observed that when a place is first occupied by many, even a single king arriving later may take possession of it.

Therefore, in that case, although the Soma sacrifice is junior in terms of both textual order (*pāṭha*) and performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), it possesses the status of being the primary element (*pradhāna*) and thus takes precedence regarding the time of the lunar festival (*parva*).

As for the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, even though they are senior in both textual order and performance, there is no compliance with the festival time in the case of the "single initiation" (*ekādīkṣā*) view.
However, in the case of the "twelve initiations" (*dvādaśādīkṣā*) view, since there is no conflict, the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* is indeed associated with the festival time.

In the case of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and others, however, there is indeed sublation (*bādha*) under all views. Therefore, in that context, since the performance on those specific days—beginning with the *sutyā* day—is established by the aforementioned injunctions as having its own specific time, the *parvan* time is accomplished through *prasaṅga* (incidental application). Thus, the discussion of sublation is incidental, occurring either through the impossibility of *prasaṅga* or through the actual sublation itself. For the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and the *soma* sacrifice do not have the *parvan* time as their fixed period, according to such scriptural injunctions as "He who [desires] with the *iṣṭi*, with the animal sacrifice, or with the *soma*... and so forth.

In this regard, since that [benefit] is impossible for two [of them], the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, being primary, would naturally receive the benefit; however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the subsidiary elements of the *Soma* sacrifice take precedence because they are the principal.
As Maḍana says: "The quality of the principal is stronger."
Śaṅkara says: "Such [subordination] exists even between the subordinate and the principal.
It is primary.
And in a conflict between the quality of the subordinate and the purpose, [the former prevails] because of its being for that purpose."
"And in the case of a conflict between the quality of a subsidiary and [the quality of] the principal" (Sūtra 161).

When the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached by means of the principle of the conflict between the quality of a subsidiary and [the quality of] the principal, the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), indicating the rejection of the prima facie view by the word "and" (*ca*), which stands in the place of the word "but" (*tu*).
This is because, when there is a conflict between the quality of a subsidiary and the quality of the principal, the subsidiary exists for the sake of the principal.
For a subsidiary (aṅga) is performed for the sake of accomplishing the excellence of the primary (pradhāna).

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the Soma-pressing (sutyā) should take place on the full-moon day (parvan), while the initiation (dīkṣā) should take place on a non-parvan day.
A "subsidiary quality" (aṅgaguṇa) is a quality belonging to a subsidiary.
From the word "subsidiary quality" (*aṅgaguṇa*), the term "principal quality" (*pradhānaguṇa*) is understood.
And that [term] ends in the third case (*tṛtīyānta*), following the word "contradiction" (*virodha*).
Thus, when there is a contradiction of the subsidiary quality by the principal quality, the application of the meaning of the suffix *iṣ* [is established].
The Vedic revelation (*vedaśruti*) situated at the beginning as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is the subject of the commentary (Su. p.

167). If the "transgression of the subordinate and the principal" (*guṇamukhyavyatikrama*) is explained as referring to a conflict between the properties (*dharma*) of the auxiliary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*pradhāna*), then one must consider how this avoids redundancy with the sūtra "And in case of a conflict between the property of an auxiliary and [the primary], [the former prevails] because it exists for the sake of that" (*aṅgaguṇavirodhe ca tādarthyāt*).

Or [as stated in] Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.21, page 814: This very section by the Bhāṣyakāra (the section on the "Transgression of the Subordinate and the Principal," 3.1.21–8) is largely redundant because it has already been covered by the twelfth section (*dvādaśādhikaraṇa*)—namely, "And in case of conflict between a subordinate quality and the principal, [the former prevails], because it is for the sake of that"—since even if the loudness (*uccaiḥ-svara*), which belongs to the subsidiary Veda, assists the principal through its subsidiaries, a deficiency in the principal remains unavoidable. Furthermore, there is a weightiness in postulating the performance of a subordinate quality based on what is heard in the principal, as it rests upon the injunction of the principal itself.

Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.218: By the statement "one should wait for the dancer," etc., the time for that [fire-laying] is prohibited because it occurs within the context of the fire-laying (ādhāna), not the time for the Soma sacrifice, since the latter is not the subject under discussion.
In this way, there is no contradiction with the principle of the subordinate quality of a subordinate element (aṅgaguṇaguṇanyāya).
For the fires are indeed subsidiaries of the Soma sacrifice, and since they are both subsidiary and principal [relative to other rites], it is logical that their time alone should be set aside.

(Pūrvapakṣa: Even on account of the contradiction with the *aṅgaguṇanyāya*, it is not proper to reject the denotability of the genus (*jāti*) by accepting that the gender (*liṅga*) is denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). [Su. p.
1414] The three [mantras] (in the *jayādi-homas* and other rites performed in the mouth of the Āhavanīya fire) ensure the absence of deficiency (*avaiguṇya*) in the rituals.

[In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): It is improper [to accept a bahuvrīhi compound], because it is studied by the Vaidikas as being indicative of a bahuvrīhi, and thus a bahuvrīhi status is understood; furthermore, since it is possible [for it to be a bahuvrīhi], it is illogical to assume a tatpuruṣa, as that would result in a deficiency (vaiguṇya) regarding the subordinate sacrifice (aṅgayāga). Moreover, if a tatpuruṣa were accepted, the word would result in having an udātta accent on the final syllable; how then can a tatpuruṣa be accepted? [This is resolved] by the principle of the conflict between a primary and a subordinate element (aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya), as in the case of the Āhavanīya fire... [sup pṛ 1483].
This must be said:
even though there is the possibility of interpreting it as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, since in common usage the accentuation can be adjusted so that the primary status [of the agent] is maintained.
(This...)

Because of the determination of the *tatpuruṣa* compound as "benefiting its own object" (*bhūtasvārthānugrāhaka*), [it refers to] the accentuation of the word-form (*śabdadharmasvara*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is according to the principle of the conflict between the quality of a subordinate element and the principal (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*). By the rule “of those that are well-purified, whose husks are removed, and which possess gender,” it refers specifically to the auxiliary *ādheya*. This is because of the explanation based on pervasion (*vyāpyatva*), as in the statement: “One should ask about the dance, not the constellation.”
3|2|10, p. 278. Because it is more logical for [the term] to denote time even in the previous case (this refers to the *pūrvapakṣa*);
according to the Bhaṭṭa school.

Because it is like an injunction for a ritual accompanied by mantras, and because of the prohibition of study on the *parvan* days; and because the secondary offerings (*anunirvāpya*) of the *devasuva* oblations are intended for the sake of the fire (*agni*).

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the rites is weak. According to the principle of the conflict between a subsidiary and its quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodhanyāya*), since [the offering] serves the purpose of the *cayana* (piling), it cannot serve the purpose of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). Therefore, the application of the mantra is logically justified by setting aside the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the [animal-cake] mantra; the connection in the statement “he offers following the animal-cake” (*paśupuroḍāśamanu nirvapati*) is solely for the sake of time (*kālārtha*), and not [an injunction for the *vaimṛdha* offering].

The statement "it should not be studied" (nādhyeyam) is of Smṛti origin; therefore, its application is restricted to the study of the Veda itself. Just as in the case of the phrase "he offers [the oblation] after the *anuyāja*," this refers to the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). Consequently, because the injunction regarding the mantra is of Śruti origin and thus possesses greater force as a constituent part of the ritual, why should the property of the *puroḍāśa* not be taken [as applicable]? It cannot be so, because their relative strength is unequal.
Soma 12.3.7: An occasion for doubt.
In the case of a simultaneous interruption, not that [one].

Where there is a conflict between the office of the officiating priest (*ārlijya*) and the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*), since both types of re-performance constitute an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), [the rule] applies there because the purificatory rite is a subordinate element of the office of the priest,
as established by the principle regarding the conflict between a primary and its subordinate qualities. 164
In the *Puruṣārthacintāmaṇi-pradīpa*:

Because it is established by the principle of "conflict between the quality of a subsidiary" (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*) that there must be a relinquishing of the scriptural statement of purpose (*arthavāda*), which is subordinate to the injunction (*vidhi*) that constitutes the primary element.

(Ko. 214|12|195.216). Between two scriptural statements that are in conflict due to the conflict between the quality of a subsidiary and its opposite, the scriptural statement of the primary (*pradhānaśruti*) is more powerful than the scriptural statement of the subsidiary's quality (*aṅgaguṇaśruti*).

According to the principle of the conflict between a subordinate element (*aṅga*) and its quality (*guṇa*), one should set aside the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is merely a portion of the meaning of the word "Brahman" as a subordinate element, and instead adopt the distinction between agent and object required by the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*). (This is the *pūrvapakṣa*. *Parimala* (on BS 4.1.3–4):

By the logic of the section on the conflict between a subordinate element and its quality (*aṅgaguṇavirodha*), since the *jatṛ* and other rites do not occur at the time of the sacrifice (*apūrvakālatva*), the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites likewise do not occur at the time of the sacrifice.
*Soma*, 7.1.1, p. 524: Because it is improper for the quality of the primary (*pradhāna*) to be sublated by the quality of a subsidiary (*aṅga*).
*Dṛṣṭa*, 4.1.3.48, p. 1224: When there is a conflict between the quality of a subsidiary and the quality of the primary, the quality of the subsidiary should be sublated.

*Bhāṣya*, 1.2.125: Regarding the phrase "of the quality of the subsidiary and the quality of the primary," when there is a conflict with the qualities of the primary—such as the time of the festival (*parvakāla*) and so forth—the rule for the sake of similarity [applies].
Furthermore, [if it were defined as that which is enjoined], then plowing and the like would also result in being subordinate parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice.

Nor can it be defined as consisting in being enjoined; for in that case, the five *prayāja* oblations involving the elements and so forth would incur the status of being subordinate parts of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), since they do not provide assistance toward its preparation.
Now, suppose that [the definition of an auxiliary] consists in not being an auxiliary to anything else.

If it is argued that even though the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are auxiliaries to the *puroḍāśa*, they would still incur the status of being auxiliaries because they are not auxiliaries to things other than the *puroḍāśa*, [we reply] that this would result in five [auxiliaries] for what is actually one.
Or, suppose that it consists in not being prompted by anything else.

If it is argued that although the *prayāja* offerings and others do assist the five-layered cake (*pañcadaśa-puroḍāśa*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because they are not prompted by it, and since they are used for purposes other than the cake, there is no contingency of them being subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the cake; [we reply: this would lead to the undesirable conclusion that the subsidiaries prompted by the archetype (*prakṛti*) are optional (*vikalpa*). Now, if it is said: "That which assists something X, while not being prompted by anything other than X, is a subsidiary of X. And 'not being prompted by anything other than X' means: being prompted by X while not being prompted by anything else," [this definition] is simpler (*lāghava*).

If "not being prompted by another" (*yad-aprayuktatva*) were included [in the definition], there would be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) regarding subsidiaries such as time and the materials to be given, which are not prompted by anything else; therefore, in the search for the absence of a qualified entity, the qualifier is "the state of being prompted by something other than that" (*yad-anyaprayuktatva*).

(Likewise, if "being prompted by something other than that" were included, there would arise the undesirable consequence of regarding the vessels used in both the archetype and the ectype as optional (*vikalpa*), because they are prompted by both; therefore, it should be understood that the qualifier is "provided that it is not prompted by that" [*yad-aprayuktatve sati*]).

And if it is argued that there is no over-narrow definition (avyāpti), because even though archetypal injunctions are prompted by something other than the ectype, they lack being prompted by the ectype itself—such that the absence of the qualifier [being prompted by the ectype] exists due to the presence of the absence of being prompted [by anything else], and thus "being prompted by nothing other than another" applies; we say: no. For this would result in the absurdity that the *puroḍāśa* pan is known [to be used] for the purpose of removing husks.

Regarding the statement, "One winnows the husks with the *puroḍāśa*-ladle," it was stated in the fourth book (4.1.12–16) that since the ladle is already established as being for the purpose of the *puroḍāśa* by the rule "one bakes the *puroḍāśa* on the potsherds" (*kapāleṣu puroḍāśaṃ śrapayati*), its prescription here for the purpose of winnowing the husks means that the *puroḍāśa*-ladle is not intended for the winnowing of husks.

Therefore, because the winnowing of husks is prompted solely by the *puroḍāśa*, there arises the logical consequence that the *puroḍāśa*-ladle would be understood as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the winnowing of husks.

If, however, that which possesses a form delimited by being a causal factor (*kāraka*) whose non-delimitation is due to being prompted by something else is considered an "auxiliary" (*aṅga*), then that [definition] would involve the concept of non-delimitation (*anavacchedakatva*). In that case, there would be no application of archetypal (*prākṛta*) auxiliaries to the ectype (*vikṛti*).
To explain:

archetypal auxiliaries do not possess a form delimited by being prompted by the archetype (such as the *samidh* fuel-sticks) as the means of assisting the ectype; for if one were to assume a separate prompting for each individual [auxiliary], such as the property of being a *samit*, it would result in the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

Rather, since all other [elements] follow along with the connection to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, there is a single assumption of extended application (*atideśa*) that "one should assist the modification (*vikṛti*) by means of those things connected to the Darśapūrṇamāsa"; thus, the assistance is provided in the form already described.

However, as for their being prompted by the archetype (*prakṛti*), this is understood through the respective individual sentences in their respective forms; therefore, it is precisely that specific form which serves as the delimiting factor for what is prompted by the archetype.

Consequently, since the original (prākṛta) subsidiaries are not known in the modified (vikṛti) sacrifice—because they possess the property of being "auxiliaries to the modification" (vikṛtyupakārakatva), which is defined by the relation to the original sacrifice that serves as the delimiting factor for their being employed elsewhere in the modification—it would follow that there is no knowledge of them in the modification. Nor, however, does it follow that there is a lack of knowledge regarding the *tuṣopavāpa* (the scattering of husks) in the case of the *kapāla* (potsherd) used for the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake). This is explained because the *kapāla* is delimited by its being employed for the *puroḍāśa*, and the status of belonging to the *puroḍāśa* (*puroḍāśīyatva*) is delimited by its being an auxiliary to the *tuṣopavāpa*; thus, it possesses the form of being an auxiliary to the *tuṣopavāpa* which is delimited by "belonging to the *puroḍāśa*"—a property that is not the delimiting factor for its being employed for the *puroḍāśa*. This is what is intended by the *Vibhāṣā*.

In that case, there would be no occurrence of the *bhedana-homa* being designated as a part of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, because only a *homa* of the same class as that which is prompted by the specific occasion (*nimitta*) of breaking [the ladle] possesses the property of being a factor that assists the *darśapūrṇamāsa*. Furthermore, in the present context, "being prompted by another" does not consist in its being a means of accomplishing what is to be accomplished (*uddeśyatā*) residing in something other than itself.

In that context, the state of being something to be avoided (*uddeyatva*) takes the form of being desired (*īpsitarūpa*), and it is not common to the five factors that are not to be adopted (*anupādeya*).

(And the state of being uncommon to the five factors not to be adopted should be understood as: while being connected with the primary object of negation (*bhāvanā*) through a relation not constituted by inherence in volitional effort (*kṛti-samavāya*), it is not an object of application for the injunction regarding the primary action.
"Place, time, occasion, result, and the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*)."

By the well-known consensus of the learned, expressed in the verse, "They say that for those who investigate [the Veda], there are five non-adoptables," it is intended that place (*deśa*) and the other factors are not to be adopted.

To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the agent (*kartṛ*) and its oneness (*ekatva*), which are intended as adoptables because they are not excluded by the injunction (*vidhi*) and reasoning (*yukti*), the first qualification is stated: "by a relation not consisting of inherence in an effort" (*kṛtisamavāyāghaṭita-sambandhena*).

It should be understood that, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to sacrifices and the like, "not being the object of the performance enjoined by the original injunction" (*prakṛtavidhibodhitānuṣṭhānāviṣayatva*)—that is, not being the object of the application of the original injunction—is what is meant.
Thus, it must be stated that such a *homa* is incapable [of serving as a substitute] when there is a cause (*nimitta*) such as the spilling of the offering.

Nevertheless, since the assistance to the *homa* is provided precisely through its being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the connection with the sense organs (*indriya*) and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the *homa* performed with curd (*dadhi*) would not be known as a *homa*.

Furthermore, because it assists the sense organ even without being delimited by its application to the *homa* sacrifice and so forth, it would follow that it is merely an ancillary (*aṅga*) to that [sense organ].

Furthermore, although the specific universals (vaijātya) that serve as the delimiters for the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites—when these are prompted by heaven—are indeed the delimiters for their being auxiliaries toward the destruction of sin, there is no distinct universal for the status of being an auxiliary toward the destruction of sin that is separate from the specific universal that serves as the delimiter for being prompted by heaven. If such a separate universal existed, it would follow that a compulsory rite (*nitya*) performed through the connection with a dharma for the sake of heaven would become an incidental (*prasaṅga*) performance.

Moreover, since the *ājyabhāga* offerings serve as auxiliaries to the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice precisely by virtue of being the sacrificial portions (*yāgabhāga*) delimited by their application to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that the *ājyabhāgas* are not known in the *Gṛhamedhīya*. For [this is not the case] in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

In the case of the *tantu* sacrifice, since the *ājyabhāga* offerings—though obtained through extended application (*atideśa*)—are related to the archetype (*prakṛti*), they serve to benefit the ectype (*vikṛti*). Here, however, because the two *ājyabhāgas* are related to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, they serve to benefit the *Gṛhamedhīya*. Consequently, the *ājyabhāgas* would not possess the status of being subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *Gṛhamedhīya* on the grounds of being prompted by something else, because they lack the specific form that characterizes their relationship to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* (which serves as the delimiting factor for what is prompted by another) and instead possess the form that delimits their status as benefiting the *Gṛhamedhīya*. This is because the injunction "He offers the two *ājyabhāgas*" found within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *Gṛhamedhīya* prescribes the *ājyabhāgas* precisely by virtue of their being *ājyabhāgas*.

In reality, even the relation to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices serves as the delimitor (avacchedaka) for being prompted by what follows a modification (vikṛti). Thus, even though that [relation] is indeed a delimitor of the Gṛhamedhīya’s capacity to provide assistance, there is no contradiction in establishing the two Ājyabhāga offerings as its constituent parts (aṅga). For this very reason, the previously mentioned consequence—that the archetypal (prakṛta) subsidiaries would result in being subsidiaries of every modification—is still in force; because the definition varies according to each specific modification, even the relation to the Darśapūrṇamāsa—which is the delimitor of the capacity to assist a particular modification—also becomes a delimitor for being prompted by what follows that specific modification.

Nor is "being for the sake of another" (parārthatva) defined as being the object of an effort produced by another; for this would be over-narrow (*avyāpti*) with respect to time and other factors that are objects of an effort.

For this very reason, it is also not the case that [being for the sake of another] consists in inherence (*samavāya*) in the agent; for even though the definition exists in the agent, it is over-narrow with respect to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

Now, [if one were to argue that] such an effort-ness [is established] through a temporal relation (*kālikānvaya-sambandha*) due to the absence of [relations like] inherence and so on—[this is rejected as follows:]

If it is argued that there is an over-narrowness (avyāpti) because such "kṛtitva" (the state of being an effort) exists in the *prayāja* offerings and so forth through the relation of being something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*), we say: no. For even in the case of [an action] consisting of a net and the like, the aforementioned "kṛtatva" (the state of being produced by effort) is absent even through any other relation; thus, there is no over-narrowness.

If it is argued that the definition of being an instrument (*kṛtitva*) as stated applies by some relation or other, leading to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as the cause (*nimitta*) and so forth, and that "being for the sake of another" (*parārthatva*) is difficult to maintain— here we reply:

That which is enjoined as the causal factor (*kāraka*) of an instrument qualified by a *deyatā* (the state of being something to be given) residing in a certain locus, through the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatva*), is subordinate (*aṅga*) to that [locus].

Just as in the case of the injunction "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," the New and Full Moon sacrifices possess the status of being the instrument (kāraka) of an effort (kṛti) qualified by a deity residing in heaven;
therefore, they are subordinate (aṅga) to that [result].

Likewise, in sentences such as "he offers the Samidh-oblation," because the New and Full Moon sacrifices—already established [in the context]—are connected as the deities, the New and Full Moon sacrifices possess the status of being the instrument of an effort qualified in that manner [by those deities]; thus, the Prayāja offerings and others are subordinate to them.

Thus, there is a distinction between substance, quality, genus, and so forth, on the one hand, as the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the agent (*kartṛ*) as the agent (*kartṛ*), and time and so forth as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*); this constitutes the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpti*).

Here, that which is enjoined as being a factor in the volitional effort (*kṛti*) qualified by the status of being the object (*uddeyatā*) residing in heaven—by virtue of its being delimited by "thatness" (*yattva*) through positive concomitance—is the status of being a subsidiary to heaven (*svargāṅgatva*). One should understand that the difference in definitions (*lakṣaṇabheda*) arises from the difference in the delimiters of the objecthood (*uddeyatāvacchedakabheda*), and not from the difference in the delimiter of the defined (*lakṣyatāvacchedakabheda*), because the latter does not enter into the definition itself.

Therefore, it should be understood that there is a single definition common to all the constituent parts of the *svarga* sacrifice, rather than a difference in definitions based on distinctions such as being dedicated to Agni (*āgneya*) or being dedicated to Agni and Soma (*iṣomīya*).

This is because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to include "being a qualifier" (*nirūpakatva*) as a mode (*prakāratā*); for if "being a qualifier" were introduced as a mode, the relation that delimits that mode (*prakāratāvacchedaka-sambandha*) would also have to be included, resulting in prolixity.

However, if it is introduced as a relation (*saṃbandhavidhayā*), there is parsimony (*lāghava*) because a relation requires another relation. Its inclusion as a relation is thus defined as "being enjoined by virtue of being the causal factor (*kāraka*) of an effort qualified by the status of being the object (*uddeśyatā*) through the relation of being its determiner (*nirūpakatva*). The purpose of this formulation is to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This is achieved by relating [the enjoined] to [the effort] through the relation of being the motivator (*prayojakatva*) of its own locus, and ultimately through concomitance such as being the object of a single cognition; for otherwise, since the status of being the causal factor of an effort conducive to the *prayāja* offerings—which are qualified by the status of being the thing to be given (*uddeyatā*) residing in heaven—exists in the *prayāja* offerings themselves, an over-extension would result.

In this context, [the definition] would suffer from over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because the properties of being the agent of an action qualified by purity (*śuddha*), being the agent of an action qualified by the objective (*uddeśyatā*), and being the agent of an action qualified by the objective residing in the primary sacrifice (*niṣṭhodeyatāviśiṣṭakṛtikārakatva*) exist in the *prayāja* offerings and in the primary sacrifice that does not have heaven as its fruit; therefore, the term "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) is included. However, the objective (*uddeyatā*) delimited by the objective-determiner (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is not [included], because it is not proximate through the relation of being a qualifier (*nirūpakatva*). Furthermore, the property of being the agent of an action conducive to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, which are qualified by the objective, exists in the *prayāja* offerings themselves; hence, that [term] is included. The mention of "action" (*kṛti*) is merely for the sake of defining the nature of the thing (*svarūpakathana*), as there is no purpose in including it [in the definition].

Nor should it be argued that the definition is formulated specifically to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as the *darśapūrṹṇamāsa* sacrifice— since the property of being the "counter-correlate" (*nirūpaka*) of the "thing-to-be-conferred" (*uddeyatā*) residing in heaven exists there as well based on the cognition "the sacrifice is the conferrer of heaven," and since the property of being its "agent" (*kārakatva*) exists even in the materials that produce it—

because in our view, the status of being an agent is uniquely determined by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), and thus is not determined by the sacrificial act (*yāga*) which is the meaning of the verbal root.

And the existence of heaven (*svarga*) [in the result] is by way of a relation other than the specific temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*) and the relation of being a qualifier of the teacher; here, even though the fitness-to-be-bestowed (*uddeyatā*) of the action having the *prayāja* offerings as its instrument exists through a temporal relation, it exists in heaven by way of the essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

Thus, there is no defect even if "fitness-to-be-bestowed" (*uddeyatva*) is not mentioned as such, because the state of being prompted by the action having the *prayāja* offerings as its instrument does not exist in heaven by way of the essential relation of being the object (*viṣayatva*).

The inclusion of "being a factor of action" (*kārakatva*) instead of "relatedness" (*sambandhitva*) is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the occasioning cause (*nimitta*) and so forth.
There is no fault, because the cause (*nimitta*) is not a causal factor (*kāraka*) in the manner that will be explained below.
For this very reason, it has been stated in various places that the locative case expressing the sense of being a cause is an "upapada-vibhakti" (a case ending used as a secondary word).
The term "prescribed" (*vihita*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to objects such as a wall (*kuḍya*).

Nor should it be argued that since the status of being a "kāraka" (participant in action) as stated [in the definition] exists even in the case of heaven (*svarga*), heaven would possess the status of being its own "aṅga" (auxiliary);
for the definition includes the condition of being a "kāraka" distinct from the "karman-kāraka" (the object).
It is precisely for this purpose that a word with a distinct meaning is included in the Sūtra.

Nor can it be argued that because the word *paropakārakaḥ* ("benefiting others") in the sentence "This Devadatta is a benefactor of others" conveys a general relation where the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is self-evident,
the difference between the members [of the compound] is presented solely by the word *para*;
for how could the difference between the members, which consists in the distinction of the object-case factor (*karmakāraka*), be understood from that?
Because the various auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are experienced through a common consciousness, their presentation [to the mind] from that [source] is possible.
Indeed, a definition in the form of "that which is the agent of an effort directed toward a heaven distinct from itself" is not possible;
for since "selfhood" (*svatva*) is not a recurring universal (*anugama*), it would follow that the definition would differ with each distinct auxiliary element.
Therefore, it is only in the case of the aforementioned distinction that there is the status of being the offspring of another.

Now, one might object: since it is cumbersome to include a distinction whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "karmatva" (the status of being an object) defined as possessing a result produced by an action—and even if *karmatva* were an indivisible property (*akhaṇḍopādhi*)—since a distinction whose counter-correlativity is delimited by *karmatva* in general would still exist in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices (which have the *prayāja* offerings as their substratum for the effort), it would be simpler to include a distinction whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "svargatva" (the nature of heaven) itself in the definition of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), rather than including a distinction delimited by the *karmatva* of the effort aimed at heaven.

If it is argued that this is not so because a difference in definition has been stated based on a difference in the intended object (*uddeśya*), we say no. For [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that cattle and other such results mentioned in sentences such as "The Jyotiṣṭoma [is performed] for all [desires]" would become subordinate parts (*aṅga*) of heaven. This is because, while being distinct from that which is delimited by heaven-hood, the meaning of the verbal root mentioned [in the injunction] is connected to the effort (*kṛti*) through its relation as an instrument (*karaṇatva*). Thus, [the definition] would fail to apply (*avyāpti*) in that case.

However, if it is considered that—because the cognition "the productive operation (bhāvanā) has sacrifice as its instrument" involves an apprehension of instrumentality as a qualifier, and because of the grammatical coreferentiality with a nominal word ending in the third case—the instrumentality indicated by the verbal root is construed with the productive operation, whereas the meaning of the root is construed only with that [instrumentality] itself; then [the rule] *proktāyām* [is applicable].

Nevertheless, following the grammatical theory accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas regarding arthavādas—which establishes a rule for the determination of case-role (prakāratā) such that "the mental presence (upasthiti) produced by the verbal root denoting *bhāvanā*, which is distinct from the gender and number expressed by the suffixes of words other than particles, prefixes, and nominal stems, is the cause [of the cognition of the object] with respect to the object itself, through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*)"—it is maintained that there is a necessary connection between *bhāvanā* and gender based solely on the contingency of their co-occurrence.

If it is argued that [the word] "in the broken" (*bhinne*) in the injunction "he offers when it is broken" (*bhinne juhoti*) serves as a condition (*nimitta*) because it possesses the sense of the locative case, and thus functions as a condition by being connected with a word other than that [which denotes the action], we say no.
This is because the state of being connected with the meaning of a case-ending that is itself connected to an activity (kṛti) consists in being a *kāraka* (participant) of that activity.

Furthermore, the status of being the meaning of a case-ending is understood through the expressive power (*śakti*) of the case-ending itself; therefore, the meanings "condition" and so forth are not grasped by taking "condition-hood" (*nimittatva*) as the primary sense. This is because the locative case has "substratum" (*adhikaraṇa*) as its primary denotation, and thus "condition-hood" lacks the status of being its primary denotation (*śakyatva*).
Nor should it be argued that "being denotable by a case-ending" means being the object of a power (śakti) as determined by a case-ending;

for even though "being the cause" (*nimittatva*) is not the object of a power as determined by the locative case, since the genitive case—by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*—denotes a general relation, it includes "being the cause" within that scope, yet it is still not the object of a power as determined by the genitive case. Thus, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the cause] being identical with the effect remains just as it was.
This objection is invalid, because what is intended here is the state of being the object of a power as determined by a case-ending, which is not delimited by a specific relation.
For the delimitor of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) power is indeed "relation-ness" (*saṃbandhatva*) itself; therefore, there is no fault.

For this very reason, it should be understood that in cases such as "seventeen [cups] for the Vaiśya," the cognition of being a cause (*nimittatva*) is indicated by the genitive through its nature as a cause.

Furthermore, even though in cases such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is indicated by the verbal root (*dhātu*), there is no fault because, in reality, its status as a word-meaning (*śakyatva*) belonging to the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not lost.

Similarly, in cases such as "he offers once" (*sakṛd juhoti*), even if one accepts a modification of the application (*viniyoga-bhaṅga*) whereby the accusative case is taken as indicating the instrument (*karaṇatva-lakṣaṇā*), there is no contradiction regarding the status of the "once-offering" (*saktan*) as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the oblation (*homa*), because in reality the capacity of that case-ending [to denote its primary meaning] is not lost.

By this very method, in passages such as "one should offer a *caru* to Soma and Rudra of *kuṇāla* rice," although the instrumentality is indicated by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-lakṣyatve*), the status of the rice (*vrīhīṇām*) as an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*yāgāṅgatvam*) must be established.

By this, even the connection of the *bhāvanā* with another [element]—which is distinct from indication (*liṅga*) and pervasion (*saṃvyāpti*) and consists merely of a syntactical string (*sūtramātra*), as in the case of "on the following day of the *dvirātra*, the *ṣoḍaśin* is taken"—is over-pervasive (*ativyāpti*) for the definition of *bhāvanā*-integration.

For in that instance, the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* is not enjoined with reference to the "following day" of the *dvirātra* sacrifice, because that would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to the qualification of the referent. Nor can it be argued that there is no split of the sentence because mutual coreferentiality (*parasparānvaya*) is established in the case of genitive constructions (*ṣaṣṭhīsthala*).

Even if that were the case, as in the example "like the subsequent oblation," there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) because the qualification "on the following day" (*uttare 'han*) cannot logically apply to the [single] day.

In reality, since a property distinct from the verbal root-meaning (*dhātu-artha*)—such as gender or number—is easily understood as being distinct from the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), the connection of even the genitive sense must necessarily be distinct from the *bhāvanā*.

Therefore, the *bhāvanā* characterized by the performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup-grahaṇa, which is related to the *dvirātra* sacrifice, is enjoined with reference to a portion of the subsequent ritual element.

Furthermore, since the latter part depends upon its correlative, it is understood as being secondary (*pārthika*) according to the maxim of the "one-year-old heifer" (*aṇaikahāyanī-nyāya*); thus, the correlative in the form of the *dvirātra* (two-night sacrifice) is obtained.

And because the latter part connected to the *dvirātra* consists of two days (*ahaḥ*), it should be understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of "day," just as in the expression: "The first day has the *aindravāyava* cup as its opening."

And thus, the objection that there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *dvirātra* sacrifice because it is connected with the meaning of a case-ending associated with an action is refuted; for there is no fault by including as a requirement the state of being the object of a power delimited by a relation specified by a case-ending.

In fact, however, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), one should accept that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has the sense of the objective (*karmatva*) by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and that the injunction is for the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with the *dvirātra* as its purpose.

Furthermore, on the very day following the second night (the *dvirātrīyottarāha*), because it constitutes the *atirātra* sacrificial form, there is an injunction for the performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup-offering based on the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) regarding the rule of optional selection. This injunction for the *ṣoḍaśin* is made with reference to the latter part of the second-night sacrifice; and since that latter part of the second-night sacrifice consists of a single day, the term "day" (*ahan*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Moreover, since the restrictive condition of "above" (*upari*) can serve as a simpler spatial delimiter, it is improper to employ a more complex delimiter for the objective referent (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the aforementioned mode [of the two-night sacrifice] serves as the delimiting factor (uddeśyatā’vacchedakatva) for the object of reference, and because the injunction—conforming to the parsimony of subsequent restrictive rules (niyamavidhi)—must have as its scope the subsequent nights, there is no need to assume a modification of the verbal root (dhātu). This is not tenable.

Since the contingency of meaninglessness arises regarding the form of the *dvirātra* sacrifice, even though—by way of the restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) concerning the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering (9.1.2)—there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here of being a means to an intermediate apūrva, and although there is no possibility of a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) for an apūrva belonging to the *ekāha* [type] within the *dvirātra*, nevertheless, in accordance with the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) consisting in non-deviation from the apūrva as assisted by the subsequent word, there is an impossibility [of accepting] that the delimiting factor of the objecthood (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) is the state of having a preceding [sacrifice] of the same class as the subsequent one.

This figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), defined as delimiting the status of being a means to the *apūrva*, is indeed necessary out of fear of meaninglessness; this applies even to those who accept the injunction for taking the *ṣoḍaśin* cup with reference to the latter day connected to the *dvirātra* sacrifice.

However, there is a distinction: according to the former view, the figurative indication of the status of being a means to the aforementioned supreme *apūrva* occurs through its connection with the sentence-meaning consisting of the "latter day" related to the *dvirātra*; whereas in our own view, the figurative indication of the status of being a means to the aforementioned supreme *apūrva* occurs through its connection with the *dvirātra* alone.

Furthermore, it should be understood that in your view, the locative case ending in *uttare ’han* denotes the objecthood (*karmatva*) of the case-meaning by means of a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its own denotable property (*svaśakyatāvacchedaka*), which is delimited by the state of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). In our view, however, the genitive case ending, which expresses a general relation, indicates [the deity] through a secondary indication based on its own denotable property. Nor should it be argued that, even so, since the dative case is directly expressive of the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradānatva*), the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) would be a meaning of the case-ending itself; consequently, in such passages as *yad agnaye ca prajāpataye ca sāyaṃ juhoti*, the deity would necessarily be a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the oblation (*homa*). This is not the case.

Since the meaning of the dative case is the status of being a recipient (*saṃpradāna*) characterized by being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*) of a substance that is being relinquished, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*)—which consists in being the intended object of a substance not [physically] relinquished—is likewise not excluded from being its meaning. Even if one were to add "the absence of being a recipient" as an additional requirement because the term "deity" is not conventionally applied to a Brahmin who is a recipient in cases such as "he gives a cow to a Brahmin" (where the Brahmin lacks the status of a recipient), this would still not be the case here; for in the present instance, deityhood is defined precisely as the status of being a recipient. Furthermore, since the deityhood of Agni and Soma is established through their recurrence [in the ritual], there is no contradiction. Thus, deityhood is stated here to be nothing other than the status of being a recipient.

In that case, let the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) consist simply in being one or another among [the categories] such as agenthood (*kartṛtva*) accompanied by purposefulness (*kṛtyanvita*).
Furthermore, there is no fault regarding the status of being a deity (*devatātva*), since that too is included within "one or another" (*anyatamatva*).
However, since causeship (*nimittatva*) and so forth are not included therein, there is no undesirable consequence of [a cause] being a *kāraka*.

And thus, even if the previously mentioned distinction between the object (*karman*) and the agent (*kāraka*) is not included in the definition, there is no deficiency; for since "objectness" (*karmatva*) is included within the category of being one or another of [the roles] such as "agentness" (*kartṛtva*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) with respect to heaven (*svarga*) and the like when they are associated with that [objectness]. It should be understood that the word in the Sūtra is intended precisely to convey this kind of "one-or-another-ness. Furthermore, "being enjoined" (*vihitatva*) consists in being distinct from an injunction (*vidhi*) whose nature is instigation (*pravartanā*); because it is only the knowledge of instigation that, by way of producing the knowledge of the means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), causes activity, [instigation] exists only in the act of activity itself. In the absence of that [instigation], it is all the more absent in its *kārakas*, and therefore [the definition does not apply to them].
For this very reason, it does not possess the quality of being produced by the cognition of an instigation (*pravartanājñāna*).

Nor does it possess the quality of being prompted by an injunction (*vidhi*), whether directly or through a causal chain; for this would result in the definition being under-extended (*avyāpti*) to universals (*jāti*) and the like.

This is because, being eternal, they lack the quality of being prompted by an injunction; and even in the case of non-eternal things such as *soma* and other materials, they lack the quality of being prompted by an injunction because they exist in an already accomplished state (*siddharūpa*).

Therefore, being enjoined (*vihitatva*) consists in the exclusion of the injunction itself. And that [exclusion] is the state of being qualified by the injunction, by virtue of being the delimitor of the delimitation of the qualificandhood (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by the modehood (*prakāratā*) residing in the injunction itself.

This [state] exists in the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, because the property of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*) and the like possesses the status of being the delimitor of the delimitation of the qualificandhood residing in the efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*), which is determined by the modehood residing in the instigation (*pravartanā*). This is because the status of being its delimitor is present therein.

Now, one might object: this [definition of being enjoined] is possible under the view that the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) characterized by the verbal root is a qualifier (*prakāra*) of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

However, under the alternative view that the meaning of the verbal root itself is the qualifier of the productive urge through a relation such as instrumentality, since the property of being the delimitor of the qualificandhood residing in the objective productive urge (*arthabhāvanā*) exists only in the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, it lacks the qualification by the injunction through the relation that serves as the delimitor of the delimitor of the qualificandhood qualified by its own qualifierhood. Therefore, the aforementioned "being enjoined" is not possible in that case. If this is argued, we say no.

This is because what is intended is being qualified by the injunction through either of the two relations: being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) of the qualificandness (*viśeṣyatā*) as determined by its own lack of a mode (*niṣprakāratā*), or being the delimiting factor of that [delimiting factor].

Nor should it be argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the definition of a *dvitva* (duality) applying to things such as the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) denoted by the suffix *su*, since that [qualification] is accepted even in those cases.

Indeed, it is not [ungrammatical] in the *nirukta*, because the aforementioned defect is absent due to the absence of being a factor (*kāraka*) of volitional effort (*kṛti*). Although, according to the view that the verbal root-meaning alone connects with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) through relations such as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), even in the case of sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, the status of being a factor of volitional effort is not possible, nevertheless—according to that very view—the connection [of the root-meaning] consists precisely in its being connected with volitional effort through one of the relations such as agency (*kartṛtva*), and in its being connected with one of the factors of volitional effort. This is because, in the case of the verbal root-meaning, there exists the state of being connected with volitional effort through the relation of objecthood (*karman*), and in the case of a factor such as *soma*, there exists the state of being connected with the aforementioned [status of being a factor of volitional effort]. Thus, there is no defect.
