In order to prevent the undesirable consequence that [the object] is connected with the effort (*kṛti*) through such relations as "being a determiner of the meaning of the sūtra," and so forth, [the relation] must be precisely "being one of the set consisting of agenthood (*kartṛtva*) and the rest.

For this very reason, in cases such as "one desiring sensory power should sacrifice with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*), even though the oblation (*homā*) is connected with the effort through a relation such as "being the locus" (*āśrayatva*), there is no risk of its being connected with the sensory power and the like.

In reality, according to the manner previously stated, since the instrumentality characterized by the verbal root (dhātu) alone is related to the productive operation (bhāvanā) as its qualifier, it is more appropriate [to define] "being an agent of effort" (kṛtikārakatva) as being either the state of having an action (kṛti) as its correlate or the state of being a "doer" (kartṛtva), and "being enjoined" (vihitatva) as being qualified by an injunction through a relation that serves as the delimitor of the delimitation of the subjecthood (viśeṣyatā) determined by the qualifierhood (prakāratā) residing in itself.

Furthermore, this "being enjoined" (vihitatva) belongs to the objectless productive urge (*bhāvanā*); for since it is impossible for the instigation (*pravartanā*) to be construed with the *bhāvanā* through the relation of being prompted (*prayojyatā*), first all the factors of action (*kārakas*) are construed with the effort (*kṛti*). Subsequently, the instigation is construed with the *bhāvanā*—which is now qualified by all those factors—through the relation of being prompted. Thus, the understanding of the word-meaning is described according to the principle of "the qualification of one thing by another already qualified."

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tantraratna* on the seventh [chapter], under the sūtra "in the five and seven" (*pañcasaptareṣu*) [7.1.13], that even when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) to a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), such as the *Viśvajit*, the assumption of a sevenfold division and so forth does not occur.

For an injunction (*vidhi*), having first secured a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) capable of being performed with all its constituent parts complete, subsequently proceeds to impel the person; then, by virtue of a requirement, it establishes subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) through the medium of the cognition of excellence (*prāśastya-jñāna*). Wherever it may reside, it remains thus.
The extended application (*atideśa*) brings [the details] into proximity;
however, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) subject to that application seizes its own constituent parts even prior to that.

At that time, because the commendatory passage (*arthavāda*) is brought into proximity—whether by direct injunction (*upadeśa*) or by extended application (*atideśa*)—and because the fruit arises together with the accomplishment of that [operation], it seizes heaven itself. Thus, the logic of heaven (*svarganyāya*) does not apply here.
(41315) Thus it is said.

However, since verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is an empirical fact even without the knowledge of fitness—occurring merely through the absence of a certainty regarding unfitness—the two [the injunction and the result] are brought simultaneously as qualifiers of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) by way of the principle "two in one. Alternatively, through the assistance of the effort consisting of common denotation (*samānābhidhāna*) and so forth, the connection of the other factors (*kārakas*) with the instigation (*pravartanā*) and the rest occurs first; subsequently, there is the connection of the factorhood (*kārakatva*) in the efficient force whose object is the thing to be accomplished (*bhāvya*). Because the instigation is clearly understood as a "means" (*itikartavyatā*) due to its being a specific qualification of the object to be accomplished, there is no requirement for the extension (*atideśa*) of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Thus, in the case of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, there is no contingency of having to postulate a fruit mentioned in an explanatory passage; this is another point.

Alternatively, since the previously stated etymological derivation is untenable and for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), "being enjoined" (*vihitatva*) consists precisely in being the object of an injunction (*vidhi*) in the form of an impulsion (*pravartanā*). And there is indeed a pervasion (*vyāpti*) [of this] in the case of a qualified productive urge (*bhāvanā*) toward such an impulsion.
Moreover, in your view, there would be the undesirable consequence that the instrumental case (tṛtīyā) and others would constitute a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the substance.

For it has been stated that the instrumental case and others serve as means of knowledge for subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*) precisely because they convey the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*), which is a constituent element of subsidiarity.
However, since your proposed definition does not include that [instrumentality], such a status would not arise.
Others, however, define *śeṣatva* (subsidiariness) as the state of being engaged for the sake of another.
By "engagement" (*pravṛtti*), there is denoted merely an activity performed by an agent, whether conscious or unconscious.
And indeed, all causal factors possess agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to their own respective activities.

Furthermore, there exists a type of objecthood (*viṣayatā*) consisting of being the intended goal (*uddeśyatā*). In that regard as well, we observe common usage such as "the wood burns for the sake of cooking" (*pākāya kāṣṭhāni jvalanti*) and "he pours water for the sake of grain" (*dhānyāya jalaṃ pralavati*).

Regarding this usage, Bhavadeva maintains that when the agent of the verbal expression (*abhidhāvyāpāra*) is an insentient word, individual instances (*vyakti*) possess the status of being the intended goal; whereas Kapila holds that when the operation has the *prakṛti* (the primordial cause) as its agent, the objects to be produced possess the status of being the intended goal.
And they say that whatever is employed with a view toward something else is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to that [latter].

Moreover, even that would result in the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice and so forth for the agent of an activity aimed at the sacrifice and so forth, simply because of the verbal root [denoting] hearing (*śru*);

and even if "being enjoined" (*vihitatva*) were included [in the definition], that [agent] would still have that as its purpose, or else the *prayāja* offerings and so forth would possess the status of being for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) even without the context (*prakaraṇa*).
Therefore, for the sake of understanding the specific intended meaning, there is first a requirement for direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Both verbal roots and nominal stems require a direct scriptural statement regarding that which is to be enjoined.
For an injunction makes known the status of the thing enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), not that of anything else.
And this injunction does not directly enjoin [the accessories] apart from the meditation itself;
rather, by taking that very meditation as its qualified object, it enforces its qualifiers as well by implication.

Even in cases where [an accessory] is already obtained in a general sense, the injunction—being perceived as having a qualified object—becomes focused on the qualifiers through the distinction between what is already obtained and what is not; and this status of being a qualifier depends upon direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

Because the commonality of cognition and designation is established through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the agency of the *sattva* (the substance) and so forth is understood as a qualification of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) upon hearing [the word], while the meaning of the verbal root is [so understood] through the mention of the result.

However, for items introduced by other words—such as the animal (*paśu*) and so forth—as well as their number, gender, and so on, this is to be inferred from the direct statement of the case-ending (*vibhakti-śruti*) and the like.

Thus, by indicating the specific subordinate (*śeṣin*) and the specific subordinate element (*śeṣa*), these causes of application (*viniyoga*), such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest, are established as providing assistance to the injunction (*vidhi*) just as the subsidiaries themselves do; this is the conclusion.
*Nyāyaratnamālā*, pp. 120–123.
Regarding the consideration of the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*), [the discussion] follows the fourth chapter.

*Vārttika* 2.2.13, p. 473: It will be stated in the eleventh [chapter] that the subsidiary and the principal share the same time (*ekakālatva*), because time is connected with the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of both the subsidiary and the principal, which is another name for "performance" (*prayoga*).
The subsidiary and the principal [acts] share the same place, time, and agent.
And their absence in the subsidiaries is due to the reference being made with respect to the primary, just as in the case of the substance and the deity.
The Commentary states: Now the subsidiaries are being considered.
Is it that for them the place, time, and agent are restricted [to those of the primary], or is there no restriction?
What is established? And there is an absence of that [the *samit*] in the subsidiaries (*aṅga*).
Why? Because of the specification with respect to the primary acts (*pradhāna*).

Since the *samits* and so forth are specified with respect to the primary acts such as the *Āgneya* as being subordinate to the injunctions of the original mandate (*codanā*), they do not apply elsewhere.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule.
Just as the substance and deity prescribed for the principal rites do not apply to their subsidiaries, so too it is with the place and other such factors.
(The pregnant woman [antarāgarbhiṇī] is to be taken elsewhere.)
"But since the subsidiaries are taught along with the principal acts, they should share the same location.

Commentary: As for what was said—that there is no restriction regarding location and so forth for the subsidiaries—in that regard, there is a restriction on location and so forth for the subsidiaries.
Why? Because the subsidiaries are also taught together with the principal act being taught for the accomplishment of the result."
How so? Because it is an injunction (*vidhāna*).
This injunction, namely the performance of the auxiliary members (*aṅga-prayoga*), is that which establishes the primary rites as having a fruit to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*).
"Injunction" (*vidhāna*), "ritual manual" (*kalpa*), and "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*) are synonymous.

Therefore, in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices," the performance of the primary rites is stated as being possessed of its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*). Just as the procedure (*vidhi*) is stated therein, so too is there an injunction for the *samits* and other subsidiaries by means of the scriptural text.
Consequently, the subsidiaries must also share the same place, time, and agent as the primary rites.

If it is argued that "the substance and the deity are likewise," the Bhāṣya states: Now, as to what was said— that just as the substance and the deity exist separately for the primary rites and the subsidiary rites, so too should the place and other factors be understood—
this must be refuted.
The Sūtra [states]: "Up to the end of the Āma. And there is no difference otherwise among those distinguished by the injunctions.
The Bhāṣya says: "This is not so."
Why? Because it is a subordinate element of the injunction of the impelling command (*codanāvidhi*).
For the injunction regarding the substance and the deity is indeed a subordinate element of the injunction of the impelling command.
Therefore, the specific substance and deity are fixed for the primary acts.
In this case, there is the fire and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), as well as the path (āyana) and the oblation (iṣṭauṣī).
Likewise, even regarding the subsidiary rites (aṅga), one performs the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) with clarified butter (ājya), and from the remnant (śeṣa), one performs the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
And it is not prescribed elsewhere.
And its application is based on the reason that there is a commonality of ritual procedure (*tantra*) due to shared factors, and so forth.
Therefore, it is unequal with respect to the substances and deities.

Because the subsidiaries are common (*tantra*) to those [actions] through their inherent connection (*samavāya*), whereas there is a distinction because of the difference in those [substances and deities], there is a division of the ritual acts.

It would apply to the performance [of the subsidiaries], because they are designated by the term "principal" (*pradhāna*), and there is likewise a scriptural indication to that effect. The Commentary states: "And if the substance and deity were common to both the subsidiaries and the principals, then, because of the co-inherence of the subsidiaries and the principals within those respective substances and deities, the lack of distinction would remain as it was; thus, the *tantra* (common performance) would apply to the principal. But there is a distinction because of that difference."
But if there is a difference between the substance and the deity, then from that difference follows a difference in the ritual action (*karmabheda*).
It would occur in the performance (*prayoga*);
for in the performance of the ritual, a distinction would arise due to the perception of specific differences.
And thus, the observation of another matter will be logical: "Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day; thirteen on the new moon day.
For this reason also, there is a difference in substance and deity.

And when time and so forth are thus supplementary to the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), then, because the originative injunction prescribes only the primary acts devoid of their subsidiaries (*niraṅga*).

Regarding the subsidiary and the primary: these factors such as time and so forth apply only to those [elements] explicitly mentioned; they do not pertain to the subsidiaries being performed at the same place, time, or by the same agent as the primary.
However, those subsidiaries may indeed be performed even at different times and so forth.
This being the position, it is replied:
... And when time and so forth are thus subordinate elements of the injunctive sentence (*prayogavākya*), the fact that the cognitions [of those things] also belong to that same time is established.

For instance, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), once understood as having its aspects of the end to be achieved (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) expressed, requires a manner of performance (*itthambhāva*).
The specific nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*) residing in the *bhāvanā* is its "manner of being" (*itthambhāva*).
And the *bhāvanā*, whose form is already known, requires [factors] such as time.

Therefore, when the manner of the *bhāvanā* is required, and the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are understood as being that manner, and when the operation of the *bhāvanā*—which is synonymous with the performance (*prayoga*)—is understood in its totality, then time and the other factors are enjoined as being subordinate to it. Thus, those very things—place and so forth—become the auxiliaries (*aṅga*) of the subsidiaries as well.

Furthermore, the substance and the deity are not enjoined as being connected to the entire performance, because they are neither required nor suitable for that purpose. For a performance corresponding to the laying of the fires (*agnyādhāna*), the spreading of the grass (*barhistaraṇa*), and so forth, has no requirement for a substance and a deity. Nor are the substance and the deity capable of effecting those [preparatory acts]. Rather, the substance and the deity are connected [to the sacrifice] because they are required and suitable for the sacrifice, which is a subordinate part of the productive operation toward the fruit (*phalabhāvanā*).

Therefore, the substance and deity connected with the primary rite belong to the subsidiaries as well. However, the distinction is that the time and other factors, being conjoined with the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) for the fruit— which consists of the entirety of the rites beginning with the *Āgneya*— belong to the subsidiaries included within that [primary] as well.

In this commentary on the *Soma*, there is an internal discussion (*antarāci-tantra*) as to whether, regarding the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*), the time, the place, and the agent are fixed by a specific injunction (*samādeśa*), or if there is no such restriction (*aniyama*).

Although words such as *amāvāsyā* (the new moon day) denote only the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*), because the second mention in injunctions such as "one should sacrifice on the *amāvāsyā*" brings about the cognition of a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) having that [day] as its instrument, it is established that place and other factors connected to that [operation] serve the purpose of both the subsidiary and the primary sacrifices—just as in the cases of "with the *pravargya* rite" and "in the waters with the *avabhṛtha* bath. Nevertheless, it should be noted that even in those cases where there is a mention of the primary sacrifice in the instrumental case by way of enjoining the place and so forth, an intermediate discussion is necessary to prove that the place and other factors serve the purpose of the primary sacrifice together with its subsidiaries.
Viśvanātha: "Whichever regions and so forth [are mentioned] as members, are they like deities and the like?
No, because there is no *ananvaya* (lack of syntactic connection); for they are included by virtue of their mention in the formal application (*prayoga*).
Maṇḍana: 'That very [thing] is not separate within the members.'"
And in the limbs [of the body], there is oneness with those who possess those limbs, such as Kāla and others.
Mī. Kau. 23.

Where there is an explicit scriptural statement regarding both the subsidiary (aṅga) and the primary (pradhāna), there even a difference in time occurs, as in: "On the day before the new moon, one prepares the altar" (Bhāṣya 1.3.12.1).
By the force of such a scriptural statement, there may also be a difference in place, time, and agent between the subsidiary and the primary.
Because the subsidiaries have the same time as the principal, their performance at another time occurs by virtue of a specific scriptural statement.
The Bhāṣya states: "It has been declared that the subsidiaries share the same time, place, and performer as the principal" (11.2.18).
And thus, this [rule] applies everywhere.
From the scriptural statement [it follows] that there is a difference in time.
Where there is a scriptural statement, there exists a difference in time, a difference in place, and also a difference in the agent.
For example: "On the previous day, on the new moon, he prepares the altar"; "They proceed with the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in the waters."
In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, it is understood that there is a different agent because of the difference in the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), as it is stated: "A mare is the sacrificial fee.
Furthermore, it has been stated that the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) must occupy the same location and occur at the same time as the primary rite (*pradhāna*).
However, where the difference in place and time of an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is stated by the scriptural injunction itself, it occurs accordingly; thus he spoke as a friend.
There is nothing here to be refuted.
In the preceding section on Soma, the commonality (*tantratā*) of time and other factors regarding the acquisition of auxiliaries was primarily established.

Now, as an exception to that [principle of simultaneous performance], having introduced the case where the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) occur at different times, the commonality (*tantratva*) of subsidiaries occurring at different places and times is being demonstrated; thus, there is a change of section (*pādāntaratva*) and immediate sequence (*ānantarya*). In such cases as "They proceed with the *avabhṛtha* bath," there is difference of place; in "On the previous day of the new moon, one prepares the altar (*vedi*)," there is difference of time; and in the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice performed in the fire, regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is said, "A mare is the fee"—thus the fee for the subsidiaries and the principal is like that of the subsidiaries.

Bhaṭṭa: It has been stated that for subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and primary rites (*pradhāna*) which are encompassed by a single injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*), there is unity of place, time, and agent;

this is because of the statement: "Whether the subsidiaries and so forth occur at the time of the primary (*mukhya-kāla*) or at their own time (*svakāla*), they are not separated from the preceding [rites]," and so on.
Furthermore, it is said that the subsidiaries and primaries, being grasped by one performance-injunction, must share the same location, time, and performer.
In some cases, even when there is an injunction, there is a difference in time, place, and agent.
For example: "On the new moon day preceding [the full moon], he prepares the altar," "They perform the Agnyupasthāna rite," and "A mare is the sacrificial fee.
In these instances, a difference in time and other factors is observed.

In some cases, even when falling within the same major ritual application (*mahāprayoga*), there is a difference of performers based merely on the distance of the *paracāra* (the movement of others); in other cases, it is by the very nature of the distinctness of the application, as in the case of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).
Furthermore, the difference of performers due to the difference in sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in rites such as the *agnyādheya* and *vājapeya* will be explained [in Sūtra 1.1.4.1].
This point, though already established, is recalled here out of friendship for the sake of the subsequent subject matter.
Maṇḍana: "In the case of subsidiaries, there is a difference in place, time, and so forth [from the primary].
Śaṃkara: "There is a difference in time between the subsidiary and the principal.
This refers to the principle that subsidiaries and primaries must share the same place, time, and agent.

(1.2.1.16.32) For when it has been determined that the Vāruṇī sacrifice is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the rite involving the acceptance of a horse, then, according to the principle governing auxiliaries and primary rites (*pradhāna*),
this [Vāruṇī] must also be performed by the very same person who is the performer of the *kratu*.
And whoever is the performer of the *kratu* is the giver of the horse.
Therefore, it must be established that the fruit belongs to the giver.

Vārttika 3.4.1.13, p. 165. It has been stated that "the performance of the subsidiaries and the primary acts is uninterrupted," as in: "But the subsidiaries, because they are enjoined, should be performed along with the primary" (1.1.2.8).
Bhāṣya 1.1.2.8.132. The non-interruption is for the sake of both the subsidiary and the primary; it is not the primary alone.

3|7|4|8: In the case of the *barhis* grass and the duties pertaining to the *barhis*, as well as the altar (*vedi*) and the duties pertaining to the altar, these serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the primary rite (*pradhāna*) in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; they do not serve the primary rite alone. 3|7|1|9–5: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the altar serves the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the primary rite.
3|7|1|7, 9: The sublation of the general rule (*prāptabādha*) characterized by the relationship between subsidiary and primary is sixfold.
For example, there are instances where a contingent element (aupadeśika) supersedes a regular one (aupadeśika).
In that regard, a specific rule (naimittika) may supersede a permanent rule (nitya), as when the *pāścādasya* [offering] of the permanent rite is superseded by the *vaidyanamīcakasāt-tadasya*.

Likewise, a desired (kāmya) act may supersede both a permanent and a specific rule, as when the *pāścādasya* of the permanent rite is superseded by the number twenty-one for the sake of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), and the *sāsadasya* of the specific rule is superseded by the same.

There is sublation of the archetypal by the modified through direct instruction, as in the case of the *prayāja* and other offerings where the purpose of the *niṣedha* (the prohibition) applies to the *prayāja* etc. [of the archetype]; and there is sublation of the archetypal by the modified through extended application (*atideśa*), as in the case of the rule "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one verses. Here, since the purpose of kindling—which is the function of the *sāmidhenī* verses—is accomplished incidentally (*prasaṅga*) by the modified *sāmidhenīs* prescribed for the optional (*kāmya*) rite which has the constant (*nitya*) recitation as its archetype, those [archetypal] *sāmidhenīs* are sublated.

Bāla, p. 123: The subsidiary meditations (*aṅga-bhāvanā*), being complete in their own constituent parts, are connected with the supreme meditation (*parama-bhāvanā*); however, their own specific functions do not cease by virtue of being dependent upon it. Vārttika 3.1.1.12, p. 732. That which has become a subsidiary is grasped by the extended application (*codaka*). Bhāṣya 3.6.16.7: And it has been stated that the accomplishment of what has become a subsidiary occurs through the commencement of the primary rite.
1|1|4|7: That which is a subordinate member (aṅga) becomes the result (phala).
1|1|3|135: There is a distinction of subordinate members due to the distinction of agents; and there is a distinction of agents due to the distinction of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
1|1|4|12: There is a distinction of subordinate members due to the distinction of time.
"Likewise, the subsidiaries belonging to the time of the Full Moon sacrifice do not assist the New Moon sacrifice due to the difference in time.
Just as with the subsidiaries, there is a sequential order for the sacrifices.

Regarding those sacrifices consisting of the *iṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and the Soma sacrifice; their performance should follow a sequential order according to the sequence of the textual recitation.
In the Vedas, those rites for specific desires (*kāmyāḥ*) that were taught and recited in a particular sequence must be performed in that very same sequence.
This is just like the sequence of performance for the auxiliary elements (*aṅgāni*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), which occurs precisely according to the order of their textual recitation.
The suffix *-vati* is applied here to the word *aṅgavat*, which ends in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), meaning "like the auxiliaries."
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
"Or rather not, because of the lack of connection.
Having set aside the prima facie view reached by the Sūtra with the word "or rather" (*vā*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
They are not to be performed according to the order of recitation, because there is no connection between them—specifically, because they lack mutual relationship.
Indeed, those ritual acts do not provide mutual assistance; therefore, the order of recitation is not authoritative in that regard. Rather, their performance may follow one's own preference.

And because they are optional. In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), this sūtra provides another reason: because those rites are optional (*kāmya*), that is, because they are occasioned by desire, and since desire is not constant, whenever a desire arises, then that rite is to be performed according to one's will, and not according to the order of the textual recitation.
The word "ca" (and) serves as a conjunction.
[The opponent] objects: "If it is argued that [the mantra] is purposeless. Thus, he raises a further doubt.

If it is argued that because there would otherwise be purposelessness—due to the consequence of the textual order being meaningless—there is no absence of sequence in performance, but rather that it must be performed precisely according to the textual order; [we reply:
like the auxiliary rites (aṅga), it would be deficient in its limbs, because it is for the sake of knowledge (vidyā) among the subsequent [stages] in its entirety.
He dispels this doubt:
even if the performance [of the rite] is according to one's desire, the recitation would still be fruitful,
because the purpose of the recitation is knowledge— that is, it serves the purpose of understanding.

Even though there is no sequential order in the performance [of the rites], the textual recitation exists solely for the purpose of knowing each respective [element]. However, if knowledge arises according to the order of the text, there is an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as the fruit;
just as, for example, from all subsequent sacrifices following the sacrifice named *Sarva*, the fruit is indeed a subsidiary (*aṅga*) through such knowledge.
The sacrifice known as the *sarvasvāra* is performed solely for the purpose of death.
Furthermore, after enjoining the *sarvasvāra* in the Śruti, many other sacrifices are prescribed;
yet it is not possible to perform those [other sacrifices] after one has died.
However, knowledge certainly arises for them even before death;
by that alone, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by that knowledge also certainly comes into being.
Thus, the recitation and trembling are useful for the sake of knowledge, not for the sake of performance.
The performance, however, follows precisely the desire [for results].

Therefore, the established conclusion is that rites performed for specific desires (kāmyakarmāṇi) are not to be performed solely according to the order of the textual recitation, but rather in accordance with the desire for their fruits;
this is like the case of the auxiliary parts (aṅga).

Just as auxiliary rites are performed in order to establish the completeness of the primary rite (*pradhāna*), and once they have been performed, that completeness is established so they are not repeated; likewise, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that a rite for a specific desire (*kāmya-karma*) should be performed only once. Bhāṣya 11.2.4.22, "Like the auxiliaries" (*aṅgavat*).

Just as the order of recitation is a restrictive rule for the *samid* and other [obligatory] offerings, it is not so for the order of recitation of optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) sacrifices.
This is like the case of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that just as there is a restriction of order among the *samid* and others because the order serves a purpose within the recitation prescribed by the injunction of Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), the same applies to another ritual manual (*kalpa*) as well.
Like the subsidiary (aṅga).

Just as in the case of "He whose sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) is made of *khadira* wood eats with the very essence of the Vedas," which is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the sake of a result, so too is the statement, "Those who perform these *rātri* sacrifices indeed become firmly established."

Bhāṣya 4.3.8.17 (18): Those syllables which are inserted by the singers while the [five] limbs are being sung—namely, those intended for the purpose of measuring the duration of the song—are not to be understood as connected to the meaning;

for the duration of the song is easily measured by means of these syllables. 9.2.10.35: The sentences of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), though complete in their own respective meanings, enter into syntactic unity with the sentence concerning the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
And it does not abandon its own nature.

(Vārttika 3.1.8.21, p. 732). The detailed sequence regarding the subsidiary sentences (*aṅgavākya*) reaching up to the fruit should be seen in the *Vārttika* on the section concerning the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Ke.:
One who is deficient in limbs (*aṅgavikalpa*), such as one who is blind and so forth, has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform the ritual action.
Even when there is a deficiency of the auxiliary factors (*aṅga*), if it is remedied by means of *aupadha* and so forth, there is indeed eligibility for the ritual action.

VI. 1|9: However, regarding a deficiency of auxiliary factors that can be rectified, if it cannot be rectified by means of *aupadha* and so forth, there is no eligibility for a ritual action performed for a specific desire (*kāmya-karman*).

VI. 6.1.10: Even when there is a deficiency of auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) that cannot be remedied by means such as substitutes (*aupadhādi*), one still possesses the qualification (*adhikāra*) for obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*).

VI. 6.1.10: The injunction regarding auxiliaries (*aṅgavidhāna*)—being connected with the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*) for the sake of its excellence (*guṇārtha*)—does not require further connection when another auxiliary is enjoined, because there is no desire to interrupt the mental focus (*buddhicchedākāmāva*). Thus, even when many auxiliaries are enjoined, there is no increase in difficulty. Su. p. 1189: The injunction regarding auxiliaries (*aṅgavidhi*).
For there can be no specific injunction regarding a subsidiary part in an action that lacks a subsidiary part;

yet there is indeed a specific injunction: "The *prastara* [grass-bundle] has *āśvavāla* [horse-tail grass] as its handle. For if there were no general category, no specific *prastara* could be enjoined.
Just as for one who has no son, no toys are made for that son; Bhāṣya 10.1.15.
The science of phonetics (aṅgaśāstra) has its purport solely upon the accomplishment of the primary [grammar].

Soma. 6|1|30. It is established in the tenth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] that archetypal auxiliary rites (*aṅgaśāstra*) are extended by their very nature to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). Su. p. 1317.

Furthermore, it will be stated under the rule "And in case of conflict between an auxiliary quality and the primary, [the former prevails] because it is for the sake of the latter" (1|2|125), p. 867, that the perfection of the primary depends upon the performance of the auxiliaries with their qualities intact.
Even if the auxiliary oblations (*aṅgahavis*) are deficient, the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the primary is not produced.

Or: 3|7|14. "And one who is deficient in a limb possesses that same [status]. A limb refers to the eyes and so forth. Sometimes, due to disease or other causes, a deficiency in a limb such as the eyes occurs; in such a case, a person deficient in a limb would be unable to perform the ritual action with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that one who is deficient in limbs has no entitlement to perform ritual acts.
However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: deficiency of limbs arising from disease and the like can indeed be remedied through medicine and other means;
for such deficiency is not invariably and permanently incurable in every case.

And thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) on the part of one who lacks the constituent parts of the rite through subsequent restoration.

In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was established that one devoid of wealth has no eligibility for ritual action because ritual action is accomplished by means of material resources. However, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was reached that the lack of wealth is not permanent; therefore, even if one initially lacks wealth, one will acquire it through effort. Thus, there is no contradiction in the eligibility for ritual action even for one who is initially devoid of wealth.

In this section, for that entire subject matter, the principle of "drawing in the subsidiary parts" (*aṅgākarṣaṇanyāya*) is applied by means of the term "their properties" (*taddharmāśabda*), and an extended application (*atideśa*) is made through the chapter on the introduction of subsidiaries (*aṅgāvatārādhyāya*).

The word "ca" (and) serves to include the case of one deficient in wealth who was previously mentioned as subject to punishment. If one deficient in a limb (*aṅgahīna*) is indeed capable of rectifying that deficiency, then he possesses the same status as the one deficient in wealth; that is, he would have the same property (*dharma*) as the one deficient in wealth—namely, the right to perform ritual acts (*karmādhikāra*) and equality [with others] in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the property is the possession of the right to perform ritual acts by virtue of having rectified the deficiency. Thus, the one deficient in a limb would possess that same property as the one deficient in wealth.

And thus, the meaning is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) there is an absence of qualification for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*), whereas in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) there is possession of qualification for ritual action. In the compound *taddharmāḥ*, the suffix *anic* is applied as a compound-final element (*samāsānta*) according to the rule *dharmādibhyaś ca kevalāt*.
On this point, see the *Sudhā* (p. 531).

When it should have been stated that "he who is capable by his power should perform [the rite]," it was instead said that "he should act in such a way as he is able," in order to indicate—by means of the very refutation—that even when there is a deficiency in the ritual requirements (*pratisamādhai vaikalye*), the qualification (*adhikāra*) remains present, as will be set forth in the sixth section (*ṣaṣṭhādhikaraṇa*) under the sūtra "And one who is deficient in limbs possesses those duties" (*aṅgahīnaśca taddharmā*).

Starting from the statement, "By two [days] the hair grows, by two the flesh," the text demonstrates that the twelve-day ritual (dvādaśāha) is the model (prakṛti) for the twelve-fold subsidiary [period] within the Gavāmayana sacrifice.
Therefore, the twelve-day rite is the archetype for all multi-day sacrificial sessions (ahargaṇa).
Śā—In multi-day sacrificial sessions (*ahargaṇa*) such as the *dvirātra* and others, there exists an additional factor of indeterminacy (*avyaktatva*) and the state of being a group (*gaṇatva*).

Therefore, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *dvādaśāha* applies. In this way, the characteristics of a group (*gaṇadharma*), such as "the days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings," are obtained.

[Objection]: But surely, in the case of the *dvirātra* and other such sacrifices, because they are unmanifest (*avyakta*), the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) must be that of the *saumya* [soma-sacrifice].

Nor can there be an application of the *dvādaśāha* procedure on the grounds of being a "group" (*gaṇa*), for if that were so, then by virtue of the lack of distinction in being a group, the procedure characterized as the *kādaśinī* (the set of eleven animals) would also undesirably apply. Thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated with its connection.

The intention is that being a group (*gaṇatva*) while remaining unmanifest (*avyaktatva*) is the defining characteristic (*liṅga*); and this does not apply to the *saumya* sacrifice, nor to the *naikadaśinī*. Nor should it be argued: "How can the *dvādaśāha* be a modification (*vikāra*) of that [the *sāhna*], given their dissimilarity—since the *dvādaśāha* is a group characterized by days (*ahaḥ*), whereas the *dvirātra* and others are groups characterized by nights (*rātri*)"? This is because both the word "day" (*ahaḥ*) and the word "night" (*rātri*) refer to the full twenty-four-hour period (*ahorātra*); thus, since both are groups based on the occasion of an *ahorātra*, there is no dissimilarity between them.

Vi—In the case of multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇas*), such as the *dvādaśāha*, the first day [of the model sacrifice] should be applied because of the connection with the days; thus, there would be only the final [modification]. Bhāṭṭa—In the sacrificial sessions (*satras*) such as the *gavāmayana*, and in the multi-day sacrifices beginning with the *dvirātra* which consist of a series of *sutyā* days, the procedure of the *dvādaśāha* applies.
This is because they share the common characteristic of being denoted by terms expressive of rites accomplished over a day and night (*ahorātra*).
For here, the word "night" (*rātri*) and the word "day" (*ahaḥ*) refer specifically to particular rites performed over a day and night.
Furthermore, because they are included within a series of pressings (*sutyāgaṇa*), they possess the character of a twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāhika*).

For this very reason, in the Gavāmayana and other rites, the injunction of twelve *upasads*—expressed through such statements as "one shaves the hair with two [verses]"—is consistent as being for the purpose of another injunction (*vidhyantara*).

Thus it is said: this word "other" (*itarat*) does not merely denote what is proximate; it also expresses what has been previously mentioned alongside [the others], as well as what remains.

For when the word "other" is employed after enumerating specific characteristics—as in, "Let two woolen blankets be given to Devadatta, silk to Viṣṇumitra, linen to Yajñadatta, and the other to Caitra"—then only that which is desired [by the recipient] is understood, not gold or silver.

In this context, after enumerating the additional properties such as the red turban (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) and so forth belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, the word "other" (*itara*) is employed; therefore, it is capable of expressing a restrictive application (*adhikāra*) here as well, and thus it functions as a statement of addition. Alternatively, if it expresses what belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma, then it functions as a statement of proximity (*saṃnidhi*). In that case, one of the two must necessarily be abandoned.

If, setting aside the sense of a heading (adhikāra), one resorts to the sense of proximity (saṃnihita), then the mere restatement (anuvāda) becomes purposeless, and the word "śyena" would have its meaning unintended. On the other hand, if one sets aside the sense of proximity and adopts the sense of a heading, no fault whatsoever arises.
Therefore, the author of the Sūtras says: "For the purpose of referring to the other.

Thus, those specific rules of the Śyena sacrifice which are additional to the Jyotiṣṭoma injunction are extended here. The meaning is that there should be a commonality; that is, there should be a word expressing equality.
And the word *śyena* is intended [to be expressed].

The *Ṭupṭīkā* (criticizing the established conclusion of the *Bhāṣya*): In common usage, the word "other" (*itara*) is not well-known to denote excess (the meaning being that such a similarity is not its denotation).
What then? Because of its applicability, that which is proximate and other than [the primary] is what is well-known.
And there are not two meanings for this word;
therefore, because it has its primary meaning, it connects with what follows, beginning with "by the injunction of the Jyotiṣṭoma" and so forth.
Having stated, "In the iṣu [sacrifice], there is the vaṣaṭkāra, the nidhana, the viśruti, and the saptaha," it concludes, "The rest is the same as the Śyena."

(Regarding the statement: "In the *pūrvāhnika*, there is a *niḍhana* with the *vaṣaṭkāra*; he performs the *viṣṭuti* in the *iṣu*; it becomes a *saptaha*"—here, in the archetypal rite, the *niḍhana* with the *vaṣaṭkāra* and the *viṣṭuti* obtained through the *codaka* rule [are present];
and here, the specific form and the *saptaha* nature of the *sāman* for the hymn are enjoined.

In that regard—) that which is obtained from the *Jyotiṣṭoma* by means of the *codaka* is referred to by the word "the other" (*itara*), and a modification (*vikāra*) related to the *Śyena* is enjoined.
Whatever is obtained from the Jyotiṣṭoma is the same as in the Śyena;
therefore, only the red turban and so forth are extended by analogy.
(He states the meaning of the Sūtra: It is for the purpose of referring to the other [rite], meaning in the case of a modification.
In the Sūtra, the phrase "the other" (*itara*) refers to the statement "the rest is the same as the Śyena" (*samānamitarat śyenena*).
The expression "or even if" (*apivā yadi*) is explained by reversing the order to "even if" (*yadyapi vā*) and applying it to the fifth [case] repetition.

Thus, the meaning is as follows: if, for the sake of obtaining an injunction of a new matter (*apūrvārtha*), the statement "the rest is the same" were intended to enjoin a modification of the qualification (*adhikāra-vikāra*) from the injunction obtained through the *codaka* from the Jyotiṣṭoma, then the word "same" (*samāna*) would denote that; in that case, a modification like that of the Śyena should be performed for those things obtained through the extended application (*atideśa*) of the name of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Thus, or alternatively: *adhikāra* means purpose (*prayojana*).
The word *artha* denotes purpose;
and the word *itarat* is a reference to the term [itself].

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: by the word "the other" (*itarat*), the elements belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma are extended [by analogy] for the purpose of enjoining a modification; and for that modification, there is an injunction within the same sentence.
Thus, because of the commonality of the injunction (*codanā-sāmānyāt*), the arrow is indeed a part of the Jyotiṣṭoma, not a modification of the Śyena sacrifice.
However, by virtue of the specific statement, the mere fact of being a modification is extended from the Śyena.

He demonstrates the specific difference in performance according to this position as opposed to the position of the Bhāṣyakāra: when the word *itarat* (meaning "other") is explained in the sense of "additional" (*adhika*), there would be an extension (*atideśa*) even to those items not part of the archetypal ritual (*aprākṛtakārya*), such as the pricking with thorns prescribed for the Śyena sacrifice, provided that the meaning is taken as "that which is other than what is similar to the Śyena," according to the Bhāṣyakāra’s interpretation.

(Regarding the phrase "again, in the case of *assa-tvakṣe*": because the word *itarat* refers to what is proximate, the statement "it is the same as the Śyena" enjoining only the modification with reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma elements, there is no application of the *kaṇṭaka-vitodana* and so forth; this is the distinction.
As for the claim that it is for the purpose of praise, he says: Praise is not tenable. (Why? Because the arrow (*iṣu*) has already been enjoined in another section (another passage).
And in another passage, there is the statement "the other is the same.
Therefore, because [otherwise] the sentence would be purposeless, the mode of expression of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) must be abandoned.
Śā—True; the word "other" denotes what is proximate, but not that alone.
However, that which was previously indicated as being present but is not actually present is what is being discussed here.

In this context, that which is present—the [elements] belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma—is not similar to what was previously mentioned, because the non-archetypal elements such as the sevenfold chant (*saptahā*) and so forth were mentioned earlier. As for those non-archetypal elements such as the red turban (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) and the like, although they do not belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma and are thus not present here, there is nevertheless a similarity between them. Therefore, since one of the two must necessarily be abandoned, the discussion concerns the elements belonging to the Śyena sacrifice, by adopting the similarity rather than the proximity [of the Jyotiṣṭoma], on account of the scriptural statement.
(Thus is the view of the Bhāṣya.

When the modification of the *viṣṭut* and other elements obtained through the *codaka* rule has already been prescribed previously by the injunction "he pierces the arrow" (*iṣuṃ viṣṇoti*), etc., then—referring by means of the word "the other" (*itarat*) to that which is obtained through the *codaka* rule—the modification consisting of the red turban (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) and so forth is extended from the *Śyena* sacrifice.
In this way, the statement will possess proximity (*saṃnihitatva*), novelty (*apūrvatva*), and purposefulness (*arthavattva*). (This is the view of the Vārtika.)
*Soma*—when one thing among those present in the intellect is apprehended by virtue of a certain attribute, that which remains is denoted by the word *itara*.
Since that [remaining thing] was initially present in the intellect by virtue of a particular attribute, there exists both similarity and proximity (*saṃnidhi*) based upon that attribute.
Thus, it is established in common worldly usage that the word *itara* refers to the existence of something proximate.

The author of the Bhāṣya also stated: "Because of the use of the word 'the rest' (*itarat*) after enumerating the Vaiśeṣika categories, there must be something proximate to them. Since both [possibilities] are impossible there, when one of the two must be accepted for the sake of making the statement meaningful, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is accepted."

According to the view of the Vārttikakāra, however, since the *viṣṭutis* and so forth are obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), they are intended for the purpose of prescribing modifications (*vikāra*). Therefore, that which is other than those [specifically mentioned], namely what belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma, should be performed in the same manner as in the Śyena sacrifice; it should be performed endowed with whatever modifications exist in the Śyena. This is because the statement "similar to the proximate" (*saṃnihita-sadṛśa-vacana*) is thus justified, and the state of proximity (*saṃnihitatva*) must not be abandoned. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: in the sentence "in the similar [case], the other is similar," there would be an application of the scope (*adhikāra*) arising from the injunction, which is the direction understood through the *codaka*.
Why? Because it possesses the character of the archetype (*prakṛti*), namely the Jyotiṣṭoma, as in the case of the *iṣu* sacrifice.
Furthermore, the statement "In the *iṣu*, everything else is the same as the Śyena" is an explanatory restatement (*anuvādaka*).
Thus, this [statement] is either an extension (*atideśa*) of the archetypal elements or an explanatory restatement.

Because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, its properties are extended from the source of those rules; thus, the *śyena* [sacrifice] takes on the characteristics of the other *śyena*. The specific features, such as the red turban (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*), are extended by that [extension].
Bhāṭṭa: The extension (*atideśa*) of direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*) is now examined (in the first section of the seventh book).
There is a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) named *iṣu*, which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

In that context, the original (*prakṛta*) *sāman* has its *nidhana* ending in *vaṣaṭ*; in the original *vidhuti*, there is the form of the *iṣu*; and in the original *stotra*, there is the *sāman* consisting of the *saptaha* and so forth (the reading "saptaha" is found in the Bhāṣyavārtika).
Then, the scripture states: "The rest is the same as the Śyena.

Regarding the inquiry whether this is a restatement (anuvāda) or an injunction of extension (atideśavidhi), since the word *itara* (the other/the rest) is well-known in common usage as denoting what is proximate (*saṃnihita*), it cannot denote the properties of the Śyena which are not proximate, because those are not present.
Rather, since they are proximate through the extension from the Jyotiṣṭoma, it refers precisely to them.

And since those [details] are obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) even in the case of the *Śyena* sacrifice, their similarity to the *Śyena* is established; thus, the purpose is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), and there is no extended application of the verbal injunctions (*vacana-atideśa*) for the subsidiaries of the *Śyena*.

This being the position reached, we reply: It is well-established in common usage that the word "other" (*itara*) denotes not only what is proximate (*saṃnihita*) but also what is similar to what was previously mentioned.

For instance, in the expression, "A woolen blanket and a silk garment are to be given to Caitra and Maitra; the other (*itarat*) is for Viṣṇumitra," the meaning is understood from the very word "other" as referring to something distinct from the two previously mentioned items.
Therefore, the Vārttikakāra’s statement that the aforementioned similarity is not denotable is indeed to be disregarded.

Consequently, that which is proximate—the archetypal (prākṛta)—is not similar to what was previously mentioned, because the non-archetypal [elements] such as the *saptadaśa* and so forth were already mentioned.
And that which is similar—namely, the *śyena* and the *vaiṣopika*—is not proximate, due to its lack of commonality with the non-archetypal.

Consequently, because of the avoidance of fault (*avadya*) in one case or the other, and for the sake of making the statement meaningful, one must abandon what is proximate and, by adopting similarity, understand that the word "other" (*itara*) refers specifically to those [acts] similar to the *śyena* sacrifice.
Otherwise, the explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) which carries the imposition of another rite would not be meaningful.

Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is: "That which possesses similarity to the *śyena*, which is similar to what was previously mentioned, and which is distinct from what was previously mentioned—that one should perform with respect to the arrow (*iṣu*)."
And similarity to a hawk (*śyena*) consists in possessing properties of the same class as the properties of the act of seizing with a hawk (*śyenanigrāhya*).

For there are indeed properties belonging to the act of seizing with a hawk—such as piercing with a thorn and so forth—and those very properties, such as "piercing with a thorn," are of the same class [as the properties of the ritual act]. Possessing these is what is meant by the literal expression. For a similarity having the hawk as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is not possible in the case of piercing with a thorn and the like.

Therefore, by way of the result, the conclusion reached regarding the *iṣu* sacrifice is that the ritual details (*dharma*) of the *śyena* sacrifice—both those similar to and those different from what was previously mentioned—must be performed; this is the extension (*atideśa*). This same principle of extension applies to the *udbhid* and other such sacrifices.
And the aforementioned similarity is based either on being non-archetypal (*aprākṛtatva*) or on being prescribed with reference to an archetypal limb (*prākṛtāṅga*).

Therefore, those novel (*apūrva*) features of the Śyena sacrifice, such as the removal of thorns (*kaṇṭakavitodana*) and so forth, are extended by analogy (*atidiśyante*) here as well; or rather, those very elements which were prescribed in the Śyena as restatements of archetypal features, such as the red turban (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) and so forth, are what are extended.

As for the statement in the *Tantraratna* that "in this view there is no restriction to these alone," that is disregarded because there is no evidence for abandoning the intermediate similarity (*avāntarasādṛśya*).

In this view, because it is impossible to enjoin multiple items by means of a single objective (uddeśya), such as the arrow and the eastern direction, the two words [“arrow” and “eastern direction”] function through secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) to enjoin, by way of the objective, merely the modification that is unrelated to the archetypal Śyena sacrifice.

Alternatively, since there is no evidence for abandoning the proximate meaning of the word *itara* (other), and since it was previously stated that even the archetypal subsidiaries are intended as the objective, the word *itara* refers specifically to other archetypal subsidiaries that are similar to and non-different from the aforementioned archetypal ones.
Because these are brought into proximity through extended application (atideśa), the injunction of similarity to the Śyena is made precisely with reference to such archetypal subsidiaries.

And in this view, similarity (*sādṛśya*) consists in possessing the same properties as those properties residing in the archetypal parts belonging to the hawk sacrifice (*śyena*). And that property is the modification—such as the red turban and so forth—prescribed in the restatement of the archetypal parts of the hawk sacrifice.
Therefore, the similarity is not defined by reference to the hawk sacrifice itself, but rather is defined solely by reference to the archetypal parts belonging to the hawk sacrifice.

Since the properties residing in the *śyena* (falcon), such as the red turban (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) and so forth, do not exist in the archetypal (*prakṛta*) rites by that very same relation which serves as the delimitor of the standard of comparison (*upamānatā'vacchedaka-sambandha*), it is a rule of comparison that [the property] must reside in the object of comparison (*upameya*) by that same relation which delimits its status as the standard of comparison.
Therefore, on this view, the word *śyena* refers to the archetypal components belonging to the falcon.
Consequently, in effect, those very properties are enjoined with reference to such archetypal components that serve as the means for the arrow-joints (*iṣu-parva*).

Therefore, by virtue of the capacity of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya-sāmarthya*), whatever modification is prescribed for a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the archetypal *śyena* sacrifice is prescribed here specifically for that very archetypal constituent part;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of performing a function not belonging to the archetype.

Consequently, on this view, according to the intended interpretation, the prescription of such a modification belonging to the *śyena* is established precisely through its connection with the arrow (*iṣu*).

And thus, because this *vacanātideśa* (extension by direct statement) is not "imagined" (*kalpita*)—unlike the *ānumānika-vacanātideśa* (inferential extension by statement)—there is no lack of evidence for its superiority over *nāmātideśa* (extension by name), even though both involve the two words "similar to the *Śyena*. This is because, while in the case of *nāmātideśa* there is a necessary metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of such modifications regarding the two words [of the name], in the case of *vacanātideśa*, there is a metaphorical indication of those very same properties already expressed by the word "similar" (*samāna*), in order to establish them as being delimited by the nature of being modifications residing in the archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries belonging to the *Śyena*. Therefore, it is superior to the latter.

*Nyāyacindu*:—In the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) called *iṣu*, the scripture states: "The rest is not the same as the *śyena*. Since the properties of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* are extended (*atideśa*) there, they would apply here just as they do in the *śyena*; thus, this [text] is a mere reiteration (*anuvāda*). This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because the word "other" (*itara*) refers to what is proximate and similar, although the *Jyotiṣṭoma* elements are proximate, they lack the aforementioned non-archetypal similarity (*aprākṛta-sādṛśya*). On the other hand, although the specific features of the *śyena* such as the red turban (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) are not proximate, by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacana*), and by accepting similarity in general, these are the injunctions for the specific features of the *śyena*.

When, by means of the word "other" (*itara*), having referred to what is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), its modification such as the red turban (*lohitoṣṇīṣa*) is extended from the Śyena sacrifice, this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "this is an extended application by means of an explicit statement.
Maṇḍana [states]: "In the case of the arrow (*iṣu*), the injunction is identical to that of the Śyena."
Śaṅkara: "The extension of the verbal injunction (*vacanātideśana*).

Extension (*atideśa*) refers to the transfer of the Soma-related ritual details (*saumika-dharma*) to the *udbhid* and other sacrifices which are unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the transfer of the Soma sacrifice's details to those [sacrifices] that are unmanifest."
The Commentary states: It is heard [in scripture]: "One should sacrifice with the Abhijit," "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit.
Such are the sacrifices of this class.
Regarding them, there is an inquiry into the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*): is this the Soma-sacrifice procedure, or is it the New and Full Moon sacrifice procedure?
Since there would be no fixed rule due to the absence of contradiction, it is said:
"But in the case of the Soma [offerings] that are unmanifest.
What is "unmanifest"? It is the absence of a specific material substance and deity.
For the sacrifice is manifested by means of the material and the deity.
And these are the injunctions regarding the material and the deity: "One should sacrifice with the Abhijit.
In the case of these unmanifested [sacrifices], the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) belonging to the Soma sacrifice should apply.
Why? Because of the commonality of being unmanifest (*avyakta*).
The Soma sacrifice also has an unmanifest injunction: "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma.
[Objection: But surely "One should sacrifice with Soma" is itself the unmanifest injunction.
Nevertheless, because there is no deity [specifically mentioned], it is unmanifest (*avyakta*).

And thus, regarding that which is enjoined as unmanifest in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Śyena," the texts show the *saumika* (Soma-related) rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and others: "At the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, gold weighing twelve *mānas* is the sacrificial fee; at the *prāyaṇīyā*, twenty-four *mānas*. Therefore, the *vidhyanta* (procedural details) of the Soma sacrifice apply to those [rites].

Śā—In the case of the *ekāhas* such as "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit" and in the *dvādaśāha*, there arises a doubt: is the procedure (*vidhyanta*) that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa or that of the Soma sacrifice? When, due to the absence of any specific indicator, a state of non-restriction (*aniyama*) would result, the rule of extension (*atideśa*) applies. This extension [is established] in the cases of the *udbhid* and others, and in the *ekādaśinas*.
(And it should not be argued: "Even in the absence of a specific regulator, why could these rites not be considered *apūrva* [original/unique], like the *darvihoma*?")
Even though *darvihoma*s are of the nature of *parvan* sacrifices, the completion of the scriptural injunction is possible because materials and deities can be obtained [from elsewhere].
However, in this case, only the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is heard, and there is no mention of the accomplishment of material or deity.

Thus, since the sacrifice could not be accomplished in the absence of material and deity from some *prakṛti* (archetypal rite), the scripture would remain incomplete; therefore, the sense is that for the sake of completing the intended meaning, it is proper that there be no restriction [regarding the source of material and deity]. It is replied: it should be *saumika* (pertaining to the Soma sacrifice), due to the commonality of being unmanifest (*avyaktatva*).
What is this "unmanifestedness" (*avyaktatā*)? It is the absence of a deity specifically enjoined for its own sake.

And in the Soma sacrifice, there is no deity enjoined for its own sake, because [the deity] is enjoined solely for the purpose of the drawing [of the cup], as in the injunction: "One draws the *aindravāyava* cup."

[Objection: Is this not improper? For even a deity intended for the purpose of being grasped has a requirement for a sacrifice, since a deity cannot exist apart from a sacrifice; and in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma," the sacrifice itself has a requirement for a deity. Since these two must necessarily be connected to one another—like a lost horse and a burnt chariot—it is therefore said: Where the deity is assigned specifically for the purpose of the sacrifice by the words of mantras intended by the seers, that [sacrifice] is *vyakta* (manifest); but the other is *avyakta* (unmanifest). (In this way, a single type of priority is obtained.)

And likewise, because it is the meaning of a *gāthā* [verse] expressed through secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) and so forth, its lack of clarity consists in its being devoid of a primary injunction regarding the deity; and that very lack of clarity exists even in the case of the Soma sacrifice.

(If one disregards the particle "only" [*evakāra*], one might object: But surely, in the case of Soma as well, the deity is enjoined by the secondary derivative itself in the statement, "He takes the Aindravāyava cup.

(Taking the particle "only" into account, the author gives the reply: It is not the case that the deity is enjoined for the sacrifice by this [statement]—namely, in the original injunction of origin (*utpattivākya*)—but rather for the act of taking (*grahaṇa*).

However, the connection of that *latā* with the sacrifice occurs subsequently through the purpose (*tādarthya*), not through an immediate syntactical relation (*anvaya*) with the sacrifice; thus, it is "unmanifest" (*avyakta*).

Some, however, say that because the deities are for the purpose of being grasped (*grahaṇārthya*), they provide assistance to the sacrifice only by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*), and not through the relationship of being for its sake (*tādarthya*).
That is not correct.

If that were the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that, like the *godohana* vessel and other such items, there would be no extended application (*atideśa*) of these elements to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

Soma: Regarding the sacrifices (*iṣṭi*), after the consideration of the archetype (*prakṛti*), the consideration of Soma—which is subsequent to that [archetype]—is undertaken with respect to its own constituent parts, such as the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and so forth, which are modifications (*vikṛti*). This constitutes the coherence of the section (*peṭikā-saṃgati*). They say that the internal coherence (*antara-saṃgati*) is stated on the grounds that, in the absence of a specific restrictive rule as in the previous case, there would otherwise be no fixed order.
In the Sūtra, the mention of the *brahmajñāna* (knowledge of Brahman) as "unmanifest" (*avyaktāsu*) is intended as a general injunction (*codanā*).
Vi— "The ritual details (*dharma*) of either the *iṣṭi* or the *soma* sacrifice should apply at the beginning of the *viśvajit*, as in the case of the *mukheṣṭi*;
they would be optional due to the lack of distinction, since even for the *soma* sacrifice, it is otherwise equal."

Bhāṭṭa: In the case of the *udbhid* and other such sacrifices, however, because of their similarity to the unmanifested (*avyakta*) nature [of the *jyotiṣṭoma*], they are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
This "unmanifested" nature consists in the absence of prescribed deities due to one's own ignorance;

for although the deities such as Indra-Vāyu, who are constituent parts of the *grahaṇa* (libation), incidentally assist the *soma-yāga*, they lack the status of being constituent parts of the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself.

Therefore, since that [extension] is established by way of being unmanifest (*avyakta*), it is easy to effect a denial by assuming that the *udbhid* and other [names] assist the deity which is a constituent part [of the sacrifice], based on the inclusion of the original instructor.

For this very reason, when the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are obtained, the injunction regarding the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)—namely, "In the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, gold weighing twelve *mānas* is the fee; in the *prāyaṇīyā*, twenty-four *mānas*"—is consistent.
(This was extracted by breaking the [text] at 8.1.3. Maṇḍana: "But in connection with the unmanifest, the properties of the Soma [sacrifice apply]."

Śaṅkara: [The rule] "from Soma, when prompted by the unmanifest" applies. There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the characteristics of the animals to be immolated (*savanīya-paśu*) to the eleven animals (*ekādaśina-paśu*), because of the observation of the two-fold girding (*dvairaśana*) belonging to the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice among those eleven animals.

The Commentary states: The animals belonging to the set of eleven (*ekādaśina*) serve as the illustrative examples; they are recorded in the text beginning with "The black-headed one is for Agni," and so forth.

For other [reciters of the Veda], there is the statement: "He causes [the sacrificer] to prosper by means of the animal for Agni, he effects a pairing by means of the one for Sarasvatī, he brings about procreation by means of the one for Soma.
Regarding these, there is a doubt: are these like the *āmikṣā* offering, or do they follow the procedure of the *savanīya* animal?
What is established? That, according to the previously stated reasoning, it belongs to the Amīṣāmīya sacrifice.
This being the position reached, it is said:
[it belongs] to the Sautya among the Ekādaśinas.
Because it occurs at the time of the *sutyā*, they call it the *savanīya*.
Its concluding ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) applies to the *ekādaśina* animals.
Why? Because of the observation of the two-fold girding (*dvairaśana*).
"One takes two ropes from the *abhigrāha* and encircles each sacrificial post (*yūpa*) with two ropes.
If [the ritual] has the *Amīṣprīya* as its archetype (*prakṛti*), this would apply to each [post] individually.
Now, how does this statement—"taking two ropes from the *abhigrāha*"—apply here?
In this regard, it is prescribed: if the girdle and so forth were also being prescribed, then there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Therefore, they are merely restated (*anūdyante*).
But surely the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been set aside; from what, then, would there be an application? It is said:

since the animal-nature is common [to both], the indicative mark—namely, the fact that it occurs at the time of the *sutyā*—is a specific characteristic (*vaiśeṣika*). From that, there is application.

Soma: But surely, in the case of the *ekādaśina* animals, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) belongs only to the two [sets], not to the *savanīya*, because the latter is itself devoid of specific ritual characteristics (*apadharmaka*).
To this it is replied: due to the predominance of the commonality of being performed at the time of the *sutyā*, there is an extension (*atideśa*) to the *savanīya*;
[this applies] to the *aindrāmādi* [animals], and the extension to the *aindra* [animal].

It is understood from the injunction of an option—that "the animal sacrifices of the seasonal rites (*ṛtupaśu*) and the *ekādaśina* animals are optionally [applied] because they are modifications (*vikāra*) and because they share the same time as the Soma-pressing (*sutyākāla*)"—that there is a dual-fettering (*dvairaśanya*).

For in the case of the *savanīya*, one arrangement is "having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-strand rope" (*trivṛtā yūpaṃ parivīya*), while another arises because it is a modification of the initiation sacrifice (*daikṣa*). Thus, there is a dual-fettering.

Here too, because of the observation of two ropes in the statement, "Two ropes reach the sacrificial post" (*raśane yūpamṛcchataḥ*), the procedure (*vidhanta*) of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice applies.

Consequently, there is the attainment of ritual details (*dharma*) such as, "He takes the clarified butter portions for the *savanīya* at the *āmīṣya* [oblation]. Objection: Should it be the initiation (*dīkṣā*) from the *saumya* [offering], or the former as before? Reply: It is the latter, due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the specific feature of the *savanīya* regarding the two ropes.

Bhaṭṭa: However, in the case of the *ekādaśina* animals, because of the greater number of days starting from the day of the *sutyā*, the greater distance between the performance (*pracāra*), and the greater number of secondary characteristics (*upadharma*), they are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice.

This statement—"Having taken two ropes at each turn (*abhigraha*), he encircles one sacrificial post with two ropes each"—is also appropriately explained as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the dual-roped nature of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice.

For this is not an injunction (*vidhi*), since "having taken two" (*abhigrahāt dve*) is itself the object to be enjoined, or because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is established by its syntactic unity with another injunction.
(8|1|3 [This was taken by piercing the middle]) Maṇḍana: "The ritual rules (*dharmas*) of the *sautya* day apply to the *ekādaśina* animals.
Śaṅkara: "The *ekādaśina* animals should derive [their rules] from the *sautya* day;
this is an extension (*atideśa*)."

Oṃ. Extension (*atideśa*): [This concerns] the extension of the ritual details (*dharma*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) to modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *aindrāgna*.
In the case of *iṣṭis*, there should be the application (*pravṛtti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
The Commentary states: An example in this regard is the passage, "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," and others of this kind.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) either that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa or that of the Soma sacrifice, or is it exclusively that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa? What is the prima facie view? There is no fixed rule; for the ritual procedure exists both in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and in the Soma sacrifice.
And these sacrifices require a specific ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*);
it has been stated that there must be a single ritual procedure [for all of them] (8.1.12).
Furthermore, no distinction is perceived when either one [of the two procedures] is restricted.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule.
This being the position reached, it is said:
in the case of the *iṣṭi* sacrifices, there is the application of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* rites.
The reason has not been stated; it is said to be "well-known. But what is that? It is the connection with the original indicative mark (*prakṛtiliṅga*) of the injunction.

What, then, is that original indicative mark? It is the instruction regarding the deity by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), the possession of potsherds (*kapālavattā*), and the word *nirvapet* (he should offer), as in: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra."
The other [text] likewise says: "A cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni";
and also: "He pours out the oblations with the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle."

Furthermore, a specific rule for the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) has been stated on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the archetype: "That which has an indicative mark [is applied] because of its connection with the purpose" (8.1.12).
Therefore, the ritual procedure belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) applies to those [offerings].
And this is shown by the text: "At each *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala*."
Even by way of embracing [the general rule], the proof is established like the "grains in the cooking pot" (*sthālīpulāka*) maxim.

As for the *Śābarabhāṣya*: in sacrifices such as "one should offer the *caru* at the *sautya* [rite]," because the procedure of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is taught through the commonality of the term "offers" (*nirvapati*), its extension (*atideśa*) applies.
Thus, this is an elaboration of the rule "that which has the indicative mark" (*yasya liṅgam*, 8.1.12); therefore, one need not strive excessively for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The same applies everywhere in what follows. Soma: "In the case of the Aindrāmā and others, should it be according to the Soma ritual or according to the additional [ritual], since both are present here? Vi: [The response follows].

[The opponent claims: "Because of the possibility [of application], it would be optional; otherwise, there would be something else here due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the potsherds and so forth.

[Bhāṭṭa: In the *saurya* and other such offerings, because they share the general nature of an *iṣṭi*, and because they share the general nature of being sacrifices, because they possess the relationship known as the ritual properties (*dharma*) starting with the act of pouring out (*nirvapati*), and because they have deities prescribed by words ending in the *taddhita* suffix, they are indeed modifications (*vikāra*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
For this very reason, there is the indicative mark: "At each *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* gold grain."
(8|1|13) Maṇḍana: "The dharma of the Darśa applies to all iṣṭis. Śaṅkara: "This [dharma] is considered to apply to the iṣṭis beginning with the Darśa.
This means that this extended application (atideśa) is held to apply to the iṣṭis starting from the Darśa.
Oṃ. Extension [of details]: the properties of the cake for Agni apply to the cake for Indra.
[Objection: It should be restricted by the sacrificial material (*havis*), because the ritual action depends upon that [material].
Commentary: This is heard in scripture: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra."
Likewise, there is the case of "the milk for Agni.

In this regard, a doubt arises: is the procedure of the *sāṃnāyya* [to apply] to the *aindra-puroḍāśa* because of the commonality of deity, and the procedure of the *aupadhika* [to apply] to the milk for Agni because of the commonality of deity—the commonality of deity being more powerful—or is it that in the latter case the *sāṃnāyya*'s procedure applies and in the former case the *aupadhika*'s procedure applies, the commonality of sacrificial material (*havis*) being more powerful? What is the prima facie view? It is stated as follows:
It is stronger because of the commonality of the deity.
Why? Because of its primacy.
The deity is the primary regulator; [the offerings] belong to Indra and to Agni.

Thus, the oblation is restricted by the secondary factor; when there is a conflict between these two, it is logical to favor the primary, because the primary functions without contradiction, whereas the secondary functions in contradiction with the primary.
