Likewise [apply] the purchasing (*krayaṇa*), mixing with curds (*āśrayaṇa*), the *puroruṅ* verses, the placing down (*upayamana*), and the covering with a cloth (*vāsopahanana*).

(The compound refers to) the purchase (*krayaṇa*), the mixing (*śrayaṇa*), the *puroruṅ* verse, the taking with the *upayāma* formula, the placing down (*āsādana*), and the wrapping with a cloth (*vāsopanahana*); the aggregate of these [is indicated]. The Commentary states: He shows that the Soma-rites beginning with the purchase apply to the *surā*: "She is to be purchased from a eunuch for lead," and "He mixes the cup for the Aśvins with *kuvala*-flour.

"There is one *puroruṅ* and one *yājyā*. "With the formula, 'Thou art taken with a support; with an unbroken [strainer], I take thee, the unbroken cup for the Aśvins,' he takes it; having taken it, he places it down."
"They dwell together for three nights;
there are linen garments, head-wraps, young sprouts, and six handfuls.
If this were the injunction, there would be sentences with multiple meanings.
They perform the purchase and other rites for tin and the like;
therefore, the ritual procedure (vidhivanta) of the Soma sacrifice applies to both.
Or rather, it should be restricted by the oblation, because [the latter] is a modification of that.
Commentary: Alternatively, here the procedure (*vidhi*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*) would be restricted by virtue of the commonality of the oblation (*havis*).
Why? Because it is a modification (*vikāra*) thereof;
that is, surā and vājina are modifications of the oblations belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Sura is a modification of an ordinary medicinal herb; Vājina is a modification of the Sānnāyya offering.
The word "Soma" is used here as a term of praise.
Commentary: Now, as for what was stated regarding "the use of that specific term."
To this we reply: this word "Soma" is for the purpose of praise (praśaṃsā), not for the purpose of an injunction (vidhi), because there is no injunctive element present.

Since Soma possesses the aforementioned fruitfulness—as in the statements "Soma is indeed the vājina" and "Surā is Soma"—there is a praise of Surā and vājina by way of their identity with it, just as one says, "Devadatta is a lion."
Thus it is for the person.
Therefore, this is not an extension of the ritual rule (*dharmātideśa*). The extension applies to the *vājina* and the *surā* offerings. 219
The other [materials] are based on explicit scriptural statement (vācanika).
Commentary: As for the others, such as lead and so forth, they are based on explicit statement because there is no [other means of] attainment;
and since there is no alternative recourse, the multiplicity of meanings of the sentences arises from the injunction of rites possessing qualities.
And the designation is likewise [indicative].
The Bhāṣya states: "One obtains the Dīkṣaṇīyā with śappa grass, the Prāyaṇīyā with tokma grains, and the Ātithyā with lion's hair.
If these were modifications of the Soma sacrifice, the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites would be obtained directly [from the archetype].
The statement regarding the attainment [of the sacrificial substance] through young grass and the like for those who have already obtained it is not tenable.
Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).
The Bhāṣya states: "And from the animal-cake, [the status of] the cups (*graha*) is heard: 'There are no cakes for these animals; for these animals have the cups as their cakes.'"
In this context, first of all, the cups (grahas) here are the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas);
they are indeed cups.
However, if they possess the characteristics of sacrificial cakes, then this [designation] is justified.
Therefore, the *pauroḍāśika* [section] is extended to them.
In the previous section on Soma, extension based on clear indicative marks (*spaṣṭaliṅga*) was stated;
for in that case, the determination of the deity and so forth is clear due to the non-extension of the deity by means of the suffix *-taddhita*.

In this case, however, because the extended application (*atideśa*) lacks a clear indicative mark (*liṅga*), there is proximity to another section (*pādāntara*) and proximity to the end of the chapter (*adhyāyāntara*).
Furthermore, since the indicatory marks to be mentioned later in the *Vājin* and other sections must be established in some way or another, they are not immediately perceived and are thus "unclear.

As for the word *soma* occurring in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it is possible to justify it as being subject to the rule (*sūtryatayā*) by taking either the performance of certain specific properties prescribed by the text or the similarity already established through perception and other means. However, just like the word *āgnihotra* occurring in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), there is no evidence that it refers here to a similarity with what is to be accomplished; therefore, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it does not constitute an extended application.

In this context, because the word *soma* (in Pāṇini 3.1.13) has been explained separately in the rule "the term *yuṣmad* becomes *yuṣmadyupapade" (*yuṣmad-upapade*), the word *yuṣmad* attains the status of an extended application (*atideśa*) precisely by way of being an injunction. Even though it is heard as a separate sentence, since it relies on the person (*puruṣa*) and the number (*vacana*), and because there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the preceding injunction (*vidhi*), it lacks injunctive force and thus lacks the status of an extended application; hence, there is no tautology. The meaning of the Sūtra is: in the case of *vājina* and the cups (*graha*) of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, there is the nature of having *soma* as their material cause (*somaprakṛtikatva*), because they possess the word *soma*.
Viśvarūpa states: "In the case of *surā* and *vājina*, [the application of the *soma* rules occurs] simply through the word *soma*."

The first [view] says: "Not so; because of the similarity of the oblation, the word *soma* is used for the sake of praise. *Bhāṣya*: It is considered whether, even though the *vājin* sacrifice has the character of a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *vājina* by-product of the *āmikṣā*, its ritual procedure (*dharma*) is extended from the *saumika* (Soma) sacrifice or from the *dāśarātrika* (the ten-night rite) with respect to its subsidiary elements. The same consideration applies to the drinking of *surā* liquor in the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice for the purpose of consecrating the deities.

In this context, regarding the statement "Soma indeed is the *vājina*, the *surā* is Soma," the word "Soma" applied to what is not Soma is for the purpose of extending the properties (*dharmātideśa*) of Soma. Nor can it be argued that, like the case of "the *upaśaya* becomes a sacrificial post" (*yūpa*), this is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and thus lacks the capacity to extend [properties], because here the name must necessarily extend [the ritual application] due to the established similarity between the two.
For this very reason, [the text] shows both the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* mantra and the consumption after having invited [others] (*samupahūya bhakṣaṇa*) in both cases.

[The opponent argues: "It shows that there is a purchase of the *surā* with lead, a mixing with *kuvala*-flour, a single *puroruc*, the mantra beginning with 'upayāma', the placing [of the cup] after having taken it, and wrapping it in a linen cloth.
And since this is so, the term 'cup' (*graha*) becomes even more appropriate.

[The Siddhāntin replies: This being the case, since the word *soma* from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) can be justified through its similarity to the nature of the fruit of the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is no evidence for a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) on the grounds that it intends to enjoin a single injunction. Furthermore, because the act of taking (*grahaṇa*) is established as being directly taught (*aupadeśika*)—just like the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice—the use of the word 'cup' (*graha*) is justified precisely in that way.

Since the indicative marks (*liṅga*) can be established even through direct scriptural statement (*vācanikatva*), the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *dāśārṇika* [offering] applies by way of extension (*atideśa*) based on the indicative mark of the injunction (*codanāliṅga*), as there is no obstruction.
Even therein, in the case of the *vājina* (curd-mixture), because it originates from an animal and possesses similarity [to milk], the ritual procedure of the milk-sacrifice (*payoyāga*) applies.
In the case of *surā* (liquor), the procedure of the cake-offering (*pauroḍāśika*) applies, because its substance is an herb (*auṣadha*).
For this very reason, the statement regarding the attainment of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice—namely, "By means of the grass-blades alone, one obtains the *dīkṣaṇīyā*"—is consistent.
Otherwise, since that [sacrifice] would be directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), a statement of its attainment would be nothing but a praise (*stuti*) and would thus be inconsistent.

Likewise, the statement—"There are no sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) for these animals; for these animals consist of cups (*graha*) and sacrificial cakes"—is consistent provided that the cups possess the characteristics of the sacrificial cake, due to the application of the word "sacrificial cake" to the cups.

And although, according to the view of the Vārttikakāra, it will be stated in the tenth book (sūtra 10.1.13) that these other subsidiary sacrifices take over the function of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*), whereby the application of the term "cake" (*puroḍāśa*) is justified precisely through the principle of "substitution by position" (*sthānāpatti*); nevertheless, even by way of such substitution, the animal-cake rituals do not yet obtain their specific properties, and thus the indicative mark (*liṅga*) remains applicable.

In reality, however, when there is a requirement for auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), since similarity consisting of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) presents itself more immediately, the extension based on the indicative mark of the injunction (*codanā-liṅga-atideśa*) is stronger than the extension by way of "occupying the place" (*sthānāpatti*). Therefore, because it has medicinal herbs as its substance (*auṣadhadravyaka*), it is indeed a modification (*vikāra*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all [such sacrifices]. For this very reason, rules such as "In the absence of these, the wise man should perform the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice," and "The *Dīkṣaṇīyā* is likewise," do not pertain to the properties (*dharma*) of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth (or the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and so forth).

However, when—according to the method of the author of the *Daśamika-sūtra-bhāṣya* (Sūtra 10.1.13)—it is taught that there is merely an injunction of a different substance, namely *surā*, in the very sacrifice of the *paśupuroḍāśa* belonging to the archetypal (*prākṛta*) ritual, then this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended solely to refute the extension of the name (*nāmātideśa*) by means of words such as "Soma" and so forth;

it is not for the purpose of establishing the extension based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of having medicinal herbs (*auṣadha*) as its substance, because even in the absence of that [extension], the status of the *paśupuroḍāśa* as a modification (*vikāra*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is established. This is how it should be understood.

*Nyāyacindu*:—In the case of *vājina* and the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifices, there is an extended application (*atideśa*) [of Soma-dharmas], because of the figurative usage: "The *vājina* is indeed Soma; the *surā* is Soma.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not prescriptive, milk-dharmas apply to the *vājina*, and the dharmas of medicinal herbs (*auṣadha*) apply to the *surā* cups.
Maṇḍana:—"There are no Soma-dharmas in the *vājina*."

Śaṅkara says: "In milk and in whey, that [is the rule]. This is the end of the section on the injunctions. 卐 Extension (atideśa): In the Viśvajit sacrifice, there is the extension of the *pṛṣṭha* chants belonging to the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*).

In the Viśvajit sacrifice, which consists of all the *pṛṣṭha* chants, the *pṛṣṭha* chants belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma are present because they are preceded by that [sacrifice], and the word *pṛṣṭha* exists [therein].
The Bhāṣya states: "It is heard in scripture: 'In the Viśvajit, there is one consisting of all the *pṛṣṭhas*.
In this regard, it is deliberated whether this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) or an injunction (*vidhi*)."
What is established? That it is a restatement (anuvāda). Why? Because for one who is not already *sarvapṛṣṭha*, the state of being *sarvapṛṣṭha* must be enjoined;
but for one who is already *sarvapṛṣṭha*, what is the point of enjoining it thus?
And this [sacrifice] has all [the stotras] at its end.
How so? Because it has that as its precedent—because it has the Jyotiṣṭoma as its precedent—the stotras belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma are obtained here.
Among those, there are four beginning with the Māhendra-stotra; all of these indeed [are included].
Therefore, this [sacrifice] has all [the stotras] as its *pṛṣṭha* [laud].
But are they not indeed the *pṛṣṭhas*? It is said: [they are].
And there is the word "pṛṣṭha"; for them there is the word "pṛṣṭha" in the expression, "The pṛṣṭhas are seventeen. Therefore, it is a restatement (anuvāda).
Or rather, [it refers] to the six-day period (ṣaḍaha), for in that case there is an injunction.
Commentary: This is not a restatement (anuvāda). What then? It is an injunction (vidhi).
A restatement that does not contribute to a specific activity would be purposeless.
Moreover, there exists the *pṛṣṭhavallama* in the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), of which this [text] would be a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Indeed, that exists in the six-day rite;
for therein are the injunctions regarding the *pṛṣṭhas*, such as "the *rathaṃtara* becomes the *pṛṣṭha*," and so forth.
Therefore, the injunction regarding the *pāḍahika* (six-day rite) elements is one of extended application (*atideśika*).

[The commentary] states: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, regarding the passage "the *rathaṃtara* is the *pṛṣṭha*," it is considered whether the word "all-*pṛṣṭha*" (*sarvapṛṣṭha*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*), or an injunction for the optional employment of both the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* *sāmans*, or an extension (*atideśa*) of all the *pṛṣṭha* stotras belonging to the six-day rite.

Among these, he refutes the first position: because only one *pṛṣṭha* has been prescribed, the word "all" (*sarva*)—which depends on plurality—would lack a referent, and thus the meaning of the sentence would be untenable.

In the *paḍaha* sacrifice, however, it is prescribed with reference to the *gāyatra* [sāman] that "all the *pṛṣṭhas* [are to be performed]"; therein, there is the state of having all the *pṛṣṭhas* as its substance.

In the *jyotiṣṭoma*, on the other hand, because the word *pṛṣṭha* is used [for the *māhendra* and other stotras] according to the "umbrella-bearer" (*chatrinyāya*) principle, it is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, by the phrase "the seventeenfold ones," the number seventeen is enjoined, not the status of being a *pṛṣṭha*.

(Candrānanda [says] "For what reason? He refutes the second position: Nor can there be a conjunction of two things that have reached the state of being mutually exclusive options, precisely because the word "all" (in the phrase *sarvapṛṣṭha*) would otherwise be redundant [given that it belongs to the Brahman-position].
This is a compound meaning "having all as its back."

And in brief, it is not difficult to enjoin multiple qualities when there is already an injunction [of the action]. (He states the solution mentioned in the Bhāṣya: Alternatively, the "entirety" (*sarvatā*) pertaining to the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] is enjoined directly.
(For it is not possible to enjoin that entirety without first enjoining the *pṛṣṭhas* themselves.)

Therefore, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), there is an injunction for the *pṛṣṭha* chants; thus, all *pṛṣṭha* chants belonging to the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) are enjoined. This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The Commentary states: Furthermore, this indicative mark (liṅga) shows [the order] within this context in a sentence intended to establish the arrangement: "He performs the Rathantara at the Pavamāna, the Bṛhat at the Ābhīśava, and the others in the middle; the Vairūpa is the Sāman of the Hotṛ, the Vairāja of the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Raivata of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and the Śākara of the Acchāvāka. This passage shows the Pārṣṭha-stotras belonging to the six-day rite (ṣaḍaha).

Ṭu—(He states the meaning of the sūtra, "And because of the observation of indicative marks"): And thus, the sentence concerning the injunction of sequence—("The Rathantara [sāman] in the Pavamāna [laud], the Bṛhat in the Ārbhava," etc.)—is appropriate in that case (the Viśvajit). The Jyotiṣṭoma possesses an established entitlement.
Bhāṣya: Now, as for what was said—"And there is the word *pṛṣṭha* (back/chant)"—to that we reply:

But in that case, the word *pṛṣṭha* is not innate; it is a designation applied to those stotras that have already arisen, namely those which are called *pṛṣṭhas*. And that [designation] is appropriate only when their status as *pṛṣṭhas* is known, yet in this case, it is not known.
How, then, is this a restatement? Because of the coexistence of the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
For it is known that there is a single *māhendra* hymn (*stotra*) therein, whereas the status of being a *pṛṣṭha* chant belongs to those [hymns] of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*).
How so? For it has been stated therein that this is a *codanā* (injunction).
In their view, the word *pṛṣṭha* has its meaning based on the Vedic text (*śrauta*);

thus, because the term *sarvapṛṣṭha* is understood to refer to the *ṛk*, *sāman*, and *dhur* [of the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice] through a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*)—as it grasps the sense of being an injunction regarding the mere arrangement—the injunction applies to those very elements.

Furthermore, the purpose of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the word *pṛṣṭha*—namely, that it is intended to explain its conventional secondary meaning (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*)—has already been described in the *Kaustubha*.

For this very reason, the view that the word *sarva* (all) prescribes a combination (*samuccaya*) of the two optional *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* chants, which are obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), is refuted.

This is because the *vairūpa* chant is directly enjoined (*aupadeśika*) for the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha*, thereby subverting those two; and because the word *sarva* implies plurality, making it impossible for it to refer to only two.
Therefore, the rule is that there is a reduction by one-fourth.

However, in the view where there is only one *pṛṣṭha-stotra* in the archetype, or two *pṛṣṭhas*, then even though it is already established [in the modified sacrifice], it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*).

And although this is not a transfer by name (*nāmātideśa*), because the word "all *pṛṣṭhas*" does not denote a quarter-part, and because in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice there is no figurative application (*gauṇatva*) of the term "pṛṣṭhas" through the *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Nor is this a case of the extension of a verbal injunction (*vacanātideśa*); for in the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice, just as in the statement "he offers the two *ājyabhāga* oblations," the status of being a subordinate element (*padahīyatva*) cannot serve as a delimiting factor for what is to be enjoined.
Nevertheless, this is indeed an original instruction (*upadeśa*) regarding the *rathaṃtara* and other [sāmans].

For this very reason, there is no performance here of the other characteristics of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), because the status of being a subsidiary to another ritual action is equally established prior to the operation of this specific sentence.

Furthermore, the commencement [of this discussion] occurs in the seventh [chapter], in the section concerning the extension (*atideśa*) of names, due to the similarity in being cognizable through words that share the same substratum as the ritual action (*karma*).

This is because, by the very maxim "the principal [element] being led [leads its accessories]," there is no necessity for the properties of the *rathantara* and so forth, such as the *ābhīśava* chants; rather, they are obtained solely as means for the *rathantara* and others which serve other functions, such as the *pavamāna* lauds.

The *Nyāyabindu* states: "In the injunction 'The *Viśvajit* has all the *pṛṣṭhas*,' there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the fourfold set of stotras beginning with the *māhendra*, which are already obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*), namely the *Jyotiṣṭoma*."
Because the term *pṛṣṭha* is employed in them in the expression "the seventeen *pṛṣṭhas*.
Alternatively, the word *pṛṣṭha* applies primarily only to the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans]; elsewhere it is used figuratively.
Therefore, with regard to those two which are obtained as options, their totality—that is, their combination—is enjoined.

Thus, in the *Bhāṣya*: since the word *sarva* (all) has multiple meanings and cannot apply to both [the *ṣaḍaha* and the *pṛṣṭha*] simultaneously, there is an extension of the injunction for the six *pṛṣṭha* chants of the *pādikas*.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Maṇḍana states: "In the *sarvapṛṣṭha*, there would be the *pṛṣṭha* chants as described in the *ṣaḍaha*."
Śaṅkara: There would be an extension (*atideśa*) to all [the subsequent rites].
That is, there is an extension of the properties of the *sānnāyya* and *payas* (milk-offering) to the *vaiśvadevī āmikṣā*.
Because it is connected with both, there would be a modification of both.
Commentary: In the case of the *vaiśvadevī āmikṣā*, there would be a modification of both curd and milk, because it is connected with both.
For it is produced by both;
in that case, no distinction is perceived such that it belongs to this one alone and not to the other. Therefore, it belongs to both.
Or rather, it is one, because the injunction is one. Commentary: Or rather, one should modify either the curd or the milk, not both;
because the injunction is one.
This single injunction, "There is an āmikṣā for the Viśvedevas," is rendered complete by a single ritual procedure (vidhyanta). Therefore, one should perform only one modification.

Because of the commonality of being a solid mass (*saṃghāta*). Commentary: As for the claim that no distinction is perceived, it is said in response: curd is a solid mass; *āmiṣkā* is also a solid mass, whereas milk is liquid.
This is the distinction:
therefore, it is a modification of curd; or rather, it is milk, because that is its primary substance, as is seen in common worldly usage, since the curd exists for the sake of that [milk].
Commentary: Milk indeed is modified for the sake of the sacrificial offering, not the curd.
This is because milk is the primary element in this mixture.
What is the primacy of the milk? Its abundance.
In that case, there is abundant milk and little curd,
because the curd is for the sake of that [milk].
And the curd is employed therein in order to cause the milk to become thickened.
As in the world.
In the world as well, it is milk alone that is taken up in order to produce curds. How so? In the absence of curd, it is produced by other sour substances such as sour gruel and the like.
And in that context as well, the word *āmiṣkā* occurs.
For the restriction to curd (*dadhi*) when [the substance] is sour would serve no unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Therefore, milk itself, having become thickened through contact with sourness, is called *āmiṣkā*.
If milk is the *āmikṣā*, it is logical that it should be a modification (*vikāra*) of milk itself. [This is] supported by the properties (*dharma*).

Commentary: The property of being performed on the same day (*sadyaskālatā*) is supported by its being a modification of milk, because the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice is characterized by being performed on the same day.
If it were a modification of curd, it would be contradicted;
furthermore, the three-day period for the Vaiśvadeva is observed, and thus its specific ritual property would be contradicted;
moreover, it indicates the state of being performed on the same day.
The Commentary states: "The curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) is the modification of the curd.

If it were a modification of the curd, then in the absence of the three-day period, it would have to be given as curd, and it could never be milk; in that case, this observation [of the text] would not be possible.
Therefore, *āmikṣā* is a modification of milk, and the curd possesses no specific ritual property (*adharmakatva*).

Extended Application (*atideśa*): [The rule] regarding the *vaiśvadevī* [offering] (Śāstradīpikā 2.2.3). Extended Application: Regarding the *śatokthya* and others, the Śāstra states: "Curd and milk mixed together are designated as *āmikṣā*.
Since the essence of both is seen therein, it consists of both."
Because no distinction is perceived, there would therefore be a modification of both.

However, in the sentence "tate payasi" (in milk that has been heated), milk is subordinate because of the locative case, whereas curd is the primary element because of its designation by the accusative case; therefore, the word *sā* [refers to the curd].
By that [designation], curd alone binds the deity;
therefore, the sacrificial offering (*havis*) is curd alone, and thus it is a modification of the *sāṃgrahaṇī* offering.
(To this objection, it is replied: In that case, however, milk is the primary substance, and the completion of the ritual action resides therein.
For when curd is being led away, it pervades that very milk;
thus, even from the perspective of the action (*karman*), it would possess primacy like the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
Therefore, the reference by means of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is appropriately understood as referring to that [milk] alone.
That very substance, having become solidified through contact with curd, is therefore the *havis* (sacrificial oblation).

Its connection with a deity is what constitutes the *āmiṣkā*; thus, for us, that very same thing remains. Consequently, it is established that the *āmiṣkā* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the morning milk-offering (*prātardoha*).

The connection [of this section] is stated as follows: even though *soma* and *payas* (milk) are not modifications (*vikāra*) of curd (*dadhi*), the *āmiṣkā* might still be considered a modification of curd.

This being established by Pāṇini 4.1.122–24, where even if curd is the primary element, it is specifically the *āmiṣkā* that is the motivator for the addition of curd, and not the *vājina*; nevertheless, the primacy of milk (*payaḥ-prādhānya*) here is treated in accordance with the actual state of things. It is appropriate to argue that the primacy of milk must be proven right here for the sake of establishing a specific extended application (*viśeṣātideśa*).
As Viśvarūpa says: "Of the two—curd and milk—the *āmiṣkā* is like curd."
Between the two, because of the predominance of the curd, it should be [the modification] of the milk.
*Bhāṭṭa*: It has been established in the fourth book (4.1.19) that the *āmikṣā* is indeed a distinct entity, yet it consists of the form of either the curd or the milk.
Therefore, there is no dispute that it is a modification of one or the other of those two.

Furthermore, when considering the specific details therein, in the phrase "when the milk has been poured out" (*tate payasi*), it is the milk indicated by the accusative case that is referred to by the pronoun *sā* ("that") in the subsequent statement "that [offering] belongs to the Viśvedevas" (*sā vaiśvadevī*), and not the milk indicated by the locative case, because the latter functions as a subordinate element.

Nor can it be argued that because the verb "ānayati" (brings) is transitive, milk—being the object being acted upon—is understood as primary even in relation to the curd; for in the case of transitive roots, since another [primary] object is determined by its status as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), when there is a desire to express a mere relationship, the genitive would apply to the general sense of relation. However, since the rule *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51) assigns the technical designation of "object" (*karman*) to such cases, the use of the accusative is understood [to indicate primacy]. Yet, even so, there is no proof for actual primacy here, because in the present context, the hearing of the locative case indicates a desire to express the status of a locus, and because there is an absence of a second accusative suffix [which would otherwise signal the primacy of the milk].
And therefore, since the *āmikṣā* has the form of curd and is a modification of curd, ordinary milk possesses the status of being the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*).

This being the position reached, [we reply]: because of the predominance of sweet flavor, and because even in the absence of curd (*dadhi*), the preparation of *āmikṣā* is accomplished through another sour substance—as established by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—and also from the wording of the mantra, "May the two yoke-mares and the milk be joined," it is understood that *āmikṣā* is designated by the term *āmikṣā* as milk itself having reached a particular state. Therefore, in accordance with that [mantra], the word [in the injunction] also refers back to the milk indicated by the locative case; thus, milk alone is the *āmikṣā*.
Consequently, it is indeed a modification (*vikāra*) of that [milk].

And likewise, in the expression "atate payasi" (in the milk being stretched), it should also be understood that the locative case indicates predominance (*prādhānya*), while the accusative case indicates the instrument (*karaṇa*) according to the rule of "sakṛd" (Pāṇini 2.1.4.12).
Furthermore, since *āmiṣkā*—which consists of a particular state—is not possible without heating (*tāpa*), there is no intention to express it [as a separate factor].
However, if *āmiṣkā* were possible in the world even without heating, then the locative case would not indicate predominance either.

Since that which is non-different from the two [milk and curd] as qualified by the state of being the substratum (*adhikaraṇatva*) is enjoined by way of being designated as a specific state (*avasthāviśeṣa*), the completion of the sentence-meaning occurs through its equality with the word expressing the subject (*uddeśya*). Furthermore, because it is precisely that [substratum] which is referred to by the pronoun *tat*, the application of the suffix [of the accusative case] is all the more appropriate.

Moreover, although the state of being the substratum itself is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) with respect to the bringing of the curd, the milk is not a subordinate element, because its purpose must be inferred; this is how it should be understood.
Therefore, because the *āmikṣā* consists of a form characterized by a specific state [of curdled milk], it is not a modification of the milk-offering (*payoyāga*).
Consequently, the ritual details such as the morning milking (*prātardoha*) apply only to the milk;
the curd (*dadhi*), however, is merely a worldly substance serving as a purificatory agent (*saṃskāraka*).
Nyāyabindu: [Objection: Since *āmikṣā* is produced from both [milk and curds], it is a modification (*vikāra*) of both;
because it is a derivative of curds, it is a modification of curds.
This being the position reached, [the reply is: because in the sentence "in milk that has been heated" (*tate payasi*), milk alone is primary, therefore milk itself is the *āmikṣā*.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that it is indeed a modification of milk. Maṇḍana [states]: "The properties of the *āmikṣā* are those inherent in milk."
Śaṅkara: "This [is] the milk of the Āmikṣā.
[This is] the conclusion.
There is an extended application (*atideśa*) of the twelve-day (*dvādaśāha*) ritual rules to the group of sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*) beginning with the *śatokthya*.
In the case of groups of sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*), that repetition (*abhyāsa*) would be understood, because of the inclusion of specific characteristics.
Commentary: Here, the groups of terminuses are the examples: "The *agniṣṭoma*, five *ukthyas*, there is a hundred *agniṣṭomas*, there is a hundred *atirātras*," and so forth.
In this regard, it is considered whether this is a repetition of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, or rather a statement regarding sacrifices characterized by such numbers and specific terminuses.
What is established? It should be understood that this is a repetition within the assemblies (saṃsthāgaṇeṣu).
This is indeed a repetition of that very original Jyotiṣṭoma.
Why? Because the defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) have been established.
These are its established characteristics: Agniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, and Atirātra.
It is through connection with these that the sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthās) arise.
He can be characterized by those [qualities];
and having characterized him, one will establish the number alone.

However, in the case of a discourse concerning various days, both the number and the [quality] are enjoined—as in, "They have the Ukthya as their conclusion, and they are five"—in which case the sentence would be split.
Therefore, this belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Or rather, by virtue of the qualification, it should be understood as belonging to the archetype (prakṛti), because the designation is based on that.
The Commentary states: "It is not thus; it is a repetition of the Jyotiṣṭoma."
How then? The archetype (prakṛti) would be qualified by that;
the days belonging to the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha) would be qualified by the specific terminus (saṃsthā).
Why? Because of the governing context (adhikāra).
These are extended here by the principle of transfer (codaka);
thus there will be an application of the transfer-rule.
But is it not the case that the Jyotiṣṭoma is directly enjoined by such terms as Agniṣṭoma and so forth?
"No," he says.
How so? Because the designation is based on that [termination].
The designation "Agniṣṭoma" and so forth is caused by the *saṃsthā* (the completion of the rite), not a designator of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.

It is capable of denoting the specific sacrifice established by each [term], not the Jyotiṣṭoma alone. As for the objection that there would be multiple meanings, it will not be so; by means of the injunction regarding the group, the mere completion (saṃsthā) of five days, which have been introduced [previously], will be prescribed.
The compound "śatāgniṣṭoma" also expresses a group characterized by both qualifiers;
it denotes a single entity, just as in the expression, "the priests wearing red turbans perform the ritual.
Furthermore, this allows for the number to reside in distinct units; therefore, there is a reference to the various days of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha).
Because they have the *saṃsthā* as their cause, these [words] are not denotative of any sacrifice;
since there is no proximity [of a specific sacrifice], there is an injunction for a group characterized by the *saṃsthā*.
Therefore, they possess twelve days.
Since the six-day procedure in the Soma sacrifice previously mentioned does not have its constituent elements well-known, whereas here they refer to the well-known Jyotiṣṭoma,
this constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: In the *saṃsthās* such as the *śatokthya* and others, the repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma is understood, because the Jyotiṣṭoma—characterized by and consisting of the *ukthya* and other elements—is what is being referred to. Regarding this, [the author] says: "In the *śatokthya*, is it the Jyotiṣṭoma or the Dvādaśāha?
By name, it is the former; because the name is applied to a composite whole, the latter would be the case."
In the *bhāṣya*, it is heard in scripture: "Without reference [to a specific sacrifice], there is a hundred *agniṣṭomas*, a hundred *ukthyas*, and a hundred *atirātras*.

In that context, since the ten forms beginning with the *agniṣṭoma* are frequently employed within the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself, the number "hundred" is prescribed by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to those forms as enjoining their repetition.

For the terms *agniṣṭoma* and so forth do not denote the general class (*sāmānya*) created by the specific terminuses (*saṃsthā*); if they did, then in passages such as "Now, therefore, with the *agniṣṭoma*, with the *prauga-stotra*," the *cayana* (fire-altar construction) would result in being inserted into the modified form (*vikṛti*) due to the distinction between the preceding and subsequent contexts.
Therefore, because it is a *jyotiṣṭoma*, there is no application (*pravṛtti*) of the *dvādaśāha* here.

Alternatively, since the terms beginning with *agniṣṭoma*—by the principle of "not grasping a qualified object when the qualifier is not intended"—denote only the *saṃsthās* (termini), and since there is no evidence for resorting to them in the present context even though they have acquired a conventional meaning (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the injunction regarding the repetition of the *śastra* is an injunction based on a reference (*anuvāda*) to the permanent and optional *saṃsthās*.
In this view, since the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself is the substratum, there is no extension of the sacrificial details (*gaṇātideśa*).
Or, let this be a distinct ritual act; nevertheless, because the referent of the other word is in the singular number, it is only one.

Since the number "hundred" pertains to the completion [of the sacrifice], it does not serve as a differentiator. Therefore, a single ritual act repeated a hundred times is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, and thus there is no extension (*atideśa*) from a group.
This being the case, there is the attainment of a single excellence.
First of all, there is no injunction regarding number with reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma or with reference to the Soma-vessel (saṃśa).
Therefore, whatever is performed as an act of gambling (akṣa) is a distinct ritual action (karmāntara).
Even that [action] is not one;
for if it were so, it would be impossible for a single action to possess multiple forms without this [distinction],
and because it is not mentioned in the scripture, such an assumption would result in an unwarranted imposition.

Therefore, in cases such as "The Agniṣṭoma is threefold" (*trivṛd agniṣṭomaḥ*) or "The Ukthya has the Vairūpa-sāman," even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti-yajña*), we must accept—on the basis of occasional usage and by means of contemporary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—that these refer to specific numerical intervals. Thus, because they differ from the number one hundred, they do not conflict with the injunction regarding the sacrifice.

In this way, the meaning of the compound is not the ritual action itself, but rather the result, understood through the etymology "that sacrifice in which there are a hundred Ukthya terminuses. This is how it should be understood.

Furthermore, that too is not the injunction for the performance of the sacrifice (*yajñavidhi*), because that would result in the undesirable consequence of breaking the unity of the sentence (*ekaprasaratābhaṅga*).

Rather, according to the intended meaning (*tātparyagati*), it is precisely the injunction for the cognition of the hundred as qualified by the [act of] offering that is meant; thus, it is logical that there is a hundredfold application (*āpatti*) based on the mention of the number "hundred.
Alternatively, there is no fault whatsoever due to its being a *dvigu* compound.

Even if the ritual action (*karman*) is one and the same, there is no contradiction regarding the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, because it can be accepted through repetition (*āvṛtti*), and thus its status as a group of pressings (*sutyāgaṇatva*) is not lost. According to the *Nyāyabindu*: "In passages such as 'it becomes a hundred *ukthya*s,' since the ten *ukthya*s and so forth constitute the name of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the injunction of a hundred repetitions is made by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to that [name]. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the conclusion is: because these terms denote the specific terminuses (*saṃsthā*) of the rite, they do not refer to the sacrifice itself.
However, it is not an injunction for a new sacrifice (*apūrva*) qualified by both number and *saṃsthā* (concluding rite), because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*).
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that, because they take the form of a group (*gaṇa*), they possess twelve days (*dvādaśāhika*).
Maṇḍana [states]: "The various *saṃsthās* and so forth are included within the days."
Śaṅkara [states]: "In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there is the *śatokthya* [rite];
that is the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
There is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *ukthya* and other stotras belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma to the *śatokthya* and other rites."
Accretion [of days] occurs from the *gaṇa* (group) because that is its archetype (*prakṛti*).
The Bhāṣya states: "It consists of a hundred *ukthyas*"; "It consists of a hundred *atirātras*"—thus it is heard in scripture.
In that case, the days belonging to the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) proceed.
And these [sacrifices] generally consist of the Ukthya form, with two Agniṣṭomas.

When it is said, "It consists of a hundred Ukthyas," there is an increase of the Ukthya-stotras for the two Agniṣṭomas in the morning; when it is said, "It consists of a hundred Atirātras," there is an increase of all the night-rounds (rātriparyāyas).
In this regard, it is considered whether the increase should be performed from the Dvādaśāha sacrifice or from the Jyotiṣṭoma.
What is obtained? An increase from the group.
Why? Because that is their archetype.
These series of sacrificial days have the Dvādaśāha as their archetype; therefore, the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) of the Dvādaśāha applies to them.
It is obtained.
If there is an increase from twelve days, thus there will be compliance with the general rule (codaka).
Therefore, the increase is from the group.
Or rather, it is from a single day, because of their equality.
It might be so. [As stated in] the Bhāṣya: "The increase is from a single day, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma, not from the Dvādaśāha."
Why? Because of their equality.
There is equality between the days of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) and the others due to their dissimilarity;
those [other days] also require a conclusion from elsewhere, and these [twelve-day days] do as well.
Nor is it the case that, according to the maxim "one beggar does not beg from another beggar," only the functions belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma are to be performed.

Nor is there an extension (atideśa) to something else; rather, since there is no evidence for a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), those [functions] for which the *ukthya* status is established are enjoined by the specific scriptural statement. Furthermore, the justification for the hymns (*stotra*) exists only in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.

In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), however, for the purpose of supplementing the specific ritual details (*dharmaviśeṣa*) by restating the hymns (*stotra*) obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), it is to be repeated in the *śatokthya* and other such rites.
And in the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*), there are two *agniṣṭoma*s on both sides, with eight *ukthya*s in the middle.
For some, there are *śatokthya* sacrifices, and the third [day] is the *ṣoḍaśī*.
Thus, in the *śatokthya* and similar rites, there are twenty *agniṣṭoma*s, and these must be increased by means of the *ukthya* sacrificial form (*saṃsthā*).

Furthermore, in the alternative view, although the increase of the *ukthya* form must be performed for the *ṣoḍaśī*, the extension (*atideśa*) that applies is that of the *ṣoḍaśī* of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and not that of the *ṣoḍaśī* belonging to the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: from the group [of days] comes the increase of the Ukthya-stotra and so forth by twelve. Why? Because all these series of days (ahargaṇas) are modifications of the Dvādaśāha sacrifice.
Therefore, due to proximity, the increase of the Ukthya-stotra must also be understood from that very same source.
Regarding the increase of hymns (*stotra*) in the *viśata* and *ukthya* sacrifices and so forth, it occurs either in a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*) or in a one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*).
The former is due to being a modification of a group (*gaṇavikāra*), while the latter is because the hymn is produced therein.
It has been stated that in the *bhāṣya* regarding the *śatāgniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, there is the application (*pravṛtti*) of the twelve-day (*dvādaśāha*) and ten-night (*daśarātra*) rites.
Furthermore, in the twelve-day sacrifice, the first and last days conclude with the *atirātra* form.
In the ten-night sacrifice, the first and last days have the *agniṣṭoma* as their concluding form (*saṃsthā*),
while the eight intermediate days have the *ukthya* as their concluding form,
and there is one *ṣoḍaśī*.

Thus, in this case, since the *śatokthya* [rite] sets aside the *ukthya* and other forms obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), there is no harm whatsoever in its being of the *agniṣṭoma* form.
As for the *ukthya* and *atirātra* forms, however, there is no doubt even regarding those cases where the status of the *ukthya* form is obtained solely through extended application.

But in those cases where the status of the *agniṣṭoma* form would otherwise be obtained, since the *ukthya* rites must be performed by virtue of the explicit injunction, the *ukthya* and *atirātra* stotras belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) must be performed, because they are the ones present [by proximity].
This being the case, there is no application of those [elements] by means of extended injunction (*atideśa*).

According to the principle that "the first [element] belongs to the first," each respective day is applied to its corresponding day through extended injunction. While those days which are modifications of the *ukthya* form of the archetype receive the *ukthya* from that source, there is no authority for such transfer in the case of those days which are modifications of the *agniṣṭoma* form of the archetype. Furthermore, since only the first and last days possess the *atirātra* form, there is no extended injunction for them; consequently, the *rātriparyāyas* (night-rounds) are even more clearly excluded from being prescribed there.

Therefore, in the Śatokthya and other such rites, the recited (vācika) stotras on those respective days must perform the very functions belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma, according to the maxim: "A beggar does not beg from another beggar.

Furthermore, there is no extension (atideśa) of other elements; rather, since there is no evidence for these being separate acts (karmāntara), they are enjoined by direct statement (vacana) wherever the term *ukthya* is established.
Moreover, the justification for the stotras exists only in the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.

In the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), however, by way of restating the hymns obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), there is an extended application of specific ritual details (*dharmaviśeṣa*); in the thirty-six-night sacrifice, it is merely that much.
Furthermore, there is an injunction by way of direct instruction (*upadeśa*) specifically for the *jyotiṣṭoma*s.

For this very reason, even though there is no extension (*atideśa*) here of the *rātriparyāya* and other such elements—which serve as alternative forms (*saṃsthā*) for the sake of the fruit within the *jyotiṣṭoma*—there is no defect whatsoever, because it is accepted that their injunction occurs precisely through direct instruction.
*Nyāyabindu*: In the *śatoktha*, there is a repetition of the ten-night period belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
And in that [sacrifice], during the first ten nights, the *agniṣṭoma* is the final form (*saṃsthā*).
Here, however, because the *ukthya* form is directly prescribed (*aupadeśika*), there is an interruption of the *ukthya* after the *agniṣṭoma* stotra.
In those *ukthya* stotras that are being performed, the interruptions of the *ukthya* from the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) are applied.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: because the characteristics of the *ukthya* are taught specifically in relation to the Jyotiṣṭoma, this [modification] is indeed a modification of that [Jyotiṣṭoma], and not a modification of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
This is according to the maxim: "A beggar does not beg from another beggar.
Maṇḍana [states]: "And the addition of the days of the sacrificial sessions (*ahargaṇa*) is what must be enjoined."

Śaṅkara says: "And there, from the *prākṛtokthya*... There, in the *śatokthya*, that *codaka* (the rule of extension) [applies]. The extended application (*atideśa*) [brings] the properties of the *ṣaḍaha* to the *ṣaṭtriṃśadrātra*.

There is also a discussion regarding the repetition over time, because of the difference in the ritual acts. The Bhāṣya states: Regarding a specific ritual act (the Ṣaṭtriṃśadrātra), it is heard in the scripture: "There are six-day periods," "There are four [six-day periods]," and "There are five [six-day periods]."

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the procedure of the twelve-day sacrifice apply, or that of the six-day sacrifice? What is the prima facie view? "Even when there is a repetition of time, [the rule applies] according to Bādari. Even when this repetition of the time of the six-day sacrifice is heard, the teacher Bādari maintained that the procedure of the days of the twelve-day sacrifice applies.
Why? Because of the difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
Here, by the word "six-day period" (*ṣaḍaha*), six Soma sacrifices characterized by days are denoted;
and a distinction between those groups of six is understood.

Regarding the phrase "four six-day periods" (*catvāraḥ ṣaḍahāḥ*), because the number is applied to distinct entities, if one were to assume a mere repetition of a single original rite—whether lateral (*pārśvika*) or internal (*ābhiprāyika*)—then it would have to be expressed as "four six-day [repetitions]" (*catuḥ-ṣaḍahāḥ*). However, when it is stated "four six-day periods," twenty-four days are understood; since this number of days serves as a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) not belonging to the archetype (*prakṛti*), it adopts the procedure of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāhika*) regarding the succession of days.
Therefore, there is no application of multiple ten-day periods;
rather, according to the teacher Jaimini, there is a repetition of that same period.
Commentary: Regarding the repetition of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) known as the *pārśvika*, the teacher Jaimini held that there should be a repetition.
Why? Because the number of days is not directly perceived.
The number twenty-four is an imperceptible number that is understood through inference.
And the inference regarding that [result] occurs precisely through four sets of six-day periods.
Therefore, one first performs those four sets of six-day periods, thereby aggregating them to the number twenty-four.
It is just as when one first perceives smoke and afterwards [perceives] fire.
Just as one achieves one's purpose through the very cognition of smoke and does not regard the cognition of fire,
so too here, by the very cognition of the six-day sacrifice (*ṣaḍaha*),

there is the extended application (*atideśa*) that establishes the characteristics of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which consists of both the *satra* and *ahīna* types, for both the *satra* and the *ahīna*.
And the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is both a *satra* and an *ahīna*, because it functions in both ways.
As stated in the Bhāṣya: "The twelve-day sacrifice consists of the *prāyaṇīya* *atirātra*, the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, the three *chandomas*, the *avivākya* day, and the *udayanīya* *atirātra*.
Thus, it bears both designations: *satra* and *ahīna*.
How is this known? From the instruction of those who are experts.
For they instruct thus: "The Sattra and the Ahīna are the twelve-day sacrifice.
And in the matter of comprehending words, the instruction of experts is the authoritative means of knowledge.
Furthermore, its designation is established by the scriptural injunctions of its specific properties (dharmas), such as:

"One, two, or even many may perform the sacrifice without deficiency; initiated priests should officiate for them"; "The householder himself [is the master], while the Brahmins are his officiating priests; they enter upon the sacrificial session (sattra)"; and so forth.
Thus, the distinction in designation arises from the difference in these properties.

For example, the Brāhmaṇa mentions the *parirāṭ* as a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). This will be explained in the tenth chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "Because of the connection with the *satra* through the injunction regarding sitting and the consumption of food, and because of the plurality of sacrificers, it is a *satra* of the twelve-day rite" (10.6.16.60); and "Because of the injunction of the root *yajati* and because the masters have not reached the state of being mere participants" (61). That [twelve-day rite] applies to the multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*) beginning with the two-night rite, according to the rule: "Of the twelve-day rite, in the groups" (8.1.9.17).

In this regard, a doubt arises: does this [rite] proceed in both ways in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), or is there a fixed rule such that it is sometimes of the nature of a *sattra* and sometimes of the nature of a *ahīna*? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? It should proceed in both ways because of the identity of the action; it proceeds as both alternatives.
Why? Because of the unity of action.
It has been stated that this action is one and of such a nature.
No distinction is perceived in its operation, such that it would be of this kind here and not of that kind there.
Therefore, it proceeds in both ways.
[Objection: But if one [power] has proceeded in two ways, there will be no second [power] for the effect.

[Response: There will be an option (vikalpa) due to the singularity of the action, just as in the case of the offering of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) in the modifications (*vikāra*) of the *Āgneya* sacrifice.

Alternatively, because of the hearing of the word "yajati" (he sacrifices), there should be an application [of the ritual] as a non-deficient (*ahīna*) sacrifice, since its verbal form is identical to that of the archetype.
Commentary: Or rather, it is not the case that in all instances there is an application in both ways.
Where the word "yajati" (he sacrifices) is heard, there the application belongs to that which has the nature of an *ahīna* sacrifice.

By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), where there is an injunction involving sitting and officiating (*āsana-upāyi-codanā*), there the application belongs to that which has the nature of a *satra*.
Why? Because the word is identical with that of the archetype (*prakṛti*). For a modification (*vikṛti*) has the same word as its archetype.
Therefore, due to the commonality of the injunction (*codanā*), there is a restriction to the archetype.

Furthermore, that which is not a *satra* is characterized by an injunction involving the root *yajati* (to sacrifice), such as: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the twelve-day rite" (*dvādaśāhena prajākāmo yajeta*).

That which is a *satra* is characterized by an injunction involving sitting and approaching, such as: "Those desiring prosperity should approach the twelve-day rite" (*dvādaśāham ṛddhikāmā upeyuḥ*) and "Those desiring prosperity should sit for the twelve-day rite" (*dvādaśāham ṛddhikāmā upāsīran*).

The fact that rites beginning with the two-night sacrifice (*dvirātra*) up to those beginning with the eleven-night sacrifice (*ekādaśarātra*) are *yajatis* is due to the injunction involving the root *yajati*.

Commentary: Here it is asked: Which, then, are those *ahargaṇa* (multi-day sacrifices) enjoined by the injunction "he sacrifices" (*yajati*) in which the nature of an *ahīna* (non-sacrificial session) prevails? Or which are those enjoined by the injunction "he sits" (*āsana*) in which the nature of a *satra* (sacrificial session) prevails? To this it is replied: From the *dvirātra* up to the *ekādaśarātra*, there is the nature of an *ahīna*; therein the nature of an *ahīna* prevails, because they are enjoined by the word "sacrifice" (*yajati*), as in: "One should sacrifice with the *dvirātra*."
In the case of the Trayodaśarātra and other such rites, they constitute *satras* because there is an injunction for sitting and officiating as priests.
The Commentary states: "Those desiring prosperity should undertake the thirteen-night sacrifice; those desiring stability should perform the fourteen-night sacrifice.
Having observed this well, the Sūtrakāra says:
Or rather, since the *ahīna* is characterized by the root *yajati*, therefore even the two-night sacrifices and others possess the nature of an *ahīna*.
For they too are injunctions for sacrifice;
since a *sattra* is an injunction for sitting [in session] as a means, therefore the *sattras* beginning with the thirteen-night rite are also injunctions of that same nature.
And this is also because of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

The Bhāṣya states: "Agniṣṭoma is indeed Prajāpati; he generated the subsequent *ekāhas*. To him, the *ahargaṇas* beginning with the *dvirātra* said, 'Do not abandon us. Therefore, their status as *ahīnas* [is established]. This demonstrates that the *dvirātra* and other such sacrifices are *ahīnas*. The Śāstra (Śabara-bhāṣya) states: "But the application of the *satra* rules to the *satras* is due to their similarity to a *satra*;
likewise, it is established that the *ahīna* rules apply to the *ahīnas* because they are easily compatible."

Because of the specific mention of *soma* and *āmikṣā*, even though there is an absence of modification of both, the connection [of the discussion] arises from the fact that in the *ahargaṇas* (multi-day sacrifices), there is no fixed modification.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: even for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which exists in both forms—as a *satra* and an *ahīna*—there would be an application without fixed restriction among the *gaṇas*, because the ritual action consisting of the twelve-day sacrifice is a single entity. [The commentary states:
"The *ahīna* is established as ending with the thirteenth day."
Or, if they were established [as distinct], there would be no distinction [between them], as each would be known by its own respective characteristic mark.
The two ends are the two piercing points (*vidhyantau*).
Bhaṭṭa says: It has been stated that among the multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*), there is the application (*pravṛtti*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
And in the twelve-day sacrifice, there are two characteristics (*dharma*): being a sacrificial session (*satra*) and being a non-sacrificial session (*ahīna*).

In that context, the status of being a *satra* (sacrificial session) is the non-literal adjunct (*alaukika-upādhi*) enjoined by injunctions such as "they should sit" (*āsīran*) and "they should approach" (*upeyuḥ*); whereas the status of being an *ahīna* (non-sessive sacrifice) is the non-literal adjunct enjoined by the injunction of the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) where the ownership [of the fruit] is not fixed. This is known from the usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).
Furthermore, when their specific nature is the cause, particular properties corresponding to them are prescribed.
Likewise, other multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇas*) designated as *satras* and *ahīnas* are also handed down in the scriptures as being devoid of [such] specific properties.
In that regard, even though there are two types [of twelve-day sacrifices], the ritual procedure (*dharma*) of a single twelve-day sacrifice applies to both.
Therefore, those elements that are not contradictory are combined (*samuccīyante*), while those that are contradictory are treated as alternatives (*vikalpyante*).

For there is no differentiation of the twelve-day sacrifice here [in this context] such that a specific injunction (*deśavākya*)—such as "like that particular twelve-day sacrifice"—could be inferred on the basis of a subordinate commonality (*avāntarasāmānya*).

Since there is no evidence for a distinction [between the two], one might assume that the extended application (*atideśa*) rule is simply "like the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāhavat*), and thus conclude that there is indeed no fixed restriction.

This being the position reached, even though the extended application occurs precisely by way of being a "twelve-day sacrifice," because the occasion (*nimitta*) consisting in being a *satra* is absent, those duties contingent upon that occasion do not apply to the *ahīna*; and because the occasion consisting in being an *ahīna* is absent, those duties contingent upon that occasion do not apply to the *satra*. Thus, in effect, the status of being the archetype (*prakṛtitva*) is established: for the *ahargaṇas* of the *satra* type, the *satra*-type twelve-day sacrifice is the archetype; and for those of the *ahīna* type, the *ahīna*-type [twelve-day sacrifice] is the archetype.

Starting from the two-night sacrifice up to the end of the eleven-night sacrifice, they are *ahīna*s; the twelve-night sacrifice possesses the nature of both; and starting from the thirteen-night sacrifice onwards, they are all exclusively *satra*s, because they possess the aforementioned characteristics and because of established usage (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*). Therefore, in those [sacrifices], there is the application of the twelve-night sacrifice in its respective form. *Nyāyabindu*:—The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the groups of days (*ahargaṇa*) called *satra*, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *satra*-form twelve-night sacrifice, whereas in the *ahīna*s, there is an extension of the *ahīna*.

Maṇḍana: "Dharma would be the establishment [of rules]. Śaṅkara: "[It would be so] because of such [a rule] in the case of the Satra and Ahīna sacrifices. [The term] "consisting of Satras and Ahīnas" refers to the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha).
Extended application (*atideśa*): the ritual properties of the potsherds used in the *Vāruṇapraghāsika* sacrifice are extended to the single-potsherd offering (*ekakapāla*) of the *Sākamedhīya*.

Regarding the cakes baked on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*), the model is that of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, because in the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices we observe the performance of all oblations, and because the *avabhṛtha* rite specifically prescribes a single portion for the offering.
In the commentary on the *sākamedha* section, it is heard in the scripture: "This is the Brāhmaṇa-text for the single-potsherd cake.
In this regard, it is considered whether this refers to the single-potsherd cake of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice or to that of the *vāruṇaprāghāsa* sacrifice.
What is obtained? We say: that which belongs to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

What is the reason? Its ritual duties have been prescribed: "Having adorned [the deity] and having offered [the oblation], one should sacrifice in a low voice; the back [of the altar] should be made manifest," and so forth.
That which belongs to the Vāruṇapraghāsika sacrifice is devoid of such duties.
In a case where specific duties have been prescribed, it is appropriate to say, "This should be performed first" or "That should be done.

Therefore, there is the inclusion of the Vaiśvadeva [offering]. Now, one might object that because of the mention of the Aindrāgna [offering], the single-kapāla cake should belong specifically to the Vāruṇapraghāsa; however, this is not a restriction, for while the mention of two offerings belonging to the same parvan is indeed possible, the mention of those belonging to different parvans is likewise not contradictory.
Therefore, it might be argued that the one-cake offering belonging to the Vaiśvadeva [parvan] is to be taken.
To this, it is replied:
the one-cake offering belonging to the Vāruṇapraghāsika [parvan] is to be taken.

Why? Because the Vaiśvadeva cake baked on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) is the archetype (*prakṛti*). How is this known? From the observation of the "offering of the whole" (*sarvahoma*) and the "non-return" (*aparyāvṛtti*) in the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice. In the Āgrayaṇa, regarding the cake on a single potsherd which is not subject to the rule of pouring in more flour (*āvāpyavidheya*), it shows both the offering of the whole and the non-return: "That he makes the offering of the whole—that is one reproach; that what has been offered returns unoffered—that is the second; one should sacrifice with clarified butter alone for those two rules. Thus, in this sentence focused on the injunction for the butter-sacrifice (*ājyayāga*), it indicates that the cake on a single potsherd is subject to the offering of the whole and the non-return.
From this observation, and because of the statement regarding the offering of the substance only once at the *avabhṛtha* bath;
furthermore, there is a restrictive rule at the *avabhṛtha* stating, "Of this very cake baked on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*), he makes two portions.
By this it is known that, indeed, elsewhere there is no taking of two portions.
And all of this has been prescribed for the single-potherd cake (ekakapāla) of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Therefore, the Vaiśvadeva single-potherd cake is the archetype (prakṛti) for all single-potherd cakes.

What follows from this? Even in the case of the single-potherd cake at the Sākamedha sacrifice, the ritual details (dharmas) of the Vaiśvadeva are already obtained; thus, their extension (atideśa) would be purposeless.
The extension (*atideśa*) of those specific characteristics (*vaiśeṣika-dharma*) of the *vāruṇaprāghāsa* sacrifice that have not yet been obtained is meaningful;
therefore, this refers to the single-potherd (*ekakapāla*) cake of the *vāruṇaprāghāsa*.
It is replied: this is merely an indicative mark (*liṅga*); from what [textual authority] is it derived?
We shall explain the answer later in the section: "The *svarasāman*, the one-pot offering, and the *āmikṣā*" (7.3.1.26).
What, then, are those properties? They are such as: "The ladles are made of gold," or "They are made of *śamyā* wood," and so forth.

Soma: Just as in the case of the statement, "These five oblations are indeed [the subject of] the Brāhmaṇas," there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the entire section (*kāṇḍa*), including its explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), which prescribes the ritual procedure along with its name, in order to achieve a broad scope for that teaching; so too here, it has been stated that there is an extension from the Vaiśvadeva section in order to achieve a broad scope. Thus, there is a logical connection (*saṃgati*) consisting of a specific investigation into the extension from the entire section, which was previously established in a general sense. This extension refers to the extension from the Sākamedha section pertaining to Indra.

[The opponent asks: "Is the instruction regarding the single *kapāla* for the *vaiśvadeva* and other offerings found in the *Sākamedha* section, specifically in the *Varuṇapraghāsa*, or rather in the *Agnimāruta*?
[We say: The former, because of the abundance of *Varuṇa*-offerings in the archetype (*prakṛti*); the latter, because of its proximity (*saṃnidhāna*)."

The Bhaṭṭa [view] regarding the discussion on the cake for Indra (aindrāmāhas) being for the sake of its purpose and its superiority: The archetype of the single-potherd cake (*ekakapāla*) is specifically that of the Vāruṇapraghāsa sacrifice, and not even that of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice as a source of ritual properties (*dharma*). This is because, as will be explained, the ritual procedure of the Vaiśvadeva is established through the extension of the injunctive mark (*codanāliṅga-atideśa*) to all single-potherd cakes.
Therefore, it is the Vāruṇapraghāsika alone that serves to provide the acquisition of certain other specific ritual properties.
And in this way, even the extension (*atideśa*) of the *aindrāmāyaṇīya* [offering] is justified.

For in that case, there is no injunction for the extension of the *dārśika* (New Moon) *aindrāmāyaṇīya*, since it is established through the extension based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the original injunction (*codanā*).
Nor is there an extension of the subsequent *aindrāmāyaṇīya* offerings, because they have not been presented [in the context].

Precisely because it is presented within the context of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, and because there is no mention of the Aindrāgna in the Vaiśvadeva [parvan], it is that of the Vāruṇapraghāsas alone.
Therefore, even though it is not recited there, the one-pot offering (ekapāla) of the Sākamedha is extended by analogy (atideśa) to the Saura offerings and others.

Why? Because the relationship between the probandum and the probans is based on the Veda;

(Samādhatte: When the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is uttered, three expectancies arise from the understanding of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*). Among these, in response to the expectancy "what?", a human goal (*puruṣārtha*)—whether directly or indirectly—is invariably implied as that which is to be brought about. The verbal root (*dhātu*), however, becomes the instrument (*karaṇa*), because the human goal functions as the object (*karman*).
Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "The subordinate status of actions is established by their own nature.

The meaning of the Bhāṣya is this: since the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) has as its goal the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), an action, when connected with it, relates to it solely as an instrument (*karaṇa*), because its own nature is not itself a human purpose.
[This is] the extended application (*atideśa*) in the case of the *saurya* sacrifice. 234

It was stated that what is called "the number of non-difference" (*abhedakatvasaṃkhyā*) is understood either as the concealment of distinction by means of oneness and so forth, or as another number common to numbers such as oneness; however, it is not [simply] one— [The text continues: ...[it is not simply one]. It was said that the term "non-difference" (*abheda*) is used because there is no distinction between the two, since both possess the quality of being a single entity; it does not mean that they are identical in every respect. For example, although the two words "cow" (*go*) and "horse" (*aśva*) are distinct, they are referred to as "non-distinct" (*abheda*) when they share the common property of being two. Similarly, while the two words "one" (*eka*) and "two" (*dvi*) are distinct, they are called "non-distinct" (*abheda*) because they share the common property of being numbers. Therefore, the term "non-difference" (*abheda*) is employed here to indicate that the two are similar in certain respects. Furthermore, the term "oneness" (*ekatva*) is used because there is no difference regarding the fact that both are singular entities. Thus, the meaning is that the two are similar in some respects, yet distinct in others. Consequently, this is designated as "the number of non-difference" (*abhedakatvasaṃkhyā*). Moreover, it was stated that this "number of non-difference" is understood as the concealment of distinction by means of oneness and so forth, or as another number common to numbers such as oneness; it is not, however, [merely] one. Now, if they are prompted by the *apūrva*, then it is as stated here.
As for the meaning of the Sūtra: [it concerns] the gender of Prajāpati, [the deities] such as Āgneya, and so forth.

Because it is common to all, its status as belonging to Agni would follow without distinction; therefore, the context establishes its specific application. What, then, is appropriate here? The unprecedented [apūrva].
Regarding the term "employed" (*prayuktā*):

for it is the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) that possesses the fruit, whereas the sacrifice itself is fruitless. As it is said: "In the case of the *saurya* [oblation], [the fruit belongs] to something else; it does not belong to the fire."
For this reason: there is no distinction [between them], because they consist of medicinal substances such as *daivakya* and the like;
furthermore, an effort prescribed toward that which yields a fruit becomes purposeful.
Therefore,
the ritual properties (dharmas) are prompted by the *apūrva*. Hereafter follows the commentary (*sūtropabṛṃhaṇa*) of the Teacher.

Bhaṭṭa: In the case of the *iṣṭis*, the principle of extended application (*atideśanyāya*) from the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices applies, because they are supplementary to the same injunction (*codanāśeṣabhāvāt*), and because [the procedure] is established as being like that [of the model sacrifice], due to its being performed and having been previously experienced.
Commentary: The collection of Dharma is a subsidiary (śeṣa) to the injunction of ritual action; that is to say, it constitutes a single part [of it].

For instance, one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), where the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consists of various acts such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) and so forth.
In that injunction, the subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) of the root *yaj* ("to sacrifice") is heard in the expression "with the New and Full Moon sacrifices."
For the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* denotes a sacrifice (*yajati*).
Here, the instrumental status of the sacrifice is heard [in the text]: "One should effect something else by means of the aggregate of sacrifices known as the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
That which is other than that [sacrifice] is enjoined as something to be performed, not the sacrifice itself.
And that [result] is unprecedented.

Now, it might be argued that only the result is heard in the sentence, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," and therefore that [sacrifice] must be performed. True, it is so heard; however, it is not accomplished by the sacrifice itself; rather, it comes into being when the sacrifice has been completed.

Something unprecedented (apūrva) is produced by that [action]; therefore, its status as something to be performed (kartavyatā) is stated. That which is to be performed is connected with the procedure (itikartavyatā).
Therefore, the dharmas are unprecedented (apūrva). And the distinction between those unprecedented [dharmas] has been stated.
Hence, that...

By this [sūtra of the prima facie view], the *saṃnipatyopakārakas* (auxiliaries that assist by direct contact, such as sprinkling and threshing) are stated to be for that purpose (i.e., for the sake of the sacrifice). Because they fall within that context, he states that even the *prajā* (progeny) and so forth are [for that purpose]. Furthermore, [the claim that these auxiliaries are] useless is contradictory.
The Commentary states: This being so, all ritual elements (dharmas) become applicable to all purposes.

Thus, the *prayāja* offerings and others exist in sacrifices such as those dedicated to Indra; consequently, their presence in the *saurya* rite is logically established by the injunction: "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* seed."
Otherwise, the *prayāja* offerings would have to be enjoined separately;
in those *prayāja* offerings, there is no black wool.
Thus, that [black wool] would serve two purposes.
Moreover, having two purposes is contradictory.

Therefore, the ritual properties (dharmas) are prompted by the root sacrifice (yajati). Since there would be no injunction regarding their origin, their application would have to depend on the primary injunction; consequently, there would be a distinction between the rituals.
The Commentary states: It is not the case that ritual properties (dharmas) are prompted by the root sacrifice (yajati);
rather, their application would follow from the injunction (codanā).
"Injunction" here is a misconception regarding the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).
Because they serve the purpose of instigation (*codanā*) and because they serve the purpose of the *apūrva*, the ritual properties (*dharma*) are connected with the *apūrva*.
The reason has been stated as "because they possess fruit.
As for the claim that the sacrifice (*yajati*) is directly perceived as the object of the ritual properties, that is an error.
It is said: because there is no injunction [to that effect].

The notion of "origination" is an error regarding the sacrifice (*yajati*). Since the two sacrifices have already been mentioned, there is no injunction stating that the ritual properties (*dharma*) are for the sake of the sacrifice.
Only sacrifices are heard of and performed;
yet by that much alone they do not have those [sacrifices] as their purpose.
It is just as when the coloring of cloth is heard of in the statement, "he dyes the cloth," and it is indeed done to the cloth, yet that [coloring] does not have the cloth as its primary purpose.
It serves either its own purpose or the purpose of man.
Likewise here too, the sacrifices being heard of and performed would have the *apūrva* as their purpose,
for the sake of their meaningfulness.
Consequently, there would be a distinction between ritual acts, because they serve the purpose of producing the *apūrva* (the unseen potency).

Furthermore, as for the fact that the sacrifice (*yajati*) is directly subordinate to the fruit, it is understood that this subordination does not occur without first producing the *apūrva*; thus, it is known to be mediated by a channel.
And even through such a channel, that by which something is accomplished is considered its cause.
For example: "He cooks with cow-dung" and "They become satisfied.
As for the claim that the fruit will arise from the sacrifice just as from drinking oil—that is an error.
Even for the drinking of oil, the fruit does not arise at a later time;
its fruit is the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātusāmya),
and that occurs at that very moment.
And as for the result—such as strength, nourishment, and so forth—that arises from the proper digestion of food;
therefore, the comparison is unequal.
Or, alternatively, it might be [the case] that [the self] possesses all attributes by virtue of its similarity to the name, just as [a word] possesses [its meaning].
