The Commentary (Bhāṣya): Although the *apūrva* is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the ritual duties (*dharma*), nevertheless, that ritual act (*padārtha*) would be accompanied by all the duties.
This is because of their commonality, just as with the name.
To begin with, the name for these is the same: "the *apūrva*."
Just like the designation, there must also be a common property (*dharma*) belonging to this [term], as in the case of the Vāhīkas.
For example, when it is said, "A Vāhīka guest has arrived; let that which is due to him be prepared," whatever Vāhīka arrives, to each of them barley-milk (*yavāgū*) is prepared.
Or, for example, as in the case where it is said: "In the Akṣayyāmeyī rite, boiled rice with lentils (mudraudana) is to be eaten; in the Udarāmeyī rite, milk is to be drunk.
For in every instance, boiled rice with lentils is indeed eaten in the Akṣayyāmeyī, and milk is also drunk in the Udarāmeyī.
Likewise here too, whatever properties are heard in connection with one *apūrva* ought to belong to all *apūrvas*.
Moreover, there are scholars known as the Aruṇaparāras; among their traditional recollections (smṛti) is a Brāhmaṇa text which begins,
"Whatever are the ritual duties (dharma) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, all those belong to the Agnihotra," and continues until, "All the archetypal and ectypal triads have been enumerated."
This indicates that very same principle in its proper sequence.

Therefore, even though [the ritual] is prompted by the *apūrva*, all ritual properties (*dharma*) serve all purposes. However, because the purpose is undivided, this would apply to the [mantras of] recitation; for the performance is as before, since the action consists of the verbal form, and the engagement [of the properties] occurs through their division and separation.
The Commentary: The avoidance of this objection is now stated. As for what was said regarding "like the Vāhīkas," that is an error;
however, because the meaning is undivided, it would be so in the case of denotations.

The object is like a Vāhīka, being connected with that region; the meaning is that it is undivided and follows through all Vāhīkas. And the specific pleasure caused by it is not caused by the person. How is this known? Because the usage is as before.
The application [of the method] is as before.
Many Vāhīkas and non-Vāhīkas have been fed.
There, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), this was understood: that the desire to eat is caused by the region, not caused by the person.
Therefore, it must be so in the case of designations such as "Vāhīka" and the like.
Now, since in this context the action (karman) consists of the word itself, it is not possible to know from any other source which property (dharma) belongs to which transcendental result (apūrva).
Furthermore, the properties (dharmas) are established and understood through the word alone.
And there would be a division of those [rites] that have not been previously [prescribed].
Therefore, there would be no application elsewhere of the remaining [elements] that have been prescribed for one place.
If it is argued that this is based on traditional authority (smṛti), [we reply:]...
Commentary: Now, as for what was stated—that it is "Smṛti"—what is the refutation of that? [The answer is: "Because it is like the previous case" (*pūrvavat*). Commentary:
For this Smṛti is "like the previous case," as he will state regarding the *codaka* which conveys the properties: "Or rather, it is like the archetype" (*vidhvanto vā prakṛtivat*, 4.4.10).
This is a restatement of those factors already established by that [rule]; it is preceded by this logic and does not enjoin what has not been established.
For this reason, the determination of factors occurs through this logic.
Since meaning is inherent in the word, and because of its connection to each specific context, its existence would otherwise be restricted solely to that pure [context].
Commentary: This is the sūtra of conclusion (*nigamana*). Conclusion is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*). That is what is being stated here.

Since this is so, therefore, because the existence of the object follows from the existence of the word, and because it is bound to each specific context, the existence [of the deity] must be derived from the word alone, as in:
"The Gandharvas and Apsarases indeed madden him who becomes mad; these Gandharvas and Apsarases are the primordial elements.
To him, svāhā! To them, svāhā!"—thus he offers the oblation.

In the context of the *abhiprāka-raṇa* (the ritual of sprinkling), there is an instruction regarding the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings: "He offers these *rāṣṭrabhṛt* oblations; he offers the *abhyātāna* oblations.
If this statement did not exist, the ritual properties (*dharmas*) would remain restricted according to their respective specific contexts.
This being the case, the *aindrāgna* and other such sacrifices would be devoid of those [general] properties.
And for that purpose, the subsequent chapter-tablet is commenced.

Therein, first by means of the seventh [chapter], it is stated that there exist ritual properties (*dharma*) for the rites dedicated to Indra and others, and that these are established through extension (*atideśa*).

Extension (atideśa) means the application elsewhere of those properties (dharmas) that have been prescribed for another [subject]. For example, having established the rule for Devadatta’s meal— namely, "Devadatta is to be fed with rice, soup, meat, and cakes"—
one extends that very same rule to Yajñadatta, saying, "Yajñadatta is to be fed just like Devadatta."

They also cite this verse: "The established rule is that *atideśa* (extended application) is that by which, from a given primary action, there occurs an extension of its properties (*dharmapradeśa*) to actions similar to it."
And that [designation] occurs either by name or by verbal expression.
In that regard, name is threefold: derivative (atideśika), ritual name (karmanāma), and conventional name (saṃskāranāma), as well as etymological (yaugika).
Furthermore, speech is of two kinds: that which is based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and that which is inferential (*ānumānika*).
Of these two, the inferential will be explained later;
that which is based on direct perception is being considered right now.
ḌuP: A name is of three kinds:

a name of an action (*karmanāmadheya*), a name of a consecration (*saṃskāranāmadheya*), and an etymological (*yaugika*) name. Among these, the etymological name does not effect extension (*atideśaka*).
How so? By the very same application (*yoga*) by which the term *prāyaṇīya* applies to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it applies to the *gavāmayana* as well.
Śā—There is no dispute whatsoever regarding the fact that ritual properties (*dharmas*) are subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the performance (*karaṇa*).
Furthermore, on the view that [the *dharmas*] follow from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), their being for that specific purpose is not tenable.
Therefore, since all *dharmas* serve every purpose, this investigation into the extended application (*atideśa*) is unnecessary.
This being the position reached, it is replied:
Indeed, the sentence of the primary injunction thus establishes, through its connection with the eternal,
the unprecedented efficient force (*apūrvabhāvanā*) for both the subsidiary and the primary acts.
Following that connection with the efficient force, what is the subsequent connection of the constituent parts?
Consequently, one might suspect that there is a lack of knowledge regarding the interval between ritual acts; for why [is this so]?

Because the two parts—the mere continuity of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the [objective] aspect—are conceived as equal, since their nature is not yet fully encompassed and because the status of subordinate and primary is possible.

Soma: Having completed the discussion on *upadeśa* (direct injunction) in the preceding section (*pūrve paṭṭake*), the discussion on *atideśa* (extended application) is now introduced in the subsequent section (*uttarapaṭṭake*) through the logical connection of cause and effect (*hetuhetumadbhāva*).

Since an injunction such as "one should do it thus" (*itthaṃ kuryāt*) is preceded by a prior injunction, the injunction "one should do that" (*tad at kuryāt*) stands in a relationship of cause and effect with the former; thus, the discussion of the latter follows the former.

Once the determination of ritual duties (*dharmavyavasthā*) in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices has been established according to their respective contexts, the seventh [section] is intended for the acquisition of those duties in the *Saurya* and other sacrifices which require such duties, by means of extended application (*atideśa*).
The eighth [section] is for the purpose of establishing the specific details [of the rule], such as: "From this action, these factors arise here.
The ninth is for the purpose of establishing the modification of the application of the extended (atidiṣṭa) ritual elements.
The tenth is for the purpose of establishing those extended ritual elements that have not yet been established.

The first section (*adhikaraṇa*) is connected because it serves as an introduction (*upodghāta*). The sequence of reflection here is as follows: whether the subsequent section (*uttarapaṭṭaka*) should be commenced or not; for that purpose, this reflection: whether ritual properties (*dharma*) apply to the *saurya* and other sacrifices by way of extended application (*atideśa*), or not; and for that purpose, another reflection: whether properties such as the *prayāja* offerings are taught as being for the sake of all sacrifices, or whether they are restricted according to their respective contexts (*prakaraṇa*).

For that purpose, another consideration arises: do the ritual properties (dharmas) have the sacrifice as their object, or do they have the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as their object? Is the connection with the *apūrva*-producing efficient force (*bhāvanā*) preceded by the connection with the sacrifice, or is the connection with the sacrifice preceded by that [connection with the *apūrva*]?

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: when there is a distinction between the primary *apūrvas*, there shall be a fixed determination of the ritual properties according to their respective entitlements (*adhikāra*) and according to their respective contexts (*prakaraṇa*), as stated in the Bhāṣya.

Why? Because of the authority of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); for the relationship of subsidiary and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*) is to be understood solely through direct scriptural statement.
[Vi— ] "Or rather, since the instructions for the *prayāja* and other [subsidiary rites] pertain to all purposes,

let the extension (*atideśa*) of everything be considered according to the principle of sacrifice (*yajñanaya*). Because there is a difference in what is understood from the connection between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*pradhāna*)."
Next, there is the consideration of the extension (*atideśa*) of ritual application (*kāryya*) regarding the subject matter at hand.

According to the Bhaṭṭa school: once the primary injunction (*upadeśa*) together with its qualification (*sādhikāra*) has been understood, there would be no establishment of *atideśa* whatsoever by means of that very primary injunction alone.
Thus, *atideśa*, whose own establishment is dependent upon that [primary injunction], is now defined.

The Bhaṭṭa text [the *Tantravārttika*] which provides the definition of extended application (*atideśa*)—beginning with "the other is similar" (*asamānam itarat*) and so forth—is cited elsewhere; therefore, it should be understood that the subsequent portion of that text is summarized here under the heading "Agnihotra" and so on, just as in the expression "Devadatta is a lion. This [summary] is either a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the established association of this topic with the discussion of extended application, or it is a restatement by adopting the very same principle (*tadyalyanyāya*).

It is being examined: Is the purpose of the instruction regarding the *prayāja* offerings and so forth already established by the archetype (*prakṛti*), or is it not? This being the point of contention, although the injunction of ritual properties (*dharma*) is made by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to the sacrifice, nevertheless, there is a common applicability to both the archetype and the ectype (*vikṛti*).

For if there were common applicability, then since an extended application (*atideśa*) is possible, and because of the rule that a reference applies to what is proximate, the [injunction] would apply only to the archetype; thus, the mention of "rice" (*vrīhi*) would be redundant—this is the introductory argument (*upoddhāta*).

In that regard, although in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, there might be an application restricted only to the archetype—as in the case of "one should sacrifice with *barley*"—and especially because the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors specifically concern only the *āgneya* and other such [archetypal] sacrifices, they possess a specific scope.
Atideśapārāyaṇa 246: Exposition of Specific Atideśas. In another context, it is said that "atideśa" refers to a location where grain is given;
by the absence of that [grain], a contradiction arises from it.
In order to establish the non-existence of that [self], it is equally applicable to all categories of objects;
this contradiction in understanding arises when there is no connection with anything else.
It does not exist in any way whatsoever as a conjunction within a single moment;
for those who do not accept the simultaneous connection of phenomena in one place.
In the section on the *apūrva*, the nature of the original injunctions as they appear in the texts is analyzed;
following that, there is a consideration of the methods for their application.
That is not tenable; for in this group of six, reflection is bound to action.
Even if the injunction were itself not an action, it would still be reflected upon for the sake of that [action].
The consideration of the fourth chapter also applies to this group of six, because it does not involve transgression;
for the purpose of the injunction is understood from the instruction according to its function.
How that [work] was taught by him will be explained by the first [chapter];
therefore, setting aside the purpose of the injunction, another task is undertaken here for the sake of meditative concentration.
This [section on] deliberation (cintā) is established as the gateway for the eight types of tasks;
by means of it, the extension (atideśa) of ritual elements is deliberated upon here in the group of six.
That very assistance, which serves as its cause, has also been shown:
through six [types of] indications, both its natural and its modified forms, for that [person] and for ordinary beings.

And thus, the sublation of those [meanings] that are not [intended as] constituent parts is employed for the sake of establishing the assistance [rendered] toward the comprehension of the principal meaning.
The archetypal [element] is not performed merely by application;
therefore, this is accepted as a transfer of function (*kāryātideśa*) rather than an instruction of the original form (*aupadeśika*).
Although this conceptualization of benefit is by nature [merely] imagined, it has been fashioned as a remedy by means of instruction that is beyond measure.
And the application [of the rule] is agreed upon by means of the instruction of the elders;
for here, "instruction" (upadeśa) refers to the composition of the treatise.
And that [injunction] is the means of valid cognition; it is restricted to the form of an action as its purpose.
Whatever object is understood from it is not merely something taught for its own sake.
Even though it exists for the sake of its own cognition, that [negation] which has a positive meaning is itself not final;
thus, this negation, being non-final, is capable of implying a positive entity.
Its status as being taught by direct instruction is logical, and it too is not contradicted by this [reasoning];
furthermore, the injunction is capable of postulating a specific benefit.
But a modified [element], like an original one, is not capable of postulating a specific benefit for a specific object,
even though it might be so capable.
It grasps [the meaning] by its very nature; lightness is the cause therein.
For when there is a conflict between what is already established and what must be inferred, the acceptance of the established is the lighter course.
This [procedure], established by the indicative marks within its own sentences, is brought into proximity;
however, the attainment of distinctness among the ritual elements cannot occur without the mediation of a contributory benefit (upakāra).
Their movement is established through their function, and their specific mode is established through instruction;
likewise, in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the properties are established through their function, and the specific mode is established through instruction.
Even when taught, the designation of an extended application (*atideśa*) is set aside; for its purpose exists in another place, which is sufficient by virtue of its own rule.
The status of being explicitly taught (*upadiṣṭa*) or not explicitly taught (*anupadiṣṭa*) is not contradictory for a single [textual unit],
for it is generally accepted that both explicit teaching and extended application (*atideśa*) are matters of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If both direct instruction (upadeśa) and extended application (atideśa) were indeed valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), then a contradiction would arise; however, this is not accepted as being the case.
From that, having obtained the instruction, one shines forth by means of the instruction;
even an extended application (atideśa) is appropriate when there is a statement otherwise regarding something else.
Instruction is [defined] by the observation of its validity as having the form of an action;
both [types of injunction], however, do not rely solely on instruction and extension.
For when there is sublation or when there is a common framework (tantra), the consideration regarding the meaning taught by way of extended application (atideśa) is not at all tenable.
But since all thoughts have their basis in the task at hand,
it is appropriate here that the thoughts be considered equal to the task.
But surely, in this way, it would follow that the meanings of words are themselves taught [by injunctions],
since even for that which possesses a result, the meaning of the injunction is said to be something else.
It is said: there would be verbal nature [of knowledge], but not the status of being an object of instruction;
this distinction between two means of valid cognition is likewise without foundation.

He who, being presented with an instruction, grasps the syntactical connection of the meaning of the sentence should be known as one who acts according to instruction (aupadeśika); and he is presented [with that instruction] in two ways.
It is presented by the verbal text itself, as well as presented by the meaning of the injunction;
it is like the assistance rendered in the archetype, or like that which is heard as something to be applied.
That which appears in two ways through its various modes is not truly present;
therefore, it is not based on instruction, but is merely bound by its effects.
In order to remove the ancient bond of [erroneous] conclusions,
Śālikanātha, the true knower, has made this effort which brings joy to the learned.
(Thus ends the Atideśapārāyaṇa in the Prakaraṇapañjikā composed by Śālikanātha; Pañjikā pp. 226–231.
The promise to set forth the specific details of *atideśa*.
Now, the definition of particularity (viśeṣa).
The Commentary states: Thus far, by means of this first chapter, the general definition of extended application (*atideśa*) has been stated.

That is to say, in the case of rites such as those dedicated to Indra for which no specific ritual details (*dharma*) have been prescribed, the ritual details are extended from those rites for which they have been prescribed, such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
In this regard, a deliberation arises: is there an extension of ritual details from all rites into a single rite, or from only one?

Since there is no distinction, it follows that [the quality] applies to all. However, once the ritual action has been rendered complete by one [quality], there is no reason for a second quality to apply.
This is true; yet it is simply not known which [quality] belongs to which [action].
For that purpose, the specific definition must be stated as "of this, in this.
This very thing is promised at the beginning of the chapter with the words, "Now, the specific definition" (*atha viśeṣalakṣaṇam*).
Now—
Now, immediately after the general definition of extended application (*sāmānyātideśa*) based on conduct (*vṛtta*), we shall state the specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
This being stated now, it should be understood according to its proper occasion.

Regarding the passage: "Is there an extension (*atideśa*) of the *dharma*s from one ritual to all rituals?"—if this is the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*): namely, whether those *dharma*s that are prescribed (*samāmnāta*) in one ritual (such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*) are extended (*atidiśyante*) to all rituals (such as the *iṣṭi*, *paśubandha*, *yajña*, and *soma*), or rather, whether there is no extension of [the *dharma*s] from one [ritual] to all rituals—this [interpretation] is highly inappropriate.
Why? Because, although the logical reasoning (*nyāya*) is not contradicted in this interpretation of the text, [it is nonetheless incorrect].
However, one *grantha* (the passage beginning with "by one being set aside," etc. is not contradicted by the other (*saṃśaya-grantha*).

If this position—that all properties are extended to a single modification—is adopted, then this answer is appropriate: once a ritual action has been rendered free of expectancy by one injunction, there is no room for a second [injunction] (and not otherwise).

Now, it is described as follows: is there an extension (*atideśa*) of all ritual properties (*dharma*) into a single rite—meaning the extension of those properties which exist in all rites—or rather not? [If one asks] "Is it thus, or [is it that] the extension is from only one [rite] into a single rite? (Even so, this is not tenable). This position—that there is an extension of the properties of all rites—has been rejected [in the *vidhyanta-adhikaraṇa*, 7.1.1].

For in that regard—having raised the objection as to why both types of duties (both worldly and Vedic) do not proceed simultaneously—the position [that they do] has been refuted by the sūtra "Because of mutual contradiction" (7.1.6).
Once [the requirement] has been satisfied by one, the second does not proceed, due to a lack of evidence.
Therefore, this position—that there is an extension of all properties—is baseless.
(Thus has been stated this doubt raised by the commentator.
Therefore,) here the following doubt is appropriate: does the obligation to perform [the rite] apply directly to anyone whatsoever without restriction, or is there some restriction?
On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no restriction.
The latter, however, is indeed restricted (*niyatā*). (One specific duty proceeds;
he states the meaning of the Sūtra: "Now, the definition of the particular" (*atha viśeṣalakṣaṇam*)—the meaning is that [duty] proceeds as restricted from one [source].
(If one asks, "In what sense? he says: "Particular" (*viśeṣa*) refers to that which is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).
If it were to proceed without restriction, then it would not be unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
Alternatively, there is another meaning of the Sūtra:
"From the particular (*viśeṣa*), the specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) proceed"—this is established.

In that regard, [one might ask] "from which specific distinction [does this follow], and of which [is it the indicator]? To this he says: "That whose gender [is determined] by connection with the meaning.
However, no doubt should be entertained in this view. (In this view, the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) consisting of the first two sūtras is to be understood).

In the section concerning the *vidhvanta* (the end of the procedure) at 7.1.1, it was stated that in sacrifices such as the *saurya*, there exists a Vedic *itikartavyatā* (manner of performance) by means of an inferred scriptural statement.
Now, its specific details are being discussed: for which [sacrifice] does the *vidhvanta* apply, and where does it proceed?

Since the extended application (*atideśa*) in general has been established following the determination of the *soma*-sacrifice, the extended application in particular is now being determined; thus, there is a logical connection between these two chapters.
In the *Bhāṣya*, the sūtra is explained thus: "We shall state the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) within the context of the general extension (*sāmānyātideśa*).

In the *Vārttika*, however, accepting that the word *viśeṣa* means "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), it is explained in the sense that "only one single procedure (*itikartavyatā*) operates. [The question is raised:
"Are they extended from some [one] fixed ritual act, or from all?"
The first [position] follows because there is no distinction; the other is established as the meaning of the treatise.
Bhaṭṭa: Thus, the threefold *atideśa* (extended application) has been defined.
Among these, the investigation of *atideśa* through direct statement (*vacana*) and by name (*nāman*) has been conducted in its entirety.

Now, however, the investigation of *codanāliṅga-atideśa* (extended application by means of indicative marks in an injunction), which was defined in general terms, is commenced for the purpose of determining its specific archetypes (*prakṛti*).

In that regard, since a single [rite] such as the *saurya* is already free of expectancy by means of a single injunction alone, even when there is a conjunction with all types of injunctions, because there is no restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), there would be an indefinite extension (*atideśa*) of multiple [elements]; however, there is no extension from the *prāyaṇīya*.
The first section [of the Sūtra] is as follows:
"1.2. (This is the second section within the Bhāṣya: Oṃ. There is no extension [of application] for the purificatory rites of the *prāyaṇīya* sacrificial post."
It would be consecrated (saṃskṛta), because it is a word [referring to a sacrificial post].
The Commentary states: It is heard in the scripture regarding the set of eleven [posts] that "the upaśaya becomes a sacrificial post" (yūpa).

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this upaśaya already consecrated for its purpose, such that preparatory rites (saṃskāra) like smearing (jopaṇa) and so forth must be performed upon it here, or not?
What is appropriate? It should be consecrated.
The preparatory rites (saṃskāra), such as the *jopaṇa* and others, must be performed here.
Why? Because of the word "that" (*tat*).
This word "sacrificial post" (yūpa) is based on consecration; it is not applicable when the consecrations are absent.
Therefore, those [consecrations] must be performed. Alternatively, [the term is used] figuratively because it is not a remnant of the sacrifice, since it denotes secondary qualities (guṇas).
The Commentary (Bhāṣya): Or rather, they should not be performed. Why? Because they are not subsidiary to the sacrifice (*ayajñaśeṣatvāt*).

These purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are performed upon this piece of wood; through this means, they are connected with the act of sacrificing (*yajati*). When the sacrifice is performed with an animal that has been employed upon wood thus consecrated, it brings about the *apūrva* (the transcendental result).
Furthermore, since no animal is led to this place of rest, the consecrations performed there would be purposeless.
[Objection: But surely, by the force of the scriptural statement, they will serve some other purpose.
[Reply: It is said:

There is no statement here that "the sacrificial post (yūpa) must be made. This is a description of a present state. But surely even a description of a present state is not possible in the absence of preparatory rites (saṃskāras)?
It is said: it will be so by way of figurative application (*bhakti*), as in the case of "The sacrificial post is indeed the sacrificer.
He asks: "In that case, it was because of similarity; but how is it here? It is replied: [it is by way of figurative application].
Because they are designations of qualities;
that is, because they are designations of the qualities of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), namely the consecratory acts (*saṃskāra*) performed upon it.
These consecratory acts of the post—such as cutting and so forth—are indeed performed silently.
By them this is designated as a "sacrificial post" (*yūpa*), even though it is actually a cake (*apūpa*).
Just as a girl who has bathed is said to be "adorned," even if she is not yet adorned with garlands,
so too, by means of a single point of identity, that which is refined by the purificatory rites is designated as "refined" through figurative praise.

Śālikanātha: The statement, "The *upaśaya* becomes the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," is a restatement (*anuvāda*) where the *upaśaya* serves the same purpose [as the *yūpa*] and does not require further consecration (*saṃskāra*).

Therefore, certain worldly characteristics of the sacrificial post, such as cutting and so forth, are extended to the *upaśaya* by virtue of this scriptural injunction; for that reason, this is a figurative expression (*gauṇa-vāda*).
Soma: The connection [of this topic] is that it has been stated that the extension (*atideśa*) from a name denoting a consecration is possible in certain cases.
The *upaśaya* is a specific piece of wood that lies near (*upaśete*) to the south of all the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*); it is itself a sacrificial post.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word *yūpa* does not extend the ritual properties (*dharma*) [of the primary posts] to it.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: the substance of the *upaśaya*, having been consecrated, should be endowed with the consecrations denoted by the word *yūpa*, because the word expressing those consecrations is heard [in the text].
Regarding the question of whether the consecration (*saṃskāra*) applies to the *upaśaya* or not—the former view follows from the mention of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
It is not so, however, because there is no joining of the animal to it; its status as a post is due only to its being cut silently.
Bhaṭṭa: Having prescribed that "one piece of wood is to be placed near the eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*)", the scripture states, "The *upaśaya* becomes a post.

In that regard, even though there is no case of "transference by location" (*sthānāpatti*), one should extend the application of the term "post" and its attendant purificatory rites—such as smearing (*jopaṇa*) and so forth—to the *upaśaya* wood by means of the rule of "transference by name" (*nāmātideśa*), because [the word "post"] is based on those purificatory rites.

This being the case, since it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) if this [passage] were to enjoin ritual properties (*dharma*) either through secondary denotation (*gauṇī śakti*) or by its own power, and since it would be impossible for it to be an independent injunction because it forms a single syntactical unit with the praise of the *upaśaya* (the auxiliary post), this is merely a praise of the *upaśaya* through a secondary application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) based on its connection with certain properties such as cutting that are already established by the sense of the context; it is not an extension of names (*nāmātideśaka*). *Nyāyabindu*: "The statement 'the *upaśaya* becomes a sacrificial post (*yūpa*)' is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) based on [properties like] cutting and so forth, and not an extension [of the name]. This is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). *Maṇḍana*: "There is no ignorance regarding the sacrificial post in the *upaśaya*."
Śaṅkara says: "The praise is the sacrificial bedpost;
'Oṃ' is the extension, not that which is named the Prāyaṇīya."

The Commentary: Is this the general rule—that every name of a rite heard elsewhere is a grasper (appropriator) of the properties of that rite? Indeed, such is the prima facie position. This [sūtra] is commenced because that is the position reached. In the Gavāmayana, it is heard: "The Vaiśvānara Jyotiṣṭoma becomes the Prāyaṇīya day."

However, on the twelfth day there is the first day, named *prāyaṇīya*, as in the expression "the *prāyaṇīya* is an *atirātra*. The distinction between those two is established by that very same principle: "At the end of a context, the purpose is limited" (2.3.12). In that case, this word *prāyaṇīya*, even when occurring elsewhere, is not a selector (*grāhaka*) of ritual details (*dharma*s).
What then? This scriptural mention [of the name] is due to two qualities.
How so? It has been stated that the name [of the sacrifice] denotes the constituent elements (dharmas) through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
And since the primary meaning (śrutyartha) is absent, the extension (atideśa) based on secondary indication does not apply to the Prāyaṇīya [offering].
The extended application (atideśa) from the Prāyaṇīya [rite] is not to be accepted here;
rather, the literal meaning of the scriptural statement (śruti) itself is possible in this case.
The word has meaning only through its quality (*guṇa*). By means of that quality, which is a connection with an action, it is joined to that ritual act by direct denotation (*śruti*) itself—
as in "it is the *prāyaṇīya* because one sets out (*prayanti*) by means of this," or "it is the *pravartanīya* because one proceeds (*pravartate*) by means of this."

And because of the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). The Commentary says: "The supplementary statements also express this very same meaning: 'He places light itself in front. The meaning of the phrase 'he places light itself in front' is that by means of which [the sacrifice] becomes a *jyotiḥ-prāyaṇīya*, by that [means] light is performed in front."
Therefore, this is not an extended application (*atideśa*).
[The discussion] begins from the section of the previous topic (*pūrvādhikaraṇa-pāda*).
By that very same reasoning, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is established.

[From the Siddhānta: It is called *prāyaṇīya* by virtue of this etymological derivation (*yoga*): "that by which they set forth" (*prayanti*) [or begin]. This designation applies to the first day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), and this same etymology is indeed present on the first day of the *gavāyana* as well.

Therefore, since the primary application of the term is established through this etymological connection, there is no transfer of ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*) by means of secondary figurative usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*).

However, where the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice is the fifth or occurs five times, because of the absence of that [specific] connection (*yoga*), it is not an example [of the previous rule]. (In that case, by the logic of the preceding section, there is indeed an extension [*atideśa*].

Therefore, such a case does not fall under the scope of the previous section. [Śābarabhāṣya: When the extension has been established, it is stated: "By whatever cause the term *prāyaṇīya* is applied—namely, its being the first—that very [cause] exists for us even in the *Gavāyana* and other such sacrifices. Therefore, since the status of being a name is possible through the Vedic text (*śruti*) based on that established cause..."

The extension (*atideśa*) of properties by way of secondary application (*gauṇatva*) is not tenable. [This is] the connection as an exception (*apavāda*). It is called *prāyaṇīya* because one sets out (*prayanti*) or begins by means of it.

By virtue of the rule of frequent usage (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *anīyara* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). "Commencement" (*prāyaṇa*) means the beginning; that which occurs therein is called *prāyaṇīya*. Since the group beginning with *veṇuka* belongs to the class of *gaha*-type words, the suffix *chaṇ* is applied. Thus, being the first is the basis for the application of the term *prāyaṇīya*.

And since that [term] is common to both the *dvādaśāha* and the *āgrayaṇika*, it serves as a name in both cases; thus, it does not function as an extension of ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*) by way of being secondary (*gauṇa*).

Consequently, where the word *prāyaṇīya* occurs on the first or the fifth day, it is appropriate for it to extend ritual properties through secondary application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), because the primary ground for its usage—the state of being "first" (*prāthamya*)—is possible there.

On this basis, the statement made by Mādhava in his *Vedabhāṣya*—that the term *prāyaṇīya*, when applied to the second day of a twenty-four-day sacrifice according to the rule "the *prāyaṇīya* occurs on the twenty-fourth," is not subject to extended application (*anati-deśa*) because it possesses primacy (*mukhyatva*) relative to the month as a whole (despite the loss of its literal meaning)—is to be considered doubtful.

For the term *prāyaṇīya* has its primary sense (*mukhyatva*) only when denoting primacy among all [days]; however, if it denotes primacy only in relation to something specific like a month, it is merely secondary (*gauṇatva*).

And thus, since a figurative sense would involve a defect, it is more appropriate that the word functions as an extended application (*atideśa*) out of a desire to establish a ritual rule (*dharma-vidhi*).

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: in the *Gavāyana* sacrificial session, this scriptural mention—the term *prāyaṇīya*—should be taken as signifying a quality (*guṇārtha*), that is, in the sense of its etymological derivation from its parts; or rather, it serves to extend the ritual properties (*dharma*) from the first day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) to the first day of the *Gavāyana*.

"Extension by analogy (atideśa) follows the previous principle; it is not so in the case of the two primary ones. Since the day is equal for both, their primacy is equal and does not arise from extension by analogy."

Bhaṭṭa: In the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, having prescribed the first day, the *prāyaṇīya*, along with its specific characteristics, it is heard in the *gavāyana* sacrifice that "the *vaiśvānara-jyotiṣṭoma* becomes the *prāyaṇīya* day.
It has been determined in the *Kaustubha* under the section on *prakaraṇāntara* (2.3.1) that these are two distinct rites due to the absence of any decisive factor [for identifying them as one].
Therefore, here in the *gavāyana* as well, the term *prāyaṇīya* serves, by the same principle as before, to extend (*atideśa*) the characteristics of the *prāyaṇīya* belonging to the *dvādaśāha*.

Nor is there a redundancy in the transfer by name (*nāmātideśa*), because its application is not already established solely through the transfer by indicative mark of the injunction (*codanā-liṅgātideśa*). Even though the "going" (*gati*) is common [to both], the *dharmas* (ritual properties) of the *dvādaśāha* occurring within the *dvādaśāha* itself are not obtained through the transfer by indicative mark of the injunction; therefore, those *dharmas* are not applicable [by that means]. This being the position reached: the application [of the term] to the day belonging to the *dvādaśāha* occurs through the connection with the quality of the *Prāyaṇīya*, namely, by way of the etymological derivation of "post" (*yūpa*) as "that by which they first go" (*yena... prathamam yanti*); for that very same reason, it applies to the *Gavāyana* as well. Thus, due to the connection with "firstness," it is primary (*mukhya*) in both cases, and there is no evidence for it being secondary (*gauṇa*).

And here, unlike the case of the *dvādaśāha*, there is no extensive application (*pracuraprayoga*) such that, by that very reason, there would be no transfer of name (*nāmātideśa*) here in the term *prāyaṇīya*. However, as for the term *vaiśvānara*, because the attributes (*dharma*) of Vaiśvānara are taught within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is a name by the principle of "recognition" (*tatpratyayanyāya*); yet, since another distinct rite (*karmāntara*) designated as *vaiśvānara* is not established [elsewhere], it does not function as a transferer at all. On the other hand, the term *jyotiṣṭoma*, being a communicator of the attributes of the Jyotiṣṭoma, indeed functions as a transferer.

Therefore, when there is a conflict with that which is similar to this, because the methods of application are not identical, the rites of the second day and subsequent days of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice do not apply; rather, they belong to the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
However, by virtue of favoring the majority, those belonging to the *dvādaśāha* alone are common [to both].
Furthermore, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) must be understood as having been intended by the author of the Bhāṣya and others regarding the term *prāyaṇīya* on the first day of the *gavāyana* sacrifice.

However, it should be understood that when the term *prāyaṇīya* is applied even to the second twenty-fourth day of the *gavāyana* sacrifice in accordance with the *Chandogasūtra*, then there is an extension (*atideśa*) [of the ritual details]. *Mīmāṃsākośa*, p. 31;

*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the term *prāyaṇīya*, which belongs to the first day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it is argued that since it is used figuratively (*gauṇa*) for the first day of the *gavāmayana*, an extension [of its details] would follow. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because the word *prāyaṇīya* possesses the primary meaning (*śakta*) there as well—based on the reason of being "first"—there is no figurative usage, and thus no extension occurs.
Maṇḍana: "The term *prāyaṇīya* does not [apply] here. Śaṅkara: "But the word *prāyaṇīya* does not [apply];
it is a case of extended application (*atideśa*)."

There is no extension (*atideśa*) of the aggregate consisting of the fruit, the restriction, and the agent from the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice; for since that ritual action does not recur [in the modified sacrifice], the aggregate of fruit, restriction, and agent is not transferred elsewhere. Bhāṣya: In this context, the aggregate of fruit, restriction, and agent serves as the illustrative example.
The fruit is heaven;
the rule is lifelong repetition;
the agent is one who desires heaven.
The *darśapūrṇamāsa* is a composite [of rites].
In this regard, it is considered whether there is an application of the composite of the fruit, the subsidiary acts (*aṅga*), and the agent to the *saurya* and other sacrifices, or not.

What is the prima facie position? It is established that there is such an application, according to the principle stated in [Sūtra] 8.1.4.11: "There is an application of the *iṣṭi* to the *darśapūrṇamāsa*."
When this situation arises, it is said: there is no engagement of the collection of the fruit, the rite, and the agent.
Why? Because the rite does not engage, and because the fruit and so forth possess that [nature of being dependent on the rite].
First of all, the rite does not proceed.
What is the reason? Ritual duties proceed by means of the injunctional supplement (*vidhyanta*).
And the action is not enjoined by the injunctional supplement; rather, it is enjoined by the primary injunction (*vidhi*).
Therefore, it does not proceed [by way of the supplement].
Because that [agent] does not engage [in the action], there is no connection between the result and the collection of factors consisting of the agent; "non-engagement" is the meaning.
Why? Because it possesses that [nature].
To begin with, the result is heard in scripture as connected with the New and Full Moon sacrifices in the injunction: "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa."
Therefore, that [result] ought to exist where the New and Full Moon sacrifices exist;
and since those two do not exist in the Saurya and other such rites,
heaven likewise does not exist there.

Likewise, the restriction regarding the ritual action (*karman*)—namely, "One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives"—how could that exist in the absence of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*? Similarly, the agent (*kartṛ*) is bound by the ritual action, as in "One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*";

how could he also exist without those two? Furthermore, the collection (*samudāya*) of the *Āgneya* and other rites does not exist in the *Saurya* and other sacrifices; thus, how could that collection exist there? Therefore, there is no application of those [elements].

*Duṣa*: Because the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the *saurya* sacrifice is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), there is no application of another instrument, as that would be merely inferential (*ānumānika*).
When there is an expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the procedure is extended by analogy (*atidiśyate*). Furthermore, the fruit (*phala*) is not the procedure.

The lifelong restriction (*niyama*) is a duty of the performer; it is extended [to other rites] from the perspective of the person's purpose. However, the performer who is pervaded by the fruit is not extended.
Because that [performer] is primary in another context due to that specific aspect, he does not possess the fruit.
Furthermore, he who is the agent in the injunction "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) performs the ritual for the sake of the result;
this [agent] is obtained through extension (atideśa).
However, where many agents are heard [in the text], there the inferred [agent] is not extended.

Even where there is a single connection, there too it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) or an extension (*atideśa*). Therefore, because the purpose is not achieved, there is no extension of the agent, even though he is a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*).
The aggregate (*samudāya*) has been beneficial by delimiting the instrument; since that delimitation is absent here, it is not subject to extension.

And by one who grasps the collection [of rites], the Āgneya and other sacrifices must be performed; if they were performed in that manner, they would accomplish heaven, and in that case, there would be a contradiction with the fruit as it is heard in the scripture.
If it is argued: "One who grasps the collection will perform the Āgneya and others as a necessary concomitant, but not as a means for accomplishing the fruit," it is replied: [this is not so].
The aggregate of these [factors] is subordinate; and a subordinate element, when being drawn along, does not bring about the primary elements, because it does not have them as its purpose.
And even in the case of their activity, it is for the sake of that [primary].
(Bhāṣya: Moreover, the activity of the properties (*dharma*) is directed toward the action (*karman*), in order to assist the action.
Furthermore, the fruit and so forth do not assist the ritual action.
To begin with, the fruit assists the person, not the action;
for it has been stated: "And the fruit [belongs to the person], because it is for the sake of the person" (3.1.3.1).

Furthermore, the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is not a property of the action; it has been stated that "this is a property of the agent" (Sūtra 2.4.12), on account of its connection with the scriptural mention of agency.
Likewise, the agent who desires heaven is not for the sake of the action; rather, the action is for the sake of the one desiring heaven.

For the one desiring heaven is not enjoined to the action by the text "one desiring heaven should sacrifice"; what then? The action is enjoined to the one desiring heaven: "one desiring heaven should sacrifice, and should do nothing else."
Likewise, the collection [of subsidiaries] does not have action as its purpose; rather, it has the fruit as its purpose, as in: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
Thus, because these [subsidiaries] would provide no assistance to the action, their performance would be purposeless.
Therefore, they do not lead to engagement [in the primary action].
Because it is not heard [in the scripture].

Bhāṣya: Here it is objected—if, due to the connection with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa), there is no application of the results and so forth, then by the same logic, since the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and others are also connected to that [sacrifice], their non-application would follow; for they too are indeed connected to it. To this, it is replied:

Although those [details] are heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they are extended by means of the "archetype rule" (*vidhyanta*) to the Saurya and other sacrifices as well (8.1.2). However, the results and so forth are not extended by the archetype rule.
If there were a direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) impelling them, then they would proceed from that.
And that [text] does not exist.
Therefore, because it is not heard [in scripture], they do not apply.
Śā— "In that case, there is extension to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) due to its connection with the original sacrifice (prakṛti)."
When it is argued that the deity is [the deity of] the prayāja and other [fore-offerings], the following is stated in reply.
Because it is eternal by its very nature, there is nothing other than it, whether through modification or by extension;
it is perceived through the possibility of its manifestation.
*Soma*—the connection [of the topic] arises from the proposition that there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the fruit and other factors as well, just as with the constituent parts (*aṅga*).

The meaning of the *sūtra*, however, is: because the action (*karman*), which is the instrument (*karaṇa*), does not apply to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the fruit and other factors, whose relationship to it is fixed, do not apply either.
[The *vṛtti* states]: "The fruit, the restriction, the agent, and the assembly—these do not exist in the *saurya* [sacrifice], or rather, the former [do]."
And [the distinction] between the *prayāja* and so forth, based on the division between the beginning and end of the injunction (*vidhyādi-vidhyanta*).

Bhaṭṭa: Thus, when the specific archetype (*prakṛti*) has been determined, [it is seen that] the fruit, the necessity, the agent, the collection [of subsidiaries], and so forth, do not [belong] to those [ectypes] by virtue of the archetype itself, because their [status] is derived through extension (*atideśa*).
To explain: first of all, the fruit of the archetype is not extended [to the ectype] precisely because the archetype itself is not extended [as a whole].

Nor can the *prakṛti* (archetype) itself be extended [by *atideśa*], because the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) of the modification (*vikṛti*) has its requirements satisfied by the very act of producing that modification.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that once the injunction to perform the *bhāvanā*—characterized solely by the specific material and deity—is established in the *saurya* and other such sentences, the extension (*atideśa*) of the archetypal *bhāvanā* arises through similarity; and that consequently, the connection with the accessories of the archetype, such as the *prayāja* offerings, is logically established, just as in the case of the *prayāja*s themselves. This is not tenable.

Since the general inference (*anumiti-sāmānya*) establishes that even a sacrifice to a deity such as the Sun must necessarily be performed because it possesses force (*balavattva*), and since this necessity implies that even a sacrifice of a different class (*vijātīya-yāga*) would be subject to the injunction of the productive urge (*bhāvanā-vidhi*), there is no requirement for an injunction [of a specific sacrifice]. Consequently, because there is no expectancy for an instrument (*karaṇākāṅkṣā*), the application by extension (*atideśa*) is untenable.

Even so, since identity and difference are not established in that way—because it would involve the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating a distinction as in the case of the *Āgneya* sacrifice—the occurrence of the *Āgneya* does not follow. This is because the difference between various distinct types is established by the repeated hearing of the injunction, assisted by the absence of any decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*). Otherwise, if the *Saurya* and other sacrifices were to result in the *Āgneya*, there would be the undesirable consequence of confusion (*sāṃkarya*) among the *Saurya* and the rest. Therefore, since the *Saurya* and other sacrifices are obtained as distinct means of accomplishment (*karaṇa*), it is established that there is no extension (*atideśa*) of those [properties]. And consequently, because of that absence, there is no extension of the fruit produced by them.

Furthermore, even in the absence of those [auxiliaries], the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) has no expectation for a fruit, because its fruit—such as spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*) and so forth—is already self-sufficient. Even in cases such as the Viśvajit sacrifice where no fruit is explicitly heard, there is still no extension (*atideśa*) of that [fruit].

For that [extension] would have to occur either through the extension of the Āgneya sacrifice by means of the original form (*prakṛticchanda*), or otherwise? It cannot be the first, because by the single statement "the modification is to be performed like the archetype," there would be a dual inconsistency (*vairūpya*): on one hand, the prescription of auxiliaries with reference to the modification, and on the other, the prescription of the modification with reference to the fruit.

Even if one were to suspect that there is no inconsistency (*avairūpya*) because the original meter (*prakṛticchanda*), by being part of the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the injunction for the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), serves to enjoin the modified productive operation (*bhāvanā*) qualified by the three constituent parts (*aṅga*), nevertheless, the inconsistency remains as it was: the same original meter would have to serve as the provider of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) regarding the constituent parts, while simultaneously serving as the provider of the objective (*uddeśya*) regarding the result (*phala*). It is not the latter case [that applies], because when the postulation of a result is already possible through the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice (Jaiminisūtra 4.1.5) as presented by its own injunction, there is no evidence for postulating a transfer (*atideśa*).
Therefore, there is no transfer of the result.

The *niyama* (restriction) is the *nimitta* (condition). Because that [condition] is not required by the modified *bhāvanā*, there is no extension (*atideśa*). For the condition is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*), such that there would be an extension as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; this is because there is a lack of authoritative evidence [for such an extension].
Furthermore, because it lacks the status of being a causal factor (*kāraka*), it cannot be a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice].

Even if this were the case, if it were to belong to the archetype (*prakṛti*), then—just like the rule regarding the breaking [of a vessel]—the occasional rite (*naimittika*) would apply only to the ectype (*vikṛti*) when the occasion arises; consequently, it would follow that the archetype is permitted [to perform it], since those [rites] are performed as subsidiaries of the ectype. But this is not the case. In no way is there an extension (*atideśa*) of the occasion, nor of the occasional rite, to the ectype.

The agent (*kartṛ*) is the qualified performer (*adhikārī*); since he is also a subordinate element (*aṅga*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is no extension (*anatideśa*) of his qualifications, such as "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*) or "having established the sacred fires" (*āhitāgni*).

For this very reason, in the case of the *sthitāgnihotra* and similar rites, the status of having established the fires is not extended. However, because qualities such as "being a king" (*rājatva*) are qualifications of the agent, and because that [qualification] is a subordinate element in the archetype, its extension to the ectype (*vikṛti*) is indeed intended.

For that [kingship] is not a qualification of the *adhikāra* (the mandate) in the archetype; for on the view that the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is desired by the verbal injunction (*śābdavidhi*), it would follow that qualifications of the subject (*uddeśya*), such as kingship, are unintended (*avivakṣā*). In reality, however, because the term "one desiring self-sovereignty" (*svārājyakāma*) refers to the fruit due to being required first, it is untenable for it to refer to the qualified person; thus, the qualified person is established only through the implied injunction (*ārthikavidhi*). Consequently, since there is no possibility of a verbal [qualification] like kingship occurring therein, kingship and the like are merely qualifications of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇa*).

For this very reason, there is the assumption of a logical and implied qualification for those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and so forth within the injunction regarding eligibility.
However, the ritualists (*yājñika*), not accepting even the status of kingship and the like as a qualification for the injunction, maintain that there is no extension [of such attributes].
"Aggregate" refers to that which is accompanied by the *prayāja* offerings ending with the *āmīṣomīya*.

Although it is a constituent part (*aṅga*) in its own archetype (*prakṛti*), because it relates to the *Āgneyī* and other offerings belonging to another archetype, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of it into the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) in the absence of that [archetype].

*Nyāyabindu*: The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since heaven, lifelong performance, the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*), and the *Āgneyī* and other groups are primary (*pradhāna*), they are not constituents of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*); therefore, there is no extension into the modified sacrifice.
Maṇḍana: "Even the results (*phala*) and so forth are not non-extended here."

Śaṅkara: "There would be no extension [of properties] from the fruit and so forth. Om. There is no extension of the qualities of the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) into the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
Because they are dependent upon the auxiliary acts (*guṇakarma*), their application would occur [only there]."

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: Here, those desiring specific results (*guṇakāma*) serve as the examples, such as "One desiring cattle should perform the libation with a milking vessel" (*godohena praṇayet paśukāmasya*), and "O men, sing unto me; one desiring a village should employ this *pratipad* verse," and so forth.
In this regard, it is deliberated whether there is an application of these desires for results in modified rites (*vaikṛta*), or not.
Following that, the introduction is made by means of the aphorism (*sūtra*).
Activity would arise because of dependence upon qualities and desires;
[activity] belongs to those who desire qualities.
Why? Because of dependence.
The *godohana* vessel is dependent upon the act of fetching water (*praṇayana*), as expressed in the injunction, "One should fetch [water] with the *godohana*.
In that case, the act of fetching proceeds;
and when the substratum proceeds, that which depends upon it also proceeds.
Just as when a cloth is pulled, the painting supported by it is also pulled;

and just as a wooden ladle (*camasa*) is employed, and just as it is said, "One should make a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of *khadira* wood for one who desires vigor," so too does the milking vessel (*godohana*) come into operation.
And when the milking vessel is being employed, the desire supported by it is also entitled to be put into effect.

There is no extended application (*atideśa*) in the case of the *soma* sacrifice. There is no extended application in the *soma* sacrifice because they are complete in themselves; since they are self-sufficient (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*), they do not require an extended application.
This being the case, since [the sacrifice] is rendered complete by the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) and so forth, extension (*atideśa*) would not apply to [rites such as] the *Sāṃgrahaṇī*.

To this, they offer the following resolution: the subsidiary offerings are heard of as occurring in the midst of the archetypal *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings [in the injunction, "He offers these two oblations with the verses beginning 'āmanamasi āmanasya devāḥ'"]. Because they are explained by words connected to those [archetypal offerings]—that is, because they are mixed with them—they are also included as falling within the context of the "how-to" (*kathaṃbhāva*).
Therefore, extension does indeed apply.

[He refutes this response: If it were explained in this way, then in a case where an *apūrva* (an unprecedented ritual act) is heard that is unconnected with the archetypal (*prakṛta*) procedure, no extended application (*atideśa*) would occur because the requirement for further details would already be satisfied by that very act itself; yet this is not what is intended. [This much is written in the *Ḍuṣaṭīkā*.

As for the subsequent portion, we adopt the printed *Tantraratna*, having compared it with the *Ḍuṣaṭīkā*: He provides the solution: "Since, if the *apūrva* nature of the *soma* sacrifice were described in this manner—namely, as being an unprecedented act consisting merely of the constituent elements present in its proximity—an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result, therefore it is explained otherwise."

How so? (In response to this inquiry: Where [a procedure] is recited in proximity and is capable of satisfying the expectancy, there, because the expectancy is satisfied by that very [procedure], there is "entirety of prescription" (*kṛtsnavidhānatā*). But here (in the case of the *soma*), those things recited in proximity which assist are capable of satisfying the expectancy. However, in the case of the *upahoma*s and so forth, because they lack the form of assistance through proximity, there is no "entirety of prescription"; therefore, the expectancy is not removed there (and thus, the extension of the rule, *atideśa*, is not obstructed).

However, because there is no further requirement for expectation (*nairākāṅkṣyāt*), there is no extension (*atideśa*); thus, the final ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) is obtained [from the Soma sacrifice itself].

He states another argument: "Alternatively, the ritual procedure is restricted by way of similarity; however, there is no similarity between the Soma sacrifice and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, because the former lacks a deity and is therefore characterized by an unmanifest injunction (*avyaktacodana*)."

Objection: Is it not the case that in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*)—namely, "One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*)—there is no mention of a deity and thus it is an unmanifest injunction (*avyaktacodana*), whereas in the performance injunction (*prayogavākya*)—where deities such as Indra-Vāyu and others are mentioned through their presence in the context (*prakaraṇa*)—there is a manifest injunction (*vyaktacodana*)? Reply: It is said:
The mention of a deity occurs in the act of drawing the cup (*grahaṇa*), not in the sacrifice (*yajña*) itself.

By way of incidental implication (*prasaṅgāt*), they bring about the sacrifice, but there is no authoritative basis (*prāmāṇya*) for their being intended for that purpose (*tādarthya*) toward the sacrifice.

The deities are connected with the act of taking [the substance] through an inferred [textual basis]; they desire the sacrifice, and the sacrifice also desires the deities; thus, the connection between the two will arise by virtue of the sense (*arthāt*).
(How so? The sacrifice, while taking the substance, takes the deity residing therein.

Just as the act of fetching [water] is conceived as requiring a means that accomplishes its own purpose—[in the context of the *paśukāma* sacrifice, since the *camasa* cup is set aside]—it takes up the *godohana* vessel for the sake of the human goal [of obtaining cattle], even though this occurs by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).
In that case, just as there is a connection between these two [the fetching and the vessel] through the force of the sense (*artha*), so it is here as well.

Therefore, because of the absence of being for that purpose (i.e., the absence of being for the sake of the sacrifice), there is an absence of a deity (i.e., an absence of a deity specifically enjoined for the sake of the sacrifice, since the sacrifice is performed for its own sake).
If this were so, then it would be an "unmanifest" injunction (*avyaktacodana*)—the sense being that its "unmanifest" nature consists precisely in the absence of a deity for its own purpose.

Therefore, the author of the Sūtras says: "But in the case of the unmanifest [rites], however, there is Soma" (8.1.9.16). [Objection: Even so, since there is no mention of a deity in the *prayāja* formula "ulūkhalasutānām," it would follow that it is unmanifest; and consequently, Soma would be the deity for that sacrifice.
It is said:
because of the wording of the mantra, the deity there is explicitly enjoined by virtue of its being the substratum [of the action]; thus it is not an unmanifest injunction.
Therefore, due to the presence of such similarity, the Soma possesses the quality of being something previously unknown (*apūrva*).

"Completeness of injunction" (*kṛtsnavidhānatā*)—this is its meaning: when a collection of ritual elements (*dharmajāta*) is recited, because it is self-sufficient (*nirākāṅkṣatva*), it does not take up what is [otherwise] obtained by implication (namely, the *iṣṭi*-type ritual procedure). Furthermore, because the statement regarding the pouring of clarified butter onto the ladle (*sugabhidhāraṇa*) is a permanent restatement (*nityānuvāda*). The commentary states: "And because of the absence of the pouring of clarified butter onto the ladle, there is a restatement in the case of the Soma sacrifice."

"The gods, having made ghee their thunderbolt, struck Soma; the two ladles were their arms. Therefore, the Soma-oblation is not poured into the ladle, nor does one sprinkle Soma with clarified butter.
This is logical if the Soma sacrifice is an independent rite (*apūrva*).
However, if it were based on the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa-prakṛti*), it would have been sprinkled with clarified butter and offered by means of the ladle.
In this regard, that view is not tenable;
therefore, it must be an unprecedented injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*).
If it is argued that it is [merely] an injunction...

The Commentary says: If you think that because there is no mention of the *sug* (ladle) in the injunction, it is a new (*apūrva*) *soma* sacrifice seen as a distinct ritual, then why is this not an injunction that prohibits the pouring from the *sug*—which is already established by its being the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices? Once the initial proposition is established, he refutes it with the Sūtra:
"No, because it is a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣatvāt*)."
The Commentary states: This is not an injunction. Why? Because it is a supplementary part of a sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*).
Another [injunction] is already established here by means of a scriptural rule.
The statement, "When he says, 'O divine Soma, may you swell in the thumb,'" is the remainder of that [preceding] sentence.
How is this known? Because it is required by it.

"They have indeed cut off this Soma when they press it; when they make his two arms the *sruva* ladles; and when they have prepared the clarified butter (*ājya*); and when he says, 'O divine Soma, may you swell in the thumb.'"
There is no extension [of the rule] to the Soma sacrifice.
Regarding the *atidhṛti*: "That which they did not make into a yoke, that they cause to swell" (some manuscripts read: "that which was not made into a yoke for it, that they cause to swell").
If this were also an injunction, the sentence would be split;
therefore, it is not an injunction.
Moreover, one hesitates because [the object] is not hot.
The Commentary states: Someone raises an objection: "If one were to depart without having fasted, they would lead him about in this world with his neck bound.
Since the [rites] belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices exist, there ought to be a mandatory fasting;
therefore, a doubt regarding non-fasting is not appropriate.
If it were something previously unknown (*apūrva*), then prior to the injunction to fast, one might depart having either fasted or not fasted;
in that case, the doubt as to whether one should fast would be appropriate.
Therefore, it is something previously unknown.
The observation [of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings] would pertain to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices.

As for the statement in the Bhāṣya—that the observation of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, taught as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the passage "Its *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s are one hundred and one"—refers to those *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s which belong to the rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, which are subsidiary parts of the Soma sacrifice; that is a statement of their cumulative performance.
What is the reason? Because the Soma sacrifice is an original (*apūrva*) rite.
Because those [factors] do not exist there in such a quantity;
furthermore, it can be said that "it" (the sacrifice) is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of "that" (the sacrificial post),
just as in the expression "the sacrificial post of the Vājapeya."

Therefore, the *soma* sacrifice is an *apūrva* (an original rite). The connection [of this section] is as follows: it was stated previously that there is an extension (*atideśa*) by means of indicative mark (*liṅga*); here, however, even in the absence of an indicative mark, the possibility of extension through the mere occurrence [of similar elements] is raised and then refuted. Regarding this, the Prābhākaras have stated that, taking the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and the Soma sacrifices as examples, the status of being a primary archetype (*mūlaprakṛtitva*)—characterized by the presence of direct instruction (*upadeśa*), assistance (*upakāra*), and completion (*samāpti*)—is investigated.

That is not correct. Because the status of being a *mūlaprakṛti* (archetype) is unestablished—due to the absence of expectancy caused by the completeness of the group of *saṃnipātin* (directly contributing) elements, and because of the application of extension (*atideśa*) which characterizes the completion of the assistance provided by the *upadeśa* (primary injunction)—the purpose of this section (*adhikaraṇa*) would be lost.

Nor can it be argued that the cessation of expectancy for assistance arises from the group of *saṃnipātin* elements alone; rather, it arises from the *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly contributing) elements as well. Since there is no means of determining the extent of those [indirect elements], when the application of extension occurs, this section is necessary to establish the status of being a *mūlaprakṛti* in order to preclude such extension. Thus it must be said.

If that were the case, it would follow that even according to the final Siddhānta, the Agnihotra—which provides assistance from a distance—would lack the quality of being *nirākāṅkṣa* (free from expectancy).

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: since the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) pertaining to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices has been applied to the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, it should likewise apply to the Soma sacrifice. [The Vi-śeṣaṇa states: "Should the *iṣṭi*-procedure apply to the Soma, or not? It should apply; there shall be its application."
Because of the dependence on what is directly enjoined (*upadiṣṭa*), the final ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) here belongs to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). [Commentary:

Where there is a complete prescription (*kṛtsnavidhāna*) in the form of an injunction that includes the totality of auxiliary means (*sāmagrī*) such as substance and deity, as in the case of the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and Jyotiṣṭoma, there is no mutual extension of properties (*dharmātideśa*) between them. This is because their requirement for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) is satisfied solely by their own independently prescribed subsidiaries, and because even such similarity (*sādṛśya*) lacks the power to act as a restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*).

Regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma, however, the response to one who—based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of prescribing the number "one hundred" by way of restating the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings already obtained from the archetype (*prakṛti*) in the text "its [sacrifice] has one hundred *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s"—thinks that because the *dākṣika* duties have been applied to the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, the *dākṣika* ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) must also apply to the Soma sacrifice situated in their midst: [the response is] that since the *prayāja*s and others being performed in the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are connected to the Soma sacrifice through a traditional sequence, the use of the genitive pronoun "its" (*tasya*) in the restatement is justified, just as in the case of "the sacrificial post of the Vājapeya. Furthermore, because the reason of "being in operation" (*pravṛttatva*) is dependent upon a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*), it lacks probative force in its absence; therefore, there is no extended application (*atideśa*) to the Soma sacrifice.

For this very reason, the passage from the *Dākṣī-kāsādana*—"The gods, having made ghee their thunderbolt, struck Soma; the two ladles were their arms; therefore, the Soma-oblation is not placed upon the ladle, nor does one sprinkle it with ghee"—is not tenable [if taken as an independent injunction]. For this is not a prohibitory injunction (*paryudāsa-vidhi*), because it is a single syntactical unit with the injunction "O divine Soma, may you swell at the thumb and forefinger," and it is therefore impossible for it to be an independent injunction while serving as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for that injunction.

Furthermore, the injunction regarding the "burning" (upoṣaṇa)—namely, "If one were to depart without having burned [the altar], they would lead him away from this world as if he were devoid of prosperity; therefore, one should depart after having burned [the altar]"—is also consistent only if there is no extension (anatideśa). Otherwise, since that requirement would already be established through extension alone, the injunction would be redundant.
Therefore, there is no extension of anything whatsoever to the Soma sacrifice.

*Nyāyabindu*: Since the procedure (*kartavyatā*) has been demonstrated for the *iṣṭi* and *paśu* sacrifices, and because the *soma* sacrifice is present [as a distinct rite], the requirements of the *soma* are not fulfilled by those [procedures] belonging to others; for it is already satisfied by its own subsidiaries that provide immediate assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), such as the *abhiṣava* (pressing) and so forth. Thus, there is no application of those [procedures] to the *soma*. As for the statement, "It has one hundred and one *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s," this is due to its connection with the *dīkṣā-yajña* (initiatory sacrifice); such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Maṇḍana: "The *soma* sacrifice does not possess the properties of an *iṣṭi*."
‘There is no extension [of the rules] from the *iṣṭi* sacrifice to the *soma* sacrifice.
4. *Atidhṛti*: [The meters] have syllables in their quarters as follows: 12, 8, 12, 8; 8, 12, 8. Example: ‘sa hi śardho na mārtam’ (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.123.6). Bāla. pṛ. 66, Ke. (Kaiyaṭa).
The *atinicṛt* [meter] consists of twenty-five syllables; in the *atirātra* sacrifice, when there are twenty-one [verses], the *atinicṛt* is a *gāyatrī*.
There are seven, six, and seven syllables in its quarters. Example: "purutamaṃ puruṇā" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.4.129).

Vāla-pṛ. 66, Ke.: Since there is no evidence for the non-commencement (*anaārambha*) of the *atipātana* (transgression), the understanding of it as such is established through the non-performance or non-completion of the sacrifice.

Alternatively, even if it were a non-commencement, since the acquisition of materials is accepted as being outside the ritual procedure (*prayoga*), and because—just as in the case of the *bhūti*, the *vanaprathā*, and other offerings—it is accepted that [the transgression] occurs at every performance even when included within the procedure, there is no inconsistency in observing the *atipāta*.
Bhāṣya 4.1.2, p. 85: The *Atirātra* sacrifice occurs either at the beginning or at the end of the *Agnīṣṭoma*.
"Every *ahīna* sacrifice is followed by an *atirātra* on another day.
(Bhāṣya 8.1.6.31). A certain *atirātra* consists of a thousand [repetitions];
"one should sacrifice with the *atirātra* accomplished by a thousand."
10|6|1|3|137. The *atirātra* is an optional (*kāmya*) specific form (*saṃsthāviśeṣa*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
This is not to be performed before the *agniṣṭoma*;
in the *atirātra*, there are twenty-one [stomas], etc. (258). In the *atirātra*, the optional *stomas* are external...
And because of the existence [of the rule]:

once this section has established the application (*āgama*) by way of being common to both the *pavamāna* and other [stotras], then just as in the case of the conclusion of the Vaiśeṣika [section], the application is established for the *pavamānas* even when they are other than those [specific ones]; nevertheless, because of the demonstration of the underlying principle (*nyāya*), and because the application is restricted to the *pavamānas* alone despite being obtained through the force of the textual recitation (*pāṭha*), repetition (*abhyāsa*) is also established for the other stotras.
Therefore, this discussion concerns all stotras in general.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: When there is an increase in the *stoma*, the completion of the number should be achieved by the repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the original (*prākṛta*) *sāmans*, because there is no injunction for others, because of the proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) established by the extended application (*codaka*), because the number alone is enjoined as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), and because no other *sāman* is heard in the text. The *Vṛtti* states: "In the case of an increase in the *stoma*, is it by repetition or by addition (*āgama*)? The former [repetition] is correct, because that alternative is not heard in the text. Do not say so; rather, the number is attained through the indicative mark (*liṅga*)."

Therefore, there is an increase [of verses] through arrival.
