may it find delight in the lotus feet of Nṛhari, so that there may never again be a rebirth for me.

*Nyāyabindu*: The office of officiating at sacrifices (*ārtvijya*) belongs to all three castes because it is based on learning and so forth. The restriction stated in the *Smṛti*—that "officiating at sacrifices is for the Brāhmaṇa alone"—is for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*).
Thus, its transgression does not result in a deficiency of the ritual (*ṛtuvaiguṇya*).

This being the case, the traditional teaching of the author of the *Yajñasūtra*—beginning with "We shall explain the sacrifice" and concluding with "The officiating of Brahmins [is prescribed]"—establishes a restrictive rule solely for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*).
For this very reason, the *Rāmāyaṇa* states: "How could the fragrant gods partake of the sacrificial oblation of that outcaste whose priest is a Kṣatriya?"
Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that the *surās* are the deities (*devatā*) and the *ṛṣis* are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Since a deity is not an enjoyer, the intended significance lies solely in the qualities of the officiating priests.
Likewise, the statement, "In this way his *ājya* is destroyed, just as the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) [is destroyed]," also serves only to indicate a deficiency in the ritual (*ṛtvaiguṇya*).
Similarly, Vedic indicative marks (*liṅga*), such as "This *havis* belongs to the Brāhmaṇas," also establish the same.
Therefore, it is established that the office of the *ṛtvij* priest belongs to the Brāhmaṇas alone.
Maṇḍana: "The office of the *ārcijya* belongs to the *brāhmaṇa* alone.
Śaṅkara: "And that [office] belongs to us, the *vipras* alone.
That is the *ārcijya*.
According to our opinion:
there is authority over ritual acts even for one who has not contributed material goods.
[The sacrifice] is for those endowed with the three [requisites], because the performance of the ritual depends upon the availability of the materials.
Commentary: Regarding the Agnihotra and other such rites, there is a doubt as to whether one who lacks the materials has the entitlement or not.
It is said in reply:

Among the three [classes]—the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—one who possesses wealth is entitled [to perform the sacrifice], not one who lacks wealth. Why? Because one who lacks wealth is unable to carry out the ritual action associated with material substances.
Therefore, there is no entitlement for one who lacks wealth.
"But because it is non-material (anila), this would not be so; for [in this case] there is a connection with a substance.
Commentary: This would not be so—that which was stated, that "one who is non-material has no entitlement.
Why? Because it is non-material.
Wind is the conjunction with a non-substance;
it is the means by which one becomes possessed of a substance.
For one who is able to sacrifice, the word "one should sacrifice" (yajeta) serves as its designator.
The word "one should sacrifice" does not authorize one who is in no way able to accomplish the sacrifice;
however, it does not exclude one who is able to do so by some means or other. And thus, the connection with the sacrificial material will occur as a matter of course.
That one will live without wealth—this is a point of contradiction;
therefore, this is stated:
consequently, the connection with the substance arises from the sacrifice itself.
"Eligibility belongs even to one who lacks wealth.
(The *Ṭupṭīkā* states: "There is no such person as 'one lacking wealth' by virtue of his caste, on account of whom others might be eligible.
Therefore, since the possession of wealth is not fixed [as a requirement], all should be eligible."
Eligibility: with respect to ritual acts.

Eligibility: in the case of the Kulāyayajña, because of the acquisition of materials already obtained from persons and others, the performance of sacrifices does not necessitate the acquisition of wealth by one who lacks it.
Therefore, just as in the case of the learned, there is eligibility for the status of a substance (*dravyatā*).
This is not equal [to the other cases].

For knowledge (*vidyā*) is directly established for the three [classes]; thus, it is logical that the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*) are possible only at that time, and they do not imply the presence of pure [knowledge] in others.

(An objection: Even in the absence of another injunction, for one who possesses wealth acquired for the purpose of eating and so forth, that very wealth suffices for the accomplishment of the ritual sacrifice; therefore, there is no implication of the requirement of wealth for one who lacks it.
To this, he says: However, the acquisition of wealth must be implied as being for the sake of the purposes of wealth for all persons.
Since there is no distinction in that regard, its implication for the rituals is not precluded, just as it is for eating and other such activities.
This would indeed be the case if there were some authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the restriction that "only eating and so forth project the substance, not sacrifices.
For eating and the like merely project the substance because they are effects of the substance; that is all.
That being so, since a sacrifice also does not differ from eating and the like in being an effect of the substance, its projecting of the substance is unavoidable.

Nor does this entail that the rule regarding the acquisition of wealth must be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), because there is an absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the like, and because the acquisition of wealth is not invariably connected to the sacrifice. Therefore, even one who lacks wealth should acquire wealth and then perform the rite. As Viśvarūpa states: "Even if there is another [means] than wealth for the sacrifice, it is by means of wealth alone that the injunction is set in motion."
Another person is entitled [to perform the rite] by appropriating the material, just as the sacrifice [is performed by one who has the means].
There is a doubt: is only the owner—the possessor of wealth—the performer, or is another also? [The answer is:
because of the purpose; because of the necessity of the purpose.

Bhaṭṭa: Since even the substance for the Agnihotra and other rites is obtained precisely through the force of injunctions regarding means such as acceptance and so forth, eligibility [for the sacrifice] arises from a substance whose production is already established by the injunctions of the rite itself through implication; it does not belong to one who possesses an unestablished substance, because of the necessity to acquire that substance.

This being the position reached, [we reply]: since even the injunction regarding the means such as receiving gifts is an injunction of permission (*anujñāvidhi*), and because the possession of wealth has already been established (4.1.2, Section 3), it follows that wealth is not prompted by an independent injunction. Consequently, just as in the case of livelihood and other such modes, it is logical that the sacrifice itself implies the requirement of wealth; furthermore, since it has been established—on the principle that even receiving gifts is prompted by enjoyment—that the sacrifice serves the purpose of the ritual (*kratvarthatva*) (4.1.3.1), it is likewise logical that the sacrifice implies the need for wealth, just as it implies the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Therefore, even one who lacks wealth is indeed entitled [to perform the sacrifice] once he has acquired wealth.

*Nyāyabindu*: "In this very way, only those who possess established wealth (*siddhadravya*) have the entitlement [to perform sacrifices], because it would be cumbersome to imply the acquisition of wealth through the sacrifices themselves.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: Since the acquisition of wealth serves a purpose, it is not contradictory to assume that sacrifices also imply such acquisition, just like eating and other such activities.

However, there is a distinction: knowledge (*vidyā*) is not obtained through mere worldly desire (*rāga*), but is understood only as established by direct scriptural injunction (*pratyakṣavidhi*). Thus is the conclusion.
Topic:
Eligibility for the Kulāya sacrifice.
Maṇḍana states: "Even one who possesses no ritual wealth (adravya) is eligible."
Śaṅkara says: "In the case of a remedy for one who lacks the means.
The meaning is that even for one who initially lacks the means, once a remedy has been provided, eligibility (*adhikāra*) for performing sacrifices becomes possible.
Eligibility exists in the Kulāya sacrifice even for those of different ritual procedures (*kalpa*).

But from the statement, the combination of two [is established] for the *sāmādēśya* sacrifice; this is the view of Pāṇinīya. Bhāṣya: They recite this: "The King and the Purohita, desiring union (*sāyujya*), should sacrifice with this.
In that regard, there is a doubt: do two Purohitas of the King sacrifice, or the King and the Purohita?
What is obtained? That there are two domestic priests for the king.
Why? Because the dual number is heard after the word *purohita*; that [dual] is capable of expressing duality of the referent of that word, and the *purohita* is indeed the referent of that word.
Not by direct statement (*śruti*),
but by the word "purohita" (domestic priest), which—
by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and by expressing a simultaneous substratum— denotes that [king].

But surely, one person cannot have two domestic priests (*purohita*), for in the injunction "he chooses a domestic priest," the singular number is expressed by the case-ending of the word being enjoined. To this it is replied:
This will come about through scriptural authority;
for what indeed would scriptural authority not authorize?
For this very reason, there will be two.

Just as by the statement "he offers with joined palms" (*añjalinā juhoti*), there are two hands for a single person—even though [the hands] are not immediately joined together—this is established in the previous section: that those of non-different ritual procedures (*abhinnakalpa*) have the entitlement (*adhikāra*). This present section is intended to demonstrate that in the case of "the king and the domestic priest" (*rājapurohitau*), those of different ritual procedures have the entitlement.

Regarding the expression "rājapurohitau" (the king and the domestic priest), there is a doubt: is this a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* with *ekaśeṣa*, or a *tatpuruṣa* with the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) having undergone *ekaśeṣa*, or a *samānādhikaraṇa-ekaśeṣa*, or a *dvandva*?
Among these, it cannot first be an *ekaśeṣa* of a compound already formed, because the word "rājan" would then be rendered meaningless.

For that [result] belongs to the king alone; and it has been stated in the Bhāṣya itself that there is no co-referential *ekaśeṣa* with the final member when *ekaśeṣa* has already been applied— [the answer being] "no," because the king does not possess the office of domestic priest (*purohita*).
The established conclusion is that there should be a combination (dvandva).
Here, the qualification applies to those of different ritual codes (kalpa);
however, because of the absence of purpose, it would not be so.
Commentary: By the word "but" (tu), the position is reversed; it would not be so that there are two domestic priests (purohitas).
Why? Because of the absence of purpose.
This purpose does not exist: namely, that there should be two domestic priests.

For a single king, there is only one domestic priest (purohita). It is heard [in scripture] that he is to be accepted as such, in the statement: "he appoints a domestic priest. Thus, singularity is intended to be expressed.
But was it not said, "because of the scriptural statement"?
It is replied: this cannot be established by the scriptural statement alone, because the word *purohita* is based on a consecratory rite (*saṃskāra*).
Even if one were appointed, he would not be a *purohita*.
And because the purposes are distinct, there is a connection with what is heard therein.

Bhāṣya: Furthermore, a distinction among the purposes is heard: "The *tejaḥ-saṃstara* is for the Brāhmaṇa; the *vīrya-saṃstava* is for the Rājanya. By these two castes, a connection with that specific result is restated. Therefore, for this reason as well, there are not two domestic priests (*purohita*) for a single king.
Because the hand is perceived as a distinct entity, it is understood that there is no [inherent] connection [between them].
Bhāṣya: Now, as for what was said—that for this very reason one person has two hands—that is appropriate in that case, because the hand is perceived as a distinct entity.
The left hand is pledged as the counterpart to the right hand in the *añjali* gesture;
without it, the *añjali* does not come to be.
Indeed, an *añjali* is never formed by two right hands alone.
Therefore, there should be both a king and a domestic priest.
Now, one might object: "In that case, the king-priest and the king-priest—meaning two king-priests—should perform the sacrifice. To this it is replied:
They do not both desire union (*sāyujya*).
That king becomes one in purpose with the domestic priest (*purohita*), but the priest does not [become so] with another priest.

For both of them, even when acting as kings, are called "priests" (*purohita*), because they do not desire that [union]; for the priest is characterized by his consecratory materials (*saṃskāra-dravya*).
[Objection: But surely there is figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) in the case of the partisan of the devotees.
[Reply: It is said:
even by means of figurative indication, linguistic usage occurs in the absence of direct denotation (śruti), as in "The fire stands" or "The pit stands."
Therefore, "the king and the domestic priest" (*rājapurohitau*) refers to the king and the domestic priest.

Śabara: Here, in this *Kulāyayajña*, because of the scriptural statement, both the king and the domestic priest have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) even though they follow different ritual procedures (*bhinna-kalpa*).
Soma: The connection [of this section] is due to its being a refutation of what preceded.

Although the same ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is possible for both the king and the domestic priest (*purohita*) in rites such as the *prajāda*, nevertheless, because the ritual procedures for the Kṣatriya are frequently mentioned—such as "O preparer of the oblation, come! and "One should give him this portion"—and because a single uniform performance by both the Kṣatriya and his priest is extremely improbable, a distinct ritual procedure is unavoidable.
[Vi]: "The king and the priest, desiring union, should sacrifice with this;
or the two priests of the king, or the two kings, both desiring the name of 'king'."

Or there may be a *dvandva* compound of two [words], for the sake of establishing the equality of the two intended [meanings]. The second [alternative] is for the sake of establishing [the meaning], while the third is for the sake of making the king’s statement meaningful.
The fourth would occur through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), as the case-ending is reduced due to the specific wording.
The *tanūnapāt* and other deities are optionally combined (*vikalpyate*) because they are equal in status.

The *Bhāṭṭa* [commentary] states: "By this same principle, in the case of the injunction ‘The King and the Family Priest, desiring union, should sacrifice,’ there is no eligibility for those following different ritual manuals (*kalpa*).

This is because the *dvandva* compound expresses a simultaneous substratum (*yugapad-adhikaraṇa-vacana*), and thus there must be secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in both words; or even if that is not accepted, since the meaning of association (*sāhitya*) is required, secondary indication in both words is necessary."
Otherwise, it would be impossible for the deities and so forth to function as a collective whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).
Therefore, this is indeed a *tatpuruṣa* compound, and its essential nature is that of an *ekaśeṣa*.
Consequently, the dual ending of the compound expresses the duality of that very referent.

Therefore, the first position is that two domestic priests belonging to two different kings should perform the sacrifice with identical ritual procedures (*samānakalpa*). Another view holds that, because the dual number is understood as not intending to qualify the specific [kings]—as established in the *Sambhūyādhikaraṇa* (6.1.12)—there may be two priests for either one king or multiple kings.

Alternatively, having applied the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), the *tatpuruṣa* compound should be formed; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of repeating both words, which would lead to an inconsistency regarding the two instances of the word "king."
For this very reason, another [proponent] maintains that there are two priests for a single king.

[He argues: since there is no evidence for a secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) in the first member of the compound, and because the king is intended as a single entity due to his identity with the object to be chosen (*upādeyatādātmya*) in the injunction "he chooses a domestic priest" (*purohitaṃ vṛṇīte*), and because a single king cannot have two priests, this must be a *karmadhāraya* compound.

This being the position reached, [the author replies: since the office of domestic priest (*paurohitya*) is heard to belong to Brāhmaṇas alone, a *karmadhāraya* is untenable; therefore, this is indeed a *dvandva* compound.

Furthermore, there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in those two words, because simultaneous expression of location (*yugapaddhikaraṇavacanatva*) has been refuted [at 6.1.12]. Nor is there indication for the sake of conveying the notion of association (*sāhitya*), since that is established even by the fact that each word refers to its own respective referent; thus, there is no evidence for indication. The distinction, however, is that in the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), there is indication of the aggregate in both words for the purpose of connecting them with singularity.

In reality, however, even in the case of an *itaretara-dvandva* (mutual conjunction), since the perception of coexistence (*sāhitya*) occurs through the relation of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), its being inferential is untenable. Although that which is necessarily perceived must indeed be understood through indication (*lakṣaṇā*), nevertheless, because such indication is equally applicable to the *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) formation as well, it is necessary in all positions; thus, by the reasoning stated previously, the formation of the *dvandva* is established.
Consequently, there is entitlement for both the king and the domestic priest (*purohita*), even when they follow different ritual manuals (*bhinnakalpa*).

The domestic priest (*purohita*) also belongs to that very same king; for since the office of *purohita* is by nature connected [to a specific ruler], it is only possible for the king to be its counter-correlative. Otherwise, the fact that the fruit of this rite is union (*sāyujya*)—consisting in falling within the same kingdom in this world—would be inexplicable. Or, let it be granted that [the fruit] may belong to another as well. Furthermore, although there is no difference in ritual procedure (*kalpa*) regarding the *narāśaṃsa* mantra—since even for the *purohita*, provided he does not obstruct the king, it is possible for him to recite the *narāśaṃsa* mantra in exactly the same way, and thus eligibility arises for both such persons alike—nevertheless, there is indeed a difference in ritual procedure regarding the Soma and the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*). Regarding these two different procedures, there is indeed eligibility [for both].
Even in that case, there is no option (*vikalpa*).
Because the king is primary and serves as the cause, Soma is set aside by that which is caused by him.

*Nyāyabindu*: "By this [principle], it is understood from what is heard in the *ahīna* sacrifice (known as the *kulāya*)—'The King and the Purohita, desiring union, should sacrifice'—" that [the rule applies].

In this regard, because there is the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, because a single king cannot have two domestic priests (*purohita*), and because a *karmadhāraya* compound is impossible, this must be a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. Therefore, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is authority for both the king and the domestic priest who follow different ritual manuals (*bhinnakalpa*).
Maṇḍana: "The king, together with his domestic priest, should perform the sacrifice.
Śaṅkara: "It would not be so in the case of a nest;
it would not be of equal status in a nest."
Oṃ. Topic: Women also have the right to perform sacrifices. Aiśāyana maintains that [the rite] belongs to men because of the specification of the masculine gender.
Commentary: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices"—thus and so forth is what is recited in the sacred tradition.

In this regard, there is a doubt: was this word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) uttered with reference to a man who desires heaven, or is there no restriction, such that it applies to either a woman or a man? What is the prima facie view? Ātreya maintains that the masculine gender is intended. Why? Because of the specification of a particular gender.
The designation is made by means of a masculine qualification, as in: "One who desires heaven should sacrifice.
Therefore, it is stated that a male should sacrifice, not a female.

However—in the section on the non-restriction of eligibility (3.1.7)—it was stated that there is no intention to express the singularity denoted by the case-ending, but not [the absence of intention to express] the gender denoted by the nominal stem.

Therefore, this is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*): just as there is an intention regarding the object even when it is being pointed out, so too is there one regarding the indicative mark (*liṅga*) expressed by it.
And because of the statement of that [mark], the mention of the fault is understood in the case of what is not yet known.

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "When an embryo is killed while it is not yet known, there is a restatement of the murder of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*); therefore, when an embryo is killed while it is not yet known, the murder of a learned Brahmin occurs."

"Bhrūṇā is one who commits evil": he who destroys that which benefits both worlds is a *bhrūṇā*; a *bhrūṇā* is a destroyer of sacrifice, for he causes the destruction of the wealth that is the means of sacrifice.
Therefore, it designates food as "ornament" (*bhūṣaṇa*).
For he supports all, or he leads to prosperity (*bhūti*); thus, the *bhrūṇā* is the one who ruins the sacrifice.
Because it refers to a male, this restatement is appropriate;
for if an embryo that is not yet known [to be male] is killed, it might happen that a male is killed.
In that case, since one who is qualified for sacrifice has been killed, the destruction of the sacrifice would constitute the sin of foeticide (*bhrūṇahatyā*).
Otherwise, if both were entitled [to perform the rite], then the slaughter of the sacrifice would occur both when [the victim] is known and when it is unknown;
in that case, one would have to assume that the mention of "unknown" is non-essential (*atantra*).
Therefore, the case-ending expresses the masculine gender as intended [by the author].

Likewise, regarding the statement, "Having killed an Ātreyī, one becomes a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā)," they say that an Ātreyī is a woman who has conceived; for [the term] *bhrūṇa* refers to what is being destroyed within her womb (*kukṣi*).
From this also, the qualification of the male is understood.
Just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśumālabheta*), only a male animal is taken because of the specification of gender, so it should be understood here as well.

But Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] it is the genus (*jāti*) [that is intended], because there is no distinction; therefore, a woman also should be understood [as eligible], since the meaning of the genus is not differentiated.
The Commentary: This being the position reached, we reply.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous view.
It is not the case that the qualification belongs to the person alone.

But the Blessed Bādarāyaṇa considers that the word "jāti" (caste) is intended [in the sūtra]. He asks: Is this word "jāti," as used in the phrase "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), understood in its conventional sense? No, he says. How then? It is etymological (*yaugika*); it functions through its connection with the desire for heaven.

By which word, then, is the genus (jāti) expressed, by which it is understood that it is the subject under discussion? We do not say at all that the word here is the subject because it denotes a genus. What then? Both the female and the male are made the subject by the word *svargakāma* ("desiring heaven").
Therefore, the masculine gender is not intended [to be significant].
Why? Because there is no distinction.
For this case-ending (vibhakti) is not able to qualify the "one who desires heaven" by means of gender.
How so? Because it is heard as being merely indicative (lakṣaṇatvena).
The word indicates that very person who desires heaven;
by that indication, such a person is designated by the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).
And that [person] characterized by that indication exists both in the female and in the male.
Therefore, it is understood that both women and men are authorized by the word.
In that case, by what is the authorization of the woman revoked?
If you say "by the grammatical case-ending," that is not so.
Why? Because it expresses the masculine; therefore, [the feminine] remains even now in the case of the feminine suffix.
If it is argued that the repeated mention of the masculine by means of a case-ending is purposeless, we reply:
even if it is purposeless, there is no exclusion of the feminine.

In the case of an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā), there is the abandonment of its own meaning, the assumption of another meaning, and the contradiction of what has already been established. Yet it is not purposeless, because it serves the purpose of providing a specific instruction.
Therefore, a woman also should be understood [as entitled], because the meaning of the genus (jāti) is not differentiated.
This is because she is enjoined, according to the literal scriptural statement (yathāśruti).

The Commentary (Bhāṣya): Now, as for what was said—that "one should sacrifice an animal" (paśumālabheta), and thus a male animal is sacrificed due to the force of the masculine gender expression; likewise here too, by the force of the masculine gender expression in the word for sacrifice, a man is qualified—this must be refuted.
To this it is replied: here, gender is not heard as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the substance.
For if it were heard as a defining characteristic, then the sacrifice would be enjoined for a woman as well, and it could not be restricted by the masculine word.
This "animal-ness" (paśutva), however, is heard in scripture as a qualification of the sacrifice;
therein, the relationship is between animal-ness and the sacrifice, not between the substance and the sacrifice.
Just as animal-ness is connected to the sacrifice, so too are masculinity (puṃstva) and singularity (ekatva).
This sacrifice, characterized by numerous specific qualifications, is heard in the scripture;
it must be performed exactly as prescribed,
because it is enjoined as something to be undertaken.
As for the scriptural mention of a fault regarding an embryo that is not yet known, and the statement that "an Ātreyī woman is killed when she is joined with a male," that must be refuted.
To this it is said: the phrase "by an embryo that is not yet known" is a restatement (*anuvāda*); the mention of an "unknown embryo" is a mere indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Likewise, for the purpose of praising the lineage (*gotra*), there is the mention of the *ātreyī* as being exempt from slaughter; yet the *ātreyī* is not one who is pregnant, for this is a [specific] lineage. Indeed, this secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) has not been produced here from the word "atrin."
For a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) arises only from those things that possess functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Now, in this case, there is no such capacity in the *adāvasya* (the water-vessel).

However, it would belong to men because they are substances (*dravya*), as [the vessel] is connected with a substance; whereas for women, their "substance-ness" consists in buying and selling, since they share a common connection with substances.
Commentary: But for men there should be eligibility, because they possess property.
For men possess property, whereas women do not.
And this ritual action is connected with property, as in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with rice" and "one should sacrifice with barley."
How is it that women lack substantiality? Because of buying and selling.
For women are connected with buying and selling;
they are sold by the father and bought by the husband.
Furthermore, they have no ownership over their father’s property because it has been sold to them, nor over their husband’s property because it has been purchased from him.
Indeed, the sale [of daughters] is heard in the scripture: "He should give [a daughter] to one who has given [a gift], or to one who has accepted [it]; in the Ārṣa marriage, a pair of cattle.
And this cannot be for the purpose of mere salutation when there is a visible purpose; rather, it must be for the purpose of securing the bride-price (*śulka*).

Thus, women possess an equal status with respect to material goods. Furthermore, there is a scriptural indication of this in another passage. The Commentary states: "She who, having been purchased by her husband, then acts with others"—this demonstrates the state of being purchased.
In such a case, however, there is the purposefulness of the action.
The Bhāṣya says: "He says, 'Whatever wealth has been acquired by her through the sale of grain, through usury, or through spinning, with that she will sacrifice.
It is replied:
Even that [wealth] is not her own; for when she belongs to another, then whatever belongs to her belongs to him alone. Moreover, the master must have work performed by her.

It is not fitting for her to perform her own work after having abandoned that [property], for whatever is acquired by her through another means ought to belong to the husband alone. Thus the Smṛti declares: "The wife, the slave, and the son—all these are indeed without property."
"Whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong," because there is no distinction in their enthusiasm for the fruit [of the action].
Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that "the woman is without property," for she possesses the nature of a substance (dravyatva), because there is no difference in her zeal for the fruit [of the ritual].

On account of the authority of Smṛti, this [Smṛti injunction] must likewise apply even to one who desires the fruit. Because of a specific scriptural statement, one who desires the fruit should sacrifice.

If, while following the Smṛti, one were dependent on others and destitute of wealth such that one would not sacrifice when told "one should sacrifice," then in that case the Śruti would be sublated by the Smṛti.
And this is not reasonable;
therefore, being desirous of the fruit, one should disregard the Smṛti and perform the sacrifice after having acquired the substance.
This is because [the substance] is inherently connected with the purpose.
The Commentary: Furthermore, she possesses ownership over property.
Thus, at the time of the gift, a formal agreement is made: "She must not be transgressed in matters of duty (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), or pleasure (*kāma*).
As for what is said—that a wife and others are without property—that lack of property even with respect to wealth is indeed unjust, because it contradicts the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Therefore, its lack of independence is stated in this manner: it is a substance established through conventional usage (*saṃvyavahāra*).
The purchase is merely a ritual duty (*dharma*);
the Commentary states: "As for the fact that purchase is mentioned in the scripture, that is merely a ritual duty; it is not [actually] a purchase."
For purchase occurs between high and low-priced goods, whereas this gift is fixed at a hundred-to-one ratio regardless of whether the girl is beautiful or unattractive;
moreover, when she exists [as a person], they do not approve of sale, as it contradicts the revealed scripture (śruti).

Therefore, this is not a sale; it is seen even in the mantras. The Bhāṣya states: "The wife indeed has authority over the household goods (pāriṇahya); by means of the husband alone, she is made the mistress of the home."

Likewise, [the text says]: "They cause the wives to shake the *ajā* cow; for the wives are indeed the buttocks (*bhasat*), and by means of the buttock they thus appropriate the sovereignty of the houses of others.
Because she has been purchased, the ownership of the master is stated to be divided.
The Bhāṣya says: An answer is given based on what has been established. The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
This is not the case; she is purchased along with her property.
For she has been purchased, because the gift of the extensive sacrificial ground is ten times [the usual] value;
therefore, that which is called her ownership is spoken of figuratively (bhaktyā),
just as one says, "Pūrṇaka is the master of the oxen."
Thus,
in this way, the wife also has authority over the property of the household;
for, because she is the recipient of the fruit [of the ritual], she is connected [to it] by way of ownership.
The Commentary states: This is not so; the purchase is the price.
Ownership is secondary.
For she (the cow) is intended for the sake of the fruit [of the ritual], and that traditional rule is not accepted as being original.
It would be so in accordance with the Smṛti; it possesses its own [independent authority] in accordance with the Śruti;
and it demonstrates its possession of fruit.
Commentary: May the husband and wife go together by means of their good deed; may they become yoked as the two bearers of the sacrifice.
Being in harmony, may they drive away the enemies; may they attain undecaying light in heaven.
Thus, [the text] demonstrates the fruit for the couple.
Therefore, it is established that both are entitled [to the rite].
[Objection: "In that regard, because of the use of the masculine gender, entitlement belongs to the man alone."
The gender is intended to be expressive of number, because it serves the purpose of the base.

It is said: "The meaning of the nominal stem (*prakṛti*) is also a qualifier of that which is intended [as the recipient], because it is governed by the same principle as number; thus, it attains the status of being intended to be expressed (*vivakṣā*)."

Nor are they [women] without means of property (*adravyalambhāḥ*), since the acquisition of wealth is possible through activities such as spinning, through inheritance from fathers and others, and through partition of the estate;

because of the traditional rule, "In the absence of a son, the daughter [inherits]," and because property acquired by the wife is common to both, according to such scriptural statements as: "She must not be transgressed in matters of duty, wealth, and pleasure," and "From the time of taking her hand, there is joint status in ritual acts, as well as in the fruits of merit and in the possession of property."

The qualification of women is clearly established by the wording of mantras such as "ye yajñapatnī vardhān" (may the wives of the sacrificers prosper), because the word *patnī* (wife) denotes a person who is logically connected [to the sacrifice] through marriage. [Objection: Just as there is no qualification for a woman regarding the *kratu* (sacrifice) with respect to eating food and so forth, so too she has no qualification here; thus, the connection [of this objection] arises from the consideration of consumption (*pratyavasāna*). However, the meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: because of the injunctions regarding the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), the commencement of eating (*annārambha*), and so forth, which pertain to one who possesses property and purpose, there should be a single performance (*aikakarmya*) and a simultaneous application (*sadyaḥ-prayoga*).
"But—[it may be argued] that it [the universal] does not exist in the feminine, or else it does exist, because it is expressed by a masculine word;
therefore, since gender is the meaning of the base (prakṛti), it is intended to be expressed like number."
Because it has not reached the horses due to being untouched by them, the meaning [of the number] is derived from the similarity with the number itself;
however, the meaning of the case-ending, the verb, and so forth, does not arise from the *ākṛti* (the generic form).

Bhaṭṭa: In the inquiry whether the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu*) belongs to the male alone or to the female as well, [the conclusion is] that it belongs to the male alone because of the hearing of the masculine gender in the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*).

This is not a qualification of the person entitled (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), because since this is a qualification of the agent (*kartṛ*) within the context of entitlement, it is untenable for it to be a qualification of the entitled person not [already] heard [in the injunction]. Therefore, just like the singularity expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the intention to express the male gender here is also not untenable.

Furthermore, because she lacks property and other such means, a woman has no entitlement [to perform sacrifices]: "The wife, the son, and the slave—these three alone are declared to be without property.
Whatever they acquire belongs to him to whom they belong."
Because of such statements as:

"One should give [a maiden] to one who possesses a mind and a chariot; in the Āryā marriage, a pair of cattle," and because she has been sold by her father to the husband for a price, she is in a state of servitude.

For this very reason, the indicative mark (liṅga) found in the statement, "One who kills an embryo is a bhrūṇahan by killing an embryo that is not yet known," is appropriate because it refers to a woman designated by the term *bhūṣaṇā* who is a sacrificer (*yajñeyī*), based on the suspicion that she might kill a male embryo.

Otherwise, even if she were known to be a woman, since there would be no difference in her being a destroyer of the sacrifice (*yajñahantṛtva*), the word "not yet known" (*avijñāta*) would be meaningless.
Similarly, there is the indicative mark in the statement, "Having killed an *ātreyī*, one is a bhrūṇahan."
The daughter of Atri (Ātreyī) is pregnant;
therefore, only a male is authorized [to perform the rite].

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), although masculinity is a qualification of the agent, nevertheless, because the woman's entitlement is established by other means of knowledge, and in accordance with the requirements of the injunction, the mention of masculinity is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of grammatical correctness, as in the case of "A Brāhmaṇa in spring," and so forth.

In the present context, however, because it is not required [by the ritual action], this [masculinity] does not serve as a qualification of the agent; rather, by virtue of its suitability, it is indeed a qualification of the qualified person (*adhikārin*).
Consequently, since that [person] is primary even with respect to the fruit, there is a desire for its qualification as the objective (*uddeśya*).

In reality, however, because it is required first, the words such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) refer exclusively to the fruit; thus, there is no possibility of the exclusion of masculinity.

Nor is there a lack of ownership for the wife, because she can acquire property through activities such as spinning; because inheritance from the father and others is established by the Smṛti; because of the Smṛti statement, "She must not transgress [her duty] in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma," which shows that even what is acquired by the husband is common to both; because of the traditional teaching, "Indeed, these women obstruct the prosperity of other households with their private parts"; because of the wording of mantras such as, "May the husband and wife go together to the world of good deeds"; and because of the traditional teaching, "From the taking of the hand [in marriage], there is joint status in ritual acts as well as in the fruits of merit. Thus, the wife also has the right [to perform sacrifices].
This is because of the traditional rule (smṛti), "The [suffix] ṅīṣ occurs after [the word] *patnī* when used in connection with [the word] *yasya saṃyoge*" (Pāṇini 4.1.33);
furthermore, the word *patnī* would otherwise be untenable in the absence of ownership (*svāmitva*).

As for the statement "wife and son" and the statement regarding her being "purchased" (*krīta*), these refer to a lack of independence (*asvātantrya*), since their meaning is sublated by another scriptural statement: "A woman does not deserve independence."

As for the taking of a bride-price (*maulyādāna*), since it is stated later that there is an absence of anything exceeding the bride herself when the purpose is not seen (i.e., no visible benefit), that [taking of a price] is also merely figurative.

And *ātreyī* refers to one born of the *atri* lineage, not one who has conceived a fetus. Even though a woman has no entitlement to perform any ritual action whatsoever, in the absence of another indicative factor, she lacks entitlement to all Vedic rites such as *japa* and so forth; therefore, this is for the purpose of prescribing a specific penance regarding the male gender when the gender is unknown.
Therefore, it is established that women also have the right [to perform rituals].

*Nyāyabindu*: "In the expression 'one who desires heaven' (*svargakāmaḥ*), because masculinity is the meaning of the base word (*prakṛtyartha*), it is intended to be significant; thus, a woman has no right [to perform rituals].
"The wife, the son, and the slave—these three alone are remembered as being without property."
Thus, because it is mentioned [in the context of] "refuge" (saraṇa),

this being the case, even though it serves as the meaning of the base (prakṛti), the masculine gender is indeed not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), because it functions as a qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya*).
However, this is not the same as [the case of] number, because it is for the purpose of forming the feminine suffix (*ṅīp*).
Nor is there a lack of wealth, since [wealth] can be obtained from one's father and others, and because of such scriptural statements as "In matters of dharma and artha...
Furthermore, the word *patnī* (wife) is established through its connection with the sacrifice (*yajña*).
As for the statement "The wife and the son...", that refers to their lack of independence (*asvātantrya*).
Therefore, the established conclusion is that women possess the right [to perform rituals].
Maṇḍana [Miśra] states: "Women have no right here. Śaṅkara [Bhagavatpāda] states: "There should be eligibility for women as well."
The qualification: the Caturhotṛ-homa is for one who has not yet established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) alone.
The oblation that is a remainder of a sacrifice preceded by an *iṣṭi* should take place in consecrated fires, because it is not intended for the sake of the primary sacrifice (*apūrva*).

Commentary: Here, among the *caturhotṛ* formulas, it is recorded: "One desiring offspring should cause [him] to sacrifice with the *caturhotṛ*; having taken four portions of clarified butter, he should recite the *caturhotṛ*; he should offer the clarified butter held over the eastern half of the fire, and that over the northern half.
In this regard, there is a doubt: are such [offerings] to be made in fires consecrated by the *pavamāneṣṭi*s, or in unconsecrated fires?
Likewise, the investigation concerning other alternative positions will also be discussed below.

What, then, is the prima facie view? Such a homa, even if not a subsidiary of a sacrifice (*akratuśeṣa*), should take place in consecrated fires. Although the *darvihomas* are *apūrva* (having no prior archetype) and thus do not require any ritual details (*dharma*) from elsewhere, nevertheless, the *āhavanīya* and other fires do require the homas and so forth, according to such scriptural texts as: "When one offers in the *āhavanīya*, by that his desired [deity] becomes pleased."

Thus, because all *homa* offerings are preceded by the *iṣṭi*, it follows that those of this class must be performed in consecrated fires (*saṃskṛtāgni*). However, by the very mention of the term *iṣṭi*, [the author] indicates that the *caturhotṛ* offerings are to be performed in unconsecrated fires. The word "but" (*tu*) in the commentary reverses the previous position.
The Caturhotṛ oblations should take place in fires that have not been consecrated.

For thus the scripture indicates: "These, indeed, are the Iṣṭis of the Caturhotṛs for one who has not established the sacred fires. Since Iṣṭis are not prescribed for one who has not established the fires, these Caturhotṛs constitute his very Iṣṭi; thus it shows that such oblations belong specifically to one who has not established the fires.
Therefore, they would apply to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) things,
because the instruction is preceded by itself.
The commentary says: But surely, the indicative mark (liṅga) establishes [the rule]; therefore, the application must be stated. To this it is replied:
In that case, here there will be an injunction for all the remaining [rites], namely, "this is the rite for one who has not established the sacred fires."
In this way, the statement will be meaningful; otherwise, it would be a mere assertion devoid of purpose.
Furthermore, this [statement] possesses the capacity for injunction (*vidhi*).
Therefore, it is an injunction regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) elements.
It belongs to all, because there is no distinction.
The Commentary says: He replies, "This is understood to be an injunction.

As for the statement "of those not subsidiary to a sacrifice," therein [the injunction applies] to all the Caturhotṛ-homas, both those that are subsidiary to a sacrifice and those that are not subsidiary to a sacrifice.
Why? Because there is no distinction.
This rule is stated for the Caturhotṛ offerings; it is not a distinction between those that are remnants of a sacrifice (*ṛtuśeṣa*) and those that are not.
Therefore, it applies to all.
However, because there is no [specific] season [for the Caturhotṛ], the mention of "all" refers to those who have not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).
The Commentary states: "Or rather, there is the exclusion of the alternative:
this rule applies only to those [rites] that are not subsidiary to a sacrifice, not to those that are subsidiary to a sacrifice.
Why? Because for one who has not established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), there is an absence of [Vedic] sacrifices."
For there are no seasonal sacrifices for one who has not maintained the sacred fires; nor would a mere subsidiary part of a season, when performed independently, serve any purpose;
nor can another fruit be postulated for it, due to a lack of authoritative evidence.
For there is indeed another purpose for the statement;
nor does this [statement] establish the qualification for the Caturhotṛ [rites].
Topic: By means of the mention of the *caturhotṛ* formulas, it is possible to establish a sacrifice for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).
Therefore, this rule applies to those [acts] that are not subsidiary parts of a sacrifice.
"Or rather, it is a muttering (japa), because it is not employed with fire.
The Commentary states: By the word "or," the position is reversed.
Such oblations (homās) would not be performed upon unrefined grains.

Why? Because the *ādhāna* (the ritual of establishing the sacred fires) is subsidiary to all [sacrifices]. But is this statement—"This indeed belongs to one who has not established the fires"—an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding those [fires], and not applicable to all *caturhotṛ* formulas?
In this way, statements such as "When one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire" will also attain their purposeful significance.
However, because it is characterized as an *iṣṭi*, the recitation (*mantra*) should be a fire-oblation (*homa*), since for others there is no mention of its application without fire.

The Commentary states: As for what was said—that "this rite of one who has not established the sacred fires is equal to an *iṣṭi*"—and that "this statement refers to the silent recitations (*japa*)," that is not correct.
Why? Because this is not the intended formulation of the statement: "That which is this rite of one who has not established the sacred fires is equal to an *iṣṭi*."
What is the reason? A mere restatement based on similarity would be purposeless;

in the alternative view, however, the injunction is meaningful. Since this sacrifice belongs to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the reference is specifically to the *homa* offerings themselves, as they are characterized by that [status].
How so? [It is] called an *iṣṭi*; this is the oblation known as the *āsecanaka*.

As for what was stated—that "all oblations [are performed] on the Āhavanīya fire"—that is not said specifically with reference to the *caturhotṛ* [oblations] alone, but rather applies to oblations in general. Since that [rule] is impossible in the case of the *caturhotṛ* [oblations], it will apply to other [oblations].
And when the Caturhotṛ formulas are being recited for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there is no Āhavanīya fire.
For both [the sacrificer with and without fires], it is like the Pitṛyajña.
The Commentary states: "It is not the case that the Caturhotṛs belong only to one who has not established the fires."
For both [types of persons], they should be performed as in the case of the Pitṛyajña.
Just as the Pitṛyajña belongs to both one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and one who has not, so too do the Caturhotṛ-homas.

How is this known? This has already been explained: when there is the position of a restatement (*anuvāda*), then it applies to the *āhitāgni*; when there is the position of an injunction (*vidhi*), then it applies to the one who has not maintained the fires (*anāhitāgni*).
The expression is understood in both ways; and a meaning that is so understood cannot be denied. Therefore, the Caturhotṛ formulas belong to both.
Or rather, it is an instruction concerning one who has not established the sacred fires, because of its connection with the commencement [of the rite].

The Bhāṣya says: "And this is not the case that, as in the Pitṛyajña, the Caturhotṛ formulas would apply to both. Why? Because this is indeed an instruction specifically for one who has not established the sacred fires."

By the statement, "This sacrifice indeed belongs to one who has not established the sacred fires," the person qualified is indicated, not one who has established the fires, due to the force of that specific designation.
Furthermore, what is stated in the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is not contradicted in that very context.
It has already been stated that the statement, "When he offers in the Āhavanīya fire," is not spoken with reference to the Caturhotṛ [sacrifice] alone.
Therefore, such types of oblations belong only to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). Regarding the Pitṛyajña, there is a repetition of what was previously stated.

The Commentary says: "Now, as for what was said—that it is like the Pitṛyajña—it is appropriate in the case of the Pitṛyajña; for there, this statement is made again concerning one who maintains the sacred fires: 'It should be performed even by one who has not maintained the sacred fires.'"
"This [rite] is for one who has not maintained the sacred fires" (*anāhitāgni*)—by this, he makes it an optional addition (*anvācaya*) even for one who has not maintained the fires.
Here, however, there is no such statement;
rather, there is a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*): "This indeed is for one who has not maintained the fires."
The word "also" (api) does not occur here.
Therefore, this is not equal to the Pitṛyajña.
Śā— "Because the statement has its own specific purpose, there is no injunction for one who has not maintained the sacred fires."
Furthermore, those [mantras] intended for that purpose are enjoined as not going elsewhere;

thus, the qualification of one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*) applies to the *Soma* sacrifices, the *Caturhotṛ* offerings, and so forth. This is primarily explained here at the beginning of the section on qualification (*adhikārapāda*), which accounts for the immediate succession to the preceding section. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: like the *Darśahoma*, even the *Caturhotṛ-homa*, though independent (*apūrva*) and not a subsidiary of a sacrifice (*akratuśeṣa*), should take place in the consecrated fires.
Nor can it be argued that [the *āhavanīya*] is not obtained from any source because it is not obtained from the *prakṛti* (archetype), as to how it could then exist in consecrated fires;

for since the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) assists all *homa*s, and since all *homa*s are applicable to those maintaining the fires (*pacamāneṣu*), the *āhavanīya* is obtained as common to all *homa*s due to the general injunction, "One offers in the *āhavanīya*. As stated in the *Cintāmaṇi*: "The *homa* with the mantra called *caturhotṛ* belongs to both [the *anvāhāryapacana* and the *āhavanīya*] when there is fire."
The fire is pervaded by ritual procedure, because it is a *homa*, like a *kratu-homa*.
Because both serve the purpose of the human agent, the third [alternative] follows from the scriptural statement;
thus, for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), [the rite is performed] only in the worldly manner.
(Bhāṭṭa: There exist mantras designated as *caturhotṛ*, such as "The Earth is the Hotṛ."
[The duties] beginning with "the *caturhotṛ* [formulas]" and so forth have been prescribed by them for recitation (*japa*) and oblation (*homa*).

Among those, as for the ritual properties (*kratudharma*) which, though serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), are nonetheless situated within the performance of the sacrifice (*kratu*) due to scriptural injunction, there is no dispute at all regarding them.

Even those optional recitations (*japa*) that are separate [from the main ritual] are indeed beyond dispute, because they are common to both those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and those who have not.

As for such oblations (*homa*), their application is governed by the rule "he offers in the *āhavanīya* fire," which establishes the *āhavanīya* as the locus for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

Regarding the qualification: since the Darśapūrṇamāsa is prescribed [for those who have established the sacred fires], the entitlement for other oblations belongs solely to those who have maintained the fires (āhitāgni).

As for the statement occurring in proximity to the Caturhotṛ formulas—namely, "This indeed is [the sacrifice] for one who has not established the fires"—this is not inconsistent; for it refers to the recitation (japa) and so forth performed by one who has not established the fires, and by way of merely restating its similarity to an iṣṭi, it intends to convey that such recitation is equivalent to an iṣṭi.

If, however, because it cannot be an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*)—as it lacks the character of a prohibition and would otherwise be purposeless—and because a similarity to a sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) in the context of mere recitation (*japa*) is in any case untenable, one were to accept the meaning that "this sacrifice consisting of the *caturhotṛ-homa*, which is composed of renunciation (*tyāga*), belongs to one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*)" and thus regard it as an injunction (*vidhi*); even so, since there is no evidence for its purpose being an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of those who have maintained the fires, it possesses eligibility for both [classes of persons], just like the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*.

This being the position reached, since the direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*) prescribes the agency of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), that very fact—due to the principle of independence (*svātantrya-adhikaraṇa*)—precludes the application of the alternative rule (*kalpa-prāpti*). Consequently, because it is impossible for the act to have the *āhavanīya* fire as its locus, the restriction (*parisaṃkhyā*) would otherwise result; thus, the entitlement belongs exclusively to the *anāhitāgni*. However, in the case of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, there is a distinction: because of the statement "in this manner for one who has not maintained the fires," even the *anāhitāgni* is permitted, and thus both possess the entitlement.

Nyāyabindu: "One should employ the Caturhotṛ [formulas]" and "One desiring offspring should offer oblations with the four Hotṛ-formulas"—thus, recitations (japa) and oblations (homa) are prescribed by means of the mantras known as the Caturhotṛs.
Among these, the oblations are for one who has indeed established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) alone.
However, the statement "This, indeed, is the way for one who has not established the fires" refers to the matter of recitation.

When it is argued that the *iṣṭi* (sacrifice) seen [in the scripture] has a gross meaning only in relation to the *japa* (muttering), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that, for the sake of making the scriptural statement meaningful, the one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) is entitled [to perform it], because of the specific scriptural injunction.
Maṇḍana says: "The one entitled is indeed the *caturhotṛ* through the *eṇagiri*."
Śabara: "In the case of the *caturhotṛ* and other [mantras], the oblations (*homa*) are certainly not auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice.
Herein begins this first section (*adhikaraṇa*), consisting of a single sūtra."
"By means of four and so forth up to ten, it is the second [offering]," according to Śrīdhara and Karabhaṭṭa;
this is the section concerning the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites, where there is only one performer accompanied by his wife.
In the performance [of rites], there should be freedom of choice regarding the person, as it serves the purpose of the person.

(The reading in the Vārttika is "prayoge 'puruṣaśruteḥ"). The Bhāṣya states: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Here a doubt arises: should one, two, or many sacrifice without restriction, or should only one sacrifice?
But was it not stated in the third [book] that "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the agent" (3.7.18)?
When it belongs to the agent, then there is equality with the cognition, as we shall explain.
Here, however, that very point is relied upon and further determined.
What is established? One may perform the ritual according to one's desire.
Why? Because of the scriptural mention of the person;
the person is explicitly mentioned in the scripture.
Having enjoined the sacrifice with reference to the person, the word does not exclude the performance of the sacrifice by one, two, or many persons.
That person is not heard of in the injunction as "one who should accomplish the sacrifice" or "one who should accomplish the fruit by means of the sacrifice.
How then? It is: "One should obtain the fruit by means of the sacrifice."
Or rather, the person is not subordinate to the sacrifice or to the accomplishment of the fruit.

For if it were subordinate to either the sacrifice or the accomplishment of the fruit, then the number, being a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), would delimit the person according to that form. However, since the word "person" is heard as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) while manifesting what is subordinate, and not as a term expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*), the expression of number is not intended there.
Regarding as many people as are both desirous and capable, it is impossible to specify them all by means of a single statement.
And how is this [injunction] primarily concerned with the teacher? There is no purpose served by the production of the fruit, nor by the production of the sacrifice;
rather, the connection with the fruit is desired by everyone for themselves.
Therefore, the action must be performed for that purpose; otherwise, even if it were being enjoined, it would not be carried out,
and in that case, the scriptural injunction would be rendered meaningless.
Therefore, there should be freedom of choice; one, two, or many may perform the sacrifice.

And thus the scripture shows: "One should use the *pratipad* verse 'yuvaṃ hi svaḥ svargati' for two sacrificers," and likewise, "'ete asupramindavaḥ' for many sacrificers. Furthermore, the mention of "two" indicates that the sacrifice [can be performed] by two.
Dūpa: But surely, since it is being employed as that which effects the sacrifice, the number is intended; why, then, is there any doubt? It is said in reply:
because he is pervaded by the fruit, the agent is the primary element.
For one who is the primary element, the number is not unintended.
In that case, because it is not a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), it brings about the sacrifice;
when there is an intention to express its primary status (*pradhānatva*), the number is not intended to be significant.
Alternatively, the agent is enjoined (*upadiśyate*) or employed (*upādīyate*) by virtue of being the one who accomplishes the performance of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, the number [of sacrifices] is intended by the instruction. What is the prima facie view? That the number is not intended.
[This is because] there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the two words "one should sacrifice" and "desiring heaven."
The agent is pervaded by heaven;
and heaven, being that which is pervaded (along with its means), becomes the primary element.
Therefore, in this word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), [the desire] is not intended to be expressed.
Topic: The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, number 294.

(In this way,) even in the case of "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), if [the singular number] is indeed not intended to be significant, then grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established (because they both refer to the same object).

If it is accepted that the number intended to be expressed belongs only to the verb and not to the other word (*svargakāma*), then there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, [the agent] exerts effort for the purpose: "May I be pervaded by the fruit. (How, then, is the performance of the rite established? To this he says: In that case, if the other [word] does not perform [the action], then one performs the sacrifice for the sake of the thought: "I shall not obtain the fruit."
If this is so, since [the person] has not been restated, how could its number be intended in the performance (*prayoga*)?

[The Sūtra states: "Because the person is not heard in the performance" (*aprayoge apuruṣaśruteḥ*). The meaning is: because the person is heard in the performance (*prayoge puruṣasya śravaṇāt*). Alternatively, it means: because the person is heard in the performance; having caused the person to be heard in the performance, the word has fulfilled its purpose.

If the instruction were of such a form as "therefore, the sacrifice is to be performed," then the number would be intended [as significant] because it serves as a qualifier for the agent (due to its subordinate status).
However, no such instruction exists. If it is argued that the force of the direct Vedic statement applies to each individual object, [we reply: no.
[Objection: "If this is so"—if you think that [the fruit] would belong to another; [Response:

If the Blessed One says this, then it being so, if one who desires heaven were to desire heaven for another, and yet another person were to perform the sacrifice even though heaven is desired by another, then the previously stated principle—"The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer" (3.1.8)—would be overturned.

Ḍuṇḍa:—If the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven) applies without distinction to either another person or oneself, who desires heaven, then (even under the view that it is a restatement), one desiring heaven for another would also have to sacrifice.
(This is the printed reading;
in the manuscript, however, the entire passage beginning with "yaḥ svarge" is present, whereas the preceding portion is not. There is no connection with any other purpose.
Commentary: It is not that one who desires heaven for another should not sacrifice, nor is it that the word "desiring heaven" does not denote [the agent] for another.
What then? It means that he does not obtain the fruit.
But how is the attainment of the fruit [established]? From the specific indication of the grammatical suffix (upagraha) in the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice).

When it is stated, "In the spring, a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires," since that [injunction] is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) by virtue of enjoining the sacrifice alone through a desire-based scriptural rule (*kāmaśruti*), there is no intention to emphasize the singularity that qualifies its agent; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) was established that one, two, or many may be the performers.

That [result] would bear fruit because a heterogeneous human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*) has not been previously established and is therefore posited as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) in each respective instance; thus, it is logical to intend (*vivakṣā*) the agency (*kartṛtva*) that qualifies it. Even if that [agency] were intended in the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven), there is no obstacle to its being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, and so it was overlooked. Otherwise, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is formulated as follows:
even if the singularity conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is intended, there may still be multiple agents.

For that [agency] inheres in the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*), but not in its substratum; otherwise, it would be impossible for it to reside collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) in a husband and wife. Consequently, since the multiplicity of those who are its substrata must necessarily include the wives, there is no obstacle to performing the rite by including multiple men as well; such is the position reached. In response to this, we say: in the absence of any specific evidence (*pramāṇa*) to indicate otherwise, and because there is no reason to bypass the first [substratum], the cognition of only one [agent] is what is experienced. Thus, even though the substratum of that [agency] may be plural, when there is no means of perceiving a distinction, the perception of a single entity occurs due to the lack of a cause for skipping over the first.
For this very reason, in cases such as the injunctions regarding numbers, recitation, and words, there is entitlement for only one person.

In that regard, if the statement beginning with "and dharma" were established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and if it referred solely to the primary ritual action (*adhikārakarman*)—given the absence of evidence for the non-inclusion of even a slave-girl (*palī*)—then the inclusion of another person would not be possible.

However, where there exists a scriptural authority (*pramāṇa*) that includes the wife, even though she possesses the status of being the locus of agency (*kartṛtva-adhiṣṭhānatva*), the singular number [of the agent] refers to the person alone; for there is no reason to bypass the primary [meaning], and because, in the absence of a specific cause, it would be untenable for the singular number explicitly mentioned in such injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," "the sacrificer, the wife, and the son should sacrifice," and "the sacrificer [is girded] with a girdle," to be a merely optional restatement (*pākṣika-anuvāda*).
Therefore, the person alone is the qualified agent (*adhikārī*).

*Nyāyabindu*: In the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), because the singularity of that [desirer of heaven] who is the objective (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), one, two, or many may perform the sacrifice. Nor is the number conveyed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) a qualifier of the agent implied by the action, because the agent falls outside the scope of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) toward the fruit prior to the arrival of the fruit itself. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the efficient force is not already established even though the desire for the fruit is, the singularity intended to be significant belongs precisely to the agent implied by that [force].
For it is not determined by worldly convention that the fruit belongs only to one who has initiated the action;
therefore, the established conclusion is that there is only one agent.
Maṇḍana states: "In the Pañcayāga, the sacrificer is one."
Śaṅkara says: "The number of agents intended [to be expressed] is that of humans alone;
the qualification [of eligibility] belongs to humans in the sacrifice of the creators of the universe, because the word 'year' refers to days."

"We shall analyze [the compound] as *śatāny āyuṣvaḥ*"; when this was said, the reply given in the Bhāṣya is: "A compound of numeral words (*saṃkhyā-śabda*) in this manner is not desired. Its meaning is: a compound is not desired with those two numeral words that end in the dual or plural numbers. By what reasoning? Because there is no evidence for the existence of numeral words ending in the dual or plural.

When the term *rājapuruṣa* is uttered, neither a dual nor a plural suffix is heard following the word *rājan*. [Objection: But even in the case of singularity, there is no evidence; how then can there be a dissolution (*vigraha*)? It is said in reply:
Singularity is with respect to the genus (*jāti*), while gender is dependent on what is not already established by the sense of the object.
Therefore, the analytical resolution (*vigraha*) occurs with a word ending in the singular number and endowed with any one of the genders;

for example, *citraguḥ* [is resolved as] *yasya citrā gāvaḥ*. When the resolution is made with a plural ending, the traditional rule of usage (*prayogasmṛti*) is the authority, because of the traditional teaching: "The suffixes *matup* and others [are applied] after words such as *bhūman*."

Since the possessive suffix *matup* is used to express abundance (*bhūman*), and the *bahuvrīhi* compound is indeed employed for that purpose, it is the *bahuvrīhi* itself that conveys the sense of abundance; thus, an analysis using the plural number is appropriate.
[This is] because such a result is not observed from a mere year’s use of elixirs (*rasāyana*). Commentary: Indeed, no connection with elixirs has ever been seen to produce such a lifespan.
Furthermore, there is no inference based on the observation of a [specific] relationship.
But surely it will be an inference from general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
For indeed, causes for a small degree of stability are observed.
When practiced in this manner, these most vigorous [exercises] will produce a firmness of the body;
for even though there is the saying that "man has a lifespan of a hundred years," it is indeed observed that one lives longer than that.
To this, it is said:
This is not an absolute rule.

Sometimes they may produce a certain degree and extent of bodily steadiness, but not for a very long time. Just as those who are practicing running attain a certain degree and extent of proficiency in their strides through practice, yet while practicing they cannot cover a distance of a *yojana* by means of human foot-steps alone.
Likewise here too, because there is no [logical] connection, it remains doubtful whether they would attain a lifespan of a thousand years or not.
And if something is doubtful, inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, an unperceived object cannot be accepted on the basis of any other means of knowledge.
Therefore, there is no doubt that there are those with such a lifespan.
And it is stated in the *Puruṣasūkta*:
"He would be the founder of a lineage," so says Kārṣṇājini, because [the birth of] many is possible from one.

Commentary: How then? The teacher Kārṣṇājini held the view that, under the position that human beings alone possess the qualification [for Vedic study], this will be a "family tradition" (kulakalpa). Why? Because [the injunction] is impossible in the case of a single person;
this is an instruction intended for men.
And one person alone is not able to complete this;
since it must be completed in such a way as is possible, many who are capable would engage in it,
so that others of that same lineage might also finish what has been begun by another.
If there were a connection with the whole [of the ritual], the performance would belong to one person alone.
The Bhāṣya states: "For it has been established that the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer.
And only he who is capable of carrying out the injunction in its entirety is entitled [to perform it]."
Therefore, the practice restricted to a specific family lineage (*kulakalpa*) is not tenable.
How then [is dharma determined]? It is concluded that dharma is established by the mere existence of a traditional transmission (*saṃpradāya*).
Thus it is heard in scripture: "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied."
If that were so, then this might be accepted on the authority of the scriptural statement that "for those performing this rite, life-span increases.
But that is not the case, because there is a lack of valid evidence;
for there is no other authoritative statement regarding this matter.
[Objection: But surely there is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), for otherwise there would be meaninglessness. [Reply: It is said: there is no meaninglessness.

For the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) will indeed result from the study itself; for it is simpler to postulate an unseen merit in a general sense than to postulate a specific unseen merit based on the particularity that "life is increased by ritual action.
Alternatively, one might as well accept the total meaninglessness [of the injunction], rather than postulating a fruit that lacks logical justification.
Now, it might be argued that three additional cognitions are initiated, so that [the sacrifice] is completed with four breaths.
Even so, the fixed measure is lost, as stated in the injunction: "Those who perform the sacrificial session (*satra*) should consist of no more than twenty-four and have seventeen spokes.
If it is argued that the measure will be set aside in order to avoid the redundancy of the scriptural statement, that is not tenable.
Because there is a fruit resulting from study, the assumption [of a reward] follows from that very fact. However,
Lāṭukāyana maintains that because of the contradiction [in the case of the *svādhyāya* injunction], one of the two must be subordinate (*guṇya*).
Commentary: How then? It must be thus: in this case, one of the two terms would have to be figurative (gauṇa).

Either the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) is used figuratively for what is not a year, or the word "fifty-five" (*pañcapañcāśataḥ*) is figurative. Why is this so? Because of contradiction; for a contradiction arises when both [meanings] are prescribed simultaneously.
How so? For the sentence would be split. If there are fifty-five *trivṛt*s, they are not years; if they are years, they are not fifty-five *trivṛt*s.
Therefore, due to this contradiction, the teacher Lāḍukāyana considered that one or the other statement must be figurative.
The mention of the Teacher (Ācārya) is for the sake of honor; it is not for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of the Āmīyas.
Saṃvatsara deliberated. The Commentary states: "It was said that one of these two statements is secondary (gauṇa); that has now been deliberated."
It is said that the expression "year" is figurative.
Why? Because it has been investigated;
for the word "year" is indeed subject to investigation.

Even the *sāvana* day, even that characterized by cold and heat, and even the lunar [day]—such a definition could be imagined as a restatement (*anuvāda*). However, this term "fifty-five" denotes a specific measure of quantity; it does not apply even when diminished by one.
The *māna* (measure) would be the archetype (*prakṛti*) because of its governing context (*adhikāra*). The *Bhāṣya* states: "Other months are the archetypes.
Regarding the months, the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) has not been mentioned [in the primary injunction]; rather, it is said: "That which is a month is a year."

Therefore, [the duration] is fifty-five months (i.e., 83 years and four and a half months). Now, it may be objected that under this view, the term "thousand-year sacrifice" (*sahasrasaṃvatsara*) would not be appropriate.
It is replied: this term "thousand-year sacrifice" is a mere name; it is not an injunction regarding a specific quality (*guṇavidhi*).
And the name is not prescribed;
and that which is not prescribed is understood through some quality or other,
yet even in that case, the genitive case is not appropriate.
For here too, that same fault remains:
there is no living for as long as it would be possible to assume this [study] in view of the wife, the fire, and the Soma sacrifice.
Therefore, while this [study] is being performed, his life would be exhausted even before it is completed; and thus, it would be assumed that he dies simply from the act of studying.
In that case, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is the archetype; thus, there will be fifty-five twelve-day sacrifices.
And so it is seen [in scripture]: "The twelve [months] are indeed the counterpart of the year.
In that regard, that fault will not occur.
It is not so;
for in that case, the word "year" is directly connected with the word "image.
Moreover, it has been stated: "consisting of fifty-five [parts]."
And the word "triṣṭubh" is seen on the twelfth day [of the sacrifice], not on the twelve-day period itself;
therefore, it is dissimilar. Or rather, [the rule applies] to the day, because it is a specific enumeration.
The Commentary: The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position.
