It is not the case that fifty-five [verses] are multiplied by twelve;
rather, it is the days themselves that are designated by the term "thirty-three."
Therefore, the word "year" refers to days.
Alternatively, it excludes another interpretation:
there are not fifty-five months, but rather days.
In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), the *trivṛt* day is the archetype (*prakṛta*).
Therein the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) is seen:
"The sun, indeed, is the all-consumer; when it rises, then it is spring; when it has set, then..."

"When it is forenoon, that is summer; when it is afternoon, that is the rainy season; when it is evening, that is autumn; and when it sets, that is winter and the cool season"—thus he brings all the seasons into the day.
And all the seasons are the year. Therefore, the day is designated by the word "year."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "fifty-five threefold [stomas]," this refers to fifty-five threefold stomas;
it does not refer to the twelve-night sacrifice,
for there is only one threefold day within the twelve-day rite.
In that case, there is no grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the number three and the twelve nights in their primary sense;
for the "threefold day" (*trivṛdahaḥ*) is characterized by the year. The "threefold day" is a collective enumeration.
Therefore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on direct statement (*śruti*) alone;
and direct statement is more authoritative than figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Consequently, the year would consist of fifty-five days.

(Now, there is a passage from the Bhāṣya which takes the form of an alternative explanation of the Sūtra, as seen in the manuscript: [this is the Bhāṣya-tippanī]. And it is as follows: The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the previous position. Nor is it the case that the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) applies to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
What then? [It applies] to the days. Why? Because of the scriptural indication: "The year is like a day," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Is it not the case that the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) is used in the context of the twelve-day sacrifice?
No, for the word "year" is certainly not used there;
rather, it is used because of its direct connection with the word "image" (*pratimā*).
"During the day there are fifty-five *trivṛt*s"—thus they are designated by the word *trivṛt*.
It is not the year [that is so designated].
Therefore, the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) is used in reference to the days.
Śā [Bhāskara]: It is stated that the *trivṛt* and so forth are the *mahaḥ* (great) characterized by specific *stomas*.
Since the term *ahaḥ* (day) is applied to the days [of the sacrificial session] (*ahargaṇa*), the presence of the year (*saṃvatsara*) is figurative.

Soma: Although there was no restrictive rule in the previous case—that only the choosing (*varaṇa*) and protecting (*trāṇa*) [are meant]—here there is a restrictive rule regarding the jurisdiction of the Gandharvas; thus, because of this counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*), there is a connection (*saṅgati*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: "A sacrificial session (*satra*) lasting a thousand years might exist among the Gandharvas, who, like humans, possess a lifespan of a thousand years. Viṣṇu Purāṇa states: "There is indeed a sacrificial session of a thousand years for the Gandharvas; furthermore, there is mention of a family-based ritual system (*kulakalpa*) for those perfected through elixirs (*rasāyana*)."
Then, even for those with a lifespan of two hundred and fifty months, there may be a reduction of years, fortnights,
or days;
this first [category] occurs only when long-lived beings among humans come into existence.
Let the second [meaning] be the cause of longevity for this [word]; let the third be the agent of contempt; let the fourth be the result when the sense is possible;
and let the fifth be so if there are twenty-four excellent *sattrins*.
"Let this sixth month be that which has declared the year;
let there be a thousand months, for they have not established [the year] otherwise; let there be reverence! The twelve nights are the image of the year."
Because of the Vedic text. Here, the term "six nights" is not a qualifier of the image;
rather, the eighth alternative is intended as the threefold (*trivṛt*) and so forth, which are the positions of one's own [sacrificial] days.

The term "mahā" refers to a day characterized by specific *stomas*, such as the *trivṛt* and others; it is not a literal day. Consequently, the nature of the year is applied to these days only figuratively.
Therefore, the entire thousand-day period is intended to be comprised of these [symbolic] days.

Commentary: It is heard in scripture: "Fifty-five threefold [days], fifty-five fifteenfold [days], fifty-five seventeenfold [days], fifty-five twenty-onefold [days]—this is the thousand-year sacrifice of the creators of the universe.
In this context, the word "fifty-five" (pañcapañcāśat) refers exclusively to a number.

However, the words "threefold" (trivṛt) and "year" (saṃvatsara) function through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) to denote that which is accomplished by the threefold hymn-form (trivṛt-stoma) and the year.
The word "fifty" is also a qualifier of the word "sound.

Therefore, the meaning realized at the time of the syntactic connection with the word *pārthika* (earthly) is that there are fifty instances delimited by the five characteristics occurring within such a produced [sound], which amounts to the number one hundred and fifty (150).

Although this [sacrifice] consisting of the *trivṛt* and other *stomas* cannot indeed be performed directly [by humans], nevertheless, because it possesses such a nature [of being a year-long cycle], it is possible even within a year; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
In that context, the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) denotes the year itself through its primary sense.

Consequently, since humans lack a lifespan of a thousand years, the eligibility for this [sacrifice] belongs only to Gandharvas and others—just as in the case of the Vedic texts—even though [the possibility of such a long life] was refuted in the section concerning animals (*tiryañc-adhikaraṇa*, 6.1.2).

However, because of the commonality of employing elixirs such as fire (*agnyādi*) and so forth, that [longevity] belongs only to humans who possess a lifespan of thousands of years through the use of elixirs;

for there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the capacity of elixirs and the like to produce such a lifespan, and because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "A person indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years. Thus, it is either the case that what was begun by one individual is completed through the lineage of sons and descendants, which is known as the *kulakalpa* (family tradition).

Because there is no evidence for an exception to the maxim "the fruit of the scripture has been declared" (3.1.8) without an explicit statement; because if all [five] were performers, the performance would be incomplete, leading to the undesirable consequence that the fruit could not arise; and because one must either assume that a lifespan of a thousand years arises from the very commencement of the sacrifice—or, since there is no evidence even for such an assumption, the number "fifty-five" refers to the sacrificers.

Therefore, even a single year consisting of the *trivṛt-stoma* is figuratively designated as "the state of being a year" (*saṃvatsaratvam*) by fifty-five sacrificers who share the same world (*sālokya*), because its duration is exactly that long.

Consequently, there is another view that this sacrificial session (*satra*) should be performed every year by two hundred and fifty sacrificers. However, this too is utterly contrary to one's desire; furthermore, it is untenable because it would result in the sublation of the prescribed measure, namely, "twenty-eight [years] for twenty-four persons."
Therefore, the qualification of human beings must be established by relying solely on the figurative sense of either the word for "number" or the word for "year.
Even in that case, since the two words for "number" are primary and possess the capacity to determine a single meaning, there is no abandonment of their own literal sense.

However, because the term *saṃvatsara* (year) is subordinate and because it is manifold due to distinctions such as solar (*saura*) and lunar (*cāndra*), it lacks the capacity to determine the specific meaning; thus, it is used figuratively (*gauṇa*).
In this regard, one view is that since we observe the statement "that which is a month is a year," the word *saṃvatsara* refers only to months.
Yet, even in that case, the application [of the term] would be entirely without purpose.
Indeed, life is not possible for more than a thousand months (eighty-three years and four months) after the *ādhāna* ceremony.
Therefore, based on the usage "the twelve nights are indeed the image (*pratimā*) of the year," another view holds that [the sacrifice] takes place during the twelve nights.
However, in this context, the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) is a qualification of the word "image" (*pratimā*); it is not the word "year" itself that is applied to the twelve nights.
Therefore, in the mantras for the twelve-day sacrifice beginning with the *trivṛt*, the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) refers to the days.

For even though the words such as *trivṛt* primarily denote only the *stoma* (the specific chant), it is the day itself that is indicated by them through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), being qualified by those chants.

Consequently, this is either a case of "signifying the signified" (*lakṣita-lakṣaṇā*), or it is a rejection [of the primary sense] due to the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of the property that delimits the status of being the signified.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the term "year" (*saṃvatsara*) in that context refers only to a day.

And this is considered as a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*), assuming that even during the intervals between the *Kṛta* and other ages, the maximum lifespan of humans is only one hundred years.

However, when the lifespan measured in many thousands of years—found in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and *Itihāsas* as the fruit of yoga and other practices for the persons under discussion—is also accepted as authoritative for the current age-cycle (*yuga-yuga*), it is precisely because of this indicative evidence that the Vedic text "A man's life is a hundred years" (*śatāyurvai puruṣaḥ*) is analyzed with the compound meaning "one whose life consists of hundreds [of years]."

Alternatively, one may resort to the fact that the Kali Yuga has commenced; in that case, when the word "day" occurs in connection with "trivṛt" and so forth, the word "year" (saṃvatsara) is to be taken exactly as it is heard, through its relationship with that [day] characterized by the *trivṛt* stoma and the like.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the term "sattra"—like the term "gauṇa" and others—refers to humans whose lifespans extend across other ages.
For, in the Mīmāṃsā system, the arrangement of the ages is not false, since the scriptural injunctions establishing the specific duties of each respective age function without obstruction.

Nyāyabindu: "Fifty-five [days] consisting of the Trivṛt [stoma], fifty-five consisting of the Pañcadaśa, fifty-five consisting of the Saptadaśa, and fifty-five consisting of the Ekaviṃśa—this is the thousand-year sacrifice of the Viśvasṛjs.

Here, the eligibility for this belongs only to Gandharvas and others who possess a lifespan of a thousand years, because it is impossible for humans due to the absence of such a lifespan. Furthermore, since there is no possibility of humans attaining a thousand-year lifespan through alchemy (rasāyana), and because there is no evidence to assume such a long life starting from the very commencement of this rite, the number "fifty-five" refers to the number of sacrificers (*yajamāna*).
Therefore, this sacrificial session (*satra*), lasting four years and performed for that purpose by those who possess wealth, is called a "thousand-year sacrifice.
This too contradicts the scriptural injunction: "They should perform the sacrificial session for a maximum of four years.
Consequently, the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) refers here to a single day.
The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that even if the duration were limited to a month, life would be impossible for so long after the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna).
Maṇḍana says: "It would be a thousand days.
Śaṅkara says: "A thousand years for men."
"Adhikāra: In the *sattra* sacrifice, those who desire the entire fruit [of the rite] individually [are the qualified agents].
This is the section concerning the purpose (*prayojana-adhikaraṇa*), according to the *Tantraratna*.
Therefore, it should be examined there, in the *Vindu*.
6|2|11–2. Topic: In the *satra* sacrifice, only Brahmins have the right to participate.
Since there is no distinction made regarding all social classes (*varṇa*), the *satras* [should be accessible] to all.
Commentary: Here, the *satras* serve as the illustrative examples.

Regarding the statements, "Those who, knowing thus, perform the satra" and "Those who, knowing thus, enter upon the satra," there arises a doubt: do the satras belong to all three social classes (varṇas), or only to Brāhmaṇas? What is the prima facie view? That the satras should belong to all classes.
Why? Because there is no distinction.
For no specific distinction is maintained such that "sattras belong to these castes" and "they do not belong to those.
Therefore, all three castes have the right [to perform them].

"Satras belong to all castes because there is no distinction," (6.3.1.16); "For ownership is not enjoined," (20). (These two sūtras, representing the prima facie view and the established conclusion, are cited here.

Regarding the sequence "Those who are the sacrificers are the officiating priests," since the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the terms "sacrificer" and "priest" is untenable, one of them must function by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In this regard, because it is primary, the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) functions according to its direct Vedic sense (*śrutivṛtta*), whereas because it is secondary, the word *ṛtvij* (priest) functions by way of indication (*lakṣaṇārtha*).
Since it is established that the words beginning with *yat* and those beginning with *tat* are respectively the subject and the correlative, the question arises: what is the meaning of the sentence?

In this context, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the priesthood (*ārtvijya*) is enjoined as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for all the sacrificers of every caste who have been both mentioned and referred back.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: it is true that all social classes (*varṇas*) are indicated by the reference and subsequent specification [of the term "all"].
This is because no specific restriction is heard in the injunction, "They should perform the sacrificial session" (*satram āsīran*).
Nevertheless, in this context, the sacrificers (*yajamānas*) are enjoined as the performers of the priestly functions (*ārtvijya*).
In this context, the primary factor is that [the sacrifice];
and two properties of it are obtained by its very nature: being performed by another agent and being performed by a Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, being performed by another agent is set aside by the explicit statement.

However, the fact that Brāhmaṇas are the performers [of the Sattra] does not abandon the status of being a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇikatva*)—which is established by the general statement [of the injunction] "those who perform their own duty, the sacrificers, should sit for the Sattra" (where the Brāhmaṇas alone fulfill the purpose)—by virtue of that duty.
As it has been stated: "And when there is a conflict between a subsidiary and a quality, [the former prevails] because of its being for the sake of that [principal]" (Jaimini Sūtra 12.1.25).
This is also because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Commentary: For this reason as well, we see that there are three *satras*.
Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

What is the indicative mark? It says thus: "One should perform the *Bārhaspatya* as the *brahmasāman* for a Brāhmaṇa, the *Pārthuraśma* for a Rājanya, and the *Rāyovājīya* for a Vaiśya. This statement regarding the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is intended for the prescription of the *brahmasāman*.
In that [sacrifice], the sight of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas occurs;
therefore, for this reason as well, all social classes (varṇas) have the entitlement.
Or rather, it is only for Brāhmaṇas, because the other two [classes] lack the status of officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Commentary: The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that all three castes have the entitlement;
rather, it should belong to Brāhmaṇas alone.
Why? Because the other two lack the status of officiating priests (*ārtvijya*). For the other two castes, the *rājanya* and the *vaiśya*, officiating as priests is prohibited.
Without officiating as priests themselves, [the sacrifice] would be defective.
Therefore, it should belong to Brāhmaṇas alone.
If it is argued that this is due to a scriptural statement— meaning,
if you think that for the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas there would result a deficiency in the ritual quality (vaiguṇya)— then [the response follows].
On account of the scriptural statement, "Those who are sacrificers (yajamāna) shall be the officiating priests (ṛtvij)," they will become priests.
But who are the sacrificers? Those who, desiring the fruit of the Sattra sacrifice, have engaged in the Sattra ritual—these include both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
For them, the duty of officiating as priests is prescribed.
In this regard, it might be argued that this injunction for officiating as priests (*ārtvijya*) applies only to those for whom such officiation is possible.
This is not so;

for just as it applies to Brāhmaṇas who are sacrificers by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement, so too will it apply to non-Brāhmaṇas who are sacrificers, precisely by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement.
Therefore, even Rājanyas and Vaiśyas, having been consecrated for the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*), may sit for the sacrificial session (*satra*).
No; for it is their status as masters (*svāmitva*) that is enjoined.
Commentary: This is not so.
Ownership is enjoined by this statement; "Those desiring this [result] should perform the sattra" is what is enjoined, not the office of the officiating priest (ārtvijya).
Now, if it is argued that the office of the officiating priest is enjoined by the statement, "Those who are the sacrificers (yajamāna), they are the officiating priests (ṛtvij)," we reply:
That too is not correct.
Why? Because here the syntactical construction is not such that "those who are sacrificers" (*ye yajamānāḥ*) is the subject (*uddeśyapada*) and "priests" (*ṛtvijaḥ*) is the predicate (*vidheyapada*).

For if that were the case, the office of the priest (*ārtvijyam*) would be enjoined as a refinement (*saṃskāraka*) of the sacrificer, rather than the sacrificers being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the office of the priest.
In that case, their status as ordinary persons would mean they could not perform the priestly functions (*ārtvijya*);
furthermore, a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) would have to be postulated,
and since that too would pertain to the sacrificer, it would result in yet another postulation.

Therefore, the ritual acts belonging to the office of the priests (*ārtvijya*) are not enjoined for those who are already sacrificers (*yajamāna*). What then? It is the non-performance by any other agent of the ritual acts belonging to the office of the priests. And this is the syntactical structure: "the priests" (*ṛtvijaḥ*) is the subject term (*uddeśyapada*), and "they" (*te*) is what is enjoined; that is, "those who are sacrificers are themselves the priests, and no others. Thus, the sacrificers are enjoined as the agents with respect to the ritual acts belonging to the office of the priests.
Because of the specific substitution, the others are excluded.

This being the case, the priestly functions (*ārtvijya*) are merely the constituent elements (*padārtha*) with their original purposes; no unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) consisting of a refinement of the sacrificer (*yajamāna-saṃskāra*) is enjoined.
Even if one were to assume the sacrificer as the agent, an unseen result would still have to be assumed for these [functions]. To this, we reply:

In the other alternative, that unseen refinement (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to the sacrificer would necessarily have to be postulated. That which is a defect in both alternatives cannot befall one of them alone. Or rather, they may both belong to the *gārhapatya* fire, as there is no contradiction.
Commentary: The Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya will perform the duties pertaining to the Gārhapatya fire.
And there is no need for them to perform the office of the officiating priest (Ārtvijya) therein.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.

Or rather, it is not so, because it contradicts the ritual manual (kalpa). The Bhāṣya states: "And this is not the case that the Rājanya and Vaiśya [should perform] the ritual act belonging to the Gārhapatya fire; for there would indeed be a contradiction with the ritual manual."
According to some, the sacrificer’s cup is made of Soma; according to others, it is the fruit-cup (phalacamasa).
Likewise, the Brahmasāman is the Gārhapatya for Brāhmaṇas, the Pārthuraśma for Rājanyas, and the Rāyovājīya for Vaiśyas.
Therefore, even this [notion] that there is a settling at the Gārhapatya fire is not established.
"Because of the observation of indicative marks [showing] that the others have ownership.
Commentary: Now, as for what was stated regarding "the observation of indicative marks," that must be refuted.
To this, it is said:
He will explain this by means of the term *satra* which is not lacking [in its application].
Since ownership (*svāmitva*) is enjoined by indicating [the sacrificer] himself,
therefore, because the officiating priests possess ownership, a *satra* is not possible for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
Therefore, there is the observation of indicative marks regarding the *ahīna* sacrifice.
Śabara says: "Sacrificial sessions (*satra*) should belong to all social classes (*varṇa*) without distinction;
for in the scriptural statements concerning those desiring prosperity and so forth, no such distinction is heard."
Since the word "yaḥ" (who) is applicable when the three castes have been mentioned,
their officiating as priests (*ārtvijya*) is utilized for the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*).
This being the position reached, we reply:

"The office of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is not stated to be a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificers; for if it were so, an extraordinary (*aprākṛta*) purpose would result for the priesthood. Therefore, even though it is logically possible [to interpret it] by means of the word *yat*, there is no reference here to the owners [of the sacrifice]."
Since that very office of the officiating priest (ārtvijya) is intended, it must be a rule for the sacrificer.
Therefore, only Brāhmaṇas should perform the Sattra sacrifice.
As in the case of Soma, here too the king has no entitlement.
Thus, the connection [of the topic] arises from this counter-objection.

Since the words *yajamāna* (sacrificer) and *ṛtvij* (priest) have distinct meanings and lack grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) based on direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), one of them must be taken figuratively. In that case, the word *ṛtvij*, being the subordinate term, is understood as indicating the officiating priests through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of their functional role, and the sacrificers are enjoined as the agents with respect to those [functions]. Nor should it be argued that the word *ṛtvij* is based on the performance of sacrifices (*ṛtayajana*) and thus primary coreferentiality is indeed possible.

In reality, although the word *ṛtvij* is based on the occasion of performing sacrifices (*ṛtayajana*), if this sentence were intended to refer to that [etymological meaning], then since the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) possess that quality [of performing sacrifices], they would be eligible for the injunction; however, this would result in the redundancy of the sentence.
This is because, if it were intended to mean "those who sacrifice for others in the ritual," there would be no primary grammatical coreferentiality (*mukhya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Thus, while the sacrificers are indeed *ṛtvij*s by virtue of the occasion of performing sacrifices, the injunction applies to them specifically regarding the duties of a *ṛtvij* performed for the sake of others.
Vi—“Is the sacrificial session (*satra*) for the three castes, or specifically for the Brahmins?
It is for the three; do not say so, for the ownership (*svāmitva*) belongs to the Brahmins, as is fitting for the virtuous.
Bhaṭṭa—Even regarding the *satra*, it is heard in scripture: “Those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), they are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).”

In this regard, the term *ṛtvij* (priest) cannot first be understood by taking its meaning as "the state of being a priest consisting in performing the sacrifice at the proper time" (*ṛtayajanakartṛtva*) on the part of the sacrificers,

because there would result from the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two nominative cases the redundancy of the sentence, according to the principle that "there are seventeen [priests] including the master" (*svāmisaptadaśāḥ*,
Jaiminisūtra 3.1.18). Therefore, in this context, the word *ṛtvij* refers to those who have been appointed as priests through the act of hiring (*parikrayaṇīkṛta*).

Furthermore, even by that [interpretation], there would be no syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "those distinct from the agent of the sacrifice," because this is sublated by the impossibility of purchasing oneself. Nor can it be argued that the word *yajamāna* (sacrificer) is connected in identity with the word *ṛtvij* (priest)—which in the archetype (*prakṛti*) denotes those agents who are actually purchased—because it would result in the undesirable consequence (*aṣṭaprasaṅga*) of two nouns in the nominative case being construed with each other; and because it is more logical that the word *ṛtvij* itself should possess a qualified indication (*viśiṣṭalakṣaṇā*), specifically indicating the priest who is purchased.
Therefore, as in the case of "he who is the *hotṛ* is the *adhvaryu*," [the word *ṛtvij*] must be understood in its secondary sense (*jaghanya*).

Having indicated that function as belonging specifically to the office of the *ṛtvij*, it is enjoined for the purpose of purifying the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), because the sacrificer alone is perceived as the objective (*uddeśya*) due to the priority of the word "yat" [in the injunction].
For this very reason, even the postulation of a non-original function (*aprākṛtakārya*) does not constitute a fault, as it follows from the statement of the result.

Thus, since there is no distinction in their desire for prosperity (*ṛddhikāmatva*), all three castes are understood to have the purpose of purifying the guest-offering (*ātithya-saṃskāra*); therefore, all three castes possess the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to participate in the *sattra*.
For this very reason, even the sequence beginning with "The Bārhaspatya [cup] belongs to the Brāhmaṇa" in the context of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) becomes logical.

And thus, since the archetypal auxiliary services (prākṛtaka-nūpakāra) are also established by the word *ṛtvij* as being solely for the purpose of purifying the sacrificer (*yajamāna-saṃskāra*), it should be understood that there is no need to procure other priests through hiring and so forth for their sake.

This being the position reached, since it is observed in common worldly usage that verbal comprehension occurs even when there is a separation due to the presence of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), and because this is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), one must avoid the faults such as the assumption of an unseen archetypal function (*prākṛtakārya*). Therefore, by accepting that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) themselves are the objects of the injunction—either by indicating the mere attainment of their own status through the word *yat* despite its separation, or by indicating the attainment of the [priestly] form itself—the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are enjoined as the agents.
Nor can non-priesthood be established by this much, because the priestly status of the sacrificers has already been proven.

The exclusion of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), which is stated in the *varaṇa* (selection) and other directions and is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), is set aside by the direct injunction (*upadeśa*).

However, this does not imply that the performance must be by one who is not a Brāhmaṇa; rather, for the sake of favoring that [injunction], the eligibility belongs to Brāhmaṇas alone. As for the *Bārhaspatya* and other offerings, they are intended with reference to the *ahīna* sacrifices.
*Nyāyabindu*:—In the *sattra* sacrifice, all three [classes] have the qualification [to participate].

According to the rule, "Those who are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)," the injunction for the *ātithyā* rite serves as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificer; thus, Brahminhood—which functions as a qualifier of the subordinate agent—is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *ātithyā*.
However, in this case, because the agent is primary, that [qualification] is set aside due to the absence of a wife.

This being the case, since it would result in the performance of a non-original function (*aprākṛta-kārya*) by virtue of being a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) within the ritual injunction for hospitality (*ātithya-vidhi*), the sacrificer is prescribed specifically with reference to that [act].
Therefore, because it has another as its agent,
there is no sublation of the Brahmin who is the agent [of the original act].
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the sacrificial session (satra) belongs to Brāhmaṇas alone.
Maṇḍana [Miśra] states: "Even non-Brāhmaṇas are entitled to the satra. Śaṅkara [Bhagavatpāda] states: "Only a Brāhmaṇa shall be entitled to the satra."

"Oṃ. The entitlement [to perform] the *sattra* belongs only to those of the same lineage as Vasiṣṭha, or indeed to the Vasiṣṭhas themselves, because of the restriction regarding the office of the *brahman*.
Commentary: This has been established—that the *sattra* is for Brāhmaṇas alone, not for Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas."

Now, this point is doubtful: does it apply to all Brāhmaṇas, or only to those of the Vasiṣṭha lineage, or to others excluding the Bhṛgus, Śunakas, and Siddhāntins? What is the prima facie view? It applies to all, because there is no distinction; for no specific qualification is adopted such as, "the sacrificial session (sattra) is for these Brāhmaṇas, but not for those."
"Therefore, for all"—
this being the position reached, we reply:
because of the rule that the office of Brahman belongs to the Vāsiṣṭhas, the sacrificial session (sattra) must be for the Vāsiṣṭhas, and not for others.
Why? Because there is a restrictive rule regarding the office of the Brahman priest: "The Brahman must be a descendant of Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, the sacrificial session (sattra) should belong to those of the Vasiṣṭha lineage and those who share that same qualification.
Or rather, it belongs to all, because of a counter-exception.
The Commentary states: "Or rather, the sacrificial session (*satra*) should belong to all [the priests], because there is no distinction.
Now, it is said that the *brahman* priest must be a descendant of Vasiṣṭha;
to this he replies, "No."
Furthermore, it is restated: "Whoever should study the *stomabhāga* [hymns], he alone shall be the *brahmán* priest.

If one asks, "What is the purpose of this instruction for the Vāsiṣṭhas?"—it is for the sake of the *stomabhāga* recitation. One who studies the *stomabhāgas*, even if not a Vāsiṣṭha, is capable of performing the duties of a Vāsiṣṭha.
Due to the restriction of the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest) to one of the Vaiśvāmitra lineage, there is no entitlement for those of the Bhṛgu, Śunaka, and Vasiṣṭha lineages.
The commentary states: "There would be no entitlement for the Bhṛgus and others. Why? Because the *hautra* is restricted to the Vaiśvāmitra lineage by the rule: 'Viśvāmitra becomes the Hotṛ.'"

Therefore, the entitlement belongs to the Vaiśvāmitras and those who share the same ritual procedure (*kalpanā*) with them. Regarding Soma: the connection [of this section] is due to the consideration of a specific detail in the preceding [section]. Vi: "The sacrificial session (*satra*) may belong to a Brahmin, or to everyone, or specifically to one of the Vasiṣṭha lineage."

Or rather, it belongs to Viśvāmitra; because of his desire for prosperity, he is the middle one. For the sake of attaining Brahminhood, [the rite] was performed by one not of the Vasiṣṭha lineage; indeed, he granted the *stomabhāga* portions for the purpose of establishing the office of the *hotṛ* priest for those equal to the Vaiśvāmitras.
The mantras beginning with "radimarasi kṣayāya tvā" are called *stomabhāgas*.
One who studies them becomes a true descendant of Vasiṣṭha (*vāsiṣṭha*) even if he is not one by birth.

According to the Bhāṭṭa school: since in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) there is an injunction—"the Brahman priest is a descendant of Vasiṣṭha, the Hotṛ priest is a descendant of Viśvāmitra"—prescribing Vasiṣṭha-lineage and others for the office of Brahman and so forth, and because those two [lineages] are mutually incompatible, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding them in the sacrificial session (*satra*).

This being the position reached, since there is an injunction for the word *dvayanapada* by means of the statement, "Whoever studies the *stomabhāga*, he alone is a Vāsiṣṭha," this [term] refers only to the study of the *stomabhāga* and so forth through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Consequently, by virtue of the primary denotation (*śakti*), the *prajāpati* [verse] belongs to those of the same lineage as Vaiśvāmitra, while the *tanūnapāt* [verse] belongs to others. Thus, some are followers of the *nārāśaṃsa* ritual procedure, while others are followers of the *tanūnapāt* ritual procedure.
In this regard, what is first established? Among many sacrificers assembled together, only those who are equal [in qualification] should perform the Sattra together.
Why? Because of the absence of deficiency (*avaiguṇya*). Otherwise, for one whose ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is not fully observed, there would be a deficiency.
Just as there is an absence of result in the archetype itself without similarity, so it is here as well. [Duh]—This section follows the order of the Siddhānta.
(This citation exists in both the printed and manuscript versions, but it is not in the *Tantravārttika*).
The section concerning the distinction of conceptualization:
"It exists" is the prima facie view.
Why? Because of the attainment of the general statement: "Those desiring such [results] should perform the sacrificial session."

"The second *prayāja* is the *nārāśaṃsa* for the Vasiṣṭhas who perform [the sacrifice]"— this was the intention stated previously. In that case, when there is a concurrence of the agency of both the Vasiṣṭhas and others, because the [agent] is not the performer of that [specific rite], and because the condition (*nimitta*) for the injunction is absent in the performance (*kṛtau*), the *nārāśaṃsa* is not an auxiliary (*anaṅga*).

(He states another view: "Because of their being the performers of that [rite]—that is, because of the Vasiṣṭhas being the performers of the Nārāśaṃsa [offering]—when it is performed by them as well, the accomplishment of the ritual for the others is achieved through the Nārāśaṃsa; this is the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position. (For the Vasiṣṭhas are the performers of the Nārāśaṃsa along with its subsidiaries, whereas the others perform the Tanūnapāt. But when there is a conjunction of both types of performers, since both possess the status of performer in its entirety, the Nārāśaṃsa is indeed performed by the Vasiṣṭha as well; thus, there is no deficiency.)

Thus, even from the perspective of the *tanūnapāt* [offering], it is indeed without defect; therefore, by whatever [priest] the sacrifice is performed with its constituent qualities (*saguṇa*), it becomes a means for the attainment of the fruit for all.

However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: in the expression "of the Vasiṣṭhas" (*vasiṣṭhānām*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) has the sense of indicating ownership (*svāmi-lakṣaṇārthā*). Consequently, it brings about the successful accomplishment of the ritual only for those whose own [portion] is the *nārāśaṃsa*, and not for others. Here too, the examples involving multiple performers are merely illustrative, since the same principle of reasoning applies.
However, the mention of "sūtra" in the Bhāṣya is for the purpose of providing an illustration.
Or, by virtue of the explicit statement, it would be like the case of the head.
The Bhāṣya [explains]: by the word "vā," the position is reversed.
And this is not the case, that only those belonging to the same conceptual class (kalpanā) are entitled [to perform the rites];
even those of different classes are entitled.
Why? Because there is no distinction.
The application belongs to all sacrificers without distinction; nor is there a prohibition against separate ritual arrangements,
for there is no deficiency in having separate ritual arrangements.
To this it is replied:
because of the scriptural statement, let even those belonging to different kalpas be included by means of the general statement;
in that case, there would be no contradiction.
Just as, by the force of the statement "so that it may serve the purpose of man," the touching of human skulls is performed even though it is prohibited by Smṛti, so it is here as well;
or else,
it is like the case of the milk-offering (āśira).

Just as in the case of the *ṛtapeya* sacrifice, because of the statement "he becomes one whose vow is not [to consume] clarified butter," when the cow that yields the *ṛtu* milk has been set aside, they prepare another cow for the *āśira* mixture;
so too will this be the case here because of the scriptural statement.
Or rather, it is not so, because there is no commencement [of a new act].
The Commentary states: This is not so; it is not the case that even those of different *kalpas* are entitled (*adhikāra*).
Only those of the same *kalpa* are entitled.
Why? Because of the absence of deficiency (*avaiguṇyāt*).
Now, as for what was said—that there is a deficiency in this [sacrifice] because of the scriptural statement—regarding that, it is because it is not commenced [as a distinct rite].
That [deficiency] is postulated on account of the scriptural statement, provided that when it is not so postulated, the scriptural statement would become purposeless.

For if this were stated with reference to sacrifices of different ritual procedures (*bhinnakalpa*), then the scriptural statement would indeed be purposeless; thus, the sacrificial session (*satra*) is accepted even as having different ritual procedures, but this is not stated with reference to sacrifices of different ritual procedures.

Its meaningfulness will apply to those belonging to the same ritual period; therefore, there is no entitlement for those belonging to different ritual periods. Or rather, it might be so, because it serves the purpose of the sacrifice, like the Audumbarī post.
The Commentary states: There may indeed be an occasion for a distinct ritual manual (*kalpa*). Why? Because the ritual manual exists for the purpose of the sacrifice;
it is the means of accomplishment for the *nārāśaṃsa* cup-offering of Vasiṣṭha and others.
And that sacrifice is common to them all in the sacrificial sessions (*satra*).
It becomes accomplished even by the measurement prescribed for another;

just as in the case of the rule, "They cut the Audumbarī post to the height of the sacrificer," the sacrifice is accomplished by the measurement of anyone at all, and thus it becomes accomplished for others as well.
It is replied: But surely the *prayāja* has a connection with the person by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*),
and that will set aside its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*yāgārthatā*) which is obtained through the context (*prakaraṇa*).
We say: no, for in that case, the fruit [of the action] will have to be postulated. But surely, even otherwise, an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) must necessarily be postulated.
To this it is replied: It is true that [the word] must be supplied, but it is by means of a valid authority (pramāṇa), namely, through syntactic unity with the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*).
On the second alternative, however, one would have to supply the word and then achieve syntactic unity with it.
To this it is replied:

In some cases there may be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with what is mentioned [in the context], yet even so, a construction based on what is not the subject matter (*aprakṛta*) and what is not directly grasped (*avyagṛhīta*) would be more cumbersome than a construction based on the subject matter (*prakṛta*). No, for that is the primary factor.
The Commentary states: This is not so, because that is the primary factor.
For this ritual procedure (kalpa) has the human goal as its purpose.
How so? Because for Vasiṣṭha and others, there is the Nārāśaṃsa cup [with the mantra] "one who knows the sacrifice."
And whatever belongs to someone for the sake of a sacrifice, that action becomes fruitful for him only when accompanied by it.
Thus, the connection is made in this way: for the Vāsiṣṭhas and others, the ritual act together with the *nārāśaṃsa* cup becomes fruitful.
This is because the two *audumbarī* posts exist for the sake of another, just like the potsherds (*kapāla*).

The Commentary: Now, as for what was described—that "as with the Audumbarī post, so it is here"—because the Audumbarī posts exist for the sake of another, the sacrificer is heard in scripture as a subordinate factor (*guṇatvena*). [Objection: But even in that case, the statement of purpose would establish the primacy of the person (*puruṣaprādhānyam*).
This is not a fault;

for even when measured by a single sacrificer, this [measurement] becomes "measured by all sacrificers. However, in this case, when the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) of one person is adopted, it does not follow that the procedure of all has been adopted.
Therefore, since the two *audumbara* posts serve the purpose of another, they are like the potsherds.
Just as it is said, "The chaff is placed by means of the sacrificial cake's potsherd," and thus the chaff is taken up by means of the potsherd which serves another purpose, so too is this case.
If it is argued that this applies even to the *āgneya* [cake], [we reply: no.

The Bhāṣya: If one views it thus—that the purpose is common with the sacrificer, and not with himself or another sacrificer—then it would follow that it is also common with whoever is the sacrificer in another performance.
This is not so, because he has no entitlement [to that other performance], and because the word is not divided [in application].
The Bhāṣya: To this, it is said.
The sacrificer is not restricted to another performance;

however, there is no specific distinction in the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) from which a restriction could arise. What then? Because singularity is intended to be expressed, the sacrifices are not to be performed by two people, and thus no other person is brought in.
He says: "Let it be so for all sacrifices in exactly the same way as for others.
This is not so;
for the statement regarding the performance of the sacrifice with its constituent parts refers specifically to one who possesses desire.
And the word "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is undivided here with respect to the two *audumbarī* posts; therefore, it will apply to both.
However, due to their conjunction, there would be a conflict of conditions, because they are taught as distinct [functions], like the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans], resulting in a contradiction.
The Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
When there are many sacrificers, there would be a destruction of the occasion [for the rite] due to their coming together. Why? Because they are taught as being distinct.

According to the Vasiṣṭhas, in the performance [of the sacrifice], the Nārāśaṃsa cup is occasional (naimittika) when there is a [specific] occasion; in another case, it is occasional when there is a "tanūpāt" [offering].
Where both types of performers act together, there is completion through their association, not by means of one alone.
Therefore, it is not performed by one alone.
If Vasiṣṭha alone is not the performer, then the rite should not be performed for his sake, nor for the sake of another;
for there would be a mutual contradiction between both cases,
as in the case of the Bṛhat and Rathantara chants.

For example, in the statement "The *pṛṣṭha* [laud] consists of the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*," it means that which produces the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, not that which has the *Rathantara* as its means; thus, in that case, neither the *Bṛhat* nor the *Rathantara* serves as the primary cause (*nimitta*). It is the same here.
Alternatively, because of the connection with the whole, there would be no contradiction, since the relationship is one of ownership.
The Commentary: The phrase "moreover" (api ca) sets aside the previous position.
There is a connection of the whole with the individual through its being the sole agent;
therefore, there is no sublation of the occasional rites.
How, then, is there agency in its entirety? It is through the connection by way of ownership.
With respect to the action, there exists a connection for Vasiṣṭha and the others solely by way of ownership;
for the action is beneficial to persons.
For each one is indeed capable of producing the result;
therefore, since each one is the agent of the whole, the occasional rite (naimittika) applies to all.
It is just as when it is said, "Let it be given to the tip [of the nose] alone."
Although she is the mother of both the beak and the morsel, nevertheless, the offering is given to her;
for she is his mother in its entirety, and motherhood is not partitioned.
In the same way, it is here with the substance as well.
Therefore, there is no entitlement for those belonging to different ritual cycles (*kalpa*).

Regarding the *sāman*: because it is connected with a portion [of the rite] for the sake of increasing the ritual action, and because it is subordinate as an object of meditation, there would be an obstruction in that case.
Commentary: Now, as for what was stated regarding "the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*," that must be refuted.
In the case of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* sāmans, there is a connection with only a portion [of the rite] due to the increase of the occasional (*naimittika*) action;
for in that instance, both [sāmans] possess the capacity as means, and this is not otherwise.
However, the connection of the two sāmans there is with a single part of the *stotra*, not with the entire *stotra*.

For in that context, the *sāman* is heard as a subordinate element (*guṇa*), while the *stotra* is the primary element. Therefore, there would be an obstruction [to the application] therein. Nor should it be argued: "In the sentence, 'For the Rājanya, the Trivṛt, the Vaidya, and the Śunaka—those praised by Kaṇva and Kāśyapa—the second *prayāja* is the *nārāśaṃsa*, not the *tanūnapāt*,' since the verbal root itself is absent, how can it be said that the meaning of the verbal root is being enjoined? [This objection is invalid.]

In this case, since an injunction (*vidhi*) must necessarily be postulated, and since that [injunction] is untenable without a verbal root (*prakṛti*), one must also postulate a verbal root; thus, the sentence results in the form: "One should perform the second *prayāja* for these [deities] as the *nārāśaṃsa*. Consequently, the injunction of the meaning of the verbal root is established.

Even if one were to postulate, "The second *prayāja* should be performed," because the term expressing general volitional effort (*kṛti-sāmānya-vācaka*) culminates specifically in the *prayāja*, the injunction of the meaning of the verbal root remains valid.
This constitutes the connection [of the present topic] by way of an exception (*pūrvapakṣa-pratibādhāt*) to the preceding section.

Even though the *prayāja* offerings and other elements are performed separately (*vi-bhinna*) in a *sattra*, those entitled to the entitlement (*adhikārin*) must be of identical ritual procedure (*tulyakalpa*). Regarding the first [view], the entitlement is common among the Vasiṣṭhas and others; in the *Sārasvata-sattra*, however, the entitlement is distinct.
Nata:

"The injunction regarding the *nārāśaṃsa* vessel is extended [to the *nārāśaṃsa* cups] by means of transference (*atideśa*), because of their proximity and because of the excellence of the quality [of the procedure], preceded by the specific owner [of the cup] in its status as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) starting from the *nārāśaṃsa*."

The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains that a difference in ritual procedure (*kalpabheda*) is heard in the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices, such as: "For those residing in the kingdom, the Nārāśaṃsa is the second *prayāja*; for others, the Tanūnapāt," and so forth. For here, having accepted that the name [Tanūnapāt] is based on its occurrence in one part [of the mantra], the second *prayāja*—which is enjoined by the statement "He sacrifices to Tanūnapāt"—lacks a fixed order. Consequently, since both the Nārāśaṃsa and the Tanūnapāt mantras generally apply to the second *prayāja* through their respective parts as options, the connection of the Nārāśaṃsa with those residing in the kingdom is merely being established.

For this very reason, the secondary derivative (taddhita) *nārāśaṃsa* constitutes the second word, which is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Consequently, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), I consider *tanūnapāt* to be [the primary term]; thus, even the statement "of others, *tanūnapāt*" is merely a restatement, just like the expression "*goducchattare*."

Nor is it reasonable for some to claim that although the three *nārāśaṃsa* verses are recited in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sūkta*, they are not recited in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; for even though the *nārāśaṃsa* mantras are recited within the *sūkta*, the specific mantra "May the *nārāśaṃsa* enjoy the clarified butter" (*nārāśaṃso agnir ājyasya vetu*) is indeed recited in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
For this very reason, Āśvalāyana and others have recited it in exactly that manner.

As for the claim that in the *nārāśaṃsa* passage, the injunction of "secondness" and so forth constitutes an injunction of being a *prāyāja*, and that because it is enjoined as connected with the *vāsisthas*, there is an absence of others—that is not correct. For if that were the case, even though "secondness"—in the form of occurring after the *samid-yāga*—is enjoined at the time of the *nārāśaṃsa*, there would be no evidence that the *vāsisthas* [perform] *tanūnapāt* and the rest; consequently, it would follow that they perform it after the *nārāśaṃsa*. Indeed, the injunction of the *nārāśaṃsa* in the word "second" is not by way of its performing that function, such that one might suspect the absence of *tanūnapāt* and the others among them.

If that were the case, even for the Vāsiṣṭhas, there would be the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) because [the deity] would be treated as a separate object of injunction. Nor can it be argued that by the statement "Tanūnapāt for others," there is likewise an application for other Vāsiṣṭhas who have Tanūnapāt as their deity; for there is no evidence to accept a syntactical split when the passage is established as a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), and because it would entail the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*), a prior injunction (*pūrva-vidhi*), and a distinct intermediate injunction (*vidhyantara*).

Therefore, one must justify the difference between the ritual alternatives (*kalpa-bheda*) by establishing the connection of the previously mentioned mantra with the Vāsiṣṭhas within the very context (*prakaraṇa*).
And that [initiation] is obtained through the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites in sacrifices such as the *satra*, which involve multiple performers.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether, in those *satra* and other rites, there is entitlement even for those of different lineages (*kalpa*)—or only for those of the same lineage—the conclusion is that there is entitlement even for those of different lineages, because there is no distinction made.

Nor does the contingency of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) for others arise when one performs the rite according to a single lineage; for in the case of the mantra "vāsijñāna," if it were restricted to the performance by those of a pure lineage alone, it would result in the subversion of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Furthermore, if this were a duty pertaining to a person qualified by the season (*ṛtu*), it would result in a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*). Although the injunction of the *vāsiṣṭha* status in the *nārāśaṃsa* mantra—given that the *haitra* [mantra] belongs to the *vaiśāmitra*—is not applicable as a direct qualifier of the performer (*kartṛ*), it is nonetheless logically consistent as an injunction regarding the connection with a *vāsiṣṭha* by way of qualifying the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*), namely the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). Otherwise, in the case of a sacrificial session (*satra*) and the like, just as there is a single measurement of the *audumbarī* post, even if one person is connected to the *vāsiṣṭha* status, a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) would arise for the others.
Therefore, the qualification (*adhikāra*) applies even when there is a difference in the ritual procedure (*kalpanā*).

This being the case, since the two mantras are obtained as optional alternatives, it is appropriate for the sentence to have a purposeful meaning by way of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Consequently, because it possesses the result of an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*)—namely, the restriction to the performance known as the *satra*—and because it is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) specifically with reference to the *vāsiṣṭhas*, this is an injunction for the application (*viniyoga*) of the *nārāśaṃsa* mantra through the medium of the second *prayāja* offering, which is an auxiliary of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices that serve as the means to achieve the results desired by the *vāsiṣṭhas*.
Therefore, the cessation of the *nārāśaṃsa* mantra from the *vāsiṣṭhas* occurs simply due to its lack of application there; thus, it is not a case of "exclusion" (*parisaṃkhyā*).
This is what constitutes the result of the operation of the sentence.

Therefore, even if there were a difference in the conceptualization [of the ritual], since the fruit would not accrue to others when only one part of the mantra is recited during the entitlement (*adhikāra*), the entitlement must consist precisely in a common conceptualization.
*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "For those residing in the kingdom, the second *prayāja* is the *nārāśaṃsa*; for others, it is the *tanūnapāt*.
That [distinction] applies to the [sacrifices] beginning with the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, as they are included therein.

In that regard, one might raise the objection: "How can there be a *nārāśaṃsa* cup when it is produced by those who have shaved their hair (*vāsiu*), and likewise for the *tanūnapāt* cup by others? Thus, relying on some such assumption, they might argue that even those with different ritual manuals (*bhinnakalpa*) could perform a *sattra*.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: The injunction regarding the *nārāśaṃsa* and other cups is for the purpose of shaving the hair and so forth; since its purposefulness is established through the medium of the ritual form (*rūpaka*), there is no need to assume a separate result. Furthermore, it is logical that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is what is to be enjoined, because of its proximity.

Therefore, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since the performance of others would result in a deficiency of the rite (*ṛtuvaiguṇya*) if they relied on a different manual, the *sattra* must indeed be performed according to a single, common ritual manual (*samānakalpa*).
Maṇḍana: "Those belonging to different *kalpas* should not [perform it together]. Śaṅkara: "A small number may perform a *satra*.
Regarding eligibility (*adhikāra*), in *satras* other than the Sārasvata, it belongs only to those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
Because of the ownership of the monastery, there would also be [ownership] of the food and other items.
The commentary states: "The *satras* themselves are the examples:
'Those who, knowing thus, sit for the *satra*'; 'Those who, knowing thus, enter upon the *satra*.'"
Regarding these, there is a doubt: do they belong to both those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnin*) and those who do not (*anagnin*), or only to those who maintain the sacred fires?
What is the prima facie view? They belong to both those who maintain the sacred fires and those who do not.
Why? Because the sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) is common to all.
For even a monastery belonging to others is available for everyone to undertake [construction or maintenance],
since its purpose is thereby accomplished;
it attains success through that person or through one belonging to him.
Therefore, it should also apply to others.
And because it is seen in the case of the Sārasvata [sattra].
The Bhāṣya says: "And in the Sārasvata sattra, there is a scriptural observation."

"The others go to the heavenly world by means of the sacrificial session (sattra), those who, though not having established the sacred fires, perform the sattra"—this indicates that even those who have not established the fires may perform the sattra. Therefore, it applies to all.
Furthermore, because an expiation is prescribed for this case.

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) states: "An expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed: 'One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivicci, if the fires of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should become mixed with other fires. This shows that there is an expiation for the mixing of fires.
That [mixing] would occur only with fires that have not been formally established (*anāhitaiḥ*), and not otherwise.
Therefore, for this reason also, the fires are permanent (*satrāṇi*)."
Because the *mātṛ* [sacrifices] must be preceded by an *iṣṭi*.
The Bhāṣya states: "The *satras* belong to those who possess the *sāmidhenī* verses, not to those who do not possess the *agni*s.
Why? Because they are preceded by an *iṣṭi*."
The status of being preceded by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice is prescribed for the *soma* sacrifices in the text:

"Having performed the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, one should sacrifice with *soma*. Thus, the *jyotiṣṭoma* has the *iṣṭi* as its preceding stage. And that [status] is extended to the *satras* through a succession of archetypal injunctions (*codaka*).
Therefore, those [rites] would not belong to those who do not maintain the sacred fires;
for they are employed for one's own purpose.
And the Bhāṣya states: "And the fires are employed for one's own purpose."
How so? Because of the distinction in the verbal suffix (upagraha).
For there is indeed a distinction in the suffix in the expression "amīn ādadhīta" (he should install the fires).
Therefore, the fires belong to one [person], and their accomplishment does not belong to another, even though the fires serve the purpose of the ritual (ṛtvartha).
And it shows the pooling [of oblations]. The Bhāṣya states: "Those who are kindling the Sāvitra fires should pool them.
From this also, it is understood that they perform the Satra sacrifices with a common purpose (sāmaya).
There may be an expiation in times of distress.
The Commentary states: Thus, in a section where the avoidance of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) was not distinguished, it is now considered elsewhere.
... Now, the avoidance of the previously mentioned indicative mark (in Sūtra 29) is being stated.
An expiation (prāyaścitta) is prescribed even for this [act].

How so? When those traveling through a forest or wilderness, or those staying there, experience terror due to fear of bandits or fear of water, or when they are struck by fire from a giver or by mutual conflict—that shall be the domain for expiation. [The opponent] says: "In that case, because the fires are for the sake of another, [the expiation applies] to whichever person's fires [are involved]."
"The ritual action accomplished by all certainly brings about its fruit.
"Not so;
for the status of the Soma-variants as having the Iṣṭi as their archetype is established."

Furthermore, those who have not performed the fire-laying (*āhitāgni*) are in no way entitled [to the sacrifice]. The fire-layer (*ādhātṛ*) has no connection with the ritual action (*kārya*), nor does it accomplish anything for others;
because, through the specific voice (*upagraha*), the fruit is connected only to the agent (*kartṛ*).
The connection [of this topic] is due to the specific investigation of the Soma sacrifice that follows immediately hereafter.

Because of the scriptural statement regarding the Sārasvata sattra, even though there is no requirement for those who do not maintain the sacred fires (anagnīn), they have no entitlement elsewhere; this is because of the lack of authoritative evidence.

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: even for one who does not maintain the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), there may be a Satra sacrifice because of another’s sovereignty over the fires of a monastery, even if those fires belong to someone else. Regarding the three [cases]: what is the proof here? It is the first, because in a single case that is established; it is not from the Ātmanepada ending [indicating] the fires belonging to the sacrificers themselves.

The Bhaṭṭa [school] maintains that, because there is no evidence for restricting the mention of "satra" in the injunction—"Those who perform a satra without having established the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) go to the heavenly world"—there is eligibility for all performers of satras, including those who have not established the fires, provided they are accompanied by those who have.
For this very reason, the plural number used in connection with the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) refers exclusively to subjects other than the Sārasvata-satra;
having understood the time for the *iṣṭi* and *soma*, one may simply expect some such performer of the *iṣṭi* and *soma*.

It is not the case that the identity of the agent for both the *iṣṭi* and the *soma* sacrifice is being enjoined there, because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This being the prima facie view, we reply: from the sentences "Having performed the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, one should sacrifice with *soma*" and "Whoever sacrifices with this *agniṣṭut* falls into a pit," there is an extension (*atideśa*) [of the rule]; and since the syntactical split is avoided by the single occurrence of the suffix *-ktvā*, it is understood that the *iṣṭi* and the *soma* sacrifice share the same agent.

In that context, because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) used in connection with the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) indicates that the act is to be performed by one who has already established the fires (*āhitāgni*) alone; and because in the injunction within the section on the *Sārasvata-sattra* regarding the offering of *vrīhi* and other grains, the same applies to the permission granted for those who have not established the fires (*anāhitāgni*), the eligibility for other *sattra*s belongs only to those who have established the fires, in accordance with the middle voice.

*Nyāyabindu*: [Objection: Even one who has not established the fires may be eligible for the *sattra*, since the purpose can be accomplished by someone using other fires; therefore, he is eligible along with others. [Reply:

This being the position, since the modifications of the *Soma* sacrifice are preceded by the *iṣṭi* (sacrificial offerings), and since one who has not established the fires lacks the *iṣṭi*, he has no eligibility.

From the middle-voice (ātmanepada) ending in the verb *ādadhīta*, it follows that the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) has the sacrificer as its agent; therefore, there is no qualification for those who do not maintain the sacred fires (*ananīn*).
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
"Qualification" (*adhikāra*) refers to the Smārta rites and so forth.
The entitlement belongs to the *puruṣa*. The entitlement belongs to the *rathakāra*.
Maṇḍana says: "One who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*) would not be entitled to the *sattra*."
Maṇḍana: "And the duties prescribed by the Smṛtis are to be performed after initiation.
Śaṅkara: "[He is] authorized for the fire-laying;
he is the one entitled [to perform the rite]."
Śaṅkara: "The restrictive rules (niyamas) apply from the time of initiation (upanayana). Eligibility for Smārta and other ritual acts belongs only to one who has been initiated;
however, those duties enjoined therein commence with birth."
Topic: (The definition of essential nature) *puruṣasya aiśvarya* 6.2.122.

Regarding the object (*karman*)—this [suffix] is employed for permission (*anujñāna*) in the context of engagement (*pravṛtti*). *Ṛjubhāṣya*: Here, the items belonging to the Smṛti tradition are presented as examples.

Page 14. Topic: Entitlement (*adhikāra*); the state of being the enjoyer of the fruit is ownership (*svāmitva*). (From here, the rules of the scripture [are given]: beginning with "The teacher is to be followed and saluted," the topic of entitlement extends only through the chapters and sections of the text).
"They are to be looked upon, saluted, and honored.
Regarding this, there is a doubt.

Context (*adhikāra*): the cessation of a cognition that is still expectant [of further specification] (such as: "Are these objects for those who have merely been born, or for those who have been initiated?"—and what is it? It consists of the form of the performance, which is the nature of the *prakaraṇa*).
Who has the entitlement? The three social classes (varṇas) are entitled to perform the ritual acts.

However, by such injunctions as, "If the fire of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should burn his house, he shall offer an eight-potherd oblation to Agni Sāmanvat," the performance of a rite is enjoined upon specific occasions (*nimitta*) such as the burning of the fire. This establishes a similarity in the result—namely, the destruction of sin produced by the rite—arising from that occasion.
Furthermore, that similarity of results is characterized by the specific qualifications of the person entitled to perform it (*adhikārin*).

See *Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*, pp. 235–36. Regarding the subject of the injunction concerning entitlement (*adhikāravidhi*), one should consult the *Vindī-bālya-prakāśā*, which states: "Injunction (*vidhi*) is of two kinds... [and so forth].

The *adhikāravidhi* (qualification injunction) itself, by the principle that "qualification occurs when the task is known," rightly functions within the scope of the *prayogavidhi* (performance injunction), as it presupposes the determination of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) necessitated by that performance injunction. (Sūtra-pṛ. 531). The cause of qualification is that which attains the status of a cause for undertaking (i.e., the cause for performance); that is the basis for being qualified (*adhikṛta*).

*Bṛhatī*, p. 30: Since the context (*prakaraṇa*), which consists of the governing authority (*adhikāra*), is the subject at hand, and because there is no abandonment of many [subsidiaries], and since there is no distinction in being the subject at hand, the simultaneous grasping [of all subsidiaries] occurs; thus, there is no difference in strength or weakness between the intermediate and the great governing authorities. *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 911: The qualified person (*adhikārī*) is one whose capacity for all constituent parts has manifested; one does not possess the authority when the capacity for the constituent parts is suppressed. *Kaṇikā*, p. 340: "Qualified person" (*adhikārī*) means standing above the ritual actions; that is to say, the sense of "equality."

Bhāṣya 6.1.13, p. 1354: To what extent must one know [the Veda] to be qualified as a learned person (vidvān) for the performance of rituals? One is qualified for rituals by knowing as much as is required for qualification;
and in the case of a ritual, there is the mantra.
He becomes capable.
