When another ritual is to be performed, knowledge of a different ritual does not serve as a visible aid."
Therefore, knowledge of another sacrifice should not be required for the entitlement [to perform] this one.
Because of the knowledge of another sacrifice, there is another sacrifice; therefore, one who knows its own constituent elements is entitled [to perform it].
Bhāṣya 3.8.1.46: "An unlearned person is not entitled to perform ritual acts. 12.4.15.42: The position is that the qualified performer is understood through a verbal injunction;
however, in reality, the qualified performer is understood only through an implied injunction.

*Bhāṭṭa*, 8.14: According to the principle that "the Veda produces valid knowledge for those who possess the qualification," the qualification (*adhikāra*) for the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence belongs only to one who possesses a correct understanding of the meanings of the individual words.
*Upadeśasāhasrī*, verse 18, commentary by Rāmatīrtha:
191. Qualification (*adhikāritva*) is the state of being a recipient of the fruit [of the action].
Maṇi, p. 86: Furthermore, that alone is a qualification of the qualified person (adhikāriviśeṣaṇa) which is heard as a qualification of the person.

For this very reason, although the injunction "A king desiring self-sovereignty (svārājya) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya" prescribes the Rājasūya with reference to self-sovereignty, it does not establish that the one desiring self-sovereignty is the enjoyer of that fruit; rather, it establishes it for one who is already a king and desires that [fruit].
Even something not heard as a qualification of the person may nonetheless become a qualification of the qualified person.

Just as knowledge established by the injunction for study [is required] for rituals accomplished by means of fire, and the possession of fire established by the rite of fire-installation (*ādhāna*) is required for rituals to be accomplished by fire—as well as the requisite capacity—even though these are not explicitly mentioned as qualifications of the person (*puruṣaviśeṣaṇa*), they nonetheless serve as qualifications for eligibility (*adhikāraviśeṣaṇa*). This is because the injunctions for subsequent sacrifices proceed only toward one who possesses the knowledge established by the injunction for study, since those injunctions imply the necessity of such knowledge; and because the injunctions for rituals to be accomplished by fire proceed only toward one who possesses the fire established by the rite of fire-installation, since those injunctions imply the necessity of such fire.
In this way, capacity (*sāmarthya*) is also a qualification for eligibility (*adhikāra*), for it is enjoined with respect to one who lacks capacity;
according to the maxim: "For those who speak of their own selves [as agents], capacity is a cooperative factor.
And that capacity, in the case of optional rites (*kāmya-karman*), pertains to both the subsidiaries and the principal act.

But one who is capable only of the subsidiaries [is not entitled]. One who is capable only of the principal act is not entitled to a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya-karma*), because the injunction for the principal act functions only with respect to one capable of performing the principal act together with its subsidiaries, since entitlement follows the application of the ritual rules (*yathāviniyogam*). For if it were to function only with respect to one who is fully capable, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural text (*śruti*); in that case, even one incapable [of the subsidiaries] would have entitlement. However, there is no such contradiction, because the scriptural text regarding "one who desires heaven" involves no contradiction when it functions only with respect to one who is capable.

On the contrary, if one were to engage in a rite toward someone incapable [of performing the auxiliaries], there would result the sublation of the requirement for the collection of auxiliaries (*aṅgasāhitya*)— which is understood through syntactic unity (*vākyaikavākyatā*) with the primary injunction (*pradhānavidhi*)— and there would follow the contingency that the auxiliaries, which are heard as being obligatory (*nityavat*), become merely optional (*pākṣikatva*). Therefore, eligibility (*adhikāra*) for a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmyakarma*) belongs only to one who is capable of performing it together with its auxiliaries (*sāṅga*).
Regarding the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), however, the principle of "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*) applies.
For these are enjoined by the scriptural injunction of "as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīvaśruti*) as duties to be performed for the duration of one's life;
yet it is not possible for anyone who possesses discernment to perform their performance (*prayoga*) for the entirety of their life.

Therefore, in the case of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), one who is capable of performing only the principal acts is qualified (*adhikārī*). As for the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), however, as many as can be performed should be carried out. Let this suffice, as the matter has been thoroughly investigated by the learned scholars (*sūri*). (Mīmāṃsā, pp. 236–241). The restriction of qualification [is] for the purpose of avoiding the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating ignorance, incapacity, or the necessity of assuming [such deficiencies].
Bhāṣya 4.1.14: "And in the context [of a ritual], there is an injunction for a mantra even among those not designated by that name, because it is taught [by scripture].

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard [in the scripture]: "He worships the Āgnīdhra fire-altar with an Āgneyī [verse]; he worships the Sadas with an Aindrī; he worships the Havirdhāna shed with a Vaiṣṇavī.

Should one worship using only the Āgneyī and other mantras already present in the archetype (prakṛta), or rather, should one take them from the Dāśatayī collection? The injunction of the mantra—"he worships with an Āgneyī"—is in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma procedure; should it apply only to those mantras designated by that name within the archetype, or to those not so designated, including even mantras not belonging to the archetype?
Because it is prescribed as being common to both the primary and non-primary [contexts] due to its being taught by the learned;
therefore, it should either be taken from the primary context, or brought in from the *Dāśatayī*,
or designated by that name, on account of both the context and logical consistency.
Setting aside the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) which was suggested by the word "or" (vā) in the sūtra, he states the established conclusion (siddhānta):

"It is designated by that. It is designated by that specific qualification; therefore, it should be understood as belonging to that very context (prakaraṇa), because of both the context and logical consistency.

In this regard, there is a *prakaraṇa* (contextual relevance) for the *āgneyya-mantra*, and elsewhere there is a logical justification (*upapatti*). By means of the possessive pronoun in the expression "Agni is its deity," the very mantra under discussion is referred to.
Furthermore, in the injunction regarding the taking of the *brahmaudana* portions and so forth, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to accept only the four mantras already present in the context.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that only the mantras belonging to the current context are to be adopted.

The instruction regarding the *anathaike* (the single [verse] for one who is without a protector) would be purposeful because of its connection with that which possesses a fruit; however, the act of standing near (*upasthāna*) does not itself possess a fruit.

The instruction, "One stands near the Āgnīdhra fire-altar with a verse addressed to Agni," would be meaningless—that is, fruitless—were there no *apūrva* characterized by the standing near the Āgnīdhra. There is no qualification (*adhikāra*) for the ritual action; indeed, there would be no qualification for anyone at all.
Because there is no connection with that which possesses a fruit, due to the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
For there is no fruit merely by means of the attendance (*upasthāna*) when it is not in proximity to a ritual (*kratu*).
Indeed, because the attendance does not possess a fruit—that is, it is not endowed with a fruit—apart from the *apūrva*.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *ṛc* addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*) which is already present in the context should be adopted. Regarding this, the *Sudhā* commentary states: "Even though [the word 'Agni'] is restricted to the ritual occasion (*ṛtu*), since the nature of the worship (*upasthāna*) is not fixed to those [specific verses] such as the *āgneyī*, it is illogical for them to serve as its defining medium (*dāraka*). Furthermore, since words such as 'āgneyī' do not have their application based on a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*), there would be no need to depend on a collection [of verses] once the specific form [of the verse] has been determined. Consequently, the result would be futility; thus, the meaning of the passage ending with 'by that which possesses a fruit'—namely, that the teaching of the nature of the worship here would be useless because the mere existence [of the verse] would fail to connect with a fruitful result—is clear."

Because [the term] is prescribed for all [of them]. The established conclusion (siddhānta) has been stated that the *āgneyī* verse enjoined by the rule "He worships with an *āgneyī* [verse]" must be taken as only that which occurs within the specific context (*prakaraṇa*).

Now, one might object: since the *āgneyī* verses recited in the context have their requirements satisfied (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) through their connection to other purposes such as the *stotra*, they [cannot be taken here].

Regarding the section on *adhiśrayaṇa* (placing on the fire) and so forth (sūtra 316): In the case of the Śākyas, where the rule for Vedic study applies to the ground, when one is placing meat for grinding, one should modify the mantra by reciting, "Thou art meat; satisfy the gods. Vi. 3.1.11. The *saṃtardana* of the two *adhipavaṇa* boards does not apply to the *ukthya* and other [sacrifices] such as the *ahīna*; however, it is not displaced from the Jyotiṣṭoma, nor is it prohibited in the Agniṣṭoma.
Bhāṣya 3.3: Even when the substratum is one, there is a difference in designation.
"Even though the substance is one, the distinction [between Indra and Mahendra] arises from the internal difference between the qualified part and the quality, etc. (i.e., Indra and Mahendra).

And it is said: “The terms ‘teacher’ (ācārya) and ‘maternal uncle’ (mātula) are observed to be used as distinct [conventions] despite the identity of the substance, due to a difference in the causes of dependence” (Vākyapadīya 2.3.1.27, p. 424). Regarding this, the *Sudhā* commentary states: Since the referent of the word ‘teacher’ is the disciple himself by virtue of his existence, he belongs to the side of the disciple; and since dependence is untenable in the absence of something to be depended upon, the disciple is the cause for the teacher’s dependence upon the disciple through reciprocal relation (*pratisambandha*).
The nephew is not the cause for the uncle's expectation regarding the nephew;
rather, even when there is identity of substance, a distinction in usage is observed due to their difference—this is the meaning of the verse of the elders (p.
653–54). Even after having studied the Veda, one must reside specifically in the teacher’s household for the sake of investigating Dharma.

VI. 1.1.1. For one who has studied the Veda and understood its meaning is qualified for the matters of the Veda, because a capacity consistent with the scriptural purpose is required. (Ke. The meaning of the root *adhī* is an action conducive to the pronunciation [of the text] from the mouth of a teacher.

Maṇi, p. 140: The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because the Smṛti rule "having studied, one should perform the *manana*" prohibits returning from the teacher’s house immediately after study, the investigation of the meaning of the Veda must not be undertaken until after the study of the Veda is complete.
The conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the Smṛti, the suffix *-ktvā* denotes merely a subsequent time and does not imply the completion of the study;
therefore, the investigation of the meaning of the Veda should indeed be performed.
Bhaṭṭa: Study is not enjoined by a separate injunction, because the injunction itself is that which is to be accomplished;
therefore, this is a principal action (*pradhānakarma*).
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 10: The purpose of study (*adhyayana*) is the attainment of knowledge through the recitation of mantras (*japayajña*) and the complete mastery of the text (*pārāyaṇa*).
* Ratnamālā*, p. 28: When the visible [result] is present, study is not for the sake of something else [i.e., an invisible result].
*Bhāṣya* 1.2.1.13: Study is for the purpose of knowledge regarding the visible object.

Śāstradīpikā, Tarkapāda, p. 6: It is stated in the *Tantraratna* in the section on the acquisition of wealth (*dravyārjana-varṇaka*, 4.1.2, second exposition) that study is neither for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) nor for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

Bālakrīḍā, p. 81: Study is obligatory because the injunction regarding the sacrifice is obligatory. Vivaraṇa-pramēya-saṃgraha, 6.2.11: Study is obligatory because its fruit—the qualification for ritual action—is necessary.
In its absence, there would be transgression due to the non-performance of obligatory and occasional rites.
Furthermore, the study of the entire Veda is indeed necessary, because it is required for the performance of the compulsory recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) and other such duties.

*Ratnamālā*, p. 28. Study, by means of the transcendental merit (*apūrva*) resulting from the observance of rules, serves as the instrument for the knowledge of sacrifices and thereby becomes the generator of the transcendental merit produced by all sacrifices without exception.
Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.1.1: There is no ritual action devoid of study, because it is impossible to perform that [action, such as the *upasthāna*] without study.
Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.6: As for the fact that the teacher recites in the presence of the pupil, that study is for the purpose of acquisition (*grahaṇa*).
This is for the purpose of excluding that which pertains to a disciple.

According to Bhāṣya 1.2.1.13, study (*adhyayana*)—for the sake of grasping and retaining [the texts] through application, rules, and so forth—is understood as being for the benefit of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
According to Vārttika 6.1.3.7, because the rites are mandatory, study is established as obligatory (*nitya*) by virtue of its result.
*Maṇi*, p. 4: Even though study does not have the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and other rituals as its purpose, it nonetheless serves the purpose of the sacrifice because it has such knowledge as its aim.
*Bhāṣya* 4.1.2, p. 82: On the other hand, heaven is the fruit of study, since the visible purpose—the knowledge of what is to be performed—is possible.
*Trikāṇḍī* 1.1.1: Study has a visible purpose.

*Bhāṣya* 1.1.1, p. 6: The obligatory nature of study is established by the statement, "Henceforth these fall [from their caste]," and by the prohibition, "Those who do not study become *vrātyas*. *Maṇi*, pp. 4–5: There is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) regarding both studying and teaching; however, there is no suspension of study when reciting mantras during the *Nitya* and other [obligatory] rites.

VI. 1.2.17: The rules regarding the study [of the Veda] include such injunctions as "one should not study on a festival day (parvan)," "one should not study when there is wind," and "one should not study when there is thunder," and so forth.

These are not rules pertaining to the performance of ritual acts (*karma*). Bhāṣya 1.2.1.18–19: Rules regarding the study [of the Veda] include such matters as eating on the ground (*bhūmibhojana*) and so forth.
The rules for Vedic study (adhyayananiyama) [apply] in cases such as the study of the Kārīrī-mantras, which are prompted by the injunction for Vedic study (Vi. 4.1.2).
The unseen potency (apūrva) produced by the rule of study serves as the basis for inferring the unseen potency produced by all sacrifices.

1|1|1. Although the collection of rules regarding the study-period (*adhyāya*) and non-study-period (*anadhyāya*), and so forth, is recited within the context of the section on Vedic study (*adhyayana-prakaraṇa*), they are of no use for the nature or the purpose of that study itself; therefore, one might think that the restriction of study (*adhyayana-niyama*)—even though not enjoined by a specific ritual context (*anārabhya-vihita*)—should produce a contradiction with the fruit and the ritual action through the knowledge generated by study. However, because this restriction is determined by proximity (*saṃnidhi*) as being enjoined by implication (*sāmarthya*) since it serves as the knowledge required for the ritual action brought about by the knowledge produced by study, and because it thus functions as a requirement for the ritual action, one might conclude that at times such as the new moon (*amāvāsya*), when the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras serve as requirements for the ritual action, these mantras should not be recited during the non-study periods. Having raised this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the sūtra: "In the case of mantras connected to a ritual action, their application should be according to their own specific rule (*svadharma*), because that rule is caused by that [connection]" (1|2|13|18), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) will be stated with the following sūtra: "Or rather, because of the injunction regarding knowledge (*vidyā*), there should be application at all times, since the application is for the sake of the ritual action" (19). The reasoning is as follows: Since there is no evidence that what is determined by the context (*prakaraṇa*) as a requirement for study is useless, and since its utility is possible insofar as it serves to complete the study without interruption, it does not function as a requirement for the ritual action. Consequently, at the time of the ritual, one should disregard the rules of study-period and non-study-period, and the recitation of the mantras required for the ritual action must be performed even during the new moon and other such occasions.
Su. Pṛ. 52: Nor do the venerable ritualists declare that there is a fruit [resulting] from the mere recitation of that [Veda].
Even regarding what they do declare, he will state an exception in the sūtra "In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals" (4.1.1).
Bhā. 1.1.1 Pṛ. 6: The injunction for study is an original injunction (apūrvavidhi) and has a visible purpose.

*Bāla.*, p. 22: The author of the *Vārttika* establishes, according to his own view, that the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) itself is the authority for the fact that everything culminates in human goals (*puruṣārtha*). *Su.*, p. 21: The *Vārttika* states as follows: "First of all, with respect to the entire Veda, the injunction of the cultivation of study (*adhyayanabhāvanā*) is prescribed by the text, 'The Veda is to be studied' (*svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ*)."

In this regard, when the expectation arises as to "what should one cultivate (*bhāvayet*)?", although "study" (*adhyayanam*) is already understood, its status as a constituent part of the cultivation is set aside because the injunctive [passage], which possesses the power to impel a person toward an action to be accomplished through an unprecedented result (*apūrva*), would otherwise be rendered incapable of impelling toward that cultivation.
Consequently, due to the contradiction with the word "study" and because of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), it is integrated into the ritual action.
When the expectation "by means of what? arises, the text reads "the grasping of syllables" (*akṣaragrahaṇam*), based on the supplementary rule "that which is possible."

"Since that [injunction] also has as its object something not previously known (*apūrvārtha*), the expectation 'What is achieved by that? arises, and thus the determination of the action (*kriyā*) presents itself. Through that [action], there is the knowledge of the word-meaning; through that, the knowledge of the sentence-meaning; through that, the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*); and through the performance, the attainment of heaven and so forth. When this much has been reached, the injunction becomes free of further expectancy. (Vārttika 1.2.1.7, p. 23). Thus, since the injunction for study requires an agent and takes only those who have been initiated (*upanīta*) as agents because of the requirement for a task to be performed, the knowledge of the meaning produced by the study prompted by the injunction for study is established only for members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*).

*Maṇi*, p. 4: The injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) applies only to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), not to the *śūdra*. *Vi.* 6.1.7: The injunction for study is intended to establish a restrictive rule regarding study, similar to the rules governing the acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*) and so forth.

Its purposefulness (*sāphalya*) is established by the assumption that one would incur sin (*pratyaveyāt*) if, while ignorant of the prohibition, one were to perform the very act of study that is prohibited.
Thus say the venerable teachers (the *Pitṛcaraṇas*).

On page 3 of the *Maṇi*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section on the inquiry into the nature of Brahman (*jijñāsādhikaraṇa*) is that the injunction for Vedic study has heaven as its purpose, according to the logic of the Viśvajit sacrifice.

This is because when a visible result is possible, there is no room for the postulation of an invisible one; thus, even though the comprehension of the meaning [of the texts] is a visible result, it is justified as being itself an invisible result [in this context].
Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Bāla. pṛ. 2. Regarding the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), "The Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied," some maintain that it culminates merely in the apprehension of the syllables. [However, others hold] that this study is enjoined for the sake of a visible purpose consisting in the knowledge of the meaning.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the meaning does not arise without inquiry;
therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the injunction (*vidhi*) is the motivator for the treatise on inquiry (Vi.
1.1.1). By the injunction for study, the rule that the Veda must be acquired through the act of study itself has been stated.

Su. Pṛ. 690: The visible purpose (*dṛṣṭa-prayojana*) of the injunction to study is the comprehension of the meaning; however, if it were for the sake of merely grasping the syllables, it would have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*). Kaṇikā Pṛ. 271: The fruit of the injunction to study consists of residing in the teacher’s house until the comprehension of the meaning is attained, as well as the performance of inquiry.

*Maṇi*, p. 4: This restriction of eligibility—that only those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) who have studied the Vedas are entitled to perform the *agnihotra* and other rites, whereas *śūdras* who have not studied the Vedas are not—is the purpose of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*).

*Jñāna*, p. 6: Bhavadeva maintains that the injunction for Vedic study indicates the *svādhyāya* (one's own Veda) as the object by means of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), which denotes a subordinate quality (*guṇa*); otherwise, there would be the fault of "dissimilarity" (*vairūpya*) in the injunction of a quality regarding the *svādhyāya*, just as in the case of the *vājapeya* sentence where it is an injunction of a quality regarding the sacrifice (*yāga*).
In this regard: "When the literal meaning of a heard sentence is subject to the assumption of [words] being deficient or excessive..."

"However, this fault—such as the presence of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) or the splitting of the sentence (vākyabheda)—does not apply when [the word] is interpreted [in its primary sense]," because it is resolved by the principle stated in the Vārttika. Bālapriyā, p. 2.
Study is impelled by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), not by the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana-vidhi*).

For when there is a requirement for a purpose regarding the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*)—which is impelled by the injunction for becoming an Ācārya—the attainment of that [Ācārya-status] itself is rightly considered its purpose, even though it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), because it is the first to arise; the knowledge of the meaning, however, is not, because it occurs later.
Therefore, since the Veda would otherwise be purposeless, the meaning is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*).
And that which is not intended to be expressed has its meaning already established, due to the absence of a purpose.
Furthermore, since there is no need for a definitive conclusion regarding what is not to be done, there can be no inquiry; thus, the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra would be useless and should not be commenced.

How is it that study is prompted by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) and not prompted by its own injunction? It is said: in the injunction regarding the Veda-study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), there is no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), and in the absence of such a person [the injunction lacks force].
It is not logical for [the self] to be the instigator, as in the case of the injunctions regarding the *prajāda* and so forth.

For it is not possible for that which lacks a specific qualification (*adhikāra*) to be an instigator of the performance of an object of injunction, as is the case with the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Furthermore, no one qualified for the injunction regarding the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) is explicitly heard [in this context].
Therefore, its status as an instigator is not possible.
Nor can it be enjoined as something to be conceptualized, like the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña);
for even when that [conceptualization] is not performed, the performance [of the rite] is nonetheless accomplished.
It might be argued that even though the person to be enjoined (niyojya) is not explicitly heard in the text, he is to be inferred, as in the case of the Pitṛyajña and similar rites.
That is not so;
for the performance of the rite is established even without inferring such a person to be enjoined.

And once that [obligation] is established, it is possible to postulate [the injunction], because there is no logical inconsistency; for an injunction (*niyoga*) is dependent upon performance, and in order to establish that [injunction], it implies a performer, since it is impossible for one who lacks qualification to be a performer, and for one who is not subject to an injunction,
[the activity] is prompted by the injunction to study.

Although it is possible that [the initiation] was prompted by the injunction for Vedic study even prior [to the age of eight], nevertheless, for fear of uncertainty regarding the time of study, it will be performed only later.
Enough of going too far.
It is established, then, that one who desires knowledge of the meaning is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) with respect to study.

However, it will be explained immediately hereafter that such a person cannot possibly be the one enjoined in the act of teaching, because the teacher’s status as such is not understood even in a general sense prior to the performance of the means [of teaching].
Furthermore, being produced by an injunction (*niyoga*) is a qualification of the person to be enjoined.
It is not logical that the cognition of the object be the same even when [the object] is with the teacher.

For it is only that which is the fruit of the *niyoga* (the injunction) that is capable of defining the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) by virtue of being desired, as in the case of liberation and so forth.

Knowledge, however, is the fruit of the study that constitutes its object; it is not produced by the *niyoga*. Therefore, if it is argued that one who desires that [knowledge] cannot be the person to be enjoined, then for that very same reason, the status of being a teacher (*ācāryaka*) would also not be a qualification of the person to be enjoined, since that too is a fruit of the object [of the injunction]. Furthermore, desire arises toward a beloved thing only when it is known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
But the status of being a teacher (ācāryatva) is not known through any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

It is your view that the status of being a teacher—which, like the Āhavanīya fire and so forth, is not apprehended by any other means of knowledge—is understood solely from the scriptural injunction enjoining the act of teaching;
and since a desire for something cannot arise regarding what is unknown, it is impossible for one who desires that [status] to be the person enjoined (niyojya).
But if, by this very statement, one were to understand that "it is desired" and thus rely on that [as the basis], there would arise the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).

For it is only when the injunction (*vidhi*) operates with reference to that which is already established as being desired that the determination of "one who desires that" occurs once this injunction has been set in motion.

It might be argued: "Performance is enjoined by virtue of the qualification (*adhikāra*), and that [qualification] exists here as well. Even though this [person] is a *niyojya* (the one to be directed), that [qualification] is indeed the direct means [to the performance].

For being a *niyojya* is with respect to the *niyoga* (the injunction); it is not the direct means for the performance of the object [of the injunction], but rather, the *niyoga* becomes something to be performed for that person who is connected to it by way of being a *niyojya*.
For he alone is the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) who understands the injunction as "this is my duty.

And for one to whom an injunction is to be performed, there arises an entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the action that accomplishes it, because that action is the means to accomplish his own duty; from this entitlement follows performance.

But where an entitlement is understood to exist even without the status of being the person to be enjoined, then since the accomplishment of performance results from that very entitlement, what is the use of the status of being the person to be enjoined?
Furthermore, there exists an entitlement (*adhikāra*) regarding teaching, because it is a means for becoming an *ācārya*.
Since this statement establishes that [teaching] is a means for becoming an *ācārya*, the performance of the act is accomplished through the acquisition of wealth for that purpose.

It is precisely by means of the study (*adhyayana*) implied by that [teaching] that the injunction of study (*adhyayananiyoga*), having attained its own nature, does not require the postulation of a further person entitled to perform it (*niyojya*).
In that case, since the non-performance of one's duty is already established by the fact that study [is mandatory],
the argumentative formulation that study is prompted by teaching is useless.

Even in the absence of being subject to an injunction (*viniyojyatva*), since the performance of study for the sake of that [knowledge] is established by the very fact of one's entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the means of attaining knowledge of the meaning, it is untenable to claim that study is prompted by the act of teaching.
Furthermore, you yourselves also accept that there is indeed an entitlement (*adhikāra*) regarding study; you simply do not accept the status of being subject to an injunction (*niyojyatva*).

The performance [of an action] cannot, on that account alone, be said to be prompted by an external injunction (*niyoga*), because the performance is obtained solely from one's own qualification (*adhikāra*).

Furthermore, even when there is a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) regarding an action that is a means to a result, the performance proceeds from that very qualification, not from the injunction itself, as is the case in the context of optional rites (*kāmyādhikāra*).
And since a result is capable of impelling the performance of the means even in the absence of a person to be enjoined, what is the use of investigating the existence of a *niyojya*?

However, in cases such as the Viśvajit sacrifice, where the attainment of the fruit is dependent solely upon the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), there may indeed be a requirement for such a person. But here, even without a person to be enjoined, study is understood as a means to the knowledge of meaning; since the performance [of study] is thus established by that very fact, it is impossible for study to be prompted by teaching.
Consequently: "The lack of being a motivator (*aprayojakatā*) is equal for both because of the absence of a person to be enjoined;
the status of being a prompter (*prayoktṛtva*) through entitlement (*adhikāra*) is likewise the same for both."

If, due to the absence of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*), the injunction to teach (*adhyāpana*) is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the subject matter of study (*adhyayana*), then, for that same reason—the absence of such a person—the injunction to study would also fail to be a motivator. Alternatively, if its status as a motivator is established because of the existence of a qualified person (*adhikāra*), then it is equally logical that the injunction to study is also a motivator due to the existence of that same qualified person. Since both are thus equal, the injunction to teach cannot be the cause of the study. Furthermore, the injunction to study is not motivated by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryaka*).
But that [prohibition] applies to the study of that [Veda] by virtue of one's own specific qualification.
The status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*), which is accomplished by teaching, may imply mere study, but not inquiry (*vicāra*), since the attainment of study is possible even without inquiry.
Therefore, when the qualification for Vedic rites produced by study can be established even without inquiry, the assumption that inquiry is required is abandoned.
In the same way, since the prompting of study itself is possible through that [qualification], no other prompter need be sought.

For by that knowledge of the meaning which serves as the fruit, the deliberation (*vicāra*), acting as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), is employed; and by that [deliberation], the study (*adhyayana*), acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*), is all the more employed.
Now, it might be argued that [the study] is prompted by the injunctions for teaching (*adhyāpana*) and studying (*adhyayana*).

The very injunction that impels the rule of study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is also the motivator for inquiry (*vicāra*); for that [injunction], while enjoining instruction after study for the sake of a specific purpose, impels such a study in order to accomplish that [purpose]. Since such [instruction] is not possible for study without inquiry, it is implied by that very [injunction].
This is incorrect, if that [injunction] pertains to a specific study.
It impels the performance [of action], because knowledge is not a subordinate factor [in that regard].

Although the injunction for teaching, by means of initiating [the student] (*upanayana*), prompts the study—and since it occurs after the initiation has begun, it prompts the performance of that very study which was not itself enjoined by the sentence [but is understood as] being for the sake of knowing the meaning—nevertheless, it prompts only the mere form [of the study] because of its utility; however, it should not be the case that the injunction for knowing the meaning must likewise prompt [the study] in that same way.
No, because the performance [of the study] is already obtained through the purpose [itself].
An entitlement is required for the sake of performance;
however, once that has been obtained, there is no basis for requiring it further.
It might be argued: "The injunction for study exists solely for the sake of entitlement, because it is an injunction, like the injunctions concerning the Agnihotra and other sacrifices."
That is incorrect.

The injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) does not have an *adhikāra* (qualification/entitlement) as its object of prescription, because it possesses its own essential nature even in the absence of such an *adhikāra*. That which acquires its own existence even in the absence of something else cannot be an injunction for that thing; it is like an occasional injunction (*naimittika-vidhi*) or an injunction for a result (*phala-vidhi*). This is because there exists a counter-reason (*pratihetu*). Furthermore, if one were to postulate an *adhikāra* on the grounds that it is seen elsewhere even when there is no logical necessity, then since it is seen in optional rites (*kāmya*) to extend up to the result, it would likewise extend up to the result in the case of occasional and prohibitory injunctions as well; yet this is not accepted here.

Therefore, the qualification for study is not established. Now, if it is argued that even though the subject matter is not the primary intent, the knowledge of the meaning is accepted as a visible purpose—alas, since the study, being perceived as teaching, does not intend the meaning when it is not the primary intent, and since what is not intended is unfit for investigation, the scripture would become meaningless. Even if it were somehow investigated, the investigation could not be established as mandatory (*vaidha*), because the injunction (*vidhi*) is not directed toward that end.
Furthermore, that which is non-Vedic cannot invalidate a Vedic injunction regarding ritual bathing (*snāna*).

If one were to hold that meditation (*dhyāna*)—which culminates in the knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*)—is what brings about the performance of the injunction, then, because the knowledge of the meaning would be dependent on such meditation, the injunction for bathing would indeed be set aside by it. However, when the injunction is fulfilled by the mere act of study (*adhyayana*) itself, then the injunction does not imply the necessity of performance through investigation (*vicāra*), as it is already accomplished by its own nature.

If, for the sake of performing subsequent rites, a person were to act according to his own will by employing worldly means—such as the words of teachers and so forth—for the purpose of acquiring knowledge of the meaning, he might occasionally engage in inquiry; and if that were the case, then when the performance of the rite has arrived and a teacher is found, he would be permitted [to inquire]. Consequently, the performance of the rite would not be established immediately following the completion of Vedic study.

[Objection: Is it not the case that reflection (*vicāra*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the study (*adhyayana*)? And since an injunction (*vidhi*) is not established by means of something that is not an auxiliary, the injunction itself, for the sake of its own fulfillment, must cause the performance of reflection; how then can reflection be considered non-obligatory (*aidhatva*)? [Reply: It is true that reflection is [an auxiliary] to the study; nevertheless, it is not employed for the establishment of the injunction, because it lacks connection with the primary purpose (*kārya*), such as the knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*). Nor is an auxiliary that serves one purpose ever employed for another purpose—even if that other purpose shares the same instrument (*ekakaraṇaka*)—as is seen in the case where the *ūrdhvabhr̥t* (the upward-moving ladle) is not employed for the *apūrva* of teaching, even though it is an auxiliary to the *saubhara* chant which is performed by one desiring rain (*dṛṣṭikāma*) or desiring a son (*putrakāma*).

Now, if it is argued that because the study of the knowledge of the meaning of injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*vidhāra*) is mandatory, it necessarily implies an inquiry (*vicāra*) into such matters through contact with the fire of the Veda—this has already been refuted by us who reject the inquiry as being enjoined by the injunction for study (*adhyāpana-vidhi*).

Even if this [study] is for the sake of knowing the meaning, nevertheless, it does not possess the status of being a means to the injunction in that specific form; rather, it is a means to it only in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
An injunction implies the performance of only that without which the injunction itself would not be accomplished, and not anything else.

Although an injunction cannot be established without investigation (*vicāra*), nevertheless, it does not necessitate the performance of that investigation, because there is no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
For such an injunction is not perceived by any person as "this is my duty"; therefore, it would not even impel one toward its own realization, let alone toward the means for its accomplishment.
For this very reason, its capacity to induce performance is not established even in the case of Vedic study (*adhyayana*).
For how could that which lacks the capacity to impel performance—because there is no person to be enjoined even when it itself is being performed—possibly possess such capacity in other cases?
Therefore, the mandatory nature (*vaidhatva*) of inquiry is not established.

It might be argued as follows: the injunction for study itself, having understood from the context that the knowledge of meaning is the purpose of study and having accepted that as its goal, implies inquiry for the sake of achieving that [knowledge].
That is incorrect.
What is the meaning of the claim that the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) accepts the knowledge of the meaning—which is already known through implication—as its purpose?

It does not, first of all, enjoin it here, because the means of achieving that [knowledge] is already understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because it is not understood as being like the injunctions for threshing and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that its being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is "permitted" (*anumanyate*), then since that being for that purpose is obtained even without permission, this is laughable: namely, that whatever is obtained even in the absence of permission is what is permitted. And since the fact that study has the purpose of knowing the meaning is obtained even without an injunction, what is the point of permission?

Therefore, since the mandatory nature (*vaidhatva*) of inquiry cannot be established in any way, one cannot effect the postponement of the ritual bath (*snāna*) on the strength of that [mandatory nature]. Since the requirement is fulfilled by mere study alone, once the performance of rituals such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* has presented itself immediately after—following the force of the Smṛti rule, "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe"—and since no other means for its determination is available, the inquiry might not even be undertaken at all. Thus, the Sūtra "Therefore, then, the desire to know Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) would not be tenable as a statement intended to establish immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

Therefore, study is not enjoined by the injunction for teaching. Teaching is the injunction regarding the [Vedic] sections (*kakṣā*), even though it is study. As it is said: "Having initiated the pupil, one should teach him the Veda."
They declare him to be an Ācārya who possesses both the complete ritual manual (sakalya) and the secret doctrine (sarahasya).
The claim that there is a scriptural injunction of this form— "one should conceive of the teacher as such through the teaching of the *upanaya* brought forward by the *smṛti*"— is incorrect;
for this sentence is not capable of enjoining the act of teaching,
because it is already established by the desire for wealth (*dravyārthitva*) and because it is connected with the word [of the *smṛti*].

Just as in the case of the injunction "One desiring food should cause [him] to sacrifice with this [offering]," where the injunction heard subsequent to the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) is itself the injunction of the sacrifice—being a word directed toward the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*) and serving as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the activity already established for the purpose of acquiring wealth—so too, the injunction "one should teach" (*adhyāpayet*) is an injunction of study (*adhyayana*) alone, not an injunction of teaching (*adhyāpana*); for [teaching] is already established as a means of acquiring wealth.
Furthermore, initiation (*upanayana*) is solely for the purpose of study, since it is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the student.
By this very [principle], the statement "one should cause a Brāhmaṇa to teach" and "one should initiate him and then cause him to teach" is explained.
Now, one might object: since the Ātmanepada ending is heard in the case of initiation (*upanayana*) there, its status as an act performed for the agent's own sake (*ātmārthatva*) is understood.
This is not so; for the prescription of the Ātmanepada suffix in the context of teaching is due to its not being intended for the benefit of the agent (*akartrabhiprāyatva*).

Otherwise, since the Ātmanepada would already be established for the accomplishment of the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*) by the rule *asvaritatriṭaḥ* itself, the sūtra *samānanapūrva* would be purposeless. Accordingly, they say: "The restatement is for the sake of [indicating] that the result does not accrue to the agent. Therefore, initiation (*upanayana*), as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to Vedic study, accomplishes the status of a teacher through the mediation of the refinement of the student; it does not exist for the sake of that [status] itself. Rather, like the curdling of milk (*dadhi*) in the case of the sprinkling of the whey (*vājina*), it brings about the status of a teacher as a byproduct.

Therefore, there is no statement enjoining teaching as a duty of the Ācārya. Furthermore, the word *ācārya* is not merely for some non-worldly purpose; it is the designator of one who, having initiated [a pupil], teaches him the Veda—just like the words *pāṭhaka* and so forth.
Even the verse beginning with "But he who, having initiated the pupil... is solely intended to explain the meaning of the word.

Therefore, since [the person] does not exist [as a qualified agent], the injunction for teaching is not applicable here; thus, study is joined with this [injunction]. Furthermore, even if teaching were enjoined as a subordinate element of either [study or reflection]—on account of the inclusion of injunctions such as "One who desires good memory studies grammar" and "He teaches"—nevertheless, because no person to be directed (*niyojya*) is heard in all those cases, and because the mere qualification (*adhikāra*) exists even in the case of study, reflection is not mandatory; thus, study is joined with the injunction for the injunction of teaching.

Someone else, however, says: even if it is possible for study to be prompted by its own specific qualification (*adhikāra*), nevertheless, that [qualification] is not logically tenable as a basis. For instance, knowledge is not, by its own power, the prompter of study;
rather, it is the *agnihotra* and other such rites which, through that [knowledge], act as the prompter.

Indeed, partial knowledge cannot itself be the motivator for study, because it is not in itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). However, rites such as the *agnihotra*—which are to be accomplished through knowledge—become motivators by means of that knowledge; yet even for them, knowledge is merely an auxiliary (*upakāra*), not the primary goal.

But in the case of the status of a teacher (*ācāryatva*), which consists precisely in teaching, it obtains the status of a motivator even through its own constituent part [the desire for wealth], whereas rites like the *agnihotra* obtain it through the medium of being an auxiliary.

Moreover, when the status of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) is already established through the door of the subsidiary (*aṅga*), it is not proper to accept its status as a motivator through the door of providing assistance (*upakāraka*), as in the case of the *vājina* offering; therefore, the study is governed by the injunction of teaching.
That is incorrect, for even though...
Knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual actions; rather, study is considered an auxiliary part of knowledge.
This [knowledge] is not an auxiliary part of teaching; therefore, it is employed for that purpose.

Even though knowledge (*jñāna*) is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to ritual action, study (*adhyayana*), however, is indeed an auxiliary to knowledge; therefore, study as employed by that [knowledge] is precisely what is connected to the injunction of being an auxiliary (*śeṣavidhiyukta*). Study is not an auxiliary to the act of teaching; thus, study prompted by that [teaching] would be prompted merely by the beneficiary (*upakārya*), and not connected to the injunction of being an auxiliary. Consequently, since it is possible for it to be connected to the injunction of being an auxiliary, the claim that it is prompted merely by the beneficiary is refuted; thus, study enjoined by the *sūtra*’s qualification (*adhikāra*) is not prompted by the act of teaching.

Although knowledge is not an end-in-itself (*apuruṣārtha*) by its very nature, it nevertheless serves as an end-in-itself because it is instrumental to the performance of ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*). Thus, since it is an end-in-itself, study can have knowledge as its purpose, just as the status of being a teacher (*ācāryatva*) does.
For that [status of being a teacher] is not desired for its own sake, but is sought by a person solely for the sake of obtaining the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Therefore, just as that [status] functions as a motivator (*prayojaka*), so too does knowledge.

The rule is that the purpose is the motivator (*prayojaka*) by virtue of its being easily accessible in its own nature; for there is no contradiction in the fact that what is desired as a means to another result—such as the state of being a knower or the status of a *paśu* (sacrificial animal)—acts as the motivator. Although it may be argued that the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the *agnihotra* and other rites is the motivator through the medium of knowledge, nevertheless, that alone is logical, not teaching (*adhyāpana*), because teaching resides in another person. Rather, it is logical that either the knowledge residing in the student or the means thereto, such as the *agnihotra*, is the motivator of study (*adhyayana*).

Furthermore, the distinction that was asserted—that the injunction to teach functions as the motivator (*prayojaka*) by way of the limbs (*aṅga*), whereas the *agnihotra* and other rites do so by way of being beneficial (*upakāraka*)—is not valid even in sixteen ways.
For in both cases, the fact that they benefit the sacrifice (*yajña*) is precisely the means (*dvāra*).
To explain:
Knowledge, because it assists the Agnihotra, prompts the study [of the Veda] since it is delimited by that [Agnihotra].

The status of being a teacher (ācāryaka), however, because it consists in the teaching of the Agnihotra, prompts the act of teaching. The status of being a teacher, moreover, because it consists in the teaching of the Agnihotra, prompts the act of teaching.
The status of being a teacher (*ācāryaka*), however, prompts the act of teaching because it consists in the teaching of the *agnihotra* and other rites; thus,
the teacher is prompted by the injunction to study.
How could the performance [of study] be prompted by the injunction for study? For a conscious being does not engage in anything other than that which accomplishes its own purpose.

If it is argued that the teacher alone, for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose, impels the student toward study by demonstrating his own entitlement—just as in the case of a messenger—and acts as the prompter of the performance therein, [we reply:

[The opponent] says: "The teacher himself, for the sake of achieving his own task, prompts [the student] toward study by demonstrating his own entitlement, just as a messenger [is prompted] by the master."

This is true; however, even so, one's own entitlement (*svādhikāra*) alone is the motivator (*prayojaka*) in that case. For the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), as established [in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra*], is based precisely on one's own entitlement. Indeed, although that [injunction] pertains to an entitlement belonging to one who is ignorant of the [Vedic] origin, it is nonetheless motivated by one's own entitlement—not by the acquisition of wealth—since it is performed by a Niṣāda through the demonstration of entitlement by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Study (*adhyayana*) is likewise [motivated by entitlement]. [In the] prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it would not be possible to demonstrate one's own entitlement.
Therefore, the fact that [the study] is prompted by the act of teaching is not established therein.
Or, let it be granted that for the boy who is being made to perform the study by the teacher—even while the teacher perceives his own entitlement—the study is prompted by the act of teaching.
Even this, however, is not possible under the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position.

In that case, there is no entitlement whatsoever for the boy; even if he were to be taught through the act of study, it would serve no purpose other than the accomplishment of the teacher's status, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

[Objection: But surely, by means of the accomplishment of the injunction (*niyoga*), an entitlement is possible even in the prima facie view. [Reply: No, because it is not something to be performed. For the injunction is not something to be performed by the boy.

By means of which [accomplishment] there could be entitlement (*adhikāra*), since there is no injunction (*niyoga*). For that which is not subject to an injunction cannot be an object of action. Therefore, through the accomplishment of that [injunction], the possibility of entitlement does not arise.

Now, even in this case [of the Viśvajit], if one were somehow to teach the Sāman and other elements within its own sphere of authority (*svādhikāra*), then, since the performance would be possible through the very priests engaged in the Viśvajit and other rites who have been so taught, it would not be necessary to postulate a person to be enjoined for the sake of establishing the qualification (*adhikāra*) in order to accomplish the performance. Alternatively, if it is argued that the priests, fearing futility, urge the sacrificer on—thinking "he is not qualified, yet he gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to them"—then that same logic applies here as well.

For when a boy is being authorized for study, he does not exclude the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth intended for the teacher; thus, that which belongs to the teacher is not desired by him. Nor is anything useless desired by a person in its own right. Furthermore, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the study belongs to the boy, and therefore an impulsion (*prayukti*) toward it by means of the study is not possible.
The statement of that [which is] unique to the [Vedic] position is intended by you [to be the definition of knowledge];
even such passages as "By the gift of knowledge, one becomes wise" (Sumati) refer to the knowledge of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
Otherwise, even the giving of knowledge regarding worldly matters or the meaning of secular treatises would lead to the world of Brahmā.

Furthermore, since study does not have human purpose as its goal according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is not possible for that [study] to be prompted by the injunction to impart knowledge which has the attainment of the world of Brahman as its fruit. Thus, it is established that study is not prompted by the injunction to study; therefore, the prima facie position is not tenable. As for the inquiry—namely, whether the purpose of study is the service of the teacher or the knowledge of the meaning—that too has already been addressed.

Is this inquiry concerning a purpose that is accessible through scriptural injunction (*vidhi*), or one accessible through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? First of all, that which is accessible solely through other means of valid cognition is not to be investigated in the treatise.
Since both [types of purposes] are accessible through other means of valid cognition, there is no occasion for such an inquiry. Nor is it [accessible] through scriptural injunction...
Only those who possess the knowledge acquired through Vedic study—accompanied by the procedural requirements such as the observance of vows and so forth—are entitled to perform subsequent rites.
This being the case, it does not follow that Vedic study exists solely for the sake of ritual action (*kratvartha*).
This point, first of all, is exactly the same for us and for the partisan of the *ekadeśin* (the partialist).
However, there is a dispute as to whether study is impelled by its own injunction (*svavidhi*) or by the injunction regarding the status of being a teacher (*ācāryakavidhi*).

Consequently, since it is not understood within a specific ritual context (*aprakaraṇa*), the prescription of study is for the sake of knowledge already acquired, which would make it for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*); rather, it is the knowledge produced by study that is for the sake of the ritual (*kṛtvartha*).
Thus it is established that, because it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), the purpose of the injunction is distinct from [the mere acquisition of] knowledge.
For it is precisely because of the attainment of purpose that the study [of the Veda] is established as having a purpose.

But how can the study of those parts consisting of meaningless sounds such as *huṃ* and *phaṭ* have a purpose? And how can there be a study by Brāhmaṇas and others for the sake of studying that portion of the Veda which prescribes the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice and other rites for which Kṣatriyas are the qualified performers? Even if one could somehow imagine that their study is for the sake of the knowledge required for officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*), nevertheless, the study by Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas of the *Vaiśyastoma*, the *Aśvamedha*, and so forth, would be either purposeless or for the sake of mere recitation.
And how is there a restrictive purpose (*niyamārthatva*) in prohibitive statements such as "one should not study during the *anugraha* [period], nor during the *natithya* [period]," and so forth?
If, first of all, the commencement of study were prompted by the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*).

An inquiry into the injunction for Vedic study can be undertaken; this [injunction] is declared for that purpose. Furthermore, by means of it, the meaning of words can be expressed, and it can be understood at the time of ritual performance. Therefore, these meanings of words are to be learned and are to be understood at the time of performing the ritual.
And no distinction is perceived to be enjoined; it is merely designated, not intended for comprehension.
Since no distinction is apprehended, it is understood that it may be adopted in either way.
In that case, it can be comprehended through this sequence and not by any other.

(There are many textual variations here. However, where a mantra is enjoined, because it serves another purpose [namely, recitation], and because the injunctive [Brāhmaṇa] statement has already fulfilled its function through the act of enjoining, the mantra alone possesses the primary authority. For this very reason, in those cases, the performance of ritual acts follows the sequence of the mantra and not the sequence of the injunction; there, the sequence of the Brāhmaṇa is utilized for purposes such as silent recitation (*japa*) and offerings of milk (*payas*). Likewise, even for those [passages] that set forth what possesses a fruit, they are employed according to the detailed sequence of that which possesses the fruit.

And even though that [Vedic study] has a visible purpose, because the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) does not have that as its sole purpose and thus lacks futility, it is understood to be for the sake of knowing the meaning.

Nor is there this rule that an injunction must be a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) only when it serves a transcendental purpose (*apūrva*), since restrictive injunctions are accepted even in cases such as knowledge and so forth, which serve human ends (*puruṣārtha*).
Therefore, in this case, it is indeed a restrictive injunction.
Indeed, for this very reason, those learned in logic speak according to the principle previously stated:
therefore, for one who has the recitation (*japa*) as his ultimate goal, the study of the Veda has its purpose already accomplished;
for this reason alone, it is obligatory (*nitya*).

This is because the entitlement to ritual action (*karmādhikāra*), which is the fruit of that [study], is indispensable; for in its absence, there is transgression (*pratyavāya*) due to the non-performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*).
Furthermore, since the study of the entire Veda is mandatory and serves as the ultimate refuge, it is indeed essential for the sake of its application.

And likewise, they record in the Smṛtis that there is eligibility for the Kṣudras, just as there is for one who has not studied the Vedas: "The twice-born who, without having studied the Vedas, exerts himself in other [pursuits], quickly falls into the state of a Kṣudra while still living, along with his lineage.
He is born equal to a Kṣudra and does not attain the Veda."
By such statements as these,

it is established that since the purpose of Vedic study is the knowledge of its meaning, and since that knowledge is impossible without inquiry, the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) must be undertaken immediately thereafter.
This has been set forth by the illustrious Jñānamitra, relying upon the opinion of the Teacher (Ācārya).
Pārthasārathi Miśra has composed the *Prayuktitalaka*,

which contains an investigation into the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*). Now, regarding the sequence beginning with the acquisition of syllables, Vedic study is enjoined for the purpose of attaining the knowledge of the meaning of sentences that arises through such a process.

Since that [study] is impossible without reflection (*vicāra*), reflection is effectively enjoined by the injunction for study itself; thus, one must remain in the teacher’s house and reflect upon *dharma*.

In this regard: "Even without an injunction, the acquisition of knowledge occurs here; therefore, its purpose [is established]. However, by the force of the injunction, heaven is to be postulated as the result, just as in the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice."

The discussion on the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) [proceeds] even without an injunction [explicitly stating] that study has its purpose through the medium of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*).
The discussion on the injunction for study.

Since that [Smṛti] is untenable, it is established that the injunction for Vedic study, by implying the necessity of inquiry, sublates the Smṛti knowledge which is contrary to it; thus, it is proven that after Vedic study, the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) must be undertaken.
(Śābarabhāṣya 2.1.1, pp. 5–7).
This concludes the discussion on the injunction for Vedic study.
The injunction for study, "One's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ*), is intended for the sake of knowing the meaning of the Vedas;
for in this injunction, the suffix *-tavya* denotes the object (*karman*).

An object may be that which is to be produced (*utpādya*), that which is to be attained (*āpya*), or that which is to be refined (*saṃskārya*), as in the examples: "He makes a jar," "He goes to the village," and "He sprinkles the rice-grains."
And according to the principle of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* (2.1.1, second exposition), study (*adhyayana*) connects as the instrument (*karaṇa*) within the efficient force (*bhāvanā*).

Since it is possible for the Veda (*svādhyāya*) to be produced by that [study], its status as an object (*karman*) consists in being either something to be attained (*āpyatva*) or something to be refined (*saṃskārya*). Consequently, the verbal formulation is either "one should attain the Veda through study" or "one should refine the Veda through study."

In this regard, since the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*)—whether unmastered or mastered through recitation—is inherently devoid of purpose, when there arises a desire for a result, the comprehension of dharma produced by the learned Veda is taken as the result because it serves as a means to heaven and other ends; and since it is improper to postulate an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) when a visible purpose is possible, one concludes that the mastery of the studied Veda has as its result precisely that purposeful comprehension of meaning, for even for one who has merely memorized the text, the study is capable of being employed toward the requirements of ritual knowledge by the very force of its own efficacy.
Consequently, the final meaning established is: "One should bring about the comprehension of the meaning by means of the studied Veda.

In this regard, although the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) lack the capacity to produce the valid cognition of *dharma* through their literal mode of expression (*vācyavidhayā*), it is established in the *Vārttika* and other treatises that the entire Veda culminates in the comprehension of a purposeful meaning; thus, the status of the Veda as a source of authority for *dharma* is justified because the injunction to study itself, by way of providing the excellence required by the injunction, functions through an implied mode (*lakṣyavidhayā*) that conveys the [meaning] by means of presenting [the *arthavādas*].

In reality, however, the injunction for self-study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) has as its purpose the acquisition [of the Veda] in the form of retaining the sequence of syllables. The comprehension of the meaning, on the other hand, occurs spontaneously once the connection between words has been grasped; the injunction for study has no operation therein. Furthermore, the comprehension of *dharma* would otherwise result in partiality, since it would be useless for a Brāhmaṇa to study the mantras and Brāhmaṇas pertaining to royal duties, given his lack of sovereignty.

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda characterized by the Agnihotra and other rites: since this knowledge exists prior to the study [of the Veda] through the instruction of a father or others—just like the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana)—it cannot be a fruit because, being already known, it lacks the quality of being something desirable to be attained. Moreover, if that knowledge were to exist prior [to the study], it could not be desired, because desire necessarily arises only toward what is already known.
Now, it might be argued: "When an object is known in a general way but remains unknown in its specific details, a desire for that [knowledge] is possible;

even when the specific details have been understood through the instruction of a father or others, such a desire is appropriate both because of a doubt regarding the validity of that instructional knowledge and because of a wish to understand further. This is not so.

For regarding the specific cognitions of the *agnihotra* and other such rites, there can first of all be no reference (*uddeśa*) to them by way of a single cognition in their specific forms, because they are infinite in number. And if they were referred to by way of a general form, then the fruit of the injunction would be the general cognition itself, rather than the specific cognition.
Therefore, since it is impossible for the comprehension of meaning to be the object of reference, it cannot be the fruit [of the injunction].

Nor should it be argued that if the injunction for study does not culminate in the comprehension of meaning, how could the Veda possess the capacity for intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding its own meaning;
for that is possible through the power of the words themselves as aided by [contextual factors] such as the introduction (*upakrama*).
Therefore, the injunction for study has as its fruit merely the acquisition of the syllables.
And likewise, there are the aphorisms of the *Puruṣārthānuśāsana* which reveal the Vedas: "If [the goal] ends with awakening, there is no further desire for study";
"He is free from desire; he attains [it] whether [the world] appears or does not appear";
"And because of the impossibility of [further] enunciation," and so forth.

And thus, in the *Paspaśāhnika* of the *Vyākaraṇa-mahābhāṣya*, in such passages as "The Veda, together with its six limbs, should be studied and known by a Brahmin without [any specific] motive" (*niṣkāraṇaḥ*), the separate injunction to know (*jñeyaśca*) found even in the Śruti becomes meaningful. However, if the injunction to study were to terminate in mere comprehension (*bodha*), then that [separate injunction to know] would indeed be purposeless.
"Without motive" (*niṣkāraṇaḥ*): a "motive" (*kāraṇa*) is that by which something is caused; it is the fruit (*phala*).
The Veda, which is independent of any visible purpose and accompanied by the grasping of words such as grammar and phonetics, is to be acquired through study and its meaning is to be understood.

This very *dharma* has no visible fruit; that is to say, it is obligatory (*nitya*). For it is recorded in the Smṛti that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in its absence: "He who, having studied the Veda, does not know its meaning, is indeed a mere pillar, a bearer of burdens," and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that the injunction [to study] is purposeless because knowledge arises spontaneously for one who has already grasped the connection between words and their meanings. For it is not established by worldly convention that one must have already grasped the connection between words and their meanings before undertaking study, as many instances of unlearned people are observed. Furthermore, even when the connection between words and their meanings is fully grasped, the meaning of the extremely profound Veda cannot be understood without an investigation into logic (*nyāya*).
Therefore, having mastered the connection between words and their meanings, the injunction eternally ordains the proper knowledge of the Vedic meaning through an investigation into logic.

That too refers only to the acquisition of those portions of the Veda that have come down through the sequence of one's own ancestors and so forth, and not to other portions of the Veda, because [if it did], the injunction for private Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) would result in its own meaning becoming redundant.
Thus, the study and the comprehension of the meaning of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) are obligatory (*nitya*).

However, the study and comprehension of other [portions] are merely incidental (*ārthika*), being prompted by the injunctions for specific rituals (*ṛtu-vidhi*); and the injunction for private Vedic study has no jurisdiction over them.

And thus, even in the case of private recitation (*svādhyāya*), the accomplishment of the ritual act is unimpeded through the knowledge of the meaning of that portion of the ritual injunctions with which one is specifically concerned.

That one should reflect upon the Supreme Person is made clear in the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika* on the third [chapter], under the sūtra: "If [the meaning] is unknown, there is no recitation; for one who is ignorant is not prescribed [for the rite]" (3.8.18).

Nor should it be argued that, although the word ‘Veda’ in the injunction for Vedic study—“The Veda is to be studied”—refers only to the text of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) by following its own literal sense, there is no evidence for such a restriction of the word ‘Veda’ in the portion “is to be known” (*jñeya*). For the word ‘Veda,’ which is determined to refer only to the text of the Veda as it occurs in the phrase “is to be studied,” acquires that same restricted meaning here too precisely by virtue of its syntactical connection (*anvaya*) with the word “is to be known. Otherwise, the composition of the *Kalpasūtras* would be purposeful only because the knowledge of the Veda’s meaning is not already mandated by the injunction for Vedic study.

And it has been stated by you in your own opinion: "Because Brāhmaṇas are numerous, because [the Veda] is incomplete in each individual recension (śākhā), because the meaning is difficult to grasp and not accessible to all people, the Teacher, for the sake of providing a clear exposition, composed the Sūtras after reflecting upon ritual action, so that everyone might attain the fruits [of their efforts]. Thus the Kalpa was begun by the Teacher.

Furthermore, how could the injunction for the recollection of the deities expressed by the mantras and the Brāhmaṇas that prescribe their application—found in the *Tāṇḍya*, *Talavakāra*, and other Śākhās, such as: "Whosoever, indeed, performs a sacrifice or teaches with a mantra whose ṛṣi, metre, deity, and Brāhmaṇa [application] are unknown, he falls upon a stump or his vehicle breaks down, he becomes worse off, or he perishes; the metres of another become his; therefore, one should know these in each mantra"—be meaningless if the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda were not essential?

Furthermore, the identification of deities within mantras is easily obtained from works such as the *Ardhānukramaṇikā* composed by Kātyāyana and others, even in the absence of knowledge regarding the meaning of the Vedas.

Moreover, knowledge of the injunctive Brāhmaṇa passages is easily obtained from the Kalpasūtras, because the Kalpasūtras consist of a compilation of injunctive Brāhmaṇa passages found scattered across various recensions.

"One should appoint only one who knows this as the Adhvaryu, not one who does not know this; one should appoint only one who knows this as the Hotṛ, not one who does not know this; one should appoint only one who knows this as the Udgātṛ, not one who does not know this; one should appoint only one who knows this as the Brahman, not one who does not know this"—such passages from the Vājasaneyaka and other recensions, which concern the selection of priests and the like, clearly demonstrate that knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas is indispensable. Who could suggest otherwise?

For this very reason, when the *Kalpasūtras* were composed as a conclusion to the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), why was it not included among those who are qualified for the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas and for ritual action?

Furthermore, in the third and fourth sections (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is raised according to the opinion of Jaimini by the sūtra: "Because it is subordinate, the statement regarding the human goal is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), as Jaimini maintains" (3.4.1.2). This view holds that knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) is a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*) by way of the agent who is subordinate to the action—just like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth—while the scriptural mention of the fruit, "The knower of the Self overcomes grief," is merely an *arthavāda*, similar to the hearing of verses concerning the absence of sin. However, by means of another sūtra, "Because of the injunction for one who possesses that [knowledge]" (3.4.16), a further argument is presented: since the performance of rituals is enjoined for one who has studied the Veda up to the teacher's house and possesses knowledge of the entire meaning of the Veda—as indicated by the scriptural passage "Having studied the Veda up to the teacher's house"—it follows from this indicative mark (*liṅga*) that knowledge of the Self is indeed a subsidiary part of ritual action. Then, establishing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the sūtra, "On account of the teaching concerning the higher [knowledge], that is the view of Bādarāyaṇa himself, because he sees it thus" (3.4.18), the author refutes this by the sūtra, "For one who possesses only the study [of the text]" (3.4.19). This states that in the passage "Having studied the Veda up to the teacher's house," the injunction for ritual action is based on the mere knowledge of the Vedic text, not on the knowledge of its meaning; for if it were based on the knowledge of the meaning, then since ritual action is enjoined for one who knows the meaning of the Veda, how could the knowledge of the Self derived from the Upaniṣads ever be a subsidiary part of ritual action?

However, the knowledge of the meaning [of the Veda] as prompted by the injunctions for rituals is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the ritual because it is merely incidental (*ārthika*), just like the knowledge of the *karma* (the act itself) and so forth in the injunction regarding *vrīhi* rice and other materials.

And thus, since the injunctions for rituals require only that much knowledge of the meaning as is obtained from the portion of the Veda one has studied, it is logical that the knowledge of restrictive rules (*niyama*) contrary to that [knowledge] should be subordinate to the ritual; this was the view held by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa.
This very point has been elaborated in many ways in the *Bhāṣya* by the venerable Śaṅkarapāda and by his commentators such as Ācārya Vācaspati and others, and therefore it is not expanded upon here.

Furthermore, having begun with "Because of the rule regarding the Pravargya in the first sacrifice; because of the rule regarding the Pravargya at the beginning," the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* cited by Āpastamba, Satyāṣāḍha, Bhāradvāja, and others—stating, "The rule for the Pravargya in the first sacrifice applies to one who is an *anūcāna* and a *śrotriya"—prescribes the rule for the Pravargya in the first sacrifice for both the *śrotriya* defined as "one who has studied a single recensional branch (*śākhā*)" and the *anūcāna* defined as "one who has studied [the Veda] along with its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*)". Therefore, since the scriptural understanding that the rule for the Pravargya in the first sacrifice does not apply to one who is not such [as defined], the notion that knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas is a subordinate part of ritual action is cast far away.
