Consequently, the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) impels the study of the mere recitation of the sacred text (*svādhyāya-mātra*). Furthermore, the injunction "and [the Self] is to be known" (*jñeyaśca*) is also an impeller for the study of the mere recitation of the sacred text.
For a person, there is spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) from following it and transgression (*pratyavāya*) from violating it.

Since those who know the *ṛtus* (sacrificial seasons) consider their purpose fulfilled merely by hearing and understanding the Vedas and their meanings, they do not at all exert themselves in the study of the Vedas and their meanings. And thus, regarding the subject matter of the *arthavādas*, since the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) does not yield a result that culminates in the [understanding of] meaning, and because the *arthavādas* would otherwise lack fulfillment through the requirement of the injunctive portion (*vidhyuddeśa*),
the conclusion stated by the author of the *Vārttika*— that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the injunctions and the *arthavādas* due to their mutual expectancy— is untenable.

However, the syntactic unity of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) with an injunction, being for the purpose of praise, is to be established solely through the mutual expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*) [between them]. To explain:

Just as in the sentence "the cloth becomes red," although the phrase "the cloth becomes" is complete in itself, the word "red" would otherwise result in meaninglessness and the redundancy of its proximity; thus, when the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) for the word "cloth" arises toward the word "red," that word "red" enters into the "cloth-sentence" by providing a qualification for the cloth. Similarly, although the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) are complete in themselves regarding their own literal meaning, the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*)—which is understood through the injunctive suffix and which requires the first constituent part (*aṃśa*) [the end to be achieved]—finds the constituent of the person's activity (*puruṣapravṛtti*) precisely in the injunction itself, and the constituent of the instrument (*karaṇa*), such as the comprehension of word-powers, obtained from grammar and other sources. However, this [verbal productive energy], requiring the third constituent, namely praise (*stuti*), cannot be established without obtaining such praise. Consequently, due to the proximity of the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) and because [the *arthavāda*] would otherwise result in meaninglessness, an expectation for the injunctive statement arises within the explanatory passages.
The view that these [Arthavāda passages] possess the purpose of praising those [injunctions] through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of their literal meaning is the easy path following the Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, just as in common worldly sentences such as "O Aupagavi, your horn will grow," so too in Arthavāda sentences like "He spoke water with his mouth" or "The cows performed this sacrificial session," the purpose is solely to praise the injunction by relying on an unreal state of affairs, and not even to convey their own literal sense; for if that were the case, the consequence would be a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
Indeed, not even a single syllable is admitted to be purposeless in the Veda.

And thus, according to the maxim "By virtue of that [quality], the others are likewise" (Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.2.123), even those other explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest," do not have their own literal meaning as their primary purpose.

Rather, through *jahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā* (indication where the literal sense is abandoned), they are intended solely for the praise of the injunction. Thus some who call themselves Mīmāṃsakas—while being secretly Buddhists, namely the Prābhākaras—assert.

The authors of the Vārttika, who are the crest-jewels of Vedic scholarship, however, maintain that in all *arthavāda* passages, one must arrive at the intended meaning by means of a non-abandoning indication (*ajahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā*) based on the literal sense of each component word.

In such cases as "He [offered] his own omentum," they hold that the Supreme Lord himself, at the beginning of creation, assumed by his own power another form—that of a sacrificial animal—and performed the ritual act as if he were a subordinate participant; thus, in every instance, the truthfulness of the literal sense should be inferred.

This is because the creation is accepted as having the Supreme Lord, who possesses inconceivable power, as its agent, based on such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," and "His power is heard to be truly manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are innate to Him.

Even in cases such as "The sacrificial post is the sun," there is a primary sense (*svārthaparatā*) due to the presence of qualities like verticality. Thus: "In case of contradiction, it would be a figurative description (*guṇavāda*); if [the primary sense] is established, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*)."

Similarly, arthavāda is considered to be of three kinds: that which states a factual reality (bhūtārthavāda), that which is for the purpose of praise (tadvadāna), and that which is for the purpose of censure (nindā).
Thus they think.

And this is correct, because by such *guṇasūtras* (subsidiary aphorisms) of the *Arthavāda-adhikaraṇa* as "But it is figurative speech" (*guṇavādastu*), "On account of form and predominance" (*rūpāt prāyāt*), "On account of being far removed" (*dūrabhūmyatvāt*), "On account of form and predominance" (*rūpaprāyāt*), "And because the agent is seen to have sons" (*kartṛśca putradarśanāt*), and "The desire for what is not immediate" (*ākālikepsā*), it is demonstrated—even in cases such as "the mind is a thief" (*stainaṃ manaḥ*)—that there is a reliance on the meaning of the constituent parts through a figurative mode of expression (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*).

Furthermore, if the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) lacked reliance on the meaning of their constituent parts, there would be a contradiction with the *guṇasūtra* located in the *Mantra-adhikaraṇa*, namely, "And the words of injunction" (*vidhiśabdāśca*).

In this regard, the supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*)—such as "O Householder, O Good Householder," etc., in the mantras, and "A hundred winters," etc., for which there is the explanatory passage "He thereby says: 'A hundred autumns [winters] you shall live'"—are established as indicators (*liṅga*) that the mantras possess their intended literal meaning.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the *Yavavarāha* section (*adhikaraṇa*) in the *Smṛti-pāda* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3.4–18; Vārttika, pp. 288–290).

In this regard, although the words *yava*, *varāha*, and *vetasa* are used in common worldly usage respectively for *priyaṅgu* (panic seed), barley, and the *jambu* fruit; and for long-tailed grass (*dīrghaśūka*), the boar, and the *vajula* tree; nevertheless, in the Veda—in the passages "the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) consists of *yava*," "they put on shoes made of *varāha* leather," and "he collects the *prājāpatya* vessels on a mat of *vetasa"—their reference to long-tailed grass, the boar, and the *vajula* tree is established by the supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*): "While other plants wither, these continue to flourish," "the cows run after the boar," and "the *vetasa* grows in water."
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the *Trivṛc-charvādhikaraṇa* (1.3.4, Vārttika p. 221–224).

In that context, the word *aśvavāla* is established as referring to *kāśa* grass by the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*): "The horse, having become glory, departed from the gods; it entered the waters; it was seized by its tail; it released its hairs and entered [them]; those hairs became *kāśa* grass.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the *Citrājyādhikaraṇa* (1.4.2, Vārttika p. 13).

In this regard, by the etymological derivation of the word *ājya* in the passage, "Because they were born from the race (*ājis*), that is the reason for the *ājya*-ness of the *ājyas*" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.9.5), and by establishing the origin of the *rathantara* and other chants from water and wind in the passage, "The waters indeed became moistened according to the season; wind moved over their surface" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.3.10.1)—where water is joined with wind—and by the etymological derivation meaning "a son born of a contest," the status of *ājya*, *pṛṣṭha*, and *dadhi* as names [of specific chants] is established.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the section [of the Brahma-sūtras], "And because of the designation of that" (1.4.14).

In this regard, [the term "hawk"] is established as a name by relying on a secondary (gauṇī) application of meaning, as proven by the supplementary passage: "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes a prey, even so does this [sacrifice] swoop down and seize the hating rival.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the section [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] concerning names, namely: "If it be argued that there is an option in the Vaiśvadeva [offering]" (1.4.10.13–16).
In that regard, the status of the word *vaiśvadeva* as a name (*nāmadheya*) is established merely by the etymological derivation: "That which the Viśvedevas sacrificed together is the *vaiśvadeva*.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the *Jātyadhikaraṇa* (Sūtras 1.4.12–23), wherein it is established that in the statement "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), the word *yajamāna* applies to the grass-bundle through figurative usage (*gauṇī vṛtti*) due to its connection with the quality of being the performer of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the *jātyadhikaraṇa* (1.4.12.23–2).

In that context, regarding the statement "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed Agni," the word "Agni" is established as referring to the Brāhmaṇa through figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), based on the connection with the quality of being born from the *muvaj* [the golden egg], as stated: "He fashioned the Trivṛt; he brought forth Agni as the deity, the Gāyatrī as the metre, the Rathantara as the Sāman, the Brāhmaṇa among men, and the goat among animals.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the *sārūpyādhikaraṇa* (1.4.12.23–3).

In that regard, [the example] "The sacrificer is the sacrificial post" (*yajamāno yūpaḥ*) is established through the figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) of the word "sacrificer" to the sacrificial post, based on its connection with the quality of verticality.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the section concerning praise (*praśaṃsādhikaraṇa*, 1.4.23–24).

Therein, in the statement "Other animals than cows and horses are non-animals; cows and horses are [true] animals," the word "non-animals" is established as applying figuratively to goats and other such animals, based on their connection with the quality of being inferior.
Furthermore, many other sections [of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtras], such as "In cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence" (JS 1.4.29), would be contradicted.
I desist here for fear of prolixity.

Therefore, in the case of explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), their purpose is to express praise by means of *ajahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā* (indication without abandoning the literal sense), without overstepping the meanings of the individual words.

27–31 | Consideration of the Injunction for Vedic Study:

In the injunction "One's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ*), within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) where study is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*) is the object to be produced (*bhāvya*). This is because, since it is not something to be performed as a subordinate act (*karmānānuṣṭhāpyatva*), it constitutes a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
If it is argued that its purpose is heaven, we say no, because that would result in its having an unseen (adṛṣṭa) purpose.

Nor is its purpose the acquisition of letters, because that is not connected to a human goal (puruṣārtha), and because grammar and the other [auxiliaries] are appropriately established as being limbs (aṅga) of the Veda.
Being a limb means being a cooperative factor (sahakāritva) in the production of the [Vedic] effect.

And this is consistent with the view that the study of the Veda is for the purpose of knowing its meaning; for grammar and other auxiliary sciences are useful for understanding the meaning of the Veda, whereas they would be useless if the study were intended solely for the sake of heaven. Furthermore, although the study of the Veda possesses a visible purpose by way of generating knowledge, it is nonetheless [regarded as] having an invisible purpose because it is a study enjoined by scripture, just like the study of the auxiliary sciences (aṅga). This is established through inference.
In this context, the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is used to exclude the deviation [of the definition] regarding the study of meaningless texts;
the term "prescribed" (*vihita*) is used to exclude the deviation regarding the recitation of mantras.
Therefore, the knowledge of meaning is that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*).

Nor does the fact that the knowledge of meaning (*arthajñāna*) is the goal to be accomplished (*bhāvya*) entail the impossibility of study, since the various rules regarding non-study days (*anadhyāya*) and so forth would be useless for either its own nature or its function; for even if they lack utility toward the function, they are useful for its own nature insofar as they serve to remove obstacles. Their utility lies in the *niyamāpūrva* (the transcendental result of a restrictive rule).

The suffix indicating purposefulness (*karmārthakatva-pratyaya*) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) in the sense of mere relation, or else it refers to the status of an unintended object (*anīpsita-karman*), as in the cases "He drinks poison" (*viṣaṃ bhuṅkte*) or "He offers groats" (*saktūn juhoti*).

"Even though it is an intended object (*īpsitakarma*), because this [injunction] is an injunction for the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) of the means characterized by the efficient-force of the sequence of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), the state of having the knowledge of the meaning as its objective (*bhāvya*) pertains to its domain"—so says someone.

Here, "Vedic study" (*svādhyāyana*) consists in knowing one's own [text]. And "one's ownness" (*svatva*) consists, through a traditional lineage, in being the object of study and the object of performance.
Therefore, the word *svādhyāya* refers to each individual branch (*śākhā*) contained within the three Vedas.
Consequently, it is established that both study (*adhyayana*) and performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) have as their object the study and performance as received through one's own specific tradition.

In that regard, when there is a requirement for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the inquiry (*vicāra*)—on account of its suitability—is connected as that very procedure; thus, the necessity of performing the inquiry is established.
And thus: "This person is indeed a mere atom, a carrier of burdens, who, having studied the Veda, does not understand its meaning;
whereas he who knows the meaning enjoys all auspiciousness and, through the lightning-flash of knowledge, attains the heavenly realm."
The *Vārttika* arises [with the argument] that the censure and praise of those who know the meaning and those who do not are thus justified, as stated in *Nirukta* 1.18.

However, the venerable teachers (*pitṛcaraṇāḥ*) maintain that even in the case of the killing [of animals] for sprinkling and other rites, since rice grains (*vrīhi*) serve as the means for the *apūrva*, the Veda itself (*svādhyāya*) is the end to be achieved (*bhāvya*), because it generates purposeful knowledge of the meaning.

Just as the acquisition of wealth is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) established in the world, so too is the knowledge of the Vedic meaning a human goal, insofar as it is instrumental to the performance of rituals, much like the acquisition of materials.
Therefore, the injunction of study is for the purpose of establishing a rule regarding study, just like the injunctions concerning the *pratīka* (initial words) and so forth.

If it is objected: "But the rule of study has no utility regarding prohibitions (*niṣedha*). For just as one who learns the meaning of an injunction through study obtains the fruit by performing what is enjoined, one might assume that one who learns the meaning of a prohibition through study avoids transgression (*pratyavāya*) by performing the prohibition; however, in this case, there would be no inclination toward the study of prohibitions. This is not so. For in that case, since the rule of study does not exist, one would assume that one who does not learn the meaning of the prohibition through study incurs transgression. Thus, the rule serves its purpose.
Nor does this much entail the status of *arthāpatti* (presumption), nor the collapse of the principle of parsimony (*vinigamanā*).

The statement, "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (*yad eva vidyayā karoti*), however, does not indicate that the knowledge of meaning is unknown; rather, it is an *arthavāda* (eulogistic statement) intended for the knowledge produced by the application of faith. Or, let it be [understood] through the force of the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) by means of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropāpavādābhyām*).

The phrase "whatever he does" refers generally to Vedic ritual action for the purpose of restricting it to the specific knowledge of the meaning indicated by the term "learning" (vidyā). The particle *san* indicates ignorance and so forth, just as in the case of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). Nevertheless, the status of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatā*) is not based solely on its producing knowledge of a meaning that must be inferred—which would imply that study results in ignorance and necessitates dependence upon context. When the Veda itself (*svādhyāya*) is the object of reference, since the singular number is not intended to be significant, there is no need to postulate another underlying Vedic text (*śruti*) as the basis for Smṛti texts such as "having studied the Vedas," provided this [present text] is the source of that Smṛti; thus, there is no burden of assuming an additional foundational scripture.

Therefore, they say that since the injunction for acquisition has as its objective precisely the generation of knowledge of the meaning through the prescribed method of acquisition, this injunction—which has knowledge of the meaning as its fruit—implies the necessity of inquiry (*vicāra*).

Consequently, dwelling in the teacher’s house until the attainment of knowledge of the meaning and the performance of inquiry are the fruits of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*); this is for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule regarding eligibility (*adhikāra-niyama*).
For instance, the study by Brāhmaṇas and others is enjoined by such statements as: "A Brāhmaṇa is initiated in the spring, a Kṣatriya in the summer, and a Vaiśya in the autumn."

In sentences such as "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age," there is an injunction for study and so forth with reference to the Brāhmaṇa; and the injunction for study, which occurs in proximity to that, stands in need of an agent.

Since the ritual requirement (*kārya*) grasps only those agents who have been brought forward by the injunction of study (*adhyayanavidhi*), it follows that when the knowledge of meaning is established for the members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) through study impelled by that injunction, the ritual injunctions (*ṛtuvidhi*)—being accompanied by the characteristic of not necessitating the acquisition of knowledge of meaning—refer exclusively to Brāhmaṇas and the other twice-born classes. Thus, one who lacks the capacity to accomplish the auxiliary (*aṅga*) consisting of the knowledge produced by the study of the Veda by an agent who has been initiated (*upanīta*) has no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to these rites.

The phrase "one should teach him" (*tam adhyāpayīta*) is a restatement of the fact that the agent is one who has been initiated (*upanīta*), as established by proximity; or else, since the two sentences concerning initiation and teaching have as their object the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), there is an injunction for the act of approaching (*upagamana*) and the act of studying (*adhyayana*), namely: "An eight-year-old Brāhmaṇa should approach [the teacher]; he should study.
The purpose of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) is established by another scriptural authority.
Because ritual acts are mandatory, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) used in the context of initiation and study indicates their obligatory nature.

Alternatively, its obligatory nature is established by the statement, "The time for the initiation of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is beyond this; after this [time], these fall," as well as by the prohibition, "Those who do not study become Brātyas.
(Maṇi, pp. 2–5).
By the reason characterized as the force of the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), it is determined that the entire Veda is a "text" (*grantha*).

(Brahma-sūtra 1.1.15).
Superimposition (*adhyāropa*) is the attribution of a thing onto that which is not its substrate.
For example, it is like the superimposition of a snake upon a rope that is not a snake, or the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl that is not silver—according to the Vedāntins.

Sublation (*apavāda*), on the other hand, is the realization that the world-appearance (*prapañca*), such as ignorance and so forth—which is a non-entity like a snake that is a transformation (*vivarta*) of a rope—is in reality nothing but the substrate itself.
The meaning is that by means of these two— superimposition (adhyāropa) and negation (apavāda)— the Brahman, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, infinite and non-dual, is manifested and expanded.
According to the principle stated in the *Sāhasrī* (verse 47), "by means of superimposition and negation," this refers to the first pair of positions.

Regarding the consumption of the remnants at the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, the *adhyūnī*—which has the form of a young shoot—belongs to the Hotṛ; this would be the *adhyūnī*-principle, without doubt.
The *adhyūnī* should be a modification of the *iḍā*-consumption; that is, it would be a modification of the other *iḍā*-consumption, which means it would supersede it.
The meaning is that there is no *iḍā* for the Hotṛ apart from the *adhyūnī*.
He manifested it.
Just as the limbs that remain from the sacrifice are obstructed by the remnants of non-sacrificial acts, so it is here.
Some say that the *adhyūnī* is a portion consisting of the hair of the victim.
Others say they are portions in the form of breasts situated above the udder.
Although there is an absence of both an udder and breasts in a male animal, the intention nevertheless refers to the lumps of flesh in those locations.
Or rather, it resides in the tail; therefore, this would be a restrictive rule for that purpose.
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position.
The *adhyūnī* is not a modification of the *iḍā*-portion;
rather, it is included in the remnant, as it is said, "They increase the *iḍā* with boneless parts," and thus its taking as part of the *iḍā* is established.

Therefore, there must be a restriction regarding her portion for the Hotṛ; they bring it to the Hotṛ alone and not to anyone else, though they do indeed provide another portion for the Hotṛ. It is like the case of the chariot.
Just as in the rule, "If he gives the chariot that has been yoked," there is a restriction of the chariot to the portion of the Adhvaryu, so it is here.
Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
It cannot be so, because it is not found in the scriptures.
The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside both the restrictive rule and the prima facie view.
In this way, there would be no restriction regarding the *adhyūnī* in the portion of the Hotṛ;

that is, there would be no rule because of the absence of such a scriptural injunction (*aśāstratvāt*). The *adhyūnī* is obtained in the *iḍā* offering, yet in the passage—"Now, what remains, he brings that as consisting of equal portions; he throws in the heart, the tongue, the breast, the udder, and the rectum"—there is no mention of the *adhyūnī*.
Therefore, that [portion] is enjoined with reference to the taking by the Hotṛ priest, in the sense that "they take the *adhyūnī* for the Hotṛ alone, and nothing else.
Consequently, it is established as a modification of the *iḍā*-consumption.
Alternatively, it may be a mere gift, because of its connection with the word "consumption" (*bhakṣa*).

The phrase "or rather" (apivā) serves to set aside the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). The *adhyūnī* is not a modification of the *iḍā*-consumption; rather, it should be merely its giving to the Hotṛ, because of its connection with the word "consumption" (*bhakṣa*).
By the word "consumption" (bhakṣa), the act of consuming is meant, because there is no connection with that [act] and no mention of it.
For she is enjoined as something unprecedented (apūrva), not for the purpose of consumption;
this is because of the lack of connection with the word "consumption," that is, the absence of any association with the term "consumption."

Therefore, it is neither a modification of the *bhakṣa* (eating) nor a restrictive rule (*niyama*); from this, a doubt arises. However, because the giver is absent, there would be a modification of the *iḍā-bhakṣa*, since [the portion] with respect to the remnant is not distinct. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of excluding the doubt regarding the giving.
There is no gift for the Adhvaryu priests,
because the giver is absent;
the sacrificer has already, at the very beginning, dedicated [the animal] to Agni and Soma for the animal sacrifice.
Thus, with respect to the remainder, the Hotṛ and the sacrificer (yajamāna) are non-distinct.
Just as the Hotṛ is not the master, so too is the sacrificer;
this lack of mastery is now non-distinct [between them].

Because the remainder is not distinct [from what has been consumed], the giver is no longer present; therefore, the *adhyūnī* should be a modification (*vikāra*) of the Hotṛ’s portion of the *iḍā*. For the Hotṛ, there is only the *adhyūnī*, and nothing else belonging to the *iḍā*.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The Adhyūnī-nyāya:
In the Agnīṣomīya animal sacrifice, the *adhyūnī* (the portion of the omentum) effects the exclusion of the Hotṛ’s entire consumption of the *iḍā*.
However, the *adhyūnī* itself should be a modification of the Hotṛ’s loud recitation and the consumption of the *iḍā*.
The Commentary: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the Agnīṣomīya animal sacrifice, [established by the rule]: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the Agnīṣomīya animal.
Regarding this, it is recited: "They carry the adhyūnī to the Hotṛ.
In this regard, the meaning is subject to doubt: is the adhyūnī a modification (*vikāra*) of the Hotṛ’s portion, or is the Hotṛ restricted [to that portion]?

How would there be a modification (vikāra), and how would there be a restriction (niyama)? If "they carry [the portion] to the Hotṛ" is enjoined with reference to the *adhyūnī* (the upper part of the breast), then there is a modification.
If, however, "they carry [it] to the Hotṛ" is enjoined with reference to the *adhyūnī*, then there is a restriction. What is the prima facie view? There would be a modification of the Hotṛ’s portion.

Why? Because the *adhyūnī* is something not previously established (*apūrva*), and since it is not a remnant of the deities (*adaivata-śeṣatvāt*), it is not obtained in the consumption of the *iḍā*; therefore, it cannot be merely restated (*anuvāda*).
Consequently, it is enjoined in connection with the taking of the Hotṛ’s portion.
Being directly perceived (*pratyakṣā*) in the taking by the Hotṛ, the *adhyūnī* sets aside the inferential (*ānumānika*) consumption of the *iḍā*.
It manifests [the result]; just as by those remnants of non-sacrifice, the remnants of sacrifice are set aside, so it is here.
Or rather, it is included in the remainder; therefore, there would be no restrictive rule.
The Commentary states: The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position, namely that it is a modification of the *iḍā*-portion.
How could it be a modification of the *iḍā*-portion? It would be so if the *adhyūnī* were something not previously [included].
For that [adhyūnī] is contained within the *iḍā*.

How so? Since it is said, "They increase the *iḍā* with boneless [flesh]," its being taken is already established; however, its connection with the *hotṛ* priest is not yet established, and that is what is prescribed: "This *adhyūnī* which they carry, that they give to the *hotṛ*, and not to anyone else.
Thus, they provide another portion for the *hotṛ*.
Furthermore, the syntactic connection with the sentence beginning with "They bring for the Hotṛ" is directly perceived.
In the other alternative, the connection "They bring for the Adhvaryu" would have to be inferred due to the intervention of the word *hotṛ*.
Therefore, there is a restriction regarding the share, as in the case of the chariot.

Just as in the case of "He gives the Yajus for the sacrifice, [placing it] in the middle of the chariot," because the chariot is obtained through another statement and there is no intervention, there is a restriction regarding the portion of the Adhvaryu; so too here, there would be a restriction regarding the portion of the Hotṛ.
[Response: This cannot be so, because it is not based on scriptural authority (aśāstra).
The Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position.
There is no restriction regarding the portion;
rather, it is a modification of the consumption of the *iḍā*.
Why? Because there is no scriptural authority by which the Adhvaryu would be the one to consume the *iḍā*.
But was it not said: "They increase the *iḍā* with bones that have no marrow"? It is replied: [No, such a text does not exist].

Because it is of the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda*) and because [the act] is already established by another statement—namely, "Now, whatever remains, that he brings to the *samavattadhānī*; what he throws in is the heart, the tongue, the breast, the nipple, and from that, the rectum"—it is understood to be a restatement.
Furthermore, the *adhvaryu* is not mentioned here.
Therefore, whether [the act] is already established or not, it is enjoined with reference to the taking [of the portion] by the *hotṛ*.

As for the claim that syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) must be assumed even though it is not attained due to an intervention, we shall assume it because of its unprecedented nature (*apūrvatva*); for, since there is no restatement (*anuvāda*) by the Adhvaryus, we will assume it in order to avoid the contingency of meaninglessness.
And in this way, the act of taking (*haraṇa*) pertaining to its own word (*svapadagata*) will be enjoined.
Otherwise, however, the designations "Hotṛ" and "Adhvaryu" would be enjoined, but the act of taking pertaining to its own word would not.
For this reason also, it is a modification of the eating.
Or rather, it may be a mere gift, because of its connection with the word "eating" (bhakṣa).
The Commentary states: "Or rather" (api vā) indicates the rejection of the previous position.

If this is so, then since the *adhvaryū* is not obtained for the consumption of the *iḍā* by another statement, it is prescribed as something new (*apūrva*) to be brought; in that case, it is not a modification of the consumption.
This—"they bring the *adhvaryū* to the *hotṛ*"—is merely a matter of giving;
here, no connection with the word "consumption" (*bhakṣa*) is being enjoined.
Therefore, it is not a modification of the portion for consumption (*bhakṣavikāra*).
However, because the giver is absent, it would be a modification of the *iḍā*-consumption, since there is no distinction regarding the remnant (*śeṣa*).
The Commentary states: the word "but" (*tu*) excludes the [previous] position; this is merely a giving, not a modification of the portion for consumption.
This is not a gift because of the absence of an owner;
for the animal has been resolved upon in this way: "Apart from the sacrifice, there is no other purpose for my body.
Therefore, due to the absence of ownership, there is no gift.
How is there an absence of ownership? Because [the status] with respect to the subsidiary is indistinguishable. Just as the sacrificer is with respect to the subsidiary, so too is the Hotṛ priest;
neither of them has mastery over the substance, and thus there is no giving.
Now, how is it that there is "eating" (bhakṣa) when there is a connection with the word "eating"? Because of the hearing of the dative case.
The dative occurs in the sense of "for the sake of that"; [it is said] "for the sake of the Hotṛ, for the sake of the Adhvaryu. Thus, the Hotṛ is intended; that [cup] assists the Hotṛ.
While being eaten, it serves to obtain a visible production of capacity, and by whatever means and to whatever extent it becomes beneficial.
In that case, the dative case-ending (caturthī-śruti) is upheld;
for otherwise, if no benefit were perceived, the dative case-ending would be contradicted.
Therefore, it is a modification of the consumption of the iḍā.

Śā—The statement "that which they carry to the Hotṛ, that [they carry] to the two Adhvaryus" subordinates the original act of carrying—which has the Hotṛ as the recipient—to the presentation of the two Adhvaryus.
Therefore, this is a modification (*vikāra*) of the consumption of the *iḍā*.

Soma—The connection [of the discussion] arises from the following: although there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the offerings to the deities (*iṣṭadevatā*) such as the heart and so forth by the offerings to the deities of the *vaiśvānarī*, there is no sublation of those [deities] who are not remnants of the sacrifice (*aniṣṭyaśeṣa*), namely the Adhvaryus; thus the point is established.
Some [hold] that the *adhvaryū* are limbs other than the hands and so forth; others [hold], based on the *Śikṣā*, that they are primarily boneless [parts],
as in "the two *adhvaryū* are the flesh of the buttocks," according to Dhūrtasvāmin.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: The modification of the Hotṛ’s consumption should belong to the Adhvaryu, just as there is a modification of the remaining portions of the side-dishes. [Objection: Is it the Hotṛ who is restricted, or does the Adhvaryu modify the Veda? [Reply: By the phrase "with boneless [flesh]," the Hotṛ is restricted in one alternative.

An *anuvāda* (restatement) is a sentence devoid of skeletal [injunction], while the *pariśiṣṭī* (supplementary rules) are those that bring about application. Regarding the phrase "the two *adhvaryus* carry it to the *hotṛ*," there arises the inquiry: having postulated the *iḍā* as obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), does the scriptural statement "the two *adhvaryus* carry it to the *hotṛ*" set aside the entire original (*prakṛta*) portion of the *hotṛ*'s *iḍā*, or not? In this deliberation, the two *adhvaryus* are here to be understood as the objects of the accusative case, because they are the recipients of the action. *Bhāṭṭa*: In the animal sacrifice, having established the *iḍā* as obtained by extended application, there is a doubt: upon hearing the scripture "the two *adhvaryus* carry it to the *hotṛ*," does this [statement] exclude the entire original portion of the *hotṛ*'s *iḍā-bhāga*, or not? In this inquiry, the two *adhvaryus* are indeed the objects of the accusative case here, as they are the ones to whom the act is directed.

With reference to that [soma], the act of taking it for the purpose of consumption, which is to be delivered to the *hotṛ*, is enjoined as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) that fulfills its original function. Although this "taking" is not technically a "giving"—since the status of recipient (*saṃpradānatva*) would otherwise be untenable because the *adhvaryu* lacks ownership—it is nevertheless an offering for the sake of consumption; and in that very context, the status of recipient is somehow established. Alternatively, because it is useful for the consumption performed by the *hotṛ*, it is intended for his benefit by virtue of his being the *hotṛ*.

In every respect, there is an injunction for the taking of the *prākṛta* [offering] by one distinguished as the *hotṛ*, as a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) for the *adhvaryu*. This is the extension (*atideśa*) of the *adhvaryu*’s duty; [it is] the *adhigupraiṣa*.
The taking [of the portion] is obtained as being dependent on that [Iḍā], and because it has the Hotṛ as its recipient, it is enjoined with reference to him.
This much is common to both views.

However, because of the statement, "They increase the Iḍā with boneless [flesh]," the boneless form of the *śikṣā* (portion) is already established for the Adhvaryu in the Iḍā; since the taking [of the portion] with the Hotṛ as the recipient is also optionally established there, it is understood as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). Thus, although the meaning is understood as "only by the Hotṛ [and not by the Adhvaryu]," this does not entail the exclusion of his other portions.
This being the position reached, [the text says]: "Now, whatever remains, that he brings into the vessel for the portions."

Because the statement, "He shall throw into the *iḍā* the heart, the tongue, the breast, the nipple, and its *vaniṣṭhu*," prescribes the throwing (*prāsana*) of only the heart and other organs into the *iḍā*, and because the present passage—"with those that are boneless"—is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that same intent (and thus lacks an independent injunction), the *hotṛ*-priest—being already established as the recipient of the *iḍā*—cannot be further restricted by that rule. Therefore, either the very form of the *hotṛ* as present in the archetype (*prakṛti*) is enjoined in connection with another object of refinement not part of the archetype, or rather, the *hotṛ* himself, as dependent on the archetypal act of taking (*haraṇa*), is enjoined in that manner.

Consequently, since that non-consumption (*anaraṇa*) serves the purpose of consumption (*bhakṣa*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the accomplishment of consumption by the Adhvaryu is also established. Furthermore, since the consumption of the *iḍā* in the archetype is already established through its being the duty of the performer as before, there is no need for it to be performed again by the Hotṛ.

For this very reason, the taking [of the portion] here is not enjoined solely for the sake of the Adhvaryu’s consecration (*saṃskāra*) with the Hotṛ as the recipient; because it is presented as serving the purpose of the archetypal *iḍā*-consumption, there is no evidence for it being a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*).
Therefore, it is established that there is an exclusion of the two Adhvaryus from the entire portion of the *iḍā* belonging to the Hotṛ.

However, when—according to the method stated by Āpastamba and others—the six substances beginning with the heart are themselves the *iḍā* portions to be offered, and the act of "increasing the *iḍā* with boneless parts" (*anasthibhir iḍāṃ vardhayanti*) is enjoined as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for them, even so, because this is a visible injunction and serves the purpose of consumption, its primary aim is indeed for the sake of eating. Nevertheless, since the statement of intention, "the *kloman*, the *śrīman*, and the *purotāt*," includes these three parts under the term "boneless," and because there is no possibility of the Adhvaryu obtaining [these] as before, their being something not previously established (*apūrva*) allows for the possibility of their being carried forward; thus, their status as a modification (*vikāra*) of the original *iḍā*-consumption is established.

Dhūrtasvāmī and others, accepting that those [sentences] are indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the remainder of the statement, argue that since the *iḍā* is increased by the Adhvaryu—who is not fixed [in his role]—and since that [increase] is thus established, they maintain that it is merely a restriction regarding the Hotṛ; however, this formulation of the view that it is for the purpose of the *iḍā*-consumption requires proof for its being indicative.
*Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), it is heard in scripture: "They bring [the portions] to the Adhvaryu and the Hotṛ."

Regarding this, since there is the statement, "They increase the *iḍā* with boneless [parts]," one might argue that the portion called *adhvaryūṅkhā*—which is included within the *iḍā* and consists of the uppermost gems—is restricted to the share of the *hotṛ*, and thus it does not exclude the consumption of the *iḍā*. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: because the phrase "with boneless [parts]" is inferred from such statements as "He throws in the heart, the tongue, the chest," and so forth; because there is no mention of the *adhvaryu* therein; and because the rule "that which he brings to the *hotṛ* is the *adhvaryūṅkhā*" constitutes an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), it indeed excludes the consumption of the *iḍā*.
Maṇḍana: "The *iḍā* is a modification of that which is to be consumed by the *hotṛ*.
[He uses the word] *bhajaḥ* in the sense of "a portion" (*bhāgasya*).
Śaṅkara: "There is a sublation of the *iḍā*-consumption by the *adhvaryu*."

Lay down his footprints turned toward the north; cause his eye to go to the sun, release his breath after the wind, the intermediate space, the quarters of heaven, and the earth for his body.

"O horse, let him cut you into one piece; let him extract the omentum even before the name [is uttered]; let him ward off what is being measured within. Make his chest like a hawk, his forearms with the *praśāsa*, his upper arms with the *śalā*, his shoulders with the *kaśyapā*, his hips with the *acchidrā*, his thighs with the *kapola*, and his joints with the *lekaparṇā*. There are twenty-six [verses] for the morning *agni-praiṣa*. (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.5).
Regarding the two *śalā* [in the phrase] "agnigau śalā," the purpose is so that the extraction may be performed in its entirety.
"Based on the statement, 'Make our limbs [strong] limb by limb' (ŚB 1.4.2.7);
the *agnipraiṣa* occurs at the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana) (ŚB 1.4.2.14);
and there is a repetition of the *agnigṛhapraiṣa* in the *prājāpatya* animal sacrifices and the seasonal (*ṛtu*) animal sacrifices at the Bṛhaspatisava, due to the difference in time."
On 1|4|2014-5-6, the commentators stated: "Food, names of kinsmen, comparisons, and the sense organs—these do not go [to the other world] with us; for that [world] is different from fire."
Vākyapadīya 1.3.8.24, p. 264: "Mother" and so forth are names of relatives;
"day-enemy" and so forth are metaphors;
"the eye is the sun" and so forth refer to the sense organs.
They do not proceed from the *bhavya* [the thing to be accomplished] by means of other types of inference (*ūha-viparyaya*).

(Su. p. 284) It should be understood that among the points of discussion found in the *agnigraha-praiṣa*, the concise final conclusions (*laghu-siddhānta*) have been set forth according to the order of the recitation (*pāṭha-krama*).
(Ke. In the passage "āśāsānā medhapatibhyāṃ medham," the term *medhapati* refers to the deity.

And likewise, according to whether there is one, two, or many deities, the formula must be modified accordingly as *medhapataye*, *medhapatibhyām*, or *medhapatibhyaḥ*. This is because such a modification of the word *medhapati* as referring to the deity is clearly enjoined in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (Ke. 1.3.12.32–40). Regarding the eleven sacrificial animals (*ekādaśina-paśu*), the singular form of the word *medhapati* is set aside; however, the dual form—namely, *medhapatibhyo medham*—must indeed be modified, because the deities are distinct and do not constitute a single group.

Bhāṣya 1.3.14.43: When there is an animal sacrifice for many deities, since the gods form a group, the mantra "medhapatibhyo medham" (the sacrificial food for the lords of the sacrifice) is optionally accompanied by the singular-ending mantra "medhapataye medham" (the sacrificial food for the lord of the sacrifice), because the group is understood through the singular number, as in the case of "one should sacrifice a barren cow to the Ādityas and to Kāma.

Vivaraṇa 1.3.13: In the *agnipraiṣa* (the call to Agni), the word *medhapati* (lord of the sacrifice) takes the dual ending when the animal has multiple deities through modification (*ūha*), and it remains unmodified with the singular ending; thus, there is an option between the two.

Bhāṣya 1.3.14.41–42: However, where the deities do not constitute a group but each possesses deity-status individually—as in the case of the *ekādaśina* (eleven) animals—the form ending in the plural, "to the lords of the sacrifice (*medhapati*) [plural], the sacrifice (*medham*)," must be modified accordingly; there is no optionality here. Vi. 1.3.14: There is no modification of the word "to him (*prāsmai*)" when the *agnīṣomīya* and the *savanīya* sacrifices share the same ritual injunction. Bhāṣya 1.3.8.22: Regarding the four *savanīya* animals belonging to the *atirātra*, one must not perform a modification of "to him" (*prāsmai*) by changing it to the plural.
This is a matter for deliberation (*kṛtvācintya*).
In reality, however, an adaptation (*ūha*) must be made. (Vi.
1.3.8) The mention of "fire" and "cow" applies to the ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī in the Atirātra sacrifice.

If the animal rites were common [to all], then the mention of the fire (*agni*) would not apply to the *sārasvatī* [offering]. If, however, they are the rites of the *agnīṣomīya*, then the mention of the fire is obtained for this [offering] through modification (*ūha*) as "for her, O Agni" (*aprasyai agne*). Bhāṣya 1.2.17.49. Regarding the two *savanīya* animals belonging to the *ukthya* sacrifice, no modification should be made to the word "for him" (*asmai*) by changing it to the dual number.
This is a hypothetical discussion (*kṛtvācintā*); in reality, however, it must indeed be performed.

[Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.3.8]: regarding the three *savanīya* animals at the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, there should be no modification (*ūha*) of the word "to him" (*asmai*) into the plural. This is a hypothetical discussion.

In the passage beginning with "O Sun, from the state of being composed of sight" (*sūrya cakṣurmayatāt*), regarding the sacrifice of two animals, no modification (*ūha*) should be made based on the dual or plural endings of words such as *cakṣus* (eye), because these words denoting substances that are composite do not refer to the physical eyeball (*golaka*). Bhāṣya 1|3|13, pp. 27–28. Regarding the word "once" (*ekadhā*), repetition should be performed for each animal; the meaning is that the mantra is recited once for each individual animal.

In that regard, when there is a ritual for two animals (*dvipaśukalpa*), the modification (*ūha*) is: "Let his skin be stripped off in one way, in one way" (*ekadhaikadhā'nayostvaccāvācyatā*); but when there is a plurality [of animals], the modification is: "Let their skin be stripped off in one way, in one way, in one way" (*ekadhaikadhaikadhaiṣāṃ tvacca ācchayatāt*). Ke. 1|3|11|29-31. Regarding the phrase "let his skin be stripped off in one way" (*ekadhā asya tvaccācchayatāt*), there is no dispute that the word "his" (*asya*) must be modified according to the context into the dual or plural forms when dealing with a group of animals. Bhāṭṭa. 1|3|11. Regarding the phrase "let his skin be stripped off in one way" (*ekadhā'sya tvacca ācchayatāt*), there is no dispute that the word "skin" (*tvacaṃ*) must be modified according to the context into the dual or plural forms when dealing with a group of animals.

1|3|11. Regarding the injunction "Make its breast like that of a hawk," the meaning is that the chest should be extracted in its entirety so that it does not perish, rather than implying the fashioning of the breast into the shape of a hawk.

Likewise, in the cases of *śalā*, *kaśyapa*, *kavaṇa*, and *sekaparṇa*, only completeness is intended to be conveyed, not the production of a specific form. Vi. 1|4|6. Regarding the phrase "The two arms as axes" (*praśāsā bāhū*), the word *praśāsā* does not mean "swords" (*asi*), but rather "praiseworthy ones" (*praśastī*).

Likewise, when there are two or many animals, the word *praśas* must be modified (*ūha*) by taking the dual or plural endings, as in "the two arms are praised" (*praśasau bāhū*) or "the arms are praised" (*praśaso bāhū*).
Alternatively, the word *praśas* refers specifically to the axe (*svadhiti*);
thus, according to the consensus of ritualists, the modification occurs only in the cognition of the axe.
In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, when there is a plurality of *svadhiti* (knives), the modification (*ūha*) is "the two arms with the *pradī* [knives]. (Ke.

1.4.4). Regarding the phrase "the two *śallā* [shoulder-blades] are the *dopaṇī*," even though there is a plurality of animals, there is no modification of the word *śallā*, because it is possible to convey the sense of similarity through a single point of comparison.
*Śallā* refers to those resembling the hair of a porcupine (*śalyaka*).
"Bhaṭṭabhāskara says they have the form of sticks; the arms are the two fire-sticks.
Regarding *agnigau kathapevāṃsā* (339):

in the case of the *praiṣa* formula addressed to the Agni-cow, namely *prāsmai 'kathapevāṃsā*, there is no modification (*ūha*) even though it refers to an animal; this is because that [term] is intended to signify completeness (*kārtsnya*).
*Aṃsā-aṃsā*. Mādhava [explains] *kathapāṃ iva* as "like tortoises.
1.4.6: In the case of *kavapāhū*, even though there is a plurality of animals (*paśu*), there is no modification (*ūha*) of the word *kavapā*, because that word refers to the whole (*kārtsnya*).
"Bhaṭṭabhāskara says that the thighs are like the *kava* and the *vatsatara*.
The *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* says they are like the *gatisādhana*, the *ādhā*, and the *sāna*.
Others say they are like the *khaṭavā*."
Ke. 1.4.25–27: "The two shoulders ending with the neck are *sekaparṇī*.
Even when there is a plurality of animals, there is no modification (*ūha*) of the word *sekaparṇī*, because it is intended to denote the accomplishment of the whole.
The two thighs are the anterior parts ending with the hips (*agnīvantau*).
They are like the leaves of the *sekaparṇā* and the *karavīra*;
"like the feathers of a parrot," says Bhaṭṭabhāskara;
"possessing fire and being high and firm," says the Bhāṭṭadīpikā.

1|4|25–27. In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, in place of the formula "The purchase price for the many-whiskered horse's legs" (*aśvamedhe bahviśitasirasya vakrakrayaḥ*), one should recite the verse "Twenty-four are the legs of the horse, the friend of the gods" (*caturviṃśadājino devabandhoḥ*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1|6|1|8) for the sake of the horse; then, for the sake of the *tupara* and the *gomṛga*, one should recite, "The purchase price for the legs of these two is fifty-two. Alternatively, a collective statement should be made: "The purchase price for their legs is eighty-six."

Bhāṣya 1.4.17–21: Regarding the passage, "Twenty-five are its ribs; lift them up one by one," [the rule is applied] such that, for the purpose of stating the number of the primary ribs according to the number of animals—as in "Fifty-two are the ribs of these two" or "Seventy-eight are the ribs of these"—the collective singular form (samastavacana) must be employed as appropriate when there are groups of two or many animals.
1.4.19–16: Regarding the passage, "Do not tear its rectum, thinking it to be the *uruka*.
Here, the word *uruka* means the omentum (*vapā*).
And likewise, in ritual modifications involving multiple animals, the word *uru* ending in the singular must be modified (*ūha*) according to the case into forms ending in the dual or plural.

In that regard, when there is duality, one must state either the analysis of the words as "thinking [them] to be two wide ones" (*uruṇī ke manyamānāḥ*) or the unification of the words as "thinking [them] to be wide" (*uruke manyamānāḥ*).
And when there is plurality, one must state either "thinking [them] to be many wide ones" (*uruṇi kāni manyamānāḥ*) or "thinking [them] to be wide ones" (*urukāṇi manyamānāḥ*).

1.4.22. Regarding the word *prāsmai* occurring in the *praisha* for the fire-altar (*agnigṛ*), there is no modification [of the mantra] when the *agnīṣomīya* and the *savanīya* sacrifices share the same ritual procedure (*samānavidhāna*).
It is likewise in the case of the *savanīya* animals at the fire-altar, provided they have the same ritual procedure.
Commentary: In the Soma sacrifice, there is the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, as stated in the text: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the *agnīṣomīya* animal."
In that context, this is recited in the *agnīdh* formulas: "O Agni, bring to him; spread the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); may his mother approve of him, his father, and his brother," and so forth.

Now, when the *agnīṣomīya* and the *savanīya* [animal sacrifices] share the same ritual procedure (*samānavidhāna*), this is deliberated upon: should the words "to him" (*asmai*) and so forth in the *agnīdh* formulas be modified (*ūhitavya*), or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? From that, the extended application (*atideśa*) is established.
"In the case of Agni and Gau, it is likewise.
In this regard, that which was the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section concerning the Lord (*patyadhikaraṇa*, 9.1.7) is the prima facie argument here;
that which was the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) there is the established conclusion here.
"Modification" (*ūha*) is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*);
"no modification" (*avikāra*) is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Regarding the third chapter, in the prima facie view that "the *saṃsthās* and the *paśus* have common injunctions" (*samānavidhānāḥ*) [Sūtra 3.6.16–43], the purpose of that which was stated as having common injunctions is here declared by this Sūtra, having been established by the preceding section.

When the ritual procedures (*vidhāna*) are identical, then even in the case of a group of *savanīya* animals on days such as those of the *ukthya* or *ṣoḍaśin*, the word ending in the respective [animal] name within the *pra-asmai* formula and so forth should not be modified (*ūhitavya*) according to the rule for the wife's [portion]; however, under the view that there is a modification (*vikāra*), it should be modified. As stated in the *Vṛtti*: "If the rules for the *agniṣomīya* and *savanīya* are the same, then the mantra beginning with *prāsmā* should not be modified according to the principle of the wife."

In ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), however, because the animals to be sacrificed (*savanīyapaśu*) are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, the modification (*ūha*) of the gender and number [of the mantra] must follow this very [model] according to the principle of the *pāśā* [mantra].

(Bhāṭṭa: Thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtupaśu*) share the same ritual procedure (*samānavidhāna*), the singular form of the word "this" (*asmai*) in the *agnipraisa* formula must be employed for them just as in the *patnīśrāddha*, and not restricted to a single-animal sacrifice based on the singular number.
The singular number can apply even to a group by virtue of the direct statement (*śruti*) itself, with the intention of referring to each individual member.

For this very reason, in a case where a masculine term cannot, by direct statement, refer to a group consisting of both males and females, there is no evidence for an extremely restricted secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, the contraction remains only among males, resulting in a disparity.

However, according to the established doctrine of "non-uniform injunction" (*asamānavidhāna*), in the case of the word *prāsmai*, one must indeed perform a modification (*ūha*) regarding both the number and the gender, such as: *prabhyo asyā agne bhara*.

This is merely a statement of the purpose for the discussion regarding the commonality of ritual injunctions (*samānavidhāna*) based on the principle of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*). In the *Nyāyabindu*: Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the animals of the concluding rites (*saṃsthāpaśu*) share the same ritual injunction, it is argued that when there is a group of two or more Savanīya animals, the singular formula contained in the *agnigṛpra* command, "prāsmai," should not be modified, just as in the case of the *patnīśrāddha*. However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), modification (*ūha*) must indeed take place; this was mentioned incidentally. As for the masculine gender of "prāsmai," because it would be utterly inappropriate [for a female], it does not apply to the *sārasvatī* animal; thus, there is a distinction.
Regarding the *medha-maṇḍana* [verse] found in the *adhigupraiṣa*: "The *adhigu* is not [recited] at the beginning of the *praisha*, because it would result in an equal application of the injunction.
Śaṅkara says: "The *adhigu* is not [recited] at the beginning of the *śaṃyuvāka*, etc., in that manner."
Modification (*ūha*). Oṃ: Regarding the singular form of the word *medha-* occurring in the *adhigu-praiṣa*, there is modification in the case of the set of eleven victims (*ekādaśinī*).
There would be a change in meaning because of the distinctness of the deities; it would not [remain] as a single collective unit.

Commentary: Regarding this set of eleven [offerings], there are injunctions such as: "He causes [the victim] to be shorn with the offering to Agni; he effects a pairing with the offering to Sarasvatī; he deposits the seed with the offering to Soma; he brings about procreation with the offering to Pūṣan," and so forth.
Furthermore, in the archetype (prakṛti), within the *adhigu-praiṣa* (the call for the slaughterer), the word *medhapati* occurs both in the singular and in the dual.
Its application here [in the ectype] is established by the rule of extension (*codaka*).
The dual number must indeed be supplied.
Now, as for the singular form, does it proceed without modification, or is it excluded?
What is the prima facie view? "Or there is an option, because of the nature of the archetype," according to the principle of the preceding section.
This being the case, we reply:
in the case of each Ekādaśinī, there is a modification, not an option;
for that very reason, the singular ending is set aside.
Why? Because of the distinctness of the deities.
For here the deities are distinct; one deity is different from another, and yet another is different from that—thus it is.
In this group, they do not constitute a single deity.
Due to the absence of that [duality], there is also no state of association.
In the *prakṛti*, these two factors constitute the cause for the application of the singular ending;
since they are absent here, there is no application [of the singular].

As it has been stated: "Even in the case of oneness, because of the removal of the quality" (9.3.13.40), that statement refers to the opponent's position (*parapakṣa*), not to one's own position (*svapakṣa*).
Therefore, there is no fault.
Śā—For one who, as before, considers the modification (*ūha*) to be intended for the group (*gaṇa*), the reply is: "Because the deity is a single self, the modification was previously declared."
Even so, who indeed could prevent this modification (*ūha*) when there is a difference?
Soma says: Since there are many deities, the modification is consistent with what was stated previously regarding the singularity of the deity as a grammatical factor (*kāraka*).

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: in another context, such as the *ekādaśina* sacrifice, there would be a modification because of the difference in the forms of the deities; since the secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) and so forth are applied to each individually, the deity must be understood as being individual for each.

Vi—In cases such as "the black-necked" (*kṛṣṇagrīva*), there is no modification (*ūha*), or rather, for this [mantra], there is no modification as in the previous case. Therefore, since the divinity belongs to the group (*gaṇa*) and not to the individual, there must be modification (*ūha*) when many [deities] are intended. Bhāṭṭa—But where there are multiple divinities (*devatātva*) while the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is either one or many, there is modification (*ūha*) even of the singular ending (of the word *medha* occurring in the *adhigupraiṣa*).

For example: "One should sacrifice an animal to Tvaṣṭṛ-Patnīvat," "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni Pāvaka," "A black-necked [animal] is for Agni," "The ewe mentioned in the Adhrigu-praiṣa is for Sarasvatī," "A brown [animal] is for Soma," and so forth.

In this case, although there is an *adhigupraiṣa* for both Tvaṣṭṛ and Patnīvat, there is a difference in deity due to the difference in the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix and the dative case ending;
however, in the third example, there is a difference in both.
Therefore, in that instance, modification (*ūha*) of both mantras must be performed according to their respective numbers.

Nor should it be argued that if both mantras are accepted as having two referents, there would result a requirement for their simultaneous use (samuccaya) in either the archetype (prakṛti) or the ectype (vikṛti), because of the difference in meaning between the deity itself and its substratum (adhiṣṭhāna).
For both mantras can appropriately be treated as optional alternatives (vikalpa), since each expresses both meanings.

Indeed, the singular form "medhapati" (lord of the sacrifice), while denoting the deity through a mediated relationship, also brings to mind the substratum by virtue of being the locus of that mediated relationship.
Because it is not the name of a deity (*abhīṣomanvat*), its presence [in the ritual] through the term *medhapati* (lord of the sacrifice) is impossible.

Even though the dual-ending form refers to the two substrates (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as "lords of the sacrifice," since the relationship of acceptance (*svīkāra*) depends upon the status of being a deity, it also brings the deity to mind. Thus, even though there is a difference in the scope (*viṣayatā*) of the two terms, both serve to bring both [the substrate and the deity] to mind; therefore, the application of an option (*vikalpa*) is justified. *Nyāyabindu*: However, regarding a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), for one who considers that the singular number is not subject to modification (*anūha*) because it intends the group as a whole, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is this: when there is a difference in the nature of the deities, there must indeed be modification (*ūha*); but when they are identical, there is no modification.
Maṇḍana: "The modification (*vikṛti*) of the *ekādaśinī* occurs there; in that context, at the word *medha*, the modification is an adaptation (*ūha*).
Śaṅkara: "The difference in deities would constitute an adaptation (*ūha*). Where there is a difference, there is an adaptation."

15. Oṃ: Regarding the word *medha-pratiśabda* occurring in the *adhigupraiṣa*, which is singular in form, there is an option for it to be in the dual when the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) is dedicated to multiple deities.
Commentary: There exists an animal sacrifice dedicated to multiple deities, as in:
"He offers these animals to the Ādityas for the sake of desire."
Likewise, there is the injunction: "One should offer the Vaiśvadeva with smoke.
However, in the archetype (prakṛti), namely the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, there is a dual number and a singular number [in the word] *medha-prati*.

Here, that which is obtained through the rule of extension (codaka) becomes a matter of doubt: should the dual number be modified (*ūhya*) and the singular number set aside, or should both be applied as alternatives to one another?

What, then, is the prima facie position? There should be a dual number, because it denotes those who are present together. There should be a singular number; it ceases [to apply] by the observation that one is unable to place [the offering], and this is the restrictive rule.
He says: "But surely, since duality is not intended to be expressed in the archetype (prakṛti), the application [of the mantra] would result in the modified form (vikārya).
It is replied:
In this case, duality is non-specific; however, it is not understood that the two [medhas] mentioned in the *adhigu* and *praisha* formulas are identical.

Furthermore, that which is being traversed is not without purpose; it establishes a number to be counted by means of the determination of another number. Thus, its purpose is indeed perceived. Therefore, there is a "many-arrangement" (*bahuvyūha*). [Objection:

Even though the previous section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*) has been established, why is this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) raised here? [Response: Because of the burning of others (*paradāhakayā*), and because of the emergence from a different doubt (*śaṅkāntarāt*).

He states the intention behind the use of the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*): [as stated] in the previous section (9.3.13.44), "Even in the case of oneness, because of the removal of qualities," however, in that [previous] instance, the non-consideration (*avikṣā*) of oneness was mentioned.
(The word "however" (*kiṃtu*) is displaced in its sequence; rather, it means that in this present sūtra, non-consideration is mentioned.
This is for the purpose of introducing the refutation with the words "that is not so" (*tan na*).)

If one asks, "In what way, then, is the purpose already established? he says: "That very same reason applies even in the case of the desire to speak. Therefore, this section concerning purpose (*prayojana*) pertains to the former [topic], while for the latter, this section concerns instruction (*aupadeśa*) and so forth.
Or rather, it is an alternative option, because it is the natural state.
Commentary: As for what was said—that a dual ending must be substituted—we accept that.
As for the argument that [the singular form] *nivarteta* (should be excluded) because it ends in the singular number, in that case:

even though it ends in the singular, it is eligible here to be optionally substituted by the dual-ending form, because it functions as the base (*prakṛti*). For it has been stated that in the original model (*prakṛti*), that [singular form] refers to the group (*gaṇa*), since the deities (*devatā*) are conjoined.
Therefore, here too, with reference to the group (*gaṇa*), the deities are established because of their association.
Soma—[answers that] there is a connection because [the deities] serve the purpose of the previously mentioned factors (*kāraka*).

For once the non-modification (*avikāra*) is established here, in the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) can be raised by this very same logic, and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) can be demonstrated by way of a counter-example; thus, this is an introduction (*upodghāta*) to what follows.
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: there would be no cessation [of the previous state] by virtue of being expressed in the singular number;
therefore, it must be a governing heading (adhikāra).
For example, in the case of "āditya," because it is expressed in the singular, the [substitution of] *ūha* for *no* or *vo* does not apply, just as in the word *ayavat*.

Because it is for the sake of the group (*gaṇa*), there is no modification (*anūha*); therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the original form (*prakṛti*). Bhaṭṭa: Where the divinity (*devatātva*) is one, but the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is either one or many, there is modification (*ūha*) in accordance with that [substratum], because the dual-ending [term] refers to the substratum.

However, for the singular-ending [term], there is indeed only the qualification (*adhikāra*), since the divinity itself is one; as in: "One should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," "One should sacrifice a smoke-colored animal to the Viśvedevas," "He should sacrifice these animals to the Ādityas," and so forth.
In this case, Vāyu is the single presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhāna*), whereas the Viśvedevas, being a collective group, are the many presiding deities.
And although sound (*śabda*) is the deity here, it is not [the deity] of the words found in the *adhigu-praiṣa*, as in the case of the Śyena sacrifice.

Although this is generally the case, nevertheless, for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of "deity" (*devatā*) and so forth, the assumption (*kalpanā*) of a sacrifice (*svīkāra*) is indeed required; for it is logical that this [usage] applies even to the meaning of "counter-correlativity to the sacrifice" as constituted by such an assumption. In this context, the term "substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) refers precisely to the "successive lineage" (*paraṃparā*) of the deity, and thus its modification (*ūha*) is established.
Likewise, in the case of the Ādityas, their status as the substratum is also plural, in accordance with the use of the plural number.

Nor should it be argued that because the word *āditya* would incur the status of being a dative case when the deity is intended, the nominal stem *āditya* itself must be construed as the deity; for even with a plural number, that [stem] indicates only singularity through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

To this we reply: even though there is secondary indication, the mode of denoting the substratum of its own primary power occurs precisely through such indication, and since plurality is logically established by that [indication] even with a single plural suffix, how can there be a multiplicity of substrata?

Therefore, in that case, there is a modification (*ūha*) of the dual ending according to the number of substrates (*adhiṣṭhāna*); however, the deityhood (*devatātva*) is one, because there is no evidence for its multiplicity. Even in the case of "to the Ādityas" (*ādityebhyaḥ*), the plural number does not apply to the deityhood itself due to the resulting change in case-ending; rather, the plurality is understood as pertaining to the objects (*ārthika*), and since it is apprehended through their connection with the purpose, the deityhood remains singular even there. Or, let it be granted that there is a distinction of deities there due to the plural number—this is the example here—but it applies specifically to the *adhigu-praiṣa*.
This should be understood as merely stating the purpose of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*).

In the *Nyāyabindu*, regarding the doubt that in rites such as the *Vaiśvadeva* there would be no modification (*ūha*) due to the force of the singular number when [the deity] is non-dual, it is stated that the purpose of the preceding section is that because [the deity] is a divinity (*devatā*), there is modification by way of being the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Maṇḍana says: "That which expresses one or two is not to be modified."
The word *medha-prati* [is used].
Śaṅkara says: "There is no need to infer multiplicity or unity.
14. Oṃ. The words such as *śyena* occurring in the *adhigupraiṣa* (the call for the Adhvaryu) manifest the extraction of the whole.

Even when words such as *śyena* (hawk) and *śalā* (rib) are mentioned, they appear in the singular number because of their proximity to well-known objects. The Bhāṣya states: In this sentence, the following is recited: "Make his chest like a hawk (*śyena*), the ribs like *śalā*, like what? Like the form of a falcon (*kavaya*); they take hold of the *sekrapaṇā*. Herein arises the doubt: Do these terms denote a generic class (*ākṛti*), or do they signify the offering of the whole [of the specific parts]?
What is established? Because of the proximity of what is well-known, it is a statement regarding the form (*ākṛti*).

When something is studied here in the vicinity of what is well-known with the thought "this is to be done," there the expression of the form is understood; for example: "These balls of flour are lions."
Others say they are similar;
the upper parts of the thighs are devoid of beauty.
[The instructions were: "Let Ṛg-verses be made," and "Let girdles be made of *arjuna* wood and *vadara* fruit."
Mādhava also says this in his *Brāhmaṇabhāṣya*:
"The mention of the shape of a lion and the mention of the shape of a girdle are understood to refer to the leaves of the *śyena* and *karavīra* plants.
Thus it is.
"Similar. Bhaṭṭabhāskara says they are "similar to parrot feathers.
However, the meaning of the sūtra is: the chest should be made in the shape of a hawk (śyena), the two arms in the shape of rods (śalāka), and the shoulders in the shape of a tortoise (kūrma).

In the case of the hawk and other [sacrificial animals], the mention of their form refers to the configuration of their parts, such as the beak and feet: the shoulders have the shape of a hawk’s wings, the thighs have the shape of its knees, and the hips have the shape of *karavīra* leaves.
This is because, when the well-known hawk or similar animal is present nearby, its very form is immediately recognized.

And there would have to be completeness [of the form], because it exists as such. [Objection: "Is it similarity or is it completeness that is intended by the mention of the hawk?"—the commentary states: "The word *pāśadaḥ* (the one who cuts the noose) sets aside the position that possesses logical consistency, but this is not the case. [End of quotation.]
Because it is proximate to what is well-known, and because that which exists [in the example] exists [in the subject], there is the comprehension of the entire object of indication.
"It expresses the form.
What, then, is intended? The extraction of the whole is what is intended. 9|4|6.
All these [parts] are extracted and fashioned into this form.
Bhaṭṭa: In that very context, in the *adhigu* injunction, it says, "Make his breast like that of a hawk," and so forth;
thus they become shaped like hawks and the like.
It is heard [in the text]: "O Father!
In that context, as in the case of the word *śyena*, one should apply the word *iva* to the breast; thus, the meaning "cut out the whole" is understood through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
There is no dispute that this is the meaning of "comparison" (upamā).
It is also agreed that the meaning of the word "as if" (iva) is similarity.
And this [similarity], when being presented here, pertains to an object of perception.
There is a purpose for those [mantras] extracted in their entirety;
for at that time, they belong to the *kṛtsnas* (entirety-mantras) alone.
Therefore:

When there is the occurrence of many [features], it is because of the presence of a few common properties that there is a lack of logical consistency; for the parts of those things which possess the form and those which do not possess that form are distinct. Therefore, the whole is understood only through its specific particulars.

And for this reason, having extracted the breast by means of cutting and so forth, and having brought it to the state of being shaped like a hawk (śyena), [the offering] is performed upon those [breasts] characterized as such, just as in the case of the animal sacrifice; for the *adhigupraiṣa* is intended for that purpose.

[Objection: Since it is obtained [as a portion] by means of a sesame seed (*tila*), even in the statement regarding the cutting-off (*avadāna*), the Bhāṣya says: "Now, from the chest... The *adhigu* formula is for the purpose of extracting the names of the limbs;

because of the hearing of the word "limbs" (*aṅgānām*), it is understood that only those [limbs] constitute the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Therefore, the purpose [of the formula] is to ensure that the entirety [of the limb] is not extracted through cutting and so forth.
How so? For it is thus:
the tantra can indeed be inferred.
By that, there arises a statement expressing similarity, namely: "Make limb by limb [the image] joint by joint."

Thinking, "May I be born from the entire *kalēdara*," it is understood that even from that [source], there is a complete extraction by means of the hawk and other [animals], precisely for the purpose of manifesting the whole *kalēdara*.
This is because, in the case of the theory of similarity (*sādṛśya-vāda*), it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*).
Otherwise, the mention of the "form of a hawk" would be redundant;
for if it were prescribed based on the wording of the mantra, there would result either prolixity or a lack of purpose.
[The Śābarabhāṣya says: "Having torn out the breast by means other than cutting, [one should fashion] the wings, feet, beak, and so forth..."

Thus, [the opponent argues that] by means of the *śalā* (pins), *dopaṇī* (handles), *kavyapākṛtī* (forms of the sacrificial cake), and *kapākṛtī* (forms of the skull-bone), as well as the *śyena-parṇā* (eagle-feathers), the form of an eagle (*śyenasaṃsthāna*) must be constructed (this is the prima facie view).
This should also be understood in the case of the passage beginning with "having points" (*śrīvantā*).
*Śalā* refers to pins or sticks.

This is not logical, because it would entail the consequence of having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), and because the chest would be maimed by the cutting. They would be like two tortoises, as in the case of Kaśyapa.
Through the rubbing, there would be the destruction of the oblation due to the movement of the means of progression and so forth.
Therefore, completeness is prescribed here. They should be similar; they should have the shape of *śyena* feathers or *karavīra* leaves.
"They are devoid of splendor, [consisting of] bone"—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
They are joined together.

This [point] applies both to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion; for in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice and others, since the comparison with Soma is intended merely as praise, it would otherwise be purposeless.

Since that [the literal sense] is necessary, and because even there, upon hearing the word *iva*, although there is a reference to totality through that [simile] in the case of "He is a lion" (*asiṃhaḥ*), there is no absence of figurative usage (*gauṇatva*)—as in the case of "Devadatta is a lion"—because it is possible for the *śyena* and other sacrifices to have as their sole purport mere similarity; therefore, there is no reference to totality through that [simile]. Thus, the connection arises because the comparison is established by the word *śyena* as performed with its chest as a distinguishing feature (*vakṣoviśiṣṭa*).
