Regarding the phrase *śalā doṣaṇī*, here *doṣaṇī* means "the two arms," and *śalā* refers to those resembling the *śalyaka* and *kalama* [types of porcupines]. Indeed, the metaphorical application (*anuha*) of words such as *śyena* and others is established by logic. [As stated: "The *śalya* is that which pierces; the *śalalī* is that which possesses *śalyas*."
Regarding the word "taśca":

although this section is not useful for the investigation of the *ūha* (modification), nevertheless, according to the *Amarakośa*, which states "śalam śalam," [the term] refers to a small stick (*śalākā*) and so forth;
thus, there is no fault, as it is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*).
Bhāskara [interprets] the two shoulders as being like tortoises; Mādhava says they are like tortoises.
The *Nyāyabindu* states, "Make his chest like a hawk," and Bhaṭṭabhāskara says the two thighs are like door-panels (*kapāṭa*).
*Khaṭvā* means "resembling a hawk";
by that method of cutting, the chest takes the shape of a hawk.

[The opponent argues: "It must be performed. This being the case, since it would result in an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*) and because the sacrificial oblation would be destroyed by the cutting, what is intended here is the entirety of the chest; that is, the whole of it.
And because of the observation of a characteristic mark;
that is, because of its similarity to a hawk (śyena).
And in this way, there is a visible purpose.
Likewise, there is the *śalā*.

The commentary states: "Furthermore, there is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*): for instance, the hands of those who associate [with the wicked] have the shape of a pair of forceps (*doṣaṇī-śalākā*);
their shoulders are like those of tortoises."
"They do not move" means that neither the mother, nor the father, nor the umbilical cord moves; the meaning is that they are like tortoises.
The thighs are like the panels of a door or like a bedstead (*khaṭvā*).
"For he is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa)"— thus, having established the vital breath as the reason for the modification,
[the text] indicates that the thighs are the two parts of the thighs preceding the hips, which are like the leaves of the *karavīra* tree.
Therefore, the associated [grains] are not enjoined.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that even the expression "resembling leaves" refers only to the totality [of the grains]. Soma says: "The word *vrīhi* [is applied] to the individual parts contained within the *nīvāra* [grain]. Maṇḍana says: "'Like the hawk' refers to the extraction of the whole."

Because the word *anantavat* lacks the capacity to refer to multiple [sacrifices], there is no modification (*ūha*). Śaṃkara raises the objection: "And in the case of the Śyena and others, there is completeness. This is the connection.

Those things which, when conjoined, become one and do not remain separate even while conjoined— like a jar and so forth— are called "conjoined" (*saṃsargin*). For example, the substances mentioned in the *adhigu-praiṣa* such as the eye,
clarified butter, oil, water, fire, and so on, are denoters of conjoined substances.
The meaning of the sūtra is this: there is no modification (*ūha*) of words such as *r̥k* with respect to the animal and its qualities among those things that are associated.
And they have not [established] the measure of an object such as fire and so forth,
because there is an absence of a fixed measure;
here, the word "measure" refers to those things associated with number, since the measure of an object is not fixed.
[The opponent says: "And thus, there is no necessity of connection among the related things. (10.28)
"Even though many have departed, there is no modification (*anūha*) because unity is still possible.
The Bhāṣya says: "In the *adhigupraiṣa*, there are connected meanings.
For example:"
Vi— "In the case of two-footed [verses], there is no modification (*ūha*) of *asu* and so forth, nor of *vaḥ*;
rather, from *paśumedas* [comes] *cakṣuḥ*, *prāṇaḥ*, and so on. [The rule] 'let the eye go to the sun' [is applied];
because the constituent element of light (*tejomātra*) is manifested as the sun and so forth, there is modification."
"Let the breath follow after him"—this [is said] regarding the quality of the animal in the case of two-footed [animals] and so forth.
Regarding the *daikṣa* *adhigupraiṣa*, [the question is]: "Should [the phrase] 'his feet directed northward' be inserted, or not? The Bhāṭṭa [position is as follows].
It is said:

But surely, because of the improper application [of the term], since the eye goes to the sun and the breath follows after the wind, this [term] should not have been used [in the singular]; for while there are two eyes, the word ending in the singular [is used].
"O dear one, the intermediate space is his breath, the quarters are his hearing, and the earth is his body"— since this is what is heard [in the scripture],
it is replied: this word "adhigu" in the *adhigupraiṣa* does not denote the *adhigu* priest.
It has been heard [in scripture].

In that context, regarding the group of animals, the singular form "of this" (*asya*) indicates the movement of the sun in the dual and plural numbers; for the sun does not move upon the physical substrate. There is no exception to the modification of the plural number for "splendor" (*tejas*); likewise, there is no modification even in the case of the word "foot" (*padaḥ*).
But this [being] is Raśmican;
moreover, that splendor is singular.
Therefore, this is not he.

However, regarding the objects of the senses such as the eye, when there is deliberation on what is to be inferred or not inferred, there is the recitation of the *adhilakṣaṇa* and *anyāyanigada*. Furthermore, in the case of modified forms (*vaikṛta*) such as the *dvipadā* verses, because of parsimony (*lāghava*), a single sense organ (*indriya*) is postulated as having a distributed function (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) across different substrates, such as "the white [animal] for Mitra."

One may obtain the black [fire] of Varuṇa at the junction of the waters and the plants, as well as food desired even by others; this [occurs] in the vital breath (prāṇavāyu). And thus, from such passages as "his desire," when a distinction in fire is understood through the classification of sacrificial animals (paśubheda), [the following applies].

Because there is oneness, the singular number is used; since this very [number] applies even when the animal is divided, it follows that there should be modification (*ūha*). But surely, it should be applied to a single animal.
As for the vital breath denoted by the term *prāṇa*, since its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is also one, those two fires are indeed distinct according to the difference of their substrates;
this is not so, it is said,
because in that case [the fire] is certainly one alone.
The direct perception of the body, however, is due to the fact that it is "to be reached by the eye of the one sun," which is light derived from what is taught by others;
for even more than that,
the eye does not function as a distributed entity (vyāsajyavṛtti), and thus the distinction of substrates is not intended when referring to a single eyeball.

Because there is a difference in the brilliance of the animal's eyes within the intervals [of the sacrifice], even if [the eye] were destroyed, there would be no impossibility of it being perceived by the eye; for the inference is that it resides in only one eyeball.
This being the position reached, we reply:
And because the object is not established among those things with which it is in contact,
since its perception occurs even without the eye [being in contact with it];
this being the position reached, [the object is distinct] because it occupies a different location and possesses a different dimension.

Although there is a distinction between animals regarding objects that come into contact, nevertheless, when there is a distinction in their substrata, one must set aside the inherent distinction of the qualities residing therein—such as color and so forth—and recognize only the contact of the rays themselves; thus, those rays become unified.
Just as it is said:
Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [the rays] existing as a distributed whole (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*).

Otherwise, if one were to assume a single eye in common for all living beings—just as small portions of water, oil, or ghee exist in various places—it would follow that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Just as distinct things become unified when in the same location, so too are the rays.
Because there is a separate sense organ for each locus;
and since that [locus] is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the word denoting them should be in the singular number, and thus there would be no modification (*anūha*).
The fact that [the mantras] such as *taijasa* are different is another matter;

and in that case, since the singular number can be justified even with the intention of referring to each individual according to the principle of the wife (*patnīnyāya*), there is indeed no modification (*anūha*).
In reality, since the sun cannot reside within the eyeball, it is only that which has emerged from it that is designated here by the term "eye.

Nor should it be argued that because the *adhigu-praiṣa* occurs only after the *paryagnikaraṇa*, the eyes and other organs are still situated within the eyeballs at that time and thus have not yet emerged;
for there is no contradiction, as the very result of the subsequent restoration of consciousness (*saṃjñāna*) is already being described even prior to that point.

And therefore, for the eye that has indeed emerged [from the socket], just like the light of a lamp, because of its unification through contact with many others, the use of the singular number in the original state (*prakṛti*) is beyond reproach. Consequently, even in the modified state (*vikṛti*), such an adaptation (*ūha*) is possible. For here, there is no assumption of a separation of locations—as in the case of lamps—among the emerged eyes; rather, when one eyeball is closed, since objects such as a jar situated in front of it are seen by the eye residing in the other eyeball, the unification of the emerged eyes is established through the assumption of their expansion (*visphāra*).

And here, just as in the case of "luminosity" (*tejasvatva*) and so forth, the eye and other organs are also a class (*jāti*) consisting of the differentiation between parts and wholes; therefore, since the whole (*avayavin*) produced by those respective bodies situated in their respective globes is also simply the eye, there is no occasion for modification (*ūha*). The same should be understood regarding the tip [of the nose] denoted by the term "prāṇa.

As for the body, although it is not possible for it to be a single entity, nevertheless, because the dissolution into the subtle earth—which serves as the cause of that which is being spoken of—is contradicted by perception, and because it is stated merely for the sake of praise within the context of the primordial material (*prakṛti*), it is not a literal truth; thus, it should be seen that there is no modification (*anūha*).
Regarding the body, some consider there to be modification (*ūha*).

The *Nyāyabindu* states: In the *adhigupraiṣa* mantra, such as "May the eye go to the sun" (*asūrye cakṣurgamyatāt*), there is modification of the dual and plural numbers in the case of the eyes. Since the singular number in the archetype refers to the "eye" (*cakṣus*)—which, being light (*tejas*), is capable of contact like water and thus cannot inherently possess number, but rather possesses it only through its substrate (*upādhi*) in the form of the animal (*paśu*)—if it were to have the substrate of the physical location (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the consequence would be duality. Therefore, the modification is determined by the specific configuration of the animal.

This being the position reached, the singular number is used with the intention that the light emerging from the substratum becomes one, and not with reference to the substratum itself, because those two [the eyes] are not connected to the sun and moon, and because they are two.

Therefore, since the stated unity is possible even when there is a difference in the animals, there is no modification (*anūha*); this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Maṇḍana says: "One should certainly not prescribe modification (*ūha*) in the case of the eyes and so forth."
Śaṅkara says: "The [words] are not [mere] associates of the Guru.
11. By the word *urūka* occurring in the *adhigupraiṣa*, the omentum (*vapā*) is denoted.
Because of its proximity to the *vaṇiṣṭha*, the omentum is denoted by the word *urūka*.
Commentary: In the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice within the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the *adhigu* formula: "Do not make its thinnest part cry out, thinking it to be an *urūka*.

Regarding this, there is a deliberation concerning the word *urūka*: does it mean "do not make its thinnest part cry out, thinking it to be like an *urūka*," or rather, "thinking it to be the *urūka*—that is, the omentum (*vapā*)—do not make its thinnest part cry out"?
What is obtained? [The phrase] "regarding it as the most excellent and wide-ranging.
How is the word *urūka* a designation for the *urūka* (a type of animal)? Because the letters *ra* and *la* function identically.
For example: *paryaṅkaḥ* becomes *palvaṅkaḥ*; *romāṇi* become *lomāni*; *aṅguṣṭhaḥ* becomes *aṅguṣṭhiḥ*.
Furthermore, because the *vaṇiṣṭhu* resembles a thigh (*urūka*), and because the omentum (*vapā*) is not commonly known by that name;

such being the case, we reply: the word *urūka* must denote the omentum. For the instruction—"Do not cut the *vaṇiṣṭhu*, thinking it to be the omentum"—would be rendered meaningless [if it did not refer to the omentum].
For indeed, due to the proximity of the term *vaṇiṣṭha*, there arises the possibility of mistakenly performing the *vaṇiṣṭha* extraction;
by precluding that, this word serves a visible purpose.
For it is not the case that the *vaṇiṣṭha* must necessarily be cut.
Thinking that the *vapā* (omentum) is located in the belly and the *kaṇāla*, one should not cut [the meat];

on the other hand, regarding the alternative view, the prohibition "do not make a noise" (*mā rāviṣṭa*) concerning the *vaṇiṣṭha* when it is to be cut would be meaningless. Furthermore, the statement resembling the word *urūka* would serve no visible purpose.
But how, when not applied to the omentum (*vapā*), will the word *urūka* cause the understanding of the omentum? It is said:
by means of the well-known meaning of its parts.
The word *urūka* is seen to denote that which is broad.
For example: "O King Aruṇa, wide [is the path]! O Tailika Aruṇa, wide [is the path]!
Likewise: "King Varuṇa has indeed made wide the path for Sūrya to follow.
And likewise: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely!"
Here too, that word is indeed used in its extensive sense;
likewise, the word *kaśā* is well known to mean fat (*medas*).
For example, in the expression "chariots drawn by *kaśās*," it is understood to mean "drawn by fat."
A portion of it, the word *kaśā*, produces the cognition of the whole.

In the case of the term *medasvinī* ("fatty one"), its *vapā* (omentum) is intended; for one who considers the fat (*medas*) to be extensive, the *vaṇiṣṭha* (the rectum), which is situated near it, is not to be cut out. Thus, the status of the term as a designation for the *vapā* is established.

What is the purpose? Under the view that it refers to the skin (vaṇiṣṭha), there is no modification (anūha) of the word *urūka* as the object of comparison; under the view that it refers to the omentum (vapā), the word *urūka* must be modified. [In the latter case], the word *kaśā* would become *uruṇī ke* or *uruṇī kāni*.

Alternatively, if "urūkam" is intended as a compound, then the connection is explained by stating that although the word "soma" in the expression "ṣaḍviṃśati-soma" consists of a compounded statement, there is no modification (*ūha*) in the word "urūka. "Vaṇiṣṭham" refers to that which is situated near the omentum (*vapā*), resembling the omentum.
It is a specific part.
The meaning of the Sūtra is:
the term *ūrūka* should denote the omentum (*vapā*), because of its proximity to the *vaṇiṣṭha*.
Because it serves a visible purpose by removing the delusion caused by the proximity of the *vaṇiṣṭha*, [the rule applies].
[The commentary says: "The two sides are the omentum (*vapā*); there is no distinction between *ra* and *la*.
The two sides are [the omentum] due to proximity; [this is said] because it removes the error regarding the prohibition."
In various modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) involving multiple omenta, the word *urūka* is subject to modification (*ūha*).
In the *Bhāṭṭa* school, it is heard in the *adhigupraiṣa*: "Do not cut its most tender part, thinking it to be an *urūka*."

In this regard, when considering whether the term *urūka* denotes the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) or the omentum (*vapā*), since the word *urūka* is not used for the omentum, and because in the Veda the letter *r* is seen in place of *l*, and because even in common usage words containing *r* and *l*—such as *romāṇi* and *lomāni*—function synonymously, the term *urūka* denotes the animal called *urūka*. Consequently, the meaning of the mantra is: "Do not cut the rectum (*vaṇiṣṭha*) with the thought that it is an *urūka*. Therefore, even if there are many omenta, there is no [application of the mantra] to two *urūkas*.
This being the case, the cutting of the *vaṇiṣṭhu* is not prohibited altogether; for, like the heart and other organs, its status as an oblation (*havis*) necessitates its being cut.
Nor is the perception of similarity to a lizard (*urūka*) at the time of cutting prohibited, as that would result in [the injunction] having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Therefore, by means of a connection with a part, the word *urūka* denotes the omentum (*vapā*) itself.

Thinking that the omentum (vapā) is located in the belly and the intestines (vapodarakaṇāle), one should not cut the rectum (vaṇiṣṭha) out of error; this is the meaning. Since the rectum is to be cut after the offering of the omentum, the statement prohibiting its cutting beforehand serves a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha).

Regarding the etymological derivation (*avayavayoga*): the word *urūka* signifies "extensive," with the long vowel being a Vedic archaism (*dīrgha-cchāndasa*). The syllable *kadā* (or *kad*) signifies "fat" (*medas*). Since the name is mentioned as a part of the whole, the syllable *ka-* also denotes that same thing [fat]. Thus, these two words form either a compound (*samāsa*) or a descriptive phrase; its meaning is "one whose fat (*vapā*) is extensive. Nor does conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) override etymology; for even in the case of the word *urūka*, there is no conventional usage for the word-form containing the letter *ra*.

Therefore, when there is a plurality of omenta (*vapā*), modification (*ūha*) must be performed in the case of the two-word reading *ūrṇā-kāni* and in the case of the compound reading *urūkaṇi*. The *Nyāyabindu* states: Regarding the passage, "Do not cut off his rectum (*vaṇiṣṭha*), thinking it to be the *urūka*," since the letters *ra* and *la* are interchangeable, the word *urūka* denotes the rectum. Thus, under the impression that it is something unseen (or unknown), there is a prohibition against cutting that specific part of the rectum.
This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the correct conclusion is]: *uru* means "broad" and *kaṃ* means "flesh"; thus, the term refers to the omentum (*vapā*).
Because of the proximity of the omentum (*vapā*) and the *kaṇāla*, the cutting of the *vaṇiṣṭhu* (rectum) was erroneously understood [as applicable]; this is now prohibited.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is modification (*ūha*) when the notion of the omentum arises.
Maṇḍana states: "The rectum is not for the *ulmuka*."
Mīmāṃsākośa 44, Śaṅkara: "And *vaporūka* [is used] in the *adhigu* [praise].
By means of the word *praśasā* occurring in the *adhigu-praiṣa*, there is praise of the two arms;
*praśasā* is a designation for the mouth."
In the commentary on that [passage] from the Veda, it is recited: "Make the arms praise" (*praśasā bāhū*).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does "praśasā bāhū" mean that one should take the word *praśasā* as being in the instrumental case (ending in *ā*), such that "the two arms are to be taken as praise," or does "praśasā" represent a dual form (with the case-ending changed to *ā*) such that "the two arms are to be made praised"? What is the prima facie view?
346. Regarding the praise by means of the *agnigupraiṣa*: since there is no purpose for the word [in question] even if it were expressive of something praiseworthy, [the reading is] *asyabhi-sulūk*.

Thus, it does not possess the quality of being frequent (*bāhulakatva*). And so it is said: "the state of being a *śalā-dhāyaka*"; this is the connection (*saṃgati*). In the Sūtra, [the term] *praśasā* [is used].
Thus, even the reading beginning with "droṣaṇī" is consistent.

And for this reason, the meaning is "by means of the word *praśasta*. Since the word *sā* denotes excellence (*praśastatva*), and since that [excellence] indicates the state of being unimpaired (*avikalatva*)—for the word *praśasā* may mean praise (*stuti*) or cutting (*chedana*).
It is not for the sake of the meaning, because the purpose has already been seen; the modification (*ūha*) is extensively obstructed. In that case as well, there is the *dasi* [suffix].
Praise (*stuti*) should be expressed in its entirety, lest the praise be interrupted.

When there is a plurality of the word *bāhu* in the original text (*prakṛti*), due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), there is a plurality of arms; thus, the means of action is two-edged swords (*dvipāśi*).
However, the sword (*asi*) is not the means for cutting.

In the modified form (*vikṛti*), just as in the case of another [word] ending in *bahutvacan* at the beginning of the section, it is a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*): the Bhaṭṭa [commentary] states that in that very injunction (*praiṣa*, specifically the *agnigupraiṣa*), there is praise (*praśasā*).
According to the maxim "when the use of a word is under one's own control," the Vedic text reads "the excellent arms" (*praśastān bāhūn*) rather than simply "arms" (*bāhū*).
Here, the word "cut off" (*kuṇutāt*) is supplied from the context. In that regard:
Such is the modification (*ūha*).

And regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), concerning the modification "praśāsaiḥ," one should consider what is meant by the term *praśasā*: does it refer to the *śāsa* (the sacrificial knife) functioning as an instrument? This is how it should be understood.

And regarding the consideration of whether this [suffix] follows from the *Mahābhāṣya-sāra* as being for the sake of "desirability" (*kānta*) or "praise" (*praśasta*), since it is not seen in the sense of praise,

and because the same logic applies even to the density (*sāndhatā*) [of the suffix], the *kvi* and *vic* suffixes do not occur. This is because it would result in the meaning of praise (*praśā*), and thus the word *praśā*— ending in the third case and with the elision of the vowel *a*— is used in its short form.
Thus, [the form] *gama* in *kṛṣāsapada* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). And having sung [the verse], the word *śāsa* denotes instruction;
for the word *śāsa* is explained as "O you are indeed the instruction" (*asi vai śāsamācakṣate*), and its meaning as "recitation" (*pragāṇa*) has been stated.
Alternatively, based on the essence of the *Mahāvārttika* and from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) such as "much" (*bahu*) and so forth, [the suffix] is one that expresses the instrument (*asivacana*).

Consequently, by means of the sword (*asinā*). If it is intended that the suffixes *kvi* and *vic* are applied to a verbal root ending in *m*, then the meaning of the command is: "Cut off the arms with the visible sword."

And although, due to its conformity with the accentuation of *svadhiti*, the root *śas*— which is taught [in the Dhātupāṭha] as having the meaning "to injure" (*hiṃsā*)— is generally prescribed for cutting (*chedana*) in the context of the Vedic verses, nevertheless,

there is a specific injunction based on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*) regarding the cutting of the arms for the *śas*-root ending in *lunaki* and appearing in the instrumental case; this is not contradicted by the general rule.

Since there is no assumption of Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), it is understood that the instrumental case is employed here because [the word] is intended for the inferior [agent], such as snow or the like. Therefore, in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, regarding the passage "a hundred golden ones,
swift-moving," the modification (*ūha*) consistent with the consensus of ritualists (*yājñika-sammatam*) and the Śākhās of the Mādhyandinas should be applied.
Since it is prescribed that "they become free from disease" by means of the injunction regarding the possession of swords in hand, there is no modification (*ūha*) following that [injunction].
However, the ritualists do not perform a modification in the word *praśasā* nor in the word *bāhu*;
rather, the modification occurs through the *rova* [sound].

This being the position reached, the Bhāṣyakāra and others have resolved it thus: [The word] "thus" (evam) refers to that which is directly prescribed; [it applies] when there is an option for shortening based on the wording of the mantra. Maṇḍana says: "Praise is the glorification of the arms."

"Out of respect, the word *praśaṃsā* (praise) refers exclusively to being praiseworthy (*praśastatva*). Of that [word], Śaṅkara himself [says]: 'And *praśaṃsā* is the state of being praiseworthy (*praśastatā*')."
Regarding the statement, "He says, 'Ten fore-offerings,' and he says, 'Bring the sacrificial knife (śāsa),'":

since this is written in the *agnigupraiṣa* as "recite those [verses] and cause them to be raised," and since the sacrificial knife (*śāsa*) is also prescribed for the animal sacrifice, it is disregarded [here].

The word *anuguya* refers to the feminine form of the effortful action (*anuṣṭhiti*). However, in reality, upon a thorough examination of all the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) such as those of Bodhāyana, the term *śāsa*— [The sentence continues: ...is [the correct reading].

According to Pāṇini 3.1.106, the suffix *aṅ* is applied [to form *śroṣage*]; since it is possible [to perform the act] even with an axe (*svadhiti*) when [the object] is cut, the term *svadhiti* applies even in the case of cutting only a finger or an arm.
Thus, from the stem ending in *a*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added, followed by the third-case singular ending.
Because the application of the case-endings is already established, there is no need to postulate another substance based on the wording of the mantra.

The indicative mark (*liṅga*)— namely, that [the word] *vaiśāsa* is explained by the rule beginning with "yat asi | sulūk" (Pāṇini 7.1.39), which prescribes a partial elision (*prādeśika-lopa*)— indicates that the *svadhiti* itself is [referred to] by virtue of its similarity to the *as*.
*uccāyayatāt*: In the injunction for the act of raising [the sacrificial post], this is the second person plural *loṭ* ending, identical [to the singular].
In the *Nighaṇṭu*, within the *agnigupraiṣa*, it appears as a synonym for *svadhiti*.
The form *uccāyayatāt* arises from the substitution of *tātaṅ* for the plural ending.
Alternatively, even if one considers the word *śāsa* to denote the instrument for cutting off the arms based on its recitation [in the Vedic text], the form is *praśā*.
The meaning is "with effort from the belly. (Ratna. 4|14|1)
That [word] is not denoted by the word-form [in question],
because the elision of the letter *t* alone is possible through its frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*),

as in the case of the *agni-guṇa-praiṣa* and the *paśu-guṇa*, where the application of the entire *ṛc* is possible; this is provided that one accepts the elision of the vowel *a* and the shortening [of the vowel] as being due to frequent occurrence.
The statement is concise for the sake of brevity.
There is an absence of valid evidence (*pramāṇābhāva*).
This is because [the term] *bāhu* is accepted as being in the dual case ending.

By means of twenty-six paths; because it is the source-material (*prakṛti*) for the quality of the animal; and because when grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, syntactic heterogeneity (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is improper. There would be no connection with the navel due to modification; the compound would not be joined with the dual ending, but the substitution of the vowel *ā* is prescribed by an independent rule (*supāṃ suluk...* / *sarvābhisaḥ*).
The Commentary states: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the Agniṣomīya animal victim;
"He who is initiated, when he immolates the Agniṣomīya animal"—here, the relationship between the two [the agent and the action] is the primary element in this mantra.
In that regard, the first position is established;
and for that relationship, the word "twenty-six" is heard in the injunction: "There are twenty-six ribs."
And there is no designator by which it might be expressed.
That which is the primary [cause], having brought together the herds of animals such as the two-sided ones with water, [is] "the white one belonging to Mitra."
Therefore, it must necessarily be explained.

In that regard, the connection [of the mantra] with its purpose is practiced: "The black [animal] belongs to Varuṇa; the mantra is recited at the junction of the waters and the plants" (with the words, "Twenty-six, twenty-six are your ribs").
Thus;
in such passages as these, the meaning is this:
is the *sandehika* [the same as] the *ṣaḍviṃśati*-...?
He states the justification for this: "In this way, when the relationship [of the parts] is primary, the word *abhyāsa* (repetition) must be applied; should it be used without modification?
Or is the mere statement sufficient, such that it will become modified?
Is it then merely *vaḍkri*, or rather the repetition of this very word, or perhaps its compounding?"
What is the connection of the word? To this he says: "And the word *vaḍkri* is a statement.
What is the conclusion? The word *ṣaḍviṃśati* is to be repeated;
it is to be understood as qualifying the word *ṣaḍviṃśatithya*.
In the case of groups of animals such as those with two wings and so forth.
What is the reason? Because in the archetype (prakṛti), there is only one.
Now, the second position.

This mantra is without a specific ritual application (*akaraṇa*). Twenty-six verses have been stated for the two *pramāda*s. Here, that quality (*guṇa*) illuminates the meaning already revealed by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).
Nor is it included within another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [For example:
"In the animal sacrifice, there are twenty-six ribs.
In that regard, if—

If there were a purpose in illuminating that which has already been illuminated by the sun, then one might employ a lamp with a modification [of its function], rather than speaking with crooked words after having already done so.
Now,
this is the point.

And thus, that which is performed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) occurs in the ectype (*vikṛti*); the statement would be made in its original form, and consequently, the word "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśati*) would be set aside. [Thus,] nothing would be sublated [and therefore there would be no modification].
In that case, however, the purpose (*āptyai*) would be sublated.
Nor by all the preparatory rites.
Now, as for the third position:
the word "twenty-six" has a connection with the animal victim.
The two animals are connected with those [parts];
nor is it qualified by both [of them]. (In this case, the *vaḍkri* and the *pādya*).
Thus, in this context, there are two sacrificial animals (paśu). Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the animal which stands in the place of the [original] animal is the primary one?"
(And thus he states that the third position is established: They are connected with the *vaḍkri* [intestines], for so it is stated in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
In the case of two [verses], the number twenty-six is manifested;
and those have been performed.

When the connection of the two animals has been established by all the *vaḍkri* [entrails], the unmodified word "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśati*) is used here to convey the name; thus, the connection of each one with twenty-six is made known.
Here—
Therefore, it is stated [as "twenty-six"] due to a confusion of the wording; he states the justification: it was not done thus in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
And since [the details] are directly prescribed in the archetype (*prakṛti*),
thus only a slight modification will occur.
(As for the phrase "but they are prescribed," it refers to the connection with the animal sacrifice in the twelfth [chapter] regarding rice.)
In this case, when a connection is being made with the number of others,

the Bhāṣya— beginning with "But if [the word] 'twenty-six' were stated in the Sūtra"— [argues that] the connection with the number of parts would be based on inference through the mediation of the meaning.
This is not so.

Having restated that, he explains: But if the word "twenty-six" (ṣaḍviṃśati) were predominant, then by necessity, the connection of each [rib] with twenty-six would be conveyed; thus, the nominative case for the "six ribs" (vaḍkrīṇām) would not be obtained. What is the intention? It would have to be twofold.
In that regard, there are indeed numerical doctrines stating, "twenty-five for one" and "twenty-seven for another. For prior to twenty, numbers are predominant; thus two perspectives are understood.
However, no such designation has been made in the present context.
Therefore, [the suffixes] beginning with *abhyasi*—
and so forth— are predominant in both [senses] after twenty;
in that regard, [the suffix] *tavya*.
When a numeral, having made itself subordinate, denotes the object to be numbered, then [the suffix] *ṭup* [is applied]. In this section there are five positions (*pakṣas*).

First: without a genitive case, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in "twenty cows" (*viṃśatir gāvaḥ*) or "twenty of this" (*asya viṃśatiḥ*), which is the analysis of the two words. Thus is the first position.
"Without modification.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, when the number is the primary element [and the thing to be numbered is secondary], it is the second case [ending].
The third [point] is that there is no modification (*ūha*) of the word "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśati*) in the phrase; this is the third.

The fourth is that there is no modification of the word "praise" (*stuti*), because it stands in grammatical apposition with the word denoting the number to be counted (*saṃkhyeya*) without the intervention of the genitive case; this is the fourth.
[And] the compound (*samāsa*): this is [the fifth].
There is no capacity [for it], as in the case of "twenty cows";
and here, number is the fifth [category].
In that regard—) the purport is the logical application of the statement of the thesis.
In your view, the ribs (*vaṅkrī*) are the primary referents and are expressed in the nominative case;
that is being defined [by the statement]:
"He has twenty-six ribs."
The intention is: how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) without the genitive case? This consists of three words forming a sentence;
therein, one alternative view holds that the relation is the primary element.
(Who? From what? To this, the author of the Bhāṣya gives the answer [in Sūtra 12]: "The connection with the indicator is stated"—namely, "he has twenty-six [teeth] of another.")
The meaning is that there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the sentence;
for otherwise, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with a word in which number is predominant would not be possible.
[Objection: Is it not observed that words denoting substances are used with reference to qualities? To this he says: Usage is indeed seen, as for example in "indra-prī devatā" (the deity Indra-prī).

When a group (a collection) is intended to be expressed as the deity, and not as the primary [referent], then even without the genitive case, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed, as in "devadatta-viṣṇumitrayoḥ ataḥ paśyat" (he sees from Devadatta and Viṣṇumitra).

In this case, the word *paryaccha* is the primary element, while the other words such as *deva* and so forth function as its qualifiers; likewise, in the Veda, there is the expression: "The year is divided into five times fifty [days].

Here, the number (*pañcāśat*) is the primary element, yet there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) even without the use of the genitive case (between the two words denoting the number, namely *mitra* and *saṃvatsara*).
Now, one might object: "In this instance, the number is intended as a qualifier of the year."
(He says, "No"—) if that were the case, the word "five" would be meaningless, whereas the word "fifty" (which has number as its primary sense) would be meaningful as the object to be qualified.
(He concludes—) therefore, the number is the predominant factor. (Now) the fourth position.
The word *vaṣaṭkāra* is specified as a qualifier for this term; thus,
here the reference back to the ribs mentioned in the statement "twenty-six ribs will be described" is made for the purpose of establishing the ritual action (*kārya*).

Therefore, they [the wives] possess predominance. However, because they are not present at the time of the primary action, there should be a designation as belonging to Agni, just as in the case of the wife (*patnī*).
[From the] Bhāṣya: The word "however" (*api tu*) serves to set aside the previous position.
This is not so; I shall speak by way of equalizing [the two].
What then? The word "twenty-six" (ṣaḍviṃśati) should be used in its unmodified form. Why? Because it does not undergo phonetic modification (asaṃnipātitvāt).
For fire is not a composite entity; it is not designated as such by way of its constituent parts (*kalpa*).

If it were designated as an instrument (*karaṇa*), then that which is manifested by it would have to be performed, and not by means of meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth; thus there would be a convergence of ritual factors (*dharmasaṃnipāta*) at the end of the mantra.
In that case, since it is impossible to perform it simultaneously in its unmodified state, it would have to be modified or repeated.

Furthermore, since this performance is being carried out at the time of leading [the animal] forward, by which animal does the injunction regarding the Agniṣṭut fall here through the force of the extended application (codaka)?
In that case, it is impossible for these [animals] to express their own respective numbers;
thus, its form is contradictory.
Therefore, it should not be said that [the word] refers to those [wives].
What then? A connection with the number twenty-six must be established.
Just as, in a ritual performance involving two wives or many wives, the word *patnī* ending in the singular does not delimit the wives by means of that number.
What then? It occurs as a unity; so it is here as well.
Therefore, the application is with modification.
Thus, in the case of no modification, the archaic form will be maintained.

(He states the meaning of the sūtra: Because it is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice by way of non-performance [of other rites], it must assist that which possesses the context.

When the expectation arises as to "how" [it assists], it is connected with the phrase "as far as one is able. Furthermore, when the expectation arises as to "what can it do?", [the answer is] that by means of this mantra—which has action as its primary focus—it performs the denotation through its words as they are recited [i.e., the mere performance of the action].

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In that regard, because of the recitation of the words beginning with 'you shall speak' (*vakṣyasi*), just as [the mantra is used] in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too in the ectype (*vikṛti*)."
But there is modification, because it is a specific location, as in the case of the *jamadagni* [mantra].
The word "but" (*tu*) in the commentary reverses the previous position. It is not without modification; rather, an adaptation (*ūha*) must be performed.

When a certain number is brought forward and then expressed by that same number, there, by virtue of the authority of the statement, even the primary meaning of a word used with a conflicting number is accepted—
just as, for example, the word *patnī* (wife) in the archetype (*prakṛti*). However, in this case, the word "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśati*) is not applied to multiple animals by being brought forward.
However, by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), the archetypal statement is obtained here.

In that case, the *codaka* will cause what is appropriate to be applied, rather than bringing in the word "twenty-six" by force. What is that which is appropriate? That which was intended in the archetype.
And it has been stated in the *Prakṛti* [section] that "of the verses" and so forth;
therefore, it is seen here as well.
But was it not said that there is no mention of the *agniṣṭoma* as an instrument (*karaṇa*)?

Thus [it is asked]: "When it is not an instrument (*karaṇa*), how can this be a statement expressing a number? Having heard [the word 'twenty-six'], it ought to be a statement expressing the number twenty-six.
It is replied:

Although there is no third-case (instrumental) indication for this [mantra], nevertheless, being adopted by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) as a means of accomplishment, it will provide a visible assistance that is required, other than through the manifestation of the portions to be cut off (*avadāna*).
To this it is replied: This [mantra] has no connection with the portions to be cut off; rather, the injunction of the performance of the sacrifice under discussion connects with the sacrifice itself.
And in that case, the mention of the oblation would serve a visible purpose;
furthermore, the "twenty-six-fold" [hymn] will also apply to that very same [oblation].
We say: it is not so.

Since, by virtue of the context, it is understood that this is an instruction for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) when there is a connection with the sacrifice in general, we determine from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that this is the instruction for the *śamitṛ* (the slaughterer). There are such statements here in the text: "O divine slaughterers and also you human ones, begin!"
Thus, [the opponent might argue]: "The word *ṣaḍviṃśati* (twenty-six) should be used because it is to be expressed as an *anuṣṭubh*.
Therefore, it would be a statement of the word itself, not a statement of the number twenty-six.

Just as with the word *yajamāna*, which expresses a single sacrificer and thus possesses its own singular number, yet when used in a context of two sacrificers, the dual is employed because it refers to its own number even in that situation—so it is here as well.

It is said in reply: If the two words *vakṣyī* and *alaḥ* (in their original form) were to possess a meaning inherent in the ritual act (*samavetārthatā*), then we might assume they have no purpose other than that which is already established.
However, there exists an inherent connection with the act of cutting out (*avadāna*), which is the function of the *vakṣyī*; thus, the word *vakṣyī* is indeed inherently connected [to the ritual].
And that [object of speech] is delimited by its own nature (in its primordial state) as having twenty-six constituents; therefore, even the word for "number" has a meaning that is inherent [to it].
Furthermore, the purification (the calming) of that object of speech is an expansion solely for the sake of a visible purpose.
Otherwise, one might recite it in a deficient manner due to forgetfulness.

Therefore, for the sake of illuminating what follows, the statement regarding the *agniṣṭut* in the archetype (*prakṛti*) applies likewise to the ectype (*vikṛti*); thus, a collective statement should be made. Because it is something not previously established, it does not apply to the wife (*patnī*).
As for what was stated in the commentary—that it is "like the wife"—[that refers to the following].

It is appropriate [to apply the term] to the wife; however, the word *patnī* (wife) is not recited there when the sacrificer has only one wife, but it does extend by application (*pradeśāt*) to cases where there are two wives or many wives.
Just as the singular number expresses the count of one wife, so too the dual and plural numbers express the count of two or many wives respectively.
Therefore, there is inequality regarding the wife;
because the prescribed modification applies to the numbers, it must extend to all parts.
The word "but" (tu) in the commentary introduces another position: that the statement does not apply to the whole, but rather there should be a combination.
Just as from this word twenty nominal stems (prātipadika) are to be employed,
so it will be in the case of no modification and in the grasping of the non-payment;
this statement is desired as if it were a quality in a distinct division.
"I shall state 'twenty-six' for these two.
[Objection: But if "twenty-six" is what is expressed, would not the nominative case not apply to the things being stated? [Reply: It is said in response:

When the twenty-six qualities are intended to be expressed as the primary object, and the number is mentioned for the sake of qualifying them, then the number is qualified by the word ending in the nominative case through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
For example: "Indra-Agni is the deity.

When the meaning of the ritual action is intended to be qualified by the quality of being two-fold, then the word *indrāgnī*—though ending in the singular—is qualified by the dual ending through secondary indication.

And thus an application is seen: "Fifty-five [are] thirty; fifty-five [are] seventeen; fifty-five [are] twenty-one. Here, the word expressing the number is qualified by the term *trivṛt* through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra are [qualified] in an assembly.
In this way, it will be stated that there are twenty-six.
Thus, there will be no modification, and it will be applicable to all [the limbs], being twenty-six years old.

(The third position: Regarding this, the Commentator, having stated that "this is primarily a quality of the number; therefore, there is a modification of the word," raised the following objection—) But surely, if "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśatī*) is what is expressed, the nominative case would not be obtained for the [limbs] (*vakṣyīṇām*).
What is the meaning of this? [The question is: "In what way does number possess primacy such that this objection arises? The answer is:
For while some word expressing a quality denotes a quality as conjoined with a substance, as in "a white cloth," others denote a quality in its abstracted form, as in "the whiteness of the cloth."
In that regard, among the words for numbers, those prior to twenty denote only a mixture of qualities, as in "five cows" or "ten cows.
However, from twenty onwards, they denote both [the quality and the substance].

Here, if the substance is the primary referent, then because of the use of the nominative plural in the word "vakṣyaḥ," the word "ṣaḍviṃśati" must also end in the plural when used in grammatical apposition, according to the rule: "The gender and number of adjectives conform to those of the substratum."
And since this [objection] is difficult to avoid for the Noble One (*ārya*), another position is adopted:
the quality (*guṇa*) extracted and made primary is designated as "the twenty-six.
[Objection: But if it is stated in this way, the nominative case (*prathamā*) would not be obtained; rather, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) ought to occur.
(Answer: This objection can indeed be resolved;

it has been resolved by the author of the Bhāṣya [by stating that "the grammatical coreferentiality is through secondary indication" (*lakṣaṇyā sāmānādhikaraṇyam*), and this was already explained by us previously under the first sūtra].
However, in this way, number would become the primary [meaning], whereas you will later state that gender is the primary [meaning].
The commentary states: "It is indeed logical that the statement 'he will speak of twenty-six' should be made.
Why is the indication given with the number as the primary element?
It is because the quality of being twenty-six is intended to be expressed as the primary meaning."
The utterance of the [words] to be mentioned is for the purpose of qualification.
Furthermore, in the primary context (*prakṛti*), the principal element is the [sacrifice], not the number.
As it has been said: "The primacy belongs to the Agniṣṭoma, because it is for its sake" (9.1.17).
"Because it is not for the sake of making them the archetype" (8).
Thus, in this way, the prescription of their being the archetype would not be established; in that case, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) alone would apply.
Therefore, the statement is indeed consistent.
"In this case, the number would indeed be primary; however, it will be stated again that [the number] is secondary"—this [sūtra] has been explained by its very recitation (it is self-evident).

(The objection previously raised is restated: "But if this were so, the plural form 'twenty-six' (*ṣaḍviṃśatī*) would result [since it is impossible for it to be in grammatical apposition with the words 'limbs' otherwise]. It is replied:

In both cases (in the word *vakṣyī* and the word *ṣaḍviṃśati*, respectively), the plurality (*bahutva*) conveyed by the suffix and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)—which is a general property—is qualified by that [number] consisting of twenty-six. In that regard, there is a single substratum (*ādhikaraṇa*) for the two: the plurality in its general form residing in the suffix (*vakṣy*), and the plurality in its specific form residing in the nominal stem *ṣaḍviṃśati*. These two together constitute one locus.
Therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of these two [words] is appropriate as a relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

As for the fact that the word "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśati*) takes the singular ending, that is because the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is singular. This is the inherent nature of words such as "twenty" and so on: they take the number residing in their own denotation, but not the number of the substance (*dravya*).
Just as in the phrase "twenty cows go," where the specific number [is subordinate],
in the *adhigupreṣa* formula,
the cows are the primary element.
Just as "twenty" is used in the singular, so it is here as well.
This objection applies equally to your position as well;
for even there, since the "curves" (*vaṅkrīḥ*) function as qualifiers of the number, the plural form is inappropriate.

Now, if it were intended that the number twenty-six is indicated subsequently by means of the ribs associated with the plural number—namely, "the number of ribs is twenty-six"—then, even in our view, the number twenty-six associated with the singular number would subsequently refer to those ribs belonging to the twenty-six [animals], as in "those which are the ribs belonging to the twenty-six.
However, there is no subsequent application of the plural number to the ribs once they have been indicated, which would result in the undesirable consequence of a plural form.
Therefore, the singular number is used because it functions as a qualifier.

Alternatively, since duality is expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) "twenty-six," once duality has been expressed, the dual ending does not apply; rather, the singular ending is used for the sake of mere indication (*nirdeśamātra*). [Objection: But in cases such as "two" (*dvau*) or "many" (*bahavaḥ*), since duality and plurality are also expressed by the nominal stem, would the dual and plural endings not fail to apply?
[Reply: It is said in response:

We shall discuss this elsewhere (in the Bhāṣya on the Kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa); it is not recited here for fear of excessive prolixity (or: it is explained later). Therefore, the statement must be made in its entirety.
For by the expression "the statement of what is not recited," the location of the substitutes for the *vaṅkris* is indicated.
The Bhāṣya states: "Indeed, even on this view, it is not the case that everything recited is spoken; rather, the mention of what is not recited is also understood, namely 'twenty-six, twenty-six'.
Now, if the dual or plural number were not employed because of non-recitation, there would be no complete denotation of those *vaṅkris*.
"Or rather, it would be repetition because there is no modification.
The Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.

It is not a statement of a compound; rather, it would be repetition, and in this way there will be no modification. In that case, the extended application (*codaka*) is favored, and what has been traditionally handed down (*samāmnāta*) will have been performed.
Only the word *atha* is repeated, and thus all the *vaṅkri*s (curved ribs) will be denoted.
In this way, the animal itself would be the primary element because the repetition is caused by it; for [otherwise] there would be a compound term.
The commentary states: the word *tu* (but) serves to exclude other possibilities.
This is not so; it is merely a collective statement.
Why? Because, were that the case, the animal would be indicated here as the primary element [of the injunction]:
"For each and every animal there are twenty-six ribs; there is no animal whatsoever that has fewer than twenty-six ribs."

Such a statement occurs only when the connection between the animal and its number is intended to be expressed; however, it has already been stated that the connection between the animal and its number was not intended in the archetype (prakṛti).
Therefore, the ribs must be mentioned in the archetype.
Here too, that very same [principle] is indicated by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer);
therefore, there is no repetition,
for that [principle] is occasioned by the animal sacrifice.
Therefore, the plural expression must be applied to the ribs.
[The Siddhānta: However, the established conclusion is that the ribs are mentioned here by way of their types in order to achieve the completeness of the sides;
furthermore, because of the subsequent reference "them" (tāḥ), they possess primary importance.
Therefore, it is logical that the collective designation alone should be used, such as "there are fifty-two ribs in these two" or "there are seventy-eight ribs in these.

[Objection: But surely this very engagement with the topic is untenable; for where a mantra is applied, there the primary object of expression is the principal element, and thus there would be no room for the various alternative positions based on multiple principals.

[Response: This would indeed be so if the application were governed by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the like; however, it is not so, but rather the application is governed by indicative power (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*karaṇa*). Since these two are common to all, the possibility of applying them to many animals arises.
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: the word "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśati*) is used repeatedly with reference to a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*).

This is because, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the number twenty-six refers to the ribs of a single animal, whereas here, the representation of the number twenty-six is distributed across each individual animal.
In that case, if the formula were applied without modification exactly as in the archetype, there would be no complete enumeration of the ribs for the entire group.
Furthermore, a collective expression is not possible because the natural state (*prakṛti*) is entirely and absolutely predominant;

and even in the case of a compound, there is no connection of a single animal with all the ribs (*vaṅkrī*). Therefore, it is argued that the statement "twenty-six ribs" would remain unmodified (*anūha*).
Or rather, it is because there is a difference in the wording even in the case of the *ūha*; or else, there is a repetition of these two [formulas] for the twenty-six [deities].
Or perhaps the whole [formula] should be used.
It is mentioned because it is perceived as the instrument for the act of "ūha";

and because, in the case of the animal sacrifice, the ribs are primary due to their being joined [to the spine]. The two sides are the fire-altars; the others are joined [to them] as subordinate parts, according to the remainder of the text.
Bhaṭṭa: In that very context, in the *preṣa* (direction) [of Atri], it is heard: "There are twenty-six ribs; having enumerated them, he should pull them out.

In this regard, even though there is no *karaṇa-mantra* (performative mantra), since it is possible for this mantra to illuminate what is present (*samaveta*), and because it is improper to assume it refers to something not present (*asamavetārthatva*), one should first consider that there is no modification (*avikāra*) in the case of a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*). When considering what kind of modification might exist, since there is no evidence for the primacy of the archetype (*prakṛti*), and because it is illogical to postulate unscripted words, [the mantra applies] to all the ribs belonging to the animals...
In the *adhigupreṣa*, for the purpose of indicating the ribs (*vaṅkrī*), there is simply the repetition of the two words "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśatiḥ* and *asa*).

For this very reason, since there is no evidence for adopting the original singular form, there is no delusion regarding the singular number anywhere; even in cases such as "Aditi, the noose" (*aditiḥ pāśam*) and "to the lord of the sacrifice, the sacrifice" (*medhapataye medham*), it is logical that all the nooses and so forth are indicated through repetition. Furthermore, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in assuming repetition because it is directly heard in the text, rather than depending on the introduction of an unmentioned dual or plural form through modification (*ūha*). Otherwise, if indication were possible through modification alone—such as by saying "twofold" or "threefold"—it would follow that even a single foot of a verse would have to be repeated.

Nor should it be argued that because [the number] is not to be designated in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as "oneness-ness" (*ekatvatva*) and so forth, and because it is manifested as a number that is a means to the *apūrva*, there can be no possibility of employing the plural number and so forth in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) for the purpose of manifesting the plurality of animals and so forth which are means to the *apūrva*. This is not to be said.

In such cases as "an animal with a black neck for Agni" (*āgneyaṃ kṛṣṇagrīvam*) and "a brown one for Soma" (*saumyaṃ babhru*), since the singularity of the individual word is not prescribed as being the means for achieving those respective *apūrvas* in multiple instances, and since in the case of "those belonging to Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyān*), the plural number is employed solely for the purpose of denoting the sacrifices, the singularity of the animal obtained through extension (*atideśa*) remains the means for achieving those respective *apūrvas*.

Therefore, for the sake of expressing that [singularity], repetition of the very word heard in the text is appropriate, rather than the insertion of another word as in the case of the word "Sūrya" and others.

As for the argument presented in the *Mūla* (the *Tantravārttika*) for the sake of establishing this position—that because the number twenty-six is the primary element in this sentence which relates the animal and the sacrificial fee (*paśubhaya*), it must be repeated for each individual animal in order to manifest that relationship separately for each—it is rejected. This is because the genitive relation (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), being subordinate, cannot logically possess primacy; furthermore, since the meaning of the sentence as a whole is not directly expressed by the words (*aśābdatva*), such primacy is even more untenable. Moreover, even if it were primary, its manifestation could be achieved through modification (*ūha*) for each animal; thus, there is no evidence for repetition (*abhyāsa*), and the argument is therefore disregarded.
Therefore, the first position is that the repetition of the two words is established by the very reasoning already stated.

As for the second [position]: since a single injunction for performance (*ekaprayogavidhi*) applies to a group of animals (*paśugaṇa*), it is understood that the numerous sacrifices, together with their auxiliary elements (*sāṅga*), must occur simultaneously.

Because the function of manifesting the meaning is also understood to occur simultaneously, one must necessarily adopt the view that the words of a single sentence occur simultaneously in accordance with that requirement; thus, there is no repetition whatsoever, even in the sense of being heard repeatedly.

In cases such as "aditiḥ pāśam," however, because there is no evidence for the repetition of the principal noun stem (*prātipadika*) in accordance with the subordinate quality (*guṇa*), there is no destruction [of the original form]; rather, there is only modification (*ūha*) of the plural ending and so forth. And although plurality is not established for anything [in this context], nevertheless, since the noun stem *pāśa* denotes multiple ropes, its inclusion is necessary for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).

Nor is the use of the singular number intended to refer to each individual object, as in the case of the word *palī* (wife) [in the compound *dvipalī*]. This is because that [singular] lacks the power to determine [the meaning], since it does not produce a cognition of either the oneness or the plurality of the bonds (*pāśa*); furthermore, it would result in a contradiction with its status as a base form (*prakṛti*), and thus it is not a determining factor.

For this very reason, even in examples such as "let the two of these be cut in two ways," although the cutting produced by effort is singular, it lacks the power to determine [the number of objects] due to its being produced by a single effort; therefore, out of necessity, the repetition of the word *ekadhā* ("in one way") is accepted.
In the present context, however, since there is no possibility of generating doubt regarding the intended meaning, it is proper to accept modification (*ūha*) for the sake of achieving simultaneity.

Even in that case, since there is no evidence for any alteration of the nominal stem *ṣaḍviṃśati*, the modification applies only to the forms *ṣaḍviṃśatī* and *ṣaḍviṃśatayaḥ*. Furthermore, because number is the primary element in this sentence, its meaning is determined as follows:
For instance, in all cases, number words such as "two" and "three" have the number itself as their primary referent,

whereas words such as "twenty" and so on have the number as their primary referent. And here, the sense of totality is present because, according to the statement "he cuts off [the portions] from both sides," the manifestation of that [totality] through the comprehension of completeness is what is suggested (vyaṅgya).
Therefore, there is no change in the primary nominal base *ṣaḍviṃśati*.

Nor does it follow that, as in the case of "twenty cows" (*viṃśatir gāvaḥ*), if the ribs were subordinate, the word *vaṅkrī* would have to end in the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; for even when number is primary—as seen in examples such as "Devadatta and others are the animals," "fifty-five years," or "years"—the word expressing number is observed to be in grammatical apposition [with the qualified object] through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, by indicating the ribs, the word *vaṅkrī* can likewise be established as being in apposition.

Nor should it be argued that there is a predominance of the crookedness (*vaṅkrī*) over the individual crooked parts through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of the expression "twenty cows.

Even if that were so, it would still be necessary to accept secondary indication in order to achieve grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "twenty-six" and the number itself.

However, if one does not accept the rule that "there is a relation of identity even at the time of the optional syntactic connection between the meaning of a noun and [another] noun," then for me as well, the connection of the crookedness with the number is possible through the relation of inherence (*samaveta-sambandha*), and thus no secondary indication is required.

Nor can the word *vaṅkrī* be taken as qualifying the number through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the ribs, such that it would fall into the singular because of their oneness; for the plural [ending] functions by way of the relation of inherence in the substrata of its own denotation (*svaśaktyāśrayasamavetavṛttitva*), and thus has the meaning of indicating oneness. Even in your own view, since the number is not primary, the singular form "twenty-six" (*ṣaḍviṃśatiḥ*) would necessarily require the indication of plurality by way of the same relation of inherence in the substrata of its own denotation.
Nor is there a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) here, because the status of being the subordinate term (*jaghanyatva*) in the word *vaṅkrī* serves as the determining factor.
Therefore, since it is impossible for the twenty-six parts— which constitute the primary subject— to be otherwise,
there must indeed be a modification of the statement as "There are twenty-six ribs in these two.

This being the position reached, [the opponent replies] that because of the reference specifically to the ribs in the words, "One should count them one by one, moving upwards and downwards," [the number remains twenty-six].
In the *adhigau* and the *savanīya* offerings (354), as well as in the *adhvarakalpā* rites, these [offerings] themselves hold primacy.
Although the number is employed as a qualifier for them, it indicates completeness; thus, there is no contingency of it being purposeless.

And thus, because the singular number in the form "twenty-six" has the sense of a general characteristic (*bahulalakṣaṇa*) and its meaning is not directly applicable (*asamavetārtha*), no modification (*ūha*) is possible. Rather, modification occurs only in the case of the word "twenty-five," because its meaning is directly applicable.
Therefore, the collective expression "there are fifty-two of these two sets" is indeed appropriate.
Furthermore, because they are the subject under discussion, thirteen ribs on each side are stated collectively by the word "twenty-six.
Thus, it is understood that here too, all [the ribs] must be manifested collectively.

And although this collective statement is established by logic as well—namely, "twenty-five in one way" regarding those who carry two [loads] twice (or "those who carry two twice," according to the Sāyaṇa commentary)—it is still stated thus.

Regarding the rule *dvirdvivahanām* (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.4.3), the commentary of Gārgya states that one should utter these two words twice for animals that have two vehicles. Although it would be appropriate to render this as a compound based on the Vedic text that serves as the source for the Ākhyāyana-sūtra, there is nevertheless no contradiction; for the Sāṅkhyāyana-sūtra, which is based on a Vedic text, permits the use of the compound even in this context, stating: *pañcaviṃśatiriti samāsaiva*. Thus, there is no conflict with the sutra's formulation.

(In fact, however, the reading in the Sāṅkhyāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.1.10 is simply: "Some say twenty-five, twenty-five," or "by way of a compound. Its commentary states: "This is the more excellent view intended by the Teacher"—referring to the view of the compound.
For this very reason, even in that alternative, the repetition occurs only twice, and not as many times as there are animals.
The same should be understood regarding the word *ekadhā* as well;
for it is only through distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) that the determination of being cut by a single effort applies to each individual animal.
Maṇḍana [states]: "The term *vaṅkayaḥ* (the ribs) should be expressed as equal."
Śaṅkara: "And such a compound should be bent [interpreted].
Likewise in the Savanīya offerings, because they are of the same injunction.
In the Agnīṣomīya animal sacrifice, there is the recitation in the *agnipraiṣa* beginning with: 'Bring forward the fire!'"

And when the position is accepted that the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice and the *savanīya* animal sacrifice have identical injunctions (*samānavidhāna*), then in the deliberation as to whether the words "prastai" and so forth should be modified (*ūhitavya*) or not, the author states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of extension (*atideśa*).
The *savanīya* animals have identical injunctions with the *agnīṣomīya* animal.

Therefore, regarding the *adhiga* call and the *agni-praiṣa* in the *savanīya* sacrifices, it should be understood that they are like what was previously stated in the preceding section concerning the *savanīya*.
Just as there is no modification (*ūha*) in the word *patnī*, so too there is no modification in [the formulas] such as *prāstaiḥ*.
This refers to the sacrifice named *adhvarakalpā*.
"In the morning, he should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati.
At midday, he should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati.
In the afternoon, he should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati."

Just as there are three *savanas* in a peaceful (*saumya*) sacrifice, so too in this [rite] there are three sets of three sacrifices within its three *savanas*; thus, due to this similarity to the *adhvara*, it is called an *adhvarakalpā*.

It is an *adhvarakalpā* because it is slightly inferior to an *adhvara*. The formation of the word is established by Pāṇini’s sūtra: "In the sense of being slightly incomplete, the suffixes *kalpa*, *deśya*, and *deśīya* are used."
Mā. 11.2.4.19: "In this way, one indeed attains the sacrifice (*yajña*). This is the fruit of the *adhvarakalpā* sacrifice. 12.4.4.19:
"He who has a rival should sacrifice with this. From Mā. 11.2.4.19, it is understood that the fruit of the *adhvarakalpā* begins with the *śyena*.
In the *adhvarakalpā*, there are the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* and *agnīṣomīya* [offerings].
Even though the *sāmidhenī* verses are prescribed in the *adhvarakalpa* and other texts, the entitlement (*adhikāra*) belongs to the three social classes (*varṇas*). (Ci.

In the *Paśu*, *Mitravindā*, *Adhvarakalpa*, and others, the fifteen-fold number (*pañcadaśya*) is enjoined by the context; it is that very number which takes its place in substitution for the fifteen-fold number obtained through extended application (*atideśa*).
And likewise, the number seventeen for the *sāmidhenī* verses applies here;
Vārttika 3.6.1, p. 1031.
"There are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses," this is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) in the *Adhvarakalpa* and other texts.
Bhāṣya 10.1.9.32: "Because of the difference in time, a distinction is perceived among the subsidiaries belonging to the three groups of three;
therefore, there is a difference."

And thus, there is no common application (*tantra*) for the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*). The offering (*nirvāpa*) prescribed by the rule "one should offer before the [morning] recitation" is a statement regarding the time for the first [rite].
This is the time for the offering of the first triad of sacrifices alone;
it is not for those of the midday and afternoon sessions,
which take place at their own respective times.

Ke. 11|2|4|22: Although there are three triads here, nevertheless, because "the fruit is one," the understanding of the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) as expressed by "he should sacrifice with this" is appropriately conveyed by a word in the singular number.
Therefore, with the three triads, there is a single sacrifice;
it is the sacrifice named Adhvarakalpā.

"In this very context [it is said]: 'One should offer an eleven-potherd oblation to Agni and Viṣṇu; Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), and there should be an offering to Bṛhaspati.

In the *Adhvarakalpā*, because the twelve-potherd oblation to Agni and Viṣṇu is a modification (*vikāra*) of the [oblation] to Indra and Agni, it follows the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*āmāvāsya*) regarding the portion of clarified butter for Sarasvatī.
The established procedure (*tantra*) of the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) is set aside.
(Bālakrīḍā, p. 141).

Although three sacrifices are prescribed in the *Adhvarakalpā*, by another statement—"One who is being afflicted should sacrifice with this very [offering]"—they are prescribed together for the purpose of neutralizing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). Consequently, all three are subsumed under a single performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*).

Bhāṣya 5.1.10: Here, first are the duties of the Bārhaspatya [offering], and then those of the Ājya; for the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is indeed more powerful than the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance).

In the injunction, "One should offer an eleven-pother portion for Agni and Viṣṇu; one should sacrifice clarified butter for Sarasvatī," the *puronuvākyās* for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are indeed fixed [by the archetype], and not the *vārtraghnī* verses, because in the absence of conflict, the first [archetype] is more authoritative.

First, there is the performance of the offering and so forth for the oblation to Agni and Viṣṇu, then that of the *caru* for Bṛhaspati, due to following the modified primary order (*mukhyakrama*), and then that of the clarified butter for Sarasvatī.
[The others] are like the ritual procedures of the *adhvara*.

(One [point]: The order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) derived from extended application (*atideśika*) is stronger than the order based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*) and the order of principal elements (*mukhyakrama*).
Because of that statement, in the case of a modification (*vikṛti*), it should follow the sequence of the principal elements (*yathāpradhānam*).

Commentary: There is a sacrifice named *Asyadhvarakalpā*; [it is prescribed that] "one should offer an eleven-potherd oblation to Agni-Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī should have the portions of the *ājya*, and there should be a cake for Bṛhaspati. In this regard, a doubt arises: are the ritual details (*dharmāḥ*) of the cake for Bṛhaspati—being a modification (*vikāra*) of the [Agni] offering—to be performed first? Is the *codaka* (the rule of extension) more powerful than the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance), or is the *prayogavacana* more powerful than the *codaka* because it is a modification of the *upāṃśuyāja*? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? In this modified sacrifice, the order should follow the primary deities, because of that specific injunction.
In the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the sequence of their direct verbal injunctions [is established];
by that, there is the inclusion of the proximate subsidiaries. For the injunction regarding performance (prayogavacana) is perceptible, whereas the injunction regarding its properties is inferential;
indeed, the latter is brought forth by the extended application (codaka).
Therefore, the explicit injunction (*prayogavacana*) is more powerful than perception;
by it, the inferential *codaka* is sublated. [The *Ṭupṭīkā*:
The third [cake] (dedicated to Bṛhaspati), because it has a single deity and its substance is the *aupadhika* [offering], is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *Āgneya*.
The second [offering, dedicated to Sarasvatī]—because its sacrificial material is clarified butter—is a modification of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
The first [offering, dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu]—because it is dedicated to two deities and because its substance is a ground offering (*caru*)—modifies the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice.
(In that case, the performance of the ritual details of the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* offering first is beyond doubt.)

But regarding the other two, there is a deliberation: should the ritual details (*dharma*) of the modification of the Āgneya [offering] (the Bārhaspatya) be performed first, by virtue of the force of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction), or should those of the modification of the Upāṃśuyāja (the Sārasvata) be performed first, by virtue of the force of the *prayoga-vacana* (the modified application injunction)?
What is the prima facie position? Because the principal acts are explicitly mentioned here, the order of the primary elements (*mukhya-krama*) is more powerful.
The other [order] is inferential because it is obtained through the *codaka* (transference rule).

Therefore, because it is inferential, the sequence grasped by the direct injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) is stronger. Or, in case of conflict, it is according to the model sacrifice (*prakṛti*), not contrary to the model.

Commentary: Or, in the case of a conflict between the order of the principal [rites] and the order of the subsidiaries, it ought to be exactly as it is in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too in the ectype (*vikṛti*). Why? Because of the difference from the archetype.

Whatever properties exist in the archetype, those very same ones ought to exist in the ectype; thus, if they were performed according to the order of the principal [rites], the ectype would not be modified from the archetype.
They would indeed exist; for the *codaka* (the rule of extension) is stronger than the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance),
as it both brings forward and causes the attainment [of the details].
Having observed what has been obtained, the injunctive statement (prayogavacana) summarizes it.

That [statement], having arisen after what was already obtained and being based on that which is already present, cannot sublate the previously obtained *codaka* (archetypal injunction), even though it is directly perceived, because it is characterized by being external [to the archetype].
Thus, it does not summarize [the ritual] beyond what has been obtained.
Therefore, first come the rules of Bārhaspatya, and then those of Ājya.

[The Ṭupṭīkā states: The two orders [of sequence] based on primary attainment are weak because they depend upon the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*); however, the authority of *śruti*, *artha*, *pāṭha*, and *kāṇḍa* is stronger because they depend upon the extended application (*codaka*).

What is the reason? When a desire for modification (*vikṛti-bhāvanā*) arises, that observation of the archetypal (*prakṛta*) elements—namely, the meaning [of the ritual acts] such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) and so forth—is called "origination" (*utpatti*) by metaphorical extension, just like actual origination (the first comprehension).
