It brings about those determined elements [and applies them] to the modification.
Subsequently, the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*), having observed [them], enjoins the completed archetypal elements and causes them to be accepted [as part of the modified rite].

What follows from this in the present context? He says: while concluding, one adopts those [elements] exactly as they are brought forward by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), and not otherwise—as in the case of the "ten" [days].
Therefore, it is precisely those characterized by the sequence [of the model sacrifice] that are obtained through the *codaka*.

Consequently, even though the direct (verbal) injunction of performance exists, it is weaker because it only acquires its own existence at a later stage, following the *codaka*—which is inferential and so forth.

(Regarding how there is weakness [of the injunction], he says: As long as there is no arising [of the action], there is no acquisition [of its result]—for indeed, the application of that which has not arisen is not possible; and as long as there is no acquisition, there is no status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*).

Once the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) has been determined, there follows the inclusion (i.e., the performance) of the proximate auxiliary by means of the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance).

Therefore, because the *prayogavacana* occurs at a later time, the sequence (*krama*) that depends upon it is weaker than its basis—the *prayogavacana*—due to the weakness of that basis when compared to the stronger *codaka* (the general injunction).

For this reason, the Commentator says: "The subsequent [injunction of performance] cannot sublate the prior [general injunction], even though it is directly perceived, because it is extrinsic (being posterior)."
The Śākhā states: "One performing the *iṣṭi* for Agni and Viṣṇu should offer an eleven-potherd cake; Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), as should Bṛhaspati.
In that case, between the Upāṃśuyāja and the offering to Agni, whose ritual details (*dharmas*) should be performed first?

Is there a primary performance of the properties of the clarified butter (*ājya*) first, by virtue of favoring the effort of the subsidiaries and the principal act as enjoined by the *prayoga-vākya* (the injunction of performance) according to the order of the principal (*mukhya-krama*), or should the properties of the clarified butter be performed first— just like the *codaka* (archetypal injunction)— followed by the properties of the Bārhaspatya oblation? In this regard, because the *prayoga-vākya* is specific to the particular instance (*auddeśika*), it sets aside the order obtained through extension (*atideśa*) by means of the order of the principal (*mukhya-krama*).
It is not so;
for it is the sequence of those constituent elements already established in the archetype that is considered here in the modification (*vikṛti*),
and they are indeed obtained here through the injunction (*codanā*) and other means as being possessed of sequence.
"Because they have no further expectancy, their sequence is fixed, and no other [sequence] is postulated for them.
Just as with arrows, since [the sequence] is already obtained here, it is logically consistent that it should be postulated.

Following the discussion regarding the relative strength between direct (upadeśika) and indirect (ātideśika) sequences, there is a thematic connection (*saṃgati*) due to the subsequent discussion between the direct and the indirect.

[Objection]: "Is it not true that, according to the twelfth [book], in the section (12.1.17) beginning with *'nanu prayogavacanaścodakāpekṣayā durbala iti dvādaśe 'jaimineḥ paratantratvāpatteḥ svatantrapratiṣedhaḥ syāt'*, it will be stated that the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is weaker than the general injunction (*codaka*), and thus there would be a prohibition of independence due to the resulting dependence? So how can the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) here be based on the strength of the injunction of performance? [Response]: True; elsewhere the injunction of performance is weak, but regarding the matter of order (*krama*), that very same injunction is strong. This is because the determination of order everywhere is dependent upon the injunction of performance—this is the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view.

The intention of the proponent of the *siddhānta* (conclusion) is as follows: because the injunction regarding performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) is dependent upon the attainment of the ritual elements (*padārtha*), and because that [attainment] is dependent upon the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), the injunction regarding performance is weaker by virtue of its reliance on the *codaka*.

Thus, even for the injunction regarding performance which lacks the capacity for independent conceptualization, since the very root of such conceptualization is severed, it cannot be the factor that establishes a different order; therefore, regarding the matter of order, the injunction regarding performance is indeed weaker.

As for the meaning of the *sūtra*: "In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the order should be according to the primary elements (*yathā-pradhāna*)," because of the force of the injunction regarding performance which prescribes the order of the ritual elements according to the order of the primary elements.
[The question is: Is the priority of the Sārasvata Ājya [offering] over the Bārhaspatya Caru, or is it the priority of those rites ending with the Ājya based on direct instruction?
[The answer is:
It is the priority of the items that involve transference, because they are obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction).
Primacy [is determined] by internal relatedness (*antaraṅgatva*) in the case of the *caru* offering in a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *Āgneya* sacrifice.

Bhaṭṭa: Now, the relative strength of the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*) in a modification is considered in comparison with the order of the textual recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) as derived through extended application (*atideśika*).

In the *Adhvarakalpā*, it is revealed in scripture: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu; there should be portions of clarified butter (*sarasrajyābhāga*), and also one for Bṛhaspati."

In this context, although three sacrifices are enjoined by means of three [separate] sentences, there is a single performance-injunction (*ekaprayogavidhi*) encompassing all three, because they are enjoined collectively for the purpose of the fruit of averting malevolent magic (*abhicāra-nirāsa*) by another sentence: "One who is being harmed should sacrifice with this very [offering]. Here, some say that because the *Āgneya* has two deities and is an offering of curd (*aupadhavyaka*), it possesses the injunctions of either the *Aindrāgna* or the *Āgnīṣomīya*.
Others, however, state that it belongs to the *Āgnīṣomīya* because it is recited as ending in a dual suffix of identical phonetic form (*samānākṣara-dvitānta-paṭhakatvāt*).
(Regarding 11.2.13, however, it is stated that the second Āgnāvaiṣṇava sacrifice, which is to be inferred from the Adhvara, is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Āgneya.

1) Because the second has clarified butter (*ājya*) as its substance, it follows the procedure of the *upāṃśuyāja*. [The third], because it has a single deity and has solid food (*aupadhas*) as its substance, follows the procedure of the Āgneya.)

In this regard, with respect to the properties of the *ājya* substance and the *kāga* animal, there arises a conflict between the extended application (*ātideśika*) of the *agnāvaiṣṇava* properties and the primary order (*mukhyakrama*). In considering whether the *agnāvaiṣṇava* properties should first be performed because of the primary order—as in the case of the conflict between the extended application and the textual order—or whether the *bārhaspatya* properties should be performed later according to the primary order or earlier according to the extended textual order: since the primary order resides in the prescriptive injunction (*upadeśika-prayogavidhi*) and is thus directly taught (*aupadeśika*), it possesses greater force than the extended application; even though it occurs subsequent to the extended application, its sublation is justified—just as in the case of the *śara* grass and other elements—and therefore the primary order is stronger.

This being the case, although the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) is based on direct instruction (*aupadeśika*), the primary order (*mukhyakrama*) cannot be established by mere nature because it would involve an improper assumption (*śaranyāyānupapatti*). Furthermore, since any such assumption must be rooted in a need (*apekṣāmūla*), that need is satisfied by the very first order obtained through textual sequence (*pāṭhakrama*) via the injunctive extension (*atideśa*), which the injunction of performance itself depends upon; thus, the requirement for an order is cut off. Consequently, in the case of the *dvaidha* [sacrifices] and others, precisely because there are various archetypal models (*prakṛti*) obtained through extension, the order obtained through the textual sequence of the extended model (*atideśikapāṭhakrama*) alone possesses greater force.

It should be understood that although this point is already established, it is stated again in the section on *krama* (order) for the purpose of clarifying the superior strength of the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) in relation to the *prayogavidhi* (injunction of performance). Nor should it be argued that, in this case, because the properties of the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* and *bārhaspatya* offerings would have to be performed according to the order of the archetype (*prakṛti*), the practice of the ritualists—who perform the offering of the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* first in accordance with the modified primary order (*vaikṛta-mukhya-krama*)—would be contradicted; for [this is not so] in the archetype...

For where the sequence is established by means of direct textual recitation (*pāṭha*) and other such authorities, there the construction of a specific sentence is indeed required: "After the object of that [first] word, the action of that [second] object and so forth must be performed. However, in the case of *mukhyakrama* (the order of the principal), due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and the force of the authority that grasps the substratum, one should simply postulate: "The duties of the subsequent principal must be performed after the duties of the initial principal," rather than a specific [sentence], nor the inclusion of the *Āgneya* and others.
For this very reason, even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the entry of the new *Āgneya* need not be postulated through another sentence; thus there is further parsimony.

Thus, even regarding the sequence of performance, one must assume a single syntactical unity (ekavākyatā) in the form: "The other ritual items are to be performed according to the sequence of performance of those whose order is already established.

Consequently, even in a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the performance of the duties of the second primary rite must follow immediately after the performance of the duties of the first primary rite; thus, the offering (nirvāpa) of the oblation to Agni-Viṣṇu comes first, and that of the oblation to Bṛhaspati afterwards.

Thus, when there is a conflict between the order of the main ritual acts (*sthānakrama*) and the order of the preparatory acts (*upākaraṇakrama*), as in the case of the *vācanika* (textually prescribed) extension (*atideśa*), then in a certain modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) where the preparatory act is textually prescribed, the acts such as tethering (*niyojana*) proceed according to the order of the subsidiary acts (*sādyaskopākaraṇapravṛtti*).

And so, regarding these two types of cases, the basis for the practice of ritualists (*yājñikācāra*) must be considered; therefore, the establishment of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) based solely on the order of the archetype (*prakṛti*) and its sequence is to be disregarded because it lacks a stated basis.
Consequently, it is established that the order of the principal acts (*mukhyakrama*) and the like are weaker only in the face of a contradiction with the textually extended (*ātideśika*) reading.
Maṇḍana: "The rule of *codaka* [extension by analogy] follows the order of strength.
Śaṃkara: "The *codaka* [rule] follows from both the sequence and the original text (*mūla*). [This is the stronger] position.
Because it is the primary [rite], being the fundamental one;
[the others] are like the sacrificial sessions (*adhvara-kalpāni*).
The rule for the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*) applies specifically to the cutting of the hair for Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-puccha*).
And specifically, because it is present according to the principle of the *adhvarakalpā* [sacrifices], its postponement occurs precisely at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Bhaṭṭa 11.2.13. [The second part of] the *adhvarakalpā* rule.
The performance [of the rites] occurs by means of the division of the constituent parts among the three groups.
This would be the case in the *Adhvarakalpa*, because the specific details pertain to a single time.
Commentary: This is heard [in the *Adhvarakalpa*]: "At dawn, one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati."
At midday, there is an offering on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a sacrificial pap (caru) to Sarasvatī, and a sacrificial pap to Bṛhaspati.
These belong to the ritual procedure of the Adhvara sacrifice.
Regarding the *adhvarakalpā* sacrifices— (the Siddhāntin says)— due to the difference in time, there is a repetition of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for each individual [rite].

Furthermore, for that [rite] whose performance in the afternoon (such as the offering on twelve potsherds) is prescribed for the morning (because the morning is the time for the primary rite), there is neither the general morning [time] nor the specific morning [time].
But for one for whom the performance is prescribed in the forenoon, only a specific time—namely, the morning—is enjoined, while the general rule remains the morning itself.
Therefore, wherever one [time] is enjoined, that one must be accepted. Or rather, it is a statement regarding the time for the first [performance].
The Commentary (Bhāṣya): As for the argument that "because the specific [act] occurs at one time," we reply to that:
this statement regarding the time—"one should offer the oblation before the utterance of speech"—refers to the offering of the first ritual act.
An objection is raised: "But surely, by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa), it would apply to all [the acts]."
Context (*prakaraṇa*) is not a differentiator of dharmas;
rather, it is an applicator (*viniyojaka*).
Its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) consists in establishing that "this [dharma] belongs here."
It is not the case that "this belongs to him" or "this belongs to that.
Furthermore, among the three offerings, it is understood that [the rule] applies only to the first one according to the established order.
Therefore, there is no simultaneity of the specific [offerings].
And there is a distinction among those actions due to the difference in time.
The word "oneness of the fruit" (phalaikatva) and so forth is as in other cases.

Regarding the commentary: as for the statement "it is an *iti*," even for distinct actions that have a single result, the singular number is used precisely because of the oneness of the fruit, since the effort culminates in that fruit.
For example, there are the Sarvapṛṣṭheṣṭi, the Mṛgareṣṭi, and the iṣṭi named Sumanā.
Regarding that [which is to be prepared according to the Adhvara ritual], what is the governing principle (*tantra*): is it the knowledge, or is it the three triads, or is it the three *rajyānīs*?
For that purpose, this is considered: in the rule "one should offer the oblation before the utterance of speech," does this apply to all offerings, or only to that of the morning?
In that case, because there is no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*), there is a withdrawal of all [the offerings] into a single performance (*sarvanirvāpakarṣa*).
Consequently, all nine sacrifices are commenced by means of a common ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Furthermore, since the conclusion follows the stated order, the subsequent rites also share this common procedure.
(To this objection, it is replied: This would indeed be so if the pouring out [of the oblation] were performed by all [the priests];
however, this specific rule is stated regarding that which pertains solely to the morning time.

Therefore, since the primary rites occurring in the morning, midday, and afternoon must have their auxiliary parts repeated in each respective instance, this is indeed a *tantra* (a single performance for multiple purposes). Soma says: "The enemy is indeed one who seizes the senses and virility; one should perform the *adhvarakalpa* offering against an enemy sacrificer; when the enemy is the sacrificer, his senses and virility are not seized. Thus, the *adhvarakalpyā* offerings are intended as counter-measures against the sacrifices performed by enemies.
In this case, although there is a difference in time for each of the three triads, there is no repetition of the subsidiaries; this is the connection [of the argument].

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: in the *adhvarakalpyā* sacrifice, there should be a common performance (*tantratā*) of the subsidiaries, just as in the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), because of the statement regarding the simultaneity of the specific ritual procedure ending with the *nirvāpa* (offering).
Vi— "The subsidiaries in the *adhvarakalpyā* [are performed] from the morning until the end."
In the three conjunctions, that very [state] would exist for the purpose of differentiation; thus, the former [is correct].

Because of the disposal of the remnants of the *upāṃśu* [offering], there is a displacement of its subsidiaries through that door; thus, one who desires the morning time for the *mukha* [opening] should perform the disposal of the remnants of the morning [offering].
Bhāṭṭa: In the *Adhvara-kalpā*, it is heard in the scripture: "The *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds in the morning... he should sacrifice with this.

And here, by the sentence "He whose rival exists should [sacrifice] with this," since there is an application to the fruit of all nine sacrifices, and because of the indicative power (*liṅga*) [of the word *āgneya*], that much constitutes a separate sentence.

Furthermore, if there were only a single sentence at the outset, then, when nine sentences were postulated based on nine substances and deities, and the injunctions for sacrifices qualified by those respective substances and deities had been established, it would follow that at the time of the subsequent [pārthika] offerings, there would also be a connection with other substances and other deities. Therefore, these nine are indeed originative sentences (*utpatti-vākya*). Moreover, due to the connection with the three periods of time—morning and so forth—there are three performance-injunctions (*prayoga-vidhi*).

Furthermore, the variety of performance at that time does not belong to the *āgneyī* [verse] itself; for if it did, there would be a requirement for a triple recitation even in the case of the *sārasvata* and *bārhaspatya* offerings. Rather, each of the three is a single modification (*vikalpa*).

Nor are the words "morning" (*prātar*) and so forth unaccounted for in all three [offerings], as they are based on the employment of one modification at each respective time. This is because, rather than assuming an unaccounted-for and unintended extension of the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*) to the performance (*prayoga*), it is more appropriate to assume a separate sentence such as "one should offer in the morning" (*prātar nirvapet*) following the injunction "one should offer" (*nirvapet*).

For this very reason, because of its endlessness, only the threefold performance is prescribed by him. This being the case, regarding the offering (*nirvāpa*) which is obtained through the general injunction "one should offer before the utterance of speech," a specific time is heard in the text. Upon reflection as to whether this [time] applies only to the oblation belonging to the morning time or to all [oblations], since there is no distinction made, it applies to all.

Nor should it be argued that—since, according to one view, the offering at the morning time (*prātaḥkāla*) entails the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) at that same time, and because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in enjoining a mere restriction (rather than a new injunction), and since the pouring out of the midday and afternoon offerings also occurs at this time even under the alternative view, enjoining it there would constitute a new injunction (*apūrvavidhi*)—therefore, in accordance with parsimony, this injunction of a specific time must apply only to the pouring out of the morning offerings. For the morning time is defined as the period subsequent to sunrise, and thus the pouring out of the morning offerings is not even prima facie applicable prior to the recitation of the *vājyā* verse; [this applies] to the Adhvaryu priest.

Because the *adhvaryu* performs the offerings for the subsequent days as modifications of the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*)— having four-syllable deities— and because it is established by extension (*atideśa*) that the entire pouring out of the oblation (*nirvāpa*) must occur immediately after sunrise; and because, when there is an abridgment of the entire pouring out, one accepts the rule of the "end-of-the-series" principle (*tadantāpakarṣanyāya*)— namely, "the performance of all constituent parts belonging to the entire ritual procedure is done once collectively (*tantra*), and the conclusion follows the same order as the beginning"— it follows that the subsequent subsidiary rites (*uttarāṅga*) are likewise [abridged].

This being the case, because the number four residing in the syllables is more proximate (antaraṅga) than the singular number pertaining to the deity, both the Sārasvata and Bārhaspatya offerings are indeed modifications of the Āgneya.

Even though they are [related to] the Āgneya, since the eight-pot-sherd offering is more proximate—due to its connection with the substance and the potsherds involved in the act of renunciation (tyāga)—and because it possesses the fourfold nature of the syllables that serve as the substratum for the deity intended as a part of the renunciation, it is indeed a modification of the Āgneya.

And for this reason, since the triad of sacrifices belonging to the morning time is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *Āgneya* sacrifice, and because that [original] sacrifice is common to both the full moon and new moon days, the status of being "prior to sunrise"—as prescribed by the statement, "One commences the ritual procedure for the full moon sacrifice when the sun has risen; for the new moon sacrifice, before sunrise"—is also applicable to the offering (*nirvāpa*). Consequently, it is logical that the offering, which must precede the pouring of the oblation (*vākyapradāna*), occurs at that very same time. Thus, even if one were to argue against it on the grounds of it being an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) rather than a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), the postponement of the morning-time offering remains unavoidable.

Nor is there an absence of the possibility of the alternative being reached even in that case, because the extended (atideśika) morning time, which precedes sunrise, is sublated by the directly enjoined (aupadeśika) morning time;

for according to the usage of the Āśvalāyana Sūtra (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 2.4.23–24), "In this way, the morning offering should be performed when [the sun] has set or when it has risen," the morning time exists even prior to sunrise.
Consequently, since there is no displacement of the offerings for the midday and the morning rites, the auxiliary elements are not performed in common (tantra).

Even when, on account of the statement in another [text], "The two portions of clarified butter belong to Sarasvatī," the middle [offering] is considered a modification of the *upāṃśuyāja*, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) must still be supported by establishing its common applicability (*sādhāraṇya*), since the *brahmavrāhmaṇa* of the Kauṣītaki school prescribes the *upāṃśuyāja* even for the new-moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*).
Maṇḍana: "It is to be understood from the fire-installation (*agnyādheya*).
Śaṅkara: "That rule applies even to the *adhvara*. It is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
The Adhvaryu, standing on the Uttaravedi, issues the command (*preṣyati*), while the Maitrāvaruṇa, standing in the Sadas, issues the command.

Saṃkarṣa 2.3.13. The Adhvaryu should recite the mantras beginning with those of the Ādhvaryava [with the thought], "I shall perform what is revealed by this," whereas the sacrificer [should do so with the thought], "I shall not be negligent."
Bhāṣya 3.8.17:
The Adhvaryu alone should offer with the *camasa* cups when he has the capacity;
however, if at any time he lacks the capacity due to being occupied with the offerings of the *graha* vessels, the *camasādhvaryus* should offer.

VI. 3.1.22: It should be understood that the sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) specified in the initiation injunctions, such as "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Hotṛ," are the [principal] priests beginning with the Adhvaryu, and not the *camasādhvaryus*.

Because the injunction "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Hotṛ" and so forth prescribes the performance of all those purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) subsequent to the initiation, there is only *kāṇḍānusamaya* (performance by sections) in the *sattra* sacrifice.
(Bhāṭṭadīpikā 5.1.3)
In the statement, "Having initiated the *hotṛ-pati*, the *adhvaryu* initiates the *brahmā*," initiation itself is not being enjoined;
for that initiation does not belong to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), nor is the *adhvaryu* its agent, since everything is already obtained through the *codaka* (the general rule of transfer).
What then? The sequence of initiation, which was previously obtained without a fixed order, is here being regulated.
Vārttika 9|1|1|1, p.

1636: "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Hotṛ, initiates the Brahman, and then the Udgātṛ," and so forth; because of the correspondence between the initiation and the application of the designations such as "Brahman" and "Udgātṛ" to the Ārṣeya and the Sacrificer respectively, in a *sattra* sacrifice, the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
The *adhvaryu* is the performer of the rites, such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, along with their constituent parts.
Bhāṣya 3.4.8.22.
[By] the *adhvaryu*.
Or rather— it is not possible to assume that the application based on name (*samākhyā-viniyoga*) is intended for those who establish such a difference in agents;
for it is not as in that case where Manu and others formulate a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding a Kṣatriya,
whereas here [the text] refers to all of them.

Thus, protection is not enjoined; that which is known as the duty of the king is asserted to be the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Is this intended for the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) performing the action, or is it intended for the purpose of all actions (*sarvārtha*)? This is understood accordingly. Here, by some [authorities], the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses and so forth is established as the duty of the Hotṛ priest. In that case as well, are they for all purposes connected with the specific sentence, or for all purposes unconnected [to a specific sentence]? It is well-known that the name [of the priest] would arise from that cause. And this being so, if the intention were for the sake of the person, that would apply to the choosing (*varaṇa*) and the supporting (*bharaṇa*).
It is determined that *samākhyā* (name/designation) is the means of application (*viniyoktrī*).

How then, in the absence of context (*prakaraṇa*), can the application of the *kṛtya*-suffixes and so forth be improper? For it has been stated: "The refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that which is connected to it [the substance] occurs through the context-particularity or through the etymological derivation of its parts; or else, due to the similarity of words, it belongs to that which possesses the measure," and so on (ŚBh 3.4.156).

But this is not incorrect; for if it were the case that [the term] "the work of the Hotṛ" and so forth [applied to all], then the author will state later: "Or rather, it should belong to the Vedic [priests] because of specific designation" (1.2.13).

Therefore, in this way, it is not the case that [the word] "you" (*tvam*) is derived from all meanings; rather, it is established by convention (*rūḍhi*) even without a relationship between agent and object. Nor can presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) postulate a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), because such a statement is already established through its conformity with passages such as, "He divides those [cakes]," where the words are joined together.
For even these [words] have their application within the context of what is directly heard.
As for those [rites] which you have mentioned, there is no connection whatsoever between the *śālā* and the *mālya* based merely on a similarity of syllables;

rather, those rites are to be performed wherever they are recited in the Veda by whoever [performs them]. And thus he will say [in 10.4.1246]: "Indeed, there is no connection with the *Rayaṃtara* such that it must be performed by another performer according to his capacity, because all [the qualities] are already employed."

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the king performs all actions"— for indeed, they are able to carry out all tasks— the term "kingdom" (rājya) is applied in this context. Thus it has been said:
In that case, they too would be able to authorize the *saṃtrava* rites;
for everything would then entail the consequence of having a beginning (*ādimattva*).

Therefore, just as in that instance, it is logical that words are eternal and that what is called "human effort" is merely an action performed by men prior to the specific verbal instruction—since both [the word and its meaning] are perceived as eternal even while being accomplished through the *saṃtrava*, and since their correctness (*sādhutva*) is established by their own inherent capacity—it is not generally the case that the word is used primarily for human purposes. Thus, after explaining the word *rājan* (king), the word *rājya* (kingship) is explained by its own power, and not for the sake of human ends.

The term *māna* is etymological; even though it is heard as being based on that [etymology], because its basis is eternal, it does not acquire the quality of having a beginning. In the same way, the determination of the action [of measuring] would arise from the cognition of the measurer (*hātṛ*) and its connection [to the act].

Since the connection is observed, there would be the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) from the word *hātṛ* [in the form] "this is his action. This is understood. But by what means is that specific action of his known? We shall infer such a statement from the observation of the conventional designation (*samākhyā*).

But surely, [the opponent might argue: from the other [source], namely the Bhāṣya—it stands established through connection with that, i.e., through connection with a specific person. This results in mutual dependence: the name (samākhyā) is dependent on that [connection], and by that [name], once the connection is established, those things which are named by a particular person must be performed by him;
thus, the name is established.
This is not a fault.
To begin with, their designation (samākhyā) will have a meaningful connection with persons;
it is directly perceived in the form of the notion of "belonging to the Adhvaryu."
But by what cause did that [activity] proceed? It was by my *adhvaryu*, the *hotṛ* priest, and the *udgātṛ* priest for the *audgātra* portion.
Just as before, it likewise requires a cause, and yet no such cause exists.
Therefore, such a scriptural statement (*śruti*) is inferred, just as [it is understood] that "the Hotṛ priest is the one who must perform this.
Or rather—the determination [of the application] would arise from the connection with the designation (*samākhyā*).

For it has been explained that among all [the means of proof], such as indicative mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, it is established in this way [only through designation]: the designation "Hotṛ" becomes meaningful for one who does not act otherwise.
Nor does it [apply] to that which has no action as its basis;
therefore, there is no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
But surely, this designation of the *hotṛ* for the *māna* is not possible?

Therefore, because no other explanation is possible, there is an application [of the mantra] based on a scriptural text (*śruti*) inferred by the rule "And the name is likewise, because it has that as its object" (3.1.6.13).
Regarding this, some say:
"This is established by the section concerning mutual sublation."

It is true that in those cases, the well-known designations of agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*) are established by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) as being independent of any contradiction or conflict;
however,

here, because of the compatibility and the specific context, the application [of the mantra] is determined by the presence of a similarity of syllables (*akṣarasāmya*) which serves as a means of justification for all purposes.

Why? Having raised an objection regarding contradiction due to the possibility of [the suffix] *tva*, he refutes it; or rather, with the intention of stating what follows: "For a conjunction already established becomes the cause [of the name];
and since this does not merely restate what was previously said, it is not redundant. Prior to the mention of the designation (*samākhyāna*), there is no other cause for the conjunction."

The word *hotṛ* [is used] because it has the *hotṛ* as its cause; thus, just like the word *rājan*, the cognition [of the suffix] is established by means of various agents. Now, this is being considered:
since both the elision (*lopa*) and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) along with the suffix (*pratyaya*) are not perceived, this is a matter of inference.
And their establishment does not exist without an established effect.
Regarding the lack of understood meaning in the *adhvaryu* [passages] (363),

since the engagement [of the agent] has been taught by such rules as "the fruit of the *soma-śāla* accrues to the performer" (3.7.8.188), this inquiry— which follows immediately after that [discussion] and its subsequent exposition— is now reached at its proper opportunity. (Thus, there is a connection based on the [proper] occasion.)
The meaning is that because they are employed in the *sūtra*, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are capable of performing all ritual acts, since they are employed by means of all those acts.
Vi— "Their function is not restricted, nor is it fixed, because they are dependent [on others].
Since they are capable, what restriction could there be as to 'who does what,' except by means of the designation (*samākhyā*)?"
"Of them"—this refers to those who are ignorant [of the specific application].

The Bhāṭṭa [responds]: In various sacrifices, for those respective performers established by authoritative means of knowledge, in the absence of a specific injunction, there would be a connection to that purpose based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the capacity [of the word], and not a restriction by the weaker designations (*samākhyā*) such as "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*).
(The state of being for that purpose remains established.)

(Continuing from the previous section: There is no contradiction here between the name (*samākhyā*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*), for these two merely establish the distribution of the agents who have not yet obtained their connection [to specific acts].
Therefore, the ritual items designated by the name *hautra* are to be performed by the *hotṛ*, those designated as *ādhvaryava* by the *adhvaryu*, and those designated as *audgātra* by the *udgātṛ*.
For whatever ritual items are prescribed in all three—the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda—these names are applied to them respectively.

These [terms] are well-known among the ritualists (*yājñika*). Furthermore, these words are etymological (*yaugika*); they cannot occur apart from a connection with the duties of the *adhvaryu* and so forth. Thus, their fitness for those respective roles establishes their status as performers (*kartṛtva*). Maṇḍana says: "Their designation is the action."

Śaṅkara: "The designation [of 'patnī'] is restrictive to the male. If it is argued that the wife of one who has been hired as an officiant (*adhvaryu*) is like the officiant herself, and thus she is hired for her husband’s sacrifice just as the officiant is—[this is refuted]. (Ratnaprabhā 6.1.4). Regarding the phrase 'like the officiant': according to the Prābhākara school, the wife possesses only the status of a permissive agent (*anumantṛ*), not that of a performer (*kartṛ*). Since permission (*anumati*) does not constitute the desire to sacrifice (*yajijñāsā*), even if she acts in accordance with that permission, it is logically untenable for her to be the performer of the sacrifice, just as in the case of the officiant."

Therefore, the renunciation of the substance for the sake of the deity must be performed not by the sacrificer alone, but by the wife as well; thus, their agency is indeed shared (*vyāsakta*). *Soma* 6.1.4. Regarding the distribution of the twelve-hundred-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the Jyotiṣṭoma according to the titles (*samākhyā*) such as "adhvaryu" and so forth:
*Bhāṣya* 10.1.3.13–55. [This concerns] the determination of the designations of the Adhvaryu and others.

Because they stand in the relationship of original form (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikāra*), [the two words] are in fact mutually independent and eternally connected with their respective meanings. Nevertheless, since the word *ādhvaryava* lacks the status of being an eternally fixed original form (*kūṭasthanityatva*), and because there is no contradiction even if an eternal term functions as a conditional one (*naimittika*), the connection of the meaning of the word *adhvaryu* serves as the basis for the application of the word *ādhvaryava* as its denotation. Thus, by metaphorically treating the word *adhvaryu* as the cause for the word *ādhvaryava*, the designation of "original form and modification" is explained.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1201)

In the expression "he yokes two oxen" (*anadvāhau yunakti*), the number two (*dvitva*) first connects with the action by way of the grammatical factor (*kāraka*); subsequently, it serves as the delimiting attribute (*avacchedaka*) of that factor.
Consequently, there is the yoking of exactly two, neither one nor many.
VI. 4.1.5. In the expression "he yokes the two oxen" (*anadvāhau yunakti*), it should be understood that duality is intended to be expressed, just as in the case of [the word] "animal" (*paśum*).

The spreading of the altar-ground (*vedi*) and so forth, which is not extended [from the model sacrifice], serves only the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). "He spreads what is not extended" (meaning: the spreading is "not extended" such that the bare altar-ground could not otherwise be seen; thus, it is a covering).
"It is not to be extended; it is not to be extended.
Bhāṣya 4.1.21, Section 2:
"Because it is not one’s own duty, it is not a practice. That ritual action in which one has one’s own qualification is a qualified action, depending upon that [qualification]."

That which is not authorized—that is, an action that does not fall within the scope of one's own authority—is "unauthorized" (*anadhikṛta*). The performance or execution of such [an action] is "unauthorized action" (*anadhikṛtakriyā*). Alternatively, the word *anadhikṛta* may function as the agentive term; thus, "action performed by one who is unauthorized" is "unauthorized action."

For example, a certain donkey, while guarding his master’s house at night, saw a thief approaching but did not bark. When questioned by the thief as to why this was so, the dog replied, "I am not authorized [to do so]; you must say nothing about this to him. Thinking that this was improper, the donkey, with the intention of waking his master, let out a loud, ear-piercing bray.
"And he received blows from his master with a staff" (Vākyapadīya 1.2.17, p.

204). "The state of having an object not previously apprehended" (*anadhigatārthatva*) consists in having as its object the state of being the object of a cognition that occurs in a moment prior to the [cognition in question] and resides in the same locus as itself.

That which has no object not already apprehended or known possesses the state of having an unapprehended object (*anadhigatārthatva*). Its own cognition—that is, the state of having an unapprehended object—is as follows:

one’s own cognition is that which does not have as its object anything residing in a locus co-referential with itself, nor anything residing in its own locus—the self—nor anything residing in a moment prior to its own locus-moment, nor anything residing in a moment prior to the moment immediately preceding its own locus-moment. Such [an object]...

The meaning is: the state of being such that its object remains accessible even during periods when study is prohibited (*anadhyāya*), etc.; that is, the capacity to produce such knowledge regarding an object not yet apprehended.
(Ke. Maṇi. pṛ. 11. The definition of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is that which makes known an object not yet apprehended.
Furthermore, its nature as an apprehension consists in the non-apprehension of what is not its own object.
Even in the case of inference, the object is the mountain as qualified by fire.
Thus, it is the capacity to apprehend an object not yet apprehended [that constitutes a means of valid cognition].
In the same way, the capacity to apprehend an object not yet apprehended should be understood to apply to comparison (*upamiti*) as well.
However, knowledge produced by worldly linguistic usage (*laukika-śabda*) is not a valid cognition (*pramā*), because it lacks the capacity to apprehend an object not yet apprehended.
Ku. 1115/5, p. 6. Bhaṭṭa Āmeśvara states that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of mantras consists in their capacity to convey a meaning not already known.
Bāla. p. 70. "If the *Mahābhāṣya* has not been studied, the *Padamañjarī* would be useless;
even if the *Mahābhāṣya* has been studied, the *Padamañjarī* would be useless."
This is the established principle (*nyāya*):
just as the desire for liberation is in vain if one fails to propitiate the Lord (*īśvara*) while propitiating another deity,
so too the desire for liberation is in vain if one propitiates another deity while failing to propitiate the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
In both instances where "syāt" occurs, the reading is "sā"; this refers to the commentary on the *Kāśikā* named *Padamañjarī*.

[The principle] "the meaning of a treatise is that which cannot be obtained otherwise" applies here: the state of not being already expressed (*anabhihitatva*) is not obtained, according to the maxim "the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise."

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa* that the bank is the meaning of the word "Gaṅgā," since its application there is possible through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone. This principle does not apply to words for which the apprehension of the primary power (*śakti*) is necessarily required.

Otherwise, since the cognition of this [meaning] could arise through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) in words such as the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it would follow that it is not directly denotable (*avācyatā*). For a word’s meaning is that which cannot be obtained by any other means; this is the principle that "the subject matter of the scripture is that which cannot be obtained otherwise" (Śābarabhāṣya 3.4.8). Bāla. pṛ. 14. *ananyalabhyaḥ śabdārthaḥ*. *ananyalabhyaḥ śāstrārthaḥ*—this is the maxim.

Regarding the nature of scripture (śāstra), it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the Pāñcarātra, and the Mūla-Rāmāyaṇa are designated as scripture.
That which is equal to these is also proclaimed as scripture."
"Therefore, any other expansion of the scripture is not the scripture itself.

Thus, by the maxim that "the meaning of a scripture is that which cannot be obtained from any other source," since difference (*bheda*) is already established [elsewhere], the scripture does not have that as its purport; rather, the *Pūrṇapraśnīya* states that the purport of the Vedic sentences lies solely in these [points].

*Sādṛśī*. 711. [Objection: On the grounds that the maxim "that which is not obtainable by other means is to be expressed" (*ananyalabhyaḥ vācyaḥ*) and "that which is not obtainable by other means is to be understood" (*ananyalabhyaḥ gamyaḥ*) has a general scope, it might be argued that the agent (*kartṛ*), though not obtainable by other means, must be expressed; thus, one might suspect that this specific scriptural authority (*āgama*) sublates the maxim. However, regarding the maxim—even one with a general scope—the phrase "of the maxim" (*nyāyasya*) implies that it proceeds more slowly than a human-authored scripture (*pauruṣeyagrantha*). (Su. p. 1486) The maxim is: "Even that which is non-different is denoted by the word 'different,' and likewise the one possesses many forms. (*ananyo'pyanyaśabdena tathaiko bahurūpavān* iti nyāyaḥ).
The meaning is that just as the Self, though being non-different, is expressed by the word "other," so too, though being one, it is said to possess manifold forms.
This is the principle stated in the *Nyāyāmṛta-advaitasiddhi-bhūmikā*, page 4: "And the timelessness [of the Self] is like the maxim regarding the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśau*). (10.8.169).

And regarding the phrase "and there is no loss," in the *Guṇasūtra*—specifically in the context of the rule "one performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between"—it will be established that because the purpose of the two *puroḍāśa* cakes (which serve as the indicators for the interval) is absent, the *upāṃśuyāja* exists on the full-moon day when only one *puroḍāśa* is offered for a Brāhmaṇa who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice, based on the statement: "For a Brāhmaṇa who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice, the *āmīmīya* *puroḍāśa* does not exist. Thus, the restriction is established for the non-*Soma*-sacrificing Brāhmaṇa.

Ku. 1.2.46: By the principle "and there is no loss [of the time]," just as in the case of a single *puroḍāśa* offering where the intervening time is characterized by two *puroḍāśas*, even when [the rites] are postponed again and again, the time characterized by the *utkīrṇa* (the drawing out) does not disappear; therefore, there is no sublation of the time in this case under the view that the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is not postponed. This is the doubt. Soma. 5.1.18: By the principle "and there is no loss of the time," just as in the case of a single *puroḍāśa* on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), the *upāṃśuyāja* is established even on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
Even in the absence of an explicit injunction for the full moon day, it is indicated by the word "full moon."

Su. Pṛ. 707: By the principle that "what is not lost [remains]," because the *ekākalasthita-homa* (the oblation performed at a single time) characterized by its specific time does not perish even at another time, the full-moon (*paurṇamāsī*) time prescribed for the portion of the *abhīṣṭoma* characterized by that [time] applies even when it is joined with a different deity.
Pṛ. 783: A non-required injunction is sublated by a required injunction;
for example, in the case of vomiting *soma*, the rule applies to the Vedic *soma*, but not to the worldly [soma].
*Bāla.*, p. 144. "Not being expressed" (*anabhihitatva*) is the absence of being expressed.
And that "being expressed" does not consist in being denoted by a *tiṅ* suffix and so forth, nor merely in being conveyed by them.

For if it were so, [the rule] would apply to forms such as *pācakena gamyate* ("he goes by the cook") and *caitreṇa bhuktvā gamyate* ("having eaten, Caitra goes"), because the agenthood is expressed by the *kṛt* suffix in the former and by the statement of common agency in the *ktvā* suffix in the latter, and thus there would be no occasion for the third case ending after the word ending in the third case.

Nor is it the state of having its number expressed; for if that were so, there would arise the undesirable consequence of using the expression "caitreṇa pācakaḥ" (by Caitra, the cook), just as one says "caitreṇa pakvaḥ" (cooked by Caitra). Furthermore, in the rule [Pāṇini 2.3.65], since the locative case ending expresses a definition (*lakṣaṇasaptamī*), and because the particle "api" in the phrase "viṣayakṣo 'pi saṃvarttaḥ svayaṃ chettum asādhu" (even a tree on the way should not be cut down by oneself) expresses the action [of cutting] rather than expressing number, there would be the undesirable consequence of the accusative case ending in "vṛkṣam". Rather, it is the state of being related to whatever case-ending is directly expressed (*śrutyā*) by the word denoting the action with which it is coreferential.

Furthermore, this is evident from the fact that in expressions such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*) and "The rice is being cooked" (*odanaḥ pacyate*), the agency residing in Caitra and the objecthood residing in the rice are conveyed by the aforementioned term [the *kṛt* suffix].

In cases such as "He is gone by the cook" (*pācakena gamyate*), the action of going alone is what connects with the person denoted by the *kṛt* suffix, and not the action of cooking, because the latter is already connected to that very person [as its agent].
And since the status of being a *kāraka* residing in him is not expressed by the case endings for object (*karman*) and so forth, the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) there is indeed appropriate.
Thus, because the phrase "by Caitra" connects with the act of eating, whereas its connection with the act of going is not admitted, the use of the instrumental case is justified.

However, in the expression "Having cooked by me alone, it is eaten by me alone," since the agent is expressed by the word "having cooked" (*paktvā*), the instrumental case in "by me" (*mayā*) and so forth does not denote the agent; rather, it denotes the instrument, as in such examples as "You know yourself by yourself" (*ātmānam ātmanā vetsi*) or "Entering by means of this very living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me manifest names and forms. Therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

In cases such as "Having cooked, rice is eaten" (*paktvā odano bhujyate*), however, when there is a requirement for an object (*karma*) subsequent to the suffix *-tvā*, the sentence is completed by supplying a word such as "rice" (*odana*) in the accusative case (*dvitīyā*). For the term *anabhihita* (not already expressed) in relation to the principal action is not meaningless.

There is no authoritative evidence for the rule that "there is an expression [of the agent] even when the action is subordinate to another," by which the sentence could be justified without supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).

If that were the case, the use of the accusative case in such examples as "Having eaten rice, the scripture is cooked" (*odanaṃ bhuktvā śāstraṃ pacyate*) and "Even though he heard it, that matter was not approved by him of evil intellect" (*śrutvāpyatha nānumatastena so'rthaḥ kubuddhinā*) would be untenable.

However, if there is a lack of confidence in the aforementioned applications, and if one accepts the following: that in the case of "by me alone having cooked, by me alone is it eaten," the first *tṛtīyā* (instrumental) occurs only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed; and in the case of "having cooked, the rice is eaten," no ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) is admitted; and likewise, having accepted the stated rule and also accepting that the suffix *ktvā* has its denotation (*śakti*) solely in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*), one accepts that the meaning of that [suffix], namely the action, is construed with the subsequent action through the relations of priority in time (*pūrvakālatva*) and common agency (*samānakartṛkatva*). Then let it be as follows: the state of being "denoted" (*abhihitatva*) is that which is conveyed by a word through its function (*vṛtti*) by a word that expresses the principal action connected to itself; the absence of that is "not being denoted" (*anabhihitatva*); and in that case, the *tṛtīyā* [is applied]. This is the summary.
Regarding this, they say:

if this were the case, then *laḥ* would have to be understood as a genitive form (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) construed with *tiṅ* and so forth, because a nominative form (*prathamānta*) cannot be syntactically connected [to them].

Consequently, there would be a pervasion of the three rules beginning with *laḥ*, and it would be untenable for the substitutes of *l*—such as *śānac* and others—to denote the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

Nor does its denotation [of the agent] follow from the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67); for even if that were the case, since the suffixes *ta* and *at* are prescribed by other rules (*karmaṇi*, *bhāve*, and *akarmakebhyaḥ*), they would simply apply accordingly. However, the agent is not denoted by them merely on that account. For, by parsimony (*lāghava*), the fact that the substance [the agent] is the referent of the word is the intended scope of the grammatical system; thus, there is no postulation of a distinct function (*vṛtti*) to denote that [agent].
It is thus established that the agent (*kartṛ*) is not denoted (*avācyatva*) by the verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), whereas it *is* denoted (*vācyatva*) by forms such as those ending in *-śānac*.
Furthermore, the rule "of *la*" (*lasya*)—which prescribes the substitution of *tiṅ* and other suffixes for *la*—is not rendered redundant.

According to the Bhaṭṭa school (Bhāṭṭa 3.4.8, pp. 322–24), the word *anabhihita* (in Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.3.1) functions through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean "when [the action] is already understood in its specific character."
Furthermore, because the words *pacati* and *pacyate* involve a connection with number, the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are understood in their specific forms;
therefore, the respective case-endings (*vibhakti*) are not applicable [to them directly].
Since the various *kārakas* are never perceived in such a specific form [when they are merely potentialities], the case-endings arise [only when they are manifested as actualized factors].

Furthermore, regarding the specific types of *kārakas*, it has already been stated that just as there is a cognition of the specific [roles] of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), so too does the connection with number occur.

As for the objection that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because of the status of a *kāraka* arising from the abstract action (*bhāva*)—as in "it is not cooked here" (*neha pacyate*) or "it is not eaten here" (*neha bhujyate*), where, when only the act of cooking is intended, the agent and object are not resorted to, since the substratum belongs to the verbal root's meaning and the efficient force (*bhāvanā*)—to that it is replied:
"That same fault, which pertains to the domain of words, applies equally even in the view that [the *kāraka*] is denoted."
The non-exclusivity (anaikāntya) of being a denoter is not accepted for that which indicates, just as [it is not accepted] for that which causes understanding.

Just as, because an action is non-exclusive, it follows that it is a non-indicator in cases where it is absent, so too, since a word denotes an object, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even in the case of "the rice is cooked" (*odanaḥ pacyate*), the word would not be a denoter.
Now, if [you argue] this is a case of deviation (*vyabhicāra*):
The instruction would be purposeless: [if one were to think] "it will digest without being breathed upon," then that vow, being performed, would be useless;
moreover, due to indigestion, the sacrificer would become ill.
Therefore, in that case, the vow would be purposeless and temporary;
one should not consume [it]. However, when there is the capacity for digestion, one may consume it.

In the preceding section, the necessity of the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) was stated; here, its non-necessity is stated, which serves to distinguish it from the former. [The word] *tu* [indicates this distinction].
[The sūtra states: "The instruction would be purposeless, because [the rite] is meaningful when connected with a fruitful [act]; for the act of standing near (*upasthāna*) is not itself fruitful."

This Sūtra is intended to refute the objection regarding the splitting of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Even though the Āgnīdhra and the other [officiants], as well as the *doha* and *havidhāna*, are invariably connected to the sacrifice (*ṛtvaikāntikatva*), their specific forms are not enjoined; nevertheless, since they are established as having been consecrated (*anuniṣṭhāditatva*), the purpose is served. However, even if they were invariably connected to the sacrifice, because the worship (*upasthāna*) of the Āgnīdhra and others is not enjoined as being non-different from their own essential nature, it would be impossible for that worship to be connected to the sacrifice through them. Furthermore, since there is no basis for a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*)—as seen in the case of the Āgnīdhra and others—and because, like the Āhavanīya fire, the name depends solely on the essential form (*svarūpa-nimittatva*) without depending on a purificatory rite, the worship would fall into futility. Thus, the Sūtra is stated to avoid this contingency.

The meaning of the portion of the sūtra ending with "phalavatā" (by that which possesses a fruit) is as follows: [if the mantra were merely for the sake of] instruction on the nature of the *upasthāna* (attendance/invocation), then since there would be no inclusion of even a single instance of such attendance as being fruitful, the instruction would be purposeless.

The portion of the sūtra beginning with "na hi" (for not... is intended to dispel the doubt that—even though the attendance of the *āgnīdhra* and others by the *daśa* (the ten priests) might not be connected to the sacrifice (*ṛtu*)—it will nonetheless possess a fruit by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

This is because, although a connection to the sacrifice is perceived through the context, if it is not enjoined (*avidhīyamāna*), it is not accomplished through performance; thus, since the general principle is itself subject to injunction, it would result in an unavoidable burden if one were to insist upon its weightiness.

The doubt that "the attendance [of the fires] following the seasons (*ṛtvanvaya*) is not fruitful" is dispelled by the portion of the Sūtra [beginning with *na*]. (Sūtra-pṛ. 1131). "Something that is not already understood, yet is required, is accepted because of its purity. (Parākrama-pṛ. 312). "The comprehension of the meaning of a treatise occurs as an indivisible whole (*anavayava*). This is the maxim (*nyāya*).
But when the instruction on dharma is established, it follows from the knowledge of the rules for its constituent parts, just as in the case of worldly and Vedic matters.
This is established. How so? Because this treatise is an instruction on dharma.

In this treatise on the instruction of Dharma, the meaning of the scripture is understood in its entirety, just as it is in worldly legal codes (*kṛtanta*). For instance, in common worldly usage, when it is said, "A Brāhmaṇa woman must not be killed" or "Liquor must not be drunk," it is not merely the individual woman or the individual liquor that is prohibited from being killed or drunk.

Furthermore, if the understanding of the meaning of a scriptural injunction were based on a single part [of it], then after having killed a single Brāhmaṇa or drunk a single draught of *surā*, one would be free to act as one pleases in other respects. Likewise, regarding the rule "one of earlier age is to be saluted," if one were to salute merely someone of earlier age, then after having saluted a single person of earlier age, one would be free to act as one pleases in other respects.
Similarly, in the Veda, in the passage "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Agnihotra and other rites," the installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) is required every spring.

If the comprehension of the meaning of a treatise were achieved through its parts individually, one would not engage in the sacrifice again after having performed it once; the same applies here as well.
[This concludes] Sāhasī 631. *Oṃ* The Principle of Non-termination (*anavasthāna-nyāya*).
The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that there is no final rest for the probandum and the probans.
Others maintain that [the application of suffixes] is dependent on an unstable succession and takes the form of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*).

However, in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.91), it is extensively deliberated: "From where does this governing authority (*adhikāra*) of the word *dhātu* extend? Does it extend prior to the substitution of *l*-suffixes, or rather until the completion of the third chapter (*tṛtīyādhyāya-vyāpya*)? Now, it might be objected: "But was it not already stated that [this rule] would apply even in cases such as *adadhanam* and *apunan*?"
This is not a fault;
once the elision has been performed, it will not occur.
But in this case, elision does not apply.
What is the reason? It is sublated by the substitution of *ī*. Here, the substitution of *ī* does not apply.
What is the reason? It is sublated by the state of being *agni*.
The substitution of *ni* for *anta* does not occur.
What is the reason? It is sublated by the substitution of *jus*.
It is not sublated by the substitution of *jus* in this case.
What is the reason? It is sublated by elision (*lopa*). Elision is sublated by the substitution of *ī* (*ītva*).
The substitution of *ī* is sublated by the final element (*anta*).

"The substitution of *ann* would result in the substitution of *jus*, and the substitution of *jus* would result in elision (*lopa*); thus, a circular argument (*cakraka*) and an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would follow"—this and more has been stated elsewhere in detail.

Furthermore, in the first chapter (*viveka*) of the *Tattvaviveka*, a work by the author of the *Pañcadaśī*, it is said: "The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must belong either to the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) or to the conceptual (*savikalpa*)."
"In the first case there is contradiction; in the other cases, there is infinite regress (*anavasthā*), dependence on a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), and so forth.
Here, self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), circularity (*cakraka*), and infinite regress (*anavasthā*) are indeed mentioned.
*Sāhasī*, p. 612. Infinite regress (*anavasthā*) occurs, for example, in the position that one must perform the *ārambhaṇīyā* rite at the commencement of the *ārambhaṇīyā* rite itself.

[Objection: But surely for that [first *ārambhaṇīyā*] there would be another *ārambhaṇīyā*, for that too another, and for that yet another; in this way, the *ārambhaṇīyā* would never reach a conclusion. [Response: In cases of infinite regress, there will indeed be a settlement by virtue of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). Bhāṣya 10.1.46: "Because all infinite regresses are settled by virtue of functional capacity."

Indeed, as many [recitations] as do not exceed the Agnikāla, the Paurṇamāsī, the Āmāvāsyā, and so forth, so many shall be performed. Vārttika 3.6.16: "He sacrifices without pausing" (anavānam yajati); by this prohibition of breathing (*śvāsa*) between the *yājyā* and the *vaṣaṭkāra*, it is understood that these two must be performed by a single agent.
Vi. [Vivaraṇa].
The form of fasting (anaśanarūpa) [is a penance] for improper conduct (anācāra). Oṃ, fasting is a penance to be performed by the sacrificer in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;

Therefore, since *irā* and the others are not taught in the Veda, they cannot possibly be equivalent to the word *irā*.

Consequently, the observation of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth would be contradicted [if it were applied to the ectype].
Therefore, it is logical that it should find its place only in the archetype, which is excluded from the process of extension (*atideśa*).

No, because of the nature of the injunction (*codanā*). The Commentary states: "It is not for the sake of the primary context (*prakṛti*); we say it is for all purposes, because it is recited equally even outside of a specific context.

As for what was said—that there is no need for an extended application (*codaka*) because the requirement is satisfied by the injunction not dependent on a specific context—that is untenable in this case.

For an independent injunction (*anāramya-vidhi*) does not satisfy the expectancy of an injunction (*codanā*). Indeed, it is only when the *sruva* ladle has been established by an injunction that the quality of being made of *khadira* wood can be enjoined by an independent injunction;
if there were no such injunction, the independent injunction would not exist at all.
Furthermore, an independent injunction (anārambhavidhi) does not bring about the ladle (sruva), nor the quality of being made of khadira wood for it.
Why? Because of the nature of the injunction.
For the injunction, "He whose ladle is made of khadira [obtains success]," has a single purpose.

And here, neither the ladle (*sruva*) nor its being made of *khadira* wood is enjoined as both. This word [of the injunction] expresses that the ladle, which already exists, is to be made of *khadira*; and that [quality of being made of *khadira*] is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*).
Therefore, the *codaka* exists.
For that [general rule], having excluded that [specific case] again and again, brings about another;
therefore, the *anārabhyavidhi* (unattached injunction) pertains to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*).
Or rather—it is not possible to exclude its universal application on this account alone.

For when an extended application (*atideśa*) is sublated in one instance, it does not become sublated everywhere. Just as, for example, even though *kuśa* grass is excluded from the door-posts, the *prayāja* offerings and other rites are not thereby excluded;
for sublation is understood to occur only with respect to that which occupies the same scope.
Therefore, the extended application (atideśa) ceases because it pertains only to the portion consisting of the requirement to be fulfilled, such as the use of *khadira* wood.
Furthermore, since the use of *khadira* wood is not of the nature of an action (*akriyātmaka*), it cannot by itself render the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) free from its expectancy.
Moreover, if it were to apply simultaneously to both the archetype (prakṛti) and the modification, it would be impossible to determine its contribution toward the ritual purpose.
However, that [injunction] is expectant because of the absence of its own object to be obtained;
nor is the obtaining of the *sruva* ladle possible without the authorization of an extended application (*atideśa*);
and this sentence is not itself the prescriber of the *sruva*.
Regarding the section on the *anārabhyādhikaraṇa*: since the primary action is not being enjoined, and because a qualified injunction would otherwise result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*),

one must therefore postulate an extended application (*atideśa*) for the *khādiratva* (the quality of being made of *khadira* wood) of the *sruva* ladle, which is established by the *anārabhya-vidhi* (independent injunction).
If it is argued that this is an "origination" (utpatti), the Bhāṣya states: If you view it thus, this is an origination by means of the injunctions regarding the archetypal form (prakṛti).
In the archetype, the subsidiary elements (aṅga) are stated both concisely and in detail.
Just as there is a concise statement, "He performs five fore-sacrifices" (*pañca prayājān yajati*), followed by an elaborate one, "He sacrifices to the *samidhs*" (*samidho yajati*) and so forth;
here too, there is elaboration in such passages as, "For whom there is a ladle made of *khadira* wood," and conciseness in such a passage as, "For whom the ladles are thus small.
Such a form of injunction is observed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), and this [ectypal injunction] is of that same form.

Therefore, the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is that it is "pertaining to the archetype" (*prākṛta*). Consequently, it is an injunction not restricted to a specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*) pertaining to the archetype.

Alternatively, a certain logician here says: "The injunction not restricted to a specific context has the archetype as its purpose, because it is enjoined both concisely and in detail, like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth."
No, because it is equal [in force].
The Bhāṣya says: "This is not so;
for an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) of this kind is not a proving factor."

There is merely a similarity here with the archetypal injunction (*prakṛti-vidhi*), but there is no authoritative evidence that this [specific detail] occurs in the archetype. Furthermore, even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) are enjoined both concisely and in detail; for example, "He offers three oblations" is concise, while "O gods, of the one who honors, of the one who honors... is detailed. Therefore, these [details] are equal to those whose scope is not specifically commenced (*anārabhya-viṣaya*) by the modified sacrifices as well.

Therefore, this is not a reason for the inclination toward primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Or rather: "The scope of such an inference does not extend [to that]"—so it has been stated (in the *Ślokavārttika*, Pratyakṣasūtra, verse 19).
Moreover, this is not even an inference, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Even in the case of a modified ritual (*vikṛti*), an injunction is perceived through both brevity (*saṃkṣepa*) and elaboration (*vistāra*).
In that regard, one might argue: "Since it has already been enjoined by one [text], either the brief or the elaborate version is not itself injunctive."
Since that [reason] is equally applicable to the *prakṛti*, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Therefore, one must necessarily provide as a reason merely the statement of brevity and elaboration, independent of whether there is an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*); and it has already been stated that such a reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Or rather:
if you say that these two sūtras are to be understood according to one's own school (meaning, according to one's own view),
and that you perceive them as having universal application, then that is incorrect.
For where there is the originative injunction of the vessels, there it is possible to enjoin their genus; but in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), there is no originative injunction. Therefore...
When that [category] is devoid of vessels, it is impossible to enjoin a class [of vessels], because of the inequality of attainment.

For if the vessels were attained equally for both the archetype (prakṛti) and the modification (vikṛti), then the injunction of a class could be established by way of non-specification (adeśena) in all instances;
but this is not the case.
Therefore, it is argued that the meaning [of the injunction] pertains only to the original context (*prakṛti*).
To this, the reply is: "No, because of equality.
In every respect, a statement not occurring within a specific context (*anārabhyavāda*) requires a basis for its application.
In this regard, whether it be an application by direct injunction (*upadeśa*) or an application by extended injunction (*atideśa*), all such application is equal to that which is already established.

Although there is a distinction between proximity and remoteness regarding direct and extended injunctions, these two determine relative strength only within their own respective domains, not in relation to a general statement made outside of a specific context (*anārabhyavāda*).
For the *anārabhyavāda* is more remote than the [direct injunction], since it reaches the ritual only through the mediation of the sacrificial vessel.
Therefore, it serves all purposes;
and the extended application (*atideśa*) arises from that.
However, because of the completeness of the injunction’s purpose and due to the contradiction with the primary [meaning], it has the sense of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
The Commentary: The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. The injunction not connected to a specific context (*anāramyavidhi*) does not apply to all purposes;
rather, we maintain that it applies to the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Why? Because of the completeness of the injunction (*codanā*).
The injunction brings about the whole [set of details];
the modified (*vaikṛta*) apūrva is not rendered devoid of expectancy by a detached rule (*anāramyavidhi*).
For that [injunction] pertains to the vessels by virtue of its syntactical connection, not to the sacrifices.
The sacrifices, because of their connection with the indicative mark of an injunction (*codanā-liṅga*), require the archetypal model (*prakṛti*); they attain syntactical unity with it.
And the archetypal elements are capable of rendering those [sacrifices] free from expectancy, whereas an unattached injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) is not.
Therefore, the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) must necessarily be brought in. And if it is argued that [this applies] not by means of a general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*),
nor does that [injunction], even if it were to operate due to the absence of a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), become connected with the modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta-yāga*).
Therefore, the *anāramyavidhi* (unattached injunction) is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) for the primary modified rite (*vaikṛta*).

When there is a conflict regarding the rule "or in the archetype" (*prakṛtau vā*), since the archetypal supplementary statement would apply by virtue of the force of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), the *anāramyavidhi* would not come into effect.
Consequently, the *anāramyavidhi* is for the sake of the archetype.
Or rather—because it is already mentioned twice in the archetype (*prakṛti*), this alone is logical.
As for the claim that "it will cause that [archetype] to be extended," that is incorrect.
Why? "If the injunction (*codaka*) were to apply to the archetypes by way of distinction..."
Therefore, it would be thus: among these, [the action] proceeds simultaneously.
Whether by the attainment of the location of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) or by the extension of the ritual procedure (*śāstra*), a distinction might occasionally arise from that source.
We shall explain in the tenth book (10.1.12) that the sacrifice is the essential operation (*tattva-vyāpāra*) and that it is what is extended (*atidiśyate*).
And because it is partless, it is extended [to all cases] simultaneously;
and by this, the section concerning the unoriginated self (ātman-anārabhyādhikaraṇa) is concluded.
For the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*), the *apūrvas* beginning with the *prājāpatya* offerings are grasped simultaneously;
and by means of those, the *prājāpatya* offerings [are accomplished],
and the *prājāpatya* offerings also [include] their own recensional branches (*svaśākhā*).

Because that extension (*atideśa*)—in the form "by virtue of being the original archetype" (*prakṛtitvataḥ*)—is uniform, its application or non-application occurs everywhere without distinction, and not merely in certain parts. This was stated in the section on strength and weakness (*balābalādhikaraṇa*, 3.3.1–14) regarding the fact that even those *kuśa* grasses which have already been obtained are set aside. Therefore, if the extension is abandoned for the injunctions concerning *khadira* wood and so forth in accordance with the *anārabhyavāda* (general rules), then it must likewise be abandoned for the *ajñāna* (unconscious errors) as well; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the rule] applying to all three types of cases.
And it has been stated therein (in this very fifth book):

"Now, if, out of deference to certain archetypal elements, the extended application (*atideśa*) of their rules is accepted as authoritative, then the acquisition of [materials] such as *khadira* wood would likewise be non-distinct; thus, a clear case of tautology (*dviruktatva*) results.

Furthermore, because they depend upon the requirements of the sacrificial procedure, we shall establish everywhere that even bypassing their own specific contexts, the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) first take up the archetypal elements."
Because that [latter] is also an uninitiated statement (*anārabhyavāda*), it attains its application through extension (*atideśa*); therefore, it possesses primacy.
Furthermore, the attainment of case-endings (*suvādi*) in the archetypal sacrifices (*prakṛti*) must necessarily be presupposed.
To the extent that case-endings do not apply there, so too [does the rule] regarding the *khādira* wood and the like; thus, it cannot be considered a subject of direct instruction (*upadeśa*).
Furthermore, their connection with the seasons is not explicit;
that too must be inferred through the principle of "presumption based on the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) by means of the *khādira* wood and other such factors.
Moreover, one who maintains that [the injunction] applies to all purposes must at least admit a connection with the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*).
And in that case, where there is no purposeful connection [to a specific rite], a connection with a modification (*vikṛti*) would lack a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).
For a connection established by extended application (*atideśa*) possesses a stronger means of valid cognition.

However, for those whose connection to a specific seasonal rite (*ṛtu*) is directly perceived, even those statements not introduced in a specific context (*anārabhyavāda*) apply to all purposes, just as in the case of: "This seventeen-fold Prajāpati indeed led the sacrifice."
Therefore, it is established that [the quality of being made of] *khadira* wood and so forth serves as the material cause (*prakṛti*).

Śā—Having concluded the discussion concerning the subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*) which arose in the context of the inquiry into detached injunctions (*anārabhyavāda*), he now resumes that very same detached injunction:
