"For the mere attainment of the *juhū* ladle and so forth is what is required by the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood and the like."
And that which is an attainment based on direct instruction, or an attainment based on extended application.
Since that [result] is identical in form to the attainment [of the fruit] by virtue of being restated in reference to it,
it is understood that the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood, which is being enjoined, serves all purposes.

[Objection: But surely, by that very extended application (*atideśa*) through which the *juhū* ladle is obtained in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood is also obtained; thus, its specific instruction would be redundant. [Reply:
It is not so, because the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not by inference (*anumāna*).
It is obtained from the injunctive statement; therefore, qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood serve all purposes.

Thus, there would be no fault of redundancy (*dvirukta-doṣa*), for there is no point in a further injunction of what has already been obtained. This would be the case if the injunctive statement were to convey the ritual elements as distinct entities.
In that context, attainment (prāpti) is appropriate; it is extended by way of its own mode. Indeed, the attainment of things occurs through their state of being qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa).
And all of those [elements] combined serve as qualifiers of the base form (prakṛti).
Therefore, as long as the attainment of the *juhū* ladle exists,
so long is the attainment of the *juhū* understood from the injunction regarding its being made of *parṇa* wood;
thus, it is already obtained along with the state of being made of *parṇa*, and is not [itself] enjoined.
The injunction regarding the nature of the *parṇa* (palāśa) wood is established as pertaining to the archetype (*prakṛti*) alone.

Soma: Because an independent injunction (*anārabhyavāda*) does not depend upon the ritual elements transferred from elsewhere, and because direct perception operates more swiftly in that case, it applies equally to both the archetype and the ectype (*vikṛti*).

As in the passage: "‘Āśrāvaya’ has four syllables, ‘Astu śrauṣaṭ’ has four syllables, ‘Yaja’ has two syllables, ‘Yeyajāmahe’ has five syllables, and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance has two syllables; this indeed is the seventeenfold Prajāpati who fashioned the sacrifice," and so forth—it should be understood that in such cases, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the modified (*vikṛti*) form of the sacrifice.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: where there are qualities (*guṇas*) based on items prescribed outside of any specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that those qualities apply to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛtis*); however, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they do not apply, according to the principle of the *ādhāna* (8.1.12).

The meaning of the sūtra is: "The quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth is for all purposes, because it is not mentioned within the context of any particular rite, and thus its universal application is logical.
[Vṛtti: "Whether in the archetype (*prakṛti*) or the modification (*vikṛti*), the injunction for one who possesses *parṇa*-wood applies."

Or rather, it belongs to the archetype itself; since the statement applies equally to both, this injunction of being made of *parṇa*-wood, depending on the *juhū* ladle, pertains only to the archetype. Since both are obtained in the ectype through the *codaka* (the rule of extension), what is the purpose of an injunction here for the ectype?

Bhaṭṭa: Regarding the passage heard as unconnected to a specific ritual context, such as "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood," this quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood is enjoined with reference to the *juhū* belonging to a sacrifice characterized by the aforementioned [qualities]. Thus, it is established that through the medium of that *juhū*, it becomes an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice accomplished by the *juhū*. In considering whether this [quality] applies equally to both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*), or belongs to the archetype alone: [the conclusion is] that it applies to all of them because of extension (*atideśa*). Nor does there arise the fault of "double-statement" (*dviruktatva*) on the grounds that it is already obtained in the ectype through extension; for if it were obtained only through direct injunction (*upadeśa*), then extension would have no scope whatsoever. Since the assumption [of extension] has as its object the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood, [extension applies].

Furthermore, since there is no extended application (*atideśa*) to the *juhū* ladle alone in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), and because that [extended application] occurs subsequent to the connection of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) with the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*), the injunction regarding being made of *parṇa*-wood first pertains to the archetypal sacrifice. Since its capacity to generate cognition is exhausted upon manifesting in the context of the archetype, it is impossible for it to generate that cognition again in the context of the modified sacrifice; thus, the section concerning what is not commenced (*anārabhyādhikaraṇa*) applies.
In the section concerning what is not commenced...
It should not be argued that this results in the fallacy of temporal inconsistency (*prātikālyavaiṣamyāpatti*).

For, as in the case of the *vaimṛdha* sacrifice and others, once it is accepted that the archetype (*prakṛti*) is complete with respect to its connection to subsidiaries other than the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood, the extension (*atideśa*) to the modified rite (*vikṛti*) becomes possible; thus, since the *parṇatā* is enjoined only subsequently, its commonality [with the archetype] is established.
Otherwise, even in the case of the Vaimṛdha sacrifice, there would be no application of the *prājāpatya* and other subsidiaries distinct from the Vaimṛdha itself.

This being the position reached, we reply: although the archetype (*prakṛti*) is accepted as complete through its connection with all its constituent parts—including whatever minor details of procedure may be present—nevertheless, when one posits an extended application (*atideśa*) for the Vaimṛdha, that extension applies only to those subsidiaries which have their own requirements satisfied by their connection to their respective parts; it does not apply to the Vaimṛdha itself, because as long as the specific subsidiaries are not understood, its productive operation (*bhāvanā*) remains incomplete.

And for this reason, since the archetype (*prakṛti*) lacks completeness without a connection to the *parṇatā* (leaf-nature) of the ladle, and because if the *parṇatā* were enjoined again immediately after the *juhū* is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), there would arise a discrepancy regarding the timing of the injunction, the *parṇatā* serves the purpose of the archetype alone.

And just as, in this case, in the rule "one cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) during the initiations" (*dīkṣāsu yūpaṃ chinatti*), there is no discrepancy regarding the timing of the injunction—since the injunction of the time of initiation applies equally to the cutting associated with the *abhīṣomīya* sacrifice, to other [sacrifices], and to the cutting [itself] by way of extended application—we shall explain that very point in [the section on] 11.3.4.

In reality, however, there is no injunction for it by way of a common rule (*sādhāraṇa*), because that which is enjoined as the meaning of the base form (*prakṛtyartha*) can be obtained even through extended application (*atideśa*).
Nevertheless, since the status of being a sacrificial post (*yūpatva*) belongs to a different time and its specific nature is not obscure, it is not inconsistent, just like other vessels.

The practical purpose (*prayojana*) is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), if the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood is lost, then in a modification (*vikṛti*) belonging to another Veda, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed in the Yajurveda would apply.
In the Siddhānta, there is no expiation when it is not specifically known, or rather, it pertains to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

This is because even expiations such as those beginning with *bhūḥ* are properties of the Veda, according to the introductory context, just like the quality of being uttered loudly (*uccaiḥ*) and so forth.
Maṇḍana states: "The [quality of] being made of *parṇa*-wood would not apply to the modified sacrifice, because of its being stated twice."
Śaṅkara: "And [the rule regarding] the leaf-vessels and so forth applies to the archetype."

(4) Having raised the objection in the *Anārabhyādhikaraṇa* by stating that since the *anārabhyavidhi* (unrestricted injunction) applies even to the *vikṛtis* (modified sacrifices), there is no possibility of the charge of "double-statement" (*dviruktatva*) arising from its application to both the *prakṛti* (archetype) and the *vikṛti*, [the opponent argues]: "If it is argued that the *codaka* (injunctive force of the archetype) is weaker than the *anārabhyavidhi* because the *vikṛti* is satisfied by the latter alone, leading to the absence of the *codaka* and thus the non-perception of the *prajā* (offering) and so forth. (5) This is refuted by the sūtra: "No, because of the unity of purpose with the *codaka*" (*na codaikyārthāt*). By this, it is explained that although the *codaka* might be weakened by the *anārabhyavidhi*—since the statement regarding *khadira* wood and the like in the *anārabhyavidhi* already fulfills the requirements of the *vikṛti* by prescribing the *sruva* (ladle) and other implements—the application of the *prajā* and other elements obtained through the *anārabhyavidhi* is still logically established as being brought about by the *codaka*. Furthermore, the claim of the partial proponent of the Siddhānta (*siddhāntaikadeśin*) that the charge of "double-statement" is unproven is addressed. *Mīmāṃsākośa*, 48.

If you argue that, by the reason of its being both concise and detailed, and by the analogy of the injunctions regarding *prajāpati* and others, one may infer through the statement "if [it be argued] by [the word] 'upa-jiti'" (Sūtra 6) that the injunctions concerning *khadira* wood and so forth have as their sole purpose the *prakṛti* (archetype), [the author] replies with "not so, because of equality" (Sūtra 7). He states that the inference is invalid because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since one observes both conciseness and detail even in modifications (*vikṛti*) such as the *āghāra* and *udvāsa*. Then, with the Sūtra "But because of the time of the injunction's purpose, and because of the prohibition of the primary injunction, [the quality belongs] to the *prakṛti*" (Sūtra 8), he concludes the final position (*siddhānta*). He does so by removing the doubt that the principle of "redundancy" (*dviruktatva-prasaṅga*)—which was raised to show that the *anārabhya-vidhi* (isolated injunction) must apply only to the *prakṛti*—is not established. He argues that since the isolated injunction possesses a qualified object (such as *khadira* wood) and depends on the *codaka* (transfer injunction) to obtain the *sruva* ladle and other implements, the *codaka* itself is more powerful. Consequently, it is illogical to exclude the subject matter of the isolated injunction; rather, the entire set of archetypal accessories (*prākṛtāṅgajāta*) already established reaches the status of being for the purpose of the *codaka*. If the isolated injunction were intended for the *vikṛti* (modification), there would arise a contradiction: the *codaka* would be subordinate to the primary modification-injunction, or the isolated injunction itself would be subordinate. To avoid this, the isolated injunction applies only to the *prakṛti*, thus resolving the issue of redundancy. This is how he summarizes the conclusion.

Su. Pṛ. 1277: In the *Anārabhyādhikaraṇa*, by means of the sūtra stating the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), "Or in the archetype" (2), the principle characterized by the consequence of redundancy (*dviruktatva*) is stated regarding the fact that the *khadira* wood and so forth belong to both the archetype and the ectype. Pṛ. 41 [of Su.]: The *pravargya* rite, which is studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), belongs to the Soma sacrifice because of its connection with the *upasad*s, as expressed in the text: "Before the *upasad*s, he performs the *pravargya*. There too, by the principle of the independent injunction (*anārabhyanyāya*), it belongs to the *jyotiṣṭoma*, which serves as the archetype; and there, due to its application during the first six-day period, it belongs specifically to the first performance of that sacrifice.
The *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), being taught as unconnected to any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to anything.

Vi. 3|6|4: Regarding the statement "On the following day, in the case of the *dvirātra* sacrifices," the Vṛttikāra's opinion is that this is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*), meaning that the *agnirāsa* occurs only in the *dvirātra* sacrifice and not in other *dvirātra* sacrifices.

10|5|13: *Anārabhya* refers to that which is taught outside of a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*). That which is stated as *anārabhya* is sublated by what belongs to a specific context (*prākaraṇika*).
Just as that which is studied as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*), such as the *pāpman-destroying* quality of the *sātatya* [leaf], [is understood thus]:

the statement "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood" establishes this *parṇa*-nature as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); its connection to the sacrifice is through syntactical unity (*vākya*), while the mention of a fruit is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). (Bāla., p. 141)

The *sābhimenīsāptadaśya* (the rule of seventeen [animals] with the *sābhimiṇī* cow), which is studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), is integrated into the *vaimṛdha*, *adhvara-kalpa*, and other such rituals.
Bhāṣya 10.8.19–19: The *sābhimenīsāptadaśya*, studied as an independent injunction, is for the purpose of the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice).

The sacrificial implements mentioned as *anārabhyādhīta* (taught outside of a specific context) are to be worn starting from the *ādhāna* (the fire-consecration ceremony) itself, and not merely starting from the *paurṇamāsī* (full-moon sacrifice). [Vi. 11.3.14] Regarding those two *anārabhyādhīta* items that do not involve a dialogue, their performance is not at every ritual juncture; rather, it occurs specifically at the morning session (*prātaḥsavana*), prior to the *dhārāgraha* (the drawing of the streams), for those whose application is contextual (*prākaraṇika*), since their performance follows directly from the injunction (*vidhi*).
"Indeterminacy [is established] by the absence of specification;
however, there is a further scriptural statement for the sake of specification.

Since both alternatives—either a single time or a repeated performance—are possible regarding the purchase [of the priests], when [the rule] "The fee is a dwarf" or "He gives ten thousand" and so forth occurs as a further scriptural statement regarding those respective parts, [it serves to specify]."
The purpose is to specify the particular mode of hiring.
The intention is that the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for a specific part [of the ritual] serves an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that from the commencement of the *rājasūya*, there is a restriction for the priests themselves until the completion of the *rājasūya*.

Ke. Oṃ: When there is a possibility of application without restriction, a prohibition in the form of an *upasaṃhāra* (restriction) occurs regarding the scope of that application; for example: "He gives a chariot yoked with a sacrificial animal at the *rathapardhya* [sacrifice]. Bāla. p. 17, Oṃ: And when there is a possibility of application both there and elsewhere, it is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*).
As it is stated in the Smṛti: "Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten. (p. 26).
Oṃ. The principle of non-restriction (aniyamanyāya).
(3|3|18|31 Brahma Sūtra): Because the principle of non-restriction (*aniyamanyāya*) applies even to meditations other than those on symbols (*pratīka*).
Śāṃbhā. 4|1|6|15: "There is no restriction for all [meditations]; there is no contradiction among the words. This is the aphorism.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether the path of the gods (*devayāna-gati*) is to be understood only in those meditations where it is heard in scripture, or whether it is to be understood even in those such as that of Śāṇḍilya where it is not heard—it should be known that this path belongs to all meditations.
Thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the path.
It is heard that [the path] belongs specifically to those in the Upakośala-vidyā and others, yet there is no such restrictive rule.

Why is this? Having heard from the scriptural statement, "Those who know thus, and those in the forest who worship with faith and austerity," and by means of inference through the Smṛti text, "The two paths, white and black," the lack of a fixed rule is established; such is the meaning of the Nyāya-sūtra.

By this reasoning, it has been stated that for all meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsanā*) and for all meditations on the "I am Brahman" (*aham-mahopāsanā*), the journey by the path of the gods (*devayāna-gati*) is accomplished without restriction.

Regarding the claim that, according to the principle of non-restriction (*aniyamanyāya*), this journey applies universally to all meditations based on modifications (*vikārālambana*) without distinction, the Commentator refutes that:
[Brahma Sūtra 4.3.6.19] "In all meditations, because of the principle of non-restriction, there is no establishment of a specific rule regarding those based on modifications."

Regarding the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) at Brahma Sūtra 4.3.6.15: "He does not lead those who rely on symbols (pratīka), but he leads those who rely on modifications (vikāra). Since both positions are thus accepted, there is no defect whatsoever in the principle that "there is no restriction for all.
This is because it is established that the word "all" refers to those other than those relying on symbols.

In *Brahma-sūtra* 3.3.6, the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) recalls the principle of the section on non-restriction (*aniyamādhikaraṇa*)—which stands within the section on the combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*)—as the underlying reason.
This very same principle of non-restriction (*aniyamanyāya*) belongs to the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*.
(Ke.)
Oṃ. There is no fixed rule elsewhere. What sequence is being considered? Elsewhere, however, there is some lack of restriction regarding sequence; that is, no fixed rule.

As, for example, in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, regarding the mantras recited by the sacrificer during the fore-offerings (prayāja) and subsequent rites, which are recorded in various Vedic branches.
This is indeed a siddhānta-sūtra.
Ke.
Oṃ. There is no fixed rule, because there is no distinction.
Regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), it has been stated: "One cow, six, twelve, a hundred, a thousand, or an unlimited number of cows.
In this regard, it was established in the preceding section that by the term "unlimited" (*aparimita*), a specific number must indeed be understood.

However, there would be no fixed rule as to whether that number should be taken as less than a thousand or more, because there is no specific distinction made and because a specific [number] would be more appropriate.
This is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa).
Or rather, it should be more than a thousand, because the word "iti" has many meanings and because of its proximity [to the preceding context].
Refuting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached through the Sūtra by means of the word "or" (*vā*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

Regarding the injunctions "a thousand should be given" and "an unlimited amount should be given," the term "unlimited" (*aparimita*) does not refer to something less than a thousand or equal to it; rather, only something greater should be understood, because the word "unlimited" has the sense of "much. Indeed, the word "unlimited" signifies abundance.
And the term "abundant" (*bahula*) should be understood as being dependent on what precedes it.

In that context, because of proximity, the word "number" (*saṃkhyā*)—which has specific qualifiers beginning with "one" and ending with "thousand"—is dependent on "thousand" when taken in its abundant sense.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that by the statement "an unlimited amount should be given," the meaning to be understood is that "more than a thousand should be given."
"And the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is meaningful for that purpose.

This sūtra is intended to establish another reason—namely, the avoidance of the fruitlessness of the explanatory passage—for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that in the context of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*), regarding the injunction "a thousand [cows] should be given" and "an unlimited amount should be given," the word "unlimited" (*aparimita*) signifies "more than a thousand.
The word "and" (*va*) expresses a conjunction of reasons.

The meaning of the word *aparimita* here is that it denotes a number exceeding one thousand. The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "Indeed, the unlimited is superior," expresses the superiority of the unlimited over the thousand; and the explanatory passage stating, "Indeed, the limited is perishable," expresses the perishability of everything up to a thousand. [The term] *arthavat* is neuter in the general sense; it means "possessing purpose" or "fruitful.
Therefore, in this context...
There is no fixed rule because there is no distinction; the established conclusion is that those whose purpose is not specified are unlimited in number, meaning they exceed one thousand. (Ke. 3.8.1)

*Oṃ. There is no restriction, because there is no specific distinction.* In the doubt as to whether the word "unmeasured" (*aparimita*) signifies an indefinite plurality or a plurality exceeding one thousand—given that a specific proximity exists due to the presence of another ritual procedure for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) involving one thousand—it follows [from the prima facie view] that it signifies an indefinite plurality.

However, since the word "unmeasured" requires a correlative and denotes a state of being much, even the proximity of something else serves as a specific determinant through its expectancy for that [correlative].

Therefore, the meaning is "less than one thousand by a small amount," as established by the sūtra: "Or it may be more, because the word 'iti' has many meanings, due to proximity. [Sūtra 5.1.20: "There is no fixed rule, because there is no distinction. [Sūtra 5.1.21: "Parākrama says: Oṃ, there is no fixed rule, because there is no distinction."

When there is a group of sacrificers (*yajamānagaṇa*) in an *ahīna* sacrifice, actions for the sake of others—such as the commencement of the fire with white [bricks] (*śuklāgnyārambhaṇa*) and the measuring of the *audumbarī* post—may be performed by any sacrificer whatsoever without restriction.
Thus, there would be no restriction regarding the sacrificer, because there is no distinction; neither a distinction based on the word nor one based on the purpose is perceived here.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the *ahīna*, there is no restriction.

[Question: Oṃ. Even when the moon has risen unexpectedly (anirukta), the performance of the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice must be carried out. Bhāṣya 6.5.12.12–15. [Answer: Oṃ. Even when the moon has risen unexpectedly, the modification (*vaikṛtya*) itself—the offering (*nirvāpa*) to the deities—must indeed be performed.

"Oṃ; one should offer [the oblation] to the original deities when it has risen while unspoken," and so forth; this is because there is a removal [of the original offerings] once the rice grains have been prepared.

Furthermore, the "Darśa-construction" (darśakalpanā) means that when the sacrifice has commenced on the fourteenth day and the moon is seen, it must be performed as the *abhyuditeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for one who has risen [after the moon was already visible]), just like the *darśeṣṭi*.
In that case, there must be a removal of the original deities and a conjunction with other deities.

In that case, when the pouring out [of the grain] has not yet been performed and the moon has risen before the pouring out is completed, one should pour out [the oblation] for the very same deities of the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*).

Thus the teacher Āśmarathya thought: "The pouring out must be performed by setting aside the archetypal deities. Why? Because once the rice grains have become *taṇḍula* (husked rice), the status of being the deity must be removed, and that removal must be performed.
After the pouring out [of the grain] and the threshing have been performed, the rice grains are produced.
Thus, it is stated that the removal of the deity occurs when the rice grains have been obtained from the *vrīhi* stalks;
however, prior to the pouring out, no such removal of the deity or similar action is mentioned.

Therefore, since there is no removal of the deities prior to the offering (*nirvāpa*), the offering is made to the very same deities as in the archetype; such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). However, [the author] states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by refuting the prima facie view reached in the Sūtra with the word "but" (*tu*), on the grounds that the removal of the deities is caused by the act of scratching out the names of those being excluded.
Action performed at the appointed time is auspicious and endowed with supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). But action performed at the wrong time is unsuccessful and thwarted (*vyuddha*).
Those deities who partake in such thwarted action are themselves thwarted (*vyuddhyamāna*).

Ācārya Ālekhana held the view that one should perform the *nirvāpa* (offering) for these deities—Agni Dātṛ, Indra Pradātṛ, and Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa—from those deities who are being excluded from the modified (*vaikṛta*) rites.

Why? Because the removal of the deities is caused by that [modification], because it effects an exclusion, and because it causes the performance of a ritual action not prescribed in the original model (*prakṛti*). Since the performance took place at an improper time, the former deities are removed.
In this regard, [the modification] has already arisen even prior to the pouring out (nirvāpa).

Thus, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that since the rising of the moon occurs even before the pouring out, the pouring out must be of the modified (vaikṛta) [offering] alone, and not of the original (prākṛta) one.
In this context, the reading "vyuddhyamānasya" is found everywhere.

Regarding the statement, "belonging to those from whom [the portion] has been subtracted (*vyuddhya*), belonging to those who do not receive the *havirśana* portion, or belonging to the modified (*vaikṛta*) [sacrifice]," the *Subodhinī* explains it thus.
However, we do not understand how the word *vyuddhya* expresses the *havirśana* and how the word *vyuddhyabhāk* expresses the state of being modified (*vaikṛtatva*).

In the *Kutūhala-sūtra*, it is written as "belonging to the portion whose time has increased (*pravṛddha-kāla-bhāgīya*)," and in the root-text of the *Kutūhala*, it is written as "belonging to that *havis* which has proceeded at an increased time (*pravṛddha-kāla-pravṛtta*)."

In that context, because the time follows the rising of the moon, its increase can be stated. Such a sacrificial oblation (havis) is understood by implication alone. Although even in the Bhāṣya the reading is indeed "vyuddhyamānasya," [the meaning remains as explained].

Although the meaning can be understood from the fact that [the suffix] functions as such that the word *vyuddhya* does not involve a temporal restriction (*akālatantrapravṛttatva*), nevertheless, they accepted the reading *vyuddhyamānabhyaḥ* with the suffix *-ya-* as being more correct.
This is because of the rule: "Suffixes whose specific meaning is not indicated apply in all three times."
The root text states: “The author of the Purāṇas, the son of Satyavīt. Regarding this, the commentary explains: the form “kartā” (author) ends in the suffix *tṛc*.

Therefore, by the maxim that “words whose meaning is not specifically restricted [to a particular time]” apply to all times, and because the action continues until its completion, his authorship of the past, present, and future Purāṇas is not contradictory.
In the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*, Rāmānanda [states]:
"When something unindicated occurs, there is the eating of what is permitted;
and when something unindicated occurs, there is the implication of the taking up of what is prohibited."
Su. 317, p. 34: The attainment of the undesirable occurs when there is the performance of prohibited actions.
Vi. 612|5: There is a prohibition against eating cultivated grains for one who seeks the undesirable.

Therefore, the prohibition—"one should not eat new grain by means of the *vāṇijāyana* method"—applies to the eating of [grain] produced by the plough, and not to the eating of rice and barley; for in the supplementary statement, "those which are produced by the plough, [one may eat them] by the other method," the term "by the other method" is restricted to that specific alternative.
Consequently, the rule concerns the consumption of domestic grains other than those produced by the plough.

This being the position reached: while it is necessary for the *vākyaśeṣa* (supplementary statement) to bring the general rule (*sāmānya*) to its conclusion in a specific case (*viśeṣa*)—since the activity [of eating] regarding barley is possible through the commonality of the substance and the existence of a cause—even so, because it is impossible to conceive that the cessation [of eating] has as its object all grains in general, the deficiency [regarding barley] is fulfilled by the *vākyaśeṣa*. Therefore, the purpose [of the *vākyaśeṣa*] is to indicate things such as "ploughed with a plough" [as exceptions]. Just as the term "umbrella-bearer" (*chatrin*) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) as a mere praise, there is thus a prohibition against eating all village-grown grains.
Saṃkarṣa 311.10: Even for one who has not attained the desired goal, there is no prohibition against using grains that have been parched.

Although a prohibition might apply to *muddrā* and other pulse-grains (*śamīdhānya*) based on the general rule regarding the consumption of husks and stalks, there is no such prohibition for them because they are unfit for sacrifice.
According to the *Saṃkarṣa*, even for one who has not performed the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, the eating of vegetables, cooked grains, and medicinal herbs is permitted at will.

Since another scriptural statement, "One should not eat grain," establishes a prohibition against eating even vegetables and the like, and since those [vegetables] lack suitability for sacrifice—beginning with the passage, "The gods cooked in the herbs; Indra and the others first conquered them"—there is a prohibition against eating new [grain]. Consequently, regarding grains that are fit to be offered to the gods, only the cooked varieties may be eaten after they have been offered to them; however, there is freedom of choice (yāthākāmya) in eating cooked green vegetables and the like, which are not fit for offering.

*Saṃkarṣa.* 312|122. The *Anīkavatī* sacrifice: it is a constituent part of the *Sākamedha* section within the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, to be performed at dawn (*prātaḥ*), and its time of performance is immediate (*sadyaskālā*).
It is prescribed by the injunction: "A cake on eight potsherds for Agni Anīkavant at dawn.
*Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya* 412|119–22. The *Prajāpati-vratas*, such as the vow of not looking [at the sun] and so forth, serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
Mā. 412|13–6. Non-established action (*anīṣṭita-karman*) is of four kinds.
Regarding the term "second" (*dvitīyā*), it should be understood as referring to the *bindu* within the *maṇi*.
That the state of being non-established (*anīṣṭitatva*) is denotable by the second case-ending is refuted in the section on Relations (*sambandhādhikaraṇa*, 2|4|12|11–12).
Su. pṛ. 1087: "For the imitation of that which is prescribed by the learned is correct"—this is the maxim.

As it is stated at great length in the Mahābhāṣya on the *ṛlak* sūtra: "Just as in the world, if someone gives a gift in such a manner, performs a sacrifice in such a manner, or studies in such a manner, and another, imitating him, gives a gift, performs a sacrifice, or studies, he is joined with prosperity.
—Sāhyī.
Anukarṣa (attraction/extension) occurs before another [element]. "Even what is not explicitly stated is inferred by a wise person"—this is the maxim.
A discerning person experiences a subject even when it has not been mentioned; such is the common practice regarding subjects.
And it has been said: "Even a beast grasps a meaning when it is uttered; horses and elephants carry [their riders] when urged.
A wise person infers even what is unspoken, for the fruit of intelligence lies in knowing the gestures of others."
Thus [it is said].
Sāṃkhyāyana 6.4.9: When there is a sequential interruption, the expiation occasioned by the subsequent interruption must be performed.
Viṣṇu 6.5.19: Regarding "following after" and so forth, [it is stated that] "the teacher is to be followed."

Regarding the injunctions— "he should be saluted," "one should rise in greeting for those who are senior," and "he should be honored"— there is a repetition [of the action] when the occasion recurs. (Bhāṣya 9.2.1) And the permission is granted by means of the mantra "upahavya."
The request for permission is made with the mantra, "Upahūtaḥ" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.5.16.42).
Furthermore, the permission regarding the consumption of Soma is intended solely for those using a single vessel, in order to avoid the faults of deficiency or excess (3.5.17.43).
Moreover, the permission for the consumption of Soma must be given through a Vedic mantra and not by means of ordinary worldly speech.
3|5|15|41. Consuming with permission.
In the Agniṣṭoma, having offered the Soma in the cup (camasa), they consume it immediately.
There, each single cup is consumed by many priests.
And they do not become defiled by that [remnant], because such is the rule.

At the time of consumption, permission is sought from the one whose cup the Hotṛ priest has just taken, using the mantra beginning with "O Hotṛ, you have been invited" (*hotopahūta*). He, in turn, grants permission with the mantra "I am invited" (*upahūtaḥ*). This is what is called the consumption of Soma with permission.
383. *Anujñāpana* (Requesting Permission): *Anunirvāpyādhikaraṇa* (a legal dispute to be settled by appeasement) is *anujñāpana* (the act of requesting permission).

When the Soma is prepared in a single common vessel, an equal division follows by the principle of *asamaṃ syādaśrutatvāt* (Jaimini Sūtra 10.3.13), as there is no scriptural injunction to the contrary. In that case, if it were drunk without being divided, it might happen that one person drinks what was intended for another.
In such a situation, a request for permission becomes possible, such as: "This portion is to be drunk for my sake; you might drink more or less than your share, so please grant me your permission."
"Conducting yourself with me from a single vessel is a means for the purification of your mind and is proper"—this constitutes a permissible authorization (*anujñā*).
Bhāṣya 3.5.17.43. Furthermore, this is the nature of seeking authorization: when one person desires to do what ought to be done by another, he says, "Please grant me your permission.
Or, one who wishes to perform an act such as eating together propitiates the mind of the other.
3|5|17|43. Having obtained permission, several [priests] should consume the Soma from a single vessel.
Bhāṣya 3|5|14|40: But in the case of non-origination, there would be a specific time, because of its connection with a purpose.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is recited: "Having offered the Paridhi sticks, he offers the Hāriyojana oblation."

In this context, the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi-praharaṇa*) is enjoined as an auxiliary part of the *hāriyojana* oblation. Furthermore, there arises the consideration that since the *hāriyojana* oblation occurs after the throwing of the enclosing sticks, the time for the oblation is thereby determined. Regarding this inquiry, the author states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). First of all, this is not an originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*), because [the rite] is already established elsewhere.

Thus, since it is not an originative injunction, the time [of performance] would be prescribed in this sentence—which is distinct from an originative injunction—since this is indeed an injunction of the time alone.
Because the *praharaṇa* (the act of striking) and the *homa* (the oblation) are connected with the fruit of the *jyotiṣṭoma*—namely, the *apūrva*—they have no mutual connection with one another.
Therefore, it is time alone that is expressed by that sentence.
The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to indicate the distinction from the origination [of the sacrifice] mentioned in the preceding sūtra.

"By desiring liberation through delusion without having procreated a son, one falls downward"—since this scriptural passage declares a transgression for one who is otherwise detached, the procreation of offspring is obligatory. (Bhāṣya 6.2.11).

If it is argued that the procreation of offspring is merely optional (kāmya) because of the statement, "Without having procreated sons, one does not go to the world [of the ancestors]," we say: not so.

"Desiring liberation while failing to procreate a son out of delusion, one falls downward"—according to this Smṛti, the procreation of offspring is as obligatory as the Soma sacrifice and as the acquisition of knowledge (Vi. 6.2.11). Even acts performed without a specific purpose are considered as having been performed if they follow their natural order (prakṛti) (Bhāṣya 1.1.13, p. 2219). The *anunirvāpyas* are those that must be subsequently offered.
*Anunirvāpyas* are certain other sacrifices prescribed after the completion of a particular sacrifice;
and between these two, there exists a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*).
Nevertheless, that assistance consists precisely in its being something entirely unprecedented (*apūrva*).
For example: "Following the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the Agnīṣomīya, he offers the oblations of the Devasū sacrifice";
or as in the case of the Anubandhyā animal, where the Devikā oblations are to be offered subsequently.

*Nirvāpya* refers to those rites suitable for being offered, that is, those which are to be performed as offerings. *Anunirvāpya* refers to certain sacrifices which are to be offered subsequently; those for which there is an injunction such as "one should offer subsequently" (*anu nirvapeta*) or "he offers subsequently" (*anu nirvapati*) are *anunirvāpyas*.

Section on the Anunirvāpya Offerings: In the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana), there is an incidental application (prasaṅga) of the ritual procedure for the animal-cake offerings to the deities of the Suvā-offerings.
In the case of offerings that are to be performed consecutively (*anunirvāpya*), there should generally be a restriction to a single performance (*tantra*) of the ritual details.
As the *Bhāṣya* states: "One offers the oblations of the *devasū* deities after the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) of the *agnīṣomīya*.
The same applies to the *devikā* oblations in the *anubandhyā* sacrifice.
In this case, the *tantra* (common performance) is determined by the majority, because the *anunirvāpyas* (subsequent offerings) are numerous.
The *tantra* would thus apply to the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*).

Furthermore, the mention of the term "Sviṣṭakṛt"—the scriptural injunction for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering seen in relation to both the animal-cake and the Devikā oblations, namely, "He cuts off [the portion] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"—is logically consistent only with a *tantra* of the *anunirvāpyas*.
But when the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *paśupuroḍāśa* applies, then there would be the term *iṣṭakṛt*.
Therefore, it would be undesirable [to apply the term *sviṣṭakṛt*].

Alternatively, because it is an adventitious element (*āgantuka*), it should have its own specific property (*svadharma*), due to the distinction of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) and because the other is the primary one.
The Commentary states: The *anunirvāpyas* (subsequent offerings) are secondary because of a specific scriptural statement.

For it is heard in scripture: "He offers the *anunirvāpyas* after the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). Since this is heard, the animal-cake comes first, and the *anunirvāpyas* come later; thus, it is the primary one, while the others are subordinate.
Therefore, because those [other elements] are adventitious and the other [the animal sacrifice] is primary, the *paśupuroḍāśa* should possess its own specific characteristics.
It retains its original position.

The Commentary states: "Moreover, the place of the *paśupuroḍāśa* is that which follows the offering of the omentum (*vapā*); here too, it must remain in that very place, because they occupy the location of the principal rite."
If there were a common ritual framework (*tantra*) for the after-offerings (*anunirvāpya*),
then those offerings would be performed in that [same] location, and the animal-cake offerings (*paśupuroḍāśa*) would have to be moved to another location.
To ensure they occupy their proper place, the ritual framework of the animal-cake offering must be performed.
If it is argued that [the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering] comes after the *śravaṇa*, the Commentary states:
this is not correct; it must be refuted.
It is a modification (*vikāra*), like the *pavamāna*.
Commentary: It is said here:

And thus, when the *paśupuroḍāśa* cake is to be offered by means of a single performance (*tantra*), and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering has reached the state of being "unexpressed" (*anirukta*), there will be no modification;
rather, one must perform the act with the specific wording: "He cuts off [the portion] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," using the word *sviṣṭakṛt*.
Just as, because of the statement "he offers to Pavamāna the foremost," an offering is made using the word *pavamāna*, so it is here as well.
Or rather, there is no modification, because with respect to the injunction it is like the archetype (*prakṛti*), owing to its existence.
Commentary: There is no modification; the formula containing the word *iṣṭakṛt* must be performed as in the archetype, due to the rule of extension (*atideśa*).
Regarding the phrase "by which statement," no modification (*vikāra*) is prescribed here.

What then? It is the equal portioning (*samavadāna*) of the *devikā* oblations, as in: "He makes an equal portion for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. In that case, if another modification were being prescribed, the sentence would be split (*bhidyeta*).
How, then, is the statement regarding Agni Sviṣṭakṛt to be understood? It is because of its existence in relation to the injunction.
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is an injunction for Sviṣṭakṛt which employs the word "Sviṣṭakṛt"; this statement is made with reference to that [injunction] as a designation for it.
Therefore, as long as there might be anyone who is a recipient of the remnant for Agni, it is said: "to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."

Just as in the cases "the sacrificial grass consists of reeds" (*aśaramayaṃ barhiḥ*) and "the clarified butter is fresh butter" (*navanītam ājyam*), the archetypal function is indicated by a word denoting a substance through its connection to the archetype, so too here, by the word *sviṣṭakṛt*, the archetypal deity is indicated through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). [Objection]: When there is a doubt as to whether the cakes offered with the *anuyāja* oblations take precedence over the *puroḍāśa* cake according to the rule of the *svadharma*, or whether it is the reverse, [it is argued] that because of their greater number, the *anuyāja* offerings take precedence. To this, the following is said in reply.
For there is no simultaneous injunction for them, nor is there a simultaneous commencement.

Rather, since the *anirvāpya* offerings are prescribed within the ritual framework (*tantra*) that has already begun with the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*), the status of the latter as a *prasaṅga* (dependent) and the former as the *tantrin* (independent) is clear; and the properties of the *tantra* must be utilized by the *prasaṅgin*.
Thus, the animal-cake offering possesses its own inherent ritual properties.

Regarding *soma*: although the majority [of elements] was of no consequence in the previous section due to the absence of contradiction, here it is stated that the determination is made by the majority; this constitutes the connection (*saṃgati*).
Here, the inquiry is not whether the *aninirvāpya* offerings constitute the *tantra* (the primary ritual framework) or whether the *puroḍāśa* does so;

for even if many [elements] are involved, the *tantra* is established by this very [discussion], since the principle of *prasaṅga* (incidental application) is already established without further deliberation.

However, while it is established that the *puroḍāśa* sacrifice is the primary ritual (*tantrin*) and the subsequent offerings (*anunirvāpyas*) are incidental (*prasaṅga*), it must be noted that this is discussed specifically in cases where there is a conflict of ritual requirements (*dharmavipratiṣedha*). The question to be considered is: when such a conflict arises, should the rule of the numerous incidental rites be adopted, or the rule of even a single primary rite? Because the primary rite proceeds by subsisting upon the rules of the incidental ones, the primary rite possesses greater force; therefore, its own rule should be adopted.
Thus, in a conflict between the rules of the animal sacrifice, the *puroḍāśa*, and the subsequent offerings, the animal sacrifice follows its own specific rule.

When there is a conflict of ritual requirements (*dharma-vipratiṣedha*) between the *puroḍāśa* cake and the offerings that are not to be set aside (*aninirvāpya*), it should be understood that the *puroḍāśa* follows its own specific ritual rules (*svādharmya*). Viśvarūpa states: "Does the *svādharmya* apply to those [offerings] that are not to be set aside, or not? Because they are numerous, it does apply. Do not say so; for since they are prescribed within the context of the main ritual (*tantra*), they are merely incidental (*prasaṅgin*)."

In the *Mādhyandina* recension and others, it is heard in the scriptural injunctions that "after the *agnīṣomīya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), one offers the oblations of the *devasū*s following the *agnīṣomīya* cake," and likewise, "one offers the *devikā* oblations" at the beginning of the *anupraṇayana* and other rites.

Since these non-officially-offered (*aninirvāpya*) oblations are numerous, they constitute the primary ritual framework (*tantra*). However, because the *puroḍāśa* is subordinate, its application is established as a case of incidental extension (*prasaṅga*).

If, however, because of the connection with the word *anu* (after), as in the case of "he subsequently offers the Vaimṛdha," there is a cognition of a subsequent time, and since that [subsequent time] is connected to the performance, it is considered that—by way of implying what is enjoined by the performance-injunction of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*)—there is a performance-injunction for those offerings to be performed subsequently to the animal-cake which are implied by themselves; then let it be that the Vaimṛdha is indeed a distinct performance, and thus there is no mutual relationship of *tantra* or *prasaṅga* between the two.

In this very context, just as the performance of the *paśupuroḍāśa*—following the injunction for the animal sacrifice (*vāyāga*)—is performed only after that sacrifice because its own performance-injunction prescribes it, and because the acts of pouring out (*nirvāpa*), the *siddhakṛt* offering, and so forth, which provide little assistance [to the main rite], are established [as belonging] to the *paśupuroḍāśa* procedure; likewise, even for the *devikā* offerings, those acts required by their own performance-injunctions, such as pouring out and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, are performed only at the time following the *saṅkāya-paśupuroḍāśa*. Thus, there is no mutual connection between them. However, since both are recited within the framework (*tantra*) of the animal sacrifice, the *prayāja* and other rites belonging to that [animal sacrifice] apply to both by way of incidental extension (*prasaṅga*).

This being the case, there is no injunction for performance here as there is in the case of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa). If that were so, then—due to the consequence of [the application of] the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in that very same manner—the section concerning the non-offering (*aninirvāpya*) in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, regarding the animal-cake sacrifice, would apply to those things not to be offered. 385. Regarding those not to be offered...

Having enjoined the quality characterized by being the *agniṣṭa-sviṣṭakṛt* through the [text] "dhāya 'tasya so'gniṣṭaḥ sviṣṭakṛt'," there would be an inconsistency with the textual context of the sentences that indicate the principal performance of the offering (*aninirvāpa*). Therefore, in this case, because the word *anu* prescribes that the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*)—which has its own specific properties as the principal—occurs immediately after those respective properties which are the principal [of the animal sacrifice], the performance of both is understood to be common (*samānatantra*); thus, there is no difference in the performance of the two.
However, regarding the injunction for the performance of the cake-offering at a time subsequent to the fat-oblation (*vapāyāga*), there is no obstacle whatsoever.

On the contrary, the injunction regarding the qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) of Agni for his *sviṣṭakṛt* offering serves precisely to indicate a difference in the performance (*prayoga-bheda*). Consequently, the factual state of affairs is as follows: in the case of offerings other than the *sviṣṭakṛt*, one performs each individual ritual act—such as the pouring of the oblation (*nirvāpa*)—after having grouped together all the constituent acts required for the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*). However, in the *sviṣṭakṛt* itself, one takes up all the portions from every vessel in sequence and performs them all at once.
Thus, in this instance, there is indeed *tantratā* (commonality of performance) among the non-conflicting subsidiary elements.

However, even though there is a multiplicity of *devikā* offerings among the conflicting elements, because the word "after" (*anu*) indicates that the quality of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is operative, one understands its independence (*tantratā*). Since it is primary and the others depend upon it, they are merely incidental (*prasaṅga*). For this very reason, after stating in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, "He takes a portion for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," the subsequent issuing of the command to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," is also consistent.

However, if the animal sacrifice were governed by the model of the *aniniṣkāsana* (the offering without the scrapings), then in each case, by the extended application (*atideśa*) from the *iṣṭi*, there would arise the injunction for the *praiṣa*: "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
It is precisely for this reason that the statement, "He cuts off [the portion] for Sviṣṭakṛt for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," is meaningful as being governed by the model of the *paśupuroḍāśa*.

As for the fact that the author of the Sūtras, having stated such a meaningful purpose, proposed an alternative view—that here only the verbal root is enjoined, while the word "Sviṣṭakṛt" has an unintended meaning—that is merely a display of boldness (*prauḍhimātra*).

Therefore, it is established that even the *puroḍāśa* is the *tantrin* (the primary performer) for the injunctions regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth, while those [offerings] not to be separately prepared (*anirvāpya*) are *prasaṅgin* (incidental).

In reality, however, since the command "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" is recited in the Kāṇva recension, it is more appropriate that even those [offerings] possess the status of being *tantrins*, resulting in an option (*vikalpa*). Maṇḍana states: "The deities do not possess independence; they exist for the sake of another."

"For the sake of another," that is, for the sake of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa). Śaṅkara says: "The connection [occurs] among the deities. This is the section concerning what is not to be offered (aninirvāpyādhikaraṇa).

Regarding the Agnicayana rite, where it is stated, "He offers the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) for the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, and subsequently offers the eight oblations of the Devasū offerings," there arises a doubt: should the characteristics of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice—such as the eleven fore-offerings (prayāja) and so forth—be adopted, or the characteristics of those sacrifices not involving an offering-material (aninirvāpya)? In this doubt, since the principle of favoring the majority (bhūyo'nugrahanyāya) [12.1.22] applies, the characteristics of the non-offering-material sacrifices would initially appear to be adopted in the Medha sacrifice. However, in a case where no distinction is perceived among all the constituent parts of the ritual complex (tantra), that is an exception to the principle of favoring the primary element (mukhyānugrahanyāya) [6.1.16–37]. Thus, the principle of favoring the majority prevails.

However, where a distinction is recognized such that one is the primary (tantrin) and the others are incidental (prasaṅgin), there the ritual properties (dharmas) of the single primary alone are to be adopted; for even though there are many incidental ones, they do not necessitate their own properties because they subsist upon that primary—this has been determined. As for Parākrama’s view: in cases where [the fire] cannot be extinguished by [a single act], there should be a restriction to the primary based on the majority.

Regarding the *agnicayana* sacrifice, the rule "he offers the eight *devasuvām* oblations following the *agnīṣomīya-puroḍāśa*" prescribes certain subsequent offerings (*anunirvāpya*). Although the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) does not extend to these subsequent offerings, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that because they are more numerous, the performance of the procedure for the subsequent offerings would apply by extension (*prasaṅga*) to the animal-cakes, thereby establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the procedure of the subsequent offerings. The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the prima facie view. [The correct conclusion is: "Because they are adventitious (*āgantuka*), they should follow their own specific rules, due to the particularity of the scriptural injunction (*śruti-viśeṣa*), and because that [original procedure] is primary (*mukhya*).
The word "or" thus refutes the previous position.

Regarding the term "aninirvāpya": because of the specific scriptural mention of the word *anu*, the *devasū* offerings and the *devikā* oblations—which are *āgantuka* (extraneous or secondary)—are distinct; whereas the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) is the primary element. Therefore, the animal-cake should possess its own inherent properties (*svadharma*). Its ritual details (*dharmāḥ*) must be performed in its own place.
That which has its own (*sve*) properties is "possessing its own properties" (*svadharman*); the suffix *an* is used here as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*).

Therefore, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *puroḍāśa* is neither restricted by the offerings not to be set aside (*aninirvāpya*), nor does it constitute a case of incidental application (*prasaṅga*). In the context of the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), it is stated: "Following the *agnīṣomīya* *puroḍāśa*, he offers the oblations of the *devasū*s," and in the case of the *anubandhyā* cow, the *devikā* oblations.
Regarding this, the following has been deliberated.
Because of the commonality of location:

in the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*), the oblations of the *devasū* deities follow the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of Agni-Soma, and the oblations of the *devikā* goddesses follow the *anubandhyā* cow.
In this regard, there is an inquiry as to which [rite] is applicable to which [oblation].

The place of the *paśupuroḍāśa* (animal-cake offering) is after the offering of the omentum (*vapā*). Therefore, the *agnīṣomīya* [offering] must take place in that very same location, because those [offerings] occupy the primary place. If there were a common ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the offerings not to be offered in the fire, then they would be performed in that location.
Regarding the *anuvāpyas* (386):
the portions for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) should be without bones.
Furthermore, they possess greater force because they occupy their own proper place.

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the ritual procedure (tantra) for the animal-cake (paśu-puroḍāśa) must be performed so that they may obtain their own proper place. [Objection: "Because of the mention of the *sviṣṭakṛt*," says the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin). He raises this doubt.

The term *sviṣṭakṛt* is heard in connection with both the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and the offerings to the minor deities (*devikāhaviṣ*), in the injunction: "He unites [the portions] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. This is appropriate within the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the after-offerings (*anuvāpyā*). However, when the animal-cake's own procedure is followed, then the word *sviṣṭakṛt* would not be used.
If the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) should say: "Therefore, the restriction applies to the *anuvāpya* offering, not to the *paśupuroḍāśa* cake;
it is a modification, like the *pavamāna* [stotra]."
It is said:

since the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for the *paśupuroḍāśa* would normally be performed with the *tantra* (the common ritual procedure) using the term "to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," there would be a modification (*vikāra*) due to the scriptural injunction, "He combines [the portions] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," whereby the word "asvitkṛt" should be used,
just as in the case of the *pavamāna*.
If it were so for those who follow [the path] without anything to be adopted, then the genus such as "beast-ness" and even "oneness" and so forth would also be non-adoptable.
No.

Because that [animal] is to be taken up (upādeya) by way of being pervaded by the act of killing (*kṛti*), whereas the individual sacrificer (*yajamāna-vyakti*) is not pervaded by his own act of killing, even by way of that [act], his specific universal (*jāti*) is not distinct from the act of killing; thus, it is indeed not something to be taken up (*anupādeya*). However, this is not the case for the *āhavanīya* fire and the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), which, although they are also to be taken up by way of being pervaded by the act of killing, [are distinct].

Because only those two [factors] established by other injunctions (*vidhyantara*) are adopted, there is no scope for the principle of "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśakti*) merely on the basis of being something to be performed by an injunction of application (*prayogavidhi*).

For this very reason, in the case of the statement "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire," it is accepted that it does not fall under the scope of the [other] principles, because of the absence of proximity (*asaṃnidhi*) due to the existence of a connection with something non-adoptable (*anupādeya*), which constitutes a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*).

Now, if the sacrificer’s own single [status], such as the caste of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, were also non-adoptable, then, due to the existence of a connection with that reality and the resulting absence of proximity, there would be a distinction [of the rite] based on a different context. In that regard, the first example is precisely: "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire."
If it is argued that even the removal of birth and so forth is manifest, we say no;
because there is no attainment of form.
He offers.
The distinction between the injunctions regarding the *anubandhyā* cow and the *vanaspati* sacrifice is established through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
However, in a matter where both direct statement (*śruti*) and indication are applicable, the direct statement is authoritative, not indication.
Therefore, the designation is not by means of just anything;
rather, it must be expressed by the word as stated, due to the force of the traditional scripture (āmnāna).
Likewise, in the case of the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) and the deity, the expression must be made using that specific injunctive word which has been stated.
Furthermore, a contradiction with the injunctions and the Vedic texts is raised;
therefore, it is argued that the designation should be made by using the word "vanaspati" (tree).
[Dūṣaṇa: However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since [the case] is the same, "vanaspati" has been cited as the example.

Regarding *soma*: if one resorts to specific mantras for the sake of favoring the water (*codaka*), then here too, for the sake of favoring it, it is appropriate to use any [mantra] whatsoever that expresses it; this is the connection. However, by the teacher Āpastamba, in the rules "Recite the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa regarding the fat of the cow's omentum" and "Issue the command (*saṃpreṣya*) for Mitra and Varuṇa regarding the fat of the cow's omentum," the restriction to the word "cow" (*go*) alone has been stated.
And that [reading] must somehow be justified by assuming a different recension in another treatise.

Here, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is simply that there is no addition to the *codaka* rule, because the purpose is served by the difference in the words of the injunction (*vidhi*) and the restatement (*nigama*).
Once the lack of restriction has been refuted by that which exceeds the purpose, the restriction of the means (*upādāna-niyama*) follows.

Regarding *anumantraṇa* (352), which is defined as the recollection of a mantra after its recitation— meaning one should recollect while uttering the mantra— this is logically consistent. However, since the defining verse specifies "when there is the state of being an instrument" (*karaṇabhāve sati*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to other instruments.
Regarding the phrase "pronouncing," there is the existence [of the action] according to the rule "what is near the present is treated as present.
Regarding the phrase "by way of being the meaning of the mantra," the meaning is "by way of being that which is expounded by the mantra.
Thus they say.
*Bāla.*, pp. 112–113. Regarding the *mantrajyāna* (the application of mantras) for the sacrificer during certain rites among the ten rituals of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*:

Bhāṣya 3.1.8.120 states that there are eleven *anumantraṇa* mantras for the *anuyāja* offerings; four each are modifications (*vikāra*) of the *barhis* and *ārāśaṃsa* offerings, while the remaining three are modifications of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. Thus, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of those respective *anumantraṇa* mantras to their corresponding instances.
However, the tenth [offering] is a modification of the first,

because the commonality of the deity is understood at the time of its original injunction (utpatti). (Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa 2.13.4–5) The mantras for recitation (anumantraṇa-mantras) have as their fruit the recollection of the performed act, in order to examine whether it has been completed or not.

Su. Pṛ. 102: In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is no fixed rule regarding the order of the *prayāja* (fore-sacrifice) formulas and other such elements recited by the sacrificers, which are completed within different breaths, such as "I gratify the spring seasons," and so forth. Bhā. 5.1.13: An inference that is contradicted by scripture (*āgama*) does not arise.

Kaṇikā, p. 304: It is thought that inference applies only to cause and effect; however, that is incorrect, because we observe that even inferences concerning things that are not in a cause-and-effect relationship—such as those regarding agriculture and the like—are causes for the understanding of non-conflicting results, such as the growth of crops.
Therefore, it is considered that the very relationship of the traversed and the traverser constitutes the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
But is it not the case that even this [relationship] is not a factor [for inference], since it exists at a time subsequent to the completion of the inference?
True.
He introduces this [reason] as an illustration of the conventional usage of inference (*anumānavyavahāra*), which is well-established subsequently when a certain relationship exists.

Alternatively, it refers to the capacity (*śakti*): for that very [relationship] is determined at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by the two—the signified (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*)—as being essentially a causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); it is precisely therein that the state of being a reason (*hetutā*) resides.
(Vārttika 1.1.26, p. 139). And inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it contradicts perception (*pratyakṣa*), provided that there is a particularity [in the object].

Bhāṣya 6.1.12, p. 1359: "Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] based on the perception of one part by a person who knows the relationship [between them].
(Commentary: The definition of inference is stated in order to show that its domain is *dharma*.

For a person who knows the relationship, based on the perception of one part—that is, the perception of one related member—there arises a cognition regarding another part, namely the other related member, which is an object not in contact; this is inference.

Just as for a person who has ascertained the necessary co-presence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between fire and smoke, there arises a cognition of the fire—which is not in contact with the senses—upon seeing one part of it, namely the smoke;
so too, because the mark (*liṅga*) related to *dharma* is not apprehended, inference is impossible. This is the sense [of Nyāyabindu 1.14].
Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of an object not present to the senses (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*), based on the observation of one part of a known relationship between two things.

It is of two kinds: that based on a relationship perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*) and that based on a relationship perceived through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*).
An example of inference based on a relationship perceived through direct perception is the cognition of the form of fire from the sight of the form of smoke.

Inference based on a relationship perceived through general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*) is, for example, the inference of the sun’s motion after having observed Devadatta’s arrival at another location preceded by his movement. (Bhāṣya, pp. 36–37). Here, in the Bhāṣya, the word *anumāna* refers to the inferential cognition (*anumiti*). It belongs to that cognizing person (*pramātṛ-puruṣa*) by whom the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*)—the relationship known as pervasion (*vyāpti*)—is known.

The meaning is: "of a person who possesses the knowledge of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*). By this, the definition of inference is stated as: "inference is a cognition produced by the knowledge of that [pervasion] and its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Where the relationship between two particulars themselves is grasped through perception, that [inference] which has those particulars as its object is called "that in which the relationship was perceived through perception" (*pratyakṣatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*).

For example, when the relationship between a specific property (*dharma*) and a specific smoke produced by it has been grasped through perception with respect to a particular substratum (*dharmin*), and subsequently, at another time, that same specific smoke is seen in that very same substratum, the inference of that same specific property whose existence was previously doubted is an inference consisting of a relationship perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasaṃbandha*).

When the relationship between the probans and the probandum is grasped by means of the apprehension of their generic forms (*ākṛti*)— as the exclusion of others— that is an inference consisting of a relationship perceived through generality (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*).
"The sun possesses motion, because it reaches another location; whatever reaches another location possesses motion, just as Devadatta.

In this case, the relationship between the two universals—motion and reaching another location—is grasped through perception, while [the presence of] motion in the sun is what is useful for the inference. This is an inference produced by a relationship perceived through generality (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
Vidyanatha, pp. 36–37. (The meaning of the *Bhāṣya*: "The knower is one who has known the relationship, or else it refers to one part [of that relationship]."
"Or rather, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound, [meaning] 'being a part of that which is related' (*saṃbandhinyekadeśatā*).

Since the relation is known by whichever cognizer [possesses it], the term 'his cognition' (*tasya buddhiḥ*) is a *bahuvrīhi* in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*). Thus he says "by the cognizer" (*pramātṛtā*).
For one who has known the relation of smoke—that is, for the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) such as a kitchen—[the cognition arises].

The proponent of the "particularist" view (*ekadeśin*) says: "The connection with fire is known as being restricted; since its one part, called smoke, is seen on a mountain and so forth, there is an increase [of that connection] in that very place, which is another part. Thus he says "ekadeśin," using a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of the genitive case.
Alternatively, this is a *karmadhāraya* compound;
and by the two words "ekadeśa," the two related members [fire and smoke] are denoted.

The relatum (*saṃbandhin*) is that which possesses pervasion (*vyāpaka*), and it exists as a single locus (*ekadeśin*); the other [relatum] is the locus (*ekadeśin*). When that relation is known, there arises a cognition of the other relatum from seeing its one part—the smoke—which is the relatum; thus he says "by the *karmadhāraya* compound" (from the *Ratnākara-saṃkṣepa*).
"Alternatively, two members of a whole whose relationship is known are perceived together;
by means of the words denoting one part [of that whole], both members of the collection are expressed.
"The relationship known" refers to the relationship between the collection of the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
The two parts thereof are the constituents of the whole.

In that case, from the perception of one constituent, there arises the cognition of the other constituent; thus, by means of the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself, it expresses a different meaning—namely, "the pair.
Here, the relationship is pervasion (*vyāpti*), wherein the property of the mark (*liṅga*) exists with the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
The pervaded (vyāpya) is the means of cognition, and the pervader (vyāpaka) is held to be the object of cognition.
Whatever is equal to or less than another in terms of space and time is the pervaded;
the pervader of that is either equal to or greater than it.
When the pervaded object has been apprehended by him, its pervader is apprehended;
for otherwise, this relationship of pervader and pervaded between the two would not exist.
Even if the pervaded is apprehended as a pervader in reality, [it remains so].
Even when there is an excess [of the reason], it would not establish the pervaded because of its lack of contradiction;
this is clearly seen in the cognition of "being a cow" and "having horns.
Because of being the pervaded, cows are the indicators, whereas having horns is not the pervader.

The pervasion [of the reason] over a certain place or time was previously defined; that very same [reason], when observed again in another locus possessing the property [to be proven],
likewise conveys the pervaded aspect for one who seeks the pervaded.
And pervasion (*vyāpti*) is to be understood through repeated observation of two general properties (*sāmānyadharma*), provided no deviation is perceived;
it is known by disregarding their differences. In some cases, however, it is known even between two specific particulars (*viśeṣa*):
having observed the rising of the Kṛttikā star, the proximity of Rohiṇī is inferred.

Among the pervaded [properties], some characteristic is the effective cause; it can be defined as "when this exists, by means of this, that [the probandum] exists. Others are dependent upon the pervasions established by others.
By those very reasons, even for one who desires [the conclusion], the determination of the pervading part (vyāpakāṃśa) is certainly not desired.

[Objection: But surely "being violence" (hiṃsatva) would lead to the inference of "unrighteousness" (adharmatva) in the case of violence such as the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, because it has a pervasion with unrighteousness in cases like the killing of a Brahmin (brahmahatyā). To this he says: "The pervasion... (vyāptireti). It is true that there is a pervasion of "being violence" with unrighteousness; nevertheless, that [mere fact of being violence] is not the determinant (prayojaka) of the pervasion with unrighteousness.
That very fact of being prohibited—which is defined as the capacity for this [act] to become prohibited given its status as unrighteousness (*adharma*)—is the actual motivator (*prayojaka*).
Others, however, such as the quality of being violence (*hiṃsātva*), merely rely on the pervasion (*vyāpti*) induced by that [primary] prohibition.
Therefore, even though the pervasion exists, they are unable to determine that the reason (*hetu*) possesses the property of the pervader (*vyāpakadharmitva*).
What, then, is the determinant (*prayojaka*)? That which is observed to have a connection with the probandum even in the absence of other properties is the determinant.
However, that which has a connection with the probandum only when accompanied by another property is not a determinant when it is ascertained to be devoid of that [other] property.

For instance, in the case of drinking liquor and the like, a connection with demerit (*adharma*) is observed for "prohibitedness" (*niṣiddhatva*) even in the absence of "the nature of violence" (*hiṃsātva*); therefore, that [prohibitedness] alone is the determinant for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by demeritoriousness.
In the cognition of a qualified object, the relationship [between them] would be inseparable;
therefore, these two— the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*)— having attained the status of qualifier and qualified, are both to be understood.
Therefore, the object of cognition (*prameyatā*) would belong to the locus (*dharmin*) as qualified by its property (*dharma*). That [cognition] belongs to the region under investigation...
Thus, it demonstrates the unity of the means of knowledge and its result here: "In the postulation of the smoke, the cognition thereof, their relation, the memory, and the validity..."
The fact that [the means of knowledge] possesses the same object as its result was previously stated on account of its operation (*vyāpāra*).

However, the author of the Bhāṣya considers the cognition of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) itself to be the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Regarding smoke, its cognition, and so forth, their status as instruments of knowledge is established; the cognition of the object of knowledge is the result, while in the case of the Bhāṣya, the cognition of avoidance (*hāna*) and so forth is the result. Their operation should be understood here, just as in the case of perception, as having the same object, because all these—smoke and the rest—operate toward the cognition of the object of knowledge.
The statement by which one’s own inference is expressed for the sake of another’s inferential cognition is called the *sādhana* (means of proof).
And that statement, having accepted the members (*avayava*)—namely, the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—purifies the proposition.
The proposition is the locus of the means of proof (*sādhanadeśa*).
And the subject (*pakṣa*) is that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). It is the locus (*dharmin*) qualified by a property (*dharma*).

This [subject], being the very object inferred for oneself, must first be stated when explaining it to another through inference alone; thus he says: "The demonstration of what has been grasped by inference is by means of that [inference] itself."
To others, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*—the thesis or proposition) should be stated exactly as it was formulated.

In that context, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is predicated with reference to the subject (*dharmin*). A restriction is postulated from its opposite (*vipakṣa*), not from that which is non-contradictory.
"Exclusion" (*niyama*) means differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*).
[This refers to] the property of being smoke (*dhūmatva*), which is not contradictory [to fire]. Hereafter, fallacious propositions (*pratijñā-ābhāsa*) are stated.

He explains the term *asaṃnikṛṣṭa* (not proximate), which occurs in the definition [of perception] given in the *Bhāṣya*, saying: "By the word *asaṃnikṛṣṭa*, two things alone are intended to be excluded:
that which is determined as being such [as it is], and that which is determined by its opposite.

A subject (*dharmin*) is "proximate" (*saṃnikṛṣṭa*) if it has been determined by a swift means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the very form in which it is desired to be inferred, or in a form contrary to that, or in some other form.
The term *asaṃnikṛṣṭa* (not already in contact) is used to exclude that [subject] from being a *pakṣa* (the subject of inference).
For when something has already been cognized, no further expectation for a means of knowledge arises;
