when an object has been determined by such [a cognition], a subsequent means of knowledge is fruitless.
"But for another [cognition], there is no room when [the object] has been determined by its opposite;
for since its very root has not arisen, its domain has been preempted by the former.

The perception of a mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is the root of inference; since that [perception] does not at all come into being [in the case of the opponent's claim], [inference] is not established.
At that very moment, the object of inference is sublated.
Once the object has been determined through a form contrary to the nature accessible to inference, there is no further need for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that contrary form.

This sublation of the mantra is not restricted solely to the domain of inference; rather, among the six means of knowledge beginning with perception—such as smoke and so forth—whichever one first determines the object by virtue of its rapid operation, by that very same means occurs the sublation of the subsequently arising mantra, characterized by the obstruction of its production. Thus he says: "And of the group of six beginning with perception, by whichever the object is determined..."
By that very [reasoning], there would be a sublation by *tara* (the comparative suffix), because [qualities] such as being subject to conceptualization (*vikalpya*) are impossible.
He states an example of contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*): "But the non-apprehensibility of sound and so forth is contradicted by perception.
He states the contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*): "[The claim that] they are not audible and so forth is contradicted by inference."
For that which is called "audibility" is not apprehended by perception;
rather, it is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the case of external objects such as color and the like.
Consequently, the inference—"Sound is non-audible because it is a quality, like color"—is sublated by an inference itself.

He states the contradiction with verbal testimony (*śabdavirodha*): “Contradiction with verbal testimony is threefold, according to the division of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth: [contradiction] with the proposition, with prior discourse (*pūrvasaṃjalpa*), and with what is established by all the world. He states that there is contradiction with the proposition merely by the utterance [itself]: “By the mere statement, ‘I shall remain silent for as long as I live,’ one is sublated.”

By means of the statement of a property (*dharma*), he points out a contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*): because even the inference “every sentence is false, because it is a sentence” is itself of the nature of a sentence. By means of the statement of the subject (*dharmin*), he says: “She who gave birth to me is my barren mother.
Here, by the statement of the subject as “mother,” there is a contradiction with the proposition.
He states the contradiction with prior linguistic convention: "For a Buddhist, the eternality of words is sublated by what was previously established.

He states the contradiction with what is established for all the world: "He who denies that the moon possesses the status of being denotable by the word 'moon' is sublated by the cognition of the moon established for all the world."

He states the contradiction with analogy (*upamāna*): "When one seeks to establish that 'this cow possesses the form of a gavaya' with respect to a cow already known [as distinct], the sublation of that [proposition] occurs through analogy (*upamāna*).
There is sublation by means of analogy.
"In the case of contradiction with presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), when Caitra— who is known to be absent from the house— is alive,

and it is being proved that he is not outside, there would be a sublation (*bādha*) by means of that very presumptive testimony. [This applies] when the probandum is the absence of fire in what burns, and when the probandum is sound, which is not produced."
And regarding the non-existence of the auditory organ and so forth, in the proof of the impermanence of sound:

the proposition of the non-existence of fire— which was postulated based on the non-perception [of smoke] in the heart— is sublated by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) through the prior cognition of its absence.

2. Regarding the proof of non-burning capacity as being like perception: the non-burning capacity, which is the absence of that power, is preceded by perception. 3. The inference of the power of denotation, conceived through the knowledge inferred from purposeful activity, is preceded by inference. 4. When the capacity of one among [the categories] such as the quarters, space, or the ear-cavity—which is inferred as the cause of the cognition of sound—is postulated, the sublation by presumption (*arthāpatti*) occurs through an inference of its absence, which is thus preceded by inference. 5. The non-injury to the impermanence that is the opposite of the eternality of sound—conceived through the impossibility otherwise of the power of denotation established by presumption—is preceded by presumption.
He states the contradiction with presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*): "In this context, there is sublation by presumptive testimony when a scriptural statement is negated;

for instance, when eating during the day is prohibited by a reason, eating at night [is presumed]. He states the contradiction with non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*): "The existence of things such as a hare's horn is contradicted by non-apprehension."
And thus, the subversions of the relationship between the property and the possessor of the property that you have cited—
concerning both the property and the possessor of the property, their essential natures and their specific qualities,
and those established by direct statement or implied by the sense— must all be shown to be contradicted by every means of valid cognition.

In this regard, he states the sublation of a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*): "When this [fire] is not established as the cause for the transformation of grass and so forth, there is sublation here by perception; thus, the sublation of that specific property [is established]. Fire is pervaded by heat; it would entail its own pervader, heat.
And because that [oil] is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it sublates the [inference]; thus, the fire itself becomes sublated.
He provides an example regarding the instruction on the nature of *dharma*: "In this world, it is said that 'unrighteousness (*adharma*) when performed produces little suffering';
however, because unrighteousness has been enjoined, there is a sublation of its very nature."
"Likewise, its specific property of being a cause of suffering is sublated.
Here, the sublation is by means of scripture (*āgama*).
He provides an example of the sublation of both the essential nature and the specific property: 'When it is said that "all things are the Dharma," there is a sublation of both.'"
Because its own nature and its specific qualities have not been proven as properties of that subject;
for here, there is a sublation of both the momentariness and the falsity [of cognition], as well as the distinction between the two:

namely, the sublation of the momentariness which is a specific quality of the nature of cognition, and the sublation of the absolute falsity which is a specific quality of its being non-conformable to reality, since this would entail the falsity of even those cognitions that apprehend them.

Thus, the fallacies of the thesis (*pratijñābhāsa*), which were excluded by the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (*asaṃnikṛṣṭa*) in the definition of the statement, have been explained in detail. Now, the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*)— namely, the unestablished (*asiddha*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), and the contradictory (*viruddha*)— are being explained in detail.

In this context, by the phrase "from the perception of one part" (*ekadeśadarśanāt*), he demonstrates the unestablished (*asiddha*) reason which is excluded by the word "perception" (*darśana*) signifying certainty: "By the phrase 'from the perception of one part,' that [reason] is set aside wherein there is either doubt or ignorance for both [parties], or even for one.
Where there is doubt, ignorance (*aghī*), or error for either the proponent or the opponent—whether for one or for both—that reason is unestablished because of its lack of certainty.

He states the non-establishment of the contrapositive for both [reasons]: "Fire is a burner of wood because it possesses the nature of being a flame; sound is impermanent because it is produced. However, in cases such as these, the contrapositive is established for both.

He states the non-establishment of the contrapositive for only one of the two: "In the case of 'being produced,' 'being a quality,' and so forth, when stated by another against a ritualist (Yājñika)."
Regarding the two types mentioned by oneself, there may be an "unestablished" (*asiddha*) reason for one or the other.

For instance, when the Vaiśeṣikas and others put forward "producedness," "quality," and so forth as reasons against the Mīmāṃsaka in order to prove the non-eternality of sound, that very same reason is unestablished for the opponent (the Mīmāṃsaka) when it is stated by him [to prove eternality]. He states this [case of] doubtful occurrence: "When there is doubt regarding its being steam or something else, for both parties or for one of them..."
If smoke were established, it would indeed be so in terms of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

(This is what was called "unestablished in terms of its own nature" [*svarūpāsiddhi*]). These same types [of fallacies] would also occur when one conceives of "unestablishedness of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
For even if [the soul] is known, it cannot be the cause of those properties that do not belong to its nature;

since [the capacity to produce effects] is observed everywhere, [the soul] must be omnipresent. Against the Buddhist, this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*); against the worldly person (*laukika*) and others, there is doubt (*saṃśaya*).
For a Buddhist, because of the certainty regarding the non-existence of a self (*ātman*), there is the "unestablishedness due to error" (*viparyayāsiddhi*).

For ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), because of doubt regarding a person distinct from the body, there is the "unestablishedness of the locus due to doubt" (*saṃdigdhāśrayāsiddhi*). By excluding [the terms] *āśraya* and *tantra* from the discussion of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and the contradictory (*viruddha*), he demonstrates the causes for doubt and error: "In this context, the causes of doubt and of being contrary have been refuted."
From the statement regarding the known relationship, there are three causes of doubt:
[the reason] being pervaded by both the probandum and its absence;
and the two contradictory relationships that exist in a single locus.

That which exists in both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)—that is, in both the probandum (*sādhya*) and its absence—is the "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).

That which is excluded from both those similar and dissimilar instances and exists only in the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*). When three reasons, each contradictory to another, are observed together in a single substratum (*ekadeśin*) with respect to other properties, that is the "contradictory-inconclusive" (*viruddhavyabhicārin*).

He illustrates the common [reason]: “The properties of being knowable, impermanence, and so forth, as well as formlessness, are common to both [sides]. [The property] of arising from what is dependent on the eternal occurs among the eternal; [the property] of arising from what is not so arises among the non-eternal, because of their respective eternality and non-eternality. [End of verse. *Ani-* [is the beginning of the commentary].
Furthermore, they maintain that inference may also employ a statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya), out of a desire for strict certainty regarding the rule of pervasion (vyāpti).
The designation of "subordinate" (upasarjana) is for the sake of establishing the meaning;
for when there is a connection of meaning,
it is from a corroborative instance based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) that the [property] is determined by the probandum (*sādhya*) itself.
Doubt is the cause.

Neither subordination (*upasarjanatā*) nor non-subordination (*anupasarjanatā*) belongs to what? Exclusion from everything else is established when there is the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).
This is seen in such instances as "gurukula" and so forth;
it is understood that "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire."

(He raises an objection: It is said in reply: For that which is pervaded, when observed, makes known the pervader because it possesses the capacity to establish the probandum; smoke, being constrained by fire, makes fire understood.
Furthermore, this genitive case in the phrase "of one whose relationship is known" (*jñātasaṃbandhasya*) is not used in the sense of being pervaded (*vyāpye*).
For [if it were], then that which is excluded from everything else—being empty—would again follow as a point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*).
Indeed, grammarians prescribe the genitive case after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) when it expresses a mere relationship (*saṃbandhamātra*).
"Just as where there is no fire, there is no smoke"—this is [an example] due to the presence of another (*anyabhāvāt*).
(The answer: It is said:
True, the genitive case is used in relation to that which is connected.
Exclusion is performed with respect to that which is not pervaded.
He refutes the opinion of some: "But [it is] weak...

For just as the genitive case occurs when there is an intention to express pervasion regarding a real entity, so too does it occur for the result, since this has been established in the same way even in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*).

The pervasive [factors]—we shall explain them in various places in the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha*). And thus say the worldly people: "Indeed, a mere state of being (*bhāva-mātra*) is excluded from the pervaded."

People designate it, saying, "This is mine," or "This belongs to another. Therefore, just as when whiteness is predicated of a cloth, there is the exclusion of its opposites; likewise, in common worldly usage, it is designated as "this is mine," and this will also serve to exclude non-common properties, but not length and so forth.
For there would be a designation by means of the battle; thus, by the genitive case, the pervasion of the relationship [is indicated].
It is said that inference is of two kinds: that which has a perceptible relationship and... [the other].

Furthermore, this [inference] belongs to others as well; thus the *Bhāṣya* states: "And there is the relation of general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa-sambandha*)," and so forth, where the specific [case] is being discussed.
Therefore, it has been stated that there is an abundance of refutations regarding the opponent's position.
Inference, which has as its object things characterized by the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*), [operates] with respect to action (*kriyā*) and power (*śakti*).
But how can there be a perception of the relationship [between two things] whose characteristics are unperceived?
It has been established below, in the discussion on *śruti* and so forth, that this occurs because one perceives the arising of its own fruit.
Therefore, inference culminates in the apprehension of a mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*).
And it has been shown in the Bhāṣya: "Devadatta’s [action] is preceded by motion. [The author asks:
What, then, is the deviation (vyabhicāra) in inference? It is like [the error] regarding mother-of-pearl and the like in the case of perception. [Objection:
But was it not just now demonstrated that [inference] is of two kinds by means of verbal testimony?
Now, one might object: "In the phrase 'that which is inferential' (*ānumānika*), it is the inferential that is to be rejected; it is not necessary to state the defense of the inferential.

What, then, is the distinction here? For even those who claim that what is inferential is non-inferential are indeed contradicting inference itself. Therefore, even in this case, the purpose of stating the definition is precisely to determine the absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)."

Furthermore, there is also confusion (non-discrimination) regarding the object of cognition (*prameya*); that too is excluded by the definition. Some hold that smoke seen in places such as kitchen hearths is not capable of establishing [the presence of fire] as a property of the mountain.
Others maintain that only specific [individual instances] are apprehended.
Still others say it is merely a memory.
(Because it is apprehended through the apprehension of the pervader along with its relatum;
since such a confusion exists—) therefore, [the author] specifies: "The cognition of another part, which is not in contact, arises for one who has known the relation from the perception of one part.
What is refuted by this? First of all, memory is set aside by the statement "in that which is in contact."
Non-apprehension is also indeed refuted by the statement that "cognition arises.
Furthermore, the apprehension of a specific [object] is also refuted by the phrase "due to the comprehension of the relationship.
Now, one might object: validity cannot be asserted based merely on the statement that "cognition arises," because there is deviation in cases such as mother-of-pearl.

However, the perception of that which lacks a relation has already been refuted by the very assertion of a relation. Furthermore, when a relation is expressed, a prior experience [of its constituents] is unavoidable.
Oh, what a great lapse of judgment on the part of this undiscerning person!

Is it not possible to have an experience of what was previously seen? And is experience not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? Furthermore, memory is one thing and experience is another. (To this he says: It is true that [cognition] arising from the sight of a connection is memory (as when smoke is perceived as being connected with fire); however, in the case of a different connection, it is indeed experience. Therefore, even though worldly people point out that they repeatedly see what is unconnected, they do not say that it is remembered.
And the status of inference and the other means of knowledge as valid cognitions is established by experience.
What, then, does "in regard to what is not proximate" mean? It means that which is devoid of the presumption of memory.
For one indeed considers the very nature of the object to be in close proximity.
But does this not result in its being equivalent to a lapse of memory?
No.
Because other causes, such as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, exist.
[Recollection is] a cognition that depends upon a prior experience.

And its dependence on that [prior experience] exists either through appearance—as in "that is the jar," and so forth, where the state of having been previously experienced is present—or through the fact that, in reality, the cognition of silver and the like is otherwise [than what was actually experienced].
Since inference has its cause in the inferential mark (*liṅga*) itself, it does not depend upon a prior experience;
therefore, this is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not recollection (*smaraṇa*).
For in this case, a prior experience is not the sole cause.
For in that case (recollection), the cause is the loss of the object of memory;
here, however, there exists a presently arisen cause such as a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, and thus its validity is established.
Therefore, it must be stated—and indeed has been stated—that whatever is a means of valid cognition does not deviate from its object.
This [definition] should also be applied to comparison (upamāna) and the other means of knowledge;
see pp. 69–81. Some maintain that inference is the mark (liṅga) as it is being known;
however, this is untenable because, if the meaning of the verbal root were not understood, the production of inferential cognition would be impossible.
It is logical to say that "it is that knowledge.
And that inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*).
That which produces the knowledge of the probandum for the person themselves—the cognizer—by means of the *parāmarśa* [reflective judgment] is for oneself.

That which produces the knowledge of the probandum (*sādhya*) for another by means of the employment of the members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*) is "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*).
And the state of being a member (*avayavatva*) consists in being a part of an inferential statement (*anumānavākya*).
These [members] are five in form: the proposition (*pratijñā*), and so forth, up to the example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*).

The definition of the *pratijñā* (proposition) is a statement that expresses the subject as qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhya*), such as "the mountain possesses fire. The definition of the *hetu* (reason) is a statement that makes known [the reason] through either an instrumental or an ablative case-ending, such as "because of possessing smoke" (*dhūmavattvāt*). The definition of the *udāharaṇa* (example) is a statement that establishes the concomitance (*vyāpti*) between the presence of the reason and the property to be proven, such as "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just like a kitchen."

The nature of the *upanaya* (application) is that of a statement which presents the subject (*pakṣa*) as being characterized by the pervasion (*vyāpti*), such as "and so is this [subject]. The nature of the *nigamana* (conclusion) is that of a statement which presents the subject as being qualified by the reason (*hetu*) which is itself qualified by the pervasion, such as "[therefore] it possesses fire, because it possesses smoke pervaded by fire.
An example (*udāharaṇa*) is of two kinds: the positive example (*sādharmya-udāharaṇa*) and the negative example (*vaidharmya-udāharaṇa*).

The second [member] is the statement of the probandum (sādhya) by way of indicating the reason (hetumat). Since the purpose is already accomplished by the first [member], there is no need for a second [statement]. Thus, when the knowledge of the intermediate sentence-meanings has been produced by the constituent sentences—namely, "the mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire," "it possesses fire which is pervaded by smoke," and "it possesses fire based on the reason of possessing smoke which is pervaded by fire"—there follows the knowledge of the meaning of the great sentence (mahāvākya).
The followers of Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyikas) maintain that the *sādhya* (the probandum) is cognized [through the members of the syllogism].

Since inference is produced by the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences consisting of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*udāharaṇa*)—namely, "The mountain possesses fire pervaded by smoke" and "It is similar to a kitchen which possesses smoke pervaded by fire"—the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) are redundant.
Nor is the application necessary for the purpose of knowing the presence of smoke on the mountain, since this is already established by the proposition and the reason alone.

The application of the conclusion (*nigamana*), however, is entirely useless. Thus, the application and the conclusion are not constituent members (*avayava*) [of the syllogism]. Alternatively, since the probandum is established by the example and the subsequent members alone, the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) serve no purpose; such is the direction of the argument.

In the *Maṇiprabhā* (pp. 39–40), inference (*anumāna*) is stated by the sūtra: "Inference is the cognition of something not in contact [with the senses] in another place, arising from the perception of one part [of a known relation] by one who knows the connection.

The meaning is this: inference is a determinate cognition whose locus possesses a doubtful probandum, which has as its object a probandum not in contact [with the senses], and which is produced by the perception of that which is qualified by the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—the pervasion being known in a general form.

Alternatively, the meaning is that inference is a cognition produced by a certain knowledge of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) characterized by the delimiting factor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka-prakāraka*).
Nor should it be argued that, just as the cognition of word-meanings arises from words, so too does the recollection of the pervader arise from the cognition of the pervaded;

for in the case of the pervader, such recollection is possible even in the absence of its direct experience. Nor should it be argued that because a single entity possesses both the nature of being disregarded and the nature of not being disregarded, the recollection would be partial while the experience would be non-partial.

Although the states of being disregarded (*upekṣātva*) and not being disregarded (*anupekṣyatva*) both subsist in the same thing due to their non-contradiction, it is possible for two contradictory properties to subsist in a single cognition.

For this very reason, mental perceptibility (*mānasatva*) has been rejected in the case of fire and the like, because of the contradiction between being visible to the eye (*cākṣuṣatva*) and being mentally perceptible;
for that [mental perception] does not exist with respect to the object "fire," since the causal complex for visual perception (*cākṣuṣasāmagrī*) acts as an obstacle to it.

Nor should it be argued that, even so, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) of that [inference], to the perception of the qualified relation (*vaiśiṣṭyapratyakṣa*), to the inference produced by a cognition similar to it, to the verbal comprehension of the qualified, and to the recollection thereof— since these are all produced by a certainty regarding the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatāniścaya*) whose qualifier is the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
This is because we intend to specify the causality as being "by way of such a certainty" (*tādṛśaniścayatvena*).

In the aforementioned instances, [the respective cognitions] function as causes: in reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), by way of being a certainty whose qualifier is the delimiting property of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedakaprakārakaniścayatva*); in analogical cognition (*upamiti*), by way of being a cognition of that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavajjñānatva*); in verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), by way of being a cognition of the meaning of an intermediate sentence (*avāntaravākyārthajñānatva*); and in memory (*smṛti*), by way of being an experience (*anubhavatva*).

Thus, since the perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣadarśana*) serves as the cause for the sublating perception (*bādhakapratyakṣa*) following error or doubt by virtue of its opposition to such error, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*); for it is not admitted that the perception which takes as its alternative the object of error or doubt is produced by the perception of a specific feature, as that is established through the convergence of circumstances (*arthasamāja*). Nor should it be argued that if both positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are followed, then by adopting one, there would be an over-extension to the other;
for the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unified by being the object of a cognition that opposes the knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

The resulting conclusion is that inference (*anumiti*) is a cognition produced by the knowledge of the presence of a property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*), where that property is qualified by a characteristic that serves as the counter-correlate to the contradiction of the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāradhīvirodhividhiyatāvacchedakadharma*).

However, the Naiyāyikas, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), state that inference is a cognition produced by the knowledge of the presence of a property in the subject, where that property is qualified by the characteristic of being the object of a positive cognition that contradicts the cognition of deviation.
This [view] will be refuted in the discussion on the theory of the final consideration (*parāmarśavāda*).
Alternatively, inference (*anumiti*) is that which possesses the universal (*jāti*) of inferentialness (*anumititva*).
This universal of inferentialness is established by experience in the form "I infer" (*anuminomi*).

The instrument (*karaṇa*) of that [inference] is inference (*anumāna*), and since inference does not arise from a middle term (*liṅga*) that is past or future, it is indeed knowledge (*jñāna*) itself, and not the cause as it is being known (*jñāyamāna*).
pp. 30–31: Inference is of two kinds: that based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa) and that based on specific observation (viśeṣatodṛṣṭa).
Each of these two types is further divided into two: for one's own sake (svārtha) and for the sake of others (parārtha).
However, the distinction between purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) and purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) [reasons] is not accepted;

for it is stated in the *Anumāna* chapter [verse 167]: "The cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) would likewise be like that [of the probandum]; it does not exist [as a valid means of knowledge] because it lacks the three characteristics," since a mark devoid of the triad of characteristics is impossible.

"Inference does not produce a false cognition, because it apprehends the pervaded [the probandum] through the absence of the non-pervader [the contradictory]. — Maṇi, p. 42. [This concerns] inference.

Some hold that smoke observed in kitchens and such places is not capable of establishing [the presence of fire] on a mountain (because when the relationship of one thing has been grasped, another thing cannot serve as a means of knowledge).

Others hold that only particulars are understood (because inference based on general observation is untenable due to the absence of a graspable relationship). Still others hold that it is merely memory (because the pervasion between the related entities was already grasped).
Vṛhatī, pp. 38–39:
Inference is sublated by direct perception and verbal testimony.
Inference is not possible regarding that which has been perceived by direct perception; this is because it possesses concomitance and other such characteristics. (*Bṛhatī*, p.
166). Inference does not arise with respect to what is already clear through direct perception, nor does it accomplish its own function [in that case].
Bhāṣya 11.16120:
"Inference as a means of valid cognition arises regarding those objects only so long as the object is not obstructed by the production of a perception of that [object]."
Furthermore, even in common worldly usage, when there is smoke from grass, it is specifically fire from grass that is inferred, not fire in general.

Just as the act of "going" (*gamana*), when adopted as the basis for the derivation of the word "cow" (*go*), is understood as the cause for the cognition [of the animal] because it possesses a dewlap (*sāsnā*) and so forth, and thus functions as the defining characteristic (*nimitta*), yet it does not have the mere act of going as its object—such is the established rule regarding the word "cow.
Likewise, even in common worldly inference, whatever reason (*hetu*) is taught in relation to the thing to be proven (*pratijñeya*)...

First of all, that [particular] is perceived by its very nature as a specific instance. However, since there is no possibility of an analogy for that which is of such a nature when it is yet to be proven, only the universal aspect is intended; this is understood precisely at the time of employing the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta). (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.130, p. 142). Inference, in common worldly usage, functions through the non-contradiction of pervasion (vyāpti), because smoke and the like are understood to serve as logical reasons (hetu) only in their universal form.

In the *Vedāntakalpataru*, however, it is stated that since an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) inferred from the impossibility of the reason (*hetu*) being otherwise established cannot possess a degree of generality (*sāmānyatva*), the reason does not thereby acquire a general form (*sāmānyarūpatā*) in accordance with it (Su.

p. 11). Inference (*anumāna*) is a worldly means of valid cognition (*laukika-pramāṇa*) (Maṇi. p. 13). Furthermore, if inference is doubtful, then "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*) is not a valid means of cognition.
"Anumāna (inference) everywhere follows what has been observed (*dṛṣṭa*).
Even *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation) is never [referred to] by the term *dṛṣṭa*.
Anumāna that conforms to what is observed does not [operate] when there is a contradiction with what is observed. (Bhāṣya 6.3.124; Ṛjuvimalā, p. 144).
*Bṛhatī*, p. 202: "And inference does not become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it contradicts perception.

*Bhāṣya* 1.2.14, p. 17: "And inference is not possible when there is a contradiction with perception. 3.3.7.14, p. 893: "Perception is sublated by inference, as [in the case of] the perception of a mirage and the like."

Or [as stated in] Vārttika 3.3.7.14, p. 895: "We consider even perception to be weak when it is accompanied by a possible error. By this very fact, the cause of error being made manifest, it is said according to the aforementioned principle that "inference is indeed stronger than even perception" (*Bṛhatī*, p.
204). Furthermore, it was stated previously (in the *Ślokavārttika* on the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra*) that inference is everywhere insufficient for the cognition of the actual existence of an object.
Vārttika 2.1.512, p. 390: By means of inference, a fallacious inference (anumānābhāsa) is sublated.
Bālakrīḍā, p. 131: The existence of the procedure (itikartavyatā) is stated to be [known] from inference;
and since that proceeds from the Āgneya [sacrifice], this is not an inference based on the Nairṛta and other [offerings].

It is replied: Since the performance of the *agnyanvādhāna* and other rites is observed to be for the sake of accomplishing the result of being a "part" (*ekadeśatva*) [of a sacrifice], and since this [Saura and other sacrifices] is also a "part," therefore it must be accompanied by the *agnyanvādhāna* and other rites.
In that regard, when two white garments are known to be for the purpose of accomplishing Devadatta's aim, those same garments are obtained even for the purpose of accomplishing another's aim.
Furthermore, those [rites] are seen to be productive of results for the ignorant among the subjects; since the Agnihotra also possesses a result, it too would have them [as its performers].
Therefore, regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), there is much that is inconsistent when relying on inference.
"Therefore, the acquisition of the property [of the model] occurs through analogy" (Ṭup.
8.1.2.12, p. 1585). "Direct perception would be a stronger cause than inference" (Bhāṣya 3.1.8.123).
The Naiyāyikas maintain that direct perception is more powerful than inference.
*Bṛhatī*, p. 204: Application based on inference is stronger.
We infer that the "king" (*rājā*) is the performer of the act of ruling (*rājya*), yet we do not perceive the word "king" being used in its primary sense with respect to a Kṣatriya.
*Bhāṣya* 2.3.13, p. 585: From inference follows the actual production of the effect.

Regarding the statement, "The sacrificial porridge (caru) is for those purified by the *nalas*," one forms an inference upon seeing that the purpose of threshing is the removal of the husks; [one infers]: "Surely the *nalas* are performing the function of the mortar and pestle. (Ṭupṭīkā 9.2.12.10, p. 1730). Furthermore, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is more authoritative than inference (*anumāna*).

"It is logical that the weak should be sublated, not the strong" (Bhāṣya 12.1.27, p. 2223). Of two things in conjunction, when one is perceived, it causes the other—which though unperceived—to be present in the mind through inference (Bhāṣya 8.1.2).
Because inference involves an extension of space and time, it is logical that it apprehends what has not been previously apprehended.
*Ratnākara*, p. 363. Dharma is not the object of either inference or perception. *Vivaraṇa* 1.2.2.
Inference has sublation (*bādha*) by perception that is distinct from comparison (*upamiti*).
*Sutras* p. 137. Inference has an object that is sublated by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).

*Kaṇikā* p. 46. For the reason (*hetu*) of inference is that which has been repeatedly observed, and it depends upon the exclusion from what is not of its own class (*asajātīyavyāvṛtti*; namely, depending on the exclusion of smoke from non-fire, which is the dissimilar class).

*Bṛhatī*, p. 83: For the sake of others, the inference of logicians does not consist of five members as [some claim], but rather only three. As it has been said: "Some say it consists of five, others of two, and we of three;
whether it ends with the example, or begins with the example, and so forth."
Thus [says] Bālakṛṣṇa, page 8. Even in inference, error is specific.
We do not say that there is no error even in inference; rather, in this case, the cognition of identity arises due to the non-apprehension of difference.
It also occurs in the *Atassindhu*:

"The *bṛhatī*," p. 204; "In inference, that which is certain is the indicator," *Śābarabhāṣya* 1.2.1, p. 77. The detailed version is "He whose sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) is made of *khadira* wood," and so forth; the abbreviated version is "He whose sacrificial ladles (*sruc*) are of such a form."

A rule is observed in such a form within the *prakṛti* (archetype), and this [rule] here is also of that same form; therefore, it is *prākṛta* (belonging to the archetype). This is an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*). Bhāṣya 3.6.16. The connection of the reasons for the Veda with the probandum is not apprehended either by way of a universal (*sāmānya*) or by way of a particular (*viśeṣa*); that must now be postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

In that case, because a particular is being adopted and because the universal is not established—since there is no possibility for abandoning it—the logical principle (*nyāya*) is restricted solely to the particular that has been adopted.
Inference (anumāna), section 403: The impossibility [of a contrary conclusion] leads one to infer that the statement of the example must indeed possess that [property].
This is because, as stated on pages 42–43, an inference contrary to worldly consensus is impossible.
Or: inference based on the perception of a particular (*viśeṣadṛṣṭam anumānam*). Vātsyāyana Bhāṣya 1.2.130, p.

142; 1.2.142, p. 109. [Regarding] those who assert that five relations—inherence (*samavāya*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and contradiction (*virodha*)—are the constituent factors of inference (this being the Vaiśeṣika doctrine in Sūtra 1.2.1), they too have been refuted.

Just as [the constellation] Kṛttikā rising [indicates] Rohiṇī, so too inference and the other means of knowledge lack validity regarding their own objects without the apprehension of a cause (*nimitta*).

(Rju-pṛ. 73). Inference and the others possess validity regarding their own objects—such as the object to be inferred—only after there has been the apprehension of causes, such as the mark (*liṅga*) or similarity (*sādṛśya*).
(When the causes, such as the mark or similarity, have been apprehended, inference and the others proceed toward their respective objects, such as that which is to be inferred.)
"Whatever negation there may be, all of it arises from non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
This, however, is untenable;
for instance:

Let it be granted for now that "when fire exists, there is smoke" is understood through perception; however, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that "when fire is absent, smoke does not exist"? Is it not the case that this is precisely an inference based on the mark of non-perception (*anupalabdhi-liṅgaka*)?
Even regarding non-perception, the absence of the object must be sought in the same manner.
That [absence], first of all, occurs through identity (*tādātmya*).
For identity is established through the necessary concomitance (anubandha) with that alone;

and the establishment of this concomitance with that alone occurs because a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) operates against the contrary case (vipakṣa). And the subverting proof is precisely non-apprehension (anupalabdhi).
Because all negations are established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*),

and because even in the case of non-apprehension serving as a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), there would result an infinite regress if another non-apprehension were required according to the aforementioned reasoning.
Nor is the establishment of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) achieved through that [non-apprehension] being logically possible.
Because it would depend upon the non-perception of the absence of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva-vipakṣatānupalabdhi*), there would result the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Thus, in this way, the establishment of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) through that very production is difficult to attain. Even in the case of identity (*tādātmya*), the identity [of the reason] depends solely on the non-perception of its opposite.
In the section on inference:
"Even though it has not been seen, the conjunction with another [cause] in relation to smoke may still be suspected based on what has been observed. It is replied:

The conjunction of smoke with fire is adventitious (*aupādhika*), for in the absence of that [fuel], the absence of the conjunction of smoke with fire indeed occurs. However, the conjunction of smoke with fire is not adventitious; how then could one suspect that it might not exist? How is its non-adventitiousness understood? Because even with effort, no adventitious character is perceived in other instances of smoke.
Thinking that this is established through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), the Teachers have maintained repeated observation as the means of proof.

[Objection: But in this way, at the very time of ascertaining the restriction of the relation (*saṃbandhaniyama*), since the connection with fire and so forth is already established for all instances of smoke and so forth, there would be nothing further to be ascertained beyond the certainty of the existence of smoke and so forth; thus, it would not differ from inference (*anumāna*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[Reply: True.
It would be so, provided that the definition of a means of valid cognition were "that which pertains to an object not yet apprehended" (*anadhigatārthagata*).
It has been stated that direct experience (*anubhūti*) is indeed the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

From smoke, the perception of fire arises through the force of direct experience, resulting in a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhikatva*). Nor can there be an assumption here of the sublation of memory, because the presence of a presently existing cause is established.

In cases such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, the sublation of memory is accepted because the cause for direct experience is absent; although it does not ascend to the level of actual perception, it is nonetheless relied upon.

However, in this case [of inference], there is no cause for direct experience—namely, the observation of a single locus characterized by a rule of connection—and thus, since the nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists of direct experience, its basis is pure. Therefore, the validity of inference is indeed logical.
Some, however, state that inference is of the nature of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), occurring beyond the limitations of space and time.
That is correct;
for space and time are transcended by the mark (*liṅga*).

However, the relationship between the mark and the object marked (*laiṅgika*), which pertains to all space and time, is ascertained precisely at the time of determining the restriction of that relationship.

Otherwise, the very restriction of the relationship would remain uncomprehended. By this, the objection that "there is no concomitance in the particular, and if it were in the universal, it would be proving what is already established" is refuted.
For, by ascertaining the rule of connection between specific places and times characterized by smoke, one concludes: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire.
"Whichever relation exists here between two things, being unconditional and established through means of valid cognition such as perception—that is held to be the indicator of the other."
This is the summary verse.
Furthermore, the fact that the restriction of the relationship between two parts has been previously known assists in the recollection [of that relationship].

For a person who recollects the restriction of the relationship regarding the object that is a part of the inferable (liṅgika), the cognition that arises from the perception of one part of that restricted relationship is inference (anumāna).
It is said to reside in one part (*ekadeśāśrita*).

In the expression "in another part" (*ekadeśāntare*), the term *ekadeśāntara* itself denotes that which is resident. Since there can be no possibility for a resident entity without its substratum (*āśraya*), the substratum is implied; yet, this does not imply a substratum distinct from the two parts, because the required implication is fulfilled by the implication of a single [substratum] alone.
Moreover, the word "also" (api) serves to establish that [the relationship] exists only when there is a common substratum.
Consequently, it is stated that the status of being the signifier and the signified pertains only to those things based upon a single substratum.

An example is as follows: from seeing smoke on a mountain—where the rule of the necessary relation between the three (the mark, the probandum, and the subject) has been known in places such as a kitchen—one gains knowledge of the smoke situated on the mountain.
But surely, because of the difference between the region above the hip and the region above the fire, fire and smoke do not reside in a single substratum; how then can there be inference?
Therefore, it is logical that what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is the conjunction of fire with the locus of the smoke, and the reason (*hetu*) is the smoke residing therein.
It is replied:
It is not the case that everyone in the world perceives it in this way; rather, people also infer fire even when it is located on a mountain and so forth.
Nor is there a difference in the locus, because the mountain, as a whole (*avayavin*), is one, and both the fire and the smoke reside within it.
However, since the upper portions of the hips are likewise constituent parts [of the body], there is no fault whatsoever.
And here, by the word "known" (*jñāta*) in the phrase "of that whose relation is known as restricted" (*jñātasaṃbandhaniyamasya*), its status as an uncommon reason (*asādhāraṇahetutva*) is expressed;
for example, [the fallacious argument]: "The kitchen possesses fire because it has fragrance."
For indeed, there is a necessary relation, characterized by inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*), between this very part called "odor" and that part called "taste.
However, that restriction of the relation has not been previously perceived,
because odor is excluded from everything other than earthhood (*pṛthivītva*).
If it is argued that this [doubt] is indeed a unique cause of doubt because the desire to know the earth is a property common to many,
that is not correct.
For whatever connection has been observed by someone, he is capable of postulating that very [connection].
And that which is recognized as being connected to the properties of both belongs to both.
Producing a memory, it brings about doubt because of the contradiction in a single thing possessing a dual nature.
However, that for which no connection whatsoever has been ascertained with anything is incapable of producing even a single recollection; thus, how could it give rise to doubt?

Therefore, even though a property (*dharma*) is common to the nature of the object itself, it is not a cause for doubt. Furthermore, it has been stated that when a connection is grasped, any subverting factor constitutes a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced.
For the property of being produced has no connection whatsoever with permanence, but only with impermanence.

This restriction of the perceived relationship, by presenting impermanence through its own presence, subverts permanence; thus, because it possesses the character of a property to be proven [in a contrary way], it is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) that acts as a subverter.
And by the inclusion of the term "restriction" (niyama), there is the exclusion of the common [inconclusive reason].
For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*).
Although the relation of knowability with eternity exists and is known, [the reason is inconclusive] because knowability is observed even in that which is non-eternal, as well as in the eternal.

Because it is a cause of doubt, because it is connected to both eternity and non-eternity, and because there is a contradiction between eternity and non-eternity within a single substratum (*dharmin*), this [reason] is called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). Likewise, regarding the phrase "from the perception of one part," [it refers to] a reason that constitutes only a part [of the whole].

In the section on inference (*anumānapariccheda*), it was stated that [the following] is a fallacious appearance (*bhāsa*): "Space is perceptible because it possesses color. The possession of color is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to space as a whole, since it exists only in a portion of space.

For when the eye is opened, whatever form is perceived in household offerings and the like is known in the world to be either fiery, watery, or earthy. Likewise, by this very reasoning, that [atom] which is claimed to have both a single location and multiple locations is also refuted; for example, [the argument]: "The Veda is artificial, because it consists of the nature of instruction. The nature of consisting of instruction does not pervade the portion that is prescriptive.
But surely smoke too would not be a valid reason (*hetu*), because it does not pervade the entire mountain?
Not so;
for in that case, the mountain is a single composite whole (*avayavin*), and the smoke exists only in one part of it.
In this case, however, there is no single entity that is the whole of the Veda; thus, it is correct that the reason is unestablished by its appearance (*bhāsāsiddhatva*).

By the mention of "perception" (*darśana*), he shows a fallacious reason that is unestablished in its essential nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), such as: "The Buddha perceives dharma and adharma through direct perception because he is omniscient.
For it has been stated that the omniscience of the Buddha cannot be apprehended by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Likewise, as long as there is no perception of even a single part of that which exists, it is equivalent [to being non-existent], just as smoke is in the dark.
By the phrase "in another part," he refutes the notion that fire and the like, as independent entities, are what is to be inferred.
And by the inclusion of the word "interior" (antar), the relationship between the signifier and the signified when they reside in different loci is rejected.

But surely, in the case of inferring the rise of the ocean from the rising of the moon, and the postulation of the proximity of Rohiṇī from the rising of Kṛttikā, how can there be a common substratum?
To this it is replied: the relationship between the rising of the moon and the rise of the ocean exists within a single time; thus, time itself is the substratum in that case.

Likewise, there is a relationship between the rising of Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī as well, insofar as both occur within the same day-and-night (*ahorātra*). Therefore, from the rising of Kṛttikā, the presence of Rohiṇī on that very same day-and-night is inferred.
By this, it is explained how, through the observation of a nakṣatra situated in the middle, one infers the arrival of the eighth nakṣatra. For in this case too, the river serves as the substratum.
As for the inference of a son’s Brahminhood based on the Brahminhood of his parents—which some maintain—the Prābhākaras do not accept it.
For when the parents themselves are Brahmins, it is the very nature of the father that constitutes the Brahminhood, not the lineage (*jāti*).

Therefore, since there is no Brahminhood other than being born from a woman and a man denoted by the word "Brahmin," there can be no relationship between a *jāti* as the probans and the inferred object.

By the term "uncontradicted" (*abādhite*), he demonstrates that inference is not admitted when the object is contradicted by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as in the case: "Fire is not hot, because it is a substance.
Now, one might object: there is no connection at all between substantiality (*dravyatva*) and non-hotness, since substantiality is observed even in fire, which is not non-hot.
Therefore, the arising of this inference is due solely to the absence of a rule of connection, and not because of contradiction.
It is said:

if inference were admitted even in a case where the object is sublated, then there would be no such thing as a restriction regarding the relation of "substance-ness" (dravyatva), because even heatlessness (*anuṣṇatva*) would be established by inference in the case of fire.
In every inference, it is the investigation of the relation that is useful, independent of the specific object one wishes to infer.

Furthermore, since the determination of the rule governing the relation between substanceness (*dravyatva*) and non-hotness has already occurred—specifically that fire alone is invariably related to non-hotness throughout—then when an inference arises by the force of that [determination], even a subsequent sublation of the rule of relation cannot establish itself.

Therefore, because the object of the inference is sublated, the inference does not arise, and thus the rule of relation is also broken. Consequently, the non-sublation of the object is a necessary cause for inference.
Hence, substanceness, having its object sublated by perception regarding fire, does not produce an inference.
Therefore, this is an example of sublation by inference (*anumāna-bādha*).
The object of the inference—"Sound is not apprehended by the auditory organ because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*)—is sublated by another inference.
For that which is the object of a cognition produced by a particular instrument—that sense-organ is said to be its apprehender.
Furthermore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is the instrument for the cognition whose object is sound.

For when the auditory organ is unimpaired, the cognition of sound arises; and when it is impaired, it does not arise. Thus, the cognition of sound follows the presence and absence of the auditory organ, and is therefore produced by the auditory organ as its instrument.
Indeed, the state of being the instrument of a particular effect consists in a necessary relationship characterized by following the presence and absence of something other than that [effect].

Therefore, when the audibility of sound has been established by the inference—"The cognition of sound has the ear as its instrument, because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of the ear"—any proponent who asserts that it does not exist is contradicted by that very inference through another inference.

One might object: "Surely, perception—which depends on the observation of one part [of the relation] for the sake of grasping the restriction of the relation (*saṃbandhaniyama*)—because it arises rapidly and because its occurrence is inevitable, obstructs the apprehension of another object even though that apprehension is independent [of perception]. Therefore, how can there be the production of that [inferential] cognition by means of inference? This is what must be addressed. It is replied:

By whoever wishes to deny that sound is perceptible by the ear, that person must necessarily first understand the relation of being perceived by the same [cognitive] faculty (*ekagrāhyatva*); otherwise, the negation would be impossible to conceive.
An object is indeed already understood when it is established in another domain, but it is not entirely unknown.

Therefore, by one who accepts the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender elsewhere, the operation of inference—which is based on a logical mark (*liṅga*) that follows the method of agreement and difference—is necessarily admitted. Thus, a swift inference, by depriving another inference of its object, functions as a sublation (*bādhaka*).

Just as inference preceded by perception occurs prior to inference preceded by inference, so too it should be understood that inference based on well-established premises (*prasiddhāṅka*) precedes inference based on premises to be proven (*prasādhyāṅka*). Furthermore, the scope of inference is sublated by scripture, as in the case of the claim: "There is no connection between action and its fruit."
And having become a fault [in the case of scripture], even scripture is approached as if it were direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
As for the statement of comparison (*upamāna*), however, it is: "A cow is not like a horse.
And by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), there is the sublation of the object of inference (*anumāna*), as in: "Devadatta, being alive and not present in his house, is also not outside."
Some, however, claim that not only the state of having a sublated object (*bādhitaviṣayatva*), but also the state of having an unestablished object (*asādhitaviṣayatva*), is a cause for inference.

They hold that inference does not operate even when the object is already established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as in the case of the heat of fire already perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This [view] is not accepted by the followers of the Prabhākara school.

It has been stated that inference has only an established object (*siddha-viṣaya*). Why, then, is it not possible for its object to be established through the maintenance of the restriction of the relation (*saṃbandha-niyama*)? However, since the cognizers have ceased their cognition in that regard, they do not apply themselves to the investigation of the restriction of the relation; thus, inference does not arise. Furthermore, if inference were not possible even when one perceives a portion of the restricted relation that has been investigated while the object remains unestablished, then the state of having an unestablished object would indeed be a cause of inference.

This is not so. Therefore, this enumeration of the causes of inference is complete: the perception of a part of a necessary relation (*niyata-sambandha*) is the means of inferential determination; such is the section on inference.
The section on inference (anumānapariccheda) [states]: "It is seen," so how can the momentum (*saṃskāra*) consisting of velocity [be inferred] by the arrow's flight through space?
In this regard, there is indeed an argument based on inference; it is not a self-contradiction of one's own words.
The conjunctions and disjunctions of the parts of light with the wind that remains there—

[conjunctions and disjunctions] inferred from the effect, namely the sound produced by the utterance [of speech]— are what initiate the non-utterance of sound; thus, it cannot be maintained that [sound] arises from anything other than those very causes of action.
The claim that "one is silent" is merely a form of inference.
However, one's own statement—that disjunction and conjunction arise—is precisely what makes the inference of action logical.
And it is not [the case that...].
No, there is no contradiction, because it was not stated that [the action] is not perceived.
For one whose action consists solely in motion, the restriction to a substance proximate to it and its effect is inferred;

and the restriction regarding connection with another location is to be observed by another through the perception of a single part of the object being moved, since for that [other observer], it lacks the status of being an effect.
And if this restriction were to apply even to that [subject],
then for that purpose an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) must be stated;
for as long as it might pertain to some locus (*dharmī*), then the effect itself would not arise.
And all that action is indeed such;

the restriction of the relation between one part and another part, established by means of valid cognition, constitutes the determination of inference— beginning with disjunction and resulting in conjunction— as set forth in the section on inference (Anumāna-pariccheda), verse 412, in the *Anumānavāda*.
It has been clarified that the use of repetition (*vīpsā*) and the like occurs when expressing a meaning;
for example: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire.

Therefore, since the relationship is properly understood through the employment of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) alone, the inclusion of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is useless.
Now it is said:
"Let there be no recourse to the fault of the example; rather, let there be an alternative analysis (vikalpa)."

For even by means of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), one points out that which lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) as being devoid of the probans (*sādhanadharma*). By excluding the probans from all things that lack the property to be proven, and thereby finding no room for the probans elsewhere, [the probans] is shown to reside only where the property to be proven exists; thus, because it establishes the necessary connection (*niyama*) with the property to be proven, its status as a logical reason (*hetu*) is indeed supported by the dissimilar instance as well. Therefore, since they perform the same function, it is logical to treat the similar and dissimilar instances as alternatives (*vikalpa*). This is incorrect.
Since one does not resort to a circuitous path when the goal can be accomplished through a direct path,

it is not logical to propose an alternative that the direct path consists in the apprehension of the non-deviation of the connection with the property to be proven (*sādhya*) as residing in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*),
while the circuitous path consists in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
Or, it may be because non-existence is incomparable. It might be thought: "Just as the inseparable connection with the probandum is the path of inference..."
Likewise, it is also excluded because of the absence of that [property];
and this is expressed by means of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), thus this is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Regarding that:
Because exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), being of the nature of non-existence, cannot possibly be a cause anywhere; it has been stated that all effects are established as positive entities (*bhāva*).
Furthermore, the exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) cannot be understood;

because the counter-examples are infinite, the restriction of the relation—consisting in the non-deviation of the connection with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—cannot be understood in the manner already described. Therefore, it is established that in all cases, only the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) should be employed.

Since it is thus similar [to the opponent's position], the refutations of the thesis are likewise: sublation by perception and other means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣādibādhitatva*), the unestablished nature of the qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), and for the reason (*hetu*): its being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhatva*), its being unestablished in one part (*ekadeśāsiddhatva*), its being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatva*), its being too-common (*sādhāraṇatva*), or its being a sublater (*bādhakatva*).

For the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is the lack of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*), the lack of the probans (*sādhanavikalatā*), the lack of the restriction of the relation (*saṃbandhaniyamavikalatā*), the absence of restriction (*niyamaśūnyatā*), and the presence of a contrary restriction (*viparītaniyamatā*).
And for the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the other members of the syllogism, there is the lack of expressiveness (*avācakatā*) and their non-employment (*aprayoga*).
Furthermore, because it shares the same nature as a proposition (*pratijñā*), this is indeed nothing other than the abandonment of a proposition (*pratijñāhāni*).
Even the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is not a distinct fault, since it is preceded by another fault;
for a proponent who has had his position refuted accepts [the opponent's] proposition.

For this very reason, even a "different proposition" (*pratijñāntara*) does not constitute a separate fallacy, because it is merely the adoption of another proposition by one whose previous proposition has already been refuted. Furthermore, "contradiction between the reason and the proposition" (*hetu-pratijñā-virodha*) is also not a distinct fallacy.

If the reason is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), the fault is simply that of the reason being unproven (*asiddha*); if it is established, then the fault lies with the thesis (*pakṣa*), since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it would also establish the thesis.
However, the fault of having an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatā*) applies even to that which has an unperceived characteristic, because it is [still] subject to inference.
Thus ends the chapter on inference in the *Pramāṇapārāyaṇa* of the *Prakaraṇapañjikā*. This concludes the discourse on inference (*anumāna-vāda*).

Having stated the non-deviation [of perception] by means of the definition established in the world— namely, that it is produced from contact with an existing object— the author of the Bhāṣya now states the very same kind of worldly definition for the sake of ensuring the non-deviation of inference and the other means of knowledge as well:
"Inference is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses], based on the perception of one part [of a known relationship] by one who knows the relationship."

Inference is that cognition which arises in one who has perceived a certain property of similarity—whether it be conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), the state of being cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇatva*), or any other relation known as being restricted to the properties of the example—with respect to a subject that possesses such a relation, provided that this subject is not determined by any stronger means of knowledge to be either similar to or the opposite of that [example]. This cognition occurs regarding a subject with which such a relation is known, whether the relation is direct or indirect.

Just as the concomitance of smoke with fire and its invariable presence in kitchens and the like is perceived through its uninterrupted upward movement, so too, upon seeing it on a mountain, there arises the cognition of fire.
But if [cognition] were dependent on the operation of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), how could there be activity toward that which has not been determined as being of such a nature?
For such is the nature of restriction.
"Wherever there is smoke, there is fire";
"Whatever possesses taste, possesses form.
If this is so, then since the nature of fire is already understood in all instances, the possibility of inference as a means of cognizing what is otherwise uncognized does not exist.

For this very reason, let it be stated that some explain the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) by the proponent [of inference] for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that [inference] is mere memory; they do so while accepting that inference indeed grasps what has already been grasped.

Nevertheless, there is no lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*), for the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not "the grasping of what was not previously grasped. Rather, its defining characteristic is "experience" (*anubhūti*).

And although inference grasps what has been grasped, it is indeed an experience because it is produced by the specific cause of the perceived mark (*liṅga*), and thus lacks the quality of being produced by memory alone (*saṃskāramātra*); therefore, its validity is logically established.
Now, from what is this lapse of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*) inferred? It is inferred from the presence of a presently arisen cause.

For, when there is the presence of a cause other than the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), as in the case of the cognition "this is silver," a lapse of memory is accepted that is distinct from a powerful valid memory.

In the present case, however, because the mark (*liṅga*)—the cause of the experience—is present, it is improper to deny the character of experience established by perception and instead accept a lapse of memory.
This, then, is their lack of causal efficiency;
it is a source of fear.

For instance, if the existence of the pervaded and the pervader were already fully understood, then one might suspect that [the cognition] apprehends what has already been apprehended; but this is not the case.

For it is only in the substrata of the example, such as the great kitchen and so forth, that the concomitance of smoke with fire is understood prior to the inference, and not everywhere, because [otherwise] no means of valid cognition would be possible.
How this impossibility arises has been explained in detail in the *Nyāyaratnamālā* itself.

In the very substrata of the examples (*dṛṣṭānta-dharmin*), the coexistence of fire and smoke is repeatedly observed; and for one who has never seen smoke even once despite searching with effort in places where fire is absent, the knowledge of fire arises regarding the substrata of the probandum (*sādhya-dharmin*).

As it has been said: "Since the coexistence of fire and smoke is well-established as being limited in space, and since their absence [in the same place] is never seen, their capacity to convey [the conclusion] is postulated."

Thus (Ślokavārttika, Arthāpatti 42): "But for me, the concomitant is the indicator by virtue of its being seen together with that [other]. And (40): "But for me, the concomitant is the indicator by virtue of its being seen together with that [other]."

Consequently, one should not understand that all things possessing smoke are possessed of fire, nor that there is an absence of smoke everywhere where there is no fire. Those who seek inference need only rely upon the frequent coexistence [of smoke and fire] and the non-observation of deviation; nothing more than this is required. This is what is meant by the statement: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire."
"Thus, this knowledge is indeed inference," it is stated in that very work (*Nyāyaratnamālā*).

Now, even if this is so, since all smoke-bearing things have already been understood as possessing fire by this very general inference, any further inference based on the observation of smoke in specific instances such as a mountain would still suffer from the same defect of apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).
[The same applies to] the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Its state of apprehending what has already been apprehended would remain exactly as it was.
Not so;
for there is a distinction between the universal and the particular.

By means of the universal, those things possessing smoke are indeed understood to possess fire; however, in the case of specific locations such as mountains, their very nature was previously unknown, let alone their possession of fire.

As for one who thinks that [the mountain] is already known, it must be stated by what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) the very nature of the mountain is known to those standing far from the mountain—
neither by perception nor by any other means of valid cognition.
And one who has not cognized the mountain is not capable of determining its possession of fire.
Furthermore, if the mountain’s possession of fire were already known at present, then one seeking fire would climb the mountain even without seeing smoke;
for there is no purpose for one seeking fire in seeing smoke once the fire has already been cognized. No one [would do so].

Furthermore, by one who asserts that the connection with fire is understood for a specific location such as a mountain characterized by smoke, it must be admitted that the connection with smoke is also understood.
For a characteristic (upalakṣaṇa) consisting of smoke whose connection is unknown is not capable of characterizing the object to be characterized (upalakṣya).

If, on the other hand, the smoke characterizes the location in general and not a specific location, then the possession of fire is also understood for that [location] in general and not for a specific location; therefore, since there is no distinction between the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin), the claim that "the mark transcends space and time, but the bearer of the mark does not" is mere idle chatter.

Moreover, by the statement "where there is contact with fuel, there is smoke," smoke is already understood; thus, nothing remains to be understood through the cognition of smoke. Enough of this talk like that of a child!
And if that which is already understood is understood again by means of inference, then inferential knowledge would be nothing but memory whose object has been forgotten.
Nor can it be argued that it is not memory because it is produced by a presently existing cause, for that reason is unestablished.
For the perception of a relation, like the non-perception of a snake, would awaken a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), since its causality in that regard is already established.
And it is undisputed that a latent impression, once awakened, produces memory.
Furthermore, the "stealing" (*pramoṣa*) of memory is well-established in cases such as the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl.
Thus, since the cognition of fire from smoke arises precisely through the established path, who indeed would postulate that the mark (liṅga) is the cause of the cognition of the marked (liṅgin)?
Or, if such a postulation were made, then because the perception of silver in a seashell is also an experience, one would have to postulate that a defect (doṣa) is the cause of that experience.
But if it is not so postulated, then here too, due to the loss of memory (smṛtipramopa), there would simply be invalidity (aprāmāṇya).
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that [inference] apprehends what has not been previously apprehended.

But surely, since it is the specific [particular] whose relation [to the mark] has not been apprehended that is the object of inference, it is only the universal (*sāmānya*) that is the object of inference; and since that has already been understood previously, how can there be the apprehension of what was not previously apprehended?
As they say: "There is no concomitance (*anugama*) with respect to the particular, while with respect to the universal, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*)."
"In this [view] which is the destruction of inference, the elephants of the proponents are submerged.
This is not a fault.

Even though the universal has already been cognized, its status as an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) is established because there is a grasping of its connection with another place and another time, which was previously ungrasped.

Furthermore, this other point must be stated by the proponent of the "partial" view (*ekadeśin*): by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is it understood that the perception of smoke is the cause of the cognition of fire?
If it is argued that it is "because of its immediate succession" (*tadānantaryāt*), [the response follows].
If it is argued that [the claim] "of experience" is untenable because [recognition] can also arise by way of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*),
[we reply: even for recollection, the conceit of being an experience is possible through the loss of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that [past experience].
In reality, experientiality (*anubhavatva*) is indeed unestablished due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For there is no other direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that serves as a means of valid cognition for the experientiality of the cognition of fire at another time; rather, such a means exists for its being a lapse of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*).

If it is argued that there would be a sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding its being a lapse of memory, and since no such sublation exists for the cognition of fire, it is therefore not a lapse of memory—this is not so.

Furthermore, because the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*) is observed here for the first time, the perception of the luster of a gem is merely a loss of memory due to the presence of the cognition of a gem; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being a misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*). Moreover, since the object exists as a gem for one who acts upon it, there is no sublation.
Therefore, if memory itself were inference, it would result in the loss of its status as a valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇya*).

And how is it that inference grasps what has already been grasped? For when [an object] is inferred in a place and time that have never before been perceived, by what means of valid cognition was it previously known? Not by perception, because that [perception] apprehends only what is present. Nor by any other [means of valid cognition].
Furthermore, you assert only this much: that the mutual relationship between fire and smoke is perceived through direct perception as being unrestricted by space and time.
However, by this much alone, the relationship of fire with other places and other times is not understood.
Therefore, inference indeed apprehends what has not been previously grasped.

What is it that has not been apprehended here? First of all, the generality of fire (*agni-sāmānya*) has indeed been apprehended, and the mountain (*parvata*) as well is known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
