It is only the mountain as qualified [by fire] that has not been apprehended by anyone; thus, it will be the object of inference (*anumeya*).
And therein, by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not, the relation alone remains as the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Just as in the case of the injunction "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), although it is an injunction of a qualified action (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), it becomes one whose purpose is the qualification because the qualified object is already established; so too here, since the qualifier and the qualificand are already established, the mere cognition of the qualified object results in a statement concerning their relationship, such as "He gives a chariot to a Yajurvedin. However, he who wishes to communicate a meaning to another through inference must employ a means of proof (*sādhana*). That sentence by which an inference is ignited for someone is called a "means of proof."
"Some [hold that] this [inference] consists of five members, others two, and we three;
it extends up to the example, or else it consists of five examples.

First, the followers of Akṣapāda consider the means of proof (*sādhana*) to consist of five members: the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).

"Sound is impermanent" is the proposition (*pratijñā*); "because it is produced" is the reason (*hetu*); "whatever is produced is impermanent, such as a jar and so forth" is the example (*udāharaṇa*); "and sound is produced" is the application (*upanaya*); "therefore it is impermanent" is the conclusion (*nigamana*). However, considering this to be overly prolix, the Buddhists hold that there are only two members, consisting of the example and the application.

For when one who perceives the mark (*liṅga*) as having its own nature connects it to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), the cognition of the marked (*liṅgin*) arises by itself. Therefore, once the rule of pervasion (*vyāpti-niyama*) of "whatever is produced is impermanent" has been recalled, and the application (*upanaya*) "and sound is produced" has been stated, the impermanence of sound is indeed understood; thus, other members [of the syllogism] are redundant.
However, such extreme completeness would only serve to cause weariness; therefore, the three-membered [syllogism] alone is logical.

"The sound is non-eternal; because it is produced; whatever is produced is non-eternal, such as a jar and so forth"—in this manner, the author of the Vārttika employs the proof ending with the example (udāharaṇa) in all cases.
Alternatively, it should be employed starting from the application (upanaya): "Whatever is produced is non-eternal, such as a jar and so forth; and sound is produced; therefore, it is non-eternal."
Even so, the means of proof remains neither deficient nor redundant.

Accordingly, the author of the Bhāṣya employs this very formulation everywhere: "Whatever is an action possesses a fruit; the oblation (homa) is also an action; therefore, it too must possess a fruit.

The defects of the thesis (*pratijñā*), such as contradiction with perception and others, as well as those such as having an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), have been explained in detail in the Vārttika.
There are three defects of the reason (*hetu-doṣa*): non-establishment (*asiddhi*), inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), and sublation (*bādhakatva*).

Among these, non-establishment is fivefold. For example, in the argument "The Buddha is a knower of dharma and adharma because he is omniscient," there is non-establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*).
This is because no such thing as the essential nature of an omniscient being exists.
The establishment of the relation [in the argument] "fire is a non-burner, because it is cold" is impossible, since there is no relation between fire and the state of being a messenger (*dautya*).
[Objection: But in that case, the rising of the moon could not be the cause for the two oceans [swelling], because there is no relation between the rising and the oceans. [Response:
[This is not so,] because both are related to the same time.
O Lord, the theory of inference would entail that the meaning [of the word] is not its own form (svarūpa), by virtue of that very same reason. Furthermore,
when the presentation of the own-form is sublated, the presentation of the object— which has that own-form as its property— is likewise necessarily sublated.

Indeed, it cannot be asserted that there is an apprehension of a different object prior to the grasping of the inclusion [of the reason in the example], precisely because that would contradict experience. In every case, a reason that is restricted by a property of the example as qualified by a specific feature of the sacrifice cannot establish the probandum itself; for, due to the contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the establishment of a subject (*dharmin*) qualified by such a specific feature is impossible. Consequently, the reason—being itself sublated by its own restriction to a contrary specific feature, and because a probandum devoid of specific features is impossible—fails to prove the very thing it is meant to prove.

Just as the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) [of production] with respect to jars and the like—established by the fact that they are produced by an intelligent agent possessing a body—is stated for the purpose of proving that bodies, sprouts, and so forth are also produced by an intelligent agent, it cannot establish that sprouts and the like have an intelligent agent as their cause. This is because such a proof would contradict the non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) of a specific body [in the case of sprouts], and because both conditions [of the reason] are present; furthermore, by that very same reason, a bodiless agent is excluded just as in the case of jars, and since an intelligent being devoid of passion and the like is impossible, the status of having an intelligent agent as cause is not proven for sprouts and the like. Thus, the contradiction of the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣavirodha*) of the reason prevents the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*), which constitutes a logical fallacy (*dūṣaṇa*).

However, a contradiction with a specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣavirodha*) is not a refutation because it does not contradict the probandum (*sādhya*); on the contrary, since it constitutes a refutation of another established tenet, it becomes a refutation for the opponent alone as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), but not for the proponent.

However, as for one who claims that even when there is a contradiction with a specific property of the probandum (sādhyaviśeṣa) in the illustrative instance (dṛṣṭānta), the reason (hetu) indeed establishes the mere probandum devoid of that [contradiction], and that this [probandum] is established by implying another specific property—then for such a person, the sun, which is invariably associated with hot fire, would establish coldness itself when it is perceived on a mountain peak, despite the contradiction with direct perception (pratyakṣa) and the presence of heat. Therefore, the fact that a reason has a specific property as its object is not at all a defect.
There are two kinds of examples: the example based on similarity (sādharmyodāharaṇa) and the example based on dissimilarity (vaidharmyodāharaṇa).

Pointing to the probandum (the possessor of the mark) as the subject, one states the apprehension of the mark-bearer: "Whatever possesses smoke, such as a kitchen and so forth, is observed to possess fire.
And when there is similarity, only similarity should be stated, not dissimilarity, because the latter is already implied.

When it becomes necessary to state it, then, pointing to the absence of the probandum, one states the apprehension of the absence of the mark: "Where fire is absent, there smoke is also absent, as in the case of water and so forth."

Where a positive entity (*bhāva*) is established by means of another positive entity, there the similarity (*sādharmya*) takes the form of an affirmation (*vidhi-rūpa*), and the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) takes the form of a negation (*pratiṣedha-rūpa*).

However, where the absence of rain and so forth is established by means of the absence of clouds and so forth, there the similarity itself takes the form of a negation, as in: "When there is no production of clouds in a certain place, then there is no rain there.
Conversely, the dissimilarity takes the form of an affirmation: "Where there is rain, there is the production of clouds."

Therefore, what was stated by the Bhikṣu— that "dissimilarity (vaidharmya) consists solely in the negation of the counter-example"— is to be disregarded. Furthermore, the fallacies of similarity (sādharmyābhāsa), such as being devoid of the probandum (sādhyavikala), and the fallacies of dissimilarity (vaidharmyābhāsa), such as not being devoid of the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāvāvaikalya), are to be examined in the Vārttika itself.
"However, that [inference] is of two kinds" (Bhāṣya, p. 36).

This statement of its twofold nature is intended to refute those who believe that inference has only the directly perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) as its object, and to demonstrate that inference likewise has as its object the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*), such as action (*kriyā*).

For the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of action is never grasped by perception; what is grasped by perception is merely the conjunction with and disjunction from preceding and succeeding locations.
From those two [the prior and subsequent states] alone, an adventitious desire and an adventitious cause are inferred; and that is called "action" (*kriyā*).
But surely, the substance itself must be the cause? No, because it exists even prior [to the action].

But surely, the substance at another moment is different, since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary? [This objection is not valid], because recognition occurs despite the fact that [the object] is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
When a preceding [moment] begins the succeeding one in the same location, it is characterized as "staying.
But when each preceding [moment] begins the succeeding one in an adjacent location, it is characterized as "going.

Just like the movement of a lamp or the movement of a shadow, because similar successive moments achieve successive locations, they serve as the cause for the appearance of motion; thus, action is established.

Furthermore, since a moment that has not yet arisen is unfit to be the locus of action, and one that has already arisen is seized by destruction, how could it initiate an action? As they say: "All conditioned phenomena are momentary; from where can there be action for those that are unstable?
We shall refute this in the section on *śabda*.
Therefore, since it is untenable [to explain change] by that alone even if stability were granted, the inference of action is logical.
This is not tenable;

for an effect requires only a cause, and that is indeed observed here. For when a result consisting of conjunctions and disjunctions with various locations arises in the body, it is perceived as being produced by a specific effort; therefore, that alone is the efficient cause.

In this case, the conjunction between the self and the body is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and the body is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*); so what is the need here for inferring an unseen cause (*adṛṣṭa*)? If it is argued: "An effect produced by a non-inherent cause occurs either in its own substratum or in that which is inherent in its own substratum, and not elsewhere—for example, a cloth [occurs] in its threads which are its own substrata due to the conjunctions of the threads, or the conjunction of the cloth with the shuttle [occurs] in the shuttle due to the conjunction of the thread with the shuttle. However, how can the conjunction of the self possessing effort (volition) with the body produce a conjunction in the ether (*vyoman*), which is not of this nature? Therefore, another cause must be postulated. [The reply is: No.
The conjunction of threads produces the cloth only in its own substratum, because the cloth pervades many threads, whereas conjunctions occur only between pairs [of substances].
Furthermore, there is the argument from inference based on the conjunction of an arrow and a bowstring.

Due to the impulsion, many actions would arise simultaneously in all the parts of the arrow and so forth, both internal and external; in that case, there would be a deviation [from the rule], because in those parts where there is no contact with the bowstring—namely, those parts which do not rest on the arrow and which are inherent in their own substrates—the contact with the bowstring initiates action.
For those [parts] are not intended to be inherent in the arrow as a whole, since they are inherent in the arrow only insofar as it is composed of them.

Furthermore, immediately after a conjunction of the self with an agentive effort (*prayatnavadātmasaṃyoga*), actions arise simultaneously in the hand—which is conjoined with that self possessing effort—the bracelet which is conjoined with it, and the gem which is attached to it. Now, in such cases as these, the production of action does not result from an impulse (*codanā*) nor from a conjunction of the self with an agentive effort; rather, it is held to result from conjunction with what is already conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*). [This occurs] because of the conjunction of the bowstring with its parts, and from the conjunction of those parts with the next part, and so on to the next.

Likewise, from the conjunction with the self there is motion in the hand; from the conjunction with that [hand] there is motion in the arm; and from the conjunction with that [arm], there is motion in the gem as well.

In that case, it can likewise be argued here: from the conjunction of the self with an effortful [soul] and the conjunction of the body with space, there arises the disjunction of the body from its previous spatial location; and from that [new] conjunction, there follows conjunction with the subsequent location. Thus, since conjunction and disjunction are established through conjunction alone as observed, the postulation of *karman* (action) is not required.
Furthermore, this is not a property of conjunction alone.
All non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) initiate their effect either in their own substrate or in what is inherent in their own substrate, and nowhere else.
Furthermore, action (karma), being inferred as a non-inherent cause (asamavāyi-kāraṇa), would have to be inferred in both [the sky and the bird];
for an effect produced by the action of the bird cannot occur in the sky.
Consequently, the cognition "it moves" would arise even with respect to the sky.
Therefore, action is not an object of inference.
Is it then the case that the reality of action does not exist at all? It does exist, because it is apprehended through perception.
But is there nothing here other than conjunction and disjunction?

For instance, when a snake is moving upon the ground, although there is no difference in the mutual conjunction and disjunction between the two—the earth and the snake—cognition grasps the idea that "everything is moving," yet it does not [grasp] the earth.
Therefore, this cognition must have as its objective basis a reality called "motion" residing in the snake.
It must be admitted that the presence or absence of the cognition "it moves" in relation to the snake and the earth depends respectively on the presence or absence of that [motion].
And it has already been stated that this [inference] cannot be merely inferential.

Therefore, this commentary (beginning with "But that is of two kinds," etc. does not have such an intention; rather, its purpose is to define the scope of inference by stating that inference has both particular and universal objects.

Furthermore, those who maintain that "in the case of a particular there would be the status of a mere atom (an indefiniteness), while in the case of a universal there would be proving what is already established" are refuted by this, because the possibility of a particular is established in both cases as well.
In that regard, when there is a following of a particular [object], it has a particular as its object; however, when there is a following of a universal, it has a universal as its object.

Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*), for this has already been explained previously: namely, that it consists in the grasping of what was not previously seen, which includes other places and other times.
Thus concludes the discussion on inference (*anumāna*).
Śābarabhāṣya, Tarkapāda, pp. 64–71.
Oṃ. Because inference is established, the [Veda] would be authoritative in connection with that.
The authority of practices is accepted on the basis of clear inference.
By whatever reason they are considered authoritative, by that very reason they deserve to be established as such.

Therefore, the *holākā* and other such rites must be performed by Easterners alone; those beginning with the *āhnīnebuka* by Southerners alone; and those beginning with the Northerners by Northerners alone.
In this regard, Prabhākara has described the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) as follows for the sake of establishing a connection:
Since the practice [of the easterners] is known by the easterners and others, it is logical that this very tradition (*āgama*) is the basis, just like the words "easterner" and so forth.

As for the words "easterner" and the rest, because their specific meanings are not determined due to their being established differently by various groups, an injunction (*codanā*) containing such words is not fixed and is therefore not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: this would indeed be the case if the injunction were inferred as possessing terms such as "eastern" and so forth; but rather, it refers generally to all rites such as the *Holikā* and the like.
And since that [general injunction] is restricted [to specific regions], there is no lack of authority.
This [position of yours], however, is inconsistent.

Is this injunction—containing terms such as "this," "what is it?," "half," "meaning," and "east"—unauthoritative because it cannot be postulated as the source [of the practice] due to the impossibility of synthesizing it through cognition? Or, if it is postulated, is it authoritative? If it is not authoritative simply because it is not postulated, then what contradiction is there? But if it is said that it is not authoritative because it is postulated, that is incoherent;
for it is impossible to postulate an injunction as the source of a practice without the synthesis of a cognition.
And once it has been so postulated, the formal discussion (*adhikaraṇa*) is introduced.
Having examined the specific detail pertaining to *smṛti* in the preceding section, the specific detail pertaining to *ācāra* (customary practice) is now considered.

Here, the intention of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) argument is as follows: since practices such as the *holākā* are observed only in connection with specific regions such as the East, the *śruti* (Vedic injunction) inferred for that region implies that the *holākā* and other such practices must be performed by the people of the East and so forth alone; thus, a specific scriptural rule (*viśeṣaśruti*) itself is inferred.
As it has been said: "Because it resides in another location, it is appropriate only for that [specific] region."
It is cognized.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the grounds for the application of words such as "eastern" (*prācya*) are themselves unstable, it is impossible to infer a fixed specific scriptural statement [regarding them].
For instance, there exists no universal (*jāti*) such as "easternness" (*prācyatva*), comparable to the universal "Brahminhood" (*brāhmaṇatva*).

Furthermore, being born in a region such as the East is not the cause for the fixed rule [of ritual practice], because even those born in the East who have gone to another country perform the *holākā* and other rites,
such as the *jambhālīlā*, while those yet to be mentioned are observed to follow the custom of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
Nor is there a restriction based on residence in regions such as the East;
for it is established that [the vision occurs] in the fourth [dhyāna] alone, so nothing is untenable.
The purpose [of this teaching] is the prior cause, because even those from other lands who reside in that land possess that vision.

According to the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), the *holākā* and other such rites should be performed only by those belonging to the eastern regions and so forth; however, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), they must be performed by all. For this very reason, factors such as being from a region of black soil or having red eyes do not serve as grounds for restriction. The Sūtra states: "The *holākā* and other rites [are to be performed] with all properties," because deviation [from regional restrictions] is observed among all people.
It is said:
It may be so.

Even though there is a deviation for each individual regarding the injunctions for rituals such as the *holākā* which establish that [the ritual] is a universal duty (*sarvadharma*), there is nonetheless a commonality among those from the East and other regions.
"Because it is logical" (nyāyavattvāt). According to the Tautātitas, there exists something common to the performance of all [rituals]; that alone shall be the cause of the restriction.
Therefore, since the determination of inference is based on the very name itself as a cause for established inference,
the means of knowledge associated with it would pertain only to a specific person connected with that name.
This may be so.
This being the case, it is replied:
now [the injunction] would apply to all dharmas, because that is the logical principle of its application.

The local customs (*deśacārāḥ*) of the Easterners consist of the *holakā* festival and so forth; those of the Southerners include the *nasya* and the *āhīnaivuka* and so forth; and those of the Northerners include the *uddava* and the *bhayaścā* and so forth. What is the intended meaning of these?
This might be so, if there were here a designation such as "eastern" and so forth.
In the deliberation as to whether these are the properties of those [specific individuals] alone or of all [of them], he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*):
there would be a cause for restriction.
For that [Smṛti], while operating as the Pāṇinian tradition,
functions in four ways in the removal of Smṛti when it serves as a mark (*liṅga*) that becomes the cause for the inferential cognition of Śruti. To explain,
its connection—

Because of the establishment of conduct (*ācāra*), which is established according to the difference of regions, [the following suffixes apply]: *so’sya nivāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.93), *tatra bhavaḥ* (4.3.53), *tatra jātaḥ* (4.3.25)—wherein the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) brought down by that conduct is connected with it—and *tata āgataḥ* (4.3.74). It should indeed be connected with the word [denoting] that very region.
‘They should perform the Holākā and other rites’: [the word] ‘āhī’ [indicates this].

For that purpose, there is the meaning: he dwells in the east, he stands in the east; the southerners should perform the Naivuka—such scriptural authority (śruti) is to be inferred. One who is born in the east, or has come from the east, is called ‘Prācya’.
Thus it has been said:
the meaning is that "a designation of place indeed proceeds by means of many types of connections."
‘By means of their dwelling, their birth from existence, and the causes for their arrival. (Vākyapadīya 1)
Alternatively, it may apply to all dharmas, because that is the logical principle (tannyāyatvāt). Even so, the designation (samākhyā) does not establish a fixed restriction.

The word "kāraṇa" (reason) [is used] because even for one born in the South who resides in the East, [the practice would persist]. The word "api vā" (or rather) is intended to refute the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
[The term] "holakādi" (the Holākā festival, etc. refers to all such practices, because the performance of the Holākā and other rites is observed [everywhere].

Now, if it were not the case that the dharma designated as "southern" (dākṣiṇātya) is the dharma for people residing in all directions— even in the absence of a specific injunction— because we observe the performance of the Āhīnavuka sacrifice [by others];
or if it is not so...
Because that is logical.
A "vidhāna" (prescriptive rule) is a word by which something is enjoined.
The designation based on the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) is the cause [of the application], but—

The principle that brings about all such phenomena (*sarvadharma*) is as follows: it is said that the worldly designation (*samākhyā*), which is entirely unrestricted (*ucchṛṅkhalā*) regarding its application to all objects, serves as the cause (*nimitta*). Thus, "the state of being that principle" (*tannyāyatvam*) refers to the existence of that principle within a particular conceptual framework (*kalpa*), a ritual injunction (*vidhāna*), or an enjoining statement (*vidhāyakavākya*). This applies even to a Southerner (*dākṣiṇātya*) who possesses a conventional name such as "Holāka" derived from the East (*prācya*) and so forth.
That is the principle; the state of being that is "the state of being that principle."

What occasion would there be for the performance [of a rite] according to the injunction? Therefore, since there is no cause for restriction, and because the logic applies equally to the easterners and others, the injunctive sentence must have universal scope; furthermore, it would entail the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) containing the word "holākā" and so forth.
The meaning is that all phenomena would begin with the letter *ka*.
An authoritative scripture (*śruti*) that establishes [the necessity of] what ought to be done is inferred;
as for that which some [hold to be] non-existent—
Thinking "this alone is to be performed," the performance [of it] is the performance of others;
its application [to those others] would arise from mere observation.
That is based solely on delusion.
And this generality is indeed perceived directly.

Now, just as some are established as having three tufts of hair (*triśikha*) while others have five tufts (*pañcaśikha*), even regarding actions prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, some perform them while others do not; likewise, practices such as the *Holikā* festival belong to some, while they belong to others in different ways.

If it is asked: "Just as [the rites] are performed even when the procedure is common [to all], why should they not likewise apply specifically to those situated in Varanasi and other such places?"—we reply: No, because the application is established by the observation of the Smṛti text: "He places the stone of the lineage and the *pravara*."

Or [one who is] from Bhava, or born in Mathurā, or come from Mathurā is called a Māthura. In that same manner, those with three ancestral lineages (tri-pravara) place three tufts of hair (tri-śikhā), and those with five ancestral lineages (pañca-pravara) place five tufts of hair (pañca-śikhā).

Therefore, it is logical that the determination [of usage] is based on designation (*samākhyā*). However, in the case of the *holākā* festival and the like, there is no such thing as [a fixed] practice (*ācāra*).
The very nature of all phenomena is the authority [for this],
because there is no mark (liṅga) for that which is eternal;
or else, it is a property of action, like a downward slope.
"Is it not the case that largeness, dark complexion, red eyes, and so forth—belonging to those residing in various respective regions—are the marks of the agent? The opponent replies:

In the regulation of practices such as the *holākā*, the characteristic of the agent will establish the restriction of the practices to specific regions, as these are properties of the ritual action."
The location might be the cause.
If it is argued that "it is that location which consists mostly of black soil," we say no;
for the mark of an agent is established as being eternal and distinct from any particular location.
"Of Āhīnavuka," and so forth.
Just as with "sloping toward the east" (*prācīnapravaṇa*), because [the quality] does not exist [everywhere],
qualities such as largeness, blackness, and the like are also not restricted to specific locations.

Because there is no specific indicative mark (*liṅga*) such as "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva" [implying a fixed location] or "a place sloping toward the east" for the obligatory (*nitya*) Vaiśvadeva, the *holākā* and other such rites are not restricted [to specific regions];
rather, like that [obligatory rite], they are auxiliary to the ritual action (*karmāṅga*), and thus their properties are common to all.
However, they are indeed properties of all [Dharma].
For [the designation] arises from connection with a place;
however, this is equal to the case of a property of the agent.
But is it not a conventional designation, such as "southerners" or "northerners"?
The proponent (siddhāntin) says:

By means of the previously mentioned qualities such as largeness and blackness, he will establish the practices (ācāra), such as the Holākā festival, as restricted by differences of region. If it is argued that this status of the region as having action as its property is equal to the property of the agent—that is, it is not [established]—we say no.

For indeed, a designation such as "Dākṣiṇātya" (a Southerner) and so forth is a conventional name (*samākhyā*). It is a designator because it arises from a connection with a region, due to its being practiced by those residing in that region.

Furthermore, a certain person from the South is called "Southern" (dākṣiṇātya) precisely because of his practice of that [custom]. Therefore, customs such as the *holākā* rite become established for all people, whether they come from the region or having previously gone eastward or northward.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In that regard, the *holākā* is well known;
and as for the *āhīnaivuka*, he indeed performs the *āhīnaivuka*.
Therefore, even by way of designation,
there is the worship of the specific lunar day according to family custom;
and for those who maintain their practice, there is the establishment of conduct out of fear of transgression.

However, customs such as the Holākā festival are *sarvadharmas* (universal duties). [The question is whether] they should be performed by those who perform the practice of worship, white rites (*śukla*), and so forth;
the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they indeed should be performed.
[This refers to] the term *veṇḍura* (in the vernacular).
Why would it not be so even in another region?
For it has been stated in the *Siddhānta* that names such as "Dākṣiṇātya" (Southerner) and the like arise from association with a particular region.
There is an absence of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of an inferred statement;
for the followers of Saṃkarṣaṇa, that [absence] appears logical there,
provided that the name [is derived] from conjunction with a location.

2|3|4. In an inferred sentence, because the specific location is not a defect, that designation [of "sentence"] would exist even in another location when that agent has departed, since it is the compound word itself that is to be inferred. It would be so.

However, even for one residing in another country, there is no lack of connection to Mathurā; rather, through this [connection], there occurs the acquisition of its function, as in: "One should not say 'gir' for 'giri'; it should be 'gaira'. Thus, the designation "Māthura" is applied because of the conjunction with that place.
Therefore, the name arises from the conjunction with the region.
This is the introduction. Here, if the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) should say, "When the word-meaning is understood, its effect is accomplished," [the reply is:
that which is desired is obtained.

Where [there is] one after-offering (anuyāja), up to as many after-offerings as there may be.

And likewise, because it is more powerful than that which is applied by context (*prakaraṇa*) as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*). Bhaṭṭa says: "Is this final after-offering (*anuyāja*) a remote auxiliary, or is it a consecration (*saṃskṛti*) like the *sviṣṭakṛt*, on account of its similarity to other after-offerings?"

Because the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of Agni as possessing the quality of being the *Sviṣṭakṛt* is purposeful, and because it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), there must be a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for another [Agni] who possesses progeny. (Bhāṭṭa)— In the *anuyājas* of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the third *anuyāja* has Agni Sviṣṭakṛt as its deity.

In considering whether this [Sviṣṭakṛt offering] is for the purpose of purifying the deity of the *āvāpika* Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice—which is a subsidiary act (*pratipatti*) of the remainder—or whether it is a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*) like the other *anuyāja* offerings, since both are understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*) to be subsidiaries of the Darśa sacrifice, there is no evidence for mutual subsidiarity; thus, it is a remote auxiliary. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: since a visible result is possible, it is improper to assume an invisible one; therefore, it is indeed for the purpose of purifying its own deity.

Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*), because the act of insertion finds its purpose solely through the sentence itself as the means for understanding the remainder; furthermore, since even the portion consisting of the abandonment (*tyāga*) depends upon the substance employed by the primary rite, its status as a subsidiary to the primary rite is understood even without a specific context (*prakaraṇa*).

As for what was stated in the *Śabdadīpikā*—that it finds its purpose through the attainment of the intended deity—that has been disregarded because, although the mantra effects the attainment of the intended deity, in the sacrifice it is the *Apūrva* [transcendental result] alone that enjoins Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt as the deity; thus, the portion consisting of the dedication (*uddeśa*) lacks the nature of being a means for recollecting the intended deity.
Nor should it be argued that even so, since the deity mentioned in the mantra is also perceived as a divinity in the *uttama-nuyāja*,

and since that [deity] lacks the status of being a divinity for the *āvāpika-sviṣṭakṛt* offering, how can [the latter] serve the purpose of consecrating that deity? For, by the statement cited by the author of the Bhāṣya— “He sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt”— which prescribes the deity just as in “He sacrifices to Viṣṇu,” the deity mentioned in the mantra is established as having the status of a divinity.
The practice of the ritualists (yājñikācāra) is rooted in disregard for this [scriptural authority].
For it has been stated in the *Kaustubha* that the authority of the deity [derived from the second case ending] is not weaker than that derived from the wording of the mantra (*mantravarṇa*).

Therefore, since the *uttama-anuyāja* is for the purpose of consecrating the deities of the *āvāpika-sviṣṭakṛt*, where there is an oblation consisting of only a single *palala* measure, there is an omission of that *āvāpika-sviṣṭakṛt*.
In that case, there is an omission of the final *anuyāja*.

Or, where the fire is the *kavyavāhana* [carrier of offerings to the ancestors] and *Sviṣṭakṛt* is the deity of the *āvāpika-sviṣṭakṛt*, even at the final *anuyāja*, there is a modification (*ūha*) of the mantra beginning with: "The divine Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, possessor of good wealth, the wise sage... and so forth; and in the act of renunciation (*tyāga*), the reference must likewise be made to him.
The ritualists (*yājñikāḥ*), however, do not act in this manner; the basis for that must be considered.
Maṇḍana: "The *anuyāja* is a subordinate element (*guṇa*) of the *sviṣṭakṛt*. Śaṅkara: "But the other *anuyāja* is a consecratory act (*saṃskriyā*)."

22. Regarding the *anuyāja* offerings, the time for their performance is prescribed by the rule: "They should be performed after the *āgnimāruta* [section]. However, this time would be merely *anuṣakta* (accidental or secondary), because it is connected with a specific purpose. The Commentary states: In the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is heard [in scripture]: "They proceed with the *anuyāja* offerings after the *āgnimāruta*; having cast away the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he offers the *hāriyojana*."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is it the fire that is enjoined, or is it the time? If the fire were enjoined, it would be a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*); if the time were enjoined, it would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, it is an injunction of an auxiliary (*aṅga*).
This being the position reached, we reply:
in the sentence concerning the *anuṣatti*, it should be a matter of time.
The *āgnimāruta* is an auxiliary of the Soma sacrifice, while the *anuyājas* are auxiliaries of the animal sacrifice.
In that case, there is no mutual connection between the two.
Likewise, the *paricaya* is a subsidiary part of the animal sacrifice (*paśvaṅga*), while the *hāriyojana* offering is the primary rite itself.

The *anuyāja* offerings and the *āgnimāruta* recitation have been established as occurring [after the animal sacrifice]; their immediate sequence is thus established, and the same applies to the *hāriyojana* and the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhipraharaṇa*).

And this being the case, no benefit whatsoever is conferred upon the *hāriyojana* by the striking of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), nor is the *hāriyojana* itself [benefited] by the striking of the enclosing sticks. Now, it might be argued that it is said that the striking of the enclosing sticks confers benefit from above. However, the striking of the enclosing sticks cannot be permitted for the sake of being "above."
This indeed exists for the sake of the animal;
and since that exists, its state of being above it also certainly exists.
Therefore, the connection is for the purpose of time.
*Soma*: The connection [of this section] is established because, as before, there is an objection that this also concerns the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*).

As for the purpose: in the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), which consists of an injunction for a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*), the *anuyāja* offerings must be performed at their own time for the sake of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice, since they are distinct from the *āgnimāruta* [offering].

In the second *pūrvapakṣa*, which consists of an injunction regarding the relationship between the subsidiary and its purpose, since the *anuyāja* offerings—which are obtained through the general rule (*codaka*)—are enjoined after the *āgnimāruta* [offering], the *anuyāja* offerings do not exist for the sake of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice; consequently, the *anuyāja* offerings are absent in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*).

In the Siddhānta, however, because the injunction in the form of a connection for the purpose of time (*kālārthasaṃyogavidhi*) prescribes the time after the *agnimāruta* [offering] for the sake of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice, there is neither a separate performance of the *anuyāja*s at their own time, nor is there an absence of *anuyāja*s in the modifications (*vikṛti*s) of the *savanīya*. Rather, that connection is for the purpose of time. As for the meaning of the Sūtra: in the sentence concerning the *agnimāruta*, there is no attainment of the ritual action (*karmānupatti*) [as a primary injunction], but rather it is the time for the *anuyāja*s. 423. Regarding the *anuyāja*s...
It would be so, because the *anuyāja* offerings are enjoined for the purpose of carrying the fire (*agnimāruta*) immediately following their own performance. [Objection:
"Should one perform the *anuyāja*s after the *āgnimāruta*? [Reply:
It must be a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), for otherwise it would be a time (*kāla*), since being for the sake of another implies subordination.

Just as the Soma sacrifice was previously known [to follow] the Āgnimāruta [śastra], so too are the after-offerings (anuyājas) intended for the animal sacrifice; their conjunction serves to establish the proper time.
Question: In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is prescribed that the after-offerings intended for the Savanīya animal sacrifice must occur after the Āgnimāruta; regarding this, the following deliberation arises.

Bhaṭṭa: It is heard in scripture: "Having thrown the enclosing sticks (paridhi), he offers the Hāriyojana oblation," and "After the Āgnimāruta section, they proceed with the after-offerings (anuyāja).

In this context, the throwing (*praharaṇa*) is a purificatory act for the enclosing sticks, as indicated by the accusative case. And although the enclosing sticks themselves do not constitute the Soma sacrifice, they are nevertheless established as such because they are included among the Savanīya offerings which are parts of that sacrifice; thus, they possess a result.

Consequently, even though this [Hāriyojana] is not the original injunction (*utpattivākya*) for the Hāriyojana itself, since no result is heard in its own original injunction, it serves as the disposal (*praharaṇa*) of the enclosing sticks.

Although this [offering] belongs exclusively to the Soma sacrifice, nevertheless, its status as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the throwing of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi-praharaṇa*)—even while other repetitions serve purposes such as heaven—is not contradicted by the repetition performed on account of the interruption (*apaccheda*) of the Udgātṛ.

Similarly, in the second sentence, although the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are not mentioned in the context of the Soma sacrifice, they are indeed fruitful as being subordinate parts of the *savanīya* sacrifice within that context.

For as long as it would take to assume [the connection] through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the status of the after-offerings as subordinate parts of the *āgnimāruta* [rite] is established by the direct statement (*vākya*) itself.

Nor is there any need here to postulate a separate word for the *vaimṛdha*, because it is logically established as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by virtue of being a qualification of the time which itself is an auxiliary.

Furthermore, the statement in the *Mūla* (Tantravārttika) that "since the *vaimṛdha* is not mentioned in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), and since the requirement for a result exists in the originative injunction, its status as an auxiliary is postulated through the context (*prakaraṇa*)" is not tenable; for even if that requirement exists in the originative injunction, once a general desirable end (*iṣṭasāmānya*) has been accepted as the object to be accomplished, the application (*viniyoga*) can be established by another sentence, making it illogical to postulate an auxiliary status based on a weaker means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

This being the case, first, as for the *hāriyojana* offering, since its fruit—consisting of heaven and so forth—is already established by the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself, there is no evidence for its being a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *praharaṇa* through the assumption of another word (*padāntara-kalpanā*) by virtue of its being a *vaimṛdhavat*.

As for the *āgnimāruta* chant, although its entirety is not established by a specific syntactical statement (*vākya*), nevertheless, since the entirety can be established solely through the force of the detailed application of indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "The *agniṣṭoma* has twelve *śastras*," it is improper to assume its entirety on the basis of a syntactical statement.

In reality, however, by this sentence there is no injunction of the *āgnimāruta* [offering] as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the *anuyāja*s, because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) between the injunction for those following the *prātaranuvāka* and the injunction for the *āgnimāruta*. Furthermore, even for the ancient authorities who maintain mutual connection [between words], there would be the fault of the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of assuming an injunction for a qualifier.
Therefore, in the expression "after the *āgnimāruta*," the two words denote by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) the time subsequent to that [rite].
Thus, [the act] is enjoined with reference to the *anuyāja* offerings.

However, in cases such as "having sacrificed with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s," one should understand that there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) because the word ending in the third case (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām*) is construed with the word *iṣṭvā*.

In reality, however, there is no *lakṣaṇā* even in the present case; for, just as in the case of "that [sacrifice] with four [verses]," even when a qualified *bhāvanā* (efficient force) is understood, the injunction results in the enjoining of the mere upwardness (*ūrdhva*), and thus there is no multiplicity of things to be enjoined.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: according to the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the *agnimāruta* hymns are to be performed at the *hāriyojana* offering—which is a modification of the *savanīya* and is not an integral part of the Soma sacrifice; according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), they are not. Maṇḍana states: "The mention of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) is for the sake of its own specific time."

15. Śaṅkara: “In the case of the Āgnimāruta [offering], there should be a combination with the *āmana* and *anumantraṇa* formulas taught for the *sāṃgameṣṭi*, along with the *atideśika* (extended) *anuyāja* offerings. (Bhāṣya 10.4.14).
When there is a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), there is a displacement of the section beginning with the after-offerings.

(10.4.12) 23–24. Since the rule for the time of the after-offerings—which serve the purpose of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice—is that they must occur after the *āgnimāruta* [offering], they are not to be performed separately at their own time; nor is there an absence of after-offerings in the modifications (*vikṛti*) of the *savanīya*. (Soma. 4.3.15) Regarding the injunction for non-pause (*anavāna*) during the after-offerings, it should not be restricted to the final after-offering alone, because it is common to all three.
*Saṃkarṣa* 4.3.15:
Among the eleven *anuyāja* offerings, four are modifications of the *barhis*, four are of the *narāśaṃsa*, and the ninth and eleventh are of the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
The statement, "He performs eleven *anuyāja*s," expresses a number pertaining to the performance (*prayoga*).
Among those, there is the optional attainment of each of the three original (prākṛta) properties; for such is seen in the case of a modification of the Āgneya sacrifice.
This being the prima facie view, [the conclusion is reached] by the principle "it should be equal" (10.3.13–53), which distinguishes the relationship between the original and its modification.

For in the science of mathematics (*gaṇitaśāstra*), when an equal division is impossible, a division is stated according to the circumstances by either adding one (*saikīkṛtya*) or subtracting one (*niraikīkṛtya*). Similarly, here too, even though [the portions] are independent, since an equal division by three is impossible, there is an addition of one. In the fourfold division, there are four modifications each for the *barhis* and *narāśaṃsa*; the remaining [portions] belong to the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
Thus, there is an extension (*atideśa*) from that context only to those [mantras] ending with the respective invocations and protections.
(Saṃkarṣa.)

Regarding the after-offerings (anuyājas): [Section] 424, the half-verse on the after-offerings. In the after-offerings, the injunction "Sacrifice to the gods" (devān yaja) is indeed common to all three [after-offerings].

In the *anuyāja* offerings, the injunction "yajña devān" (sacrifice to the gods) is prescribed; however, this refers exclusively to the *barhis* sacrifice, because a different injunction, "yaja yaja" (sacrifice, sacrifice), is prescribed for the *narāśaṃsa* and *triṣṭupka*. The plural number, moreover, is intended to express the plurality of the objects.
Because it is seen to be so in the *uparava* mantras;
for if it were for all purposes, since the two *praiṣas* occurring simultaneously could not be combined, the result would be an option (*vikalpa*).
This being the position reached, the purpose of the *praiṣa* is indeed common to all three.

Because the *uparava* mantras are enjoined as the instruments (*karaṇa*) [of the action], and since plurality is possible for each individual *uparava*, even though the plural number might not be intended [in other contexts], here the plural number is indeed possible; this is because of the sequence of [mantras] suitable for that, according to the principle of the "grass-starter" (*tṛṇārambhiṇī*). Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the combination (*samuccaya*) of even those [mantras] that are directly contributive (*saṃnipātinaḥ*), according to the maxim of the grass-starter.
This is because it will be explained in the sixteenth [book] that after stating generally, "Bring the gods for the sacrificer," one then states the particulars, such as, "Bring Agni."

For this very reason, another Śruti passage is consistent: "Having said, 'Sacrifice to the gods,' he says, 'The meters are indeed the gods; thus he sacrifices to the meters. When he sacrifices to Agni Āgnīdhra, he sacrifices to the Gāyatrī; when he sacrifices to Narāśaṃsa, he sacrifices to the Triṣṭubh; when he sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, he sacrifices to the Jagatī. By this, the statement "he performs two insufficient after-sacrifices (anuyājas)" is explained. Since the *barhis* sacrifice lacks the *yejyā* formula, the direction for Narāśaṃsa results from both the modification (*ūha*) and the combination (*samuccaya*) of the formulas "O goddess, sacrifice, sacrifice" and "O Narāśaṃsa, sacrifice. (Saṃkarṣa 2.3.1). In the after-sacrifices, the prohibition of the *yejyā* formula is by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

Regarding the two statements, "I perform the *yejyā* [offering] in the *anuyājas*" and "I perform the *yejyā* in the *yajatis*," there is a unity of intent; thus, by means of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), the performance is understood as: "The *yejyā* is to be performed in those *yajatis* that are distinct from the *anuyājas*.
(Vi. 10.8.2). In all *anuyājas*, there is indeed no *anavāna* (pausal breath), not merely in the last one.
Regarding the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), it is heard in scripture: "He offers without taking breath.
In another scriptural passage, it is heard: "He should breathe out at the last one.

In that case, there is an application (*upasaṃhāra*) of the *praiṣa* (direction) and the non-breathing to the last [offering] by virtue of the sequence of the after-offerings as handed down in the tradition.

This being the case, the statement "uttamena" (with the last) does not possess the status of a restrictive rule (*upasaṃhāra*), because it lacks the character of a specific injunction (*viśeṣavidhi*) due to its being a mere restatement (*anuvādakatva*).
The Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) also maintains that the word "anuvāda" in the Sūtra must be understood in this sense.

Since there is no fixed rule regarding the omission of breath (*anavāna*) between the *barhis* and *narāśaṃsa* offerings—given that such omission occurs only occasionally when they are not explicitly mentioned—the non-omission of breath is here enjoined as a restrictive rule.

Since the *sviṣṭakṛt* offerings, the *anuyāja* offerings, and the *yājyā* verses are excessively long, it would necessarily follow that one must recite them without pausing (*anavāna*) in the middle; therefore, this is prohibited.
Consequently, because they pertain to different subjects and consist of the nature of a prescription and a prohibition respectively, there can be no sublation of one by the other.

Even this being the case, although one who practices breath-control (*prāṇābhyāsa*) might occasionally fail to obtain [the result] even during a long sacrifice, the status of this as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*)—on the grounds of its occasional applicability (*pākṣikaprāpti*), just like the injunction "one should tie the animal to the *paridhi* post"—is possible even in the case of the third after-offering (*anuyāja*) and cannot be refuted.

Therefore, by explicitly restating the figurative *anavāna* (non-pause), which is already established by the principle "one should recite once; even so, [it should be] without pause," the Śruti—through the injunction "he sacrifices without pausing" (*anavānaṃ yajati*)—interprets the term *anavāna* as applicable to both the figurative and the primary senses. Consequently, the injunction accepts the three *anuyāja* offerings as its scope.

Thus, since this is already established by that [injunction], the prohibition [of pausing] is incapable of being restricted to them merely because of the restatement (*anuvāda*); such is the intention.
(Saṃkarṣa.)

1.1.3.16–54: In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the rule "he performs the *anuyāja*s with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*)" prescribes *pṛṣadājya*, which is distinct for each individual *anuyāja*. 10.1.6.17.64: In the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the quality of *pṛṣadājya* prescribed by the rule "he performs the *anuyāja* with *pṛṣadājya*" is distinct for each individual *anuyāja*.
10|16|17|64. In the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are modified by way of time and quality.
*Ṭup.* 1|2|1|12. In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the clarified butter held in the *aupabhṛta* ladle serves as the portion for the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings.
*Bhā.* (Bhāṣya).
The distinction of *anurajhaka* (425): the sacrifice following the *vaṣaṭkāra*.

The distinction of *anurajhaka* implies a distinction of *anurajhaka*, because there is no cognition of exclusion from another *bhāvanā* without a separation of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) from the *bhāvanā*; for it would follow that there is a contradiction with the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of a single *bhāvanā*, and thus it is impossible for multiple *anurajhakas* to coexist within a single *bhāvanā*.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 704). As for that which is called *anurūpa*, it refers to the *ṛk* beginning with "dvitīyayā" in the *bahiṣpavamāna* of the Jyotiṣṭoma, and so forth; this is a *daivata-stotra*.
The first is named *pratipad*, while the third is named *paryāpta*;
this is the designation used by ritualists (*yājñika*) for the *anuvacana* recitations belonging to the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ priest).
In that context, the *anuvacanas* (recitations) when performed separately belong to the *hotṛ*, whereas the combined *praiṣa-anuvacana* (direction and recitation) belongs to the *maitrāvaruṇa*.
(Vi. 3.1.21). There is a designation as *hautra* (belonging to the *hotṛ*) for all *anuvacanas*.
(Vā. 3.1.21.43). Among the *anuvacanas*, the agency of the *maitrāvaruṇa* applies only to those ending with a *praiṣa*.
Bhāṣya 3.7.2.143–45: In the *anuvacana*s, the Maitrāvaruṇa is a modification of the Hotṛ.
10.7.16.19: The place for the prescription of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is for the purpose of the *anuvacana*s.
The *anuvaṣaṭkāra*.
When the Adhvaryu performs the oblation of Soma, the Hotṛ recites the *yājyā*; at the end of the *yājyā*, the *vaṣaṭ* call is uttered.
Immediately thereafter, the Hotṛ recites the mantra "O Agni, enjoy the Soma," and then the Adhvaryu offers the remaining Soma once more.
This mantra is called the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*.
The deity of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is Agni. (Vi. 3.1.16).
The injunction for the sacrifice of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*. Section 426: The Topic of the *Anuvaṣaṭkāra*.
Like a section (anuvāka), there is the recitation of the invitatory verses (anuvākyā);
this will be explained in the first section of the Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa under the rule "it is enjoined" (vidhīyate). Kū. 3.2.16.35.

And because [the deity] cannot be obtained [elsewhere], therefore even in a modified sacrifice (vikṛti), it is by the very deity of the primary sacrifice. Om. This is the rule for the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* sacrifice.
Those who have entered into that state of being its effect (the *vaṣaṭ*-offering) are to be indicated [as the deity], not the deity of the *anuvaṣaṭ*-offering.

For it is heard in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: "He performs the after-offering with the mantra, 'O Agni, eat of the Soma. Maṇḍana says: "But she [the deity] is not to be indicated in the sacrifice performed with the *vaṣaṭ*-call."
In this sentence, there is an injunction for the mantra with reference to the Soma sacrifice.
By the word "iti," [it indicates] the instrument;
Śaṅkara says: "At the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* of the deity..."
It should not be raised.
By the word *anu*, there is the mention of a subsequent effect.
"Oṃ, like an *anuvāka*": for that which is spoken of as "three *anuvākas*" [is so called].

When it is thus established that either the recitation of the mantra after the sacrifice (*yāgottaramanumantraṇa*) is enjoined, or [the mantra] is to be recited during the sacrifice itself— [the opponent says]:
"Let it be recited," and having begun from the beginning and completed it, he [recites it] again.

For another sacrifice that has been established, there would be the prescription of the pair of *anuvākyā* verses at a time subsequent to the Soma sacrifice, and thus the qualities of standing and sitting would be enjoined.
VI. 10|4|22. There is an option between two pairs of *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras in the rite dedicated to Indra and Bṛhaspati.
One pair is: "This oblation is for you both"—"O Indra and Bṛhaspati, [this is] dear"; the other is: "This Soma remains for you both"—"O Indra and Bṛhaspati.
Bhāṣya 12|4|2–4. The Section on the *Anuvākyā*.

3|1|123. A contradiction of the sequence by the sentence is observed, because the *ajñāvatāra*—which had been set aside by the section on the prohibition of warding off (*vāraṇādhikaraṇa*)—is revived by the section on the *anuvākyā* (see "the *vācanī-adhikaraṇa*," Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 1072). Following the *anuvākyā*, the Hotṛ's recitation continues up to the *yājyā*.
"One should not speak out against the *yājyā* and the *anuvākyā*.
(Saṃkarṣa).
A sound is perceived from afar as a repeated utterance (*anuvāda*).
Bhāṣya 1.1.6.23, p. 80: An explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) that does not produce a specific modification in activity would be purposeless.
Bhāṣya 7.3.7; 8.4. *Anuṣaṅga* (syntactic connection), section 430: The Section on Syntactic Connection (*anuṣaṅgādhikaraṇa*).
That by which one might supply a word by ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*)—

if, however, one should desire to employ ellipsis solely for the purpose of avoiding a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), he may indeed do so. But in that case, because of the injunction of the term "having performed" (*caritvā*), it would follow that the performance of the *upasad* rites must continue as far as the ellipsis extends.

And this is undesirable because there is no syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with the Veda. Now, if it were argued that the fulfillment of all requirements is achieved by performing the *agnihotra* itself first, then—in that case—the utterance of the words would likewise remain situated as such, assisting [the ritual] in accordance with the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) of the *agnihotra* and other rites; thus, there would be no need for *anuṣaṅga*. (Vārttika 2.3.124, pp. 614–15). *Anuṣaṅga* is not applicable to a *ṛk* mantra, as established in the section on Mantras (*Mantrādhikaraṇa*).

In the verse "amyak sā ta indra," in the subsequent verse "laṃ tū na indra" and "taṃ ryaṃ dāḥ," that [phrase] is to be understood as being supplied by *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation); thus, this is a case of *pūrvānuṣaṅga* (supplementation from what precedes).
Bāla. pṛ. 60. *Anuṣaṅga* is of two kinds: *anuṣaṅga* and *anukarṣa*.
*Anuṣaṅga* is the supplementation of what precedes after what follows, and *anukarṣa* is the supplementation of what follows before what precedes.
*Anuṣaṅga* (supplementation): This refers to the supplementation from another proximate location.
*Maṇiprabhā*, p. 71. Regarding the *anuṣaṅga*:

"May your breath unite with the wind, your limbs with the joints, and the lord of glory with the blessing. Here, because the middle mantra is unsuitable to be connected with the plural form "limbs" (*aṅgāni*), and because the mental proximity (*buddhi-sannidhāna*) is interrupted by that [middle mantra], there is no *anuṣaṅga*.
VI. 2|3|188. *Anuṣaṅga* (supplying an ellipsis) is of two kinds according to another classification: by the requirement of the principal (*śeṣin*) and by the requirement of the subordinate (*śeṣa*).
Examples of the former are "ayāśayā rajāśayā harāśayā" and so forth;
examples of the latter are "citpatistvā punātu vicchidreṇa pavitreṇa" and so forth.
*Ke.*: *Anuṣaṅga* (supplying a word from a previous context) is the act of utterance at the time of explanation, even for that which has been stated only once.

*Su.*, p. 170. Even when one among several expectant [sentences] has been rendered free of expectancy through connection with a single supplement (*śeṣa*), *anuṣaṅga* is improper due to mutual expectancy.
p. 695. By means of *anuṣaṅga*, *adhyāhāra* (supplementation of a missing word) is set aside.
As in "O Agni, that [mantra] of yours which dwells in the dust" (*yā te agne rajāśayā*), and so forth (Bāla. pṛ. 144). Through *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation), an injunction becomes an injunction.
There is *anuṣaṅga* from before (*purastāt-anuṣaṅga*) and *anuṣaṅga* from after (*parastāt-anuṣaṅga*).

Among these, the first is as follows: "If a Brāhmaṇa should win, having placed the Vāīspatya [cup] in the middle, he should offer oblation after oblation and dedicate this [conquest] to him; if a Rājanya, [he should dedicate it] to Indra; if a Vaiśya, to the Viśvedevas.
Here, the phrase "having placed in the middle" and so forth is supplied after "to Indra" and "to the Viśvedevas.
The second is as follows: "Now this is the Jyotis; now this is the Viśvajyotis; now this is the Sarvajyotis; with this, one should sacrifice, giving a thousand as the sacrificial fee."

Here, the phrase beginning with "by this" (etena) is to be supplied to the three preceding sentences (pūrva-vākya-traye), as it is improper to supply a word when its application is possible. (Vārttika 10.3.1557).
The section on *anuṣaṅga* (supplying ellipses).
The principle of *adhyāhāra* (supplying missing words). The principle of *adhyāhāra-anuṣaṅga* (supplying both missing words and ellipses).

"Carry-over" (*anuṣaṅga*) means the completion of the sentence; for it applies equally to all [the mantras]. The Bhāṣya states: "O Agni, that body of yours which lies in the wood (*ayāśayā*), most excellent, dwelling in the depths—[with this] word I have driven away [evil]; the brilliant word I have driven away, *svāhā*! O Agni, that body of yours which lies in the dust (*rajāśayā*)... O Agni, that body of yours which lies in the fire-embers (*harāśayā*)... Here there is a doubt: should the phrase "that body of yours which is most excellent" (*tanūrvarṣiṣṭhā*) be carried over into all [the subsequent mantras], or should a worldly (non-Vedic) syntactical supplement be supplied?

What is established? That "O Agni, that form of yours which dwells in the dust" (yā te agne rajāśayā) does not have "tanūr varṣiṣṭhā" as its syntactic remainder (vākyaśeṣa), for this [latter phrase] is not employed subsequent to it. This being the case, we reply:
The "anuṣaṅga" (supplementation) constitutes the completion of the sentence, as in the case of the verse "tanūrvarṣiṣṭhā.

For just as this [supplementation] follows immediately after "yā te agne'yāśayā," so too does it follow after "yā te agne rajāśayā" and "yā te agne harāśayā. If it is argued that the phrase "harāśayā" is separated [from the preceding], we say no; for there is no separation from the collective whole.
The compound "rajāśayā" (dust-filled) is an uninterrupted [compound].

Since there is no syntactic connection with the remainder of the sentence by means of the whole compound, the connection must be with the meaning of the whole. Furthermore, no specific distinction is understood through the meaning of the whole.

Therefore, the connection applies everywhere. Furthermore, a sentence-remainder (vākyaśeṣa) that is heard—being complete and capable in meaning—is a supplement to that which is expectant, whether it occurs subsequently or antecedently.
What, then, is the duration of this proximity? It is said: it is as far as both [the expectant part and the remainder] are able to require one another.

What is this? Is it that there is an intervention by a related word in the case of immediate succession (*ānantarya*)? For in such a case, both [the preceding and following elements] are able to maintain their mutual expectation.
Indeed, even when there is an intervention by a related word, the prior mental impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) does not depart because of that very relationship.
Even where there is an intervention by something else characterized by expectancy, a relationship still exists there as well.
For the opponent expects that the function of both must be stated;
if it were not so expected, one of them would be a redundant reading.
And it is possible for that [function] to be expected.
Therefore, just as it is in the case of one [word], so it is with the other;
for both are not separated by unrelated words and both possess expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
And this much alone is the cause for the connection with a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*).
There is no immediate succession;
for even when there is an interruption, a connection occurs in the absence of a separation.
Therefore, there is an *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of a missing word).

Now, this must be so: where a complete and efficient [formula] is heard in the proximity of those that are already devoid of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣāṇām*), such as: "May the Lord of Thought purify you; may the Lord of Speech purify you; may the divine Savitṛ purify you with an unbroken strainer, with the rays of the bright Sun. For here, the [formulas] ending in "purify" (*punātu*) are complete and do not expect anything further. But does it not expect the word "with an unbroken [strainer]" (*acchidreṇa*)?
It requires truth; even though it requires this, it requires only one, for by that one alone it becomes free from requirement (*nirākāṅkṣa*).
For once it has been made free from requirement by one, it will not require another. It requires [another] because of meaninglessness, but once connected with one, it does not become meaningless.
Therefore, the one does not require the other, nor does the other require it, because both are complete in themselves.

Now, it might be argued that in this supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), not even a single instance of requirement is perceived; by what would it be made free of requirement, and by what not? Thus, since no distinction is apprehended, it would be connected with all [of them].
He says: This is not so.

It is understood that there is a distinction, namely that it connects with that which is perceived internally by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, it does not connect with everything in between, and thus there is no universal application (*anuṣaṅga*) everywhere.
He says: This is not so.
The word *punātu* is perceived as being in direct proximity to this [mantra], and the word *punātu* itself is also [in proximity] to such [phrases] as *citpatistvā*.
This single word *punātu* is repeated again and again;

therefore, wherever the word *punātu* is employed, because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with it, [the phrases] such as *acchidreṇa* are expectant (*sākāṅkṣāḥ*) without that word *punātu*.
Furthermore, those [words] require the word *punātu*; and that word *punātu* is qualified by the term *acchidreṇa*.
Therefore, by means of that word *punātu* together with its *anuṣaṅga*, all [subsequent words] must necessarily be rendered complete.
Consequently, because there is an equal connection among all of them, the completion of the sentence (*vākyaparisamāpti*) is established through *anuṣaṅga*.
Or rather: in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, at the beginning of all three Upasads, an Āgneyī verse is prescribed, namely "agnim īḷe".
Therein, in the sequence for the first [Upasad], the mantra "yā te agne'yāśayā" is recited as being self-sufficient (nirākāṅkṣa).
However, for the two subsequent ones, the mantras "yā te agne rajāśayā" and "yā te agne harāśayā" are recited as being expectant (sākāṅkṣa).

In that context, the instruction for the eradication of the female gender is not complete without something ending in the word *śrī*; nor is practical application possible with what is incomplete. Therefore, by the principle of "presumption from the impossibility otherwise" (*arthāpatti*), a supplementary portion of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) possessing full capacity must necessarily be inferred.
Why? Because the use of incomplete sentences is never resorted to in the Veda;
whatever portion remains missing must be sought out with diligent effort.
Indeed, for Vedic statements, perception alone is not the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for inference and the other means of valid cognition are likewise valid.
And it is only upon the cessation of all means of valid cognition that non-existence (*abhāva*) is determined by means of verbal testimony (*śabda*).
Therefore, in this case, when a portion of the text is perceived through direct observation, one should not stop with that alone.
If even inference and the other means of knowledge were to cease [at that point], then we would conclude that this mantra consists of only this much.
However, if something is understood through them, then we determine that this mantra is complete only when accompanied by that [additional portion], whereas prior to it, it was deficient.
Thus, here, by means of *arthāpatti* (presumption), one must first determine in a general sense that there exists some "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

Consequently, since there is no occasion for anything other than the *amāvāsyā* [mantra], this sentence is incomplete and unfit for ritual application. Therefore, when there is a requirement for a specific [textual supplement], one must consider whether a worldly (*laukika*) one is to be supplied, or whether a Vedic one—such as the preceding mantra beginning with *tanūrvarṣiṣṭhā*—is to be supplied by *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation). In this doubt, he says it is the worldly one. For it is said: "A Vedic composition does not venture to go elsewhere."
But a worldly object is for all purposes subject to disposal according to one's will.

Just as the Vedic fires, such as the Āhavanīya and others, do not function beyond the specific purposes assigned to them, so too is the Vedic subsidiary (śeṣa): that which is enjoined by the text within a particular context cannot be employed elsewhere because it is bound by that very context. The worldly (laukika) [fire], however, being unbound, serves all purposes; even when restricted for the sake of fulfilling every requirement, it is not contradicted.
Therefore, it is the worldly one [that is used].

In that case, if one employs even a Vedic word—considering it to be non-Vedic and merely worldly because it was composed and because its usage is more recent than the non-Vedic—no one prevents him from doing so; however, one should not entertain the notion of its being Vedic therein.

For it has been said: "One employs those very same Vedic phonemes as they appear in the *Mahābhārata* and other works, having abandoned their status as objects of Vedic study, by virtue of worldly understanding."

If, however, because there is no distinction in their being infinite, a connection were also admitted with the word *rajāśayāḥ*, then, due to the application according to the specific instruction, the application would result in occurring only before [the *rajāśayāḥ*].
Therefore, for this reason as well, it is not a Vedic subsidiary (*śeṣa*).
This being the position reached, it is said in reply:
When the pervasion [of the Vedic injunction] has been released, there is the occasion for worldly [matters];
that is the section on *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation), as well as the release from its operation once all searching has ceased.

Only a Vedic sentence is capable of completing a Vedic statement as its supplement, not a worldly one, due to the rule that Dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*). However, when the Veda, even when searched for in every way, is seen to have abandoned its function, then it permits even a worldly [supplement]. And that search proceeds according to proximity.

In that regard: "If the intended meaning is not perceived in the suffix, it is sought again in the word itself; if found within its own word, it need not be sought in another word. If it does not exist even within its own sentence, then it must be sought in another sentence."
If [the required connection] is not found even within another sentence, it must be sought in another context (*prakaraṇāntara*).

When a single meaning has been expressed—whether by a verbal root (*prakṛti*) or by a suffix (*pratyaya*)—and there exists another meaning capable of being related to it, it is "delightful" (*ramaṇīya*) if that [connection] is seen right there.
If, however, it is not seen, then one should abandon negligence and indolence and search for it within the root or the suffix.
If it is not found even among these three, then one should look for it in another word occurring immediately after or before;
if it is not found in the immediate [word], then in one separated by one, two, or more [intervening words].
However, if it is not found within its own sentence, then by that same sequence, one should look for it in another relevant sentence.

However, even in another sentence, if [the required word] is not found, one should seek it according to the requirements of the object of meditation within a different context. But when it is not found there either, then one should look for it in common worldly usage.

If it is not found even in the world, then having determined that it does not exist, one should fulfill the requirement by imagining its presence as being proximate, thereby rendering the expectation satisfied.

And in all cases, if [the remainder] is not found in what is proximate, even that which is remote according to the Veda may be used; however, if it is already obtained in what is proximate, that alone shall be used, even if it is non-Vedic. Therefore, since the remainder is not obtainable here within its own word or its own sentence—namely, in the sentences regarding the *rajāyāhara* and the *āśaya*—it is certainly concluded from another sentence.

And that [mantra], being required in such a manner, is perceived immediately before it in one instance, while in another it is separated by an interval. Although this mantra, having its purpose already fulfilled in the first ritual act (*prathama-mantra*), does not itself require those two [subsequent acts], those two—being impossible without it—are brought into proximity with it; and since it is impossible to recite it once in the vicinity of all [acts] because it would otherwise be obtainable through other means of knowledge, it is repeated again and again. Thus, this subsidiary (*śeṣa*) is recited for the sake of both of us; it should not be assumed to have been recited solely due to the specific proximity of one, as if it were intended for him alone.
Thus it is said.
And although it is recited earlier, nevertheless, it is applied only where it is required by those two [the *mantra* and the *brāhmaṇa*].
Why? Because it is recited in that specific location merely for the sake of being understood.

Due to its suitability, however, the placement [of the mantra] is seen to be as in the case of previous mantras. For that [mantra], being recited only once, cannot be recited in all the desired locations simultaneously; thus, it is recited according to the sequence for one [location], and for the other two, it reaches the range of the intellect and is grasped. Once grasped, it is itself incapable of remaining in another location, yet it is required by those two through their syntactic connection (*anvaya-vṛtti*). Furthermore, since its efficacy has been observed by its presence both before and after [the other two], it is placed precisely at the subsequent [location].

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), however, having stated that because the [text] is read between the first and second [sections], no specific distinction is perceived and thus the "remainder" (śeṣa) is connected to both since it is recited for both; and having raised the objection that there is no connection with the third [section] due to the intervention [of the second], he established—on the grounds that the purpose (artha) is not different—that the intervention of the parts is resolved by forming a collective whole (samudāya) of both. Then, raising the further objection that in that case the remainder would belong to the whole rather than the individuals, he explained that since the whole is unfit for ritual application, the connection must be with the individual members of the whole that are fit for application. Furthermore, because those two [individuals] possess primacy, and because otherwise the absence of expectancy (nairākāṅkṣya) could not be established, he declared that the connection of the entire remainder is established with each [member] individually, and then began another argument.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the proximity of that which has expectancy" (*sākāṅkṣasya saṃnidhau*), there is the previous explanation: "because all [auxiliaries] possess an equal connection" (*sarveṣu tulyayogitvāt*), meaning that among all the auxiliaries (*śeṣa*), there is an equal connection with the remainder (*śeṣa*) through proximity; and there is another explanation: "because they possess an equal connection with expectancy, proximity, and capability" (*tulyākāṅkṣasaṃnidhiyogyatāyogitvāt*).
Thus says the *Sudhā* (p. 693).
In this regard, some have maintained that these are merely alternative explanations (*vyākhyānavikalpa*).
(He states his own view: Others, however, say that the latter [position] was formulated because of dissatisfaction with the former.
What is the reason? "The state of being a collection (*samudāyatva*) of those two is not established by anything;
furthermore, no cause for their individual production is perceived."
For the state of being a collective (*samudāyatva*) would arise either through performing a single function or through being designated by a single word; yet neither of these exists here.
