[Objection: But surely this "single function" is what is called the inclusion of a single supplementary portion of the sentence (*ekavākyaśeṣagrahaṇa*). [Response:
Oh, how little the function of mantras (namely, the illumination of ritual procedure) has been understood!

For in that case, there would have to be a mutual dependence between the two. How so? It is said: since those two are the remainder, it is not logical for them to attain the status of a "collection" (*samudāya*) upon being perceived.

Since even from the individual leaf (*pattra*) its connection is desired as being only in the state of a collection (*samudāyatva*), the state of being a collection is not obtained from the very beginning.

And if it were to attain the state of a collection, then there would again be a connection with each [leaf] individually; thus, the "play of the king’s only son" (*rājaikaputrakrīḍā*) results. (As the commentary *Sudhā*, p. 693, notes: "Just as a play is extremely unjust—because [the son] is so exceedingly dear that he cannot be restrained by his parents, yet because he is the king's only son he cannot be restrained by others—so too is this [proposed interpretation]. Furthermore, the section concerning the "addition by connection" (*anuṣaṅgādhikaraṇa*) occurs precisely hereafter.
The application [of the rule] would follow, because such a thing exists within the aggregate;
or rather, it is not the case that there is no apprehension of a distinction, because there is a distinction caused by the difference in location.
For the first [syllable] stands in the position desired, but not so the two subsequent ones.
Therefore, this alone is the correct explanation.
(If one asks, "What is that? he says: "Expectancy, proximity, and compatibility—these three are established as the causes of syntactic connection; there is no separate *śruti*."

For when something is mentioned once as being connected with many, it necessarily possesses proximity (*ānantarya*) with one of them; however, that [proximity] alone is not then relied upon as the cause of the connection, because even in that case, the establishment of the connection arises from the same three causes [of expectancy, compatibility, and proximity].
Rather, due to a specific proximity, there arises an illusion through the cognition of that substratum.
That illusion, however, ceases upon seeing another related element that is both proximate and connected to the expectant [word].
Just as there is an understanding of an injunction regarding the meaning of the verbal root and so forth by virtue of the capacity for the inclusion of accessories and the like,

so too it is understood therein that this [injunction], being recited in its entirety, is read in proximity to some one [element] because a common connection with all [elements] is possible and because of the unity of the sentence.
Therefore, immediate sequence is not the cause [of the injunction's application].
"Proximity" (*saṃnidhi*)—this is a term from the *Bhāṣya*—means "delimitation by the intellect" (*buddhiviparicchitti*).
(This is its meaning.

Since it is impossible for a single cognition qualified by all qualifiers to arise without the persistence of cognitions regarding the qualifiers and the qualificand, the persistence of the cognitions of the qualifiers and the qualificand is required until the production of the qualified cognition, because [the cognition] depends on the finality of the qualifiers and the qualificand; thus says the *Sudhā*, p. 694.

And that [connection] occurs both in immediate succession (*ānantarya*) and in the intervention of a related word (*saṃbandhapadavyavadhi*). Even the intervention of a related word is simply a variety of immediate succession.
How so? "The connection would be with what is immediately following; for even what follows another is also immediate."
Then, having ascended that [connection] again, one attains immediate succession (*anantarya*).

By means of the verse "O Agni, that [power] of yours which is royal at the beginning," the required supplement, not found subsequently, is obtained by looking back to what precedes: "tanvīryaiṣṭā" (the sacrifice performed with the body).
And when one has ascended there, then [the word] "harādāyā" becomes immediately contiguous and is likewise joined again even with the third [verse].
Thereafter, however, it is exhausted by that very much which is not mentioned in another [text].

In every case, it is exactly thus: having flowed forth further and further, it reaches its limit in one place; these [mental modifications], becoming immediate, hold fast as long as they are required, until nothing more suitable remains and something unsuitable is perceived.
Then, having reflected upon everything and withdrawn, it ceases.

And although proximity and remoteness are perceived due to sequential utterance, nevertheless, since it is understood later that for the doctrine of eternality, both the immediate and the distant are simultaneously related, there is no difference in their authority.

Thus, the relationship between words in a sentence, and between sentences in a context, exists as long as there is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and fitness for connection; even when separated by another capable word, the relationship remains provided it is not intervened by something incompatible.

Regarding the Bhāṣya statement, "even when there is no intervention, even if there is a separation": the meaning is that a connection occurs even when there is a distance [from the word] provided there is no intervention by a contradictory word.
Therefore, the completion [of the sentence] is established. *Anuṣaṅga* means that which is attached (*anuṣajyate*).
*Samāti* (completion) means that very [subordinate element] is completed by that [principal element].
This applies where the principal (*śeṣin*) is still expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*).

However, where there is no further expectancy—where among all the principals only one subordinate (*śeṣa*) is recited as being expectant, such as the passage "May he purify the defects" followed at the end by "the flawless," and so forth—in that case, how is it?
What is established? [The answer is: "The fulfillment of the purpose of the subordinate elements (śeṣas) occurs through their connection with the immediately following [principal element].
And since the principal elements (śeṣins) are already devoid of expectancy, what could be the cause for the cognition of *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a missing word)?
It is replied:

"If this were a supplement to the immediately preceding sentence, then it would be so; however, this [sentence] pertains to everything because of its connection with the meaning of the verb. For, by virtue of its specific proximity, this [word 'punaḥ'] is connected with the word 'punātu'."
That [agent] is indeed one and the same in all three sentences.
Because of its oneness, the meaning is also one.
Nor does its difference arise from a difference in the grammatical factors (kāraka), such that it would be connected with *cippati* and so forth; thus its non-difference is established.
Nor is this action such that it is "without flaw" in a way that it would be satisfied by a single connection.
Therefore, because its purpose is action, its status as something to be employed lasts only as long as it is being employed,
just as wood has utility only so long as it is used for cooking.

Now it is argued: "Even though this [action] is one, that connection with an instrument which is heard in scripture as qualified by a particular agent must be joined with that very [agent] who is qualified by it.

Just as, although the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice is one, the mixing with milk (*payasā śrayaṇam*) enjoined for it does not apply excessively when it is qualified by the performance of the *maitrāvaruṇa-graha*; and just as in this very case, actions such as throwing (*kṣipati*) and so forth do not occur everywhere.
To this it is replied:
For the restriction of the *śrayaṇas* (milk-offerings) is indeed distinct; it is prompted by what has not been previously established.
Furthermore, because other agents are already occupied, there is no confusion regarding the acts of pouring (*cipati*) and so forth.
Since the great sacrifices such as the *Aindrāgna* serve multiple purposes, it is appropriate that the restriction of the *śrayaṇas* be determined according to their respective Vedic branches.
For there is no such cause [for this distinction], since an instrument is employed for the sake of an action;
rather, that very action is manifested again by means of the manifestation of the instrument. And because it is undifferentiated everywhere, that action requires manifestation.

And just as the verbal root *ci* (to collect), which possesses an operation identical to that [of the act of collecting] due to its being brought into connection with a sentence, is non-worldly (*alaukika*), so too is the [act of] composition (*anibandhana*) non-worldly.

This being the position reached: it functions according to what is required; however, there is no hearing of another instrument (*karaṇa*) that has an unbroken purifier (*achidrapavitra*) as its counter-correlate, for such a thing is established by the Veda in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) regarding its form. Nor is the instrument prompted by the agent, such that a supplementary element would need to be sought, as that would lack any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*).
It is established by that distinction:

because the factors of action (*kāraka*) are dependent upon the ritual act, the purpose of the *para-soma* [offering] is primary in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since there is no connection with the incongruity of the remaining mantras or the expiations.
But even so, would the states not still exist through other mantras?
In the established doctrine (siddhānta), however, its existence [is affirmed];
for if it were connected with the word "punātu" [in the phrase] "yadā adhyā-", this fault would not arise.
There is no such defect.

Since the remnant of the *laukika* [worldly] offering taken at the *darśa* is not accompanied by a mantra, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), its application is established as being restricted—just like the properties of the *barhis* grass used in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. (Just as the recitation [of the mantra] is not to be performed at the time [of the actual cutting], but rather its mental coordination [is required]; for, due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), the properties of the objects belong to the *barhis* of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, because it is possible to form the cognition of them as a single whole.)

For this very reason, there is no application [of the mantra] to the *varhis* (sacrificial grass) used in the *chinna-pitṛyajña*, such as in the case of "iṣe tvā" and so forth; likewise, even for this remainder, the word "damī" and so on from the context is not performed by the ritualists (*yājñika*) at the time of practical application. This is because, since the word *punātu* has already been recited, its occurrence is understood as such. However, if there were an *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of a missing word) of a mantra, then because it would be a mantra, its utterance at the time of application would also have to be performed; thus, there would be the contingency of connecting the word *punātu* contained within that [mantra].
*Sudhā*, p. 696): Regarding the word "here" (*iha*):

some, however, say that even for a word supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*), there is indeed an actual utterance; thus, having commenced with the *yajñiya* [mantras], they claim that the performance of the *pūtu* and other [mantras] follows from the function of the word *pūtu*, and that the performance of the *achidra* and others is done without formal intent (*anāsthayā*).
As for the meaning of the Sūtra: we perceive directly that the qualification is one and the same in both mantras.

"Anuṣaṅga" means that which is attached; it is the completion of a sentence. It does not apply to another mantra, because its purpose is to effect the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of both the distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) and the distinct [mantra] itself. It is the completer among all the remaining [mantras], since the remainder of the sentence cannot be understood simultaneously [with each]. [Objection: But if this is so, then because they serve a single purpose, would it not follow that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the mantras?

[Response: An option here is indeed appropriate, just as in the case of the "division mantras" (*vibhāga-mantra*). This is established because [the rule] "when one recites... attaches [to each part], and because such [mantras] are prescribed with specific numbers.
In this context, the word "laukika" (worldly) serves as an indicator for that which is not [Vedic];
there is a conjunction at the end of the Veda.

Even though there is no faith in the words of the outsiders, the requirement for completion should not be sought in other [non-Vedic] mantras; rather, it is to be supplied by means of the Veda—this is the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*).

Even if it were subordinate to something else, there would be the consequence [of its application everywhere]; thus he says: "In all cases, the presence of contrary characteristics is found in the intellect and the ear, but the worldly [perception] is not like that.
(2.1.16.48). It might be possible [there], but not in other mantras; this is the distinction. Therefore...
There is no connection or further attachment for one whose purifier (*pavitra*) is unbroken; these two are the primary objects (*śeṣin*).

Although this word *punātu* exists in all mantras, it is not brought over here by all [of them] because there is no expectancy (*anākāṅkṣatvāt*) for the phrase "with an unbroken purification" (*achidrāpavittistva*). Furthermore, that [word *punātu*], being possessed of its own requirement, does not depend on anything else.
It is connected with all [the rites] ending with the *abhyāsa* (repetition). Instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) is dependent upon action (*kriyā*), and action occurs only once.

Because it is beneficial, flawless, beginningless, and has no other recourse, when [it is applied] to the two mantras, therefore, through that door, it is attached as a supplement (*anuṣajyate*) to everything.

2|1|17|48. When the word *śabda* (the verbal form) is accepted, then, in the case of the imagined [mantra] "punātv acchidreṇa," where there is a requirement for many subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*), that which is immediately subsequent to the first [element] is the very same [element] that is subsequently connected; namely, the word *punātu* itself is the previously mentioned subsidiary element. Just as in the case of "yā te agne ayāśayā," at the time of observing the connection with the instrumental case (*pi*), it connects [with the action]. Following the word "kriyāḥ" (actions), there is "tanūrviprapā" and so forth.

The two subsequent items being existent, they depend upon that [preceding mantra] and thus reach it along with the *āsādana* (placing) mantra: "O Agni, that [form] of thine which lies in dust (*rajāśayā*)," and "O Agni, that [form] of thine which lies in heat (*harāśayā*). Thus, in every respect, there is an *anupaṅga* (supplementation). Or rather, it should be employed with such an *anuṣaṅga*.

In that case, for the two subsequent [mantras] which require a supplement, this very supplement is used; for those [mantras] which are employed by way of a common ritual framework (*tantra*), that [supplement] serves merely as a mark.

It will be explained later that it is not the worldly [usage], because [the word] has not been supplied when [the ellipsis] was filled. Nor is it the case that, since there is no distinction in the *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of an elided word) from the remainder of the sentence, it is connected with what precedes; for that which is fixed in one place cannot be led elsewhere. As for the claim made by some that it is connected through *anuṣaṅga* with all [preceding parts], that is because it is traditionally taught as being established in a specific context.
Furthermore, it should not be understood that it is merely required immediately after the first [word].
Because it is recited in that [same] section, its identity as such is possible.
Here too, it is the very measure of the *yajus* that is being considered, because [otherwise] it would be unfit for the ritual action; and because it is not distinct [from the others].
Even though they sit [there], there is no connection; rather, the coherence consists in having a single object.

For [the connection] is bound in one place, since the nature of the syntactic linkage (*padānvaya*) is indistinguishable everywhere. Indeed, that which is Vedic by virtue of its belonging to the *samāmnāya* (the traditional collection) is not to be transferred elsewhere as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Proximity (*ānantarya*) alone is the cause of the relationship; for even in the absence of that [proximity], verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) occurs.

Because there is no basis for [the application of] a non-abiding word (*asaṃśridha-pada*) in the absence of a specific injunction; since all [mantras] are included in the remainder (*śeṣa*), the occasion for a penance (*prāyaścitta*) arises through the distinction of the *yajus* formulas. ... Thus, because it is impossible to recite the *dhāna* [formula] only once, its status as something to be enjoined arises from expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Furthermore, since it is recited in proximity (*saṃnidhi*) to many [formulas] that have arisen with such expectancy, it is logical to understand it as being for the sake of all of them. It has been stated in the first section (*prathamavarṇaka*) that the remainder (*śeṣa*) is applied everywhere, whether it is recited repeatedly or recited at the end of all.
Because it is impossible to produce [the result] by rising [from one's seat];

and because a subsidiary element (*śeṣa*) recited in proximity to many [principal elements] that require its presence at a specific location is understood—by means of indicative power (*liṅga*)—to be applicable everywhere, since the scripture is known to have a universal purpose.
(This was stated in the second section.)
In this case, there is indeed no *anuṣaṅga* (supplying of an elided word).
Nor is it the case that, even if non-interruption (*avyavadhāna*) were not a cause [for *anuṣaṅga*], *anuṣaṅga* would be established upon the intervention of a word connected to another word;

for an objection arises from the fact that the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*) according to the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), and even if that were not the cause, the illustrative example is the section on intervention (*vyavāyādhikaraṇa*).

Kau. 2|1|18|5–50. Because it is accepted that there is an absence of a restrictive factor (*niyāmakatva*) in cases of doubt; however, in the present case, since the requirement for a restrictive factor arises from the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) for a specific [meaning]—as the sense of being for all purposes is understood through the context after merely stating a connection with something else—it has been explained in the section on *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) that [the word] "goes as far as the end. Therefore, supplementation (*anuṣaṅga*) alone is appropriate.

And therefore, even in the case of its omission, [the rule applies] because the cessation of the cognition [is required]; for it has been stated in the section on *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) that the expiation for the breaking of the *yajus* formula follows from its proximity (*saṃnidhi*).

Where, at the end of many principal elements (*śeṣin*) that are already free of expectancy, a supplementary element (*mantraśeṣa*) is recited that is itself dependent—such as the remainder of the mantra "cittisunātu punātu," which, although made free of expectancy by being revealed through the supplementary portion of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), becomes expectant again because of the other mantra portions beginning with "tistvanā" and "devasavitā savitā"—and thus, being expectant, it connects once more with the previously uttered phrase "achidreṇa pavitreṇa," where it assumes the role of illuminating the mantra-remainder through proximity and fitness; in such a case, since there is no distinction between them, the supplementary connection (*anuṣaṅga*) applies to all, according to the section on *anuṣaṅga* (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.49–50).

And it has not been established that they must be extracted [from their context]. (p. 1224) As many words as exist, because they fulfill their purpose through a single syntactic unity due to the requirement of proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*), all those [words] which are separated by distance [from one another]—the justification for their restrictive application is established by the principle stated in the section on *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation). Even when the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is aroused by the expectancy for the remainder (*śeṣa*), the proximity and distance of the non-initial [word] converge simultaneously according to that path.

Because the subsidiaries (*śeṣas*) are subordinate, and since there is no determining factor [to restrict them], all of them are indeed subsidiaries. Consequently, because the injunction is understood as the "grasper" (*grāhaka*) having reached the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*)—which is qualified by all the subsidiaries and is fit for performance—the immediate sequence [of the subsidiaries] is not a restrictive factor.
Therefore, the injunction is completed.

And that [injunction], by means of a single effort, enjoins that very qualified [efficient-force] for the sake of all the subsidiaries read in proximity to the various sacrificial acts; thus, there is no fault of assuming multiple potencies.
Or rather, it is you alone.

And therefore, regarding these [passages] on pages 316 and 485 concerning the purification of the knees, ankles, and so forth, this is a counter-example to the section on *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation); for even a remainder (*śeṣa*) is admitted in mantras because of its connection with each primary element.
The section concerning separation (*vyāvāyādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the section concerning non-continuation due to intervention (*vyavetānanuṣaṅgādhikaraṇa*), one should consult Maṇḍana’s statement: "In cases such as *rājaśayā*, the completion [of the sentence] occurs through ellipsis (*anupajya*)."
Śaṃkara [Mīmāṃsāsūtrabhāṣya 2.1.17.49]: "Now, *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) is described.

As for the nature of the section on *anuṣaṅga*: 'In the absence of another [word], there is supplementation to complete the sentence; it should be connected equally to all [preceding words], as it is adjacent to the subsequent one as well. Furthermore, it is established upon that [subsequent word] because of its connection.'"
"Subsequently, that immediate succession is admitted.
(Sūtra-bhāṣya, p. 1069).

"O Agni, that body of yours which lies within wealth, which is far-reaching and hidden—let this word [be uttered]. (RV 2.1.16.48). However, according to the Sūtra-commentary (*Sūtrārthika*), it is stated: "Then, having mounted that again, he should recite: 'He has struck away this word; he has struck away, svāhā!
O Agni, that [body] of yours...'; thus the third quarter is recited. Who [says this]?

"O Agni, those [embers] which are thy dark-red abodes," and "those which are thy ash-colored abodes. In this regard, there is a doubt (in the section concerning *anuṣaṅga*): In the case of *anuṣaṅga*, should the phrase "tanūrviprapā" be appended everywhere according to the Vedic text; or rather, since *anuṣaṅga* possesses the common characteristic of serving all purposes, should a supplementary portion of the sentence—whether Vedic or worldly—be supplied? Herein lies the clarification of the subject: just as the status of being a *mantra* is established by that very fact, so too the status of being a *yajus* is appropriate for the *yajurdvaya*. As before, the consideration of the measure of the *yajus* follows the sequence of the comparison in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "There are indeed three *upasads* with a single oblation."
In the Vedic tradition, there is a universal syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
Three types of actions are heard [in the texts] regarding the *ām* offerings.
And for these, the three factors of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*saṃnidhi*)—which serve as their auxiliary elements—are the cause [of their connection].
The *prayājās* have Agni as their deity; they are established by such scriptural injunctions as "Agni is the face" (*agninīkam*).
In the sequence of these [rites], three mantras are recited.
Among them, for the first *iṣṭi*, the mantra "O Agni, that which is thy desire" (*yā te agne'yāśayā*) is complete and thus free from expectancy.

Regarding the second and third [formulas], *yā te agne rajāśayā* and *yā te agne harāśayā*, these two are incomplete and thus possess a syntactic expectancy (*sākāṅkṣau*). In this regard, the first doubt is as follows: Is the explanatory statement beginning with "the injunction for the purpose of the body" (*tanvarthavidhi*) and so forth untenable after the completion of the first mantra? Or, having established the extent of the *yajus* by means of a digression regarding the worldly [completion] of a formula, is the incomplete *yajus* now completed through a similar digression by means of an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), or rather, is it untenable?

In this regard, the intention of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: First of all, it is not possible for the passage beginning with "tanvarthavidhiḥ" to be a supplement to "yā te agne'yāśayā," nor can it be a supplement to "yā te agne'yāśayā" and "yā te agne harāśayā," because it has been taught by the rule governing Vedic study (*adhyāyanavidhi*) precisely as a supplement to the preceding sentences.

This is just as the *āhavanīya* fire, being a supplement to the oblation (*homa*), is understood from the Veda as distinct from the performance of the ritual act of "placing the fire" (*agnyanvādhāna*).

1012122155–56. Since performance is dependent upon injunction (*vidhi*), it is untenable without an injunction. *Sūtra-bhāṣya*, p. 734: "The recollection of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) of the performance, which necessarily occurs during the act, is accomplished by means of mantras that have no other purpose and no other means of accomplishment."

Since it is not possible to perform what has not been perceived at the time of execution, one necessarily relies on a recollection that is bound to occur; and because of this dependence on a suitable means, one begins to take up some means such as the performance of a certain Brāhmaṇa passage, or the review of a preceding ritual act, or a Sūtra text, or sentences containing the word "one's own" (ātman), or an observer, and so forth.

In that context, when one perceives mantras being recited in a particular section (*prakaraṇa*) that have no other apparent purpose, and which are grasped by the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) in a general sense as "something must be done with these," one recognizes that they possess such a form as would require a scriptural text (*vākya*) for the purpose of establishing their remembrance (*smṛti*). Once it is understood that these [mantras] are of such a nature, and they are applied through a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) whose scope is determined by indicative mark (*liṅga*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), it is realized that their purpose is denotation (*abhidhāna*). Consequently, since other means [of remembrance] lack authoritative basis, they are set aside. Furthermore, the invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*) is thereby established.

Is one offering the *samidh* fuel-sticks for the sake of the ritual act (*kṛtyartha*), or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)? Likewise, should one speak the untruth for the sake of the ritual act, or for the sake of the person?
And if it is indeed for that [ritual] purpose, then the word "untrue" (*anṛta*) is merely a qualifier of that which is to be spoken.
And at the time of negation, the injunction is subordinate to that [negation]; thus, the remainder is determined as "not speaking untruth.

Consequently, in one case (where the negative particle *nañ* has the purpose of negation regarding the *liṅga*), the statement is expressed as: "One should perform that which is speaking untruth for the sake of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). But in the other case (where the *nañ* has the purpose of negation regarding the ritual), it is expressed as: "That which one might speak as untruth for the sake of the ritual (*ṛtvartha*), that he should not do."
And since this entire [discussion] depends upon the determination of the verb (*ākhyāta*), the following inquiry will arise from that: "Is the agent denoted by the verb, or not?

(From here until the end of the section titled "The Inquiry into the Designation of Verbs and Nouns" [Vārttika text, p. 908, l. 7], the passage has been extracted and inserted into the *Kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*). What is the prima facie view? Since speech is generally characterized by untruthfulness, the prohibition applies specifically to that falsehood which is prone to occur when a person speaks for their own sake; [it is] for men.
Why? Precisely because of a different connection.
That indeed is a restatement (*anuvāda*) which reiterates what is already established by being identical in meaning.
Furthermore, there is a difference in purpose—and thus a difference in substance—between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*).
How so? "For an injunction, when it operates, operates for the sake of accomplishing what is beneficial;
a prohibition, on the other hand, turns one away from evil, owing to their distinction."
For in this cultivation (*bhāvanā*) expressed as "one should speak the truth," the expectation of a purpose is satisfied by heaven and the like, because all injunctions have human goals as their end.
Therefore, the meaning is this: "When one engages in worldly transaction through two modes of speech, by engaging in truthful speech, one becomes connected with prosperity.
In that case, heaven accrues to one who speaks the truth.
Furthermore, for one who speaks untruth, there is neither merit nor fault.
Likewise, by the prohibition "one should not speak untruth," the consequence of falling into hell arises from speaking untruth; yet from speaking truth, there is neither fault nor merit.
Therefore, both [speaking truth and avoiding untruth] constitute injunctions (*vidhi*) that are not redundant, as they lead to prosperity (*abhyudaya*).
He said: This would be a different connection (*saṃyogāntara*) if, in the Smṛti, only "one should speak the truth" were stated.
But in that case, just like the injunction to speak the truth, the prohibition of falsehood is also understood as distinct.
Therefore, there is no different connection.
It is said:
"Because it is a vow of Prajāpati, and because of the logical principle regarding the prohibition of looking,
it is understood that there is an injunction for truth by way of exclusion (paryudāsa)."
For even there, it is restricted by the rule, "one should indeed speak untruth";
thus, this constitutes a different connection.
Indeed, in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is no application of the word *vrata* to the prohibition against speaking untruth, nor does any contingency of optionality arise.

For it will be stated (10.8.116) that an option applies only to prohibitions that are established by scriptural injunction, and not to those preceded by what is already established by the nature of things;
therefore, this is a mandatory injunction.

(Refuting the interpretation of the *saṃyogāntara* [different connection] offered by the Commentator under the view that [the prohibitions] serve solely the purpose of the person, he himself proposes an interpretation of the *saṃyogāntara* under the view that they serve the purpose of the person engaged in the sacrifice: But if it is thus maintained that "there exist such prohibitions even apart from the Prajāpati-vows," then that very *saṃyogāntara* must be explained as follows: "The Smṛti-based connection pertains to the person in general for the sake of accomplishing his own ends; this [Vedic connection], however, serves the purpose of the person engaged in the sacrifice for the sake of another result."
"Now, by this very reason, it would be appropriate to regard the particular as a restatement (anuvāda) in view of the attainment of the general;
this is not so,
because of the difference in result, just as before."
For that which is a prohibition against falsehood based on Smṛti leads only to this much being understood: "In order to avoid the fault of falsehood, a person must not speak untruth.

In that case, when one transgresses it even during the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, then, like a transgression regarding external duties, there would be for him merely a personal sin (pratyavāya), but no obstruction of the fruit of the ritual act.
For the seasonal sacrifices (ṛtavaḥ) do not fail because of transgressions concerning the duties of the pure individual.
For instance: "If one who is in the midst of a sacrifice should eat *kalañja* and other forbidden foods, there is no deficiency in that sacrifice, because it is accomplished exactly as prescribed."
For the seasons, depending upon the injunctions and prohibitions pertaining to themselves,
become defective when those are transgressed.
As for the injunctions and prohibitions pertaining to the person, they remain indifferent to his presence or absence, just as they would be toward someone situated in another season.

They are not distinct. For there is no cognition of them as subordinate factors (*guṇa*) within the context of the sacrifice, such that a cognition of deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) would arise upon their transgression.
Therefore, one who speaks an untruth during the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices would both incur hell and obtain the fruit of the Darśapūrṇamāsa without any alternative.
The meaning is "for the sake of remembrance.

However, since the Vedic [prohibition] is a duty pertaining to the person as connected with the context (*prakaraṇa*), this meaning is understood regarding that Vedic prohibition: "The *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices accomplish their fruit when performed by a person who has avoided speaking untruth.

For, by the force of the context, untruth is prohibited after characterizing it as being a means to the *apūrva* residing in the person; therefore, upon its transgression, the *darśapūrṇamāsa-apūrva* itself would not arise due to the defectiveness [of the rite], but there is no sin for the person alone.
For at that time, a transgression (*pratyavāya*) being postulated cannot be postulated as pertaining to an independent person;
therefore, there is a different connection [in the case where it is a duty of the person engaged in the sacrifice].
Thus is the injunction.

In this way, even in the view that it pertains to the *ṛtudharma* (the duty of the season), a different connection (*saṃyogāntara*) should be explained, because there is no difference in the cognition regarding the person for whom the sacrifice is intended.

(Even in the view that it pertains to the sacrifice itself, when one transgresses a prohibition pertaining to the sacrifice, it is possible for the result to be the avoidance of the sin arising from the deficiency of the rite.
Therefore, because it is a perpetual restatement (*nityānuvāda*), [the prohibition] does not apply.
As for the distinction between [the fruit] being a property of the season (*ṛtudharma*) and a property of the person to whom it is given (*dattapuruṣadharma*),
that distinction of the fruit we shall explain later.

(As stated in the Vārttika at the end of the section: "For even that which is not the subject matter [is included]," p. 143). Since the injunction is established in both ways, it is not said that it is of no use now.
"Later on, [it will be said] that this is a rule regarding rice.

For the very reason stated previously, we say it is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*). Now, two prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*) are presented: one, that the injunction of truth is a duty of the person alone through a different connection; and the other, that it is a duty of the person as associated with the ritual (*ṛtu-yukta-puruṣadharma*).
To this, the following reply is given:

(From here onwards, the *Vārttika* beginning with "In all verbal forms, of the agents... on page 913 up to "...therefore the agent is the denotable [meaning]" on page 940 is to be found in the *Kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*).
The *Bhāṣya* (p. 940): Therefore, it is not directly expressed by the word (*śrauta*).
[This concerns] the operation of the causal factor (*kāraka-vyāpāra*).

If it is not directly expressed by the Vedic word (*śrauta*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) will not be sublated. As for the argument that human effort would become purposeless because, under the view that the action is a property of the ritual (*karma-dharma-pakṣa*), its performance is already enjoined by the injunction of application (*prayoga-vacana*), that is now addressed.
Being unknown, it would have to be grasped within the context [of the ritual procedure],
yet that which is not prescribed does not become part of the procedure.
Therefore, because it is unknown, it must be enjoined even in this alternative view.
Therefore, we consider this to be a prohibition concerning the primary subject.
Consequently, that which was given to one who is ignorant must not be spoken of;
thus, whatever was intended by him, that is what is "ignorant" [of the recipient's lack of knowledge], and that alone should be performed.

Having resolved upon one made of rice (*brīhimaya*), a cake (*puroḍāśa*) made of barley (*yavamaya*) is not to be offered. He asks: "When it must not be stated that [the offering] is not made of rice for either of the two positions, then for what purpose is this deliberation? It is replied: [It is for the sake of determining the correct course].
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is a property of the person; in that case, when there is a transgression, the expiation is [that prescribed for the person].
In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is a property of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice; in that case, when there is a transgression, the expiation is that belonging to the Yajurveda.
Or—therefore (page 940).

Because the agent is not denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), and because the operation of the factor (*kāraka*) lacks direct scriptural status (*śrautatva*), the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not sublated.

As for the argument that, under the view that [the act] is a property of the ritual (*karmadharma*), the proximate injunction would be purposeless since it is already enjoined by the injunction of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, and therefore it must serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatā*), we reply: "As long as there is contact with an injunction, that much alone constitutes its purpose;
and without that, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not understood to be an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*ṛtvaṅga*)."

For the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), being devoid of an injunction (*vidhi*), while itself attaining the status of something to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*), cannot be grasped as part of the procedure (*kathaṃbhāva*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices because its purpose is not required. Nor can it be enjoined by that very performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*).

Therefore, having first made known the benefit to the person—either directly or indirectly—by means of the injunctive rule (*vidhi*), and having treated the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as the instrument (*karaṇa*), when there remains a requirement for a further purpose, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) must be postulated through its connection with the benefit of the proximate *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; otherwise, there would be a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*), namely: "because it is an auxiliary, there is an injunction [for it]," and "because of the injunction, it is a specific auxiliary. Thus, the injunction regarding the auxiliaries is meaningful.
And thus, by the word "should speak" (*vadet*), this much is understood: "One should accomplish the benefit for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices by means of speaking.
Then, by the force of the word "untruthfully" (*anṛta*), it follows: "Whatever one might do by means of speaking, that should be done untruthfully.
Furthermore, through the connection [of the context], the statement is revealed as: "That which would benefit [the sacrifice] by truthful speaking, that [benefit] is not [to be achieved here]."

Therefore, regarding that which is spoken for the benefit of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, if falsehood should result, its prohibition is enjoined. Consequently, in every instance of conversation pertaining to the purpose of the ritual, falsehood must be avoided.
Thus, having told the Adhvaryu priest, "A cake made of barley is to be prepared," [one should say] "May my barley be fit for the sacrifice."
"Therefore, let [the oblation] be made of rice"; one must not contradict [the injunction] in this way.
Furthermore, because it precedes that [act], one would be contradicting the very "intention" (saṃkalpa) by speaking thus.
Alternatively, having caused the Adhvaryu himself to form the intention by means of his own words—this should be seen as the nature of a double-tongued person.

He asks: "When there is a restatement of what is already established by tradition (smṛti), and when the injunction arises from a different connection, the point that 'one should not speak untruth' is common to both cases; what then is the purpose of this inquiry? To this it is replied: "For if it were a restatement of what is established by tradition, the occasional rite would be based on tradition; but in the case of the view that it is an injunction, this [prohibition] becomes a Vedic action because of its injunction in the Yajurveda."

And regarding the Smṛti, if it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), then the very same expiation prescribed for speaking falsely (*anutavadana*)—namely, "one should mutter the *gāyatrī* while supporting oneself" (*gāyatrībhṛte japet*)—must be performed.

However, if it is an injunction (*vidhi*), then because it belongs to the Yajurveda, it possesses superiority; since "the sacrifice is based on the Yajurveda," one should offer the oblation into the *anvāhāryapacana* fire with the mantra "Bhuvaḥ svāhā.
Furthermore, in the Smṛti, because it cannot be determined which [Veda] is its source, there would be no fixed determination of the expiation occasioned by a Vedic command.

Thus, even if the relationship of root and derivative is accepted, by the very fact of [the rule] "one should not speak untruth" (*nānṛtaṃ brūyāt*), its objects (i.e., the prohibited acts) and the transgression thereof are established as being "untruthful"; therefore, the expiation for that [transgression] is precisely that prescribed by this [Vedic injunction].
[Objection: But for you as well, according to the Yajurvedic statement, shouldn't this very same expiation apply?
[Reply: This is not so.

For this very reason it is said: because its subject matter concerns those who maintain the sacred fires (*vanīyādi*), it depends upon the qualification of one who has established the fires (*āhitāgni*); and since the prohibition of falsehood (*anṛta*) is a duty for every human being, it applies even to one who has not established the fires (*anāhitāgni*) and is thus not restricted [to the former alone].
Therefore, in his case, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must necessarily be required.

If such an expiation were required, then for one who has established the fires, where fire is the instrumental cause, that same [Vedic expiation] would be appropriate; thus, there is an absence of Vedic expiation [for the latter].
Furthermore: "When any one of the auxiliary sciences of the Veda (*vedāṅga*) fails during a sacrifice, an occasional rite (*naimittika*) is prescribed by scripture;
however, in the case of the destruction of something that is not an auxiliary of the sacrifice, there would be no occasion for it."

For the entire injunction, "If the sacrifice should suffer ruin through the *ṛc*," is heard as being conditioned by anything connected to the sacrifice. And since the [subsidiaries] are connected to the Jyotiṣṭoma due to the context (*prakaraṇa*),

the context would indeed have to be set aside here because the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger— according to the principle stated in (3.3.18), "Because of the connection with the Veda, it is not set aside by the context"— but this does not constitute a reason for excluding the connection to the sacrifice itself.
Therefore, even though the specific Vedic text has been understood and it concerns a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*), an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should not be performed on that account.

However, when—due to the absence of an assumption of a result (*phalakalpanā*) and because of the context (*prakaraṇa*)—it is the prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) that such items are duties of the person connected with the sacrifice (*ṛtuyuktapuruṣadharma*), whereas the final conclusion (*siddhāntaṃ*) is that they are purely sacrificial duties (*śuddhaṛtudharma*), then in both cases the expiation is triggered solely by the excellence of the Yajurvedic sacrifice; thus, another purpose must be stated.
That is stated as follows:

"For even those who possess knowledge, having become purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) under the previous position, would all belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), because they possess the nature of the purificatory rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*)."

For all the *samid* and other [fore-offerings], occurring at another time, are purificatory rites for the person who is the proponent of the prima facie view regarding the limbs of the *stotra* and *śastra*.
And these would belong to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) by virtue of the section [sūtra] stating, "They belong to the sacrificer because they are performed by him, like the main ritual acts" (3.8.14).

In that regard, since the *samid* and others consist of sacrifice, they belong to the sacrificer in both ways—by means of the act of relinquishing the substance (*dravya-tyāga-vyāpāra*) and by being [part of] the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and so forth; thus, even for the purification of the sacrificer, their performance is done in common (*tantra*), and no distinction is observed.

However, those [recitations] which consist of the *stotra* and *śastra* verses, being subordinate to the agent who performs them, would—by setting aside the recollection of the primary [ritual] beginning with the *pradhāna-uttara* for those authorized by the primary injunction regarding this "mine" (*mamārtha*)—be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), like the *dantavyavana* and other such acts.

And since, in the case of the purification of the sacrificer, a single performance (*tantratva*) is not possible according to the principle of the renunciation of common property (*sādhāraṇadravyatyāga*), they must be repeated for each individual sacrificer.

Furthermore, when even in the case of a prohibition the injunctive element is determined in this way—"false speaking is [an act] that assists the person engaged in the seasonal sacrifice"—then, because this very [prohibition] is a negation qualified by falsehood, it follows that this becomes a harmful consequence: "If something is spoken by the sacrificer during the performance of the *āsīḥ* and other rites for the sake of self-purification, then, in the case of optional determinations, one must not perform [the speech] through its essential nature; otherwise, however, there would be the speaking of whatever one pleases by others."

However, regarding the prohibition of the pure *kratu*-dharma, the meaning is: "Whatever is prescribed for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) or the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) during the sacrifice—whether performed or not performed—all that must not be done," because there is no difference in their being included within the *kratu*.

Therefore, just as the sacrificer, having resolved upon an offering of rice (*vrīhimaya*), must not give an offering of barley (*yavamaya*), so too the Adhvaryu and others, having said, "We shall perform [the rite] according to one or the other alternative," must not, out of a desire for brevity, revert to the original injunction.
Furthermore, whatever else is for the sake of the ritual performance (*saṃskāra*), even that which is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) must be avoided by him according to this [text].

Now, one might argue: "In the case of a prohibition, the person is subordinate; therefore, by the restrictive power of the compound *adhyartha* (for the sake of the sacrifice), the Adhvaryu would incur the prohibition of the carrying of the *praṇītā* water. This is true, provided that the object of the prohibition were something that required permission.
However, since this [prohibition] consists in the absence of permission, it does not depend upon a specific agent.

Furthermore, the prohibition is established by the Vedic text itself—specifically through the indication characterized by its co-occurrence with the word to be prohibited—and this [prohibition] is consistent with the attainment of that which is to be prohibited.
Wherever that [prohibition] is obtained, it proceeds within its own domain and cannot be set aside by the name (*samākhyā*).

Now, one might argue: "The mere injunctive portion, 'one should speak,' when being undertaken, is restricted by the name; therefore, since the prohibition follows that [injunction], it too will be restricted. This is not so.
For when the meaning of the scripture has been fully determined and there remains a need for reasoning, the name (samākhyā) comes into play.
However, the mere word "one should speak" is not understood as the full meaning of the scripture;
rather, because it is connected with a prohibition, it stands merely as a restatement (anuvāda).

Furthermore, it has been established in the *Grahādhikaraṇa* (3.1.7) that even when something is being inferred (*anuvamāna*), it does not become a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) even if it is heard [in the text].
How much less so in the case of a name (*samākhyā*), which is restricted solely to the mere agent of the ritual action being enjoined?
Therefore, because it is being inferred, the act of speaking is not qualified.
Even a negation that contradicts it cannot establish any distinction whatsoever.

Therefore, it is established that there is a purpose in every case, and thus it has been correctly investigated. Śā—Injunctions belonging to the context of a sacrifice (*kratuprakaraṇa*) prohibit those ritual items that would otherwise be applicable by implication to both the sacrifice and the person;
this is the illustration here.

In connection with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in scripture: "One should not speak untruth. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this an injunction concerning the person as such (*puruṣadharma*); or is it a restatement (*anuvāda*) concerning the person engaged in the ritual (*ṛtuyuktapuruṣadharma*); or is it an injunction concerning the person engaged in the ritual; or is it a restatement concerning the ritual alone (*śuddhakratudharma*); or finally, is it an injunction concerning the ritual alone? (Soma: Is this an injunction or a restatement? If it is an injunction, is it an injunction concerning the person as such, or concerning the person engaged in the ritual, or concerning the ritual alone?)

Likewise, even in the case of the position of restatement (*anuvāda*), the refinement of the doubt is as follows: Is this a duty of the person associated with the sacrifice (*ṛtuyukta-puruṣadharma*), or is it a duty of the pure sacrifice (*śuddha-kratudharma*)? For that purpose, the action being prohibited must be examined: for what purpose is it prohibited—is it for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)?

Furthermore, it must again be examined whether the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes the agent or not. In this regard: "Because of [its] cognition, because of traditional memory (*smaraṇa*), and because no separate mention is heard regarding a specific agent..."
It is determined that the verbal suffix expresses the agent.
Because the agent is understood from the verb "should say" (*vadet*), according to the grammatical rules:

"The suffix *kṛt* denotes the agent" and "The suffixes *la* denote both the object and the agent. Furthermore, in expressions such as "Devadatta cooks," the verb possesses a specific agent, since words like "Devadatta" are not heard separately [from the verb], but are used together with it in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
That [prohibition] consists of that purpose; for while it appears to state directly that [the act] is beneficial to the person, it actually establishes its very opposite.
Therefore, having heard [the Vedic text], the prohibition—having set aside the context—is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
As for the Smṛti-based prohibition, this same [Vedic text] is its source; such is one view.

Since there is no contradiction between the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*), this is a duty for the person engaged in the ritual sacrifice, meaning "one performing the rite must avoid untruth.
This is the second position, which holds that it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is already established by Smṛti.

The third position is that the prohibition is indeed for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) as an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), yet it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). To this, it is replied: "Even if it is for the sake of the sacrifice, as for the claim that it is a restatement, that is understood to be just like a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) due to the difference in its connection (*saṃyogabheda*)."
Now, it remains to be determined whether dharma belongs to the person engaged in the sacrifice, or rather, whether it is the property of the pure sacrifice itself.
To this, it is said: "All verbal suffixes denote action;
for that very reason, the agent is not understood as the primary denotable object."

The word *smṛti* does not have as its object the expression of number when it denotes an agent; furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of words like "cow. Thus, since there is no contradiction with the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), this prohibition is indeed for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). And because it constitutes a different connection (*saṃyogāntaratvāt*), it is not a restatement (*anuvāda*); [that is,] the connection for the sake of the sacrifice is one thing, while the connection for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) is distinct.
Soma—The connection [of this section] arises from the refutation of the restatement of what was previously mentioned.

As for the meaning of the Sūtra: the non-performance of action, namely the practice of not speaking untruth, intended for the context of the sacrifice (*kratu*), should be a mandatory restatement (*nityānuvāda*); because, according to Smṛti, it is connected to the person from the time of initiation (*upanayana*) onwards. Vi— "One should not speak untruth": is this a scriptural injunction (*vaidha*) or a duty of man (*puṃdharma*)? It is a statement of restatement (*anuvāda*).
When the ritual injunction applies to a person who is either attached or pure, it applies to the ritual itself.
Because it serves a human purpose, such a prohibition regarding non-existence is [valid];
it is a direct restatement based on masculinity, due to the force of both the Vedic text and the ritual procedure.
When not explicitly stated, there is no mention of a person; offspring is produced only during the fertile season.
Another says: "In the case of the *saktu* offering, there is a dispute; therefore, the injunction regarding the conjunction [of the act] applies to the sacrifice."
The first position is that the prescribed prohibition is a duty for men (*pumdharma*), serving the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

The second [position] is that, since [the act] occurs in a man, the prohibition is a duty for the man associated with the *ṛtu* (seasonal period), while the scriptural statement (*vākya*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). The third position—the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—is that it pertains to the pure sacrifice (*śuddha-kratu-dharma*), and the scriptural statement is a restatement.

Bhaṭṭa: The inquiry is whether specific injunctions and prohibitions situated within the context of particular sacrifices—such as "He offers the *samidh* oblations" and "One should not speak untruth"—are duties of the person in general (*śuddhapuruṣadharma*), or duties of the person engaged in the sacrifice (*ṛtuyuktapuruṣadharma*), or duties of the sacrifice itself (*śuddhakratudharma*).

Furthermore, although for a prohibition, since its agent is engaged in action for the sake of another, it is difficult to establish its status as a subsidiary (*aṅgatva*) in the form of being something to be enjoined.

Even if the object of the prohibition—the act of turning away, or the absence of an effort conducive to speaking—is connected [to the rite] through some other relation, it lacks the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) for the effort (*kṛti*), just like a cause (*nimitta*) and so forth; therefore, since "subsidiariness" (*aṅgatva*) is pervaded by "being helpful" (*upakārakatva*), it is impossible in the absence of that pervader.

As for the prohibition of speaking and the like, since they do not apply to a person engaged in the sacrifice (*kratu-yukta-puruṣa*), they are as far removed from being [subsidiaries] as a broken vessel (*kuṇḍa*) and such things, precisely because they are not prescribed.

Therefore, precisely because it is possible for [the prohibition] to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*), an investigation into those specific locations is impossible; nevertheless, what is called the "person-centeredness" (*puruṣārthatva*) of a prohibition consists in its being the object of an action that generates an effort residing in the person. Its being a "dharma of the person associated with the sacrifice" (*kratuyuktapuruṣadharma*) consists in its being the object of an action that brings about the capacity residing in the person through proximity to the sacrifice. Its being a "pure dharma of the sacrifice" (*śuddhakratudharma*), however, consists in its being the object of an action that causes a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in the sacrifice.
And this [principle applies] wherever a prohibitive act is not specifically enjoined by the scripture, as in the example under discussion.

However, where it is specifically enjoined—as in the case of the taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup and so forth—even in the absence of the specific mention of the thing to be prohibited, the capacity of the sacrifice to produce its fruit is implied by the prohibition itself; thus, it should be understood that the prohibition serves the purpose of the sacrifice precisely by being an indicator (*arthātumāpaka*) of the aforementioned meaning. For this very reason, since subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) is the subject matter of the chapter in a manner common to both primary and secondary [meanings], there is no inconsistency regarding the definition.

In this regard, even though the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) denotes the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) according to the principle of the locus of an action (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇanyāya*), the agent (*kartṛ*) is also denoted by it; for, just like singularity and other numbers, the agent is perceived as residing therein.

This is because, just as the rule *kartari kṛt* (Pāṇini 3.4.67) establishes that the suffix *kṛt* denotes the agent, the rule *laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69)—which is taught for the purpose of expressing the agent, the object, and the state—establishes that the verbal suffix (*l*) also denotes the agent, the object, and the state. Furthermore, this is so because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "Caitra" in the expression "Caitra cooks."

And although, according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "the verb has the action as its primary meaning," the connection [of the object] with the *bhāvanā* is as the thing to be accomplished (*bhāvya*)—just like oneness and so forth—and not with the ritual act (*karman*), because the latter is understood more slowly;

nevertheless, it is accepted that even that which is perceived as subordinate may attain primacy when there is a requirement for a purpose, as in the case of the deity and other factors in the animal-sacrifice cake-offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and so forth (PMS 10.1.19).
This same logic applies equally to injunctions and prohibitions regarding their own objects, even when there is a change in the attainment of their respective locations and so forth.

Therefore, if it is an injunction (*vidhi*), everything [is for the sake of the sacrifice]; and if it is a prohibition (*niṣedha*), the fruit of the action belongs solely to the person (*pratyaya*) by virtue of the direct statement (*śruti*) and the rule of co-referentiality (*samānābhidhāna*), and not "assistance to the ritual" (*ṛtūpakāra*) by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*). And thus, even though the agent is not denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), nevertheless, the word—whether implied by the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) or directly indicated by the suffix—is the means of bringing about the deficiency of that [agent].
Therefore, since the time of her pure menses (*śuddhar-tu*) has arrived, there is no fault in postulating that [the injunction] is for that purpose.
Consequently, it is logical that it is indeed a duty (*dharma*), even under the view that the agent is expressed by the verbal suffix.

In reality, however, as in the case of [the *vaimukhya* rule at] 4.3.11, because it is a duty of the pure person (*puruṣadharma*) according to the principle of context (*prakaraṇa*), its status as the expressed meaning [of the suffix] does not hold; for its cognition is established through other means as well.
[This refers to] the context.

And at that time, because the prohibition of speaking untruth is [connected] with initiation (*upanayana*), it is as follows: from the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), the agent, the effort (*kṛti*), and so forth, such as singularity, are understood; and since these are the basis for the activity of prompting, it is undisputed that this very same [suffix] is the source for the prohibition of speaking untruth for one's own sake as well.
In that regard, the first position is that in every case where a word conveys multiple meanings, [the suffix is the source].

The second [position], however, maintains that even though the person (*puruṣa*) is primary, there is *śakti* (direct expressive power) in one case and *ākṣepa* (implication) and so forth in the other; thus it is the same. For, compared to the assumption of heaven, dissolution, and so on, when the principle is understood from this [text], there arises the fault of assuming multiple powers (*aneka-śakti-kalpanā*). Furthermore, in that context, since an accessory (*guṇa*) is seen in the world to imply a primary element through the requirement of fitness for the principal act—which is understood from the context (*prakaraṇa*)—and because of the necessity of purification (*parisaṃskāra*), [the meaning is established] by direct statement (*śruti*).
The principle of various kinds of clothing and dwellings (450): the principle of the pregnant woman in between;

Parākrama, p. 12: "The maxim of the butter residing in another house being inferred from [the presence of] butter in a different house.
That which is the object to be established and has become the subject of doubt is the *pakṣa* (the thesis). For example, in the statement "the mountain possesses fire," the mountain is the *pakṣa*.

In that case, if [the reason] resides in the subject (*pakṣa*), yet it exists elsewhere as well, and if by means of that the probandum is intended to be proven, then this principle is stated: "One who possesses smoke from another house is inferred to be present in a different house.
For example: "Devadatta is learned; Viṣṇudatta has studied extensively.
Here, the study which is the proof of learning resides in Viṣṇudatta alone, who is distinct from the subject, Devadatta.

The *sāhasī* [commentary] states: "By the maxim, 'Having observed the knowledge of validity from another source, the injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) ordains [the details],' the injunction of performance—just as it is obtained—functions to establish the proximity of the auxiliaries to the primary act" (Ku. 5/1/8/16). Following the worldly maxim, "When [an element] is obtained from another source, the agent and the object are not to be expressed," the meaning of the sūtra beginning with "dvitvekyayoḥ" becomes established. On page 1426 of the *Sukhabodhinī*: "Through the determination of one alternative, there arises an implied determination of the other alternative."

Furthermore, that [exclusion] has both existence and non-existence as its objects. Among these, the first is as follows: "A Brāhmaṇa indeed belongs to Agni by virtue of his deity; through the Soma sacrifice, he becomes one belonging to Agni-Soma. When that Paurṇamāsa oblation is offered, then he belongs to both deities. Thus, when the Agnīṣomīya sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is established as pertaining to a man who has performed the Soma sacrifice, it follows by implication that its absence pertains to a man who has not performed the Soma sacrifice.
[As the text says: "In the previous state, he prepares the altar."

"Because of the *atirātra* [sacrifice] being internal" (460) means that by performing it otherwise; since the *vaidikaraṇa* has been established for the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) sacrifice on the preceding day, it follows by implication that the *vaidikaraṇa* is established for the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) sacrifice after the covering of the oblation (*havirabhivāsana*).
Bāla. pṛ. 19.
Oṃ. Because it has an Atirātra on one side, the Pañcadaśarātra and the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana are *ahīnas* (non-sacrificial sessions), since we observe that those which consist of them are *ahīnas*.
Regarding the dispute as to whether the Pañcadaśarātra and the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana are *ahīnas* or *sattras* (sacrificial sessions), he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The Pañcadaśarātra—a specific sacrifice accomplished in fifteen days and nights—and the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana—a specific sacrifice bearing that name—must be *ahīnas*, not *sattras*.
Because it has an Atirātra on one side.
"On one side" means that it is of such a nature as to have an Atirātra sacrifice either at the beginning or at the end.
And having an Atirātra on one side is the defining characteristic of an Ahīna sacrifice.
And that [quality] belongs to two [others], hence it is *ahīna* (non-deficient).

For in the scriptural passage, "Because it has an *atirātra* on one side, therefore it is *ahīna*," we observe the state of being *ahīna* in those things which consist of that [namely, having an *atirātra* on one side].
Furthermore, it is because of the term *ahīna* itself.

The *pañcadaśarātra* is an *ahīna*, which is a specific class of sacrificial sessions (*ahaḥsamūha*) consisting of a collection of days, and not a *satra*; this is another reason stated for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction.
By the scriptural statement, "Insofar as it has an *atirātra* on either side, therefore it is an *ahīna*," the *ahīna* nature of the *pañcadaśarātra* is explicitly declared.

Thus, because of the statement that it is "not an Ahīna," the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the Pañcadaśarātra is an Ahīna. [The author] states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Or rather, it is a *satra*, because of the injunction regarding the *upāyi*."
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the prima facie view.
Both the fifteen-night sacrifice and the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana would be *satras*, not *ahīnas*,
because of the injunction regarding the consumption [of the Soma].

"Those who desire prosperity should undertake this fifteen-night sacrifice," and in the context of the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, "those desiring wages should undertake it"—these two are enjoined by means of the verbal root *iṇ* (to go) in the sense of "undertaking.
Therefore, both of these are indeed *satras*.
As for the statement, "Insofar as it has an *atirātra* on either side, it is therefore an *ahīna*," this is not an injunction; rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended for praise (*stuti*).
Furthermore, praise characterized by the marks of a *ahīna* sacrifice— namely, being an *atirātra* on one side— is not applicable to the *ahīna*,
because every *ahīna* indeed has an *atirātra* on one side. However, it is applicable to the *satra*.
Because it possesses an Atirātra on either side, this is an Ahīna; yet, by its essential nature, it is a Satra.
Since it thus possesses a dual character, it is the most excellent.
Therefore, the Pañcadaśarātra is indeed a Satra.
And it shows an indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the *satra*:
in the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana*, [the text] "The Subrahmaṇya priest, the Subrahmaṇya priest" shows an indicative mark of the *satra*.
For the householder (*gṛhapati*) is prescribed in the *satra* as the officiating priests who perform the duties of the sacrificer.
Therefore, the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana is a sattra;
likewise, the Pañcadaśarātra is also a sattra. The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that both are indeed sattras and not ahīnas.
Regarding the rule for determining which [of two options] applies when one is obtained: "For the Vāsiṣṭhas, the second *prayāja* is the *nārāśaṃsa*; following that, it belongs to others.
For here, according to the order of the recitation of the injunctions, the second [option] must be taken as it follows that [preceding rule], and not the *nārāśaṃsa*.

Or, for example: "If the Soma sacrifice has the Rathantara as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; if it has the Bṛhat as its *sāman*, [one should draw] those beginning with the *śukra*.
Here too, by virtue of the textual recitation (*pāṭha*), it is established that the cups must begin with those for Indra and Vāyu, not with the *śukra*.
(Bālakrīḍā, p. 18).
When there is a mutual requirement between two things, the requirement of both is stronger.
(Mīmāṃsā, p. 171).
Indeed, the established principle is that what has already fulfilled its purpose in one place may be further explained in another.
(Regarding the matter that the carrying away of Soma-related substances at the *avabhṛtha* bath is a *pratipatti* [disposal], etc.
Bhāṣya 4.2.8.22:
"But another [result] to be accomplished is indeed the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), for one who performs sacrifices and other rites."

By the principle stated in the *Ślokavārttika* (Codanāsūtra, verse 192), "The designation 'dharma' [is applied] to that which possesses it," it is understood that only that which consists of sacrifice and the like is dharma; thus [the author] has accepted this.
(*Sannātana-dharma-pradīpa*, Prāmāṇya-prakāśa, p. 71).
Furthermore, the general is one thing and the specific is another.
"One should sacrifice" is the general; "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]" is the specific. Bhāṣya 7.1.13.

"Modification in the Sūtra" is as follows: "In the case of the injunction regarding the commonality of animals and so forth, the *satra* itself is modified otherwise" (*Ślokavārttika* 1.1.156). Regarding the injunction for the characteristics of the animal in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there arises a doubt: are these rules common to all three animals, or only to the *savanīya*, or to both the *agnīṣomīya* and the *savanīya*, or only to the *agnīṣomīya*? On this point, the Sūtra states: "The injunction for the animal applies to all, because there is no distinction in the context" (3.6.178).
This [Sūtra] means that the rule is common to all—this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

Furthermore, regarding its "otherwise-making" (*anyathākaraṇa*): because it prescribes something different, it serves as the introduction to the "forest-pakṣa" (*āraṇyapakṣa*). Consequently, there arises the risk of [confusing] the logical connection of the rule beginning with *sthānācca pūrvasya* (JS 3.6.20). Therefore, having set aside the first pakṣa—which was formulated without a sūtra—as the basis for that connection and its purpose, and having applied it differently within this pakṣa concerning the *savanīya*, [the author states]: "The injunction for the animal sacrifice (*paśuvidhi*) would apply equally to all, if there were no distinction of context (*prakaraṇaviśeṣa*); however, such a distinction of context does exist. This is the principle: "In the case of its otherwise-making, there should be a removal [of the rule] from many [cases]."

If it is argued that the portion [of the *Āyurveda*] consisting of instructions on Vedic rites for pacification (*śāntika*), nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), expiation (*prāyaścitta*), austerity (*tapas*), yoga, charity (*dāna*), oblations (*homa*), and so forth, is not authoritative—[this being a Buddhist objection]—we say no, because it shares the same status regarding validity (*tulyayogakṣematvāt*). [The meaning is: the medical portion (*cikitsā-bhāga*) would also be non-authoritative. If it is argued that this very point is unproven because there is the possibility of interpolation (*prakṣepa*), we say no; for [the text] has been handed down through an uninterrupted tradition (*saṃpradāya*) from the time of its composition, according to the maxim: "In the case of [a text] whose continuity is established, there is no possibility of alteration."
In the *Pramāṇaprakāśa* of the *Sanātanadharma-pradīpa*, page 246:

Oṃ, the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*). Objects such as the decapitation [of Rāvaṇa], which occurred at different places and times experienced during the day, are remembered due to the force of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) awakened by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); through the influence of the defect consisting of sleep, they appear as residing within the self (*ātman*).
And thus, for those things known as cognitions of another [object], their appearance as cognitions of another is like the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell;
this indeed is what is called *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension).
Nor should it be asked how there can be such an appearance, given that at that time the mind has no connection with external objects.

There is no fault, because proximity in the form of the characteristic of knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇā*) is accepted, and because the cognition of that [object] with its specific operation is admitted as being lost.
(Maṇi, p. 26).
Otherwise, it would be logical for the status of being a cause for apprehension and so forth to belong only to a cognition characterized by the production of a false appearance (*anyathākhyāti*).
Page 27.

Oṃ. In the postulation of alteration, there is the fault of transformation (*vipariṇāma*), the fault of postulating an intervention (*vyavahita-kalpanā*), and the fault of postulating a conventional usage (*vyavahāra-kalpanā*). In this regard, the example of proof is the sentence concerning the *Āgneya* [oblation].

In the second [case], regarding the phrase "those who are established" (*pratiṣṭhāsanti*), there is a displacement of the word *pratiṣṭhāsanti* from its position after *rātrīpeyuḥ* to before it, resulting in the construction "those who are established" (*ye pratiṣṭhāsanti*). (Cāla. pṛ. 4).
Oṃ. It is "impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti). Indeed, impossibility otherwise is not apprehended through direct perception;
rather, it is apprehended through the non-deviation of the effect [from its cause].
And non-deviation [of the probans] is preceded by repeated observation.
(Bṛhatī, p. 85).
Om. "The impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti) is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
And that [inference] is not capable of postulating anything more than what is established as being the cause;
for otherwise-unaccountability (*anyathānupapatti*) occurs only when all other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have ceased to apply. (Vādavidhi 1.2.4.30, p. 142)
1|2|17, p. 119: "The postulation of a result in the Viśvajit sacrifice is based on the impossibility [of the injunction otherwise].
7|1|12, p. 1526: "And that (the *apūrva*) is established by the means of knowledge known as 'impossibility' (*anupapatti*).
Since it is possible through the postulation of a single *apūrva*, there is no basis for postulating another unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)."

For he who postulates many unseen principles (*apūrva*) must necessarily postulate at least one; and if that one is established—since the purpose of the sentence is thereby fulfilled—the "presumption of the otherwise inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*) is exhausted and does not serve as a means of valid cognition for any further unseen principle.

Oṃ. There are three types of "being established otherwise" (anyathāsiddhatva). Among them, the first consists in being a property that does not conform to the positive and negative concomitance of another [cause] which has been apprehended. The second consists in being the object of the apprehension of being a prior existence of the effect, where that prior existence is caused by the negative concomitance of something else that is already established as a prior existence.
The third [condition] is the state of being accompanied by the positive and negative concomitance with something else that has already been postulated (*klṛpta*).

Here, it should be intended as "not following the positive and negative concomitance with something else that has not been postulated" (*aklṛptānyavyatirekānuvidhāyin*); by this, there is no *anyathāsiddhi* (redundancy) for another cause, and the knowledge of God (*īśvara-jñāna*) and so forth are included, because that [knowledge] follows the positive and negative concomitance with the direct perception of the material cause (*upādāna-pratyakṣatva*) and ownership (*svatva*).
Maṇi, p. 45.
*Oṃ*. The maxim: "One thing is auspiciousness (*śubha*), another is dharma.

Just as, for instance, when an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) performed for the destruction of ignorance (*vidyā-nivṛtti*) is composed for the purpose of instructing the disciple, the author of the Siddhāntin has stated therein that auspiciousness is the cause (*kāraṇatā*) with respect to the cessation of ignorance.

In this regard, the proponent has stated: "Indeed, auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is neither the cause of the destruction [of obstacles] nor the cause of completion, because even without auspiciousness, we observe the obstacle-free completion of works by atheists (*nāstika*) and others. Against this position of the proponent, the fault of an undesirable consequence (*ayuktavattāpatti*) arises from the very principle under discussion, namely, that it follows [from his own premise] that [auspiciousness] is not the cause of completion.
The rash one. 271.
