"Oṃ. The principle of the section [sūtra] *anyalabhyatvam*—'The cake on one potsherd (*ekakapāla*) has the Vaiśvadeva as its archetype' (7.1.5.23)—is the logic of this section.
[This refers to] the principle of this section, namely *anyalabhyatva*.
Bhāṣṭa 7.1.15.
Oṃ. Because of the injunction of another [substance], there would be no eating of forest-grown food, for both are intended for the purpose of sustenance.

Since, in the context of the Soma sacrifice, another food is enjoined by the statement, "Milk is the fast-food for the Brāhmaṇa, gruel for the Rājanya, and curdled milk (āmikṣā) for the Vaiśya," the eating of forest-grown grains such as *śyāmāka*—which is obtained through the force of the extended application (*codaka*) from the Darśapūrṇamāsa—is precluded.
This is because both [the milk and the forest-grown food] serve the same purpose.
Various other verses (462) and grains such as *syāmāka* are for the sake of stability alone;
even with just one [type of grain], subsistence— that is, living— would indeed be possible.
In that case, there is no requirement for the combination of both.
Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that there is an exclusion of the ordinary forest-wood. [The question is:
"What are the other verses?"
Nor should it be argued that the expansion of the *ṛc* itself might occur by reciting one triplet (*tṛca*) and then taking up another subsequent verse;
for such a possibility is ruled out by the expression "one after another" (*anyā-anyām*).
Therefore, in the *pragāthas*, there is only an expansion of the *pāda*.

Bhāṭṭa 12.16, Section 4, p. 111. The maxim: "The state of being various distinct words. Why? He says: In that act of denotation (*abhidhāna*) where the word is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the object possessing the dewlap (*sākṣāt*) is the object (*karman*); and in that [act] where it is the object, the word is the instrument. When this rule is understood, if by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) it is perceived that one and the same word has a different meaning as its denotable object, or that a different word is the denoter of a particular meaning, then even the rule already understood is sublated.
Thus, there arises the contingency of contradicting the established rule (*niyama-bādha-prasaṅga*).

Ratnākara, in his *Saṃbandhākṣepavāda*, verse 13, page 501, states: "'The state of having various distinct words for a single [object]' (13.8.26). This logic does not hold, because similar words, while entering into a single meaning, all belong to an uninterrupted tradition (*avicchinnaparaṃparā*). Therefore, among these, one is beginningless (*anādi*), while the others are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*)."
In cases such as "hastaḥ," "karaḥ," and "pāṇiḥ," however, because of the instruction of experts, the relationship between these words and their meaning is beginningless (anādi).
Bhāṣya 13.8.26. Just as it is illogical for a single word to have multiple [meanings], so too is it illogical for a single meaning to have multiple words; this is also a logical principle.
Therefore, the two words "jyotiṣṭoma" and "agniṣṭoma" are not denoters of a single ritual action.
*Kalpataru* 3.1.1: *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya*. The maxim "the state of having various distinct words for different things" (*anyānyānekaśabdatvam*) is presented as an illustration in the *Prakāśa*.
*Parimala*: [The maxim] "the state of being variously distinct" (*anyānyānekatvam*).

Bhāṣya, pp. 301, 410, 748, 1340, 1266, 1550. The author of the *Bhāṣya* read the sūtra "the state of having various distinct words" (*anyānyānekaśabdatvam*) by emending it to "the state of being in an improper place" (*anyāyasthānakatvam*).

Su. pṛ. 356. The seed for the [objection] that "there would be a plurality of distinct [meanings]" consists of three things: the consequence of an unstable relationship (*anavasthita-sambandha-prasaṅga*), the consequence of having to postulate multiple word-meaning capacities (*aneka-śakti-vācakatva-kalpanā-prasaṅga*), and the consequence of the faults of alternative options (*vikalpa-doṣa-prasaṅga*).

As it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "The unity of meaning for a single word is not established by [that reasoning], because of the consequence of the faults of an unstable relationship, the postulation of multiple word-meaning capacities, and alternative options.
Page 301, line 30: "Mutual multiplicity" means that the primary status [of a word] resides in only one [meaning], not in both.
Soma. 7.2.2: A single word might have multiple meanings; what fault would there be in that? When the word is uttered, there would be doubt, and no certainty regarding the meaning.
In that case, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would not be established.
The employment of words is for the purpose of practical usage (vyavahāra),
or else another cause, such as a different mode of expression, must be expected. However, when there is identity of meaning, the cognition of the object is independent [of such factors].
Therefore, it is unreasonable for [the word] to have multiple meanings. Bhāṣya 7.3.14.36, pp. 1533–37: There is no evidence that this [word *paurṇamāsam*] denotes a different ritual action;
rather, it is directly perceived as denoting the ritual action under discussion.
And that which is properly measured is what is to be grasped;
there is a mutual multiplicity [of cognitions]. (5.4.4.14, p.
340) A measure is not perceived as distinct from the object of cognition.
How is this understood? It has been stated [in the Sūtra]: "The multiplicity of distinct [powers]... (3.2.1.9, p. 748).

The principle that "there is a multiplicity of distinct [powers]" applies only where there is a postulation of separate powers due to a difference in meaning; it does not apply merely because of a difference in meaning within the scope of a single power.
Since an alternative explanation is available, it is improper to assume a commonality of verbal expression [for multiple powers]. (Soma. 7.3.2)

"Multiplicity of distinctness" (anyānyānekatvam). Vārttika 5.4.4.18 states: "For multiplicity is illogical"—by this principle, since the names such as *Kāṭhaka* and others are distinct names, their application to the ritual action is justified only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Sūtra 2.4.2.10: Even when in proximity, a new name perceived for the sake of non-repetition constitutes an exception (*utsarga*) according to the principle of "multiplicity of distinctness. It is well-known in the world that [a new name], because it denotes a different object, sets aside the previous cognition and generates a new cognition.
*Bhāmatī* 3.1.1 (*Brahma Sūtra*): "For multiplicity is illogical" (bhā.
7.3.14.4); "Indeed, having two meanings is illogical" (10.1.1.42, 37); "Indeed, having two meanings is illogical."

10|1|1|42: "A single word cannot have two meanings. (Ṭupṭīkā 7.3.16, p. 1536). Others, however, [hold that there is] no modification because of its being established on the bank and because of its lack of distinction; therefore, in this case, regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma (*āgneyomīya-paśu*), the *pāśa-mantra* is recited in the Taittirīya tradition with the word *pāśa* in the singular: "O Aditi, release the bond" (*aditiḥ pāśaṃ pramumoktv eta*). In the Maitrāyaṇīya and Kāṭhaka traditions, it is recited with the word *pāśa* in the plural: "O Aditi, release the bonds" (*aditiḥ pāśān pramumoktv etān*).

In a sacrifice involving two animals (*dvipaśuka*), the application of a mantra containing the word *pāśa* in the plural number without modification—that is, without changing it into the dual form—is improper;
it is devoid of logic (*nyāyaśūnya*).
The same applies to a mantra containing the word *pāśa* in the singular number.

In that context, regarding the singular form used in the archetype (prakṛti) for a sacrifice involving a single animal, there is no perceived obstruction; that is, there is no perceived contradiction in the application of this mantra to a single tethering post (pāśa). Here, from the term "unperceived obstruction" (adṛṣṭapratighāta), the sense of possession (matvartha) is to be understood.
Alternatively, the reading *adṛṣṭapratighātatvāt* (because it has no perceived obstruction) should be accepted; in that case, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Now, in the *Kāṭhaka* and *Maitrāyaṇīya* [recensions], even in the case of a single animal sacrifice (*ekapaśuka*) involving a single noose (*ekapāśaka*) dedicated to Agni and Soma, a mantra containing the word "nooses" (*pāśāḥ*) in the plural is prescribed.

Although this is an irrational connection—since the use of the plural for a single noose is devoid of logical justification—it must nevertheless be explained as being justified by the force of the injunction (*vidhivalāt*), on the grounds that although the noose is a single unit, there is a plurality of its constituent parts, which the plural form intends to express.
And thus, even in that case, it is possible to know that there is no perceived obstruction.

So, while the archetype (*prakṛti*) stands with one animal and one tethering-rope (*pāśa*), there arises an inquiry regarding a sacrifice (*yāga*) with two animals: what is to be applied? What is to be omitted? Where is there modification (*ūha*)? Where is there no modification?
In that regard, the mantra expressing the singularity of the tethering-rope does not apply in the performance with two animals, because its purpose is perceived to be obstructed.

The first position is that another mantra, just as it is employed without modification in the case of a single tethering post, can likewise be employed in the case of two tethering posts; therefore, it proceeds without modification (*anūha*).
The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside what was stated in the first position. [The correct view is: there must be modification (*vikāra*), because the mantra is for that purpose.

Regarding what was stated—that there is no modification—therein [we reply]: a modification must indeed be made, because the mantra serves that purpose, namely, the purpose of the ritual application for releasing the bonds (*pāśa*).
That modification, however, should be made only in the mantra expressing the singularity of the bond, as follows: "May Aditi release these two bonds.

As for the other mantra, since it is possible for it to express the whole, this [present] mantra expresses only a part; thus, because its expression is incomplete and it reveals only those bonds whose number is not intended to be specified, it does not apply. This is the second position.
However, because of the connection with an improper application, it should function according to its literal meaning even in subsequent cases, just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*).
This excludes the second position regarding the word "amītu.
Because of the connection with an improper application—that is, due to the connection with a mantra that expresses a plurality of nooses—it proceeds without modification, just as in the archetype.

Just as multiplicity of parts is applied metaphorically to the whole in the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too in the case of other modified animal sacrifices (*vikṛti-paśu*)—even though they differ from the archetype—the mantra denoting the plurality of cords (*pāśa*) should be used without modification (*anūha*), provided it does not deviate from its literal meaning; however, the mantra denoting the singularity of the cord should be applied with modification (*ūha*). This is the third position.
But in accordance with the true meaning, since injustice is not enjoined [by scripture],
he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
By the word "but" (*tu*), the reasoning stated in the preceding sūtra is refuted.

In accordance with the actual meaning, without overstepping the referent, the dual ending must be substituted for both mantras that express either the singularity or the plurality of the fetter (*pāśa*). Since it is not enjoined that the recitation be modified according to the model (as would be the case in the *prakṛti*), the application must therefore be modified; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
However, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), it remains as it is observed.

[Objection: But surely, just as in the archetype (*prakṛti*), even when there is only one rope (*pāśa*), the mantra expressing the plurality of ropes functions—and this despite its lack of connection with other [rope-less] instances—so too should it function in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) involving two animals.

To this, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) replies: In the archetype, although there is only a single rope, the mantra composed of the word *pāśa* in the plural number is prescribed by that very [plural] expression itself.
Thus, in the Vedic tradition, a mantra seen [in scripture] must be accepted exactly as it was seen.
There, the untying of the fetter (pāśamocana) is to be performed;
there, no purpose is served by [considering it] as either a singular or a plural entity.
But in a modification (*vikṛti*) involving two animals, there is no such direct injunction;
therefore, it must be performed in accordance with logical reasoning (*nyāya*).
Consequently, an adaptation (*ūha*) must be made in the modification.
This is the maxim: "That which is undertaken for one purpose serves another purpose as well.

For example: irrigation channels are constructed for the sake of rice; from them, water is drunk, ablutions are performed, and the rice is cultivated. The same applies here. Amara states: "A *kulyā* is an artificial river."

In the Mahābhāṣya on the sūtra *bahugaṇavatuḍati saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini 1.1.23): "A thousandfold [sacrifice] (*sāhasī*) [is so called]. Vi. 12.1.1: "Observation of another purpose" (*anyārthadarśana*) refers to the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) regarding another matter in sentences that have begun to enjoin something else. For example, the fact that the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) receives assistance from the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and other rites intended for the sake of the bird-offering (*pakṣya*). Vi. 12.1.1. "Observation of another purpose" is the observation of a sign in statements engaged in enjoining one thing, regarding a different matter.

Ku. 2.4.8, p. 233: *Anyārthadarśana* (Observation of a Different Purpose). A certain sentence conveys a meaning entirely different from the subject matter at hand; nevertheless, by the very observation of that sentence with its different purpose, some utility arises even for the meaning of the primary sentence.
Something is inferred regarding the subject matter through that which has a different purpose.

The observation of such a statement is called "observation of another matter" (*anyārthadarśana*). For instance, the statement, "Fourteen oblations are offered at the full moon sacrifice; thirteen at the new moon sacrifice," establishes how many oblations there are in the *darśa* and *paurṇamāsa* sacrifices.
By this, it is understood that at the *darśa* and other sacrifices, the *āgneya* and other principal rites (*pradhāna*), as well as the *prayāja* and other subsidiary rites, [are present].
"Observations of other purposes" (anyārthadarśanāni) [refer to passages such as]: "The other priests shall be ignorant," and so forth.
This is an observation of another purpose regarding the subordinate status of the offspring and other such factors.
The same applies to others as well.

What are these "observations of other purposes" (*anyārthadarśana*)? Those which have no other possible application (*ananyagati*); their status as an inferential mark (*liṅgatva*) will also be stated [in the following]. Vārttika 3.1.7.4, p. 841. An inferential mark in the form of an observation of another purpose indicates some meaning through the relationship of concomitance (*sāhacarya*).
And that [inference] becomes an auxiliary to another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) only when such a primary means already exists; it does not, by itself, produce the ascertainment of any object.
(Ābharaṇa 3.1.2.15). The capacity of a mark (liṅga) consisting in the observation of something else to be self-evidently determinative is not accepted by the experts of the system (tāntrikas).
(Soma).
The principle that "the proximity of another object functions as a qualifier by virtue of expectancy" is established in the *aparimitādhikaraṇa* (6.1.10).
[Regarding] the phrase "he cuts from two sides that are not deficient," the understanding of the animal's entirety [is derived] from this statement. (Parākrama, folio 27/2).
Commentary on 1.4.1:
There is a logical principle that the prescription of one thing occurs by means of another.
For example, in Devadatta’s presence, Yajñadatta provides rice with a bowl; likewise, he provides for battle with elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
This was stated in the commentary on the sūtra "yena vidhis tadantasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.72):
"Eating with a ladle. Sāhasrī, 605.
The other priests would be as in the archetype.
In a *sattra*, there should be other priests than those who are themselves the sacrificers; this is because it follows the archetype.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that just as in the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice according to its original form (*prakṛti*), there are officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) other than the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), so it should be here. However, the meaning of the word "apivā" (or rather) is: "Or rather, they should be the sacrificers themselves, because of their connection with the designation of 'officiating priests'; thus, the status of being a sacrificer belongs to them.
In a *sattra*, there are no officiating priests other than the sacrificers."

However, the sacrificers themselves should be the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). This is because of the connection with the designations of the priests; for in the initiation passages such as "Having initiated the master of the house (*grahapati*), he initiates the Brahman priest," we observe a connection—that is, a relationship—between those designations of the priests and the sacrificers.
Therefore, they should possess the status of both sacrificer and officiating priest, and the office of officiating priest should belong to the sacrificers alone.
If it is argued that the consecration pertains to the agent because of the scriptural statement—
namely, that in a *sattra* sacrifice the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—

and because of the statement, "Having initiated the master of the house, he initiates the *brahmā* priest," then the consecration would be a refinement of the agent, consisting of the initiation of the agents who are indeed the officiating priests.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) would argue: "By means of the designations [of the priests] associated with the agent (*kartṛ*), their consecration (*dīkṣā-saṃskāra*) is enjoined through the force of the statement, just as in the case of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*). Just as in the fire-installation, by the statement, 'He who intends to install the sacred fires (*agni*) for the first time should observe a vow for that night; he should not eat meat, nor approach a woman,' a restriction is enjoined for the installer, namely the Adhvaryu priest; or just as in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, by the statement, 'All [the priests] fast on the day of preparation (*upavasatha*),' the fasting of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is enjoined—in the same way [here]."
It might be so in the case of the object, because that is the logical principle, as in the case of the material cause (*prakṛti*).
[The author] refutes with a distinction the example stated by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*)—namely, "because of being the establisher"—by stating:
"The vow would belong to the establisher, because it is an injunction of something not previously established (*apūrva-vidhi*) by means of a scriptural statement."

However, regarding the doubt as to whether in a *sattra* sacrifice the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) or not, it is proper that the sacrificers alone are the priests, because of that principle, according to the rule: "Or rather, they [the sacrificers] should be the priests, because of their connection with the designation of the priests" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 10.6.15).

The analysis of the compound is as follows: those for whom that principle applies are "those characterized by that principle" (*tannyāyāḥ*), namely the sacrificers; the state of being such is "that-principle-ness" (*tannyāyatvam*); and [the conclusion follows] because of being of such a nature.

Because of the nature of the archetype (*prakṛti*): just as in the archetype, the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the function of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), so too in the *satra*, by the statement "Having initiated the *gṛhapati*, he initiates the *brahmā*," the refinement of initiation would be prescribed for the sacrificers alone.

As for the injunction regarding the fasting of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the injunction regarding the vows of the consecrators (*ādhātṛ*), those will occur by virtue of specific scriptural statements; thus, the example is dissimilar.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in the *satra*, the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests.
If it is argued that they should bear the names of their masters, as in the case of the "Lord of the Cup" (*grahapati*), [we reply:
in the initiation passage, "Having initiated the Lord of the Cup," the designations such as *adhvaryu* and *brahman* are the names of the masters;
they would indeed be the names of the masters.
If the opponent should argue: "All those [functions] belong to the master alone, while the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) must be different;
just as the designation 'householder' (*gṛhapati*) belongs to the master alone and not to the officiating priests, so it is here. Thus would the proponent say.
No, because the well-known [terms] are used for that which is connected with their respective properties.
In the sentence concerning initiation (*dīkṣā*), words such as *adhvaryu* and *brahmā* denote the master;
thus, they would refer to the sacrificers (*ṛtvij*), not to those who are subordinate to another.

What was stated by the opponent is not correct, because of the inclusion of well-known [names]; that is, because the names are included as being well-known among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who perform the duties of the *ādhvaryava* and other offices, based on those very duties.
The suffix *-tva* is used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*).
Therefore, those are the names of the masters (*svāmin*).

The designation "householder" (gṛhapati), however, belongs to the patron alone who is not connected with the duties of a priest—that is, by virtue of his own specific duty—thus it is appropriate for it to denote the sacrificer.

Even in the archetype sacrifice, this word "householder" is employed in reference to the patron, as in the injunction, "The householder should sacrifice. Therefore, the established conclusion is that in a sacrificial session (sattra), the sacrificers themselves are the priests, and the priests themselves are the sacrificers.
Furthermore, a specific designation among many is not tenable when they are equal.

In the case of a *satra*, where the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are equal solely by virtue of being priests and the sacrificers (*yajamāna*) are equal by virtue of being sacrificers, the specific designation "of many" in the statement, "He who is indeed the householder (*gṛhapati*) of many sacrificers is the leader of the *satra*; for he [attains] sustenance through the most abundant [offerings]," would not be tenable. A specific designation such as "householder" is tenable only when there is inequality among similar householders, not when they are equal.

If all [the participants] were to become householders (*gṛhapati*) by virtue of being priests (*ṛtvij*), they would perform [the rites] without any distinction of action; consequently, since there would be no distinction, the specific mention of the householder would be untenable. From this specific statement, it is understood that in the *sattra* sacrifice, the priests themselves are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*).

Furthermore, the designation of "consecrated" (*dīkṣita*) and "unconsecrated" (*adīkṣita*) would not be possible, because those states are inherently and constantly present [in the case of the priests].

The designation and reference "those who have been initiated (dīkṣitāḥ) perform the Satras; those who have not been initiated (adīkṣitāḥ) perform the Ahīnas" would be untenable if the Satras lacked self-performed agency, because the two states— being initiated and not being initiated—
are invariably present in both the sacrificer and the officiating priest (ṛtvij), depending on whether the purpose is one's own sacrifice or a sacrifice performed for another.

Because the act of sacrificing for one's own sake exists in the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), while the act of sacrificing for the sake of another exists eternally in the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*); therefore, based on the designations "initiated" (*dīkṣita*) and "uninitiated," the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in a *sattra* sacrifice, the agency belongs to oneself. This is because there is no distribution of sacrificial fees (*adakṣiṇatvāt*).

"They say that sacrificial sessions (*satra*) are without sacrificial fees (*adakṣiṇa*), because neither a cow, nor a garment, nor gold is given therein. Since the sacrificial sessions lack sacrificial fees—meaning they lack the desire for such fees—the sessions are performed by the participants themselves.
However, if the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) were distinct [from the participants], the absence of sacrificial fees would not be possible.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that in a sacrificial session, the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests.
The state of not being an object for a cognition that depends on the search for something else is the principle of "the full moon [is known] by its complete lack of luster" (6.1.9.4).
Sūtra-pṛṣṭha, p. 1220.
Reciprocal non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*): "That which is the absence of a horse in a cow is reciprocal non-existence"—so say the ancients (*jīrṇa*).

Regarding this reciprocal non-existence, the ancients maintain that it is a pervading occurrence (*vyāpyavṛtti*), whereas the moderns (*navya*) maintain that it is a non-pervading occurrence (*avyāpyavṛtti*). (Ślokavārttika, Abhāvapariccheda, verse 3).

*Maṇi*, p. 34: Mutual absence (*anyonyābhāvatva*) is the state of being an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by identity (*tādātmya*) or by relation (*saṃsarga*); or it is the state of being an absence that is the object of a cognition produced by the superimposition of identity; or it is the state of being an absence that is co-located with its counter-positive, delimited by the same space and time that delimit the counter-positive. *Maṇi*, p. 155: They say that mutual absence is the state of being the object of a cognition produced by a word denoting a relation between a counter-positive and an inferential subject (*anuyogi*) expressed by terms in grammatical apposition (*samānavibhaktika*).
Thus they have said.

In the absence of the co-occurrence of the negative particle (*nañ*), there is a grammatical rule (*vyutpatti*) whereby two words denoting a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and a substratum (*anuyogin*)—which are understood through different case-endings (*vibhakti*)—express a relation of identity (*abheda*). When that same negative particle is co-occurrent with those words, it brings about the cognition of mutual absence.

The fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayānyāya*). The meaning is that [the object] is of a nature such that its apprehension depends on the apprehension of that which depends on its own apprehension.

As it is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* regarding the essence of the rules concerning *buddhi*, *ādeca*, *bahusvara*, and so forth: "When one does not apply effort toward mutually dependent effects in the treatise, it is like a boat tied to another boat; it does not serve for the sake of crossing over."

And so it has been stated by another: "In the rule *halantyam* and the rule *ādirantyena sahetā*, a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*) arises for the mutual understanding of the terms *hal* and *ic*.
This is the summary. [End of] the *Sāhasrī*.
The maxim is: "That which is subordinate (*upasarjana*) to one thing does not connect with another.
The meaning is that whatever is a subordinate qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of one thing does not undergo syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with another.
(Ke.)

As for the claim that—because it is the essence of the *Nyāyāsudhā* treatise—one must accept a lakṣaṇā (indirect indication) of the meaning qualified by the word, even though the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) denotes the object itself, in order to effect its connection with the status of being the recipient (*uddeyatva*), and that consequently the deity expressed by the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) is understood as "the deity as qualified by the word," this is to be disregarded. For, since the status of being the recipient—as expressed in "one should utter [the name]" and so forth—is sublated if applied to the meaning qualified by the word, and because the meaning of the word functioning as a qualifier is not independently produced [as a primary referent] according to the maxim "that which is produced for another [is subordinate]," [this view] must be set aside.
Or rather, there would be a connection; [this is] the *anvādhāna*.

Or it may be someone else, due to the knowledge of the preparatory rite (*parikriyā*). This point is also deliberated upon as an exception to the [general rule of] designation (*samākhyā*): whether the preparatory rite is to be performed by persons designated as such because of its recitation in the context of the Teacher (*ācārya*) and others, or rather by the master (*svāmin*). Once this is established, the statement "or someone else" is to be understood.
Or [the alternative view]:

"Or there may be another [agent], because of the knowledge of the performance" (vā 3.8.19). In this regard, it will be stated that the status of being the performer belongs to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) due to their ignorance [of the primary agent]. (Su. p. 1498). Connection (*anvaya*) is not possible without a relationship of subordinate and principal; for, since two subordinate elements lack mutual expectancy, no connection is observed between them.
The same applies to two principal [words] as well.
Therefore, because pervasion is possible, there is the status of action and factor; otherwise, just as words [are such], so too is the word "the state of being a residual defect" included therein.
Since concomitance (anvaya) is based on having a single object, the cognition of a single object cannot occur without the use of words ending in the same case-suffix.

(Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 832). The logic of positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatirekanyāya): when X exists, Y exists—this is positive concomitance; when X is absent, Y is absent—this is negative concomitance.
"In this case, there exist positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Thus, one proceeds to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of both positive and negative concomitance regarding the logical reason (*hetu*).
For example, when fire is the probandum (*sādhya*), the possession of smoke [is the reason].

Wherever there is smoke, there is fire—this is positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*); where fire is absent, smoke is also absent—this is negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), as in the case of a kitchen and so forth.

By the logic of positive and negative concomitance stated in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* (1.3.10), it is pleasure alone that is the denotation of the word "heaven" (*svarga*); it is not logical for the word "heaven" to denote a substance other than that.

6.1. By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): when there is knowledge of the form (*ākṛti*), there is knowledge of the individual (*vyakti*); in the absence of knowledge of the form, there is an absence of knowledge of the individual. Thus, the form alone is the meaning of the word, not the individual. Similarly, when pleasure (*prīti*) exists, the word "heaven" (*svarga*) is employed; in the absence of pleasure, it is not. Therefore, pleasure alone is what is denoted by the word "heaven. [Ke: Through positive and negative concomitance, the relationship between the signifier and the signified is understood.
Or [it is said]: "By means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the distinction between word and meaning is understood" (Vārttika 2.1.2, p. 586;
Bhāṣya 3.2.1).

Page 747: "The impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvaya-anupapatti*) is the seed of indication (*lakṣaṇā-bīja*), but not the impossibility of the intended meaning (*tātparya-anupapatti*), because that [latter] is impossible in the case of the Veda.

Maṇi, Page 76: Regarding the statement, "Every day he gives one hundred and twelve [cows]," since the giving of one hundred and twelve is prescribed as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of each day within the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice—which is of the nature of an *ahīna*—the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) here does not serve the purpose of the entire performance.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is as follows: this injunction does not indicate that the gift is for the sake of the primary sacrifice; rather, its purpose is solely to exclude [other gifts] such as the one hundred and twelve [cows] and so forth.

The phrase "every day" (*anvaham*), however, is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the fact that the gift is for the sake of the primary sacrifice, which is obtained through extension (*atideśa*). Since the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is already established by the general rule, it would follow from the injunction of giving it again that it should be performed only once; therefore, the phrase "every day" establishes its repetition.

If [the term] were intended as an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the days beginning with the *aśā*, there would be the consequence of the meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*) of the word "daily" (*anvaham*).
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

(Bhāṭṭadīpikā 10.6.17). By the word "daily," the time for repetition (*āvṛtti-phalaka-anvahakāla*) is enjoined for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), because if the twelve-day sacrifice itself were also being enjoined, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
In [Mānava Śrauta Sūtra] 6|7|8, by the term *anvaham* ("daily"), it is stated that even when the gift is distributed day by day, there is no difference in the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) itself.
In Mānava Sūtra 11|4|1, "He gives thousands daily; in the Catuṣṭoma, a thousand horses," there is a prescription for the thousand horses on the tenth day.
However, according to Pārthasārathi Miśra, there is no such division as "a thousand cows daily, but the thousand horses on the eleventh day."

Therefore, in the *Pauṇḍarīka* sacrifice, having given a thousand horses on the tenth day, there is a distribution of thousands of cows for the remaining days. (10.6.17). "Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) must be performed every day"—this is the rule.
(Bhāṣya 7.2.1).

By the statement, "One should sacrifice one [animal] each day; on the twelfth [day], the first," the option of shifting the performance (*vihāra*) is prescribed for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
Bhaṭṭa 10.6.17. The placing of fuel (*anvādhāna*);
the placing of fuel for the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*).

The *adhvaryu* or the sacrificer, having sat down behind the *gārhapatya* fire in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), places three large fuel-sticks (*samidh*) upon it three times with the three *dhaman-mantras* accompanied by the utterance of *svāhā*. Then, having sat down before the *dakṣiṇāgni* with his right knee raised and having placed the sticks in the same manner, he stands at the north-western quarter (*vāyavyadeśa*) between the *gārhapatya* and the *āhavanīya* fires; remaining there, he likewise places three fuel-sticks upon it.
Then, standing in that very place, he performs the ritual worship (*upasthāna*) with the tenth *ṛk*-mantra.

All this ritual activity, being conducive to the rite that is about to be performed, is called *anvādhāna* (the preparatory piling) by virtue of its etymological derivation as "the placing of fuel-sticks" (*samidhām ādhānam*).
For what purpose is the *anvādhāna*? It is for the purpose of establishing the fires (*agnyādhāna*).
Furthermore, that maintenance [of the fires] prior to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites is accomplished precisely through the *saumika* ritual procedure (*viharaṇa*).
Therefore, there is no *anvādhāna* (the ritual piling of fuel) in the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and subsequent rites.
(Vi. 12.1.10). There is an option (*vikalpa*) as to whether the *anvādhāna* is performed on the day of sacrifice or on the preceding day;
it is not a case of a fixed difference in time.

Saṃkarṣa 3.1.5: Regarding the mantra used for the *anvādhāna* (the placing of fuel), the fruit mentioned therein belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*). [The *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice is performed] at 467; the *anvāhārya* [rice] is [offered] in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.

VI. 3.8.14. Between the *anvādhāna* (the preliminary rite of adding fuel) and the principal sacrifice (*pradhāna*), there is a prohibition of other offerings (*iṣṭi*) in the case of occasional (*naimittika*) sacrifices such as the *kṣāgneyī* and others, but not when they are constituent parts (*aṅga*) of a larger rite.

however, in a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *sadyaskalā*, it is indeed employed with the words "atha yajñāya."

The theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related).

Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) are the factors that cause the expression of the related—what is termed "grasping by the grasper"—but not even the fact of being conveyed by words.

For if that were the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the assistance provided by the *prakṛti* (archetype) prior [to the modification], which is not expressed by words, could not be expressed as related by the modified injunction (*vaikṛtavidhi*).

And it has been stated by Śālikanātha: "The modified object itself connects with the archetypal assistance through the performance injunction; thus, the injunction is said to be 'invited' (invitant)."
Whatever is desired and appropriate comes into proximity; thus, the meaning accompanied by each of those [factors] is expressed by its own word alone.
And the meaning of the injunction, being of the nature of that which is to be accomplished, requires an auxiliary;

"Thus [it is said]:

However, regarding the fifth [section], there is no verbal designation for this which has "excess" (*vitati*) as its characteristic; thus, the dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) mentioned is irrelevant, because in the theory of *anvitābhidhāna*, the verbal designation is not the determining factor. *Bāla.*, p. 42: Since even the theory of the expression of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*) has been refuted regarding words, including both stems and suffixes, a suffix expresses its own meaning only as something already associated with its grammatical connection (*kṛtānubandha*). *Su.*, p. 708: The critique of the theory of the expression of related meanings (*anvitābhidhānavāda*) is carried out by means of determining the meaning of a sentence;
therein, the theory of the relation of what is already expressed (*abhihitānvaya*) is also established.
Proponents of various doctrines understand the root of the cognition of sentence-meaning in many ways.
Among these, the path regarding other meanings has been demonstrated in the *Vārttika*.

In that regard, some maintain that the sentence itself is indivisible and possesses the nature of a suggester (*vyañjaka*); it is understood through the various forms of phonemes and words, and thus serves as the communicator of each respective sentence-meaning.

Others, however, maintain that the sentence is precisely such knowledge (jñāna), and that immediately following it, the meaning of the sentence is cognition itself appearing as various universals (jāti), qualities (guṇa), substances (dravya), and actions (kriyā); furthermore, they assert that the relationship between the sentence and its meaning is one of cause and effect.
In both these positions, the means [of understanding] is the acquisition of the conventional usage of words and their meanings through conceptual construction.
Others, however, hold that just like a word, a sentence is also the final phoneme accompanied by the impressions (saṃskāra) of the preceding phonemes.

By the path beginning with "the denoter" (*vācaka*), they maintain that the denoter of the sentence-meaning is precisely that which possesses parts, serving as the means for the cognition of word-meanings produced by words that have acquired their relations and constitute its own parts.
The venerable authors of the *Ṭīkā* hold that the words themselves denote their own meanings as connected with other word-meanings.
The masters of Nyāya hold that the word-meanings, once denoted by the words, themselves bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning.

In this regard, the theory that the sentence and its meaning consist of cognition (*jñānātmaka-vākyavākyārthavāda*) has already been refuted within the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), because it contradicts the principle that an action cannot operate upon itself and because it lacks any functional efficacy.

As for the alternative view that the sentence and its meaning are distinct from the words and their referents (*padapadārthavyatireka-vikalpa*), its resolution lies in resorting to the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*).
For a "sentence" is nothing other than a collection of words intended to convey a single qualified object.

Even the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is nothing but the word-meaning (*padārtha*), because it exists within a single [composite] object; thus, although it is impossible to assert either absolute non-difference or difference, nevertheless, by virtue of its existence as a subordinate constituent, that [sentence-meaning] can be subsumed under the [word-meaning] as something external to it.

If it is argued that the doctrine of the partless sentence (*nirbhāga-vākya-vāda*) is also refuted simply by the admission of parts—just as in the case of words—the answer is no, because that [admission of parts] is unproven.

In this regard, it might be argued as follows: Just as, even though there is a division of phonemes (*varṇa*), because the status of being a single word is possible through their similarity, and because the cognition of individual parts is untenable and false, one has resorted to the view that the word, as a whole without parts, is the denoter of the word-meaning; so too should it be for the sentence. For in that case as well, there is the reflective awareness, "This is one sentence," which precludes plurality, since plurality and unity are contradictory. Furthermore, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning leads one to postulate the sentence itself as being partless. To this we reply: in that case, the illustrative example is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For we do not perceive a word as distinct from its phonemes;
rather, that which is referred to by the cognition "one word" is the cause for the comprehension of a single meaning even when it consists of many [phonemes].
Indeed, even among many things, there is unity when they accomplish a single purpose, as in the case of "an army" (*senā*) or "the Rājasūya sacrifice."

For this very reason, for those who do not recognize the unity of meaning, there is no apprehension of a single word. However, the unitary nature of the word-form as something unconditioned would appear to those who have mastered it merely through its continuous recitation (*saṃhitā-pāṭha*), just as it appears to those whose senses are not impaired; and in that case, because of the manifestation of a single word, the existence of a word distinct from the phonemes would be established. On the contrary, its non-existence is determined precisely by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible. Nor is a distinct word established even by the comprehension of meaning.
For that [cognition of meaning] arises from other phonemes and is certainly not caused by something else.

Since it is established that the phonemes alone are the objects of sensory cognition and nothing else, the comprehension of meaning arising from those other phonemes is understood to have them as its sole cause.

Furthermore, because an intermediate entity is excluded by both perception and non-perception, its status as the expressive agent (vācaka) is cast far away; it cannot be postulated even on the grounds of presumptive necessity (*arthāpatti*).

Therefore, since it is observed that meaning is understood immediately following those very phonemes—which have been produced by a single speaker, are uttered without interruption, possess specific accents, are combined, and are characterized by a particular sequence—it is determined that such [phonemes] alone are the denoters of meaning.
But how can there be simultaneity (*sāhitya*) for those that exist sequentially? We reply: "By virtue of an intermediate operation.
For each preceding phoneme, as it is perceived, generates an intermediate operation known by the name of a "disposition" (*saṃskāra*).
Another phoneme, accompanied by that [impression], produces the comprehension of the meaning.
If this is so, then many impressions would have to be postulated for each individual phoneme; therefore, it is simpler to postulate a single property of "word-ness" (śabdatva).
He says: "No."

Indeed, its existence should not be accepted as something whose reality has been refuted by the non-perception of what is perceptible; however, postulating a *saṃskāra* (latent impression) for the sake of explaining what is observed does not cause much embarrassment. Even if many [factors] are to be postulated as providing the observed assistance, nothing whatsoever is contrary to what is observed. When there is no postulation of other unestablished *saṃskāras* here, the very *saṃskāras* established as causes of memory are these very ones.

If it is argued that those [cognitions], being conditioned by experience, produce memory only with respect to that [object] and not a comprehension of another object, we reply: no other function of theirs is admitted apart from these memories; rather, while producing that very memory, they also serve as conditions for the comprehension of the object, because syllables are denotative only when they are remembered.
But even if they are remembered, how can the comprehension of the object arise from the syllables occurring in a sequence, since [the sequence] does not exist [simultaneously]?

Furthermore, if there were simultaneous recollection even of things experienced sequentially, then words uttered even out of order would be expressive, because they too would generate the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) that cause recollection. Moreover, setting aside error, recollection occurs simultaneously for all [words] due to its logical possibility.
If, however, the sequence of utterance is also required as a factor, then that amounts to the same assumption of an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
For even a residual impression (*saṃskāra*), which is the cause of memory, certainly arises even when there is a different order [of sounds], and memory occurs on account of that [impression].

In that case, what further function could a specific order perform beyond the postulation of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*)? Nor can an unseen potency be postulated, because even without the actual pronunciation or its performance, one understands a specific meaning from the words *jarā* and *jarāḥ*—which are respectively a noun and a verb—once they have ascended to the level of memory.

If the word (*pada*) were merely the phonemes (*varṇa*), then, because there is no difference in the phonemes between the words *rāja-* and *jarā*, and because the sequence of pronunciation and the experience produced by it do not exist when [the words] are unpronounced, and because a single recollection—even when it is held to have multiple phonemes as its object—lacks sequence, how could there be a determination of a difference between words? How much less, then, could there be a comprehension of a difference in meaning? Furthermore, the phonemes are not eternal and omnipresent in their own nature such that they would possess a sequence conditioned by space and time; for if that were so, this [sequence] would be something entirely different.
Those who know the reality of sound maintain that the reality of the word (*padatattva*) is that which causes one to perceive the manifestation of a distinct word.
To this, it is replied:
[This is so] because the property of the manifesting phonemes, though superimposed upon the phonemes themselves, [is perceived as such].
The sequence [of recollection] is accepted for the sake of the object, just as it is for non-duality, certainty, and so forth.

As for the view that in those successive recollections there is an impossibility of acting in concert—just as there is no simultaneous experience—that may be granted; however, the recollection of all [objects] occurs simultaneously, even when they were experienced sequentially, just as it does with other objects such as jars and cloths.
As for the objection that "even if this is so, there would still be comprehension of the object," that is incorrect, because the sequence itself is not a cause.

Even if there is no simultaneity in the mind regarding recollection, and in reality there is no sequence among the phonemes (*varṇa*)—which are omnipresent and eternal—nevertheless, because the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*) occur in a sequence, that sequence is perceived as superimposed upon the phonemes being manifested by them, just as length and so forth are [superimposed] upon the phonemes, or like smallness and largeness are superimposed upon the face in a mirror. Consequently, even the subsequent recollection apprehends only those phonemes whose bodies are characterized by a specific sequential order; thus, the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of the related) is refuted. [The theory of *anvitābhidhāna* is refuted.]
This is the opposite case, because the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the word "cow" does not cease in the absence of a [corresponding] cow.

Now, one might argue that even in that case, the expectancy would cease through actions such as standing, which are perceived directly by means of the stone and other objects; thus, when the object is established by another means of knowledge and a horse is present, upon being told "Let the cow be brought," one understands the meaning of the sentence to be "The cow stands; let the horse be brought here. This is not so, because it is understood that they constitute a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*).
For it is observed in the world that when as many words as possible are employed in combination, they are intended to convey a single qualified meaning through that very combination.
And this is accomplished only when there is a syntactical connection (*anvaya*) among the *śruti* texts themselves; otherwise, it is contradicted.

Furthermore, since the cessation of expectancy regarding the offering can be achieved by means of one [text] alone, it is improper to assume a connection with multiple [texts], due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*).

Therefore, it is the words themselves, expressing the related meanings, that constitute the means of valid cognition for the sentence-meaning. To this, it is replied: even this view is not tenable, for in this view, one would have to assume a greater degree of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
Furthermore, because it would entail the contradiction of what is perceived [in experience], the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the expression of related meanings) is superior.
Where there is conformity with what is perceived and the conceptual construction is more parsimonious, that theory is preferred.

For, according to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of already related meanings), even when a word is analyzed into its components, another meaning—acting as a qualifier—is expressed by each individual word.

Otherwise, the arising of the cognition of the related (*anvita*) would be impossible. Consequently, the postulation of two powers—one for the relation and one for the related—would involve a much heavier postulation of the unobserved (*adṛṣṭa*).
Now, it might be argued: "The power is not postulated as distinct for each relation; rather, only a single power is postulated, which extends up to the related."
That is not correct; for how could both be denotable if there were oneness of power?
It is true that there is only one qualified object, while the other is merely a qualifier.

For although the qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*) itself [is what is expressed], nevertheless the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is indeed distinct from the qualified; if that [qualifier] is not apprehended, it is impossible to apprehend the qualified object as characterized by it.

Nor is there any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) to apprehend it; thus, if one were to maintain that the word expresses the qualified object only after first denoting that [qualifier], there would be the fault of conceptualizing two powers (*śaktidvaya*).
Therefore, it is logical that [the word] denotes only its own form (*svarūpamātra*).

Nor is there any inconsistency in the cognition of the sentence-meaning [in this way], because even when the intrinsic nature [of a word] is denoted, the cognition has a qualified object as its domain.
For the cognition of a particular is established without effort from the universal.

Since the form of the word-meaning, which consists of the universal of all states, is denoted by the word, the cognition of the specific state associated with that [universal] is established from that very source; therefore, it is not possible to postulate a further power of denotation.

And this being the case, in the instance "Let the white cow be brought," since there is no [expressed] agent (*kāraka*), and because action implies only its factors (*kārakas*), it follows that by necessity the cow is connected with the bringing, and the bringing is connected with the cow; thus, the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is refuted.
The refutation of the theory of the expression of the related.
But [it exists] in its own nature alone; thus, there is a great distinction.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of the absence of dependence, we say no, for even when such dependence exists, it is not observed.
It might be argued as follows: we do not assume that the common word-potency (*pada-śakti*) is restricted by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).

How then does the denotation of what is connected (*anvitābhidhāna*) with another meaning not occur? [The answer is: because of the absence of mutual requirement (*apekṣā*). For that [requirement] is the defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the denotation of what is connected.

Furthermore, there is no requirement for action and its factors (kriyā-kāraka) to be perceived through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, there is such a requirement for two [words] heard [in proximity], and that requirement is also removed by their mutual relationship; thus, there is no contingency of connection with some other meaning. In this regard, because no such connection is observed when there is a requirement, there can indeed be a situation where, in a certain place, one desires to know a specific action of a horse—such as whether it is going or standing—upon hearing a sound like neighing (*heṣā*).

Furthermore, in another instance, having inferred motion from the sound of footsteps, one desires to know the specific agent, wondering, "Is it a horse that is going? At that moment, someone utters the words "A cow stands. In that case, if syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) were not accepted as the restrictive factor, then because the horse—inferred from sounds such as neighing—requires a specific action, and the action understood from the word "stands" requires a specific agent, there would be a mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) between them, such that [the sentence would mean] "The horse stands."

Likewise, since movement—inferred from the sound of the footstep—is dependent upon an agent, and since the cow perceived by the ear is dependent upon an action, there would be a mutual syntactic connection (anyonyānvaya) such as "the cow goes.
However, the connection "the cow stands" would not be established by rule, because proximity is common to all [words] and lacks the specific requirement [for a particular connection].
And yet, it is not so observed.
Nor should it be said that the capacity of a word itself is the determinant for the cognition of its own meaning as connected with the meanings brought forward by other words;
for even [the word] "horse" and so forth would then entail the expression of what is already connected. Consequently, the restriction of the capacity of words is not established.

Therefore, unity of sentence alone is the refuge for determining the meaning and for the cognition of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) through words that denote [objects] as already related; and since that [unity] is established by the word-meanings themselves through their inherent capacity to convey the syntactic relation—provided there is no contradiction—it is excusable. Thus, enough with this obsession with the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "dhava-khadirau" and so forth, since it is accepted that "a *dvandva* compound occurs when there is a simultaneous [connection] with a common substratum," and because the connection with the denotative power occurs simultaneously, the *dhava* tree—while connected with the dual number—indicates its own self as being accompanied by a second [entity], rather than denoting it directly. If it were possible for it to be connected with a second entity through any [other] means whatsoever, why would it indicate its own self as being accompanied specifically by the *khadira*? If you argue that this is because of the nature of the sentence (*vākyatva*), then in that case, that very [sentence-nature] would everywhere be the cause through the indication of the objects of words as having a mutually connected essence; thus, there would never be the postulation of anything not already established.

Even though the postulation of a capacity (*śakti*) would be equal [in both views], it is nevertheless more reasonable to accept that the word-meanings (*padārtha*) alone are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), rather than the words themselves, because there is no sequence among sentences.

For even in the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna-vāda*), the knowledge of the sentence-meaning arises only after the word-meanings have been understood through the words; otherwise, proximity (*saṃnidhi*) would be difficult to establish.
However, there is a dispute as to whether those [word-meanings] are expressed (*abhihita*) by the words or merely recalled (*smārita*).
In every respect, it is beyond dispute that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs after the words have been apprehended and their respective word-meanings have been understood.

Consequently, it is not logical to assume that words which are separated by the intervening word-meanings experienced immediately prior could be the cause of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever for the existence of a renewed recollection of the words.
Furthermore, it is simply impossible to maintain the connection [of meaning] in extremely long sentences;
and even in the absence of such a connection, it is a matter of common experience for everyone that the sentence-meaning is understood through the mere connection of word-meanings.

Therefore, by virtue of conforming to what is observed, the sentence-meaning is caused solely by the word-meanings, and not by the words themselves, as that would entail the undesirable consequence of contradicting what is observed.

Regarding this, he says: "Even though the capacity of word-meanings is something being understood, because it follows immediately [upon them], the sentence-meaning does not relinquish its status as their cause."

Thus, it should be understood that by this [argument], the claim that the capacity for connection resides in the words themselves— which is generally associated with the theory of *kāraka*s— is actually established as its opposite. Furthermore,

as for the statement that it is logical for the words themselves to directly convey the connected meaning through their *tātparya*, that would lead to the absurd conclusion that firewood which does not require flames could be the means of cooking, or that sacrifices such as the *Āgneya* could be the means of achieving the ultimate result without those intermediate operations.

Now, in that case, the supreme *apūrva* (unprecedented result) which arises when [the constituent acts] have been concealed by means of forms such as the *āgneya* sacrifice cannot be produced directly by them; yet, because they serve that purpose, it is said that even those which accomplish it through an intermediate operation do so "without obstruction. This is the same here as well.

For here too, while the words themselves are concealed, after the recollection of the word-meanings, the word-meanings alone are the direct means for the sentence-meaning—which is not otherwise apprehended—whereas the words are the means only by way of those meanings, and not directly.

[Objection: But in that case, words would not possess denotative power (*abhidhāyakatva*), because the individual nature of word-meanings would be lost; since they would denote their own forms and so forth, let them be merely indicative (*sāraka*) rather than denotative.
[Reply: Let it be so, if you wish. And thus:
first of all, the word reminds one of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) through its own form, as is seen in common worldly usage.
Even a word is distinguished from a mere indicator because it possesses denotative power.
Even these [words], when not remembered, do not lead us to understand the meaning of the sentence;
therefore, their status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) exists only when they are recollected in their proper connection.

Thus they say. Others, however, say: the cause of remembrance is proximity (*pratyāsatti*); yet there is no proximity between a word and its meaning by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), or the like, from which remembrance could arise.
If it is argued that [the word] possesses denotative power (*vācakatva*), we say no, because that power is innate.
It might be thought: "Just as denotative power exists even in the absence of another relation, so too will there be the capacity to cause recollection (*smārakatva*)."
In this regard, it is thus: because denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) is inherent.

For denotative capacity is indeed the state of being a word (*pratyayatva*), and that is established even by way of an innate power (*svabhāva-śakti*), as is the case with the eye and other senses regarding color-form and other objects.
[Objection: But even there, a relation characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) certainly exists.
True;
however, that [truth] is common to pleasure and the other [feelings].
But in the case of potency (*śakti*), being a cause for cognition is the uncommon [defining characteristic].

In the same way, a word will also possess the capacity to convey meaning through its own inherent power (*svābhāvikī śakti*), whereas its function as a reminder (*smārakatva*) occurs through the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Nor can that [inherent power] be awakened by means of perceiving another relationship, because such a relationship is never observed anywhere.

[Objection: But even the status of being a cause of cognition (*pratyayatva*) is never seen in something that lacks a relationship, for even the eyes and other senses, though endowed with inherent power, convey their objects only through a relationship; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving curd even when it is not being offered.
But the word has no connection whatsoever with its meaning.

How, then, can it be a means of cognition (*pratyaya*)? If you say that even though it is not [directly] perceived, it is postulated as such in this very case, then why is it not postulated rather as a mere reminder (*smāraka*)? Or, the distinction must be stated.
That is now explained.

In any case, even though it has not been observed elsewhere, one must postulate either that a word is a reminder (*smāraka*) or that it is a cause of cognition (*pratyaya*) for something unrelated [to it]. Between these two, the postulation of its being a cause of cognition is superior.

Since we observe the cognition of an object immediately following a word, it is logical to postulate that the word is the cause in that instance; however, it is not logical to postulate that the word merely awakens a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

It is logical that there is a cognition of the meaning of that [word], because there is no evidence for its being a mere recollection. Therefore, a word is indeed expressive (*abhidhāyaka*) and not merely a reminder (*smāraka*).

If it is argued that the cognition produced by a word is nothing but memory because it apprehends what has already been grasped, that is incorrect, because it does not possess the defining characteristics of memory.
The characteristic of a *saraṇa* (re-cognition) is not the grasping of what has already been grasped; rather, it is being produced solely by a mental formation (*saṃskāra*).

On the contrary, that cognition which is produced by a previously existing mode [of apprehension] and grasps what has already been grasped is called an "anuvāda" (re-statement), not a *smṛti* (recollection).

How then is the statement of the *Vārttika* to be understood? It is indeed consistent; for even an *anuvāda*, by virtue of its grasping what has already been grasped, is not distinct from recollection.
"Repetition [of the word] brings about cultivation (*bhāvanā*), as is seen in common worldly usage" (*Ślokavārttika*, *Vākyādhikaraṇa* 248); such is the figurative usage.

And likewise, he says: "Even a word is not distinguished [from a sentence] because it lacks anything additional and because it is merely a reminder" (*Ślokavārttika*, *Śabdapariccheda* 107); this shows that it is not [merely] a reminder.
Therefore, it is logical that a word possesses denotative power (*abhidhāyakatva*) even when its expressed object is the mere nature of the thing itself.
"That which is the cause of primacy is also a means for proving the meaning;
those [arguments] regarding the non-existence of intentionality and denotation are also rendered inconclusive.
This is the summary verse.

Furthermore, if the state of being related (anvitattva) were understood solely through direct denotation (abhidhāna), then how could there be a comprehension of the bank and so forth—which are indicated by secondary signification (lakṣaṇā)—as being related to the hamlet in such expressions as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā"?
For even the essential nature of that [bank] is not the primary denotation of the word "Gaṅgā," much less its being related [to the hamlet].

Now, it might be argued: [this text exists as a certain [view] of the proponent]: "When the nature of the object, which serves as the cause, is recalled by the word *gaṅgā*, the word *ghoṣa* denotes its own meaning as connected with that nature of the bank which is recalled through its relation to that [primary object]; the word *gaṅgā*, however, is useful merely for the recollection of the bank.

But in a case where, as with all words, every term has only a metaphorical meaning and no primary meaning exists at all, how can there be a cognition of the related [meaning]? Or does such a sentence even exist that is true [but lacks a primary meaning]?
The action, or that which is associated with it, is what the earth moves toward;

indeed, for all words, the denotable object is either the action itself or that which is associated with it. For verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*), the denotation is the action; for others, however, it is that which is associated with the action.

In the world, there is observed the use of words concerning accomplished facts (*siddhārtha*) that takes the form of a response to curiosity but is devoid of any [further] purposeful action (*kāryaśūnya*), such as: "Who is this going? or "He is going on the ground," and so forth.
Or, for poets, because of the description of specific objects (*arthaviśeṣa*), as in: "The women, with eyes like blue lotus groves, move about with cranes."
"Clad in silk, they are as beautiful as kadamba flowers," and so forth; for it is your own established doctrine that such [usage] is indicative (lākṣaṇika).
And even in that case, there is only the cognition of the related [meaning].
Nor does this [cognition] deserve to be produced by words, because they do not denote that [relation];

for since the word *bhūmipa* (king) does not denote its own meaning as connected with an action (*kāryānvita*), its own meaning cannot be denoted as connected with the sense of "going" even when [the sentence] possesses expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth; likewise, the sense of "going" is also not denoted as connected with that [king]. Thus, the cognition of a relation cannot arise based on words. Therefore, one must necessarily admit that this cognition of a related [meaning] is obtained through the nature of the meanings brought forward by the words—which serve as the cause—by means of the characteristics of expectancy, semantic competency (*yogyatva*), and syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*).

And if that were so, let it be thus in all cases; what is the point of postulating that words denote [objects] as related? Or, do you maintain that in those cases cognition arises through inference having the related object as its domain, and not through words nor through word-meanings?

Just as in the case of accomplished objects (*siddhārtha*), the cognition of the sentence-meaning is not caused by the words, so too it is not caused by the word-meanings; rather, it is caused by inference. For the composition of a sentence, being a human product, leads one to infer its author's prior knowledge regarding the specific meaning. That [composition] in turn causes one to infer the specific cognition that served as its cause. Thus, when the object is established through inference, there is no capacity in all the individual word-meanings to convey the connected sense (*anvita*).
It cannot be established [that the meaning is] determined.
For instance: even in cases where there is a cognition of the effect, the same consequence follows;
the capacity of words is not established on the basis of their being connected [with other words].

Even in cases such as "Bring the cow," since the understanding of a specific action is established through a succession of inferences according to that very logic of verbal expression, it is not easy to maintain that words possess the capacity to denote meanings already related (anvitābhidhāyitva).
To this, it is replied: That object which constitutes the subject matter of a sentence is inferred by means of that [sentence].
The determination of the power of words cannot be established [as referring] to something else that is not associated [with them].

For it must necessarily be admitted that for one engaged in linguistic usage, the cognition of that very [associated object] arises through the observation of usage directed toward a qualified object;
and this is not established by the mere sentence, but rather from the comprehension of the qualified sentence.
And its specific distinction lies precisely in its capacity to denote an object.

For, by means of a sentence that conveys a specific sentential meaning, the listener infers the speaker’s intention regarding that subject; then, through the inference of a cognition directed toward that specific object, the elder listener understands the particular object and proceeds to engage in linguistic activity concerning that specific object, which would not be possible otherwise.
Therefore, one must necessarily admit that a sentence possesses the capacity to convey a specific object.

And since this [capacity] is necessarily established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) as residing only in the words themselves, it is proven that words denote objects as related (anvitābhidhāyitva). For instance: even in sentences whose referents are already established (siddhārtha), because there is a comprehension of a qualified meaning, and because the words themselves lack such capacity, the word-meanings serve as the cause (nimitta).

For even from sentences whose meanings are already established, such as "The king goes" and so forth, there arises a cognition whose object is a specific meaning—namely, the king's going and the like—and this [cognition] results from inferring the speaker’s specific knowledge.
Furthermore, the composition of a specific sentence serves as the inference for that kind of knowledge;
and the particularity of a sentence can only consist in its capacity to convey that specific meaning, and not otherwise.

Therefore, it must be admitted that a sentence conveys a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*). In that case, since words lack the capacity to denote their own meanings as already connected to an action (*kāryānvita*), it must be accepted that they convey a qualified meaning by means of the word-meanings (*padārtha*) themselves. If it were argued that the inference of the cognition regarding that [qualified object] does not necessarily depend on a sentence that conveys a connection, because a qualified inference can be obtained from a collection of words that merely recall specific objects;

For such is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of consciousness: "Whoever utters words that express certain objects which are capable of mutual connection, that person possesses knowledge of those objects in relation to one another.

And thus, even without the objects themselves being expressive of a connected meaning, since it is possible to infer a specific effect regarding established facts through the inference of knowledge by means of the particular arrangement of words alone, it does not follow that the sentence has the word-meanings as its cause.
If this is so, then the same would apply to sentences whose meanings are effects (*kāryārtha*).
Therefore, the cognition of the sentence-meaning would not be established [by the mere denotation of word-meanings].

For even in sentences such as "Bring the cow," since words possess the capacity to convey the individual forms of their respective word-meanings, it is possible to infer the specific sentence-meaning only after first inferring the qualified cognition [of those meanings]; thus, the status of words as "denoters of the related" (anvitābhidhāyitva) is established.

Even without the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), since words uttered by someone [as] non-denotative of those word-meanings—which, though mutually compatible, consist merely of their own forms (*svarūpa*)—are pervaded by the possibility of inferring a qualified cognition of the form: "That which is connected with this [object] is other than that," [the inference is possible].

Furthermore, even the mere form is not the denoted object; for, just as a specific word is the expressive [signifier], it is possible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through a cognition whose object is the qualified meaning.

For just as the denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) of each word is grasped with respect to its specific meaning—such as that the word "cow" denotes an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth, and the word "horse" denotes a steed—so too can the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of each respective word by a cognition whose object is the meaning connected with that [other word] be grasped, [in the form]: "The arrangement of the word 'cow' is preceded by a cognition of an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth, which is connected with another suitable and desired meaning.

Consequently, even the fact that words denote the intrinsic nature of objects (*arthasvarūpa*) is not established; how much less so their denotation of [objects] already connected (*anvitavācitva*). Therefore, the authority of the Veda [is maintained].

For it is not possible for the Vedic sentence to convey the meaning of the sentence through the inference of the speaker’s knowledge—since [the Veda] is without a speaker—and thus its validity would be established.

It might be argued as follows: having observed the activity of the elder who is prompted [to act] immediately after hearing the words, one infers that he possesses a cognition whose object is a specific meaning.

And because that [cognition] arises from the internalization of the word, it is understood as being produced by that very cause; thus, the capacity of the word to denote that [meaning] is postulated. Subsequently, however, upon observing someone acting toward an object not previously mentioned, he reflects: "How did the elder who is being prompted arrive at a certain cognition of the meaning from a sentence that appears to be inconsistent? Having reflected, he determines this: "Surely this person has understood the meaning in this way based on this very [sentence]; these words are not grasped as unrelated; therefore, surely another cognition has been known by him. Thus, he concludes that the sentence possesses the capacity for inference based on cognition.

However, it is not considered false that the capacity to denote was present previously; rather, it is the capacity to denote as established by that [usage] which is intended. This is not correct, for the capacity of a word is not inferred from its being produced by an effect.
It might be argued that there is an error regarding its being produced by that [word], and that this error must be removed.

For the understanding of the elder who is prompted [to act] following the word is not produced by the word itself—such that one would postulate a causal power (*śakti*) for it—since it is produced by the inferential mark (*liṅga*) which is the speaker’s cognition inferred from the word.
Nor can an effect already accomplished through another cause constitute a power belonging to something else.
[The opponent] imagines [this], but that leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
