Even though, in that state, one might mistakenly perceive the word's status as being produced by a word—due to its continuity like inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and due to the proximity of the word—and thus mistakenly perceive the word's capacity (*śakti*), nevertheless, later on, when one realizes it is not produced by that [word], the error regarding its being produced by it ceases; consequently, the capacity based upon it, or the error itself, is indeed sublated. This is like the cognition of smoke arising from a "smoke-elephant" (*dhūmamahisha*) that is merely emitting smoke;
for that [cognition], although superimposed in its own form, ceases precisely because it lacks the nature of a valid logical mark (*liṅgatva*).
Likewise, the assumption that a word possesses denotative power must also be abandoned, because it is determined that the effect [of cognition] is not produced by it.

Now, one might argue that even after an inference has occurred, a word could subsequently function as a denoter by restating it. To this we reply: no, because there is no evidence for its being a restatement.
For there is nothing inconsistent that would necessitate the assumption of its being a restatement (*anuvādakatva*).

If it is argued that it is a restatement because it possesses expressive power (*śakti*), then that is a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*): expressive power depends on being a restatement, and being a restatement depends on expressive power.
Therefore, its status as a denoter (*vācakatva*) is not established.
If, furthermore, expressiveness [of words] is for the sake of establishing the inference of knowledge whose object is the specific ultimate reality,
then there follows the refutation of the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna) at 478,
and the defense of the theory of the expression of the related at 479.

Now, he says: "The word-meanings, having been expressed, bring about the cognition of the sentence-meaning; this [cognition] is of an internal nature, and it is logical that even though it is being expressed, it does not [manifest externally]. *Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the theory of *sphoṭa*. The phrase "ayedānīṃ" likely introduces a new point regarding the relationship between word-meanings (*padārtha*) and the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). The argument suggests that while individual word-meanings are conveyed, the resulting understanding of the whole sentence is an internal, mental realization rather than a further verbal expression.*
As for the explanation given of this—
that the denotation of the universal enters into the unconnected individual— it is not the case that the universal is merely the individual itself.

The word denotes [the universal] alone, not the connection; for if it were to denote the connected form, then by virtue of entering into the denotable object, the individual (vyakti) would also become denotable.
This is because the connection has already been understood.

The meaning of this is as follows: just as the form (ākṛti) is [the universal], so too the nature of that which is connected is its state of being connected; thus, when that is denoted by the word, the individual (vyakti) is perceived along with the form being denoted by the word. It is [this individual] that is born from the word.
The inclusion of the positive concomitance (anvaya) would necessarily occur [in the denotation].

Therefore, there too, there is a power (śakti). Even though it is within the scope of cognition, it is said to be "comprehensible through form" (ākṛtigamya); in that regard, it is "comprehensible through form."
It must be postulated.

Now, if it is argued that by the word "endowed" (*anvita*), the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the word-meanings is indicated—since that [nature] is the cause for the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*), and not merely the generic form (*ākṛti*) alone—[then we reply: no.
It is said that [the universal] perishes, and that it is impossible to express one thing without expressing the other;
it is understood through the word, and thus it is logical that the individual (vyakti) is likewise [understood].
But if it is so, then the cognition of another [thing] by means of the word is not established.
Not like a genus (jāti), because a genus is denotable in each individual instance;
for this [denotability] is indeed the very nature of the configuration (ākṛti).

Without an underlying continuity (anvaya) within the individual instance (vyakti), the essential nature of the word-meaning cannot be defined; for it is by means of that [continuity] that the form [of the meaning], which culminates in the individual instance, is capable of ascending to the level of cognition through the word.
Now, just as the universal (jāti) is not [separate] from the individual (vyakti),
nor is there a cognition of form when the possessor of form is absent— if such a thing were to exist...
Nor is it cognized as devoid of any individual instance; likewise, the word-meanings themselves would not even exist as forms [if they were not so cognized].
Therefore, the universal (jāti) is perceived together with the individual instance.
In some cases, [words] are found to be devoid of mutual connection; ultimately, they are employed in the sense of existence (*astyartha*).

Furthermore, it is maintained that the cognition of the form (*ākṛti*) is the cause for the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*), yet even so, there is no co-referentiality (*anvitatva*) of all word-meanings in every instance.
That too is refuted.
For what reason? Because a word, by its own power, [denotes] the genus—
Since [the meaning] is established from the very cessation [of the operation], it is not the denotable object.
True; it denotes only the positive concomitance (anvaya), but because it is impossible to cause comprehension without the individual (vyakti) [which is excluded by that concomitance].

It is understood from the non-termination [of the word]; however, its specific [form] cannot be [known] without explicit designation. Because it possesses this nature, it also causes the individual (vyakti) to be conveyed.
Therefore, this is the inherent capacity of the word.

It ascends to verbal cognition; therefore, since the word denotes the related [meaning], the cognition of the action (kṛti) follows, and the cognition of the individual (vyakti) is caused by that. Due to the complexity of postulating a [separate] power, [the word] denotes only its own form (svarūpa).
How, then, is it so?
It is said that the cognition of the form (ākṛti) is the cause for the cognition of the individual (vyakti);
as the author of the Bhāṣya states: "The second case-ending arises from the nominal stem (prātipadika)."

But it is not the case that the form (*ākṛti*) is first understood by means of the word and only afterwards does the word cause the individual (*vyakti*) to be cognized; rather, he says [in Pāṇini 1.2.64] that "the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is the qualifier. (1.1.725)
Likewise, [it is said] "by the word through the expression of the related" (p. 99).
Why is it stated that the cognition (*pratyaya*) expresses the related?
Because it is impossible to cause the understanding of the related without [the cognition of] the other; therefore, the relation—

Or, in your view, how is it that when [the sentence] causes the cognition [of meaning], it is said to be "caused by the word-meanings" (*padārthanimitaka*), while in the Bhāṣya, when there is a distinction, the disappearance of that [word-meaning] is stated? By that [reasoning]...
It is said that [a word] is "connected" (anvita) by means of a word; the connection is with the word-meaning of the sentence.
Because they are in accordance with the connection, other words denote their own mere forms;
the meaning is that they cause the sentence-meaning to be understood as connected, and they cause another [meaning] to be understood as connected.
However, it must be established that [the word] possesses the quality of denoting what is already connected (*anvitābhidhāyitva*). Alternatively,
"the state of conveying what is connected" means nothing other than "the state of conveying [something else]."
Nor is it said that the suffix (*pratyaya*) does not denote what is connected [with the stem]; what then?
This is not an explanation of the text by way of a convoluted path.
When its own meaning is expressed by means of a suffix, it shines forth in accordance with the meaning of the verbal root as understood through its power;
and this is what constitutes the "denotation of the related" (anvitābhidhāyitva) of words.

Since it is understood that [the word] refers specifically to blood, in that case, the meaning is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the primary subject;
this is supported by logical arguments.
Thus, the commentary on the text is provided even by means of a difficult method.
And by the speaker's own will, [the meaning] arises from the suffix and the base-part in the aspect of affection;
thus it would come to be.
The individual word-meanings expressed by the words [constitute] the sentence-meaning.
When it has been established that co-utterance itself is the cause for the cognition of attachment to another word-meaning, then [the words] are logically connected as conveyors of that meaning.
It is said:
just as in the case of perception and recollection, [recognition] does not arise in this way through perception alone.

And the cause for the cognition of the related [object] is that the sensory aspect has the sense-faculty as its cause, while the recollective portion has the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as its cause,
as stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).
By this commentary, that which is rooted in it is implied;
and when the springtime is apprehended as qualified by the absence of the sound of cuckoos, the specific qualification is stated.
Even though it is fixed,
those who do not perceive it as equal [to all] are favored by his compassion;
therein, he asserts the meanings of sentences— both the primary and the secondary— as having the nature of intentional discourse regarding the purpose of the task.

In this regard, it must be established that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is indeed something unprecedented (*apūrva*). Its foundation lies in the fact that even the meanings of the individual words are of such a nature; therefore, he first examines that very [sentence-meaning]. Here, he makes a formal declaration (*pratijānīte*) in order to refute those who claim that the sentence itself—whose division into words is perceived—is the conveyor of the sentence-meaning, as well as those who hold that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are the sentence through their connection, and those who maintain that the word-meanings denoted by the words bring about the mutual connection for themselves: "Just as the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from the words alone..."
In this way, we establish the doctrine of the teacher Prabhākara:
[the meaning] arises from the words themselves as a sentence, neither from the letters of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*), nor from the word-meanings.
He begins to explain that method: "By means of the words alone, whose capacities are exhausted by merely conveying their own meanings as related [to one another]..."
When the meaning of the individual words has been understood, the meaning of the sentence is likewise grasped by the intellect.

For, since words alone are not the means for the cognition of the sentence-meaning, the sentence as a single unit is postulated as that means through the principle of "presumption based on the impossibility otherwise" (*arthāpatti*). Although the meaning of a word is not understood independently of its relation [to other words], and although the derivation of meaning occurs here because the Vedic *kārya* (duty/task) is an eternal means [of knowledge] dependent upon sentences and their constituent parts, nevertheless, it is accepted that one understands the sentence from the sentence itself, which has been refined by the mastery of the meanings of individual words.

Alternatively, if words and word-meanings are merely conceptual (kalpanika), then because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for them, and because meaning is not understood from the utterance of each individual phoneme, nor is simultaneous hearing possible for those phonemes uttered in sequence, another phoneme—accompanied by the mental impression (saṃskāra) produced by the preceding phonemes—is what is directly perceived. And the view is accepted that the conventional understanding of ultimate words and word-meanings serves as its auxiliary cause (sahakārin). Or else, it is maintained that words, whose meanings are easily understood through convention yet remain unconnected [to one another], convey the sentence-meaning by expressing their own respective referents.

If, however, it can be established that words themselves denote their own meanings as already connected, then, because the meaning of the sentence has been understood, these [other] hypotheses find no footing.

But how is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning established if words convey only their own meanings as already connected? To this he says: "The connection is one of primary and subordinate elements; the wise declare that the sentence-meaning is indeed the meaning of the word."

[Objection: "But surely, because they are so numerous, there would be many sentence-meanings and many sentences. To this he says: "Although the individual meanings of the words are numerous, they are each distinct; yet, by virtue of their purpose, they are merged into a single sentence-meaning.
Because it is understood as a single sentence-meaning, it is spoken of individually [as one]."
But how, then, can there be a single purpose for many? To this he says: "For the qualities of comprehension have a single primary purpose.
If that which is the primary element is indeed to be understood as distinguished, then the presentation of the qualities is for the sake of that very end.
Therefore, the purport (tātparya) lies in that very [sentence] alone;
that alone is the object of cognition (prameya).

Since the authority of a word is accepted only with respect to its purport, and since the comprehension of such a [purport] does not depend upon a single word, the sentence alone is the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) in that regard.
For this very reason, it has been stated by means of the genitive case: "In a sentence, there is no such thing as a word, nor are there any such things as word-meanings within the sentence-meaning.

The meaning is that there is no separate entity called a word that serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and there are no separate word-meanings that serve as objects of valid cognition (*prameya*).
And this has been clearly stated in that very same [work].

Now, in order to refute those who claim that only the sentence is the signifier of the sentence-meaning, and those who claim that it is only the phonemes connected within the sentence [that signify], he says: "In linguistic transactions involving elders, which occur upon hearing sentences, the determination of the expressive power of words is made through the process of insertion and deletion. Although all acquisition of linguistic competence is preceded by the linguistic usage of elders, and such usage occurs solely through sentences, nevertheless, when a certain portion of meaning is inserted with the insertion of a word, and is deleted with its deletion, it is precisely through that [correlation] that the expressive power of that very word is established for that specific meaning.

Nor is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning thereby rendered untenable, for the logical principle will be stated later by which one might postulate a single sentence as a product, while disregarding the distinctness of the phonemes perceived through direct perception. Furthermore, for these sentences— “O child, bring the cow,” “O child, tie up the cow,” “O boy, bring the cow,” “O boy, tie up the cow,” “O infant, bring the cow,” “O infant, tie up the cow,” “O little one, bring the cow,” and “O little one, tie up the cow”— eight [distinct] expressive capacities would have to be postulated.

The proponents of the word (*padavādin*), however, maintain that there are seven powers for true sentences. Following this same method, in the case of the word *śuklām* (the white one), the proponents of the sentence (*vākyavādin*) must postulate eight further [powers],
whereas for the proponents of the word, there is only one.
Furthermore, it must be considered: if the division of words is not ultimately real, upon what basis does the acquisition of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) rely as its means?

Moreover, even in the view of those who assert that the phonemes (*varṇa*) within the syntactical connection of a sentence possess denotative power (*vācakatā*), the acquisition of proficiency is indeed possible, because the division of words and word-meanings remains ultimately real in their system.
Now, it is said that the acquisition of proficiency consists precisely in the grasping of the relationship between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*).
Furthermore, for those who maintain that sentences do not denote individual phonemes, a word is not the denoter of a word-meaning;
therefore, even in their view, the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) would be devoid of an object.
To this it is replied:
It is not by way of a definitive determination, because the relationship between cause and effect is accepted [as existing].
What, then, is the causality of the substrate (*adhas*) in this case?
It is not a fault at all.

For when a word is not employed within a sentence, and a certain meaning connected with others is understood as part of the sentence-meaning, that word is merely the cause for that meaning and not its direct denoter.
However, even in that view, the complexity of postulating a [separate] expressive power (*śakti*) is exactly equal to the [previous] argument already presented.

As for those who claim that it is the sentence itself, as it has ascended into memory, that conveys the meaning of the sentence—for them too, the aforementioned burden of conceptualizing an impossible succession remains.

Furthermore, the statement of the Commentator, "another letter, accompanied by the impressions produced by the preceding letters, is the cause of cognition" (1.1.5, p. 46), would be rendered objectless. Moreover, the simultaneous recollection of a large sentence is impossible.

Therefore, the expressive power must be attributed to the words themselves. On this point, some raise an objection: "Indeed, it is not even possible to determine the expressiveness of words within a sentence employed in the linguistic usage of elders; for human sentences lack the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding their meaning, as they lack any indicative mark (*liṅga*). For from the sentence, which is the effect, one infers the speaker’s prior cognition—which is the cause—having that meaning as its object, through the effort [required to produce the utterance]."

And since that [word] is non-deviant with respect to what is to be praised and what is to be known, it depends upon the remaining objects [as its cause]; thus, there is no need to postulate its status as a denoter (*vācaka*).
To this it is replied: surely you have not properly grasped the meaning set forth in the *Nītipatha* (the treatise titled *Nītipatha*).
For this is explained there:

when a child is learning, he understands that the specific activity of the elderly person who employs him—which occurs immediately after hearing a word—is a cognition of an object caused by that word.
Having thus learned, he at some point hears from someone a sentence consisting of words whose meanings are mutually connected.

And for one who perceives it in this way, this reflection arises: "How could this sentence, consisting of words whose meanings are not yet perceived as connected, have produced a certainty regarding its meaning for an elder?
For even in the case of an elder person, the suspicion that the words might not express a connected meaning is possible, just as it is for me."

When such doubt arises, this certainty is produced once again: "Surely this speaker has been determined to be thus; he employs words whose meanings are connected [to one another]. Since no other [cause] is possible for this restriction in the employment of such words, which is not otherwise perceived, it is established through inference that there is no other [cause]. And when the other [the speaker] is ascertained, this sentence becomes a mere restatement (anuvāda) of him.

If it is thus considered that the statement is merely a restatement of that meaning and is therefore a valid sentence, such that the prior cognition of the expressive power [of the words] is not erroneous; yet, one has simply not realized that previously there was a determination of the object preceded by inference—then even this inference of the specific speaker’s knowledge based on the unestablished connection is not possible through the mere comprehension of the forms of the words alone, but rather through the comprehension of their specific [meaning].
And no specific feature of the words other than their expressive power is perceived.

Therefore, because this person also possesses the expressive power for these words just as I do, he is swift; thus, by the employment of words that express a qualified relation (*viśiṣṭānvaya*), he has inferred the speaker’s prior cognition regarding that [relation].
This great ocean of logic is profound.

On this point, some say: "Granted that there is knowledge of the word-potency (*śakti*) of words with respect to word-meanings, nevertheless, the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is not established."

For instance, because the counter-correlates (pratiyogins) are infinite, there is no positive concomitance (anvaya); and since they are not non-different [from one another], those things already conjoined would likewise not be non-different, making it difficult to grasp the relationship. Furthermore, a word whose relationship has not been grasped cannot be expressive, as that would entail the absurd consequence of all meanings being understood from a single word. Moreover, the denotation of universals is certainly not impossible, since the connection with particulars is understood from sentences.

Furthermore, even when there is the expression of the mere intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) [of a word], the cognition of the sentence-meaning occurs; for if one resorts to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of what is already related), it involves the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a separate power (*śakti*).

Likewise, it must be considered whether a word, while expressing its own meaning as already related, expresses it as related to another word-meaning that has been expressed, or to one that has not been expressed. If it were related to an unexpressed word-meaning, the employment of other words would be useless, and there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cognition of all meanings arising from a single word-meaning.

If it is argued that [the word] denotes [the object] as already expressed, then that word too, by virtue of denoting what is already connected (*anvitābhidhāyitva*), would require the denotation of another word-meaning; thus, a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*) results.
Therefore, words perform the function of denoting the mere essential nature (*svarūpamātra*) of the word-meanings.

And those word-meanings, having been thus denoted by the words, bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning when they possess expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*).
One should not suspect that they require the apprehension of a collective whole (*saṃgraha*), because this is a property of words (*pada-dharma*), not a property of meanings (*artha-dharma*).

Thus says the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "For words, having denoted their respective meanings, cease their operation; then, the word-meanings, being thus expressed, cause the sentence-meaning to be understood" (1.1.25, p. 96). He begins to refute this [view] as follows: "Their own meanings are deposited and measured out, possessing nothing else..."
The capacity of words is understood to reside precisely in those [words] that are not themselves connected [to a meaning].

To this, it is said: It is true that insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*uddhāra*) have as their object only word-meanings already connected; nevertheless, the denotation of the connected (*anvitābhidhāna*) is impossible.
That is stated by way of a traditional succession (*pāraṃparyeṇa*).

For instance, a word-meaning conjoined with others, when expressed, becomes the cause for the cognition of that which is so conjoined; thus, words possess causality toward the conjoined meanings through a mediated process.
As the venerable authors of the Vārttika have said: "The capacity [of words] is not lost even regarding the sentence-meaning for us;
it is understood from the word-meanings once they have been determined by those [words] alone."

Thus, as stated in the *Vākyādhikaraṇa* (Ślokavārttika 229): "The presentation of word-meanings (*padārtha*) is the internal operation of words joined together for the sake of comprehending the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*); it is precisely this that is conventionally designated as 'the presentation [of the meaning],' which is an indispensable concomitant of them, just as flame is of wood in the act of cooking."
(343) Thus [it was said].

Anticipating this very doubt, he first dispels another objection: "I have relied upon the following linguistic convention: words express their own meanings as connected with other meanings that are obtained through expectancy, proximity, and compatibility."
Likewise, due to non-difference and non-deviation, there is no fault whatsoever.

As for what was stated— that because a word is non-different [from its universal], the apprehension of its specific form is untenable, and that if it were denotative despite having its power ungrasped,
there would be the consequence of deviation— that is untenable;
for even when resorting to an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), the cognition of the relationship is easily accomplished.

The linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) is established as follows: "A word expresses its own meaning as connected with that which is expected (*ākāṅkṣita*), capable (*yogya*), and proximate (*saṃnihita*). Therefore, "the meaning of a word is that which is connected with whatever is expected, capable, and attains proximity."
The establishment of the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhānavāda).

And the establishment of the theory of the expression of the related is proven by the word-meanings under discussion, even though they are presented as indivisible wholes; thus, the expression of the related is established.
Just as with expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), even in the case of proximity (*saṃnidhi*), the sequence [of words] should be understood to follow the very order of that which brings about the proximity.
And in accordance with that, the denotation of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) likewise proceeds in the same way.
Proximity arises solely from the word; it is not a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) in the process of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*).
For even with a noble who has been brought here today, one observes a relationship in the world.
These two do not occur simultaneously for all the correlates of proximity;
rather, they occur sequentially, following the order in which the causes of their manifestation appear.
In whatever manner the proximity of counter-correlates arises,
in that very same manner, through the sequence of words, there occurs the cognition of the related [object].
These are the summary verses.

The meaning is that those two—expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and proximity (*saṃnidhi*)—as previously described, are connected with another word-meaning that is expected, proximate, and capable (*yogya*). But what is this so-called "capability"? It is the fitness for connection.
How is it understood here that [the word] is capable of expressing a relation? Because it is observed as having the nature of a relation.
[Objection: If that is so, then how can there be the expression of a word as connected with an apūrva (unprecedented) effect in the Veda?
On this point, others say:

"This is not indication (lakṣaṇā), because it involves the abandonment of its own primary meaning (svārtha). For indication is observed in cases such as the Ganges only through the abandonment of its own primary meaning."
However, those within the Mīmāṃsā school, maintaining their own specific position, say this:
"Indeed, there is neither the abandonment nor the inclusion of one's own primary meaning through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

[The rule] *sṛṣṭīrupadadhāti* is also accepted as an instance of indication, because the possessors of the quality (*guṇin*) are what is being indicated, and because the meaning of *sṛṣṭi* is included within them."

Similarly, because the singular number in the expression "he sacrifices on the full moon day" (paurṇamāsī yajate) would otherwise be untenable, the word *paurṇamāsī* denotes the sacrifice itself for the purpose of indicating the collection of sacrifices.
Nor does the inclusion of the collection imply the abandonment of the individual [sacrifices], since the collection is dependent upon them.
Likewise, because the dual and plural numbers would be untenable in the other two cases, that which is characterized by the things to be expressed along with their meanings is resorted to.
Furthermore, there is no abandonment of the primary meaning (*avaya*).

Thus, in the *Niṣādasthapati* section of the *Pūrvapakṣa*, it is stated that there would be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sense of the genitive case; yet, even there, the abandonment of the primary meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) does not occur.
Similarly, in the expression "by the sound of the chariot" (*rathaghoṣeṇa*), there is no abandonment of the chariot (*ratha*).
Likewise, by means of a collective indication (*gaṇalakṣaṇā*), the word *medhām*, which ends in the singular number, is to be applied to the mantra in its original form (*prakṛti*).

Nor is it improper to employ a collective indication even when there is an abandonment of the two individual [meanings], for it is indeed appropriate to abandon the primary sense in favor of a collective one.
To this, it is replied:
Furthermore, what is this indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?
It is defined as follows: "The impossibility of a connection between the expressed meaning and the sentence-meaning;
indication is said to occur because of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) of that [meaning] which has been brought about by virtue of its connection with the former."
This refers to the subsequent verse.

Since the literal primary meanings (śakti) of words such as "Ganges" in the expression "A hamlet on the Ganges" cannot logically cohere with the meaning of the sentence, they are set aside. Instead, the bank—which attains proximity to the mind through its connection to that [primary meaning]—is determined to be what coheres with the sentence-meaning.
For this very reason, it has been said: "Indication (lakṣaṇā) occurs through incompatibility and through a relationship."

And in cases such as "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), there is no lack of compatibility with other [meanings] for the directly expressed (*śrauta*) sense, nor is there a lack of connection due to its being already connected [with another word], because the meaning already connected cannot possibly be connected with anything else.

Now, it might be argued: "Let this not be *lakṣaṇā*; rather, the action brings about the understanding of a state consisting of the mention of the factors of action (*kāraka*) once they have been understood, by virtue of their inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
To this, we reply:

First of all, the nature of the word (*śabdatva*) is not the means for understanding anything else; rather, it is accepted as being within the scope of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

Likewise, the comprehension of a specific syntactic connection (*viśiṣṭānvaya*) would become groundless if it were impossible [otherwise]. If, however, one resorts to that [specific connection] on the grounds that linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is untenable without a specific syntactic connection—and thus the utterance of words would be purposeless—then even so, the comprehension of a specific syntactic connection arises from the speech of those who act with deliberation and employ sentences solely for their own sake.
However, since there is no evidence that the Veda cannot be understood as having a sequential connection (*anvaya*), a specific [meaning] can indeed be discerned.

Nor does it follow that [the Veda] would be purposeless even in common worldly usage; for this reason alone, it is not logical to conclude a specific sequential connection based merely on the adoption of certain means and so forth.
For the fact that the taking up of water by one who intends to burn is purposeless does not imply that the power to burn resides in the water.

Granted that there is a lack of purpose regarding desire and pride, yet there is no lack of connection with a particular [object] in the case of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

Now, if it is argued that the capacity of words to convey a connection with a desired, relevant, and fit particular is understood through the usage of elders, and that consequently the understanding of the connection with a particular follows from such linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*),
that is not so.
In that regard, how indeed can the intentionality (*tatparatā*) of either words or word-meanings be established within the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) as a means?
We consider that such reflection is untenable without the postulation of a power (*śakti*) belonging either to the words or to the word-meanings.

And he states that this [power] belongs to the words alone: "Because of primacy, because of being the designator (*abhidhātṛ*), and because it provides the understanding of the intended meaning (*tātparya*)."
Let the capacity be admitted as belonging to the words themselves.
It is not proper to assume that this [sentence-meaning] is understood by discarding the words that arise first.
Furthermore, it is undisputed that words denote their respective meanings;
therefore, since their power of denotation is well-established, it is easier to postulate that this very power extends up to the point of syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
Rather, the power to signify the meanings of words must be postulated.

Therefore, since the postulation of a property (*dharma*) is better than the postulation of a further property, it is more appropriate to postulate that words themselves possess the power of denoting the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*).

Furthermore, it is accepted that words are denoters; if they were to produce a cognition of word-meanings whose object is merely their own form, then their status as denoters would be lost, because such a cognition arises from the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) that cause the understanding of word-meanings, which occurred at the time of grasping the relationship [between word and meaning].

For it must necessarily be admitted that there is an awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding the related meaning, in order to establish the recollection of the relationship [between word and meaning].

Therefore, if one accepts that words convey a meaning already associated [with others]—which was not apprehended at the time the relationship was grasped—it is only by so accepting this that the capacity of words to denote the associated meaning (*anvitābhidhāyaka*) can be maintained.

As for the claim that "a word does not differ from a mere reminder because it lacks any additional element," in that case, the word first awakens that [latent impression] which resides within the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).
Observing the statement of the Teacher (Vātsyāyana), "And like worldly usage," he says that words possess denotative power only insofar as they are reminders; to that [objection], he replies:
"Because it also results in the comprehension of the intended meaning.

Even by that opponent who would maintain that words function merely as reminders regarding word-meanings, it must be admitted that words have the purpose of conveying the sentence-meaning; otherwise, it would follow that the sentence-meaning is not derived from verbal testimony (*aśābdatva*).

If this is so, let the power to directly convey the meaning of the sentence belong to the words themselves; what is the use of [postulating word-meanings], which leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence?

Therefore, for those who claim that words possess a denotative function (*abhidhāyakatva*) toward word-meanings distinct from their mere capacity to remind, there is an unnecessary postulation of a power.
First, there is one...

There is the power of words to denote [their own meanings], and another power residing in the word-meanings to instill the capacity for syntactic connection (*anvaya-yogya-śakti*), as well as the power of word-meanings to make known that syntactic connection.

For those who maintain that words merely cause recollection (*smārakatva-vādinaḥ*), it is more logical—by the very reasoning already stated—to postulate the power in the words themselves rather than abandoning the power of denotation and postulating a separate power.
Therefore, it is established that words denote their meanings as unconnected (*ananvitābhidhāyīni*).

Now, in order to avoid the previously mentioned fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), he demonstrates how the meaning of a sentence is understood from words: "The entire collection of words, having been heard, causes the meanings connected [with one another] to be remembered."
That which, having first brought about individual cognitions through logical means, subsequently conveys the meaning of the sentence.

First, one who has not grasped the relationship [between word and meaning], or for whom the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) from grasping that relationship has not arisen or has perished, is not qualified for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

However, one who possesses the latent impression from grasping other words, upon hearing a word, first recollects this: "This [word] is the designator of that [object] as connected with a correlate that is expected, proximate, and compatible.
And thus, by the one who recollects, the very form [of the word]—though unconnected—is manifested in memory.
No one maintains that the meaning of a sentence is understood upon hearing only a single word.

For even according to the proponents of the theory of "relation of the expressed" (*abhihitānvayavāda*), as long as another word does not present another object, there is no comprehension of the relation; this is because an object denoted by a word requires another object for its cognition, and because a relation is dependent upon its correlate. Therefore, even in their view, all words denote their own meanings as already related to others.

Subsequently, one must accept that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning arises from all those [words] once they have ascended to memory. As the venerable author of the *Bṛhatī* has said: "Since even those [words], when not remembered, do not lead us to understand the sentence-meaning, it is therefore through their remembrance alone that there is validity with respect to the collection [of words]."
Thus [it is said].
For this very reason, the definition of a sentence by the venerable Ācārya is: "A sentence is words that express a meaning by combining together.
Now, one might ask: how can there be a comprehension of the sentence-meaning for one who maintains the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of related meanings)?
For how could a meaning that is not understood by a word being heard become "contained" within it?
It is replied:

even for the proponent of the theory of the connection of the expressed (abhihitānvayavādin), there is no such rule that only a subsequent letter, accompanied by the impressions produced by the preceding letters, conveys the meaning of the word. This is because one observes the comprehension of the Vedic meaning even from what is subsequently remembered, despite the fact that the knowledge of the syllables was not previously ascertained due to having been studied during childhood.
Therefore, there is no fault even in this being a means of comprehension for that which has ascended to memory.
For it is not the case that the word being heard does not first denote its meaning—already associated with the counter-correlate and similarity—due to the absence of auxiliary factors;
rather, it is denoted subsequently. Thus, everything is logically consistent.

To those proponents who say: "Only one word is expressive of the related meaning (anvitābhidhāyaka), while the other words function merely to bring about the presence of the counter-correlates (pratiyogin); nor is there a grasping of a specific [meaning], because the specific is grasped through its primacy or its status as the principal word. For this very reason they say, 'The principal word is the sentence,' or 'The first word is the sentence,'" he replies to them:

The word "all" (sarva) would belong to the first [item] alone, if it were connected with the meaning of the first item among all items. But this is not a fixed rule, because in the case of "He purchases Soma with a ruddy, one-year-old, tawny-eyed cow," the word "all" is connected only with the act of purchase.

Furthermore, since there is no fixed order of sequence among the words in a sentence, it would not be logical to claim that at one time a particular word is the first to express the related meaning while at another time it is not.
Likewise, it has been stated that even the principal word possesses the status of a sentence,
because all the other words are syntactically connected with the word *soma*.

Although all [factors] such as the *aruṇā* (redness) and so forth possess a purpose directed toward the *soma*, nevertheless, in this sentence, the purpose of the *aruṇā* and others is restricted solely to the act of purchase (*kraya*), and their syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs through the relation of action and instrument (*kriyā-kāraka-bhāva*). However, by means of the purchase, they possess merely a purpose directed toward the *soma*. Now, if a sentence is that which contains the most predominant term, it is called "principal" (*pradhāna*); but here, it is the act of purchasing itself—characterized by its requirement for all the constituent factors—that is being propounded.
Therefore, the word "purchases" (*krīṇāti*) alone is the principal term, and all other words, such as *aruṇā* and the rest, are subordinate to it.

To this it is replied: The purport of a sentence is fixed in each case. In some instances, it resides solely in the verb, as in "He performs the Agnihotra sacrifice" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*); in others, it resides in a subordinate quality, as in "He performs the sacrifice with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*).

Therefore, since the status of being the principal term applies to all words, it must be acknowledged that all words possess the power to express meaning through syntactic connection (*anvitābhidhāna*). This being the case, it is not contradictory even in those instances [where a word is used alone]. Furthermore, this is exactly the same regarding the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*) as well.

But if this were so, all words would become mutual synonyms, such as in the case of "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), where there is denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) by the word "cow" just as there is by the word "bringing. To this it is replied:
There are these two meanings: that the *gola* is associated with *ānayana*, and that the *āyana* is associated with *go*.
Since each term denotes one of these [meanings] individually, how could there be the contingency of synonymy?
This is the same even in the case of the referent (*padārtha*).

[Objection: But surely, since the meaning of "purchasing" (krīṇāti) would be expressed as connected to the giving of the redness (aruṇya), there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) characterized by repetition (āvṛtti).
[Reply: No, because of the simultaneous utterance (tantravāraṇa).
Furthermore, because it is untenable for there to be dependence (*tantratā*) upon a change in form (*vairūpya*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

What is this "individualization (*vyakti*) brought about by logic"? As long as the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) is being established by logic, the collection of words does not convey the meaning of the sentence. [In the world...]

The impossibility of linguistic usage (*vyavahārānupapatti*) is meaningful in the Bhāṣya: as long as one does not deliberate upon such matters as "this is the injunction," "this is the correlative," "this is the primary," "this is subordinate," "this is intended [by the speaker]," or "this is unintended," no one at all understands the meaning of a Vedic sentence. As it has been stated by the venerable author of the Vārttika: "Doubt indeed persists regarding a Vedic sentence that has been heard only so long as its mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) is not clearly determined."
"And having understood the explicit meaning [of the Veda], those who were hesitant regarding Mīmāṃsā—
all doubts concerning the meaning of the Vedic sentences completely dissolve.
Thus [it is said].

For this very reason, in the Mīmāṃsā, the comprehension of Vedic sentences constitutes the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance). As those very [authors] have stated: "When dharma is being cognized by means of the Veda acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the Mīmāṃsā shall fulfill its role as the *itikartavyatā*."
[Objection: But surely in the world, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence occurs immediately and does not depend on an intermediate causal complex.
[Reply: It is said:
this might indeed be so in the case of sentences that are extremely well-practiced.

Since even in the world, various disputes arise regarding statements such as those concerning memory (*smṛti*) in relation to things never seen before, how can there be an immediate ascertainment of the meaning? Moreover, due to the absence of a [reliable] cause, people lack this discrimination.
As it has been said: "Based on the distinctions of many classes, qualities, substances, and actions..."

Due to the nature of conditions, people do not wish to determine with certainty those things that are characterized as objects of knowledge and whose essence consists of the knower, because of the absence of a [definitive] cause. The science of grammar exists for the purpose of establishing the relative strength and weakness [of linguistic elements].
Thus [it is said].
If it is asserted that all words denote their meanings without mutual connection (*ananvitābhidhāyitva*), that applies to all words whose meanings are expressed through direct denotation (*śrauta*).

However, when there is a substitution of words for those whose meanings are indicated by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇika*), then only that word which expresses its meaning through direct denotation is what denotes the connected meaning (*anvitābhidhāyaka*).

The other word, however, is intended solely to bring the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) to mind. Since its denotative capacity has not yet been ascertained here, its own meaning is also non-denotative at that time, because it cannot yet enter into syntactic connection (anvaya).

Rather, when its own meaning is recalled, that which is related to it—whether by similarity or otherwise—and which is itself fit for syntactic connection, is brought to mind; the word then denotes its own meaning as connected with that [recalled object]. This is the secret of the philosophical system (darśana-rahasya).

Nor is it faultless to claim that all words in a sentence can possibly be either figurative (*lakṣaṇika*) or secondary (*gauṇa*); for in some cases direct denotation (*abhidhāna*) is the cause, while in others it is this [figurative function]—this is the meaning. Furthermore, what was stated as "and so forth" (*iti ca*) is intended to show the secondary [function] characterized by what has been already expressed (*abhihitalakṣaṇa*), which is brought to mind by the word "and so forth."

But how can a word that expresses [the meaning] as related (anvitābhidhāyin) be able to cause recollection by its mere own form? To this he says: "Even when there is the expression of the related, the own form exists;
therefore, the word produces recollection even with respect to the mere own form.
Thus, the recollection of the own form has been explained up to the limit of the means of knowledge consisting of the heard text (*saṃdhava*).

Now, he states that even the mere recollection of the word's own form is not untenable only because of the word itself: "Just as in some cases one's own word is recalled by an object that is not a means of valid cognition,
so too will the object be made to be recalled by a word that is not a means of valid cognition."

For that which is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not necessarily the cause of recollection; rather, it is a means of valid cognition when there has previously been a perceived proximity between something and another. That [proximity], by means of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) or through a defect, can produce a verbal recollection regarding that object.

And since the word itself also possesses a proximity with its own form—namely, its inclusion within the denotation of that word—it is capable of producing a verbal recollection there as well, just like the object.

Just as the mere nature of an object perceived in a non-conceptual state (nirvikalpaka-daśā), though itself inexpressible, causes the word to be remembered, so too does the word [cause] the object; what is there that is illogical? By this, it has been demonstrated that immediately after the utterance of a word, there is the cognition of the nature of the word-meaning. Even for the proponent of the theory of "connection of the expressed" (abhihitānvaya-vāda), that [cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), because there is no determination of any additional meaning, given the accepted tenet that a valid means of knowledge must consist of an object not previously apprehended.
As it has been said: "The authority of all [words] regarding an unperceived object consists in its being a recollection (smṛti) through association" (Ślokavārttika, Pratyakṣasūtra 11).

If, however, this were not admitted to be a recollection, then—since no other mode of comprehension is accepted apart from valid cognition, recollection, doubt, and error—it would have to be stated wherein the cognition of one's own referent from a word is to be included.
For this very reason, even in the theory of expressed association (abhihitānvayavāda), the status of being a recollector is acknowledged.
He now resolves this objection of mutual dependence: "By means of the meanings brought to mind through memory, every word expresses its object; thus, there is no mutual dependence.
For in the mere recollection of its own meaning and essential form, a word does not depend upon another word.
This [word] is indeed present as being brought near by memory;
therefore, there is no mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva).
But surely, linguistic proficiency (vyutpatti) arises from the usage of elders?
And linguistic usage is based upon the comprehension of related meanings;
therefore, from the observation of that [usage], it is only the comprehension of related meanings that can be accepted,
and not merely the connection of unrelated word-meanings.
It is said:

the very impossibility of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) and the impossibility of otherwise understanding the limit (*tānta*) is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which has a connected meaning;
for this has already been demonstrated.
"The cognition of a related [meaning] is not possible for others unless there is a prior cognition of the unrelated [meanings].

Regarding this, someone says: "If the denotation of the related is performed by words based on what is brought to mind through memory, then, since memory is established upon proximity and since proximity can exist between many objects, there would be no distinction among those objects brought to mind; consequently, in the case of 'He cooks in a pan' (*sthālyām pacati*), only the object currently being cooked (*pacyamāna*) would be denoted as related."

For since it is recorded in the Smṛti that "she (the wife) indeed [participates] even when [the rite] is accompanied by the offering of water-libations," she would be designated as being accompanied by that [rite] even when it is so stated.
Likewise, since "you two cook" is understood through the medium of the act of cooking and so forth, it would be designated as being accompanied by cooked rice due to the recollection of that [act].
However, this fault does not apply to the theory of the non-connection of what has been expressed (*abhihitānvaya-vāda*),
because each individual meaning is that which is to be expressed.
To this, it is replied:

First, the cognition of the word-meaning from the word cannot be said to be distinct from recollection; therefore, it must be accepted that the capacity to convey the syntactic relation belongs to the meanings as they are being recollected.

And thus, the fault is equal [in both views]. As for this [objection regarding] the word: since it conveys the syntactic relation of those meanings already recollected, and because such is observed in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), there is no fault; this remains equally true even under the other theory.
Nor is this an absolute rule, for it has been stated that even in the usage of elders, we observe the expression of a relation through a word whose meaning is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*).

Now, if the objection is raised: "The meaning of the word [is understood] within its own referent; however, by which among those [meanings] is the cognition of the relation brought about?", then in the theory of the expression of the related (*abhihitānvaya-vāda*), it is indeed appropriate that the cognition of the relation occurs through the expressed meanings.
That, however, is incorrect.
What other denotative function is there besides that of reminding, which could be called "establishing"? Now, it might be argued:
"The nature of being a reminder is based on proximity."
Therefore, one must accept a proximity characterized by the relationship between the signifier and the signified that exceeds that [mere sequence].
This is not so;
for in the linguistic usage of elders, it is observed solely as a means of recollection, and thus it falls under the category of being a reminder.

For the capacity to cause comprehension is precisely the relationship between the signified and the signifier; and although that capacity is observed to fulfill other relations such as denotation (*abhidhā*) and so forth, nevertheless, it is not accepted as such in the case of the word.
Rather, its status as a signifier arises solely from the acquisition of the quality of being a signifier.
Likewise, its status as a reminder arises solely from the acquisition of the quality of being a reminder; what is the use of resorting to another distinct relation?

Moreover, for one who maintains that words denote meanings already connected (anvitārthavādin), this [denotation] is established as being restricted; it is not possible [to claim otherwise], because a word is remembered as denoting its own meaning as connected with another word-meaning, since it is observed in the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) only as thus connected.

Even in cases where there is no such usage, the attainment of the denotation of a specific connection occurs through the force of proximity (*saṃnidhāpaka*); this is known from common worldly experience itself, so there is no fault whatsoever.
This much has been understood: that the meaning of the sentence is that which is connected with that word.

If there were also an expression of connection (anvitābhidhāna) by this [word], then there would be a split in the sentence (vākyabheda). And such a split is not logical when the status of a single sentence is possible.
As it has been said: "When a single unified sentence is possible, a split of the sentence (vākyabheda) is not desired.

Therefore, since a split of the sentence is undesirable when a unified sentence can be established in some way or another, it is precisely because of such a split that figurative (lakṣaṇā) or secondary (gauṇī) functions arise in common usage.
Otherwise, why would one split the sentence and explain it in a different sense, rather than simply accepting all the words in their primary (mukhya) meanings?

In the Vedas as well, precisely because of the requirement for syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), one resorts to figurative descriptions (*guṇavāda*) in the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), or describes the transposition of case endings; or, as in the *Audumbara-adhikaraṇa*, somehow interprets [the word "udumbara"] as denoting cattle; or, as in the *Citrā-adhikaraṇa*, abandons the conventional meaning in favor of some derivative sense, such as [interpreting "citrā"] as "that which causes intelligence," just as in the phrase "there are fifteen verses" (*pañcadaśāny ājyāni bhavanti*); or, as in the *Vājapeya-adhikaraṇa*, accepts the status of a name (*nāmadheya*) precisely because it would otherwise result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*); and as in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*, because the injunction of multiple qualities would result in a syntactical split.

The establishment of the [meaning] by way of restating the whole is seen in many places: in the section on "another context" (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*), the description of the figurative nature of the word denoting the subject matter due to the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*); in the section on the "cup" (*grahādhikaraṇa*), the non-intentionality of syntactic unity; in the case of "he plants half within the altar and half outside the altar," the indication of location (*deśalakṣaṇā*); in the section on the "linen cloth" (*kṣaumādhikaraṇa*), the injunction regarding the *puṇḍrī*; in the section on "the purpose" (*ārthādhikaraṇa*), the non-intentionality of both words, as in the case of the scrapings of the *vāruṇī* and the husks which indicate independently; and in the section on "exclusion" (*paryudāsādhikaraṇa*), the figurative nature of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—and much more is observed.

In that case, if the denotation of the word being supplied were abandoned and its connection were instead indicated with something else, then even the status of being a single sentence would be lost. It is for this very reason that it is stated: "the individual [meaning] is consistent with logic. For what is called "being a single sentence" (ekavākyatva) is indeed a great syntactic connection (mahāvākya).
The meaning that follows from that [usage] is what must be relied upon here as the sentence-meaning.

Since the comprehension of word-meanings arises from the linguistic usage of elders, those logical principles (*nyāya*) which are known to be the causes for comprehending sentence-meanings within the usage of elders must not be abandoned when extracting the sentence-meaning; thus, there is no room for [the objection] that one would have to search through the entire body of scripture.
Let it be, then, that there is expression through connection (*anvitābhidhāna*) with another word-meaning by virtue of the force of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*).

Therefore, why does the expression of the related meaning (*anvitābhidhāna*) not also occur through another meaning that is either recalled by that [word] itself or recalled by it, provided it is consistent with being part of the same syntactical unit?
It is replied: because the expression of the related meaning is established through the word’s status as a linguistic unit (*padatva*), once the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) has been presented.
Now, if the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) is not pacified, then who indeed could prevent the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) therein?

For this very reason, when a single word is uttered, among many meanings that are present through memory by virtue of their connection with that [word's] meaning, the denotation of the related occurs only with respect to that meaning whose specific distinction is grasped in some manner;
however, when no specific distinction is grasped, there is simply no cognition of non-relation (*ananvaya*).

For this very reason, in the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), when a similarity is perceived with something that recalls the assistance provided by a particular element in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the fulfillment [of the requirement] occurs through that very assistance.

Therefore, only in cases where a similarity is proposed based on a unique restriction for the sake of many such elements is the inclusion of its specific assistance justified, because it leads to a rapid recollection. However, in the case of *darbha*-grass offerings, since all [elements] are present without distinction, it is impossible to apprehend a specific [similarity].
Thus, since there is no determination (*anadhyavasāya*) regarding the primary assistance (*upakāra*), the status of being an assistant (*upakārakatva*) resides in that very [assistance].

Just as the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs according to the understanding derived from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), in that context, for a person who has grasped the relationship through non-separation (*anavagraha*), it is observed that the denotation of another word occurs only with that which is invariably recalled by the word, and not by anything else.
This is the justification for the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhānavāda*).
For every word, by its very nature, invariably directs those who remember the relationship toward its own meaning, not toward another meaning.
Consequently, there is no fault whatsoever in the fact that a word conveys its own meaning as already connected with the meanings of other words.

Furthermore, if it is admitted on the basis of experience that the connected own-meaning is conveyed even when [the relation] has been expressed, and if the specific connections are not otherwise possible, then let it be postulated that words also possess the power of denoting the connected (anvitābhidhāna).
If it is argued that [the word] simply falls into the state of being meaningless, let it be so; there is no fault whatsoever.

The preceding word merely expresses its own meaning as connected [to something], but because it does not encounter another object denoted by a subsequent correlative word, it expresses that meaning as connected to that [subsequent word]; thus, there is no fault. Even in this way, for one who holds the view of proximity (*āsannamatena*), there is a parsimony in the postulation of capacity, since the postulation of capacity [for the sentence] occurs alongside the capacity residing in the word-meanings themselves to convey the connection.

Even when the assumption of a capacity is equal [in both cases], it is more appropriate to rely on the words themselves as possessing the power to convey the related meaning (*anvitabodhana*), rather than on the word-meanings, because the words are apprehended first and because the intention (*tātparya*) is understood to reside in the sentence-meaning.
How then is this Bhāṣya passage—"For the words... (p. 96.8)—to be explained? To that he replies: "a..."

Regarding the investigation of *anvitābhidhāna*: [it is stated] "the mantra for seeking," and likewise, "the verb (*ākhyāta*) has being (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning. Because of this principle of *anvitābhidhāna*, it is said that even in words ending with possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*), there is *anvitābhidhāna*.

“Even possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) denote only a specific [qualification]; indeed, no other denotation for them is established. In the case of ‘the priests wearing golden garlands’ (*hiraṇyamālina ṛtvijaḥ*), the golden garland which serves as the qualifier is already expressed by the base word itself, and the priests who are the qualificands are also expressed by their own word; what else, then, could the possessive suffix denote apart from the qualified entity?
In that very same passage, two views have been stated regarding the fact that even within a single word, there is no *anvitābhidhāna* (expression of the related).

In that regard, how is it then that the author of the Bhāṣya (p. 99, ad 1.1.62–72), having raised the objection according to the view of the Guru—namely, that when he says, "the second case-ending arising from a nominal stem is a qualifier of the nominal stems," he is stating that the suffix expresses [its meaning] as already connected (anvitābhidhāyitva)—provides a twofold resolution?

Or, in your own view, since all words denote [their meanings] as already connected (*anvitābhidhāyitva*), how is it specifically stated that the suffix (*pratyaya*) functions therein? Therefore, because it does not conform to the treatise, you must establish the following distinction: that other words denote only their own individual forms (*svarūpamātra*), whereas the suffix denotes [its meaning] as already connected.

Alternatively, it is not by this [statement] that the suffix is said to denote the related meaning; rather, when the suffix denotes its own meaning, that very meaning is understood as being already present within the meaning of the base (prakṛti). In that regard, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is explained that both the base and the suffix possess their respective parts of "attachment" (anurāga) toward their own meanings, and that the cause for the attachment of word-meanings is precisely the syntactic connection (sambhidhyāhāra) between the base and the suffix, which is equivalent to the syntactic connection between different words.
Therefore, since the cognition of the affectionate aspect is established through the very act of denotation (*samabhidhyāna*), the suffix has no power (*śakti*) with respect to that;
it denotes only its own primary meaning (*svārtha*). As it is said regarding words: "When it is said that the stem and the suffix denote the meaning of the suffix together..."
Even though it is expressed through differentiation, this is stated as such because of its predominance;
there exists no other power of the word apart from the powers of its constituent parts,
by virtue of which the comprehension of a qualified object could arise from a single [word].
"A cognition does not always proceed toward a specifically qualified object;
rather, it does so because of the qualification by a specific meaning of the base (prakṛti) previously known.
Thus [it is said].
In this matter, only the second position is ultimate.
Thus, Bhaṭṭa Someśvara has explained the Siddhāntavārttika of the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa* (2.1.1.9) with this intent:

"Since it is an established practice that the base and the suffix denote their own respective meanings, and since they necessarily possess a fixed sequence, the suffixes—encountering those cognizers who have already grasped the meaning of the base expressed earlier—denote their own meaning as being accompanied by the connection [to that base] produced thereby; therefore, [the suffix does not denote its own meaning in isolation]."
Sometimes the meaning of the suffix alone is apprehended in its purity.
As it has been said: "The second case-ending, which follows after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), states that the meaning of the nominal stem is a qualifier.
Thus, this method explained for words ending in *su*-suffixes and *tiṅ*-suffixes is also stated to apply to words such as *pācaka* and the like.
"The root *pac* denotes the cooking (*pāka*), while the suffix *aka* denotes the agent;
however, the agent as connected with the cooking is not denotable by either one [of them] alone.
(The reading for the fourth quarter of this verse in the *Vākyapadīya* is: "By which part is it not denoted?")

This same principle applies even in the case of *devatātaddhita* suffixes and those expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) and so forth. Therefore: "The efficient force (*bhāvanā*), being constrained by the more powerful injunctive text (*vidhiśruti*) than the word-text (*padaśruti*), is not capable of taking a sacrifice or the like as its object of attainment (*bhāvya*)."

In such passages as these from the *Śābarabhāṣya* and others, the usage of the term "direct denotation" (*śrutitva*) regarding the word by Miśra and other commentators in the *Svargakāmādhikaraṇa* and elsewhere is not based on the theory of "expression of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*).

Nor should it be argued: "How can there be an expression of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭābhidhāna*) without the expression of its qualifiers? For it has been said: "The apprehension of the qualified [entity] is not desired [as being expressed] through the qualifier Agni-Soma."

However, there is no disagreement regarding whether [the word] denotes [the agent] or not; for this is established according to the method stated in the *Vārttika* on the section concerning the agent (*kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*, p. 9.15). Now, one might object: "In such expressions as *yajeta paśunā* ('one should sacrifice with an animal'), the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is a direct denotation (*śruti*) merely because it denotes a qualified [object]; therefore, since a name (*samākhyā*) is equal to that, it too would result in being a direct denotation. Consequently, in that particular section (*adhikaraṇa*), there was a suspicion that it might be a direct denotation, and thus the citation of the verse by Harisvāmin—'But the root *pac* itself expresses the cooking'—is inappropriate, because [if the suffix were a direct denotation], the name would lack the status of a direct denotation due to its failure to denote the syntactic relation (*anvaya*). [Response: This is incorrect. For the suffix does not denote the qualified [object] through the mere expression of its own meaning; rather, it denotes the qualified [object] by way of expressing the action (*bhāvanā*). And since the action is not denoted by the noun (*nāman*), the suffix cannot denote the qualified [object]. Therefore, the suffix is not a direct denotation (*śruti*) with respect to the qualified [object]. Furthermore, even if it were to denote the qualified [object], it would still not be a direct denotation with respect to the syntactic relation (*anvaya*), because the syntactic relation is not expressed by the suffix itself. Thus, the objection is refuted. Moreover, the name (*samākhyā*) is not equal to the suffix, because the suffix denotes the action, whereas the name does not. Consequently, the name is not a direct denotation. Therefore, the aforementioned position is indeed correct. As for the argument stated there [in the *Śābarabhāṣya*] immediately following this—namely, "Even if the name (*samākhyā*) were to express the relationship, even then it would not be an authority (*pramāṇa*) therein"—that very same point is addressed in the passage beginning with, "We say that the direct statement (*śruti*) and the others do not express subservience to another; rather, when conjoined with an injunction (*vidhi*), they cause the understanding of subservience to another" (*Śābarabhāṣya* 3.1.2).

Bāla, p. 50:

With reference to the injunction "He carries forward the water," it is heard [in the scripture]: "With an earthen vessel for one desiring stability. Is this earthen nature optional (kāmya) and thus not part of the obligatory performance (nityaprayoga)? No; rather, because of the injunction "He carries forward the water," some other vessel must be taken.
By the injunction "one should bring forward water with a *camasa*," the *camasa* itself, being prescribed as a constant requirement, is to be employed in the obligatory performance.

Regarding the statements "he brings forward water," "he mixes the oblation with the *praṇītā* waters," and "he should pour out the *praṇītā* waters within the altar," the sole purpose of the *praṇītā* waters here is the mixing of the oblation; the pouring out within the altar, however, is a disposal (*pratipatti*). Thus, the mixing of the oblation is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the *praṇītā* waters, while the pouring out is not a motivator.

Bhāṣya 3.6.1.10:

In the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, which is connected to a single [set of] waters, the status of being an *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is not established by the [general] context (*prakaraṇa*).

‘It would be displaced from the twelve [days] because of the lack of syntactical connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma, since the syntactical unity with the Ahīna is directly perceived.

(Bhāṣya 3.3.8.16). Regarding displacement (*apakarṣa*): certain sentences located within the *bhakṣa-mantra* might be displaced before the sentence concerning the consumption, due to both their form and explicit instruction; however, there is no displacement of the Soma-related acts such as the carrying forward of the *abhiṣava* and *praṇayana*, nor even of the act regarding the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) during the initiations (*dīkṣā*).
Śābarabhāṣya 5.1.14:

There is no displacement [of the altar] to the previous day on the new moon day; for even regarding the displacement of the altar, there is no evidence for the displacement of the entire collection of offerings ending with the *abhivāsana*.

"The altar being prepared does not remove the seat, just as the oblation [does not remove] the vessel;

There is no displacement of the offering; even when the drawing of the cups for the Aśvins and others is displaced to the new moon festival (*amāvāsyā-parvan*), [the offering remains].

The rule of displacement serves the common purpose of the performance of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as an auxiliary to both the *āgnīṣomīya* (offered to Agni and Soma) by direct instruction (*upadeśa*), and the *savanīya* and *anubandhya* (offered at the pressing and the concluding rite) by extended application (*atideśa*), as expressed in the injunction: "One cuts the sacrificial post during the initiations" (*dīkṣāsu yūpaṃ chinatti*).

Even in the event of a deficiency— meaning either destruction or non-availability— there is no substitute for the deity, the word *agni*, or the ritual action.

Bhāṣya 6.3.1.18–19: In the event of the non-availability of a prescribed substance, another substance similar to the one heard in the scripture should be taken as a substitute; however, a substitute for a substitute is not to be accepted. 6.3.1.32: In the event of the non-availability of the primary substance, upon the subsequent availability of that primary substance, only the primary substance itself should be employed. 6.3.1.35: In the event of the non-availability of the prescribed substance such as *nīvāra* rice, an optional substance such as barley (*yava*) should not be taken as a substitute.
