Regarding the *apaciti* sacrifice (No. 494), in the case of the *apaccheda* [of the two priests] during the *apaciti* sacrifice, both the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [Sāmans] [should be used], because there is no loss of the connection with the previous ritual element of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Furthermore, one should perform the second [rite].

In that case, regarding the *upavatī* [verse] at the *bahiṣpavamāna*, it is not for the purpose of excluding the agent of the initial performance; this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belongs to that very [performance] as its constituent part. Rather, it is something else entirely.
(The term *upavatī* is appropriate because it means "singing near" [the sacrificer]; it is not a constituent part of the initial performance.
The fire to be addressed by the one who performs the initial performance is called *anuprayuj*.)
Bhāṣya 10.1.16:
Because there is no purpose for the accomplishment [of the sacrifice] through [the performance of] another;

for the application of another [rite] belongs to the officiating priests (ṛtvij). In the case of the *apaciti* [sacrifice], which is a one-day rite (*ekāha*), the *bṛhat* and *rathaṃtara* [sāmans] are combined and applied to the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha* [laud]. [The second [element] is] the consecrated [priest] (the sacrificial fee, the agent), who is the performer of the application of another. Combined, they are established [therein].
10|6|8|24–26: "And the limb of what has been discarded" (*apagasya cāṅgam*)—this is a novel argument (*apūrvā yuktiḥ*).

Consequently, when there is an omission of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in that [sacrifice], the properties such as the *rathaṃtara* [sāman] are established according to the model sacrifice (*prakṛtitvat*) in the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*).
The expiation (*prāyaścitta*) also pertains only to the limb of the second performance, not to the limb of the first performance—9|2|17|49–50—in the *apaciti* one-day sacrifice.

Because it is not contradictory, it is non-sublated (*abādhya*). Here, in the case of a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, sublation is characterized by the non-arising of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Sublation of the property (*dharma*) consists in the cognition of the word-meaning through the assumption of a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) in the concluding passage, rather than by accepting the literal meaning as in the introductory passage.

In the case of the obligatory (*nitya*) and the occasional (*naimittika*), or the obligatory and the optional (*kāmya*), there is sublation of the former by the principle based on the sequence of the cognition of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*). Regarding general and particular rules, the application of the effect occurs for that which rests on the general through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by the particular,
whereas for that which rests on the particular, it occurs through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Direct denotation (śruti) sublates that which is obtained through indication (lakṣaṇā); in that case, there is a sublation of the cognition of the relationship with the expressed meaning.
However, in the case of optionality (vaikalpya), because they both rely on a single cause, there is no mutual sublation;
for since the unseen potency (apūrva) is the instigator and the cause of the ritual duties, there is an absence of temporal sequence [between them].
But here, it is said that [the sacrifice] is to be bound on the previous day;
even when there is simultaneity of the Soma-cutting (apaccheda), even in the case of simultaneity of the cuttings.
In one case of preparatory action, there is one *kalpa*; in the other case, it will be the latter.
Thus, there is no contradiction.
Therefore, both are expiations.
Nor [is it possible] from a single conjunction.
The Commentary says: But this is not so.
Why? Because of the connection with a single [act].
That very same sacrifice would have to be performed again.

If it were thought that there is a deficiency (vaiguṇya) when one or the other is absent, then even when all [the rites] are performed, the sacrifice would be deficient because of the absence of the *adakṣiṇya* (non-giving of the sacrificial fee).
One performance, while being carried out, does not authorize another performance.
Furthermore, neither the *adakṣiṇya* nor the giving away of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*) possesses primary importance.
The ritual action must be connected with a qualified performance;
therefore, there is no option [between them].
Śā—In a single performance, both would result, which is impossible to combine; thus, there is an option.
The connection [of this section] is due to its dependence on what precedes it regarding the Soma sacrifice.
As for the two types of expiation, there is either a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*); this is the settled conclusion.
In the former performance, there is an absence of sacrificial fees (*adakṣiṇyatva*), whereas in the latter, there is another [rule].
In the final application, there is no sign; therefore, those two are attained in a single application, and thus, due to their contradiction, they are to be understood as alternatives.
Commentary: In the case of simultaneity, because there is no contradiction between the two expiations, they must be performed in combination.

It is indeed possible to perform the gift of all one's possessions (*sarvasvadāna*), which is occasioned by the interruption of the *pratihartṛ*, even during the subsequent performance occasioned by the interruption of the *udgātṛ*.

Alternatively, that [gift] occasioned by the latter is merely the repetition of the performance characterized by the increase of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā-utkarṣa*); for the absence of fees (*adākṣiṇya*) is also [included], since it is a subject of restatement (*anuvādya*) by implication (*arthāpatti*).

Therefore, there is no contradiction even in the case of giving away one's entire property during the *pūrvaprayoga* (the first performance). This being the position reached, it is not the case that such giving of all one's property occurs in the *pūrvaprayoga* itself; for even if the lack of a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇya*) were merely a contingent occasion (*naimittika*), the increase of the fee (*dakṣiṇotkarṣa*) would be untenable in the *pūrvaprayoga* if the giving of all property were to take place then.

Nor does the giving of all property occur in the *punarprayoga* (the subsequent performance), because the rule for the dismissal of the *pratihartṛ* priest is prescribed specifically with respect to that [subsequent] performance.

Otherwise, if the *pratihartṛ* were to be dismissed during a single performance, because there would be no distinction in the state of the sacrifice (*kratu*), it would follow that one must give away all one's possessions in all subsequent performances as well.
Furthermore, if the occasional rite (*naimittika*) were not performed in a performance where its occasion (*nimitta*) arose, it would follow that it must be performed even in another performance.
Therefore, due to this contradiction, [the rule regarding] the absence of fees (*adakṣiṇya*) and the giving of all...
When it is argued that everything obtained through the injunction (*codaka*) should be permitted,
we reply:

because of the restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyāna*) stating, "He offers the *ājyabhāga* oblations with the *apsumant* verses," only as much as is explicitly mentioned should be permitted, not everything.

VI. 10|7|15. Regarding the statements, "He performs the *prayāja* offerings with Apabhraṃśa words" and "The two *anuyāja* offerings are also [performed] with Apabhraṃśa," this does not actually prescribe four *prayājas* and two *anuyājas* distinct from those [already established] in the *saumika* *avabhṛtha* rite. Rather, according to the principle of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is an injunction for specific *prayājas* and *anuyājas* by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), and not merely the performance of *prayājas* and *anuyājas* outside [the standard ritual].
(Bhaṭṭa). *Apabhraṃśa*: For one who speaks using non-Sanskritic words, it becomes a means to heaven and fame.

Furthermore, for one who utters corrupt words (*apaśabda*) during a ritual action, as if speaking untruth, there arises the contingency of a deficiency in the sacrifice caused by the performance of what is prohibited;
as it has been said: "One who knows the application of speech is corrupted by corrupt words."
Or rather: [Vārttika 11.8.27, p. 281] "The scriptures of the Śākyas, Jains, and others consist predominantly of corrupt words.
Because they are like a collection of false paintings, their status as authoritative treatises (*śāstra*) is not recognized.
For they are indeed explanations consisting mostly of corrupt words, such as those of the Māgadhī, Dākṣiṇātya, and other Apabhraṃśa dialects."
"For indeed, monks, my doctrine is that all things are subject to causality (*savatthika*).
Likewise: "When a jar is overturned, there is a cause; when it is set upright, there is no [external] cause.
"In experience, these conditioned phenomena arise with a cause; they perish without [further] cause."
‘The cause of non-arising,’ and so forth.
(“For even for me, O monks, all action proceeds.
“When the stirred-up [impurity] has been cast out, there exists a cause for its upward movement.”)
"There is no cause for falling; these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have a cause for their experience—they arise with a cause, and they perish without a cause.
"Non-arising as a cause" is a [term] formed by *saṃskṛta*.
(Therefore, since they are non-existent, how could there be truthfulness in those words? From what source could truthfulness come to them?)
How could there be beginninglessness in those forms which are seen to be corrupt (*apabhraṃśa*)?
[Page 237, *Apabhraṃśa*:

This very same word (such as *go*, etc.), following upon various manifestations—due to differences in ancient incapacity, negligence, causes, and so forth, and due to the displacement, addition, or alteration of the sequence of its phonemes—is apprehended in the form of a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*) and conveys that very same meaning. Thus, there is no establishment of another expressive word (*vācakaśabda*) as a synonym (*paryāya*), nor is there any difference in their status as linguistic conventions.

Furthermore: "Regarding names such as Devadatta and others which are beyond doubt, since they are not perceived by children in the form of 'that-ness' (tattā) and so forth, there is uncertainty [regarding their denotative power].

For even with respect to words like 'that-ness,' one who perceives the cognition of the referent Devadatta and so on—whether from a word used by a child or from a word used by an adult who imitates that child—how indeed could he conclude its denotative power based solely on the observation of usage and cognition?"
"And whatever Apabhraṃśas there may be among people, such as *gāvī* and the like— these too, by virtue of their form as *gāvī* and so forth, would be subject to deviation [from correct usage].
Since *gāvī* and similar forms are corrupted only in certain instances, there might arise, through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the delusion that they possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*)."

However, as for those words such as *abhinava-gāvī* which are currently being employed in a form that is largely unintelligible to the dull-witted, yet are perceived as conveying meaning either through the modification of their original forms (*prakṛti*) or by means of convention; since there is indeed observed usage and comprehension even in these cases, [your reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Consequently, this reason put forward by you is also subject to fault;
due to the defect of inconclusiveness, it is not capable of proving [your point].

Furthermore, a word being uttered otherwise becomes corrupt (*apabhraṃśa*), as stated at page 276–77 [of the work cited]. Corrupt forms such as *gāvī* and others are not authoritative with respect to the object possessing a dewlap and so forth.
One word alone—possessing an uninterrupted tradition and denoting the meaning—is the true linguistic item; all others are corruptions.

Bhāṣya 11.8.24: Among words that are directed toward a single meaning, one is beginningless; the others are corruptions (apabhraṃśas). 11.8.26: By someone desiring to utter the word "go" (cow), it was impossible [to do so], and thus "gāvī" was uttered.

Another person understands that what he intends to express is the animal possessing a dewlap and other such features; desiring to utter the word "go" (*gauḥ*) for that purpose, he instead utters "gāvī.
Thereafter, others also, being lax, utter "gāvī" when they intend to express that same animal possessing a dewlap.
Thus, the animal possessing a dewlap is understood from words such as "gāvī."
For *gāvī* and the like are indeed appropriate for the word *go*.
(11.8.28) Those who know this—the knowers of reality—recognize that *gāvī* and other such forms are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) of the word *go*.
For them, even from words such as *gāvī*, the cognition of the meaning arises; they understand the object through the word *go* itself, as stated by Vyāḍi.
*Bṛhatī*, p. 237: All these corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśas*) have a beginning.
In this regard, a certain elder, desiring to utter the word "cow" (*go*), uttered "gāvī" through inadvertence.

Thereupon, another elder, having understood his intention from the fact that he was attempting to convey a meaning, thinks: "This man, wishing to utter the word 'cow,' has uttered 'gāvī'. Thus, one understands the object such as a cow from the very word "cow" intended to be uttered, and not from the word "gāvī."
*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 238: "For words corrupted by regional dialects (*deśabhāṣā*) or linguistic decay (*apabhraṃśa*) cannot be distinguished [from correct forms].

*Vākyapadīya* 1.14–5.10, p. 226: "Linguistic corruption (*śabdāpabhraṃśa*), semantic corruption (*arthāpabhraṃśa*), that arising from negligence (*pramādaja*), and that arising from incapacity (*aśaktija*).
Regarding *apabhraṃśa*, see the section on the "Immeasurable" (501).

"Just as a confusion regarding the expressive word arises even among those produced by [innate] power due to negligence because of their conformity to correct forms, so too does it arise in the speech of barbarians (*mleccha*).
It is precisely from the corruption of words that corruptions of meaning arise, caused by the employment of figurative usage, error, and the like."
They are able to be examined by means of the merit and purposes for which the noble practice of the treatise itself remains unimpaired. (11.4.19, pp. 219–20).
A certain specific [usage] is observed in each region through the use of Apabhraṃśa;
for example—the term *rauhiṇikā* for a cow.
Page 919, verse 3|4|413: The utility of Apabhraṃśa words lies in their containing the essence of correct (sādhu) words.
Maṇi, page 151:
Corrupted (apabhraṣṭa) words convey meaning by following the path of correct words.

"From the perception of words such as *gāvī*, there arises the recollection of the word *go*; from that, an animal possessing a dewlap and other characteristics is understood. (Bhāṣya 1.1.8.29). Furthermore, in the texts of the Śākyas and others, whatever has been employed by those lacking discernment with the intention of using incorrect words—even though it consists mostly of usages such as *prasṛti*, *visita*, *padayāti*, and *atiṣṭhat*—only a very small portion of it can be found to be correct.
How much more so, then, those corrupted forms such as *bhikkhave* and others, which are well-known even among the corrupt regional dialects (*apabhraṃśa*).
For while a Prākṛt word ending in *e* is seen in place of the second-person plural, it is not seen in the nominative plural, even when it is a proper name.

Furthermore, in place of a Sanskrit word—such as *saṃskṛta* becoming *sakata*, *saṃkaḍa*, or *sakaḍa*—only the doubling of the letter *k*, the elision of the *anusvāra*, and the mere substitution of the vowel *ṛ* for *a* are observed in Prākṛt and Apabhraṃśa; there is not even the occurrence of the letter *ḍ*.
Or [as stated in] Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 11.6.12, pp.
238–39: the rule regarding the time, beginning with the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa), for the rites for the ancestors (pitṛkarmāṇi).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the vow during the latter part of the night is not constant.
Bhāṣya 6.8.129.
"In the afternoon, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a pap to Bṛhaspati, in the case of the lower ritual alternative.
This is the *bhāṣya*.
It refers to the maxim of the shadow in the afternoon (*aparāhṇacchāyānyāya*).

Just as the shadow in the latter half of the day is first short and later becomes long; and as it has been said: "The friendship of the wicked and the virtuous is like the shadow of the forenoon and afternoon of a day—different in that the former is heavy at the start and gradually diminishes, while the latter is light at first and increases thereafter."
Thus [it is said]. It is impulsive. 332. And there is the maxim: "That which is unlimited goes to the principal."

In that [mantra] and so forth, where there is no specific mention or acceptance (*parigraha*) of any particular deity—that is *aparimita* (unspecified). And that which goes to what is primary means that which expresses it; this is the meaning.
This is the principle stated by Durgācārya in the *Nirukta* 7.4, p. 629:
"And that which is unspecified goes to the best."

Even in that view where the sacrifice is considered "praise of men" (naraśaṃsa), in that view as well, the excellence of the sacrifice follows from the fact that all things originate from the sacrifice;
this is the principle of *apari-gāmi*.
Durgācārya, *Nirukta* 7.4, p. 627.

Regarding the rule *parimāṇe ca śiṣṭasya* (with the variant reading *aparimita-śiṣṭasya*) at Pāṇini 6.2.121, which concerns the locative case, it has been determined in the discussion on the various ritual options for the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā-kalpa-bheda*) at the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*)—where it is heard: "One [cow] should be given, six should be given, twenty-four should be given, a hundred should be given, a thousand should be given, or an unlimited amount (*aparimitam*) should be given"—that the word *aparimita* refers to a variety of sacrificial fee options beyond eleven, signifying a state of abundance.
Parākrama, p.

212: "'An unlimited amount should be given'—this is a direct prohibition of a specific quality (*guṇa-pratiṣedha*) intended as a gerundive (*kṛtyārtha*) in the context of the fire-consecration (in the prima facie view)."
*Bāla.*, p. 12: "Immeasurability" (*aparimitatva*) means that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) exceeds one thousand.
*Bhāṣya* 6.7.1223–25: "Immeasurability" means that at the fire-consecration, the gift consists of a number different from those previously mentioned.
6.7.121–22: The word "immeasurable" (*aparimita*) is conventionally used for many things when their measure cannot be determined.

It is understood that his wealth is "immeasurable" (aparimita) in the sense that it is "much," just as one is called "skilled" (kuśala) or "proficient" (pravīṇa). Like the word "aśakya" (impossible), in the case of the word "aparimita," the conventional meaning of the whole overrides the etymological meaning of its parts. This is the section concerning the immeasurable (aparimitādhikaraṇa).
In the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), by means of the statement regarding the "unlimited" (*aparimita*), there is an injunction for the giving of a different number.
The "unlimited" is a prohibition of [specific] numbers because it is directly heard in the scripture (*śruti*).

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: Regarding the fire-consecration, it is heard in the scripture: "One should be given; six should be given; twelve should be given; twenty-four should be given; a hundred should be given; a thousand should be given; the unlimited should be given."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is it that a prohibition of "giving" is enjoined with respect to whatever limited quantity—such as one and so forth—is prescribed, or is it that something called "unlimited" (*aparimita*) is enjoined as the object of giving? What is the prima facie view? It is a prohibition of number regarding what has been prescribed; that is, a prohibition of the numbers such as one and so forth which have been prescribed. This is the section concerning the unlimited (*aparimita*).
Whatever number [is mentioned], that is what is prohibited. Why? Because of the direct scriptural statement (śruti) of that.
From the word "limited" (parimita), a calculated number is understood, just as in the case of the word "arrow" (vāṇa).
And that [negation] pertains to the singular and so forth;
its negation is performed by the word "na" (not). In this way, the literal meaning of what is heard is established.
Otherwise, the established usage of the word "aparimita" (unmeasured) would be abandoned;
one would have to assume its meaning to be "plurality" through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

For in the previous case, the act of giving was enjoined by the hearing of the word "to be given" (*deya*); here too, there is the hearing of the word "to be given. That word, being heard, is capable of enjoining the act of giving.

Corrupt words:

In the neuter singular forms ending in *takāra* (such as *patham*), used here and there by Maśaka (the author of an ancient Sāmavedic Kalpasūtra), we find the expressions: "The rest is the same as the Jyotiṣṭoma" (*samānamitaraṃ jyotiṣṭomena*) and "The rest is the same as the one-day Gavām Ayana" (*samānamitaraṃ gavā aikāhikena*). The Bārhaspatya [rite] is recited in the Gavāmayana; the Amīvatī in the Jyotiṣṭoma; and the Pārthurasameya in the Aśvamedha.
Because they are not mentioned in the same context [as the subject under discussion], they are not examples.
(Therefore, because they are mentioned in a single context, "milk is the fast-food" and so forth are indeed the examples.)

It is not so, because it is a rite performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*).
The Commentary states: This is the refutation.
Because it is optional;

For that [vow] is not to be undertaken independently of any specific scriptural injunction;

This is determined because even regarding the vow, a connection is observed in the statement: "Curdled milk (mastu) is for the Śūdra."
In the case of a Śūdra, there is only whey (*mastu*—that is, the thin liquid remaining after curds have been churned).
Therefore, all four social classes (*cāturvarṇya*) would be entitled [to perform the sacrifice]. Furthermore, in the matter of consecration (*saṃskāra*), that [the class] is the primary factor.

The Commentary: And here a distinction is understood, namely, that [the person] is predominant. For in the vow (*vrata*), the person is indeed predominant. What follows from this fact that the person is predominant? This follows: a consecration (*saṃskāra*) whose primary focus is the person cannot, if it is not applied [to him], set aside his entitlement (*adhikāra*).

How is that so? For when it is enjoined that "one who desires heaven should sacrifice," how is it understood that a Śūdra desiring that [heaven] is not intended? Does he perhaps fail to accomplish that which is to be accomplished by the person through the sacrifice? "Or rather, it should be understood that [the study] applies to those other than Śūdras, because of the mention of 'feeling' (vedana). Commentary: It was stated that the scriptural texts do not establish [the eligibility of all]; however, it can indeed be argued that they do establish it."
Nor was that [exclusion] specified by the author of the Sūtra;

for even regarding those [cases] which are contingent (*naimittika*), it would have been possible to state the exclusion of the Śūdra, yet he did not do so. Instead, another reason (*hetvantara*) has been specified.

Even this being the case, when there is an incidental mention of Brāhmaṇas and others, the eligibility belongs only to those who are not Śūdras. Why? Because of the mention of the Veda.

Since he lacks the Veda, the Śūdra is incapable;
therefore, he would not be entitled [to perform sacrifices].

Regarding the statement, “In spring, one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa [into Vedic study] when he is eight years old from conception,” the spring season, the age of eight years from conception, and other such rules are auxiliary to the act of study.
Furthermore, for the person, the injunction “One’s own Veda is to be studied” prescribes study, not [the study as part of] a sacrifice (due to the absence of scriptural evidence for that).
Therefore, the acquisition of the Veda through such a specific procedure is for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha).

Since the Veda is required for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratu*) in order to accomplish one's own purpose, the study of that Veda serves as the *prayojana* (purpose) which, by way of context, renders [the sacrifice] free from expectancy. Therefore, because the sacrifice is rendered free from expectancy by such a form of study, and because the Śūdra lacks the capacity for study, he has no entitlement [to perform sacrifices]; this is the underlying intention.

The proponent of the final conclusion says: "The eligibility [for Vedic study] does not include the Śūdra. [Objection: "Because he desires the quality [of knowledge]. "In this way, his capacity will be produced. [Dvivedagaṅga: But the other, not understanding the intention, says: "If it is argued that it is for the sake of the qualities (guṇa), then study is a subsidiary part of the sacrifice (kratvaṅga); therefore, it is possible even for a Śūdra who has not been initiated."
Therefore, one who has not been initiated will study [the Veda].
Because the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) is for that purpose, the mention of the person (*puruṣa-śruti*) occurs in the context of the two-fold [initiation].
The Commentary says: It is replied.
This mention of "man" refers to knowledge itself,
because the sacrament of initiation has that as its purpose.
One is brought into the presence of the teacher for the sake of knowledge, not for some invisible (transcendental) purpose, nor to build a difficult wall or the like.
This mention of a person in the context of knowledge is indeed for a visible purpose.
How is this understood?
Because this [Vedic passage] is studied as pertaining to the office of a teacher.
Why? Because the middle voice (ātmanepada) is observed.
But how, then, does the root *nī* signify "making someone one's teacher" (*ācāryakaraṇa*)? Because its meaning is heard in that sense;
for the rite of initiation (*upanayana*) is connected with making someone one's teacher.
And by teaching the Veda, one becomes an Ācārya;
therefore, the prosperity of Brāhmaṇas is heard of in connection with the study of the Veda.
For a Śūdra, the study of the Veda is not heard of [in the scriptures].

Therefore, because he lacks knowledge, the Śūdra is incapable and cannot be entitled [to perform rituals]. Durga says: "The sacrament is for the sake of knowledge, and knowledge serves the purpose of the person; in this regard, the same reasoning as previously stated should be observed."

For this has been explained: study, up to and including the knowledge of the meaning, is enjoined by the injunction for the recitation of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*); however, it does not extend through that medium to the prior sacrificial rites (*kratu-pūrva*), because the purpose is attained even by its termination at that point alone. It should not be carried further beyond that to reach the distant prior sacrificial rites. Therefore, because it is enjoined by the injunction for the recitation of one's own Veda, knowledge is established even by those scriptural passages concerning the desire for knowledge (*vidyā-kāma*) which aim at knowledge.
But for a *śūdra*, there is no entitlement [to such knowledge], because he lacks the knowledge prompted by the injunction for the recitation of one's own Veda.

If it is argued [that the Śūdra is not entitled] because of the instruction regarding knowledge—the commentary says: if you view that the Śūdra is unqualified due to his lack of knowledge and incapacity, this is not a valid objection; for there is an instruction regarding knowledge.
He points out the knowledge:
"Even that which has not been stated will be studied."
For it is possible to study [the Veda] even if it has not been explicitly stated [to be so].
Therefore, there is eligibility for all four castes as well. [Duh: Those initiatory rites such as the *upanayana* which have been prescribed for someone would apply to him.
But the other, being uninitiated, will study;
and there is no deficiency in the sacrifice, because initiation and the like serve the purpose of the person.
Or rather, due to his lack of learning, he would be excluded from the ritual act.
The Commentary states: "And this is not the case—that a Śūdra would study. Study is prohibited for him by the injunction, 'A Śūdra must not study.
Even if he were to study, he would not obtain the fruit of study, and a fault would arise."
Therefore, a Śūdra is non-learned (*avaidya*);
it is established that his absence [of qualification] applies to the ritual action.
Even if he were established as learned, nevertheless, due to the absence of the sacred fires (*anagnitva*), he would not be eligible for the ritual action.
Now, how is it that fire is not [the subject]? For there are indeed scriptural injunctions for Brāhmaṇas and others regarding the establishment (ādhāna) of the fires.

But is it not the case that the sentence "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire" is the injunction for the act of establishment? In that regard, the injunction is understood from the direct Vedic statement (śruti), "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fire," and from the Vedic statement, "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire."
That which is based on inference is weaker than what is directly stated in the revealed scripture (śruti).
Therefore, the statements are merely indicative;
consequently, the Śūdra lacks the qualification [for Vedic study].
*Ṭup-ṭīkā*: In the case of studying by one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), there is a deficiency in the sacrifice (*kratu*).

How so? Since the injunction "One's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" establishes study as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) through such means as restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), it is precisely that kind [of study] which the sacrifice takes up by way of incidental application (*prasaṅga*).
Nor is it implied by some other logical necessity (*anyathānupapatti*), because it is established even otherwise.
Therefore, because the requirement has been satisfied by a specific study, the study performed at another time is not accepted.

Just as the *godohana* vessel, having its requirement fulfilled by the *praṇayana* that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, becomes defective when used for the external *praṇayana*, so too the sacrifice (*kratu*) becomes defective through irregular study.
Hence the Bhāṣya says: "Even for one who studies, the fruit of study does not accrue."
This same principle applies even to the requirement of acquiring wealth (*dravyārjanākṣepa*).

(Just as when there is no knowledge of the fire-sacrifice (*agni-vidhi*), one is not prompted by the injunctions for the ritual (*kratu-vidhi*s), so too wealth acquired for the sake of human ends is accepted by the injunctions for the ritual, but it is not required by them.
And thus, there is the observation of another purpose.
The Commentary states: There is also an observation of another purpose, namely, "there is no study by a Śūdra.

Therefore, the qualification [for Vedic study] belongs to those other than Śūdras.

[The Śāstra asks: Is there eligibility for all four castes in the Agnihotra and other rites, or only for the three [upper] castes, excluding the Śūdra?

[Objection]: Since the performance [of rituals] is established through the injunctions for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and since action implies knowledge (*vidyā*)—just as the mantra implies it—and since there is a connection through the Śūdra’s status as the agent of the ritual action, let there be eligibility for the Śūdra because the implication of knowledge is possible; this is the counter-argument [in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*]. Regarding this, [the following is considered]: "Is even a Śūdra entitled to sacrifice or not? Bhaṭṭa: Although the injunctions regarding desire (*kāmaśruti*) apply without distinction, nevertheless, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), it was established in the second book that these injunctions depend upon the injunctions for the installation of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and Vedic study (*adhyayana*). Consequently, it is illogical to assume that they would imply [the performance of rites by] a Śūdra; furthermore, because there is a prohibition against a Śūdra hearing even a syllable of the Veda, only the three [higher] castes have the entitlement, not the Śūdra, with respect to Vedic rites whether accomplished by means of fire or not so accomplished. Since this section serves as a mere application (*prayojana*) of what was already established in the second book, there is no great need for a formal prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) here.
For this very reason, throughout the Veda, there is mention of only the three [twice-born] castes.

As for the mention of "curdled milk for the Śūdra" after having enumerated the three castes in such passages as "milk is the vow of the Brāhmaṇa," that indicates that curdled milk is the appropriate food for the Śūdra who lacks [Vedic] entitlement, and not for the Brāhmaṇa and others; thus, the flow of milk and so forth pertains to his senses.

(In reality, however, since the Śūdra in general possesses the entitlement for the *ādhāna* of the *rathakāra*, for the *raudra* sacrifice of the *niṣāda*, and for non-Vedic rites such as propitiatory ceremonies (*śānti*), it would be more appropriate to say that the statement "there may be [an offering] of a Śūdra" will be meaningful precisely in those cases. Maṇḍana: "The Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice and the like.

This is the *adhi-kriyā* (the topic under discussion).

The section concerning those other than Śūdras (*apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*) is for the purpose of establishing that there is no entitlement (*anadhikāra*) to perform rites accomplished by means of fire (*agnisādhya*) due to the absence of fire, even though there is no explicit scriptural prohibition regarding one's entitlement to ritual action (*karmādhikāra*). [Ko. 2.4.2.19]

In the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, it is stated that the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), requiring an agent because its agent has not been specified, accepts only the Brāhmaṇas and others—who have already been introduced by the rite of initiation (*upanayana*) and who themselves require a purpose, such as "for what purpose have we been brought here by this instruction?"—and enjoins study for them alone, not for the Śūdra. (Rasāyana, p. 62). Furthermore, the injunctions for the *agnihotra* and other rites entitle only those of the three higher castes who are learned.
This restriction of eligibility (*adhikāraniyama*), which will be discussed in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, is established by the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*).

(The *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* is the section that establishes the principle that the right to perform Vedic rites, the right to study, and the right to know the meaning of the Vedas belong only to the three higher castes, excluding the Śūdras. [Ke. Śābara Bhāṣya 1.3.1, p. 6. In the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, study is explained as having the attainment of the syllables (*akṣarāvāpti*) as its defining characteristic.

[This is] an ornament [to the argument]. (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.11–22). Furthermore, teaching the Śūdra is not possible in this way. This is because, from Vedic mantras such as "He who generates the syllables... and "I [perform] the New and Full Moon sacrifices according to the sacrifice," it is understood that the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) has its proper purpose; because of the prohibition of the Śūdra from sacrifice, namely, "Therefore, the Śūdra is not perceived [as entitled] to the sacrifice"; because there is no injunction for the study of the Vedas for the Śūdra; and because of the prohibition of his [access to] knowledge, namely, "A Śūdra should not study the Veda. This will be made clear in the sixth book (*adhyāya*), in the section concerning those other than Śūdras (*apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*).

Having explained the portion of the sūtra, *ku.* 2|3|14, *avidvān na hi*, as meaning "because one who is ignorant is not ordained [to perform rituals] by virtue of being an agent," on the grounds of the reasons to be stated in the *apasūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning Śūdras), [the author states]:

*su.* 3|7, p. 62, "The logic of the removal of fire from the ground (*apasāritāgnibhūtalanyāya*): just as even when the fire has been removed from the ground, heat is still perceived there, so it is in this case."
The rash one. 287. Removed—this is the logical principle. The heat experienced on the surface of the earth indicates that fire has arrived at the surface of the earth.
This is the summary.

"The seasons have their impurities removed; indeed, that sun (Āditya) removes the impurity of these [seasons]; therefore, one should not approach him with sexual intercourse during the day. For this very reason, it will be stated later that by the phrase "then one should study," there is a restriction of time specifically regarding the *ādhāna* itself.
(Bhāṭṭadīpikā 5.4.3). The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is an injunctive *śruti* in the form of a case-inflection (*kāraka-vibhakti*).

Both components of the definition are included to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to a neutral jar or a leaf.
The secret. Page 112. The meaning of the fifth case (pañcamī) is the state of being the *apādāna* (ablative).
This is according to the rule: "The fifth case is used for the *apādāna*.
And the state of being the *apādāna* consists in being the locus of a separation produced by an action inherent in another [entity].

The meaning of that [definition] is: being the substratum of disjunction while not being the substratum of the action that causes disjunction. The final conclusion (*niṣkarṣa*) is as follows: it is the state of being the locus of such an action—which produces a result delimited by its respective [specificity]—while not being the substratum of that very action; or else, even in the case of hearing the praises of the virtuous and so forth, it is the name, which consists in being the relator (*nirūpakatva*) produced by such an action and being the relator of such an action.

Maṇi, p. 140: It will be explained in the *Parṇamayī-adhikaraṇa* that there is no fruit for those things such as hearing the verses of the sinless one (*apāpaśloka*) which are mentioned for the purpose of praise.

(10.8.1.4). Here again they cite [the example]: "Just as this prohibition (*na prathamayajñe pravṛñjyāt*—'one should not perform the *pravargya* at the first sacrifice') would be so."

Such exclusions (*paryudāsa*) are of this nature, as will be stated in the tenth [book] under the sūtra "api tu... (Vārttika 3.3.12.33, p. 878). Śābarabhāṣya 6.7.4: According to the principle of the tenth chapter, eighth section, and fourth quarter, [the phrase "not in the *anuyājas*"] functions as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion). In the phrase "not in the *anuyājas*," the negative particle *na* would be a supplement to the word *anuyāja*, which is but a single portion of the sentence.)

Because conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is not intended, the word "anuyāja" and so forth—accompanied by the negative particle *na*—should be a partial specification (*ekadeśa*) of injunctions such as "one performs the *yeyajāmaha* in sacrifices. This is the meaning of the Nyāya-sūtra: "In sacrifices that are not *anuyājas*, one performs the *yeyajāmaha*. However, since the status of this as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) will be stated in the Siddhānta-sūtra: "But because it is a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), there should be an exclusion of the other" (10.8.7.15), [the former view is rejected]. (Su. pṛ. 950). The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: the word "but" (*api tu*) serves to set aside the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The prohibition, "The initiated one does not give, does not offer oblations, and does not cook," is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the statements, "One should give every day," "One should offer oblations every day," and "One should expect a guest. Thus, because it is a supplement to these statements, there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the other case—that of the uninitiated.
The meaning of "the initiated one does not give" and so forth is "the uninitiated one gives" and so forth.

If a prohibition were accepted in such cases as "the initiated one does not give," then because the act would be both enjoined and prohibited, there would be an option (*vikalpa*), and that is improper. [The sūtra states:
"Or rather, because the agent is common, inference shall be the means of knowledge" (1.3.1.2). This very principle applies to *smṛti* as well.
"Alternatively, since the agent is the same, whatever logic applies to the authority of Smṛti also applies equally to the Veda regarding Kṛṣṇa."

Or rather. (Vā. 1.3.127, p. 286). The meaning of the Nyāya Sūtra is as follows: the word "api vā" (or rather) sets aside the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the lack of authority of tradition (*smṛti*). Tradition is inference, because it possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by following the revealed scripture (*śruti*).

And thus, inference based on tradition (smṛti) would be a means of valid cognition regarding dharma. Why? Because of the identity of the agent; that is, because the agents of the Vedic injunctions and the agents of the traditional recollections are the same, being one and the same.
However, the meaning is not that there is identity of the agent between the revealed scripture (śruti) and the tradition (smṛti).
Because that would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*),

since the non-human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas has already been proven. Furthermore, even in the absence of the principle of "repetition for each primary act" (*pratipradhānānuvṛtti*) which will be stated in the eleventh book— namely, [Jaimini’s Sūtra] "Or rather, because the acts are distinct, there should be an instruction of them along with their subsidiaries, since they are enjoined therein" (1.3.13)— [the objection does not hold].
Su. Pṛ. 734. The meaning of the Nyāyasūtra is as follows: the phrase "api vā" (or rather) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Since the two rites, the *darśa* and the *paurṇamāsa*, are distinct due to the difference in their times, there is no single performance (*tantra*) of their auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), but rather a repetition for each primary rite (*pradhāna*). However, in the case of the two triads of primary rites, because those auxiliaries are prescribed by way of a single performance (*tantra*), there would be an instruction for the primaries together with their auxiliaries.
Therefore, there is no commonality (*tantra*) among the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the two triads; however, within each individual triad, there is indeed a commonality among the constituent parts.
Thus [it is said]: "Or rather, it would be merely a matter of time" (4.4.13).
The two *puroḍāśa* cakes should not be enjoined with reference to a performer who is not an *asomayājin*.
Why? Because that same principle applies.

For that is the principle which was stated: "Or rather, it would be merely a matter of time for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices"; here too, that very same principle applies: "At the time of the *asomayāga*, these two *puroḍāśa* cakes belong to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices."
Bhāṣya 10.8.14.14: The meaning of the Nyāya-sūtra is as follows—the phrase "apivā" (or rather) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

By the statement, "Before the Upasads, he proceeds with the Soma," only the time would be prescribed, because no specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) or difference is perceived compared to other prescriptions regarding time.
Or rather, it may be a name, because it is something new at its origin and lacks injunctive force.

And here, since the single section on injunction (*vidhi*) contains both types of inquiry, there is a separate presentation. Once it has been established that [the term] enters into the constituent part of the means (*sādhana*) by being included within the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), the following is now considered: does its entry into the constituent part of the means occur as an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), or as a name (*nāmadheya*)?
In this regard, the following is the prima facie intention:
because it possesses an established meaning and because it prompts a specific course of action, it is more appropriate that this [sentence] be an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi).

For instance, although there is no conventional usage (*samudāya-prasiddhi*) for it in the world, nevertheless, through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*)—namely, "it pierces upwards" (*ūrdhvam minatti*)—an instrument such as a spade is indeed understood from the word *udbhid*.
This being the case, the meaning of *udbhid* possesses purposefulness (*arthavattva*), because it conveys a meaning distinct from the meaning of the root *yaji* (to sacrifice).
Thus, because the meanings are distinct, there is a specific distinction even regarding the engagement of the person [in performing the ritual].

As it has been said: "Because of its greater established authority, because it serves a purpose, because it is additional, and because it prompts activity, that which is of the nature of a quality is enjoined."
Thus [it is said].
(Vārttika 1.4.1, p.
321) But if it is a name, even though that is understood, the etymological derivation of its parts constitutes its meaningfulness.
Likewise, there is no meaninglessness [of the word] because its referent is not distinct from the referent of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
Precisely because its referent is not distinct, it does not serve as a qualifier even when [the action] is undertaken.

Now, one might object: "When a quality (*guṇa*) is being enjoined, must it be enjoined with respect to a fruit (*phala*), or with respect to the ritual act (*karman*)? In this regard, it cannot be enjoined with respect to a fruit—unlike the case of the *droha* and *hiṃsā* [in the *aindravāyava* injunction]—because, unlike the case of *praṇayana* (carrying forth), there is no established substrate (*āśraya*) for it within the context.
Nor can it be with respect to the action, precisely because there is no action under discussion.

Nor should it be said that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) by means of referring to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice as "one whose eyes are difficult to guard," in the same way that the Āhavanīya fire is enjoined by referring to the oblation as "one whose eyes are difficult to guard.
This is because it is impossible to enjoin another quality in an action that has already become free from expectancy through the presence of a quality enjoined at its origin (*utpattiśiṣṭaguṇa*).
However, in the case of the injunction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire, the injunction is valid because there is no contradiction with an exclusion (*avarodha*).
Nor should it be argued that the injunction of a quality is possible even in the absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) due to the restatement of a quality extracted [from another context];
for since a restatement refers to a matter already previously understood, and upon such recollection, there remains an absence of expectancy due to the exclusion of other qualities.
And this distinction must be established precisely in the *Citrā-adhikaraṇa*.

Furthermore, even in the Jyotiṣṭoma, because of the scriptural mention of the accessory consisting of Soma in the injunction "One should sacrifice with Soma," it is indeed a case of *udbhid-tva* (the naming of a sacrifice by its accessory).
Therefore, even by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to that [Jyotiṣṭoma], there is an injunction of an accessory.

And this being the case, one should not say, "Let it be thus, for it is simply an injunction of an action qualified by a quality," because that would entail the fault of excessive injunction (*vidhi-gaurava*) and because it would result in the undesirable implication of a possessive indication (*matvartha-lakṣaṇā*) in the word *udbhidā*.
As it has been said: "Even when a quality is being enjoined, it must either pertain to the fruit or to the action;
or else, through the cognition of a qualified injunction—it is not tenable in any way."
Thus it is said.
(Vārttika 1.4.1, p.
323) It is replied: in this way, there is indeed a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

Nor does such a procedure entail the fault of excessive injunction (*vidhigaurava*) or the fault of indicating a possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), because there is no such contingency since all specific particulars are excluded. If it is argued that one resorts to such a method there out of necessity, then that [necessity] is equal in the case of the non-attainment [of the object].

Therefore, just as in the case of "He cleanses the cup with the *daśāpavitra*," and so forth, there is an injunction of a qualified entity even through the force of the suffix, in the same way, here too, there is indeed an injunction of an action qualified by such things as the capacity for digging up and sleepiness.
This being the case, it is replied:

this is the intended meaning. This [qualified injunction] might indeed be resorted to through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) as a last resort, if there were no other way by means of [the term] being a name (*nāmadheya*).

For instance, because the word *udbhidā* ends in the instrumental case, it expresses a connection with the sacrifice as the instrument; therefore, grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*) is perceived.
Even that [coreferentiality] would be lost if *udbhid* were a conventional term (*rūḍha*) for something other than its own meaning, like *vrīhi* (rice) or *soma*.

Furthermore, there is an etymological derivation based on its parts: just as in the case of an implement such as a spade, where one "pierces upwards" (*ūrdhvaṃ minatti*), so too in the case of the sacrifice, it is by means of this [rite] that the attainment of cattle (*paśūnām ṛddhi*) is brought about.
Therefore, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), words such as *udbhid* are indeed names of sacrifices.

As it has been said: "A word whose established meaning is unknown is determined by its connection with a well-known meaning through direct Vedic statement; however, that which is conventionally fixed (*nirūḍha*) is not removed from its own primary sense."
Thus, since the same logic applies even to the establishment of the constituent parts (*avayava*), the objection raised regarding the lack of purpose (*anarthakya*) has first been refuted.

Furthermore, as for the claim that [the name] is purposeless because it does not exceed the meaning of the root *yaji*, that is incorrect; for the name possesses purpose by virtue of being the cause for the cognition of a specific type of sacrifice (*yajiviśeṣa*).

For this very reason, it is also appropriate to say that [the negative particle] does not produce a specific activity, because it produces a specific activity precisely by conveying a specific abandonment of the injunction. Now, an objector might say: "Indeed, a word becomes related to another word only when it conveys a specific property, as in the cases 'a blue lotus' or 'a white cloth'."
Furthermore, a name is not something distinct from the sacrificial act itself;
therefore, how could it serve as the cause for the cognition of a specific sacrifice?
Nor can a name, by its own nature, be either verbal or non-verbal, since it is impossible for it to have a connection with a meaning.

Now, if it is argued that the name itself indicates its own self for the purpose of establishing the property of being a word (*śabdatva*), that too is like a man fleeing from five [enemies] falling again into the hands of his pursuers.

For the status of being a name was accepted out of fear of the "indication of possessive meaning" (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), having regard for the possibility of it being an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Now, since this very same indication is admitted even when it is a name, what has the injunction of a quality done wrong?

Furthermore, even when there is a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) involving a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), the general principle of possessiveness is not abandoned; however, in this case, because there is an indication of the self (*ātmalakṣaṇā*), it is even more inferior than that. Therefore, the view that it is a prescription of a quality is superior.

It is replied: This would indeed be so if there were the misconception that a name (*saṃjñā*)—like the word "blue" (*nīla*) and other such terms—qualifies the named object (*saṃjñin*) by way of indicating its own expressed meaning as a qualifier.
But rather, a word which is co-referential with a word expressing a universal...
Alternatively, it is a name (nāmadheya): when the sacrificers apply a specific designation to that which has been incorrectly brought [into the ritual], that is called a "name" (saṃjñā).
For example: "Devadatta is a Brāhmaṇa."

And that particularity, because it is presented by a certain qualifying name-word (*saṃjñāpada*), is characterized by the exclusion of this word [from other objects] through the exclusion of the scope of another name; thus, it is the connection with an existing qualifier that is denoted by the name-word by its own power alone. Therefore, this particular sacrifice is understood as being exactly of such a nature [as defined by the name], and not as qualified by a qualifier.
Since that which serves as the locus possesses an existing qualification, the form qualified by that qualification is established;
therefore, nothing is logically tenable.

In this context, although there is no fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication of possession) in the injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)—since the originative sentences (*utpattivākya*) are intent upon the meaning of that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), nor is there the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) required for the reason of being a name (*nāmadheya*)—nevertheless, at the stage of syntactic unity with the sentence of entitlement (*adhikāravākya*), the fault of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* does arise because of the possibility of another interpretation, namely: "by means of the *udbhid* sacrifice [one attains] heaven. It is with this intention that the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) did not introduce the word denoting the fruit (*phalapada*) here, in order to demonstrate the application of all originative sentences.
The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: if the former position holds, the sacrifice is performed with substances such as axes and the like;

however, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is performed with the substance *soma* itself, as in the Jaimini-sūtras 8.1.16 and others which state, "But in the case of the *avyaktas*, [the sacrifice is] of *soma*.

As for the Sūtra: "In the case of origination—that is, at the first cognition—if there is something unprecedented (*apūrva*) that is not well-known like the words *soma* and so forth, such as *ṛgbhid* and the like, that should be a name (*nāmadheya*)."
Because no quality [of the sacrifice] is established elsewhere, there is "no injunction" [of such a quality].
(Tautā.
Furthermore, because it is a new matter (*apūrva*) other than that, the statements regarding the obligatory (*nitya*) [rite] would be merely reiterative (*anuvāda*). (7.4.15)

In the case of the *saurya* sacrifice and others, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the worldly procedure of the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka* applies by way of extended injunction (*atideśa*), because its application is seen in the *āgrayaṇa-sthālīpāka* and similar rites. To this, the following is said: in the *vārhaspatya* sacrifice, there is the observation of the cutting of grass in the phrase "he cuts the *vārhaspatya* grass"; and in the *saurya* sacrifice, there is the observation of the *prayāja* offerings in the phrase "at each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala*. These would thus be connected to Vedic procedures through extended injunction. However, regarding such cases, the author will resolve the prima facie view with the sūtra beginning "Or rather" (*api vā*). Therein, the cutting of the *vārhaspatya* grass is directly prescribed; therefore, it is a rule for a specific purpose (*arthavidhi*). The prohibition of choosing a *hotṛ* priest is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*). And the sentence concerning the *prayāja* is for the purpose of prescribing the *kṛṣṇala* offering within the context of the *prayāja* itself—thus the proponent of the prima facie view will respond.

(In the Sūtras: "In the case of [rites] such as the Saurya sacrifice, the Vedic *itikartavyatā* (procedure) does not apply because it is based on something else (*anyāpūrvatvāt*). Where there are statements that are constant restatements (*nityānuvāda*), the indicative mark (*liṅga*) based on reasoning (*nyāya-pūrvaka*) serves as the means of cognition therein.

Alternatively, [the mantra] should belong to the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*), because of its connection with the word denoting the primary [rite]; since the mantra is subordinate, it should follow the primary rite.

(10.8.13–14). By this sūtra, it is stated that because the primary rite—the *upāṃśuyāja*—is connected with the time of the full moon through the scriptural statement, "One should sacrifice silently on the full moon day," the *upāṃśuyāja* must indeed be performed on the full moon day.

Furthermore, although the mantra in the form of the *anuvākyā* for Viṣṇu and Agni is recited in the sequence of the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*), it should nevertheless occur on the full moon day in accordance with the primary rite.
*Sūtra* 6.1.12: *Apivā’pyekadeśe syāt* (For when the primary purpose is accomplished, there is disregard for the mere accessory, because [the accessory] exists for the sake of that).

Even though there is an intention [to perform all parts], by the rule *apivā*, just as some other subsidiary part is omitted due to incapacity, so too the singularity of the sacrificer might at times be set aside, and two or many might sacrifice. (Thus it was stated.)
The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: even if there is a deficiency in some part [of the ritual], the performance of the obligatory rite (*nityakarman*) should take place;
for when the principal (*pradhāna*) is performed, the accomplishment of the purpose—the fruit—occurs.

Anything other than the principal is merely a subordinate element (*guṇamātra*) for those ignorant [of the details], because it exists for the sake of that [principal], namely, for the sake of the principal.
Therefore, even an imperfect obligatory rite (*nitya-karman*) should be performed.
Thus [say] the followers of Ke.
(Kevalāmnāyins).

Alternatively, according to the principle of the second section on Mantras (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.1.6.1), which states that "on account of the capacity for performance, the mantra should be expressive [of the action]," since the assumption of a ritual application (*ṛtikalpa*) depends upon semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), and since primary denotation is understood through independent capacity, it is that very [capacity] derived from the Vedic text (*śruti*) which effects the application.
(Sūtra-pṛ. 1084). As for the meaning of the Nyāya-sūtra: the word *apivā* excludes the position that the mantra is injunctive (*vidhāyaka*).
Even though a mantra is distinguished by a verbal form (*ākhyātapada*), it should be expressive of the action (*abhidhānavācī*), not injunctive.
"Because of the efficacy of the mantras in the performance and in the recollection of the purpose of the performance.
Thus, by this principle— "or rather, because of the efficacy in the performance"— the mantras, for the sake of application to the subject matter, first postulate a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

Vārttika 3.1.1, p. 750: When mantras are mentioned in proximity to that which possesses a specific context (*prakaraṇavat*), it is understood that the meaning they express serves as a means (*sādhana*) for that [context].
Vārttika 3.1.14, p. 843: This very point has been explained under the sūtra "api vā prayoga... (Vārttika 3.1.12). Vārttika.

Alternatively, there is the principle: "Or rather, they [the priests] would be the sacrificers, because of their connection with the designation [of 'sacrificer']" (*teṣāṃ syād yajamānatvam*, 10.6.1.5).

Regarding the doubt as to whether, in a *sattra* sacrifice, those very same individuals are both the sacrificers and the priests, or whether they are different persons, it is logical that they are indeed the same.
It has been stated here that "or rather, because there is no difference" (JS 3.1.512). Furthermore, the principle regarding the action of the substance is expressed as "or rather, the sacrificers.
By this principle, we see that they are indeed those very same individuals.
Bhāṣya 10.6.15.54: The word "api vā" (or rather) found in the Nyāyasūtra excludes the distinctness of the priests from the sacrificer.

The priests themselves should be the sacrificers; for in such passages as "The Adhvaryu, having initiated [himself], initiates the Brahman priest," there is seen a connection—namely, a relationship—between the sacrificers and the priests through their designations.
Therefore, those priests would possess the status of sacrificers, and the office of priesthood would belong to the sacrificers alone.

(6.3.12) "Or rather, because there is no difference [in the ritual], and because there is no distinction in the form and the word, there would be oneness of action, as in the case of 'cowness'; and it is a name, like the term 'being'.

[This means: When there is a substitution for the prescribed substance, even though there is a difference in the substance, there is no difference in the sacrifice because there is no distinction; and because there is no difference in form, there is no difference in sacrifices such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
Therefore, even when the rite is performed by means of a substitute, there would be oneness of action.
Regarding the distinction between individuals:

embodied deities do not exist for you [the Mīmāṃsakas]; rather, even in the absence of fire and other such elements, there is a modification (*ūha*) in rites such as the *saurya* sacrifice because of the existence of the *apūrva*.

(9.1.4) *Apūrva* is either a potency produced by the ritual action that results in fruits such as heaven, or it is the subtle state of the fruit, such as heaven, existing prior [to its manifestation].
This very thing is what is called the "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*).
What is it? It is either an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of the sacrifice known as *apūrva*, or some kind of potency (*śakti*) produced by the sacrifice that inheres in the agent. (Vi.
2.1.2) Furthermore, the *apūrva* exists, because starting from this [injunction], it is taught: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."

Otherwise, the injunction would be purposeless, because the sacrifice would have been destroyed. Bhāṣya 2.1.2.5, p. 390. [This refers to] the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as the intermediate operation of the action which is the means to the fruit, and of the auxiliaries which are the means for accomplishing the assistance toward that fruit. The process here is as follows: first, there is the injunction of the action as the means to the fruit, namely, "One should effect heaven by means of the sacrifice."

When the question arises, "How can a result be produced by that which is perishable? it is said: "By producing the *apūrva*. When the question arises, "How is the *apūrva* produced? it is said: "By way of the performance of the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*).

Therefore, because the sacrifice—which has been made the object of the operations of the auxiliaries—cannot possess the status of being a means to the *apūrva* in its own essential form, another *apūrva* is also postulated.

In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, however, because the two groups occurring in the two fortnights are undertaken simultaneously for the sake of the fruit, each individual sacrifice is conceived as having its own distinct apūrva (unseen potency). When there is a requirement for the "how" (*katham-bhāva*) of that sacrifice, the various subsidiaries such as the *āghāra* libation are enjoined. That [requirement] is fulfilled by those [subsidiaries] together with their respective preceding and following subsidiaries, as was explained before; it is not possible [to fulfill it] by the mere intrinsic nature [of the main act alone]. Therefore, three additional *utpatty-apūrvas* (origination-potencies) are postulated.

If, however, the *apūrvas* were postulated as preceding the words from the very first with respect to the six sacrifices, then—because they would serve the purpose of the *apūrva*—six further *apūrvas* would have to be postulated for the sake of accomplishing the *apūrva* from those sacrifices which are primary and whose nature is unknown; thus there would be prolixity (*gaurava*).
Therefore, there is only one *phalāpūrva* (the *apūrva* of the fruit).
The *utpattyapūrvas* (the *apūrvas* of origination), however, differ according to each primary act.

Likewise, since even the auxiliary rites (*aṅgas*), though accepted as being helpful to the sacrifice, are momentary, they are unable to provide assistance by remaining together in their own form; therefore, intermediate operations (*avāntaravyāpāra*) in the form of *apūrvas* are first initiated.

Then, all of them, acting together, produce for the principal rite (*pradhāna*) an awakening of its capacity—an assistance consisting of the primary form that initiates the fruit—which is designated as the supreme benefit.
In this regard, however, there is the following distinction.

The *saṃnipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing) auxiliaries, by means of refining the substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*), bestow an excellence of power upon the essential nature of the sacrifice; they operate toward the establishment of the *apūrva* residing in that [sacrifice], and through that medium, toward the *phalāpūrva* (the fruit-apūrva).
The *ārādupakāraka* (remotely contributing) auxiliaries, however, contribute directly to the production of the *phalāpūrva* from the *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-apūrvas).

Thus, despite this difference in modality, all auxiliaries are accepted as being of a single form in their manner of functioning (*itthambhāva*) as supporters in the production of the sacrifice’s *apūrva*.
Therefore, this is unprecedented.

Śābarabhāṣya 2.1.2. Soma: But surely, just as for the primary rites (*pradhāna*) such as the Āgneya and others, a single "fruit-apūrva" (*phalāpūrva*) is first postulated—which is to be accomplished by all the primaries—in order to effect the means for the fruit; and subsequently, individual "origination-apūrvas" (*utpattyapūrva*) are postulated for the sake of establishing the mutual association of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), so too, for the sake of effecting the production of the ritual assistance (*kratūpakāra*) for all the subsidiaries, a single apūrva produced by all the subsidiaries should be postulated, and subsequently, intermediate apūrvas in the form of operations should be postulated for the sake of establishing their mutual association. Why, then, is it not stated in the section [dealing with] the single apūrva produced by all the subsidiaries?
And this has been accepted in the very same way by the authors of the *Nyāyasudhā*. To this it is replied:

just as heaven (*svarga*) occurs at a later time, the assistance to the sacrifice (*kratūpakāra*) produced by the subsidiaries does not occur at a later time, because that [assistance] arises immediately after the performance of the subsidiaries ending with the satiation of the Brahmins.

Furthermore, since there is no inquiry here as to how a single, all-encompassing *apūrva*—which would be the fruit to be accomplished by all [the rites]—should be postulated (in the manner of the *apūrva* of heaven), because there is no inquiry into how a fruit in the form of heaven occurring at a later time is to be achieved through the Āgneya and other [rites], nor an inquiry into how the assistance to the sacrifice (*kratūpakāra*) occurring at a later time is to be performed by all the subsidiaries (*aṅga*s); rather, the inquiry here is simply: "How is the conjunction of these momentary [factors] to be brought about?
And that inquiry is satisfied merely by the postulation of individual *apūrva*s.

However, among these, because the desire for the fruit (*phala*) is more intense and because that fruit occurs at a later time, it is precisely the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) regarding the means to accomplish it that arises first.
There is a disparity [between primary and subsidiary rites] because everything that is to be accomplished must first be postulated as the means to accomplish the fruit for all [the rites].
...The assistance to the primary rite (*pradhāna-anugraha*) produced by the subsidiaries consists in the awakening of the capacity to generate the fruit; it is nothing else.

And this alone is the supreme benefit (*parama-upakāra*), for all the constituent parts (*sarvāṅga*) join together with one another to achieve this end; such is the understanding of those who possess knowledge.

And thus, the intention of the author of the treatise is that the intermediate benefit (*avāntara-upakāra*) consists precisely in the accomplishment of the visible and invisible results (*dṛṣṭā-dṛṣṭa-sampādana*) produced by acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*) and the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*).
2|1|2. It is understood from these [words] that only words denoting an action (*bhāva-śabda*) convey the *apūrva*, not words denoting substance (*dravya*) or quality (*guṇa*).
Bhāṣya 2.1.2.1–4: The *apūrva* desires the ritual properties (*dharma*) by means of the sacrifice as its instrument.
Ṭupṭīkā 2.1.5.47, p. 1035: Since the *apūrva* is cognizable solely through injunction (*vidhi*), it is differentiated according to the differentiation of the injunctions.
Vivaraṇa 10.4.1: That the *apūrva* exists is understood from the word itself.

It is not enumerated by any means of knowledge other than the word prior to [the word]; Bhāṣya 9.1.2.3, Section 2, page 1646. Regarding the *apūrva*, it is [known] through the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) as *apūrva*.
Or it is understood through scriptural presumption (śruty-arthāpatti).
Vi. 9.1.4: The *apūrva* possesses constituent parts.
"In the chapter on repetition, purification (*saṃskāra*) occurs through false superimposition (*mithyādhyāsa*) in due order."
In the same way, it will exist in the form of parts within the apūrva.
Nor must that which is incorporeal possess parts;
for by this very presumption (arthāpatti), it can be asserted that it is perceived in the form of subtle parts.

Or [as stated in] Vākyapadīya 2.1.2, p. 399: *Sudhā*—Since formless things such as the Self (*ātman*) are observed to be partless (*niravayava*), the unprecedented [entity] must be described as partless due to its formlessness. However, formlessness is not the determinant for partlessness, because even material atoms (*paramāṇu*) are observed to be partless; otherwise, one would have to postulate multiple determinants. Rather, the intention is that [partlessness consists in] the absence of the nature of being a configuration of parts. (This is said even while tentatively accepting the existence of parts for the sake of argument.)
Page 611: For the *apūrva* is both the motivator and the cause of the ritual acts.
