What is this investigation of the *apūrva*?

(Since an action perishes very quickly,) there arises a certain excellence (*atiśaya*) of the action—which is characterized by the disappearance of the action itself, which is produced when the previously non-existent [result] is attained, which possesses a distinct nature acquired through space and time, and which transcends even the immediate sequence of the action—and this excellence, residing in the agent (the eternal self), is said to be the means for the fruit that occurs long after the action has ceased (according to the school of the Buddhists).
Therefore, that [past action] does not exist at the time of the [present] action;
and even though it exists at its own time, because the action has already passed away, it is not perceived as being connected with the action through direct perception.

As it has been said: "At that time, it does not exist in the form of a means to the fruit. Its state of being future belongs to the time of the ritual action (*karman*), while at the time of that [action], the action itself is absent.

[The opponent] objects: How then can there be the status of the action as a means [to the result]—since that [unseen potency, *apūrva*] inheres in something else [namely, the self, whereas the action inheres in this agent]?

[The opponent] objects: "Because it is produced by that [action]—that is, because it is deposited in the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*) by that action—there is no rule that an instrument must reside only in its own substrate.

That [unseen force, *apūrva*], which is to be inferred from its effect, is rightly applied to that which is capable of producing the effect. Because it is produced by that [action]—because it is deposited by that action—it is the power of that action; that is, the *apūrva*."
Nor is the status of being an instrument of an action merely figurative, for it is established as such in the case of firewood and the like.
Indeed, even firewood and such do not directly serve as the means for cooking; rather, they do so through their first conjunction with fire, which depends upon heat.
And yet, in the expression "they cook with firewood," the status of being an instrument belongs to the firewood in its primary sense.
Even in the case of a mass of immeasurable rice grains, the conjunction with fire is preceded by that [prior state].
The same applies to sacrifices and other such acts.
Now, some maintain that this *apūrva* does not exist, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

But surely, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the connection between an action and its fruit, because that would undermine the authority of the injunction (*codanā*).

For at that time—prior to the postulation of the *apūrva*—the connection between the action and its fruit is not established by the injunction; rather, it attains establishment through presumptive testimony. Thus, [the connection] would have presumptive testimony as its cause (i.e., it would be established by the means of knowledge that is presumptive testimony). Otherwise, if the connection between the action and its fruit were established from the word independently [of other factors], there would be no occasion for presumptive testimony.
Once that [connection between the sacrifice and the fruit] is established, why would one postulate that *apūrva* by depending on something else (the *apūrva*) which is itself untenable?
For a cognition that is independent does not have the power to bring about what is to be postulated.

Even if there were such dependence, if the cognition of the connection between the sacrifice and the fruit were to depend on some other entity (*arthāntara*), how could that [connection] be cognized when that [other entity] is not cognized? (For the cognition of the establishment of the connection between the ritual act and its fruit occurs only when the other entity is cognized; for a sentence-meaning cannot exist when its constituent word-meanings are not cognized.)

If it were to depend upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), its independence (*anapekṣatva*) would be contradicted. Furthermore, the heard sentence would be untenable due to its dependence, as in the case of "one who has known [the self] should sacrifice," because of the lack of explicit mention of that which must be supplied (*adhyāhārya*). [That is to say, the word *svargakāma* ("desiring heaven") is what must be supplied; because of its non-mention, there is dependence. [The opponent asks: Is it the sentence that is untenable, or is it the meaning (*artha*)?
In the previous case (the position that the sentence is untenable),
[the injunctions apply] to various unprecedented [results] by means of a specific unprecedented [result].

[One might argue that] there must be the postulation of a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣakalpanā*). [But] in reality, there is no such inconsistency, because the meaning of the sentence is fully established through the denotation of the individual word-meanings by the words [of the injunction], "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Furthermore, if a supplementary part were required, it would follow that the *apūrva* is produced prior to the sacrifice, on the basis of the phrase "having produced the *apūrva*."

From the two-fold application of the verb *yā*—namely, "having produced the *apūrva* by means of the sacrifice" (*yāgena apūrvaṃ kṛtvā*) [and] "one should produce the fruit by means of the sacrifice" (*yāgena phalaṃ kuryāt*)—the aforementioned fault would follow: that the same sacrifice by which the *apūrva* is produced would also subsequently produce the fruit. This is because it is logically impossible for an action to operate after having ceased its activity.

That is to say, by means of another sacrifice; and thus, since the result would be produced prior to the sacrifice, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the production of the *apūrva* before the sacrifice—this is the aforementioned defect. Furthermore, if [the result] is not logically possible as something directly stated (*śrutatayā*), then the very same alternative previously mentioned [must apply], because it is equally logical [in that case]. If it is impossible through any other nature, then the postulation of an *apūrva* for the sake of an object established by direct statement (*śruti*) would be incorrect.

Regarding this prima facie argument concerning the unprecedented subject, it was concluded in the *Kaṇikā*: "This multitude of refutations is to be countered by the crest-jewels of the gods themselves; thus, the Teacher [Maṇḍana] did not elaborate upon them. For who are we there? The great majesty of those for whom 'you' and 'I' have been exhausted therein."

Vi. Pr. 230–34. The ritual details (dharmas) such as the *prayāja* offerings, which are connected with a specific *apūrva* or with a specific sacrifice that serves as its instrument, remain restricted to that very context in which they are recited, provided that the context exists and does not extend beyond the ritual details. Vi. 7.1.1.
The capacity of persons to attain a result, produced by sacrifices and the like, is what is denoted by the term *apūrva*.

Because it does not exist prior to the performance of the sacrifice and arises after the performance has taken place, it is designated by the word *apūrva* (the "unprecedented") precisely due to its etymological derivation. In all cases, that which is capable of being the material cause for [attaining] heaven and so forth—the general capacity—is what is denoted by the word *apūrva*. (Su. p. 352). The connection with the *apūrva* implies the injunction of an action (*karmavidhi*) in order to bring about a distinction. (p. 827). The purpose of being delimited by the designation *apūrva* is as follows: if words denoting substances and qualities also enjoin the *apūrva*, then there can be no substitute (*pratinidhi*) in the case of a substance or a quality; this is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). (upādātvayaḥ yathā tatraivaṃ pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ).

Thus, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the ritual performance must be carried out by substituting either a substance or a quality. (Bhāṣya 2.1.1.5). Furthermore, the purpose for which even the establishment of names is intended is as follows: whatever in this treatise depends upon the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), such as the injunctions regarding the meaning of unknown terms and so forth—all that is to be understood [as having this purpose]. (Vārttika).

The distinction between those *apūrva*s has been stated;
therefore, because there is no difference between them, the ritual properties (*dharma*) remain restricted according to their respective contexts.

Bhāṣya 7.1.1.3. As for those properties that provide immediate assistance (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*), it is established that they too are for the sake of the *apūrva*, and thus [the objection] is refuted.
Dup. 9|1|1|2, p. 1638: "Or rather, that very result arises in the form of a subtle power (*sūkṣmaśaktyātmaka*).
Every effect, such as curd and the like, when being produced, does not immediately manifest in its gross state;
what then? It first undergoes various subtle forms.
In this way, even heaven and the like attain a state of "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) that stands in the place of a sprout or similar effect.

Thus, by virtue of being in the process of arising, they themselves become what has arisen. (Vārttika 2.1.2, p. 395) It is precisely where actions are primary with respect to substances and so forth, that there is the establishment of the *apūrva* caused by them.

1|2|1|1|8, p. 371. Even the *apūrvas* of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), though residing in the self and being connected with the primary rites (*pradhāna*) through a single purposeful conjunction, are established as *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly contributing) because they lack the status of being subsidiary to the substratum (*āśraya*).
Vārttika 2|4|5, p. [blank].

The six sacrifices beginning with the *Āgneya*, occurring at different moments and being perishable, are unable to produce the result collectively; therefore, one postulates six intermediate *apūrvas* belonging to the *Āgneya* and others that are capable of producing that result.
These very [apūrvas] are called the "originating apūrvas" (utpattyapūrva).
However, the intermediate apūrvas of the Āgneya and other sacrifices possess results indirectly, because they serve to accomplish the ultimate apūrva (paramāpūrva).
Nor are they established prior to the [ritual] acts, nor are their means and measures determined.

(Vārttika 2.1.4.8, p. 669). The *apūrvas* arising from the primary acts (*pradhāna*) and the *apūrvas* arising from the subsidiary acts (*anuṣaṅga*) come into existence only immediately after the performance of the primary acts.
(Sudhā, p. 1512). In the case of the *apūrva* resulting from restrictive rules (*niyama*), it is not produced by the action itself.
Vārttika 2.1.1, p. 371: Alternatively, the restriction that "the husking must be performed by that [threshing] alone" is to be enjoined as having an *apūrva* (unseen merit) as its cause;
this is called the "restrictive *apūrva*" (*niyamāpūrva*).
Vivaraṇa 2.1.3: That which directly produces the fruit is considered the "fruit-*apūrva*" (*phalāpūrva*).

This alone is called the *paramāpūrva* (the supreme apūrva). Among these, the *saṃnipatyopakāraka* (directly contributing) rites, such as threshing (*avaghāta*) and others, produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in the essential nature of the sacrifice by means of purifying the substance and the deity; thus, they function toward the accomplishment of that [sacrifice] which is to be approached. On the other hand, the *prayāja* and other [auxiliary rites] operate directly toward the accomplishment of the *phalāpūrva* (resultant apūrva) from the *utpattyapūrvas* (originative apūrvas).
The Section on the Unprecedented (Apūrvādhikaraṇa).
"But the injunction is the commencement.
The commentary: How, then, is it understood that this *apūrva* exists? It is said: "But the injunction is the commencement."
Regarding the term "codanā," we speak here of the *apūrva*.
Furthermore, the *apūrva* exists, because an undertaking is enjoined in the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."

Otherwise, there would be a separate injunction for the sacrifice after it has been destroyed by breaking and so forth. If the sacrifice were to perish through some other means, the result would not occur in the absence of the causal basis.
Therefore, [the injunction] says, "produce [it]."
If, however, it is postulated that "that very [action] does not perish" on the strength of the statement regarding its fruit, this cannot be maintained.
For we do not perceive anything other than action [that produces the result].
That which causes the substratum to reach another location is called "action."
That [action] is not inherent in the self, because the self is omnipresent. The perception of an effect everywhere is the mark (liṅga) for its existence everywhere.
But surely, that itself is the coming from another location?
(Answer: Indeed, no contradiction with consciousness is observed even in the absence of [the object's] arrival.
That substance which was inherent [in the substrate] here is that very same substance;
because it has been destroyed, it is understood that the [substrate] itself has also perished.
If it is argued that the substratum also remains undestroyed, [we reply] no, because of its reduction to ashes.
If it is argued that it exists even when there are ashes, [we reply] no, because it is not perceived even when conditions for perception are present.

If it is argued that the mark [of inference] is the performance of an action (*phalakriyā*), then, this being the case, one must consider the possibility of non-perception due to subtlety and so forth. If it is thought that one of these—subtlety and the rest—will be present, then something imagined will exist; in that case, one might imagine either that [mark] or something prior to it. Since there is no reason for such a non-specific imagination, there is no basis for a specific imagination (*viśeṣakalpanā*). If it is argued that the action will be unconditioned (*anāśrita*), that too is exactly the same.
By postulating a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it does not reach another location; thus, it remains exactly as it was.
Therefore, the sacrifice is a "breaking" (*bhaṅgī*); because it is a "breaking," the *apūrva* exists.

What is the purpose of this inquiry? If substances, qualities, and so forth also prompt the *apūrva*, then in the performance of substances and qualities, no substitute should be adopted, just as in the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

If, then, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), whether it be a substance or a quality, that which is to be substituted must be performed as the primary [original], then—having accepted that [substitution] as established—one might ask: why this investigation into the specific verbal expressions for its representation (*pratipatti*) regarding the *apūrva*?

Its establishment itself is unproven; therefore, that very point must first be demonstrated. To this he says: "The action enjoined for the sake of a fruit is momentary, yet it leads to a result that extends over a long duration."
Its establishment cannot be through either [of those two ways]; thus, it is understood in relation to the *apūrva*.

Because the connection with heaven and so forth, as presented by the Vedic sentences, would otherwise be inexplicable, the *codanā* (injunction) itself will also enjoin the *apūrva*; thus, it possesses a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavat*).
Therefore, the *apūrva* exists.

On this point, others who consider themselves clever state their refutation: "Because it is not known through the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the previously unknown is the object of a sixth [means].
Therefore, it is understood as a real entity (*vastu*) precisely by its being so designated.
The five means of valid cognition, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), serve the purpose of making known the nature of a real entity.
Thus, that wherein those [means of knowledge] do not operate is understood through their absence, by its very nature of non-existence.

Furthermore, those [means of knowledge] do not operate with respect to the *apūrva*. Therefore, because it is preceded by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the *apūrva* must be understood as having the form of non-existence (*asadrūpa*) precisely by virtue of its etymological meaning.

In this regard, it is first of all not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is not perceived by the eyes and other senses as having a nature consisting of form and so forth. Nor is it apprehended by inference based on measurement (*unmāna*), because its connection with any particular cognizer has never been observed;
for no relation of this [self] with anyone has ever been experienced, either specifically or generally.
And it has been stated previously that, in every respect, [the Brahman] exists as a reality from the time of study until the attainment of direct realization:
"We do not hear of this [Brahman] being denotable by words anywhere;
therefore, its being accessible through words is simply not tenable."
Furthermore, its status as being based on scripture (*āgamikatva*) would have to be asserted either by means of a word or through what is understood from a sentence.
In that regard, there is no word whatsoever that directly denotes this [apūrva].
As for the term "the unprecedented" (*apūrva*), because it signifies something else [namely, the absence of prior existence], it actually further subverts its very existence.
Furthermore, a word does not function with respect to an object already known through another means of valid cognition,
nor is it established that a word is an independent means of valid cognition.
And thus, because the sentence lacks denotative power, it is not authoritative. Furthermore, no word-meanings are heard [in the Veda] whose connection could constitute the *apūrva*.

Even those categories of words such as "direct statement" (*śruti*), "indicative mark" (*liṅga*), and so forth, serve as causes for a distinction or an application regarding an entity established by its own nature; they do not establish the existence of anything at all. Therefore, they are not a means of valid cognition with respect to the *apūrva*.

Furthermore, since there is no extended application (*atideśa*) when the specific instruction (*upadeśa*) has already occurred, and because the entire Veda pertains to injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*), it does not serve anywhere to establish the intrinsic nature of an existing entity; thus, the *apūrva* (the unseen force) is not cognizable through scripture (*āgama*).
Alternatively, by virtue of its similarity to things like a hare’s horn which are not perceived, it would follow that it is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), comparable to such things.
Therefore, it cannot be compared even to *adūrva*.

This is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as well: "This [result] does not exist at all," because the connection with the fruit, the sacrifice, and so forth, is established even otherwise.

First, the presumption based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*)—which [others] maintain exists because of the very existence of *dharma*—must also be refuted here by the proponent of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*), since that too falls within the domain of destiny (*daiva*) bestowed by God.

As for presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), of what kind would it be? It occurs where an inconsistency is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, the postulated meaning is not contradicted by anything, as in the case when it is said, "He cuts with a sacrificial ladle" (*suveṇāvacayati*); for it is impossible for meat, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth to be cut with it in any way, because this is known through direct perception.
Moreover, even in that case, it is conceived by means of perception itself as belonging to the fluids;

nor is this conception contradicted by anyone, because there is no abandonment of what is heard [in scripture] and no assumption of what is not heard. But the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is never conceivable as the means of accomplishing the fruit, since its establishment by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) would only occur when other causes have been excluded.
"If, however, a remainder is postulated merely through the exclusion of others,
why is it not understood that fruits have a rabbit's horn as their cause?

For the status of having the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as the cause is not established by the mere negation of other causes, because [such a reason] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntyāt*) due to instances such as a rabbit's horn."

Moreover, if the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is intended to be the goal accomplished by the sacrifice, then one would be abandoning the heaven (*svarga*) mentioned in the scripture and postulating something not mentioned therein.
If, on the other hand, it serves as the means toward the fruit, then the same consequence follows from abandoning the sacrifice mentioned in the scripture;
nor can it be defined in any other form.
Therefore, by virtue of the authority of scripture (āgama), the result must arise from the sacrifice itself.
If it is asked, "How can that which has perished be the means of accomplishment?"—
if it is understood from scripture alone, what contradiction does this pose for you?
What is the proof that the result must be accomplished by means of something being heard [in scripture]?

Furthermore, why do things such as space (*ākāśa*), which abide eternally, not accomplish the result? If it is postulated that the result is accomplished by means of the *apūrva*—on the grounds that no other state of existence is possible apart from what is heard—then it would be better to postulate space itself; for its actual existence is already well-established, and one need only assume its status as the cause of the result.

In the case of an *apūrva*, however, everything from its existence onward would have to be postulated without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, if the intention is that the fruit must be given by something established that is connected to the sacrifice, even so: "It is better to posit the status of being the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) for the sacrificer himself, who is connected to and persists through the sacrifices; for in that case, there is simplicity (*lāghava*)."

If the fruit, being accomplished by another entity related to the sacrifice, is thereby considered accomplished by the sacrifice, then for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), it would be better that it be accomplished by the self alone through the sacrifice that has already passed away.
Or rather, this very destruction of the ritual act (*karman*) will accomplish the fruit for us;
for it is postulated with effort because of the injunction of a perishable sacrifice.
For when an action that perishes is enjoined, what is observed? The action has perished, yet it is determined by the scripture that the fruit will arise at a later time.
Furthermore, it is established that whatever cognition arises with respect to something, that thing is its cause.
Therefore, let the fruit have non-existence itself as its cause.
This might be so;
however, it is not maintained that the reality of consciousness (cidvastu) is something to be accomplished (sādhya).
To this, it is said:
Or rather, it is because of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency),
for which there is the section on *apūrva*, that at that time there exists the cause for the knowledge of the non-separation between the ritual action and its fruit.

And as for that which was not excluded because it was included within the scope of the treatise at the time of its commencement, why is it determined only at a later time? Furthermore: "Because of his capacity regarding all acts of agency, his possession of qualities is recognized; and because he is obstructed by that [agency], the presumption of meaning (arthāpatti) pertains to the *apūrva*."

Thus, this very state of having an intermediate result is merely a minor deficiency in the causal factors; therefore, one need not postulate an *apūrva* (unseen potency) for the sake of establishing a result at a later time.
For in that case, the presumption (*arthāpatti*) would be inconclusive, as it might also postulate a deficiency in the ritual procedure itself.
Nor is the postulation of an *apūrva* useless simply because the result occurs in another birth.

Why? Because: "Even when births are equal in being composed of pleasure and pain, heaven and hell would here [in this world] result spontaneously immediately after the action. For heaven and hell cannot be of the nature of unsurpassed pleasure and pain, nor can they be particular locations, such that one would not experience them right here in this very life; for it would otherwise be impossible for there to be the desire to abandon or attain things that are not of this world.
As for those worldly pleasures and pains that are intense, they are understood to arise from other actions alone; thus there is no distinction [in this regard].
Furthermore, [this is so] because of the diversity and variety of the fruits of prohibitions.
Furthermore:
"Even in the case of a subsidiary (aṅga), there could be a discussion [of its application] as being a cause of assistance;
however, because it is established by incidental occurrence (prasaṅgasiddhi), there would be no application of what is unknown in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti)."

Since the *prayāja* and other such subsidiaries are also momentary (*kṣaṇika*), their assistance to the primary sacrifice must indeed be rendered while they are present in their own form. Thus, that assistance also occurs through the agent alone, as there is no separate *apūrva* (transcendental potency) for them.

In that case, for one who has performed the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries in the archetype (*prakṛti*), because that assistance remains present in the ectypes (*vikṛti*), there exists the characteristic of *prasaṅga*—whereby the result is achieved even without the performance of the ritual procedure (*tantra*)—and therefore the subsidiaries need not be performed again.
Consequently, in instances such as "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala*," one should not apply [the rule of repetition].
Surely, this objection follows from the difference in time;
however, he will provide the answer to this with the statement: "Because the purpose remains unchanged" (1.2.1.14).
For that very form of assistance which is intended toward the subsidiaries that are proximate is the same even in a modification (*vikṛti*) situated at a distance; thus, there is no distinction.
The intention is that this will hold true even in the view that [the apūrva] is the destruction of karma.

For in that case as well, since the destructions of the applications of various auspicious and inauspicious karmas—whether single or multiple—have ceased when the sacrificial cakes (apūpa) have been offered, the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) will not be precluded; thus, there is no fault.
And in this very manner, the contradiction regarding origination is to be resolved.
And it has been said: "In the chapter on error, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises sequentially;
likewise, in the case of the *apūrva*, it will exist in the form of the constituent parts of the sentence."
Furthermore, that which is formless cannot possess parts through its own parts. Indeed, it is by this very presumption (*arthāpatti*) that one can say it is perceived in the form of subtle parts.

Even when its existence prior to manifestation is revealed because that which is absolutely non-existent cannot arise, even then, its manifestation—distinct from sound and other objects—consists in being appropriated by each individual through their actions and being directed toward the production of results.
For it is said: "The manifestation of entities is perceived as their formlessness;
therefore, its manifestation will occur through the closing of the eyes while remaining within the self.
Or rather, the self is held to be eternally existent by nature, capable of pervading all things."
However, whatever obstruction this [Apūrva] has due to karmas is removed by it;
therefore, it is indeed Apūrva (the unprecedented).
Furthermore, we do not perceive any other purpose for it that exceeds its primary nature.

Therefore, beginning from this point, the section concerning the unprecedented [doctrine] has been stated by Yājñavalkya (in the Sāvitrī-upākhyāna of the Mahābhārata): "Yama forcibly dragged out the person the size of a thumb."

Thus, even that [statement] should be understood as intended for the purpose of enhancing poetic beauty and for the sake of clearly praising the conduct of death, within a sentence primarily devoted to extolling the *pativratā* (faithful wife), by means of the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of "Lord of Creatures" (*prajāpati*).

For in that very same way, the state of being present in all things is described in the *Gītā* and other texts in a single manner. Furthermore, if there were omnipresence, it would follow—just like space—that there is only one Self in all bodies.
This is not a fault, because of the multiplicity of bodies and because we observe a fixed distribution of the experience of pleasure and pain for each individual body.
For if [the subtle body] were other [than the one], its purpose would be fulfilled by a single body alone, and thus multiple bodies would be useless.
If it is argued that this is no fault, as in the case of bodies in other births;
No;
for in that case, there would be a different experience due to the influence of other actions, because of their repeated commencement.
Furthermore, the perception of pleasure and so forth occurring in every body would have to exist for each individual body.
Furthermore, there would be the perception of one's own nature and so forth by means of the sense organs belonging to another, due to [the soul] residing within another body;
and because of demerit and the like, there would be no fixed order of castes, nor would there be any distinction regarding the cessation of karma.

For it is possible for a single self to be connected with various bodies because it is omnipresent; however, there is a slight objection regarding its being manifold. Even if all selves were omnipresent, they would occupy the same location because they are devoid of material form.
And precisely because it consists of the nature of consciousness (*caitanya*), there is the conventional usage of "oneness of self" (*aikātmya*) in the Upaniṣads.

If it is asked: "But even if there is no plurality [of selves], how is it that all do not experience the pleasure, pain, and so forth belonging to others due to the connection with all bodies?"—to this he says: "Just as even within a single body, there is a restriction of pleasure and so forth among those who are merely described as being in the mother's womb, so too will there be a restriction everywhere."

It is said that this same fault applies even to the proponent of the doctrine that the self is equal in size to the body; for since that [self] also occupies the same space as the self in the womb, it would perceive the pleasure and other sensations belonging to the mother's body.
Whatever solution is offered for that case will certainly apply to all bodies in every instance, provided there is no distinction.

Just as consciousness is perceived, however, the mere fact of falling into parity with the opponent's position is not a valid proof, because both of those [positions] are ultimately terminated by something else.

Furthermore, because its [the soul's] size is limited to that of the sense organs, even though the self is immeasurable within the space of the body, it still possesses contact with the maternal womb via the body of the embryo and so forth; thus, there would be an equal fault [for both positions].

Therefore, it should be refuted in this way: "If the enjoyability of pleasure and the like were held to depend upon reaching a specific location, then the aforementioned fault would follow; however, since the object of experience is determined by its suitability, there is no fault."
For if the cause of connection and experience were held to be solely the fact that the self and pleasure and so forth occupy the same location, then this fault would arise.
But here, the connection between the eyes and other organs and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is characterized by fitness (yogyatā).
In that regard, just as...

Just as there is no perception of color and other qualities by the sense of touch when they occupy the same location as that touch, so too there is no perception by one self of the merit, demerit, pleasure, or pain belonging to another.
Therefore, because the relationship of owner and owned is established for each respective self, there is no fault.
Thus, due to its omnipresence, the immobility of the self is proven.
Now, [the opponent might argue that] the *apūrva* does not perish along with the self, but rather perishes together with the substance; to this, he says: "That has perished.
Nor is there a lack of its destruction, because a different substance contrary to it is perceived.
Furthermore, there is no cause for the obstruction of its apprehension by which it would not be perceived.

If, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), one were to postulate an obstruction to its perception and so forth, even then, while the *apūrva* exists, one would have to postulate that which is contrary to what is observed: namely, that it remains undestroyed for that long, yet is not perceived; likewise, the cause of its obstruction, and the cause for that [obstruction] also being unperceived—thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, if action (*karman*) is momentary, one must postulate both its persistence and the cause of its non-perception; thus there is prolixity (*gaurava*) in this way when postulating the persistence of an action that is not supported [by a substrate].

Now, if it were the case that conjunction, disjunction, and so forth existed merely as inherent in the self without producing any effect, then even in that case, there would be both the perception of the contrary and the assumption of something unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, it is established that one must indeed assume something previously unknown (*apūrva*).

The purpose of this fundamental section (*mūlādhikaraṇa*) is that when substances and other factors are connected with a result, because they serve an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there is no fixed restriction [on their application], just as there is none for ritual actions (*karman*).

Regarding the connection between action and its fruit, however, since substances and the like serve a visible purpose through the production of the action, there is a substitute (pratinidhi) based on the knowledge that they perform the same function.

How then is it that the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) avoids the fault of leaving an undertaking incomplete? The action must indeed be completed by means of whatever substance is available.

However, one need not strive to obtain a substitute that is strictly similar, because a result can be obtained even from something merely similar; furthermore, when no specific means has been prescribed for an action, a substitute is said to be "one located in the same place as the desired object," since similarity serves another purpose.

For the original substance was intended for the sake of the primary result, whereas the substance now being brought in is for the sake of completing the action undertaken for a contingent result (naimittika-phala) through the mediation of the substitute.
Moreover, the establishment of the name [of the ritual] is also indeed a purpose.
That [reason], however, has not been demonstrated here because it was already stated previously.

Since the verbal root *su-* denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) whose fruit is [heaven], the fact that words such as *śyena* stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it establishes their status as names (*nāmadheya*); this is also a practical application of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
For the relationship between the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) is indeed heard in the scripture regarding heaven and the sacrifice.
If another entity were to exist, scripture itself would be contradicted.
Therefore, even when the sacrifice has perished, it is that very [sacrifice] which accomplishes the fruit; this is the section concerning the *apūrva*.
Or rather, it should be understood from the authority of the scriptures that [the fruit] persists until the result is attained, and not as something new (apūrva).
This being the position reached, we reply:
"The commencement of an effect by that which has perished and is non-existent is impossible."
Since that which is established as momentary cannot logically have a non-abiding [state], something entirely new (apūrva) must be postulated. Thus,
there is a connection with the prima facie view regarding the Soma sacrifice.

The purpose, however, is that everything here in this treatise—such as the knowledge of the meaning of the *apūrva* (the unprecedented) and the fact that it is for the sake of the *apūrva*—is to be understood.
As for the meaning of the sūtra: the *codanā* (injunction) pertains to the *apūrva*, because it is heard that the commencement of the fruit of ritual actions [occurs] through it.

If there is doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of the *apūrva*, it does not exist, because there is no means of valid cognition [for it]. The fruit would be established from the sacrifice by virtue of the authority of the scripture;
however, this involves the postulation that the destruction of a momentary thing is accompanied by a cause.
Let there be no contradiction with the internal [scriptural authority].
The postulation of something not previously known is for the sake of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*).
What is called the "intermediate operation" (*avāntaravyāpṛti*) or "capacity" (*śakti*) is said to belong to the sacrifice.

That it is "unprecedented" (apūrva) should be understood from the Veda through its ritual procedure (*prakriyā*). Once it is established according to the Bhaṭṭa school that there is indeed such a thing as the *apūrva*, the inquiry arises as to whether this *apūrva* actually exists or not. In this regard, since even a momentary sacrifice can be established as the means to attaining heaven by way of the destruction of its own past potentiality (*tāvad-dharma*), there is no need to postulate an *apūrva*, as that would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Nor can it be argued that because destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is eternal, the scriptural statements—"Dharma does not perish through recitation" and "Even very great sins are destroyed by expiation"—are logically untenable as grounds for the destruction [of karma] through recitation or expiation; for recitation and the like function as obstacles to fruition and thus act as destroyers [of the causal efficacy of karma]. Furthermore, there is no fault in postulating a cause other than the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice characterized by its non-self-nature (i.e., the apūrva) resulting from recitation.
Therefore, there is no evidence whatsoever for an *apūrva*.
This being the position reached, we reply: an *apūrva* must indeed be postulated, because the assumption of complexity (*gaurava*) is not a fault when it pertains to the result itself.

Therefore, when the primary rite (pradhāna) is to produce a fruit such as heaven, the *apūrva* is its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*). And when a subsidiary rite (*aṅga*) is to produce its own fruit in the form of a capacity conducive to the fruit of the primary rite and so forth, that [capacity] is its intermediate operation.
Furthermore, like the fruit itself, it resides in the self (*ātmaniṣṭha*).
Furthermore, there is no proof for anything other than the serpent (*nāga*) and so forth being an intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*).

Therefore, in this context, where there is only one principal act (*pradhāna*), there arises from that principal act—due to its preceding and succeeding states—an intermediate *apūrva* (unseen potency) distinct from it; and at the conclusion of all the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), another, supreme *apūrva* arises. Thus, there are two *apūrvas*. Likewise, even when there is a plurality of principal acts, it should be understood that while there is a distinction of production-*apūrvas* (*utpattyapūrva*) for each principal act, the supreme *apūrva* is one.

In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, by the two statements, "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day" and "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day," it is understood that the three constituent sacrifices possess a collective efficacy (sāhitya) independent of any intervening interval. Since this collectivity is logically untenable without being defined by a single final effect, there arises a distinct intermediate Apūrva for each group, and by means of that, the ultimate Apūrva. Thus, nine Apūrvas are established. In the same manner, the postulation of Apūrvas in other cases—such as the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and the Dvādaśāha—is to be understood.

Regarding the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), however, those which provide assistance by direct contact (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) are employed in producing a fitness conducive to the generation of the "origination-apūrva" (*utpattyapūrva*) within the primary act itself;
and the destruction of that fitness residing in the final primary act constitutes their cessation.
As for those generating assistance from a distance (*ārādupakāraka*), they are employed in producing a fitness conducive to the generation of that immediate effect residing in the origination-apūrva.
And when the collective apūrva exists, the immediate effect is that very [apūrva].
In its absence, it resides in the supreme apūrva, and from that indeed comes heaven;
in this case, destruction occurs due to the final fitness [for fruition].
If, however, it is suspected that there is no such evidence for a supreme *apūrva*, then let that be non-existent.

But for the subsidiary acts (*ārādupakāraka*) which are not known [to produce results directly], let their function be to generate a capacity conducive to the fruit within the very *utpattyapūrva* (origination-apūrva) when it assumes the state of a collective *apūrva* (*samudāyāpūrva*).
In any case, the *apūrva* is established.
Maṇḍana: "The establishment of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) follows from the force of the injunction (*vidhi*).
Śaṅkara: "For us, there is no *apūrva* at all.

Thus, first, it is established that the *apūrva* exists; furthermore, it is established that the *apūrva* arises precisely from the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), and also that substances and the like serve the purpose of that [verbal meaning] insofar as the verbal meaning generates the *apūrva*.

The refutation of that [view] occurs in the *Tadadhikaraṇa* (Kau. 2.1.4.7, p. 630). In the *Apūrvādhikaraṇa* (1.2.4.42, p. 71), it will be argued that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating restrictive rules (*niyama*) rather than postulating an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by action.

Indeed, this has been thoroughly discussed in the *Kaustubha* under the section on *Apūrva* (Bhāṭṭa 4.2.7): "Otherwise, in the case of not using the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*), there would be the contingency of assuming that it destroys the purpose of the sacrifice; furthermore, there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the causality of non-performance and so forth.

For once this section (the section on Heaven, establishing that the fruit is distinct from the action and is eternal) is established, then in the section on *Apūrva*, the accomplishment of an effect distinct from the action follows simply because [the fruit] possesses properties other than those [of the action].

[In passages such as] "He offers the *samidh*s" and "He offers the *tanūnapāt*," because they intend different meanings and because there is a difference in the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the establishment of distinct names occurs; and by the logic of the section on the unprecedented (*apūrva-adhikaraṇa*), the establishment of a distinction between *apūrva*s follows.

Since it is impossible for an action to be the cause of a result that occurs at a later time, the postulation of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is made; however, the locus of this *apūrva* is established upon the accomplishment of the result. [Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 3.1.1]. And the prior [action] is the original form (*prakṛti*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), whereas the modification (*vikāra*) is the subsequent. Page 528. The prior, however, is the modification.
(From here on, the term *apūrva* generally refers to the ritual action. Thus, the *gṛhamedhīya* rite among the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices is an *apūrva*.

Bhāṣya 10.7.124–33: "And if the archetype (*prakṛti*) were to have the same ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) as [the modification], then because of its non-permanence (*anityatva*), the *apūrva* would be purposeless.

If the archetype were to have the same ritual procedure as the modification (*vikṛti*), then the modification-specific (*vaikṛta*) ritual procedure would apply to the archetype as an *apūrva*, due to the non-permanence of the modification."
When some desire arises for a particular sign, a modification occurs.
And that which is occasioned by a sign (naimittika) always sets aside the regular rule.
For if it did not set it aside, then the modified, the occasional, or the optional rite would indeed be purposeless.

Therefore, because it is a modification (*vaikṛta*), the archetype (*prakṛti*) would be subject to the principle of extension (*prasaṅga*). This is a hypothetical consideration (*kṛtvācintya*). In reality, however, there is no case at all where the archetype shares the same ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) with its modification (*vikṛti*).
*Apūrva* refers to that action which has no prior [cause];
it is its very own nature, such that for it there exists no other nature whatsoever— such is the *apūrva* consisting of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice.
"By enjoining a previously unknown matter, it will possess purposefulness.
(Bhāṣya 3.1.6.12) "It will enjoin a previously unknown matter, and thus it will effect a specific engagement [of the agent]—[this is the injunction, as indicated by the phrase] 'the rest is the same.
If it were a mere restatement, it would not effect a specific engagement and would therefore be purposeless."
The *upāṃśuyāja* in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is a new (*apūrva*) rite, as stated in the injunction: "One performs the *upāṃśuyāja* in between.
(Vi.
2.4.4). Likewise, the *avabhṛtha* in the *jyotiṣṭoma* is a new rite.
As much as has been stated must be performed.

"A novel ritual element (*apūrva* padārtha), when being displaced, does not serve to displace those that precede it"—this principle is established in the section beginning with *tathāpūrva* (Śābarabhāṣya on PMS 5.1.26.19).

Śābarabhāṣya 5.1.9: In the case of the animal and Soma sacrifices not previously mentioned, there are the injunctions: "One should sacrifice with Soma" and "One should immolate the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Viṃśatikā 2.1.6: Similarly, [the rites] such as the Āghāra-libations are original: "He pours the two Āghāra-libations" and "He performs the Agnihotra oblation."

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Upasad is thus an original (apūrva) rite; only that which is explicitly stated should be performed. In the case of original rites, there may likewise be an option regarding this [performance], because they possess all functional capacities.

In the context of the *abhicayana* (the piling of the fire-altar), many mantras for the purpose of shaking (*ādhunana*) the *ukhā* (the sacrificial pan) and for the purpose of sowing seeds (*bījavapana*) have been recited.
In that regard, it is stated: "He offers with seven [mantras]" and "He scatters with fourteen.

Regarding this, the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) position—which is contrary to the sūtra—is that the number fourteen must be understood from the very beginning according to the order of the recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of refuting that [view].
Therefore, numbers such as three and so forth are *apūrva* (unprecedented), not established by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding those unprecedented numbers, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) as to whether they should be placed at the beginning, in the middle, or from any point whatsoever.
There is no restriction that it must be "from the very beginning" here;
in this way, all *ṛcs* and all mantras would possess meaning.
However, if one were to take them only from the beginning, the additional [mantras] would be rendered purposeless.

Therefore, the established conclusion is that there must be an option (vikalpa) for the sake of making all [of them] meaningful. [Objection: But would it not be a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda) regarding something unprecedented?

Regarding the *ājyabhāga* offerings in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice, nor at the *soma* sacrifice.

In that regard, since the *soma* sacrifice is an original (*apūrva*) archetype, the statement heard concerning the *soma* sacrifice—"nor at the *soma* sacrifice"—would be an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the rule "one does not perform those two at the animal sacrifice.

Just as the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are not performed at the *soma* sacrifice, so too they are not performed at the animal sacrifice; thus, this is a praise of the prohibition of the *ājyabhāga* offerings at the animal sacrifice.

Or. 3|1|13|8 | An original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) is fourfold, according to the distinction between the originative injunction (*utpattividhi*), the applicatory injunction (*viniyogavidhi*), the qualification injunction (*adhikāravidhi*), and the performance injunction (*prayogavidhi*).
An originative injunction is one that makes known the essential nature of a ritual act (*karma*); for example, "One performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice."
The injunction that makes known what was previously unknown is the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), such as "One offers with curd.

The injunction that makes known the connection with a result is the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*), such as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice. The injunction that makes known the primary rites along with their subsidiaries and ancillaries is the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vidhi*).

And that [obligation] is distinct from the two [types of injunctions], namely the injunction of origin (*utpatti-vidhi*) and the injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*), and it is also the sustainer (*jīvaka*).
It should not be asked, "For what purpose is its postulation?
because it is not obtained through anything else, as it possesses the same locus, time, and agent.
Because it is necessary for the attainment of that [result].

Others hold that the *prayogavidhi* (injunction of performance) is precisely the cognition of the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the injunctions regarding the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) and the principal (*pradhāna*) rites.
*Maṇi*, p. 99. The *apūrvavidhi* (injunction of what is not otherwise established) is fourfold.

The injunctions are: the injunction of genus (*jāti-vidhi*), the injunction of substance (*dravya-vidhi*), the injunction of quality (*guṇa-vidhi*), and the injunction of action (*kriyā-vidhi*). Among these, an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) regarding genus is: "One desiring vigor should make the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of *khadira* wood. An original injunction regarding substance is: "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a cow-milking vessel (*godohana*)."
Because the word *godohana* is etymological (*yaugika*), it denotes a substance.
An injunction for a quality that is not previously established is, for example: "If one should desire, 'May there be rain,' one should erect the sacrificial shed low.
An injunction for an action that is not previously established is, for example: "One performs the *agnihotra* oblation."

The injunction regarding the deity (*devatāvidhi*) is also included within the *apūrvavidhi* (injunction of what was not previously established); for although the deity serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice, it is nonetheless known solely through the injunction. Furthermore, the injunction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth—which serve as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the oblation—is also included within the *apūrvavidhi*; for although the *āhavanīya* and so forth serve a visible purpose by way of being a locus, it has been stated in the *Ādhārāgnihotrādhikaraṇa-vārtika* that they possess an invisible purpose because they are not implied by the injunction for the oblation itself.

The rule for deities (*devatāvidhi*) is also fivefold, based on the distinctions of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), the dative case, the wording of mantras (*mantravarṇa*), the accusative case, and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). The Theory of Exclusion (Apohavāda): "By those who have postulated that the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*) is the universal (*sāmānya*) denoted by words, it is clearly stated— though using the term 'exclusion' (*apoha*)— that 'cowness' (*gotva*) is indeed a real entity (*vastu*)."
For it has been established previously that non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed a distinct entity (*bhāvāntara*).
In that case, let it be explained: what kind of entity is this whose nature consists in the cessation of the non-cow and so forth?
The *Ratnākara* [verse] refutes the universal (*sāmānya*) as having the form of exclusion (*apoha*), which is established in the Buddhist system: "The cessation of the non-cow," etc.
However, those who say: "An essence (ātman) that conforms to individual characteristics (svalakṣaṇa), which are mutually exclusive and absolutely distinct, is not possible;
nor do individual characteristics, because they are non-conceptual, receive the status of being denotable by words through either identity or non-deviation.

Therefore, the meaning of a word is simply the exclusion of what is other than that (atadvyāvṛtti), which permeates all [particulars]. Just as the exclusion of the non-cow applies to a brindled cow (śābaleya), so too does it apply to a black-spotted cow (bāhuleya)."
As they say: "Whatever form belongs to a brindled cow or a black cow does not exist in that [other] one; therefore, the exclusion of what is other than that form applies equally to both."

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "That which produces a semblance (*sādṛśya*) among things that are absolutely distinct is observed to consist in the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*); for example, the dewlap [which produces a semblance] among cows, horses, and elephants. Likewise, the conceptual form (*vikalpa-ākāra*) 'this is a cow' produces a semblance among the absolutely distinct individuals such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Therefore, the universal (*sāmānya*) denoted by the word is simply the exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*), and not a separate entity. By them [the Buddhists], the universal of "cowness" (*gotva*) has been stated as a real thing (*vastu*) itself under another name; it is not a different object.
And this is a summary verse regarding the arguments for non-identity that will be explained below.

The word "tu" (but) [indicates an exception]. In a ritual context, when a scripture is recited as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*) within no specific section, it remains unmodified exactly as recited; yet, if it is heard in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti-yāga*) regarding a particular modification, it serves the purpose of prohibiting the archetypal elements (*prākṛta*), that is, for the purpose of prohibiting those elements obtained through the rule of transfer (*codaka*).

Just as the scriptural injunction, "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," which is stated without reference to a specific context, is heard in relation to particular modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) such as the *vaiguṇya* and others; by this, the previously established *sāmidhenīs* obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*), which were otherwise unknown [in those contexts], are set aside. The sense is: "In the *vaiguṇya* and other such rites, one should recite seventeen *sāmidhenīs*, and one should not perform any other archetypal (*prākṛta*) rite.

"But in the case of a modification, it would be for its sake.

Nor is it the apprehension of the ground as possessing the absence of a jar, because that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya).

Indeed, it is not the case that this [perception] is the means for establishing the conventional usage of the non-existence of something unperceived; rather, it is precisely that [perception] which is its cause—this is the correct view. For otherwise, since the perception of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) would be impossible without being preceded by the non-perception [of the absence], the perception of the bare ground in a place like a jar-less location could not be the cause for determining the absence of the jar. This is because even that which is unknown can be seen as a means of knowledge, just like the eyes and other sense organs.

Thus, even against one's will, one must accept that the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the ground arises from the absence of the jar; for that very [absence] is what constitutes the determination of the conventional usage of non-existence. [Objection: But in this way, you have accepted that [the ground] is a means (*upāya*) merely by its existence (*sattāmātra*), and that is untenable, because it has been stated that if there were no non-perception (*anupalambha*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cognition of that [non-existence] arising. [Response:
What end is served by such a multitude of arguments regarding the absence of the jar?
That very [argument] is incorrect;
for there is no existence of a real entity,
since its establishment depends upon non-perception.
[Objection: But surely, in this case, mere perception [of the locus] cannot be the cause for the cognition of absence;

rather, when one perceives Caitra upon being asked "Was this Caitra here?", how could Maitra—who possesses the same capacity for perception—be perceived while his counter-positive (the absent Caitra) is not? [Reply: True, he perceives Caitra, and that is accepted as the cause. Thus it is said: "Having remembered the counter-positive," but not remembering its prior existence there on the floor.
"No"—by this, he indicates that it is merely a non-apprehension; for since memory is an apprehension with respect to reality, its absence would also be impossible as a non-apprehension.
Nor is it simply the perception of the ground, which has become associated with a single cognition, that constitutes [the non-apprehension] of the jar.

Therefore, it is now appropriate [to state] that the non-apprehension of that which is fit for apprehension is the "non-perception of its absence. It is not the case that the means of seeing the elements (bhūta) as they were previously perceived and combined is [the cause]; for if that were so, even if those [elements] are currently being apprehended, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-perception of a jar, even though the jar has been perceived [before]. At that time too, the prior existence of Caitra, who was moving about, was [present] on the floor.

In that case, since at midday there is the perception of the recollection [of the jar], and the non-perception of the jar is distinct from that, [one might argue]: "The absence of recollection of the object on the previous day is established by the fact that 'it is not remembered'; this non-perception, whether it is itself perceived or not, must be the cause for producing a cognition of existence regarding the previous day's object. Is it perceived or unperceived? It cannot be perceived, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Nor is it the case that the proof of non-existence occurs solely through the non-perception of perception.
For that [non-perception] as well, since it is of the nature of a positive perception, must currently be established by another non-perception;

because the means of proof is the non-perception of a perceptible means of knowledge. Therefore, it too must be perceived, and thus there would be an infinite regress due to requiring yet another non-perception.

However, if there is no establishment [of the object], then inference and the like would not arise. But if the sun has already passed over the Makara sign (Capricorn), then its existence could serve as the logical reason (*hetu*).

And so, when this [reason] is present in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, and because the existence of the act of worshipping a shrine (*caityavandana*) and the like is characterized by the nature of being perceived through a ladle (*darviṇopalambha*), and because there is the possibility of cognizing the ground, even then, since there is no obstruction to the commencement of a continuous series of similar [moments]—such as the hearing of a sound that is established merely by the arrival of the resonance (*dhvani*) and the pastness of the *apūrva* of the sacrifice—at that time, the absence of Caitra is established on the mountain slope characterized by Caitra who has recently arrived.

One who maintains that perception occurs only through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntaropalambhavān*) is asked: "O Amaitra, did this Caitra exist previously? [The opponent replies: "Even for a memory that lacks a [corresponding] means of valid cognition, there is a capacity regarding its own object. At that time, he possesses an inquiry arising from that [memory]. Since the previous state of the subject is not perceived, and because the visibility of Caitra—who was present at heart—is determined to be non-existent at that very moment, it is logical that the cognition arises only from a cause that brings about the result.
And in the absence of that [perception], he states inference and so forth: "O long-lived one, Caitra was here previously. In that case, it is because of the cessation [of perception];
for it serves as the means of establishing the non-existence of the object to be inferred.
For it is not established through inference, because at that time there was no non-perception of that [object] due to its being perceived then.
Nor is there an absence of the objects' status as objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*).

Furthermore, a prior non-perception, which would remove that [status], is possible only when all other efforts are complete except for the object itself; and when that [non-perception] exists, it is capable of producing the cognition of its absence now.

Indeed, it is not on the basis of being a cause (*nimitta*) that the conventional usage of the cognition and its absence—namely, "seeing" and "not seeing"—is established; for such usage is possible even in the absence of a contradiction between the two cognitions.
Nor does one see color at present by means of the non-existence of the object [in the past].
Therefore, even when there is a connection within a single cognition, the completeness of other conditions—including the contact between the sense organ and the object—is required.

Since that very [cognition] is impossible in the absence of an object, it has been stated that something is experienced even in the absence of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, is this conventional usage of non-existence absent? [No; its fitness for being remembered is established.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction between apprehension and non-apprehension, because they establish the existence and non-existence of things at different times; thus, it is untenable for them to have distinct objects.
