It might be argued: "If non-existence were established by mere existence [of its absence], then even the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of 'existence' would be subject to negation. To this, it was stated that the non-perception [of the object] possesses visibility (*dṛśyatva*), and thus, for the sake of establishing the cognition of that [non-existence], both [visibility and non-perception] are described as being of the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is objected that this is not so, [we reply: no.
There would be no desire to investigate subtle insects, thorns, and the like.
Not so;
for that [investigation] occurs because they are perceived as having the nature of being excluded from real entities (sadvayāvṛtti), and it serves to establish their own subordinate visibility.
Because the reality of that which is commanded by the Lord is untenable;
because no distinction is perceived;
and if it is argued that this is due to its being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), we say: no.
[This refers] to the knowledge [of the object], not for the sake of knowing its visibility.

Or, let it be that the knowledge of visibility is the reason; yet this would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that it applies to potencies and so forth as well. For indeed, their difference is not like the cognition of a bare ground; what, then, follows for non-perception? Indeed, it is not light...
It is being examined:

since the determination of that [object] consists in the non-difference of the object's capacity from its cognition and so forth, that which is being cognized must be the cause; this must likewise apply to the eye.
If it were not so—

Nor is it the case here that the distinction between those [cognitions] is determined by the difference in their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*); thus, smoke is understood to be the cause of inferential knowledge, and so too is the mind.
Everything is clear. (Kaṇikā, pp. 68–92). The cause must be known.
Therefore, since non-apprehension of the real is the cause for the cognition of absence, there is no infinite regress;
nor does it follow that absence must itself be an object of cognition distinct from the absence of the object of cognition.
Indeed, being an object of cognition is not the same as existence, for we accept its existence as a unique property (*kaivalya*).

Since the non-perception of Caitra implies the absence of his existence—even though he is non-dual with the ground—due to the exclusion [of his presence], the opponent [the proponent of non-existence] states that it has a cause: "The non-apprehension of the object is due to the non-existence of the thing itself. He says: "To say 'non-existence is an object of cognition' is well-said! (i.e., it is a fine statement).

[The opponent asks: "If it does not exist, then what is the cause for the cognition of its absence other than the recollection of its counter-positive? And how is it cognized? (A certain mock-skeptic objects: "Just as even when those [threads] exist, a cloth sometimes appears; therefore, it was established that non-existence is not the object of cognition in the case of thorns and the like—how then can there be a production of a distinct conjunction? When the counter-positive is perceptible, if it is being recollected, then how is the linguistic usage 'it does not exist' possible? (The mock-skeptic says: "When there is the apprehension of a real entity, there is the linguistic usage of non-existence."
We perceive that conventional usage is non-existent;

for you have indeed defined this contradiction as the long-term coexistence of that [usage] with the cessation of its cognition. As for this activity or cessation of worldly people regarding something, thinking "it does not exist" in a certain place—[this is what we observe].
This is the meaning. 1) Furthermore,

regarding that which precedes [the result] (*purastāt*)— namely, the worldly practice characterized by the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired— is this due to a lack of discernment, or rather, because of the existence of something else that has been determined?

(He concludes the topic under discussion: Therefore, [is it] due to the exclusion of something else, or rather due to the determination of its absence? If [it were] based on non-determination, then even if it were not based on a valid cognition (*pramiti*), nor based on an invalid cognition (*apramiti*), they would not seek to know the absence of what is desired, simply because of that non-determination.
"Desirable does not exist, desirable does not exist"—thus [arise] engagement and withdrawal.
Withdrawal occurs precisely because of the non-delimitation of the undesirable; however, engagement (the desire to know) is based on the apprehension of absence.

[He] asks: "Indeed, pride (*māna*) would also result in being indefinable; apart from that, what object of knowledge has been described for [the state of] non-existence? [Another says: Because the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyabhāva*) belonging to the body of pride is entirely incomparable."

Nor is it [known] through the mere apprehension of the nature of something else, because that would entail the occurrence of activity on a ground where a subtle thorn or the like has been grasped merely by its own nature, as there would be no possibility for an inquiry preceded by effort.
Likewise, if non-existence were an object of knowledge (*prameya*), then inference regarding even things such as a rabbit’s horn would become unimpeded.
Therefore, non-existence is an object of knowledge.
And this cognition of non-existence is not perceptual, because it is not produced by contact with the sense organs.
But one might object: "Just like the cognition of existence, how can it be said not to be produced by the sense organs, given that it too arises from contact with the sense organs?"
It is said:
this determination of non-existence is preceded by the apprehension of existence;
and since that apprehension of existence occurs through the sense faculty, its occurrence in dependence upon that [faculty] is established by another means (anyathāsiddha).

If it is asked what the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this is: [it is perception], because we observe the cognition of absence even in one who has grasped the mere nature of the absent object, whose sensory activity has ceased, yet who has developed a desire to know due to other causes arising while he has gone to another place.
Nor is it inference, because the apprehension of the necessary relation (*sambandha*) cannot occur;
for indeed, when the related term (*sambandhin*) is not grasped, the comprehension of the relation is not easily achieved.
Furthermore, there is no apprehension of that which possesses non-existence as its correlate.

Thus, this other means of valid cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva*) has been defined by this Bhāṣya. *Bṛhatī*: (The Teacher asks: What is understood by this? (The Opponent replies: It was stated that "the meaning is 'it does not exist'. (The Teacher refutes: And what exists therein? (The Opponent replies: The state of being an object of knowledge belonging to the means of valid cognition.
(Ācārya: Therefore, the status of non-cognition as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) appears almost superhuman.

Ṛju: Surely, let it be that that which is not cognized does not possess the quality of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*); however, its non-existence—which, like the relation of absence, has the ground as its locus—may well be the object of cognition.
No, it is said in reply.
Indeed, non-existence is nothing other than the very state of not being cognized; there is no other.
For even one who asserts that non-existence is a distinct entity must necessarily admit that the positive entity itself is indeed being cognized;
for it is only in this way that the conventional usage of "non-existence" is logically established. What, then, is the purpose of postulating a separate entity?
Nor is the object of cognition (prameya) merely the state of not being cognized, because the non-cognition of that object consists in the self’s experience of it as unassociated [with other objects].
And that state of the self is established by itself (*svataḥsiddha*).
Therefore, nothing remains to be an object of cognition.

Furthermore, even for one who asserts that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the very cause for the arising of the cognition thereof is the connection with its non-existence. And this [non-existence] does not produce cognition by its mere presence while remaining unknown— like the eyes and other sense organs— because even when the ground and so forth are currently being perceived, there is observed the cognition "this was previously here" due to the non-perception of something else, even though it is absent.
Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that the present cognition of non-existence arises solely from a previous perception now ascended into memory.

Consequently, let non-existence be defined simply as "perception of the solitary" (kevalopalambha); what is the point of positing a separate entity? Furthermore, that quality of the self which consists in being associated with the perception of the solitary occurs in some cases due to the deficiency of the causal complex for perceiving an object, and in others due to its completeness.
In this regard, it is precisely by connecting that very state which brings about the conventional usage of non-existence that the conventional expression "there is no jar on the ground" proceeds.
Nor is there any over-extension here, such that the conventional usage of non-existence would apply even when [the jar] is in contact [with the ground],
because the perception of the object alone is different from the perception of it as conjoined.

Furthermore, even an inquiry preceded by deliberate effort may conclude that "this is the state [of non-existence]" regarding subtle thorns and the like on the ground, despite the completeness of the causes for perceiving an object; what inconsistency is there in this? Otherwise, if one were to suspect that "this state belongs to the self because of its subtlety," the unhesitating practice of the term "non-existence" would be impossible.

And since this very proof of non-existence—which serves as the counter-position—is established, inference does not proceed regarding the horns and so forth associated with rabbits and the like; thus it is proven that non-existence is not a separate category of objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

*Ṛjuvimalā*, p. 92–93. *Bṛhatī*: "Even a definition is a state of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabhāva*); thus, it defines [the object] precisely as 'the state of being a means of valid cognition'.
(The opponent: "And this is a well-known fact:
among the Mīmāṃsakas, what is this sixth means of valid cognition?"
Nor is its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) determined from anything else in the world;
therefore, we do not know what the seed of its established authority is.
(The Siddhāntin: What is it that is not known here? First of all, its very nature as a means of valid cognition is determined from the text itself.

When it is said that "it does not exist," ordinary people understand this as the non-existence of its very status as an object of cognition (*prameyatva*). (Opponent: What, then, is the purpose of defining it in this way? This undertaking is for the sake of understanding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for how else could there be a determination of the object in accordance with those means?
(Proponent: Precisely for this reason it is stated: because this undertaking is for the sake of understanding the absence of the means of valid cognition.

(Opponent: Is the nature of the aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) determined by this [text]? (Proponent: That which cannot be determined by the very definitions (*svalakṣaṇa*) previously stated—that is what is determined by this [text]. This treatise is a commentary on the designations and explanations of those specific definitions.
For the status of a cognition as a means of valid cognition with respect to its object is not determined merely from its arising.
Therefore, because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone is denoted, there is certainty,
since the own-nature (*svarūpa*) of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is what is being apprehended.
Consequently, because the effect is directly perceived, the statement "it does not exist" expresses that the previously mentioned definition itself is what is to be proven (*sādhya*).

What, then, is this "established convention" (*prasiddhi*)? Established convention is like the established convention regarding the act of carving. If, however, they consider there to be a difference in the cause because of a difference in linguistic usage, what can we do?
If certain Mīmāṃsakas [namely, Bhaṭṭapāda] maintain that there is a difference in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what can we do about it?
Human effort does not adorn those who are utterly deluded; thus, no consideration should be given to them.
Indeed, the establishment of a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not follow from a difference in conventional usage.
Therefore, this is nothing other than the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
And this very [definition] is its characteristic.
*Bṛhatī*, pp. 91–95. The Section on Non-existence (*Abhāva-anupalabdhi-pariccheda*).

(Śā. "Non-existence, too, is the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*), for the sake of establishing the meaning 'it does not exist' which is otherwise unestablished," so says the *Bhāṣya*.
But how can the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) be a definition of a means of valid cognition, since it is the opposite?
This word "means of valid cognition" refers to the five means of valid cognition previously mentioned, such as perception which apprehends an existent object.
And since the absence of those five is the definition [of the sixth], there is no inconsistency.

What is its object of cognition (*prameya*)? It has been stated: "of the object [expressed as] 'it does not exist'. For every entity is twofold, consisting of both existence and non-existence. When an entity exists in a certain place in its form of existence (*sad-rūpa*), it is then cognized there as "existing" through perception and other means of knowledge. However, when it exists in that same place in its form of non-existence (*asat-rūpa*), because it is impossible for the means of knowledge—such as perception—which cause the cognition of the form of existence, to produce a cognition of that form of existence, there occurs a non-arising even though the conditions for such arising would otherwise be present. This non-arising, which is the opposite of "non-perception of what is perceptible" (*dṛśyādarśana-yogyānupalambha*) and so forth, is what is designated by the term "absence of a means of knowledge" (*pramāṇābhāva*) in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*).
By that very means—namely, through the sense organs and so forth—the absence [of an object] is cognized, as in the case of "there is no jar here on the ground.

As for one who, denying non-existence, claims that there is no sixth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because of the absence of an object of cognition (*prameya*), what is the objective basis (*ālambana*) of the cognition that arises immediately after the non-perception of the perceptible, such as "there is no jar here on the ground"? It cannot be the ground, for if it were, such a cognition would occur even when a jar is actually present.

Likewise, regarding the cognition "this cow is not a horse" and the cognition "color is not taste," what is the basis for such [cognition]? If it is held that the cause is the perception of another location (*deśāntaragrahaṇa*), then one would have to say that the cowness residing in a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow) does not exist in a *bāhuleya* (a black cow), and even bamboo stalks situated within one pillar would have to be treated as non-existent in another pillar despite being threaded through it. Therefore, it is the absence itself (*abhāva*) that is the cause for the linguistic usage "it does not exist," and not the existence elsewhere.
This means that the cause for the linguistic usage "it does not exist" is the non-perception of something that is being remembered as having existed previously.
No;
for even when an object is being perceived, there is the linguistic usage of its absence in the surrounding space.
Furthermore, regarding a jar that has been brought [to a place] and is currently being perceived, there is the linguistic usage of its prior absence, such as: "Previously, this was not here."

Now, in your own view, how can there be a cognition of the prior absence of a jar that is currently being cognized? For the non-existence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) regarding an entity is indeed the cause for the cognition of its absence. And when something is being cognized, the non-existence of a means of valid cognition is not possible.

If it is argued: "Even though the jar is being cognized at present, it is not cognized as being related to the prior time; therefore, since the means of valid cognition for the jar's relation to the prior time has not arisen, the cognition of its absence at that [prior] time is entirely appropriate."
No;
because it is not possible.

For a connection with a prior time is not now a fit means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, it is the absence of a fit means of valid cognition that is the cause for the knowledge of non-existence, not the mere absence of a means of valid cognition.

However, in the prior time, there was simply the non-arising of the valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) appropriate [for it]; for at that time, although the absence of the jar existed, it was not cognized, because the counter-positive—the jar—was not reflected upon (*aparāmarśa*), and the knowledge of absence depends upon that [counter-positive]. For this very reason, it is not tenable to say that "the absence of the jar is now remembered," since what has not been cognized cannot be remembered. Just as this non-arising of the valid cognition belonging to the prior time has now perished due to the arising of the valid cognition, it is unable to produce an absence, just as an eye that has just been plucked out is incapable of producing the cognition of form.
Now, even though it has perished, smoke from yesterday—though destroyed—may indeed serve as the cognition of the location of the hand when it is being remembered.

This would be so if the absence of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*), by virtue of being known itself, were to make known the absence of the object of knowledge (*meyābhāva*), just as a logical mark (*liṅga*) here makes known the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
But that is not possible, because it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

For in order to know the state of non-existence of the object of cognition (*prameya*), the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) must be known. That [absence], too, being itself an absence, must be known by another cognition of absence; that [second one] by yet another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, it must be admitted that the absence of a means of valid cognition produces the cognition of absence by its mere existence, like the eye and other sense organs. Consequently, it must be explained how there can be a cognition of the prior non-existence of a jar that is currently being cognized.

It is said: It has been correctly stated that the mere existence [of non-perception] makes known the absence of knowledge and the absence of the object of knowledge; however, there is indeed now the non-arising of a capable cognition regarding the connection with a prior time even for this jar being perceived. For although it is fit to be remembered as having a connection with a prior time, it is not remembered.

Nor is it necessarily only the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) that makes known an absence; rather, the non-arising of a memory-cognition itself, provided it possesses the capacity [to arise], certainly makes known an absence.

Therefore, if the jar being seen now had existed previously, it would necessarily have been perceived by someone standing there; and having been perceived, it ought to be remembered now. Even though this is the case, it is not remembered. This very non-arising of remembrance regarding all true objects currently existing produces at present a cognition whose object is the absence [of that jar] at the previous time—is this not intelligible? Furthermore, in the *Bhāṣya*, the term "absence of means of knowledge" (*pramāṇābhāva*) is intended as an indicator for the "absence of remembrance" (*smaraṇābhāva*) as well. The same applies in the *Vārttika*.

Alternatively, since the result of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is remembrance, it can be said that its absence is also, by virtue of its result, simply the absence of a means of valid cognition.

Now, it might be argued that it is logical for non-perception of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*) to bring about the cognition of absence merely by its existence; for even when such non-perception is present, the cognition of absence sometimes does not arise, while even when it is absent, the cognition of absence sometimes does arise.

For instance, when a person, with both hands, feels all around a portion of a room containing a pair of fingers, then, because he has felt every part, a non-perception of the object as it is fit for perception (*yogyānupalabdhi*) has indeed occurred. Nevertheless, doubting whether every part of the space was felt or whether some part might not have been felt, he does not ascertain the absence of the fingers due to the lack of certainty regarding that non-perception, even though it exists.

Sometimes, even when one has not actually perceived an object anywhere, one mistakenly concludes through the non-perception of what is perceptible that it is indeed perceived everywhere; having determined this through that very error, one then ascertains the absence of the finger-ring in that very place.
Therefore, it must be admitted that the non-perception of the perceptible is the cause of the cognition of absence precisely by virtue of its being known.
And thus, there follows the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, the non-existence of the visible counter-entity is merely the cognition of that [surface] alone, and not a separate reality. (The proponent says: But surely, if non-existence is not admitted, the cognition of that alone can never be determined; nor is the cognition of that alone simply the cognition of the ground, because even the cognition of a [ground] conjoined with something else would result in being a cognition of that alone, since the nature of the ground appears there as well. Therefore, the cognition of the ground which occurs when there is an absence of the perception of a jar and so forth is the cognition of that alone.
And thus, since you accept the absence of cognition, the apprehension of non-existence is rendered purposeless.
How, then, should this be defined? It is stated as follows:
the non-existence of a jar and so forth exists as an object of knowledge (*prameya*).

The non-arising of a cognition of something fit [to be perceived] indicates its absence by its mere existence, like the eye and other organs, and not by being known, for that would lead to an infinite regress.

As for the fact that there is no ascertainment of absence even when there is a fit non-perception, while there is ascertainment when such [non-perception] is absent, that is caused by the cognition of the fit [object].
For the fit non-perception is the cause; in that regard—
Section on Non-existence (Abhāvapariccheda): Refutation of Non-existence as a Means of Valid Cognition (Abhāvapramāṇanirāsa).

Capability (*yogyatva*) is a cause only through being known, not by its mere existence. Therefore, capability, though always present, does not determine non-existence when it is at times unknown; however, at other times, having erroneously determined that capability—which is actually non-existent—to be present, one determines non-existence. In the case of perception (*upalabdhi*) and so forth, [the cause] is by way of mere existence, not by way of being known; thus, there is no consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Everything is clear.
Therefore, its object of cognition (*prameya*) is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
Nor is that [non-existence] perceptible by the senses, because the cognition of it is seen to arise even in the absence of sensory operation.

For example, when someone who was at home in the morning is asked at midday, "Did any man from Mathurā—wearing white clothes, tall, and dark-complexioned—arrive at this house this morning?", he determines the non-existence of that person during the morning time at that very moment, even without the operation of the senses, due to the failure of a suitable recollection to arise.
Nor should it be argued that the absence perceived in the morning is what is being remembered at that time;
for at that moment, the counter-positive (the person from Mathurā) does not arise in the mind in any way whatsoever, and because an absence cannot be known if its counter-positive is not present.

Thus, even in cases where an absence existing in a proximate space and time is perceived right now through the operation of the sense organ due to non-perception, since the cause can only be the incapacity consisting in the non-arising of a cognition of the fit object, it is impossible to postulate the sense organ as the cause.
Therefore, non-existence is not perceived, nor is it inferable; for since it is unknown, there is no apprehension of any mark (*liṅga*) by which it might be grasped.

As for what some here say—that "the existence of an imperceptible thing is pervaded by its perception, and thus, through the cessation of that pervading perception, the cessation of the pervaded imperceptible thing is inferred"—that is refuted.

By inferring the cessation of the pervaded through the cessation of the pervader, one must necessarily first comprehend both cessations in the instances of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) and ascertain the invariable concomitance (*niyama*) between them; then, in the subject (*pakṣa*), which is the locus of the probandum, the absence of perception—which serves as the means of proof—must be apprehended by some means within itself, and from that, the absence of the perceptible (*dṛśyanivṛtti*) must be inferred. However, since cessation is of the nature of non-existence, its apprehension through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is impossible. If it were to be inferred by another cessation, then that too, being of the nature of cessation, would have to be inferred by yet another cessation, and that again in the same way; thus, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, the non-existence [of consciousness] must necessarily be cognized through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Once that has been cognized, inference follows afterwards.
Thus, the status of non-existence as a separate means of valid cognition is established.
However, those [means of knowledge] such as verbal testimony (*śabda*) and analogy (*upamāna*) need not even be suspected [as additional categories].
Therefore, it is established that the sixth means of knowledge exists,
and these alone are the [valid] means of knowledge.

As for that additional probable measure, such as the number "thousand" understood from its constituent part, the number "hundred," which is asserted by some, that is in fact nothing but inference, because it is based on the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Furthermore, traditional lore (*aitihya*) such as "Vaiśravaṇa dwells in the banyan tree" is not a valid means of knowledge at all, due to the absence of any definitive certainty.
Even if it were valid, since it is included within scripture (*āgama*), it is not a separate means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

As for intuitive cognition (*prātibhājñāna*)—which some consider a means of knowledge, citing such examples as "I have heard, I have heard, I shall hear"—that too is produced by fallacious signs (*liṅga-ābhāsa*) and the like; because it lacks definitiveness, it is not a valid means of knowledge.
Therefore, that which is asserted by the followers of Kaśyapa—that intuitive cognition is the means for perceiving dharma and adharma—is baseless.
Worldly renown (*lokaprasiddhi*) is also included within perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is therefore not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, there are only six means of valid cognition.
Accordingly, it is said in the *Bhagavadgītā*: "O Rāma, that by which everyone in the world is led astray."
Thus ends the doctrine of non-existence (abhāvavāda), pages 83–87.
Refutation of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) (the refutation of non-apprehension).
Now, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for non-existence (*abhāva*) is refuted.

If it is argued that the linguistic usage and practical activity of "it does not exist" would otherwise be untenable without another means of valid cognition, we say no; for this is established simply through the specific features of the ground (*bhūtala*) and so forth.

But surely, the ground—which is the object of the linguistic usage of existence—is not the objective support (*ālambana*) for the linguistic usage of non-existence, because it would follow that the same object belongs to both the usages of existence and non-existence.

This is not so; for even by the proponent who maintains that there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) whose nature is non-existence, the fact that the non-existence of that [object] is the referent of the linguistic usage "it exists" must be admitted. Otherwise, it would follow that the non-existence of non-existence itself would be non-existent.
Consequently, non-existence too would not be the referent of the linguistic usage "it does not exist.

Now, one might argue: "Even if non-existence is the referent of the linguistic usage 'it exists' in relation to something else, it is nevertheless the referent of the linguistic usage 'it does not exist' in relation to a jar."

If that is the case, then even the ground (bhūtalam) is, in relation to something else, the object of the conventional usage "exists," and in relation to a jar, it is the object of the conventional usage "does not exist. Why, then, is a distinct reality (tattvāntara) admitted? Because [you claim] the ground alone is the object [of cognition]. But if so, what is the "isolated" (kevala) object?
If it is the ground itself, then the same consequence (prasaṅga) follows even when a jar is present there.
If it is something other than that, then it must be admitted as a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*).
If you say it is the bare ground (*ekākī bhūtalama*), then since "bare" means "without a companion," it follows that you have admitted the absence of a companion.

If you argue that even when the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is being remembered, the ground is the objective support (*ālambana*), whereas when it is being perceived, there is no linguistic usage of non-existence simply because there is no memory [of the counter-correlative], then in that case, when a place in another location is being perceived, there would be no linguistic usage of the absence of that [object] in the other location.

Furthermore, even in that case, since the locus possesses the status of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) by virtue of its connection with another location, it would be impossible to remember it as being connected to that [other location], and thus the conventional usage of "non-existence" could not occur.

Now, if it is argued that when the counter-correlate is the object of inquiry, the ground (*bhūtala*) is the objective support (*ālambana*), whereas in the case of a jar, because the counter-correlate is already known, there is no such inquiry; [we reply:]...

It is not so, because even when a beloved son or similar object is already known, a further desire to know (*jijñāsā*) does not arise, and [if it did] it would lead to an infinite regress of worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, it is observed that the cause of a distinct type of transaction is the cause of a distinct type of cognition; therefore, in the case of the desire to know a jar, the cause for the transaction of its non-existence occurs only through the determination of the absence of the jar as something distinct from the ground. Thus, a separate reality (*tattvāntara*) is admitted. Now, one might argue that this is simply the perception of the ground qualified by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) other than that [for perceiving the jar], whereas in the case of the jar being present, such a complex is absent, and thus there is no perception.

What is this "being distinct from that"? If it means being other than that, then since that possibility exists even in the cognition of a conjoined object, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence [of the jar] not occurring.
If it means the absence of that [jar], then a distinct reality (tattvāntara) has indeed been accepted.
For this reason as well, this cognition of the mere ground is not the cause; rather, it is a specific cognition of the ground.
And that [cognition] is indeed distinct from the cognition of a composite [object].

Nor is it a cognition of non-existence (*abhāva*), because a distinct cognition is admitted as the cause for the cognition of non-existence, such as "there is no jar" and so forth; therefore, for one who accepts that which produces the cognition of non-existence, by that very [cognition] there is worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

This is not so. For a cognition that is devoid of the cognition of non-existence does not have as its object something over and above the ground (*bhūtala*); even if it has the ground alone as its object, it does not possess the nature of being a cognition of the non-existence of a jar associated with that ground, due to the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

However, the non-perception of the jar is a cooperative cause; therefore, it is the cognition of the mere ground, qualified by that non-perception, which brings about the cognition of the absence [of the jar].
If it is argued that in that case, that [mere ground] alone is the cause of linguistic usage, we say no, because there is no difference in the object (*viṣaya*).

For even when it is merely the ground, the production of a different cognition is possible due to the presence of the cooperation of perception, just as there is a difference in cognition regarding a single jar depending on whether it is seen with the eye or touched by the hand.
Therefore, because it produces a cognition distinct from that of the mixed [surface], its status as the cause of the knowledge of absence is established.

For you, however, a distinct linguistic usage cannot arise from the mere cognition of the ground assisted by non-apprehension; for distinct linguistic usage is observed to have a distinct object, just as in the case of the linguistic usages "jar" and "cloth.
Consequently, since the linguistic usage of absence must have the very cause of the knowledge of absence, the counter-argument is not established.
To this it is replied:

Even though the linguistic usage of non-existence has as its cause the cognition of non-existence, the cognition of that [locus] alone is accepted by the proponent of absence (*abhāvavādin*) as being caused by non-existence; and that [cognition] is accepted as distinct from the cognition of a qualified object consisting of a related positive entity.
As it has been said: "Having perceived the existence of the locus and having remembered the counter-positive..."
"In this state, the mental cognition of non-existence arises."

Thus, the establishment of distinct linguistic usage occurs precisely through the qualification of that specific cognition which consists in the apprehension of the existence of the real object; therefore, there is no undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) even regarding a jar, because in that case there is an absence of the cognition of mere distinctness.
Even though difference [of objects] arises from the difference of their causes, [the distinction in usage is not based on that].

If it is argued that, nevertheless, difference produced by the object itself is the cause of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), we reply: True; in cases such as the cognition of mere distinctness (*vilakṣaṇamātra*), its being the object must necessarily be admitted as a form of distinctness, because the relationship between object and subject is a form of difference.
Therefore, the conventional usage of "distinct" is justified.
Just as from the cognition of mere distinctness the knowledge of the absence of non-distinctness arises, so too for us the conventional usage of "distinct" occurs; thus there is no fault.

As for what was stated—that a distinct linguistic usage based on a difference in the nature of the causes is not observed in the case of a difference in cognitions, as in the example of visual and tactile perceptions directed toward the same object—that is extremely weak; for from visual perception one can employ the expression "the cloth is white," and from tactile perception "the cloth is soft"; thus, even in that case, there is a distinct linguistic usage.

Furthermore, the distinction between different types of linguistic usage (*vilakṣaṇavyavahāra*) is also weakly established on the basis of the determination of distinct objects; for the two distinct usages, "the absence of the jar does not exist" and "the jar does not exist," are non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*), as they are both based solely on the determination of a mere absence (*abhāvamātra*).

If it is argued that even in those cases there is no distinction because the object of usage is indeed one and the same, then, since the usages "the ground exists" and "the jar does not exist" would likewise be identical, their difference could not be maintained.

[Objection: Surely, when there is a desire to know the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of this [non-existence], there is a distinction from the cognition of that alone; and since the cause of a distinct linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) arises only from a distinct determination (*pariccheda*), it follows that one must admit a distinct cognition of absence.
[Reply: Not so. The desire to know is not itself the cause of linguistic usage; rather, it is specifically the cognition of that alone which is the cause of linguistic usage.
Some [such cognitions] follow immediately after the desire to know the counter-correlate, while others do not.
And those specific features which occur immediately after the desire to know the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) are the causes of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
Furthermore, the desire to know the counter-positive is included here as part of the defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), not as the actual cause of usage.

For even according to your own view, the desire to know the counter-positive is not the cause of the cognition of absence; rather, it is merely a defining characteristic with respect to the "mere-cognition" (*mātrabuddhi*) which is the cause of that [cognition of absence], since it has been stated that the apprehension of the existence of the thing itself and the recollection of the counter-positive are the causes.

As for what was said—that "even when the beloved is known, further desire to know does not arise; therefore, there is deviation even in the case of a secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa)"—that applies equally to the opponent as well.
Nevertheless, it is replied:

it is not merely the desire to know the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) that constitutes the secondary characteristic; rather, it must be specified as the desire to know the counter-correlate when that correlate is being cognized elsewhere. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.

Now, what is the cause of your [opponents'] cognition of "mere that" (*tanmātra*)? Nor can a single, fixed cause be asserted; for in some cases there is the blow of a mallet, in some a divided pot, in some a series of shards, in some the exclusion by the means of knowledge of non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), in some the reduction of parts to powder during the *Atirātra* sacrifices, and in some the remaining in another location. Therefore, because the causes are not fixed, the cognition of "mere that" is one and the same. In the view of those who maintain non-existence (*asat*), however, non-existence itself is the cause of the cognition of non-existence.

It is not so; for even in your own view, there is antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) in one place, destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) in another, and mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) elsewhere—thus, the restriction of the causes for the cognition of non-existence is exactly the same [for both of us].

Now, if you argue that although non-existence is established simply as that which has a jar as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), a distinction between causes is justified by postulating internal subdivisions, then let us also postulate internal subdivisions for us, even though [non-existence] is a single entity in the form of the cognition of the jar and its mere absence.

Now, if there is no distinction of genus, then since non-existences (*abhāva*) themselves are the causes and are opposed to existence (*bhāva*), they would possess only oneness; in that case, it would be impossible to establish multiple non-existences through their opposition to existence by means of their oneness. Furthermore, regarding the "non-perception of the perceptible" (*yogyānupalabdhi*) which is intended as the cause: is its causality due to its being desired [as such], or due to its being known? It cannot be due to its being known, because since that [non-perception] is itself a non-existence, it would entail the necessity of apprehending another non-perception, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Nor is it the case that sentient beings possess the nature of being a cause, because even in their absence, there is the observation of the cognition of non-existence.

Furthermore, even while Devadatta is being perceived, one observes, "Previously, this [object] did not exist here"; thus, the objection regarding the non-perception of the non-perception [of the cause] is refuted by perception itself.

Now, [it may be argued that] the refutation is based merely on the non-perception of what is perceptible, due to the fact that [the object] was previously perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It is not [the case that non-existence is known] merely through non-apprehension; therefore, since non-apprehension is possible even when that [object] exists, it cannot be the knowledge of its absence. This is not so, because we observe the knowledge of absence even in the absence of such [non-apprehension]. For instance, one who has seen Devadatta at midday might think in the evening, "This very person was not here this morning. By that evening cognition, the apprehension of his memory is excluded by the recollection of his being at midday.
Furthermore, by the very act of perceiving him in the evening, his apprehension [at midday] is likewise excluded.

Therefore, because mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it cannot serve as a logical reason (*hetu*) for existence. Now, if it is argued that apprehension sublates the non-apprehension belonging to that same time, but not the morning non-apprehension, and thus non-existence is grasped in the form "it did not exist before because it was not apprehended in the morning"— in that case, since non-apprehension of the very nature of an entity is one and the same insofar as it is the absence of apprehension, the mere non-apprehension perishes once apprehension has occurred.

Even for those existing in the morning, destruction occurs precisely from the perception of the morning [objects]. Therefore, antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva), which persists as long as the moment of perception lasts, perishes through that very perception.

Otherwise, even in the case of destruction by a blow of a mallet, the pot would be considered destroyed only at the time of the blow; it could not be said to have been destroyed in the preceding moments either, yet this is not observed to be the case.

[Objection: Even if the non-apprehension [of an object] results from the removal of the apprehension [of its absence], nevertheless, since the morning apprehension itself is not apprehended, it remains unapprehended; therefore, let there be the grasping of its non-existence. [Reply: It is not so.
Because that apprehension is eternally void (*tuccha*), even a non-apprehension that would be incompatible with it does not exist.
To explain: it is not perceived in the morning, nor before, nor after; thus, it lacks the very nature of being an apprehension.
Therefore, since that which is unperceived lacks existence, its status as a cause is also utterly discarded.
Thus, it is established that there is no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence" (abhāva). (Praviv., pp. 67–69)
The *ṣoḍaśin* is taken in all *atirātra* sacrifices.
Regarding the *dvirātra* sacrifice of the Aṅgirases, it is heard in scripture: "On the previous day, the *ārbhavānasa* is the *sāman*; on the subsequent day, there is the *ṣoḍaśin*.

In this regard, when considering whether this is an injunction for the *ṣoḍaśin* or an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyāna*) of it from the morning [service], since the *ṣoḍaśin* is already obtained through the general rule (*codaka*), its absence [from the morning service] is established; thus, by the statement "the *ṣoḍaśin* is taken on the subsequent day of the *dvirātra*," the *ṣoḍaśin* is taken in all *atirātras*.

Therefore, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that this is an injunction for something not otherwise obtained. Alternatively, since this optional drawing of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup at the archetypal *atirātra* sacrifice is already obtained through its optionality in all *atirātra*s, it would be restricted by the rule: "It is drawn on the second day of a two-night [sacrifice].

Once that restriction is made, because of its absence in other *atirātra*s—and because it is stated that "the *ṣoḍaśī* is [drawn] on the latter day" specifically regarding the two-night sacrifice of the Aṅgirases—it becomes mandatory in that context.

Thus is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). Alternatively, there is a connection because it is prescribed as an independent injunction (*anārabhya-vidhāna*). The word "or" (*vā*) serves to set aside the prima facie view.

In all *dvirātra* sacrifices, there would be the application of the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* on the subsequent day, because the statement "on the subsequent day of the *dvirātra*, it is taken" serves the purpose of a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*).

The statement "the *vaivānasa* is the *sāman* on the previous day, and the *ṣoḍaśin* on the subsequent day" is an injunction for the purpose of restriction. This is an application (*upasaṃhāra*) made with respect to what was already established by the general rule (*anārabhyavidhi*), "on the subsequent day of the *dvirātra*, it is taken."
That which is taken on the second day of a *dvirātra* sacrifice is taken on the second day of the *dvirātra* of the Aṅgirases, and not elsewhere.

Alternatively, in all *dvirātra* sacrifices, the *sāman* is connected with the *ṣoḍaśin* on the second day; for there is a general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) stating, "It is taken on the second day of the *dvirātra*."
The statement "the Ṣoḍaśin is on the subsequent day" is not an injunction for the Ṣoḍaśin itself.

What then? It is the Vairāja Sāman that is enjoined by the rule "on the previous day," while it is stated that "the Ṣoḍaśin is on the subsequent day" because [the Ṣoḍaśin] is already established by means of an unattached injunction (anārabhyavidhāna).
Therefore, this is a reference to the Ṣoḍaśin as something already established.
Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Here, each preceding explanation is according to the opinion of the Vṛttikāra, while each succeeding one is according to the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra.
(Ke.)
*Abhikramaṇa*,
the basis for *abhikramaṇa*,

refers to moving toward the Āhavanīya fire from its vicinity at the time of the *prayāja* offerings; in reality, however, *abhikramaṇa* is a slight shifting toward the Āhavanīya at each successive *prayāja* offering.
(Ke. VI. 3.1.10. Stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) is to be applied only to the *prayāja* offerings, not to the entire context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). Bhāṣya on VI.
The Section on Stepping Forward (*abhikramaṇādhikaraṇa*).
The *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) finds its place only within the *prayāja* offerings of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
However, if it were a quality of the agent, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because it could not be inherent in the action.
The Commentary states: "In the *prayāja* injunction of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, it is heard: 'One performs the oblation while stepping forward for the sake of victory.'"
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) to be inserted only within the *prayāja* offerings, or rather throughout the entire context?

What, then, is the prima facie position? We argue that if the stepping forward were a subordinate element of the agent, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because one action cannot be connected with another action;
for the act of stepping forward is formless (*amūrta*).
That ritual act is not able to accomplish the oblation;
therefore, it attains syntactical unity with it.
Consequently, it is included within the entire context.
"Because there is no distinction in the connection and because there is no distinction in the context" (3.1.18).
Now, it might be argued that for this very reason, [the rule] should not be applied elsewhere either. To this, it is said:
Elsewhere, it is connected with persons. But is it not the case that even in the *prayāja* offerings, it is connected with persons?
This is not so.
For by this very word, "he offers" (*juhoti*), it is possible to enjoin the human effort, but not the connection between the person and the stepping forward.
But is it not the case that elsewhere too there is an injunction of the connection between the person and the stepping forward?
This is not a fault.
Otherwise, since its non-existence is established by its not being mentioned in the context (*prakaraṇa*), the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) will declare its necessity;
therefore, the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) finds its place in the entire context.
Or rather—thus have the purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), substances (*dravya*), and qualities (*guṇa*) been examined.
Now, that action which, while being heard as related to another action, acquires by implication the status of a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), is here examined.

In this regard, concerning the term *abhikramaṇam* (stepping forward), because the suffix *ṇamul* indicates repetition (*vīpsā*) and so forth, when the expectation arises—"having stepped forward repeatedly, what does one perform?"—the subsequent verb *juhoti* (he offers) is seen to take up the previously mentioned *prayāja* offerings. Therefore, is the stepping forward connected with that [verb] alone, or with the entire context (*prakṛta*)?

And since a doubt has arisen upon hearing [the text], this section is commenced again with this specific distinction— namely, for the purpose of setting aside and resolving that doubt— just like the *aruṇā* section (PMS 3.1.12–16), because the substance is immaterial and because the sentence establishes its own connection [with the action].

In that case, even a substance which stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is not restricted, because its connection with the action to be accomplished is established through logical necessity (*upapatti*).

Here, however, it is that very [substance] which possesses the status of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Furthermore, the quality (*guṇa*) required as a delimiting factor is one whose mode of connection with the action is already known.
But here there is no separate performance;
furthermore, while in that case there are various distinct substances for different actions, here, however, in all the rites, that same Adhvaryu priest is the performer—thus there is no redundancy.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That it is for the sake of all [the rites].
Why? Because it is not perceived that an action can be accomplished by another action, owing to its immaterial nature;
therefore, setting aside the connection with the *juhuyāt* (he should sacrifice), [the result] is enjoined.
It cannot be said that one performs the oblation while stepping forward;

therefore, it is not connected with the *prayāja* offerings. Consequently, as in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the locus of the stepping forward, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

"Is it not the case that by this very reason—namely, the commentary stating, 'therefore there is no application elsewhere' (p. 730)—the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* itself is [already] established? The meaning is that the objection regarding the purpose of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (p. 685, ll. 4–5)—namely, 'Now, if it is not connected with the word "red" (*aruṇā*), but is instead connected within that same sentence with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), then there will be no split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*)'—is precisely what has been set forth here."

And the rebuttal is this: because [the agent] is subordinate to the action denoted by the verb, the act of stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) would necessarily result in a connection with the *homa* offering.
There is no connection of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth with the agent as grasped by the root *hu* (to sacrifice).
However, in other cases, there will be no contradiction in the connection of the agent—who is grasped by the context (*prakaraṇa*)—with the primary action.
"But there would be syntactic unity because of mutual expectancy, for it is not identical with the preceding.
The Bhāṣya says: "It is not as was stated—that the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is to be inserted into the context; rather, it must belong to the *prayāja* offerings themselves.
Why? Because it has syntactic unity with them."
Since this sentence is expectant of a preceding word and remains incomplete, it finds its conclusion in the statement "he offers the *abhikramaṇa*.
And because a direct syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), the *abhikramaṇa* is thus assigned to the *prayāja* offerings themselves.
Now, it was argued that the *abhikramaṇa*, being immaterial, is incapable of effecting the completion of the oblation.
It is said:
[The word "approaching"] being connected with the agent, even though it is not directly denotative of the object, will be able to bring about its accomplishment.
How? By means of the approach, the agent reaches the Āhavanīya fire.
Both are means for the oblation: one may offer with the hand from a distance according to one's intention, or one may sit down at the place of stepping forward;
[this is] the section on stepping forward.
By means of approaching [the fire].
Therefore, it is understood that approaching assists the oblation;
hence, its placement is within the *prayāja* offerings themselves.

Or rather—in any case, the word *abhikramaṇam* (stepping forward) does not become independent of further action (because the suffix *ṇamul* is prescribed under the rule governing verbal root connection). For this [word] does not state how it should be connected with a substance.

Therefore, because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the verb *juhoti* (he offers) which introduces the context of the *prayāja* offerings under discussion, its purposefulness (*tādarthya*) is understood.
And it is capable of assisting that [action] by means of proximity to the agent;
furthermore, proximity to the *āhavanīya* fire is required for the two *prayāja* offerings.
Or rather, just as in the case of "redness" (*aruṇatva*), there is a connection with the substance by virtue of the sense of the matter itself.

Thus, even though the agent (*kartṛ*) is subordinate (*upasarjana*), there is no fault whatsoever. And in this way, it is also established that even the object (*karman*), by way of being a benefit (*upakāra*), is something to be accomplished through action (*karmasādhya*). (This has been explained following the *Bhāṣya*. Now, he speaks according to his own view.)
But when, because of its excessive length, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is formulated by breaking the word *abhikramaṇam* alone, such that it is not [to be recited] at all;

How, then, is it so? Because the injunction of *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is made through the mention of the word "juhoti" (he offers) as it occurs throughout the entire context (*mahāprakaraṇa*), and because there is no intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) [to override it], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) relies on the application of the great context. In that case, regarding the stepping forward as a subordinate quality of the agent (*kartṛguṇa*), since it does not coexist with the action of the *prayājas* (fore-offerings) brought to mind by the intermediate context, there would be a "split of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*) consisting merely in the absence of syntactic unity with that context. Having stated this, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is declared by means of the principle "but [it is] expectant" (*sākāṅkṣaṃ tu*), whereby the intermediate context itself—through its state of expectancy for the sentence containing the injunction of the *prayājas*—is established as being in syntactic unity with it.
As for the statement, "For from this, by the preceding," that is intended to show that the sentence is not yet complete.

What, then, is the meaning? "From this" refers to the intermediate section (avāntaraprakaraṇa), and "by the preceding" means by the injunction regarding the nature of the *prayāja* offerings themselves. [This is] because there is another subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of the *prayājas* subsequent to the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*).
Therefore, the procedure for the *prayāja* offerings will be established as residing within that context.

Because, since the performance of the *prayāja* rites would be impossible due to the contradiction arising from the [unqualified] approach (*abhikramaṇa*), there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) and the sentence concerning the *prayājas* would lose its propriety. [Objection:

Since the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*) concerns the specific details once it has been established that the [subordinate] status of the *prayājas* is reached because their connection with the verbal action is untenable due to the resulting meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), the immediate sequence of connection (*anantara-saṃgati*) is clear.

Page 1091. [Vi]: "He offers with the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward)"—is this connected with the entire [sacrificial act] by the agent, or only with the *prayāja* offerings? It would apply to the whole performed by the agent.
Because both the *prayāja* offerings and the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) are actions, they lack a mutual relationship;
thus, even these two are not co-present.
If it is argued that there is no fault because of its connection with the agent, then this [connection] would be equally applicable [elsewhere].
Consequently, due to its proximity to the *prayāja* offerings, its conjunction must occur right there.

This is according to the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra. Alternatively, according to the opinion of the Vārttikakāra: "Or rather, like the *bali* offering, that [krama] exists within the context (*prakaraṇa*) due to proximity;
it would belong to the *darśa* and other sacrifices studied within the *prakriyā* of the *krama* because of its connection with them."
There is a sub-context beginning from "He offers the *samidh*s";
because it is read within that [context], its status as a subsidiary to the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) is established through that [sub-context].
Thus [says] the Bhāṭṭa: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the injunction "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikrāmaṃ juhoti*) is heard near the *prayāja* offerings.

Since *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is incorporeal, it cannot otherwise be connected to the *prayāja* offerings denoted by the verb *juhoti*. Furthermore, as in the case of the quality of redness (*āruṇya*), because no substance in the form of an agent is mentioned here, there is no possibility of connection even through that medium. Therefore, being separated from its immediate context, it becomes an auxiliary to the oblations of the *havir* materials belonging to the *prayāja* offerings within the *prakaraṇa*, by means of the function of securing the presence of the agent and the *āhavanīya* fire.

This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the author of the *Bhāṣya* established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *prayāja* oblations; for even though [the word "having sacrificed"] is not explicitly mentioned (*anupātta*), its existence is understood through the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-gamya*), and by means of that very [suffix], its syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the root *hu* (to sacrifice) is logically possible.

However, the author of the *Vārttika* explained it otherwise: because this form ending in the suffix *-ṇamul* lacks the necessary expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) for a connection with *juhoti* due to its relation to priority in time (*pūrvakālatā*) and so forth; and because there is no evidence that the root *hu* refers exclusively to the *prayāja* oblations; and because the status of being a *prayāja* has already been settled by the section concerning the eight [syllables] (*aṣṭaṇādhikaraṇa*).

Even if there were a connection with the *vākyīya-homa* (the oblation mentioned in the specific sentence), there is no evidence for such a restriction; therefore, just as in the case of "on the altar, over the oblation," this [rule] applies as an auxiliary to all oblations within the context (*prakaraṇa*). This is because a connection based on a specific sentence (*vākya*) cannot justify the function of a subordinate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*), which serves to restrict the scope of the primary context. For if, in such a connection, the text had simply said "he steps forward" (*abhikrāmati*), then it might indeed be an auxiliary to the *prayāja* offerings within that subordinate context.
In reality, however, there is no such thing as a "context" characterized by the *itikartavyatā* (procedure) and so forth among the auxiliaries themselves, because they lack a fruit of their own.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the *prayāja* offerings and the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) would become subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the *anuyāja* offerings.

Furthermore, since the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) postulated for the purpose of establishing a connection with the subsidiary parts mentioned in the text would grasp only those [subsidiaries], it would be illogical for it to grasp the *abhikramaṇa*.

This being the position reached, we reply: because expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is established even in the case of the subsidiary productions (*aṅga-bhāvanā*)—which are themselves productive of the primary result—through their connection with the [primary] production (*bhāvanā*), this same [expectancy] belongs to the subsidiaries as well.
That [subordinate element] is obstructed by the superior strength residing in the primary [element], due to its proximity and syntactical connection.
Therefore, there is no contingency of mutual subsidiarity (*parasparāṅgatva*).

At that time, its cessation occurs either through extended application (*atideśa*), or through the fulfillment of requirements by implication (*ākṣepalya*), or by means of common elements such as sipping water (*ācamana*) and so forth.

However, where there is a connection with subsidiary elements (aṅga) based on explicit scriptural statement (vācanika), the fulfillment of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) occurs through the initial [statement], and the cessation of that expectancy occurs through the final one. But it is not the case—as in the instance of the *maṇi* and other such items—that each individual scripturally stated subsidiary acts as an excitant (*uttejaka*), because that would involve the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) regarding the requirement of the absence of all such factors, and because, unlike those cases, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) here.

Therefore, when there is a connection with subsidiary elements based on explicit scriptural statement, the relationship of being a subsidiary to a subsidiary (*aṅgāṅgatva*) belongs to those [subsidiaries] mentioned in the text by virtue of the stronger intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).

In the present case, however, since *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) is enjoined as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *homa* (oblation), and because there is the risk of its injunction being purposeless (*ānarthakya*) with respect to the essential nature of the *homa*, one must resort to the status of a "subordinate context" (*avāntarādhikāra*) consisting of a textual connection with a subsidiary element (*vācanikāṅga-saṃbandha*), which serves to indicate that the intention is to characterize [the stepping] as a means to the *apūrva*.
It is not, however, a "principal context" (*pradhānādhikāra*) or a "context of both subsidiary and principal" (*aṅgapradhānādhikāra*), as is the case with the word "on the altar" (*vedyām*).

And this subordinate context exists here, because after beginning with "He pours clarified butter into the *juhū* ladle," *abhikramaṇa* is enjoined in the middle, and subsequently we hear: "He sprinkles the sacrificial offerings with the remnants of the *prayāja*."
Therefore, the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) is indeed an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *prayāja* offerings.

Nor can it be argued that because there is no actual pouring (*homa*) in the *prayājas*, the stepping forward cannot be an auxiliary; for according to the usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*) accompanied by the ritual throwing (*prakṣepa*) is the very meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). Consequently, since the *prayāja* is heard [in the injunction] as a mere sacrifice (*yajati-mātra*), it is logical that the pouring (*homa*) is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*).
Maṇḍana [states]: "The stepping forward is an auxiliary of the *prayājas*."

9. Śaṅkara: "The stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *prayāja* offerings. In the section concerning the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇādhikaraṇa*), a specific introduction to the auxiliaries was stated (Su. p. 1072). Even though it is connected with words denoting the *prayāja* and other such auxiliaries, it is established in the section on the stepping forward that the stepping forward and so forth are auxiliaries of the *prayāja* within the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*), because they are enjoined following the persistence of an emergent expectancy (*udbhūtākāṅkṣā*) even when not explicitly connected to those [auxiliaries]."
Ku. 3.2.12: 29. Intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) consists precisely in the extraction [of a portion] by means of a doubt;
and that does not exist at all in the case of the primary [action] (*prakṛti*).
However, regarding the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*), which are auxiliary members of the primary action, it was stated in the section concerning the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*).

Bāla, p. 11: Furthermore, when an action already established by another sentence can be characterized by yet another sentence, it is not possible to reject the context (*prakaraṇa*) on the grounds that the injunction would fail to be fulfilled—since even that action obtains its form from another sentence and thus the injunction is logically sustained. With the intention of avoiding such a connection with the injunction, one cannot dismiss the context;

for instance, in the case of "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikramaṃ juhoti*), the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) is remote, and it must be stated that it does not belong to that [context] merely because of its recitation within it.
And that [position] is untenable because it will be refuted in the section concerning the stepping forward (*abhikramaṇādhikaraṇa*). (Su. p.

737) In the section concerning the stepping forward, it will be demonstrated that even for the *prayāja* offerings recited in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there exists a subordinate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). (p.

764) In the statement "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikraman juhoti*), the stepping forward possesses the status of being a subsidiary element of the *prayāja* oblations, as expressed by the word "offers" (*juhoti*).
Stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*) is enjoined as a subordinate element (*anuvāda*) to the oblation (*homānuvādena*).

Śābarabhāṣya 3.1.10: "He offers while stepping forward" (*abhikramaṃ juhoti*)—this is the *ṇamul* suffix used as an injunctive scriptural statement (*viniyoga-kratṛ śruti*) according to the view of Someśvara (Bālakrīḍā, p. 48).
"He offers while stepping forward" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) by means of the root *hu* (to offer) of the *prayāja* and other rites enjoined by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
Thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), Bhāṣya 3.4.18 states:
"Even though the word 'he offers with a step forward' (*abhikramaṃ juhoti*) is a general term, it refers specifically to the *prayāja* offerings because of its restrictive scope.
Vārttika 3.1.10.21, p. 870, notes: "The sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) and the *anvāhārya* rice are performed for one who is *svādin* (one who eats well)."
For it is by means of the *svādu* (sweet/savor) that one assists in the purchase (*parikraya*).
Bhāṣya 10.3.10.38. The pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*) is a characteristic of the portioning (*avadāna*).
"He spreads [the butter] underneath, having taken two portions of the oblation, he pours [butter] over [them], and offers the fourfold portion."
10.8.12.30–31: The sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) should not be performed as a subsidiary act for that which is not a sacrifice, such as the garment (*vāsas*) or the calf (*vatso*).
10.3.10.38: Both the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) should not be performed in the *kṛṣṇala* oblation.

[Reason: The under-spreading is performed so that the pure, fine flour of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) may not become mixed; the sprinkling is performed so that the entire oblation (*havis*), being pure and unadulterated, may fall [into the fire] exactly as it was.
But there is no connection with the *kṛṣṇala* [gold grain].
(10.2.12) Furthermore, in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) must indeed be performed on the *ekakapāla* cakes among the *tryambaka* offerings.
As for the Mīmāṃsā discussion regarding whether they "should be sprinkled" or "should not be sprinkled," it concerns an equal purpose.
Regarding the *tryambaka-homa*: because it is not previously established (*apūrva*), the act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) is enjoined as something new. [Vi.
10.8.18] The sprinkling consists of spreading clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *juhū* ladle, placing the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) upon it, and again placing clarified butter on top of that.
This sprinkling is the third ritual action. [Vi. 10.8.12]
The sprinkling (abhighāraṇa) is performed solely with the intention of making an offering.

Bhāṣya 5.4.2.3: The sprinkling with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings must first be performed for the *āgneya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and thereafter for the *sāṃnāyya* (curdled milk), because the order of principal items (*mukhyakrama*) is stronger than the order of procedure (*pravṛttikrama*).
5.4.2–4: There is no sprinkling with the remnant of the *prayāja* for the animals dedicated to Prajāpati in the *vājapeya* sacrifice.

4|1|4|13–30. The sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) with the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings is both a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificial oblations (*havis*) and a disposal (*pratipatti*). It is thus a refinement of both what has been used and what is about to be used. [Question: Even though there is a smear of both the sprinkling and the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*), how is the four-fold portion (*caturavatta*) accomplished for the *havirājya* (clarified butter as oblation) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices? [Answer: Bhāṣya 10|8|133–34 states that because of the separation in the act of sprinkling, there should be a different vessel, as in the case of the *anuyāja* offerings.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, both the seasonal animals (*ṛtupaśu*) and the animals dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyapaśu*) are commenced together at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). Following the tenth fore-offering (*daśamaprayāja*), the animals dedicated to Prajāpati are set aside; then, after pausing until the end of the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite, they are resumed at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*) at the time of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsi-sāman* and the ritual of immolation (*ālambha*) and so forth is performed. However, the subsidiary oblations (*aṅgahoma*) are performed after all the Soma offerings have been completed. There is another view, according to which the performance of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati—including up to the offering of their omenta (*vapāhoma*)—is carried out simultaneously with the seasonal animals.
This discussion is based on the first position.

First, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) of the seasonal animal sacrifices (*ṛtupaśuyāga*) was performed with the remnant of the animal-offering oblations (*paśuprayāja*).

Now, if the sprinkling of the Prājāpatya animal sacrifices were to be performed at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina*), then the remnant of the morning oblations would have to be retained; however, since the *juhū* ladle is occupied elsewhere, it would be impossible to retain the oblation-remnant there, and thus another vessel would have to be taken.

In this regard, there arises the inquiry: "Should the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) with the *prayāja* remnant be performed for the *prājāpatya* victims, or not? And if it is to be performed, should a separate vessel be prepared for the purpose of holding that *prayāja* remnant? Regarding this, the author states the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) view: If the *prājāpatya* animals are to be sprinkled with the *prayāja* remnant, then for the sake of holding that *prayāja* remnant—which serves as the means for the sprinkling—there must be a distinct vessel. This is because the *juhū* ladle is already occupied at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) for the purpose of the *ājyabhāga* offerings and so forth; without a second vessel, it would be impossible to hold the *prayāja* remnant. Therefore, a separate vessel should be taken.

It is like the *anuyājas*. In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, the *anuyājas* are performed using the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter). Just as there, for the purpose of holding the *pṛṣadājya* used in the *anuyājas*, a *pṛṣadājya-dhānī* (a vessel for spotted butter) is set apart from the *ājya-dhānī* (the vessel for clarified butter), so it is here. It is like the *anuyājas* in the *anuyājas*.
In the case of *abhicāraṇa* (sprinkling),
there is a removal [of the substance] because it is a single portion;
it is inferred that this remnant is a single portion of the clarified butter (*ājya*) intended for the *prayāja* offerings which has been employed.
And that [act of holding] has fulfilled its purpose in the case of the Ṛtu cups and the animal-sacrifice cups;
likewise, since there is no subsequent [use] as a remnant (śeṣa), for whose sake would another vessel be required for the purpose of holding? Therefore, a distinction of vessels need not be made.
This is also because the joint performance [of the acts] is based on a logical reason.
He states another reason for the aforementioned superiority.
The word "and" (ca) serves to combine the reason consisting of being a cause for simultaneous application with the previously mentioned reason of being a single part.
Furthermore, there is unworthiness for this reason as well.

Because the simultaneous performance (*sahaprayoga*)—the joint execution of the seasonal animal sacrifices (*ṛtupaśu*) and the animal sacrifices dedicated to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyapaśu*)—is the cause for the absence of the sprinkling of clarified butter (*abhicāraṇa*). This is shown by the statement in the *Vātapeya* sacrifice regarding the animal dedicated to Prajāpati: "The morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) is indeed a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); since the animals are seized at the morning pressing, they seize them at the ford so that they may have their place of origin (*sayoni*), and also for the sake of the non-overpowering of the omenta (*vapā*).
Therefore, since there is no requirement for a remnant (*śeṣa*), what is the purpose of the vessel?
And because of the perception of non-existence.
He states another reason for that very point:
"These omenta are indeed 'with-a-side' (savyā) at this time, when they have not been anointed with ghee."

What is that designation by virtue of which one says that "touching" (*abhimarśana*) is a quality? Therefore, wherever its performance benefits either the *paurṇamāsī* or the *amāvāsyā*, it should be performed there.
Whatever is touched—whether directly or through the primary sacrifice—at the *paurṇamāsī* or the *amāvāsyā*, its performance there benefits those two.

Therefore, [the sprinkling] must be performed for both the primary oblations and the subsidiary oblations. Or rather—the second case ending indicates that the touching is understood as being subordinate; therefore, it serves all purposes.
Since its subordinate status is established, the specific nature of that [subordination] is now to be considered.
Furthermore, in accordance with the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), only the principal oblation (*havir-mātra*) is understood through the sense of the accusative case.
Therefore, this alone is the logical conclusion (*upapatti*).
