Therefore, it must be stated as follows: since the time, the action, and their combination are not to be touched in the injunction "one should touch the full moon," the term "paurṇamāsī" (full moon) must be used in a figurative sense.

In that regard, although it is maintained that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is secondary because the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is primary, nevertheless, even by that much, since the understanding arises that it serves as a qualifier for that which is to be touched (*abhimṛṣṭavya*), and since a doubt regarding the scope of the entire [term] such as *lava* and so forth might arise, the specific distinction must be obtained from another source. Thus, because there is an expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), and for the sake of resolving the doubt, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is construed in its primary sense alone—that is, in the sense of the nominal stem—and specifically in the locative sense (*saptamy-artha*), as in "on the full moon day" (*paurṇamāsyām*).
And that alone is what is required here, because the specific object to be touched—namely, the sacrificial offering (*havis*) and so forth—is determined by the injunction as being proximate.

Therefore, this scriptural statement is intended solely for the purpose of defining [the act] either by way of time or by way of the performance; thus, it refers to the touching of every sacrificial offering.

In the case of the sentence, "Having pressed and having offered, they shall eat," the completion of the sentence (*vākya-parisamāpti*) occurs with respect to the aggregate [of actions].

Bhāṣya 3.6.12, p. 697. However, when the action is primary, the completion of the sentence occurs with respect to the aggregate of the objects qualified by that action, as in: "The hundred-fine for the Gargas, the oblation, and the overcoming of the enemy."
Or: The consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the sacrificer is part of the command for the *rājasūya*. Vi. 5.2.60.
The consecration occurs during the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) in the Soma sacrifice known as the *rājasūya-abhiṣecanīya*, following the *māhendra-stotra*.
4.4.2. Because it is the consecration, the performance of the gambling (*videvana*) and other rites takes place prior to it in the *rājasūya*.

Bhāṣya 5.2.10.21: Since the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) is displaced [from its original position] to the *Abhiṣecanīya* rite within the Rājasūya, the gambling (*videvana*) and other such elements are also displaced earlier. Vārttika 2.3.13, p. 582: The *abhiṣecanīya* is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.

4.4.1: There are thirty-two *pavamāna* chants for the *abhiṣecanīya*; among them, nine are *rājasāman*s, eleven are *rājasāman*s, and they call the *balaughaśravas*, the *vaśiṣṭhasya janitri*, and the *traiśoka* the *sākaṃpravedana*s.
Regarding the pure and impure, and the instruction on the flow [of the ritual], [it is argued]:

although the acts such as gambling (videvana) and others are recited in proximity to the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice, by virtue of the power of the context (prakaraṇa), they are subsidiary to the entire Rājasūya,
and not subsidiary to the Abhiṣecanīya alone.
The location for the performance is that of the *abhiṣecanīya*. (Vi.

3.1.10) Regarding the *abhiṣecanīya*, the simultaneity of the agreement for the purchase of the Soma with the agreement for the purchase of the Soma for the *daśapeya* sacrifice is stated as: "He purchases both Somas together.
The distinction is that the *abhiṣecanīya*, which is to be performed with the *saṃsapa* [chant], is performed first, whereas the *daśapeya* follows later according to its name.
1|1|2|14: At the *abhiṣecanīya* [sacrifice], during the *māhendra-stotra*, the *ābhra* [offering] intended for presentation must be performed by means of anticipation (*apakarṣa*).
3|1|10: "He gives ten thousand cows at the *abhiṣecanīya*.
Bhāṣya 1|1|4|17: The *abhiṣecanīya* and the *daśapeya* are part of the *rājasūya*.
In that context, on the tenth day of the Abhiṣecanīya sacrifice, the Daśapeya is completed. (ŚB 5.1.2.14–16). These two Soma sacrifices occur within a single season.
The purchase of the Soma for both occurs at one and the same time, as determined by the verbal formula.
But those performed for a specific purpose occur at different times:
first the *Abhiṣecanīya*, then the *Daśapeya*; there is no other sequence of birth.
57. The ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the *abhiṣecanīya* and the *daśapeya* sacrifices is distinct.
In the *daśapeya*, the postponement [of the purchase] is counteracted by the purchase; therefore, for those [rites] prior to it, there should be a common *tantra*.
Commentary: In the *rājasūya*, the *abhiṣecanīya* and the *daśapeya* are both one-day (*ekāha*) sacrifices.
Regarding these two, it is considered whether their performance is by way of a single *tantra* or separately.
What is established? That the ritual procedure (*tantra*) for these two is common.
Why? Because the purchase of the *daśapeya* is drawn forward [in time], according to the text: "One purchases the Soma together for both the *abhiṣecanīya* and the *daśapeya*.
Since the *abhiṣecanīya* occurs at an earlier time, the purchase of the *daśapeya* is drawn forward to that time of purchase.

When that [rite] is being withdrawn, it withdraws the constituent elements (*padārtha*) occurring prior to it, according to the rule: "The withdrawal should extend from that point onward until the end of what was heard" (Pāṇini 5.1.3.12.24).
Therefore, the commencement (*prakrama*) is common (*tantra*) to those two one-day rites (*ekāha*).
Since they have commenced with a common procedure, their performance must likewise conclude with a common conclusion (*tantra*).
Therefore, they belong to the same system.
The statement regarding "samāna" (the common) is likewise.

The Bhāṣya states: "This sacrifice is indeed the same, namely the Daśapeya and the Abhiṣecanīya. Because the *tantra* (the common ritual framework) is identical, the two sacrifices are identical; however, they are distinct by virtue of their individual natures (*ātman*). Alternatively, there is no postponement because it is for the sake of the purpose; rather, their simultaneity is enjoined.
The Commentary (Bhāṣya): Or rather, there is no withdrawal of the purchase. Why? Because it is for the sake of the purpose. There are these two purchases.
One [act] is caused by the purpose, while the other is produced by the word.

That which occurs prior to the commencement of the ritual, at the time of procuring the sacrificial implements—namely, the conversation with the Soma-seller, the purchase of the Soma, and the determination of its price—that must necessarily be performed for the sake of the purpose.
Without that being done, the commencement of the ritual itself would not be appropriate.

Why? Because at the time of the season, it might happen that there is no Soma, or there might be no seller of it, or he might not give it for half the price; likewise, the season itself might not coincide.
This simultaneous occurrence is stated for his sake.
What is the reason? Because of its primary importance.
And in that very context, the purchase is virtually accomplished; the mere offering of the price constitutes the enclosure (paridhi).
Whatever else occurs there, such as "I buy you for a sixteenth part," and so forth, is merely a ritual formalization (*dharmamātra*), because the seller is dependent on another.
This being the case, the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) belonging to two different times will occur precisely according to their respective times.

And in that corroboration, the usage of the root *krī* (to buy) for the purpose of purchasing is observed in the statement: "We have bought Dhanya together with Devadatta; the agreement has been reached.
Therefore, it is a corroboration of that [purchase], and it occurs outside of the ritual (*ṛtu*).
Therefore, there is no withdrawal [of the ritual procedure].
Because of the difference in time, the distinction of the *tantra* (ritual framework) is exactly as stated,
since the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is observed in the former case.
The Commentary states: In the preceding *abhiṣecanīya* sacrifice, there is the observation of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding purificatory bath).
How so? "They indeed break this sacrifice in common when they descend for the *avabhṛtha* of the *abhiṣecanīya*.
Thus, this observation of the *avabhṛtha* would be appropriate in the preceding sacrifice only if the ritual procedure (*tantra*) proceeds separately.
Otherwise, the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) would take place at the end of the Daśapeya,
and [the same would apply] to the latter of the consecrations (dīkṣā).

The Commentary states: Furthermore, there is the observation of separate initiations for the Daśapeya sacrifice, as in the text: "In that manner, they should extend the initiations of the Abhiṣecanīya so that the Daśapeya is completed on the tenth day; he initiates immediately, and he purchases the Soma immediately.
Otherwise, the initiations of the Daśapeya would also occur within the Abhiṣecanīya itself, and in that case, this observation would not be tenable.
This is because the time is identical.
Regarding the commentary which states, "That [statement] of equal number is because it is like that," we reply:
These two Soma sacrifices occur within one season, and thereafter for two years. It is with reference to this equality of time that that statement of equal number is otherwise justified.

Therefore, there is a difference in the ritual manuals (*tantra*). In the previous case, because the possibility existed for the postponement of the immolation (*ālambha*), the entire sequence ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa* was performed every year. Here, however, since there is no commonality of ritual manual (*samānatantra*) between the *Abhiṣecanīya* and the *Daśapeya*, it is stated [that they are distinct]; this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*).

In this context (regarding what was stated as "the dialogue with the seller of Soma"), by the word "dialogue," the dialogue between the buyer and the seller— consisting of such exchanges as "I buy you for a sixteenth part" and "King Soma is worth more than that"— which is prescribed as a duty to be performed at the time of the purchase of Soma, is not intended [here],
because [it is sublated] by the Abhīvarta [chant] in the Abhiṣecanīya and Daśapeya sacrifices.

If that were the case, since the [purchase] would be excluded by that very name, it would follow that its commencement must necessarily be avoided. However, if at the time of the sacrifice (*kratu*) no Soma-seller can be found, or if even one who is found demands an excessive price, then with the thought that "the sacrifice itself will not be accomplished," just as one procures other means for the performance of the rite, the worldly determination of the price made with the seller is what is intended here. And because that [price] is fixed according to the lunar month (*cāndra*), it does not necessitate simultaneous performance. As stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "In the *Daśapeya* and the *Abhiṣecanīya*, is there a common ritual procedure (*tantra*) or a distinction?"
The system of being devoid of purchase is differentiated by the distinction of time.

Bhāṭṭa: In the Rājasūya, all the sacrifices—the *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices, and *soma* sacrifices—are of distinct ritual procedures (*bhinnatantra*). This will be explained by [the fact that] in some cases there is a difference in time, in some a lack of difference, and in others a difference in the number of preparatory rites (*akṣaṇā*).

Among these, there is a *soma* sacrifice named the Abhiṣecanīya; after that, the "offerings of the Saṃsṛps" (*saṃsṛpāṃ havīṃṣi*); and after that, again, the Daśapeya *soma* sacrifice is prescribed in the scripture.

Regarding the inquiry as to whether these two, the Abhiṣecanīya and the Daśapeya, have the same ritual procedure (*samānatantra*) or different ritual procedures (*bhinnatantra*), [it is stated]: "He buys the *soma* together for the Abhiṣecanīya..."
The distinctions between the rules of permission (*abhyanujñā*) and injunction (*vidhi*): "One should give only through repeated practice; one need not give at the [specific] time.
In this context, "one need not give" during the state of poverty constitutes a permission (*abhyanujñā*) itself, because there is only a slight fault in not giving under such circumstances.
*Bāla*, p. 33. Oṃ. The distinctions between the rules for permission (*abhyanujñā*) and injunction (*vidhi*) are to be seen in the *Vidhiviveka* and the *Bālaprabandha*.
Oṃ. There is the maxim: "The parts [constitute] the whole internally.
Just as a tree moves by means of its constituent parts moving together, so too should it be understood in the present case.
"In this *Mahābhāṣya* on *Pratyāhāra*, etc.
[refers to] Sāhasī 828: "Om! For it is a logical principle (*nyāya*) that a part is indeed included within the whole.
For example, 'when a tree moves, it moves by means of its parts. This was stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.1)."
Likewise, it is suggested by another method in the Mahābhāṣya on the Vārttika "Grammar is a definition" (*alakṣaṇaśloke vyākaraṇam*) as follows:
"For words that are applied to a whole also apply to its parts.
For example: 'the eastern Pañcālas,' 'the northern Pañcālas,' 'oil has been eaten,' 'ghee has been eaten,' and [the adjectives] 'white,' 'blue,' and 'black'."
Thus, the term *vyākaraṇa* (grammar), though applied to the whole (*samudāya*), is also applied to its parts (*avayava*).
The same applies here as well.
[Sāhasī 445]. *Oṃ*: "That which is more venerable comes first"—this is the maxim.
"alpāntaram" is a Vārttika on Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.2.34.
"Abhyarhitam" means that which is worthy of honor, venerable, or principal. That [term] should be placed first in a *dvandva* compound, as in "Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna" (*kṛṣṇārjunau*), and so forth.

By relying on the maxim that "that which is more worthy of honor comes first," the sequential relationship between the eleventh and twelfth chapters— which respectively establish the *tantra* (the common application) and the *prasaṅga* (the incidental application)— has been established.
[End of] the introduction to the twelfth chapter.

Although the *sāmidhenī* verses were mentioned previously as being to be performed, nevertheless, according to the grammatical principle that "that which is more worthy comes first" (*abhyarhitaṃ pūrvaṃ*), because the *prayāja-yājyās*—which are the causes of satisfaction—are more worthy, he prescribes those very *āghāras* first. This is the principle: "That which is more worthy comes first. Furthermore, the possibility of enjoining another quality that contradicts a quality already established by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*) will be demonstrated in the *Vaiśvadevādhikaraṇa* (1.4.11–16, 22); it is mentioned here for the purpose of adding another reason.

However, in this case, the very contingency of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*)—which is expressed by the term "instruction of a subordinate quality" (*guṇopadeśa*)—is the primary reason [for the word order], and thus it should be indicated according to the maxim "that which is more venerable comes first" (*abhyarhitaṃ pūrvaṃ*). Since there is no relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgi*) between the *ādhāra* and the *agnihotra*, the rule "that which is more venerable is placed first" (*abhyarhitaṃ pūrvaṃ nipatati*) does not apply; therefore, in the rule *ādhārāgnihotram* (Pāṇini 2.1.13), the word *ādhāra* is appropriately placed first because it begins with a vowel (*atvāccaratvena*). (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 419)

On page 788, regarding the sūtra *paśusomayoḥ* (2.1.17), there is a concern that since the word *paśu* ends in the suffix *vyat* and because the suffix *kṛt* ending in *vyat* is subject to irregularity in its placement as a prior member according to Pāṇini 3.1.26 (*alakṣaṇahetoḥ kriyāyāḥ*), it would be improper for *paśu* to be mentioned before *soma* due to *soma*'s primacy and its status as the more venerable (*abhyarhita*). Anticipating this objection, he states that in a science established on logic, even when something is not the primary object of attention, it is proper for *paśu* to be placed first because it is the more venerable of the two by virtue of being logically superior. On page 788, the *abhyātānas* are indeed oblations; they are *darvihomas*.

3.4.13. The Abhyātāna oblations are subsidiary to Vedic rites, not to worldly activities such as agriculture and the like.

At the time of throwing the *paridhi*, it must be performed with the mantras beginning with "Śrāvaya" and "Śrauṣaṭ.
Bhāṣya 1.2.10.26: *Abhyāsa* (repetition) is a restatement [of a rule] when there is no distinction [in the context].
VI. 2.4.1. Repeated mention (*punarvidhāna*).
Su. p. 820. Repetition (*abhyāsa*) is a means of proof for the differentiation of ritual acts (*karmabheda*).
Bāla. p. 8. Repetition is a means of proof for the differentiation of properties (*dharmabheda*).
Maṇi, p. 13: Repetition (*abhyāsa*) of acts such as threshing, which have a visible purpose, continues until the accomplishment of the intended result.
Bhāṣya 1.1.5.27: Repetition of threshing continues until the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*) are produced.
11.1.5.27: Repetition is stronger than even a concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*), because the latter is improper when it contradicts what has occurred many times.
*Parākrama*. 8. Repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the word *ekadhā* occurring in the section on the *agnipraigha* [is prescribed] in the *padyuṇe* [section].
Bhāṣya 1.3.129–26. Repetition (*abhyāsa*) of a desired rite (*kāmya-karman*) is performed out of a desire for the ground of its fruit.
1.1.4.20–26. Repetition (*abhyāsa*) is one of the means of chanting (*gīti*).

9|2|729: Repetition [is required] in the piling [of the fire-altar], not for all [the bricks], so that it may be accomplished; such is the meaning. 11|1|16 28: Repetition [occurs] three times in the *sāmidhenī* verses; this is a property of the first and last [verses], not a property of the *ṛc* itself.
1|1|9|33: Repetition of the grinding [of grain] continues until the completion of the ground flour.
Repetition (abhyāsa):
By repetition, however, Oṃ, the repetition of the *sāmidhenī* verses, due to its being first, should be a property of the position (*sthānadharma*).

Regarding the *sāmidhenīs* in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in scripture: "He recites the first verse three times; he recites the last verse three times."

In this regard, there arises the inquiry: is the tripling of the utterance a property of the *ṛc*—meaning that the *ṛc* "pra vo vājā," even when occurring elsewhere, must be recited three times—or is it a property of the position, meaning that whichever [verse] is first uttered, even if it is another, must be recited three times? Regarding this discussion, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):
This repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the first *sāmidhenī* verse that has been mentioned is a property of the position; it is a property of the position.
That *ṛc* which is uttered in the first position is what must be recited three times.

Because of its priority— due to the rule "he recites the first three times" which indicates that the *ṛc* is to be repeated, and because the priority is stated in reference to the *ṛc*— it follows that this is not a property of the *ṛc* itself, but rather a property of the first position. Therefore, wherever there might be only a single *sāmidhenī*, even if it is distinct from the *pravovājīyā*, that too must be recited three times.
Ke. Oṃ: Repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses would be a property of their position (*sthāna-dharma*), because of their being first.

Regarding the statement, "He recites the first three times and the last three times," since the words "first" and "last" refer to the initial and final positions due to their being uttered first, does this [repetition] not, by virtue of its greatness, refer to the specific verses characterized by those positions—namely, the *pravovājā* and *ājuhotā* verses? (Su. p. 469). Repetition of the *sāmans* occurs in the *vahiṣpavamāna* at a sacrifice with a conflicting *stoma*.
(Bhāṣya 10.5.126). Repetition occurs through the increase of position in the *tryanīkā* sacrifices of the *gavāmayana*.
10|5|2|83–87. *Oṃ*. By repetition (*abhyāsa*), however, there is the completion of the number in the case of the *sāmidhenī* verses, because that is their original nature (*prakṛti*).

Desirable (*kāmya*) variations of the *sāmidhenī* verses for the New and Full Moon sacrifices are heard in such injunctions as: "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one," and "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should recite twenty-four.

In that regard, should the number exceeding eleven be completed by the introduction (*āgama*) of additional *ṛc* verses, or by the repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the first and last verses, or by repeating as much as prescribed and then introducing the remaining six or so verses?
Such is the inquiry.
Here, the fundamental number is eleven; the first prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the completion of the number is achieved by the arrival of ten and the others.
The word "tu" (but), however, serves to refute that.
Regarding the optional *sāmidhenī* verses, the fulfillment of the required number should be achieved through the repetition of only the first and the last verses until that number is reached;
this is because they have repetition as their archetype.
The term "abhyāsaprakṛti" is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for which repetition is the archetype (*prakṛti*) in the original ritual."
Their state is that of being the natural form resulting from repetition; therefore.
In the archetype (*prakṛti*), there are indeed only eleven *sāmidhenī* verses. Therein, by repeating the first and last verses three times, the number fifteen is achieved.

That being the case, since the *sāmidhenī* verses have repetition as their archetype (*prakṛti*), the completion of the number in the twenty-one-fold and other such configurations would occur solely through the repetition of the first and last verses.

For instance, by repeating the first and last of the eleven verses three times each, there would be fifteen; by repeating them six times each, twenty-one; and by repeating the first six times and the last nine times, twenty-four, and so forth.
This is the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
If it be argued: "Oṃ, [it would apply] without distinction.

When the proponent has stated that in the optional *sāmidhenī* rituals of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, such as those involving twenty-one verses and so forth, the completion of the number must be achieved through repetition, someone might say: "Oṃ, because there is no distinction, since it would follow that there is no distinction between the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*), the completion of the number is not to be done by repetition. [The response is: "Oṃ, it should indeed be so, because it is a property (*dharma*); like the archetype, one should repeat until the number is completed."
Regarding the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he states the reply:
There should be repetition (abhyāsa), because that is its characteristic; for the modification (vikṛti) possesses the characteristics of the archetype (prakṛti).
Therefore, one should repeat it until the number is completed; that is, as many times as necessary, the repetition of the first and the last [verses] must be performed.
"As in the archetype" means that it is repeated just as it is in the archetype until the number fifteen is completed.
Or rather, "only as much as is stated," because its limit has been fixed.
With the word "or" (*vā*), he sets aside the second prima facie view and states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

As it has been stated regarding the practice of eleven verses—"He recites the first thrice and the last thrice"—once this has been said, the number fifteen is achieved through repetition; any number exceeding that must be completed by the arrival of additional verses. Having stated the limit of the repetition as "he recites the first thrice and the last thrice," it is not possible to perform the repetition more than that number of times.

Therefore, having practiced what has been stated, there is the traditional authority (āgama) for the remaining [points]. Oṃ. And because more [points] are observed, he states another argument for the established conclusion (siddhānta).

Since it is observed that in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, which has seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses, two additional *ṛc*s—"*apṛthupājāḥ*" and "*taṃ sravāḥ*"—are introduced, it is understood that elsewhere as well, the completion of an increased number is achieved by the introduction of additional *ṛc*s.
The plural "of the additional ones" (*adhikānām*) is used as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
[This concludes] the section on the repetition of the *sāmidhenī* verses (568). The section concerning repetition.
If someone should say: "It applies to ritual actions as well;

if, in the case of optional rites such as those involving twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses, the required number were to be completed by bringing in [additional verses], then there should likewise be no repetition in the *dhuri-sāman* rituals which take the form of specific *gāyatra* verses."
No, because it has been challenged. The proponent states the final position:
this is not so.
In the *dhuri* sacrificial acts, because the repetition is enjoined by the rule, "The *dhuryu* is praised repeatedly," such repetition is appropriate.

Therefore, in the optional (*kāmya*) ritual procedures for the *sāmidhenī* verses involving twenty-one and so forth, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that while it is stated, "He recites the first three times and the last three times," any number exceeding that must be completed solely by the addition (*āgama*) of further verses.

Regarding this, the constant number fifteen of the *sāmidhenīs* is prescribed for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) through the repetition of the first and last verses, according to the rule: "He recites the first three times and the last three times."
Bhāṣya 10.1.8.27: From repetition there is a distinction in mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and by that, a distinction in the ritual action (*karma*).
Vi. 2.2.2: From repetition there is a distinction among the methods of arriving at conclusions.

Saṃkarṣa 3.1.16: It is logical that repetition, characterized as a re-enactment of an injunction, possesses the power to differentiate [an action], because it is possible for the injunction not to have been previously operative; otherwise, since [the action] would be already established from another source, the status of the injunction as an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) would result.
Su. P. 820. And in the case of repetition, there is a repetition of that [act], because of the repeated performance of the ritual action.
In the Gavāmayana sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "They perform the recurring *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite.
That which is heard in the context of the Dvādaśāha—"Having completed the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite, one should eat barley or ghee"—is extended [to the Gavāmayana] by the rule of transfer (*codaka*).
In that case, during the repetition of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), there should be a repetition of the honey-consumption (*madhubhojana*) at the end of each first day (*pratipad*).
This is because the ritual action—the six-day rite itself—is performed again and again.
Furthermore, the consumption of honey is prescribed at the conclusion of the six-day rite.
Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the honey-consumption (*madhubhojana*) occurs at the end of each *pratipad* during the performance of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*).
Alternatively, it should occur at the very end, because the time has been specifically fixed:

"When the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite is completed, one should cause [the sacrificer] to eat honey or ghee. This meal prescribed for the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) is extended here by the rule of transfer (*codaka*); since the six-day rites have been performed consecutively, the act should be done only once at the final conclusion, not at the end of every individual *pratipad*.
Because the time has been fixed.
For the time for the meal has indeed been determined as "when the six-day period has concluded" (*saṃsthite ṣaḍahe*).
*Saṃsthāna* means completion.
It is the cessation of the activity pertaining to the *ṣaḍaha*.
Furthermore, one who is performing the *ṣaḍaha* again is not said to have ceased from the activity pertaining to the *ṣaḍaha*;
nor does the *ṣaḍaha* conclude merely upon the cessation of the agent.

Therefore, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that at the end of all the six-day periods performed in succession, the midday *śastra* is recited only once, not at the end of each individual day.
The word "or" (*vā*) serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). This concludes the section concerning repetition (*abhyāsādhikaraṇa*).
The principle of repetition;
the principle of the section on repetition;
through repetition, there is a distinction of ritual acts.
Furthermore, [the word] "ekastha" (occurring in one place) would serve as a qualification for the subsequent scriptural statement (*śruti*).

Or rather—the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding repetition (*abhyāsa*), presented by way of an illustrative example from the section on "Different Words" (*śabdāntara-adhikaraṇa*), is easily stated; thus, its commencement follows immediately after that. In this regard, having set aside words such as "samidh" in passages like "He offers the *samidhs*, he offers to *tanūnapāt*," etc., the question is raised concerning the word "he offers" (*yajati*), which is stated five times: does it denote a single action, or many? This is the illustrative example.
That is raised as follows:
"The word *samit* and so forth must be either a quality (*guṇa*) or a name (*nāmadheya*);
and since the distinction [of the action] arises from those two alone, what will repetition (*abhyāsa*) accomplish here?"
All six causes of differentiation exist as distinct entities;

they must be shown to have as their fruit the mere removal of one's own limited capacity. Therefore, as long as the differentiating nature of the qualities and names is not removed here, there can be no attainment of the supreme goal through practice; this must be illustrated.
And yet, that is not possible.
Why? "For no verbal root (ākhyāta) is ever employed in the Vedas in isolation;
and if any name (nāman) is employed, its two possible courses have already been explained."
For all [injunctions] such as "He takes the draught for Indra and Vāyu" are distinct from one another due to their connection with inherent qualities (*autpattika-guṇa-yoga*).

Likewise, [injunctions] such as "He offers when [the vessel] is broken" and "He offers when [the oblation] has spilled" are also distinct, because—by the principle stated in *PMS* 2.3.12 (sūtra 25), "And [an action] which has a fruit [is separate] when not in proximity to another action"—they are undertaken with respect to a specific occasion (*nimitta*). Since they are directed toward the existence of the occasion rather than toward repetition (*abhyāsa*), they do not constitute a single performance.

As for those who cite the repetition in the *Pañcaśarādīya*—namely, "having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa* for them, having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa* for them"—for them, that [repetition] possesses the capacity to extend as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) *paryagnikaraṇa*.
Furthermore, the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is not heard here, such that a distinction [of acts] might arise from its repetition; thus, this is not a valid example.
As it has been said: "That which possesses dependence is as one desires."
Therefore, that very [consciousness] is first established as the cause of both difference and non-difference.
Those nominal words whose meanings are to be adopted are, for their part, dependent upon the verb; therefore, following its lead, they await its operation.

If that [verb] is already established in the context, then the nominal word is either a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*) for that very [action], or else, if an unprecedented result (*apūrva*) has been postulated by that [verb], then the nominal word is subordinate to that. Thus, when the alternatives of difference and non-difference have been resolved, the subsequently occurring word such as *samit* remains ineffective; therefore, having set that aside, one investigates the mere verb alone.
But if this is so, does it not follow that there would be no distinction between a name (*saṃjñā*) and a collection (*gaṇa*)?

In those cases where a verbal form (*ākhyātapada*) is not operative, those two serve as differentiators; as he will illustrate with the examples: "Now this is the Jyotis" and "The whey for the Vājins."
In the case of the *vājina* [offering], no verbal form (*ākhyāta-pada*) is even heard.

Even in cases such as the *jyotiṣṭoma*, where it is possible for the verbal form to enter into the context through its operation in connecting a quality with a result, a distinction will nonetheless arise due to its prior application, as if there were a doubt.

Furthermore, even where a quality is enjoined because it cannot otherwise fit into the context despite the verbal form naturally admitting entry into the contextual action—as he will state in this very work during the discussion of the accepted position: "This connection with the deity, being enjoined," and so forth—even there, that [quality] is a differentiator.

And since that occurs when the power of differentiation has been enjoined in the verb (*ākhyāta*), that very point is first examined. In the *Bhāṣya*, the question "Is there one new potency (*apūrva*)? is an introduction to the distinction between the difference of actions based on their results. That is to say: does one action enjoin a single new potency, or do all the actions enjoin multiple new potencies?
What is established? That there is one new unseen potency (*apūrva*).
Why? "Even though the meaning of the suffix is the same, it differs according to the difference in the verbal root;
even when the verbal root is the same, by what is its difference understood?"
Moreover: "Previously, by that very word, the object was deposited in the intellect;
it does not attain a state of difference through subsequent hearing, because of recognition."

Just as the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), having been employed once, is not differentiated when uttered again because of the recognition that "it is the very same one," so too is its meaning. Furthermore, just as the direct perception produced by the mental effort (*buddhi*) regarding this very [act] cannot constitute a different verbal expression even if it is purposeless, so too a repeated scriptural mention (*punaḥśruti*) does not constitute a different meaning. Indeed, that which is purposeless cannot be included within the category of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And whatever the Veda makes known, that alone must be accepted as authoritative by those who follow it and others. Therefore, in this case, if one were to imagine a difference when non-difference has been understood through the Veda by means of the word "one," he would be rendering the Veda itself invalid.
Furthermore, futility (meaninglessness) as understood through a valid means of knowledge does not constitute a defect.
And this is also a possible interpretation: a word that has been touched by the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) is itself grasped as being employed for the purpose of expressing the meaning.
Alternatively, there will be repetition (*abhyāsa*) for the sake of illuminating the *āmīdha* and other such elements;
for in common worldly usage, repetition occurs to whatever extent is necessary to manifest the intended meaning, even beyond the mere doubling of a word.
And likewise, in the narrative of Pañcendra, regarding the prayer of the Buddha-child, the repetition five times of the words "Give me a husband" is heard.

And just as in that case there was no deception on the part of the deity, so too here there is no such thing for anyone, by which one might imagine five sacrifices (for the five, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others).
Alternatively, when the injunction is accepted in all the utterances, the unity of the ritual action is understood, as in other scriptural systems (Mīmāṃsākośa 72).
In the case of sentences concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices,
because those which have an identical purpose are optional alternatives, that very same ritual action will at one time be designated by the name *samid* and at another time by the name *tanūnapāt*.
For it is not understood that rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), despite having the same function, serve as means for different purposes simply because they occupy the same position [in the ritual].
Alternatively, because the purpose is to enjoin deities such as Tanūnapāt and others, it does not have another meaning.

For if there were an injunction of an action, it would be a name; however, in the case of a restatement (anuvāda), an injunction of a name is not possible, and thus it must be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi).
Therefore, for this reason also, it is not a separate ritual action.

Furthermore, even in another instance where those very same word and meaning are recognized (*pratyabhijñāyate*), it is impossible to assert that they are different entities—just as in the case of the recognition of a sacrifice-fire that has gone out and been reborn—how much more so here, when the cognition is constrained by an immediately preceding and powerful recurrence?
Moreover, if there were a difference in the object with every utterance, it would follow that the meaning of the word is an impermanent individual manifestation.
Furthermore, "Just as in the case of *gatva* and so on, the nature of sacrifice (*yāgatva*) does not differ among these [individual acts]."
And once its true nature has been ascertained, how could there be another action?
Section on Repetition (Abhyāsādhikaraṇa) 572: By means of the chapter on repetition, Śabara [states]: "The oneness of the word is established through direct perception and recognition;
because of that oneness, its referent object also does not undergo division."

"Therefore, there is one sacrifice; and because of that oneness, there is also oneness of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) and the transcendental result (*apūrva*). This being the position reached, it is replied: "This nature of being an injunction consists in impelling one who has not yet acted. And that [impulsion] is understood through direct statement (*śruti*) to belong only to the meaning of the verbal root and the efficient force."

Therefore, due to the difference in the sacrifice (*yāga*), there is a difference in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*); and due to that difference, there is a difference in the transcendental result (*apūrva*). [Objection:

Since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is different, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is also different; thus, because it is easy to establish the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by way of a counter-example, there is an immediate connection [to the next topic].

[Soma: As for the meaning of the Sūtra: even the repetition of a single [text] is a differentiator, just like a different word (*śabdāntara*), because there is no distinction, as in the case of curd (*dadhi*) and so forth, since there is no specific thing to be enjoined.
Otherwise, the sentence itself would be meaningless. [Bhāṣya:
"In such cases as 'He offers the *samidhs*,' is there oneness or is there difference? Whence can there be oneness or difference between the verbal root and the suffix?"
"Due to repetition, there is a distinction of acts here; because it is a name, it is an injunction regarding a quality.

The status of being an injunction appears from direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), whereas [the status of] restatement (*anuvāda*) appears from proximity (*saṃnidhi*); and that [proximity] is weaker than the direct statement.
— Bhaṭṭa: In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, [it is said]: "He performs the *samidh* sacrifice."
He performs the offering to Tanūnapāt;
he performs the offering to Iḍas; he performs the offering to Barhis.
In such passages as "He performs the *svāhākāra* sacrifice," there is no difference in the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) because the sacrifice itself is recognized and thus remains non-different.
Nor does repetition (*abhyāsa*) cause a difference in the sacrifice; for repetition is a single entity, and as such, it is not contradictory to unity.

Nor does this [word *samit*], which consists of the repetition of an injunction, possess the quality of being a differentiator by way of being something to be enjoined; for, as in the case of "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), its power is transferred to the deity and the person, and thus it has the sacrifice as its object.

Nor is there an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) by means of the subsequent sentence due to the obstruction of the quality residing in the originative sentence of the sacrifice, because—due to the lack of any other recourse—the word *samit* found in the initial sentence is accepted as a name (*nāmadheya*) according to that principle.
In reality, however, if the *samit* offering were derived from the wording of the *yājyā* mantra, then that [offering] would be no different for those who do not recite that [mantra].

Therefore, the injunction of the five deities occurs either by way of a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *upāṃśuyāja* or by way of a restatement of the action enjoined by the sentence containing the word "viddhat.

Nor is there any possibility of redundancy; for since the deities such as Spring (*vasanta*) can also be obtained optionally from the *anumantraṇa* mantras—just as from the *yājyā* mantras—it is logical that these [injunctions] constitute restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*).
Consequently, because there is no repetition of an injunction already heard elsewhere, there is a difference between the ritual acts (*karmabheda*).

This being the case, since it is immediately apparent that only those mantras possessing the power of mutual expectancy (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*)—namely, the *yajyā* and *anuvākyā* mantras—are capable of determining the deity, whereas it is impossible for mantras possessing the power of one-sided expectancy (*anyatarākāṅkṣā*) to determine the deity, the words such as "samidh" do not serve as determinants of the deity.

Consequently, because the meaning of the accompanying word (*upapada*) has a possibility of being already established, and because it is perceived through direct word-hearing (*padaśruti*) and other means to be the object of the objective-efficient-force (*arthabhāvanā*) as something to be enjoined, it is improper to enjoin what has already been enjoined; thus, its distinctness (*vaijātya*) is established by virtue of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the state of being enjoined.

Nor is it the case that the distinction [of rites] is established merely through doubt, because the names such as *samit* and so forth would be established as names by the principle of "being perceived as such" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), and the refutation of their being injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) would occur via the principle of "not being perceived as such" (*tadakhyanyāya*). For once the unity of the ritual act is established, the function of a name is fulfilled by a single name; since it would follow that multiple names are redundant, it is appropriate to conclude they are merely restatements of qualities (*guṇānuvādaka*), and thus the determination of them as names is not reached. However, when the difference between rituals is established through repetition (*abhyāsa*), each individual ritual requires its own name to be meaningful; thus, the determination of them as names [is reached].
The *prayojana* (purpose) is the purpose of the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*).
Other purposes are set forth in the *Kaustubha*.

In the *Kaustubha*: first, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the injunction of deities, since there is an option (*vikalpa*) based on their having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), the performance of the rite (*karmānuṣṭhāna*) occurs only once.

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the injunction for repetition (*āvṛtti*), however, even in a particular modification (*vikṛti*) where the quality of the *samidh* offerings serves an unprecedented purpose (*apūrvārtha*), there is performance five times because the inherent [repetitions] such as the *tanūnapāt* are obtained as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the repetition of the *samidh* offerings; likewise, there is the performance of all five repetitions of the quality intended for a result (*phalārtha*) which rests upon the *samidh* offerings. Furthermore, in that specific modification, only the *samidh* offerings mentioned again [in the text] are to be performed, and the optional (*kāmya*) quality should be permitted therein.

Maṇḍana: "The repeated scriptural mention (*bhūyaḥśruti*) distinguishes the *samit* and other [fuel-sticks].
Śaṅkara: "Even from repetition, the action is distinct.
[It is] distinguished.

Even though there is a distinct name (*saṃjñāntara*), because [the action] is connected with a quality (*guṇa*) or a fruit (*phala*), the injunctive [element] is occupied with the desire for that quality or fruit; thus, there is no operation toward the meaning of the root *yaj* (sacrifice). Consequently, since the root-meaning is joined with a different object through the repetition of the chapter (*abhyāsādhyāya*), how could the sacrifice be subsumed by that [name]? Anticipating the objection that "there would be a distinct name for a distinct named entity," [the author replies]: Since a name serves to indicate a specific thing to be enjoined (*vidheya-viśeṣa*), and since the root-meaning cannot be the thing to be enjoined independently of the productive energy (*bhāvanā*), it would follow that [the name] is meaningless unless there is a distinction in the productive energy to be enjoined (*vidheya-bhāvanā-bheda*). (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 822–823)

Anticipating the objection that "the distinction [of the sacrifice] will arise from the difference in the mental cultivation (bhāvanā) due to the repetition of the study," it is stated: Since an injunction (vidhi) has the inherent nature of impelling one toward what has not yet been undertaken, and since there would otherwise be the consequence of it being a mere restatement of what is already established, it is logical that this [injunction], characterized by its re-enjoining, possesses the power of differentiation. However, because a name (saṃjñā) lacks the inherent nature of impelling one toward what has not yet been undertaken, it does not have the capacity to differentiate based on the repetition of the study; such is the intention. (Sūtra-pṛṣṭha 820). [Regarding the unity of the Indra-Agni injunction...]

Regarding the section on repetition (abhyāsādhikaraṇa), [sūtra 2.2.2]: "Repetition [constitutes a separate injunction] because it is not subordinate to another action; for in that case, the sentence regarding the new-moon day (āmāvāsya) is merely a restatement (anuvāda) of its own meaning. Since there is no apprehension of a specific distinction and no repeated hearing of an injunction, the principle of repetition does not apply here. The counter-example (pratyudāharaṇa) for the section on repetition is the section on number (saṃkhyādhikaraṇa, 2.2.20).

Kau. 2.1, p. 720, p. 232. [Objection]: In the *Abhyāsa-adhikaraṇa*, if it is argued that a name (*saṃjñā*) mentioned in conjunction with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not a differentiator [of acts], we reply:
It is true that a name mentioned in conjunction with a verbal root whose meaning is not intended for anything else is not a differentiator.

Tautā. 2.3.4.1, *Pūrvapakṣa*: According to the principle of the *Abhyāsa-adhikaraṇa*, the essential nature of the principle is that a repetition (*punar-śravaṇa*) which is not intended for anything else necessarily functions as a differentiator.

In this context, the distinction between rituals (*karmabheda*) is declared through the repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the word "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), as in: "He sacrifices to the *samidhs*, he sacrifices to *tanūnapāt*, he sacrifices to the *iḍas*, he sacrifices to the *barhis*, he sacrifices with the *svāhā*-utterance.

Although it could be argued that a distinction in the productive urge (*bhāvanābheda*) follows from the repetition of the sacrifice—just as there is a distinction in the sacrifice itself—it has not been presented here because such a distinction can also be established by means of "differentiation by words" (*śabdāntara*), which is not its exclusive characteristic.
(Kauṣītaki-bhāṣya 2.2.2)

And this distinction pertains not only to the individual instances (*vyakti*), but also to the genus (*jāti*) residing therein, because it is a general rule that when there is a difference in what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), there must be a difference in the delimiting factor of that injunction (*vidheyatā’vacchedaka*).

(Ku. 2|3|27): Even though there is a confusion of the things to be enjoined (*upadheya*), the logical principle (*nyāya*) remains unconfused; for in the case of repetition, the function consists solely in establishing the status of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*) as the object of injunction (*vidheya*), while disregarding its status as something to be adopted (*upādeyatā*) through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

Therefore, in that case, proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is the restrictive factor (*pratibandha*), but it is not a restrictor in the case of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*). Oṃ. Repetition is enjoined as a human goal because it is not a subsidiary part of an action.
The repetition that has been mentioned for the lifelong Agnihotra by the word "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīvam) is enjoined as a human goal.
Because it is not a subsidiary part of an action—that is, because it does not serve as a subsidiary to any other ritual act—it is established as an end in itself.

Therefore, the *homa* must be performed continuously, not merely in the evening and morning; this is the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) view. In the *Kutūhala*, however, it is explained that there is an option (*vā*): "repetition" or "not repetition," because [the action] is either a subsidiary part of the ritual (*karmaśeṣatvāt*) or not a subsidiary part of the ritual (*akarmaśeṣatvāt*). This is because the evening and morning timings pertain to optional (*kāmya*) performance and pertain to occasional (*naimittika*) performance. Somanātha has explained that the word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of negation: this is not a mere repetition because it is not a subsidiary part of the ritual; rather, it is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), and consequently, the performance must be carried out continuously.
In that case, it follows by implication that [the sacrifice] is impossible;
for although the *agnihotra* must be offered continuously throughout one's life,
it is not possible to offer it continuously during that entire period because of the occurrence of sleep, bathing, eating, and other such activities.
Thus, the application [of the rule] is impossible.

That is to say, by the elision of the sense (*tyalopa*), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) indicates that the sacrifice should be performed continuously at the remaining time, having set aside the times for sleep, bathing, eating, and so forth.
That is to say, by implication (*arthāpatti*), the sacrifice must be performed continuously at all times other than those occupied by sleep and the like.

Thus, this is indeed the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). [The opponent argues: "The [Agnihotra] is not taught as being restricted by specific times; rather, according to the two sūtras stating that 'the Agnihotra is to be performed for as long as one lives' and 'it must be offered continuously, setting aside times such as sleep,' the prima facie view is established. Refuting this prima facie view, the author sets forth the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the following sūtra.
The fire sacrifice (homa) must not be performed constantly at times other than those prescribed for sleep, bathing, eating, and so forth;
or rather, having set aside the times for sleep, bathing, and the like, it must not be performed constantly at any other time.
Why? Because specific times are taught: "The Agnihotra is to be offered at dusk, and at dawn in the morning."

Furthermore, just as the times for the Agnihotra are taught, so too are times taught for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices in such injunctions as: "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsī on the full moon day," "One should sacrifice with the Amāvāsyā on the new moon day," and "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa as long as one lives.
And it is not possible to perform different rituals at a single point in time.
Therefore, the lifelong performance of the Agnihotra occurs at both evening and morning, and the lifelong performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa occurs on the full moon and new moon days.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The sūtra “for time is indeed taught” is cited in the *Kutūhala*;
for since a specific time is taught, therefore the oblation is not to be performed continuously.

This is the meaning of that. Alternatively, the *prayāja* offerings are repeated; for when there is an *abhyudaya* (transference of the sacrifice), one observes a transgression of time, and thus the injunction regarding the time is established through the indicative marks of the time.
In the Siddhānta, this sūtra is for the purpose of showing indicative marks (liṅga).

It should be understood that because of the observation of temporal marks—marks that indicate specific times—there is an injunction regarding time, meaning an injunction for the sake of performing the *homa* and other rites at specific times such as evening and morning.
As it is said: "Verily, he who, being engaged in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, should let the full moon day or the new moon day pass by, falls away from the heavenly world."

If the *homa* were to take place at any time while [the substance] exists, then what would constitute its transgression? Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no constant application [of the rite], but rather it must be performed at the prescribed time.
The phrase "kāla-vidhānam" does not appear in the Ya and Ku manuscripts;
nor is there any necessity for it.
Alternatively, [the repetition] is like the *prayāja*s; it is a partial [repetition] for the sake of other deities.

In the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, regarding the animals dedicated to the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra, one might raise the objection that it is impossible for them to serve as purificatory rites (*saṃskāraka*) for the animal deities dedicated to Indra, Savitṛ, and Varuṇa. To refute this, the Sūtra states: "There is repetition. Regarding this, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakṛt) will state that in the case of the animal sacrifice, the number eleven is prescribed for the five *prayāja*s obtained through the extended injunction (*codaka*), and since that number cannot be achieved without repetition, the *prayāja*s are repeated. Thus, he will explain that through repetition, the entire apūrva is accomplished.
