7|1|1|1, p. 1523. Regarding the *abhyudayeṣṭi*, there arises a question concerning the transgression of time, as in the case of the *pañcaśarāva* offering. In the sacrifice performed when the moon has risen, the inquiry is: is another sacrifice enjoined on account of the transgression of the [prescribed] time, or is it merely a contingent removal of the original deities from the *darśa* rite itself? In this regard, the following is the sūtra of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position.

Thinking that the time for sacrifice was precisely at this point, the commencement of the New Moon (darśa) iṣṭi was made; however, if the moon rises after that, a lapse of the prescribed time occurs. Due to this lapse of time, there is the injunction for a different sacrifice from the New Moon, as expressed by the rule: "He should divide the rice grains into three parts: those that are of medium size he should offer as a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dātṛ; those that are the largest, as a pap of curdled milk to Indra Pradātṛ; and those that are the smallest, as a pap of boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. This is the injunction and rule for a separate sacrifice.

Just as in the case of the five-platter rice offering (*pañcaśarāva odana*) dedicated to Indra at the *havirāta* sacrifice, an injunction for a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*) is prescribed through the connection of substance and deity; so it is here.
Or rather, it is a removal (*apanaya*), because [the original substance] is already present.
Having set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) reached by the Sūtra through the bond of sublation, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In this case, there is no injunction for a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), because it is impossible to enjoin another deity when the sacrificial offerings (*havir*) are already occupied by the archetypal deities (*prākṛtadevatā*).
Therefore, here the removal of the archetypal deities is performed;
and having effected that removal, other deities are enjoined in those very same offerings, since the archetypal offerings remain present.
And because words have that as their purport.
He states another reason for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

"Because words such as 'One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni the Giver' have that as their purport; that is, they have as their purport the injunction of another deity preceded by the removal of the previous deity."
The particle *ca* serves to include another reason.
*Apanaya* means the removal or abandonment of corruption (*apabhraṃśa*).
This is because we observe the repetition of the *ātaḥ* [substitution] in the case of *bhā*.
The sūtra provides another reason that does not establish the opponent's conclusion. The addition of previously prepared curd to milk for the purpose of producing curd is called *ātañcana*.

Because we observe the repetition (*abhyāsa*)—that is, the recurrence—of this process, it is not established that a separate ritual (*karmāntara*) is enjoined by the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* passages; rather, a different deity is enjoined in connection with those very same oblations.

"If one should fear that [the moon] will rise, one should offer the oblations at the end of the night. One should wait with the husked rice grains; one should set aside half of the curd for the purpose of the *ātaṅghna* offering and not the other half. If [the moon] should rise, one should proceed with that *ātaṅghna* [offering]. If not, one should feed the Brahmins in the morning with this"—by this, the repetition of the *ātaṅghna* is stated.

If the removal of the original deities is conditional (*naimittika*), then since the *caru* has been prepared for that original curd, one must again perform the *ātañcana* (curdling) upon the milk of the new moon sacrifice (*āmāvāsya*).
Thus, the observation of this *ātañcana* is appropriate as an injunction regarding the deity, not as an injunction for a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate another reason.

Thulyasthi was told by Somanātha: "If the sacrificer thinks, 'Since the New Moon sacrifice (*darśayāga*) has been commenced by me on the fourteenth day itself, then the moon will rise directed toward me,' and thus there occurs a transgression of time (*kālāparādha*) regarding the rising; then, at the great night—when the night is divided into three parts—he should, with his intellect, commence the ritual procedure and perform it up to the stage of the *phalīkaraṇa* (threshing), remaining there while awaiting the non-rising of the moon."

In that case, whatever curd is contained within the evening oblation should be divided into two parts. One half should be set aside for the purpose of the ten-fold offering to be performed at its own time on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*); the other half should not be set aside for the sake of the *ātaṅghna* offering, but rather should be preserved silently.

This being so, if the moon should rise [while the sacrifice is still pending], then one should perform the sacrifice using the morning milk that has become *ātaṅghna*, combined with the fresh curd that was set aside for the *ātaṅghna* offering.
"If the moon should not rise, then one should feed the Brahmins with curd placed for the purpose of warding off evil spirits.
Also, in the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā*: "One should fear—that is, have apprehension—before the rising of the moon during the late night."

One should wait—that is, one should expect—for the sake of destroying the [defect], for the purpose of the *darśa* sacrifice performed at its own proper time, and for the purpose of the curd (*dadhi*) used in the *ātānana*.
It is not merely half; rather, that [curd] should be set aside for the oblation offered when the sun has risen, and it is not restricted solely to the *sānnāyya* sacrifice.
By this, it is explained that [the act] was performed for the purpose of warding off misfortune (*ātighna*). Precisely because it was established for the purpose of warding off misfortune,
it constitutes an original injunction (*apūrva*), since such a rule did not previously exist.

[Objection: "But surely, just as in the case of the injunction: 'He who desires cattle, having performed the New Moon sacrifice, should set aside the entrails; those which are the largest, he should make into a cake on eight potsherds for Agni the Giver; those which are of medium size, he should make into a cooked rice-oblation in milk for Agni Śipiviṣṭa; those which are the smallest, he should make into a curd-oblation for Agni the Bestower,' another distinct rite (*karmāntara*) is enjoined, so too in the present case, it must be another distinct rite. To this, [the author] replies: Because the New Moon sacrifice for one desiring cattle is *apūrva* (unprecedented), and because it enjoins a previously unknown sacrifice, it would indeed be the injunction of a distinct rite.

In the present case, however, the *darśa* sacrifice remains the very same as that which was established; and since it is merely the connection of the already established substance with this particular deity that is enjoined therein, there is no status as a separate ritual action (*karmāntaratva*).
Because of the defect in the milk, the other [substance] in the *pañcaśarāva* offering is indeed not defective.
He thus refutes the *pañcaśarāva* argument stated in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Because of a defect in the milk—specifically, because a defect consisting of its destruction or the like has arisen from the milk or the curd—the prescription of a separate ritual (*karmāntara*) in the case of the *pañcaśarāva* offering is appropriate. However, the other, the original *candrābhyuditeṣṭi*, as well as the original curd and boiled milk, are not defective; indeed, since they are not defective, there is no prescription of a separate ritual here due to the disparity between the two examples.

Alternatively, the word *hi* may stand in place of the word *tu*, as in: "For [the former] is not defective, but the other is indeed defective. If it is argued that the same applies to the *sānnāyya* offering, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) raises this objection once again.

If, due to a defect in the sacrificial offering (*havis*), the injunction for a separate rite (*karmāntara*) is possible in the case of the *pañcaśarāva* [offering], then in the present case as well, there should be a separate rite.
How so? Because in the case of the *sānnāyya* (curdled milk offering) as well, a state of defect has arisen just like the occasion for the *pañcaśarāva*;
likewise, in the case of the curd (*dadhi*) and the boiled milk (*śṛta*), a state of defect has arisen due to the defect of the rising of the moon.
If the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) should say, "Therefore, even in this case, there must be a separate ritual act," [the reply is:
No, because that [reason] is not defective; for the cause is no different.

Just as in the example of the *pañcaśarāva* offering, which is a substitute for the *sānnāyya* consisting of curd and boiled milk, the argument made by the proponent—that it is defective due to the defect of the moon's rising—is incorrect.

Because that *sānnāyya* is not defective—that is, it is free from blemish—whereas in the case of the *pañcaśarāva* (the five-plate offering), the substance is indeed defective by its very nature; however, here it is not so. [Objection:
But surely it is defective due to the transgression of time; [Response: It is not rendered defective.
For the cause is indeed non-distinct and equal;
thus, the prescription for expiation applies even when [the curd] is spoiled, as it also applies when it has risen due to a lapse of time.
Indeed, there is no defect in the essential nature of the curd and so forth merely because of a lapse of time.
However, for that which has commenced at an improper time, there is a prescription of deities; but this does not apply to the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) when it has been spoiled.
Therefore, this is not a prescription of a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*). The scriptural statement is intended as a secondary characteristic (*lakṣaṇārtha*).
Regarding the conclusion that in the *abhyudayeṣṭi* (the sacrifice performed when the moon has risen) there is no injunction of a deity with reference to the original material (*prākṛtadravya*),

because the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) has not been performed at the time of the *abhyudaya*, and thus the original material lacks the state of being cooked (*śṛtatva*)— making it impossible for it to be the object of reference— that is incorrect. For, since the word "cooked" (*śṛta*) is used as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇārtha*) for milk characterized by the properties intended for the purpose of cooking— which are concomitant with the act of boiling— the term "cooked" does not fail to apply.

In every respect, the *abhyuditeṣṭi* is not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), but rather merely the prescription of a connection with different deities preceded by the removal of the original deities. [Question: At the time of the *abhyudaya*, should the removal of the milk-offering (*doha*) retain its own specific properties (*svadharma*), since it has already been set in motion?

"He deprives him of offspring and cattle, and increases his rival, for whom the moon rises while the sacrificial oblation has already been set out. He should divide the rice grains into three parts: those that are of medium size he should offer as a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dātṛ; those that are the largest he should offer as a pap of curdled milk to Indra Pradātṛ; and those that are the smallest he should offer as a pap of boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. Thus is described the *candrābhyuditeṣṭi* (the sacrifice performed when the moon has risen). In the Śruti, the prefix *vi-* signifies the removal of the fault (*doṣāpanaya*) in the case of the moon rising [after the oblation has been prepared]. 576. [This concludes the section on] the *abhyuditeṣṭi*.
This is connected with the word "ardhayati" (he diminishes).

For whichever sacrificer the *dārśika* oblation has been set aside (*nirupta*), if at that time the moon rises in the east— having risen before the oblation was set aside, meaning the risen moon is seen after the setting aside—
such a moon causes that sacrificer to be separated (*vyayuta*) from offspring and cattle.
Furthermore, this [act] increases the enemy who is a rival in the lineage, both in terms of progeny and cattle.
Such being the case, this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed by the sacrificer to remove the fault arising from performing the rite at an improper time.

Regarding that, it is said: that sacrificer should divide the rice grains prepared through threshing and other processes into three parts—namely, the sacrificial portions (*havir*), the middling, and the smallest—and should separate them for the various deities according to the method to be described.
For example, those rice grains which are of medium size—one should offer a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) prepared in earthen vessels with water for the donor of the middle-sized grains;
a cake of medium-sized grains is to be made, and it is for the donor.
Likewise, one should offer a cooked oblation (caru) of the smallest and most coarse grains for Indra, the recipient of the gift.
This *caru* is to be cooked in curd.
Thus, one should offer a *caru* of the finest, most minute rice grains to Viṣṇu, characterized by the attribute *śipiviṣṭa*.
And it is heard in the scripture that this *caru* is to be cooked in prepared, boiled milk.

In this regard, concerning the inquiry as to whether the ritual rules for offering curd and milk (*dadhi-payas*) should be performed when [the moon] has risen during the *śruti* [rite], the author begins with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

When the rising of the moon is the occasion (*nimitta*), there is this removal of the defect (*doṣa*) mentioned in the scripture—the removal or separation from the deities of the tenth day; that very removed defect consists of the curd and milk. It should be such that it possesses its own properties (*svadharma*), meaning it possesses the properties of its own defect.

The suffix *anic* is applied as a compound-ending by the rule *dharmādibhyaś ca kevalāt* (Pāṇini 5.1.124). Why? Because they proceed from their own specific properties (*svadharma*). This means that because the curd (*dadhi*) and the milk-sacrifice (*śruti*) have already proceeded [with their respective rites], therefore, even in the case of the *abhyudaya* sacrifice, the ritual properties (*pradānadharmāḥ*) belong to the curd and the milk-sacrifice; this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
And because of the instruction regarding the hundredfold oblation (*śatopadeśa*).

Regarding the *candrābhyuditeṣṭi*, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the ritual properties (*dharma*) pertaining to the offering—namely, the milking away of the calves (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) and so forth—must be performed for the curd (*dadhi*), he states another reason:

"Because of the instruction regarding the cooked rice (*caru*) as if it were already accomplished" (*śrute carum*). From this, it is understood that the ritual properties intended for the sacrifice must be performed for both the curd and the milk.
The term *śruta* (boiled) is applied to milk when the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) has been accomplished.

Although these two sūtras (41–42), by virtue of the word *tu* (but), appear to set forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding what is about to be stated, while the subsequent two sūtras establish the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) because they refute [the former], thus suggesting that all four sūtras constitute a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), nevertheless, the authors of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) have explained the four sūtras by treating them as distinct topical sections.

Although that [objection] was refuted in the *Codanāsūtra* of the *Ślokavārttika*, it should nevertheless be understood that the same [position] was established in the *Ṭupṭīkā* because it does not contradict the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhādhyāya*) of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā*.

Regarding the *Abhyuditeṣṭi*: since there is a difference between the two rites mentioned in the *Darśa* scripture, they cannot exist as a single unit; therefore, one must adopt the position that one should perform both sacrifices, and not the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* alone. (*Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*)
1.2.9. The *Abhyuditeṣṭi* is a performance of the *Darśa* itself, occasioned by the rising of the moon; it is not, however, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the omission of the *Darśa*.
Therefore, having performed the occasional (*naimittika*) performance of the *Darśa* even when the moon has risen, one must subsequently perform the regular (*nitya*) *Darśa* performance for oneself.

Vi. 6.5.1: When the *Darśa* rite has commenced and the rising of the moon serves as the occasion, that very same *Darśa* rite must be performed as the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* by way of an occasional rite; it does not become a different ritual action altogether.

6|5|1: Regarding the *abhyuditeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for one by whom the moon has risen [during the preparation]): when the sequence of curd is underway, even if the moon rises before the pouring (*nirvāpa*), the rite must be performed at the appointed time, because the commencement of the ritual action takes place at that specific time.
In the *abhyuditeṣṭi*, if the moon rises after half of the pouring has been completed, the remaining pouring must be performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*).
There is no removal of the handfuls of grain, because they are subordinate to that [act of pouring].
The Commentary: When the pouring out of four handfuls has been commenced but remains incomplete, a doubt arises.
Is that which has been poured out fixed as such, while the remainder is to be poured out from the original (prakṛti) offerings, or from the modified (vaikṛta) offerings, or perhaps silently?
What is the prima facie view? "When poured out" means when half-poured out.
In that case, there would be no removal of the deity.
Why?
Because it possesses those qualities.
The deity is a quality of the act of pouring out (nirvāpa), not of the handfuls (muṣṭi). And that pouring out has the deity as its object.
Why?

Because the number four is intended to be complete, only the repetition must be performed; and that mere repetition is performed again. Since the offering was already made previously, the deity has not been removed.

This very same [offering] is performed again; when it is performed once more, the deity must remain the same as before, and thus the offering should be completed according to the original model (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, the subsequent handful (*muṣṭi*) is not a separate ritual act (*padārtha*) such that there would be a removal of the deity.
This is done merely to complete the required number of offerings.

Therefore, it is "not to be removed. In the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, there is the offering of half [the oblation]; for in the *upāṃśuyāja* of the *abhyuditeṣṭi*, there is a connection with that which is not the original form, because it occupies its place.
The commentary states: One need not desist from the natural (*prākṛta*) [rites]. Then from what? From the modified (*vaikṛta*) optional rites.
Why?
A conjunction with a specific, non-ordinary deity is heard in the scripture, not with the one entitled [to the original rite].
The injunction "one should divide the rice grains into three parts" is prescribed by detaching [the grains] from the ordinary [offerings] and assigning them to the modified offerings.
These [modified offerings] now take the place of those [original ones].

Therefore, when the etymological explanation has ceased, the deities have departed, and others have arisen in their place. Consequently, the remainder of the offering should be performed by means of the modified [deities]. This would be so because of the absence of the other.
The Commentary states: Because of the absence of any other object associated with a deity, there can be no offering (*nirvāpa*) associated with a deity.

If, in the act of offering, one half were for another deity and the other half for yet another deity, then the offering would not be one belonging to the original deity (*prākṛta*), nor would it be one belonging to another deity (*vaikṛta*).
Therefore, it must be offered silently (*tūṣṇīm*).
Necessarily, there must be a distinction in intention elsewhere.
The word "ca" has the sense of "ḍupa," "tu," and "śabda. Otherwise, the word "ca" would express a mere conjunction (*samuccaya*).
And that is incorrect;
for the non-existence of anything among those previously mentioned cannot possibly serve as a reason.
Furthermore, with respect to the act of offering (*nirvāpa*), the connection [of the mantra] was already established at the first handful, based on the constituent elements of the offering.

It is said that "one should divide" when there is a cause for its elevation; this refers to division. Considering it to be a constituent element (*padārtha*), what was previously connected [with the archetypal deities in the act of pouring out] is now separated as to one part.
And it is possible to separate it, because separation depends solely upon that which is conjoined.
Furthermore, it is not possible to establish a connection with another deity, because that [connection] depends upon the ritual substance (*padārtha*).
The remaining portion of the handful is but a part of that substance.
Therefore, due to the cessation of the original [procedure] and the absence of a connection with a modified [deity], the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is performed silently.

In other cases as well, if the referent is a constituent part (*avayava*), this same principle applies. For example, in the case of the *pradāna* (offering), its constituent parts include the recitation (*anuvacana*) and the *preṣya-yājyā*.

When [the procedure] is removed from the archetypal (*prakṛti*) rites and not connected with the modified (*vaikṛti*) ones, the remaining act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) must be performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*).

Soma: Even though the oblation has already been set forth here, the counter-argument—that there is either the removal of the original deity due to the *abhyudaya* (transformation) or the association with another deity—is the point of connection (*saṃgati*).

The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: when the presiding deity (*sāmin*) has been determined and four handfuls have been measured out, there is no removal of the original deity from even a portion [of them]; because the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) is subordinate to the deity, it is impossible to remove a portion [without removing the whole].
Vi—In the case of *abhyudaya*, when there is a removal from the original [deities], one should offer the remaining rice-balls (*ṣaṇḍulān*).
One should perform [the rites] here either from the archetypal (*prākṛtī*) or from the modified (*vaikṛtī*) ones;
from the archetypal because they are the primary procedure, and from the modified because of a specific occasion (*nimitta*).
Since the remaining purpose is not established by the context, the latter [option] prevails here due to its connection.
Bhaṭṭa: When the rising of the moon or the sun is known to be directed toward the object [of the sacrifice], the remaining [offerings] need not be performed with the original materials (*prākṛta*).
This is because there is no obstacle to the application of the contingent removal (*apanaya*) of the ritual act, since the contingency (*nimitta*) exists.

Nor can they be performed with the modified materials (*vaikṛta*); for since a portion of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) has not been prescribed [for that specific case], the connection with another deity does not apply there.

For just as prohibitions such as "one should not eat the fruit" operate by targeting specific parts [of the whole] through their non-commonality with the parts, so too does a prohibition consisting of removal.
And just as injunctions such as "one should give the fruit" operate upon the whole alone, so too does the connection with another deity.
Therefore, the offering (nirvāpa) of the remainder must indeed be performed silently.

The ritualists (*yājñikas*), however, accepting that even a single part of a ritual act may have its own specific purpose and extension, perform only those [acts] belonging to the modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta*).
Maṇḍana says: "The purpose also [is fulfilled] by half a cubit, silently.
Śaṅkara says: "[It is done] silently at the half-brick."
In the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, there is also the removal of the deities from the *upāṃśuyāja*.
Regarding the *upāṃśuyāja*, because there is no specific scriptural statement, it remains as in the archetype (*yathāprakṛti*).
The Commentary states: regarding that very same rising of the moon, there is a doubt—whether there should be a removal of the deities even in the *upāṃśuyāja*, or not.
What is established? In the *upāṃśuyāja*, it should be according to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Why? Because there is no specific injunction.

For instance, in those [other sacrifices] there is an injunction: "A cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ from the middle-sized grains; a pap in curd for Indra Pradātṛ from the smallest grains; a pap in boiled milk for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa from the finest grains"—but such an injunction does not exist for the *upāṃśuyāja*.
Therefore, it could be as one wishes.

Regarding this, the Vṛttikāra intends to say that "the Upāṃśuyāja occurs only at the Full Moon, not at the New Moon" (10.8.17–54), and he does not desire this to be considered a discussion of the *kula* (lineage/branch). Thus, the commencement of a new section (*adhikāra*) would be inappropriate.
Or rather, it is logical, because the *upāṃśuyāja* is clearly enjoined by a direct statement in the *Bahuvacanabrāhmaṇa* (the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 3.6).
How then is the statement in the tenth book independent? This is merely a matter of reasoning (*nyāya*).
Or else, there is no contradiction due to its application, as is the case with the others.
The Commentary: The word "or" (vā) excludes the fifth [alternative].
There is also the removal of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
For what reason? Because of the application (*pravṛtti*).
The application of the *tantra* at an improper time is the cause for the removal [of the oblation].
Why? Because here no division of the oblation by means of the *abhyudaya* (sunrise) is prescribed for the afternoon.
How is this understood? From the hearing of the general statement: "For him whose [moon] rises [while the oblation has been set aside]."
For the sun rises for everyone in the afternoon,
and the afternoon is not the proper time for the commencement of the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
This being the case, it is not possible to distinguish [the specific sacrifice] by means of those rice grains.

Therefore, there is also a division of the *upāṃśu-yāja*. For by this sentence, "One should divide the rice-grains into three parts," the removal of the deities is effected. Indeed, the injunction here—"one should divide"—means that one should perform the division.
"How so? The subsequent sentences are intended for specific divisions, stating: "This and that substance is for this deity; this and that is for her.
Even for that substance for which there is no specific division, there is a general division, namely: "one should divide it. Therefore...

In the context of a connection with the *dharma*, the fact that the subject matter is a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) of the *apūrva* is not the determining factor due to its complexity; rather, it is simply the state of being connected to the *apūrva* for the sake of establishing the great scope of the scripture.
For this very reason, even a mantra such as "Agnim" has as its purpose the fruit to be accomplished by the *apūrva*.
And in the present case, that connection consists in being the means for cooking (*śrapaṇa*).
This is the summary.

Now, an objection is raised: although curd and milk are means for cooking rice, they do not acquire the properties of the *praṇītā* water; for the *praṇītās* are enjoined specifically for the purpose of mixing (*saṃyavana*), and in the present case, since there is no mixing, that [application] is impossible.

For this very reason, in the *caru* offerings to Sūrya and others, because there is no cooking with the *barhis* grass, just as the placement on potsherds is determined by the absence of such cooking, so too, due to the absence of mixing, the properties of the *praṇītās* are simply excluded.

If this is argued, [we reply: even though the statement regarding the *praṇītā* waters conveys their function as the means for mixing the sacrificial balls (*piṇḍa*), their status as a means for incidental cooking also exists; therefore, the properties of the *praṇītā* waters are applicable both in the *saurya* oblation and in the present case.
Alternatively, this discussion may be considered a *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical inquiry).

Furthermore, it should be understood that although there is no difference in the ritual action itself, the application of the properties of the *praṇītā* waters to *dadhi* and *śrita* occurs solely through "substitution" (*sthānāpatti*)—because their role as the means for cooking the *āgneya* oblation is equally occasional (*naimittika*)—and not by way of the *vrīhi-yava* principle (where one is a substitute for the other) according to *PMS* 3.5.15 and 12.3.4.10.
13. Maṇḍana: The ritual properties of the *praṇītā* water should apply to the curd. 21. Śaṃkara: One should consume [the curd] according to the ritual properties of the *praṇītā* water.
25. In the *Abhyuditeṣṭi*, the performance of the ritual properties for the substances to be offered applies to both the curd and the whey.

In the case of an auspicious rising (abhyudaya), there should be the removal of the defect through one's own duty, because it has already commenced. The Commentary states: This is handed down in the tradition: "Verily, he deprives him of offspring and cattle, and increases his rival, for whom the moon rises while the sacrificial oblation has already been set aside. He should divide the rice-grains into three parts: those that are of medium size, he should offer as a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Dātṛ; those that are the largest, he should offer as curdled milk to Indra Dadhikrāvan; those that are the smallest, he should offer as cooked rice in boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa."
The example is "one should prepare a *caru* offering in boiled milk and curd.

In this regard, the meaning is subject to doubt: should the properties of milk intended for the *iṣṭi* sacrifice be performed in both the boiled milk and the curd, or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That they should not be performed.
Why? Because it is not for the purpose of being offered, because it is prescribed for the purpose of the *praṇītā* water, and because it is not equal to the *caru*, there is no commingling with it.
This being the position reached, we reply:

when the occasion of the *abhyudaya* (the moon rising while the sacrifice is still in progress) occurs, this milking which has been diverted from its original deity should retain its own inherent characteristics (*svadharma*).
And in that case, the properties of milk apply for the purpose of the sacrifice; in the Abhyuditeṣṭi, curd and whey are to be used. In the Abhyuditeṣṭi, the rites of the Darśa must be performed.
Why? Because that milk and curd were indeed set forth for the purpose of sacrifice.
And since they are for the purpose of sacrifice, therefore the ritual properties (dharmas) belonging to the sacrifice have already been applied to them.
There is a reason for the application of those properties, but none for their removal.
[Objection: Is it not the case that curd and milk are enjoined for the sake of the prepared offering? [Reply: No, he says;
for in that case the sentence would be split (vākyabheda) if curd and milk were intended both for the sake of the deity and for the sake of the sacrificial pap (caru).
[Objection: But surely the connection with the deity applies equally to the curd and the milk as well; thus there will be no split of the sentence.
It cannot be so;
for the preceding statement, "One should divide the rice-grains into three parts," has already established that a division must be made.

Immediately following that, this subsequent sentence—"Those which are the largest, those he should offer as *dadhiśru* to Indra Pradātṛ; those which are the smallest, those as *śṛtacaru* to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa"—is intended to specify the particular nature of that division.

In this case, since there is no distinction made, it must be stated that curd and milk are also to be divided. Furthermore, if curd and milk were to be mentioned for the purpose of the *praṇītā* water even while they themselves are being divided, then the sentence would become split (*vākya-bheda*).
Therefore, these two are not enjoined for the purpose of the *praṇītā*.

And when that meaning is not being enjoined, the base-meaning (*prātipadikārtha*) is the connection of the deity; by the power of the sentence (*vākya-sāmarthyāt*), both the curd and the milk are connected with the deity, as well as with the *caru* (gruel).
"The *caru* in the curd: one portion is for Indra Pradātṛ"—just as it might be said when various substances are being divided: "The jewels collected in a golden vessel: one portion is for Devadatta."
"Just as in the case of 'Gold placed in a silver vessel is the other share of Viṣṇumitra,' two shares are understood along with the vessel because the sentence is intent upon a specific division;
and since the vessel is distinct, the locative sense is understood as a restatement (anuvāda).
Likewise here, because the sentence is intent upon a division and because curd and milk are distinct, it is understood that 'one share' [belongs to the sacrificer]."
Furthermore, since the meaning is already established, the locative case will be a mere restatement (anuvāda).
Therefore, curd and milk are for the purpose of offering;
and the properties of curd and milk must be performed for the purpose of the offering.

And there is the scriptural instruction. The Commentary states: For this reason as well, the ritual duties (dharmas) intended for the sacrifice must be performed upon the curd and the milk when they are offered. Why? Because there is an instruction regarding them as if they were already established: "the sacrificial pap (caru) in boiled milk" and "the sacrificial pap in curd. This is only logical if those ritual duties are already present.
In this case, since cooking (*śrapaṇa*) is not performed, the scriptural instruction given there as if [the substance] were already established would be untenable.
Therefore, for both curd and milk, the properties of curd and milk intended for the sacrifice must be performed.

Ṭup—(Leaving aside the unity of the topic (*ekādhikaraṇya*) which is obtained by the natural force of the Sūtra, why has the author of the Bhāṣya resorted to a division of topics? To this he says: True—) these two Sūtras (*abhyudaye* and *śrute*), being devoid of the words *tu* and *vā*, [by their very nature] present curd and milk as possessing the properties [of the sacrifice] in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the two subsequent sūtras (*uttare*), by means of the word "or" (*vā*), [the authors] set aside this position—that the two sūtras have the purpose of providing a definition—and establish the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that curd and milk are not joined with the properties of an offering (*pradānadharma*).

Thus, having discarded the system of the author of the sūtras (and thereby discarded the unity of the topic as previously accepted), the commentator (who is indeed the author of the Bhāṣya) composed an exposition that is not in conflict with the sixth [book].

For it has been stated therein that this very same New Moon sacrifice (*āmāvāsya*) is the rite; only the substance is removed from the previous deity and joined with another deity, yet its essential nature as a sacrificial act remains unchanged.
How then could it not possess the characteristics of a sacrifice?

Indeed, for this very reason, the author of the Sūtras has determined that the milkings are solely for the purpose of offering, having set aside the view that they are for the sake of preparing the *caru* (boiled rice), stating: "Because it is not a preparation for that" (6.5.16).

Therefore, by means of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the preceding section—namely, that "curd and milk [are for the purpose] of cooking, as indicated by the locative case" (*saptamī-śrutā śrapaṇādyai dadhi-payasī*)—these two [initial] sūtras constitute the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Likewise, the subsequent sūtras are also [prima facie positions] formed in the same manner against this very conclusion.

Thus, because the subsequent sūtra and its section (*adhikaraṇa*) serve as an exception (*apavāda*) to the logic of the preceding prima facie position, their commencement is more appropriate on account of this logical consistency.

(Now, why is the statement regarding the *paśukāmeṣṭi* not cited at the very beginning? For if that were done, the textual order would not contradict the logic, and the Sūtras would be explained according to the literal text as forming a single coherent whole. To this, he says: Otherwise (if one does not resort to the distinction between separate topical sections), the example of the *abhyudaya* (Sūtra) would have to be discarded.
(He states the established conclusion of the present topical section: "But the logic is the same" (as that which was [stated] in the sixth [book]).

*Soma*—(This is an intermediate connection in the form of an illustration. Nor should it be argued that this section is redundant because this matter has already been established in the sixth book (*adhyāya*). Even so, there might be some confusion on the part of someone who, due to the hearing of the locative case ending (*saptamī*) used in the preceding section, might think that the milk belongs to the *praṇītā* water; therefore, it is not redundant because it serves to dispel that misconception. The meaning of the Sūtra, however, is as follows: "In the case of the *abhyudayeṣṭi*, there is a removal of the milking; the milking from which the deity has been removed should possess the characteristics of what is to be offered (*pradeya*), because the milking is desired as something to be offered."

Vi—‘If they [the clouds] do not exist when the sun has risen, they would not have existed even before; since they have already begun to appear, they must exist like other things, as it is merely stated that their appearance depends on divine destiny. ‘Like other things’ means like rice grains.

11. Bhāṭṭa: In that case, regarding the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice (just like the *prāyaṇīyeṣṭi*), because of the use of the locative case (*saptamī*) in reference to the curd (*dadhi*) and the heated milk (*śrita*), they would possess the characteristics of the offering material (*pradeya*), since they function as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, the statement "he cooks together" (*saha śrapayati*) can also be explained as a mandatory restatement (*nityānuvāda*) for the same reason as before. Nor should it be argued that the curd and other substances are the offering material simply because the deity alone is enjoined there with reference to substances such as *kṣodra*; for if the status of being a substratum were also enjoined, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result.
It cannot be said that the curd and so forth are the offering material, because even if the substances were enjoined, the problem of syntactical split would remain as it was.
Therefore, it is better to accept that the seventh [case-ending] is heard [in the text] precisely as a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) caused by multiple subordinate factors (*anekaliṅga-nimitta*).

In reality, however, since in that view a distinct *bhāvanā* (efficient force) itself is accepted, there is no syntactical split even regarding the injunction of the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*).

This being the position reached, [the author replies]: "If the offered oblation (*havis*) should be consumed by fire, then at that time these very rice grains, well-purified, as well as curd and milk... and so forth. Since this specific removal (*apanaya*) is heard in the scripture, and because it has been established in another context that even when there is a different mental realization (*bhāvanā*), curd and milk—which belong to the original sacrifice—are to be taken up solely as things to be offered (*pradeya*), it is untenable to intend them as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Therefore, the properties of the thing to be offered (*pradeyadharma*) certainly apply. 9. Maṇḍana: "They would exist again upon its rising"; "they" refers to the properties of the thing to be offered.
Śaṅkara: "The state of being offered arises at the time of the rising [of the moon].
11. Regarding curd and whey:

in the *Abhyuditeṣṭi*, even if the moon rises after the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*) has begun but before the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) of the oblation, the pouring out for the deities occurs precisely at that time of the moon's rising.

Since the original [deities] have not been set aside and the [new deities] have arisen, and because of the removal of the rice-grains that had become the object of the original rites—according to the *Bhāṣya*: "It is established that the occasion [of the rite] has merely commenced"—there arises a doubt: regarding the occasional removal of the deities and the association with other deities, should these be performed after the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), once the rice-nature of the oblation is established, while the pouring out itself remains directed toward the original deities, now that the sunrise has been recognized; or should they be directed toward the modified deities alone? This is the doubt.
What, then, is the prima facie position? The Teacher [Bādari] held that one should perform the offering with the ordinary materials even when the moon has risen after they have been set aside.
Why? Because the removal is heard of in respect to those things that have become rice-grains; for the scriptural text says:
"If the sacrificial oblation of one who has already set it aside is overtaken by the rising of the moon..."

In the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, [the text] states: "In the *Abhyuditeṣṭi*, one should divide the rice-grains into three parts. This prescribes the division of the rice-grains immediately after the realization that the moon has risen. That [division] is not possible for those [grains] which have not yet become rice.

Therefore, because the rice grains are absent in the undesirable [result], the original deities are removed; thus, one should offer the oblation using only the original [deities]. Having set aside [the portion]—because the removal of the deities is caused by the non-drawing of its share.
Commentary: The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position.

The teacher Ālekhana held the view that one should offer oblations to those deities who, having been excluded [from the *candrodaya* sacrifice], still perform their ritual duties. Why? Because the removal of the deity is caused by the performance of that [excluded] act at an improper time; therefore, since the deity has been removed, one should offer the oblation to the deities who have been excluded from the *vyūha*.
In this sūtra, the reading *vyūhyabhāgamya* is seen everywhere;
and this same reading is clear in the Bhāṣya.
In the manuscript *ya*, the reading *kutastulyau ca vyūhyabhāgamyaḥ* is clearly evident.
In the *Āpastamba-Śrautasūtra* and Rudradatta’s commentary (*Vyākhyā*), the reading "vyūhya-bhāgasya" has long since disappeared; thus, there is no co-existence [of the two substances].
Now, if it were argued that after first taking a portion of milk, the offering of the *caru* is placed therein, and in this way the *caru* will exist both in the milk and in the curd—
That also is not so;
for in this *avadāna*, no other motive is heard.
What then? A division is prescribed upon the rising [of the sun].
Furthermore, it is not possible to set aside the curd or the milk for the *caru* prior to the verbal injunction.
Therefore, this must be understood as follows: in the section concerning the *abhyuditeṣṭi*, there is an injunction prescribing simultaneous cooking in the statement, "He cooks together.
Consequently, when simultaneity is being established, the locative sense—which is already implied by the context—is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
However, a qualified injunction (viśiṣṭavidhāna) occurs by way of [specifying] the means of exit and the avoidance of faults.
In the case of "to Indra, for the sake of giving, in curd, a sacrificial pap (caru)," a productive operation (bhāvanā) qualified by five elements is enjoined.
As for the sacrifice, which is the meaning of the verbal root, it is already present in proximity.
If it were not present, there would be a separate action;
however, it does exist.
Nevertheless, this was not accepted by the authors of the Bhāṣya, because, since it serves multiple purposes, they considered it to be nothing other than a syntactical split (vākya-bheda).
(Regarding this, the *Tantraratna* states:

[there is] a productive urge (*bhāvanā*) qualified by the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) prepared through division, by Indra, and by the state of being the giver; [furthermore], a productive urge qualified by milk as characterized by sixteen substances—[that is, by milk and by the sacrificial porridge prepared from the portions obtained from the sixteen staffs]—and by Viṣṇu, and by the word "etc. [meaning] by the state of eating and drinking, is enjoined. [This is so] because of the flowing out of the middle and other [portions] (the meaning being "by means of the middle and other substances").
And thus, because of the injunction of the productive urge, the non-separation of many objects (is established as their injunction by a single injunction alone).)
With the desire to explain the Bhāṣya, the *adhikaraṇa* is described according to the Bhāṣya.

Here, according to the Bhāṣya’s view, since the sacrifices under discussion and the substance are not yet divided, the injunction "one should divide" (*vibhajet*) prescribes only the division among the deities—that is, one should divide the substance, such as the rice-grains, among the deities. [Objection: If this is the case, how is the status of being *caru* (cooked sacrificial food), which is indicated by the locative case-ending, set aside? To this, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "In that context, the status of being *caru* is already established by the fact of cooking; thus, in this sentence, it is understood along with the meaning of the locative case, which is itself already established by the sense."
[The opponent] objects: "This is true; since there is cooking (*śrapaṇa*), the status of being a *caru* is indeed obtained.
However, there is no cooking of the curd. It is replied: "By virtue of the scriptural statement, there will be cooking [of it], for [the text says] 'he cooks together' (*saha śrapayati*)."
[Objection: Is it not the case that by this [text], the cooking together with another is being enjoined? [Response: No;
because of parsimony, the state of being together is already established.
By this statement, however, the cooking of the curd itself—which was not otherwise established—is what is enjoined.

The beauty [of the milk] is obtained through its purpose; it has the sense of the locative case (and therefore it is a separate action from the churning), because the repeated practice of curdling is observed.
The Commentary states: It also demonstrates the practice of curdling.
How so? Thus it is heard in scripture: "If one thinks, 'He will vomit,' one should offer the oblations at the dead of night;
one should wait even until the rice-grains have been husked."

One should set aside curd for the purpose of mixing with the sacrificial offering; one should not [set it aside] otherwise. Even if he were to proceed with the sacrifice using that [curd], it would be improper; if he does not, he should feed Brāhmaṇas with it in the morning.
Thus:
if another action were to be adopted [as the primary object], then rice, curd, and ghee would be so;
therefore, it is the worldly [substances] that are to be adopted.

For this is not the function of the primary elements at that time. Since the curd has already been prepared [on the previous day], when the New Moon sacrifice is performed on the following day, the curd is already present; thus, the act of churning (atañcana) does not need to be repeated. In that very same Abhyuditeṣṭi, curd is prescribed; therefore, there would be no need for churning.

Now, if there is the removal of the deity due to a specific omen, and consequently a *caru* offering is prepared in that curd, then the act of adding the coagulant (*ātañcana*) must again be performed at the subsequent new-moon milk-offering.
Thus, the observation of the repeated addition of the coagulant is consistent with the injunction regarding the deity;
for since this is a case of something not previously established, it must be an injunction.

The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): Now, as for what was stated—that just as in the *Paśukāmeṣṭi*, there is a separate ritual [action]—[it is argued that] since these occasional rites (*naimittika*) consist of mere futile activity, they cannot serve the purpose of destroying the defects incurred by the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited; therefore, it is considered that these occasional rites have only a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*). If that were the case, then let there be a combination (*samuccaya*) [of the occasional rites with the regular ones].

As for the objection that the defect resulting from carrying [the fire] outside the altar—which applies under the alternative of performing the *praṇayana*—does not apply to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices, and therefore this [act] cannot have the purpose of removing that defect:
this being the position reached, we reply that there is no separate ritual action (*karmāntara*) because there is no evidence to distinguish it [as such].

Nor is there a qualifying attribute (*guṇa*) that would necessitate a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); for since the deity alone is enjoined by means of the substance and the location, that does not entail a syntactical split.

And since the deity requires a sacrifice that brings it into existence, just as in the case of the *aindrāgna* and similar offerings, it is logical that only those sacrifices under discussion (*prakṛta*) serve as its originators; thus, according to the very method you have stated, the two sections [of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra*] are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of what is already established by the sense of the text.

Because of the use of the word "yat" (which), there is the inclusion of the deity of the middle [fire], etc., as the object of reference (*uddeśya*), even though they are not under discussion. Since the form of the deity is one, the term "abhi" is accepted as indicating the intended meaning through a relationship of mutual qualification and qualified, or because a qualified entity is understood through the employment of a single word.
590. Justification of the Section on the Abhyuditeṣṭi: In the performance of the Abhyuditeṣṭi, only a single causal factor (*kāraka*) is to be enjoined.
Furthermore, in the context of the Abhyuditeṣṭi, there is the statement: "He cooks [the oblation] together" (*saha śrapayati*).
Because of the identity of the deity for the curd (*dadhi*) and the *śrta* (boiled milk), the scriptural text prescribes their simultaneous cooking with the *agniṣṭoma*.

Consequently, the status of being a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) and the status of being the substratum (*adhikaraṇatva*) for the curd and the *śrta* are established by implication and are merely restated.

However, since only the specific deity and the object of the action (*kāraka*) are prescribed in relation to the archetype (*prakṛti*), namely the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); thus, this is not an injunction for a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*).
The initiated [scholars] raise this objection:

since the connection between each substance and the deity is understood in both the sentence concerning curds (*dadhivākya*) and the sentence concerning what is heard (*śrutavākya*), syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is difficult to avoid; thus, the position that these are distinct rites (*karmāntara*) is difficult to maintain.

Furthermore, it was accepted in the sixth book itself (6.1.22–23) that, in order to avoid the contingency of syntactical split, the sentences are intended as injunctions of distinct rites by means of the indicator of context (*prakṛtatāgrāhaka*).

Just as in the case of the text, "If both oblations of one who has suffered damage should perish, he should offer five-platter porridge to Indra," because there is an injunction for the porridge, an injunction for the measure of five platters, and because Indra—who is already optionally available alongside Mahendra—is enjoined as a constant requirement, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that this very sentence, by avoiding the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and the abandonment of the original ritual, prescribes a different ritual occasioned by the damage to the milk offering.

Otherwise, having tolerated a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the case of *abhyudayeṣṭi* as if it were a mere injunction of another deity, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself would have to be overturned here in the case of "one for whom both [are spoiled]" (*yasyobhayam*), where it would instead become an injunction for a substitute (*pratinidhi*) for the *ārtadoha*.
This is merely a scare tactic against those who do not overstep the principles of Mīmāṃsā.
For instance:
Even a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is more powerful than meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), because that would result in a loss of authority (*aprāmāṇya*).

For this very reason, it has been stated regarding the direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof: "For those [means of proof] obstructed by meaninglessness, the relative strength and weakness are reversed.

Therefore, since there is no syntactic unity with another injunction here, the rule "he cooks together" (*saha śrapayati*) is an injunction for simultaneous cooking; otherwise, if the *abhyudaya* passage were an injunction for a separate ritual action, simultaneous cooking would not be established merely from the words "curdled milk" (*dadhiśruta*) and "cooked rice in a pot" (*śrute carum*), and thus [the rule] would be meaningless.

Nor should it be argued that, just as in the primary injunction "One desiring long life should offer a *caru* of ghee in the form of a hundred *kṛṣṇala*-weights" there is a reference to the ghee already established by the subordinate injunction "he cooks it in ghee," so too in the *abhyudayeṣṭi* (the sacrifice for prosperity), there would be a reference to the *caru*-nature already established by the injunction for simultaneous cooking (*sahaśrapaṇa*) even in the case of a separate rite.

For it has been stated in the *Jāghanī-adhikaraṇa* (3.1.10) that the injunction of simultaneous mention applies when both [the substance and the action] are already established, or when neither is established.
Furthermore, if there is a reference to the *caru*, the establishment of the connection with its deity follows from the injunction of that [connection].

Therefore, in order to avoid the futility of the injunction for simultaneous cooking, and because the intention [of the text] is grasped precisely through its force, the phrase "one should offer" (*nirvapet*)—even though it is not explicitly taught as such—is intended to enjoin the connection with the deities for both *sviṣṭakṛt* and *cid* which are heard in the text. Consequently, even if one accepts a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) for each substance, it is not proper to abandon the contextually relevant ritual (*prakṛtakarma*) and to enjoin a ritual not present in the context (*aprakṛtakarma*).
As it has been said: "Whether it be figurative (*gauṇa*), indicative (*lākṣaṇika*), or even through a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), [the meaning is established] by itself."
"Who indeed would oppose that which the Veda itself relies upon?
(Vākyapadīya, p. 223).
For such is the only example for the acceptance of sentence-split (*vākyabheda*) as stated in this Vārttika, and no other.
The example of secondary indication (*gauṇatva*) is: "Just as one seizes two birds with a sling.
The example of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), however, is precisely the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

But in the case of the *ārtavākya*, because there is no indicator of intended meaning due to its pointlessness—just as in the injunction for simultaneous cooking—it is more logical to enjoin a separate ritual action in order to avoid splitting the sentence; thus, there is a difference [between the two cases].
The performance of the *abhyuditeṣṭi* [offering] occurs even if the moon rises prior to the pouring out of the oblation (*nirvāpa*) following the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
"It should be when [the grain] has been poured out, because of its connection with that.

The Bhāṣya states: Regarding this very example, there is a doubt: if the rising of the moon is understood after the grain has been poured out, then is it the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, or even if it has not been poured out? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It should be the *abhyuditeṣṭi* when it has been poured out and [the moonrise] is understood.
Why? Because of its connection with that.
For there is a connection with the pouring out [of the oblation], as in the text: "whose oblation has been poured out.
Therefore, this injunction does not apply when [the oblation] has not been offered.
Ṭup—In the previous case, a minor quality (*guṇa*) occurring within another word was examined;
here, an action (*kriyā*) occurring within another word is being examined.
This much is the difference.
Or, [it applies] when [the ritual] has commenced, for one who is intent on its completion.
The Commentary states: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
This injunction would apply merely to the commencement of the ritual procedure at an improper time.

For the occasion (*nimitta*) is indeed obtained by that much alone: "for whom the oblation (*havis*) rises" (*yasya havir abhyudeti*). Here, the mention of the "oblation" (*havirgrahaṇa*) serves as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). The rising characterized by the oblation—"the oblation of whom rises"—is the occasion; it characterizes the oblation as something already in operation, not as something indifferent. Therefore, when it is said, "the oblation rises," it is understood that the oblation which is already in operation rises.
For it is not possible to qualify [the injunction] by saying "for whom the oblation has been set aside" (*nirupta*);
for in that case, the sentence would be split.
Without regard for the phrase "for whom the oblation has been set aside," one could enjoin: "if the oblation rises while being carried."
Therefore, even regarding that which is undesirable, there is a desire for it.
The performance of the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice [is required]; the other [details], such as the new moon (*amā*) and the great digit (*mahākalā*), are merely characteristic marks.

The Commentary: Now, as for what was said—that there is a connection with the *nirupta* (that whose oblation has been set aside) in the statement "for whom the oblation is *nirupta*"—this term *nirupta* is merely a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*). The meaning is that [the rite applies] when some particular ritual act has commenced.
And likewise, there is an observation of another purpose.

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "Even with another purpose, this [scriptural passage] demonstrates this very point: 'If the sun should rise while the oblation has not yet been taken, that is well known; then this is the rule of conduct (*vratacaryā*): they prepare the curd-oblation from the previous day's grains; they wash the vessel; they prepare those very same [grains] again; in the afternoon, he removes them with a *parṇa*-branch. Just as the new-moon oblation is well known today, so indeed is that. Whether the rule of conduct is not observed, or if the sun should rise after the oblation has already been taken, then one should act otherwise: [using] these very rice-grains, well-purified. By prescribing a different procedure when the oblation has not been taken, it shows the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) even for an undesirable sunrise when the oblation has already been taken."

Śālikanātha: Since the mere occurrence at an improper time is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*), the occasional rite (*naimittika*) must indeed be performed even before the offering, once the rising of the moon is known. Soma: [Objection: Even here, there would be non-performance [of the rite] because of the consumption [of the oblation] after it has been placed on the mouth [of the fire]. Śālikanātha: By the rule *abhir āme* (Pāṇini 1.4.19), the word *abhi* functions as a *karmapravacanīya*. Consequently, the oblation denoted by the word ending in the second case—which serves as the occasion—is the qualifier of the rising of the moon, which acts as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, there is a connection [between the two].
Vi— "Above [the time of] moonrise, after the offering to the Lord (iṣṭinirvāpa), and even before it;
the first [alternative] is as stated, while the final position is by way of excluding the night."

Bhaṭṭa: Because of the scriptural statement, "He whose offering has been set forth" (*yasya haviḥ nirvṛtam*), the rising of the moon subsequent to the setting forth (*nirvāpa*) is the occasion (*nimitta*). Furthermore, since the commencement of the sacrifice on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is prescribed to take place before sunrise, this expiation does not apply when the moon rises before the setting forth. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the Siddhāntin replies]: By the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), the occasion is simply the beginning of the day delimited by the phrase "the offering should rise over him" (*havir abhyudiyāt*). Moreover, since the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) is obligatory (*nitya*), it cannot logically serve as an occasion; therefore, by process of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), this rule pertains exclusively to the new moon sacrifice (*darśa*).

For this very reason, even the indicative mark (liṅga) in the text, "If the oblation has not been taken up and the moon should rise," becomes appropriate. Maṇḍana [says]: "Even when the moon rises after it has risen, there is still a sacrifice. Śaṃkara [says]: "Because the pouring out [of the oblation] is not distinguished [from the case where it was already taken]."
In the consumption of the *abhyunīta* Soma, there is also the mention (*upalakṣaṇa*) of Indra. (Vi.
3.1.12) Because it is accepted [as a rule], for it cannot be said that a reason is defective even if its [logical] connection (*adṛṣṭa*) is not perceived.
*Bṛhatī*, page 130:
Because it serves the purpose of covering [the coals] for the sake of subsequent cooking.
Regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is revealed in scripture: "With the *veda* [grass-broom], he covers the coals with ashes."

In the investigation of whether that which is obtained by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) should be performed in the *saurya-caru* sacrifice or not, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it should be performed; the aphorism stating the established conclusion (*siddhānta-sūtra*) follows.
From the sūtra "na vā'rthāntarasaṃyogāt" (or rather not, because of connection with a different purpose), the word "not" (*na*) is understood to carry over.
The particle "ca" (and) serves to conjoin this with the previously mentioned characteristics of the animal sacrifice.

In the *saurya* oblation of rice, the practice of *abhyūha*—as stated in the injunction, "He pours the embers together with the *veda*-grass over [the vessel]"—is not to be performed. This is because *abhyūha* is for the purpose of further cooking; specifically, *abhyūha* consists of placing embers along with the *veda*-grass on top of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) to ensure proper baking.
And that [repetition] is not necessary in the case of the *caru* offering; thus, it should not be performed.
Furthermore, incessant repetition of the name is even worse than ignorance.
(*Bṛhatī*, p. 227).
Now follows the collection of four mantras for the taking up [of the fire] at the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*). (According to Amarasimha: *adhi* means "a woman," "wood," or "a pickaxe.

Regarding the mantras for kindling the fire (*abhyādāna*), because the ritual action is performed as a collective at the conclusion of the entire set, there is no option (*vikalpa*) to perform them individually with each mantra.
Alternatively, they may be performed at the end of the first mantra.
In that case, the first mantras function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by means of a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*), while the others function directly.
The mantras for the deity are four: "Thou art Agni," "Thou art Vahni," "Taking [the child] by the hand," and so forth.

Certain mantras are capable of being employed as introductory invocations; these are the examples cited in the section on Mantras (Mantrādhikaraṇa), Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 2.1.24–27. O Goddess, Mahākālī is said to be sixteen times greater than Amā.
Supreme illusion is established within the embodied being, assuming the form of the body.
O fair-faced one, those very digits of the moon, beginning with the new moon (amā) and ending with the full moon (paurṇamāsī),
are declared to be the sixteen lunar days (tithis).
In that regard, a month consists of two fortnights, namely the bright and the dark, in sequence;
the bright fortnight is that which causes the moon to increase, while the dark fortnight is characterized by the waning of the moon.

The lunar days known as the "waxing fortnight" (pakṣati) are fifteen in number; they end with the new moon (darśa) in the dark fortnight, while those of the bright fortnight end with the full moon (pūrṇamā).
From such statements as these, [it follows that] the lunar day (*tithi*) is not a mere absence of the moon;

rather, *amāvāsyā* (the new moon) occurs when, among the lunar digits remaining after the *kalā* has passed, the separation of each individual digit from the solar disc—from the initial separation of one part up to the separation of the other parts, or from the initial conjunction of one part up to the conjunction of the other parts—occurs over a certain duration of time. That duration of time, corresponding respectively to the bright and dark fortnights, is what is designated by the terms *pratipad*, *dvitīyā*, and so forth.

Therefore, it should be understood that the words *tithi* and *pratipad* and so forth have their primary denotative power (*śakti*) only with respect to the lunar phases (*kalā*), while their application to time is by means of a restricted metaphorical indication (*niruddha-lakṣaṇā*). (Bhāṭṭadīpikā 5.4.7). Furthermore, because of a scriptural injunction, there is a difference in time between the subsidiary and the principal rites: the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is on the later day, while the altar (*vedi*) is on the earlier day.
On the day before the new moon, one prepares the sacrificial altar (vedi).
[Bhāṣya 1.3.12.1] "The new moon kills the teacher; the fourteenth day kills the pupil;
the eighth day and the full moon kill the Veda; therefore, one should avoid them."
By such statements as these, there is a recollection of the teacher (*adhicārya*) regarding the class of phenomena (*dharmajāta*) that constitutes the subject matter of study (Su. p.

53). On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between the non-appearance of the moon and the time of the new moon, which is fixed by its specific measure according to the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
This sacrificer (p. 730); this is he who possesses a thousandfold human power (594), for he is indeed that.
From that [he offers] on dry grass;
having given dry [grass],
they support nourishing foods, like water supports an island.
In the sense of the sentence, however, there is a connection between the first, third, second, and fourth words.
Therein, the word *yat* (which), being supported by the pronoun *sā* (as indicated by the phrase *sāṅkhyata-dākṣitaḥ*, meaning "supported by that word"), is supplied in the third case-ending.
Just as fire blazes upon dry grass, so too is that spear (*ṛṣṭi*) which is observed as your constant companion—that spear, O Vaddhamā, belongs to us alone through your grace.

Even these Maruts, who scatter the ancient water in the form of rain and sustain foodstuffs like waters sustaining an island— being dear to you as they are— they too belong to us alone. Therefore, being thus possessed of common property with us, grant us immortality (and not merely wealth).

Vārttika 1.2.4.14, pp. 1.7–1.8: Regarding the reading "this sacrificer" (*ayaṃ yajamānaḥ*), a modification of the reading to "this sacrificer who has pressed and will press the Soma" (*ayaṃ sutāsuti yajamānaḥ*) is directly prescribed in the *maitrāvaruṇa-praiṣa* mantra obtained through the *codaka* rule for the *savanīya-paśu*.
On the tenth day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), the worship of the *āhavanīya* fire must be performed with the verse "This [is] Sahasramānava," sung to its melody.
Now, there might be an option [between the two] because of their being one, since both serve that same purpose. 9.2.8.29. Section 2.
Commentary: Or rather thus.
On the tenth day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), after the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and before the *mānasa-stotra*, there is the worship of the *āhavanīya* fire.

As stated in the *Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa* (4.9.1): "Having risen after the *patnīsaṃyāja*, the wise one approaches the *āhavanīya* with the verse, 'This [Soma] of a thousand men... In a certain specific ritual, it is heard: "He worships the *āhavanīya* with this [verse], 'This [Soma] of a thousand men...
Regarding this, the meaning is subject to doubt: should the worship be performed with the verse unchanted (*apragītā*) or chanted (*pragītā*)?
What is obtained? Is it [the result] by means of a chanted verse or by means of an unchanted one?
Why? Because there is no specific instruction. This very same ṛc is both chanted and unchanted.
For they record it in both ways;
therefore, no distinction should be observed.
And if there is no distinction, then because it is a matter of praise, there is an option between the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.
With the verse, "This Sahasramānava," one worships the Āhavanīya fire; thus, there is recognition of its application whether it is sung (pragītā) or un-sung (apragītā).
Whether sung or un-sung, it can accomplish the worship or the praise. Therefore, there is an option (vikalpa) between the two.
The application [of the mantra] would be based on the explicit statement.
Commentary: This being the position reached, we reply: it is only when chanted that it should be applied, not when unchanted.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement.
What is the statement? "With this verse, 'This one is a thousandfold man' (RV 10.90.5)," is the word used in the context;
and in the Sāmaveda, that [verse] occurs as a chanted (pragīta) one in its original form.
The phrase "by this" is connected to that [verse].
But is it not the case that even a non-sung (apragītā) verse is recited there?
True; however, that [recitation] is for the purpose of establishing a connection with the singing (pragāṇa).
For it is not possible to perform chanting (*pragāṇa*) upon that which has not already been chanted;
the study of the *ṛc* is for the sake of the *sāman*,
as it is understood that the accomplishment of the *sāman* does not occur without the *ṛc*.
However, even without the *sāman*, the *ṛc* is accomplished;
the *ṛc* does not require the *sāman*.

Therefore, when it is said in the Sāmaveda that one "approaches" (*upatiṣṭhate*) or "praises" (*stauti*), the understanding arises only with respect to the *ṛc* that has been set to melody (*pragītā*), and not with respect to one that is not set to melody (*apragītā*).
He says: If there is a conviction regarding the sung [verse] because of the context, then by virtue of the explicit statement, it applies to the unsung [verse].
For the unsung [verse] is also recited in another scripture;
therefore, setting aside the context, it is grasped by the syntactical statement (*vākya*).
It is said:
the *ṛc* is not grasped by means of the entire sentence; for this is merely the citation of a representative portion (*pratīka*).
In the phrase "with this [verse] beginning with 'ayaṃ sahasramānavaḥ'," the word *ṛk* primarily denotes the specific verse under discussion;
in your view, however, the mention of the opening words (*pratīka*) would involve figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
And between direct denotation (*śruti*) and figurative indication, direct denotation is the more logical, not figurative indication.
Therefore, one should perform the attendance with a song already sung.
This being the position reached, we reply:
the word "with this" (*etayā*) refers to that which is proximate.
And the *pragītā* (chanted) version is proximate. Although the *apragītā* (un-chanted) version is also proximate, nevertheless, only the *pragītā* is to be accepted.
Why? Because the recitation of the *apragītā* version is for the sake of another purpose.
For it is not possible to produce the *sāman* when [the verse] is not chanted.
But is it not the case that even the unchanted form is recited in the scriptures, and thus it is grasped by the sentence?
It is replied:

In that case, the connection must be inferred through context (*prakaraṇa*); in the other case, however, it is established by the direct statement (*śruti*). Thus, the word "with this" (*etayā*)—which denotes what is proximate—is not sublated.

Soma: Although there was no option (*vikalpa*) in the preceding case, an option is stated here. Now, because [the *saṃhitā*] is recited at the end of the *saṃhitā* that is not yet chanted (*apragītā*) [Sāma Veda 4.9], its recitation is solely for the purpose of chanting; for the *saṃhitā* text serves the purpose of chanting by means of preserving the original form of the *ṛc*. "With what is not a *yajus*, one should drive away the calves" [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.3]; this is a separate injunction regarding the *ayana* sacrifices.

There is no restrictive rule regarding chanting (*gāna*) when approaching the fire; for even if the name is not modified, there is indeed a deviation from the subject matter (*prakṛta*). Therefore, the approach is performed with the chant (*pragīta*).

Bhaṭṭa: In a certain specific rite (on the tenth day of the twelve-day period within the Gavāmayana), this verse, "This [man] of a thousandfold lineage" (*ayaṃ sahasramānavaḥ*), is recited both as a chanted (*pragītā*) and an unchanted (*apragītā*) hymn.

Furthermore, it is enjoined by the rule: "Having performed the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, the wise one, having risen, worships the Āhavanīya fire with this [verse], namely 'This [man] of a thousandfold lineage' (using the *aticchandas* meter)" (Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa 4.9.1).
Since it is recited in two ways (by means of these two methods), both forms are employed as optional alternatives (*vikalpa*).
This being the case, the recitation of the unchanted verse is solely for the purpose of chanting;
for neither chanting nor comprehension of meaning is possible when the nature [of the text] has not been determined.
However, since the chanted verse requires no other purpose and is thus available, it is that which should be adopted for the rite of *upasthāna*.

The reading of that very [verse] as *pragīta* (chanted) in another scripture is also solely for the purpose of making known its specific form (*ṛksvara*) to those who follow that tradition; thus, there is no contradiction with the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the chanting found in the other scripture.
Maṇḍana states: "The worship is performed with the *pragīta* [verse].
Śaṅkara states: "And the meaning of the mantra is that it is indeed *pragīta* along with the *sahasra*."

In the *Pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument) stated at Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 4.1.4, it is argued that the statement, "He drives away the calves with a non-Yajus formula" (*ayajuṣā vatsānapākaroti*) and "The cow that yields milk for the evening [milk] is without a strainer" (*apavitravatī gāṃ dohayed dhi*), which speak of driving away the calves in the morning, is indeed a restrictive injunction (*paryudāsa-vidhi*) excluding the use of Yajus formulas and so forth.

Furthermore, in the passage, "Beans (*māṣa*), *varaka*, and *kodrava* grains are indeed unfit for sacrifice" (*ayajñiyā vai māṣāḥ varakāḥ kodravāḥ*), the term "unfit for sacrifice" (*ayajñiya*)—by its effort to convey the sense of being unworthy—is a prohibition against their being used as sacrificial means (*sādhana*). Consequently, one understands a prohibition of beans and the like in every instance other than those where they are specifically prescribed.
One should not negate them;
rather, it should be understood that they must indeed be apprehended when there is an absence of a commonality of substance (dravyasāmānya).
Bhāṭṭa 6.1.6.3.

"One should offer a *caru* of mudga beans for one desiring cattle"—in this case, it might be argued that since beans (*māṣa*), chickpeas (*caṇaka*), and *kodrava* are unfit for sacrifice, they serve as substitutes (*pratinidhi*) in the absence of mudga beans, because they are capable of performing the function of the *caru* (the cooked rice offering). Furthermore, there is no prohibition against using them.
If this is argued, it is not so.
Because the statement, "Beans and the like are indeed unfit for sacrifice," results in a prohibition of those grains, beans and so forth are [excluded] when they would otherwise be obtained.
In the case of the *ayana* sacrifices, there is a distinct injunction because of the attachment of a specific name.

Because of the observation of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the statement, "In the *ayana*s there is a separate injunction due to the application of a distinct name," it follows that for the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* and others, there is a separate performance consisting of the *prasthānahoma* together with the *sāṃnāyya* vessels. Oṃ, the analogy of the magnet. This [analogy] pertains to the commencement of action while remaining indifferent;
it consists of a group of characteristics such as the transition to another location.
They are prescribed in proximity to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

Thus, its status as a modification (vikāra) is established.
