thus one enters into the destruction of the objects of the sense of agency,
just as an immutable witness or a magnet [attracts iron].
They do exist;
moreover, it is possible to designate them by these words because they are used in their etymological sense:
"One desiring offspring should sacrifice," and "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya."

therefore, it is not a separate ritual act.

[Sāhasī 919] The *dākṣas* are the descendants of Dakṣa; their *ayana*—that is, their performance characterized by repetition—is the *Dākṣāyaṇa*.
Is the fruit [of the action] due to a quality of the two Full Moon sacrifices themselves, or is it an injunction for a separate ritual act?
[The answer is:
The connection with the name is due to a quality.
Oṃ. The maxim of the magnet and the needle. It is said that the Supreme is devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka).
Thus, the departure together with the two *sāṃnāyya* jars is [the view] in the *sākaṃprasthāyīya*.
Regarding the deliberation, he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the solstices (*ayana*), such as the *dākṣāyaṇayajña* and others.
As for what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view— that this refers to a different ritual action because of the attachment of a specific name—

that is explained as a mere departure [from the previous topic], according to the analogy of the magnet and the needle, since the Lord lacks the status of being the cause of the world's birth and so forth.

Likewise, regarding the transfer to the location of the Āhavanīya fire, this "transfer" is a separate injunction and a distinct ritual act; it does not, however, constitute a modification (*vikāra*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. To this, the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) provides the following reply.
However, there is the attachment of a designation (*saṃjñopabandha*).
In that regard, it is said that the status of being the cause of the world belongs to that which has been superimposed [upon the substrate] by virtue of the existence of that [designation].
Therefore, just as in another statement, [the sacrifice] is denoted by the word *ukthya*.
Why? Because of the attachment of a name (*saṃjñopabandhāt*), specifically through a new name such as the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* and others;
it is not because it is a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), but rather because of a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
"Ayana" means "returning";
this is possible.
Śrīkara 1.1.19 (Brahma Sūtra).
Of iron, directly;
when a specific form is shown in its proximity, [it is understood] because of the connection with the designation "one desiring cattle should take the Ukthya. Because of the connection.
For it is designated by an unprecedented name:
these priests of the sacrificer Dakṣa are "Dākṣas."
Even in the absence of an explicit injunction, that [result] follows from mere proximity;
thus, even for the well-known ritual element of the *ukthya*, there is a connection to the fruit.
These *ayanas* are thus linked [to their respective results].
Therefore, it is a different ritual action.
The *Dākṣāyaṇayana* is [called] *Dākṣāyaṇa*.
But who is Dakṣa? He who is energetic (*utsāhī*).
It moves the needle of the magnet; likewise, there is a specific arrangement of the magnet here as well, so this is not untenable.
But is it not the case that the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is not seen here? [The word] *dakṣa* is derived from the root *dakṣ*, which signifies the action of exertion.

And it is heard in the scripture that those who worship the body and so forth, as well as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), set out together with curd and milk, like the maxim of the needle and the thread, [attaining] uninterrupted and eternal [results]; thus it is called "Dākṣāyaṇa."
What then? It is by means of this [term] "dākṣāyaṇa.
And the injunction for the ritual action is devoid of a specific quality;
the simultaneous setting forth of the cooking-pots (kumbhīs) is the quality.
Thus, in the vicinity of the *āhavanīya* fire,

for those who possess the excellence of having reached the culmination of severed meditation (*dhyāna*) and the performance of the *gāriṣṭha* rites, and who are in their final bodies, [the result follows] from that very action; since it is understood that the action itself is the means, how could a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) be the cause of the fruit?
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he states another reason with the word "ca" (and):
"even when there is a cutting off of the qualities."
Transference (*saṃkramaṇa*) is the quality (*guṇa*).
In the *saṃkramayajña*, thus [it is performed] by virtue of that quality; [hence the name] *Dākṣāyaṇayajña*.
The identity [of the individual soul] with the Śiva-jyotir-liṅga has been taught [in the scriptures].
[Objection: What is the means [to that realization]? It is said: Śrīkara. 3.1.18 (Brahma-sūtra). [Answer: It is stated.
Even though this is so, nevertheless, regarding the specific [case],
he states the traditional teaching that "it is not a subordinate element" (*aguṇa*),
beginning with: "One should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña," and so forth.
There is a connection with the notions [of the qualities],
according to the analogy of the magnet and the needle, because of the existence of the qualityless Brahman;
for, as in the case of "red turbans" and so forth, they are primarily qualifiers, since [Brahman] is incapable of being employed [in ritual action].
The injunction regarding speech is indeed for the purpose of impelling action;
and that impulsion is distinguished by the completion of qualities rather than being devoid of qualities.
Because there is a flaw in the non-dualist position which asserts that *prakṛti* is the cause of the world;
for those very same scriptural passages establish only the connection with the fruit for those [who perform the rites],
and are devoid of any injunction [regarding the cause].

Even if a connection with the qualities (*guṇa*) is accepted, the injunction for the sacrifice remains as stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*): "The sentence is completed with respect to the fruit" (2.3.26). [This applies] to the insentient *pradhāna* alone, according to the analogy of the magnet and the iron needle.
For instance, the ritual action under discussion is not first enjoined with respect to the fruit, as in [the statement], "To all... (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 4.3.13);
the meaning is that it certainly exists.
To this, he states the reply.
Completion (*samāpti*) is the conclusion of the sentence.
Even if one accepts that Brahman is the cause of the world, its quality of being devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*) is compromised.
By the very statement "the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]," their fruitfulness is already established.
And the sentence regarding the fruit is completed; it is not distinct. As for those other sentences which are beyond doubt.
2|1|29 Brahmasūtra: [The Self] is not [the agent], because it is self-established according to the analogy of the iron needle and the magnet, and because another designation would be redundant;
nor is it a different action, because [it is] the subject under discussion...
In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states another reason:
the sentences concerning the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* and others result in being injunctions of a fruit [attained] through a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of progeny (*prajā*).

[This is] because it would contradict the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the fourfold karma of those whose minds have been rendered continuously auspicious by the grace of the Lord, and because it would entail the undesirable consequence of an excessive burden of specific injunctions (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).
By him [it is said]: "The section on the two fruits is completed. For the sake of the fruit consisting of progeny and so forth, [one performs] the Dākṣāyaṇayajña."

[The sūtra] "One should offer [the oblation] for the sake of desire," and so forth; by these [passages], it is determined that [the fruit] is not undifferentiated, for there is destruction [of the merit]. (Brahma Sūtra 4.1.13)

Because it is impossible to apply the ritual action [to another context], the quality (guṇa) is enjoined as a qualification for the fruit; having thus accomplished its purpose, the sentence [is exhausted]. Therefore, this is an injunction of a distinct ritual action.
They are distinct and of different characteristics, yet they are indeed equal to those [others]. *Oṃ*, this is the principle of the unasked ornament (*ayācitamaṇḍananyāya*),
and the principle of the non-wakeful engagement (*ajāgarapravartananyāya*).
It is argued: "Nor is it untenable for these [mantras] to have the primary ritual action as their substratum on the grounds that they lack the capacity to be means of accomplishment;
rather, there is modification, because of the context."
The sentences beginning with "yaṇ" [also] state that the fruit results from a subordinate element (guṇa).
Therefore:
An object obtained without even a request is called *ayācita* (unasked).

For it is evident that, in the sequence of setting out together, those two [the unasked and the *sahārtha*] serve as the means for accomplishing that ritual act. Thus, he sets aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the statement.
This is not a separate ritual action;
rather, the Dākṣāyaṇayajña and others are modifications (*vikāra*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
*Maṇḍana* means adornment or decoration.

[The section] on the unasked and the unannounced (598): by means of a ruddy, one-year-old female calf, there is the designation of both sets of deities— the deities of the fore-offerings (prayāja) and the after-offerings (anuyāja).

For this very reason, the statement from another scripture—“That which [is recited] as ‘yadayāḍ devānām ājyapānām,’ that belongs to the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s”—is appropriately understood as a restatement of what is established by logic (*nyāya*). Therefore, even in the *udayanīya* sacrifice, which is not a *prayāja*, there is no omission of that [mantra]. (Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa 4.3.1)

In that context, for every handful [of grass], there is a repetition of the cutting mantra, "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods," and not a single recitation.
(The term *ayuk* refers to odd-numbered handfuls of *darbha* grass; *yuk* refers to even-numbered handfuls).

Bhāṭṭa 6.1.1, p. 218: There were scholars named Aruṇaparāśaras. Vārttika 11.6.1, p. 231: “*Aruṇayā*” is an injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding a quality (*guṇa*). Bālam Bhaṭṭī, p. 24: Since the word *aruṇā* is connected with an instrumental case-ending expressing the instrument (*karaṇa*), it indicates the identification (*abhimāna*) with the redness; therefore, redness (*aruṇimā*) is the instrument.

Su. Pṛ. 1429. In the case of the word *aruṇā* (red), its connection with the purchase is established by way of delimiting the substance. Vā. 3.2.3, p. 762: "He purchases Soma with a red, one-year-old, yellow-eyed [cow]"—this is heard in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. In this context, the word *aruṇa* denotes either the quality of redness or the genus of redness, but it does not denote a specific individual.

And the third [case-ending] expresses the instrumentality of that which is capable [of performing an action], but for that purpose, there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a substance. *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 3.1.6. In the case of "He buys with a red one" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*), there are three means of proof (*pramāṇa*)—namely, direct statement (*śruti*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), and context (*prakaraṇa*)—for the fact that redness (*āruṇya*) serves as the means to the effect that accomplishes the transcendental result (*apūrva*). Even among these, the power of application (*viniyojakatva*) belongs to direct statement alone, not to the others. *Bhāṭṭadīpikā* 3.1.7, p. 255. In such cases as "He buys with a red, yellow-eyed [cow]," the individual (*vyakti*) does not appear from the word at all; for it is established that only the genus (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*) serve to delimit the individual and function as the instrument.

The connection between the genus (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*) belongs to the word-meaning through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with gender and number alone; therefore, the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) occurs there precisely by way of that connection.

(PMS 1.3.10). In the case of "aruṇayā piṅgākṣyā ekahāyanyā" ("with a red, yellow-eyed, one-year-old [cow]"), although [the qualities] are not mutually connected, they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) because of their connection with the verb "to purchase" (*krīṇāti*).
(Vārttika 3.2.9, p. 769): "aruṇayā piṅgākṣyā ekahāyanyā."
By means of the two [qualities] of tawny eyes and self-luminosity, the constituent parts consisting of qualities are characterized;
by those, the substance composed of parts is indicated,
and that arises from a combination.

3|1|6|12, p. 638: "He buys Soma with a reddish-brown, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow. Here, the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*) pertains specifically to the one-year-old cow used in the purchase, and not to the general context of the act of buying itself. Bhāṣya 3|1|6|12, p. 673: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the [quality] beginning with "reddish" (*aruṇādi*) is subordinate (*śeṣa*). This is the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (Topic of the Red Cow), numbered 599.
It is heard [in the scripture]:

therein, the word *aruṇā* denotes the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*). By the direct statement of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), its status as the means for the purchase of Soma is understood.
Although a quality (*guṇa*) is formless, nevertheless, it is the quality itself that is stated here to be the means (*sādhana*) by virtue of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*).

Since that [status as a means] is not possible without a substance (*dravya*), its function as a delimiter of the substance is postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Thus, the two qualities, which are directly connected with the purchase (*kraya*), are subsequently connected through presumptive testimony as mutual delimiters of one another.
That being the case, it results in the conclusion that "one purchases [the cow] with a one-year-old female cow characterized by redness. Thus, the red color and so forth are subsidiary (śeṣa).

By direct statement (*śruti*), there is a connection with action in general; by syntactical connection (*vākya*), there is an application to its specific instance; and by context (*prakaraṇa*), it belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

Even though there is a coexistence of direct statement and context as scriptural injunctions, there is no contradiction because they serve to mutually assist one another; thus, in the investigation of relative strength and weakness, this [conflict] does not arise.
Vārttika 3.1.7.14, p. 822. This is the *aruṇādi*-nyāya (the principle concerning the "red" [cow], etc.).

The *aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the *aruṇādhikaraṇanyāya*, the *aruṇānyāya*, the *aruṇāśabdanyāya*, and the *anekahāyananyāya*— by these terms, a single topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) [Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.6–12] is understood.
According to the *aruṇādi-nyāya* (3.1.6–12), because multiple words are taken up within a single sentence, the fruit (*phala*) is the *apūrva* [transcendental result] belonging to them collectively.
Vārttika 2.1.1.1, p. 373: The Section on the "Aruṇā" (The Red One).

In the word *aruṇā*, the base ending in a feminine suffix first denotes, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), a substance qualified by that quality. Although the substance is thus understood, because its denotation is secondary, the heard instrumental case-ending expresses the quality itself as the instrument with respect to the purchase (*kraya*).

In reality, however, the word *aruṇa* denotes a substance through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) while functioning primarily as a mere quality; for when the primary sense is possible, it is improper to resort to secondary indication. Nor should it be argued that, given this, the feminine designation *aruṇā* is untenable—based on the principle “the gender and number of words denoting qualities depend on their substratum” (*guṇavacanānām āśrayato liṅgavacanāni*), which implies that only words like *śukla* (white) denote a substance where the quality is subordinate and thus take the gender of the substance. This objection is not valid.

The meaning of that [sūtra] is indeed this: "There is a connection with gender for those words capable of denoting a substance as a subordinate element of a quality, which are connected with an action by way of delimitation.

And in cases such as *aruṇākṣaḥ* ("red-eyed"), the word *aruṇa* necessarily denotes both the quality and the substance; thus, even though it is a word denoting a quality alone, its connection with gender occurs through the female animal (*hāyanī*), which serves as the delimiter. However, since words such as *rūpa* (form) are never used to denote a substance without suffixes like *matup*, they do not possess the gender of the delimited substance—as in the case of *baṭo rūpaḥ* ("the boy's form").
Thus, there is no possibility of such usage [as "the white exists in the water"].

In the expression "white exists in the water," words such as "white" (śukla), which connect with the action by way of delimitation (*pariccheda*), do not take the gender of the qualified substrate (*guṇin*). However, those that connect with the action by way of the delimited object (*paricchedya*) do take the gender of the qualified substrate, as in "the white universal" (*śuklā sāmānyam*), and so forth; this is the meaning.

Thus it is established that the word *aruṇā*, even though it ends in a feminine suffix, denotes a mere quality (*guṇavacana*). And the third case (*tṛtīyā*) expresses that redness (*āruṇya*) as an instrument (*karaṇatayā*). While expressing it thus, because of its identity with the quality of redness, it does not directly possess the capacity to be a means for accomplishing the action; rather, it rests upon the quality’s inherent capacity to delimit a substance, which, by way of the delimited substance, serves as the means for accomplishing the action through a mediated process.
And the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is capable of being delimited by the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*);
for delimitation is indeed a specific cognition of the substance as that which is to be delimited.

Thus, the meaning of the sentence is the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of purchase, which has as its instrument the substance—a one-year-old, reddish-brown-eyed cow—as delimited by the quality of redness.

Thus, since there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the instrumentality implied by the instrumental case-ending is understood to be conveyed by the primary nominal stem (*prakṛti*) itself, and it is adopted as the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

However, if there were a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), the instrumental case in "aruṇā" would merely be restating (*anuvādinī*) the instrumentality residing in the substance, which is the secondary meaning of the nominal stem.
And when syntactic unity is possible, it is not proper to resort to a split in the sentence.

Nor should it be argued: "Why should redness (*āruṇya*) be included in the purchase solely because it delimits the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), since its status as a means for the purchase is established even through any substance whatsoever"? For, compared to its role as a delimiter, the one-year-old cow is syntactically connected with the quality [redness] within a single sentence; and since the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) of the quality—which requires a delimited object—is satisfied by the one-year-old cow mentioned in its own sentence, it is necessary to describe the satisfaction of that expectation through another quality or another substance.

It is precisely with this intention that the restrictive rule (*niyamapada*) was established in the Sūtra (6.1.122): "From each one, there should be a *cit*. Otherwise, he would have simply said, "From each one, there should be an *anvaya*. Nor should it be argued that because substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) have the same referent, there should be an option (*vikalpa*) between them, as in the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*).

Indeed, the mere fact of having a single purpose (*ekārthatva*) is not the seed for an option (*vikalpa*), because that [purpose] serves as the unifier only when there is identity of the means (*dvārakatva*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an option even among the sacrificial pan (*kapāla*), winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), fire-pot (*uddhvana*), pestle (*musala*), and so forth, regarding their function in the *puroḍāśa*.
For rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*) share a single means in the sacrifice, namely the form of producing the *puroḍāśa* and other offerings.

In the present case, since both [the substance and the quality] serve as means for the purchase— the substance by way of bringing about the bending down [of the cow], and the quality by way of delimiting the substance— and since both are subordinate to the substance,
there is an option (vikalpa) between them, as in the *aruṇā* section.

Now, even if this were so, in the cases of "He buys with the red [cow]" (*aruṇā krīṇāti*) and "With a one-year-old red cow" (*aruṇaikāhayanyā*), there would not be the impossibility of both [the quality and the substance] being connected simultaneously, because a single word heard only once cannot logically have simultaneous connection with both.
Nor can there be a connection with both by way of alternation (*paryāya*); for from a single verb heard only once, it is impossible to derive two successive meanings.
If this is argued, it is not a fault.
The syntactic connection (*niveśa*) of redness (*āruṇya*) with the one-year-old cow (*ekāhayanī*) is not verbal (*śābda*), but rather implied (*ārthika*).

For first, when the productive urge of purchase (*kraya-bhāvanā*)—which has both the quality of redness and the substance of the one-year-old cow as its instruments—is understood through the constraints of the words, one considers the absence of any statement that redness is a direct means of accomplishing the purchase. Consequently, one establishes its status as a means to the action by way of delimiting the substance of the one-year-old cow.
Thus, because the connection of redness with the one-year-old cow is an implied connection, there is no occurrence of the "two sets of three contradictory factors" (*viruddha-trikadvaya-doṣa*).
And even so, how is it that the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is restricted only to the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), given the injunctions:
"He buys with a goat," "He buys with gold," "He buys with a cow," "He buys with a bull," and "He buys with a draft-ox"? [This is] like the discussion on the redness (*aruṇādhikaraṇa*).

Because there is no capacity for mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) by way of *nayi* (the suffix -tā), there would be an impossibility of forming compounds in such cases as "bring the blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam ānaya*) or "fetch water with the blue jar" (*nīlaghaṭena jalam āhara*).
Nor can that capacity be established through a subsequent mutual connection, because that itself is difficult to maintain.

For a verbal cognition of mutual connection is not produced by the word itself, since it is impossible for a quality-word uttered once to terminate simultaneously in both an action and a substance; this is because words, cognitions, and actions do not possess a function that ceases and then resumes (*viramya-vyāpāra*).

Nor should it be argued that once the connection between the quality and the possessor of the quality with the action has first been understood through the constraints of verbal syntax, a subsequent mental synthesis of their mutual relationship is then postulated due to the requirement for a delimiting relation (*pariccheda*) and a delimited object (*paricchedya*).
For the mutual connection between the quality and the possessor of the quality is what necessitates a compound (*samāsa*), since the rule for forming compounds applies only to such words.
However, when the words "blue" (*nīla*) and "jar" (*ghaṭa*), which denote those two, are heard as being connected to the action, there is no mutual connection between them.

Therefore, since the two imagined [entities] possess a common substratum in the form of the word-meanings (*pārthika-anvaya*), the expressive power must be attributed to the two words as they are actually heard.

For in that case, the imagination of the two words denoting the quality and the qualified must be of those ending in case-terminations, and not of those devoid of case-terminations, nor of those in compound (*samāsa*). It cannot be the first [option], because there can be no mutual connection between two words ending in case-terminations that express [their meanings] as qualified by specific grammatical relations (*kāraka*).

Not the second [alternative]; for those two words, being devoid of case-endings (*vibhakti*), are unfit for usage and unsuitable for composition (*samāsa*), since a *karmadhāraya* compound—prescribed under the governing rule *sup supā* and so forth—is impossible between the words *nīla* and *ghaṭa* when they are not joined [by a case-ending].

Nor the third; for semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) must be understood as a mutual connection (*parasparānvaya*) based on the consideration of the compounded words, and the compound itself depends upon the knowledge of that competency; thus, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Furthermore, if one were to assume such a cognition in every instance, and consequently postulate a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in accordance with it, and further postulate a synthesis (*anusandhāna*) based on the assumed word-meanings, there would be great complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, by accepting that even the word *aruṇā* has a primary denotation (*śakti*) consisting of the form of a linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) directed toward a qualified object (*guṇaviśiṣṭaparatva*), there is no fault whatsoever, as a qualified factor (*viśiṣṭakāraka*) is enjoined by restating the sacrifice (*ṛtu-anuvāda*). Nor should it be argued: "If the word *aruṇā* refers to a qualified object, how can this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*) proceed? For the commencement of that section is also easily established.

For instance, since the word *aruṇā* does not possess a figurative (secondary) meaning when applied to a substance qualified by a quality, it must be explained in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the same manner as the previous [case]. The establishment of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) proceeds by demonstrating that the primary power (*śakti*) [of the word] is distinct [from its figurative sense].

The Sūtra, however, should be construed as follows: because there is a single action—meaning, because the verb is one—and because there is unity of purpose, which constitutes syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is not logical.

Therefore, there is a restriction between the substance and the quality—wherein the word *ekahāyanī* has the substance as its primary meaning and the word *aruṇa* has the quality as its subordinate meaning—and their syntactic connection (*anvaya*) occurs in the act of purchase (*kraye*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*), as they both convey a qualified object.
This is the general direction [of the argument]. This is the path accepted by the Prābhākaras, the Grammarians, and the Ritualists.

The *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* establishes that, because no substance is explicitly mentioned in the sentence “One purchases Soma with a reddish-brown, yellow-eyed [cow],” the quality of redness (*āruṇya*) must be construed with the very substance mentioned within its own sentence.
In the *Bhūṣaṇasāra*, under the determination of the meaning of verbal roots, verse 2, in the section on the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (3.1.6.2), the application of the quality is explained.
And that [is established] by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

In the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (PMS 3.1.4–7, p. 665), it is stated that the restriction of qualities occurs through their connection with what is directly stated in the remainder of the text (*śrutaśeṣasaṃyoga*).
However, in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the explicit mention of the thing being restricted by its own word is not part of the logical conclusion (*nyāyarāddhānta*).
However, it is simply a figurative application (upādāna) in some manner or other.

Bāla. p. 167. And it has been stated by Bhavadeva in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*: "The entire [process] is through indication (lakṣaṇā), because the very act of denotation (abhidhāna) has as its purpose the imposition of an inseparable relation with the thing denoted.

(*Bhaṭṭālaṃkāra*, p. 31). Now, it might be argued that in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated that there is a prescription of a staff (*daṇḍa-vidhāna*), saying, "the subordinate meaning is what is prescribed."
Since [the application] is obtained everywhere by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the two recitations (*anuvacana*) are specifically pointed out; thus, there is no contradiction.

(Vārttika 4.1.6.8, p. 1237). Now, an objection is raised: from the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in the term *āgneyatā*, it appears that even the relation (*saṃbandha*) is denoted as being inseparable (*avibhaktatā*). And that [denotation of the relation] is improper, because it is equivalent to the prohibition of expressing a relation established in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*. This is the doubt.

Su. Pṛ. 462: It was stated in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (Vārttika 3.1.7–14, p. 715) that the act of purchase (*kraya*), which has the enjoined [substance] as its basis, does not qualify the substance being connected with the quality.
This is because, in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, the connection understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is designated as being derived from syntactical connection (*vākyīya*).

Su. 3.7, p. 70, from the fifth application: the reason given is "because there is no connection with its qualifiers. This is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because even though words denoting universals (*jāti*) and qualities (*guṇa*)—such as "the cow is white" (*goḥ śuklaḥ*) or "the red female" (*aruṇā strī*)—do not possess knowledge of specific individuals or substances, their denotation of the individual substance has been refuted in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* and *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*. (p. 1460) Even if it were argued that while there is no connection with a qualifier for that which is merely implied, and therefore denotation occurs because such a connection is observed, that too has been refuted by the fact that both [alternatives] are seen in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* and *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*.

Or rather: when a connection is heard, the resolution of doubt and the removal of contradiction are to be understood as in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (Sūtras 3.1.10–20), because [the term] sequentially assumes its own connection through syntactical unity (*vākya*) and by the principle stated in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa-vārttika* (p. 603).

Page 729, 3|1|10|19: In the *Vārttika* on the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, it is established that a *bahuvrīhi* compound possesses denotative power (*śakti*) itself with respect to the meaning of the external word (*anyapadārtha*), and not merely figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

*Soma.* 3|1|20: Furthermore, the claim that the case-ending of an adjective serves solely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvārthatva*) is also incoherent; for this is accepted by the Naiyāyikas—who postulate identity (*abheda*) as the meaning—and by the Mīmāṃsakas, who accept the theory established in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* that each [quality] connects [with the action] individually.

(Duṣyanta 1.2.8.21). (Bālakrīḍā, p. 166). By the principle of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*.

The relationship between the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). [Durmādhava, 1.2.1.1, p. 1627]. By the logic of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the substance denoted by the two derivative terms *ekahāyanī* and *piṅgākṣī* with the genus (*jāti*) denoted by the word *go*. [Bālambhaṭṭī, p. 167]. When there is a conflict between the force of the words (*śabda-sāmarthya*) and the force of the thing itself (*vastu-sāmarthya*), it is proper that the determination be based on what is supported by the force of the words, according to the logic of the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* (in the prima facie view).

Kau. 1|4|20|30, p. 299. Furthermore, co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two [words] can only be postulated if they both have the same object. Therefore, if Devadatta and others were denoted by the word *pacati* (he cooks) in a general sense, then co-referentiality with them would be obtained.

If it is argued that this will occur through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), according to the logic stated in the *Ākṛti* and *Aruṇā* sections, we say no; for it is impossible to indicate [the agent] by means of the cooking residing in the rice-grains.
Indeed, only that which is inherent in the same substrate (*samaveta*) as the cooking can be indicated—such as oneness and so forth—not that which inheres in something else.
